units.tr: Setting forth briefly and clearly the causes, occasions and progress of these disturbances, together with a synopsis of the agreement so far reached.

units.tr: Excerpted from the writings of both parties most worth knowing, the chief of which are now for the first time faithfully translated into Latin and inserted.

units.la: Addita est Ecclesiæ Scotiæ ad Helveticas reformatas Epistola, quâ compendio res tota perspectiuè exhibetur.
units.tr: Added is the Epistle of the Church of Scotland to the reformed Churches of Helvetia, by which the whole matter is set forth comprehensively in brief.

units.la: Prodiit non ita pridem in lucem brevis narratio motuum praesentium Scoticorum, deducta ad Kalend. Octobris anni trigesimi octavi post millesimum sexcentesimum: quacum obviis multorum ulnis acciperetur & fidem datam efflagitarent importunius: visum fuit eorundem motuum descriptionem continuare, quantum ex scriptis utriusque partis scitu dignissimis colligi posset: ut exteris rerum harum cognitione certa flagrantibus consuleretur, quorum aures dubiis & vagis rumoribus pro relatorum indole hactenus repleta fuerunt. Quae in subitarium hoc σχεδίασμα relata sunt, amicis per modum epistolarum, obvio & sponte nato dicendi genere expedita, primitus destinabantur, quorum studio publici juris nunc fiunt. Rudes commentarios, συνόψεις, aut collectanea, non vero justam historiam conscribere authori institutum unquam fuerat; neque alio quam commentarioli titulo succisivam hanc operam dignam judicavit, quicquid typographo & amicis contra visum sit, quorum culpam praestare non renetur, si opus lemmatis dignitati usque quaq[illegible, ~4 letters] respondeat.
units.tr: Not long ago there appeared a brief narrative of the present Scottish troubles, brought down to the first of October in the year 1638. Since it was received with open arms by many and they demanded more insistently that the promise be kept, it seemed right to continue the description of these disturbances, as far as could be gathered from the writings of both sides that are most worth knowing, so that foreigners, who burn to have certain knowledge of these affairs, might be provided for. Their ears have hitherto been filled, according to the character of those who reported, with doubtful and vague rumours. What is here set down in this hasty sketch, expressed in a plain and spontaneous style of speaking, was at first meant for friends in the form of letters; at their urging it is now made public. The author never intended to write a true history, only rough commentaries, outlines or collections. He judged this idle labour worthy of no title other than that of a little commentary. Whatever the printer and friends thought otherwise, he is not bound to answer for their fault, if the work does not in every respect match the dignity of its title [illegible].

units.la: Quin conatus hic diversa hominum judicia subiturus sit, ac plures fortasse judices & censores quam lectores inveniet, vix dubitandum erit: aliis nimiam festinationem & tantum non abortum incerto adhuc esse differentibus, donec sublatis temporum impedimentis gravissimis prodirent peritiores, qui argumentum hoc amplissimum copiosius & felicius tractarent, rerumque quae nostris temporibus mirabiliterpaene[?], certe non sine conspicua Dei manu, contigerunt, memoriam posteritati consecrarent, stylo materiam aequante. Eadem & nobis olim mens; & hodie fuisset; nisi constaret, conatu hoc felicioribus illis ingeniis accuratioris historiae laudem non praereptam esse, subjectam materiam tanquam in sylvam hic colli-ligi, & forte excitari posse alios qui Spartam hanc pro rei dignitate exornabunt.
units.tr: There is hardly any doubt that this attempt will meet with diverse judgements of men, and will find perhaps more judges and critics than readers. Some will complain that it is too hasty and almost premature, and they will defer it until, with the gravest obstacles of the times removed, more skilled writers appear who would treat this ample subject more fully and happily, and consecrate to posterity the memory of the things that have happened in our times, things almost wonderful and certainly not without the plain hand of God, with a style equal to the material. The author once had the same mind, and would still have it today, had he not judged that by this attempt no praise of more accurate history is snatched from those more gifted writers. Here the material is gathered together as into a forest, and perhaps others may be stirred up who will adorn this Sparta as its worth deserves.

units.la: Sed neque operi huic manum admovisset author si per alios quiescere licuisset, qui omnes operam & studium in eo collocare videntur, ut bonorum animos praejudiciis praeoccuparent, neque ut illud assequerentur, orbi Christiano perfuasum essent, eos quibus nihil aliud unquam propositum fuit, quam privilegia à majoribus suis ab omni aevo transmissa vindicare, ac religionis puritatem frequentissimis & expressis amplissimorum regni ordinum statutis sancitam, à coenaputidarum[?] traditionum & ipso Antichristianismi nucleo afferere, idque ex vi foederis solemnis cum Deo olim initi; hos, inquam, si vel ad inculpatam suam tutelam contra apertam vim aliis omnibus modis saepius frustra tentatis pertrahantur, immani & nunquam satis damnanda rebellione authoritatis regiae jugulum ipsum petere, optimi fui regis jugum excutere, ab ecclesiis aliis omnibus divortium petulanter facere, religionem reformatam conculcare & hosti ludibriis & sannis exponere, pontificiis ludos facere, seditionem movere, Iesuitismum recoctum[?], reponere, Deo denique & hominibus bellum indicere. Hæc sunt quæ in libellis suis toties ingeminarunt venales illæ animæ, quæ ad eas partes se contulere per quas honoris & pecunia uberior spes affulget, viperarum instar, quæ nasci nequeunt nisi denata matre. Atrocium id genus criminum infamia intoleranda est iis qui honoris & existimationis suæ apud probos curam omnem penitus non exuerunt; An vero commentariis hisce abstersa satis sint, Lectori partium studio non excæcato haud difficile erit judicatu, vel ex tumultuaria eorundem lectione. Nam videbit fonticas motuum horum causas fuisse, quod Scoti dissiciliores se præstitissent ad dura obscurorum paucorum hominum imperia subeunda, qui suam tantum causam subdole agentes quæsito regia authoritatis egregio velo, quà fraude quà vi nihil ad summam diligentiam reliqui fecerunt, ut Scotis liberorum subditorum jus, & religionis puritatem extorquerent, quosque blanditiis corrumpere non potuerunt, belli funesti calamitatibus in foveam defossam tandem præcipitarent. A turbulentis hisce consiliis (serenis.[?] rege, cujus gratia per summum nefas turbones isti abusi sunt, quam longissime abesse, innata Majestati clementia, & indoles æquitatis studiosa statuere jubent. Omnium sæculorum annales docent, non nunc primum irrepsisse in optimorum principum aulas incendiorum artifices, qui delationibus & calumniis non secus ac in pelago ventorum turbines, ingentes procellas commovent, quorum mores ex veteri ecclesiastica historia suis coloribus depingit Clariss. Vedelius, de prudentia veteris ecclesiæ. lib.2.cap.5.para.1.& sæpius: Libellus lectu dignifsimus hisce praesertim temporibus, comprobatis & certis documentis ostendens quomodo principum optimorum ista pestes & in negotio religionis simulatores detegi possint.
units.tr: But the author would not have laid his hand to this work if it had been permitted to others to keep silent. They seem to have devoted all their effort and zeal to this end: to forestall the minds of good men with prejudices, and to persuade the Christian world of this, that those men, to whom nothing was ever proposed except to vindicate the privileges handed down to them from their ancestors through all ages, and to defend the purity of religion, sanctioned by very frequent and express statutes of the most distinguished orders of the kingdom, from the foul traditions of men and the very core of Antichristianism, and that on the strength of the solemn covenant once entered into with God, that these men, I say, when they were driven, for the sake of defending their blameless position against open force, after every other means had been tried often and in vain, to attack with an inhuman rebellion, never sufficiently to be condemned, the very throat of royal authority; to cast off the yoke of the best of kings; to make wanton separation from all the other churches; to trample underfoot the reformed religion and expose it to the enemy for mockery and scorn; to make sport for the Papists; to stir up sedition; to bring back rehashed Jesuitism; and finally to declare war on God and men. These are the things that those venal souls have repeated so often in their pamphlets, souls who have gone over to whichever side offers a richer hope of honour and money, like vipers, which cannot be born except by the death of the mother. The infamy of crimes of this kind is intolerable to those who have not wholly cast off all care for their honour and reputation among good men. Whether these commentaries have wiped away such charges sufficiently will not be hard for a reader, not blinded by partisan zeal, to judge, even from a hasty reading of them. For he will see that the chief causes of these disturbances were that the Scots proved less pliant in submitting to the harsh commands of a few dark men, who, pursuing only their own cause craftily, under the excellent veil of royal authority, left nothing undone, by fraud or by force, to wrest from the Scots the rights of free subjects and the purity of religion. And those whom they could not corrupt with flattery they at last thrust, as into a dug pit, into the calamities of a deadly war. Let the most serene king, in whose favour these disturbances have been abused by a supreme wickedness, be placed as far as possible from these turbulent counsels; the innate clemency of His Majesty and his disposition devoted to equity bid us so to judge. The annals of all ages teach that the artificers of fires have not now for the first time crept into the courts of the best princes. By accusations and calumnies they stir up huge storms, as winds stir whirlwinds on the sea. Their manners are painted in their own colours from the old ecclesiastical history by the most distinguished Vedelius, On the Prudence of the Ancient Church, book 2, chapter 5, section 1, and often elsewhere. It is a book most worth reading, especially in these times, showing by proven and certain documents how such pests of the best princes, and pretenders in matters of religion, may be detected.

units.la: Aliis forte non arridebit humi repens ac demissius dicendi genus & phrases quaedam minus tersa & de foro arreptae, in quarum locum si substituta fuissent alia quae auribus magis arrisissent, tum vel longiores & ingratae periphrases admittendae, vel argumentum prorsus negligendum fuisset, quod cum magna sui parte sit Theologicum, (praesertim plenior illa narratio Synodi Glasguensis a pagina 83. ad 296.) vocibus & phrasibus apud Theologos receptis iisque quidem significantioribus utendum fuit, uti & locis illis, quibus jus Scotorum municipale excutitur, propria τεχνολο-[?] [illegible, ~6 letters] exprimere oportuit: addita fere semper explicatione commoda ne vocabuli exotici obscuritas legentis impetum sisteret. Adde quod authoris institutum fuerit, ipsissima quae & qualia utrinque narrarentur quam fieri potuit graphice depingere, atque eo fine scripta quaedam utriusque partis è re nata vernaculo sermone edita in linguam Latinam transferenda erant, ut ex ipsis fontibus causa status peti posset. Quae ab aliis feliciter satis translata erant, ne actum ageret, de verbo in verbum inserunt suis locis.
units.tr: Perhaps some will not be pleased by a style of speaking that creeps along the ground and is rather low, and by certain phrases less polished and taken from the marketplace. If other words had been put in their place, words that would have pleased the ears more, then either longer and unpleasing circumlocutions would have had to be admitted, or the subject would have had to be neglected altogether. Since a large part of the subject is theological (especially the fuller account of the Synod of Glasgow, from page 83 to 296), terms and phrases received among theologians had to be used, and those more expressive ones. The same holds for those passages in which the municipal law of the Scots is examined; there it was necessary to express the proper technical terms [illegible]. Almost always a convenient explanation was added, so that the obscurity of a foreign word would not stop the reader's progress. Add to this that the author's purpose was to depict as vividly as possible the very things, and the kind of things, narrated on each side. For this end certain writings of each party, produced by the occasion and published in the vernacular, were to be transferred into Latin, so that the cause of the state could be sought from the very sources. Those that had already been translated well enough by others, so as not to do the work twice, they insert in their places word for word.

units.la: Atque hi & quotquot hoc genus scripta unquam aggressi sunt, satis norunt quam difficile sit ita verbis verba reddere (quod fidelis interpretis munus est) ut orationi interim sua vis ac constans gratia servetur, & a sententia nihil recedatur. Verborum mangonibus delicatulis, quibus nihil sapit quod palaestram & oleum non redolet, sicuti nec iis qui nunquam æquis animis ferre possunt versutiam & artes suas detectas, hæc non scribuntur, verum veritatis & candoris studiosis, qui pro æquitate sua typothetarum negligentiam Authori à prælo absenti vitio non vertent, quin potius errata arrepto calamo corrigent.
units.tr: These men, and all who have ever undertaken to write things of this kind, know well how difficult it is to render words by words (which is the task of a faithful translator) in such a way that the force and steady grace of the speech is kept and nothing departs from the sense. These things are not written for dainty wordmongers, to whom nothing tastes good that does not smell of the wrestling-school and the oil lamp; nor for those who can never bear with equanimity having their cunning and tricks exposed. They are written for lovers of truth and candour, who, in their fairness, will not blame the author, absent from the press, for the carelessness of the printers, but will rather take up the pen and correct the errors.

units.la: Denique ne nimiis præfationum anfractibus in ipso limine fastidium lectori ad negotii huius certam cognitionem anhelanti creetur, hic finiam, si prius suggessero, cum Deo optimo maximo precibus seriis contendendum esse, ut spiritus pacis & Christiana prudentia Regum ac subditorum corda regat, tempestatemque hanc florentissimis ecclesiis formidabilem in Halcedonia vertat, ac pacis & solidæ concordia remoras ocius submoveat. Sic utere præsenti hac opella, ut calamitatum quibus alii premuntur sympathia ad preces in eorundem gratiam fundendas exstimulet, ac paterna illa in alios severitas ad salubrem pœniten-tiam & seriam vitæ emendationem deducat. Det ille in cuius manu omnium corda sunt ut ulciscendi crudelitate, dominandi libidine, ac nocendi cupiditate deposita, omnes Deum pacis & veritatis caste colentes, paratis animis Christianam concordiam alamus, & persequamur etiam fugientem. Vale, & conatibus nostris fave:aut si quid nosti rectius istis, Candidus imperti,
units.tr: Finally, lest by excessive windings of prefaces at the very threshold a weariness be created in the reader, who is eager for a sure knowledge of this affair, I will end here, after I have first suggested that we must earnestly contend in prayer with God, the best and greatest, that he may rule the hearts of kings and subjects with the spirit of peace and Christian prudence, and turn this storm, dreadful to the most flourishing churches, into halcyon calm, and remove quickly the obstacles to peace and solid concord. Use this present little work so that the sympathy for the calamities by which others are oppressed may stir you to pour out prayers for their benefit, and so that that fatherly severity towards others may lead to salutary repentance and a serious amendment of life. May he in whose hand are the hearts of all grant that, with cruelty of revenge, lust of domination and eagerness to harm laid aside, all of us who purely worship the God of peace and truth may, with ready minds, nourish Christian concord and pursue it even as it flees. Farewell, and favour our endeavours; or, if you know anything more correct than these things, kindly impart it.

units.la: HISTORIA RERUM NUPER IN REGNO SCOTIÆ GESTARUM.
units.tr: THE HISTORY OF THE RECENT TROUBLES IN THE KINGDOM OF SCOTLAND.

units.la: UT[?] quæstionum quibus exagitatur, & motuum qui hodie in Ecclesia & Regno Scotiæ fervent, solida habeatur cognitio; Notanda inprimis sunt ipsorum causæ, occasiones, initia, & quousque hactenus progressum sit. Initia porro & causæ nequeunt commodè percipi, nisi primum ostendatur, quæ fuerit Ecclesiarum Scoticarum ab initio reformatæ ibidem religionis legitima administratio, regni legibus & frequentium nationalium Synodorum constitutionibus sancita, & quibus quasi gradibus à disciplinæ puritate primitus receptæ recessum fuerit. Et quia accuratam Ecclesiæ Scoticæ historiam propediem prodituram spes est, summatim nunc ea solum attingam, quæ præsentibus controversiis lucem aliquam afferre possunt.
units.tr: So that a solid understanding may be had of the questions that are being disputed, and of the disturbances that now rage in the Church and Kingdom of Scotland, their causes, occasions and beginnings must first be noted, and how far they have progressed to this point. Their beginnings and causes cannot be properly grasped unless it is first shown what the lawful administration of the religion was in the Scottish Churches from the beginning of their Reformation, sanctioned by the laws of the realm and by the decrees of the frequent national Synods, and by what steps they gradually departed from the purity of discipline first received. Since there is hope that an accurate history of the Scottish Church will be published shortly, I shall now touch only briefly on those matters that can throw some light on the present controversies.

units.la: Postquam Deus mirabili sua dextra laboribus primorum reformatorum in Scotia, Knoxii, Willoci, Vinrami, &c. benedixisset, religionique suæ primæva & Apostolica puritas restitueretur: cum omnes ex vicinorum malis experti essent, non diu conservari posse doctrinæ puritatem, nisi disciplinam christianam ad regulam SS. scripturæ conformandam haberetur ratio; ideo omnes piorum Doctorum aliorum conatus, co tum tendebant, ut optima ecclesiæ disciplina stabiliretur, Ecclesiis non minus cessaria[?] quam murus civitati, quam castris val-luni,[?] lum, quam horto maceria, verè Μ[?]ήτηρ [?]τῶν ὄντων [?]ἡ ἀ-σφάλεια, ut frequenter eam vocat Nazianzenus.
units.tr: After God had blessed with his wonderful right hand the labours of the first reformers in Scotland, Knox, Willock, Winram and others, and the original and apostolic purity of the religion had been restored, all of them, having learned from the troubles of their neighbours, saw that the purity of doctrine could not long be preserved unless account were taken of framing Christian discipline according to the rule of Holy Scripture. For this reason all the efforts of the other godly teachers were directed to establishing the best discipline of the Church. Discipline is no less necessary to the Churches than a wall to a city, a rampart to a camp, or a hedge to a garden; it is truly "the mother of all things, security," as Nazianzen often calls it. [μήτηρ τῶν ὄντων ἡ ἀσφάλεια]

units.la: Negotium itaque conscribendi politiæ exactissimam formam mandatum fuit pastoribus; quorum sententia fuit, Ecclesiam per conventus plurium regendam; etenim unius arbitrio rem neutiquam committendam censuerunt ecclesiasticam: & exactam regiminis formam senatui supremo offerunt; videlicet, ut regeretur Ecclesia per sessiones (seu consistoria) presbyteria (seu classes) synodos provinciales & nationales.
units.tr: Accordingly the task of drawing up the most exact form of polity was committed to the ministers. Their opinion was that the Church should be governed by a number of assemblies together. They judged that ecclesiastical affairs should by no means be left to the will of one man, and they presented to the supreme council an exact form of government, namely, that the Church should be governed through sessions (or consistories), presbyteries (or classes), and provincial and national synods.

units.la: Atque ubicunque per pastorem colligi potuere Ecclesiæ, in iis erectæ sessiones, quæ constabant ex Pastore, Senioribus, & Diaconis: huic conventui semper præsidebat pastor. Statutum, ut plures vicinæ Ecclesiæ simul convenirentur, quæ presbyterium seu classem facerent, cui conventui tunc seniores (ut vocant) Laici interesse debuerant à particularibus Ecclesiis deputati: ad conventum hunc (qui singulis septimanis in primaria vicina urbe habendus esset) pertinere dixerunt judicium omnium appellationum à consistoriis, potestatem decernendi de sententia excommunicationis, pastorum admissionem, suspensionem, depositionem, Ecclesiarum visitationes, & hujus generis similia, quæ ad Ecclesiarum sic unitarum commodum facerent.
units.tr: Wherever a congregation could be gathered under a minister, a session was set up there, consisting of the minister, the elders and the deacons; the minister always presided over this assembly. It was ordained that several neighbouring congregations should meet together to form a presbytery or class, and at this meeting the so-called lay elders, appointed by the individual congregations, were to take part. They said that this gathering, which was to be held every week in the principal neighbouring town, had authority to judge all appeals from the consistories, to decide on sentences of excommunication, and on the admission, suspension and deposition of ministers, the visitation of the congregations, and similar matters that served the good of the churches thus united.

units.la: Statutum etiam, ut in istis cœtibus, qui hebdomatim conveniebant, pastores omnes per vices dona sua exercerent, utque duo proponerent, quorum primus Textum scripturæ aperturus fuit, alter locos doctrinæ & usus familiariter propositurus, singulis vero mensibus caput aliquod controversum inter reformatos & pontificios vernaculo sermone publicè discuterent, ac dein populo dimisso idem contra symmystas defenderent. Atque hoc exercitium presbyteriale vocatum fuit. Porro præsidentia fuit vel vicissitudinaria, vel per electionem.
units.tr: It was also ordained that in these weekly meetings all the ministers should in turn exercise their gifts: two of them would propose, the first to open a passage of Scripture, the second to explain familiarly the points of doctrine and their use; and each month they would publicly discuss in the vernacular some disputed head between the reformed and the Papists, and then, after the people had been dismissed, defend the same against their opponents. This exercise was called the presbyterial exercise. Moreover, the presidency was either by rotation or by election.

units.la: Censuerunt etiam Ecclesiis utilissimum futurum, si Synodi provinciales haberentur, singulis annis bis; in quibus de iis quæ in minoribus conventibus peragi non potuêre, disceptaretur: ubi etiam diligens instituenda fuit Cleri censura, & hisce conventibus Præsides seu Moderatores per plurimorum suffragia eligebantur.
units.tr: They also judged it would be most useful for the Churches if provincial synods were held twice every year, in which matters that could not be dealt with in the smaller meetings would be debated; there too a careful censure of the clergy was to be instituted, and at these synods presidents or moderators were chosen by the votes of the majority.

units.la: Denique quia plurima sæpius occursura essent, quæ totius ecclesiæ nationalis statum tangerent, & quæ in provincialibus Synodis transfigi non possent; ideo Synodi nationalis necessitatem & utilitatem proponunt, ad quam conventuri essent ex singulis Presbyteriis Pastores aliquot (postea numerus incertus ad tres redactus est) cum unico Seniore, seu deputato Laico istius presbyterii; ex singulis regni urbibus unus, ex Academiis etiam aliquot. Huic conventui eligebatur plurimorum suffragio Moderator seu præses.
units.tr: Finally, since many matters would often arise that touched the state of the whole national Church and could not be settled in the provincial synods, they proposed the need for and usefulness of a national synod. To it each presbytery would send some ministers (the number was later reduced to an uncertain three) together with one elder, or lay deputy, of that presbytery; from each town of the realm one, and from the universities also several. At this synod a moderator or president was elected by the majority of votes.

units.la: Horum quatuor conventuum ὑπερτύπων[?] Senatui regio exhibuerunt, cujus mandato & authoritate labor ille susceptus fuit. Veruntamen communibus & concordibus senatorum & magistratuum suffragiis tum non muniebatur: omnia tamen de consistoriis, Synodis provincialibus, nationalibus, satis arridebant. Illud solum de presbyteriis in actum redigi vix potuit; etenim procerum multi Ecclesiæ bona, quæ invaserunt, sic sibi ereptum iri augurati sunt: alii disciplinæ jugum aversabantur. Accedebat, quod tunc magna erat Doctorum & Pastorum infrequentia: postea tamen publica ordinum regni authoritate, in comitiis anni 1592. omnia plenè sanciebantur.
units.tr: They presented an outline [ὑποτύπωσιν] of these four assemblies to the royal Council, by whose command and authority that labour was undertaken. Yet at that time it was not supported by the united and agreed votes of the councillors and magistrates. Still, everything concerning the consistories, the provincial and national synods pleased them well enough. Only the matter of the presbyteries could hardly be put into effect; for many of the nobles, anticipating that the Church's property which they had seized would thus be taken from them, were alarmed, and others shrank from the yoke of discipline. Moreover, the number of teachers and ministers was then very small. Later, however, by the public authority of the estates of the realm, in the parliament of 1592, everything was fully sanctioned.

units.la: Quare cum hisce de causis erigi tum non potuerint Presbyteria, ut defectui huic interim subveniretur, statutum, ut eligerentur Superintendentes. Si enim ministri (quorum tum magna fuit raritas; sicut ubique esse solet, veritate ex tam crassis tenebris ignorantiæ & superstitionis caput primitus emergente) egregiis donis à Deo locupletati, particularibus quibusdam ecclesiis omnes addicerentur, regni pars maxima ministerii beneficio destitueretur; quo non solum obmurmurandi materia ecclesiis pastoribus idoneis destitutis daretur, sed multorum etiam salus, periculo certo exponeretur. Quare ex paucis pastoribus qui tunc Euangelium pure prædicabant, eligendi erant duodecim, quibus provinciæ assignandæ erant, in quibus ecclesias fundarent, & ea omnia (in consilium adhibitis semper vicinis pastoribus) peragerent, quæ liber primus de disciplina (nam sic delineatio illa disciplinæ, de qua prius, vocabatur) ad presbyteria proprie pertinere declarabat. Porro munus hoc Superintendentium vel inde constat fuisse tantum temporarium, donec major esset in provinciis Pastorum frequentia; nam ubi frequentiores fuere in vicinia pastores, & Ecclesiæ melius constitutæ, nihil ibi negotii fuit cum Superintendentibus. Eligebantur autem isti Superintendentes ab Ecclesiis quas curabant; ac Synodis tenebantur rationem reddere omnium actionum, quarum judicio se submiserunt[?]. Specialiter tum iisdem mandatum, ne regimini politico sese immiscerent, etenim, cum ordinarii Pastoris munus totum hominem requireret, impossibile judicarunt, eum cui tot Ecclesiarum cura incumberet, posse secularibus negotiis, in aula aut Senatu regio vacare. Sed numerus hic duodecim Superintendentium, propter stipendiorum inopiam impleri non potuit, quare in eorum locum electi sunt ex doctissimis & prudentissimis pastoribus quidam, quibus Commissariorum nomen inditum: & horum numero ascripti quidam ex Episcopis, qui deserto Papatu, reformatæ prosessioni se adjunxerant, iis tamen omnibus hoc non fuisse concessum constat; Nam Alexander Gordonus Gallovidianus Episcopus, post ejuratum Papismum, licet gauderet titulo & reditibus Episcopi, ac serio ambiisset, ut sibi liceret suis Gallovidianis superintendere, repulsam tamen tulit, & alius Pastor ipsius provinciae praepositus fuit. Habitae tunc fuerunt frequentes Synodi, & in Synodo nationali anni 1566. chirographis pastorum in Synodo congregatorum, comprobata fuit confessio Ecclesiarum Helveticarum, ubi Episcopatus pro commento humano declaratur,
units.tr: Because for these reasons presbyteries could not then be set up, it was decided, to meet the deficiency in the meantime, that superintendents should be elected. For if the ministers (of whom there was then great scarcity, as is always the case when the truth first emerges from such thick darkness of ignorance and superstition), endowed with outstanding gifts from God, were all bound to particular congregations, the greater part of the realm would be deprived of the ministry; and so not only would there be grounds for complaint from congregations left without suitable ministers, but the salvation of many would be certainly endangered. Therefore twelve were to be chosen from the few ministers who then preached the gospel purely, and to each of them a province was to be assigned in which they would plant churches; and they were to carry out, always taking the advice of the neighbouring ministers, all those duties which the first book of discipline (for so that outline of discipline mentioned earlier was called) declared properly belonged to the presbyteries. Indeed, it is clear from this that the office of superintendents was only temporary, until there should be a greater number of ministers in the provinces; for where ministers were more numerous nearby and the churches better established, there was no business at all with superintendents. These superintendents were chosen by the churches they looked after, and they were bound to render account of all their actions to the synods, to whose judgment they submitted themselves. It was especially enjoined on them that they should not meddle in civil government; for since the ordinary office of a minister requires the whole man, they judged it impossible that one on whom the care of so many churches lay could be free for secular business at court or in the royal council. But this number of twelve superintendents could not be filled because of the lack of stipends; so in their place some of the most learned and prudent ministers were chosen, and they were called commissioners. To this number were added some bishops who, having deserted Popery, had joined the reformed profession. It is certain, however, that not all of them were granted this. For Alexander Gordon, bishop of Galloway, after he had abjured Popery, although he enjoyed the title and revenues of a bishop, and seriously sought that he might be allowed to superintend his own Galloway, was refused, and another minister was placed over that province. Frequent synods were then held, and at the national synod of 1566, by the signatures of the ministers gathered in the synod, the Confession of the Helvetic Churches was approved, in which episcopacy is declared to be a human invention.

units.la: Et quia in illis conventibus saepenumero deliberatum fuit serio, de vindicandis decimis aliisque reditibus Ecclesiasticis, à privatis quibusdam magnatibus praeter jus & aequum occupatis, ac fine ulla juris vel speciei, in privatum paucorum patrimonium conversis: Ideo eorum quidam qui nullo justo titulo, se bona Ecclesiastica possidere intellexerunt, ut sibi prospicerent, excogitarunt hanc artem, ut Pastores ipsorum clientes & propinqui, ad Episcoporum titulos eveherentur, quibus minutula redituum portio concessa fuit, ut reliquum ipsis in praedam cederet. Atque ut hoc obtinerent, licet nihil intentatum reliquissent, nunquam tamen titularibus illis Episcopis concessa fuit jurisdictio Ecclesiastica; iisdemque etiamsi munere ullo Ecclesiastico fungi vellent, omnis civilis jurisdictio interdicta. Mirum tamen quas turbas titulares illi Episcopi Ecclesiis dederunt, & in omnibus Synodis frequentissimae exhibitae querelae, contra Episcoporum illorum segnitiem & malos mores, quod Ecclesiam jam adultiorem eo adduxit, ut serio disceptari coeptum fit, an functio illa ulla lege ferenda esset in Ecclesia; ac tandem decretum unanimi consensu in Synodo Taodunensi anno 1580. authoritatem illam quam in Ecclesias sibi arrogarunt Episcopi, esse Antichristianam usurpationem, per quam Antichristus in Christi cathedram surrepsit. Authoritate etiam Synodica fecundus liber, de disciplina editus fuit. Et quia nondum ubique erecta fuerunt presbyteria diligenter negotium illud urgebat ferenissimus Rex Iacobus beatæ memoriæ; mittendo ad Synodum, cum nobili quodam viro, & eodem tempore confessionem Domus Regiæ, (de qua pluribus posthac dicturi sumus) & diagramma quinquaginta presbyteriorum, locis totius regni maximè opportunis, constituendorum, uti in libris de disciplina conclusum fuit; ac denuo Episcoporum, tam in sæcularibus quam Ecclesiasticis, usurpatio fuit damnata.
units.tr: And because in those assemblies it was often seriously debated that the tithes and other ecclesiastical revenues should be recovered from certain private nobles who had occupied them contrary to law and right, and had turned them, without any legal title or pretext, into the private patrimony of a few men, some of those who understood that they possessed Church goods without any just title, devised this trick, in order to provide for themselves: their own clients and relatives, who were ministers, were to be raised to the titles of bishops, to whom a small portion of the revenues was granted, so that the rest might fall to them as plunder. And to secure this, although they left nothing untried, the titular bishops were never granted ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and any civil jurisdiction was forbidden them, even if they wished to exercise any ecclesiastical office. Yet it is remarkable what disturbances those titular bishops caused the Churches, and in all the synods very frequent complaints were made against the sloth and bad morals of those bishops. This led the Church, now grown more mature, to debate in earnest whether that office should be tolerated at all in the Church; and at last, by unanimous consent, the Synod of Dundee in 1580 decreed that the authority which the bishops had arrogated to themselves over the Churches was an Antichristian usurpation, by which Antichrist had crept into the chair of Christ. By synodal authority the second book of discipline was also published. And because presbyteries had not yet been set up everywhere, the most gracious King James of blessed memory urged this business diligently, sending to the synod, with a certain nobleman, both the Confession of the King's House (of which we shall speak more at length hereafter) and a plan of fifty presbyteries to be established in the places most convenient throughout the whole realm, as was concluded in the books of discipline; and again the usurpation of bishops, both in secular and ecclesiastical affairs, was condemned.

units.la: Sed qui Episcopatui evertendo maximam operam navarunt, postea aulicorum gratiâ Episcopatus ambiunt, qui eos quærebant, quos minimo ad illud nomen conducerent, ut lautiori præda securius frui possent, avaris quibusdam Ecclesiasticis, ad ejusmodi consilia promovenda nimium pronis, cum scirent, plus ex ruderibus Episcopatuum se posse corradere, quam ex tenui sacerdotio. Omnes tamen ipsorum conatus (licet muniti specie consensus trium ordinum) fuere irriti, & presbyteriis tandem postliminii jure in plenis regni comitiis 1592. statuto 114. restituta fuit authoritas. Ac per aliquot annos usque adeo coercebatur Episcoporum titulo tenus fastus, ut Ecclesiis turbas creare non fuerint ausi, donec infœlices quasdam controversias, inter Regem & Synodos nationales ortas, conspexerunt, occasione comitum quorundam Papanorum, qui cum Hispano, ad res novas moliendas, conspiraverunt. Hos ab Ecclesiis excommunicatos, Rex volebat recipi; renitente Ecclesia eos pro Ecclesiæ membris agnoscere, qui nullum poe-
units.tr: But those who had worked hardest to overthrow episcopacy afterwards courted it for the sake of the courtiers. The courtiers sought men whom they could hire at the smallest cost to bear that title, so that they might enjoy the richer plunder more safely. Some greedy churchmen, too inclined to promote such schemes, knew they could scrape more from the ruins of the bishoprics than from a meagre priesthood. Yet all their efforts, though protected by the appearance of the consent of the three estates, came to nothing. At last, by the right of postliminy, in the full parliament of 1592, act 114, authority was restored to the presbyteries. For some years the pride of the bishops was so restrained, in name only, that they did not dare to stir up disturbances in the Churches. Then they saw certain unhappy controversies arising between the King and the National Synods, on the occasion of some Papist earls who conspired with the Spaniard to bring about revolution.

units.la: nitentiæ signum ad averruncandum priorum scelerum scandalum, dederunt; quos etiam Papismum fovere nimis apertis indiciis constaret. Hic itatim, qui latebant, Aulici, nova consilia Regi optimo suggessisse feruntur; nunquam pacem solidam regno futuram, nisi antiquatâ hac ecclesiasticorum Cyclopica paritate, eam politiæ Ecclesiasticæ formam constituat, qua cuncta Regis arbitrio dirigi possint. Serio tum de erigendis Episcopatibus deliberatum in aula, politicis consilia illa sedulò promoventibus; quibus Regem in Anglia Ecclesiasticis gratiorem futurum, non malè augurabantur; quorum ope, coronam regni illius jure hæreditario debitam, facilius sine cæde, & sanguine adipisceretur. Nam aliter metuendum erat, ne mitris suis metuentes, à Rege Iacobo nato & enutrito, in ea Ecclesia, in qua ministrorum paritas vigeret, paulò alieniores se ostendissent. Nunc vero omnem ejusmodi metum discuti, Rege serio allaborante, ut Episcopatum, frequentium Synodorum decretis ejectum, rursus introduceret. Sed quia rem plurimis motibus occasionem daturam præsenserant, & nondum memoria excidisset tumultus ille Edinburgenus, anno 1596. suadent; ut non confestim, & momento, sed per intervalla, & pedetentim negotium hoc promoveret, ne res agi videretur. Imprimis vero dandam operam esse, ut oblatâ lucri, aut dignitatis spe, Ecclesiasticorum quorundam animos sibi devincirent, nec consiliis eventus defuit.
units.tr: The King wished these men, excommunicated by the Churches, to be received back. The Church, resisting, refused to acknowledge as members those who gave no sign of repentance to make amends for the scandal of their former crimes, and who were clearly shown to be fostering Popery. Then the courtiers, who had been lying in hiding, are said to have suggested new plans to the excellent King: that peace would never be firm in the realm unless this ecclesiastical Cyclopean equality were abolished and a form of ecclesiastical polity set up by which everything could be directed by the King's will. Then, with politicians vigorously promoting these plans, the court seriously deliberated about erecting bishoprics. They reasoned well that the King would be more agreeable to the churchmen of England, and that with their help he would more easily obtain, without slaughter and bloodshed, the crown of that kingdom due to him by hereditary right. Otherwise it was to be feared that the bishops, fearing for their mitres, would show themselves less well disposed toward King James, who had been born and reared in that Church in which parity of ministers flourished. Now, with the King labouring earnestly to reintroduce the episcopate, which frequent synods had cast out, all such fear was to be dispelled. But because they foresaw that the matter would give rise to many disturbances, and the tumult at Edinburgh in 1596 had not yet faded from memory, they advised that the business be promoted not at once and all together, but by intervals and step by step, lest the thing seem to be actually being done. Above all, care was to be taken to bind to themselves the minds of certain churchmen by holding out the hope of gain or dignity, and the outcome did not fail their schemes.

units.la: Et quia usque adeò exosus fuit episcoporum fastus, ut vix absque famæ dispendio licuerit eos nominare, nusquam eorundem tum facta mentio, contenti hoc à Synodo obtinuisse, ut unicuique liceret, dubia de externo Ecclesiæ regimine proponere. Deinde laboratum, ut aliquot eligerentur deputati, qui Synodi nationalis nomine, gravamina Ecclesiarum parlamento proponerent. Et hi inter alia, ausi sunt propria authoritate urgere, ut jus suffragii, in supremo illo regni ordinum conventu, pos[?]tliminio Ecclesia reciperet. Ac licet sagacioribus suboleret, quid astutiae illis consiliis machinarentur Aulici, gratiamque hanc intempestivam Ecclesiae ingens damnum daturam, non male augurati sint; quia numero vincebantur, in plurium sententiam inviti concessere.
units.tr: And because the pride of the bishops was so hateful that it was scarcely possible to name them without loss of reputation, no mention was made of them at that time. The courtiers were content to obtain from the Synod that each man might be free to propose doubtful points concerning the external government of the Church. Then they laboured to have some deputies chosen who, in the name of the National Synod, would present the grievances of the Churches to parliament. These men, among other things, dared on their own authority to press that the right of voting in that supreme assembly of the estates of the realm should be restored to the Church. Although the wiser sort suspected what cunning the courtiers were plotting with these measures, and rightly foresaw that this untimely favour would bring great harm to the Church, they gave way unwillingly to the opinion of the majority, since they were outnumbered.

units.la: Sed ne deputati secularium quorundam vestigia premerent, qui usurpatis Praelatorum titulis, in publicis regni comitiis, pro Ecclesia non ita pridem se venditabant, & saepius contra Ecclesiae commodum, suffragiis abutebantur; ne, inquam, idem a deputatis illis fieret, eas cautiones Synodus poni statuit, quae Episcopaturientibus frenum injicerent, quales sunt inter plures hae. I. Ne qui ad suffragii jus eligeretur, aliquid in Comitiis proponeret, nisi de Synodi nationalis consilio; cui actorum omnium rationem redderet, cujusque censurae se submitteret, sub poena depositionis & excommunicationis. II. Ut assignata a Rege portione & stipendio contentus viveret. III. Ecclesiae particulari praeesset, ut alii omnes Pastores; eamque sedulo curaret, ac Classicali seu presbyteriali censurae se non subduceret. IV. In jurisdictione Ecclesiastica, ne quid supra Collegas usurparet. V. Ut si Synodus nationalis, provincialis, classis, eum ab officio Pastoris deponat, suspendat, jure suffragii simul se privatum agnosceret, in omnibus denique conventuum Ecclesiasticorum judicio se submitteret. Atque has conditiones omnes & singuli deputati, se religiose observaturos, juramento & chirographo polliceri tenebantur. Acris tum fuit disputatio de nomine, quo compellandi essent: Nemo Episcopi nomen vel leviter insinuare ausus fuit, & execrationibus dirissimis deputati ipsi sæpius professi sunt sibi nunquam statutum Pontificii aut Anglicani Episcopi jugum Scoticis Ecclesiis imponere; videbant quam infœliciter illud Adamsono Andreapolitano titulo tenus Archiepiscopo cessisset. Agitata etiam tum fuit quæstio alia, de duratione hujus muneris; aliis ut aulæ gratia potirentur, non renuentibus; quin deputatorum ad jus suffragii in comitiis regni munus esset perpetuum, ad vitam aut culpam, aliis vero summa ope contra nitentibus. Etenim si perpetuum foret, frustra cancellos poni, quibus commissionarii hi (nam sic vocandos statutum) circumscriberentur. Et si litem, ob rem male administratam, contra eos intentaverit Ecclesia, hos regia authoritate fretos, Ecclesiæ judicium despecturos, beneficia retenturos, ac, tempore sibi maximè opportuno, vindictam in Ecclesiam meditaturos esse, æquum etiam esse nè in deteriori statu ponatur Ecclesia, quam quo alii Regni ordines (excepto nobilium majorum ordine) sunt, quibus concessum, legatos singulis vicibus ad comitia eligere. Et multa hujus generis urgebantur; ita ut nihil de perpetuitate tum statutum fuerit : & deputati illi, seu commissionarii in quaslibet conditiones assentiebantur, modo jus suffragii sartum tectum concederetur.
units.tr: But lest the deputies should follow in the footsteps of certain laymen who, having usurped the titles of prelates, had lately been presenting themselves in the public assemblies of the realm as representatives of the Church, and had all too often abused their votes against the good of the Church, the Synod resolved that safeguards be laid down to curb those who aspired to bishoprics. Among several, these were the following. I. No one chosen to have the right of voting should propose anything in parliament except with the counsel of the National Synod, to which he was to render an account of all his acts, and to whose censure he was to submit, under penalty of deposition and excommunication. II. He should be content with the portion and stipend assigned by the King. III. He should preside over his particular Church, like all other ministers, and should diligently care for it, and should not withdraw himself from the censure of the classis or presbytery. IV. In ecclesiastical jurisdiction he should not usurp anything above his colleagues. V. If the National Synod, a provincial synod, or a classis deposed or suspended him from the office of minister, he should acknowledge himself at the same time deprived of the right of voting; and finally, in all matters he should submit himself to the judgement of the ecclesiastical assemblies. All and each of the deputies were bound to promise, by oath and by signed bond, that they would observe these conditions faithfully. Then a sharp dispute arose over the name by which they should be addressed. No one dared even lightly to suggest the name of bishop, and the deputies themselves repeatedly declared with the most dreadful curses that they would never allow the yoke of a Papist or Anglican bishop to be imposed on the Scottish Churches. They saw how unhappily that had turned out for Adamson, Archbishop of St Andrews in name only. Another question was also raised at that time, concerning the duration of this office. Some, who did not object to the courtiers' favour, wished that the deputies' office of voting in the assemblies of the realm should be perpetual, for life or until fault; others strongly opposed this. For if it were perpetual, it would be pointless to set up barriers within which these commissioners (for so it was decreed they should be called) would be confined. And if the Church should bring a suit against them for maladministration, these men, relying on royal authority, would scorn the judgement of the Church, keep their benefices, and, at a time most convenient to themselves, plot vengeance against the Church. It was also fair that the Church should not be placed in a worse state than the other orders of the realm (except the greater nobles), to which it was granted to elect representatives to the assemblies on each occasion. Many arguments of this kind were pressed, so that nothing was then decided about perpetuity; and those deputies, or commissioners, agreed to whatever conditions were laid down, provided the right of voting were granted to them safe and sound.

units.la: Sed quas sacro juramento & solenni chirographo ratas tunc habuerunt cautiones, postea apertè professi sunt, se iis non teneri[?]; utpote quod iisdem pro tempore tantum assentiti fuissent, quo rixosis contendendi ansa præriperetur : non animo in perpetuum observandi; quod omnibus subsequentibus actionibus re ipsa comprobarunt. Nam cum ægre ferrent, tam arctis cautionum stipulatarum cancellis se concludi : nec si eosdem transilirent, Synodorum censuram (quibus obitę legationis rationem reddere tenebantur) sine perjurii manifesti macula effugere posse, omni conatu allaborarunt, ne tam frequentes Synodi coirent, translata omni authoritate indicandi Synodum nationalem in Regem, cum notabili damno Ecclesiæ, cui pro re nata sæpius & singulis annis semel convenire concessum fuit, Rege aut Regis deputato, si quis adesset, tempus & locum subsequentis Synodi indicente, & expressa lege sancitum fuit in comitiis regni anno 1592.
units.tr: But the safeguards which they then held to be binding by sacred oath and solemn bond, they afterwards openly declared they were not bound by. They had assented to them only for the time, namely so that the occasion for quarrelsome disputes might be taken away, not with any intention of observing them for ever. This they proved in fact by all their later actions. For since they took it ill to be shut up within such narrow confines of the stipulated safeguards, and since they could not escape the censure of the Synods, to which they were bound to render an account of their embassy, without the stain of manifest perjury even if they leapt over those limits, they laboured with all their might that such frequent synods should not assemble. All authority to appoint the National Synod was transferred to the King, to the notable loss of the Church, to which it had been granted that it might meet, as occasion required, often and once a year, with the time and place of the following synod being appointed by the King or his deputy, if one were present; and this was expressly enacted by law in the parliament of the realm in 1592.

units.la: Quod cum continua etiam praxi receptum esset ab initio reformationis, iniquè admodum tulerunt Ecclesiæ, hisce artibus sibi eripi: nec videbant quibus mediis obviam iri posset Episcoporum tyrannidi, receptæ libertatis Ecclesiasticæ ruinam minitanti, itaque quandoquidem Rege consentiente, in Synodo nationali Edenburgi habita anno 1602. decretum fuisset, sequentem Synodum habendam Abredoniæ, ac Rex deinde novo mandato diem statutum mutaverit, alio certo substituto, tandem cum rescripto altero regio, conventus ille Abredoniæ habendus in diem incertum prorogatus esset, quem Regem nunquam indicturum verebantur multi, nisi de Consilio eorum qui Episcopaturiebant, quibus certum, nullam Synodum expetere, donec potentia & dignitatibus auctiores, Synodos quo vellent, pro arbitrio flecterent[?]; hac inquam de causa, pastores quibus Ecclesia chara, deputati à classibus, Abredoniam conveniunt, ad diem illum certum, quem Rex edicto publico primitus destinaverat. Porrò quas pœnas Regi dederint, testatur multorum exilium, post diuturnum carceris squalorem. Atque in hæc tempora incidebat Andreæ Melvini, Jacobi Melvini, Ioannis Forbesii, Duncani, Fermii, Welshii, Durei, Sharpii ac aliorum exilium,
units.tr: Although this had been the continual practice from the beginning of the Reformation, the Churches took it very badly that they were robbed of it by such tricks. Nor did they see by what means the tyranny of the bishops could be resisted, a tyranny threatening the ruin of the liberty the Church had won. Therefore, although with the King's consent it had been decreed at the National Synod held at Edinburgh in 1602 that the following synod should be held at Aberdeen, and the King afterwards, by a new mandate, changed the appointed day, substituting another fixed date, at last, by a second royal rescript, the assembly to be held at Aberdeen was postponed to an uncertain day. Many feared that the King would never appoint it except on the advice of those who aspired to bishoprics, who knew for certain that they would not seek a synod until, made greater by power and dignities, they could bend synods wherever they liked at their pleasure. For this reason ministers, whom the Church held dear, and deputies from the classes, met at Aberdeen on that fixed day which the King had first appointed by public edict. What penalties they paid the King for this is shown by the exile of many men after a long squalor of imprisonment. It was in these times that the exile of Andrew Melville, James Melville, John Forbes, Duncan, Ferme, Welsh, Dury, Sharp and others fell.

units.la: Quum jam sic stabilitum jus suffragii in Comitiis effet, ut convelli non posset, ad invadendam Ecclesiasticam in sympresbiteros jurisdictionem se comparant, tempore, negotio huic promovendo, opportuno; pastoribus, qui remoram injicere insurgenti tyrannidi vellent, aliis in exilium, aliis carceri, aliis, ut intra propriæ cui inserviebant, parochiæ limites se continerent, damnatis; habetur tunc conventus eorum Ecclesiasticor.quorum nomina regiis literis erant expressa Limnuchi Anno 1606. adsunt imprimis deputati illi seu Commissionarii, quorum quibusdam jam tituli beneficiorum Episcopalium regia munificentia concessi fuere. Ac licet in omnibus præcedentibus Synodis nationalibus ii soli suffragii jure gauderent, qui à Classibus seu Presbyteriis, civitatibus, Academiis, legitimè deputati fuerant, nulla tamen hic deputationis habita fuit ratio. Quare, dum conventus ille primum haberetur, qui regiis literis evocati, negabant conventum illum habendum pro Synodo nationali: Statim tamen ac dimissus fuit, celebrem fuisse Synodum venditant, ejusque decreta presbyteriis obtruduntur sub pœna perduellionis; Videlicet, ut deputatos seu Commissionarios Ecclesiarum, pro Classium præsidibus agnoscerent, & quos Rex titulo & reditibus Episcopatuum ornaverat, Synodorum provincialium præsides seu Moderatores essent; licet multi qui conventui illi intererant, confidenter affirmaverint, nihil tum agitatum aut conclusum fuisse de Synodorum provincialium præsidibus: neque ipsi Episcopi ubique conventus illius statuta executioni mandare ausi fuerunt; Etenim in Synodo provinciali Fifana non multò post dimissum Lymnuchensem conventum, non concessum fuit Gladstono Archiepiscopo Andreapolitano, ut vigore istius decreti, præsideret. Conventui huic Lymnuchensi electus fuit Moderator Nicolsonus, paulò ante titu-lo & beneficio tenus factus Episcopus Caledonius, quem usurpationis hujus feriam licet feram inceffisse poenitentiam referunt. In cujus rei fidem circumferuntur versus non illepidi, compositi à Theologo magni nominis D. Lindesio, Brechinensê primum, dein Edenburgensi Episcopo. ipsi proxima affinitate juncto; qui, quæ præsens audiit prosa, sic metro constrinxisse fertur:
units.tr: Now that the right of voting in the Assemblies was so firmly established that it could not be overturned, they prepared to seize the ecclesiastical jurisdiction over their fellow presbyters, at a time they judged favourable for advancing this business. The ministers who wished to check the rising tyranny were condemned: some to exile, some to prison, and others to remain within the bounds of the parish they served. Then a gathering of those ecclesiastics was held at Linlithgow in 1606, whose names were specified in the royal letters. Above all, the deputies, or Commissioners, were present, and some of them had already been granted the titles and benefices of bishoprics by royal generosity. Although in all previous national synods only those had enjoyed the right of voting who had been lawfully chosen by the classes or presbyteries, cities and universities, no account was taken of election in this case. So when that gathering was first held, those summoned by royal letters denied that it could be regarded as a national synod. Yet as soon as it was dismissed, they boasted that a famous synod had been held, and its decrees were forced upon the presbyteries under penalty of treason. Namely, they were to acknowledge the deputies or Commissioners as presidents of the classes, and those whom the King had adorned with the title and revenues of bishoprics were to be presidents or moderators of the provincial synods. Yet many who attended that gathering confidently affirmed that nothing had then been discussed or concluded about the presidents of provincial synods, and the bishops themselves did not dare to put the decrees of that gathering into effect everywhere. Indeed, at the provincial synod of Fife, not long after the Linlithgow gathering was dismissed, Gladstone, Archbishop of St Andrews, was not allowed to preside under the force of this decree. Nicolson was chosen as moderator of the Linlithgow gathering, a man who shortly before had been made Bishop of Caithness in title and benefice; they report that he later repented, though late, of this usurpation. As evidence of this, some rather witty verses are in circulation, composed by the famous theologian Dr Lindsay, first Bishop of Brechin and then of Edinburgh, closely connected to him by marriage. He is said to have put in metre what he had heard said in prose at the time:

units.la: Solatur frustra conjux, solantur amiciEt medicum accersi sedulo quisque jubetSed dare solamen nemo, dare nemo salutemTe præter, potuit, Rex Iacobe, mihi. Quae corpus gravat atque animam tantum eximé mitraeHuic caput: hujus onus me premit & perimit,
units.tr: In vain the wife console, in vain the friends console him, and each man bids the doctor be sent for with all diligence; but no one can give comfort, no one can give health, but you, King James, could give it to me. The mitre that weighs on the head burdens the body and takes away the soul; its weight oppresses me and destroys me.

units.la: Pastorum quidam inviti (qui sub poena perduellionis cogebantur) decretum hujus conventus, de presbyteriorum seu Classium perpetuis moderatoribus, admiserunt; sub certis tamen conditionibus, donec ea de re plenius, in Synodo nationali libera disputiretur: Alii vero qui admittere nullatenus voluerunt, duriter tractati; quibusdam in exilium ejectis, aliis carceri mancipatis, nondum tamen arcem caufæ obtinuerunt; ideoque huc jam omnes conatus collimant, ut jurisdictionem Ecclesiasticam plenè obtinerent.
units.tr: Some ministers, unwillingly (for they were compelled under penalty of treason), admitted the decree of this gathering concerning the perpetual moderators of presbyteries or classes, but under certain conditions, until the matter could be discussed more fully in a free national synod. Others, however, who would by no means admit it, were harshly treated: some were cast into exile, others were consigned to prison. Yet they did not gain the chief point of the cause, and so now all their efforts are aimed at obtaining full ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

units.la: In hunc finem Mense Februario anni 1610. quam Ecclesiarum consensu se nunquam adepturos noverant, jurisdictionem in fratres compresbyteros à Rege obtinent, sub titulo Commissariorum Regis in jurisdictione Ecclesiastica seu judicum celse Commissionis, qua armantur potestate exauctorandi ministros, suspensionis censuram irrogandi, excommunicationem decernendi, & ad ferendam sententiam aut latam denunciandam, quemvis Ministrum co-gendi, gendi, potestate mulctandi, in carcerem conjiciendi, & persequendi contumaces poena rebellionis; &c.
units.tr: To this end, in February 1610, they obtained from the King jurisdiction over their fellow presbyters, which they knew they would never obtain with the consent of the Churches. It was under the title of Commissioners of the King in ecclesiastical jurisdiction, or judges of the High Commission. They were armed with the power to depose ministers, to inflict the censure of suspension, to decree excommunication, to compel any minister to pronounce or proclaim a sentence once passed, to fine and to throw into prison, and to prosecute the contumacious under the penalty of rebellion; and so on.

units.la: Atque, ut speciem aliquam consensus Ecclesiarum obtinerent, Synodus indicitur Glasguæ, mense Iunio anni ejusdem 1610. ubi aderant, non (ut legibus statutum, & continua praxi receptum) a presbyteriis liberè deputati, sed Moderatores presbyteriorum (quos in conventu Lymnuchensi ab Episcopis electos diximus) pensiuncula annua inescatos, & spe lautioris fortunæ lactatos cum binis ex singulis presbyteriis pastoribus, quos minis aut præmiis facilius se pellecturos sperant; eoque nomine missus mandato regio Comes Dunbarensis, tanquam Regis deputatus, stipatus satellitibus Regiis. Coram hoc deputato agendum erat de Episcopis, qui civilibus dignitatibus onusti, pinguissimorum beneficiorum patroni, stipendiorum Ministris debitorum moderatores, ut alios spe auctioris stipendii ad se pertraherent, alios si flectere non possent, minutiore frangant, armati etiam ancipiti gladio celsæ commissionis. Et ii sententiam dicturi erant, qui ab ipsis electi & evocati, ac satellitio Regio obsessi fuerant.
units.tr: And in order to obtain some appearance of the consent of the Churches, a synod was summoned at Glasgow in June of the same year, 1610. There were present, not men freely chosen by the presbyteries (as the laws prescribed and continuous practice had established), but the moderators of the presbyteries (whom we have said were chosen by the bishops at the Linlithgow gathering), enticed by a small annual pension and cheered by hope of a more comfortable fortune, together with two ministers from each presbytery, whom they hoped would be more easily drawn over by threats or rewards. For this purpose the Earl of Dunbar was sent with a royal mandate, as the King's deputy, attended by royal guards. Before this deputy the matters concerning the bishops were to be treated. These men, laden with civil dignities and patrons of the richest benefices, moderators of the stipends owed to ministers, were to draw some to themselves by hope of a larger stipend, and to break others, if they could not be bent, by smaller means, armed also with the two-edged sword of the High Commission. And those who were to pronounce the sentence were men chosen and summoned by the bishops themselves, and besieged by the royal guard.

units.la: Non mirandum ergo, si omnia ad Episcoporum libitum hic concessa fuerunt; videlicet, ut nulla ordinatio Pastorum sequentibus temporibus rata esset, nisi actum ordinationis consummaret Episcopus; nullus Minister exauctorandus nisi probante Episcopo, Omnium presbyteriorum seu classium, Episcopi Præsides essent, si adfuerint, & quos ipsi vicarios constituerent si abfuerint: essent Episcopi, aut ipsorum vicarii, Synodorum provincialium Præsides perpetui, dioecesios[?] visitatio ipsis committitur.
units.tr: It is no wonder, therefore, that everything here was conceded at the bishops' pleasure: namely, that no ordination of ministers would be valid in later times unless the act of ordination were completed by a bishop; that no minister could be deposed unless the bishop approved; that the bishops should be presidents of all presbyteries or classes, if present, and of those whom they appointed as their vicars if absent; that the bishops, or their vicars, should be perpetual presidents of the provincial synods; and that the visitation of the dioceses was committed to them.

units.la: Summa, quæcunque antea ad presbyterium pertinebant, ea Presbyteriis erepta, Episcopis concederentur. Interim Ecclesiasticorum in eo convenru mens non fuit, licuisse Episcopis actus illos jurifdictionis per se, exclusis Presbyteriis, exercere: sed negativam ad summam potestatem Episcopis concedunt, conjunctam cum classe seu Presbyterio; cujus voculæ suppressionem subdole urgent, ejusque loco vocem conventus ministrorum poni suadent, ne Regis aures offenderent, qui Presbyterii prolationem iniquo animo laturus diceretur. Sed revera, ut eventus docuit, Presbyteria prorsus eversa volebant, quorum loco liberum esset, quos vellent deligere Pastores, qui actibus istis jurisdictionis interessent. De consecratione Episcoporum, nulla tunc mentio; quia nec fraude nec vi sciebant se nunquam potuisse persuadere aut cogere conventus illius partem maximam, ut statuerent jure divino differre Episcopum à presbytero seu ordinario pastore: neque jure Divino posse Episcopum, quod non possit presbyter. Quo tamen eorum studia collimasse, statim à dimisso conventu, demonstrarunt, tribus eorum in vicinam Angliam excurrentibus, ut in Episcopos consecrarentur, qui reversi alios consecrarunt, Ecclesiis & Synodis inconsultis; ac in omnibus actionibus ita se gesserunt, quasi <bl>ἀποστολικὸν</bl> illam Ecclesiis non acceptam ferrent, sed quasi ea ipsis jure Divino competeret, utpote à spiritu Sanćto creatis & consecratis. Atque hi gradus illi sunt, quibus pedetentim & per intervalla jugum Hierarchiæ Anglicanæ Ecclesiis Scoticis imposuerunt, quo facilius farraginem cæremoniarum Anglicarum introducerent. Quod malum prudentiores maximè terrebat; cum scirent, eos, quibus plus licet, quam par est, sæpius plus velle quam licet.
units.tr: In short, whatever had previously belonged to the presbytery was snatched from the presbyteries and granted to the bishops. Meanwhile, it was not the mind of the churchmen at that gathering that the bishops might exercise those acts of jurisdiction by themselves, with the presbyteries excluded. Instead they granted the bishops a negative power over the highest authority, joined with the class or presbytery. They craftily pressed for the suppression of this little word, and urged that the phrase "gathering of ministers" be put in its place, so as not to offend the King's ears, since he was said to take it ill that presbyteries were mentioned. But in truth, as the outcome showed, they wanted the presbyteries utterly overthrown, so that in their place it would be free to choose whatever ministers they pleased to take part in these acts of jurisdiction. Of the consecration of bishops there was then no mention, because they knew that neither by fraud nor by force could they persuade or compel the greater part of that gathering to decide that by divine right a bishop differs from a presbyter or ordinary minister, nor that by divine right a bishop can do what a presbyter cannot. Yet immediately after the gathering was dismissed, they showed to what end their efforts were aimed: three of them ran over to neighbouring England to be consecrated bishops, and on their return they consecrated others, without consulting the Churches or the synods. In all their actions they so conducted themselves as if they did not hold that [apostolic] office as received from the Churches, but as if it belonged to them by divine right, as men created and consecrated by the Holy Spirit. These were the steps by which they gradually, and at intervals, imposed the yoke of the English hierarchy upon the Scottish Churches, so that they might more easily introduce the mass of English ceremonies. The more prudent men were especially alarmed by this evil, since they knew that those who are allowed more than is fitting often want more than is allowed.

units.la: Nec vanus fuit hic metus. Etenim Episcopi cum se solos omni jurisdictione Ecclesiastica vestitos cernerent; neque quenquam esse, qui contra hiscere auderet, nisi utriusque gladii aciem experiri vellet; quumque Regi optimo unicè in votis fuisse compertum haberent, ut mutatis simplicibus ritibus cultus Divini Ecclesiæ Scoticæ, Anglorum multiformes in eorum locum sensim introduceret, quo regnorum firmior esset unio. Denique cum sine cæremoniis illis hierarchiam suam jam adolescentem vix stabiliri posse putarent, quæ aliter instar ignis sine alimento & fomite expiraret, ad mutationem simplicium rituum cultus Divini, in quibus conformis fuit Ecclesia Scotica, Ecclesiis reliquis reformatis transmarinis sed Anglicæ Ecclesiæ dissormis, animum serio intendunt Episcopi; & cum frustra se laboraturos cernerent, si universos simul & semel abolerent aut introducerent, paucos seligunt, maximè plausibiles, ut sic cuneatim cæteris recipiendis viam sternerent. Regi itaque gratificandum suadent, in admissione quinque articulorum, videlicet, genuflexionis in Sacœna, celebrationis § [?] dierum sacrorum (nativitatis, passionis, resurrectionis, ascensionis Christi & descensus Spiritus S.) privati Baptismi, privatæ administrationis sacræ coenæ, & confirmationis Anglicanæ; quæ cæremoniæ, quia promotæ per Synodum Perthensem (quæ habita fuit Perthæ Anno 1618) vulgo Perthenses cæremoniæ dictæ. Et quia Synodi illius historia utrinque exstat; aliis vituperantibus, tanquam non uno nomine nullam, in qua debita Synodis libertas deputatis negata, ac ad quam jure suffragii admissi qui à presbyteriis se minimè deputatos fassi sunt. Aliis verò eandem approbantibus & tuentibus. Ideò de ipsa Synodo ejusque forma nunc supersedendum duxi, Lectore hujus rei cupido, remissio ad libellos ea de materia editos. Qualiscunque demum fuerit Synodus, in ea tamen admissæ sunt § [?] illæ cæremoniæ, à multis pacis gratia (sicut antea Episcopatus intra limites & cautiones multiplices inclusus) præsertim cum solenne tunc daretur promissum, Regem non statuisse, reliquam farraginem cæremoniarum Anglicarum urgere. At alii, sive, quia promisso huic non satis siderent (revocatis in memoriam frequentissimis pollicitationibus & execrationibus, dum de admissione Commissariorum agitaretur, hierarchiam Anglicanam non intendi) satiusque putarent non admittere, quam postea, cum experti essent quantum damni Ecclesiis daturæ essent, ejicere; sive, quia in conscientia putabant, singulas ad indifferentium categoriam simpliciter referri non posse, ideo constanter sese iis opposuere.
units.tr: Nor was this fear vain. For when the bishops saw that they alone were clothed with all ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and that there was no one who would dare to murmur against them unless he wished to test the edge of both swords, and when they found that it was known to be the most excellent King's sole desire that, with the simple rites of the worship of God in the Scottish Church changed, he should gradually introduce the many-formed rites of the English in their place, so that the union of the kingdoms might be firmer, then at last, since they thought their hierarchy, still young, could hardly be established without those ceremonies (otherwise it would die like a fire without fuel and kindling), the bishops seriously turned their minds to changing the simple rites of the worship of God, in which the Scottish Church agreed with the other reformed Churches beyond the sea but disagreed with the English Church. And since they saw they would labour in vain if they abolished or introduced them all together at once, they chose a few, the most plausible, so that they might pave the way for receiving the rest one wedge at a time. Accordingly, they urged that the King be gratified by the admission of five articles, namely: kneeling at the Lord's Supper; the observance of certain holy days (of Christ's nativity, passion, resurrection, ascension, and the descent of the Holy Spirit); private baptism; private administration of the Lord's Supper; and English confirmation. These ceremonies, since they were promoted by the Synod of Perth (held at Perth in the year 1618), were commonly called the Perth Articles. And since the history of that synod survives on both sides, some condemn it as null and void in one respect, because the freedom due to synods was denied to the deputies, and because men were admitted to the right of voting who confessed that they had not been chosen by the presbyteries at all. Others, however, approve and defend the same synod. For this reason I have thought fit to say nothing more now about the synod itself and its form, the reader eager about this matter being referred to the pamphlets published on the subject. Whatever kind of synod it was, nevertheless those ceremonies were admitted in it, and many accepted them for the sake of peace (just as the episcopacy had been admitted before, enclosed within limits and many safeguards), especially since at that time a solemn promise was given that the King did not intend to press the rest of the mass of English ceremonies. But others, either because they did not sufficiently trust this promise (recalling the very frequent pledges and curses made while the admission of the Commissioners was being debated, to the effect that the English hierarchy was not intended), and thought it better not to admit them than afterwards, when they had found out how much harm they would do to the Churches, to cast them out; or because in conscience they thought the individual ceremonies could not simply be classed among things indifferent, therefore they steadfastly opposed them.

units.la: Qua sententiarum varietate schisma in Ecclesiis ortum est, quod in hodiernum diem sopiri non potuit; Aliis Synodum illam rejicientibus, ut spuriam: aliis ut legitimam probantibus.
units.tr: By this variety of opinions a schism arose in the Churches, which to this day has not been able to be quieted: some rejecting that Synod as spurious, others approving it as lawful.

units.la: Multarum calamitatum seriem, quas occasione hujus Synodi perpessi sunt plures, nihil attinet narrare; hoc tamen prætereundum non est, coram celsa illa commissione multos citatos, ab eaque damnatos, Iunioribus etiam cum Sacro ministerii munere inaugurantur, necesse Synodum illam, ut legitimam, tueri, prædictaque quinque cæremonias defendere: & Episcopatus Regimen, sicut nunc est in Ecclesia Scotica, approbare: & hisce similia quæ ad Episcoporum regimen stabiliendum faciunt ac quæ faciliorem reliquis cæremoniis Anglicanis introducendis, viam sternunt.
units.tr: There is no point in narrating the series of calamities which many suffered on account of this Synod; yet this must not be passed over: many were summoned before that lofty commission and condemned by it; younger men were also inaugurated into the sacred office of the ministry. It was necessary to uphold that Synod as lawful, to defend the aforesaid five ceremonies, to approve the government of bishops as it now is in the Scottish Church, and the similar matters that serve to establish the rule of bishops and that pave an easier way for introducing the remaining English ceremonies.

units.la: Siquis huic juramento se submittere nolit, rejicitur. Si vero juramenti semel dati immemor, prædictis se opposuerit, citatur in jus; non coram Synodis aut conventibus Ecclesiasticis: sed coram celsa commissione; quod forum est politico Ecclesiasticum, ratione personarum jus ibi dicentium; ubi summo jure cum reis agi potest, exhibito iis juramento ex officio, quo tenentur semet accusare, prodere; quod primitus introductum fuit in Ecclesiam Anglicanam, sub Henrico 4. postulantibus Episcopis ad detegendos Lollardos; quam sanguinariam legem vocat Foxus ipse Anglus, contra scripturam, quæ vetat, accusationem contra presbyterum admitti, nisi sub duorum aut trium testimonio: contra veterum Romanorum statuta; nam & Trajanus, licet fidei Christianæ hostis, statuit tamen etiam in Christianorum causis, quod sine authore certo propositi libelli; nulla crimina locum habere debeant; nam, inquit, & pessimi exempli res est, nec nostri seculi. Unde illud ex ipsis iuris naturæ penetralibus vulgatum, neminem cogi debere contra se testes producere; Ergo multo minus cogendus inofficiosò [?] hoc iuramento contra se testimonium præbere. Adde quod Tribunal illud Scotis plane extraneum sit, neque unquam ulla lege civili aut Ecclesiastica munitum; quod multarum querelarum contra Episcopos materiam dedit.
units.tr: If anyone is unwilling to submit to this oath, he is rejected. But if, forgetful of the oath once given, he opposes the aforesaid things, he is cited to court, not before synods or ecclesiastical assemblies, but before the lofty commission, which is a political-ecclesiastical court, with its judges chosen by reason of persons. There the case may be pursued with the full rigour of law, the oath ex officio being offered to the accused, by which they are bound to accuse and betray themselves. This was first introduced into the English Church under Henry IV, at the demand of the bishops, to detect the Lollards; Foxe himself, an Englishman, calls it a bloody law, contrary to Scripture, which forbids that an accusation be admitted against an elder except on the testimony of two or three witnesses, and contrary to the statutes of the ancient Romans. For even Trajan, though an enemy of the Christian faith, nevertheless decreed, also in the cases of Christians, that no charges should have a place when the written accusation lacks a certain author; for, he says, this is a thing of the worst example and not of our age. Hence that principle, spread from the very innermost parts of natural law, that no one ought to be compelled to produce witnesses against himself. Therefore much less ought one to be compelled by this oath, contrary to duty [?], to give testimony against himself. Add that this tribunal is quite foreign to the Scots, and was never fortified by any civil or ecclesiastical law, which has given occasion for many complaints against the bishops.

units.la: Dum fervent dissidia Ecclesiastica circa illas Perthenses cæremonias, moritur Rex optimus & prudentissimus Jacobus, quumque de serenissimi regis Caroli voluntate, certiores essent: aut (ut alii) Regem optimum ad demortui parentis (ut præ se ferebant) consilia promovenda flexissent, telam orsam pertexere statuunt; præsertim cum egregium specimen piissimus Rex dedisset, quo animo esset erga Ecclesiasticos, tum in Anglia, tum in Scotia; Decreto illo vero regio de revocatione donationum bonorum Ecclesiasticorum, inprimis decimarum, quæ dono parentis olim minorennis, concessa fuere nobilibus quibusdam. Atque licet successum tam egregio conatu dignum res ea non obtinuerit, quibusdam tamen Ecclesiasticis, qui se Episcoponum machinationibus favere ostendebant, aliquid emolumenti accrevit.
units.tr: While ecclesiastical quarrels were raging over those Perth ceremonies, the most excellent and prudent King James died. When they had certain knowledge of the will of the most serene King Charles, or (as others say) when the excellent King had yielded to promote the counsels of his deceased father (as they professed), they resolved to weave the web they had begun, especially since the most pious King had given a distinguished specimen of the disposition he bore towards ecclesiastics, both in England and in Scotland: namely, by that royal decree concerning the revocation of grants of ecclesiastical property, above all tithes, which had been granted by the late father's gift, while still a minor, to certain nobles. And although that matter did not achieve the success such an excellent undertaking deserved, some profit accrued to certain ecclesiastics who showed themselves favourable to the machinations of the bishops.

units.la: Redit in Scotiam Rex post triginta fere anniorum absentiam Anno 1633. ac tum omnium ordinum regni comitia habentur, Rege ipso præsente. Si unquam, tum aliquid audendum erat; quo regi innotesceret, quantum in Republica ac Ecclesia possent Episcopi; ac simul experiundum ipsis erat, an alii omnes cervices ipsorum jugo sponte submissuri essent. Inhunc finem proponitur articulus, quo concederetur Regi, mandare quem vellet habitum omnibus publico officio, seu in republica seu in Ecclesia, fungentibus; & urgetur hoc tanquam connexum regalis privilegii, quare uno & eodem articulo utrumque conjungitur, & respondendum erat categoricè, affirmando aut negando.
