Cum ars hæc Nobilibus quibusdam suboleret, & Episcopos ac aulæ officiarios pronos in affirmativam absque scrupulo ruentes viderent, articuli partes nullo nexu sibi invicem hærentes, dividunt; & quandoquidem esset πολυζήτησις, quæ unico responso in captionem deduceret respondentes, primam articuli partem de regali privilegio concedunt, negant secundam de vestitu præsertim Ecclesiasticorum in sacris, tum quia (ut ingenuè profitebantur) non videbant, qua ratione firma aut probabili ad res illius naturæ extendi posset ac debeat Regale privilegium; tum quia metuebant, ne prætextu hujus articuli Pontificius Sacerdotum vestitus in sacris, uti sunt, superpellicium seu lintea illa vestis candida, rochetum, capa, epitogia, caputia, pilei quadrangulares, & id genus aliæ vestes, pastoribus invitis obtruderentur, quas tamen Ecclesia Scotica ab initio reformationis abjecit, cum reliquis omnibus Antichristi, cujus inventum fuerunt, reliquiis: Metus etiam fuit, ne succedentibus seculis, (quæ ad deteriora fere semper vergunt) Principes flagitiosorum novatorum male feriatis consiliis seducti, statuti hujus prætextu, libertatem sibi sumerent obtrudendi alias Papismi sordes[?] ab Ecclesia Scotica fœliciter profligatas .
units.tr: The King returned to Scotland in the year 1633, after an absence of nearly thirty years, and then assemblies of all the orders of the kingdom were held, the King himself being present. If ever something was to be attempted, it was then, so that it might become known to the King how much the bishops could do in the commonwealth and the Church; and at the same time they had to test whether all the others would willingly submit their necks to their yoke. To this end an article was proposed, by which it would be conceded to the King to order whatever dress he wished to be worn by all who discharge public office, whether in the commonwealth or in the Church; and this was pressed as connected with the royal privilege, so that the two were joined in one and the same article, and an answer had to be given categorically, by affirming or denying. When this trick was smelt out by certain nobles, and they saw the bishops and the officials of the court rushing headlong into the affirmative without scruple, they divided the parts of the article, which clung together by no bond; and since it was a matter of much debate, which by a single answer would lead the respondents into a trap, they granted the first part of the article concerning the royal privilege, and denied the second concerning especially the dress of ecclesiastics in sacred functions. They did so partly because (as they candidly professed) they did not see on what firm or probable reason the royal privilege could be, or ought to be, extended to matters of that nature; and partly because they feared that under the pretext of this article the Papist dress of priests in sacred functions, such as they are — the surplice, or that white linen vestment, the rochet, the cope, the epitogia, the hoods, the square caps, and other garments of that kind — would be forced upon the ministers against their will, which the Scottish Church had nevertheless cast off from the beginning of the Reformation, together with all the other relics of Antichrist, of whose invention they were. There was also a fear that in later ages (which almost always tend toward the worse), princes, led astray by the ill-advised counsels of shameless innovators, might take for themselves, under the pretext of this statute, the liberty of imposing on the Scottish Church other filth of Popery, happily put to flight.

units.la: Sed pluralitate suffragiorum totus articulus Regi concessus fuerat ; Masculus tamen ille & apertus procerum illorum animus Regi clementissimo non admodum placuit, Episcopis nobilium illorum actiones etiam innocentissimas in deteriorem partem traducentibus, quasi contemptum authoritatis regiæ, seditionem in Republica & schisma in Ecclesia spirarent. Ita ut proceres illos tunc Rex non solum publice increpuerit, verum etiam (ut terrorem cæteris injiceret) propria manu eorum nomina, qui totum articulum simpliciter non concederent, notarit; tanquam subditorum Regiæ dignitati minus quam par esset deferentium. Quare proceres illi cum hac arte de Regis gratia immerito se dejectos dolerent, communicatis consiliis consultissimum esse statuunt supplici libello Regi humiliter ostendere, se privatis affectibus in hoc negotio non indulsisse, atque unicam & solam causam cur posteriori articuli parti assensum non præbuissent, fuisse conscientiæ dictamen. Libellum hunc supplicem à Guilielmo Haig Sollicitatore regio formatum ipsorum mandato, ac diligenter ab omnibus revisum, fidei & diligentiæ Comitis Rothusii & Domini de Laudoun commiserunt, ut omnium nomine, captata opportunitate, Regi offerrent : Qui cum multis indiciis perspexissent, ingratum Regi futurum quicquid à se oblatum esset, satius esse judicarunt, eundem Regi tunc non exhibere,rati temporis tractu aversionem hanc de Regis animo obliteratum iri, ac fidelitate & submisso obsequio; Regis gratia tandem potituros esse :, sed improvido unius, & improbo ac maligno alterius consilio, libelli hujus exemplar furtive descriptum in Episcoporum manus pervenit, qui anno 1634. Regem statim monent, rem esse capitali supplicio dignam ,
units.tr: But by a majority of votes the whole article was granted to the King; yet that manly and open spirit of those nobles did not greatly please the most clement King, the bishops twisting even the most innocent actions of those nobles to the worse sense, as if they breathed contempt of royal authority, sedition in the commonwealth, and schism in the Church. So much so that the King not only then publicly rebuked those nobles, but also, to strike terror into others, marked with his own hand the names of those who had not simply granted the whole article, as subjects who paid less deference to the royal dignity than was fitting. Wherefore those nobles, grieving that they had been unjustly cast out of the King's favour by this device, agreed among themselves that it was most advisable to show humbly to the King, in a supplicatory petition, that in this business they had not indulged private feelings, and that the sole and only cause why they had not given assent to the latter part of the article was the dictate of conscience. This supplicatory petition, drawn up by William Haig, the King's solicitor, at their command and carefully revised by all, they entrusted to the good faith and diligence of the Earl of Rothes and Lord Loudoun, that they might offer it to the King in the name of all, when an opportunity was seized. But when they had perceived by many signs that whatever was offered by them would be unwelcome to the King, they judged it better not to present it to the King at that time, reckoning that with the passage of time this aversion would be wiped from the King's mind, and that by fidelity and submissive obedience they would at last attain the King's favour. But by the ill-advised counsel of one, and the wicked and malicious counsel of another, a copy of this petition, secretly transcribed, came into the hands of the bishops, who in the year 1634 at once warned the King that the matter was worthy of capital punishment.

units.la: ac confulto à Nobilibus illis hierarchico regimini non fatis faventibus, libelli hujus supplicis exemplaria dispersa fuisse, ut pastores ad aflumendum vestitum illum in sacris difficiliores redderent, quos aliter fatis æquos & paratos sese habituros jactabant. Etenim Regi persuasisse feruntur Episcopi, Pastores Ecclesiarum libenter affumpturos quem vellet Rex habitum in sacris imperare, sed cum re ipsa edocti effent, Pastorum fere omnium animos ab omni novatione alienos esse, veriti ne vanitate hac Regis gratia exciderent, calumniam hanc ipsi cum asseclis (hominibus ad dignitates supra meritum aut genus subito evectis) fabricarunt, ut regis iram capitibus suis debitam in alios innocentes derivarent, ac simul ulciscerentur quam sibi putabant scripto eo illatam injuriam, in quo questi fuere proceres illi, ab Episcopis nobiles quosdam pontificios electos fuisse Dominos articulorum, (quibus articulos omnes in parlamento concludendos, formandi & disponendi provincia committi solet) quod effet contra statuta plurima parlamentaria, quibus expressè interdicitur Pontificiis quibufliber, ne fedeant tanquam membra cujuflibet fori, cui suprema competit jurisdictio. A Rege tandem importunis horum sollicitationibus obtinetur rescriptum, quod paucis quibusdam seleCtis personis, nomine deputationis immediatè à Rege (quam vocant Scoti, A Committee) potestas concedebatur, procedendi contra auctores & fautores illiùs libelli supplicis, quasi rei effent seditionis & læsæ majestatis regiæ: quod cum innotuisset Guil. Haig ejusdem formatori licet sibi minimè conscius effet eorum criminum, quia tamen eosdem habituru effet Iudices & accusatores, fuga opportuna vitæ suæ consuluit, in absentem tamen lata fuit sententia, ejusque bona omnia in fiscum redacta fuerunt. Nobilium vero, quorum intererat, quidam, in quæstionem vocati sunt, inter quos Dominus de Balmerino (sub cujus custodia libellus delituit) post arctam multorum mensium custodiam capitis damnatus fuit, ab optimo tamen Rege clementer eidem indultum, cum ex quatuordecim viris more Scotico, ad causam capitis disceptandam & definiendam electis, septem iisque nobilissimi ac maximæ dignitatis, reum absoluissent, alii verò nobiles forum illud ut incompetens declinando evaserant.
units.tr: And it is reported that the nobles, who were not sufficiently favourable to the hierarchical government, had deliberately caused copies of this supplicatory petition to be scattered, so that they might make the ministers more difficult about assuming that dress in the sacred office, whom otherwise they boasted would be fairly compliant and ready. Indeed, the bishops are reported to have persuaded the King that the ministers of the Churches would willingly assume whatever dress the King commanded in the sacred office; but when they were taught by experience that the minds of almost all the ministers were alien to every innovation, fearing lest these men should fall from the King's favour through this vanity, they and their followers (men suddenly raised to dignities beyond their merit or birth) fabricated this calumny, so that they might turn the King's anger, due to their own heads, upon other innocent men, and at the same time avenge the injury they thought had been done them by that writing in which those nobles complained that certain Papist nobles had been chosen by the bishops as lords of the articles (to whom the task of forming and arranging all the articles to be concluded in parliament is usually committed), which was contrary to many parliamentary statutes, by which it is expressly forbidden to Papists of any kind to sit as members of any court to which supreme jurisdiction belongs. At length, by the importunate solicitations of these men, a rescript was obtained from the King, by which power was granted to a few select persons, in the name of a deputation immediately from the King (which the Scots call a Committee), to proceed against the authors and abettors of that supplicatory petition, as if they were guilty of sedition and of treason against the King's majesty. When this became known to William Haig, its drafter, although he was not at all conscious of those crimes, he nevertheless, because he would have as judges and accusers those same men, took timely flight to look to his life; yet sentence was pronounced against him in his absence, and all his goods were confiscated to the treasury. Of the nobles concerned, some were called into question, among whom Lord Balmerino (under whose custody the petition had lain hidden), after many months of close confinement, was condemned to death; yet the most excellent King mercifully granted him a pardon, when fourteen men, chosen in the Scottish manner to hear and decide the capital case, had acquitted the accused, seven of them being the most noble and of the greatest dignity; while the other nobles escaped by declining that court as incompetent.

units.la: Interea diligenter sudatum est ab Episcopis informandis novis Canonibus Ecclesiasticis, & libro liturgico, certa spe, neminem ausurum sese iis opponere, nisi nobilium illorum fortunam experiri vellet, & majori terrore omnes concutiendos sperabant ex promotione Archiepiscopi Andreap. Regni primatis, senis capularis & septuagenarii, ad munus Cancellariatus quæ suprema est dignitas totius regni in secularibus, Summi vero thesaurarii, (quæ secunda est dignitas) officium spe inani jamdudum devoraverat Episcopus Rossensis, nunc in flagranti gratia apud Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum: Cumque sint tantum quatuordecim in Scotia Episcopi, novem tamen fuere ex sanctiore Regis senatu, & multi in Camera rationum, summo divitiarum fulgore, & opulentiæ splendore, ad quæ nuper subito evecti fuerant, nihil quod vel in repub. vel in Ecclesia ausuri essent, impervium aut difficile fore, nimis credula, & regno & Ecclesiæ noxia fallacia sibi persuasere. Excuditur tandem liber Canonum in usum Ecclesiæ Scoticanæ, authoritate regia non solum ratus haberi, verum etiam jubentur omnes subditi in Regno Scotiæ, in omnibus articulis semet subjicere Episcopali censuræ. Per constitutiones uno ictu, tota disciplina[?] Ecclesiasticæ, (hactenus cum fructu in Ecclesia Scotica observatæ, & frequentibus legibus in omnium trium ordinum Regni conventu supremo,
units.tr: Meanwhile the bishops worked hard at shaping the new ecclesiastical canons and the liturgical book. They were confident that no one would dare oppose them unless he wished to try the fate of those noblemen. They also hoped everyone would be struck with greater terror by the promotion of the Archbishop of St Andrews, primate of the realm, an old man of seventy who wears a skull-cap, to the office of Chancellor, the highest dignity in the kingdom in secular affairs. The Bishop of Ross had long since devoured in vain hope the office of Lord High Treasurer, the second dignity, and he now stood high in favour with the Archbishop of Canterbury. There are only fourteen bishops in Scotland, but nine of them sat in the more sacred royal council, and many were in the Exchequer. Lately raised suddenly to these posts, dazzled by the glitter of wealth and the splendour of opulence, they persuaded themselves, too credulously, that nothing they dared attempt in the commonwealth or the Church would be impregnable or difficult, a fallacy harmful both to the realm and to the Church. At last the book of canons was printed for use in the Scottish Church. Not only was it to be held valid by royal authority, but all subjects in the kingdom of Scotland were ordered to submit themselves to episcopal censure in all its articles. By these constitutions the whole structure of ecclesiastical discipline, which had hitherto been observed with profit in the Scottish Church and established by frequent laws passed by the supreme assembly of all three orders of the realm,

units.la: seu parlamento, latis, fancitæ) structura evertitur, consistoria seu sessiones, Classes seu presbyteria conventiculorum loco habentur, rejiciuntur seniores laici & diaconi, omnes causæ Ecclesiasticæ ad Episcopi solius tribunal revocantur. Jam pridem disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ nervos inciderant, quædam tamen facies licet elanguida manebat, per illa restantia rudera, ostendens qualis olim Troja fuisset, spem etiam faciens, quam gloriosum ædificium extrui possset, si Deus oculo misericordiæ vastatam suam vineam respicere dignaretur: licet post infælicem illam Synodum Perthensem, nullus conventus aut Synodus nationalis fuisset, manebant tamen provinciales Synodi, præsbyteria, sessiones, quibus (licet vanis fere nominibus) se mutuo solabantur viri boni: At monstroso hoc canonum partu in lucem extruso ipsum nomen ablatum, neque dubitabant quin omnium ulnis libenter suscipseretur; Sed quam vana spe se lactaverint subito patuit, etenim ubique male formatus hic partus rejectus est, tum propter absurda literis quasi majusculis in fronte notata, qualia sunt, quod omnes vetentur sub pœna excommunicationis, aliquid in dubium vocare; quod in libro Canonum aut in libris Liturgiæ & Ordinationis (tum nondum impressis) contineretur, licet liber ille canonum habeat, quicquid Anglorum liber continet, quæ Episcopi non potuerunt ignorare, vocari in dubium quotidie à Scotis & aliis fere omnibus reformatis Ecclesiæ, sed & multa nova superaddita sint de quibus in Anglorum canonibus nec vola nec vestigium, quorum pauca speciminis loco exhibebo, uti sunt cap.18.9. Sacramentalis confessio & absolutio, literis etiam majusculis, qua verendum est, ne auricularis confessio Ecclesiis obtrudatur, præsertim cum in libro liturgico jubentur omnes semel saltem in anno participare Sanctæ cœnæ, & ad alia omnia Sacramenta accedere, quid prohibebit, quo minus inter alia Sacramenta ad quæ adultioris ætatis homines jubentur accedere, ponatur Pœnitentiæ Sacramentum ? Cujus pars primaria est auricularis confessio ; ideo dicta Sacramentalis, & præter hujus generis plurima, quæ vel cæcis spectanda offerunt ; ambiguitatibus libellum illum scatere queruntur Scoti, sub quibus mysteria quædam occultantur, quæ solui desiderant, ut sunt, Dum jubentur pastores urgere operum necessitatem, quasi impudentia ipsa aulit quempiam Pastorum in Ecclesia Scotica reum agere contrarii dogmatis. Sed quid si efficacem necessitatem operum ad justificationem intelligant canonum fabri; nec sine causa tale quid de quibusdam eorum suspicari licet, nam licet dogma sit aperté Pontificium, totam humanæ salutis per Christum partæ structuram convellens, à multis tamen hodie resorbetur, & tractatus ea de re publicè prostant in vicina Anglia, sine ullo auctorum papaturientium damno, aut censura, ad quam heterodoxiam amplectendam queruntur Scoti, contribulium suorum quosdam plenis velis ferri, sic cap.8. §4. insinuant, disciplinam sicut nec doctrinam ad reformationis perfectionem nondum pervenisse, ideoque sedulo videntur cavisse, ne ullibi mentio haberetur de receptis Ecclesiæ Scoticæ consessionibus fidei : Quod ; quid aliud est, quam omnibus novitatibus in doctrina portam patentissimam aperire. Porro cum defectus illos in doctrina compertes habeant Episcopi (alioqui ejusmodi suspitionibus non gravarent) cur non aliis amicè monstrant ? Sed illa fortasse mysteria sunt Eleusina, iis solis aperienda, qui cœcæ obedientiæ specimine exhibito, sese ejusmodi Doctoribus, discipulos dignos præbuerunt, nec dubitandum, quin tempore opportuno in atria & ipsum cubile deducendi sint, ubi Calvinum, fanaticum illum Puritanum (nam hisce clogiis ab Hierarchicis, heroes illi vulgo appellantur) videbunt ad partes vocatum, & magisteriali virgula flagellatum, quod ausus fuerit sanctissimum papam Antichristum vocare, quod nulla spiritualis communio, cum idololatrica illa Ecclesia Romana, habenda sit, quod non expectata ordinatione Genevensis Episcopi ausus sit cathedram pastoralem Genevae conscendere, licet petitus votis civium & suffragiis honorabilium, quod hoc suo audaci coepto viam straverit aliis, praesertim Iohanni Knoxio Scoti discipulo, qui non expectata Episcoporum ordinatione (qui tunc intentissimis animis Christi teneram Ecclesiam in Scotia diflipabant) ausus fit pro Pastore fe gerere, licet a plebe petitus (quam maxime potestatem habere, vel eligendi dignos Sacerdotes, vel indignos recusandi, atque illud de Divina authoritate descendere, olim testatus est Cyprianus) & a legitimo presbytero Iohanne Rough ordinatus: etenim ii jure Divino ordinatio Pastorum Episcopis competit, totus fere beatus chorus reformatorum injustae intrusionis rei peragentur, & mirandum illud divinae benignitatis opus in Ecclesiis reformandis in dubium vocabitur. Audiet etiam alia majoris momenti, quam iniquè scilicet & rigidè fe gesserit Augustinus contra Semipelagianos: Calvinus & Genevenses contra Castalionem, Synodus Dordracena contra Remonstrantes, quam utile sit Imagines in templis locare, signo crucis signari, coram altari genu flectere, quam nullius momenti sint controversiae, inter reformatos & Pontificios agitatae, quam facilis partium reconciliatio, nisi paucorum puritanorum obstaret pertinax morositas. Verebantur etiam ad haec Scoti, ne sub obscuris ejusmodi verborum involucris, ea Ecclesiis Scoticis obtruderentur, quae alibi hactenus publicè & cum multorum applausu docentur, quererbantur etiam in istis canonibus Episcopos sibimet ipsis indulgere, ac durius cum Pastoribus agere, quam Pontificii Episcopi cum clero sibi subdito agere soleant: ereptum[?] pastoribus jus liberorum regni civium: tum, dum licet verbis, concedatur appellatio, ab injusta ordinarii præsulis sententia, ad Regem: negetur tamen libertas appellationem prosequendi, nisi primum petita & concessa licentia à præsule parte adversa; tûm etiam, quod pastorum virginitatem colentium, aut aliorum fine liberis decedentium testamenta non sint rata, nisi prius observetur conditio quam præscribunt Episcopi, Ecclesiam maxima bonorum parte dotandam.
units.tr: that is, the parliament, was overthrown at a single blow. Consistories or sessions and classes or presbyteries were regarded as mere conventicles. Lay elders and deacons were rejected, and all ecclesiastical causes were referred to the court of the bishop alone. Indeed, the sinews of ecclesiastical discipline had been cut long before, yet a certain face of it, though enfeebled, still remained. Through those surviving ruins it showed what Troy had once been, and it gave hope of how glorious a building could be raised again if God deigned to look upon his ravaged vineyard with the eye of mercy. Although after that unhappy Synod of Perth no national assembly or synod had met, provincial synods, presbyteries and sessions remained, and good men comforted one another with these names, however nearly empty. But now this monstrous birth of canons had been brought into the light, and the very name of these bodies was taken away. The bishops did not doubt that it would be gladly welcomed by all, but how vainly they had flattered themselves was soon apparent. This ill-formed offspring was rejected everywhere. Some of its absurdities were noted in large letters on its front, such as that all are forbidden, under pain of excommunication, to call in question anything contained in the book of canons, or in the books of the liturgy and ordination (not yet printed at that time). Yet although that book of canons contains whatever the English book contains, which the bishops cannot have failed to know, the Scots and almost all the other reformed Churches question it every day. Moreover, many new things have been added of which there is neither word nor trace in the English canons. I shall give a few of them as a sample, such as chapter 18, section 9, Sacramental confession and absolution, also in capitals. There is reason to fear that auricular confession will be forced upon the Churches, especially since the liturgical book orders all to partake of the holy Supper at least once a year and to approach all the other sacraments. What will prevent the sacrament of penance from being placed among the other sacraments to which men of riper age are ordered to come? Its chief part is auricular confession, and so it is called sacramental. The Scots complain that, besides very many things of this kind which offer themselves to be seen even by the blind, the little book teems with ambiguities under which certain mysteries are hidden, which they desire to be unfolded. For example, while ministers are ordered to press the necessity of good works, as if such impudence were itself to bring any minister in the Scottish Church to trial for holding a contrary doctrine. But what if the framers of the canons mean by necessity of works their efficacy for justification? One may well suspect this of some of them. For although the doctrine is openly Papist, overturning the whole structure of human salvation obtained through Christ, it is nowadays widely absorbed by many, and treatises on this subject are published openly in neighbouring England, without any loss or censure to the authors who are aspiring to the Papacy. The Scots complain that some of their fellow countrymen are carried under full sail toward embracing this heterodoxy. Thus in chapter 8, section 4, they hint that discipline, like doctrine, has not yet reached the perfection of reformation, and so they seem to have taken care that nowhere should mention be made of the confessions of faith received by the Scottish Church. What else is this than opening the widest gate to every novelty in doctrine? Further, since the bishops are aware of these defects in doctrine (otherwise they would not be burdened with such suspicions), why do they not show them kindly to others? But perhaps those are Eleusinian mysteries, to be revealed only to those who, having given proof of blind obedience, have shown themselves worthy disciples of such teachers. And there is no doubt that at the opportune time they will be led into the courtyard and even into the bedchamber, where they will see Calvin, that fanatical Puritan (for the Hierarchs commonly give these heroes that name as an epithet), summoned to account and whipped with the magisterial rod, because he dared to call the most holy pope Antichrist, because he held that no spiritual communion was to be had with that idolatrous Church of Rome, and because, without waiting for the ordination of the Bishop of Geneva, he dared to mount the pastoral chair at Geneva, though he was sought by the votes of the citizens and the suffrages of honourable men. Because of this bold enterprise he opened the way for others, especially John Knox, a disciple of the Scots, who, without waiting for the ordination of bishops (who at that time were with the most intent minds tearing apart Christ's tender Church in Scotland), dared to pass himself off as a minister, though sought by the people. Cyprian once testified that the people have the greatest power to choose worthy priests or to refuse unworthy ones, and that this comes down from divine authority. Knox was ordained by the lawful elder John Rough. For by divine right the ordination of ministers belongs to bishops, so almost the whole blessed chorus of the reformed will be charged with unjust intrusion, and that wonderful work of divine goodness in reforming the Churches will be called into doubt. They will also hear of other matters of greater moment: how unjustly and harshly Augustine behaved against the Semipelagians; how Calvin and the Genevans behaved against Castalio; how the Synod of Dort behaved against the Remonstrants. They will hear how useful it is to place images in churches, to sign oneself with the sign of the cross, and to kneel before the altar; how of no moment are the controversies argued between the reformed and the Papists; how easy the reconciliation of the parties would be, were it not for the stubborn peevishness of a few Puritans. The Scots also feared that under such obscure wrappings of words, things would be thrust upon the Scottish Churches which elsewhere have hitherto been taught publicly and with the applause of many. They complained too that in these canons the bishops indulged themselves and dealt more harshly with the ministers than Papist bishops are accustomed to deal with the clergy subject to them. The ministers were deprived of the right of the free citizens of the realm. Although an appeal from the unjust sentence of the ordinary prelate to the King is allowed in words, the liberty of pursuing that appeal is denied unless permission has first been sought and granted by the prelate on the opposing side. Furthermore, the wills of ministers who keep virginity, or of others who die leaving children, are not to be valid unless the condition prescribed by the bishops, that the Church be endowed with the greater part of the goods, is first observed.

units.la: Pium hunc præsulum affectum in Ecclesiam laudant,sed qui aliis tam comiter viam monstrant ipsos præire jubent, ut qui primi sunt in decernendo primi sint in conferendo, verborumque liberalitati, respondeat rerum largitas, ut in simili causa loquitur Salvianus, Nec æquius quid ab Episcopis in hoc negotio fieri poterit, quam ut ex superfluitatibus aliquid seponant in pios usus, saltem pecunias illas, quas ex venundatione officiorum curiæ Commissionariatus corradunt, præsertim, cum nullum officium publicum, cui jus dicendi potestas competit,in toto Regno venum exponatur, iis solis exceptis, quæ ad Episcoporum forum pertinent.
units.tr: They praise this pious affection of the prelates toward the Church. But those who show others the way so courteously should be told to go first themselves, so that those who are first in decreeing are first in bestowing, and the bounty of deeds answers the liberality of words, as Salvian speaks in a similar cause. Nothing more just could be done by the bishops in this matter than to set aside something from their superfluities for pious uses, at least the money which they gather from the sale of offices in the court of the Commissariat, especially since no public office to which the power of judging belongs is put up for sale in the whole kingdom, except those which pertain to the bishops' court.

units.la: Hujus generis multa ab Ecclesiasticis objecta,sed Laici, quibus libertas patriæ chara, impatientius fremebant, dum canonibus hisce, durissimum injectum jugum conscientiis viderent, ita ut vix liberioris aurae haustus restaret, nisi actiones suas ad nutum paucorum ambitiosorum præsulum componerent,Si vel in dubium vocarent,rubricam aliquam in libris edendis & editis, paratum in sua capita excommunicationis tremendæ fulmen videbant; sed durissimum longe judicabant aliis eandem poenam decerni, qui conversati fuerint cum excommunicato; praesertim cum metuendum sit, ne excommunicationis fulmen vibretur in homines innoxios, ac ignaros quid rerum agatur, saepe ob non satis fideliter solutas decimas, aut expensas Curiae Episcopalis: vocabant in memoriam, quam servili jugo premerentur ipsorum majores sub papatu terrore excommunicationis, ob res vilissimas, neque spem esse, mitiores futuros Episcopos hodiernos, qui licet cap.18.§2. Excommunicationem summariam damnent, quae legitimis citationibus non praecedentibus lata sit, cap. tamen 8.§4. Quosdam ipso facto excommunicatos dicunt, quam excommunicationem juris, seu latae sententiae Canonistae papales vocant, in qua summam Tyrannidem latere ingenue professus est Spalatensis Archiepiscopus. Et quia legibus regni Scotiae excommunicatorum bona, nisi intra praescriptum tempus, Ecclesiis se submiserint, in fiscum redigenda statuuntur, Ideo videbant omnes suas fortunas & quicquid hominibus carum esse solet, praesulum arbitrio exponi, in quos peccare durius esset, quam in ipsum Regem. Neque Panicum hunc fuisse timorem, fidem faciebant acta praesentia Episcopi Gallovidiani, qui, ut rudimentum poneret flagrantis zeli, quo fervet ad omnes non solum Ecclesiae Anglicanae caeremonias, verum etiam papaturientium heterodoxias promovendas in Scotia, habita celsa commissione in propria dioecesi, absentibus Archiepiscopis, ejus fori praesidibus, & pauculis assessoribus sibi adscitis; omnes fere, qui magistratu fungebantur in oppido Kirkudbrigh in jus vocat, quod proprium pastorem virum octuagenarium, audierint concionantem postquam Episcopali sententia a functione Ministerii depositus aut suspensus esset, quod difficilem se exhibuisset in recipiendis cæremoniis Perthenfibus, &c, quod fidem fere superat, Pastoris illius filium oppidi tum Consulem (seu, ut vulgo vocant, Balivum) in carcerem trahi jubet, quod reum & citatum patrem foro huic non exhibuisset, uti ferebatur. Eodemque tempore, nobilem quendam primariæ in ista provincia familiæ & dignitatis, pecunia prius bene mulctatum in remotiffimam à propriis ædibus urbem relegatum misit, quia forum illud tanquam extraneum, nullis Parlamenti statutis munitum declinaverit. Ex hoc uno audaci facinore discebant omnes omnino laici, cujuscunque ordinis & dignitatis essent, quid sibi à clementia Episcoporum expectandum esset; interim quia nondum severe urgebant omnes ubique Episcopi librum hunc canonum in Synodis provincialibus, omnia in publico statu fuere pacata, nullus publicus motus exortus, sed manifesta maximorum tumultuum indicia cernebant ubique prudentiores, si prout cæpissent pergerent Episcopi, quibus nisi mature obviam iretur, fumus ille in flammam erumperet, quæ Ecclesiæ & Regno ruinam tantum non allatura esset.
units.tr: Many objections of this kind were raised by the churchmen. But the laymen, whose love of their country's liberty was strong, grew more and more impatient. They saw a very harsh yoke laid on their consciences by these canons, so that hardly a breath of freer air remained unless they shaped all their actions to the nod of a few ambitious prelates. If anyone questioned any rubric in the books being published or already published, they saw the dreadful thunderbolt of excommunication ready to fall on their heads. But they judged it far harsher that the same penalty should be decreed against those who had dealings with an excommunicated person. This was especially so because there was reason to fear that the thunderbolt of excommunication would be hurled at harmless people who knew nothing of what was going on, often over tithes not paid faithfully enough or over the expenses of the episcopal court. They recalled how their forefathers under the papacy had been held in servile bondage by the terror of excommunication, even for the most trivial matters. They had no hope that the present bishops would be any milder. Although they condemn in the canons (chap. 18, §2) the summary excommunication pronounced without prior lawful citation, yet (chap. 8, §4) they say that some are excommunicated ipso facto. The papal canonists call this excommunication of law, or excommunication by sentence already passed, and the Archbishop of Spalato openly confessed that great tyranny lies hidden in it. Moreover, since by the laws of the kingdom of Scotland the goods of excommunicated persons are to be confiscated to the exchequer unless they submit to the Church within the prescribed time, everyone saw that his whole fortune, and whatever usually matters most to men, would be left at the mercy of the bishops. And that this fear was not groundless was shown by the recent conduct of the Bishop of Galloway. To make a start on the blazing zeal with which he burns to promote not only the ceremonies of the English Church but also the popish heterodoxies of those who crave the papacy in Scotland, he took a high commission in his own diocese, the archbishops being absent. He summoned before him, with a few assessors whom he had brought in, nearly all who held office in the town of Kirkcudbright. He summoned them because they had heard their own minister, an old man of eighty, preaching after he had been deposed or suspended from his ministry by episcopal sentence, because he had been difficult in receiving the Perth ceremonies, and for other things which almost pass belief. He ordered the son of that minister, who was then the town's provost (or, as the common people call him, bailie), to be dragged to prison because, as was reported, he had not produced his father, who was accused and summoned, before this court. At the same time he sent into exile, in a most remote town far from his own home, a certain nobleman of a leading family and rank in that province, who had first been well fined, because he had refused that court as foreign and not protected by any statute of Parliament. From this one bold deed all the laymen, of whatever rank or dignity they were, learned what they had to expect from the mercy of the bishops. Meanwhile, since not all the bishops everywhere had yet pressed this book of canons hard in the provincial synods, everything in the public state remained calm and no public disturbance arose. But the wiser men saw everywhere clear signs of great tumults to come, if the bishops went on as they had begun. Unless they were met in time, that smoke would break out into a flame which would bring ruin almost upon the Church and the kingdom.

units.la: Sed hæc Episcopi contemnentes, ut statuerant, excudi curant librum liturgicum, seu communium precum in usum Ecclesiarum Scoticarum, nullo præeunte consensu Ecclesiarum, quibus, regio mandato imperatur, ut omnes eundem reverenter recipiant, tanquam unicam divini cultus publici formam, tempus etiam definitum, videlicet Paschatis festum anni 1637 ad quem diem Senatus regius statuit, ut unaquæque Ecclesia, duo ad minimum exemplaria emeret in usum Parochiæ, & pretium satis liberale, libris illis coëmendis destinatum, in eorum Episcoporum utilitatem, qui fætui huic formando maximam operam navarant.
units.tr: But the bishops, despising these warnings, did as they had determined. They had a liturgical book printed, that is, a book of common prayers for use in the Scottish churches, without the consent of the churches beforehand. By royal command the churches were ordered to receive it reverently, all of them, as the only form of public worship. They also set a fixed time, namely the Easter festival of the year 1637, by which day the royal Senate decreed that each church should buy at least two copies for the use of the parish. A fairly generous sum of money was set aside for buying these books, for the benefit of those bishops who had taken the greatest pains in forming this offspring.

units.la: Porro liber ille idem fere est cum libro communium precum in Anglia si mutationes quasdam exceperis, paucis quidem in melius sed pluribus in deterius, lectiones librorum apocryphorum non sunt hic tam frequentes quam in Anglia, quae tamen apocryphorum capita retinentur, ea ut plurimum iis diebus destinantur, in quibus frequentissimus fieri solet (aut imperatur) populi conventus. Dein, cum in Anglia retineatur translatio versionis vulgatae Latinae, præsertim in Psalmis, hic vero adhæretur versioni poltremae, quae dicitur Iacobi Regis, atque hae sunt mutationes in melius.
units.tr: Further, this book is almost the same as the Book of Common Prayer in England, with some changes. A few changes are for the better, but more are for the worse. The readings from the apocryphal books are not as frequent here as in England. Yet the chapters of the Apocrypha are retained, and for the most part they are appointed for those days on which a very crowded assembly of the people usually takes place, or is ordered. Next, since in England the translation of the Latin Vulgate is retained, especially in the Psalms, but here the most recent version is adhered to, which is called the version of King James, these are the changes for the better.

units.la: At in deterius frequentissimæ sunt; specimen tantum exhibebo in administratione sacræ cœnæ, ubi expressa mentio pomposi apparatus altaris, seu mensæ (quibus vocibus promiscuè liber utitur) situs altaris juxta murum ad orientem, stabit Presbyter ossiciaturus, ad partem seu latus altaris boreale, locum hunc occupaturus tantum in principio actionis, & dum legitur offertorium, staturus postea eo in loco, in quo majori facilitate utraque manu uti posset: hæc loci mutatio tantum est inchoanda, dum dicitur precatio consecrationis elementorum (porro locus hic nullus alius esse potest quam ante altare, facie à populo aversa) Diaconus (non qui in usu Belgarum aut Scotorum & reformatorum in Gallia, sed tertius ordo cleri) populi collectas presbytero adducet in pelvim congestas, summa cum reverentia, qui coram Deo humiliter præsentabit, & altari imponet. Tum presbyter offeret & locabit panem & vinum sacramento destinatum super dominica mensa. In prima precatione post finitum offertorium, fit lucu-lenta mentio mortuorum, pro quibus Deo gratiæ aguntur. frequens mentio, pastorem debere se aliquando ad populum convertere (aliquando ergo avertitur.) In oratione consecratoria, quę in Anglico clara fuêre contra transsubstantiationem, omittuntur, eorumque loco ea ponuntur, quæ Pontificiorum, Vbiquitariorum sensum ferre, absque ulla deflectione possunt, Audi nos benigne[?] Pater, & pro omnipotenti tua bonitate concede, ut ita benedicas & sanctifices verbo tuo, & spiritu tuo sancto hæc tua dona, has tuas creaturas panis & vini, ut sint nobis corpus & sanguis dilecti filii tui, &c. quæ sunt formalia verba Canonis Missæ. In eadem precatione margini apponuntur hæc, Presbyter officiaris sumet seu tollat patinam in manus, dum hoc est corpus meum repetitur, & calicem, dum dicitur hic est sanguis novi Testamenti, finita consecratione immediatè subjungitur memoriale, seu oratio oblationis (quæ in missali Romano vocatur oblatio rememorativa) in qua dicitur, Christum voluisse nos illud memoriale celebrare in memoriam, non solum beatæ passionis, sed & potentis resurrectionis, gloriosæ ascensionis, &c. &, ut verbo dicam, quantum declinat hic liber ab Anglico, tanto propius accedit ad missale Romanum, plurimas alias mutationes in deterius observarunt Scoti, & profitentur apertè, se probaturos omnes materiales partes canonis missæ, seminaliter ibi positas, & parvo temporis intervallo missam posse inde fabricari.
units.tr: But the changes for the worse are very many. I will give only one example, in the administration of the Holy Supper. There the book expressly mentions the elaborate furnishing of the altar, or of the table (the book uses these words interchangeably): the altar is to be placed against the wall to the east; the minister who is to officiate shall stand at the north side or flank of the altar, occupying this place only at the beginning of the action, and while the offertory is read he shall afterwards stand in that place where he can use both hands with greater ease. This change of place is only to be begun while the prayer of consecration of the elements is said (and this place can be none other than before the altar, with his face turned away from the people). The deacon (not the kind who is found among the Dutch or the Scots and the reformed in France, but a third order of the clergy) shall bring the people's alms to the minister, heaped in a basin, with the greatest reverence; he shall humbly present them before God and place them on the altar. Then the minister shall offer and set the bread and wine appointed for the sacrament upon the Lord's table. In the first prayer, after the offertory is finished, there is a notable mention of the dead, for whom thanks are given to God. There is frequent mention of the minister being bound at times to turn towards the people (so at other times he turns away). In the prayer of consecration, which in the English book was clearly framed against transubstantiation, these things are omitted, and in their place are put words which can carry the meaning of the Papists and the Ubiquitarians without any deviation: Hear us graciously[?], Father, and by thy almighty goodness grant that thou mayest so bless and sanctify with thy word and thy Holy Spirit these thy gifts, these thy creatures of bread and wine, that they may be to us the body and blood of thy beloved Son, &c. These are the formal words of the canon of the Mass. In the same prayer these notes are placed in the margin: the officiating minister shall take or lift the paten in his hands while the words this is my body are repeated, and the cup while it is said this is the blood of the new testament. Immediately after the consecration follows the memorial, or prayer of oblation (which in the Roman missal is called the commemorative oblation), in which it is said that Christ willed us to celebrate this memorial in remembrance not only of his blessed passion, but also of his mighty resurrection, his glorious ascension, &c. And, to put it in a word: the further this book departs from the English one, the closer it comes to the Roman missal. The Scots have also made very many other changes for the worse, and openly profess that they will approve all the material parts of the canon of the Mass, which are there sown as seeds, and that from them a Mass could be built up in a short time.

units.la: Sed redeo ad narrationem, defunctus necessaria hac excursione, quia librorum horum in sequentibus frequentissima futura est mentio, utpote, quod omnibus hisce dissidiis causam dederint, Episcopis omni conatu urgentibus, ut ab Ecclesiis reciperentur, nullo præeunte Synodi Nationalis examine aut judicio, cujus consensum se nunquam obtenturos sciebant, itaque denuo, ad supremum Regis senatum confugiunt, cujus mandato omnes jubentur regio mandato parere, cum certificatione (ut ita loquar) nisi in usum Parœciarum singuli Pastores duo exemplaria comparent, se interdicturos eis aqua & igni, rebelliumque poenas non evasuros. Interim vero quidam Episcoporum, non expectato die à Rege præfinito (Paschatis festo) statim ea li-tur. turgia in cathedralibus Ecclesiis usi sunt, præsertim Roffensis & Dumblanensis Episcopi, librorum istorum primarii authores, & Ecclesiis antea de ἐπεγδήξι᾽α valde suspecti. Alii cum Synodis Provincialibus egerunt, in quibus respondebant Pastores, non posse se tam insignem cultus divini publici mutationem probare, nisi re-bene perpensa & examinata, iniquum esse, ea tam magni momenti Ecclesiis invitis obtrudere, de quibus nulla unquam habita sit in Synodis Nationalibus deliberatio aut censura, quibus suprema in rebus hujus materiæ competit potestas: Canones Ecclesiasticos nullibi unquam latos aut sancitos fuisse, quam in Synodis, agnoscentibus & statuentibus illud Hierarchicorum doctissimis, præsertim Lanciloto Wintoniensi Episcopo in concione de jure & potestate convocandi conventus, & Bilsono. æquum ergo esse, ut res hæc Nationalis Synodi judicio submittatur. Ad hanc exceptionem varie responsum, quibusdam Episcopis silentio supprimi satagentibus omnem Synodorum Nationalium mentionem; à quibus tam metuebant quam ab œcumenicis Pontifices Romani. Aliis vero apertius affirmantibus, omnem canonum & rituum Ecclesiasticorum sanciendorum authoritatem sibi solis, ut Ecclesiam repræsentantibus competere; Pastoribus cæteris, seu solis, seu congregatis, obedientiam solum relictam esse: in quibusdam tamen Provincialibus Synodis, deliberandi tempus ex gratia concessum, ad Synodum Provincialem proximam, quæ mense Octobri habenda fuit, anni currentis 1637. præsertim in diœcesi Edinburgena (quam ad novum Episcopatum erexerat Rex anno 1633.) sed quorundam præcipitantium impetu qui omnem moram fervidis suis consiliis damnosam putabant, procuratur novum à Rege serenissimo mandatum, quo Ecclesiæ urbis Edinburgenæ
units.tr: But I return to my narrative, having digressed for this necessary reason, because mention of these books will be very frequent in what follows, as they gave cause for all these quarrels. The bishops pressed with every effort that they be received by the churches, with no prior examination or judgment of the National Synod. They knew they would never obtain its consent. So they again took refuge in the supreme senate of the King, by whose command all were ordered to obey the royal command, under the warning (as I may put it) that unless the individual ministers procured two copies for the use of their parishes, they would be forbidden fire and water and would not escape the penalties of rebels. Meanwhile some of the bishops, without waiting for the day fixed by the King (the Easter festival), at once used that liturgy in the cathedral churches. This was especially so with the Bishops of Ross and of Dunblane, the chief authors of these books, who had long been highly suspected of popery by the churches. Others dealt with the provincial synods, in which the ministers replied that they could not approve so remarkable a change in public worship unless it had been well weighed and examined. They said it was unjust to force on the churches, against their will, things of such great importance, on which no deliberation or censure had ever been held in the National Synods, to which supreme power in matters of this kind belongs. They said that ecclesiastical canons had never been enacted or sanctioned anywhere except in synods, as the most learned of the hierarchical party acknowledged and laid down, especially Lancelot, Bishop of Winchester, in a sermon on the right and power of calling assemblies, and Bilson. It was therefore fair that this matter should be submitted to the judgment of the National Synod. To this objection various replies were made. Some bishops laboured to suppress in silence every mention of National Synods, fearing them as much as the Roman pontiffs fear ecumenical councils. Others affirmed more openly that the authority to enact canons and rites of the Church belonged to themselves alone, as representing the Church, and that the other ministers, whether alone or assembled, were left only with obedience. Yet in some provincial synods, a time to deliberate was granted as a favour, until the next provincial synod, which was to be held in October of the present year 1637. This was especially so in the diocese of Edinburgh (which the King had erected into a new bishopric in 1633). But by the rash impetuosity of some men, who thought every delay harmful to their fiery plans, a new mandate was obtained from the most serene King, by which the churches of the city of Edinburgh (which is the metropolis of the kingdom) were ordered to admit this liturgy at once, without any delay. By virtue of this mandate the ministers of that town were summoned. Those who refused were at once silenced, without any lawful process, and those who promised obedience to the public reading of the liturgical book on the Lord's day before the morning sermon…

units.la: (quæ regni metropolis est) jubentur liturgiam hanc statim omni mora posthabita admittere, cujus mandati vigore convocantur oppidi illius Pastores: renuentibus, absque omni legitimo processu statim indicitur silentium, qui obedientiam spondent ad libri liturgici lectionem publicam, die dominica ante matutinam concionem se comparant.
units.tr: (which is the capital of the kingdom) are ordered to admit this liturgy at once, without any delay. By virtue of this command the ministers of that town are summoned. Those who refuse are immediately silenced, without any lawful process, while those who promise obedience prepare themselves on the Lord's day, before morning sermon, to read the liturgical book in public.

units.la: Ad insolitum hoc spectaculum magnus fuit populi concursus, cumque vidissent, libros illos ab Episcopo productos (qui primum actum in cathedrali Ecclesia peragi per se æquum putabat) ingentem edunt fremitum, ac Templo excedunt, non sine diris imprecationibus in capita Episcoporum & alseclarum[?]: clausis ostiis peragitur sacrum, quæ, sibi à plebe metuentes Episcopi, qui frequentes intererant, occludi curarunt per magistratum urbis: finitis sacris, egrediente templum Episcopo ingens oritur populi tumultus, à verbis devenerunt mulieres ad verbera, à quarum furore nisi mature subductus fuisset, præsentissimum vitæ periculum, non effugisset. In cæteris oppidi templis aut cogebantur lectionem intactam relinquere, aut interrumpere.
units.tr: A great crowd of people gathered for this unusual spectacle. When they saw the books brought forth by the Bishop, who thought it only fair that the first act should be performed in the cathedral church, they raised a huge outcry and left the church, not without dreadful curses against the heads of the Bishops and their followers. The service was held with the doors shut, because the Bishops, who attended in large numbers and feared the common people, had the city magistrates secure them. When the service was over and the Bishop was leaving the church, a great tumult of the people arose. From words they came to blows, and the women's fury would have brought the Bishop into the most immediate danger of his life had he not been hurried away in time. In the other churches of the town, the ministers were either forced to leave the reading untouched or to interrupt it.

units.la: Cogitur statim regius Senatus à prandio, qui indignitate rei motus, statuit diligentissimè indagandos tumultus authores, ac sub pænis severissimis omnibus interdicitur, ne aliter quam honorificè & reverenter de Episcopis, eorumque actionibus, ac libris hisce loquantur; statutum quoque, ut continuaretur liturgiæ lectio: sed sacris pomeridianis finitis, major oritur sævientis populi contra Episcopum fremitus: non defuere quæcunque furor arma procaci & irritatæ plebi ministrat: sed ille curru magnatis tectus evasit, injuriam hanc vindicaturus. Nam omnia ad Regem delata fuere, non sine amplificationibus, quibus clementissimum ipsius animum ad extremam vindictam irritarent; nisi Senatus regius literis mollioribus (quibus cives spectatos, & alicujus nominis, liberabant, culpa in procacem plebem, mulieres, praesertim viliores, rejectà) ad clementiam flexissent. Interim tamen nulli habiti fuerunt conventus sacri diebus hebdomadariis; nec ad publicas preces, aut conciones (uti antea fieri consuevit) integri mensis spatio patebant templa, ita ut oppidum quasi interdicto Ecclesiastico subjectum fuit, quod furorem populi, sat hactenus saevientis, inflammavit.
units.tr: The royal Senate was at once summoned from dinner. Moved by the outrage of the matter, it resolved that the authors of the tumult should be sought out with the utmost diligence, and under the severest penalties it forbade anyone to speak of the Bishops, their actions and these books other than honourably and respectfully. It also decreed that the reading of the liturgy should continue. But when the afternoon services were finished, a greater outcry against the Bishop arose from the raging people. There was no lack of whatever weapons fury supplies to a bold and provoked mob, but he escaped, sheltered in a nobleman's carriage, intending to avenge this insult. For everything was reported to the King, not without exaggerations designed to rouse his most merciful spirit to the utmost vengeance. Only the royal Senate, by milder letters (in which it freed the respectable citizens of some standing and placed the blame on the bold mob, especially the lowlier women), softened him toward clemency. Meanwhile, however, no sacred assemblies were held on the weekdays, nor were the churches open for a full month for public prayers or sermons, as had been customary before. The town was thus, as it were, placed under an ecclesiastical interdict, which inflamed the people's fury, already sufficiently raging.

units.la: In aliis regni partibus, haud minori diligentia urgentur omnes ab Episcopis, ut librum liturgicum reciperent; & quia praesens periculum, omnium, qui resistebant, capitibus imminebat (nam Senatus regii edicto omnes terrebant Episcopi) ideo ne ignavo silentio, sibi atque Ecclesiis deesset Pastores; ii maximè, cum quibus acrius instabant Episcopi, Senatum regium supplices adeunt, ac rogant, ne tam manifesta vi Ecclesiam opprimi finerent, se paratos mutare, quicquid in recepta à majoribus disciplina & liturgia, vitiosi à quoquam ostendi posset: summa capita errorum, in hisce libris contentorum notant, ac disputationem, seu amicam collationem super iis offerunt, ostendunt quantorum malorum res sit, mutationes in Ecclesiis introducere, etiam in melius vergentes; quas plus novitate turbare, quam utiliter prodesse, (licet veterum exempla non ostenderent) miseram praesentis Ecclesiae sub schismate gementis, faciem declarare dicebant: violenta obtrusione liturgiarum pessundatas fuisse Austriacas reformatas Ecclesias; notabant etiam infoelices illas controversias, quibus vexata fuit Ecclesia regnante Carolo Magno, aliis Ambrosianae liturgiae adhaerentibus; aliis in illius locum Gregorianam seu Romanam promoventibus; ac quibus calamitatibus Hispaniae regnum olim concussum fuerit, regnante Alphonso 6, qui consilio legati Pontificii veterem Mozarabicam liturgiam, antiquaturus, ut Gregorianam introduceret; omnibus ordinibus regni reclamantibus. Denique quam fragili loco res Ecclesiæ starent; si ad paucorum, aut Principis libitum, cultus innocens hactenus cum magno piorum fructu observatus, sine prævio consensu Ecclesiarum mutaretur; idque in cultum non uno nomine vitiosum. Si hæc nunc permittantur, posse à posterioribus principibus deteriora in horum locum introduci; nam nunquam defuturi sunt ex Ecclesiasticorum[?] ordine; qui ut aulica gratia fruantur purpuram[?] instar Ecebolii colant.
units.tr: In other parts of the kingdom, all were pressed by the Bishops with no less diligence to receive the liturgical book. Since the present danger hung over the heads of all who resisted (for the Bishops terrified everyone with the edict of the royal Senate), the ministers, lest they fail themselves and their churches by a cowardly silence, approached the royal Senate as suppliants, especially those with whom the Bishops were pressing most fiercely, and asked that it not allow the Church to be oppressed by such manifest force. They said they were ready to change whatever faults anyone could show in the discipline and liturgy received from our fathers. They noted the chief errors contained in these books, and offered a disputation, or a friendly conference, on them. They showed how great an evil it is to introduce changes into the Churches, even changes tending toward the better, which by their novelty rather disturb than usefully benefit, though the examples of the ancients did not show this. They declared that the wretched face of the present Church, groaning under schism, made this plain. The Austrian reformed Churches, they said, had been ruined by the violent imposition of liturgies. They also noted those unhappy controversies by which the Church was troubled under Charlemagne's reign, some adhering to the Ambrosian liturgy, others promoting the Gregorian or Roman liturgy in its place. They noted too the calamities by which the kingdom of Spain was once shaken under Alphonso VI, who, on the advice of a papal legate, wished to abolish the old Mozarabic liturgy in order to introduce the Gregorian, all the orders of the kingdom protesting. Finally, they pointed out how fragile the Church's position would be if an innocent form of worship, hitherto observed with great spiritual profit by the godly, were changed at the pleasure of a few men or of the Prince, without the prior consent of the Churches, and that in a worship faulty in more than one respect. If these things were now permitted, they said, worse things could be introduced in their place by later princes; for there would never be lack of men from the ranks of the clergy who, to enjoy courtly favour, would cultivate the purple like Ecebolius.

units.la: Optima quidem de serenissimi Regis pietate omnibus esse persuasum: sed omnium regnorum historias abunde docere, successionem plurium Regum, eodem modo erga cultum divinum affecto-rum, raro occurrere, interim non esse, quod hæ mutationes in regem rejiciantur ab Episcopis; qui ante quadriennium regno inauguratus, solenni & sacro juramento se obstrinxerit, ne quid in regno hoc Scotiæ mutaret; nisi legitimo, quorum interesset, præeunte consilio & consensu. Quare senatum regium enixè & humiliter obtestantur, ut malis hisce obviam ire velit, ac severi hujus decreti rigorem lenire.
units.tr: It was indeed generally believed that the most serene King was of the best piety. But the histories of all kingdoms show abundantly that a succession of several kings equally inclined toward the worship of God is rare. Nevertheless, there was no reason for the Bishops to reject these changes on the King's account, since four years earlier, when he was inaugurated to the kingdom, he had bound himself by a solemn and sacred oath not to change anything in the kingdom of Scotland unless by lawful counsel and consent of those concerned. Therefore they earnestly and humbly beseech the royal Senate to wish to meet these evils and to soften the rigour of this severe decree.

units.la: Annuit senatus, ac declarat, sibi per decretum illud nunquam in mentem venisse, ut in praxin publicam deducerentur libri illi: hoc se solum voluisse, ut singuli pastores exemplaria compararent in usum privatum, ut diligenter inquirerent, quid in iis fit, cur admitti non debeant, si serenissimus Rex postea urgeat.
units.tr: The Senate assented and declared that it had never intended by that decree that those books should be put into public practice. It had wished only this: that individual ministers should procure copies for private use, so that they might carefully examine what is in them and why they ought not to be admitted, should the most serene King later press the matter.

units.la: Quam gratiam pastoribus illis à senatu concefsam, animo non satis æquo tulisse Episcopos relatum est; nam cum antea omnem invidiam ex obtrufione librorum ortam in Senatum regium cessucessuram sperassent, nunc se, à senatu derelictos, tanquam piacularem hostiam omnium furori objectos vident; Ac pro solita prudentia, quâ hactenus usi fuere, putabant rerum periti quieturos eos, donec melior offerretur opportunitas: sed veriti ne Regi tandem innotesceret, se ipsius majestati vanis promissis imposuisse, (cui persuaserant, negotium hoc sine publico motu facile promoveri posse, plurimosque omnium ordinum subditos summis votis libros illos expetere;) ne inquam hæc fraus statim pateret, secunda vice rem tentandam censent: sed irrito conatu, nam nihil intentatum reliquerint, quo blandis pollicitationibus aut vi pastores in suam sententiam pertraherent; nihil tamen effecere, nisi quod piscatores istos sapere docuerint; qui videntes, se antiquato illo senatus regii mandato, quotidie ab Episcopis premi, ad senatum denuo confugiunt, ardentibusque precibus rogant ut se & alios qui adhuc domi se modestè continent liberare velit, à justo metu introducendarum novitatum, via tam iniqua; Episcopisque mandaret ne Provincialibus pastoribus negotium facesserent, sub horum librorum prætextu quos erroribus apertis & subdolè tectis scatere se probaturos dicebant, cum senatui Regio visum erit. Aderat tunc pastorum numerus frequentior ex omnibus regni partibus, simul cum senioribus Ecclesiarum, ut senatoribus regiis confiaret, non esse solos Pastores, quibus libri illi displicerent. Multi tum exhibiti libelli supplices (nam sigillatim adhuc agebant causam hanc communem) quidam moderatiori stylo compositi, tradebantur illustrissimo Ducì Lenoxiæ, (qui non ita pridem ab aula regia venerat, ad matris exequias faciendas Pasleti in Scotia, ac tum statim in Angliam revertisurus erat) ut Regi in manus traderet. Responsum tum etiam iisdem datum à Senatu, interdictum esse Episcopis, ne ulterius libros illos obtruderent: se etiam serenissimum Regem certiorem fecisse de ipsorum postulatis; ac responsum, voluntatemq; regiam cum acceperint, communicaturos. Gratiis Senatui actis, supplices omnes tum pastores, tum Ecclesiarum seniores Laici, ut vocant, (qui omnes fere nobiles primariae dignitatis aut primarii urbium magistratus fuere) laeti domum se contulerunt, ac precibus privatis, publicisque supplicationibus ac jejuniis cum Deo egerunt omnes, ut Regis piissimi consilia, in bonum publicum Ecclesiae & regni converterentur; hostiumque conatus, cuniculis sat hactenus quassatam Ecclesiam subfodientium, irritos redderet.
units.tr: It was reported that the Bishops did not take this favour granted by the Senate to those ministers with a very even temper. For although they had earlier hoped that all the odium arising from the imposition of the books would pass over to the royal Senate, now they see themselves abandoned by the Senate and exposed, like a sacrificial victim, to the fury of all. And, by the customary prudence they had hitherto used, those skilled in affairs thought they would keep quiet until a better opportunity offered. But fearing lest the King should at last learn that they had imposed on his majesty with empty promises (for they had persuaded him that this business could easily be advanced without public disturbance, and that most of his subjects of every order eagerly desired those books), they judged that the attempt must be made a second time, lest this deceit be exposed at once. But the attempt was in vain, for they left nothing untried by which to draw the ministers to their opinion, by flattering promises or by force. Yet they achieved nothing, except that they taught those fishermen to be wise. Seeing that, with the old mandate of the royal Senate set aside, they were pressed every day by the Bishops, these men again fled to the Senate and with fervent prayers asked it to free them and the others who still quietly kept to their homes from the just fear of innovations introduced by so unjust a means. They also asked it to order the Bishops not to trouble the provincial ministers on the pretext of these books, which they said they would prove to teem with open errors and cunningly concealed ones, when the royal Senate saw fit. A larger number of ministers from all parts of the kingdom was then present, together with the seniors of the Churches, so that it might be made clear to the royal senators that the ministers were not the only ones who disliked those books. Many supplications were then presented, for they were still pleading this common cause one by one. Some, composed in a more moderate style, were handed to the most illustrious Duke of Lennox (who had not long before come from the royal court to perform his mother's funeral rites at Paisley in Scotland, and was then about to return to England at once), that he might place them in the King's hands. Then the Senate also gave an answer to the same men: the Bishops were forbidden to press those books any further, and the Senate had informed the most serene King of their requests; when they had received the King's answer and will, they would communicate it. With thanks given to the Senate, all the suppliants, both ministers and the lay seniors of the Churches (as they are called, who were almost all nobles of high rank or the chief magistrates of the towns), went home joyfully. They dealt with God in private prayers, public supplications and fastings, all of them, that the counsels of the most pious King might be turned to the public good of the Church and kingdom, and that he might render null the attempts of the enemies who, with mines, were undermining the Church, already shaken so far.

units.la: Cum accipiunt regium ab aula tabellarium venturum, illico Edinburgum frequentes convolant; ubi loco benigni responsi, severum contra eos vibratur edictum regium, Octobris 18, quo omnes sub rebellionis poena jubentur Edinburgo discedere intra paucarum horarum spatium; quasi ipsorum praesentia plebem Edinburgenam ad tumultus excitasset. Et quia Edinburgeni bis ausi fuere Episcopis librum liturgicum introducentibus sese opponere, ac in Episcopum Edinburgenum impetum facere, poenae loco removentur inde omnia tribunalia juridica; videlicet senatus regius, Camera rationum & Sessio: (Sessio porro, quam vocant, est supremum tribunal civilium causarum omnium ad quod appellationes omnes deferuntur, institutum a Jacobo V. Scotorum Rege, ad similitudinem Parlamenti Parisiensis cujus propago est.) Et quia nullibi commodus locus inveniri potuit, nulla fuit in foro eo causarum civilium dijudicatio, quo justitio[?] non solum urbs Edinburgena, sed omnes regni subditi graves Regi poenas dedere.
units.tr: When they hear that a royal messenger is coming from the court, they flock to Edinburgh in large numbers. There, instead of a kindly reply, a harsh royal edict is hurled at them, dated 18 October, ordering everyone to leave Edinburgh within a few hours on pain of rebellion, as though their presence had stirred the people of Edinburgh to tumult. And because the Edinburgh people twice dared to oppose the bishops who were introducing the liturgical book, and made an attack on the bishop of Edinburgh, all the courts of law are removed from the city as a punishment: namely the royal Senate, the Chamber of Accounts and the Session. (The Session, as they call it, is the supreme tribunal for all civil cases, to which all appeals are brought. It was established by James V, King of the Scots, on the model of the Parliament of Paris, of which it is an offshoot.) And since no convenient place could be found elsewhere, civil cases could no longer be judged in that forum, so that not only the city of Edinburgh but all the subjects of the kingdom incurred heavy penalties from the King.

units.la: Promulgatio horum edictorum mirum quam omnium ordinum supplices incenderet, qui cum cognitum se habere dicerent, per Episcopos solos stetisse quo minus Rex pro consueta sua benignitate postulatis ipsorum clementer responderet & loco levaminis, iniquissimorum gravaminum, sub quibus patienter adhuc gemebant, novo onere presseftit, ac urbe excedere iussit quasi eorum praesentia seditionibus viam sterneret, gravem querimoniam contra Episcopos Senatui regio offerunt Octobris 19. Atque cum libri illi canonici & liturgia semina superstitionis & idololatriae continent; Rogant, ut cum Episcopis eorum auctoribus solis jure agere· sibi liceret, quos aliorum etiam criminum reos se peracturos profitentur, quae nisi liquido probent, nullam recusant poenam, capitibus, honori, bonis infligendam.
units.tr: The publication of these edicts so inflamed the petitioners of every rank that they declared they knew the King would have answered their requests kindly, as is his custom, had the bishops alone not stood in the way. Instead of relief from the most unjust burdens under which they still groaned in patience, they were laden with a new load and ordered to leave the city, as though their presence were paving the way for sedition. On 19 October they therefore presented a grave complaint to the royal Senate against the bishops. They argue that those canonical books and the liturgy contain the seeds of superstition and idolatry. They ask that they be permitted to bring legal action against the bishops alone, as the authors of these things, and they profess that they will prove the bishops guilty of other crimes too. If they fail to prove them clearly, they refuse no penalty, to be inflicted on their heads, their honours and their goods.

units.la: Libello huic supplici ingens omnium ordinum numerus subscripsit, ratumque habuere quibuscunque animus fuit, Ecclesiasticam libertatem & puritatem cultus divini vindicare à tyrannide Episcoporum & mixtura superstitionis, uti loquebantur. Singuli antea separatim causam hanc agebant apud Senatum, quo omnem adversariis calumniandi ansam praeriperent; quasi ostentata[?] multitudine & per seditionem, vi, à Rege, gravaminum levamen extorsuri essent, nunc vero, cum moderatissimae ipsorum actiones in deteriorem partem traherentur, regisque clementissimi aures falsis & fictis ad invidiam criminationibus occlusas aequissimis subditorum fere universorum totius Regni postulatis cernerent, quasi prae paucitate contemnendi essent, seditiosi isti puritani (quibus titulis probrosis defamantur ab Hierarchis, omnes, quibus ministrorum paritas, rituumque Apostolicorum simplicitas arridet) consultissimum itaque censebant, ut communis haec Ecclesiae causa, junctim ageretur, quo Regi innotesceret. non paucos esse, (ut mentiebantur adversarii) sed quamplurimos omnium ordinum, Deo Regique fideles subditos, quorum summa desideria eò contenderent. Senatui etiam modestè ostenderunt, se non posse Edinburgo discedere, donec via aliqua monstretur, qua à præsentibus & imminentibus gravissimis periculis liberarentur.
units.tr: A huge number of people of every rank signed this humble petition and approved it, all those whose wish was to defend ecclesiastical liberty and the purity of divine worship from the tyranny of the bishops and the admixture of superstition, as they put it. Previously each man had pursued this cause separately before the Senate, so as to deprive their adversaries of any pretext for slander. The adversaries claimed that they would extort relief from the King by force and sedition, by a show of numbers. Now, however, since their most moderate actions were being twisted for the worse, and since they saw that the ears of the most merciful King were closed to them by false and fabricated accusations, and that the most just requests of almost all his subjects throughout the kingdom were being despised because of their small numbers, these seditious Puritans (for so the Hierarchs slander them with disgraceful titles, all who favour equality among ministers and the simplicity of apostolic rites) thought it most expedient that this common cause of the Church be pursued jointly, so that the King might learn that there were not a few (as their opponents falsely claimed) but very many loyal subjects of every rank, faithful to God and the King, whose chief desires tended this way. They also respectfully showed the Senate that they could not leave Edinburgh until some way was pointed out by which they might be freed from the present and impending very grave dangers.

units.la: Mansere itaque admodum frequentes, & numerus indies crevit, omnibus ex remotissimis Regni Provinciis Edinburgum convolantibus, ut in causa communi consilia conferrent: & quia non sine causa verebatur Senatus regius, ne tumultus aliquis & graviora mala ex tanta frequentia orirentur, rogat, ut supplices semet separarent, sigillatimque gravamina quisque proponeret, nam sic divisos facilius placari aut everti posse sciebat. Nec ignotum Episcopis, qui Senatus magnam partem faciebant, inde natam Britannorum olim ruinam per Romanos; de quibus Tacitus: dum singuli pugnarent vincebantur universi: sed fatalia ejusmodi consilia, causæ ruinam minitantia, aspernabantur libertatis Ecclesiasticæ vindices, nec ullis artibus aut minis adduci potuerunt, ut se separarent: multis colloquiis ultro citroque habitis, tandem inter Senatum regium & eos convenit, ut frequens hic conventus dimitteretur, sed ea conditione, ut ante dimissionem liceret supplicantibus ex suorum numero, quibus maximè fiderent, aliquot eligere, qui pro legitimis deputatis à Senatu regio haberentur, quibus liceret, omnium supplicum nomine, actionem hanc contra Episcopos prosequi, & pro ut res ferret, consilia communicare, ac ea omnia agere, quæ ad causam hanc communem promovendam conducerent: quos etiam se certiores facturos, senatus spoponderit de voluntate regia circa hanc causam. Vigore hujus conventus eliguntur ex majoribus Nobilibus (hoc est Comitibus, Vice-comitibus. Baronibus majoribus regni, jure nascendi Senatoribus, vulgo Dominis Parlamentariis) quatuor, totidem ex mi-nore nobilitate, tanquam Provinciarum deputati, totidem civitatum legati, ac quatuor denique Pastores Ecclesiarum, tanquam classium deputati, ordinem etiam statuunt, quo alii per vices in horum locum substitterentur, ac quo omnibus per universas regni Provincias innotesceret, quis esset rerum status. Hisce constitutis, pacatè singuli ad propria se conferunt; omnibus primum ferio monitis, & sa-crosanctè pollicentibus, vitæ ac morum emendationem, ac seriùm precum ac jejunii usum, quo Deum, precatis populi in sensum, propitium redderent, ut Regis piissimi & æquissimi cor ad ea consilia flecteret, quæ divinam gloriam, coronæ stabilimentum, & honorem, civiumque salutem & pacem promoverent.
units.tr: So they remained in very large numbers, and their number grew daily, as people came flocking to Edinburgh from the most distant provinces of the kingdom to confer together on the common cause. Because the royal Senate had good reason to fear that some tumult and worse evils might arise from so great a crowd, it asked the petitioners to separate and for each man to put forward his grievances individually, for it knew that divided they could more easily be appeased or overthrown. The bishops, who made up a large part of the Senate, were not unaware that the ruin of the Britons long ago at the hands of the Romans had arisen from just such a policy; of which Tacitus says: "while they fought singly, they were all conquered." But the champions of ecclesiastical liberty rejected such fatal counsels, which threatened the ruin of their cause, and they could not be persuaded, by any tricks or threats, to separate. After many conferences held back and forth, at last it was agreed between the royal Senate and them that this large assembly should be dismissed, but on this condition: that before the dismissal the petitioners might choose from their own number some whom they trusted most, who would be regarded as lawful deputies by the royal Senate. These would be allowed, in the name of all the petitioners, to pursue this action against the bishops, to share counsel as circumstances required, and to do everything that would advance this common cause. The Senate promised that it would also inform them of the royal will concerning this cause. By virtue of this agreement there were chosen: from the greater nobility (that is, earls, viscounts, and the greater barons of the kingdom, who are Senators by birth and are commonly called Lords of Parliament) four; as many from the lesser nobility, as deputies of the provinces; as many as envoys of the towns; and finally four ministers of the churches, as deputies of the presbyteries. They also fixed an order by which others might take their places in turn, and by which it would be known throughout all the provinces of the kingdom what the state of affairs was. With these arrangements made, each returned quietly to his own home, having first been earnestly admonished by all and having solemnly promised the amendment of life and morals, and the use of earnest prayers and fasting, by which they would make God, whom the people had asked, favourable, so that He might turn the heart of the most pious and most just King toward those counsels that would promote the divine glory, the stability and honour of the crown, and the safety and peace of the citizens.

units.la: His ad Regem delatis, eoque per Senatum monito, omnes hosce motus inde natos, quod vererentur omnium ordinum plurimi, introductione eorum librorum actum esse de antiqua libertate, & contaminatam reformatæ religionis puritatem (quæ omnibus ipsa vita charior effet) Senatui interdicit, ne harum controversiarum judicio se interponeret, quarum examen ac decisionem in se suscepit. Præconis etiam voce publicè omnibus significari mandat, non esse sibi statutum, ullam vel legum libertatis aut Religionis mutationem introducere &c. Publicatum fuit hoc edictum mense Decembri anni 1637.idcirco cum supplicum deputati sæpius Senatum interpellassent, ut tandem aliquando liceret actionem contra Episcopos instituere, respondissetque Senatus, sibi à Rege mandatum, ne quos libellos supplices acciperent, in quibus aliquid effet,
units.tr: When these things had been reported to the King, and he had been so advised by the Senate, he forbade the Senate to interpose itself in the judgment of these controversies, whose examination and decision he had taken upon himself. These disturbances had arisen because very many of every rank feared that by the introduction of those books the ancient liberty had been destroyed and the purity of the reformed religion (which was dearer to them than life itself) contaminated. He also ordered it to be publicly declared by the voice of a herald to everyone that it was not his intention to introduce any change in the laws, liberties or religion, and so on. This edict was published in December of the year 1637. Therefore, when the deputies of the petitioners had often petitioned the Senate that at last they might be allowed to bring their action against the bishops, the Senate replied that it had been commanded by the King not to accept any petitions in which there was anything that touched those books or the bishops.
