units.la: quod libros illos aut Episcopos tangeret, quo responso, delusos, ac vana spe lactatos, cum se cernerent deputati, nomine omnium Regni civium, quibus haec res cordi fuit, protestationem contra Senatum regium parant, seque, pacificis omnibus mediis frustra tentatis, Ecclesiis deesse non posse declarant, si quis porro exoriretur in prosecutione causae hujus tumultus, soli Senatui ob negatam justitiam imputandus esset.. Quod cum Senatui regio suboleret, nec ignoraret, quam proxima fumo esset flamma, Episcopis (ut fertur) primum monitis, ut se à Senatu pro tempore subducerent; deputatis comparendi licentiam concedit, qui quia sciebant difficilem esse in Senatum ingressum, ante januam Pallatii Dalkethensis (quo in oppido tum cogebantur) praestolabantur, ut Senatoribus saltem egredientibus protestationem insinuarent.
units.tr: With this answer the deputies saw themselves deluded and kept on empty hope. In the name of all the citizens of the kingdom to whom this matter was dear, they prepared a protest against the royal Senate, declaring that, since all peaceful means had been tried in vain, they could not fail the churches. If any tumult should arise in the prosecution of this cause, it would be imputed solely to the Senate, on account of justice denied. When the royal Senate came to know of this, and did not fail to see how close the flame was to the smoke, it first (so it is said) warned the bishops to withdraw from the Senate for the time being. It then granted the deputies permission to appear. Since they knew it would be difficult to enter the Senate, they waited before the door of the Palace of Dalkeith (where the court was then assembled in that town), so that they could at least hand their protest to the Senators as they came out.

units.la: Vbi comparuere Deputati in Senatu, omnium nomine verba fecit nobilis Dominus de Lowdon, Vicecomes Avrensis, singulari facundia & animi constantia explicabat, quid ab initio libellorum supplicum Senatui exhibitorum actum fuisset, quae ipsorum causae, quam modeste ac patienter Regis optimi clementiam expectassent, & quorum artibus quod ea non fruantur factum sit, paratos se contra Episcopos actionem instituere, institutamque prosequi, qua se probaturos suscipiunt eosdem gravissimorum criminum reos esse, idque sub capitum, honorum, fortunarum suarum periculo, & poena, si in probatione deficient, aut coram aequis judicibus causa cadent, aequitatem itaque postulare, ut a Senatu regio excluderentur Episcopi, donec de ipso- rum innocentia constiterit: esse absurdum, eosdem habere judices & adversarios, denique. Senatores regios obtestatur, ut procrastinationibus omnibus posthabitis, tandem aliquando aliquid hac in causa facerent, quo toti Regno & posteris ostenderent, quam chara ipsis esse Religionis puritas & justitia, duo pacis & felicitatis regnorum omnium firmissima Columina.
units.tr: When the deputies appeared before the Senate, the noble Lord of Lowdon, Viscount of Ayr, spoke on behalf of all of them. With singular eloquence and constancy of spirit he explained what had been done from the beginning with the petitions presented to the Senate, how modestly and patiently they had awaited the clemency of the best of kings, and by whose arts it had come about that they did not enjoy it. He said they were ready to bring an action against the bishops, and to pursue the action once begun, by which they undertook to prove that the same bishops were guilty of the gravest crimes, and this at the risk of their heads, their honours and their fortunes, and under penalty if they failed in the proof or lost the case before fair judges. He therefore asked for justice: that the bishops be excluded from the royal Senate until their innocence had been established, since it was absurd that they should be both judges and adversaries. Finally he entreated the royal Senators that, setting aside all delays, they should at last do something in this cause, so as to show the whole kingdom and posterity how dear to them were the purity of religion and justice, the two most firm pillars of peace and the happiness of all kingdoms.

units.la: Hanc ejus orationem subsequutus est Pastorum Ecclesiae deputatus. Merozitarum maledictionem horum capitibus imminere demonstrabat, qui Ecclesiae laboranti auxilium illud tempestivum praestituri non sint quod omnium votis ab ipsis expectatur, Deum se honorantes honorare; Contemnentes vero se, viles & leves facere. Si tempore hoc tam periculoso, Ecclesiae Christi manum auxiliarem non porrigant respirationem & liberationem aliunde exorituram ei, quae tria S.Sanctae Scripturae loca, praesenti occasioni appositè convenientia graviter premebat, usque adeo ut Senatoribus quibusdam lachrimas e[?]licuerit; respondit Senatus sibi causam hanc, quam commendatissimam futuram, sed, quia expresso Regis mandato vetetur circa hanc controversiam ulterius aliquid agere, dolere se, quod Deputatorum votis, nondum satisfacere posset, rogare itaque ut parvi temporis moram, aequis animis ferrent, donec regiam majestatem denuo de omnibus certiorem faceret.
units.tr: This speech was followed by the minister appointed by the ministers of the Church. He showed that the curse of Meroz hangs over those who will not bring the timely help that everyone expects from them to the suffering Church, and that God honours those who honour him, while those who despise him are made worthless and contemptible. He urged that if they did not stretch out a helping hand to the Church of Christ in this perilous time, relief and deliverance would arise for her from elsewhere. He pressed three passages of Holy Scripture, which fitted the present occasion so well, so forcefully that some of the senators were moved to tears. The Senate replied that the cause was most commendable, but that, since a express command of the King forbade them to do anything further about this controversy, they grieved that they could not yet satisfy the votes of the deputies. They therefore asked them to bear patiently a short delay until they could again inform His Royal Majesty about everything.

units.la: Quare ad Regem scribit Senatus, ac monet, omnia media à se hactenus tentata esse, quibus motus hosce sedari posse sperabant, eos tamen indies augeri, nec eorum sedandorum ullam restare spem, nisi subditis supplicantibus aliquid concederet, atque cum harum controversiarum judicium sibi soli reservaverit Rex, obsecrantur, ut Senatorum regni Scotiae aliquot quibus maximè sideret, ad se vocaret, cum res haec majoris sit momenti, & quae per literas transfigi non possit, uti suo maximo cum dolore hactenus sint experti. Itaque in Angliam vocatur à Rege Comes Traquarius, magnus Regni thesaurarius, cujus opera antea fideli in magnis sæpè negotiis usus fuerat, licet tum variis per Episcopos eorumque fautores suspitionibus gravatus, & ut fertur, coram ipso rege ab iis accusatus, quod in odium Episcoporum (cum quorum primariis graves inimicitias exercere diceretur) nobilibus supplicantibus nimium faveret. Quomodo causam ille suam in aula regia egerit, ac se accusationibus illis liberaverit, nondum satis vulgo notum: hoc tamen omnibus quam notissimum, omnem movisse lapidem quosdam Episcopos, quo regis gratia excideret, quod fortasse eum coegit parcius supplicum causam Regi repraesentare, nec multorum de eo conceptæ opinioni respondere.
units.tr: Accordingly the Senate wrote to the King and warned him that every means they had so far tried, by which they hoped these disturbances could be calmed, had not only failed but were growing daily, and that there was no remaining hope of calming them unless he granted something to his supplicating subjects. Since the King had reserved the judgment of these controversies to himself alone, they begged him to summon to himself some of the senators of the kingdom of Scotland in whom he especially trusted, since this matter was of greater weight and could not be settled by letter, as they had painfully found to their great sorrow. Accordingly the King summoned to England the Earl of Traquair, the great Treasurer of the kingdom, whose faithful service the King had often used in important affairs before. Yet at that time he was burdened with various suspicions raised by the Bishops and their supporters, and, as is reported, was accused by them before the King himself of favouring the noble petitioners too much, out of hatred of the Bishops, with whose leaders he was said to be waging bitter enmity. How he pleaded his case at the royal court and freed himself from those accusations is not yet well enough known to the public; but this is very well known to all, that certain Bishops moved every stone to make him lose the King's favour. This perhaps compelled him to represent the cause of the suppliants to the King more sparingly, and not to match the opinion that many had formed of him.

units.la: Dimissus ab aula in Scotiam redit, ac mense Februario Anni 1638. regium mandatum, quod secum detulit Sterlini (qua in urbe tum cogebatur Senatus) publicandum curat, Cujus hæc summa fuerat, immerito accusari Episcopos, tanquam librorum illorum authores, quum quicquid ab iis in hoc negotio præstitum sit, id se auctore & mandante factum, libros porro illos, à se diligenter evolutos, in quibus post accuratam lectionem, nihil invenerit, quod antiquis legibus, aut receptæ in Scotia religioni noceat, quin contra sibi persuasum, aptissimos esse ad pietatem solidam promovendam, & incrementum Papismi impediendum: à quo quantum abhorreat, quotidianæ actiones testantur: damnare se omnes subditorum conventus hactenus habitos, ad exhibendum libellos supplices, contra hos innocentes libros, & Episcopos eorundem promotores, sicut etiam omnes subditorum, cujuscunque demum ordinis, subscriptiones in eundem finem, tanquam manifestas conspirationes, ad turbandam pacem publicam, legibus regni frequenter vetitas, concedere tamen omnium præteritorum veniam iis, qui posthac, ab iisdem religiose abstinebunt, ac pœnam rebellionis, & læsæ majestatis regiæ in contumaces, qui ejusmodi illicitos conventus in finem prædictum habituri sint, se statuere, Clementer tamen, se fidelium subditorum suorum querelas auditurum, modo nec in materia, nec in forma peccent, hoc est, in jus regale non impingant.
units.tr: Dismissed from the court, he returned to Scotland, and in February of the year 1638 he saw to it that the royal command he had brought with him was published at Stirling, where the Senate was then gathered. Its substance was this: that the Bishops were unjustly accused as the authors of those books, since whatever had been done by them in this matter had been done on his authority and command; that he himself had carefully read through those books, and after close reading had found nothing in them that harmed the ancient laws or the religion received in Scotland, but on the contrary was persuaded that they were most apt for promoting solid piety and hindering the growth of Popery, from which he abhorred, as his daily actions bore witness. He declared that he condemned all the assemblies of his subjects held hitherto for presenting supplicatory petitions against these innocent books and the Bishops who promoted them, and likewise all the subscriptions of his subjects, of whatever rank, made to the same end, as manifest conspiracies to disturb the public peace, which the laws of the kingdom had often forbidden. Nevertheless he granted pardon for all past offences to those who would henceforth refrain from such things, and he decreed the penalty of rebellion and treason against the royal majesty for the obstinate who should hold such unlawful assemblies for that stated purpose. Yet he would graciously hear the complaints of his faithful subjects, provided they did not offend either in matter or in form, that is, did not encroach upon the royal prerogative.

units.la: Verum medicina hæc ad morbum sanandum parata eandem auxit, nam cum libertatis Ecclesiasticæ vindicibus edictum hoc promulgatum iri suboleret, protestationem parant, & quia rumoribus seu veris, seu falsis delatum esset, suggestum regi consilium, de summis papaverum capitibus demetiendis (allatis tum ex historia exotica, tum domestica exemplis, & præxi Mariæ Reginæ contra Magnates, qui cum Rege Henrico, Regis avo, conspiraverunt, in eadem fœdissimi nebulonis & Sycophantæ, Davidis Rixii Pedemontani) & quia locus ad insidias aptus fuit, ideo frequentissime conveniunt, ac modesta protestatione utuntur, ut posteris saltem constaret, bonam causam silentio à se non fuisse proditam, cujus protestationis hæc summa fuit, I. Semina superstitionis & Idololatriæ, in illis libris contineri, præsertim ad regulam opinionum, hodie in Ecclesia Anglicana, publicè defensarum, exponendi sint. II. Licet priora illa fœmina Idololatriæ & superstitionis non inessent, manifestas tamen esse novitates, quæ à Scotis admitti non possunt, nisi cum violatione libertatis, legum, ac Religionis receptæ; præsertim cum Scotis invitis obtrudantur, nullo præeunte Synodi Nationalis judicio, penes quam, suprema semper, in ejusmodi negotiis Ecclesiasticis, potestas esse consuevit.
units.tr: But this remedy, prepared to cure the disease, made it worse. For when the defenders of ecclesiastical liberty heard that this edict was about to be published, they prepared a protest. And because it had been reported, whether truly or falsely, that the King's council had advised cutting off the chief heads of the nobles (with examples brought from both foreign and domestic history, and the practice of Queen Mary against the magnates who conspired with King Henry, her grandfather, and the same most foul scoundrel and sycophant David Riccio of Piedmont), and because the place was suited to ambush, they met very frequently and used a modest protest, so that at least posterity would know that they had not betrayed the good cause by silence. The substance of this protest was as follows. I. Seeds of superstition and idolatry are contained in those books, and they are to be set out especially by the rule of the opinions now publicly defended in the English Church. II. Even if those former seeds of idolatry and superstition were not present, there are nevertheless plain novelties which the Scots cannot admit without violating their liberty, their laws, and the religion received, especially since they are forced upon the unwilling Scots, without any prior judgment of the National Synod, in whose power the supreme authority in such ecclesiastical matters has always customarily lain.

units.la: III. Iniquum esse negare libertatem accusandi Episcopos, quos multorum criminum reos esse probabunt, reipublicæ etiam & Ecclesiæ, quam maximè interesse, ne in eminentiori loco constitutorum, scelera dimittantur impunita. IV. Protestantur contra usum celsæ Commissionis, cum fit Tribunal nullo juris fundamento nixum, nulla lege municipali statutum, ab Anglorum consuetudine contra leges Regni fundamentales, Scotis obtrusum, nec alium se videre illius usum, quam, ut Episcoporum tyrannidem stabiliret, merum porro esse germen Hispanicæ inquisitionis. V. Episcopos se rejicere tanquam iniquos judices eorumque se non posse admittere judicia, donec de ipsorum innocentia constiterit in foro competenti. VI. Omnes ipsorum conventus, subscriptiones libellorum supplicum, ad Senatum regium, in id solum institutos, ut cultus divini hactenus recepti, puritatem, contra obtrusas novitates, Ecclesiarum libertatem, contra Episcoporum tyrannidem tuerentur, esse licitos: sibique statutum, ad eosdem fines sanctos prosequendos ejusmodi modestos conventus frequentare; nec se posse bona conscientia ab iisdem desistere, nisi gloriæ divinæ, honoris Regii, libertatis regni, & Ecclesiæ proditores haberi se velint. Protestatio hæc lecta fuit, in foro publico Sterlinensi ejusque exemplar publicè affixum.
units.tr: III. It is unjust to deny the liberty of accusing the Bishops, whom they will prove to be guilty of many crimes; and it is especially in the interest of the commonwealth and the Church that the crimes of men placed in higher positions should not go unpunished. IV. They protest against the use of the High Commission, since it is a tribunal resting on no foundation of law, established by no municipal statute, imposed on the Scots from English custom against the fundamental laws of the kingdom; and they see no other use of it than to establish the tyranny of the Bishops, and it is simply a sprout of the Spanish Inquisition. V. They reject the Bishops as unjust judges, and they cannot admit their judgments until their innocence has been established in a competent court. VI. All their assemblies and subscriptions of supplicatory petitions to the royal Senate, instituted solely so that the worship of God received hitherto might be defended in its purity against the novelties forced upon them, the liberty of the Churches against the tyranny of the Bishops, are lawful; and they have resolved to attend such modest assemblies to pursue these holy ends, nor can they with a good conscience desist from them, unless they wish to be held traitors to the glory of God, the honour of the King, and the liberty of the kingdom and the Church. This protest was read in the public square of Stirling, and a copy of it was publicly posted up there.

units.la: Porro quia jam satis perspexere supplices, quorsum extrema illa consilia tenderent, & cum omnibus imperatum fuisset à Senatu regio, ut Sterlino statim discederent, quibus nihil privati negotii ibi fuerat, ideo frequentissimo numero Edinburgum se conferunt monitis ὁμοψήφοις[?], ut eò quam citissimè confluerent, deliberaturi, quæ ad omnium salutem facerent, cumque calamitatum quibus olim & hodie premerentur primariam causam fuisse violationem fœderis nationalis cum Deo initi & sanciti, in mentem revocarent communi ac unanimi sententia conclusum fuit, fœdus illud solenniter renovandum esse, quod vulgo Confessio minor Ecclesiæ Scoticanæ, seu Confessio familiæ regiæ vocatur. Quum vero hujus frequentissima futura sit mentio, aliis propugnantibus, aliis vero teterrimis convitiis oppugnantibus; De verbo in verbum à veritatis studiofo fideliter translatum, subjiciendum duxi.
units.tr: Moreover, since the supplicants had already seen clearly where those extreme counsels were tending, and since the royal Senate had ordered everyone who had no private business there to leave Stirling at once, they went in very great numbers to Edinburgh, summoned by unanimous admonition [ὁμοψήφοις], to gather there as quickly as possible and deliberate about what would serve the common safety. And when they recalled that the chief cause of the calamities under which they had long suffered, and still suffered, was the violation of the national covenant made and sworn with God, it was concluded by common and unanimous judgment that this covenant must be solemnly renewed, the one commonly called the Shorter Confession of the Church of Scotland, or the Confession of the royal household. Since its frequent mention will occur, some defending it and others attacking it with the foulest abuse, I have thought it right to append it, faithfully translated word for word by a lover of the truth.

units.la: Confessio fidei Ecclesiæ Scoticanæ, Regis chirographo ejusque Familiæ primum approbatæ, Anno Domini, 1580. Postmodum ab omnium ordinum regni civibus, Anno 1581. ex senatusconsulto, & Synodi nationalis decretis. Cui demum subscripserunt omnium conditionum Cives, Anno 1590. ex novo senatusconsulto, postulante id Synodo nationali: addito insuper communi fœdere, de vera religione & Majestate Regia tuenda. Quam denique, Anno hoc 1638. Nos Proceres, Barones, reliquique Nobiles, urbium Municipes, verbi Dei Præcones, aliique regni Cives, chirographis consignavimus, una cum firmo animi nostri proposito, pacto promissoque (propter rationum quæ suo loco memorabuntur momenta) purioris religionis & Majestatis Regiæ propugnandæ, ad ejusdem Confessionis, & sanctionum regni præscriptum, quarum formulæ sequuntur.
units.tr: The Confession of faith of the Church of Scotland, first approved by the King's signature and that of his family, in the year of the Lord 1580. Afterwards by the citizens of all ranks of the kingdom, in the year 1581, by decree of the Senate and the decrees of the National Synod. To which at last the citizens of every condition subscribed, in the year 1590, by a new decree of the Senate, at the request of the National Synod; with the common covenant added concerning the defence of the true religion and of the Royal Majesty. Which finally, in this year 1638. We, the nobles, barons, the rest of the gentry, the burgesses of towns, the heralds of the Word of God, and the other citizens of the kingdom, have set our hands to, together with a firm purpose and promise of our minds, bound by covenant (on account of the weighty reasons which will be recalled in their place), to defend the purer religion and the Royal Majesty, according to the prescription of that Confession and the sanctions of the kingdom, whose formulas follow.

units.la: Nos universi, & singuli subscribentes profitemur, postquam de Religionis controversiis diu multumque apud nos deliberatum esset, cunctis ad lydium veritatis Divinæ lapidem accuratius examinatis, in veritatis certa persuasione per Dei verbum, & Spiritum sanctum animos nostros acquiescere: Ideoque corde credimus, ore confitemur, consignatis chirographis testamur, & constanter asserimus, Deo teste invocato, & universo genere humano in conscientiam appellato, hanc unicam esse fidem, & religionem Christianam Deo acceptam, hominique salutarem, quæ nunc ex immensa Dei misericordia, per Euangelii prædicationem mundo patefacta, à multis Ecclesiis, gentibusque clarissimis, præsertim ab Ecclesia Scoticana, Rege nostro serenissimo, tribusque regni hujus ordinibus, ut æterna Dei veritas, & unicum Salutis nostræ fundamentum, recepta, credita, & propugnata est, explicata etiam uberius in Fidei Confessione majori, plurimis Comitiorum publicorum actis confirmata, Regisque serenissimi, & universorum hujus regni civium publica multorum jam annorum professione approbata: Cui Nos confessioni, cultusque Divini formulæ, ut veritati Divinæ, certissima sacrarum literarum auctoritate subnixæ, libentissimis animis in singulis assentimur: omniaque adeo contraria de religione dogmata aversamur: præsertim vero Papismum universum, & singula ejus capita, quemadmodum hodie Dei verbo confutata, & ab Ecclesia Scoticana damnata sunt. Nominatim detestamur Antichristi illius Romani in sacras Scripturas, in Ecclesias, in Magistratum politicum, in hominum conscientias, sacrilege vendicatam autoritatem, nefarias omnes de rebus adiaphoris leges, libertati Christianæ derogantes; impium de sacrarum literarum, de legis, de officii Christi, de beati Euangelii imperfectione dogma; perversam de peccato originis, de naturæ nostræ impotentia, & in legem Divinam contumacia, de justificatione per solam fidem, de imperfecta nostra sanctitate, & obedientia legi præstanda, de natura, numero, & usu sacramentorum doctrinam; quinque adulterina sacramenta, omnesque ritus, ceremonias, falsaque traditiones genuinorum sacramentorum administrationi citra autoritatem verbi Divini accumulatas, crudelem de infantibus sententiam ante baptismum morte præreptis; districtam & absolutam baptismi necessitatem; blasphemam de transubstantiatione & corporali præsentia Christi in cœnæ Dominicæ elementis, cujus etiam impii fiant participes; atque orali ejusdem manducatione doctridoctrinam ; juramentorum , perjuriorumque gratiam faciendi arrogatam potestatem; matrimonii in gradibus verbo Dei interdictis permissionem; crudelitatem erga innocentes matrimonii nexu solutos, diabolicam missam; sacrilegum sacerdotium ; abominandum pro vivorum mortuorumque peccatis sacrificium , hominum indigetationem seu canonizationem ; angelorum mortuorumque invocationem, crucis, imaginum, reliquiarumque venerationem , in creaturarum honorem dicata fana, dies sacratos, vota nuncupata, purgatorium, pro defunctis deprecationem ; ignotæ linguæ in precibus sacrisque usum ; sacrilegas supplicationum pompas ; blasphemam litaniam, mediatorum turbam , ordinum ecclesiasticorum multiplicem varietatem ; auricularem confessionem ; incertam & desperationis plenam pœnitentiam ; generalem & ancipitem fidem ; peccatorum per satisfactiones humanas expiationem; justificationem ex operibus; Opus operatum ; operum supererogationem; merita, indulgentias,peregrinationes & stationes; aquam lustralem; campanarum baptizationem, exorcismos, bonas Dei creaturas cruce obsignandi, lustrandi, ungendi, conjurandi, & consecrandi superstitionem ; politicam ipsius monarchiam, impiamque hierarchiam, tria vota solennia, variasque rasurae sectas ; impia & sanguinaria concilii Tridentini decreta, omnesque atrocissimæ illius in Christi Ecclesiam conjurationis populares & fautores: Denique inanes omnes aversamur allegorias, omnesque ritus & signa, traditiones omnes, præter aut contra autoritatem verbi Dei Ecclesiæ obtrusas, & doctrinæ hujus Ecclesiæ verè reformatæ repugnantes: Cui nos Ecclesiæ reformatæ, in doctrinæ capitibus,fide, religione, disciplina, & usu sacramentorum, ut viva illius sub Christo capite membra, libentes nos aggregamus: Sancte promittentes, magnumque & tremendum Domini Dei nostri nomen jurantes, Nos in Ecclesiæ hujus doctrina & disciplina constanter perseveraturos, & pro cujusque vocatione ac viribus, ad extremum spiritum defensuros, sub pœna omnium in lege maledictionum, æterniqué cum animæ tum corporis exitii periculo, in tremendo illo Dei judicio.
units.tr: We, all and each of the undersigned, profess that, after the controversies over religion had been long and carefully debated among us, and all things had been examined more closely by the touchstone of divine truth, our minds have come to rest in a firm persuasion of the truth, through the Word of God and the Holy Spirit. Therefore we believe with the heart, confess with the mouth, testify by our signed hands, and steadfastly assert, calling God to witness and appealing to the conscience of the whole human race, that this is the one Christian faith and religion, acceptable to God and salutary to man. Through the immeasurable mercy of God it has now been made known to the world by the preaching of the gospel, and it has been received, believed and defended as the eternal truth of God and the sole foundation of our salvation by many churches and most famous nations, above all by the Scottish Church, by our most serene King, and by the three estates of this kingdom. It has also been explained more fully in the Greater Confession of Faith, confirmed by very many acts of public assemblies, and approved by the public profession of the most serene King and of all the citizens of this kingdom for many years now. To this Confession, and to the form of divine worship, as to divine truth supported by the most certain authority of the Holy Scriptures, we assent in each point with the greatest willingness of mind. We likewise turn away from all doctrines contrary to this religion. Above all we turn away from the whole of Popery and each of its articles, as they have today been refuted by the Word of God and condemned by the Scottish Church. By name we detest that Roman Antichrist's sacrilegious claim to authority over the Holy Scriptures, over the Churches, over the civil magistrate, and over men's consciences; all his wicked laws concerning indifferent matters, which detract from Christian liberty; his impious doctrine of the imperfection of Scripture, of the law, of Christ's office, and of the blessed gospel; his perverse doctrine of original sin, of the impotence of our nature and its obstinacy against the divine law, of justification by faith alone, of our imperfect holiness and of the obedience to be rendered to the law, and of the nature, number and use of the sacraments; the five adulterine sacraments; all the rites, ceremonies and false traditions heaped upon the administration of the genuine sacraments without the authority of the divine Word; the cruel judgment concerning infants snatched away by death before baptism; the strict and absolute necessity of baptism; the blasphemous doctrine of transubstantiation and of the bodily presence of Christ in the elements of the Lord's Supper, and of the impious who become partakers of them, and the doctrine of oral manducation of the same; the arrogated power of granting dispensations from oaths and perjuries; the permission of marriage within the degrees forbidden by the Word of God; cruelty toward innocent persons freed from the bond of marriage; the diabolical mass; the sacrilegious priesthood; the abominable sacrifice for the sins of the living and the dead; the canonizing or enrolling of men as saints; the invocation of angels and of the dead; the veneration of the cross, of images and of relics; temples dedicated to the honour of creatures; holy days; vows made in words; purgatory; prayer for the dead; the use of an unknown tongue in prayers and sacred rites; the sacrilegious pomp of processions; the blasphemous litany; the crowd of mediators; the manifold variety of ecclesiastical orders; auricular confession; repentance that is uncertain and full of despair; a general and doubtful faith; the expiation of sins through human satisfactions; justification by works; the opus operatum; works of supererogation; merits, indulgences, pilgrimages and stations; holy water; the baptizing of bells, exorcisms, and the superstition of marking, washing, anointing, conjuring and consecrating God's good creatures with the cross; the political monarchy of the Pope and his impious hierarchy; the three solemn vows and the various sects of the tonsure; the impious and bloody decrees of the Council of Trent, and all the popular supporters and favourers of that most atrocious conspiracy against the Church of Christ. Finally, we turn away from all empty allegories, and from all rites and signs, and all traditions thrust upon the Church beside or against the authority of the Word of God, and repugnant to the doctrine of this truly reformed Church. To this reformed Church, in the heads of doctrine, faith, religion, discipline and the use of the sacraments, we willingly join ourselves, as living members of her under Christ the Head. Solemnly promising, and swearing by the great and dreadful name of the Lord our God, we shall steadfastly persevere in the doctrine and discipline of this Church, and shall defend them to our last breath, each according to his calling and strength, under the penalty of all the curses of the law, and at the peril of eternal destruction of both soul and body in that dreadful judgment of God.

units.la: Quumque sciamus non paucos à Sathana, & Antichristo Romano subornatos, promissionibus, subscriptionibus, & juramentis se obstringere, & in usu Sacramentorum cum Ecclesia orthodoxa ad tempus subdole contra conscientiam communicare, versutè constituentes; obtento interim religionis velo, in Ecclesia verum Dei cultum adulterare clanculum, & per cuniculos labefactare, tandem per occasionem apertis inimicitiis oppugnare; vana spe propositâ venie[?] dandæ à Pontifice Romano; cujus rei potestatem contra veritatem Divinam sibi arrogat, ipsi perniciosam, cjusque affectis multo magis exitiosam: Nos igitur, ut simulationis erga Deum, ejusque Ecclesiam & insinceri animi suspicionem omnem amoliamur, cordium omnium inspectorem respectamur, huic nostræ confessioni, promissioni, juramento & subscriptioni animos nostros usque quaque respondere; nulloque rerum terrestrium momento, sed indubia & certa notitia ex amore veritatis Divinæ per Spiritum sanctum in cordibus nostris inscriptæ ad eam nos inductos esse: Ita Deum propitium habeamus, eo die quo cordium omnium arcana palam fient.
units.tr: And since we know that not a few are suborned by Satan and the Roman Antichrist to bind themselves by promises, subscriptions and oaths, and craftily, for a time, to communicate with the orthodox Church in the use of the sacraments against their conscience, devising these things deceitfully; that meanwhile, under the veil of religion, they secretly corrupt the true worship of God in the Church, undermine it through tunnels, and at last, when the occasion arises, attack it with open hostility, with the vain hope held out of a pardon to be granted by the Roman Pontiff, a power which he arrogates to himself against divine truth, and which is pernicious to himself and far more deadly to those who are devoted to him: therefore we, in order to remove every suspicion of pretence toward God and his Church and of an insincere mind, we who regard the searcher of all hearts, declare that our minds respond in every way to this our Confession, promise, oath and subscription. And we declare that we have been led to it not by any consideration of earthly things, but by a certain and indubitable knowledge, inscribed in our hearts by the Holy Spirit out of love for the divine truth. So may we have God propitious to us on that day when the secrets of all hearts shall be made manifest.

units.la: Cum vero nobis constet per eximiam Dei gratiam huic regno præfectum esse Regem nostrum serenissimum, ad Ecclesiam in eo conservandam, & justitiam nobis administrandam, cujus incolumitate & bono exemplo secundum Deum religionis & ecclesiæ tranquillitas ac securitas nitatur, sanctè ex animo, eodem adacti sacramento, eademque pœna proposita pollicemur, & consignatis chirographis promittimus, sacratissimi Regis nostri incolumitatem & autoritatem in beato Christi Euangelio defendendo, in libertate patriæ asserenda, in justitia administranda, in improbis puniendis, adversus hostes quoscunque internos sive externos, quovis etiam bonorum & vitæ discrimine Nos constanter oppugnaturos. Ita Deum nostrum optimum, maximum, potentem & propitium conservatorem habeamus in mortis articulo, & adventu Domini nostri Iesu Christi, Cui cum Patre, & Spiritu sancto, sit omnis honos & gloria in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Now since it is clear to us that, by the singular grace of God, our most serene King has been set over this kingdom to preserve the Church in it and to administer justice to us, on whose safety and good example, under God, the tranquillity and security of religion and the Church depend, we solemnly and from the heart, bound by the same oath and under the same penalty, promise, and by our signed hands pledge, that we shall steadfastly contend against all enemies, internal or external, for the safety and authority of our most sacred King, in defending the blessed gospel of Christ, in asserting the liberty of the country, in administering justice, in punishing the wicked, even at the risk of our goods and lives. So may we have our God, the best, greatest, mighty and propitious Preserver, at the moment of death and at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be all honour and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: Quinetiam complura publicorum regni nostri Comitiorum, seu Parliamenti (ut vocant) statuta antiquant, abrogant, & irrita esse jubent, in universum omnes leges, senatusconsulta, constitutiones canonicas, civiles, ac municipales, cuncta denique placita, instituta, & poenarum irrogationes, quibus verae religioni, ejusque professoribus, aut verae ecclesiae, ejusdem disciplinae, jurisdictioni & libertati præjudicium fiat, aut quæ idololatriæ & superstitioni, aut ecclesiae Romanæ patrocinentur, (ut Lex 3. & lex 3 r. Parliamenti 1.l. 23.p.11.l.114.p.12. Iacobi 6.) omnemque papismum, & superstitionem funditus extirpari jubent, ex sententia statutorum conventus ordinum memorata lege 5.[?]p.20. Iacobi 6. Atque adeo in papanos omnes & sacrificulos, tanquam verae religionis, in ecclesiis hujus regni legibus constitutae, hostes, multis poenis, quà civilibus, quà ecclesiasticis animadverti jubent, l. 24. p. 11. Iacobi 6. Imo tanquam omnes regiminis Christiani hostes publicos, l.18.p.16. Iacobi 6. & ut perduelles, & serenissimi Regis nostri autoritatis impugnatores, l.47.p.3.ut idololatras,l.10.p.7.Iacobi 6. Præterea & ipsa fidei Confessio, & complures praeterea leges, nominatim pontificis Romani autoritatem & jurisdictionem damnant, & ex hoc regno prorsus eliminant: ejusque propugnatores poenis coerceri jubent, l. 2. p. 1. l. 51. p. 3. l. 106. p. 7. l. 114. p. 12. Iacobi 6. Haereticam Papæ doctrinam, omnesque in doctrina errores, verè Christianæ fidei publicè apud nos receptæ, & legibus constitutæ, vel minimo in apice repugnantes damnant, simulque in ejus generis librorum, schediasmatum, elucubrationum, epistolarum scriptorumque quorumlibet autores & disseminatores animadverti jubent, l. 46. p. 3. l. 106. p. 7. l. 24. p. 11. Iacobi 6. Baptizationem omnem secundum ecclesiæ Papanæ ritus, & Missæ idololatriam damnant, omnesque missificos, Missæque ultroneos auditores, & quicunque sacrisiculos, Iesuitas, negotiatores Romanenses, clam fovent; auxilio juvant, tectove excipiunt; nullâ exceptione factâ, poenis multari jubent, L. 5. p. 1. l. 120. p. 12. l. 164. p. 13. l. 193. p. 14. l. 1. p. 19. l. 5. p. 20. Iacobi 6. Omnes item libros, omniaque scripta damnant errores in doctrina contra veritatem religionis publicè receptæ, aut superstitiones, ritus, ceremoniasve pontificias complectentia, quibus mirificè populus effascinatur, gravesque poenas in eorundem importatores irrogant, l. 25. p. 11. Iacobi 6, Superiorum quoque temporum idololatriæ monumenta & vestigia damnant, ut cruces invisendi, sanctorumque ferias celebrandi pravam consuetudinem, hujusque generis ritus papanos superstitionem redolentes, quibus honori Divino derogatur; vera religio contemptui habetur, & graves in plebe foventur errores. In harum superstitionum crimen si quis iterato relabatur, eadem illi poena statuitur quae idololatris, Lege 104. Parl. 7. Iacobi 6.
units.tr: Moreover, the statutes of the public assemblies of our kingdom, or of Parliament as they are called, very many of them, they declare to be annulled, abrogated and void; in general, they order that all laws, decrees of the senate, canonical, civil and municipal constitutions, and finally all decisions, institutions and imposition of penalties which do prejudice to the true religion and its professors, or to the true Church, its discipline, jurisdiction and liberty, or which favour idolatry and superstition or the Church of Rome, be wholly rooted out (as Act 3 and Act 3 of the Parliament of 1, c. 23, p. 11, c. 114, p. 12 of James 6.), and all Popery and superstition, according to the sentence of the statutes of the said assembly of the estates, Act 5 [?], p. 20 of James 6. And so they order that all Papists and sacrificing priests, as enemies of the true religion established by the laws in the churches of this kingdom, be punished with many penalties, both civil and ecclesiastical, Act 24, p. 11 of James 6. Indeed, they are to be treated as enemies of all Christian government, Act 18, p. 16 of James 6. and, as traitors and opponents of the authority of our most serene King, Act 47, p. 3, and as idolaters, Act 10, p. 7 of James 6. Besides, the Confession of Faith itself, and several other laws, expressly condemn the authority and jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff and utterly banish them from this kingdom, and they order that his defenders be restrained by penalties, Act 2, p. 1; Act 51, p. 3; Act 106, p. 7; Act 114, p. 12 of James 6. They condemn the heretical doctrine of the Pope and all errors in doctrine that conflict, even in the least point, with the true Christian faith publicly received among us and established by law, and they order that the authors and disseminators of books, pamphlets, writings, letters and whatever writings of this kind be punished, Act 46, p. 3; Act 106, p. 7; Act 24, p. 11 of James 6. They condemn all baptizing according to the rites of the Papal Church, and the idolatry of the Mass, and they order that all who secretly foster and assist the saying of Mass, the willing hearers of Mass, and all sacrificing priests, Jesuits and Roman agents, or who receive them under their roof, be punished by penalties, with no exception made, Act 5, p. 1; Act 120, p. 12; Act 164, p. 13; Act 193, p. 14; Act 1, p. 19; Act 5, p. 20 of James 6. Likewise they condemn all books and all writings containing errors in doctrine against the truth of the religion publicly received, or containing papal superstitions, rites or ceremonies, by which the people are wondrously bewitched, and they impose grave penalties on the importers of the same, Act 25, p. 11 of James 6. They also condemn the monuments and traces of the idolatry of earlier times, such as the custom of visiting crosses and celebrating the feasts of saints, and rites of this kind smelling of Papal superstition, by which divine honour is diminished, the true religion is held in contempt, and grave errors are fostered among the common people. If anyone should relapse again into the crime of these superstitions, the same penalty is laid down for him as for idolaters, Act 104, Parliament 7 of James 6.

units.la: Permultis etiam conventús publici statutis religionis verè Christianæ conservationi, ejusque in doctrina & sacramentis puritati consulitur, ecclesiæ quoque prospicitur libertati in Synodis nationalibus & provincialibus, presbyteriis, consistoriis parrochianis, totaque politia, disciplina & jurisdictione, uti hæc religionis puritas, ac ecclesiæ libertas usu recepta fuit, exercitio confirmata, verbo prædicata, & professione declarata, ad præscriptum reformatæ religionis in regno Scotiæ, id constat lege 99.p.7.l.23.p.11.l.114.p.12.l.166.p.13.Iacobi 6. quæ etiam confirmantur lege 4. serenissimi Regis nostri Caroli. Ita ut Lex 6.p.1. & l.68.p.6. Iacobi 6. in anno 1579. veram & sanctam Iesu Christi in hoc regno Ecclesiam definiant esse beati Euangelii Ministros, à Deo tum excitatos, aut postea etiam excitandos, cum iis qui tum vivebant, in doctrina & Sacramentorum administratione consentientes, una cum populo Christum, uti tum per Euangelium offerebatur, profitente, & in usu Sacramentorum secundum ritus in ecclesia reformata hujus regni tum receptos, & doctrinam in Confessione Fidei comprehensam, communicante: Omnesque adeo à societate hujus ecclesiæ, & veræ religionis publicè receptæ excludant, quicunque vel contradicunt Euangelii doctrinæ publicè approbatæ, explicataeque Fidei Confessione in conventu publico. Anni 1560. omnium ordinum professione confirmatâ, & in acta primi parliamenti Iacobi 6. relata, quamque sexti hujus parliamenti autoritas ratam esse jubet; vel usum Sacramentorum, quibus tum ritibus celebrantur, respuunt, quamdiu in ea secessione perfistunt. Quin & ea, quæ sequitur lex 69.p.6. Iacobi 6. nullam aliam ecclesiæ aut religionis faciem agnoscendam esse pronunciat, quam quæ illo tempore per Dei bonitatem, in hoc regno constituta fuerat., quæ propterea verè, divinæ, Christianæ, & absolutæ religionis elogiis constanter insignitur, ad cujus professionem omnes hujus regni cives, permultis comitiorum publicorum legibus obstringuntur, omnesque ejus articulos, ipsamque adeo fidei confessionem chirographis approbare, erroresque omnes & doctrinas iisdem articulis repugnantes ejerare tenentur lege 49.p.1.ll.45.46; & 47.p.3.l.71.p.6.l.106.p.7.l.24. p.11.l.123.p.12.ll.194.&197.p.14. Iacobi 6. Omnibusque provinciarum Præfectis, aliisque Magistratibus imperatur, ut cunctos secus facientes investigent, comprehendant, & afficiant, lege 5.p.1.l.104. p.7.l.25.p.11. Iacobi 6. Nulla habita ratione privilegii à Rege in contrarium impetrati: cujusmodi privilegiis, quæ exercendis in papanos & sincerioris religionis adversarios legum sanctionibus ulla ex parte præjudicant, fides omnis & robur abrogatur, lege 106.p.7.Iacobi 6. & contra lex. 47.p.3.Iacobi 6. purioris religionis Divinæ, & sacræ autoritatis regiæ causam arctissimis vinculis ita complicatam esse pronunciat, ut utriusque semper damna sint communia; adeoque neminem fidem & religionem instauratam non confitentem, & publice profitentem fidelem civem, & autoritati Regiæ obsequentem esse, sed perduellionis supplicio teneri: Omnes etiam in apostasiam prolapsos ad Fidei Confessionem revertentes, perseverantiam deinceps in eadem fide, autoritatis Regiæ propugnationem, verosque Evangelii Ministros & professores adversus inimicos quoscunque & oppugnatores tuendi, & pro cujusque viribus adjuvandi studium promittere jubet: Nominatim adversus omnes cujuscunque demum nationis, conditionis, & ordinis, Tridentinæ conjurationis socios, omnesque qui sanguinaria illius concilii decreta adversus Evangelii professores exequi conabuntur, aut ad ea exequenda auxilium conferent. Quæ sanè lex totidem omnino verbis repo-nitur. nitur in capitibus Pacificationis Perthensis, 23. Februarii 1572. (quam quidem Pacificationem Comitia ultimi Aprilis 1573. approbarunt, Comitia Anni 1587. ratam esse iusserunt, quamque etiam lex 123. p. 12. Iacobi 6. commemorat) addita clausula quae cives cunctos teneri asserit, omni perduellioni, & hostili, adversus puriorem religionem ejusque professores, aut regiam autoritatem, molitioni resistere,
units.tr: Many public statutes also provide for the preservation of true Christian religion and for the purity of its doctrine and sacraments; care is taken for the freedom of the Church in national and provincial synods, presbyteries, parish consistories, and the whole polity, discipline and jurisdiction of the Church. As this purity of religion and the liberty of the Church have been received in use, confirmed by practice, preached in the word and declared in profession, according to the prescribed form of the reformed religion in the kingdom of Scotland, this is established by the law 99, p. 7, l. 23, p. 11, l. 114, p. 12, l. 166, p. 13, of James 6, which are also confirmed by the law 4 of our most serene King Charles. Thus the law 6, p. 1, and l. 68, p. 6, of James 6, in the year 1579, define the true and holy Church of Jesus Christ in this kingdom to be the ministers of the blessed Gospel, raised up by God then or afterwards to be raised up, agreeing with those who then lived in doctrine and the administration of the sacraments, professing with the people Christ as then offered through the Gospel, and communicating in the use of the sacraments according to the rites then received in the reformed Church of this kingdom, and in the doctrine comprehended in the Confession of Faith. And they exclude from the fellowship of this Church and of the true religion publicly received all who either contradict the doctrine of the Gospel publicly approved and explained in the public assembly by the Confession of Faith, or who reject the use of the sacraments as they were then celebrated in those rites, for as long as they persist in that secession. Moreover, the law which follows, 69, p. 6, of James 6, pronounces that no other face of the Church or of religion is to be acknowledged than that which at that time, by the goodness of God, had been established in this kingdom; and for this reason it is constantly marked with the titles of true, divine, Christian and absolute religion. To the profession of this religion all the citizens of this kingdom are bound by very many laws of the public assemblies, and they are obliged to approve all its articles, and indeed the confession of faith itself, by their signatures, and to abjure all errors and doctrines contrary to those articles, by the law 49, p. 1, ll. 45, 46; and 47, p. 3, l. 71, p. 6, l. 106, p. 7, l. 24, p. 11, l. 123, p. 12, ll. 194 and 197, p. 14, of James 6. And to all the governors of the provinces and to the other magistrates it is commanded that they search out, apprehend and punish all who act otherwise, by the law 5, p. 1, l. 104, p. 7, l. 25, p. 11, of James 6, without regard to any privilege obtained from the King to the contrary. For every faith and force is revoked from such privileges as in any way prejudice the sanctions of the laws to be exercised against the Papists and the opponents of the purer religion, by the law 106, p. 7, of James 6; and, on the contrary, the law 47, p. 3, of James 6, declares that the cause of the purer divine religion and of sacred royal authority is so tightly bound together that the losses of each are always common to both. Hence no one who does not confess and publicly profess the restored faith and religion is to be regarded as a faithful citizen obedient to royal authority, but is held liable to the punishment of treason. It also orders all who have fallen into apostasy and return to the Confession of Faith to promise thereafter perseverance in the same faith, the defence of royal authority, and the protection of the true ministers and professors of the Gospel against all enemies and assailants, and to pledge zeal in helping them according to each one's strength. Especially against all, of whatever nation, condition or rank they may be, the associates of the Tridentine conspiracy, and all who attempt to carry out the bloody decrees of that council against the professors of the Gospel, or who lend aid to carrying them out. Indeed this law is repeated in exactly the same words in the chapters of the Pacification of Perth, 23 February 1572 (which indeed the assembly of the last of April 1573 approved, the assembly of the year 1587 ordered to be held valid, and which the law 123, p. 12, of James 6 also recalls), with the added clause which asserts that all citizens are bound to resist every treasonable and hostile attempt against the purer religion and its professors, or against royal authority.

units.la: Pariter etiam Cives omnes sereniffimi Regis incolumitatem & autoritatem defendere tenentur, uti & autoritatem superioris ordinum conventus, sine qua neque ulla lex potest constitui, neque legitimi judicii forum, lege 130, 131. p. 8. Iacobi 6. Tenentur & civium tueri libertatem, qui non alio jure vitam instituere, non alio gubernari debent, quam sanctionibus Regiis, seu publicis regni legibus, l. 48. p. 3. Iacobi 1. l. 79. p. 6. Iacobi 4. quae sanctio repetitur lege 131. p. 8. Iacobi 6. Quod si publicae regni leges & libertates innoventur, si quid iis derogetur, Delegatio data de uniendis Scotiae Angliaeque regnis (quae unica fuit sanctio parliamenti 17. Iacobi 6.) tantam rerum perturbationem orituram pronunciat, ut omnis liberae monarchiae ratio in hoc regno penitus tollatur. Quippe quod fundamentalibus hujus regni legibus, antiquis privilegiis, muneribus publicis & immunitatibus, non majestas tantum & autoritas stirpis Regiae per tot secula conservata fuerit, sed & populo quoque praediorum, possessionum, munerum, libertatis, dignitatis, omniumque fortunarum jura sarta tecta permanserint. Ut ergo sincerae religionis, legibus & libertati hujus regni sua constet integritas, lege 8. p. 1. repetita lege 99. p. 7. approbata lege 23. p. 11. & l. 114. p. 12. Iacobi 6. & l. 4. Regis Caroli, statutum est, ut Reges omnes imperium ineuntes in diadematis & imperii fuscep-tione, sancto interposito juramento religiose promittant, Deo æterno teste invocato, se per omnem vitam Deo ex verbi sui præscripto pro viribus inservituros, necnon ad ejusdem verbi normam sincerum religionem Christianam, verbi Divini prædicationem, genuinam Sacramentorum administrationem, uti tum in usu, Confessioni Fidei ab Ecclesia Scoticana receptæ consentaneam, conservaturos: omnesque doctrinæ errores huic fidei repugnantes abolituros; populumque suæ fidei commissum ex Dei voluntate per verbum patefacta, & receptis in hac republ. legibus, & institutis verbo Dei non repugnantibus gubernaturos; omnique studio curaturos, ut Ecclesia Dei & populus Christianus sincera & firma pace deinceps fruatur, omnesque hæretici & purioris religionis hostes pravitatis istius nomine ab Ecclesia verà damnati e ditionibus suis eliminentur. Quod à serenissimo nostro Rege Carolo, regni hujus diadema suscipiente præstitum fuit Edinburgi, Anno 1633. uti ex coronationis formula constat.
units.tr: Likewise all citizens are bound to defend the safety and authority of the most serene King, as also the authority of the assembly of the higher estates, without which no law can be established nor any lawful court of justice, by the laws 130, 131, p. 8, of James 6. They are also bound to protect the liberty of the citizens, who ought to order their lives under no other right and be governed by no other rule than the royal sanctions or the public laws of the kingdom, law 48, p. 3, of James 1; law 79, p. 6, of James 4; which sanction is repeated by the law 131, p. 8, of James 6. But if the public laws and liberties of the kingdom are violated, or anything is taken away from them, the Commission granted concerning the uniting of the kingdoms of Scotland and England (which was the only sanction of parliament 17, of James 6) declares that such a great upheaval of affairs would arise that every rational basis of free monarchy would be utterly destroyed in this kingdom. For it is by the fundamental laws of this kingdom, its ancient privileges, public offices and immunities that not only the majesty and authority of the royal line have been preserved through so many ages, but also the rights of the people over their lands, possessions, offices, liberty, dignity and all their fortunes have remained intact and secure. Therefore, so that the integrity of the sincere religion and of the laws and liberty of this kingdom may stand, it has been enacted, by the law 8, p. 1, repeated by the law 99, p. 7, approved by the law 23, p. 11, and law 114, p. 12, of James 6, and law 4 of King Charles, that all kings entering upon rule, at the receiving of the crown and the government, shall solemnly promise under a holy oath, with the eternal God called as witness, that they will serve God throughout their whole life according to the prescription of his word as far as they are able, and that they will maintain the sincere Christian religion, the preaching of the divine word and the genuine administration of the sacraments, as agreeing with the Confession of Faith received by the Scottish Church, as it is now in use; that they will abolish all doctrinal errors contrary to this faith; that they will govern the people committed to their trust according to the will of God made known through the word, and according to the laws received in this commonwealth and the institutions not contrary to the word of God; and that with all zeal they will see to it that the Church of God and the Christian people enjoy a sincere and firm peace thereafter, and that all heretics and enemies of the purer religion, condemned by the true Church under the name of this depravity, be removed from their dominions. This was sworn by our most serene King Charles, when he received the diadem of this kingdom at Edinburgh in the year 1633, as is evident from the form of the coronation.

units.la: Quod ergo Deus Opt. Max. præcepit, quod superioribus sæculis pii factitarunt, quod exemplo laudatissimo nobis præmonstrarunt Majores nostri sincerae religionis studiosi, multique etiamnum superstites senatusconsulti insuper autoritate nixi, omnibus regni hujus Civibus mandantis, ut communibus syngraphi tabulis consignatis, universi cujuscunque demum ordinis, aut conditionis, mutuum fœdus paciscantur: Quod duabus de causis initum fuit: altera erat afferendæ veræ religionis ergo, uti à corruptelis omnibus tum vindicata, atque explicata in Fidei Confessione, de qua supra, aliaque insuper prolixiori Confessione, quam compluribus sanctionibus, tum Ecclesiæ conventus nationales, tum ordinum regni comitia confirmarunt, quam catechismi publici enarrant, quam à multis annis Deo cœlitus benedicente Pastores promulgarunt, regnique Cives universi, ut indubiam Dei veritatem una verbi Divini auctoritate fultam suo testimonio confirmarunt. Causa altera fuit, ut serenissimi Regis incolumitas, & autoritas illæsa conservaretur: Cum ea sit purioris cultus Divini & majestatis Regiæ arctissima conjunctio, ut una consistant & corruant; communesque sint utriusque hostes & amici: Denique quod nobis conscientia dictitat, & ore confitemur, nos, & posteros omnes ad nationale hoc jusjurandum & fœdus inviolabile conservandum obstringi: Nos subscribentes regni Scotiæ Proceres, Barones, reliquique Nobiles, urbium Municipes, verbi Dei Præcones, aliquæ regni Cives, agnoscentes quantopere cum alias sæpenumero, tum præsertim hac tempestate periclitetur religionis puritas, Regiæ Majestatis dignitas, & publica hujus regni tranquillitas, ex multis variisque innovationibus & malis, de quibus cum in genere, tum nominatim, per libellos supplices & protestationes nuper questi fumus, Profitemur, Deo teste invocato, & beatis angelis, ac universo genere humano conscio palam declaramus, nos concordi omnium sententia ex animo statuere verae huic religioni ad extremum usque spiritum constanter adhærere, eamque pro virili propugnare, quæque in rebus ad cultum divinum pertinentibus jam novata sunt, una cum corruptelis ecclesiastici regiminis, & ecclesiasticorum in civilibus potestate & magistratu, nulla ratione approbare, donec liberis Synodorum & Comitiorum regni judiciis examinata & probata fuerint, omnique licito conatu & molimine, ut pristina religionis nostræ puritas & libertas quæ ante supradictas innovationes lege constituta, & pu-blica blica professione recepta fuerât, recuperetur, operam dare. Cumque diu multumque rationum momentis examinatis & perpensis, exploratum nobis sit, novationes ante memoratas, de quibus supplices quaesti & protestati sumus, nulla verbi Divini auctoritate niti, supradictis confessionibus earumque doctrinæ repugnare, religionis apud Nos instauratorum sententiæ, & supra positis Comitiorum legibus adversari ; ad papisimum, & Antichristi tyrannidem postlimino restituendam, ad puriorem religionem subvertendam, ad omnium libertatem & fortunas, ad regni leges evertendas manifesto gradum facere, Declaramus universi supradictis confessionibus non minus damnari innovationes omnes ante memoratas, & mala in Ecclesiam introducta, quam si singula disertè in iisdem expressa fuissent, nosque pariter ab iis abhorrere obstringi, atque à cæteris papismi capitibus ibidem ejeratis ; Quamobrem conscientia officii Nostri erga Deum, Regem, & patriam permoti, nullo ad hoc inducti rerum terrestrium illicio, quantum humana fert infirmitas, Deo propterea ad uberiorem gratiam assequendam precibus interpellato, sanctè pollicemur, & verendum Domini Dei nostri nomen juramus, nos ad extremum vitæ halitum in purioris hujusce religionis professione & obedientia constanter perseveraturos, pro ejus defensione staturos, omnemque corruptelam, omnesque errores illi adversantes, unumquemque pro muneris sui conditione totis viribus fortiter oppugnaturos. Eadem quoque animi sinceritate Deum hominesque testamur, tantum abesse nos ab omni consilio aut voluntate quippiam adversus Dei gloriam, Regiæve Majestatis amplitudinem & autoritatem moliendi, ut è contra polliceamur, & sanctè juremus, omnibus viribus, quovis etiam bonorum & vitæ discrimine, augustissimi Regis nostri incolumitatem & autoritatem, in religionis puritate, & patriæ nostræ libertate, ac legibus asserendis & confervandis nos propugnaturos: Atque in hac causa religionis, & supradictæ autoritatis Regiæ defendendæ, mutuum auxilium adversus quoscunque adversarios communicatis viribus, consiliis, ac opibus invicem allaturos: Ita ut quicquid in hac causa adversus ullum nostrum designabitur, id perinde habeamus, ac si in universos & singulos designatum foret. Denique in beati hujus foederis societate, Nos cà fide & constantia perstituros, ut nemo omnium ullis artibus, ullis illecebris, aut terroribus rectà vel obliquè ab eà se divelli patiatur, aut communia consilia in tam honesta causa prosequenda ullis objectis impedimentis remoretur, sed è contra, ad eam quisque promovendam omni honeste studio incumbat: quod si quo consilio, sive coram, sive per literas, ad societatis hujus desertionem quispiam nostrum solicitabitur, illud si fieri potest in ipso ortu extinguturos, ne ad alios pertingat; aut si res postulet, ad publicam deliberationem statim relaturos, ut mature obviam eatur. Neque est quod nos perduellionis, conjurationis, aut alia id genus probra & convicia deterreant, quibus nos infamare adversariorum improbitas & versutia conabitur, cum ad hæc consilia justissimis causis descenderimus, & firmissimis nixi rationibus; serio præsertim studio purioris cultus Divini, Majestatis Regiæ, & tranquillitatis publicæ confervandæ impulsi, ut felicitate publica, & ipsi & posteri fruamur.
units.tr: Therefore, what Almighty God commanded, what the pious did in earlier centuries, what our forefathers, zealous for sincere religion, showed us as a most praiseworthy example, and what many still living have done, supported moreover by the authority of a decree of the Senate ordering all the citizens of this kingdom, of every rank and condition, to enter into a mutual covenant, the common documents being signed: this covenant was undertaken for two reasons. The first was to assert the true religion, as vindicated and explained from all corruptions, both in the Confession of Faith mentioned above and in the fuller Confession, which the national assemblies of the Church and the estates of the realm have confirmed by several sanctions, which the public catechisms expound, which the ministers have promulgated for many years with God blessing them from heaven, and which all the citizens of the realm have confirmed by their testimony as the indubitable truth of God, resting on the sole authority of the divine Word. The second reason was that the safety and inviolate authority of our most serene King might be preserved, since the bond between the purer worship of God and royal majesty is so close that they stand or fall together, and have common enemies and friends. Lastly, we declare what conscience tells us and what we confess with our mouths: that we and all our posterity are bound to keep this national oath and inviolable covenant. We, the undersigned, nobles of the kingdom of Scotland, barons, other gentlemen, burgesses of the towns, preachers of the Word of God, and some citizens of the realm, recognising how greatly the purity of religion, the dignity of the royal majesty and the public tranquillity of this kingdom are endangered, both at other times often and especially in this present age, by many and various innovations and evils, of which we have lately complained in general and by name through supplicatory petitions and protestations, profess, calling God to witness, and openly declare, before the blessed angels and the whole human race as witnesses, that by the unanimous judgment of all of us we have resolved from the heart to adhere constantly to this true religion to our last breath, and to defend it to our utmost power; that we will in no way approve those things in matters pertaining to divine worship which have now been changed, together with the corruptions of ecclesiastical government and the power of churchmen in civil affairs and the magistracy, until they have been examined and approved by the free judgments of the synods and parliaments of the kingdom; and that we will apply every lawful effort and endeavour so that the former purity and liberty of our religion, which was established by law and publicly professed before the aforesaid innovations, may be recovered. And since, after the weight of reasons has long and carefully been examined and weighed, it is clear to us that the innovations mentioned above, about which we have complained and protested in our supplications, rest on no authority of the divine Word, are contrary to the aforesaid confessions and their doctrine, are opposed to the opinions of the religion established among us and to the laws of Parliament set out above, and that they manifestly lead towards restoring popery and the tyranny of Antichrist, overthrowing the purer religion, and subverting the liberties and fortunes of all and the laws of the kingdom, we declare that all the innovations mentioned above, and the evils introduced into the Church, are condemned by the aforesaid confessions no less than if each had been expressly named in them; and that we are likewise bound to abhor them, and the other heads of popery there rejected. Therefore, moved by the conscience of our duty towards God, the King and our country, induced by no allurement of earthly things, as far as human weakness allows, having called upon God to obtain his richer grace, we solemnly promise, and swear by the reverend name of the Lord our God, that to our last breath we will persevere constantly in the profession of and obedience to this purer religion, will stand up in its defence, and will strenuously assail with all our strength every corruption and every error opposed to it, each according to the condition of his office. With the same sincerity of mind we also testify before God and men that we are so far from any plan or will to devise anything against the glory of God or the greatness and authority of the royal majesty, that on the contrary we promise and solemnly swear that with all our strength, even at the risk of goods and life, we will defend the safety and authority of our most august King, and will vindicate and preserve the purity of religion, the liberty of our country and its laws; and that in this cause of religion and the defence of the aforesaid royal authority we will bring one another mutual aid against whatever adversaries, with our combined strength, counsels and resources, so that whatever is plotted in this cause against any one of us we shall regard as plotted against all and each. Finally, in the fellowship of this blessed covenant we will persevere with such faith and constancy that none of us allows himself to be torn from it, directly or indirectly, by any arts, enticements or terrors, or delays the common counsels in pursuing so honourable a cause by any objections or obstacles; but on the contrary each will apply himself with every honest zeal to advancing it. And if anyone of us is solicited, by any scheme, whether in person or by letter, to desert this fellowship, we will, if possible, stamp that scheme out at its very beginning, lest it reach others; or if the matter requires, we will at once bring it to public deliberation, so that it may be met in good time. Nor should we be deterred by charges of treason, conspiracy or other such reproaches and insults, by which the wickedness and cunning of our adversaries will try to defame us; for we have undertaken these counsels for the most just causes and rest on the firmest reasons, impelled above all by a serious zeal to preserve the purer worship of God, the royal majesty and public tranquillity, so that we and our posterity may enjoy public happiness.

units.la: Cumque sperare non liceat consilia nostra & conatus secundaturum Deum, si ad professionem & fœderis consignationem ea non accedat vitæ probitas & integritas, quæ Christianos deceat, fœderis cum Deo instaurati reos, sanctè, cum nostro ipsorum, tum familiarum & clientium nomine, pollicemur, qua publicè in propria quemque familia, qua privatim in sua persona singulos, omni studio advigilaturos, ut intra Christianæ libertatis limites quisque se contineat, aliisque pietatis, temperantiæ, & justitiæ, omniumque officiorum erga Deum hominemque exemplo præluceat. Denique, ut conjunctionis hujus vinculum religiose conservetur, Deum immortalem, cordium inspectorem sinceritatis & bonæ fidei testem nobis appellamus.
units.tr: And since we cannot hope that God will prosper our counsels and endeavours unless this profession and the signing of the covenant are accompanied by that uprightness and integrity of life which befits Christians, we solemnly promise, both in our own name and in the name of our households and dependants, that we will each take care, in our own family publicly and each in his own person privately, to keep himself within the limits of Christian liberty, and to set an example of piety, temperance and justice, and of all duties towards God and man. Finally, that the bond of this union may be religiously preserved, we call upon the immortal God, the searcher of hearts, as witness of our sincerity and good faith.

units.la: Ita Domino nostro IESU CHRISTO acceptæ sint rationes nostræ in tremendo judicio; Quod si huic fœderi non steterimus, iram Dei sempiternam in futura vita, atque in hoc sæculo honoris omnis & dignitatis jacturam nobis imprecamur: Supplicissimis interim votis Deum obtestamur, ut ad hæc præstanda Spiritu suo sancto nos confirmet, studia & incepta nostra felici exitu, atqz omni benedictionum genere accumulare dignetur: Ut in patria hac nostra religio vigeat & justitia, idque in Dei gloriam, Regis nostri honorem, publicamque omnium pacem & solatium. In quorum omnium fidem appositis chirographis ista consignavimus, &c.
units.tr: So may our reckoning be accepted by our Lord Jesus Christ at the dreadful judgment. But if we do not abide by this covenant, we invoke upon ourselves the eternal wrath of God in the life to come, and in this age the loss of all honour and dignity. Meanwhile, with most humble prayers, we beseech God to confirm us by his Holy Spirit in performing these things, and to deign to crown our undertakings and endeavours with a happy outcome and every kind of blessing; so that religion and justice may flourish in this our country, to the glory of God, the honour of our King, and the public peace and comfort of all. In witness of all which, we have set our hands to these things, &c.

units.la: Fœdus hoc cui à supplicibus subscriptum & in cujus verba juratum, tribus constat partibus principalibus, primâ habet de verbo in verbum vetus illud fœdus compositum an. 1580 munitumque auctoritate regia, Regii Senatus, duarumque Synodorum nationalium, pro religionis reformatæ puritate; in doctrina & disciplina, contra omnes & singulos Pontificiorum errores, qui speciatim rejiciuntur & abjurantur, articuli pro disciplinâ sunt admodum succincti, nam in genere, & cumulo quasi, rejicitur & abjuratur tota Hierarchia Papalis, & omnes ejus ritus superadditi sacramentorum primævæ institutioni. Adjungitur etiam mutuum fœdus pro defendenda religione reformata, & tuenda pérsona & dignitate regia, Renovatum fuit illud fœdus denuo, anno 1590. omnibusque regni subditis utroque tempore mandatum eidem ut subscriberent. Fœderis hujus sanciendi, hæc olim dicitur fuisse prima causa, quia major, Ecclesiæ Scoticæ Confessio, ab ordinibus regni in comitiis anni 1560. 17 Augusti approbata, & statutis Parlamentariis inferta, veram doctrinam nudè proponit, paucis erroribus aut anti-thesibus notatis aut nominatis, multi Pontificii (magnates præsertim) sub generalibus illis phrafibus, latere fe posse considebant, ac simulantes fe reformatos esse, quo aditus ad dignitates & munia, facilior concederetur, interim Pontificiorum errores, quos ipsi in sinu fovebant diligenter spargebant, quare ut hisce larva detraheretur, inventa fuit illa minor confessio, & quia hypocrisis hæc, quosdam Regis Iacobi (tunc adolefcentis) piæ memoriæ, familiares infecifle dicebatur, à tota ipsius familia, Rex confessioni huic subscribi mandavit, ipso (pio & vere regio exemplo) cæteris præeunte, quam deinde ad Synodum nationalem rex transmisit, in qua denuo post Synodum Taodunenfem, plenis suffragiis, nemine contradicente, decretum fuit, episcoporum auctoritatem, ex scripturis nullam esse, Episcopisque vetitum, sub pœna excommunicationis ne jurisdictioni Ecclesiasticæ sese immiscerent. Ac simul cum hâc fidei confessione obsignanda, per legatum misit diagramma seu formulam 5o Presbyteriorum, seu Classium, locis regni maximè opportunis conftituendorum renovare jussit Rex foedus illud anno 1590. quo etiam anno, in Synodo nationali decretum fuit, ut denuo ministri in singulis parochiis curarent, confessionem hanc obsignandam chirographis civium cujusvis ordinis. Statutum etiam, ut per presbyteria singula, omnes qui rem sacram tractaant, in omnia capita disciplinæ, (quæ in duobus libris de politia Ecclesiastica continentur) subscriberent ante sequentem Synodum. In Synodo 1587. decretum (& Synodis aliis inter annum 1580 & 1590) Ne Academiarum rectores, discipulos maturioris ætatis, in disciplina reciperent eorumque nomina albo seu matrici inferrent, aut quemquam ad gradus Academicos promoverent, nisi in hanc, confessionem prius juratum. Denique mutui illius fœderis pro defendenda Religione & persona regia, hanc fuisse causam dicunt, quia utrique à Pontificiis jultus metus fuit, qui horrendum aliquid, ubique contra reformatæ Religionis profeffores omnes, præsertim vero fereniffimos Principes Britannicos, machinabantur, quorum conatus omnes in Scotia, per hoc fœdus Deus illusit, ac in historia Anglica meminit Cambdenus, nobiles Anglos tale fœdus inter fe pepigisse pro tutela Religionis & persona Elizabethæ Reginæ, atque hæc pro prima fœderis hujus parte.
units.tr: This covenant, which was subscribed by the supplicants and sworn to in its words, consists of three principal parts. The first contains, word for word, that old covenant drawn up in 1580 and confirmed by royal authority, the Privy Council and the two national synods, for the purity of the reformed religion in doctrine and discipline, against all and each of the errors of the Papists, which are specifically rejected and abjured. The articles on discipline are very brief, for in general, and as it were in a heap, the whole Papal hierarchy and all its rites added to the original institution of the sacraments are rejected and abjured. To this is joined a mutual covenant for defending the reformed religion and protecting the person and dignity of the king. This covenant was renewed again in 1590, and at both times all the subjects of the kingdom were ordered to subscribe it. The first cause of enacting this covenant is said to have been this: the larger Confession of the Church of Scotland, approved by the estates of the realm in the assembly of 17 August 1560 and inserted in the parliamentary statutes, sets out the true doctrine plainly, with few errors or antitheses noted or named. Many Papists, especially the magnates, believed they could hide under those general phrases, pretending to be reformed so as to gain easier access to dignities and offices, while meanwhile they diligently spread the errors of the Papists, which they nursed in their own bosom. So that this mask might be torn away, that lesser confession was devised; and because this hypocrisy was said to have infected some members of the household of King James, of pious memory (then a youth), the King, with a pious and truly royal example, ordered the whole of his household to subscribe this Confession, himself going before the others. He then sent it to the national synod, in which again, after the Synod of Dundee, by full votes and with no one contradicting, it was decreed that the authority of bishops has no basis in Scripture, and that bishops were forbidden, under pain of excommunication, to meddle in ecclesiastical jurisdiction. At the same time as this confession of faith was to be signed, he sent by a legate a plan or form of the presbyteries or classes, fifty in number, to be set up in the most convenient places of the realm. The King ordered that covenant of 1590 to be renewed; in that same year, in the national synod, it was decreed that the ministers in each parish should see to it that this Confession was signed by the hands of citizens of every rank. It was also enacted that, through each presbytery, all who handle sacred things should subscribe to all the heads of discipline (contained in the two books on ecclesiastical polity) before the next synod. In the synod of 1587 (and in other synods between 1580 and 1590) it was decreed that the rectors of the universities should not admit students of more mature age to discipline, nor enter their names in the roll, nor promote anyone to academic degrees, unless he had first sworn to this Confession. Finally, they say the reason for that mutual covenant for defending the religion and the royal person was this: both were under a just fear of the Papists, who were everywhere plotting something horrible against all professors of the reformed religion, and especially against the most serene British princes; God mocked all their efforts in Scotland through this covenant. Camden, in his English history, also records that English nobles made such a covenant among themselves for the protection of religion and the person of Queen Elizabeth. This is the first part of the covenant.

units.la: Secunda pars continet enumerationem omnium statutorum seu legum fancitarum, in supremo trium ordinum regni Scotiæ conventu (quem Parlamentum vocant) in favorem Religionis reformatæ tum in doctrina, tum in disciplina, & contra papismum.
units.tr: The second part contains a list of all the statutes or laws enacted in the supreme assembly of the three estates of the kingdom of Scotland (which they call Parliament) in favour of the reformed religion, both in doctrine and in discipline, and against popery.

units.la: Tertia pars fœderis habet applicationem antiqui fœderis & legum ad præfentem rerum statum; in ea exponunt, per ritus Pontificios in veteri fœdere abjuratos, intelligi, omnes illas novitates in libris canonum Liturgiæ & ordinationis obtrufas; fertur, laboraffe tum supplicum multos, quam dilgentiffimè, ut eadem nota insignirentur 5. cæremoniæ Perthenfes, & regimen Episcopale, sed qua magna Pastorum pars, illa inter ἀδιάφορος[?] referebat eorumque praxi assueta fuit, nec videbant, quomodo hoc consistere possit cum subscriptione & juramento, Episcopis praestito, dum primum ministerii functione inaugurarentur, ideo in istis duobus temperamentum quoddam inventum fuit, videlicet, ut omnes, qui foederi, & scripto huic subscriberent, abstinerent à praxi quinque istarum Perthensium cæremoniarum,donec de earum natura plenius in libera Synodo Nationali agitaretur ac,ut operam sedulam sponderent, in Synodo revocandi ad examen corruptionis Ecclesiastici regiminis, inter quas an episcopatus numerandus esset liberæ Synodi maturo judicio remitterent,denique pro tutela personæ ac auctoritatis regiæ, sibi invicem mutuum contra omnes auxilium spondent, ac sacrosancte pollicentur, ita ut quod minimo creabitur hoc nomine à quolibet periculum, id omnes omnino tangere profitentur, hæc summa hujus foederis.
units.tr: The third part of the covenant applies the ancient covenant and laws to the present state of affairs. In it they explain that the Popish rites renounced in the old covenant are to be understood as all those novelties forced upon us in the books of canons, the liturgy and the ordination. It is reported that many of the suppliants laboured most diligently to have the five Perth articles and episcopal government marked with the same brand. But a large part of the ministers referred those matters to the category of [ἀδιάφορα] indifferent things, and were accustomed to their practice, nor did they see how this could be reconciled with the subscription and oath given by the bishops when they were first inducted into the function of the ministry. Therefore a certain compromise was devised in these two respects, namely that all who subscribed to the covenant and this written document should abstain from the practice of the five Perth articles until their nature was more fully debated in a free National Synod; that they should promise diligent effort to bring back to the Synod the examination of the corruption of church government; and that the Synod should decide in its mature judgment whether episcopacy was to be counted among these matters. Finally, they pledge to one another mutual help against all for the protection of the royal person and authority, and sacredly promise that whatever danger is threatened to any one of them in this cause, they all declare that they are wholly touched by it. This is the sum of the covenant.
