units.la: Cui ab omnibus ferè libertatis vindicibus, subscriptum fuit, qui Edinburgi tunc præsentes fuerunt, mense Februario anni 1638. exemplaria ejusdem ad absentes mittuntur, omnibus regni incolis communicanda; ut quibus Religionis puritas cordi esset, in foedus hoc jurarent, quod à quamplurimis libentissime factum, ita ut ante finitum Aprilem, vix pro reformatæ professionis homine haberetur, qui foederi huic non subscriberet, omnes tamen nondum subscripsisse constat. Itaque res hæc Ecclesiam & Regnum in foederatos & non foederatos divisit. Non foederati sunt inprimis omnes Pontificii, quorum numerus in Scotia admodum exiguus est, vix excedens 600. in quorum capita, ut hi motus eant, faba hæc cudetur, deinde sunt & politici quidam, novi homines, subito ad dignitates evecti, aut qui ad eas anhelant, denique sunt quibus Reformata religio cordi est, sed vel ritibus Anglicanis addictiores, libris canonum, liturgiæ & cæteris favent, paucis quiquibusdam minutulis mutatis, ex quorum numero, Abredonenses, tum Theologi, tum politici, perhibentur esse, nam reliquis Ecclesiis, à motuum horum principio, nunquam se adjunxerunt, nec aliquid adhuc fecere, quo ostenderent sibi non probari novitates illas obtrusas, Alii vero sunt, quibus, nec ritus Anglicani placent, nec modus ipsos introducendi, interim foederis subscriptionem detrectant, hisce præsertim rationibus moti.
units.tr: It was subscribed by almost all the defenders of liberty who were then present at Edinburgh in February 1638. Copies of it were sent to those who were absent, to be communicated to all the inhabitants of the kingdom, so that those to whom the purity of religion was dear would swear to this covenant. This was done most willingly by very many, so that before the end of April hardly anyone was considered a man of the reformed profession who did not subscribe to it, though it is certain that not all had yet subscribed. Thus the matter divided the Church and the kingdom into covenanters and non-covenanters. Among the non-covenanters are first of all all the Papists, whose number in Scotland is quite small, scarcely exceeding 600; upon whose heads this bean will be struck, so that these disturbances may proceed. Next there are certain politicians, new men suddenly raised to dignities, or those who long for them. Finally there are those to whom the reformed religion is dear, but who are more attached to the English rites, and favour the books of canons, the liturgy and the rest, with a few small changes. Of this number the men of Aberdeen, both theologians and politicians, are said to be; for they never joined the other churches from the beginning of these movements, nor have they yet done anything to show that those forced novelties do not please them. There are others who dislike both the English rites and the manner of introducing them, yet refuse to subscribe the covenant, and are moved especially by these reasons.

units.la: Quarum prima est, quia non putant sibi licere detrectare obedientiam legibus debitam, ad quam juramento & subscriptione, dum sacro ministerii munere initiarentur, obligati fuerunt. Porro foederi huic subscribentibus promittendum est, se abstenturos à praxi quinque caeremoniarum Perthensium, quæ sancitæ fuerunt in Synodo Nationali Perthensi, & rata statuto Parlamentario. Respondent foederati, Episcopis non licuisse per leges, ejusmodi juramentum exigere, ideoque ab initio invalidum fuisse, non licuisse dicunt, quia nullum aliud Pastoribus initiandis juramentum offerri debuit, quam quod legibus regni sancitum est, nulla porro lege unquam Episcopis concessa fuit potestas, juramento adigendi Pastores in praxin illarum caeremoniarum. Etenim nihil ea de re exstare, constat ex actis Synodi Perthensis, cujus mentem non fuisse obligare ad praxin caeremoniarum illarum, testatur ipsa Episcoporum praxis, qui confirmationem Anglicanam nondum in praxin redegerint, ex quo liquido constare posset, unicam Synodi illius intentionem fuisse, declarare rituum illorum, in se ἀδιαφόρων[?]. Addebant multi, graves se habere causas propter quas, illius Synodi judicium merito rejiciendum sit tanquam multis nominibus illegitimæ: quia tempore debito non indicebatur: nec omnes vocati, quorum Synodo adesse intererat; quod non fuerit ibi, rite electus
units.tr: The first of these is that they do not think it lawful for them to refuse the obedience owed to the laws, to which they were bound by oath and subscription when they were initiated into the sacred office of the ministry. Moreover, those who subscribe this covenant must promise that they will abstain from the practice of the five Perth articles, which were enacted in the National Synod of Perth and ratified by a parliamentary statute. The covenanters reply that by the laws bishops were not permitted to exact such an oath, and therefore it was invalid from the beginning. It was not lawful, they say, because no oath other than that enacted by the laws of the kingdom ought to be offered to ministers being admitted, and no law has ever granted bishops the power to bind ministers by oath to the practice of those ceremonies. Indeed, that nothing exists on this matter is clear from the acts of the Synod of Perth; and the intention of that Synod not to oblige anyone to the practice of those ceremonies is attested by the very practice of the bishops, who have not yet put the English confirmation into practice. From this it could clearly be established that the sole intention of that Synod was to declare those rites to be indifferent [ἀδιάφορα] in themselves. Many added that they had weighty reasons why the judgment of that Synod should rightly be rejected as illegitimate in many respects: it was not announced at the due time; not all who ought to have attended were summoned; the president was not duly elected; the Archbishop of St Andrews thrust himself in and conducted himself as president without any votes of the members of the Synod preceding; many who were not deputed by the churches enjoyed the right of voting; and the votes of many were not free but extorted by threats. With such matters they argued that the authority of that Synod should be made void. Therefore, although that Synod was approved by parliamentary authority in 1621, it could never be persuaded to the greater part of the churches to admit those ceremonies. For, they affirm, both in the Synod and in Parliament it was made clear to the deputies that the King was not concerned about the practice, but only that the indifference of those rites should be acknowledged. They said that a solemn promise was then added by the King's deputy, and in the King's name, that by this concession the Scottish Church would be freed from fear of the remaining English ceremonies; and that unless this promise had been given, the estates of the kingdom would never have ratified that Synod. But now, since it is agreed by all that no account is taken of that solemn promise, and since a most open door has been made, by the practice of those ceremonies, for the rest of the English rite, and even for the Popish apparatus which the English still lack, to be introduced without any warrant of any law whatever; and finally, since by the practice of these ceremonies a greater good, namely the peace of the Church and the spread of the Gospel, is hindered, and courage is added to obstinate Papists, while the weaker are scandalised; they demand equity, lest the sacrament of godliness become a hindrance to godliness. Therefore, notwithstanding that oath, they may abstain from the practice.

units.la: Præses, Archi-Episcopo Andreapolitano sese intrudente & pro Præside, nullis præeuntibus Synodalium suffragiis, sese gerente, quod complures, ab Ecclesiis non Deputati, jure suffragii gavisi sunt; quod suffragia multorum non fuerint libera, sed minis extorta, & hisce similia producebant, ut Synodi illius auctoritatem irritam redderent, quare licet illa Synodus, auctoritate Parlamentaria anno 1621. approbata fuerit, Nunquam tamen perfuaderi potuit Ecclesiarum potiori parti, ut cæremonias illas admitterent. Nam tum in Synodo, tum in Parlamento, significatum fuisse deputatis affirmant, de praxi non laborare Regem; tantum ut rituum illorum indifferentia agnosceretur. Additum tum a Regis deputato solenne promissum dicebant, idque Regis nomine, liberatum iri hac concessione Ecclesiam Scoticam à metu reliquarum cæremoniarum Anglicanarum, quod promissum nisi accessisset, Synodum illam ordines regni nunquam ratam habuissent. Nunc vero, cum omnibus constet, solennis illius promissi nullam haberi rationem, ac cum cæremoniarum istarum praxi, patentissima porta aperta sit ad reliquum Anglicanorum ritum, quin & Pontificiorum etiam, quibus adhuc carent Angli, apparatum, absque ulla legis cujuslibet vel specie introducendum, denique, cum praxi istarum cæremoniarum majus bonum, videlicet Ecclesiæ pax, ac Evangelii dilatatio impediantur, ac obstinatis Pontificiis animus addatur, infirmiores scandalizentur, æquitatem postulare, ne facramentum pietatis, sit impedimentum pietatis, quare juramento illo non obstante, posse eos à praxi abstinere.
units.tr: The President, with the Archbishop of St Andrews thrusting himself in and acting as President, without any prior votes of the members of the synod, meant that many men who had not been appointed by the churches enjoyed the right to vote. The votes of many were not free but extorted by threats, and they adduced similar objections, so as to render the authority of that synod void. Therefore, although that synod was approved by parliamentary authority in 1621, it could never be persuaded to the greater part of the churches to admit those ceremonies. For, they affirm, it was declared to the deputies both in the synod and in parliament that the king was not concerned with the practice, but only that the indifference of those rites should be acknowledged. They said that a solemn promise was then added by the king's deputy, and in the king's name, that by this concession the Scottish Church would be freed from fear of the remaining English ceremonies. Had that promise not been added, the estates of the realm would never have ratified that synod. Now, however, since it is evident to all that no account is taken of that solemn promise, and since by the practice of these ceremonies a wide door is opened to the rest of the English rite, indeed even to the Popish apparatus which the English still lack, to be introduced without any law of any kind, and finally since by the practice of these ceremonies a greater good, namely the peace of the Church and the spread of the Gospel, is hindered, and courage is added to obstinate Papists while the weaker are scandalized, they demand equity, that the sacrament of piety should not become an impediment to piety. Therefore, notwithstanding that oath, they could abstain from the practice.

units.la: Secunda ratio non fœderatorum hæc erat, omnia fœdera mutua inter subditos, jure municipali regni Scotiæ illicita sunt, nisi regis mandatum, foedus approbantis, accesserit, atque foedus hoc est subditorum inter se, Rege nec conscio, nec mandante. Responderunt foederati, Regni quidem legibus municipalibus vetari foedera inter subditos inita, in Reipublicæ totius, aut cujuslibet damnum, non vero, quæ ad Dei gloriam, Regii honoris, regni, libertatis publicæ conservationem facta sunt, cum salus populi suprema lex esse debeat, ad quam leges aliæ omnes interpretandæ sunt. Dein, se non esse destitutos auctoritate regia, ad foedus hoc ineundum, quandoquidem, beatæ memoriæ. R. Iacobus hujus foederis author fuerit, annis 1580 & 1590, ac Senatus regii Synodorumque decretis, tum omnibus regni incolis, subscriptio mandata fuit, unde impositum nomen foederis, seu confessionis Nationalis; ac licet multorum supina negligentia, in purioris religionis damnum, ac Papismi incrementum, executio intermissa sit, vigere tamen affirmant continuam ejus praxin in omnibus regni Academiis, in quibus confessioni huic seu foederi subscribitur, ab omnibus, qui gradum aliquem scholasticum consequuntur.
units.tr: The second reason of those who refused to subscribe the covenant was this: all mutual covenants among subjects are unlawful by the municipal law of the kingdom of Scotland unless the king's command, approving the covenant, has been added, and this covenant is among subjects themselves, the king neither knowing of it nor commanding it. The covenanters replied that the municipal laws of the realm forbid covenants entered into among subjects to the harm of the whole commonwealth or of anyone, but not those made for the glory of God and the preservation of the king's honour, the realm and the public liberty, since the safety of the people ought to be the supreme law, to which all other laws are to be interpreted. Next, they said that they were not without the authority of the king for entering into this covenant, since King James, of blessed memory, was the author of this covenant in the years 1580 and 1590, and by the decrees of the royal Senate and of the synods, subscription was enjoined on all inhabitants of the realm; whence the name covenant, or National Confession, was given to it. And although, through the careless negligence of many, its execution was interrupted to the loss of the purer religion and the increase of Popery, they affirm that its practice continues in all the academies of the realm, in which this confession or covenant is subscribed by all who obtain any scholastic degree.

units.la: Tertia ratio eorum, qui detrectant foederi subscribere, hæc est, Qui foederi huic subscribunt, mutuum sibi invicem in hac causa contra omnes auxilium spondent. Itaque si Rex vi armata acturus sit, tenentur confoederatos etiam armis defendere contra Regem. Porro nondum sibi constare dicunt, licere subditis cujuscunque demum ordinis, aut dignitatis sint vel omnibus in unum conjunctis Principe & Monarchæ absoluto (qualem esse dicunt Regem in Regno Scotiæ) in causa Religionis, aut libertatis legum, vi armata sese opponere, in cujus rei confirmationem, omnes ii sacræ scripturæ loci allegantur, qui principibus obedientiam suadent, citatis etiam multorum patrum, scholasticorum, doctorum reformatæ Ecclesiæ, & eorum etiam jurispetitorum, qui pro jure Regum scripsèrunt contra Iesuitas, testimoniis: mirum quam in hoc spatioso campo triumpharint multi: Sed respon-derunt foederati, quæstionem hanc maxima semper exercuisse ingenia, neque se libenter eam discutiendam suscipere, cum Rege optimo & equissimo rem nunc esse, qui majorum vestigiis insistens, infinita illa potestate (quam Regibus multi, commodis suis velificantes, licet cum ruina legum tribuunt) non statuerit uti: sed potestate legitima, quæ legum receptarum ambitum non excedat: paratos se semper esse, omnimodam legibus Regni imperatam obedientiam præstare, sibique perfuasum quam alienissimum esse à Regis animo, eam obedientiam postulare, quæ cum pietate in Deum, aut Regni privilegiis pugnet; quibus tuendis se sacrosancto juramento, inaugurationis tempore (anno 1633.) obstrinxerit. Sed cum modestum hoc responsum, multis non satisfecisset, cogebantur foederati fusius respondere, præsertim propter novatores quosdam, qui, ut audicam gratiam adipiscantur Regiæ dignitatis promotores strenuos se simulant, ut facilius Orthodoxis os obstruant, itaque dicebant, aliam esse rationem subditorum merè privatorum, aliam eorum, qui ita subditi sunt, ut tamen magistratus officio gaudeant, quorum officii est populi sibi subditi jus & privilegia tueri. Notum illud Trajani, cum pugionem præfecto prætorii traderet, hoc pro me utere, si recte impero, si male, contra me. Apostolorum monita, obedientiam suadentia, etiam improbis magistratibus, licet generaliter prolata, tacitam tamen habere exceptionem summæ necessitatis, Assertores Regii imperii fortissimos, non negare populo universo aut insigni ejus parti, jus se armis tuendi contra principem supremum, mum, in quibusdam casibus. Etenim, si collectivo quasi regni alicujus corpori, defensionem armatam, contra publicæ libertatis invasores, demas, eodem pacto omnibus Tyrannorum injuriis expones. Oculos Convertendos in antiquum jus Regni Scotici, populum Scoticum, à primo in Britanniam adventu (quem historici referunt ad Alexandri Magni tempora, 330 fere anno ante natum Christum (Hibernorum λαηεολογήματα[?] hic flocci facio) se in societatem civilem, sub Fergusii primi authoritate non confociasse ea conditione, ut mori præoptaverit quam ullo casu vim superiorum armis arceret, quod omnium ætatum historiæ gentis Scoticæ testantur, nec negligendum esse οὐ βίᾳ ἀλλὰ νόμῳ in Scotos obtinuisse imperium Fergusium primum; quod & in Gallia & Germania olim factitatum fuisse observat Tacitus, cum serviret Syria, Asiaque. Porro non deesse luculenta hujus exempla, in omnibus fortè regnis Europæis, post Romani imperii eversionem, non in Germania solum, ubi precario regnare debet imperator, sed & in Gallia & ditionibus familiæ Burgundicæ, & Dania ac Suecia notum esse, quid ubique à subditis in causa libertatis patriæ reformatæ religionis sæpius, premente necessitate, factitatum, quos rebellionis Iesuiticæ ita temerè damnare esset crudele & contra πολιτικωτάτων[?] uniforme judicium. Regem Iacobum, cui magistratus jura optimè cognita fuerunt, pro reformatis in Gallia & Belgio causam dixisse, ac fusè ostendisse, quam immane diferant Iesuitarum doctrina & praxis, ab innocua & necessaria defensione reformatorum ibidem. Denique longè diversam esse rationem belli defensivi, per majorem populi partem, & belli offensivi. Neque hæc à se prolata dicebant foederati, quasi Regi optimo Carolo notam aliquam inurerent, cui illud solum justum, quod legibus conforme, in cujus pectoris sacrario, crario,nisi faterentur æquitatem, pietatem in Deum, totumque virtutum verè regiarum chorum sedes fixisse, ingratissimi merito habendi essent. Disputationum harum summam, unico tenore ponendam censui, ne series narrationis interrumperetur. Profstant porro hæ disputationes, & plura alia scripta eristica super hisce materiis, quæ magna quidem animorum concertatione agitatæ fuerunt, ita tamen, ut fœderatorum numerus indies cresceret & animi confirmarentur.
units.tr: The third reason of those who refuse to subscribe the Covenant is this: those who subscribe it pledge mutual aid to one another in this cause against all. So if the King should act with armed force, they are bound to defend their fellow confederates even with arms against the King. Further, they say that it is still not settled for them whether subjects of any rank or dignity whatever may, in matters of religion or the liberty of the laws, oppose by armed force even all of them together against a prince and absolute monarch (which they say the King in the Kingdom of Scotland is). To confirm this they cite all those passages of Holy Scripture which urge obedience to princes, along with the testimonies of many Fathers, scholastics, and teachers of the reformed Church, and also of those jurists who wrote in defence of the rights of kings against the Jesuits. It is remarkable how many have triumphed on this broad field. But the Covenanters replied that this question has always exercised the greatest minds, and that they did not willingly take it up for discussion, since the matter now concerns a most excellent and most equitable King, who, following the footsteps of his ancestors, has resolved not to use that unlimited power which many, favouring their own interests, grant to kings even at the cost of the ruin of the laws, but only that lawful power which does not exceed the bounds of the received laws. They said they were always ready to render complete obedience to the laws of the Kingdom, and they were persuaded that it was as far as possible from the King's mind to demand that obedience which conflicts with piety towards God or with the privileges of the Kingdom, which privileges he had bound himself by a most sacred oath to protect at his inauguration (in the year 1633). But since this moderate answer did not satisfy many, the Covenanters were compelled to answer more fully, especially on account of certain innovators, who, in order to win the favour of the court, pretend to be vigorous promoters of royal dignity, so that they may more easily stop the mouths of the Orthodox. Thus they said that there is one reason for subjects who are purely private persons, and another for those who, though subjects, nevertheless enjoy the office of magistrate, whose duty it is to defend the rights and privileges of the people committed to them. Famous is the saying of Trajan, when he handed a dagger to the prefect of the praetorians: use this for me if I rule rightly, against me if badly. The admonitions of the Apostles, urging obedience even to wicked magistrates, although stated in general terms, nevertheless have a tacit exception in cases of the greatest necessity. The most resolute defenders of royal authority do not deny that the whole people, or a distinguished part of it, has the right to defend itself by arms against the supreme prince in certain cases. For if you were to deny armed defence against the invaders of public liberty to the body of a kingdom, as it were collectively, you would in the same way expose it to all the injuries of tyrants. Let us turn our eyes to the ancient law of the Kingdom of Scotland: the Scottish people, from its first arrival in Britain (which historians refer to the times of Alexander the Great, about 330 years before the birth of Christ; I care little here for the Irish [λαηεολογήματα] babblings), did not join itself in civil society under the authority of Fergus the First on the condition that it would rather die than in any case repel by arms the violence of superiors. All the histories of the Scottish nation in every age bear witness to this, and it must not be overlooked that Fergus the First gained dominion over the Scots not by force but by law [οὐ βίᾳ ἀλλὰ νόμῳ]. Tacitus observes that this was once also done in Gaul and Germany, when Syria and Asia were in servitude. Moreover, that clear examples of this are not lacking, in almost all the European kingdoms after the overthrow of the Roman Empire, is known not only in Germany, where the emperor ought to reign only at the pleasure of others, but also in France, in the dominions of the house of Burgundy, and in Denmark and Sweden: what has been done everywhere by subjects, under the pressure of necessity, often in the cause of the liberty of the fatherland and of the reformed religion, and to condemn these rashly as Jesuitical rebellion would be cruel and contrary to the uniform judgment of the most politic. King James, to whom the rights of magistrates were very well known, pleaded the cause of the reformed in France and in the Low Countries, and showed at length how immensely the doctrine and practice of the Jesuits differ from the harmless and necessary defence of the reformed there. Finally, the Covenanters said, the reasoning of a defensive war carried on by the greater part of the people is very different from that of an offensive war. Nor did the Covenanters put forward these points as if they were branding some stain upon the best of kings, Charles, for whom only that is just which is in accordance with the laws, and in the sanctuary of whose breast equity, piety towards God, and the whole chorus of truly royal virtues have fixed their seat; they would deserve to be considered most ungrateful if they did not acknowledge this. I thought the sum of these disputations should be set down in a single line, so that the sequence of the narrative would not be interrupted. These disputations, and many other polemical writings on these matters, still survive; they were indeed debated with great contention of minds, yet in such a way that the number of the Covenanters grew daily and their spirits were strengthened.

units.la: Senatus regius, cum omnia in deterius vergere conspiceret; sedulo de omnibus Regem certiorem facit, misso in hunc finem ineunte Martio mense Senatore, qui imminentis periculi, ac nisi à Regia clementia remedium tempestive adhiberetur, jamjam erupturi, Regem coram moneret; quod à Senatore fideliter peractum fuit, quare Rex, tres ex primariis Regni Senatoribus ex Scotia ad se vocat, eo etiam multi Episcoporum, licet non vocati, convolant, rati, dum tantum capitibus immineret periculum, non esse sibi secure dormiendum, cumque Regis animum ad clementiam flecti cernerent, omnia sua & fautorum opera ad extrema & violenta consilia deducere satagunt: declarant res non adeo esse desperatas, quin si Rex causam vi acturus sit, certissimi sint de felici & optato exitu: paucorum quorundam Puritanorum seditiosorum insolentiam severitate compescendam esse, nisi imperii majestatem contemptui exponeret: posse se etiam in ipsa Scotia, præsertim in partibus Regni Borealibus, ac familiis montanis, fortissimorum virorum, non contemnendam manum colligere, quibus si mediocres Anglorum copiæ jungerentur, facillimum esset in ordinem cogere omnes qui ejusmodi supplicationibus, protestationibus, conjurationibus auctoritatem regiam lacessere ausi fuerunt: & quia tres illos nobiles à Rege vocatos violentis hisce suis consi-liis non consensuros sciebant; Alios, quibus à simili tempestate in Anglia metus esse posset, submittunt, qui eadem consilia suggererent: Gravissimam etiam accusationem coram Rege instituunt contra Comitem Traquarium Regni Scotiæ summum Thesaurarium, cujus clandestinis consiliis & connivëntia, omnes hosce motus ortos dixerunt: Et ille, solam tumultuum causam fuisse Episcoporum quorundam non ferendam superbiam & temeritatem, quibus multa etiam alia objiciebat, verane an falsa, dies docebit.
units.tr: The royal Council, seeing that everything was tending for the worse, diligently informed the King of everything, sending in early March a senator for this purpose, who was to warn the King in person that the impending danger was about to break out, unless a remedy was applied in good time by royal clemency. This the senator faithfully carried out. Consequently the King summoned three of the leading senators of the Kingdom from Scotland to himself; many bishops, though not summoned, also flocked there, thinking that while danger hung over their heads they should not sleep securely. And when they saw that the King's mind was being inclined towards clemency, they strove by every effort, their own and their supporters', to drive matters to extreme and violent counsels. They declared that affairs were not so desperate that, if the King should act by force, they would not be most certain of a happy and desired outcome. The insolence of a few seditious Puritans was to be checked by severity, unless the majesty of the empire was to be exposed to contempt. They could also gather, in Scotland itself, especially in the northern parts of the Kingdom and among the mountain families, a not contemptible band of most brave men; if moderate English forces were joined to these, it would be very easy to bring to order all who had dared to assail royal authority with such supplications, protests, and conspiracies. And because they knew that the three noblemen summoned by the King would not consent to these violent counsels of theirs, they sent in others, who might feel fear from a similar storm in England, to suggest the same counsels. They also brought a most grave accusation before the King against the Earl of Traquair, the Lord High Treasurer of the Kingdom of Scotland, saying that all these movements had arisen through his secret counsels and connivance. He replied that the sole cause of the disturbances was the intolerable pride and rashness of certain bishops, and he objected to them many other things; whether they are true or false, the day will show.

units.la: Dum hisce diversis consiliis distineretur ac distraheretur aula, nobiles foederati in Scotia, ad familiares quosdam nobiles Scotos in Anglia hærentes literas mittunt cum articulis Ecclesiarum gravamina continentibus, obsecrantes ut Regi eos insinuarent, cujus aures fidelium subditorum æquissimis postulatis nondum occlusas sperabant: & Rex multorum consiliis varie agitatus, aliis moderata & pacifica, aliis violenta & extrema suadentibus, tan-dem pro innata & hæreditaria clementia moderationibus consiliis utendum statuit, ut æquissimis: Marchionemque Hamiltonium nobilissimæ familiæ Principem & magnæ in Scotia clientelæ, cum tribus illis nobilibus Senatoribus quos ad se in Aulam vocaverat, in Scotiam dimittit, cum mandatis, ut paci studerent.
units.tr: While the court was being distracted and pulled in different directions by these various counsels, the noble Covenanters in Scotland sent letters to certain noble Scots friends remaining in England, with articles containing the grievances of the Churches, begging them to bring these to the King's notice, in the hope that his ears were not yet closed to the most equitable demands of his faithful subjects. And the King, variously troubled by the counsels of many, some urging moderate and peaceful measures, others violent and extreme ones, at last resolved, out of his innate and hereditary clemency, to use the most moderate counsels. He sent into Scotland the Marquis of Hamilton, prince of a most noble family and of great clientage in Scotland, together with those three noble senators whom he had summoned to the court, with instructions that they should work for peace.

units.la: Statim ad iter se accingit Marchio regius Deputatus, cumque Dalketham oppidulum Edinburgo vicinum, venisset, ibi aliquamdiu hæsit, causatus se non nisi cum detrimento auctoritatis regiæ Edinburgum accedere posse, quod arx regia à foederatorum vigilibus sollicitè custodiretur. Contra vero, foederatorum deputati nullis rationibus adduci potuerunt, ut Dalkethæ cum Marchione agerent. quarum suspicionum hanc perhibent fuisse causam: Edinburgo Regni Scotiæ Metropoli imminet Arx regia munitissima, sita in rupe declivi; sed ut in alta pace fieri solet, quibus cura providendi commissa fuit, in armamentario & re frumentaria procuranda negligentiores fuere, itaque deerat fere pulvis tormentarius & alia arci defendendæ necessaria. Huic malo ut obviam iretur, navis quædam Londino mittitur, cum omnis generis apparatu bellico ad arcem instruendam, qui nocte intempesta exponitur, & in Dalkethense pallatium defertur, ut inde sine suspicione[?] Arci opportunius inferri posset; quod cum cognitum haberent fœderati, ac suspicionibus in deterius omnia detorquentibus ubique ferverent, extra arcem Edinburgenam vigilias disponunt, quibus mandatum, ne quid apparatus bellici inferri sinerent; etenim, si pace motus hosce componendos statuerit Rex, cui bono tanta apparatus bellici copia munienda erat arx? neque sibi tutum, deputatos ad Dalkethense Pallatium mittere: Tandem post paucorum dierum moram Marchio Edinburgum se confert (fœderatis publicas arcis vigilias remittentibus) mense Iunio, cui obviam processit omnium ordinum frequentissimus numerus; aderant in ea turba 700 Pastores Ecclesiarum.
units.tr: The Marquis, the royal Deputy, immediately set out on his journey, and when he had come to Dalkeith, a little town near Edinburgh, he stayed there for some time, alleging that he could not enter Edinburgh except to the detriment of royal authority, since the royal castle was carefully guarded by the sentries of the Covenanters. On the other hand, the deputies of the Covenanters could not be induced by any arguments to treat with the Marquis at Dalkeith. They report that the cause of these suspicions was this. Over Edinburgh, the metropolis of the Kingdom of Scotland, looms the most strongly fortified royal castle, set upon a steep rock. But, as usually happens in deep peace, those to whom the care of providing had been entrusted were rather negligent in procuring the armoury and the stores of grain, so that there was almost no gunpowder and other things necessary for defending the castle. To remedy this evil a certain ship was sent from London with every kind of military equipment to supply the castle; it was unloaded in the dead of night and carried to the palace at Dalkeith, so that from there it might be brought into the castle more conveniently and without suspicion. When the Covenanters learned of this, and with suspicions turning everything for the worse, they were in a ferment everywhere, they posted sentries outside the castle of Edinburgh with orders that they should allow no military supplies to be brought in. For, they argued, if the King had decided to settle these movements by peace, for what good would so great a store of military equipment be needed to fortify the castle? Nor did they think it safe to send deputies to the palace at Dalkeith. At last, after a delay of a few days, the Marquis made his way to Edinburgh in June (the Covenanters withdrawing the public sentries from the castle), and there went out to meet him a very large crowd of all orders; in that throng were present seven hundred ministers of the Churches.

units.la: Cum fœderatis sério egit tum Marchio, ut fœderi renunciarent, alioqui nullam esse spem obtinendi Synodum Nationalem; (quam illi unicum malis hisce curandis, & flammæ restinguendæ remedium summis votis expetebant.) Responsum à fœderatis, hoc concedi non posse, nisi cum manifesto perjurio, & divini nominis profanatione: Et quia partem illam fœderis, qua mutuum sibi invicem auxilium in causa hac spondent, à quibusdam distortam esse intelligebant; quasi conspirationem contra regiam majestatem denotaret; ideo exhibito scripto, omnes ejúsmodi scrupulos Marchionis animo eximere studuerunt. Etenim cum omnibus subditis persuasissimum Rex esse voluit, sibi statutum esse, reformatam Religionem & leges à majoribus sancitas, tueri, quomodo possunt eorum verba, quibus ad religionis, & legum, ac dignitatis regiae tutelam contra omnes se obligant, torqueri, quasi aliquid contra authoritatem regiam molirentur? Addebant, eos potius læsæ majestatis regiæ reos esse, qui ejusmodi consequentias nectendo, contra foederatorum expressam mentem & clara verba, in subditorum animis satis hactenus commotis, iniquas suspiciones excitant; quasi, quod Rex sacrosanctè pollicitus sit, reipsa fortasse præstare non constituerit: Neque alio spectare Episcoporum consilia, quàm ut dissidii semina inter optimum regem & fideles subditos sata, foveant, quo poenam facinoribus suis debitam effugiant. Denique Marchionis postulata omnia obtulerunt, obsecrantes, ut ea Regi clementissimo serio commendaret.
units.tr: The Marquis also pressed the Covenanters earnestly to renounce the Covenant, saying that otherwise there was no hope of obtaining a National Synod, which they desired above all as the one remedy for these evils and for quenching the flames. The Covenanters replied that this could not be granted except with manifest perjury and profanation of the divine name. Because they understood that a part of the Covenant, in which they pledge mutual help in this cause, had been twisted by some as if it signified a conspiracy against the royal majesty, they presented a written paper and strove to remove all such scruples from the Marquis's mind. Since the King wished all his subjects to be thoroughly persuaded that it was his resolve to defend the reformed religion and the laws sanctioned by our forefathers, how could their words, by which they bind themselves to defend religion, the laws and the dignity of the king against all, be twisted as if they were plotting something against royal authority? They added that rather those who, by drawing such inferences contrary to the expressed mind and clear words of the Covenanters, stir up unjust suspicions in the minds of subjects already sufficiently agitated, are the ones guilty of treason against royal majesty, as if what the King had solemnly promised he had perhaps not decided to fulfil in fact. Nor do the Bishops' counsels aim at anything but to foster the seeds of discord sown between the best of kings and his faithful subjects, so that they may escape the punishment due to their crimes. Finally they offered all the Marquis's demands, earnestly begging him to commend them seriously to the most gracious King.

units.la: Ante discessum Marchionis in Angliam publicatur edictum regium, mense Iulio; Cujus hæc sunt capita, I. profitetur Rex, se quam maximè à superstitionibus Papisticis abhorrere; ac sibi statutum, reformatam religionem, prout in Scotia exercetur, tueri. II. Se nolle urgere libros Canonum, liturgiæ, aut aliquid ejus notæ, nisi iis legitimis mediis, quibus omnibus constet, mutationem religionis aut legum à se non intendi. III. Se rectificaturum celsam commissionem. IV. Sibi cordi fore omnia, quæ pertinent ad Ecclesiam, & regnum sedandum. V. Sibi statutum esse captata commoda opportunitate Parlamentum & Synodum indicere.
units.tr: Before the Marquis's departure for England, a royal edict was published in July. Its heads were these: I. The King professes that he utterly abhors Papist superstitions, and that it is his resolve to defend the reformed religion as it is practised in Scotland. II. He does not wish to press the books of canons, the liturgy, or anything of that kind, except by those lawful means by which it is clear to all that no change of religion or laws is intended by him. III. He will rectify the High Commission. IV. All matters pertaining to the Church and to the settling of the kingdom are dear to him. V. It is his resolve to call Parliament and a Synod when a convenient opportunity has been seized.

units.la: Finita per præconem edicti lectione, statim publicè protestationem suam per advocatum in suprema curia legunt foederati, cujus capita ( post[?] brevem prætéritorum narrationem, qua motuum horum causam in Episcopos rejiciunt) hæc fuerunt.
units.tr: When the herald had finished reading the edict, the Covenanters at once publicly read their protestation through an advocate in the High Court. After a brief account of past events, in which they throw the cause of these disturbances back upon the Bishops, its heads were these.

units.la: I. Se nunquam in quaestionem vocasse piam & sinceram optimi regis intentionem erga religionem reformatam, & contra idololatriam horrendam papismi. II. Mandatum hoc, malis hisce, quibus involvuntur, curandis, non sufficere; quia nullam mentionem facit abolitionis librorum illorum obtrusorum contra legum municipalium auctoritatem, omniumque ecclesiarum reformatarum prax-in, quos tamen libros superstitionibus papisticis scatere, ex parallelo & collatione papismi & librorum horum, præsertim prout à navatoribus hodiernis explicantur, facile se demonstraturos profitentur; quia frustra fit mentio rectificationis (ut ita loquar) celsæ[?] commissionis, quam abolere penitus ratio postulat, cum nulla publicæ legis in conventu ordinum regni sanctitæ, vel specie muniatur. III. Cum mandatum hoc ipsorum conventus damnet, protestantur omnes eos conventus esse necessarios & legitimos, & quicquid adhuc à foederatis in publicio gestum fit, esse legibus conforme; immerito itaque odiosis verbis esse exagitatos. IV. Sibi statutum prioribus gravaminibus exhibitis adhærere, nec posse causam hanc tam piam; tam justam deserere, donec per legitimam & liberam Synodum Nationalem Ecclesiæ puritati & paci provideatur.
units.tr: I. They have never called into question the pious and sincere intention of the best of kings towards the reformed religion and against the horrible idolatry of Popery. II. This mandate is not sufficient for remedying the evils by which they are beset, because it makes no mention of abolishing those books thrust upon them, which are contrary to the authority of the municipal laws and to the practice of all the reformed Churches. They profess that these books are full of Popish superstitions, and that they will easily demonstrate this from a parallel and comparison of Popery with these books, especially as they are explained by the present innovators. Mention is made in vain of the rectification (so to speak) of the High Commission, which reason demands be utterly abolished, since it is supported by no sanction of public law in an assembly of the estates of the kingdom, nor even by the appearance of one. III. Since this mandate condemns their assemblies, they protest that all those assemblies are necessary and lawful, and that whatever has so far been done in public by the Covenanters conforms to the laws; they have therefore been unjustly assailed with hateful words. IV. It is their resolve to hold fast to the grievances previously presented, and they cannot abandon so pious and so just a cause until provision is made for the purity and peace of the Church through a lawful and free National Synod.

units.la: In Angliam excurrit Marchio, ut regem de rerum statu, coram faceret certiorem, obitæque legationis rationem redderet, rediturus in Scotiam ad statum diem, videlicet 12 Augusti. Interea solennia jejunia celebrantur à Scotis, iis præsertim diebus, quos causæ huic agitandæ de eaque deliberandi per Senatum suum aulicum destinaverat Rex, & quia Synodi Nationalis indictionem, tam celerem quam praesentia mala requirebant, à Rege vix sperabant, scriptum edunt foederati, quo probare conantur, Ecclesiis in tali statu licere sibi prospicere, potestatem indicendi Synodum, si magistratus fidei hostis sit, aut negligentior in Ecclesiae bono procurando penes ipsam Ecclesiam esse, quae hanc potestatem à Christo suo domino accepit, quaque absque scrupulo ullo usa fuit, omnibus illis saeculis inter Christi mortem & Nicaenam Synodum. Quod si quis putet, accessione Principum ad Ecclesiam, omnem illam potestatem Ecclesiae ereptam, & in Principes collatam, nae ille longe fallitur, nam sic Regum & Principum accessio ad Ecclesiam non esset promissum & benedictio, Isaiae 49. 23. sed in damnum Ecclesiae cederet, contra expressa Dei verba quibus non vult minui sed augeri & corroborari ecclesiae authoritatem sub Christiano magistratu, cujus auctoritatem in Ecclesia, esse cumulativam non privativam indicat, ad Ecclesiae aedificationem non destructionem, cujus ruinam subsequi necesse erit, si urgentibus malis Ecclesiae subversionem minitantibus impediatur Synodorum indictio, & à magistratu qualitercunque affecto simpliciter pendeat. Porro quaecunque Synodi indictionem unquam requirebant, ea omnia nunc in Ecclesia Scotica concurrere, ut sunt.
units.tr: The Marquis hurried into England to inform the King in person of the state of affairs and to render an account of his mission, intending to return to Scotland by the appointed day, namely 12 August. Meanwhile the Scots celebrated solemn fasts, especially on those days which the King had set aside for this matter to be debated and deliberated upon by his privy council. Because they scarcely hoped that the King would call a National Synod as quickly as the present evils demanded, the Covenanters published a writing by which they try to prove that the Churches, in such a state, may provide for themselves. The power of calling a Synod, if the magistrate is an enemy of the faith or too negligent in procuring the good of the Church, lies with the Church itself, which received this power from Christ her Lord, and which she used without any scruple in all those centuries between Christ's death and the Nicene Synod. If anyone thinks that by the accession of princes to the Church all that power was snatched from the Church and conferred upon the princes, he is greatly mistaken. For then the accession of kings and princes to the Church would not be a promise and a blessing (Isaiah 49. 23), but would turn to the Church's loss, against the express words of God, by which he does not wish the authority of the Church to be diminished under a Christian magistrate but increased and strengthened. He indicates that its authority in the Church is cumulative, not privative, for the building up of the Church and not its destruction. That ruin must follow if, while evils threatening the subversion of the Church press upon it, the calling of Synods is hindered and everything simply depends on a magistrate affected in whatever way. Moreover, all the circumstances which ever demanded the calling of a Synod now concur in the Scottish Church, namely:

units.la: I. Corruptio doctrinae per Papismum, ejusque furculum geminum Arminianismum. II. Multiplicatio abusuum regiminis Ecclesiastici per Episcopos. III. Subversio disciplinae Ecclesiasticae legibus frequentibus sancitae. IV. Loco pacis & unitatis regnat schisma. V. Sedibus moti sunt fideles quamplurimi Pastores, Episcoporum tyrannide, quibus beneficium appellationis est ademptum, cum nullae multis hisce annis praeteritis habitae sint Synodi Nationales. VI. Tantum abest, ut censura aliqua notati sint Pastores, Doctores, Episcopi manifesto rei praedictarum corruptionum, ut contra, primariae dignitates in eos cumulentur, tanquam rei bene gestæ præmia, eorundemque exemplo alii ad similia perpetranda animentur, ita ut de ecclesiæ salute fere conclamatum sit, nisi per liberam synodum remedium protinus afferatur. Hæc illi fuse in tractatu de Synodorum necessitate, in quo ad contraria, quæ objici solent argumenta, pro jure magistratus etiam Ecclesiam negligentis respondent.
units.tr: (1) The corruption of doctrine by Popery and its twin offshoot, Arminianism. (2) The multiplication of abuses in ecclesiastical government by the Bishops. (3) The subversion of church discipline by frequently enacted laws. (4) Instead of peace and unity, schism reigns. (5) Very many faithful ministers have been driven from their charges by the tyranny of the Bishops, and the benefit of appeal has been taken from them, since no National Synods have been held in all the years past. (6) So far are the ministers, teachers and Bishops from being subjected to any censure as manifestly guilty of the aforesaid corruptions, that on the contrary the highest dignities are heaped upon them as rewards for a well-done work, and by their example others are encouraged to commit similar acts, so that concerning the salvation of the Church it has almost been cried out that unless a remedy is brought at once through a free synod, it is lost. They set these things out at length in their treatise on the necessity of Synods, in which, answering the arguments usually raised to the contrary, they also defend the right of a magistrate who neglects the Church.

units.la: Ante statutum & præfinitum diem redit in Scotiam Marchio Hamiltonius Regis Deputatus; fœderatis articulos quosdam offert, quibus consentiendum erat, si Synodi Nationalis aut Parlamenti indictionem vellent, sed ab iis rejecti fuerunt, utpote, quod ab Episcopis inventos scirent, ut, aut Synodi convocationem impedirent, aut convocatam inutilem redderent, cujus libertati ubique per præli-mitationes officiebant: & quia metus fuit, ne fœderati tam frequentium procrastinationum pertæsi, non exspectato regis consensu (quem frustra hactenus sæpius expetiverant) Synodum Nationalem indicturi essent; itaque cum eis serio egit Deputatus ut convocatione Synodi supersederent, donec ipse ab aula rediret, ad quam denuo iter suscipiebat, ut Regi persuaderet Synodi liberæ indictionem, quod tandem concessum fuit à fœderatis, licet multi ad id ægrè adduci potuerint, propter mala quæ præsentem medicinam poscebant. Præfitutus[?] tamen fuit dies 22. Sept. ad quem, nisi revertetur Marchio, liberum esset fœderatis, rebus suis consulere.
units.tr: Before the appointed and fixed day, Marquis Hamilton, the King's Deputy, returned to Scotland. He offered the Covenanters certain articles, with which they were to agree if they wished a National Synod or Parliament to be called. These were rejected, since they knew them to have been devised by the Bishops, so that either the convocation of the Synod would be prevented or, once convened, it would be rendered useless; in every way the articles hampered its freedom by limitations. And since there was fear that the Covenanters, weary of such frequent delays, would call a National Synod without waiting for the King's consent (which they had so often and so far in vain sought), the Deputy pressed them earnestly to defer the convocation of the Synod until he himself returned from court, to which he was again setting out in order to persuade the King to permit the free calling of a Synod. This was at last granted by the Covenanters, although many could hardly be brought to it, on account of the evils which demanded a present remedy. However, the day of 22 September was fixed, after which, unless the Marquis had returned, it would be free for the Covenanters to look to their own affairs.

units.la: Sed ille singulari diligentia diem prævertit, & die præfinito mandatum regium per præconem publicè legendum curat, cujus hæc fuerunt capita. I. Regem abrogare omnia Senatus regii decreta, pro libris canonum & liturgiæ (nam libri ordinationis & homiliarum nondum prodierant) II. Abrogare tribunal celsæ commissionis. III. Liberam relinquere praxin quinque articulorum seu ceremoniarum · Perthensium. IV. Episcopos Synodali censuræ subditos esse. V. Nullum aliud Pastoribus initiandis jutamentum præstandum esse, quam quod legibus Parlamentariis inseritur. VI. Ac ut omnis scrupulus subditorum animis eximeretur, quasi Rex à reformatæ religionis professione alienus esset; mandare se, ut renovetur minor illa consessio, cui olim Anno 1580. à Rege Iacobo ejusque familia & regni civibus subscriptum fuit: cum speciali mandato ad Senatum regium, ut huic Senatores ipsi primum subscriberent, ac deputatos in singulis Provinciis constituerent, qui omnium regni incolarum subscriptiones promoturi sint. VII. Regem indicere Synodum Nationalem Glasguæ ad 21. Novembris, Anni hujus 1638. & Parlamentum, seu ordinum regni conventum habendum Edinburgi, ad diem 15 Maii anni 1639. Denique, ut firma Ecclesiarum & regni pax solide statuatur, oblivioni se tradere declarat omnia, quæ à subditis suis, in hac causa, secus quam oportuit, acta fuere.
units.tr: But he, with singular diligence, anticipated the day, and on the appointed day he had the royal mandate publicly read by a herald. Its heads were these: I. The King revokes all decrees of the royal Council concerning the books of canons and the liturgy (for the book of ordination and the book of homilies had not yet appeared). II. He abolishes the tribunal of the High Commission. III. He leaves the practice of the Five Articles, or the Perth ceremonies, free. IV. The Bishops are made subject to synodal censure. V. No oath other than that contained in the Parliamentary laws is to be taken by ministers being admitted. VI. And that every scruple might be removed from the minds of the subjects, as if the King were alien to the profession of the reformed religion, he orders that the lesser Confession be renewed, which was once subscribed in 1580 by King James, his family and the citizens of the kingdom; with a special mandate to the royal Council that the councillors themselves subscribe first, and that they appoint deputies in each province to promote the subscriptions of all the inhabitants of the kingdom. VII. The King will call a National Synod at Glasgow for 21 November of this year 1638, and a Parliament, or assembly of the estates of the kingdom, to be held at Edinburgh on 15 May 1639. Finally, so that firm peace of the Churches and kingdom may be solidly established, he declares that he consigns to oblivion all that his subjects have done in this cause otherwise than they ought.

units.la: Quam prægestierit fœderatis animus gratissimo hoc pacis nuncio, vix dicas; sed in ipsa verba penitius introspicientes videbant, omnes suas præcedentes actiones tacitè damnatas, justam libertatem Synodo Nationali præreptam, itaque ne arte & vafritie Episcoporum ( à quibus omnia hæc mandata regia diligenter revisa sciebant, qui panem oftentantes subdolè lapidem regerent, cujus impetu ex improviso colliderenter ) ne inquam horum artibus egregii ipsorum conatus frustrarentur, protestationem parant, non quod aliquid sinistri de candore piissimi Regis foverent, sed quia non satis iis fide erant, qui in florenti gratia apud Regem fuerunt, quorum violentis consiliis factum esse querut tur, quod hanc eandem clementiam a principio experti non essent: Protestationis vero, quæ publicè post auditum mandatum regium lecta fuit, hæc sunt capita. I. Post gratias Deo & Regi humiliter actas, mandatum hoc non esse sufficiens remedium malis præsentibus dicunt, quia omnes hosce motus processisse dicit a Panico metu, ne mutaretur religio aut leges, cum tamen metus fuerit justissimus, ejusque causa non imaginaria, sed realis mutatio tam religionis quam legum, per libros canonum, liturgiæ, &c. in quibus Papismi nucleus continetur.
units.tr: One can hardly say how eagerly the Covenanters welcomed this most welcome news of peace. Yet on looking more closely into the words themselves, they saw that all their previous actions were tacitly condemned, and the just liberty of the National Synod was taken away. So, lest the cunning and craft of the bishops (who, they knew, had carefully reviewed all these royal commands, and who, offering bread, slyly threw a stone, by whose blow they might be struck unexpectedly) should frustrate their earnest efforts, they prepared a protestation. They did not do this because they harboured any suspicion about the sincerity of the most pious King, but because they had no great trust in those who stood high in the King's favour, and whose violent counsels, they complained, were the reason that they had never before experienced such clemency. The heads of the protestation, which was read publicly after the royal command had been heard, are these. I. After thanks humbly rendered to God and the King, they say that this command is not a sufficient remedy for the present evils, because all these disturbances arose from a panic fear that religion or the laws would be changed; yet the fear was most just, and its cause was not imaginary but real: a change both of religion and of the laws, through the books of canons, the liturgy, and so on, in which the kernel of Popery is contained.

units.la: II. Quia mandatum hoc vetat tantum praxin illorum librorum, cum tamen præcedentibus mandatis regiis mensibus Februario & Iunio anni 1638. & aliis 1637. singulari commendatione iidem ornentur, tanquam aptissima media ad veram religionem promovendam, & Papatum demoliendum, quæ mandata rescindi necesse est, non solum quatenus praxin imperant, verum etiam quatenus tam honorifico elogio libros illos ornant, alioquin non defuturos prurientes novatores, qui continuas Ec-clesiæ turbas creaturi sunt. III. Quædam esse in mandato hoc, quibus justa libertas futuræ Synodi adimitur, dum videlicet Perthensium ceremoniarum indifferentia extra quæstionem supponitur ac hierarchiæ Episcopalis corruptiones approbantur; quasi liceret Episcopis ab Ecclesiis non deputatis suffragium in Synodo ferre, iisdemque quatenus Episcopis, suffragium in supremo ordinum conventu, Ecclesiis inconsultis, compereret; quæ cum inter præcipua gravamina sint, de quibus querantur fœderati, abundè patere dicunt, mandato hoc, tanquam plenè satisfactorio, se non posse acquiescere; præfertim, cum ad Synodum Nationalem proprie pertineat de his sententiam ferre, quæ Ecclesiis conducibilia sunt, quæ noxia. IV. Quia mandatum hoc regium imperat omnibus subditis, ut confessioni a Iacobo Rege obsignatæ annis 1580 & 1590. subscribant, atque ut omnes jure jurando se obligent ad doctrinam & disciplinam præsentem tuendam.
units.tr: II. Because this command forbids only the practice of those books, whereas by the earlier royal commands of February and June 1638, and by others of 1637, the same books are adorned with singular commendation as most fitting means for advancing true religion and demolishing Popery. Those commands must be rescinded, not only in so far as they enjoin the practice, but also in so far as they adorn those books with such honourable praise; otherwise there would not be lacking itching innovators who would stir up continual troubles in the Church. III. There are in this command certain provisions by which the just liberty of the future Synod is taken away, namely in that the indifference of the Perth ceremonies is put beyond question and the corruptions of the episcopal hierarchy are approved; as if it were lawful for bishops to cast a vote in the Synod on behalf of churches that had not deputed them, and as if the same men, as bishops, could in the supreme assembly of the estates obtain a vote without the churches being consulted. Since these are among the chief grievances about which the Covenanters complain, they say it is abundantly clear that they cannot acquiesce in this command as if it were fully satisfactory; especially since it belongs properly to the National Synod to pass judgment on those matters which are helpful or harmful to the churches. IV. Because this royal command orders all subjects to subscribe the confession sealed by King James in 1580 and 1590, and to bind themselves by oath to defend the present doctrine and discipline.

units.la: Cui fœderi & confessioni a Rege nunc imperatæ, se non posse bona conscientia subscribere declarant;
units.tr: To this covenant and confession, now imposed by the King, they declare that they cannot in good conscience subscribe.

units.la: I. Quia hoc subtili stratagemate, aliis frustra tentatis, obliterabitur omnis memoria confessionis, subscriptione & juramento hactenus obsignatæ, mense Februario, anni hujus 1638, fœdusque illud quod æternum statuebant, vix erit paucorum mensium.
units.tr: I. Because by this subtle stratagem, after other attempts have failed, all memory will be erased of the confession, the subscription and the oath sealed hitherto in February of this year 1638; and that covenant, which they had established as eternal, will scarcely last a few months.

units.la: II. Quia si fœdus illud, in cujus verba jurandum esse omnibus rex imperat, idem sit cum fœdere, in quod hactenus juratum est, tunc juramenta non necessaria erunt multiplicanda, & nomen Dei in vanum & frustra assumetur.
units.tr: II. Because if that covenant, to whose words the King commands everyone to swear, is the same as the covenant hitherto sworn to, then oaths would have to be multiplied needlessly, and the name of God would be taken in vain and to no purpose.

units.la: III. Quia qui fœderi regio nunc subscribunt, tacitè fatentur, priorem subscriptionem fuisse illegitimam, quia a Rege non imperata; & juramentum, quo tum obsignabatur, fuisse temerarium; cujus fœderatos jam pœnitebit.
units.tr: III. Because those who now subscribe to the royal covenant tacitly confess that the earlier subscription was illegitimate, since it had not been commanded by the King, and that the oath by which it was then sealed was rash; the Covenanters will soon repent of this.

units.la: IV. Quia manifesta est differentia, inter fœdus hoc a Rege imperatum, & fœdus illud, cui sponte collectivum quasi regni & Ecclesiæ corpus hactenus subscripsit; nam in fœdere regio nulla mentio applicationis ad præsentes errores, quibus Ecclesiarum pax turbata est; nec reformationis vitæ & morum; cum tamen in fœdere obsignato mense Februario utriusque aperta mentio facta sit; prioris præsertim, propter illos errores, quibus libri canonum & liturgiæ scatebant; quos tamen cum confessione à Rege imperata, confirmare posse putant librorum illorum authores, qui frequenter declararunt, articulos Perthenses, Episcoporum hierarchiam, & alias omnes novitates obtrusas aut obtrudendas, non repugnare confessioni, quam anno 1580 obsignaverat Rex.
units.tr: IV. Because there is a manifest difference between this covenant commanded by the King and that covenant to which the body, as it were collective, of the kingdom and the Church has hitherto subscribed of its own accord. For in the royal covenant there is no mention of its application to the present errors by which the peace of the churches has been disturbed, nor of reformation of life and morals; whereas in the covenant sealed in February there was an explicit mention of both, especially of the former, on account of those errors with which the books of canons and the liturgy were riddled. Yet the authors of those books, who have often declared that the Perth articles, the episcopal hierarchy, and all the other novelties thrust upon them or to be thrust upon them do not contradict the confession which the King had sealed in 1580, think that they can confirm these with the confession commanded by the King.

units.la: At fœderati contradicunt, & omnes illas novitates virtualiter tum abjuratas clamant; cujus probationem ad Synodum Nationalem referunt. Adde quod in foedere, in cujus verba rex adigit, desint quaedam quae in foedere anni 1580 & 1590. clarè extant, videlicet, Pontificios illos esse, à quibus religioni & personae regiae immineret periculum, (& merito, nam juxta formalia verba statuti 47. Sancti in parlamento anni 1572. Quo vero religionis hostes, declarantur esse regis & regiae authoritatis hostes.) Quorum loco generales quasdam phrases, data opera, insertas dicunt, quas non dubium est, quin captatis occasionibus, detorturi sint adversarii in foederatos, quos hactenus (licet immeritissimè) pro iis habeant, à quibus plus periculi religioni & authoritati regiae immineat, quam ab ipsis Pontificiis, quia scilicet ad paucorum placitum, qui Regis gratia abutuntur, à recepta religionis reformatae puritate se divelli non patiuntur. V. Qui foederi huic à Rege imperato cum novis illis additamentis subscribunt, tenentur subscribere, foedusque illud tueri secundum mentem & expositionem Regis in foedus adigentis; nam qui jurat, tenetur jurare secundum sensum & opinionem ejus, qui juramentum exigit; praesertim cum constet, quis sit in juramentum adigentis sensus: Atque constat, Regis opinionem esse, quicquid in libris canonum, liturgiae, ordinationis obtrudiuur[?], non repugnare confessioni fidei: Quod si foederati facturi sint, horrendi perjurii reatu manifesto se involvent; utpote quod novitates illas abjurarint, & declararint, esse impios ritus in Ecclesiam introductos ab Antichristo ejusque praecursoribus, sine ullo divini verbi mandato, & caetera. Plura hujus notae in scripto satis prolixo, & typis excuso, congesserunt; quae omnia publicè perlecta fuerunt 22 Septembr. anni 1638 in frequentissima omnium ordinum corona, ac protestationis exemplar feciali obtulerunt.
units.tr: But the Covenanters contest this, and cry out that all those novelties were then virtually abjured; they refer the proof of this to the National Synod. Add to this that in the covenant to whose words the King binds them, certain things are lacking which clearly stand in the covenants of 1580 and 1590, namely that those are Papists from whom danger threatens to religion and to the person of the King (and rightly so, for according to the formal words of the statute of St. Sancti in the parliament of 1572, the enemies of religion are declared to be the enemies of the King and of royal authority). In place of these, they say, certain general phrases have been deliberately inserted, which without doubt the adversaries will, on any occasion they seize, twist against the Covenanters, whom they hitherto (though most undeservedly) regard as those from whom more danger threatens to religion and royal authority than from the Papists themselves. This is because, at the pleasure of a few who abuse the King's favour, they do not allow themselves to be torn away from the purity of the reformed religion that has been received. V. Those who subscribe to this covenant commanded by the King, with those new additions, are bound to subscribe and to maintain that covenant according to the mind and interpretation of the King who imposes it. For he who swears is bound to swear according to the sense and opinion of him who demands the oath, especially since it is clear what the sense of the one imposing the oath is. And it is clear that the King's opinion is that whatever is thrust upon us in the books of canons, the liturgy, and the ordinances does not contradict the confession of faith. But if the Covenanters were to do this, they would manifestly involve themselves in the guilt of horrible perjury, since they have abjured those novelties and declared that the impious rites introduced into the Church by Antichrist and his forerunners, without any warrant of the divine Word, and so on. They have set forth many points of this kind in a fairly lengthy writing, which was printed; all of these were read publicly on 22 September 1638, in the very crowded assembly of all the estates, and they gave a copy of the protestation to the herald.

units.la: Eodem die Senatus regius confessioni & fœderi, per Regem imperato subscribit, hisce verbis; (quæ quia gravissimis concertationibus ansam præbuisse feruntur, diligenter notanda sunt.) Senatus regius approbat, subscribit, ac jurat in confessionem fidei supra scriptam, secundum tenorem ejusdem, cum primitus prodierat 5 Martii 1580, ac prout tunc publicè professio ejus fiebat in regno hoc, &c. ac statuit, ut omnes subditi Confessioni huic subscribant, addita ubique hac clausula, secundum tenorem & receptam publicam professionem, quæ in regno Scotiæ vigebat Anno 1580. unde orta fuit quæstio difficilis: quænam anno illo fuisset publica professio, præsertim de Episcopatu; nam extra controversiam apud omnes erat, nullam tum mentionem fuisse in Ecclesia Scotica articulorum Perthensium, aut aliarum istarum novitatum obtrufarum in libris Canonum, Liturgiæ &c. quas subscriptione hac ejectas esse de Ecclesia plurimi putant; licet in abjuratione specialiter non designentur. At Hierarchiæ Episcopalis fautores aliter de Episcopatu statuendum censebant; ejus tamen ruinam veriti omni studio allaborarunt, ut scriptum quoddam obsignarent Senatores regii; quo semet obligarent, ad tuendum Episcoporum in Ecclesia Scoticana regimen: neque Episcopatum Confessionis & fœderis subscriptione eliminari de Ecclesia: quin contra magis eadem stabiliri. Sed conatus ille irritus fuit; quare, propter diversitatem sententiarum nihil ea de re tum in Senatu regio statutum.
units.tr: On the same day the royal Senate subscribed to the confession and covenant commanded by the King, in these words (which, because they are said to have given occasion for the most serious disputes, must be carefully noted). The royal Senate approves, subscribes to, and swears to the confession of faith written above, according to its tenor, as it was first published on 5 March 1580, and as its profession was then publicly made in this kingdom, etc.; and it decrees that all subjects shall subscribe to this Confession, with this clause added everywhere, according to the tenor and the received public profession which prevailed in the kingdom of Scotland in the year 1580. From this arose a difficult question: what the public profession was in that year, especially concerning episcopacy. For it was beyond controversy among all that at that time there was no mention in the Scottish Church of the Perth articles, or of those other novelties thrust upon it in the books of canons, the liturgy, and so on, which many think were cast out of the Church by this subscription, although they are not specifically named in the abjuration. But the supporters of the episcopal hierarchy judged otherwise about episcopacy; nevertheless, fearing its ruin, they laboured with every effort that the royal senators should seal a certain writing by which they would bind themselves to defend the government of bishops in the Scottish Church, and that episcopacy should not be eliminated from the Church by the subscription to the Confession and covenant, but rather that it should be the more firmly established by them. But that attempt was in vain; therefore, because of the diversity of opinions, nothing was decided in the royal Senate on that matter at that time.

units.la: Præsbyteria seu Classes ad synodum Glasguæ habendam justo numero deputant, videlicet ex singulis tres pastores cum unico seniore; mandata, quibus instruendi erant, concipiunt, ac de Ecclesiarum gravaminibus ad synodum deferendis sedulo deliberant; In jus ubique vocant pastores, Papatus &c
units.tr: The presbyteries, or classes, appoint for the synod at Glasgow the due number of members: three ministers from each, with one elder. They draw up the instructions with which these members were to be equipped and deliberate carefully about the grievances of the churches to be brought before the synod. Everywhere they summon the ministers to judgment for publicly spreading Arminian heterodoxies, for Popery, and so on.

units.la: Arminianismi heterodoxias publicè spargentes, aut qui flagitiosis moribus actionibusque improbis Ecclesiæ offendiculo fuerunt, ut si qui forte presbyteriorum judiciis se gravatos exististimarent, ad synodum nationalem provocarent: In quibusdam presbyteriis acres obortæ fuerant concertationes, quod seniores post quadraginta plus minus annorum continuam intermissionem suffragium in presbyteriis seu Classibus sibi vendicarent, durissimum hoc quibusdam visum ut pari fere cum pastoribus numero interessent, quo non solum obrutum iri pastores, verumetiam omnia seniorum illorum suffragiis circumagenda fore questi sunt, præsertim cum seniores ut plurimum sint viri nobiles magnæ authoritatis: Qui seniorum jus propugnabant, respondebant; Secundum primitivam ecclesiæ Scoticæ disciplinam, senioribus hisce jus hoc tributum esse, in eum finem loca quædam ex libro secundo de disciplina expromunt satis diserta; Presbyteria etiam juxta illius libri præscriptum constituta, sanciri expressa lege parlamentaria Iacobi 6. parlam. 12. anno 1592. Afferebant, Ante luxatam episcopaturientium artibus ecclesiæ hanc disciplinam, Classibus semper interfuisse seniores, neque hoc purioribus illis temporibus à quolibet in controversiam unquam vocatum fuisse; paucorum itaque annorum intermissionem non debere nec posse præscribere politiæ communibus omnium suffragiis receptæ ac legibus sancitæ, præsertim cum nullo canone ecclesiastico, nulla lege politica hactenus relicta sit: neque magis verendum né sic obruantur pastorum suffragia in presbyteriis, quam in singularum ecclesiarum sessionibus seu consistoriis, quibus quatuor aut sex ut plurimum seniores pro unico pastore intersint: Absurdum esse quod de seniorum qualitate objicitur, quasi vero exclusis nobilibus prudentia & morum nun[?] elegantia supra alios conspicuis, ecclesiarum gubernationi tenuioris fortis homines admovendi essent: neque minuendum esse pastoribus ne nobiles illi[?] authoritate sua, omnia pro arbitrio circumagant, cum conventibus semper praesint pastores, ac in dicendis sententiis praeant.
units.tr: Or for those whose wicked morals and shameless conduct were a stumbling block to the Church. If any of them thought they were wronged by the judgments of the presbyteries, they could appeal to the national synod. In some presbyteries sharp disputes had arisen, because the elders, after an interval of about forty years, claimed for themselves the right to vote in the presbyteries or classes. To some this seemed too harsh: that they should sit in nearly equal numbers with the ministers, so that the ministers would be overwhelmed and everything would be swung round by the votes of the elders. They complained of this especially because the elders were for the most part noblemen of great authority. Those who defended the elders' right replied that, according to the primitive discipline of the Scottish Church, this right belonged to these elders. To prove this they cited several passages, quite clear ones, from the second book of the Discipline. They also pointed out that the presbyteries were set up according to the provisions of that book and were given sanction by an express act of parliament, the 6th Parliament of James, c. 12, in the year 1592. They argued that before this discipline was overthrown by the intrigues of those who aspired to bishoprics, the elders had always sat in the classes, and that in those purer times no one had ever questioned this. A lapse of a few years therefore could not and should not cancel a polity received by the common votes of all and confirmed by law, especially since no ecclesiastical canon or political law had hitherto repealed it. Nor was there more reason to fear that the votes of the ministers would be overwhelmed in the presbyteries than in the sessions or consistories of the individual churches, where four or six elders usually sit for each minister. It was absurd, they said, to object to the character of the elders, as if, with noblemen excluded, men of lesser rank should be brought in to govern the churches, though those noblemen were conspicuous above others for prudence and elegance of manners. Nor should the ministers be diminished, lest those noblemen by their authority turn everything at their own pleasure, since the ministers always preside at the meetings and lead the voting.

units.la: Proxima cura fuit de citandis Episcopis, ut in synodo rationem redderent eorum quae ipsis objicienda essent. Regis quidem edicto mandabatur Archiepiscopis & Episcopis ut synodo interessent, quasi iis ex officio jus suffragii competeret; eodemque edicto ipsorum personae synodo subjiciebantur; Verum foederatis quam certissimum fuit, jus illud suffragii Episcopis nulla ratione deberi; Generalem illam in edicto regio declarationem, qua omnes subditi parlamenti & synodi judicio subjiciebantur, ad plenam citationem non sufficere, & facile etiam eludi posse: Quare cum regis deputato serio[?] & submisse agunt foederati, ut literis citatoriis Episcopos tanquam reos sigillatim adesse juberet; Quod cum ille constanter renuisset, ne defectu legitimae citationis synodi judicium & censuram subterfugerent episcopi, ad insolitum citandi modum recurrere coguntur foederati: Classibus videl: se sistunt, graves contra Dicecesos[?] illius Episcopum, & alios omnes quotquot sint in regno Scotiae, deponunt querelas, quod intra limites a synodo praescriptos in potestatis ecclesiasticae exercitio se non continuerint; sed in omnibus se gesserint tanquam ecclesiae dominos & principes, ac intoleranda tyrannide ecclesiarum jura invaserint; (atque hic speciatim longum catalogum eorundem subjiciunt) quod Arminianorum heterodoxias, & plurima Pontificiorum damnata dogmata aut publice defenderint, aut alios noxias ejusmodi heterodoxias spargentes legitimis censuris non solum non coercuerint, verumetiam unice foverint; accusantur etiam ebrietatis, perjurii, ordinariae profanationis nominis divini & diei Dominicae, fcortationis, simoniae, sacrilegii, & cæt: & quia in unam factionem simul conspirasse omnes Episcopos quam certissimum fœderatis fuit, ideo consultissimum iis videbatur, omnes συνάψιν[?] iisdem literis citatoriis includere, addita tamen clausula; Respective, ne queri possent Episcopi, singulos omnium criminum infamia gravari. Classis seu presbyterium perlectis & perpensis libellis illis supplicibus contra Episcopos; quia judicavit rem esse majoris momenti quam quæ peragi posset ab alio quovis ecclesiastico conventu, quam synodo nationali, causæ hujus cognitionem ad synodum nationalem refert; &cum ignoraret, quonam profugissent Episcopi, decrevit eosdem libellos supplices sibi oblatos, die dominico de pulpito prælegendos, & hac prælectione publica citari Episcopos declarat, ut synodo nationali se sistant ad diluendum objecta crimina, aut subeundam synodi censuram: Qui inveniri potuerant in Scotia Episcopi (nam multi in Angliam se subduxerant) literarum harum exemplar traditur, qui facile præsagire potuerunt, quam infaustum hoc esset insignis alicujus calamitatis omen, & quam male sibi consuluissent; si deputato regio authores fuerunt illius consilii, ne Episcopis ordinaria citatione diem diceret, quæ constans fuit multorum opinio.
units.tr: The next concern was to summon the bishops, so that they might give account in the synod of the things that were to be brought against them. By the king's edict, the archbishops and bishops were indeed ordered to attend the synod, as if they had a right to vote by virtue of their office. By the same edict their persons were made subject to the synod. But the Covenanters were quite certain that this right of voting was in no way due to the bishops. They held that the general declaration in the royal edict, by which all subjects were made subject to the judgment of parliament and the synod, was not sufficient for a full summons and could easily be evaded. So the Covenanters, with the royal deputy, pressed him earnestly and humbly to order by letters of summons that the bishops be individually cited to appear as accused persons. When he steadfastly refused, lest the bishops escape the judgment and censure of the synod through the lack of a lawful summons, the Covenanters were forced to resort to an unusual method of citation. Namely, they presented themselves to the classes and laid serious complaints against the bishop of the diocese, and against all others, however many there were in the kingdom of Scotland, that they had not kept within the limits prescribed by the synod in the exercise of ecclesiastical power. Instead, in everything they had acted as lords and princes of the churches, and with intolerable tyranny had usurped the rights of the churches. (Here they set out at length a long catalogue of particulars.) They had either publicly defended the Arminian heterodoxies and many condemned dogmas of the Papists, or, though they spread such harmful heterodoxies, had not only failed to restrain them by lawful censures but had actually cherished them. They were also accused of drunkenness, perjury, the habitual profanation of the name of God and of the Lord's Day, fornication, simony, sacrilege, and so on. And since the Covenanters were quite certain that all the bishops had conspired together in one faction, it seemed most prudent to them to include all of them [συνάψιν] in the same letters of summons, but with the added clause "respectively", so that the bishops could not complain that each one was burdened with the infamy of all the crimes. The class or presbytery, after reading and weighing those supplicatory libels against the bishops, judged the matter to be of greater importance than could be dealt with by any other ecclesiastical assembly than the national synod. So it referred the cognizance of this cause to the national synod. And since it did not know where the bishops had fled, it decreed that these supplicatory libels, presented to it, be read publicly from the pulpit on the Lord's Day, and declared that by this public reading the bishops were cited to present themselves to the national synod to refute the charges, or to submit to the synod's censure. Copies of these letters were delivered to whichever bishops could be found in Scotland (for many had withdrawn into England). They could easily foresee how ominous this was, a sure sign of some great calamity, and how badly they had advised themselves, if (as was the common opinion of many) the king's deputy was the author of that plan, so that he would not give the bishops a regular summons.

units.la: Veruntamen ut gravem hunc ictum declinarent, cui ferendo impares se noverant, in omnes formas se vertunt, ac toties icti in prædecessoribus suis, aciem liberæ nationalis synodi evitare laborabant, veluti infames scopulos, ubi exuvias de majorum suorum naufragio natantes cernebant; ideoque nihil reliqui ad summam diligentiam faciunt, ne præfinito tempore coiret synodus; cum fautoribus & af-
units.tr: Nevertheless, to ward off this heavy blow, which they knew they were unequal to bearing, they turned themselves in every direction. Often struck in the persons of their predecessors, they tried to avoid the battle line of a free national synod, as they would avoid infamous rocks, where they saw the wreckage of their ancestors floating.
