The second difference, he said, arises from this: the Dutch ministers sent to that synod, although in private conversations, public sermons and even in published books they had declared that the opinions of the Remonstrants did not please them, never went so far as to condemn those opinions by any judicial sentence. Much less did they bind themselves by sacraments and other holy agreements to one side of the controversy, or conspire against the heads of the party holding the contrary opinion, as the bishops complain was done by the delegates to this synod. To this the president replied. All the controversies between the Remonstrants and the Contraremonstrants, especially if they do not go beyond the limits of the five articles, are not, and are not to be considered, about fundamental doctrines. The Remonstrants had indeed erred gravely, but it has not yet been persuaded to us that every heterodoxy is heresy. God forbid that we should deny that discipline is called changeable in the article of the Confession cited; but that statement must be understood of accidental circumstances, about which the Word of God has laid down nothing. For he showed that the authors of that Confession did not put the essentials of discipline (that is, what the Apostles, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, prescribed to the churches for their instruction) among things changeable. Indeed, in article 19 of the same Confession, discipline formed to the exact rule of the Word of God is called, after the Word and the sacraments, the third mark of the true visible Church. From this it follows that, although discipline is not simply [ἀπλῶς] necessary to the being of the Church, so that any church which does not have discipline in all points conformable to the Word of God is not to be regarded as the true Church of Christ (far be such a harsh judgment from us, which must be left to the ancient Donatists, the modern Anabaptists, and their genuine offshoots today), nevertheless, I say, although it is not simply necessary to the being of the Church, it is necessary to the integrity and perfection of the visible Church. It is necessary also for judging the Church from its effects, at least a posteriori, and finally it is the ordinary means and help without which the salvation of the Church cannot be obtained so easily. When Robert Montgomery, pseudo-archbishop of Glasgow, denied this necessity in the year 1528 and laid down that discipline was changeable, he paid heavy penalties to the Scottish Church on that account. If these considerations are not enough to demonstrate the immutability of those things which are essential to discipline, let at least this be remembered, which is recorded in the acts of the National Synod for the year 1596. The question was then asked whether it was lawful for the prince or the ministers to raise doubts about the external articles of discipline, on which nothing was expressly stated in Holy Scripture either affirmatively or negatively. The synod answered that it is lawful for the prince, either in person or through his envoys, to propose what he doubts, or what he judges should be reformed in the particular matter of external order. It is equally lawful for anyone to do this, provided it is done with modest study, decently, in the proper place and time, and with the intention of building up and not of tearing down. The synod further added that certain matters must be placed beyond the chance of doubt and controversy, when it went on to say these words: "Since the substance of external ecclesiastical administration is delivered most fully in the Scriptures." By this clause the synod, while judging the accidentals to be changeable according to the variety of circumstances, declares in what sense that article of the Confession is to be understood: there are nonetheless certain immovable things in discipline. And the bishops themselves do not deny that the dispute between the bishops and the Churches is about these matters and not about those, since they hold that government of the Church by bishops is necessary and instituted by Christ, and that his commands bind everyone everywhere and always. Therefore anyone can easily infer that the first supposed difference between the Dutch bishops and the Remonstrants is no difference at all. Another, David Dogelisius, minister of Cupar in Fife, added this: the bishops are being summoned to judgment because they privately cherish, and publicly promote, very many heterodoxies of the Papists and errors of the Remonstrants (to put it very mildly). Since he himself acknowledges these to be fundamental, at least on that ground the case of the bishops is like that of the Remonstrants, since the crime which stains them is the same. But grant (he said) that the question concerns only the heads of discipline. It would certainly be unjust to deprive the ministers deputed to this synod of the right to give their opinion in the synod on those matters about which, before the synod was convened, they had declared their judgment plainly and openly. Let the practice of the Church against the schismatics Novatus and Donatus be an example, whose heterodoxies and errors in ecclesiastical discipline were condemned in synod by those who, before the synods were held, had manfully opposed them both privately and publicly. Add to this that if only neutral persons can be judges here, and there is no minister in the Scottish Church who has not shown himself to lean to one side or the other of the controversy, then where, I ask, are judges of these controversies to be sought? If you say that foreign and overseas churches should be consulted, this opinion will suffer the same inconvenience and it will be necessary to stumble on the same stone. Besides, in that way hardly any churches would be fit to settle disputes arising among themselves. As to the second difference, the president answered briefly. There was certainly no need for great effort to refute long arguments of this kind, since at first sight it is plain to anyone weighing the comparison fairly that in this cause the bishops are as like the Remonstrants as milk is like milk. As for what the delegates bound themselves to, by sacraments, against the bishops, this will be answered at length in the synod's reply to the bishops' protest. As to the bishops' second exception, whether the elders have a definitive right of voting in synods, there was no debate. The president, to cut off all occasion for foolish quibbles, stated the point of the controversy thus: "Whether the elders, by the statutes of the Church of Scotland, have a right of voting." And so an end was put to this controversy, since no one came forward to attack the right of the elders.

units.la: Ad ipsam protestationem tandem ventum est; Quandoquidem (inquit præses) Synodi judicium declinent Episcopi, consultum esset, omnium sententias perrogari; an synodus hæc, non obstante protestatione, legitimus judex censenda sit? nam ad nullum alium judicem res hæc deferri poterit, cum suprema potestas determinandi controversias ecclesiasticas in qualibet ecclesia sit penes synodum nationalem: Tum deputatus regius occasionem hanc oblatam nactus, exequendi postrema regis mandata, (ex aula per Episcopum Roffensem, multorum opinione, delata) gravi & ornata oratione Synodum affatur: Diutius (inquit): fortasse apud vos hæfiffem, nisi importuna quæstionis hujus determinatione vel invitum discedere cogeretis; Etenim quantum video, statutum vobis videtur synodum hanc legitimam declarare; nec jure Episcopos ejus judicium declinasse, quod probare neutiquam possum, si ullam officii in Deum aut in Regem rationem habuero. Quare quanto gaudio perfruebatur animus, cum coactam synodum hanc cernerem, in qua re ipsa præstiturus essem quicquid regis nomine subditis hujus regni pollicitus sum, contra multorum sententiam, quibus suggestum fuit regem hæc nunquam serio intendisse; tanto majori* anxietatis æstu nunc crucior, cum spem omnem deploratam conspiciam, implicitum hoc negotium per synodum hanc feliciter expediendi. Synodum liberam toties à vobis efflagitatam, tandem adepti, ita tamen circumscripsistis ut libertatis vix umbra aliqua appareat. Interim ut omnibus constet, quam religiose rex promissa factis exprimere statuerint, charta hæc signata mea manu vel me tacente fatebitur; quam, in constantem pietatis & clementiæ regiæ memoriam publicis synodi registris inferi jubeo, verum cum hac protestatione, facto hoc minime a me approbari, quæ hactenus statuta sunt, aut quæ posthac statuenda erunt in hac synodo. Chartam illam publice à Scriba synodi prælectam, eadem continere compertum fuit quæ edicto regio ad mensem Septembris concessa fuerunt, quæ inde petenda sunt. Præses synodi nomine, serenissimo regi ab omnibus merito gratias immensas agendas profitebatur ob singularia hæc in Ecclesiam genitricem beneficia, fœlicia & prospera regiæ familiæ vovebat: tandem ad authoritatem summi magistratus delapsus, quousque se in rebus ecclesiasticis extenderet, demonstrabat; qua oratione Deputato regio & cæteris regni senatoribus ita satisfecit, ut omnibus tum constaret, meras esse calumnias quæ de pastoribus ecclesiarum, & reliquis libertatis vindicibus spargebantur, quasi cum Pontificiis magistratum supremum omni alio circa religionem officio exuerent, quam ut ecclesiasticorum statuta executioni mandaret: Extrema hic certe, si alibi unquam, ut præcipitia periculosissima cavenda sunt, in quæ non solum ii incurrunt, qui se libertatis Ecclesiasticæ patronos venditant, verum etiam qui præjudiciis excæcati causam suam agunt, aut aliis adulantur scenæ servientes, quasi illi soli politicæ potestatis esse(?) strenui vindices, jurisque regum acerrimi defensores, qui magistratuum supremorum arbitrio non solum negotia civilia, (quod ab omnibus concessum est) verum & ecclesiastica omnia, etiam extra synodum per se aut pauculos à se solis delectos, simpliciter definienda esse statuunt: ignari se Christo unico Ecclesiæ Monarchæ, principatus jus αὐτο-κεφαλ[illegible, ~4 letters], rerum spiritualium intuitu, eripere; quod non sine immani sacrilegio invaserant Pontifices Romani, eoque ad Antichristianæ tyrannidis ἀκμὴν[?] nihil sibi deesse ostenderunt, susque deque etiam habentes quantam perdendis ecclesiis, si quando impios & pseudochristianos principes nactæ fuerint, fenestram aperiant patentissimam: Sic Cæsari danda quæ Cæsaris sunt, ut Deo interim jus suum illibatum constet.
units.tr: At last they came to the protest itself. Since (said the moderator) the bishops decline the judgment of the Synod, it would be advisable to ask everyone's opinion: whether this Synod, notwithstanding the protest, is to be regarded as a lawful judge. For this matter cannot be referred to any other judge, since the supreme power of determining ecclesiastical controversies in any church rests with the national Synod. Then the royal commissioner, seizing the opportunity offered to him, and carrying out the king's final instructions (which, as many believed, had been brought from the court through the Bishop of Ross), addressed the Synod in a grave and elaborate speech: "I would have stayed with you longer (he said), perhaps, had not the unwelcome determination of this question compelled me to leave against my will. For, as far as I can see, it seems to be your decision to declare this Synod lawful, and I cannot possibly prove that the bishops were wrong to decline its judgment, if I have any regard for my duty to God or to the King. So, when I saw this Synod assembled, in which I was to fulfil in fact whatever I had promised in the king's name to the subjects of this kingdom, my spirit was filled with joy, although many had suggested that the king never seriously intended these things. Now I am tormented by a far greater storm of anxiety, since I see every hope abandoned of settling this tangled business happily through this Synod. You have at last obtained the free Synod you have so often demanded, but you have so hedged it about that scarcely a shadow of freedom appears. Meanwhile, so that everyone may know how faithfully the king has resolved to match his promises with deeds, this charter, signed with my hand, will bear witness, even if I say nothing. I order it to be entered in the public registers of the Synod, in lasting memory of the king's piety and clemency. But let it be on this condition, that by this protest it is in no way approved by me, whatever has been enacted so far, or whatever shall be enacted hereafter in this Synod."* The charter was then read publicly by the clerk of the Synod, and it was found to contain the same things that had been granted by the royal edict of September, and which are to be sought from there. The moderator, speaking on behalf of the Synod, professed that immense thanks were rightly due from all to the most serene king for these singular benefits to the mother Church, and he prayed for happiness and prosperity for the royal family. Finally, passing to the authority of the supreme magistrate, he showed how far it extended in ecclesiastical affairs. With this speech he so satisfied the royal commissioner and the other senators of the kingdom that it became clear to all that the calumnies spread about the ministers of the churches and the other defenders of liberty were mere lies, as if they, together with the Papists, would strip the supreme magistrate of every duty concerning religion except that of executing the decisions of the churchmen. Here, if anywhere, extremes must certainly be avoided as most dangerous precipices. Into these fall not only those who pose as champions of ecclesiastical liberty, but also those who, blinded by prejudice, pursue their own cause, or flatter others, serving the stage, as if they alone were the vigorous defenders of political power and the most fierce champions of the rights of kings. These men maintain that not only civil business (which is granted by all) but also all ecclesiastical matters, even outside the Synod, are to be settled simply by the will of the supreme magistrate, or by a few men chosen by him alone. They are ignorant that they are snatching from Christ, the sole Monarch of the Church, the right of sovereignty [αὐτοκεφαλ…] in spiritual matters, which the Roman Pontiffs invaded not without monstrous sacrilege, and by which they showed that nothing was lacking to the very summit [ἀκμὴν?] of Antichristian tyranny. Caring nothing for it, they open the widest door for the destruction of the churches whenever they have found impious and pseudo-Christian princes. Thus let to Caesar what is Caesar's, so that meanwhile God's right may remain unimpaired.

units.la: Serio etiam urgebat præses, ut ad controversiæ hujus definitionem, An Synodus hæc legitima & in membris suis rite constituta esset? in suffragia irent Synodici. Respondit Deputatus regius, ut supra; Et quandoquidem libertati synodi usque adeo præjudicatum (inquit) sit, declarat integrum sibi non esse cœtui huic diutius adesse; ac dicta hæc, quam illi tristia essent, manantes de genis lachrymæ, & effusi gemitus fidem faciebant; inter alias rationes quibus synodi libertati præjudicatum dicebat, hæ duæ erant præcipuæ. 1. Quia deputatorum ad synodum electio libera non fuit, sed circumscripta à fœderatis (quos Edenburgi tribunal novum & inauditum erexisse dicebat,) in cujus fidem duo protulit scripta a fœderatis illis, seu saltem fœderatorum antesignanis, ad eos quos causæ suæ fautores & zelotas noverant, missa, alterum ad pastores, alterum ad nobiles seniores; quibus (inquit) mandant ut illi soli ad Synodum delegentur, qui fœderi impense favent; nec ut consanguinitatis aut affinitatis ulla hic habeatur ratio; utque illud commodè fiat, consultum esset, priusquam convocetur presbyterium ad deputatos eligendos, ut cum intimis & fidis consilia communicent, eorumque quos in presbyterio deputatos delegari cupiunt, nomina designent, ut minori obstaculo iidem illi postea designentur communibus & publicis suffragiis: ut deputati sic electi Edenburgum conveniant ante aperturam synodi; quo eorum numerus quibus causa hæc cordi est, innotescat, ne nostra ignavia hostibus & vicinis ludibrio simus: Moneantur etiam pastores, ut quam diligentissime se præparent ad disputandas quæstiones: De potestate supremi magistratus in ecclesiasticis, præsertim in convocandis Conciliis, de senioribus, de Episcopatu, de juramento, de liturgia & corruptelis ejusdem: Summa denique nunc omnibus danda est opera, omniqué animi contentione adnitendum, ne oblata opportunitas libertatem tam politicam quam Ecclesiasticam recuperandi, nostra negligentia elabatur: An non scripta hæc satis monstrant à vobis (inquit deputatus regius) omnem libertatem synodo ademptam esse: Secunda ratio fuit; Quod temere & præcipitanter ad jus suffiragii in synodis laicos seniores admiserint: Ad hæc in ter alios respondent Comes Rothusius, & Laudonus: Duo scripta illa esse suppositicia, quibus falsa plurima a se nunquam excogitata, continerentur; neque se negare quin Ecclesiarum deputati Edenburgi hærentes, (quos ad invidiam & odium conflandum, novum & inauditum tribunal erexisse hostes calumniantur) instructiones ad presbyteria undequaque transmiserint, non ut authoritate & mandatis cogerent, sed ut fraterne in causa hac communi, eaque gravissima, monerent quid facto consultissimum esset; quod plusquam necessarium jam fuisse dixerunt, quandoquidem pauci sint quibus synodorum nationalium forma legitima cognita sit, propter earundem quadraginta hisce annis elapsis infrequentiam: Accedebat etiam Episcoporum astuta vigilantia, qui per emissarios suos, omnia turbandi occasiones sedulo exquirebant; quibus ut obviam irent, prudenti cautione per ejusmodi instructiones opus fuit: Instructionum a se missarum exemplaria proferunt, quarum æquitatem si quis in quæstionem vocet, se statim demonstraturos prositentur: Ad secundam illam de Senioribus laicis exceptionem respondent; aliud jus iis in synodis non esse concessum, quam quod verbo Dei, rationibus firmis, nec Scoticæ solum hujus ecclesiæ, verum aliarum etiam omnium rite reformatarum ecclesiarum laudabili praxi, iisdem competere demonstrabunt: Nec satis se mirari dicunt, cur quæstionem hanc in dubium nunc trahat Deputatus regius, cum ante indictam synodum ipsi abunde compertum fuerit, inter alias liberæ synodi nationalis conditiones, hanc imprimis ursisse libertatis vindices; quorum desideriis cum se plenissime satisfecisse dicat, facile intellectu est, concessione liberæ nationalis synodi, concedi etiam jus illud seniorum, nisi una manu datum altera eripiat; quod cum ægre sibi persuaderi patiantur,cum ipsius æquitate & honore consistere posse, coguntur oculos in Episcopos deflectere, mutationis hujus authores;qui synodi,(cujus indictionem & aperturam impedire non potuerunt) dissolutionem urgent, ac omnia tumultibus impleri ac misceri cupiunt, ut criminum,quorum urgentur,censuram effugiant: quibus solis, quaecunque ex dissolutione synodi mala oborirentur, merito imputanda declarant. Hæc tamen deputatum regium à dissolutione synodi dimovere non poterant, quam denuo imperat, omnibus severe monitis, nisi gravissimum læsæ majestatis crimen subire vellent, ut quam maturrimè à coetu hoc quem jam illicitum declarat, se subducerent.
units.tr: The moderator also insisted earnestly that, to settle this question, "Whether this Synod is lawful and duly constituted in its members," the members of the Synod should go to a vote. The royal commissioner replied as above: "And since the freedom of the Synod has been so much prejudiced (he said), I declare that I am not free to remain any longer in this assembly." His words, and how sad they were to him, were attested by tears flowing down his cheeks and by his deep sighs. Among the other reasons by which he said the freedom of the Synod had been prejudiced, these two were the chief: (1) because the election of the commissioners to the Synod was not free, but restricted by the Covenanters (whom he said had set up a new and unheard-of tribunal at Edinburgh), and in proof of this he produced two writings sent by those Covenanters, or at least by the leaders of the Covenanters, to those whom they knew to be supporters and zealots of their cause: one to the ministers, the other to the elders of the nobility. In these, he said, they order that only those be chosen to the Synod who strongly favour the Covenant, and that no regard be had to kinship or affinity. And so that this may be done conveniently, it would be wise, before the presbytery is called together to elect the commissioners, for them to confer with trusted and intimate friends, and to name those whom they wish to be chosen as commissioners in the presbytery, so that these same men may afterwards be designated with less obstacle by common and public votes; and the commissioners so chosen should meet at Edinburgh before the opening of the Synod, so that the number of those for whom this cause is dear may become known, lest through our sloth we become a mockery to our enemies and neighbours. The ministers are also to be warned to prepare themselves as diligently as possible for disputing the questions: on the power of the supreme magistrate in ecclesiastical matters, especially in calling councils; on the elders; on episcopacy; on the oath; on the liturgy and its corruptions. Finally, all effort must now be given, and every exertion of mind must be made, lest, through our negligence, the opportunity offered of recovering liberty, both political and ecclesiastical, slip away. "Do not these writings sufficiently show (said the royal commissioner) that all freedom has been taken from the Synod by you?" (2) The second reason was that they had rashly and hastily admitted lay elders to a right of vote in the Synods. In reply to these charges, among others, the Earl of Rothes and Lauderdale answered: that those two writings were forgeries, containing many falsehoods which they had never devised; nor did they deny that the commissioners of the churches, staying at Edinburgh (whom the enemies slander as having set up a new and unheard-of tribunal in order to stir up envy and hatred), had sent instructions to the presbyteries on all sides, not to compel by authority and commands, but to advise in a brotherly way, in this common and most weighty cause, what would be most prudent to do. They said this was more than necessary, since few people know the lawful form of national Synods, because of the infrequency of those Synods in the forty years that have now passed. Added to this was the crafty vigilance of the bishops, who by their agents diligently sought every occasion for disturbing matters; and to meet these, prudent caution through such instructions was needed. They produced copies of the instructions they had sent, and professed that if anyone should call their fairness into question, they would at once demonstrate it. To the second objection, concerning the lay elders, they replied that no other right had been granted to them in the Synods than that which they would demonstrate by firm reasons to belong to them, not only from the Word of God and the praiseworthy practice of this Scottish Church alone, but also of all other duly reformed churches. They also said they were not surprised enough that the royal commissioner now calls this question into doubt, since before the Synod was convened it had been fully known to him that among the other conditions of a free national Synod, the defenders of liberty had insisted first of all on this one. Since he says he has fully satisfied their desires, it is easy to understand that, with the grant of a free national Synod, the right of the elders was also granted, unless one hand gave it and the other took it away. Since they could not bring themselves to believe that this could be consistent with his own fairness and honour, they were forced to turn their eyes to the bishops, the authors of this change. These men, who could not prevent the calling and opening of the Synod, now urge its dissolution, and wish everything to be filled and thrown into confusion with tumults, so that they may escape the censure of the crimes with which they are charged. To them alone, they declared, must be rightly imputed whatever evils might arise from the dissolution of the Synod. Yet these things could not turn the royal commissioner from dissolving the Synod, which he now again ordered, with severe warnings to all that, unless they wished to incur the most grievous crime of treason, they should withdraw as quickly as possible from this assembly, which he now declared to be unlawful.

units.la: Hic Comes Argathelius senator regius, & à rege destinatus Marchionis assessor, synodum alloquitur. Mandatum sibi à rege dicebat, ut synodo huic interesset, in qua quam honeste se gesserit, prout muneris impositi ratio postularet, conscientiam suam & aliorum abundè testari: Nunquam se privatis rationibus inductum fuisse, ut regi in hoc negotio palpum obtruderet, aut extrema consilia suggereret: Ex improviso mandatum de dissolvenda synodo sibi accidisse; Exceptionem illam de laicis senioribus, suo judicio, non validam esse, in qua tamen arcem causæ suæ ponere videntur qui synodum nullam cupiunt. Addebat regis expresso mandato se cum aliis regni senatoribus subscripsisse fœderi & confessioni, sed hac expressa cautione, ut exponeretur secundum mentem majorum fœdus illud anno 1580. primitus sancientium: Quare synodum obtestabatur, ut sedulo caveret, ne alienus sensus eidem affingeretur: Cujus orationi subserviebat Comes Rothusius; Operam hanc declarandi sensum fœderis pernecessariam esse; propter varia & sibi invicem contradicentia multorum de eo judicia ; aliis propugnantibus, fœdus illud bene consistere non folum cum omnibus novationibus hactenus introductis, verum cum iis etiam quæ in libris Canonum, liturgiæ, ordinationis obtrudebantur ; aliis vero judicantibus quasdam excludi ; aliis denique, omnes: ac redeundum esse ad disciplinæ, rituum, & doctrinæ puritatem & simplicitatem, quæ anno illo 1580 viguerat. Deputatus regius dicebat, eo labore defungendum esse, cum rex sententiam suam declaraverit, quo sensu velit fœderi huic a subditis subscribi: Interim nunc dissolvendam esse synodum, idque se regio nomine omnibus mandare : Quo cum senatoribus exeunte, protestationem prælegit scriba synodi contra mandatum illud; de qua fusius suo loco.
units.tr: Here Earl Argathelius, a royal senator and assessor appointed by the king to the Marquis, addressed the assembly. He said that the king had ordered him to attend this synod, and that his conduct in it, as the duties laid on him required, bore sufficient witness to his conscience and to that of others. He had never been moved by private motives to flatter the king in this business or to suggest extreme measures. The order to dissolve the synod had come to him unexpectedly. The objection about lay elders, in his judgement, was not valid, although those who want no synod seem to rest their whole case on it. He added that, by the king's express command, he had subscribed the covenant and the confession along with the other senators of the realm, but with this express proviso: that the covenant of 1580, by which it was first sworn, should be explained according to the intention of its framers. Therefore he begged the synod to take care that no alien meaning be attached to it. Earl Rothusius supported his speech. He said that this work of declaring the sense of the covenant was very necessary, because of the many varied and mutually contradictory opinions about it: some maintained that the covenant agreed well not only with all the innovations introduced so far, but also with those forced upon us in the books of canons, the liturgy and the ordination; others judged that some of these were excluded; and others again, that all were. The church must return to the purity and simplicity of discipline, rites and doctrine that flourished in that year, 1580. The royal deputy said that this labour must be left aside, since the king had declared his opinion on the sense in which he wished his subjects to subscribe this covenant. Meanwhile, the synod was now to be dissolved, and he ordered all present to do so in the king's name. As the senators left, the clerk of the synod read out a protest against that order, which will be treated more fully in its place.

units.la: Vbi nullis rationibus nec precibus Deputatum regium de sententia dimoveri posse, ac frustra reditum expectari, cerneret Præses; multa, quibus ecclesiarum deputatis, inopinato ac repentino hoc discessu tantum non dejectis, animum adderet, eleganter dicebat, aliisque quibusdam omnium ordinum nominatim designatis ad idem officium præstandum suo exemplo præivit; quorum concors sententia fuit: Quandoquidem Illustrissimus deputatus regius (summis laudibus prosequendus) regi usque adeo fidelem se servum præstet, regiisque mandatis ita stricte adhæreat, ut nullis rationibus ab iisdem vel tantulum se dimoveri passus fit; maiori certe sollicitudine nobis deputatis ecclesiarum incumbendum esse, servis Omnipotentis Dei, cujus imperio & reges ipsi subditi sunt, ne in hominum gratiam ab ipsius mandatis vel tantillum deflectamus: Ipsius præsentiæ fidendum esse, quam ab hujus negotii, utpote Christi sui, primordiis, opportune semper experti sumus; hujus arbitrio omnia committentibus ex animi nostri sententia omnia se con-secturum secturum certo sperare jubet: nec dispondendum esse animum quibuslibet objectis impedimentis, iis praesertim quibus abunde cognitum fit, quam daminosum hoc Satanae & Antichristi regno opus sit, & quam Christo agonothotae gratum, dilectae suae Sionis ruinas reaedificare.
units.tr: When the president saw that the royal deputy could be moved from his opinion neither by arguments nor by entreaties, and that it was vain to expect his return, he sought to encourage the deputies of the churches, who had been all but cast down by this sudden and unexpected departure. He spoke eloquently and, by his own example, led the way for certain others of every rank, each named individually, to perform the same office. Their united opinion was this: since the most illustrious royal deputy (worthy of the highest praise) shows himself so faithful a servant to the king and adheres so strictly to the royal commands that he has not allowed himself to be moved from them the least bit by any arguments, we deputies of the churches ought surely to apply ourselves with all the greater care, as servants of Almighty God, under whose command kings themselves are subjects, not to turn aside even slightly from his commands to win men's favour. We must trust in his presence, which we have always found timely from the very beginnings of this business, since it is his own work of Christ. Committing all things to his will, he bids us firmly hope that he will bring about everything according to our mind. Nor should we despair because of whatever obstacles are set before us, especially since it is well known how damaging this work is to the kingdom of Satan and Antichrist, and how pleasing to Christ, the umpire of the contest, to rebuild the ruins of his beloved Zion.

units.la: Orationibus hisce non solum deputatis erecti animi, verum & multis astantibus spectatoribus, inter quos fuit ex prima nobilitate adolescens magnae spei, Dominus Areskinus, Nobiliss. Comitis Marrii[?], Senatoris regii, primogenitus: qui cum lachrymis ad foederis & confessionis subscriptionem admitti postulat; ingenue fassus conscientiam aurem sibi saepius vellicasse, ac monuisse, ut quam primum causae huic optimae se adjungeret, quod quia huc usque neglexerit, sentire se Deum sibi iratum, quem omnium precibus placari flagitat: Hunc subsequuti sunt complures alii. Omnes hoc certum divini favoris argumentum exosculabantur, quod, quando metuendum maxime fuerat ne pusillanimitate multorum animi fracti desciscerent; eodem temporis articulo quasi Θεὸς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς[?] posthabitis omnibus periculis, quorundam corda ita confirmarentur, ut in foederis societatem ascribi peterent.
units.tr: These speeches raised the spirits not only of the deputies but also of the many onlookers present, among whom was a young man of great promise from the foremost nobility, Lord Erskine, eldest son of the most noble Earl of Marr[?], a royal senator. Weeping, he asked to be admitted to subscribe the covenant and the confession. He frankly confessed that his conscience had often pricked him and warned him to join this excellent cause as soon as possible; because he had neglected it until now, he felt God to be angry with him, and he begged that God be appeased by the prayers of all. Several others followed him. All of them embraced this as a sure sign of divine favour. At the very moment when the greatest fear had been that the spirits of many would be broken by cowardice and would desert, the hearts of certain men were so strengthened, all dangers set aside, as if by a god from the machine [Θεὸς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς], that they asked to be enrolled in the fellowship of the covenant.

units.la: Et quia metus fuit ne importunis sollicitationibus quorundam constantia vacillaret, ac terrore minatum zelus algeret, opportune omnium deputatorum sententias sciscitandas judicavit praeses ante dimissam hanc sessionem. An, non obstante deputati regii mandato, quo Synodi dissolutionem imperabat, statuerent Synodum non relinquere usque dum de omnibus ad ecclesiae pacem necessariis conclusum esset? Respondent omnes Affirmative, pauculis exceptis, qui clausulam literis fidei infertam causabantur, per quam deputato regio absente, sibi non liceret Synodo interesse: Quibus secedentibus, secundo quæsitum, An Synodus hæc non obstante Episcoporum protestatione legitimus Episcoporum judex censeri debeat? Respondent omnes uno ore & concordibus calculis Affirmative.
units.tr: And since there was fear that the constancy of some would waver under the importunate pressure of others, and that zeal would grow cold under threats of terror, the president judged it timely, before this session was closed, to ask the opinions of all the deputies. Notwithstanding the royal deputy's order, by which he commanded the dissolution of the synod, did they resolve not to leave the synod until everything necessary for the peace of the church had been concluded? All answered yes, except a few who objected to a clause inserted in the letters of commission, by which, if the royal deputy was absent, they would not be permitted to attend the synod. When these had withdrawn, a second question was put: whether this synod, notwithstanding the protest of the bishops, ought to be judged the lawful judge of the bishops? All answered with one voice and with unanimous votes, yes.

units.la: Responsio Synodi ad Episcoporum protestationem.
units.tr: The Synod's answer to the Bishops' protest.

units.la: Ac priusquam ulterius progrediar, Synodi responsionem ad scriptum illud Episcoporum, quo ejus authoritatem declinabant, paucis quantum fieri poterit, subjungam: Impressa fuit Edinburgi, cum ecclesiarum deputati accepissent Episcoporum protestationem Londini typis excusam fuisse: cujus summam invenies ad sessionem 6.
units.tr: Before I go further, I will add, as briefly as I can, the Synod's answer to that writing of the Bishops in which they sought to decline its authority. It was printed at Edinburgh after the commissioners of the churches had received the Bishops' protest, which had been printed in London. You will find a summary of it under the sixth session.

units.la: Ad præfationem quæ duo continet, Synodorum nationalium necessitatem, & penes quem sit jus eadem convocandi, respondent.
units.tr: They reply to the preface, which contains two points: the necessity of national synods, and in whose power it lies to convene them.

units.la: Episcoporum protestationem de Synodorum necessitate, esse facto contrariam, cum per Episcopos solos fateretur, quod Ecclesia Synodis nationalibus destituta fuerit annis plurimis elapsis, à quibus tam sibi metuebant, quam ab œcumenicis liberis conciliis pontifices Romani. Dein, penes quem sit nationalem Synodum convocandi potestas: hic (inquit Synodus) regi adulantur Episcopi, privatam suam causam agentes. Etenim licet ingenue fateamur licere supremo magistratui cum velit Synodum convocare: nequaquam tamen omne jus convocandi sic ei tributum dicimus, ut seditionis & læsæ majestatis rei sint omnes in Synodum coeuntes sine ejus expresso mandato & consensu: alioqui horum criminum rei essent Christiani primis tribus sæculis: Quod si excipias disparem esse ecclesiæ rationem sub Christiano magistratu; respondent, nec illud se negare, ideoq; ipsius consensū omnibus modis enixe expetendum; sed quid si renuat ecclesiæ periclitanti dexteram hic porrigere, quid si officiū hoc præstare fastidiat aut negligat, quid si cesset officii facere in manifesto ecclesiæ periculo? an seditionis & viola&c violatæ majestatis crimen incurret ecclesia, quæ medio hoc necessario, quo urgentibus malis occurri possit, utatur? Paria sunt non apparere & non esse; & error cui non resistitur approbatur; & veritas cum minime defensatur opprimitur; negligere imperium cum possis deturbare perversos nihil aliud est, quam fovere, dist. 83. can. error: Si magistratus pietatis hoc officium ecclesiæ exhibere nolit; Ecclesia tamen tam libere jure suo uti nunc potest quam olim usi fuere primi illi Christiani: Adde quod saniores Pontificii, non tantum authoritatis Romano Pontifici, (quem tamen Ecclesiæ monarcham statuunt) in convocandis conciliis tribuant, quam Regibus Episcopi. vide Antonium de Rosellis I. V. D. in Monarchia parte 2. cap.30. & parte 3. cap.3. qui temporibus Frederici tertii Imperatoris obiit anno 1467. Antonium de Dominis, Archiepiscopum Spalatensem lib.2. de Republic. ecclesiastic. cap. 7. num. 18. Iacobum Almainum Theologum Sorboniftam, qui vixit anno 1510: Quorum sententia est; vel reluctante Pontifice Romano licere ecclesiæ in synodo convenire; posse per viam requisitionis vel monitionis, denunciativè, non per viam authorizationis præceptivè, vel invito pontifice Synodum convocare; hujusque sententiæ hoc fundamentum ponitur, quia jus tale indictionis est jure divino penes ecclesiam, Si quid hæc contra aulæ Romanæ Gnathones valeant in causa universalis synodi; multo fortius stringent pro jure ecclesiæ in nationalibus synodis convocandis, utpote magis necessariis: Nec hoc negatum Richardo Feildo, hierarchicæ dignitatis strenuo defensori: lib. 5. de ecclesia cap. 52. Primates olim convocarunt nationales synodos; quos tamen non legimus speciatim singulis conventibus consensum à regibus postulasse: quia tacite consensum præbuisse putantur Imperatores & Principes, dum Christianam religionem ipsi amplectuntur, eamque publice protendi libertatem subditis concedunt: Nam principali concessio, accessoria omnia concessa videntur, sine quibus principale sartum tectum conservari nequit. Hinc illud eruditi authoris de libertate ecclesiastica pro Venetis contra Pontificem. Imperatores cum libertatem religionis edictis suis Ecclesiæ concesserunt, simul jus liberè cogendi synodos illis attribuisse, nam cultus Christiani hæc pars est prorsus necessaria & συνῳδῆς[?]. Quare cum lege municipali ecclesiæ hæc libertas sancita sit in publicis regni comitiis anno 1592, non necesse est subinde à rege novum ad eam rem mandatum peti. Sed urgent Episcopi, utcunque hoc olim receptum fuerit in Ecclesia Scotica, jam tamen sine manifesta legum sancitarum violatione fieri non posse, nam in comitiis anni 1592. Regis esse declaratur per se aut deputatos locum & tempus synodi defignare, quod in comitiis anni 1612. repetitur. Cui respondet Synodus: Titulum statuti illius anni 1592. esse Sanctionem libertatis & privilegiorum veræ ecclesiæ: ideoque licet declaret regis esse tempus & locum futuræ synodo designare, addit tamen si adsit; qua clausula insinuatur Ecclesiæ per synodum repræsentatæ, rege aut deputato regio absente, jus illud competere, nullatenus vero intelligi possunt illa de jure aliquo privativo regi competente; quasi in ipsius potestate relictum esset synodum indicere aut non: nam sic corpus statuti lemmati & titulo contradiceret; etenim hoc esset Ecclesiam jure suo spoliare, non ipsius jus sancire & ratum facere: Reliqua, inquiunt Synodici, petenda sunt ex peculiari hac de re tractatu edito, de quo prius mentio facta est.
units.tr: As to the Bishops' claim that a national synod is necessary, they say the fact contradicts it, since the Bishops themselves admit that the Church has gone without national synods for many years, and the Roman pontiffs feared these as much as they feared free ecumenical councils. Next, on in whose power it lies to convene a national synod: here (says the Synod) the Bishops flatter the king, pleading their own private cause. For although we frankly admit that the supreme magistrate may convene a synod whenever he wishes, we by no means say that the right of convening is given to him in such a way that all who assemble in a synod without his express command and consent are guilty of sedition and treason. Otherwise, the Christians of the first three centuries would have been guilty of these crimes. If you object that the situation of the Church under a Christian magistrate is different, they reply that they do not deny this either, and that his consent is therefore to be sought earnestly by every means. But what if he refuses to hold out his hand to a Church in danger? What if he disdains or neglects to perform this duty? What if he ceases to act when the Church is manifestly in peril? Will the Church, which uses this necessary means by which pressing evils can be met, incur the crime of sedition and violated majesty? Things that do not appear are as good as things that do not exist; an error that is not resisted is approved; truth that is not defended is oppressed; to neglect the authority to overthrow the wicked when you are able is nothing other than to foster them (Dist. 83, can. Error). If the magistrate refuses to perform this office of piety for the Church, the Church may nevertheless now use its own right as freely as those first Christians once did. Add to this that the more sensible Papists grant to the Roman Pontiff, whom they nonetheless set up as monarch of the Church, no more authority in convening councils than Bishops grant to kings. See Antonius de Rosellis, doctor of both laws, in Monarchia, part 2, chap. 30, and part 3, chap. 3, who died in the time of the Emperor Frederick III, in the year 1467; Antonius de Dominis, Archbishop of Spalato, On the Ecclesiastical Republic, book 2, chap. 7, num. 18; and James Almain, Sorbonne theologian, who lived in the year 1510. Their view is this: even if the Roman Pontiff is unwilling, it is lawful for the Church to meet in synod; it may convene a synod, even against the pontiff's will, by way of request or admonition, declaratively, not by way of authorizing with a command. The foundation of this opinion is that such a right of calling is by divine right in the power of the Church. If these arguments count for anything against the courtiers of the Roman court in the case of a universal synod, they will bind much more strongly for the right of the Church to convene national synods, which are the more necessary. Nor is this denied by Richard Field, a vigorous defender of hierarchical dignity (book 5, On the Church, chap. 52). Primates once convened national synods, yet we do not read that they asked the kings for consent to each particular meeting. This is because emperors and princes are thought to have given tacit consent when they embraced the Christian religion themselves and granted their subjects liberty to profess it publicly. For when a principal grant is made, all the accessories are considered granted, without which the principal cannot be kept safe and sound. Hence that learned author's statement on ecclesiastical liberty, written for the Venetians against the Pope: When emperors granted the Church liberty of religion by their edicts, they at the same time granted it the right to convene synods freely, for this part of Christian worship is absolutely necessary and in harmony [συνῳδῆς]. Therefore, since this liberty of the Church was sanctioned by municipal law in the public assembly of the realm in the year 1592, it is not necessary to seek a fresh mandate from the king for this matter each time. But the Bishops press the point that, however this was once received in the Scottish Church, it cannot now be done without a manifest violation of sanctioned laws, for at the assembly of 1592 it is declared to belong to the king, either in person or through his commissioners, to appoint the place and time of the synod, which was repeated at the assembly of 1612. To this the Synod replies: the title of the statute of 1592 is Sanction of the liberty and privileges of the true Church. Therefore, although it declares that it belongs to the king to designate the time and place of a future synod, it adds if he is present. By this clause it is implied that the right belongs to the Church represented in synod when the king or his royal commissioner is absent. Nor can those words be understood as referring to any private right belonging to the king, as if it were left to his power whether or not a synod should be called; for in that case the body of the statute would contradict its motto and title. Indeed, this would be to strip the Church of its right, not to sanction and ratify it. As for the rest, they say, it must be sought in the separate treatise published on this matter, which was mentioned earlier.

units.la: Defuncti præfationis examine, ad recusatæ synodi rationes deveniunt.
units.tr: Having examined the preface, they turn to the reasons given for refusing the synod.

units.la: Ad primam, literas missionum abunde testatas fuisse, meram esse calumniam: nam omnes datae fuerunt post diem quo indicebatur synodus, adde quod cum spes certa synodi habeatur, semper liceret presbyteriis seu classibus deputatos eligere ante indictionis diem, nec posse Episcopos ipsos denegare, si in memoriam revocent modum electionis deputatorum ad Synodum Andreapolitanam anno 1617.
units.tr: As to the first, the charge that the letters of commission were not sufficiently attested is mere calumny, for all of them were issued after the day on which the synod was announced. Moreover, since there was a firm expectation of a synod, it was always lawful for the presbyteries or classes to elect their commissioners before the day of the announcement, and the Bishops cannot deny this if they call to mind the manner in which the commissioners were elected to the synod at St Andrews in 1617.

units.la: Ad secundam, Municipalem illam legem sancitam parlamento 3. Iacobi 6. ad annum 1572. in desuetudinem jampridem abiisse: cujus sanciendae causa fuerat, quod tum quidam addicti Mariae reginae, Iacobi regis matri, regem Iacobum viva matre agnoscere noluerint, cum cujus morte obliterata est lex illa: quare si haec exceptio synodalium incompetentiam inferat; Episcopis ipsis & quotquot sacro ministerii munere post ipsam defunctam inaugurati sunt, laborandum erit ut ab hac labe se purgent.
units.tr: As to the second, that municipal law sanctioned by Parliament in the sixth year of James's reign, in 1572, has long since fallen into disuse. It was enacted because some who were attached to Mary the queen, mother of King James, were unwilling to acknowledge King James while his mother was alive, and with her death that law was forgotten. Therefore, if this exception implies that the synod lacks competence, the Bishops themselves, and all who have been inducted into the sacred ministry since her death, will have to work to clear themselves of this stain.

units.la: Dein statuti illius verba non omnes in genere verbi pastores tangit, verum eos solum qui beneficio & titulo gaudent ecclesiastico. Denique si quid hic a pastoribus omissum fit, imputandum Episcoporum oscitantiae & supinae negligentiae, statutum illud executioni non mandantium: Pastoribus autem verbi hoc minime vitio vertendum esse, nisi pertinaciter obedientiam legibus illis recusent; quod nemini merito objici potest, utpote quod in promotionibus Academicis, & nupera Confessionis subscriptione, juramentum illud fidelitatis lubentissime praestiterint.
units.tr: Next, the words of that statute do not in general touch all ministers of the Word, but only those who enjoy a benefice and ecclesiastical title. Finally, if anything has been neglected here by the ministers, it is to be imputed to the carelessness and idle negligence of the Bishops, who did not put that statute into execution. The ministers of the Word are by no means to be blamed for this, unless they stubbornly refuse obedience to those laws, which no one can rightly charge them with, since they most willingly took that oath of allegiance at their academic promotions and at the recent subscription to the Confession.

units.la: Ad tertiam, Si confessioni a rege imperatae alienus sensus non fuisset ascriptus, videl: quod bene illi conveniat cum novationibus omnibus introductis; nec repagulum ponat aliis novitatibus introducendis; subscriptionem confessionis istius nunquam detractassent: quare pro pertinacibus habendi non sint quoad demonstretur majores suos confessionis istius primogenios authores, sic explicasse prout rex jam declarat: nam ad horum sensum subscriptores teneri, satis declarat regii senatus statutum mense Septembri.
units.tr: As to the third: if the sense imposed on the Confession by the king had not been attributed to it, namely that it agrees well with all the innovations introduced and does not place a barrier in the way of other novelties to be introduced, they would never have refused to subscribe to that Confession. Therefore they should not be considered obstinate as long as it has not been shown that their forefathers, the original authors of this Confession, explained it in the way the king now declares. For that the subscribers are bound to this sense is sufficiently declared by the statute of the royal Senate in September.

units.la: Ad quartam, Cum veteri majorum instituto, omnes majores Præsulati, hoc est, tam Abbates, Priores quam Episcopi, tertium illud ordinum regni membrum composuerint, non magis reos esse violatarum legum eos qui Episcopos impugnent, quam qui Abbates & Priores: Quod ad leges illas attinet, quibus Episcopis dignitates in integrum sint restitutæ, præsertim anni 1584. Respondent; antiquatas fuisse anno 1587, statuto illo annexationis (ut loquuntur) ac in Episcoporum & Abbatum locum repositos fuisse provinciarum ad Comitia deputatos, Barones videl: minores, qui ordinum regni membra olim & hodie dicuntur, ex quibus etiam Articulorum Domini pari numero cum aliis duobus comitiorum membris eliguntur, ad supplendum defectum Ecclesiasticorum, qui tunc exclusi; Neque posteriora comitia Baronibus minoribus unquam jus hoc adimisse: Sed detur Episcopos solos tertium ordinum regni membrum constitutos esse, an illi læsæ majestatis rei qui ipsorum vitia taxant, & synodi censuræ subjici debere docent? quod etiam in Pseudo-synodo Glasguensi anno 1610 ab ipsis conclusum fuit: & cujus censuræ obnoxios declaravit rex edicto Septembris: An vero usque adeo indivulsa sint Episcoporum vitia, & Episcopatus, ut illis in quæstionem vocatis, hic æqui judicis censuram non effugiet: & parcendum sit Episcopis multorum criminum reis, ut Episcopatui sua dignitas constet, qui alias ad ravim usque clamitant distinguenda esse hominum vitia ab officiis, cur eadem hic confundunt? Sed hoc certe anxios eos tenet, quod μορμολυκείῳ[?] illo Hierarchici Episcopatus non diutius deterreantur fideles Dei servi, quin ligonem ligonem libere vocent.
units.tr: As to the fourth: since, by the ancient custom of our ancestors, all the prelates, that is, the Abbots and Priors as well as the Bishops, formed that third order of the realm, those who attack the Bishops are no more guilty of violating the laws than those who attack the Abbots and Priors. As for those laws by which the dignities of the Bishops were restored in full, especially those of 1584, they reply that these were abolished in 1587 by that statute of so-called annexation, and that in place of the Bishops and Abbots there were installed the commissioners of the shires to the assembly, namely the lesser barons, who were and still are called the members of the realm's estates. From among these, together with the two other members of the assembly, the Lords of the Articles are elected in equal number, to supply the lack of ecclesiastics who were then excluded. Nor did later assemblies ever take this right away from the lesser barons. But grant that the Bishops alone constituted the third estate of the realm: do they really hold that those who censure their faults are guilty of treason, and must be subject to the censure of the synod? This was also concluded by them in the so-called Synod of Glasgow in 1610, and the king declared by his September edict that those who were liable to its censure were subject to it. But are the faults of the Bishops and the Episcopate so inseparable that, when these are called into question, the Bishops will not escape the censure of an impartial judge, and the Bishops, accused of many crimes, must be spared so that the dignity of the Episcopate may stand? They keep crying out that the faults of men must be distinguished from their offices; why do they here confuse the two? But this surely troubles them anxiously: that the faithful servants of God will no longer be deterred by that hierarchical bugbear [μορμολυκείῳ] from freely calling a spade a spade.

units.la: Ad quintam, quod presbyteria seu classes exciderint libertate eligendi aut mittendi deputatos ad synodum, quia Moderatores ab Episcopis constitutos, juxta canones synodi Glasguensis anno 1610. abdicarint; Respondent: In ipsa pseudo-synodo quae moderatorum classicalium electionem Episcopis concessit; expresse pactum fuisse ab Ecclesiis, ut annuae Synodi nationales haberentur, conditione itaque hac non praestita, cecidisse jure illo concesso Episcopos: dein[?] canones illos statuere, ut in Synodis provincialibus, Episcopi praesentes presbyteriis moderatores designent, quibus cum deputatos suos praesidere jubeant, cui non perspicuum, ad antiquos possessores jus illud legitime devolutum esse? nisi ostendat eorum deputatis eandem tum potestatem concessam esse, quod demonstratu impossibile erit: Adde quod moderatorum classicalium plurimi sponte se hoc munere abdicarint, quo casu synodus ista Glasguensis, classi permittit jus alios substituendi; plures vero ab Episcopis constituti eo munere adhuc defungantur: Denique licet omnes loco movissent presbyteria, nullus praeter eos quibus praejudiciis fascinati sint mentis oculi, colliget, omni libertate privanda esse presbyteria; sed ad summum, digna quae gravi aliqua censura pro reatu allegati criminis notentur.
units.tr: To the fifth charge, that the presbyteries or classes have lost the liberty of electing or sending deputies to the synod, because they have renounced the moderators appointed by the bishops according to the canons of the Glasgow synod of 1610. Their answer: In that very pseudo-synod which granted the bishops the election of classical moderators, it was expressly agreed by the Churches that annual national synods should be held. That condition not having been fulfilled, the right granted to the bishops lapsed. Next, those canons decree that in provincial synods the bishops present shall appoint moderators for the presbyteries, and order them to preside over the presbyteries' deputies. Who does not see that this right has lawfully devolved back to its former possessors, unless they show that the same power was then granted to their deputies? That will be impossible to demonstrate. Add that many of the classical moderators have voluntarily laid down this office, in which case the Glasgow synod itself allows the class the right to substitute others; but many appointed by the bishops still discharge that office. Finally, even if the presbyteries had all removed their moderators, no one except those whose mental eyes are blinded by prejudice would conclude that the presbyteries must be stripped of all liberty. At most they deserve to be marked with some serious censure for the crime alleged.

units.la: Ad sextam, quod electioni clericorum ad synodum delegatorum interfuerint laici seniores &c. Resp. quandoquidem Nobiles, quique in Ecclesiis maximae dignitatis sunt, ab initio reformationis eligantur ecclesiarum particularium seniores: quid vetabit quominus cum pastoribus ad classem delegentur? prout non solum in aliis reformatis ecclesiis, praesertim Belgicis & Gallicis fieri consuevit, verumetiam lege in ecclesia hac statutum sit: videatur liber secundus politiæ ecclesiasticæ, in hanc sententiam expresse; & sæpius: Ita ut admiranda sit Episcoporum impudentia illud negantium; nam canonibus synodi nationalis anni 1582. mandatur verbi ministris ut seniorum præsentiam in presbyteriis sedulo urgeant, præsertim cum de rebus majoris momenti instituendæ sint deliberationes; inter quas facile primas tenet, deputatorum ad synodum nationalem Electio: in synodo Taodunensi, anno 1597. designatur numerus deputandorum à presbyteriis ad Synodum tam seniorum quam clericorum, ut loquuntur Episcopi; quæ presbyteria tum constabant tam ex senioribus quam pastoribus; Ita ut sine seniorum eorum consilio nihil ageretur in Ecclesia; uti de primitivæ ecclesiæ statu testatur Ambrosius in 1. ad Timotheum cap. 5. Quod si frequentibus canonibus sancita consuetudo hæc exoleverit, episcopaturientium artibus quia ambitioni suæ remoram esse videbant; intermissio tamen ista paucorum annorum præscribere non potest politiæ communibus omnium suffragiis & subscriptionibus receptæ, præsertim cum nullo canone ecclesiastico demonstrari possit, senioribus hisce jus hoc unquam imminutum fuisse. Cum autem periculosum sit in rebus divinis, ut quis jure suo ac potestate cedat; ac jus hoc seniorum verbo Dei consonum esse declaret liber secundus de politia ecclesiastica; cur illis vitio verteretur quod jure suo usi fuerint, quo præsens damnum religioni intentatum depellerent?
units.tr: To the sixth charge, that laymen, elders, etc., took part in the election of the clergy delegated to the synod. Answer: Since nobles, who hold the highest dignity in these Churches, have been chosen as elders of the particular churches from the beginning of the Reformation, what would prevent them from being delegated to the classis along with the ministers? This is customary not only in other reformed churches, especially the Belgian and French, but is also enacted by law in this Church. See the second book of the Polity of the Church, which says so expressly and often. So the shamelessness of the bishops in denying it is remarkable. For by the canons of the national synod of 1582, ministers of the Word are commanded to press diligently for the presence of the elders in the presbyteries, especially when matters of greater moment are to be deliberated; and among these the election of deputies to the national synod easily holds first place. At the synod of Dundee in 1597 the number of deputies to be sent to the synod by the presbyteries was fixed, of elders as well as of clergy, as the bishops put it; and those presbyteries then consisted of both elders and ministers. So that nothing was done in the Church without the counsel of those elders, as Ambrose attests on 1 Timothy chapter 5 concerning the state of the primitive Church. But if this custom, sanctioned by frequent canons, has fallen into disuse, because the arts of men aspiring to bishoprics saw it as a hindrance to their ambition, still such an interruption of a few years cannot prescribe against a polity received by the common votes and signatures of all. This is especially so since no ecclesiastical canon can show that this right of the elders was ever diminished. Since it is dangerous in divine matters for anyone to yield his right and power; and since the second book on ecclesiastical polity declares this right of the elders to be consonant with the Word of God, why should it be held against them that they used their right to ward off the present harm threatened to religion?

units.la: Ad septim. Cum nullum designant pastorem qui tribunitiis concionibus subditos ad rebellionem excitaverit, neque classes delegantes, aut synodus ad quam delegentur, quempiam præsentium hujus criminis reum sciant, pro pura puta calumnia habendum esse; neque facile existimandum Episcoporum pectora charitate in pastores perfusa, reorum, si quos scirent, nomina supprimere velle, ut eorum famae scilicet parcerent, quos perjuros, perduelles, diabolicarum calumniarum authores & fautores, schismaticos, tertio quoque verbo criminantur: Sed dolosum in generalibus versari, vetus est dictum.
units.tr: To the seventh. Since they name no minister who stirred up the subjects to rebellion by tribunician sermons, and since neither the classes sending delegates nor the synod to which they are sent know any of those present to be guilty of this crime, the charge should be regarded as pure calumny. Nor is it easy to think that the bishops, with hearts drenched in charity toward ministers, would wish to suppress the names of offenders, if they knew any, in order to spare the reputation of those whom they call perjured, traitors, authors and abettors of diabolical calumnies, schismatics, every third word. But it is an old saying that deceit lies in generalities.

units.la: Ad octavum, ejusdem esse commatis dicunt: Nec schismaticos dicendos esse pastores, quod tyrannidi Episcoporum ecclesiae libertates impudenter pessundantium, & rancidas Antichristi sordes per fas & nefas obtrudentium, modeste sese oppositerint: Nec perjuras; si impium illud & nulla lege munitum juramentum non praestiterint: in quod ab Episcopis adacti fuerunt complures, ignari politiae legibus sancitae; ac studii Episcoporum, quo Ecclesiae puritatem corrumpere satagebant. Etenim sine perjurio semper licuit in malis promissis fidem rescindere: Porro juramentum illud in quod Episcopi inaugurandos S. ministerii munere adigebant, tum veritate in re, tum justitia in causa destituta fuit: Causae justitia defuerat, quia eo solum fine urgebatur ut tyrannidem suam in Christi Ecclesiam firmius communirent: quod poenitenda experientia vel caecis hodie patet, quae licet prima facie sese tunc non prodderet, nunc tamen emergens & inevitabile Ecclesiarum damnum secum trahens, ab infamia perjurii omnes liberat, praesertim cum juramentum illud de rebus fuerit sua natura (ut Episcopi fatentur) adiaphoris, quae cum majus bonum impediant removendae sunt, nulla jurisjurandi habita ratione, ne sacramentum pietatis, ejusdem fit impedimentum: Quod ad rei juratae veritatem attinet, videl. Synodum Perthensem legitimam fuisse, articulosque quinque per eam Ecclesiæ obtrusos, simul cum Diœcesano Episcopatu ejusque appendicibus, cum hujus Scoticæ Ecclesiæ constitutionibus primitivis bene consistere, licet multi olim vera hæc putarent, ignorantia scilicet invincibili decepti ; nunc tamen productis in lucem authenticis Synodorum registris, salsissima esse compertum habent : Addequod juramentum hoc in quod adacti fuerunt ab Episcopis pastores, Ecclesiarum juri & libertati præjudicet, & repugnet juramento legitime prius præstito, à pastoribus omnibus tum in patrum personis, tum repetito ab ipsorum singulis cum ad gradum magisterii in Academiis promoverentur: Quare cum ejusmodi temeraria juramenta non ligent, nullatenus habendi sunt pastores pro perjuris, si non præstent ; nam injusta vincula rumpit justitia. Sed quid si propria vineta cædant hic Episcopi, Qui negare non sunt ausi, conditiones (ad quarum religiosam observationem in Synodo ad montis Rosarum anno 1600. juramento solenni obstricti sunt ecclesiastici illi ad jus suffragii in Conciliis regni admissi ) à se, ut Episcopatu potirentur, fœdè violatas, quem tamen seu Anglicanum, seu Romanensem sacramentis tum abjurabant, & quod hominum fidem fere superaret, nisi ab ipsorum Coryphæo typis commissum esset, fatentur se in conditionum illarum nonnullas (verius omnes) pro tempore magis quam animo in perpetuum observandi, assensisse: Rima certè per quam Ethnicos ipsos elabi puderet, apud quos explosum illud, Iuravi lingua, mentem injuriam gero. Quod ad illud de deputatis quibusdam pastoribus, censura ecclesiastica ab Hibernicis Episcopis notatis, Respondent ; Tres solum aut ad summum quatuor esse de quibus hoc affirmari posset, eosque natione Scotos, professione pastores Ecclesiæ Scoticæ: censuræ causam unicam fuisse, quia simplicitati rituum Ecclesiae Scoticae adhaerentes, non passi sunt sibi persuaderi minis, & vi, hierarchiam Anglicanam ejusque liturgiam esse verbo Dei in omnibus consonam: Quare licet censura ecclesiastica ibi hoc nomine notati essent, non ligatur Ecclesia Scoticana, quae pastorum paritatem & simplicem cultus divini puritatem colit, quin ad publica munia rite vocatos pro legitimis pastoribus habeat: praesertim cum censura ea non liget extra terminos jurisdictionis Hibernicae. Ad illos vero pastores quod attinet quos censura notatos dicunt in hac ecclesia Scotica ; nullos tales synodo cognitos esse; nam censuras in foro celsae commissionis latas ipso facto nullas esse dicunt: cum forum illud ab initio illegitimum fuerit, ob id solum institutum ut fidelibus Dei servis os obstrueretur; & verum est illud Gelasii cauf. 11. quaest. 3. Apud Deum & ejus ecclesiam neminem posse gravare injusta sententia : ita ergo ea se non absolui desideret, quia se nullatenus perspicit obligatum. Denique quod omnes pastores depositionis a ministerii functione dignos dicant Episcopi, probationem solidam requirere se aiunt, quae tam atrocis sententiae justitiam declaret: Calumniatorum artem probe edoctos Episcopos ; Calumniare audacter, nam semper aliquid adhaesurum putant:
units.tr: To the eighth, they say it is of the same kind: Ministers should not be called schismatics, because they modestly opposed the tyranny of the bishops, who shamelessly overthrow the liberties of the Church and force on it the rancid filth of Antichrist by fair means or foul. Nor perjured, if they did not take that impious oath, which had no warrant in any law, into which many were driven by the bishops, ignorant of the laws sanctioned by polity, and by the zeal of the bishops who strove to corrupt the purity of the Church. For without perjury it has always been lawful to rescind faith in bad promises. Moreover, that oath into which the bishops forced those to be inducted into the holy ministry lacked both truth in the matter and justice in the cause. Justice in the cause was lacking, because it was pressed only with the aim of more firmly fortifying their tyranny over Christ's Church. This is plain today, to be regretted by experience, even to the blind. Though it did not reveal itself at first sight, it now emerges, bringing with it inevitable damage to the Churches, and it frees everyone from the infamy of perjury. This is especially so since that oath was by its nature (as the bishops themselves confess) an indifferent matter, which, when it hinders a greater good, must be set aside without regard to any oath, lest the sacrament of godliness be hindered by it. As to the truth of the matter sworn, namely that the Synod of Perth was lawful, and that the five articles forced on the Church through it, together with the diocesan episcopacy and its appendages, agree well with the primitive constitutions of this Scottish Church: many once thought this true, deceived by invincible ignorance; but now, with the authentic registers of the synods brought to light, they have found it to be most false. Add that this oath, into which the bishops drove the ministers, prejudices the rights and liberty of the Churches, and contradicts the oath lawfully sworn earlier by all ministers, both in the persons of their fathers, and repeated by each of them when they were promoted to the degree of master in the universities. Therefore, since such rash oaths do not bind, the ministers are by no means to be held perjured if they do not take them; for justice breaks unjust chains. But what if the bishops here cut their own vines? They have not dared to deny that, in order to obtain the episcopate, they shamelessly violated the conditions, to whose religious observance those clergy admitted to the right of vote in the councils of the kingdom were bound by solemn oath at the synod at Montrose in 1600. These conditions they had then sworn to with sacraments, whether as Anglicans or as Romanists. And what would scarcely be believable to men, were it not printed by their own chief, they confess that they assented to some (more truly, all) of those conditions for the time rather than with intent of observing them forever. Surely this is a crack through which even the heathen would be ashamed to slip, among whom that saying is exploded: "I swore with my tongue; I bear the wrong in my mind." As to what they say, concerning certain deputed ministers, noted with ecclesiastical censure by the Irish bishops, they reply that there are only three, or at most four, of whom this could be affirmed, and these are Scots by nation and ministers of the Scottish Church. The sole cause of the censure was that, adhering to the simplicity of the rites of the Scottish Church, they would not allow themselves to be persuaded, by threats and force, that the Anglican hierarchy and its liturgy were in all things consonant with the Word of God. Therefore, although they were noted with ecclesiastical censure under this name, the Scottish Church, which cultivates the parity of ministers and the simple purity of divine worship, is not bound, so as to cease to hold as lawful ministers those duly called to public functions. This is especially so since that censure does not bind beyond the limits of Irish jurisdiction. As for those ministers whom they say were censured in this Scottish Church, the synod knows of no such men. For they say that censures pronounced in the court of the High Commission are null of themselves, since that court was illegitimate from the beginning, instituted solely so that the mouths of faithful servants of God would be stopped. And that saying of Gelasius (cause 11, question 3) is true: "Before God and his Church no one can be burdened by an unjust sentence; therefore it does not desire to be absolved, because it does not see itself bound in any way." Finally, as to the bishops' claim that all ministers are worthy of deposition from the ministerial function, they say that a solid proof is required, one that would declare the justice of so atrocious a sentence. The bishops are well trained in the art of calumny: "Calumniate boldly, for something will always stick."

units.la: Ad Nonum, Quod seniioribus laicis ut vocant jus suffragii definitivi in synodo nationali concedant, &c. Respondet synodus. 1. Seniores qui jurisdictioni intenti sunt, male Laicorum ordini accenseri; cum in libro de politia ecclesiastica, Ecclesiasticorum nomine semper veniant: neque immerito, etiam Clerico[?] dicendos, licet e populo electi sunt, & provincia sua defuncti in ejusdem ordinem redeant, nam vocatio ad functionem ecclesiasticam, ejusque administratio clericos facit, si Gratiano canonum compilatori fides habenda, qui distinct. 21. cap. Cleros, ex Isidoro, & causa 12 q. 1. cap. duo sint genera, ex Hieronymo probat, Clericos sic dictos quia sorte electi sint, ut in Christi ecclesia deserviant: si enim laici existimandi sunt quando ministerii onere deposito rursus in eorundem numerum veniunt; certe perperam iis accensentur dum adhuc Ecclesiæ onus sustinent, & publicam personam gerunt.
units.tr: Concerning the ninth point, that they should grant to the senior laymen, as they call them, the right of definitive vote in the national synod, etc. The synod replies. First, the elders who are engaged in jurisdiction are wrongly counted among the laity, since in the book on ecclesiastical polity they are always included under the name of Ecclesiastics. Nor are they rightly called laymen even though they were chosen from the people, and when they have finished their office in their province they return to the same order. For the calling to ecclesiastical function and its administration makes men clerics, if credit is to be given to Gratian, the compiler of the canons, who in Dist. 21, chapter Cleros, following Isidore, and in Causa 12, q. 1, chapter Duo sint genera, proves from Jerome that clerics are so called because they are chosen by lot to serve in the Church of Christ. For if men are to be regarded as laymen when, having laid down the burden of the ministry, they return to the number of the laity, then certainly it is wrong to count them among the laity while they still bear the burden of the Church and act in a public capacity.

units.la: 2. Si hæc exceptio admittenda sit, facessant omnes quotquot unquam habitæ fuerunt Synodi nationales ab ipsis reformatæ ecclesiæ in Scotia primordiis, ad hunc usque diem, ne corruptis quidem illis exceptis, in quibus semper sine controversia admissi fuere ad jus suffragii seniores: Proferant Episcopi vel unicam, ex qua exclusi unquam fuerunt; aut igitur jus suffragii senioribus in synodis debetur, aut si horum ad suffragia admissio synodum nullam facit; Illegitimæ fuerunt omnes antehac in ecclesia Scoticana synodi, etiam temporibus purissimis; nec ulla exterarum & transmarinarum ecclesiarum Concilia nationalia legitima ab Episcopis censeri possunt: quæ impudens assertio severa animadversione digna est, licet aliorum criminum rei non essent: neque ab hac absurditate sese extricant Episcopi, dicentes se Laicos simpliciter non excludere, verum jus suffragii definitivi eisdem lubenter deferre, dummodo a supremo magistratu ad id delegentur: nam sic ecclesiam libertate sua spoliant, quæ liberam potestatem mittendi quos voluit, semper exercuit; notum id esse etiam in veteri ecclesia, cujus praxin imitata est ecclesia hæc Scotica, in qua laici illi (quos per contemptum sic vocant) semper a presbyteriis deputati sunt, idque expresse cautum esse in synodo nationali ann. 1597. ad Taodunum, in qua non solum deputatorum ex singulis presbyteriis numerus certùs præscribitur, verumetiam penes presbyteria esse deputatorum electionem & missionem definitur: Olim piis principibus satis suisse ecclesias serio monere quibus dotibus ac virtutibus instructi esse deberent deputandi, delectum autem eorum qui mittendi essent, ecclesiis reliquisse, quibus jure competere sciebant. Ad verba illa ex synodo Chalcedonensi citata, quæ Patrum illius Concilii esse dicunt, Mitte foras superfluos, Quibus non satisfacit Whitthakeri responsum: Superfluos illos fuisse Clericos, Monachos & Laicos, qui Eutycheti favebant, quos ad turbas vitandas repelli decebat, cum à nullis legitime deputarentur; quibus si nobiles ad synodum legitime deputatos accenseant, næ illi contumeliam nobilissimis proceribus inurunt, non ferendam: Quibus inquam hoc responsum non placet; at episcopis saltem arrideat Matthæi Sutlivii acerrimi hierarchici: De conciliis lib. 1. cap. 34. argumentum hoc Bellarmini quo Laicos extruderet, in Bellarminum nervose retorquentis: Verba hæc non esse patrum Synodi Chalcedonensis, sed sic clamasse Dioscorum & Ægyptios, hæreticorum fautores, Atque ita inquit cum nunquam reperisset Bellarm. in orthodoxorum testimoniis tutum latibulum, ad hæreticos confugit, eorumque auxilium implorat: Similiter factum hic ab Episcopis incertissimum desperatæ causæ argumentum; quibus talium Episcoporum & patrum authoritatem non invidemus. Quod ad vocem illam Theodosii junioris, si rigide & κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν [?] accipiendum sit, videl: illegitimum esse, eum, qui non sit in ordine sanctissimorum Episcoporum ecclesiasticis immisceri [?] tractatibus; quomodo sartum tectum conservabitur magistratui supremo jus definitivi aut deliberativi suffragii, contra Pontificios telum hoc vibrantes, quo magistratus supremi authoritatem in rebus ecclesiasticis oppugnent? quomodo etiam presbyteris verbi seu pastoribus, contra eosdem Pontificios jus suffragii conservari poterit ? nam hos non esse in sanctissimorum Episcoporum ordine jurabunt Episcopi, nec Athanasio parcendum erit; qui in Synodo Nicena licet tum non ex ordine Episcoporum; ecclesiasticis tamen tractatibus contra Arrium se immiscuit: ut infinita alia exempla praeterea. Sed quid si in concilio illo Ephesino Ecclesiasticis tractatibus sese immiscuerit Theodosius ? An non pronunciat omnia illius concilii acta esse irrita ? Atque licet non interfuerit, Candidianum tamen misit, qui de omnibus Imperatorem certiorem fecit: Quare fictum hoc esse, & suppositititium sibi videri dicit Whittakerus: cum non habeatur in antiquis exemplaribus: & quia in se aperte falsum esse constat: denique male translata ex Græco hæc esse dicunt: τὴν ἐγὼ § ἡγεμόνας τῶν ἐπισκόπων[?], eorum qui non sunt in ordine Episcoporum: cum reddenda sint eorum qui extra catalogum Episcoporum, h. e. eos solum in concilio sententiam ferre oportere, qui in Catalogo inscripti erant eorum qui ab ecclesiis ad concilium erant delegati & ab Episcopis recensiti ex literis authoritatis publicæ, quas solebant exhibere, uti à Junio observatum.
units.tr: Second, if this exception were admitted, all the national synods that have ever been held by the reformed Church in Scotland from its beginnings to this day would have to go, and not even those corrupted ones excepted, in which the elders were always admitted without controversy to the right of voting. Let the bishops produce even one synod from which the elders were ever excluded. Either the right of voting is owed to the elders in synods, or, if their admission to the votes makes a synod no synod at all, then all the synods hitherto held in the Scottish Church were illegitimate, even in the purest times; nor can any national councils of foreign and overseas churches be judged legitimate by the bishops. This shameless assertion deserves severe rebuke, even if they were not guilty of other crimes. Nor do the bishops extricate themselves from this absurdity by saying that they do not simply exclude laymen, but gladly grant them the right of definitive vote, provided they are delegated to it by the supreme magistrate. For in this way they strip the Church of its liberty, which has always exercised the free power of sending whom it wished. This is known to have been the case even in the ancient Church, whose practice the Scottish Church has imitated, in which those laymen (whom they contemptuously so call) have always been deputed by the presbyteries. This is expressly provided for in the national synod of 1597 at Dundee, in which not only is a fixed number of deputies from each presbytery prescribed, but the choice and sending of the deputies is defined as resting with the presbyteries. In former times pious princes were content that the churches should seriously admonish what gifts and virtues those to be deputed ought to have, and left the choosing of those who were to be sent to the churches, to whom they knew it rightly belonged. As for the words cited from the Council of Chalcedon, which they say are spoken by the Fathers of that council, Cast out the superfluous, Whitaker's answer does not satisfy those who object: he says those superfluous ones were clerics, monks and laymen who favoured Eutyches, whom it was proper to repel to avoid disturbance, since they were not lawfully deputed by anyone. If the nobles are counted among these as legitimately deputed to the synod, then those people bring an insult upon the most noble peers that is not to be borne.
