This answer, I say, does not please me; but at least it should please the bishops, the most bitter hierarchist Matthew Sutcliffe, On Councils, book 1, chapter 34, who turns against Bellarmine with vigour the argument by which Bellarmine would thrust out the laity: These words are not of the Fathers of the Synod of Chalcedon, but were shouted thus by Dioscorus and the Egyptians, the supporters of heretics. And so, says he, since Bellarmine never found a safe hiding place in the testimonies of the orthodox, he has fled to heretics and implores their aid. The bishops here have made a similarly most uncertain argument from a desperate cause; we do not begrudge such bishops and such fathers their authority. As for the saying of Theodosius the Younger, if it is to be taken rigidly and according to the letter [κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν], namely that it is unlawful for one who is not in the order of the most holy bishops to mix himself in ecclesiastical deliberations, how then will the supreme magistrate keep his right of definitive or deliberative vote, when the Papists hurl this weapon against him, to attack the authority of the supreme magistrate in ecclesiastical matters? How also will the right of vote be preserved for the ministers of the Word, or pastors, against the same Papists? For the bishops will swear that these are not in the order of the most holy bishops, and Athanasius will not be spared, who at the Synod of Nicaea, although at that time not of the order of bishops, nevertheless mixed himself into the ecclesiastical deliberations against Arius; and there are countless other examples besides. But what if Theodosius himself had mixed himself into ecclesiastical deliberations at that Council of Ephesus? Does he not pronounce all the acts of that council void? And although he was not present, he sent Candidianus, who informed the Emperor about everything. Therefore Whitaker says this saying is made up and seems spurious to him, since it is not found in the old copies, and because it is plainly false in itself. Finally, they say these words are badly translated from the Greek: τὴν ἐγὼ § ἡγεμόνας τῶν ἐπισκόπων [as printed, garbled], of those who are not in the order of bishops; whereas they ought to be rendered of those outside the catalogue of bishops, that is, that only those should give judgement in the council who were inscribed in the catalogue of those who had been delegated by the churches to the council and were listed by the bishops from the letters of public authority which they were accustomed to present, as Junius has observed.

units.la: Ad mandatum illud Pulcheriæ Imperatricis respondent; æquum illud fuisse, cum quos expelli jubere[t] Imperatrix, sine legitima missione, importunè se ingerebant: quod de senioribus ad hanc synodum dici nequit: Adde quod concilio illi Chalcedonensi interfuerint laici, ab Imperatore minime delegati, quos scilicet secum episcopi duxerunt, quod aliis negatum, hisce concessum fuit, videl. ut interessent, quorsum autem interfuissent si in decernendo jus nullum habuissent ? Denique ad illud Martini Archimandritæ, non esse suum sed Episcoporum subscribere: Ideo Abbas hic subscriptionem subterfugiebat: quia Eutycheti hæretico tum condemnato favebat, eo etiam exemplo constare dicunt tempore Chalcedonensis concilii receptum fuisse, ut alii quam Clerici definitivo in synodis suffragio gauderent: alioquin cur abbatis monachorum subscriptionem postulasset synodus? Etenim alia est monachorum causa alia Clericorum inquit Hieronymus: Clerici oves pascunt, ego pascor: & idem alibi: Monachus non docentis, sed plangentis habet officium: Et ab his ipsis Chalcedonensis Synodi patribus decretum, ne monachi ecclesiasticorum officium attingerent: quia scil. erant laici, & diaconis aliisque ecclesiae ministris minores: Sed licet omnia ita sese haberent ut volunt Episcopi, non sequetur tamen synodum hanc esse eo nomine illegitimam, quia quaestio non est, an ordinanda sit haec synodus ad normam & Idœam synodorum quae corruptis illis ecclesiae temporibus coactae fuerunt; verum an constitutionibus & praxi ecclesiae Scoticae, seniores à presbyteriis legitime deputati admittendi sint ad jus suffragii definitivi in synodis nationalibus: quae contra objiciunt Episcopi, omnia sunt ex Pontificiorum armamentario depromptá: quibus abunde à Reformatae Ecclesiae doctoribus satisfactum est, ita ut episcopos puderet recoctam hanc cramben reponere, ac deserta reformatorum causa, cuius alias se strenuos defensores simulant, pontificiis sese adjungere; & clericis solis jus definitivi suffragii concedere; quasi hisce solis in synodo competeret, haereses & abusus irrepentes tollere, & de negotiis quae totam ecclesiam attingunt deliberare, ad quod ossicium praestandum cum alii praeter pastores idonei sint, donis & vocatione ab ecclesiis legitima instructi, cur quaeso excludendi sunt? an quia laici? sed ex horum numero etiam summus magistratus est, & quos ab eo deputari posse, antea confessi sunt Episcopi.
units.tr: To the command of the Empress Pulcheria they reply that it was fair, since those whom the Empress ordered to be expelled were pushing themselves in without lawful sending; which cannot be said of the elders at this synod. Add that laymen, not at all deputed by the Emperor, were present at that Council of Chalcedon, whom of course the bishops brought with them. What was denied to others was granted to these, namely that they might be present; but to what end would they have been present if they had no right to decide? Finally, to the saying of Martin the Archimandrite, It is not his business to subscribe, but the bishops': this abbot was therefore shirking subscription, because he was favouring the heretic Eutyches, who had then been condemned. They say that by this very example it is established that at the time of the Council of Chalcedon it was the custom that persons other than clerics should enjoy a definitive vote in synods; otherwise why would the synod have demanded the subscription of an abbot of monks? For the cause of monks is one thing, and the cause of clerics is another, says Jerome: clerics feed the sheep, I am fed; and elsewhere: The monk has the office not of teaching, but of mourning. And by these very Fathers of the Synod of Chalcedon it was decreed that monks should not touch the office of the Church, because, namely, they were laymen and inferior to deacons and the other ministers of the Church. But even if everything were as the bishops wish, it would not follow that this synod is illegitimate on that account, because the question is not whether this synod is to be ordered according to the norm and idea of those synods which were gathered in those corrupt times of the Church, but whether, according to the constitutions and practice of the Scottish Church, elders lawfully deputed by the presbyteries are to be admitted to the right of definitive vote in national synods. What the bishops object to on the other side is all taken from the Papists' armoury; and this has been abundantly answered by the teachers of the reformed Church, so that the bishops should be ashamed to bring back this reheated cabbage, and, abandoning the cause of the reformers, whose strenuous defenders they otherwise pretend to be, join themselves to the Papists and grant the right of definitive vote to clerics alone, as if to these alone it belonged in synod to root out heresies and abuses that creep in, and to deliberate on matters that touch the whole Church. Since other men besides pastors are fit for this office, being furnished with gifts and by lawful calling from the churches, why, pray, are they to be excluded? Because they are laymen? But the supreme magistrate himself is among their number, and the bishops have previously admitted that men can be deputed by him.

units.la: Sed quia tam confidenter gloriantur Episcopi scripturam S. rationem sanam, & antiquitatem puriorem totam, in hanc suam sententiam, pronam accedere, age, singula haec paucis percurramus; ut etiam pateat majores nostros, quorum vestigia religiose premimus, S. scriptura, rationibus, & ex suprema antiquitate deductis testimoniis, non destitutos fuisse, dum seniores domis & vocatione instructos ad jus suffragii definitivi admiserint. Praeat suo merito Scriptura, in qua mentio fit synodi Hierosolymitanae, Act. c. 15. quae aliarum omnium norma esse debeat; qui locus ab omnibus reformatis doctoribus urgetur, ut probent contra Pontificios, non solis clericis competere jus suffragii, nam verf. 4. quaestio ad totam ecclesiam delata est, & coram ea expositia; quorsum quaso illud, nisi ad omnes pertinuisset caussam illam definire? verf. 7. multa erat disceptatio, verf. 12. Tacuit tota multitudo; ergo alii praeter Apostolos & Presbyteros loquuti sunt, verf. 22. Tunc visum est Apostolis & presbyteris cum tota ecclesia delectos ex se viros mittere Antiochiam: [illegible, ~5 letters] tam Laicis quam Apostolicis & senioribus accommodatur, & vocem definitivam arguit: verf. 23. missae fuerunt literae synodicae Apostolorum, Presbyterorum & fratrum nomine: sententiam itaque dixit populus, & subscripsit: subscriptiones autem certissima suffragii ferendi indicia sunt, rursus verf. 25. & 28. illud visum est nobis, repetitur: ex quibus testimoniis Ludovicus Cardinalis Arelatensis in synodo Basiliensi colligit: Alios quam Episcopos habuisse vocem in Synodo definitivam. Vindicationem hujus loci contra pontificios, ejus sententiam ex corrupta consuetudine suspendentes, si quis postulet, adeat omnes nostros Doctores, qui de conciliis contra Pontificios scripserunt.
units.tr: But since the bishops boast so confidently that Holy Scripture, sound reason and the whole purer antiquity incline to their opinion, let us go through each of these points briefly. That will also show that our forefathers, whose footsteps we devoutly follow, were not without Scripture, reasons and testimonies drawn from the highest antiquity when they admitted elders, equipped with gifts and a lawful calling, to a definitive right of voting. Scripture rightly goes first, in which the synod of Jerusalem is mentioned (Acts 15), and which ought to be the rule for all others. All the reformed teachers press this passage against the Papists, to prove that the right of voting does not belong only to the clergy. For at verse 4 the question was referred to the whole church and laid out before it. Why, I ask, was this, unless it concerned everyone to settle that matter? At verse 7 there was much debate. At verse 12 the whole multitude kept silent, so others besides the apostles and elders spoke. At verse 22 it seemed good to the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men from among themselves to Antioch. [illegible] This applies to laymen as well as to apostles and elders, and it indicates a definitive vote. At verse 23 the synodal letters were sent in the name of the apostles, the elders and the brethren. The people therefore gave their judgment and subscribed, and subscriptions are the most certain signs of casting a vote. Again at verses 25 and 28 the words "it seemed good to us" are repeated. From these testimonies Louis, Cardinal of Arles, concluded at the Council of Basel that others besides bishops had a definitive voice in the synod. If anyone wants a defence of this passage against the Papists, who suspend its meaning on the basis of corrupt custom, let him consult all our teachers who have written about councils against the Papists.

units.la: Idem suadet sana ratio: nam cum synodus nationalis universam ecclesiam illius nationis repræsentet, consistere debet ex omni genere & ordine hominum, quia quod ad omnes pertinet, firmum esse non potest sine consensu omnium: & quod omnes tangit ab omnibus tractari & approbari debet: quod in hanc causam à Iuello citatum est, nomine Regulae in Concilio Chalcedonensi à Theodosio sancitae: quam in natura & ratione fundatam dicit Fieldus: Res autem in synodis tractandae ad omnes pertinent: & ecclesiae cives sunt tam Laici quam Clerici, quibus Deus saepe donum interpretationis aeque, aliquando uberius largitur quam quibusdam pastoribus; quod cum in totius ecclesiae commodum concessum sit, iniquum esset talentum illud sub modio condi. At quis locus aptior ad doni hujus exercitium quam synodus? cujus judicium non est imperatorium sed inquisitorium ligans propter probationem ex verbo Dei allatam; quod si Laicis convenire potest tam quam Clericis, & vero ex delegatione publica accedat authoritas; quis ipsorum praesentiam in synodis merito aegre ferat? Si quis autem putet dona haec solis ecclesiasticis concessa, meminerit gravis quaerelae Nazianzeni contra sui temporis Episcopos, qui licet rustici, idiotae, illiterati, nulla sacrarum literarum scientia praediti, nec in rebus sacris exercitati, in Synodis tamen ausi fuerint judicium ferre, quare illas synodos merito Nazianzenum detestatum fuisse scribit Spalatensis, lib. 7. cap. 3. & quae Marsilius Patavinus in defensore pacis, parte 2. cap. 9. de majoribus & minoribus saeculi sui clericis notat, Et Deo (inquit) teste & fidelium multitudine, sacerdotes plurimos abbates & praelatos quosdam me vidisse & audiisse memini adeo diminutos, ut nec grammatice quidem congruum scirent proferre sermonem, ideoque suadet generale Concilium per non sacerdotes integrari, prolato Apostolorum exemplo, & Isidori authoritate. Quam male itaque ecclesiae consulunt, qui neglectis Laicis doctis, solos ex Clero, saepe ignaros & imperitos ad synodum mittendos statuunt: Plura vide sis apud Spalatensem lib. 7. de repub. ecclesiast. cap. 3. per totum. Praxin si quis desideret veteris ecclesiæ; etiam post invalescentem Episcoporum ambitionem, post corruptam disciplinam, invectam superstitionem, inveniet satis frequentem: & consuetudinis hujus adeo expressa vestigia, ut obliterari non potuerit; Theodoretus Cyri Episcopus, epistola 81[?]. synodum desiderat, quæ non constat ex solis Episcopis, sed ex judicibus & aliis dignitate eminentibus, rerum divinarum peritis. Isidori mercatoris sententiam citat & approbat Marsilius Patavinus loco supra citato: Deinde (inquit) ingrediantur & Laici, qui electione Concilii interesse meruerunt: multo magis igitur literati & in lege divina periti (addit Marsilius) quanquam non exstant sacerdotes.
units.tr: Sound reason also argues the same. For since a national synod represents the whole church of that nation, it ought to consist of every kind and rank of men, because "what concerns all cannot be firm without the consent of all, and what touches all must be dealt with and approved by all." This rule, cited against the Papists by Jewel, is put forward as a principle of the Council of Chalcedon, enacted by Theodosius; Field says that it is founded in nature and reason. Matters to be treated in synods, however, concern everyone, and laymen are citizens of the church just as clergy are. God often gives to them the gift of interpretation as freely, and sometimes more abundantly, than to some ministers. Since this has been granted for the good of the whole church, it would be wrong to bury that talent under a bushel. But what place is more fitting for the exercise of this gift than a synod? Its judgment is not imperious but inquisitive, binding only by reason of proof brought from the Word of God. If this can belong to laymen as much as to clergy, and authority comes from public delegation, who could rightly take offence at their presence in synods? But if anyone thinks these gifts were granted only to churchmen, let him remember the serious complaint of Nazianzen against the bishops of his own time, who, though rustic, untaught, illiterate, possessing no knowledge of the sacred letters and not practised in holy matters, nevertheless dared to pass judgment in synods. For this reason, Spalatensis writes (book 7, chapter 3), Nazianzen rightly detested those synods. Marsilius of Padua, in the Defender of Peace, part 2, chapter 9, also notes this about the greater and lesser clergy of his age: "And, God and the multitude of the faithful being my witnesses, I remember having seen and heard of many priests, abbots and certain prelates so diminished that they did not even know how to speak grammatically correct Latin." He therefore urges that a general council be made up of non-priests, citing the example of the apostles and the authority of Isidore. How badly, then, do they consult the church who, neglecting learned laymen, decree that only clergy, often ignorant and unskilled, be sent to the synod! See more on this in Spalatensis, book 7, On the Ecclesiastical Commonwealth, chapter 3, throughout. If anyone wants the practice of the ancient church, even after the ambition of bishops grew strong, after discipline was corrupted and superstition introduced, he will find it fairly frequent. The traces of this custom are so clear that they could not be erased. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, in letter 81[?], desires a synod that does not consist only of bishops, but of "judges and others eminent in rank, skilled in divine matters." Marsilius of Padua, in the passage cited above, cites and approves the opinion of Isidore the merchant: "Then let laymen also enter, those who have deserved to take part in the council by election." Much more, then (Marsilius adds), should learned men who are experienced in divine law, although there are no priests present, take part.

units.la: Decretis secundi Concilii Arausicani illustres & magnifici viri subscripserunt, Magdeburg. Cent. 5. cap. 9. Concilio Colonien si habito 887. aderant laici, quorum consensu decreta concilii illius promulgantur. Concilio Metensi sub Arnulpho intererant plurimi Comites, viri nobiles & alii laici Deum timentes: initio primi capitis sic loquuntur patres. Episcopi, presbyteri & fideles laici qui ante nos fuerunt, juxta sacram canonum authoritatem sæpius in Christi nomine convenientes, justitiam Dei statuerunt, & idcirco suis diebus pacem habuerunt: Plura hujus generis apud Spalatensem libro & capite supra citatis exstant. Author revisionis Concilii Tridentini, licet Pontificius, tuetur tamen lib. 1. cap. 8. ab omni seculo post receptam Christianæ nominis professionem, laicis suffragium definitivum competivisse in conciliis: in cujus sententiæ confirmationem producit non solum testimonium Lucæ ex Act. c. 15. 23. Verumetiam Synodos Gallicanas, Hispanicas nationales satis frequenti numero. Concilio Constantiensi interfuerunt 24 Duces. 140 Comites, plurimi à civitatibus & Academicis delegati, juris Doctores & Professores, omnes Laici; Major & frequentior fuit Laicorum numerus in concilio primo Pisano. Si altius ascendere placeat ad Cypriani ætatem, videbis non solos Episcopos, presbyteros & diaconos conventibus ecclesiasticis interfuisse, verum etiam populum seu totum, seu ejus maximam partem. Denique (ut inquit Sutlivius Hierarchicus de conciliis l. 1. c. 8. parag. ult.) nulla lege aut consuetudine vel principes, & docti viri à suffragiis decisivis in concilio excluduntur: neq; aliquid contra eos investigari potest, licet omnes angulos perreptet Bellarminus, & quicunque post illû desperatæ hujus causæ patrocinium suscipiunt; Quare cum merè Laicis, donis & vocatione instructis, jus decisivi suffragii in quibuslibet Conciliis, etiam generalibus competere testentur authores hi, quo juris titulo ab eodem jure repellentur Seniores ecclesiarum? qui ratione officii Ecclesiasticis accensendi sunt, & non per contemptum tertio quoq; verbo Laici vocandi: Reformatarum Ecclesiarum praxin universalè hic non negligendam, & doctorum ejusdè, nobis palam συνωδίλων: quos si quis cum fastu repudiet, Augustini illud audiat, Qui contempta veritate præsumit consuetudinē sequi, aut circa fratres invidus est & maligrus quibus veritas revelatur, aut circa Deū ingratus cujus inspiratione ecclesia instruitur: Atq; hæc de exceptione.
units.tr: Illustrious and distinguished men subscribed to the decrees of the second Council of Arles (Magdeburg Centuries, century 5, chapter 9). At the Council of Cologne held in 887 laymen were present, and the decrees of that council were promulgated with their consent. At the council of Metz under Arnulf many counts, noble men and other laymen who feared God were present. At the beginning of the first chapter the fathers speak thus: "The bishops, presbyters and faithful laymen who came before us, gathering often in the name of Christ according to the authority of the sacred canons, established the justice of God, and for that reason they had peace in their days." Many more examples of this kind exist in the book and chapter of Spalatensis cited above. The author of the revision of the Council of Trent, though a Papist, nevertheless maintains (book 1, chapter 8) "that from every age after the profession of the Christian name was received, laymen have had a definitive vote in councils." To confirm this opinion he produces not only the testimony of Luke, Acts 15:23, but also the national synods of Gaul and Spain, which are quite frequent. At the Council of Constance there were present 24 dukes and 140 counts, very many delegates from cities and universities, doctors and professors of law, all laymen. The number of laymen was greater and more frequent at the first Council of Pisa. If one wishes to go back further, to the age of Cyprian, one will see that not only bishops, presbyters and deacons took part in ecclesiastical assemblies, but also the people, either the whole or the greater part of them. Finally (as Sutcliffe, Hierarchicus, on councils, book 1, chapter 8, last paragraph, says): "By no law or custom are princes and learned men excluded from decisive votes in council, nor can anything be found against them, even if Bellarmine and all who after him take up the defence of this desperate cause search every corner." Therefore, since these authors testify that laymen simply, equipped with gifts and a calling, have a right of decisive vote in any councils whatever, even general ones, by what legal title will the elders of the churches be shut out by that same right? They are to be counted among ecclesiastical persons by reason of their office, and are not to be called "laymen" with contempt, as the third word. The practice of the reformed churches should not be neglected here, and the agreement of its learned men is plain to us [συνῳδῶν]. If anyone disdainfully rejects them, let him hear that saying of Augustine: "Whoever, despising the truth, presumes to follow custom, is either envious of the brethren to whom the truth is revealed, or ungrateful towards God by whose inspiration the church is taught." So much for this objection.

units.la: Ad decimam, Quod synodus hæc sit pars adversa, &c. Repetenda hic sunt quę disputata fuerunt inter præsidem & D. Balcanquellum, sessione 7. Quibus addenda sunt sequentia. Cum synodum nationalem ut partem causæ suæ adversam recusent Episcopi, cur se Ecclesiæ Scoticæ membra vocant? quandoquidem synodus hæc per deputatos ecclesiarum, repræsentet omnes & singulas ecclesias Scoticas: quarum membra esse non possunt, qui omnes & singulas pro parte adversa habent: Dein synodus nationalis cum sit suprcsupremum tribunal ecclesiasticum, vesti tum suprema authoritate ecclesiasticas controversias determinandi, recusati nequit. Theologi magnæ Britanniæ in Synodo Dordtacena, aun.. 1618. 1619. Neque valent exceptiones contra supremum judicem productæ: Tertio, licet ante indictam synodum condemnarint deputati ecclesiarum de quibus in synodo postea erit agendum, fecerunt quod sui erat officii, hoc est, doctrinæ & disciplinæ primitus receptæ adhærentes, utramque corrumpentibus sese opposuerunt pro ratione muneris, quod omnibus pastoribus incumbit; quod non vetabit, si quid in contrarium ab Episcopis aut quolibet proferatur ex verbo Dei, quin mutato judicio libenter sint illud arrepturi. 4. Probari non potest, quidlibet à deputatis privatim condemnatum, quod non sint parati demonstrare jampridem damnatum fuisse in Ecclesia Scotica: Etenim Episcopatum simpliciter non prædamnarunt, sed an inter corruptiones ecclesiastici regiminis censeri debeat nec ne, ad synodi nationalis judicium retulerunt: Quinque illos articulos Perthenses non abjurarunt tum simpliciter, verum ab eorundem praxi se abstenturos usque dum Synodus declararet, an inter errores in confessione nationali damnatos referendi essent. Neque ullius valoris est quod afferunt de primis reformatoribus Concilii Tridentini judicium declinantibus, Nam præterquam quod usque adeo dispar sit utriusque synodi ratio, ut puderet quamlibet reformatam synodum cum impuro illo conciliabulo conferre, in qua judices Episcopi, servilia Papæ mancipia, judicii norma Pontificis voluntas, cui gratificando in omnibus juramento obstricti erant, quod ita religiose ab iis observatum, ut sententiam de rebus leviffimi momenti nullam ferre ausi fuerint, nisi prius tabellarii manticis inclusa Româ Tridentum mittetur: retur: Alia etiam est ratio priorum illorum reformatorum & horum Episcoporum: Nam reformati illi doctores non professi fuerunt unionem cum Ecclefia Pontificia quæ sola ibi repræsentabatur, cui jamdudum nuncium remiserant & res suas sibi habere jusserant, ut Synagogæ Antichristianæ; Episcopi autem hujus Ecclesiæ Scoticæ se membra esse profitentur; Quare si hoc exemplo causam suam promoveri cupiunt Episcopi, à communione hujus Ecclesiæ sese potius abscindant est necesse: Quod de quibusdam orthodoxis patribus, provincialibus, iisque ἀντεχόμενος synodis interesse renuentibus, male tractatur ad Episcopos nationalem legitimam hanc Synodum recusantes; præsertim citatos ut gravissimorum criminum infamia se purgent. At, inquiunt, Ecclesiarum deputati quorum judicium recusatur, declararunt se partem esse adversam, nulli autem tali permittitur esse judicem, quādoquidem sit in propria causa: Cui resp. Causam propter quam injus vocantur Episcopi, non esse pastorum propriam, sed totius ecclesiæ; Episcopos etiam anno 1600 pactos fuisse, se synodi nationalis ecclesiam repræsentantis judicio sese submissuros, si stipulatarum conditionum limites excederent. Quare cum pacto conventum sit ut pars offensa simul habeat judicatum, exceptio illa inter frivolas reponenda est. Ad 11. De odio illo hostili quo feruntur deputati in Episcopos ipsos, probationem* (inquiunt Synodici) desideramus; Verum quidem esse, libertatis vindices fœdus illud nationale laudabili majorum exemplo renovasse, sed non eo animo ut quempiam haberent, ne Episcopos quidem ipsos, si ab objectis criminibus se expedirent; fœdere itaque eo odii in vitia, non in homines, demonstratur. Quod ad libellum illum citatorium attinet, quo publice citabantur Episcopi; quem odii in Episcopos testem omni exceptione majorem dicunt.Respondet fynodus. Litteras illas citatorias criminum duo genera continere, alia de quibus fama clamosa, & flagrans ubique serpebat scandalum. Alia vero usque adeo notoria fuere,ut dubitatum fuerit in causa tam perspicue evidenti an testes essent producendi: & si cui scrupulus adhuc hæreat, facile eximetur hujus protestationis vel tumultuaria & perfunctoria lectione. Crimina personalia quædam evidenter probata Ecclesiarum deputatos ita tædio & pudore affecerunt, ut in cænosis istis sordibus diutius hærere, vix tutum putarent; quorundam etiam atrocium criminum objectorum Episcopis in litteris illis citatoriis omissa fuit probatio, partim temporis brevitate, partim quia testes longius aberant; non vero quasi conscientia nostra testaretur de ipsorum innocentia; etenim si ita constitutum sit Episcopis, ut velint ulteriorem de his instituí[?] examinationem, per nosquidem licebit,sed verendum ne accusationem exarmare non possint:At inquies, quicquid sit de istis criminibus ; cur publicè in omnibus regni fere templis prælectus fuit ille libellus ? nequaquam certè ut eorum flagitia populo innotescerent ; quibus plus satis manifesta antea fuerunt, verum quia Episcoporum aliis absentibus,aliis in obscuro latentibus, modus hic citandi tutissimus videretur,& pane unicus, Deputato regio renuente Episcopos citare, ut defectu scil. citationis censuram effugerent: neque est quod hic paratragædientur, lædi fraternam charitatem, contemni monitum Apostoli & cæt.ut sibi misericordiam,& nobis hostibus (quos vocant)odium conflent:Etenim multitudinem peccatorum sic operit discreta charitas,ut justitiæ suum etiam locum tribuat, quæ publica & flagrantia crimina publice redargui jubet , Salus etiam ecclesiæ totius quin omnibus charior esse debeat turbonum & seductorum fama, nullus dubitat. Monitum illud Apostoli Seniorem ne increpato, praescribere modum privatae correptionis erga ætate seniores, non vero publicæ; nam publice peccans publice corripiendus est, cujuscunque demum fuerit ætatis: ne-que ullam dignitatis diminutionem passum esse quodlibet ordinum regni membrum; cum contra Episcopos, non contra Episcopatum instituta sit accusatio: sed de hoc prius in responsione ad excep-tionem quartā. Falsum etiam esse dicunt, Episco-poscitatos super inquirendis ut vocant, nam speciali crimina ubique designabantur, quæ nulla tergiver-satione celari possunt. Ternas citationes omissas quæruntur, sed frustra, quandoquidem ordinaria praxi restringantur ad inferiora tribunalia sola quæ stata & frequentius habentur, neque ullo modo consistere possint cum supremis; præsertim cum synodo nationali, quæ cum singulis annis semel solum ordinarie habeatur; reis triennii impunitatem concederet. Sed cur quæso hac exceptione utuntur Episcopi? An ut se non citatos causentur; at protestatio hæc ante synodum apertam compositā, & ab iis subscripta qui extra limites regni jam degunt, eorum-que nomine synodo exhibita docent, citationis illius minime fuisse ignaros: Citatio vero (ut inquiunt Iurisperiti) contumaciam inducere potest, si scientia citationis apprehenderit citatum, atque ita comperiatur malitiose aut dolose latitare: Ejusdem farinæ est cum objiciunt citationes ab eo foro (vid. synodo) in quo causa disceptanda est; debere emanare: nam ut ut locū habeat hæc exceptio in foro inferiori & subalterno, nequaquam in supremo procedere potest: neque unquam in ecclesiastico judicio ulla illius habita fuit ratio, nam cui incognitum perpetuam hanc esse hujus ecclesiæ praxin, ut legitime ad classem seu presbyterium citatus habeatur, quem citavit seniorum confessus seu consistorium, & ad synodum tum provincialem tum nationalem, quem citavit presbyterium; a solis Episcopis hoc primum in dubium vocari constat: ut defectu insolitæ & inauditæ solennitatis ab omni censura synodica se liberent: Denique excipiunt contra libellum illum citatorium, quod omnes συνοδικῶς[?] citet, & singulis omnium accusationes impingat: Cui respondet Synodus. Illud factum fuisse quia omnes simul in unam factionem conspirarunt, ac quorundam criminum specialiter designatorum pariter omnes rei essent: additam tamen clausulam fuisse, vid. Respectivè quà declaratur omnium criminum reos non esse singulos. Ad 12. Episcopis qua talibus, ab Ecclesiis ad synodum non delegatis, jus suffragii non competere, decretum fuit expresse: in synodo ad Montem Rosarum ann. 1600.[?] & anno 1597. cautum fuit, ut quicunque seu pastores, seu seniores ex provincialibus ecclesiis deputati essent, à presbyteriis delegarentur: qui duo Canones nondum rescinduntur, nec rescindi debent; quia in jure naturali fundantur, & in continua aliarum reformatarum ecclesiarum praxi sunt, apud quas ii soli ad definitiva suffragia admittuntur qui ab ecclesiis legitime mittuntur: quia scilicet ecclesiam repræsentat synodus, quare qui ab Ecclesiis ad synodum deputati non sunt, ecclesiam nullam repræsentare possunt: nisi forte cum Bellarmino dicant repræsentari ecclesias ab Episcopis, sicut Respub. à principe: cujus crassam absurditatem multis explodit argumentis Whitakerus de conciliis controverf. 3. quæst. 3. Adde quod receptum sit apud omnes Reformatæ Ecclesiæ doctores, oportere eos quibus definiendi in synodis partes committuntur donis necessariis & justa vocatione instructos esse; justa autem vocatio quæ sit, explicant, ut vid. ab Ecclesia electi, & ad id munus specialiter designati sint: fine qua nefas erit publici ministerii munera obire in synodis: Si vocationem hanc habeant Episcopi, cur ejus tabulas non proferunt, si ad veterum conciliorum praxin confugiant, meminisse debuerunt, veritati à nemine præscribi posse; neque ad exemplar eorum conciliorum formandas esse Scoticæ ecclesiæ Synodos, utpote quod hierarchiam illam humano consilio in ecclesiam olim introducam, quia Antichristo viam stravit; penitus exstirpaverit; nec probari potest in qualibet libera synodo postmodum restitutam esse, licet vanis dignitatum istarum titulis sese jactent nostrates: Ad 13. merito primatibus & metropolitanis, &c. denegari ab hac synodo præsidentiam ecclesiasticam: cum in politia hujus ecclesiæ cautum sit, ut in omnibus conventibus ecclesiasticis præses communi fratrum consensu eligeretur: libertatemque hanc illibatam mansisse, usque dum anno 1616. in Pseudosynodo Abredonensi, sese præsidem obtrufisset Andreapolitanus Archiepiscopus, sine ulla juris aut receptæ consuetudinis specie, nec est quod hoc sine exemplo fieri clament, cum in frequentissima synodo Antiochena sub Galieno & Aureliano Imperatoribus contra Paulum Samosatenum habita præsidisse Malchionem presbyterum Antiochenum, etiam multis Episcopis præsentibus testentur historiæ Ecclesiasticæ Magdeburgensium. Nam quod de Niceni, & Antiocheni Concilii Canonibus, ut & Justiniani Novella citant, nihil ad quæstionem facit; cum veterum Conciliorum illorum ἐφεσινῶν, de disciplina Capitula apud reformatas omnes ecclesias, in desuetudinem venerint, neque Justiniani aut cujuslibet exteri principis statuta politica, Ecclesiæ Scoticæ, quæ ejus legibus non gubernatur, præscribere possunt: neque libertatem hanc legibus regni nunicipalibus munitam, eripere. Si hoc sibi jure competere petere demonstrante vellent Episcopi, ex verbo Dei, aut constitutionibus ecclesiasticis probandum quibus licet penitus destituti sunt, ne tamen sine aliqua saltem rationis specie insanire viderentur; citant Acta Parlamentaria anni 1606. & 1609. quibus Episcoporum restitutio in integrum (ut loquuntur) sancitur: At si statuta illa diligentius evolvissent, viderent fuisse restitutionem saecularium dignitatum, reddituum, ac privilegiorum temporalium in repub. nulla prorsus Ecclesiasticae dignitatis mentione facta: quod inde constat, quia ut ordinationis & jurisdictionis potestate eminerent, cogendae fuerunt postea Synodi, anno 1606. & 1610, in quibus tamen praesidentiam hanc nunquam arripere ausi fuerunt; gnari scilicet nullis fidiculis, ex statutis illis unquam erui posse, memores etiam Pseudosynodum illam Limnuthensem anno 1606, diserte constituisse, Ut nationalis synodi praeses, ecclesiae deputatorum in synodo suffragiis eligeretur: Quod contraria illa constitutione ecclesiastica in hodiernum usque diem, antiquatum non esse Episcopis compertum est; Itaque relictis statutis parlamentariis, & Synodalibus constitutionibus, ex quibus praesidentiam hanc tam facile elicies quam aquam ex pumice: Ad jus divinum se conferunt, & à Christo solo [illegible, ~9 letters] hanc & exortam potestatem sibi concessam dicunt, cui soli acceptum ferunt quicquid spiritualis eminentiae qua in reliquum clerum vestiti sunt: Sic scilicet in pejus solent proficere, popularium suorum in Anglia exemplo audentiores facti, qui inter [illegible, ~9 letters] tuentur hierarchiam suam esse juris divini: quod paradoxum citius amputationibus quam disputationibus confirmabunt: hisce ducibus, quem diris olim detestati fuerant Episcopatum, postea tolerabilem; nunc necessarium non solum jure Apostolico, verum & divino; quod cum tam confidenter crepent, cur ex divinorum testamentorum tabulis locum nullum producunt, ex quibus solis quæ juris divini sunt, intelligi possunt, fatentibus ipsis Canonistis qui Ius divinum esse dicunt quod continetur in lege & evangelio, atque immutabile semper permanet, lib. 1. Iure Canon. tit. 2. & quas solas, perfectum & omni numero absolutum controversiarum ecclesiasticarum judicem agnoscunt qui cumque ex animo Synagogæ Romanæ nuncium remiserunt: Nec dubitandum quin si quid ex his in causæ suæ patrocinium adferre potuissent, statim produxissent, nisi forte ex eorum numero sint, qui ut alibi sic hic Cassandri vestigia religiose premunt; importuna antiquitatis & Catholicorum traditionum admiratione capti, in quibus jus divinum fundari asserant; de quibus verè nimis vaticinatum fuisse Clariss. Chamierum, miser ecclesiarum statum hodiernus docet: Nisi (inquit) horum semipapistarum conatus compescat Deus, verendum ne id perficiatur, non ut sint papistæ correctiores, sed ut nos simus corruptiores: Quibus antiqui patris tam veram quam seve[?]ram si reposueris censuram, Diaboli cum vid. esse, extra divini scripturarum authoritatem, aliquid divinum putare: pro singulari quo in antiquitatem & patres feruntur studio, æquius ferent: sed de hisce alias. Interim, licet à Christo vocationem habeant ad Episcopatus, qua tamen authoritate ipsis hactenus licuit jurisdictionem illam episcopalem exercere in Ecclesia Scotica, cum illius erectioni nunquam consenserit, nec eam seu Synodis ecclesiam repræsentantibus, seu parlamentariis regni statutis acceptam ferunt; pro usurpatoribus habendi sunt, ob quod inter alia crimina in jus vocantur: Sed legitimam (dicunt Episcopi) vocationem habemus, per liberam Capituli electionem, & Episcopalem consecrationem, per regis consensum; secundum laudata statuta&c antiquā regni hujus confuetudinē. Respondet Synodus. Si per statuta illa& antiquam consuetudinem, intelligant leges crassissimis papismi temporibus sancitas, & morem tum observatum; lubenter seiis legum illarum patrocinium concedere; verum hac postica usurpationis crimen non effugient, cum leges illae omnes saepius refixae sint, & posterioribus statutis rescissae; Posteriora autem derogant prioribus; Ostendant etiam vel ex corruptissimis synodis Ecclesiae Scoticae, umbram minimam, qua Episcoporum electio Capitulo mandetur, aut ulla consecrationis Episcopalis mentio levissima facta sit: contra diserte in Synodis damnantur Capitula illa cathedralia, & Episcoporum per eadem electio: tanquam praxes Pontificiae, Nugae porro sunt de libera electione per capitulum, nam electio omnis proprie comparativa est, qua a pluribus unus eligitur, cujus tamen nullam rationem hic habere possunt eligentes si maxime vellent: nam in electione per Capitulum quem rex per litteras nominat Episcopum eligendum, hunc solum possunt ad Episcopatum evehere: Capitulo nihil hic relictum, praeter simplicem consensum, quem principum commendationibus, quorum preces sunt armatae, negare neutiquam audebunt: Nulla hic vel levissima ratio habetur populi quem partes suas temporibus antiquis habuisse in Episcoporum electionibus nullus hierarchicorum negabit: sic electum fuisse Cornelium Episcopum Romanum testatur Cyprianus, & alios sui temporis Episcopos, nec aliter eligi debere, cum ex divina ordinatione discendat ut ipsa plebs maxime potestatem habeat vel eligendi dignos sacerdotes, vel indignos recusandi: Ubi ille Canon, inquit Athanasius, ut a palatio mitteretur Episcopus. Si quis plura in imaginariam hanc & ligatam electionis speciem desid[?]eret consulet Spalatenfem de repub.lib, 3.c.3.Quare cum legitima hac Cleri & populi electione, quæ Cypriani temporibus floruit, destituti sint Episcopi, ac nihil solidi in medium afferre possint quo usurpationis crimen eluant, cum per fas & nefas ecclesiarum libertates invaserint ac nihil minus quam quod Cypriani ætate Episcopos decebat, faciant, non est quod Cypriani illa sententia utantur: Audiant potius magnum illum Nazianzenum, de πρεσβεια[?] & philarchia Episcoporum. Propter hanc (inquit) res omnes nostrae jaftantur & concutiuntur, propter hanc fines orbis terrae versantur in fufpitione, & bello, eoque surdo, & ne nomen quidem habente: propter hanc periculum est ne magnum illud & NOVVM nomen amittamus, utinam neque effet praesidentia, neque loci prelatio, neque violenta praeeminentia, ut ex sola virtute cognosceremur. Nunc autem dextrum hoc latus & sinistrum, sublimior & inferior sedes, & illa praecundi vel eodem gradu incedendi invecta consuetudo multas nobis clades nequicquam intulerunt,&c. quæ sequuntur: Quod autem fit magnum illud & Novum nomen, explicabit Augustinus, epist. 19. ad Hieronymum: Secundum honorum vocabula quæ jam Ecclesiæ usus obtinuit, Episcopatus presbytero major est. De Episcopatu vero loquitur qui suo sæculo, non re sed titulo, non potestate sed honore à presbyteratu differebat: Quid dicturus si typhum sæculi Episcoporum tyrannide in Ecclesiam invectum hodie cerneret.
units.tr: To the tenth objection, "that this synod is a party to the cause," etc. What was argued between the moderator and Mr. Balcanquhal in the seventh session must be repeated here, and the following must be added. If the bishops refuse the national synod as a party adverse to their cause, why do they call themselves members of the Scottish Church? For this synod, through the deputies of the churches, represents all and each of the Scottish churches, and those who regard all and each of them as a party adverse to themselves cannot be members of them. Next, since the national synod is the highest ecclesiastical tribunal, endowed with supreme authority to determine ecclesiastical controversies, it cannot be refused. The divines of Great Britain at the Synod of Dort, in 1618 and 1619, did the same. Nor do the objections raised against this supreme judge have any force. Third, although the deputies of the churches, whose judgment is now being discussed, condemned certain things before the synod was called, and the synod will deal with them later, they did what belonged to their office. That is, adhering to the doctrine and discipline first received, they opposed those who corrupt either, as their duty as ministers requires of all pastors. This will not prevent them, if anything to the contrary is brought forward by the bishops or by anyone else from the Word of God, from gladly changing their judgment and embracing it. (4) It cannot be proved that anything was condemned by the deputies in private, which they are not ready to show was condemned long ago in the Scottish Church. For they did not simply condemn episcopacy outright, but referred to the judgment of the national synod the question whether it ought to be counted among the corruptions of ecclesiastical government or not. They did not simply renounce the five Articles of Perth, but promised to abstain from their practice until the synod declared whether they should be counted among the errors condemned in the national confession. Nor is there any worth in what they allege about the first reformers who declined the judgment of the Council of Trent. For, apart from the fact that the procedure of the two synods is so unlike that any reformed synod would be ashamed to be compared with that impure conventicle, where the judges were bishops, servile slaves of the Pope, whose will was the rule of judgment, and who were bound by oath to gratify him in everything (an oath so religiously observed that they dared to pass no sentence even on matters of the slightest importance unless the decision had first been sent from Rome to Trent in a courier's bag), the position of those first reformers and of these bishops is also different. For those reformed teachers did not profess union with the Papal Church, which alone was represented there, and to which they had long since sent word and bid it keep its own affairs, as they would a synagogue of Antichrist. But the bishops of this Scottish Church profess themselves to be its members. Therefore, if the bishops desire their cause to be advanced by this example, they must of necessity cut themselves off from communion with this Church. What is said about certain orthodox fathers, provincial synods, and those who refused to attend synods, adhering to them, is wrongly applied to bishops who refuse this lawful national synod, especially since they have been summoned to clear themselves of the infamy of most grave crimes. But, they say, the deputies of the churches, whose judgment is refused, have declared themselves a party adverse to the bishops, and no such person may be judge, since no one may judge in his own cause. To this we reply: the cause for which the bishops are summoned to judgment is not the cause of the ministers alone, but of the whole Church. Moreover, the bishops agreed in 1600 that they would submit themselves to the judgment of the national synod, which represents the Church, if they exceeded the limits of the stipulated conditions. Therefore, since it was agreed by pact that the offended party should also hold the judgment, that exception must be counted among the frivolous ones. (11) As to the hostile hatred with which the deputies are said to be borne against the bishops themselves, the synodists say, "We demand proof." It is true that the defenders of liberty renewed that national covenant following the praiseworthy example of their ancestors, but not with the intention of having any man as an enemy, not even the bishops themselves, if they cleared themselves of the crimes laid against them. The covenant therefore shows hatred of vices, not of men. As for that citatory libel by which the bishops were publicly summoned, which they call a witness of hatred against them beyond all exception, the synod answers: those citatory letters contain two kinds of crimes. Some were such that clamorous report and blazing scandal crept about everywhere. Others were so notorious that, in a cause so plainly evident, it was doubted whether witnesses should even be produced. And if anyone still has scruples, they will easily be removed by a hasty and cursory reading of that protest. Certain personal crimes, plainly proved, so filled the deputies of the churches with weariness and shame that they thought it hardly safe to linger long in those filthy muck-heaps. In some of the atrocious crimes laid against the bishops, proof was omitted in those citatory letters, partly from the shortness of time and partly because the witnesses were far away. This was not as if our conscience bore witness to their innocence. Indeed, if the bishops are content that a further examination of these matters be instituted, it will be allowed by us, though we fear they may not be able to disarm the accusation. But you will say: whatever the truth of those crimes, why was that libel read publicly in almost all the churches of the kingdom? Certainly not so that their shameful deeds might become known to the people, which were already more than sufficiently manifest, but because, since some bishops were absent and others lay hidden, this mode of summoning seemed safest, and almost the only one, the royal deputy refusing to summon the bishops, so that they might escape censure through lack of summons. Nor is there reason here for pompous complaints that fraternal charity is wounded, the admonition of the Apostle despised, and so on, that they may gain mercy for themselves and hatred for us, whom they call enemies. For discreet charity covers the multitude of sins in such a way that it also gives justice its place, which orders public and blazing crimes to be publicly reproved. No one doubts that the safety of the whole Church, and indeed the reputation of disturbers and seducers, ought to be dearer to all. The Apostle's admonition, "Rebuke not an elder," prescribes the manner of private correction towards those older in years, not public correction. For one who sins publicly must be publicly rebuked, whatever his age may be. Nor has any member of any order of the kingdom suffered any diminution of dignity, since the accusation was instituted against the bishops, not against episcopacy. But of this more has been said in the reply to the fourth exception. They also say it is false that the bishops were summoned "to inquiry," as they put it. For specific crimes were named everywhere, which cannot be concealed by any evasion. They complain that three citations were omitted, but in vain. For, by ordinary practice, such citations are restricted to the lower tribunals alone, which are held regularly and more often, and can in no way be consistent with the supreme ones, especially with a national synod, which is held ordinarily only once a year, and which would grant the accused a triennial impunity. But why, I ask, do the bishops use this exception? Is it so that they may complain they were not summoned? But that protest, drawn up before the synod opened and subscribed by those who now live beyond the borders of the kingdom, and presented to the synod in their name, shows that they were by no means ignorant of that citation. "A citation, however" (as the jurists say), "can produce contumacy if the cited person has knowledge of the citation, and it is thus found that he hides maliciously or fraudulently." Of the same kind is the objection that citations must issue from the court (namely, the synod) in which the cause is to be pleaded. For although this exception may hold in a lower and subordinate court, it can by no means proceed in a supreme one. Nor was any regard ever had for it in ecclesiastical judgment. For who does not know that the constant practice of this Church is that one is legitimately held cited to the classis or presbytery by the one who cites him, the session or consistory of the elders, and to the provincial or national synod by the presbytery who cites him? It is clear that only the bishops have first called this into doubt, so that by the lack of an unusual and unheard-of solemnity they might free themselves from all synodical censure. Finally, they object against that citatory libel that it cites all "synodically" and fastens the accusations on each of them individually. The synod replies: this was done because they had all conspired together into one faction, and because all were equally accused of certain specifically named crimes. Yet a clause was added, namely the phrase "respectively," by which it is declared that they are not each the guilty party of all the crimes. (12) It was expressly decreed that bishops, as such, not delegated to the synod by the churches, have no right of voting. At the synod of Montrose in 1600, and in 1597, it was provided that whoever were deputed from the provincial churches, whether ministers or elders, should be delegated by the presbyteries. These two canons have not been rescinded, nor ought they to be; for they are founded in natural law, and are in the continuing practice of the other reformed churches, where only those are admitted to decisive votes who are lawfully sent by the churches. For the synod represents the Church, and therefore those who have not been deputed to the synod by the churches cannot represent any church. Unless perhaps they say with Bellarmine that the churches are represented by bishops as the commonwealth is by the prince. The gross absurdity of this is exploded by Whitaker in many arguments, On Councils, controversy 3, question 3. Add to this that it is received among all the teachers of the reformed churches that those to whom the task of deciding in synods is committed must be furnished with the necessary gifts and with a just calling. What a just calling is, they explain: that they be chosen by the Church and specially designated for that office, without which it will be wicked to discharge the offices of public ministry in synods. If the bishops have this calling, why do they not produce its documents? If they flee to the practice of the ancient councils, they ought to remember that no one can prescribe to the truth, nor are the synods of the Scottish Church to be formed on the pattern of those councils, since that hierarchy, once introduced into the Church by human counsel, paved the way for Antichrist and was thoroughly rooted out. Nor can it be proved that it was later restored in any free synod, however our countrymen may boast with the empty titles of those dignities. (13) It is rightly denied by this synod to primates and metropolitans, etc., to hold ecclesiastical presidency. For it is provided in the polity of this Church that in all ecclesiastical assemblies the moderator shall be chosen by the common consent of the brethren. This liberty remained unimpaired until 1616, when at the pseudo-synod of Aberdeen the Archbishop of St Andrews thrust himself into the presidency, with no appearance of right or received custom. Nor is there reason for them to cry that this was done without precedent, since the most crowded synod of Antioch, held under the emperors Gallienus and Aurelian against Paul of Samosata, was presided over by Malchion, presbyter of Antioch, as the Magdeburg Centuriators testify in their Ecclesiastical History, even with many bishops present. For what they cite from the canons of the Councils of Nicaea and Antioch, and likewise from Justinian's Novels, has nothing to do with the question. For the chapters of those ancient Ephesine councils concerning discipline have fallen into disuse in all the reformed churches. Nor can the political statutes of Justinian or of any foreign prince prescribe to the Scottish Church, which is not governed by his laws, nor take away this liberty, which is protected by the municipal laws of the kingdom. If the bishops wished to demonstrate from the Word of God or from ecclesiastical constitutions that they have this right, which they are wholly destitute of, then, so as not to seem to rave without some appearance at least of reason, they cite the Acts of Parliament of 1606 and 1609, by which the restoration of the bishops "to their integrity," as they put it, was sanctioned. But if they had unrolled those statutes more carefully, they would see that what was restored was secular dignities, revenues, and temporal privileges in the commonwealth, with no mention at all of ecclesiastical dignity. This is clear from the fact that synods had afterwards to be compelled, in 1606 and 1610, so that the bishops might stand out in the power of ordination and jurisdiction. Yet in those synods they never dared to seize this presidency, knowing well that it could never be drawn from those statutes by any cords, and also mindful that the pseudo-synod of Linlithgow in 1606 had expressly enacted that the president of the national synod should be elected by the votes of the deputies of the churches in the synod. That this ecclesiastical constitution, contrary to them, has not been abrogated down to the present day is known to the bishops. Therefore, leaving aside the parliamentary statutes and the synodal constitutions, from which they could draw this presidency as easily as water from a pumice stone, they betake themselves to divine right, and say that this power was conceded to them by Christ alone [illegible, about nine letters], and that they owe to Him alone whatever spiritual eminence they are clothed with over the rest of the clergy. Thus, as usually happens, they grow worse, having become bolder by the example of their fellows in England, who maintain that their hierarchy is of divine right. They will confirm this paradox more quickly with amputations than with disputations. Under these leaders, episcopacy, which they once detested with dire curses, and later tolerated, is now declared necessary, not only by apostolic right but by divine right. Since they boast so confidently, why do they not produce a single passage from the tablets of the divine testaments, from which alone what is of divine right can be understood? The canonists themselves admit this, who say that divine right is "what is contained in law and gospel and remains always unchangeable" (Canon Law, book 1, title 2). And these same men acknowledge as the only perfect and fully complete judge of ecclesiastical controversies the Scriptures, which they have renounced on behalf of the Roman synagogue. Nor is there doubt that if they could have brought anything from them in defence of their cause, they would have produced it at once, unless perhaps they are among those who, here as elsewhere, religiously tread in the footsteps of Cassander, captivated by an importunate admiration of antiquity and of Catholic traditions, on which they assert that divine right is founded. The present wretched state of the churches shows that the most illustrious Chamier prophesied truly, and too truly, about these matters. "Unless God," he says, "restrains the endeavours of these semi-Papists, it is to be feared that it will come to pass, not that the Papists may be made more correct, but that we may be made more corrupt." If you set against them the judgment of an ancient father, as true as it is severe, "It is of the devil to regard anything as divine outside the divine authority of the Scriptures," they will take it with less favour, for all their singular zeal for antiquity and the fathers. But of these matters elsewhere. Meanwhile, even if they have a calling from Christ to the episcopacy, by what authority has it hitherto been lawful for them to exercise that episcopal jurisdiction in the Scottish Church, since it never consented to its erection, and they do not claim it either from synods representing the Church or from the parliamentary statutes of the kingdom? They must be held as usurpers, for which crime, among others, they are summoned to judgment. But the bishops say, "We have a lawful calling, through the free election of the chapter and episcopal consecration by the king's consent, according to the statutes cited and the ancient custom of this kingdom." The synod replies: if by those statutes and the ancient custom they mean laws sanctioned in the grossest times of Popery, and the custom then observed, we would gladly grant them the protection of those laws. But they will not escape the crime of usurpation by this later plea, since all those laws were often revoked and rescinded by later statutes, and later statutes derogate from earlier ones. Let them show, even from the most corrupt synods of the Scottish Church, the least shadow of a commission of the election of bishops to the chapter, or the faintest mention of any episcopal consecration. On the contrary, those cathedral chapters and the election of bishops through them are expressly condemned in the synods as Popish practices. Idle too is their talk of free election by the chapter, for every election is properly comparative, by which one is chosen from several, yet the electors could have no regard for this here even if they wished to. For in an election by the chapter the one whom the king names by letter as bishop to be elected is the only one they can raise to the episcopate. Nothing is left to the chapter here except a bare consent, which they will by no means dare to refuse to the recommendations of princes, whose prayers are armed. Here no regard is had, even the slightest, for the people, whose part in the election of bishops in ancient times no hierarchist will deny. Thus Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome, as Cyprian testifies, and other bishops of his time; and they ought not to be elected otherwise, since it is learned from divine ordinance that the people themselves have the greatest power either to choose worthy priests or to refuse unworthy ones. "Where is that canon," says Athanasius, "that a bishop should be sent from the palace?" If anyone desires more on this imaginary and bound species of election, let him consult the Spalatensis, On the Commonwealth, book 3, chapter 3. Therefore, since the bishops are destitute of that lawful election by clergy and people which flourished in the times of Cyprian, and can bring forward nothing solid by which to wash away the crime of usurpation, since they have invaded the liberties of the churches by right and wrong alike, and do nothing less than what befitted bishops in the age of Cyprian, there is no reason for them to use that saying of Cyprian's. Let them rather hear that great Nazianzen on the precedence (presbeia) and love of rule (philarchia) of bishops: "Because of this," he says, "all our affairs are shaken and tossed about; because of this the ends of the earth are in suspicion, and at war, and that a deaf war, which does not even have a name. Because of this there is danger that we lose that great and NEW name. Would that there were neither presidency, nor preference of place, nor violent pre-eminence, so that we might be known by virtue alone. But now this right side and left side, the higher and lower seat, and that custom introduced of going before or walking in the same rank, have brought upon us many disasters in vain," etc. What that great and new name is, Augustine will explain, in letter 19 to Jerome: "According to the terms of honour which the use of the Church has now established, the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate." But he speaks of an episcopate which in his own age differed from the presbyterate not in reality but in title, not in power but in honour. What would he say if he saw today the pride of the bishops of this age, brought into the Church by the tyranny of bishops?

units.la: Ad 14. Non negat synodus permissione Ecclesiasticæ ordinationis potestatem Episcopis antiquis concessam fuisse; inde tamen non sequi affirmant, eandem potestatem commissione Dominica hodiernis Pseudo-Episcopis solis in Scotia competere: Dein si non possint Episcopi à pastoribus judicari, quia ab iis ordinati fuerunt, nec potuere presbyteri Alexandrinæ ecclesiæ ab ipsorum Episcopo judijudicari, utpote quem ordinarunt, si Hieronymo fides habenda, qui de Alexandrinæ ecclesiæ presbyteris testatur, eos semper unum ex se electum, & in ex-celsiore gradu collocatum, Episcopum nominasse, vel hoc unum os obstruere posset, mira confidentia perpetuum antiquitatis consensum obtendentibus, quod soli Episcopo ordinationis jus adjudicatum sit: denique quia olim à presbyteris judicati non fuerunt Episcopi, ideo in Ecclesia Scotica idem fieri debet; quæ omnes Ecclesiasticos nationalis synodi judicio subjectos declarat, est eorum argumentum qui politiam ecclesiæ relictis constitutionibus receptis, ad inveteratam consuetudinem revocare volunt: Et mera principii petitio: nam quis concedet consuetudinem præsentem ab incunabulis reformationis semper frequentatam, obtentu antiqui alicujus canonis abolendam esse. Ac ne omne judicium subterfugere exstimentur Episcopi, ab iis judicari petunt, à quibus veterum quorundam conciliorum Canones, Episcopos judicandos statuerunt: quæ omnia frustra sunt; cum (ut sæpius dictum) synodus hæc, ordinanda non fit ad exemplar eorum temporum; etenim si in ecclesiasticorum judiciis, omnia ad veterum conciliorum amussim exigenda sint, tum nullus episcopus legitime condemnabitur, nisi coram 12. episcopis: accusatione probata 72. testibus idoneis: Causa 2. quæst. 5. Canone. Nullam damnationem, & Præsul non damnetur, & ne antiquitatem desideres, referuntur hæc ad Synodum Romanam, sub Sylvestro Pontifice, regnante Constantino Magno habitam: quo etiam inclinant Episcopi, citatione Concilii 2. Carthaginensi can. 10. Si ad has formas judicia institui appetunt Episcopi, quando unquam causam tanquam rei dicturi sunt? nam in nationali Synodo formalitates hæ nunquam inveniendæ sunt; quarum defectu Censuram omnem evadent: quod ipsorum unicus scopus est.
units.tr: To the fourteenth point: The synod does not deny that the power of ecclesiastical ordination was granted to the ancient bishops by permission, but they affirm that it does not follow that the same power belongs by the Lord's commission to the present pseudo-bishops alone in Scotland. Next, if bishops cannot be judged by ministers because they were ordained by them, then neither could the elders of the Alexandrian church be judged by their bishop, since he was ordained by them. If we may trust Jerome, who testifies of the elders of the Alexandrian church that they always chose one from among themselves, placed him in a higher rank, and called him bishop, this one point could silence them, though they put forward their remarkable confidence in a perpetual consensus of antiquity, namely that the right of ordination was granted to the bishop alone. Finally, the bishops argue that because bishops were not formerly judged by elders, the same should be done in the Scottish Church. But this argument, which declares all ecclesiastics subject to the judgment of the national synod, belongs to those who, having set aside the constitutions received, want to recall the church's polity to an long-established custom. It is a mere begging of the question: for who will grant that a present custom, which has been constantly observed since the beginnings of the Reformation, should be abolished on the pretext of some ancient canon? And lest the bishops seem to escape all judgment, they ask to be judged by those whom the canons of certain ancient councils declared should judge bishops. All of this is vain, since (as has often been said) this synod is not to be ordered according to the model of those times. For if all the judgments of the church were to be measured by the rule of the ancient councils, then no bishop could be lawfully condemned except before twelve bishops, with the charge proved by seventy-two suitable witnesses (Causa 2, quaest. 5, canon: Let no condemnation be made, and let a prelate not be condemned). And that you may not look for antiquity, these matters are referred to the Roman synod held under Pope Sylvester, in the reign of Constantine the Great, to which the bishops also incline, citing the Second Council of Carthage, canon 10. If the bishops seek to have judgments instituted in these forms, when will they ever be going to answer as accused persons? For in a national synod these formalities are never to be found, and by their absence they would escape every censure, which is their one aim.

units.la: Quare cum omnes hæ exceptiones frivolæ sint; Protestationes ipsorum scripto subjunctæ ejusdem generis sunt; Quod ad illam clausulam, de necessitate regiminis ecclesiastici per Episcopos, mirari se dicit Synodus hominum impudentiam: quiillud necessarium vocant; cujus necessitatem nullo apice Scripturæ unquam demonstrare aggressi fuerunt hierarchicorum ἀναγκαῖον. Nam nec necessarium est ἀπλῶς & absolute cum Ecclesiæ floruerint, in quibus Episcoporum ἐξουσία sic dictorum nulla mentio, necnomen ratione utilitatis; tum quia ἐξουσία hæc Episcoporum licet sincero animo primitus instituta fuerit à patribus, viam tamen iis minime advertentibus stravit ambitioni, uti Nazianzenum graviter differentè audivimus, quid vero dicturum fuisse arbitremur, si sæculis postmodum secutis, atque adeo nostro hoc in Scotia vixisset, ubi malorum omnium lerna ambitio omnes modestiæ limites transgressa est, nunc etiam fremens, quando se in ordinem ac intra cancellos copi animadvertit ne in ecclesiam diutius grassetur: sed quid dico Ambitioni, Cæcus est qui hac patentem portam Antichristo apertam esse non videt: nam politia ecclesiæ Aristocratica; quæ Apostolico sæculo viguit, consensione perpetui primatus ordinis uni presbyterorum, paulatim mutata est in oligarchiam: qua paucí illi potestatis supereminentiam sibi arripuerant, ac tandem in tyrannidem unius œcumenici. An vero utilis exstiterit procurandæ Ecclesiarum paci, vel hujus laceræ ecclesiæ luctuosissima facies indicet; quæ σωτηρία illa ἀλλάγμα in schismatis remedium humano consilio primitus institutam, ejusdem veriffimum fomitem à primo quo obtrudi cœpit momento experta est; nihil etenim quod ita ecclesiam divellere posset, quam præsidendi ambitio: quod in Pontifice Romano ad primatum suum vendicandum, nimis conspicuum est; cujus caput aliis quam Episcopalibus humeris niti non potest: Risum etiam vel Democrito moveat quod se hanc protestationem exhibere dicant nomine ecclesiæ Scoticæ, quasi vero sex Episcopi, (nam cæterorum subscriptio non exstat) cum paucis pastoribus asseclis, iisque vel largitionibus corruptis, aut minis territis, vel falsis narrationibus deceptis, uti complures eorum cum lachrymis ingenue agnoverunt, Ecclesiam Scoticam constituant: Cujus authoritatem, & synodos omnes legitime hactenus habitas portentosis hujusmodi protestationibus annihilare conantur; Sollicitos se jam declarant ne quid in hac synodo determinetur, quod libertati hujus ecclesiæ, dignitati regiæ, aut vicinis reformatis ecclesiis damnum aut infamiam creare posset: quorum licet nullam rationem Episcopos hactenus habuisse nimis liquido constet: importune tamen hæc ingerunt, ut oblique synodum perstringant, & in serenissimi regis ac vicinarum ecclesiarum odium immeritum trahant; cum synodo nunquam statutum sit, dignitatem & authoritatem regiam vellicare; aut infamiæ notam aliquam vicinis Ecclesiis inurere; quæ pro æquitate sua haud ægre ferent, si ecclesia hæc ad primævam reformationis suæ puritatem aspirans; quæ cum ipsius laudabilibus constitutionibus consistere non posse deprehendentur, rejicienda censeat, licet ab aliis forte recepta sint, quibus uti nihil præscribere vult Ecclesia Scotica; sic nec aliarum exemplo sibi præscribi judicat, earum præsertim quæ adhuc intemperiem nonnullam è reliquis sentiunt morborum, quibus ex Romana contagione ita graviter vexatæ fuerunt, ut plane convalescere nondum potuerint: Rainold. in thesibus de ecclesia, thes. 5.[?] parag. 29. Et hæc hactenus quibus abunde protestatio illa Episcoporum refutata est.
units.tr: Therefore, since all these objections are frivolous, their protestations appended in writing are of the same kind. As to that clause about the necessity of ecclesiastical government by bishops, the synod says it marvels at the impudence of these men, who call it necessary, a necessity which the hierarchs have never attempted to demonstrate from any point of Scripture [ἀναγκαῖον]. For it is neither simply nor absolutely necessary, since the churches flourished in which there was no mention of the so-called authority [ἐξουσία] of bishops, and it is not necessary even on grounds of usefulness. Moreover, although this authority of bishops was introduced at first by the Fathers with sincere intent, it nonetheless paved the way for ambition, which they did not foresee, as we have heard Nazianzen gravely declare. But what would he have said, we may suppose, had he lived in the ages that followed, and indeed in this our Scotland, where ambition, the hydra of all evils, has overstepped every limit of modesty, and now even rages, when it sees itself brought into order and confined within its bounds, lest it run riot in the church any longer? But why do I speak of ambition? He is blind who does not see that the gate has been thrown open wide to Antichrist. For the aristocratic polity of the church, which flourished in the apostolic age, through the consent of a perpetual primacy of one order of elders, was gradually changed into an oligarchy, in which a few men seized for themselves a preeminence of power, and at last into the tyranny of one universal bishop. And whether this so-called salvation, that exchange [σωτηρία; ἀλλάγμα], devised at first by human counsel as a remedy for schism, has proved useful for securing the peace of the churches, the most mournful face of this torn church shows; for from the first moment it began to be imposed, it has experienced the most true fuel of schism itself, since nothing can so divide the church as the ambition to preside. This is too conspicuous in the Roman Pontiff in claiming his primacy, whose head cannot rest on shoulders other than episcopal ones. It would even make Democritus laugh that they say they put forward this protestation in the name of the Scottish Church, as if six bishops (for the subscription of the rest is not extant), together with a few ministers, their followers, corrupted either by bribes, or frightened by threats, or deceived by false reports, as many of them have frankly acknowledged with tears, constituted the Scottish Church. They try to annul its authority and all the synods lawfully held hitherto by such monstrous protestations, and they now declare themselves anxious lest anything be determined in this synod which could cause damage or infamy to the liberty of this church, to the royal dignity, or to the neighbouring reformed churches. Although it is all too clear that the bishops have hitherto paid no regard to these things, they press these points unseasonably, so as to strike obliquely at the synod and draw undeserved hatred upon the most serene king and the neighbouring churches. Yet it has never been resolved by the synod to pluck at the dignity and authority of the king, or to brand the neighbouring churches with any mark of infamy. These churches, in their fairness, will not take it amiss if this church, aspiring to the primitive purity of its reformation, judges that things which are found incompatible with its own praiseworthy constitutions should be rejected, even if they have perhaps been received by others. The Church of Scotland does not wish to prescribe to others the use of these things, and so it does not judge that it should be prescribed to itself by the example of others, especially of those which still feel some remnant of the diseases with which they were so gravely afflicted by Roman contagion that they have not yet been able to recover fully. Rainold, in his theses on the church, thesis 5.[?] paragraph 29. And so far, by these arguments, that protestation of the bishops has been sufficiently refuted.

units.la: Digressio qua veteris et hodierni Scotici Episcopi dissimilitu- do varia ostenditur, seu Antitheses variæ inter veteres et hodiernos Scotiæ Episcopos.
units.tr: A digression in which the various differences between the ancient and the present Scottish bishops are shown; or, various antitheses between the ancient and the present bishops of Scotland.

units.la: Porro cum hodierni Episcopi toties inculcent singularem pietatem, prudentiam, doctrinam veterum Episcoporum, quasi ab iis genus ac originem deducerent, & per suum latus confodi clamitent veteres illos heroes, quasi hodiernus Episcopatus impugnari non posset quin eodem telo petantur sanctissimi illi viri, ecclesiæ splendidissima lumina Christianæque reipub. firmissima columina, Ignatius, Polycarpus, Cyprianus, Athanasius, Augustinus, Ambrosius, aliique complures: Age, digreffiuncula hac instituatur comparatio inter veteres illos & hodiernos episcopos: nam ab illis ad hos concludi nequit nisi primum ostendatur hodiernos Episcopos priorum illorum veram effigiem & imaginem reddere, quod si vero dissimilitudo sit multiplex, nec ulla antiqui Præsidis Episcopi lineamenta in hodierno Principe Episcopo appareant, præter solum Episcopi nomen, manifestum erit quam futili commento dignitatem suam tueantur, ac quam fallaci impostura fallant, Tertiam columnam paralelli hujus facerent Episcopi Pontificii, nisi labore hoc nos liberassent hodierni Episcopi, qui nullam aliam differentiam inter se & Pontificios episcopos, quantocunque sint acumine excogitare possunt, quàm quod hi à Pontifice Romano dependeant; cui nostri videri volunt nuncium remisisse; Etenim perspicua sunt quæ Archiepiscopus Andreapolitanus in epistola dedicatoria præfixa refutationi libelli de regimine Ecclesiæ Scoticanæ, in hancrem diserte loquitur: omnia etiam argumenta eorumque amplificationes de verbo vere in verbum à Pontificiis mutuantur decertantibus de dignitate & jurisdictione ac privilegiis suorum Episcoporum.
units.tr: Since the present bishops so often press upon us their singular piety, prudence and learning, as though they derived their descent and origin from the ancient bishops, and cry out that those old heroes are being stabbed through their side, as if the present episcopacy could not be attacked without those most holy men, the most splendid lights of the Church and the firmest pillars of the Christian commonwealth, being struck with the same weapon (Ignatius, Polycarp, Cyprian, Athanasius, Augustine, Ambrose and many others), let us, then, in this little digression, set up a comparison between those ancient bishops and the present ones. For no conclusion can be drawn from the former to the latter unless it is first shown that the present bishops render the true likeness and image of those earlier ones. But if the dissimilarity is manifold, and no feature of the ancient president-bishop appears in the present prince-bishop beyond the bare name of bishop, it will be plain with what flimsy contrivance they defend their dignity, and with what deceitful trickery they deceive. The Papist bishops would make a third column of this parallel, were it not that the present bishops have freed us from that labour. However sharp their wits, they can devise no other difference between themselves and the Papist bishops than that the latter depend upon the Roman Pontiff; and our men wish it to appear that they have sent him away. Indeed, what the Archbishop of St Andrews says plainly in the dedicatory epistle prefixed to the refutation of the book on the government of the Scottish Church, speaking in this very manner, is clear enough. All their arguments, and their amplifications of them, are borrowed word for word from the Papists, who contend about the dignity, jurisdiction and privileges of their bishops.

units.la: Dissimilitudo veterum Episcoporum ab hodiernis.
units.tr: The dissimilarity of the ancient bishops from the present ones.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Veteres,
units.tr: The ancients,

units.la: Præsides tantum fuerunt presbyteriorum : neque se presbyteros vocari indigne ferebant: utpote quod nomina presbyteri & Episcopi indistincta fuerint, ut testatur Hieronymus ad Oceanum : quod non negat Georgius Doimamus[?] in concione de Episcopatu & presbyterio : & Irenæus in epistola ad Victorem apud Eusebium lib. 5. c. 24. Pontifices Romanos, Anicetum, Pium, Hyginum, presbyteros vocat, neque sibi Episcopi nomen ita vendicabant ut ad reliquos presbyteros non extenderetur, nam Gregorii Nazianzeni seculo, hoc est anno Christi 370. uti in oratione post suum in urbem reditum testatur, episcopi nomen præsidibus illis specialiter attributum vocat Novum, & Augustinus epistola 19. ad Hieronymum, usu & consuetudine Ecclesiæ qui tum recens obtinuit, nomina illa distincta fuisse : neque se solos Apostolorum successores exclusis presbyteris dicebant. Nam sicuti in gradu extraordinariæ functionis nullos habuisse Apostolos successores agnoverunt, ita in potestate tota ordinaria pastoralis ministerii reliquos presbyteros Apostolis successisse testatum reliquerunt, Ignatius ad Trallianos, coetum presbyterorum vocat conjunctionem Apostolorum Christi. Irenæus lib. 4. cap. 43. dicit, presbyteros in ecclesia ab Apostolis
units.tr: were only presidents of the presbyteries. Nor did they count it an insult to be called presbyters, since the names presbyter and bishop were not distinguished, as Jerome attests in his letter to Oceanus; Georgius Doimamus, in his sermon on episcopacy and the presbytery, does not deny this; and Irenaeus, in his letter to Victor, cited in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 24, calls the Roman Pontiffs Anicetus, Pius and Hyginus presbyters. Nor did they claim the name of bishop for themselves in such a way that it did not extend to the other presbyters. For in the age of Gregory Nazianzen, that is, in the year of Christ 370, as he testifies in his oration after his return to the city, he calls the name of bishop, specially attributed to those presidents, a novelty. And Augustine, in letter 19 to Jerome, says that those names were distinct by the usage and custom of the Church which then had recently prevailed. Nor did they call themselves the sole successors of the Apostles, to the exclusion of the presbyters. For just as they acknowledged that the Apostles had no successors in the grade of their extraordinary function, so they left it on record that the other presbyters succeeded the Apostles in the whole ordinary power of the pastoral ministry.
