Ignatius, to the Trallians, calls the college of presbyters the union of the Apostles of Christ. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 43, says that the presbyters in the Church were appointed by the Apostles.

units.la: Hodierni
units.tr: The present bishops

units.la: Volunt esse principes cleri, & presbyteri appellationem ut dignitati & pompæ inferiorem fastidiunt, & sibi solis episcoporum nomen arrogant, sequeque solos Apostolorum successores jactitant. stolis successionem habere. Cyprianus lib. 4. epistola 9. OmnesPraepositos. (quorum nomine presbyteros solet comprehendere, nam eorum plures uni ecclesiae assignat) vicaria ordinatione Apostolis succedere. Hieronymus in 2. cap. Michae, citatus a Gratiano in decretis distinct. 35. cap. Ecclesiae. Licet presbyter tantum esset, tamen de seloquens[?], si in Apostolorum (inquit) loco sumus, non solum sermonem eorum imitemur, sed etiam conversationem, & abstinentiam. Denique Augustinus serm. 36. ad fratres in Eremo, eosque presbyteros: Vos, inquit, estis sal terrae, Apostolorum successores.
units.tr: want to be the princes of the clergy. They scorn the name of presbyter as beneath their dignity and pomp, and they arrogate the name of bishop to themselves alone, boasting that they alone have the succession of the Apostles. Cyprian, book 4, letter 9: all the prelates (under whose name he usually includes the presbyters, since he assigns several of them to one church) succeed the Apostles by vicarious ordination. Jerome, on the second chapter of Micah, cited by Gratian in the Decretum, distinction 35, chapter "Ecclesiae": although he was only a presbyter, yet, speaking of himself, he says: if we stand in the place of the Apostles, we should imitate not only their speech but also their conduct and abstinence. Finally, Augustine, sermon 36, to the brothers in the desert, and to those presbyters: You, he says, are the salt of the earth, the successors of the Apostles.

units.la: Veteres
units.tr: The ancients

units.la: Olim Episcopi eligebantur per clerum, seu totum presbyterorum collegium: Hieronym. in epistol. ad Evagrium. Alexandriae à Marco Euangelista usque ad Heraclam & Dionysium Episcopos, presbyteri semper unum ex se electum, in excelsiori gradu collocatum, Episcopum nominabant, & necesse fuit ut accederet populi
units.tr: Of old, bishops were elected by the clergy, that is, by the whole college of presbyters. Jerome, in his letter to Evagrius: at Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to Heraclas and Dionysius as bishops, the presbyters always chose one from among themselves, placed him in a higher rank, and called him bishop; and it was necessary that the consent of the people should be added.

units.la: Hodierni
units.tr: The Present Practice

units.la: Sic eliguntur. Cum regi significatum fuerit per Decanum capituli, Dioecesin orbatam esse Episcopo, obsignato diplomate concedit capitulo facultatem eligendi, & simul mittit literas quibus nominat episcopum eligendum. Atque sic capitulo nihil aliud relinquitur quam umbratilis quaedam & imaginaria nominati electio. consensus. Cyprian. lib. 1. epist. 4. nomine synodi Africana. Videmus de divina authoritate descendere, ut sacerdos plebe praesente sub omnium oculis deligatur & dignus atque idoneus publico judicio ac testimonio cŏprobetur. Et ibid. Diligenter de traditione divi-
units.tr: Thus they are chosen. When the king has been informed by the dean of the chapter that a diocese is bereft of its bishop, he grants the chapter, under sealed warrant, the power to elect, and at the same time sends a letter naming the bishop to be elected. So nothing is left to the chapter but a kind of shadowy and imaginary election of the nominee. consent. Cyprian, book 1, letter 4, in the name of the African synod. We see that it descends from divine authority that a priest be chosen with the people present, under the eyes of all, and be approved as worthy and fit by public judgement and testimony. And ibid. Carefully, from divine tradition-

units.la: ctio. Denique sic ele-ctum comprobat, ac mandat Archiepiscopo ut eum in Episcopum consecret: Hac ratione Episcopi saepius obtrusi qui provincialibus suis prorsus incogniti vel de facie; aliquando gregis sermonem non intelligunt, ut in Episcopatibus Argathelienfi, Insularum, Rossensi, & Catanesiae saepius usu venit.
units.tr: -tion. Finally, having thus approved the one chosen, he orders the Archbishop to consecrate him as bishop. In this way bishops are often foisted on dioceses, men who are utterly unknown to their own provincials, or even by sight; sometimes they do not understand the language of the flock, as happens quite often in the bishoprics of Argyll, of the Isles, of Ross and of Caithness.

units.la: na & Apostolica observatione tenendum est, quod apud nos quoque & fere per provincias universas tenetur, ut,& caet. Episcopus deligatur, plebe cui ordinatur praesente, quae singulorum vitam plenissime novit,& uniuscujusque actum de ejus conversatione perspexit. Sic Cornelium Romanae Ecclesiae Episcopum electum fuisse testatur idem Cyprianus lib.4. epistol. 2. & Sabinum in Basilidis locum successisse, lib.1. epist.4. & Fabianum Romanum Episcopum, annotantibus Magdeburgicis in centuriis historia Ecclesiastica. Gratianus distinct. 62. can. Nulla. Nulla ratio finit ut inter Episcopos habeantur qui nec à clericis sint electi nec à plebibus expetiti. Sic electus fuit Ambrosius à civibus Mediolanensibus, & Flavianus ab Antiochenis,& Chrysostomus à Constantinopolitanis: Porro usque adeo religiose observatus fuit hic electionis mos, ut cum postea Imperatores Episcopos obtruderent nulla cleri & populi electione præcedente, indignissime tulerint episcoporum doctissimi. Ubi ille canon, inquit Athanasius, ut à palatio mittatur is qui futurus est Episcopus, in epistola ad solitariam vitam agentes: Non negandum quin imperatoribus & regibus ad fidem Christianam conversis suæ partes fuerint in Episcoporum electionibus, eosque assensum præbuisse Episcopis rite electis, uti in Chrysostomi electione facilitatum fuisse testatur Sozomenus. lib. 8. cap. 2. verum sui juris totam electionem fecisse, nullibi legitur apud pri-orum sacrorum scriptores: Tandem Caroli magni & Ludovici filii saeculo, electio post multas quas multorum [illegible, ~8 letters] passa est corruptelas, ad primitivam suam formam revocatur. lib. 1. cap. 84. Capitulum illud continetur in Gratiani decretis. Distinct. 63. Can. Sacrorum. Sacrorum Canonum non ignari, ut Dei nomine sancta ecclesia suo liberius potiatur honore, assensum ordini ecclesiastico præbemus, ut Episcopi per electionem cleri & populi secundum statuta Canonum de propria Dioecesi (remota personarum & munerum acceptione) ob vitae meritum & sapientiae donum eligantur, ut exemplo & verbo sibi subjectis usque quaque prodesse valeant.
units.tr: The Apostolic observance, then, ought to be kept, and not merely by us but almost throughout all the provinces, that a bishop be chosen in the presence of the people to whom he is to be ordained, who knows most fully the life of each and has observed the conduct of each person. Thus Cornelius was elected Bishop of the Roman Church, as the same Cyprian testifies, book 4, letter 2, and Sabinus succeeded in the place of Basilides, book 1, letter 4, and Fabian the Roman bishop, as the Magdeburg Centuriers note in their ecclesiastical history. Gratian, distinction 62, canon "Nulla". No reason allows those to be counted among bishops who have been chosen neither by the clergy nor sought by the people. Thus Ambrose was elected by the citizens of Milan, Flavian by the Antiochenes, and Chrysostom by the Constantinopolitans. Moreover, this custom of election was so religiously observed that when afterwards the emperors thrust bishops upon the Church without any preceding election by clergy and people, the most learned of the bishops took it very badly. Where is the canon, says Athanasius, that he who is to be bishop should be sent from the palace? In his letter to those living a solitary life: It cannot be denied that the emperors and kings, once converted to the Christian faith, had their share in the elections of bishops, and gave their assent to bishops duly elected, as Sozomen testifies that the election of Chrysostom was made easier thereby, book 8, chapter 2. But that they made the whole election their own right is nowhere read in the writers of the earlier sacred history. At length, in the age of Charlemagne and his son Louis, the election, after suffering many corruptions, was recalled to its original form. Book 1, chapter 84. That chapter is contained in Gratian's Decretum, distinction 63, canon "Sacrorum". Not ignorant of the sacred canons, so that the holy Church may enjoy its honour more freely in the name of God, we grant our assent to the ecclesiastical order, that bishops be chosen by the election of the clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, from their own diocese (setting aside the acceptance of persons and offices), for the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may be able to benefit those subject to them in every way by example and word.

units.la: Veteres. & Hodierni.
units.tr: The ancients and the moderns.

units.la: Olim qui cleri & populi suffragiis electi fuerunt, ad Episcopa-
units.tr: In former times those who were chosen by the votes of the clergy and people were ordained by bishops,

units.la: Sic electi conserunt se ad Archiepiscopum, à quo solo consecrari pof-sunt. tum ab aliis episcopis promovebantur; aliquando à meris presbyteris: & si concederetur Timotheum fuisse ordinarium Episcopum; consecratio tamen non fuit per Archiepiscopum, nec Episcopum, sed per coetum presbyterorum. 1. Tim. 4: 4. Ab abbatibus insulae S. columbani qui Presbyteri tantum fuerunt, refert Beda histor. lib. 3. cap. 5. Episcopum electum & missum fuisse Arcanum.
units.tr: and so chosen they turned to the archbishop, by whom alone they could be consecrated. Sometimes they were promoted by other bishops, and sometimes by mere presbyters. Even if it be granted that Timothy was the ordinary bishop, his consecration was not by an archbishop or a bishop, but by a company of presbyters (1 Tim. 4:14). Bede, in his History, book 3, chapter 5, reports that the abbots of the island of St Columba, who were only presbyters, sent out a bishop elected and dispatched, Arcanus.

units.la: Veteres. Hodierni.
units.tr: Ancient writers. Modern writers.

units.la: Nullam aliam agnoverunt consecrationem seu ordinationem quam presbyterorum ef-set. Episcopi & presbyteri una & eadem est ordinatio, inquit Ambrosius, in 1. ad Timoth. cap. 3. & Albinus Alcuinus (natione Scotus qui floruit favore & gratia Caroli magni ad quem ab Achajo Scotorum rege missus fuit circa annum 800. & cujus opera aperta primum fuerunt Academia, Parisiensis in Galliis, & Ticinensis in Italia: hic) libro 3. De divinis officiis sic loquitur. Qualis autem esset antiquitus consecratio Episcoporum ostendit Hieronymus in epistola ad Evagrium, Alexandriae inquiens, à Marco Evangelista usq; ad Heraclam & Dionysium episcopos, presbyteri semper unum ex se electum, in excelsiori gradu collocatum Episcopū nominabant, quomodo si exercitus imperatore faciat, & Diaconi eligant de se quem indu-
units.tr: They acknowledged no consecration or ordination other than that of the elders. The ordination of bishops and elders is one and the same, says Ambrose, on 1 Timothy chapter 3, and Alcuin the Albinus (a Scot by birth, who flourished through the favour and grace of Charlemagne, to whom he was sent around the year 800 by Achaius, king of the Scots, and through whose efforts the academies of Paris in Gaul and Pavia in Italy were first opened) speaks thus in book 3 of On the Divine Offices. What the consecration of bishops was like in antiquity Jerome shows in his letter to Evagrius: at Alexandria, he says, from Mark the Evangelist down to Heraclas and Dionysius the bishops, the elders always named one chosen from among themselves, placed in a higher rank, and called him bishop, just as an army makes a general emperor; and the deacons chose one of their own number and called him archdeacon. The archdeacon has the same consecration as the other deacons, but is set over them by the choice of the brethren. Therefore the bishop once had the same consecration as the elders.

units.la: Diversam habent consecrationem à presbyteris: quia ordine dif-ferre se dicunt à Presbyteris. strium[?] noverint & Archidiaconum vocent: Archidiaconus vero eandem consecrationem habet quam cæteri Diaconi, sed electione fratrum præponitur: ergo eandem olim habebat Episcopus consecrationem quam presbyteri.
units.tr: Bishops have a consecration different from that of the elders, because they say they differ from the elders in rank. The archdeacon has the same consecration as the other deacons, but is set over them by the choice of the brethren. Therefore the bishop once had the same consecration as the elders.

units.la: Quod ad ritus & ceremonias in consecratione usitatas, iidem fere prorsus sunt cum iis qui in papatu adhibentur, quos antiquis illis Episcopis prorsus incognitos fuisse hospes prorsus in historia Ecclesiastica est, qui ignorat.
units.tr: As for the rites and ceremonies customarily used in consecration, they are almost entirely the same as those used among the Papists, which were quite unknown to those ancient bishops, as anyone who is not a complete stranger to ecclesiastical history knows.

units.la: Veteres.
units.tr: Ancient writers.

units.la: Nullam singularem potestatem in ordinatio-nibus pastorum sibi ar-rogabant: nam nec nominabant per se exclusò cle-ro & populo ordinandum: sic Ambrosium plebs Mediolanensis Episcopum nominat cujus postulatis acquie-verunt præsentes Epis-
units.tr: They claimed no sole power over the ordination of ministers: they did not nominate on their own the man to be ordained, excluding clergy and people. Thus the people of Milan named Ambrose bishop, and the bishops present acquiesced in their demands.

units.la: Hodierni.
units.tr: Modern writers.

units.la: Singularem ordinatio-nis presbyterorum pote-statem, exclusò clero, sibi solis vendicant, atque hanc sibi maxime peculiarem & propriam, non fratrum presbyterorum voluntario consensu, sed jure divino, aut saltem Apostolico: ideoque impositione manuum in ordinatione, gratiam internam conferri dicunt.
units.tr: They claim for themselves alone a sole power of ordaining elders, excluding the clergy, and they regard this as most especially their own and proper right, not by the free consent of their fellow elders, but by divine right, or at least by apostolic right. Therefore they say that internal grace is conferred by the laying on of hands in ordination.

units.la: copi. Theodoret. histor.eccles.lib.4.c.6.Sic Augustinum Episcopum sibi præponi postulat Hipponensis Ecclesia Valerio Episcopo præsente, Possidon. in vita Augustin. Et Augustinus ipse maxima licet authoritatis, nihil tamen egit solus pro imperio in nominatione Eradii quem sibi successorem cupiebat, nam ipse testatur epist. 110. Populum sibi adsedisse in negotio hoc peragendo, & Eradium adftitisse: & Petrum à Clero & populo Alexandrino per suffragia nominatum fuisse refert Theod: hist. eccles. lib. 4. cap. 20. Et à Gratiano in decretis relatum dist. 63. can. plebs: Decrevisse Gelasium Papam ut ad electionem sacerdotum ex singulis parœciis & Presbyteri & Diaconi & universa turba convocentur, Verum quidem est populo praivisse (Clerum[?], actionemque totam direxisse prasidem; interim sibi soli nominationis & electionis quae prima ordinationis pars est, jus non transcripsit. Nec Episcopi soli nominatum examinabant, aut de ejus sufficientia judicabant exclusis caeteris presbyteris, Assensusque Ecclesia usque adeo necessarius fuit, ut non licuerit Episcopo consecrare nisi post electionem cleri & populi: Secundam ordinationis partem, videl. initiationem quae per ritum impositionis manuum, electus in ministerio confirmatur, in solidum sibi non vendicarunt Episcopi; etenim Eusseb. histor. Eccles. lib. 6. cap. 43. narrat presbyteros interdixisse Episcopo ne Novatum presbyterum ordinaret; Episcopum vero obsecratum fuisse omnes ut hunc solum χειροτονεῖν[?] sibi permitterent; quo exemplo patet in actu hoc ordinationis nihil potuisse Episcopum sine consensu reliquorum presbyterorum: neque initiandi pastores jus; saeculo illo in universum presbyteris ademptum fuisse: & Ambrosius in Ephes. cap. 4. & Augustinus vel author quidam antiquior lib. quaestionum veteris & novi Testamenti quaest. 101. sua adhuc memoria testantur, presbyteros in Ægypto ordinasse ; seu consignasse vel consignasse, quod intelligi non potest de consecratione eucharistiæ, quam nemo dubitat quin omnes ubique pastores possent non in Alexandria modo & per totam Ægyptum : In concilio Carthaginensi 4. can. 22. Decretum ut Episcopus sine clericorum suorum consilio clericos non ordinet, & can. 3. Presbyter cum ordinatur, Episcopo eum benedicente aut manum super caput ejus tenente, etiam omnes presbyteri qui præsentes sunt manus suas juxta manus Episcopi super caput illius teneant: neque hoc decretum esse ut actioni gravitas quædam concilietur, aut ut ordinando animus adderetur, sed necessario fieri debere præcedentia ostendunt. Extat Canon concilii Ancyrani, Chorepiscopis non licet presbyteros aut Diaconos ordinare, sed nec presbyteris civitatis sine præcepto Episcopi in unaquaque parœcia: ex quo colligi potest antea licuisse presbyteris civitatis in aliena parœcia ordinare, sicuti olim licebat, Chorepiscopi quos presbyteros solum fuisse afferunt Hierarchicideni[?] non cohiberi ne in propria parœcia ordinent. Tertio, venia episcopi posse, ergo ritus ordinationis sæculo illo ad solos episcopos non pertinebat: Denique ex prædictis patet, Episcopum peregisse ritum illum totius presbyterii nomine, cum presbyterorum primus esset, sicuti in collegiis politicis solent iis qui ordine ex omnium consensu primi sunt, partes quædam demandari, quibus tamen non ex proprio arbitratu, sed præeunte collegarum judicio defunfunguntur. Et quid quæso est illa manuum impositio, aliud nisi oratio (rectius ritus orationis) super hominem, Gratianus in Decretis. cauf. 1. quaest. 1. cap. manus ex august. hanc autem orationem presbyteris tum illicitam fuisse, cui erit credibile, quandoquidem presbyteri in benedictione cum Episcopis consortes ministeriorum sunt ut inquit author epistola de septem eccles. ordinibus. Si quis objiciat can.6.concilii2. Hispalensis; quo dicitur Episcopum sacerdotibus &ministris solum dare posse honorem, id est ordinare. Respondebit Gratianus in Decret.cauf. 15.quaest.7. can. Si autem. Per illud Solum excludi alios Episcopos non proprium clerum. Adde quod concilium illud recentius sit neque in censum veniat illius sæculi de quo jam vertitur controversia. Etenim nullus negat sæculo tertio & quarto ac sequentibus in honorem Sacerdotii ut loquuntur veteres, administrationem ritus illius in ordinatione episcopis principaliter attributam fuisse, unde illud Hieronymi in Epistola ad Evagrium.
units.tr: The bishops did not seize this power. Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History book 4 chapter 6. Thus the Church of Hippo demanded that Augustine be set over it as bishop, with Bishop Valerius present (Possidius, in the Life of Augustine). And although Augustine himself was of very great authority, he did nothing alone by his own authority in the nomination of Eradius, whom he wished as his successor; for he himself testifies in letter 110 that the people sat with him in carrying out this business, and that Eradius was present. Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History book 4 chapter 20, reports that Peter was named by the clergy and people of Alexandria by vote. It is also related by Gratian in the Decretals, distinction 63, canon "plebs": Pope Gelasius decreed that for the election of priests, both elders and deacons and the whole crowd should be called together from each parish. It is true that the people went first, and the presiding bishop directed the whole proceeding; yet he did not transfer to himself alone the right of nomination and election, which is the first part of ordination. Nor did the bishops alone examine the nominee or judge his fitness, excluding the other elders. The assent of the Church was so necessary that a bishop might not consecrate unless after the election by clergy and people. The second part of ordination, namely the initiation by which the one elected is confirmed in the ministry through the rite of the laying on of hands, the bishops did not claim wholly for themselves. For Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History book 6 chapter 43, relates that the elders forbade the bishop to ordain the elder Novatus, and that all besought the bishop to permit that he alone should cheirotonein [χειροτονεῖν] him. By this example it is clear that in this act of ordination the bishop could do nothing without the consent of the other elders, and that the right of initiating ministers had in that age been taken away from the elders in general. Ambrose on Ephesians chapter 4, and Augustine, or some older author, in Questions on the Old and New Testament question 101, still testify in their own memory that elders in Egypt ordained, or, as the text has it, "sealed" or "sealed"; this cannot be understood of the consecration of the eucharist, which no one doubts that all ministers everywhere could perform, not only at Alexandria but throughout all Egypt. In the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 22, it was decreed that a bishop should not ordain clergy without the counsel of his clergy; and canon 3: when an elder is ordained, while the bishop blesses him or holds his hand over his head, all the elders who are present should also lay their hands beside the bishop's hands upon his head. That this decree was not made to give some solemnity to the action, or to add spirit to the ordainers, but that it must necessarily be done, the order of events shows. There is a canon of the Council of Ancyra: chorepiscopi may not ordain elders or deacons, nor may the elders of a city, without the bishop's command, in any parish. From this it can be gathered that formerly elders of a city were permitted to ordain in another parish, as was once allowed; and that the chorepiscopi, who, they say, were only elders, were not forbidden to ordain in their own parish. Thirdly, the bishop could do so with permission; therefore the rite of ordination in that age did not belong to bishops alone. Finally, from what has been said it is clear that the bishop performed that rite in the name of the whole presbytery, since he was the first of the elders, just as in political colleges it is customary to commit certain duties to the one who by the consent of all is first in rank; yet these duties are discharged not by his own judgment but by the judgment of his colleagues going before. And what, I ask, is that laying on of hands, other than prayer (more properly the rite of prayer) over the man? Gratian in the Decretals, cause 1, question 1, chapter "manus," from Augustine. But who will believe that prayer in blessing was then forbidden to elders, since, as the author of the letter On the Seven Orders of the Church says, elders are partners with bishops in the ministries of blessing. If anyone objects canon 6 of the Second Council of Seville, which says that a bishop can give honour only to priests and ministers, that is, ordain, Gratian will reply in the Decretals, cause 15, question 7, canon "Si autem": the word "only" excludes other bishops, not their own clergy. Add that this council is more recent and does not belong to the age of which the controversy now speaks. For no one denies that in the third and fourth centuries and afterwards, in honour of the priesthood, as the ancients put it, the administration of that rite in ordination was chiefly assigned to bishops; hence the saying of Jerome in his letter to Evagrius: What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not do? For the testimony of Chrysostom, Homily 11 on 1 Timothy, which the hierarchs so often cite, is plainly corrupt; and even if it stood as the hierarchs wish, he speaks of the custom of his own age, and says that bishops possess this privilege by the voluntary consent of the elders. What does this have to do with bishops who presided before the First Council of Nicaea? For after that council, especially in the more famous churches, bishops gradually increased their dominion over the churches, not content with that paternal pre-eminence which they had obtained by the voluntary concession of the elders. And then they decreed that ordinations made by elders should be void, though from the beginning it was not so. So much for ordination; there follows the difference in jurisdiction between

units.la: Quid facit excepta ordinatione episcopus quod presbyter non facit. Nam testimonium Chrysostomi homil. 11. in 1.Timoth. quod toties ab hierarchicis reponitur corruptum plane est; & licet ita se haberet ut volunt hierarchici; loquitur tamen de sui sæculi consuetudine, & privilegium hoc possidere episcopos dicit voluntario presbyterorum consensu: quid hoc ad præsides Episcopos ante concilium primum Nicenum: nam post illud in celebrioribus præsertim ecclesiis episcopi paulatim imperium in ecclesias sibi augebant, non contenti paterna illa praelatione quam voluntaria presbyterorum concessione obtinue-rat. Ac tum decrevere ut ordinationes facta à Presbyteris irrita fierent, verum à principio non fuit ita. Atque hæc de ordinatione, sequitur dissimilitudo in jurisdictione inter
units.tr: What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that an elder does not do? For the testimony of Chrysostom, Homily 11 on 1 Timothy, which the hierarchs so often cite, is plainly corrupt; and even if it stood as the hierarchs wish, he speaks of the custom of his own age, and says that bishops possess this privilege by the voluntary consent of the elders. What does this have to do with bishops who presided before the First Council of Nicaea? For after that council, especially in the more famous churches, bishops gradually increased their dominion over the churches, not content with that paternal pre-eminence which they had obtained by the voluntary concession of the elders. And then they decreed that ordinations made by elders should be void, though from the beginning it was not so. So much for ordination; there follows the difference in jurisdiction between

units.la: Veteres. &
units.tr: The Ancients.

units.la: Nullam delegationem interna huius jurisdictionis ab Episcopis ad Presbyteros agnoverunt: nam Ambrosius in 1. Tim. 5. & Chrysostom. hom. 17. in Matt. diserte vocant presbyteros, Christi vicarios, & Cyprian. lib.4. epist. 8. dicit: Dominum sacerdotes sibi in sua Ecclesia eligere & constituere dignatum esse: Nam Deus est Dominus messis, & ille operarios in messem
units.tr: We recognise no delegation of this internal jurisdiction from bishops to presbyters. For Ambrose on 1 Tim. 5 and Chrysostom, homily 17 on Matthew, plainly call presbyters the vicars of Christ, and Cyprian, book 4, letter 8, says that the Lord has deigned to choose and appoint priests for himself in his Church. For God is the Lord of the harvest, and he sends labourers into the harvest.

units.la: Hodiernos.
units.tr: The Moderns.

units.la: Iurisdictionem in fo-ro interno, seu in foro conscientiæ presbyteris quidem competere dicunt, sed commissam tantum & delegatam ab Episcopo, cujus vicarii sunt, cum ille solus totius Dioeceseos pastor sit: Quare exercitium hujus jurisdictionis in foro conscientiæ Episcopis subditum esse volunt, ita ut Presbytero ordinato non liceat concionari aut sacramenta administrare nisi facultate ab Episcopo prius concessa. emittit, hinc à Deo constituti in Ecclesia, à Christo dati dicuntur, legationeque Christi nomine non Episcoporum fungi referuntur: Verum quidem est ab hominibus ordinatos esse, facultatem tamen & authoritatem ministrandi Ecclesiæ à Deo habent: cujus sunt œconomi: quare nunquam invenies veteresillos Episcopos, appellantes presbyteros quibus praeerant, legatos suos; etenim cum se solum Christi legatos agnoverint, & vero delegatus non potest subdelegare, videl. in iis muneribus quae peritiam & fidem requirunt; uti in jure Canonico saepius repetitur; absurdum fuisset Presbyteros, suos indigetasse legatos; Quod si collegas agnoverint, tum totius dioecesis pastores non fuerunt: neque ita circumscribebant presbyteros ut non licuerit eis exercere actus pastorales seu presbyterales sine ipsorum venia. Clara sunt quae habet author quisquis est epistol. de 7. Ecclesiae ordinibus. Nemo hinc (inquit) Episcoporum diabolicae tentationis invidia inflatus, irascatur si presbyteri in Ecclesiis praedicent, si plebibus ut scriptum est benedicant. Etenim abnuenti mihi ista sic dicam: Qui non vult presbyteros facere quod jubentur à Deo, dicat quis major est Christo. Mandatum illud Christi Ite, praedicate &c. Matt. 28. presbyteros adaeque ac Episcopos includere nullus unquam negavit; Missio autem haec seu commissio lusoria[?] prorsus esset, si non liceret exercere id, ad quod presbyteri committuntur: ac qui sentiunt, (Christum sic quasi loquentem volunt, Iubeo vos praedicare, mitto vos ut annuncietis verbum Evangelii, praedicandi tamen exercitium vobis minime concedo: quo quid dici posset ineptius.
units.tr: They say that jurisdiction in the internal forum, or the forum of conscience, belongs indeed to presbyters, but only as committed and delegated by the bishop, whose vicars they are, since he alone is the minister of the whole diocese. Hence they wish the exercise of this jurisdiction in the forum of conscience to be subject to bishops, so that an ordained presbyter may not preach or administer the sacraments unless he has first received permission from the bishop. They are said to be set up by God in the Church and given by Christ, and are described as acting in the name of Christ, not of the bishops. It is true that they are ordained by men, but they have the power and authority of ministering to the Church from God, and they are its stewards. So you will never find that the ancient bishops called the presbyters over whom they presided their legates, for since they recognised themselves as the legates of Christ alone, and a delegate cannot subdelegate, at least in those offices which require skill and faith (as is often repeated in the Canon Law), it would have been absurd for them to appoint presbyters as their own legates. If they had acknowledged them as colleagues, then they were not the ministers of the whole diocese. Nor did they so limit the presbyters that the latter could not perform pastoral or presbyteral acts without their permission. What the author of the letter on the seven orders of the Church says is clear, whoever he is: "Let no one of the bishops, puffed up with the envy of the devilish temptation, be angry (he says) if presbyters preach in the churches, if they bless the people as it is written. For to answer those who refuse, I will say this: let him who does not wish presbyters to do what God commands say whether anyone is greater than Christ." No one has ever denied that the command of Christ, "Go, preach," etc. (Matt. 28), includes presbyters equally with bishops. But that mission or commission would be utterly idle if it were not lawful to exercise that to which the presbyters are commissioned. And those who hold otherwise make Christ speak as if saying: "I bid you preach, I send you that you may announce the word of the Gospel, but I by no means allow you to exercise preaching." Nothing could be more absurd than that.

units.la: Ajurisdictione fori interni ad jurisdictionem externam seu externi fori progrediamur, cujus potestas vel est δογματικὴ[?], vel ἀλκετικὴ[?], vel denique κεφαλικὴ[?], . querendum in singulis qu[?] in genere, inter
units.tr: Let us now pass from the jurisdiction of the internal forum to external jurisdiction, or the jurisdiction of the external forum, whose power is either dogmatic [δογματικὴ], or [ἀλκετικὴ], or finally [κεφαλικὴ]. To be inquired into in each case, in general, among

units.la: Veteres
units.tr: The Ancients.

units.la: Sibi solis externa ju-risdictionis potestatem non usurparunt, quam sibi cum presbyteris commune dicebant: Ignatius (cujus supposititia scripta magni faciunt hierarchici) in epistol. ad Trallianos presbyteros vocat senatum Dei, & non consiliarios solum, sed & assessores episcopi: eorumque praesentiam in omnibus deliberationibus usque adeo necessariam, ut iis assensum non praebentibus nihil ordine & decenter peragi potuit ab Episcopo in ecclesia gubernatione, uti idem Ignatius epistol. ad Ephesios loquitur, sic coaptetur presbyterium episcopo, quomodo chordas (inquit) in cithara colligatas cernimus; etenim nisi omnes nervi ab imo s fit disparitas. Et primum
units.tr: They did not claim the power of external jurisdiction for themselves alone, which they said was held in common with the presbyters. Ignatius (whose spurious writings the hierarchists value highly) in his letter to the Trallians calls the presbyters the senate of God, and not merely counsellors but assessors of the bishop, and their presence in all deliberations was so necessary that without their assent nothing could be done in good order and decently by the bishop in governing the church. As the same Ignatius says in his letter to the Ephesians: the presbytery is fitted to the bishop as the strings are bound to a cithara (he says), for unless all the strings are tuned from the bottom up, there is discord. And first...

units.la: Hodiernos.
units.tr: The Moderns.

units.la: Hi omnem externi fori jurisdictionem exclusis presbyteris vendicant sibi solis : ita ut eosdem consulere dedignentur, quod si eorum consilio aliquando utantur , illud non ex necessitate sed libera sua voluntate fieri dicunt & presbyterorum suffragia tum nolunt esse decisiva, sed solum deliberativa & con-sultiva, quibus numerandis non astringitur, sed ab ipsius solius arbitrio pendet num majorem aut minorem partem sequi velit : quod ne quis hoc iis per calumniam affictum esse calumnietur , ecce Dounami ipsius verba non magis (inquit) detrahit Episcoporum dignitati uti prudentum & eruditorum consilio, quam majestati regum consulere prudentes & fidos viros, qui sunt eis à consiliis : & quotidianæ ipsorum pradad summum recte intenduntur, interque se consentiant, incongruum sonum edet cithara. Irenaus lib. 4. cap. 44. vocat principes, Augustinus serm. 36. ad fratres in Eremo. Patronos & rectores terræ, Epiphanius contra Arium negare non potest, sedisse in thronis sicut & Episcopi, quorum etiam mentionem facit Nazianzenus, in oratione habita in laudem Basilii qui floruit anno Christi 370. Ecclesiis præsedisse, sicut Episcopi, diserte narrat Chrysostomus in 1. Timoth. hom. 11. munusque docendi & præsidendi ecclesiæ, simul accepisse dicit. Cypriani sæculo extra controversiam est, presbyteros simul cum episcopis exercuisse potestatem jurisdictionis externa, ipsque à primordio episcopatus sui statuerat nihil sua privatim sententia gerere, sine presbyterorum consilio: atque ad hoc se debito & officii vinculo astrictum fuisse lib. 3. epist. 10. indicat. Cum ad vos per Dei gratiam venero (inquit scribens ad presbyterum) tunc de iis quæ vel gesta sunt vel gerenda, sicut mutuus honor postulat in commune tractabimus.
units.tr: These claim for themselves alone all external jurisdiction, excluding the presbyters, so that they disdain to consult them. And if they ever make use of their counsel, they say this is done not out of necessity but of their own free will, and they do not want the votes of the presbyters to be decisive, but only deliberative and consultative. They are not bound to count them, but it depends solely on their own judgement whether they will follow the greater or the lesser part. Lest anyone accuse them of making this up as a slander, look at the words of Downame himself: "Consulting prudent and learned men does no more detract from the dignity of bishops (he says) than consulting prudent and faithful men, who are of the council, detracts from the majesty of kings. And if their daily prayers are rightly directed to the highest, and they agree among themselves, the cithara will give out an unharmonious sound." Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 44, calls them princes; Augustine, sermon 36 to the brethren in the desert, calls them patrons and rulers of the earth; Epiphanius, against Arius, cannot deny that they sat on thrones as bishops did; Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration in praise of Basil, who flourished in the year of Christ 370, mentions them as well; Chrysostom, on 1 Timothy, homily 11, plainly says that they presided over the churches just as bishops did, and that they received the office of teaching and presiding over the Church at the same time. In the age of Cyprian it is beyond dispute that presbyters exercised external jurisdiction together with the bishops. He himself had determined from the beginning of his episcopate to do nothing on his own private judgement without the counsel of the presbyters, and he shows in book 3, letter 10, that he was bound to this by the bond of duty: "When I come to you by the grace of God (he writes to a presbyter), then we shall deal together, as mutual respect requires, with those things which have been done or are to be done."

units.la: Quod idem est cum illis Hieronymi, Episcopos debere in communi cum presbyteris regere ecclesiam. Et ex eodem Hier. Gratianus in Decretis. Caus. 16. quæst. 1. cap. Ecclesia, de consuetudine sæculi. Ecclesia habet senatum presbyterorum sine quorum consilio episcopis nihil agere licet: Et in epist. ad Evagrium. Quid facit excepta ordinatione episcopus quod presbyter nō facit? Notandum imprimis hoc testimonium, nam Hieronymi seculo anno 390. Ambiebant singularem hanc potestatem quidam Episcopi, sed frustra, Hisce adderem locum quendam ex Chrysostom. Hom.11. in 1.Timoth. non quod in se aliquid firmi contineat, cum vitiosæ interpretationi innitatur; sed quia quicquid in interpretatione est vitii, deglutiunt Hierarchicis locus sic se habet, τὴν χειροτονίαν μόνην [?] βεβαιωσαι [?]. Sola manuum elevatione superant eos, aut potius suffragio, quia primus presbyter in χειροτονία reliquis præibat. Sola (inquit) ordinatione superiores illis sunt, nempe Episcopi: Ergo, argumento ad hominem, Episcopis in jurisdictione æquales sunt presbyteri, iisque sæculis causarum & litium Ecclesiasticarum dijudicatio presbyterorum & Episcopi communi consilio peragebatur; neque Episcopis competivisse vocem (ut loquuntur) negativam, quæ irrita redderet majoris partis presbyterorum suffragia: nam sic vere regalem & monarchicam potestatem exercuissent, qua uti possunt principes sæculares in senatu suo, nec fuissent presbyterorum collegæ, prout se vocat Augustinus, epist. 137. & Concil. Chartaginense 4.can. 35. (cujus canones hierarchicorum antecsignani, promptuarium vocant Ecclesiastica disciplinæ ab antiquioribus usu receptæ, & ad pristinam consuetudinem revocatæ, quam merito ipsi viderint) Duo hic sunt quæ remoram quandam afferre possūt; alterum, videl. Canones frequentissimos prohibere ne quid tentent presbyteri sine Episcopo: sine Episcopi sententia, conscientia, præcepto, consensu: magno certe apparatu objectionem hanc instruunt, quae sine strepitu facile solvi potest: nam apud eosdem veteres cautum fuit antiquitus, ut ipse Episcopus nihil faceret absque consensu presbyterorum: uti in hac sectione superius accepimus: & perspicue in Canon. 23. Concil. 4. Carthaginens. Irritæ declarantur omnes sententiæ Episcopi quæ præsentia Clericorum non confirmantur: non tamen sequitur presbyteros eminuisse singulari aliqua potestate supra Episcopum. Sic apud veteres extat Canon, ne quid in generalibus synodis fieret sine consensu Romani Pontificis; male tamen inde concludere Pontificios Reformatæ Ecclesiæ Doctores omnes tuentur, Authoritatem & supereminentiam jurisdictionis externa habere Romanum Pontificem supra reliquos Apostolos. Summa, cum perpetua præsidentia uni presbyterorum olim concessa fuerit, iniquum certe fuisset non requirere assensum illius. At isthis phrasibus si quis urgeat singularem authoritatem Episcopi ut principis, meminerit similes canones extare de Episcopis ne quid faciant nisi consensu presbyterorum: & ut antea dictum, nihil sine consensu Romani Pontificis. Alterum quod objicitur est [?]πολύψυχον illud Hieronymi adversus Luciferianos. Nisi exors quædam & ab omnibus eminens detur potestas, tot in Ecclesiis efficientur schismata quod sacerdotes: Si quæratur in quibus illa consistat, statim subjungit ibidem, Inde (inquit) venit ut sine Episcopi jussione neque presbyter neque Diaconus jus habeat baptizandi : Atque supra vidimus veteres episcopos ante Hieronymi ætatem illud sibi non vendicasse, & ipse Hieronym. epist. 2. Nepotia. Pessimæ inquit consuetudinis est in quibusdam ecclesiis tacere Presbyteros & præsentibus Episcopis non loqui. Itaque exors illa potestas in quibusdam tantum ecclesiis obtinuit: an vero laudanda sit, demonstrat, cum rem pessimæ consuetudinis esse dicit, & ad Rusticum Narbonens. quod citatur etiam à Gratiano Dist. 95. cap. Gratia. Episcopos illud sibi arrogantes, dicit, Diabolicæ tentationis invidia inflatos esse, & subdit. Propterea (inquit) hæc scribo ut si præteriti temporis error non potest jam revocari, vel ad præsens in Ecclesiis servetur humilitas, ut presbyteri hoc in ecclesiis suis faciant quod Romæ, in Italia, in Creta, in Oriente, Cypro, Africa, Illyrico, Hispania, Britannia, quod in omnibus locis ubi humilitas perseverat. Denique non quæritur, an Episcopis illis antiquis potiores quædam regiminis partes, per se collegiis [?] omnibus communes, cedant, quasi propriæ, nam cum ordinis præsidentia, regiminis aliqua dignitas necessario cohæret, neque quispiam ordine collegio alicui præesse potest, nisi simul ejus onera aliquot nobiliora omnium nomine in se recipiat: Hoc si quis exortem potestatem vocet, per me licebit: Sed quæritur an hac exorti potestate potiantur necessario, functionis suæ jure, sine collegarum voluntario consensu hodierni Episcopi affirmant: Hieronymus negat. In Comment. in Tit. 1. Sicut presbyteri sciunt se ex ecclesiæ consuetudine ei, qui sibi præpositus fuerit esse subjectos, ita Episcopi noverunt se magis consuetudine quam dispositionis dominicæ veritate majores esse. & August. epistol. 19. ad Hieronym. Secundum honorum vocabula quæ jam ecclesiæ usus obtinuit, episcopatus presbyterio major est: Ex quibus patet, neque omnem Jurisdictionis potestatem, neque semper, neque ab omnibus illis Episcopis vendicatam fuisse ut sibi solis propriam exclusis presbyteris: multo minus hæc sibi à Christo commissa esse profitebantur prout hodierni de se jactitant. Atque hæc de jurisdictionis potestate in genere: Sequitur ut ostendatur quanam sit differentia inter veteres & hodiernos episcopos, ratione partium illius jurisdictionis. Et primum de potestate δυναμικὴ, quæ versatur in judicandis causis fidei & religionis.
units.tr: This is the same as those words of Jerome that bishops ought to rule the Church in common with the presbyters. And from the same Jerome, Gratian in the Decretum, Causa 16, question 1, chapter "Ecclesia, de consuetudine saeculi": "The Church has a senate of presbyters, without whose counsel bishops may do nothing." And in the letter to Evagrius: "What does a bishop do, apart from ordination, that a presbyter does not?" This testimony is especially to be noted, for in Jerome's age, about the year 390, some bishops were seeking this singular power, but in vain. I would add to these a passage from Chrysostom, homily 11 on 1 Timothy, not because it contains anything firm in itself, since it rests on a faulty interpretation, but because whatever fault there is in the interpretation, the hierarchists swallow down. The passage stands thus: [τὴν χειροτονίαν μόνην βεβαιῶσαι]: "They surpass them only in the lifting of hands, or rather in the vote, because the first presbyter went before the others in the ordination [χειροτονία]." "They are superior to them by ordination alone, namely the bishops." Therefore, by an argument ad hominem, presbyters are equal to bishops in jurisdiction, and in those ages the judging of ecclesiastical causes and disputes was carried on by the presbyters and bishops together by common counsel. Nor did the bishops possess what is called a negative voice, which would make void the votes of the greater part of the presbyters, for in that case they would have exercised a truly regal and monarchical power, such as secular princes can use in their own senate, and they would not have been colleagues of the presbyters, as Augustine calls them in letter 137, and as the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 35, does too. (The hierarchists' vanguard calls its canons a storehouse of ecclesiastical discipline, received by the ancients in use and restored to the former custom, which they may rightly regard as their own.) Two things here may seem to cause some hindrance. The first is that the canons very often forbid presbyters to attempt anything without the bishop, without the bishop's judgement, knowledge, command or consent. They build this objection with great show, but it can easily be resolved without noise. For among the same ancients it was provided from antiquity that the bishop himself should do nothing without the consent of the presbyters, as we have heard above in this section, and plainly in canon 23 of the Fourth Council of Carthage: all the decisions of a bishop are declared void which are not confirmed in the presence of the clergy. Yet it does not follow that the presbyters stood out with some singular power above the bishop. So among the ancients there is a canon that nothing should be done in the general synods without the consent of the Roman Pontiff. But from this it is wrongly concluded, as all the teachers of the Reformed Church maintain against the Papists, that the Roman Pontiff has authority and pre-eminence of external jurisdiction over the other apostles. In sum, since a perpetual presidency was once granted to one of the presbyters, it would certainly have been unjust not to require his assent. But if anyone presses these phrases to show a singular authority of the bishop as a prince, let him remember that there are similar canons about bishops, that they should do nothing without the consent of the presbyters, and, as said before, nothing without the consent of the Roman Pontiff. The second objection is that multi-souled saying of Jerome against the Luciferians: "Unless some exceptional power were given, standing out above all, there would be as many schisms in the Churches as there are priests." If one asks in whom that power resides, he immediately adds in the same place: "Hence it comes that neither a presbyter nor a deacon has the right to baptise without the command of the bishop." And above we have seen that the ancient bishops, before Jerome's age, did not claim this for themselves. Jerome himself says in letter 2 to Nepotian: "It is a very bad custom in some churches for the presbyters to be silent and not to speak when the bishops are present." So that exceptional power prevailed only in certain churches. Whether it is to be praised he shows, when he calls it a matter of very bad custom, and in his letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, which is also cited by Gratian, Distinction 95, chapter "Gratia": he says that bishops who arrogate this to themselves are puffed up with the envy of the devilish temptation, and adds: "Therefore I write these things, so that if the error of past time cannot now be revoked, at least for the present humility may be kept in the Churches, so that presbyters in their own churches may do what is done at Rome, in Italy, in Crete, in the East, in Cyprus, in Africa, Illyricum, Spain, Britain, and in all places where humility endures." Finally, the question is not whether some greater parts of government, common to all the colleges by their nature, pass to those ancient bishops as their own. For with the presidency of an order some dignity of rule necessarily goes, and no one can preside over a college unless he takes upon himself, on behalf of all, some of its more honourable burdens. If anyone wishes to call this an exceptional power, that is his affair. But the question is whether, by the right of their office, the present bishops affirm that they must hold this exceptional power without the voluntary consent of their colleagues. Jerome denies it. In his commentary on Titus 1: "As presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one who has been set over them, so bishops know that they are greater by custom rather than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement." And Augustine, letter 19 to Jerome: "According to the names of honour which the usage of the Church has now obtained, the episcopate is greater than the presbytery." From these things it is plain that not all power of jurisdiction, nor always, nor by all those bishops, was claimed as their own exclusively, to the exclusion of the presbyters. Much less did they profess that this had been committed to them by Christ, as the moderns boast of themselves. So much for the power of jurisdiction in general. It remains to show what the difference is between the ancient and the modern bishops with respect to the parts of that jurisdiction. And first, concerning the dynamic power [δυναμικὴ], which is concerned with judging causes of faith and religion.

units.la: Veteris. & Hodierni.
units.tr: Of the Ancient and the Modern.

units.la: Jus judicandi de rebus fidei sibi solis non transcripserunt: sed in presbyteris & Synodis cui frequentes inter-e-rant causas eas definen-das proponebant. Ruf-sin. lib. 1. Eccl. hist. c. 14. refert Alexandrum Alexandriæ episcopum
units.tr: They did not claim the right of judging matters of faith for themselves alone; rather they brought such questions to the presbyters and the synods, where they were often held, to be decided. Rufinus, in book 1 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 14, reports that Alexander, bishop of Alexandria,

units.la: Vix hic sibi constant, nam aliquando sibi solis omnem jurisdictionem externi fori vendicant: exclusis presbyteris, sic Dunamus[?] in concione. Presbyteri non guber-nant populum particularis sui gregis in foro ex-terno, hoc ad majoritatem Episcopalem pertinet: Interim alias conretulisse ad clerum quid statuendum esset de baptismo per Athanasium puerum inter ludendum administrato. & Cyprian. epistol. ad Quinti.testatum reliquit presbyteros una cum Episcopis convenisse in synodum, ut sententiam ferrent de baptismo haereticorum & schismatico- cedit locum & sententiae dictionem presbyteris simul cum Episcopis in synodis & presbyteriis: In quibus notius est quam ut probationi insita, de causis fidei & religionis disceptari solere: Sed facile haec conciliari possunt, interesse presbyteros ut consiliarios, non ut judices;quorum sententiam admittere aut rejicere potest pro arbitrio Episcopus. rum.Malchion,qui presbyter solū fuit Antioche-na Ecclesia, non solum interfuit ut judex Antiocheno concilio secundo,contra Paulum Samosatenum Episcopum Antiochenum convocato, sed cum eloquentia & singulari eruditione emineret ut ait Eusebius Eccles. hist. lib.7.cap.28.eidem concilio interfuit, & haereticum notariis omnia excipientibus quaestionibus ursit. Ejus etiam nomen in Epistola Synodica reperitur,quaescripta fuit nomine Episcoporum presbyterorum & Diaconorum. Aderant autem quamplures magni nominis Episcopi. Hierosolymae, Caesarea Palestinae, Caesarea Cappadociae Tarsensis, Iconiensis, quorum longum Catalogum ex Eusebio recensent authores centuriarum Magdeburgicarum. cent.3.c.9.parag. è penultima.Et hoc omnes reformatarum Ecclesiarum Doctores mordicus contra Pontificios tuentur. Quare cum in synodis. jurisdi-ctio[?] Ætio δυναμικὴ[?] exerceri solita fuerit: atque in iis omnibus decisiva suffragia tulisse presbyteros æque ac Episcopos, reformatis omnibus certum sit: evidenter sequitur potestatem dogmaticam veteres illos episcopos sibi solis non vendicasse.
units.tr: Here these men hardly agree with themselves, for at times they claim all jurisdiction of the external forum for themselves alone, excluding the presbyters. Thus Dunamus[?] in a sermon: "The presbyters do not govern the people of their particular flock in the external forum; this belongs to the episcopal majority." Yet at other times they have reported to the clergy what should be decided about baptism administered by Athanasius, a boy, while at play. Cyprian, in his letter to Quintus, has left it on record that the presbyters came together with the bishops in a synod to pass judgment on the baptism of heretics and schismatics. The presbyters yield their place and their voice in judgment to the bishops, together with the presbyters, in synods and presbyteries. It is better known than needs proof that causes of faith and religion were usually disputed there. But these matters can easily be reconciled: the presbyters are present as counsellors, not as judges, and the bishop may admit or reject their opinion as he pleases. Malchion, who was only a presbyter of the Antiochene church, not only took part as a judge in the second Antiochene council, convened against Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, but also, since he excelled in eloquence and unusual learning, as Eusebius says in book 7, chapter 28 of his Ecclesiastical History, he was present at the same council, and questioned the heretic while notaries recorded everything. His name is also found in the synodal letter, which was written in the name of the bishops, presbyters and deacons. Many bishops of great name were present: those of Jerusalem, Caesarea in Palestine, Caesarea in Cappadocia, Tarsus, and Iconium. The authors of the Magdeburg Centuries, century 3, chapter 9, near the end of the paragraph, recite a long catalogue of them from Eusebius. All the teachers of the reformed churches defend this stoutly against the Papists. Therefore, since it is established among all the reformed that in synods the power of judgment was customarily exercised, and that in all of them the presbyters as well as the bishops gave decisive votes, it evidently follows that those ancient bishops did not claim the dogmatic power for themselves alone.

units.la: Sequitur potestas διακτικὴ[?], quæ exercetur in iis quæ ad externum regimen ecclesiæ pertinent; & externis ceremoniis cultui divino administrando accommodatis. Atq; hic exsurgit nova differentia,nam
units.tr: There follows the power διακτικὴ[?], which is exercised in those matters that pertain to the external government of the church, and to the external ceremonies adapted to the administration of divine worship. Here a new difference arises, for

units.la: Veteres.
units.tr: The Ancient.

units.tr: They judged that this power was common to them with the presbyters. Therefore, by the common votes of all, in synods they drew up the διατυπώσεις[?], that is, the formulas of the Agenda, and the chapters (as they wished,

units.la: Hodierni.
units.tr: The Modern.

units.la: Sibi solis omnem vendicarunt, ac presbyteris ne quidem consultis, Canones fabricarunt, & Presbyteris pro imperio obtruserunt:uti & novam liturgiæ formulam antiquata veteri.
units.tr: They claimed all of it for themselves alone, and without even consulting the presbyters they framed canons and imposed them on the presbyters by command, and likewise introduced a new form of liturgy, with the old one set aside.

units.la: cant) fecerunt. Quin & crassissimis Papismi tenebris non licuit Episcopis sine presbyterorum consensu Agendarum istarum receptas formulas mutare. Nota est illustris illa disceptatio inter Episcopum Andegavensem, & Canonicos aliquot S. Trinitatis collegii ibidem, quos presbyterio veteri successisse nullus negat: quæ hunc successum habuit ut sententia senatus regii definiretur, Episcopo non licere breviarium & missale ibidem usitatum mutare. Vide amplissimi Thuani historiar. lib. 129. ad annum 1603.
units.tr: did so). Indeed, even in the thickest darkness of Papism the bishops were not permitted to change those accepted forms of the Agenda without the consent of the presbyters. That famous dispute is well known between the bishop of Angers and some canons of the college of the Holy Trinity there, who no one denies succeeded the ancient presbytery. The outcome of this was that by a decision of the royal senate it was determined that the bishop was not allowed to change the breviary and missal used there. See the most distinguished Thuanus, Histories, book 129, under the year 1603.

units.la: Superest potestas γενικὴ[?] in exercitio disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ posita, multiplex hic se prodit dissimilitudo: nā-
units.tr: There remains the power γενικὴ[?], which consists in the exercise of ecclesiastical discipline; here a manifold dissimilarity shows itself, for

units.la: IO.
Veteres. & Hodierni.
units.tr: The Ancient and the Modern.

units.la: Nullam disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ partem soli exclusis presbyteris exercuerunt, sed omnia eorum consilio & suffragio administrabant, quippe quod presbyteris æque ac sibi disciplinam commissam sciebant: Tertull. in Apologet. Ibidem (id est in cœtu publico ecclesiæ) exhortationes, castigationes, & censura divina, inter quas refert relegationem à communicatione orationis, conventus & omnis sancti commercii, hoc est, quod vulgo nunc vocatur excommunicatio major. Iam accipe per quos administraretur: Præsident probati quique seniores, honorem istum non pretio sed testimonio adepti. Et ante illum Irenæus adversus hæres. lib. 4. cap. 44. Presbyteris iis obediri oportet qui successionem ab Apostolis habent, & sanam doctrinam præbent ad informationem & correctionem aliorum. Loci illius series satis ostendit intelligi correctionem judicialem, quam non exercuere presbyteri deputatione episcopali, sed virtute sui presbyteratus, in quo Apostolorum successores fuerunt. Cyprianus frequentissime in epistolis. lib. 3. epist. 5. Non defuit presbyteris sacerdotii vigor, ut quidam disciplinæ minus memores
units.tr: The ancient bishops did not exercise any part of ecclesiastical discipline by themselves, excluding the presbyters; rather they administered all of it by the counsel and vote of the presbyters, since they knew discipline was committed to the presbyters equally with themselves. Tertullian, in his Apology: There (that is, in the public assembly of the church) are exhortations, rebukes and divine censure, among which he mentions exclusion from fellowship in prayer, from assembly, and from every holy association, that is, what is now commonly called major excommunication. Now hear by whom it was administered: Certain approved elders preside, who have obtained that honour not by payment but by testimony. And before him Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 4, chapter 44: One must obey those presbyters who have succession from the Apostles and who provide sound doctrine for the instruction and correction of others. The sequence of that passage shows well enough that judicial correction is meant, which the presbyters did not exercise by episcopal appointment but by virtue of their presbyterate, in which they were the successors of the Apostles. Cyprian, very often in his letters, book 3, letter 5: The vigour of the priesthood was not lacking in the presbyters, to restrain certain men who were less mindful of discipline.

units.la: Excommunicandi potestatem sibi solis arrogant, ut & solvendi a sententia excommunicationis lata. Soli clericalem disciplinam exercent aut per se, aut per officiales, cancellarios, à se deputatos, qui sacro presbyteratus ordini nunquam initiati fuerunt. comprimerentur. Itaque ad episcopi & mancipiorum ejus forum non fuit recurrendum ut, hodie fit. Et lib-2. epistol. 7. Lapsorum causa consuevit tractari facta conciliorum collatione cum Episcopis & presbyteris. Ita quidem, ut firmum decretum esse non poterat quod plurimorum consensum habuisse non videbatur. ibid. Cum ad eum delata esset querela; placuit, inquit, presbyterium contrahi. Nempe, religio illi fuit a primordio Episcopatus, sibi soli rem communem vendicare, & quae mutuus honor communi presbyterorum consilio peragenda postularet, privatim administrare. lib. 3. epistol. 10. & 19. Eadem mens Hieronymo, in epist. ad Heliodor. Mihi ante presbyterum sedere non licet, illi, si peccavero licet me tradere Satanae ad interitum carnis, ut salvus fiat spiritus. In Synodis quibus intererant presbyteri, anathema dictum haereticis: Depositi episcopi, ut Samosatenus in Antiochena & Marcellinus in Sinuessana sententia 30. presbyterorum Romanorum damnatus. Quin & veteres Episcopi, seniores, seu presbyteros gubernantes ab administratione disciplinae non excludebat: sine horum concilio nihil agebatur in ecclesia, donec doctorum superbia excluderentur, inquit Author commentariorum in 1. Tim. c. 5. quae nomine Ambrosii circumferuntur. Ius ligandi & solvendi ὁμοίως[?] ex aequo omnibus pastoribus & doctoribus tributum esse a Christo, asserit Basilius Magnus Archiepiscopus Caesariensis quod nec Lomb: negat sententiar. li. 4. dist. 19.
units.tr: The Modern claim the power of excommunicating for themselves alone, and likewise of absolving from a sentence of excommunication once pronounced. They alone exercise clerical discipline, either in person or through officials and chancellors appointed by themselves, who were never ordained to the sacred order of the presbyterate. So it was not necessary to appeal to the court of the bishop and his servants, as happens today. And in book 2, letter 7: The case of the lapsed was customarily handled by a joint gathering of the councils with the bishops and presbyters, so that a decree could not be firm if it did not seem to have the consent of most of them. Also ibid.: When a complaint had been brought to him, it was decided, he says, that the presbytery be convened. Indeed, it was a matter of conscience for him, from the very beginning of the episcopate, to claim for himself alone a common matter, and to transact privately what the mutual honour owed to the presbyters demanded be done by common counsel of the presbyters. Book 3, letters 10 and 19. The same mind is found in Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus: It is not lawful for me to sit before a presbyter; if I have sinned, let him hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. In synods in which presbyters were present, anathema was pronounced against heretics; bishops were deposed, as Samosatenus in Antioch and Marcellinus in Sinuessa were condemned by the sentence of thirty Roman presbyters. Indeed, the ancient bishops did not exclude from the administration of discipline the elders who governed; nothing was done in the church without their council, until the pride of the teachers shut them out, says the author of the commentaries on 1 Timothy, chapter 5, which circulate under the name of Ambrose. Basil the Great, archbishop of Caesarea, asserts that the power of binding and loosing was granted by Christ equally to all pastors and teachers; the Lombard, Sentences, book 4, distinction 19, does not deny this.

units.la: Verum sicuti hodierni Episcopi sibi solis potestatem hanc vendicant, ita in alios sacrilege transtulerunt, & per vicarios suos, officiales, Archidiaconos, Cancellarios, Antichristi excrementa omnes disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ partes, quin & excommunicationem ipsam administrant: atque sic non solum per se tyrannidem in ecclesiam exercent, sed sub servos hosce suos in miserrimam servitutem redegerunt; qui in nullo ordine sacro constituti sunt, sed homines mere sæculares: Annon propria vineta cadunt Hierarchici alias reformatas ecclesias damnantes, quod administrationi disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ ex Apostoli præscripto & purioris sæculi exemplo, (nequicquam contra fremente D. Hallo & Symmistis) admoveant seniores gubernantes, homines laicos, hoc est, qui vocationem sæcularem sequuntur? etenim si illicitum est hujus conditionis homines pietate & prudentia conspicuos simul cum pastoribus seu verbi presbyteris disciplinam administrare, quam indecorum est novitiam istam prolem officialium & cæt. Scriptura & antiquitati penitus incognitam, per se solam nobilissimos actus jurisdictionis ecclesiasticæ exercere? Videsis doctissimum illum tractatum, cui titulus Altare Damascenum, cap. 5. de Episcoporum dignitate & potestate & cap. 6. De vicariis & officialibus, cujus auctori ut acceptum feras enixe rogo, si quid Antithesibus hisce adjutum te cernas. Infœlicis certe ingenii esset, ut ait ille, non fateri per quos profecerim; neque clarissimus ille author, quisquis sit, agre feret, gratiam hanc sibi à me multorum nomine ingenue repositam. Difficilia ista temporacum quibus colluctatus est, literato orbi au-ctoris nomen suppresserunt.
units.tr: But just as the modern bishops claim this power for themselves alone, so they have sacrilegiously transferred it to others, and through their vicars, officials, archdeacons and chancellors, the excrements of Antichrist, they administer all parts of ecclesiastical discipline, and even excommunication itself. Thus they not only exercise tyranny over the church in person, but have also reduced these servants of theirs into the most wretched servitude; these men are appointed to no sacred order but are mere laymen. Do not the hierarchs, who condemn the other reformed churches because they admit to the administration of ecclesiastical discipline, according to the Apostle's prescription and the example of the purer age (though Dr. Hall and the Symmists rage against it in vain), governing elders, that is, men who follow a secular calling? For if it is unlawful for men of this condition, distinguished for piety and prudence, to administer discipline together with the pastors or presbyters of the Word, how unseemly it is that this novel breed of officials, unknown to Scripture and to antiquity altogether, should by themselves exercise the most noble acts of ecclesiastical jurisdiction? See that most learned treatise entitled The Damascene Altar, chapter 5, On the dignity and power of bishops, and chapter 6, On vicars and officials; I earnestly ask you to credit its author, if you find anything in these Antitheses helped by it. It would certainly be the mark of an unhappy intellect, as that man says, not to confess through whom one has advanced; nor will that most distinguished author, whoever he is, be displeased that I have openly set down this favour to him on behalf of many. Those difficult times with which he struggled have hidden the author's name from the literate world.

units.la: Omnem supra presbyteros honoris prærogativam, voluntario eorundem consensui ascribe-bant; seque mera con-suetudine, non vero dominicæ dispositionis veritate iisdem majores esse, Eundem esse jure divino Episcopum & presbyterum: ex æquo utrumque Apostolis successisse, uti antithesi prima ostensum fuit. Quæ ad potestatem ordinis & jurisdictionis spectant, utrisque ex æquo competivisse, & eadem junctim administrasse, ut antithesi. 7. 8. 9. 10. probatum fuit.
units.tr: They ascribed every prerogative of honour above the presbyters to the voluntary consent of the presbyters, and they claimed to be greater than them by mere custom, not by the truth of the Lord's arrangement. The same man is, by divine right, both bishop and presbyter: both succeeded the Apostles on equal terms, as was shown in the first antithesis. What belongs to the power of order and of jurisdiction equally belonged to both, and they administered the same jointly, as was proved in antitheses 7, 8, 9 and 10.

units.la: Hinc Irenæus lib.4.c. 43. qui vixit anno Chri-
units.tr: Hence Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 43, who lived in the year of the Christian era

units.la: Ast hi singulares illas prærogativas supra presbyteros & presbytero-rum collegia, jure divino sibi vendicant: ita ut ne-fas, & sacrilegium fit vel scrupulum unicum exortis hujus potestatis præ-sulibus abradere: à Spiritu S. episcopos se con-stitutos jactitant, neque episcopatum suum seferre acceptum ecclesiæ e-jusque synodis; neque regibus; nempe, vocatio-nem habent à Christo, solam permissionem ex-ercitii hujus potestatis à principe. Inde Episcopatum necessarium esse dicunt, & presbyteros a-liarum ecclesiarum refor-matarum ἀκέφαλος vocant, & ecclesias episco-pis hisce destitutas, vel eo nomine laborare defectu ftianæ ara. 180. Oportet eis qui in ecclesia sunt obedire presbyteris, qui successionem habent ab Apostolis sicut ostendimus, qui cum Episcopatus successione charisma veritatis acceperunt. Scholastici doctores in enumerandis ecclesiæ ordinibus, episcopatum & presbyteratum unum tantum ordinem faciunt, vide citatos fuse à Clariss. Gersomo Bucero, dissertationis de gubernatione ecclesiastica parag. 70. & celeberrimo D. Voetio in Desperata causa papatus lib. 2. sect. 1. cap. 9. Verum quidem est Æriū ab Epiphanio inter Hæreticos relatum, quod dixerit Episcopum jure divino nihil differre ab Episcopo. Sed si hoc hæreseos nota dignū, quo pacto ab eadem [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: But these men claim those singular prerogatives above the presbyters and the colleges of presbyters by divine right, so that it is impious and sacrilegious to scrape away even a single scruple of this power from the bishops who have been set over them. They boast that they were constituted bishops by the Holy Spirit, and they do not admit that their episcopate was received from the Church and its synods, nor from kings; they have their calling from Christ, and only the permission to exercise this power from the prince. Hence they say that the episcopate is necessary, and they call the presbyters of the other reformed churches headless (ἀκέφαλος), and say that churches destitute of such bishops labour under a defect of the Christian era 180. It is necessary for those who are in the Church to obey the presbyters, who have succession from the Apostles, as we have shown, and who with the succession of the episcopate have received the charism of truth. The Scholastic doctors, in enumerating the orders of the Church, make the episcopate and the presbyterate one order only; see those cited at length by the most distinguished Gerson Bucer, in his dissertation on ecclesiastical government, paragraph 70, and by the most celebrated D. Voetius in Desperata causa papatus, book 2, section 1, chapter 9. It is true that Aerius was listed by Epiphanius among the heretics, because he said that a bishop differs in nothing by divine right from a presbyter. But if this is worthy of the mark of heresy, how is it that from the same [illegible]

units.la: œconomico, male constitutas esse; & receptum est axioma Cantuariensis scholæ. Irritam[?] esse [?]ns scholæ, [?]ritiam ene omnem presbyterorum ordinationem quæ ab Episcopis non administratur, quia scil. legitimus ordinationis minister ex juris divini præscripto est solus Episcopus. Si quis contra hiscere ausus fit, hæreticum vocant Ærianum, paritatem vero presbyteri & Episcopi, omnium Calvinianum, & dogma antiquitati explosum. Etenim, ut huius erroris fontem aperiam, non ignorabant boni illi viri corruituram necessario Episcopatum, si fragili humanæ authoritatis fulcro solummodo inniteretur, utpote quod receptum sit juris axioma. Jura positiva cum incipiunt corrumpere viam suam sunt antiquanda. Et Consuetudines (humano videl. consilio receptæ) quæ ecclesiis noscuntur gravamen inducere nostra nos decet consideratione remittere, uti bene Ambrosius, Augustinus, & nubes illa patrum, citante Bellarm. lib. 1. De clericis cap. 15. ex Medina. Et quicquid nunc garriant Canonistae, notum tamen est in ecclesia duos tantum fuisse ordines sacros, presbyteratum & Diaconatum. vide Gratiani decreta: distinct. 60. Can. nullus: Hieronymus usque adeo aperte hoc tuetur in comment. in Titum. cap. 1. ad illa verba: Ut constituas presbyteros sicut ego disposui,
units.tr: economic, were badly constituted; and the axiom of the Canterbury school is accepted. ... that every ordination of presbyters that is not administered by bishops is void, because, namely, by the prescription of divine law the only lawful minister of ordination is the bishop. If anyone has dared to murmur against this, they call him an Arian heretic, and they call the equality of presbyter and bishop Calvinist, and a doctrine exploded by antiquity. For, to lay open the source of this error, those good men did not fail to see that the episcopate would necessarily fall if it rested only on the fragile prop of human authority, since that is an accepted axiom of law. Positive laws, when they begin to corrupt, must be made ancient. And customs (received, that is, by human counsel) which are known to bring burden to the churches, it befits us to remit by our consideration, as Ambrose, Augustine and that cloud of Fathers rightly do, citing Bellarmine, book 1 On the Clergy, chapter 15, from Medina. And whatever the Canonists now chatter, it is nonetheless well known that in the Church there were only two sacred orders, the presbyterate and the diaconate; see the Decrees of Gratian, distinction 60, canon "Nullus". Jerome defends this so openly in his commentary on Titus, chapter 1, on those words, "That you should appoint presbyters as I have directed,

units.la: sanxit Gregor.Magn.lib. 1.Epist.64. Et orbi Christiano non solum praecedentium saeculorum tristi exemplo, verumetiam praesentis aevi lugubri experientia plusquam manifestum est praesulum istam vel moderatam προστασίαν[?] fomitem esse & fuisse ambitionis, & ex ea pullulantium schismatum & haeresium. Atque hinc est quod in desperatae suae causae patrocinium ad jus divinum recurrant, licet frustra, & reclamante universo reformatorum choro.
units.tr: Gregory the Great sanctioned it, book 1, letter 64. And to the Christian world it is more than manifest, not only from the sad example of preceding ages but from the mournful experience of the present age, that this prostasia [προστασία] of bishops, whether moderate or not, is and has been a kindling of ambition, and of the schisms and heresies that sprout from it. And hence it is that, to defend their desperate cause, they have recourse to divine right, although in vain, and with the whole choir of the Reformed protesting against them.

units.la: & in epistola ad Evagrium; Ut Hierarchici affirment errasse hic Hieronymum; & parum abest quin albo haereticorum, uti hoc nomine Epiphanius Ærium, asscribant: flosculos tantum exscribam: Locis illis praedictis agens de ecclesiastica politia ratione non solum qua Apostolorum aetate, sed qua eam proximae subsecuta est, Communi presbyterorum consilio ecclesiam gubernatam fuisse dicit; Ergo indistincta tunc fuerunt episcoporum & presbyterorum officia ut & nomina: quandoquidem gubernationis praerogativa sese efferant episcopi supra presbyteros, ea vero olim utrisque communis fuerit, quid quaso restare poterat quo a se invicem tunc distinguerentur? Et hoc plurimis SS.script:locis perspicue probat: thesfeos[?] sua repetitione subjungens, ostendimus apud veteres eosdē fuisse presbyteros quos & episcopos: postea paulatim ad unū omnis sollicitudo est delata ut dissensionum plantaria evellerētur: An vero medicina morbo responderit, eventus docuit. Et Alphonsus de Castro advers. hæreses lib. 6. titulo Episcopus; Aperte negat pastorum inæqualitate plantaria diffensionum exstirpari : de mutatione hac politejas ecclesiastica sicMusculus in locis communibus. Profueritne, vel secus consilium hoc ecclesiæ Christi, melius est posterioribus sæculis declaratum, quam dum hæc consuetudo primum introduceretur, cui debemus omnem illam principalium & equestrium episcoporum insolentiam ac tyrannidem, imo omnium ecclesiarum Christi corruptionem, quam si Hieronymus cerneret, dubio procul consilium agnosceret non Spiritus Sancti ad tollenda schismata, sicuti prætexebatur, sed ipsius Satanæ ad vastanda & perdenda prisca pascendi dominici gregis minis-teria: quo fieret ut haberet ecclesia non veros doctores, pastores, presbyteros & episcopos, sed sub nominum istorum larvis, otiosos ventres & magnificos principes, qui non modo non pascant ipsi populum domini doctrina fana & Apostolica, sed & improbissima violentia caveant, ne id per quemquam alium fiat:
units.tr: and in his letter to Evagrius: that the Hierarchists affirm Jerome erred here, and they come close to enrolling him in the roll of heretics, as Epiphanius did Aerius under that name. I shall copy only the flowers: in the places mentioned, treating of the arrangement of ecclesiastical polity, not only as it stood in the age of the Apostles but as it followed soon after it, he says the Church was governed by the common counsel of the presbyters; therefore the offices of bishops and presbyters were then undistinguished, and so were their names. For since the prerogative of governance raises bishops above presbyters, but that was once common to both, what, I ask, could remain by which they were then distinguished from one another? And he proves this clearly from very many passages of Holy Scripture, by repeating it and adding, "We have shown that among the ancients those were presbyters who were also bishops; afterwards, little by little, all care was transferred to one, so that the seedbeds of dissensions might be uprooted." Whether the medicine answered the disease, the outcome has shown. And Alphonsus de Castro, against heresies, book 6, under the title Bishop, plainly denies that the seeds of dissension are rooted out by the inequality of pastors; on this change in ecclesiastical polity, see Musculus in his Commonplaces. Whether this counsel was beneficial or otherwise to the Church of Christ has been declared better in later centuries than when this custom was first introduced, to which we owe all that insolence and tyranny of princely and knightly bishops, indeed the corruption of all the churches of Christ. If Jerome were to see it, he would doubtless recognise a counsel not of the Holy Spirit for removing schisms, as was pretended, but of Satan himself, for laying waste and destroying the ancient ministries of feeding the Lord's flock; with the result that the Church would have not true teachers, pastors, presbyters and bishops, but, under the masks of those names, idle bellies and magnificent princes, who not only do not feed the people of the Lord themselves with sound and apostolic teaching, but with most wicked violence take care that no one else does so:

units.la: Et Whitakerus de pontifice Roman.quaest. 1. cap. 3. paragraph. 26. remedium hoc morbo ipso pene pejus fuisse, utpote quod primus fuerit gradus monarchiæ pontificiæ , annotante Illyrico parte. 1. Clavis scriptura in voce, Episcopus. Rursus ibid. Hieronymus. Presbyteri sicut sciunt se ex ecclesiæ consuetudine esse subjectos ei qui sibi præpositus fuerit , ita Episcopi noverint, se magis consuetudine quam dominicæ dispositionis veritate presbyteris esse majores , & in commune debere ecclesiam regere. Ab Hieronymo ad Chrysostomum transeamus; Is hom. II. in 1. Tim. capit. 3. quærit, cur de Episcopis differens, omisso presbyterorum ordine, ad Diaconos transfilierit? Respondet. Quia medium (videlicet interveniens inter Episcopos & Diaconos) non multum, etenim illi (presbyteri) & docendi munus susceperant & præsidendi ecclesiæ, & quæ de Episcopis dixit eadem de presbyteris (dici.) sola enim horum electione ascenderunt; sensus est, Episcopos habere a presbyterorum electione quod ordinis causa præsint presbyterio, atque uniea [?] hac ratione a presbyteris differre: Eandem semitam terit Sedulius presbyter Scotus, qui eodem sæculo vixit quo Paladius, qui missus a Celestino pontifice Romano Episcopos in Scotia primus creasse dicitur, verba formalia Hieronymi citat & approbat, in expositione epistolarum ad Titum & Timotheum.
