Ambrosius eodem inclinat. in Comment. in 1. Timoth. cap. 3. Quare (inquit) post Episcopum Diaconatus ordinem subjecit? Nisi quia presbyteri & Episcopi una ordinatio est. Uterque enim sacerdos est, sed Episcopus primus est, ut omnis episcopus presbyter sit, non tamen omnis presbyter Episcopus, hic enim Episcopus est qui inter presbyteros primus est: Redolentne hæc quæso principatum potestatis debitum episcopis iure divino; An potius primatum ordinis ab ecclesia introductum? primus, inquit, erat presbyter; cui loco illustrando subserviat illud ejusdem Ambrosii comment. in cap. 4. ad Ephes. Non per omnia (inquit) conveniunt scripta Apostoli, ordinationi, quæ nunc in ecclesia est, Nam & Timotheum à se creatum presbyterum, episcopum vocat, quia primi presbyteri episcopi appellabantur, ut recedente eo sequens ei succederet. Unde colligitur præsidentiam illam ordinis, cum primum institutum hoc obtinuisset, non fuisse perpetuam, sed succedaneam, hoc est, primatus ille ordinis olim nulli fuit perpetuus, nec ad vitam certa persona annexus, prout Ambrosii sæculo obtinuit, sed omnibus presbyteris communis, utpote quod sibi invicem in præsidentia succederent: Augustino eadem mens tom. 2. operum epistol. 19. ad Hieronymū. Quanquam, inquit, secundum honorum vocabula quæ jam ecclesiæ usus obtinuit, Episcopatus presbyterio major sit, tamen in multis rebus Augustinus Hieronymo minor est. Præceptoris sui vestigia pressit Primasius in Comment. ad Epistolam ad Tit. Quæ fuerit venerabilis Bedæ sententia, aperte explicat in commentariis Actorum Apostolicorum, ad illa verba: In quo Spiritus S. vos posuit episcoepiscopos: vide Albini Alcuini sententiam supra, antithesi. 4. ejusque σύγχρονος[?] Rabanus Maurus, quem Scotum natione vocant non solum historici Scoti in vita regis Achaii à quo in Gallias ad Carolum Magnum missus fuit, sed & Angli ipsi, Balæus in scriptoribus ecclesiasticis magna Britanniæ: multosque variarum nationum & saeculorum authores magni nominis. Rabanum hunc Scotiæ vendicantes, citat Dempsterus in libro cui titulus, Mendicabula Hibernorum repressa & cæt. & David Camerarius lib. 3. De Scotorum pietate in Menologio Scotorum sanctorum ad diem 4. Februarii, videantur ipsius Rabani commentaria in epist. Pauli ad Philippenses & ad Timotheum: cujus verba quia eadem fere sunt cum Chrysostomi & Hieronymi supra citatis, non exscribam: Porro cum omnes hi paritatem presbyterorum & episcoporum ex scripturis asserunt neque nomina solum utrisque fuisse olim communia, verum etiam munia, paradoxum illud hodiernorum hierarchicorum, principatum potestatis supra presbyteros jure divino vendicantium, merito explodendum est: At Apostolici saltem juris fuisse putabant veteres Episcopatum (inquient hierarchici:) At quo argumento illud persuadebunt? Etenim cum splendidissima illa patrum nubes ex scriptis Apostolicis presbyterorum & episcoporum paritatem astruxerit, probabile cuiquam erit eosdem imparitatem hanc Apostolis authoribus transcribere posse? præsertim cum perspicue testatum reliquerint, nihil pro Apostolico habendum quod in scriptis Apostolorum non reperiatur. Hieronymus in Haggæum cap. 1. Quæ (inquit) absque authoritate & testimoniis scripturarum quasi Apostolica traditione sponte reperiunt, atque confingunt, percutit gladius Dei: & ejus æqualis Theophilus Alexandrinus: in Epistola 2. Paschali. Diabolicum est extra scripturarum divinarum authoritatem aliquid divinum putare: At quod Apostolicum est divinum est: Nisi fortasse ecclesiis reponere velint pontificium illud Apostolorum traditiones alias suisse scriptas, alias vero non scriptas: inter quas si hanc de Episcopatu numerent, age examinetur ad regulam illam Augustini contra Donatistas lib. 4. capit. 24. Quod universa tenet ecclesia, nec conciliis institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. At Episcopatum Diœcesanum universa ubique ac semper tenebat ecclesia, nec conciliis institutus fuit, id est, conciliorum authoritate introductus. Quam falsa hæc minor sit precedentes & subsecuturæ antitheses demonstrant: Adde quod Hieronymus aperte testetur, episcopatum à conciliis primitus sancitum. Comment. in Tit. 1.
units.tr: And Whitaker, On the Roman Pontiff, Quaest. 1, chap. 3, para. 26, says that this remedy was almost worse than the disease itself, inasmuch as it was the first step toward papal monarchy, as Illyricus notes in part 1 of the Clavis Scripturae, under the word Episcopus. Again in the same place, Jerome: "Just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one set over them, so let bishops know that they are greater than presbyters by custom rather than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement, and that they ought to rule the Church in common." Let us pass from Jerome to Chrysostom. In Homily 2 on 1 Timothy, chapter 3, he asks why, in speaking of bishops, he passed over the order of presbyters and went on to deacons. He answers: because the intermediate order (that is, the one between bishops and deacons) is not large; for presbyters had received both the office of teaching and the office of presiding over the Church, and what he said of bishops he said also of presbyters, for they rose to office by election alone. The sense is that bishops have from the election of presbyters that they preside over the presbytery for the sake of order, and by this reasoning they differ from presbyters. Sedulius, a Scottish presbyter, treads the same path. He lived in the same century as Palladius, who was sent by Pope Celestine and is said to have been the first to create bishops in Scotland. In his exposition of the Epistles to Titus and Timothy he cites and approves Jerome's very words. Ambrose leans the same way, in his Commentary on 1 Timothy, chap. 3: "Why (he says) did he place the order of deacons after the bishop? Unless because presbyters and bishops are one ordination. For both are priests, but the bishop is first, so that every bishop is a presbyter, yet not every presbyter is a bishop; for he is bishop who is first among the presbyters." Do these words, I ask, smell of a power of rule owed to bishops by divine right, or rather of a primacy of order introduced by the Church? "He was first," he says, "a presbyter." To illustrate this, Ambrose's own commentary on chapter 4 of Ephesians serves: "The writings of the Apostle do not agree in all things with the ordination which now exists in the Church. For he calls Timothy, whom he himself made a presbyter, a bishop, because the first presbyters were called bishops, so that when one withdrew, the next succeeded him." From this it is gathered that the presidency of order, when it was first instituted, was not perpetual but successive. That is, the primacy of order was once held by no one permanently, nor attached to a fixed person for life, as it prevailed in Ambrose's century; it was common to all presbyters, since they succeeded one another in the presidency. Augustine holds the same view, in volume 2 of his works, Letter 19, to Jerome: "Although," he says, "according to the titles of honour which the usage of the Church has now established, the episcopate is greater than the presbytery, yet in many things Augustine is less than Jerome." Primasius followed the footsteps of his teacher in his Commentary on the Epistle to Titus. What the venerable Bede's opinion was he plainly explains in his commentaries on the Acts of the Apostles, on the words: "In which the Holy Spirit has placed you bishops." See the opinion of Alcuin above, antithesis 4, and of his contemporary [synchronos] Rabanus Maurus, whom not only the Scottish historians, in the life of King Achaius, from whom he was sent into Gaul to Charlemagne, call a Scot by birth, but the English themselves, Bale in his Ecclesiastical Writers of Great Britain, and many authors of great name of various nations and centuries. Dempster, claiming this Rabanus for Scotland, cites him in the book entitled The Mendicant Irish Repressed, and David Camerarius, book 3, On the Piety of the Scots, in the Menology of the Scottish saints, at 4 February. Let his commentaries on the Epistles to the Philippians and to Timothy be consulted; since his words are almost the same as those of Chrysostom and Jerome cited above, I will not copy them out. Moreover, since all these writers assert from Scripture the equality of presbyters and bishops, and since not only the names but also the functions were once common to both, that paradox of today's hierarchists, who claim a principate of power over presbyters by divine right, is rightly to be exploded. "But at least the ancients thought the episcopate to be of apostolic law," the hierarchists will say. But by what argument will they persuade us of this? For since that splendid cloud of Fathers has established from the apostolic writings the equality of presbyters and bishops, will it be probable to anyone that they could have transcribed this inequality from the Apostles as authors? Especially since they have plainly left it on record that nothing is to be held as apostolic which is not found in the writings of the Apostles. Jerome on Haggai, chap. 1: "Those things which they spontaneously discover and invent, without authority and testimonies of Scripture, as if by apostolic tradition, the sword of God strikes." And his contemporary Theophilus of Alexandria, in his Second Paschal Letter: "It is diabolical to think something divine outside the authority of the divine Scriptures; but what is apostolic is divine." Unless perhaps they wish to hold, with the papists, that some apostolic traditions were written and others were not written; if they count episcopacy among the unwritten ones, let it be examined by that rule of Augustine against the Donatists, book 4, chap. 24: "What the whole Church holds, and what has not been instituted by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority." But the whole Church everywhere and always held the diocesan episcopate, and it was not instituted by councils, that is, introduced by the authority of councils. How false this minor premise is, the preceding and following antitheses show. Add that Jerome plainly testifies that the episcopate was first sanctioned by councils, in his Commentary on Titus, chap. 1.

units.la: Postquam unusquisque eos quos baptizaverat suos putabat esse non Christi, in toto orbe decretum est ut unus de presbyteris delectus superponeretur cæteris, ad quem omnis ecclesiæ cura pertineret. Dein idem Hieronym. in epistol. ad Euagrium: Primatum hunc episcoporum, Alexandriæ primum cœpisse, post mortem Marci Euangelistæ ; hancque consuetudinem uno impetu ab aliis omnibus ecclesiis receptam fuisse cui verisimile? præsertim cum addat ibidem, Paulatim, ut dissensionum plantaria evellerentur, omnem sollicitudinem ad unum delatam fuisse: si paulatim, certe non universaliter & semper obtinuit & consuetudinem hanc Alexandrinæ ecclesiæ Sozomenus lib. 1. cap. 15. civitatis consuetudinem vocat; quia videlicet apud alias ecclesias non obtinuit, Epiphanio ipso fatente: Haresi.86. de Miletianis. Non habuit Alexandria duos episcopos ut aliæ urbes: Cur itaque hic cum Hieronymo in eadem ad Enagrium epistola, Alexandrina ecclesia singulare exemplum objicientibus, respondere non liceat? Quid mihi profers unius urbis consuetudinem, quid paucitatem de qua ortum est supercilium in leges ecclesiæ, vindicas: Denique cui incognitum multas ecclesias duos simul episcopos habuisse præterioribus[?] illis sæculis. Clemens in constitut. lib. 7. cap. 46. refert. Euodium & Ignatium, non successive, sed simul uno eodemque tempore Antiochenæ ecclesiæ episcopatum adeptos fuisse: Nam explodendum insanum illud Baronii delirium, asserentis, duplicem fuisse Antiochia ecclesiam, ratione dissidii à Luca in Act. Apost. cap. 15. commemorati, inter eos qui fuerunt ex circumcisione, quos Nazaraos vocabant, & qui ex gentibus ecclesiæ nomina sua dederunt: sicuti postea factum esse commemorant ecclesiastica historiæ scriptores in iis civitatibus, quæ simul ab orthodoxis hæreticis aut schismaticis incolebantur : quasi vero Euodius aut Ignatius hæreticis publica Apostolorum sententia in Synodo Hierosolymitana damnatis. Act. 15. ministerii sui operam commodare voluissent : Prodigiosa illa varietas in nominando Petri successore in Episcopatu Romano, apud Ecclesiastica historiæ scriptores, aliis Linum, aliis Anacletum, aliis Clementem locantibus., nulla ratione reconciliari poterit, nisi concedatur plures Episcopos simul sedisse, ac pari authoritate ecclesiam gubernasse. Ecclesiæ Smyrnensi præfuit Polycarpus, Johannis Apostoli discipulus, ac ejus ecclesiæ episcopum ab Johanne ordinatum testantur Ignatius, Irenæus, Eusebius : at Clemens constit. Apostol. lib. 7. cap. 47. Aristionem primum fuisse Smyrnae episcopum, ejusque successorem Strateam, istiqué tertium Episcopum successisse alterum Aristionem : & Suidas in voce Polycarpus, Bucolum primum fuisse Smyrnensis ecclesiæ episcopum : Infinitum esset omnia hujus generis exempla coacervare ; Præsentia satis docent plures Episcopos uni ecclesiæ simul præfuisse ; Atque in hodierno episcopatu nihil ejusmodi cernitur, utpote quod inter propria ejus γνωρίσματα[?] hoc primum locum habeat ; Quod in Diœcesi Episcopus sit singularis, nam si plures admitterentur, altum iri clamant de unitate Ecclesiæ ; [?]Dunamus in concione Lambethana : utpote quod inter pastores ecclesiæ æqualitatem dicant esse schismatum & hæresεôn seminarium : quasi obliti essent illius Augustini in Psalm. 105. Nonne inquit, Episcopi fuerunt authores schismatum & haeresium? & illius apud Chrysost. hom. 58. ad populum Antiochenum : cum de priscis monachis sermonem faceret, Quoniam apud eos aequalitas multa fuerat, multa etiam fuit virtutis facilitas. Et unitatem in ecclesia conservari posse aliis mediis docet Cyprianus. lib. 3. epist. 13. copioso vid. corpore sacerdotum concordiae mutuae glutine & unitatis vinculo copulatum. Cohærentia porro hæc, docente Spalatensi, De Repub. eccles. lib. 3. cap. 1. parag. 14. paritatem supponit neque admittit subordinationem unius ad unum, sed ad plures, videlicet. Collegium, & Gregorius per humilitatem ecclesiae unitatem custodiri asserit. Priusquam sectioni huic finem imponam, eximendus est scrupulus quidam, quo fortasse quidam tenentur, ne prioribus sine haesitationis aestu subscribant: In historia ecclesiastica vident series episcoporum deductas à primis ecclesiarum incunabulis; ideoque colligunt unum semper singulariter, durante vita, praefuisse: Verum in rei hujus causas sollicite inquirentibus, haec occurrent quibus nubes haec dispelli commode possit: videlicet. Veteres scriptores unius tantum Episcopi mentionem ordinarie & ut plurimum fecisse, partim quia illis solis propositum fuit temporum rationem edocere, quod assequuti fuerant nominatione unius, qui propter doctrinam, aut virtutum ornamenta rerumve experientiam celebris essent: partim vero quia ad sui saeculi consuetudinem, quando unius ἐπισκοπῆς[?] praevaluit, scribendi ratiorationem mutuabantur. Sed de his hactenus fusius quam instituti ratio postulabat; ad reliquas antitheses progrediendum: in potestate extensiva, muneris exercitio, & vitæ habitu. Dissimilitudo ratione extensiva potestatis hæc est.
units.tr: After each one thought that those whom he had baptized were his own and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and set over the rest, to whom the entire care of the Church would pertain. Then the same Jerome, in his letter to Evagrius: "This primacy of the bishops began first at Alexandria, after the death of Mark the Evangelist." And how likely is it that this custom was received all at once from all other churches, especially since he adds in the same place: "Gradually, so that the seeds of dissensions might be plucked out, all care was transferred to one"? If it was gradual, then certainly it did not prevail universally and always. Sozomen, book 1, chap. 15, calls it a custom of the city, because clearly it did not prevail among other churches, as Epiphanius himself admits, Heresy 86, on the Meletians: "Alexandria did not have two bishops as other cities did." Why, then, may it not be answered here, together with Jerome in the same letter to Evagrius, to those who object the single example of the Alexandrian church? "Why do you bring me the custom of one city? Why do you claim as law of the Church a paucity from which arose pride?" Finally, who does not know that many churches in earlier centuries had two bishops at the same time? Clement, in the Constitutions, book 7, chap. 46, reports that Euodius and Ignatius obtained the episcopate of the Antiochene church not successively but simultaneously, at one and the same time. That mad delirium of Baronius must be exploded, who asserts that the church of Antioch was double, by reason of the dispute mentioned by Luke in Acts 15, between those who were of the circumcision, whom they called Nazarenes, and those who gave their names to the church from the Gentiles; as the ecclesiastical historians record was later done in those cities which were inhabited at the same time by orthodox and by heretics or schismatics. As if Euodius or Ignatius would have wished to lend the service of their ministry to heretics condemned by the public judgment of the Apostles in the Synod of Jerusalem, Acts 15! That prodigious variety in naming Peter's successor in the Roman episcopate, among the ecclesiastical historians, some placing Linus, others Anacletus, others Clement, can in no way be reconciled unless it is granted that several bishops sat at the same time and governed the church with equal authority. The church of Smyrna was presided over by Polycarp, a disciple of the Apostle John, and Ignatius, Irenaeus and Eusebius attest that he was ordained bishop of that church by John. But Clement, Apostolic Constitutions, book 7, chap. 47, says that Aristion was first bishop of Smyrna, that Strateas succeeded him, and that as third bishop another Aristion succeeded; and Suidas, in the word Polycarp, says that Bucolus was first bishop of the Smyrnean church. It would be endless to heap up all examples of this kind. The instances already given teach sufficiently that several bishops presided over one church at the same time. And in the present episcopacy nothing of the kind is seen, since among its own marks this holds the first place: that the bishop in a diocese is single. For if several were admitted, they cry out at once about the unity of the Church, Dunamus, in the Lambeth sermon, since they say that equality among the pastors of the church is a seminary of schisms and heresies [haireseōn]. As if they had forgotten that saying of Augustine on Psalm 105: "Were not bishops the authors of schisms and heresies?" and that saying of Chrysostom, Homily 58 to the people of Antioch, when he spoke of the ancient monks: "Since there was much equality among them, there was also much ease of virtue." And Cyprian, book 3, letter 13, teaches that unity in the church can be preserved by other means: "joined together by the glue of mutual concord and the bond of unity in a copious body of priests." Moreover, these bonds, as the Spalatensis teaches, On the Commonwealth of the Church, book 3, chap. 1, para. 14, presuppose equality and admit no subordination of one to one, but of one to several, namely a college. And Gregory asserts that unity is kept in the church by humility. Before I end this section, a certain scruple must be removed, by which some may be held back, lest they subscribe to the foregoing without any hesitation. In the ecclesiastical histories they see series of bishops traced from the earliest beginnings of the churches, and therefore they infer that always one alone, for life, presided. But to those who diligently inquire into the causes of this matter, these considerations will occur, by which this cloud may conveniently be dispelled. The ancient writers mention only one bishop, ordinarily and for the most part: partly because their purpose was only to teach the order of the times, which they achieved by naming one who was famous for learning, or for the ornaments of virtue, or for experience of affairs; and partly because they followed the manner of writing of their own age, when the rule of a single bishop had prevailed. But these matters have been discussed more fully than the plan of this work required; we must proceed to the remaining antitheses, in extent of power, exercise of the office, and habit of life. The dissimilarity in extent of power is this.

units.la: Veteres. & Hodierni.
units.tr: The Ancients and the Moderns.

units.la: Olim oppidatim fere fuerunt episcopi, nec majori intervallo inter se distincti; quod vel inde liquet, quod in concil. African. cap.20. refertur. Oportere, videl. ad examinandam causam presbyteri accusati, ut ex Episcopi ex vicinis locis adjungerentur episcopo: Et multo, ante Cypriani ætatem, tempore, in Concilio Lambesitano nonaginta episcoporum sententiis damnata fuisse privatum veterem hære-
units.tr: Formerly there were almost bishops in every town, and they were not separated from one another by any great distance. This is plain from the Council of Africa, canon 20, where it is laid down that, to examine the case of an accused presbyter, bishops should be called in from neighbouring places to join the bishop. Much earlier, in Cyprian's time, at the Council of Lambesis, the verdicts of ninety bishops condemned Privatus, an old heret-

units.la: Singularem illam jurisdictionis potestatem quam sibi jure divino vendicant, extendunt in plures integras provincias. Unius hodierni Episcopi dicecesis amplioris circuitus est, & plures subjectas habet ecclesias quibus imperat, quam olim decem Episcopi. v. g. in Scotia Episcopatus Glasguensis ambitu suo comprehendit provincias undecim, Glottianam, Lennoxiam, Renfroanam, Cuningamiam, Carislam [?], Coilam, Nithiam, Eusdaliam, Esdaliam, Annandiam, Tuediam,
units.tr: They stretch that singular power of jurisdiction, which they claim for themselves by divine right, over whole provinces. A single bishop today has a wider diocese and more churches under his rule than the ten bishops of former times. For example, in Scotland the Bishopric of Glasgow comprises within its bounds eleven provinces: Glottiana, Lennoxia, Renfroana, Cuningamia, Carisla [?], Coila, Nithia, Eusdalia, Esdalia, Annandia, and Tuedia.

units.la: ticum testatur Cyprianus. Libr. 1. epistol. 3. Eodemque testante lib. 1. epistol. 4. Universam fraternitatem convenisse ad Sabini episcopi electionem, Ac veterum historias legentibus passim occurrent vilissimi & ignobiles pagi, gnobiles pagi, ac frigidissima oppida; indigna qua Geographis in tabulis locarentur; qui tamen unum Episcopum habuerunt, Nazianzon oppidum licet Cæsarea vicinum celebris tamen fuit magis illius Theologi Gregorii Nazianzeni Episcopatu. Chrysostomi quoque tempore obtinuit ut Episcopi Diœcesis non plures una civitate contineret. hom. 3. in acta Apostolorum. Nonne terrarum orbis imperium tenet imperator? hic autem unius civitatis est Episcopus. Sozomenus histor. ecclesiast. lib. 7. cap. 19. dicit, se comperisse in pagis Episcopos ordinatos apud Arabes & Cyprus.
units.tr: ic, as Cyprian attests, in book 1, letter 3. And in book 1, letter 4, the same Cyprian testifies that the whole brotherhood assembled for the election of Bishop Sabinus. Readers of the ancient histories will everywhere come across very base and obscure villages and most frigid towns, unworthy of being placed on the maps of geographers, which nevertheless had a bishop of their own. Nazianzus, though it lay near Caesarea, became famous chiefly through the episcopate of that theologian, Gregory Nazianzen. In the time of Chrysostom too, it was the rule that a bishop's diocese should not contain more than one city. Homily 3 on the Acts of the Apostles: Does not the emperor hold dominion over the whole world? Yet this man is bishop of one city only. Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 19, says that he had learned that bishops were ordained in villages among the Arabs and in Cyprus.

units.la: Verum quidem est invalescente ambitione, (quæ facit ut semper magis elaborarent homines late quam bene præ-esse) & typho sæculi, vetitum fuisse ne in villis constituerentur Episcopi, mutationis hujus causam nullam aliam proferunt Canones & Canonum expositores, quam ne vilesceret nomen & authoritas Episcopi, quia scilicet tenuiores pagi non tantum suppetebant, quantum sufficeret ad pompam quam affectabant: Quasi vero pluris faciendus esset splendor & secularis unius Episcopi magnificentia quam ecclesiæ ædificatio: Erasmus antiquitatis sedulus indagator late extensas has Episcoporum pontificiorum Diœceses sic taxat lib. 1. Ecclesiast. Multorum præsulum ditio tam late patet, ut si quam maxime forent expediti omnibus mundanis negotiis, non possent tamen in omnibus oppidis concionari, cum hodie una civitas complures requirat ecclesiastas. Et si cui minus arrideat Erasmi censura, saltem audiat illud Hooperi Episcopi Glocestriensis, & martyris, in explicatione Decalogi ad præceptum. 8. Si jam inquit vigeret antiquus ille erga populum amor, agnoscerent ipsi plus in una civitate negotii esse, quam quod facile ab optimis expediri possit: Satis norunt primitivam ecclesiam nullos ejusmodi Episcopos habuisse ante Sylvestri primi tempora. Addit, Episcopum uni civitati tantum præfici debere. Et dum magistratus (inquit) in hunc ordinem eos redegerit, tam impossibile erit Episcopo pie & sobrie in omni religionis scripturam transvadere quam Camelum adigi per foramen acus.
units.tr: It is true that, as ambition grew strong (which makes men always more eager to preside widely than well), and as worldly pride increased, it was forbidden to appoint bishops in villages. The canons and their expositors give no other reason for this change than that the name and authority of the bishop would be cheapened, since the smaller villages could not supply enough to meet the display they desired. As if the splendour and worldly magnificence of a single bishop were to be valued above the building up of the Church! Erasmus, a diligent investigator of antiquity, thus censures these widely extended dioceses of the Papist bishops in book 1 of his Ecclesiastes: The rule of many prelates extends so far that, even if they were entirely free from all worldly business, they could still not preach in every town, since today one city needs many preachers. And if Erasmus's censure is less to someone's liking, let him at least hear that of Hooper, bishop of Gloucester and martyr, in his explanation of the Decalogue on the eighth commandment: If that ancient love for the people were now in force, he says, they themselves would recognise that there is more business in one city than the best men can easily manage. They well know that the primitive Church had no bishops of this kind before the time of Sylvester I. He adds that a bishop should be set over only one city. And, he says, when the magistrate has brought them back to this order, it will be as impossible for a bishop to get piously and soberly through all the writings of religion as it is to drive a camel through the eye of a needle.

units.la: Veteres. & Hodierni.
units.tr: The Ancients and the Moderns.

units.la: Verbi prædicationem inter præcipua officii sui munia collocabant, memores illius. Pauli ad Tim. 1. 5. 17. in eaque strenue sese exercebant, ἀκαίρως εὐκαίρως[?].
units.tr: They counted the preaching of the Word among the chief duties of their office, mindful of Paul's words to Timothy, 1 Tim. 5. 17, and they applied themselves to it vigorously, "in season and out of season" [ἀκαίρως εὐκαίρως].

units.la: Docendi officium omnium præcipue ut insit Episcopis est necesse, Theophyl. in 1 Tim. 3.
units.tr: The office of teaching must especially belong to bishops, Theophylact on 1 Tim. 3.

units.la: Raro concionantur: ac munus ecclesiastæ tanquam fastigio suo indignum in alios rejiciunt, plebem vid. per deputatos pascentes, nullo linguæ vitio aut senio impediti, sed fastu corrupti & verbi divini fastidio correpti, cujus mali fontem subsequens antithesis aperiet,
units.tr: Today they seldom preach, and they cast the office of preaching onto others as if it were beneath their rank, feeding the people through deputies. They are not hindered by any defect of speech or by old age, but are corrupted by pride and have grown weary of the divine word. The following antithesis will reveal the source of this evil.

units.la: in 1 Tim. 3. Quod non negant patres in conciliabulo illo Tridentino. Vsque adeo manifestum hoc est, ut probationibus insistere, e
units.tr: On 1 Tim. 3. The Fathers do not deny this even at that Tridentine conciliabule. It is so manifest that to insist on proofs would be superfluous.

units.la: Est in v Veteres.
units.tr: The Ancients.

units.la: Crasse ignarum esse oportet aut gnaviter imprudentem, qui negabit hoc non quam longissime abfuisse ab antiquis illis Episcopis: vide quae infra tractanda erunt ad sessionem 2 5. ex Canonibus Apostolicis, Clemente Romano, Cypriano, Synesio, Hilario & cæt. in hanc rem fusè, quibus adde testimonium Ammiani Marcellini. lib. 27. de habitu vitæ, beatorum quos vocat Episcoporum, ipse licet ethnicus: Tenuitas edendi, potandique parcissimè, indumentorum vilitas, & supercilia humum spectantia, perpetuo numini, verisque ejus cultoribus eos ut puros commendat & verecundos. Damnatum etiā set Soli lucem fœnerari.
units.tr: One must be grossly ignorant, or stupidly careless, to deny that this was very far from those ancient bishops. See what is to be treated below at session 25, from the Apostolic Canons, Clement of Rome, Cyprian, Synesius, Hilary and others, at length on this point. To these add the testimony of Ammianus Marcellinus, book 27, on the way of life of those whom he calls the blessed bishops, though he was himself a pagan: Their eating and drinking was very sparing, their clothing was cheap, and their eyes were cast down to the ground. He commends them to the eternal divinity and to its true worshippers as pure and modest. He also condemned them for lending out the light of the sun at interest.

units.la: & Hodierni.
units.tr: And Present-Day Bishops.

units.la: Omnium oculis se ingerit pompa illa sæcularis merum typhum & fastum redolens ; nullo alio nomine salutari volunt quam quo majores Barones parliamentarii.
units.tr: That worldly pomp, reeking of pure arrogance and haughtiness, thrusts itself upon everyone's eyes. They want to be greeted by no other title than the one by which the greater barons in parliament are addressed.

units.la: My Lord. In omnibus privatis & publicis congressibus , imò in ipsis comitiis parlamentariis Archiepiscopus Andreapolitanus ut regni Scotiæ Primas , vendicat sibi secundum à Serenissimo rege locum, Archiepiscopus Glasguensis supra omnes Comites , & cæteri Episcopi supra Dominos Barones. Palatia inhabitant: Amplissimarum Barohiarum sunt Domini : Sæcularibus administrationibus publicis se mancipant, sunt Cancellarii regni , aucupantur esse Thesaurarii. Sunt ordinarii senatores regii , ac supremæ curiæ quam vulgo Scoti
units.tr: My Lord. In all private and public gatherings, indeed even in the parliamentary assemblies themselves, the Archbishop of St Andrews, as Primate of the kingdom of Scotland, claims second place after the most serene King. The Archbishop of Glasgow claims precedence over all the earls, and the other bishops over the lords barons. They inhabit palaces. They are lords of the most distinguished baronies. They devote themselves to secular public offices; they are chancellors of the kingdom and angle to be treasurers. They are ordinary royal senators, and of the supreme court which the Scots commonly call

units.la: in Paulo Samosateno, maximo licet Episcopo quod mundanas dignitates usurpaverit, & Ducenarius magis quā Episcopus vocari voluerit, quod per forum incedens numerosam catervam satellitum partim praecedentium, partim subsequentium, circa se habuerit, ita ut fides nostra, invidiae & odio propter fastū & superbiam cordis illius, facta est obnoxia. Eusebi li. 7 ca. 29. Vide Canonem Synodi Carthaginensis 4. Canonem hunc in corpus Decreti retulit Gratianus. Dist. 41. Can. Episcopus & Clerici. Episcopus (inquit) non longe ab Ecclesia hospitiolum, vilem suppellectilem & mensam ac pauperem victum habeat, & dignitatis suae authoritatem fide & meritis quaerat. Videatur Posidonius in vita magni Augustini Hipponensis Episcopi. Mensa (inquit) frugali usus est & parca, quae quidem inter olera & legumina, etiam carnes aliquando propter hospites vel quosque infirmiores continebat: cochlearibus tantum argenteis utens, caetera vasa quibus mensae inferebantur cibi, vel testacea vel lignea vel marmorea erant. Item. Testamentum nullum fecit, quia, unde faceret, Christi pauper non habebat: & de Basilio magno Caesarea Episcopo refert Sozomenus lib. 6. cap, 16. respondisse imperatoris
units.tr: in Paul of Samosata, although a very great bishop, because he usurped worldly dignities, and wished to be called a Ducenarian rather than a bishop, because, walking through the forum with a numerous troop of attendants, some going before him and some following, he kept around himself, so that our faith became exposed to envy and hatred on account of the pride and arrogance of his heart. Eusebius, book 7, chapter 29. See the canon of the Fourth Council of Carthage. Gratian placed this canon in the body of the Decretum, Dist. 41, Can. Episcopus & Clerici. The bishop, (he says), should not have a small lodging far from the church, humble furnishings, a table and poor fare, and should seek the authority of his dignity by faith and merits. See Posidonius in the life of the great Augustine, Bishop of Hippo. He used a frugal and sparing table, which, among vegetables and pulses, sometimes included meat on account of guests or of weaker persons. He used only silver spoons; the other vessels in which food was brought to the table were of earthenware, wood or marble. Likewise. He made no will, because he had nothing from which to make one, being a poor man of Christ. And Sozomen, book 6, chapter 16, reports that Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea, answered the emperor

units.la: Collegium Iustitiae vel sessionem vocant: & in Camera rationum regiarum plures adoptantur. Quid memorem profusi luxus ostentationem in vestitu, famulitio & similibus. toris præfecto interminanti bonorum publicationem : Horum nihil me cruciare potest ; equidem opes non habeo præterquam laceram vestem & paucos libros : Complures pagina replenda effent fi testimonia patrum adjicerem qui acriter invecti sunt in facularitatem , luxuriam , typhum Episcoporum. Vide præsertim Bernardum. lib. 2. 3. 4. ad Eugenium & sermone 76. & 77. super Cantica. Saculo corruptissimo : Quod si objiciat equestre illud & heroicum sacerdotum genus , uti Lutherus festive eos vocat. Non ad superbiam aut pompam hæc à se fieri , sed ut sic ornetur in suis ministris ecclesia , & sic honorata crescat in sua authoritate , prout Episcopi Gerfonis saculo se tuebantur ; Respondebit idem Gerson , in tractatu de temperantia citato & approbato ab Archiepiscopo Spalatensi acerrimo Hierarchico , de repub. ecclesiast. lib. 9. cap. 5. parag. 44. cujus verba non pigebit transcribere , nam valde interest qua manu vibretur telum : Vel enim (inquit) pompam in vestibus, in ferculis , in servitoribus, & cæt. quærunt ecclesiastici ad placendum Deo, vel ut proficiant proximo , vel ad ecclesiæ honestatem & authoritatem. Non primum , quia ex Hieronymo, non tenera vestis , sed munditia mentis facit ornatum clericorum ; & quia plus placent Deo opera pietatis , in quibus possent expendi ea quæ talis pompa requirit. Non secundum, quia plus scandalizat laicos pompa hæc clericorum quam ædificet, plus ad indignationem, invidiam & murmur eos excitat, quam ad amorem, & plus auget in eis avaritiam & superbiam quam extinguat, neque potest sacerdos pompaticus verbo & exemplo humilitatem, frugalitatem, & sobrietatem aliis persuadere. Non tertium, quia honor debet dari in testimonium virtutis, non propter exteriores divitias & ornatum. Sicque populum inducunt in errorem dum ille ab eis discit honorare ecclesiam propter temporalia ista, & non propter bona futura & spiritualia: Alioquin Christus & ejus Apostoli non sufficienter ornassent ecclesiam & honorassent, quando talia in se contempserunt, & aliis spernenda suaserunt. Addit Spalatensis, ejusdem cap.parag.
units.tr: They call it the College of Justice or the Session, and several are chosen for the Chamber of the Royal Accounts. Why should I mention the display of lavish luxury in clothing, in servants and the like? To the prefect threatening confiscation of goods, he said: None of these things can torment me. Indeed I have no wealth except a torn cloak and a few books. Several pages would have to be filled if I added the testimonies of the Fathers who sharply inveighed against the worldliness, luxury and pride of bishops. See especially Bernard, books 2, 3 and 4 to Eugenius, and sermons 76 and 77 on the Song of Songs. In a most corrupt age. But if someone should object that equestrian and heroic breed of priests, as Luther jokingly calls them, these things are done not out of pride or for show, but so that the church may be adorned in its ministers and grow in honour and authority, as the bishops of Gerson's age defended themselves. The same Gerson will answer this, in his treatise on temperance, cited and approved by the most fierce advocate of hierarchy, the Archbishop of Split, in On the Ecclesiastical Commonwealth, book 9, chapter 5, paragraph 44, whose words it will not be tedious to transcribe, for it matters greatly with what hand the weapon is hurled. For (he says) either ecclesiastics seek pomp in clothing, in dishes, in servants and so on, to please God, or to benefit their neighbour, or for the honour and authority of the church. Not the first, because according to Jerome it is not fine clothing but purity of mind that adorns clergy, and because works of piety please God more, and the money such pomp requires could be spent on them. Not the second, because this clerical pomp scandalises laymen more than it edifies them; it stirs them more to indignation, envy and grumbling than to love, and it increases avarice and pride in them more than it quenches them. Nor can a pompous priest persuade others of humility, frugality and sobriety by word or example. Not the third, because honour ought to be given as a testimony of virtue, not on account of external riches and ornament. Thus they lead the people into error, while the people learns to honour the church for these temporal things and not for future and spiritual goods. Otherwise Christ and his apostles would not have adorned and honoured the church sufficiently, when they themselves despised such things and advised others to scorn them. The Spalatensis adds, in the same chapter, paragraph

units.la: 39. Reverentia quam nobis exhibet populus ob splendorem solum externum, est popularis, plausibilis, tota vana & spiritui nihil proficua, & splendor hic, ut dicebat Bernardus, admirationem non devotionem excitat: Si itaque collapsa jam spirituali reverentia, quæ ad spiritualem populi profectum plurimum valet, quid ad spiritum, si populus me tanquam divitem & in mundo potentem ac honoratum mundano solum honore revereatur? Pereat & hæc reverentia, ne ex ea & per illam populus etiam in errorem inducatur, ut ex carnali etiam carnalior fiat. Unde (inquit Bernardus serm. 77.) 77. in Cantica.) hanc illis (videl: præsulibus seu episcopis) exuberare existimas rerum affluentiam, vestium splendorem, mensarum luxuriem, congeriem vasorum argenteorum, & aureorum, nisi de bonis sponsæ, id est, ecclesiæ. Inde est quod illa pauper & inops & nuda relinquitur, facie miseranda, inculta, hispida, exangui. Non est hoc ornare sponsam sed spoliare, non est custodire sed prodere; non est defendere, sed exponere; non est instituere sed prostituere, non est pascere gregem, sed mactare & devorare: eAtque hæc sufficiant retundenda importuna jactationis Scoticorum Episcoporum, qui per suum latus lancinari veteres illos Episcopos magnis clamoribus ingeminant. Claudo digressiunculam hanc verbis Isidori Pelusiota qui patrocinium Hieracis ad Episcopatum electi, sed eum detrectantis sic peragit, epistol. 223. floruit vero sub Theodosio Iuniore anno 482. cum primatus ille ordinis nondum lege lata in principatum potestatis & κατακυριευόμενον [?] degenerasset. Illud (inquit) fortasse ignorare videmini lenitatis & mansuetudinis dignitatem in tyrannidem transiisse. Nam si ostendere potestis veterem pascendi gregis rationem nunc quoque vigere, maximè quidem eum qui se huic negotio imparem esse arbitratus est, ac propterea in fugam se dedit, à vobis laudari æquum fuerit. Sin vero res in contrarium cessit, ab eo poenæ minimè expetantur: Tunc enim salutis omnium causa mortem oppetebant, nunc autem pastores ovibus mortem inferunt, non corpora jugulantes (levius enim hoc malum esset) verum animis offensiones afferentes. Tunc jejuniis corpus castigabant, nunc autem ut luxu ac delitiis exultent, efficiunt. Tunc bona sua egentibus distribuebant, nunc autem pauperum bona in rem suam vertunt. Tunc virtutem colebant, nunc virtutum cultores proscribunt & eliminant. Verum cum ostendam quantum inter vetus ministerium, & præsentem tyrannidem intersit, quæ tandem causa est, quamobrem æqualitatis amantes, coronis non redimitis. Sed redeamus tandem ad Synodi progressum.
units.tr: 39. The reverence that the people show us for external splendour alone is popular, showy, wholly vain and of no profit to the spirit; and this splendour, as Bernard said, excites admiration, not devotion. If, then, spiritual reverence, which contributes greatly to the spiritual progress of the people, has now collapsed, what does it matter to the spirit if the people revere me only with worldly honour, as one rich, powerful and honoured in the world? Let this reverence perish too, lest through it the people also be led into error and become more carnal from being carnal. Hence (says Bernard, sermon 77 on the Song of Songs): you think that this abundance of wealth, splendour of garments, luxury of tables and heaps of silver and gold vessels belong to the prelates, that is, the bishops, unless they come from the goods of the bride, that is, the church. Hence she is left poor, needy and naked, of pitiable face, unkempt, bristly and pale. This is not to adorn the bride but to despoil her; not to guard her but to betray her; not to defend her but to expose her; not to instruct her but to prostitute her; not to feed the flock but to slaughter and devour it. And let these suffice to repel the importunate boasting of the Scottish bishops, who with great clamour repeat that those ancient bishops were torn at their side. I close this little digression with the words of Isidore of Pelusium, who pleads the cause of Hierax, elected to a bishopric but refusing it, and so he proceeds, letter 223. He flourished under Theodosius the Younger in the year 482, when that primacy of order had not yet been enshrined by law into a principate of power and being lorded over [κατακυριευόμενον] [?] had degenerated. He says: Perhaps you seem to be unaware that the dignity of gentleness and meekness has passed into tyranny. For if you can show that the old manner of shepherding the flock still flourishes now, then it would be fair for you to be praised for him who judged himself unequal to this task and therefore fled. But if things have turned out otherwise, then no punishment should be sought against him. For those men once faced death for the salvation of all; now, however, shepherds bring death upon their sheep, not by slaughtering bodies (for that would be a lesser evil) but by bringing offences upon their souls. Then they chastised the body with fasts; now they make themselves exult in luxury and delights. Then they distributed their goods to the needy; now they turn the goods of the poor to their own use. Then they cultivated virtue; now they banish and eliminate the cultivators of virtue. But since I shall show how great the difference is between the old ministry and the present tyranny, what then is the reason why, lovers of equality, we are not crowned with garlands? But let us at last return to the course of the Synod.

units.la: 29. Novemb. Sess. 8. Die Iovis.
units.tr: 29 November. Session 8. Thursday.

units.la: PRæses, cum Nobiliss. Comitem Argathelium, senatorem regium synodo adesse conspiceret, omnium nomine impense rogat, ut actionibus synodicis oculatus spectator interesse dignaretur, quo testari posset quam legitime omnia procederent: Ad quod se persuaderi passus est: non sine ingenti multorum gaudio, non tam quod ille inter potentissimos regni nobiles, & prudentissimos senatores emineret, quam quod hujus consilii tum regem tum Deputatum regium non ignarum fuisse suspicarentur; sed vanam hanc fuisse conjecturam protinus patuit, nam apertis indiciis declarabat sereniss. Rex Comitis in Synodo præsentiam sibi admodum displicere, neque quidquam deputato regio ingratius accidere potuit; cum in hoc lubrico rerum statu a primariis quibusdam, regni senatoribus se derelictum cerneret; quorum octo Comites Argathelius, Marrius, Wigtomensis, Kingornius, Gallovidianus, Naperus, Almonius, Blackhalius, synodo declarant; subscripsisse se Confessioni à rege imperatæ, secundum sensum & praxin anni 1580 cujus declarationem genuinam ex solis synodalium registris promendam esse censebant.
units.tr: The Moderator, seeing the most noble Earl of Argyll, a royal councillor, present at the Synod, earnestly asked him on behalf of all to attend the synodal proceedings as an eyewitness, so that he could bear witness how lawfully everything was carried on. He allowed himself to be persuaded, to the great joy of many. They were glad not so much because he stood out among the most powerful nobles of the kingdom and the wisest councillors, as because they supposed he was not unaware of this plan, either of the King or of the royal Commissioner. But this guess was soon shown to be empty, for the most serene King made it plain by clear signs that the Earl's presence at the Synod displeased him greatly, and nothing could have been more unwelcome to the royal Commissioner. In this unstable state of affairs he saw himself abandoned by some of the chief councillors of the kingdom. Eight of them, the Earls of Argyll, Mar, Wigtown, Kinghorn, Galloway, Napier, Almond and Blackhall, declared to the Synod that they had subscribed the Confession imposed by the King, according to the sense and practice of the year 1580; and they held that its genuine declaration should be drawn only from the synodal registers.

units.la: Porro quia pastores quosdam ad Synodum deputatos, ecclesiasticis censuris notatos in Hibernia, aut in Scotia objiciebant Episcopi, de iis agi coeptum est; quatuor qui ex Hibernia profugi in Scotia sedes suas fixerant, fusè coram synodo demonstrant, censuris illis se notatos eo solum nomine fuisse, quod puritati disciplinæ adhærerent: nec probarent multiformes illos ritus quibus ecclesiæ Hibernicæ onerentur: Censuras etiam ipsas illegitimè inflictas. Tres alii censura celsæ commissionis in Scotia notati ab eadem ita se perspicuè expediverunt; ut omnibus abunde satisfactum esset: censuras illas injustas, & illegitimas fuisse. Deinde à synodo ex omni ordine delecti fuerunt, quibus mandatum fuit ut summa diligentia expenderent verum & genuinum sensum confessionis anni 1580: an novi illi ritus, & mutatio quam disciplina passa est, cum eadem Confessione consistere possint, an vero eandem evertant: aliis vero mandatum ut libros Canonum, Liturgiæ, ordinationis penitius excuterent; utrisque, ut diligentiæ suæ rationem maturè synodo redderent. Denique aliis commissum ut ecclesiarum ad synodum gravamina colligerent, disponerent, ac suo quæque loco publicè agitanda proponerent.
units.tr: Next, since the bishops objected that some ministers who had been sent to the Synod had been censured by the ecclesiastical courts, in Ireland or in Scotland, the matter was taken up. Four men who had fled from Ireland and settled in Scotland showed at length before the Synod that they had been censured for no other reason than that they adhered to the purity of discipline; and they proved that the bishops could not justify the many forms of ritual with which the Irish churches were burdened. They also showed that the censures themselves had been unlawfully inflicted. Three others, censured in Scotland by the High Commission, cleared themselves so clearly that everyone was fully satisfied that those censures had been unjust and unlawful. Then the Synod chose men from every order, to whom it was entrusted to weigh with the greatest care the true and genuine sense of the Confession of 1580: whether those new rites and the change which discipline had undergone could stand with the same Confession, or whether they overthrew it. Others were ordered to examine closely the books of the Canons, of the Liturgy and of the ordination; and both groups were to report promptly to the Synod an account of their diligence. Finally, others were charged with gathering the grievances of the churches for the Synod, arranging them, and laying each before it in its proper place to be discussed publicly.

units.la: Urgebant Episcoporum accusatores ut tandem aliquando liceret litem Episcopis intentatam contestari. Initium factum est ab Episcopo Gallovidiano, cujus accusatio prælecta, continebat, præter ea quæ ipsi communia erant cum cæteris Episcopis (violationem conditionum stipulatarum in synodo
units.tr: The accusers of the bishops pressed that at last it might be permitted to bring the suit against the bishops to a formal hearing. A start was made with the Bishop of Galloway. His accusation was read out, and it contained, besides those charges which he shared with the other bishops (the violation of the conditions agreed at the Synod

units.la: 1600 ad Montis Rosarum, & usurpationem libertatis ecclesiasticæ:) personalia plurima crimina, tam in moribus quam in doctrina: inter quæ fuerunt, Aperta & ordinaria diei Dominicæ profanatio; negligentia pastoralis muneris, supina tyrannis in pastorem & alios inaudita,quod papistas pertinaces ab Ecclesiis excommunicatos in intimæ familiaritatis societatem admiserit, in reformatæ religionis odium,professus Pontifitios illos licet excommunicatos multo sibi chariores puritanis (quo nomine traducere soliti sunt hierarchici eos qui puritati reformationis adhærent.) Plurimorum pontificiorum & omnium Arminianorum dogmatum publica & privata defensio, quorum specialem designationem literæ illæ accusatoriæ continebant. Causæ hujus profecutio & determinatio ad subsequentes sessiones dilata fuit.
units.tr: of Montrose in 1600, and the usurpation of ecclesiastical liberty), many charges personal to himself, both in morals and in doctrine. Among these were: open and habitual profanation of the Lord's Day; negligence of his pastoral office; a haughty tyranny, unheard of, towards the minister and others; that he had admitted obstinate Papists, excommunicated by the churches, into the society of his close familiarity; that he showed hatred of the reformed religion, professing that those Papists, though excommunicated, were far dearer to him than the Puritans (the name by which the hierarchs were wont to slander those who adhere to the purity of the Reformation); the public and private defence of many Popish doctrines and of all the Arminian doctrines, which the accusatory letters set out in particular detail. The prosecution and determination of this cause were deferred to the following sessions.

units.la: Verebatur interim synodus ne sicut heri in fynodo, sic hodie, solemniter & publice dissolutionem ejusdem imperaret deputatus Regius; Nec frustra: nam 29. Novemb. Edictum Regis nomine publicari jussit, quo terrore pœnæ læsæ majestatis in pertinaces, absolutam synodi dissolutionem imperabat: cujus edicti typis postea excusi, & 18.Dec.cū multis additamētis, denuo promulgati hæc fere summa fuit.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Synod feared that, as yesterday in the Synod, so today too, the royal Commissioner would solemnly and publicly order its dissolution. Nor was the fear groundless. On 29 November he had an edict published in the King's name, by which, with the threat of the penalty for treason against the obstinate, he commanded the absolute dissolution of the Synod. Later this edict was printed, and on 18 December it was promulgated again, with many additions. Its substance was roughly as follows.

units.la: Mandati regii de dissolvenda synodo summa.
units.tr: Summary of the royal mandate for dissolving the Synod.

units.la: Post prolixam omnium quæ hactenus à Sereniff. rege concessa fuere commemorationem; ut omniū animis suspicionum radices penitus evellerentur, omnibusque constaret quam singulari constantia religionem amplecteretur; Regem Synodum nationalem indixisse, eamque liberam. Conventum tamen hunc pro synodo legitima non agnoscere. 1.
units.tr: After a lengthy recital of all that had hitherto been granted by the most serene King, so that the roots of suspicion might be utterly torn from everyone's minds, and it might be plain to all with what singular constancy he embraced the religion, the King had indeed called a national Synod, and a free one. Yet this assembly he did not acknowledge as a lawful Synod. 1.

units.la: Quia ex iis constet qui ausi fuerunt publice protestari contra edictum regium. 22.Septemb. promulgatum, quo tamen omnia concedebantur quæ ad pacem solidam ecclesiæ & regni stabiliendam excogitari potuerunt, 2. Quia non destiterunt arces regias usque adeo sollicitè custodire ut nihil apparatus bellici, aut alterius cujuflibet necessarii, inferri permittant. 3. Quia illicitos conventus cogant, ac novum tribunal Edenburgi erexerint, in manifestum summæ authoritatis ac legum contemptum.4. Quod ex deputatis fuere quidam in Hibernia, & Scotia censuris ecclesiasticis notati, alii à ministerii functione legitimè suspensi, alii ad ministerium illegitimè promoti, omnes denique juramento constricti ad regiminis Episcopalis subversionem. 5. Quia liberæ delegandorum ad synodum electioni præscripserunt; privatim ubique monentes & jubentes, ut prætermissis iis qui animitus non favè[?]rent omnibus ipsorum consiliis ii soli deputarentur; de quorum zelo constaret. 6. Quia Glasguam advenerunt locum Synodo præstitutum armis lege vetitis accincti, ac comitatu frequentissimo, nulla habita edicti illa speciali[?]ter vetantis ratione. 7. Quia peremptorie abnuerint sex assessoribus à rege designatis, jus suffragii definitivi. 8. Quia obstinatè renuebant ne Episcoporum protestatio prælegeretur, ante præsidis electionem & literarum fidei examinationem. 9. Quod regia declaratione registris Synodicis ad perpetuam memoriam inserta, non contenti, eo collimarent omnia ipsorum consilia, ut Episcopatum ipsum penitùs everterent, adeoque tertium ordinum regni membrum amputarent: & fundamentales regni leges refigerent: Quæ cum manifestum Monarchici regiminis damnum secum trahant, ejusmodi conventui non potuisse Deputatum Marchionem diutius interesse; ideoque inde discessisse, 28. Novemb. quando licet anxiè rogitasset, ut actionem illam precibus clauderent, pollicitus, se die crastino rediturum ut responsurum ecrundem ad hæc objecta audiret, & examinaret.
units.tr: Because it is clear from those who dared publicly to protest against the royal edict published on 22 September, by which nevertheless everything was conceded that could be devised to establish a firm peace in the Church and the kingdom; 2. because they have not ceased to guard the royal castles so carefully that they permit no military equipment or any other necessary supplies to be brought in; 3. because they compel unlawful gatherings and have set up a new tribunal at Edinburgh, in manifest contempt of supreme authority and the laws; 4. because some of the deputies were censured with ecclesiastical penalties in Ireland and in Scotland, others were lawfully suspended from the ministerial function, others were unlawfully promoted to the ministry, and all were finally bound by oath to the overthrow of episcopal government; 5. because they prescribed the free election of delegates to the Synod, privately warning and ordering everywhere that, with those set aside who were not favourable to their designs in their hearts, only those should be deputed in whose zeal they could be confident; 6. because they came to Glasgow, the place appointed for the Synod, armed with weapons forbidden by law, and with a very large retinue, paying no heed to the special reason given in the edict forbidding this; 7. because they peremptorily refused the right of a definitive vote to six assessors designated by the King; 8. because they obstinately refused that the protest of the bishops be read out before the election of the moderator and the examination of the letters of faith; 9. because, not content that the royal declaration had been inserted in the synodal registers for perpetual remembrance, they aimed all their plans at this, to overthrow the episcopate utterly, and so to cut off the third order of the kingdom, and to annul the fundamental laws of the realm. Since these things carry with them manifest harm to monarchical government, the Marquess, the royal Commissioner, could not remain at such an assembly any longer; and therefore he withdrew from it on 28 November, when, although he anxiously asked them to close that action with prayers, he promised that he would return the next day to hear their answer to these objections and to examine them.

units.la: 10. Æquum tamen hoc postulatum obtinere non potuit, quin contra inauditam protestationem prælegi curaverint, qua ausi fuerunt regiis senatoribus, qui suffragiis suis conventus hujus illegitimi dissolutionem ratam habuissent, diem dicere, ut coram parliamento ejusdem rationem redderent: 11. ac posthabito deputati regii peremptorio mandato, sessiones suas continuaverint; in quibus injusta plurima fanciverint.
units.tr: 10. Yet they could not obtain this fair demand without having the unheard-of protest read out against him, in which they dared to summon before the parliament the royal councillors who, by their votes, had approved the dissolution of this unlawful assembly, to give an account of their conduct; 11. and, disregarding the peremptory order of the royal Commissioner, they continued their sessions, in which they enacted many unjust things.

units.la: Quare. 1. Regem non solum illegitimam pronunciare hanc synodum, verum etiam subditos omnes serio admonere ingentis periculi in quod se præcipitaturi sunt, qui synodum hanc sibi probari seu sermonibus seu factis declarabunt: Quod si cuilibet damni quidpiam ex recusatione synodi hujus creatum fuerit, se (regem) id præstiturum, eorumque personas, famam, bona protecturum. 2. Præcise omnibus imperare ut confessioni & fœderi subscribant, secundum declarationem & expositionem à Marchione, suo nomine publicatam. & cæt.
units.tr: Therefore: 1. the King not only declares this Synod unlawful, but also seriously warns all his subjects of the great danger into which they will throw themselves if they declare by word or deed that they approve this Synod; and if any loss arises to anyone from refusing this Synod, he (the King) will make it good and will protect their persons, reputations and goods. 2. He commands all, without exception, to subscribe the Confession and the Covenant, according to the declaration and explanation published in his name by the Marquess, etc.

units.la: Responsio Synodi & protestatio contra illud mandatum.
units.tr: Response of the Synod and protest against that mandate.

units.la: Edicto huic protestationem objecerunt Synodici, primum Glasguæ, dein Edenburgi, quam prælo commiserunt; Qua ad singula capita fuse responderent, quorum plurima hactenus, præsertim in responso synodi ad Episcoporum protestationem pertractata sunt, quo remittendus est lector, ne repetitionibus nobis labor non necessarius, tibi vero tædium crescat.
units.tr: The Synodical men lodged a protest against this edict, first at Glasgow and then at Edinburgh, and committed it to the press. In it they answered each point at length. Much of this has already been treated, especially in the synod's response to the Bishops' protest, to which the reader is referred, so that the labour is not needlessly repeated for us and the tedium does not grow for you.

units.la: Ad 1. Fuse se ostendisse dicunt æquitatem & necessitatem protestationis illius contra edictum, Septemb. pag.
units.tr: To 1. They say they have shown at length the equity and necessity of that protest against the edict of September, p. ...

units.la: Ad 2. Ex omnibus actibus[?] regiis, solam esse Edenburgenam, extra quam custodias & vigiles posueposuerunt , quibus impediebant apparatus bellici submissionem ; ne terrore arcis bene munitæ , civium Edenburgensium animi à causæ communis profecutione abalienarentur , ac reliquorum libertatis vindicum pernecessarii conventus in loco tam opportuno impedirentur , quæ subvectione bellici hujus apparatus, fe effecturos olim jactitabant religionis hostes: Naturæ leges ab omni criminis focietate eos liberare, qui tam ingens prævisum & impendens periculum amoliri studeant: Ac ratione omni abhorrere ut arces in regni securitatem contra externos hostes exstructæ, in civium regni præsentem perniciem converterentur: Salutem reipub. & populi supremam legem esse : Legibus etiam municipalibus quicquid à se factum sit approbari. nam Iacobi 2. parliamento 2. statuto 3. provinciarum vice-Comitibus mandatur ut ingruente tumultu omnem operam adhibeant , ne provincialibus damnum aliquod daturi sint arcium munitarum incolæ; quod si neglexerint vice-Comites, quid quæsoiniqui,à subditis provincialibus fieri dicas, si hi, in quorum pratiam & tutelam lex ea fancita fuerat, saluti & tranquillitati suæ consulant , diligenter præcaventes, ne quid ab ejusmodi munitis arcibus damni accepturi sint : Quæ coronæ regiæ primitus annexæ fuerunt, in regni totius utilitate. Iac.2.parl. 1 r. statuto.41. nec ab eadem abalienari possunt, nisi regni ordinibus liquido constet ingens reipub. commodum ibid.inter quas arxEdenburgena cum facile primas obtineat; de ea magis solliciti fuere majores nostri,quam familiæ Areftinæ traditam fuisse meminerūt,hac lege expressa&Editione,ut nulli nisi conventum ordinum reposcenti traderent,inquit Thuanus. Cui custodiendæ publici sumptus ex tertiis beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum ordinum consensu adjudicati sunt,utpote quod hujus & aliarum omnium diligens custodia ad regni utilitatem referatur. Iacob. 6. parl. 1. stat. 10. ejusdem parl. 9. statuto 9. & parl. 12. statut. 121. quo illud referendum quod regni Claves dicantur. Iacob. 6. parl. 7. stat. 125. quæ omnia satis declarant penes collectivum regni corpus, ejusque potiorem partem esse, providere ne, quod à majoribus suis in regni tranquillitatem constitutum fuit, in ejusdem manifestam pernitiem tendat, cui jamdudum involveretur, nisi maturè hoc consilio subvectio appparatus bellici in arcem Edēburgenam impedita fuisset. Idem sæpius laudabili exemplo à majoribus suis factitatum, ut aliorum regnorum frequentissima exempla missa faciant, quibus nunquam ab iis vitio versum fuit, aut crimini datum.
units.tr: To 2. Of all the royal fortresses, they say, only Edinburgh's was guarded, with sentries and watchmen posted around it, to prevent military preparations from being used to subdue the country. This was so that the citizens of Edinburgh should not have their spirits alienated from the pursuit of the common cause by the terror of a well-fortified citadel, and so that the most necessary assemblies of the other defenders of liberty should not be hindered in a place so convenient. The enemies of religion had once boasted that by bringing in this military apparatus they would achieve these ends. The laws of nature free from any fellowship in crime those who strive to avert a great danger foreseen and impending. And it is abhorrent to all reason that citadels built for the security of the kingdom against foreign enemies should be turned to the present ruin of the kingdom's own citizens. The safety of the commonwealth and of the people is the supreme law. Even by municipal law, whatever they have done is approved. For in the third statute of the second parliament of James II, the sheriffs of the provinces are commanded that, when tumult threatens, they take every care that the inhabitants of the fortified castles do no harm to the provincial people. If the sheriffs neglect this, what unjust treatment, I ask, do you say the provincial subjects suffer, if those for whose benefit and protection that law was enacted look to their own safety and peace, taking careful precautions that they suffer no harm from such fortified castles? These castles were originally annexed to the royal crown for the benefit of the whole kingdom (James II, parl. 11, statute 41). Nor can they be alienated from it unless it is clear to the estates of the realm that there is a great advantage to the commonwealth (ibid.). Among these, the castle of Edinburgh easily holds the first place. Our ancestors were more anxious about it than about the one which, they recall, was handed over to the family of Arran, with this law expressed and published: that it should be given to no one except one who demanded it at a meeting of the estates, as Thuanus says. For its custody public money was assigned, with the consent of the third estate of the ecclesiastical benefices, since its careful keeping, like that of all the others, is referred to the utility of the kingdom (James VI, parl. 1, statute 10; the same parliament, statute 9; and parl. 12, statute 121). To this belongs the fact that the keys of the kingdom are so called (James VI, parl. 7, statute 125). All of these sufficiently show that it rests with the collective body of the kingdom, and its greater part, to provide that what their ancestors established for the tranquillity of the kingdom should not tend to its manifest ruin. The kingdom would long ago have been involved in that ruin had the bringing of the military apparatus into Edinburgh castle not been hindered in time by this counsel. Their ancestors did the same very often, as a laudable example, and the very frequent examples of other kingdoms may be set aside. These were never blamed on them or made a crime.

units.la: Ad 3. Immerito novi tribunalis erectionem sibi exprobrari, quasi in contemptum senatus regii, non munera solum illius, verum & nomen usurparent: Etenim licet libertatis vindices ad necessariam religionis & puritatis cultus divini tutelam modestè conveniant, ut communicatis consiliis causam hanc communem junctim agerent, senatu regio non connivente solum, verum etiam institutum hoc approbante, mense Novembri anni 1637. Nunquam tamen ab illis conventibus emanarunt decreta quælibet de rebus ecclesiasticis aut civilibus; contenti scilicet consilia [?]suggessisse, quibus subditorum gravamina Regi, parlamento, & synodo præsentarentur commodius: Quod si legibus regni municipalibus subditorum ad pacis publicæ violationem, & regiæ authoritatis diminutionem conventus prohibeantur, malè istis accensebuntur. Conventus hi necessarii tum à senatu regio, tum à deputato regio approbati ad Dei gloriam, & solidam subditorum pacem promovendam instituti; per quos certè secundum Deum stetit, quód ingentes hi animorum motus in tumultus jampridem non processerint. Neque ostendi potest vim ullam, aut injuriam, seu verbo seu facto cuilibet mensibus hisce retroactis per conventus hos illatam fuisse, quicquid quidam conscientiæ furiis territi causentur quo fugam ex patria,ut ecclesiarum malitiosam desertionem pallient.
units.tr: To 3. It is unjust to charge them with erecting a new tribunal, as if in contempt of the royal senate, and usurping not only its functions but its name. For although the defenders of liberty met modestly for the necessary protection of religion and the pure worship of God, so that they might act together and share counsels in this common cause, the royal senate not only connived at this but even approved the arrangement, in November 1637. Yet no decrees on ecclesiastical or civil matters ever issued from those assemblies. They were content simply to suggest counsels by which the grievances of the subjects might more conveniently be presented to the King, the parliament and the synod. If the municipal laws of the kingdom forbid assemblies of subjects as violating the public peace and diminishing royal authority, then they are wrongly accused. These necessary assemblies, approved both by the royal senate and by the royal deputy, were set up to promote the glory of God and the solid peace of the subjects. Through them, under God, it has come about that these great movements of minds have not long since broken out into tumults. Nor can it be shown that any force or injury, by word or deed, was inflicted on anyone through these assemblies in the months just past, whatever certain men may allege, terrified by the furies of conscience, to excuse their flight from the country and to cloak their malicious desertion of the churches.

units.la: Ad 4. De pauculis Pastoribus in Hibernia aut Scotia Episcoporum & celsæ commissionis censura notatis, actumsuperius in responsione ad 8 & 9 caput protestationis Episcoporum.
units.tr: To 4. As to the few ministers in Ireland or Scotland marked by the censure of the bishops and the High Commission, this was dealt with above, in the response to the eighth and ninth heads of the Bishops' protest.

units.la: Ad 5. Prout in Synodo responsum fuit Deputato regio, simpliciter negant, ejusmodi mandata quibus præscriberetur libertati electionis Deputandorum ad Synodum, à conventibus publicis unquam prodiisse; sed ab adversariis suis conficta esse; ideoque ut fidei aliquam speciem facerent vera quædam falsis miscuisse; uti sunt illa; serio monita suisse Presbyteria ut quantum commode & legitime fieri posset, caverent, ne ad Synodum delegarentur pastores ii qui praxi sua novitates obtrusas in libris Canonum & liturgiæ approbarunt, quales fuerunt novi illi Sacellani capellæ regiæ, & qui membra sunt Capituli Cathedralium ecclesiarum, Item Pastores eirenarchæ. Quorum tamen quibusdam cum à classibus rite delegarentur, locus in Synodo sine ullius contradictione concessus est: Et quid quæso hic atrocis malitiæ inesse potest, cum non sit tutum ut sedeant judicaturi in Synodo de iis rebus, quas neglectâ ecclesiæ authoritate, (ut nihil asperius dicatur) ad Episcoporum lubitum se approbasse testati sunt: Alterum verum monitum, suppositive illis scriptis insertum est, quod presbyteriis fuggestum fuit, ut pastores ad Synodum deputandi, essent ex doctissimis, ac diligenter controversias illas studerent de quibus speratum fuit disceptationes institutum iri, videlicet, de Episcopatu, de Senioribus, Senioribus , de potestate supremi magistratus in Ecclesiasticis , praesertim in convocandis Conciliis : Immerito haec oblique perstringuntur , nomine odiofo Thematum periculosorum [?] : quasi de omni Thematte [?] Ecclesiastico non liceret deputatis ad Synodum, modeste sententiam proponere ; Sed quo plus periculi in controversiae alicujus determinatione inest , de ea sententiam publice dicturum , tanto instructiorem esse convenit : praesertim cum spes effet Theologos Abredonenses ad Synodum venturos , ut receptam ecclesiarum sententiam de prioribus capitibus impugnarent.
units.tr: To 5. As was answered to the royal deputy in the synod, they flatly deny that any mandates prescribing limits on the freedom of electing deputies to the synod ever came out from the public assemblies. They say these were invented by their adversaries, who therefore mixed some true things with false ones to give the charge some appearance of credibility. Such a true item is this: presbyteries were earnestly warned to take care, as far as could be done conveniently and lawfully, that ministers who by their practice had approved the novelties thrust into the books of canons and the liturgy should not be deputed to the synod. Such were those new chaplains of the royal chapel, and those who are members of the chapters of the cathedral churches, and likewise the ministers who serve as justices of the peace. Yet when some of these were duly deputed by the classes, a place in the synod was granted to them without any objection. And what atrocious malice, I ask, can there be here? It is not safe for men to sit in the synod as judges on those matters which, neglecting the authority of the Church (to say nothing harsher), they testified they had approved at the pleasure of the bishops. Another true admonition was falsely inserted into those writings: it was suggested to the presbyteries that the ministers deputed to the synod should be among the most learned, and should study diligently those controversies about which it was hoped disputations would be held, namely on episcopacy, on elders, on the power of the supreme magistrate in ecclesiastical matters, and especially in the convoking of councils. These points are unjustly touched on obliquely, under the odious name of dangerous topics, as if deputies to the synod were not allowed to propose modestly their opinion on any ecclesiastical theme. But the more danger there is in settling some controversy, the better instructed one ought to be when giving one's opinion on it in public. This is especially so since there was hope that the Aberdeen theologians would come to the synod to impugn the accepted opinion of the churches on the earlier heads.

units.la: Ad 6. Deputatos ad Synodum, Latronum in tractu illo , per quem iter facturi erant , grassantium metu, armis accinctos Glasguam venisse , exemplo etiam eorum qui in comitatu Deputati regii fecerunt; Quam pacifice sese gesserint, experientiam satis edocuisse.
units.tr: To 6. The deputies to the synod came to Glasgow armed, girded with weapons for fear of robbers prowling along the road they had to travel. They also followed the example of those who did the same in the retinue of the royal deputy. How peaceably they conducted themselves, experience has sufficiently taught.

units.la: Ad 7: Assessoribus à rege designatis non potuisse synodum jus definitivi suffragii concedere ; nisi cum manifesto Ecclesiasticae libertatis damno: Cum in nulla legitima Synodo nationali hujus ecclesiae unquam admissi fuerint Assessores ad jus suffragii ; & literae Illustriff. Deputati regii, Marchionem solum & unicum regis Nomine Deputatum nominaverint:
units.tr: To 7. The synod could not grant the assessors designated by the king the right of a deciding vote without manifest damage to ecclesiastical liberty. Assessors were never admitted with the right of voting in any lawful national synod of this church, and the letters of the most illustrious royal deputy named only the Marquis, and he alone, as deputy in the king's name.

units.la: Ad 8. Ante praesidis electionem, & examinatas Delegatorum literas fidei ; concedi non potuisse Protestationis Episcoporum nomine exhibitae praelectionem; quibus peractis & synodo tum primum formaliter in membris suis constituta, statim praelecta fuit;
units.tr: To 8. Before the election of the moderator and the examination of the delegates' credentials, the reading of the protest presented in the name of the bishops could not be granted. When these things had been done and the synod was for the first time formally constituted in its members, the protest was read out at once.

units.la: Ad 9. Regiam illam declarationem non esse satisfactoriam , nec à se probari posse tanquam sufficiens & plenum remedium quod praesentia omnia mala curaret, & à recidiva in haec aut graviora liberaret; rationibus plurimis in procestatione ad Edictum Septembris demonstrasse se dicunt: Ad illud quod eversione Episcopatus, (quo omnia Synodalium studia collimasse dicuntur) amputetur, tertium ordinum regni membrum; de eo fusius & ex professo tractabitur infra ad sess.
units.tr: To 9. That royal declaration was not satisfactory, and they could not approve it as a sufficient and full remedy that would cure all the present evils and free the kingdom from relapse into these or worse ones. They say they demonstrated this by many reasons in the protest against the September edict. As to the claim that the aim of all the synod's efforts was the overthrow of episcopacy, and that the third estate of the realm would thereby be cut off, this will be treated more fully and expressly below, at the session.

units.la: Ad 10. Negant se vel levissimis indiciis unquam potuisse colligere, Propositum fuisse Deputato regio redire ad Synodum, Cui diutius adesse integrum sibi non esse profitebatur; Quare quod unum ipsis relictum fuit; cogebantur protestari, non solum contra discessum Deputati è synodo, & mandatum de synodo dissolvenda, verumetiam contra Senatores eos qui suffragiis suis mandatum illud approbarent, idque secundum leges regni municipales: nam Iacob. 4. parl. 2. statut. 12. expresse cautum est, ut Senatores regii teneantur Consiliorum suorum rationem reddere Regi, ac regni ordinibus in parliamento congregatis, à quibus tum eligebantur: & edicto regio mensis Septembris, anni huius declarantur omnes omnino subditi, judicio nationalis synodi, & parliamenti subjecti, ideoque nullum esse qui ad parliamentum citari non possit, si criminis alicujus reus habeatur; nisi forte quis putet Consilium illud crimen non esse, quo regnum universum omniaque fere ejus membra præsentissimo periculo expoununtur; dum conspicerent, omnium ordinum gravamina de religionis puritate stabilienda, eamque corrumpentibus novitatibus, negligi, ac deploratam esse omnem spem, flagitiosos publica authoritate in ordinem cogendi.
units.tr: To 10. They deny that they could ever have gathered, even from the slightest indications, that the royal commissioner intended to return to the Synod, at which he professed he could not remain present for long. What was therefore left to them was to protest, and they were compelled to do so, not only against the commissioner's departure from the Synod and the order to dissolve it, but also against those senators who approved that order with their votes. This was so under the laws of the kingdom. For in Jac. 4, parl. 2, statute 12, it is expressly provided that the king's senators are bound to render an account of their counsels to the King and to the estates of the realm gathered in parliament, by whom they were then elected. And by the royal edict of September of this year, all subjects without exception are declared subject to the judgment of the national synod and of parliament, so that there is no one who cannot be summoned to parliament if he is held guilty of any crime. Unless perhaps someone thinks that this counsel is not a crime, by which the whole kingdom and nearly all its members are exposed to the most imminent danger, while they see that the grievances of all orders concerning the establishment of the purity of religion, and the novelties corrupting it, are being neglected, and that all hope has been abandoned of bringing the scandalous to order by public authority.

units.la: Ad 11. Quod conventum hunc continuaverint, posthabito dissolutionis mandato. Respondent.
