He has not done so for any other nation, and so they do not know his judgments." 8. In the collect for the feast of St Michael, that Michael, prince of the angels (Rev. 12.7), is counted among the created angels, although he is Jesus Christ. 9. In the rubric before communion, the preparation seems to consist in this: that those about to communicate signify their names to the elder the evening before, or on the very morning when the Lord's Supper is administered; although it is then impossible for the minister to institute an inquiry into the life and morals of those about to communicate, or to settle so suddenly scandals, controversies and quarrels. 10. The same rubric admits to the Lord's Supper a person guilty of a notorious scandal, provided he resolves and professes within himself that he will make satisfaction afterwards. Does not this directly oppose the institution of Christ, who commands that the brother who has been wronged must first be sought out and reconciled to him? 11. Just as this book is wholly destitute of all ecclesiastical authority, so on p. 29 it orders that homilies to be composed by public authority be received. From this it follows that the preaching of the Word and the prayers depend entirely on that public civil authority, and that in all matters of religion this Church is bound to blind obedience, and that the foundation of faith is an edict procured, or to be procured, from the court. 12. The prayer of the offertory contradicts the title prefixed to it, which reads: "Let us pray for the whole Church of Christ, militant here on earth." But in the prayer itself there is a commemoration of the dead, and the name Saints is restricted to those who now enjoy glory. And thus the way is paved for the canonization and invocation of the saints. Add that in the same place prayers are made for the dead, who have finished the course of their life in faith and now rest from their labours; in just this way Bellarmine admits that the souls in purgatory are best described. 13. Auricular confession is thrust upon the consciences of the people (p. 204), and absolution is expressly offered. 14. Provided three or four are present, communion may be celebrated (p. 214); these will perhaps be a deacon, a subdeacon and a clerk, even though no one from the people is present. What, I ask, does this differ from the private mass of the Papists? 15. In the same place it is commanded that all approach communion three times a year, especially at Easter. This is Jewish; nor is it read that Christ bound this sacrament to any special time, but he said, "Do this as often as you eat," and so on. 16. To persuade the people of the necessity of baptism (p. 216), they cite those words of Christ: "Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit," etc., which nevertheless are not to be understood of the baptism of water. And in the same place it is said that God has sanctified the font, altogether without any testimony of Scripture. 17. In the exhortation after the signing of the cross in baptism, this foundation is laid down as indubitable: that all who are baptized are regenerated; and on p. 224: that infants who are baptized have all things necessary to salvation. This is the axiom of those who defend the total and final apostasy of the truly holy. 18. In the questions proposed for the examination in private baptism (p. 223), they presuppose that those can baptize who are entirely ignorant of both the form and the matter of baptism. 19. It is said on p. 231 that Christ redeemed me and the whole human race. This phrase, since nowhere throughout the whole book is it softened by any suitable explanation, prepares the way for a universal redemption of the reprobate as well as the elect. 20. It is said on p. 235 that there are two sacraments generally necessary to salvation. By this it is implied that the others are, although less necessary, still to be counted; and among their number it will afterwards be shown that order, matrimony, penance and confirmation are placed. 21. On p. 236 the inward parts of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper are said to be the body and blood of Christ, which are truly received in the Lord's Supper; yet nowhere, either in the liturgy of the Eucharist or in the Catechism, is there any little word by which this phrase is explained or distinguished from the fiction of transubstantiation. 22. Confirmation (pp. 237, 238), according to the definition of a sacrament proposed in the Catechism inserted there, will be a sacrament, namely an external and visible sign of the inward and spiritual grace conferred upon us, instituted by Christ as the means by which grace is received and as a pledge by which we are made certain of that same grace. And here the external and visible sign is the laying on of hands by the bishop, who alone can confirm. The inward and spiritual grace is defence and strength against all assaults of the devil, sin and the world. And in the little prayer after the hands are laid on, the bishop says: "We pour out our supplications to you for these children, upon whom, after the example of your Apostles, we have laid our hands, that by this sign we may make them more certain of your gracious will towards them." From this it follows that the laying on of the bishop's hands is a sealing sign and the means by which grace is conferred. Add that, by reason of the minister, who is the bishop alone, it is preferred to the two genuine sacraments, and this confirmation is often called necessary. How do these things differ from the Papists? 23. What forbids that matrimony also be tacitly numbered among the sacraments? For the ring, sanctified by the touch of the elder's book, will be a sacred symbol of grace, signifying that those joined in matrimony must live in mutual love and peace, and according to the precepts of Christ. 24. In the celebration of matrimony (p. 242), the bridegroom is instructed by the elder to say to the bride: "I make you partaker of all my goods, or I enrich you with all the fortunes of my goods, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit." By these words the husband is bound to share with his bride all his goods, movable and immovable, unless he wishes to be a perjurer and to abuse the most holy name of God. 25. In the order of the visitation of the sick (p. 253), the sick person is ordered to make a particular confession of his sins before the elder, from which he will be absolved by the elder; this inclines towards auricular confession. 26. When plague or any other contagious disease is raging, it is permitted to celebrate the Lord's Supper with the sick person alone; and if with one sick person, why not with any other one? 27. It is said on p. 267: "In the primitive Church there was a pious discipline, that at the beginning of Lent manifest sinners were compelled to public repentance, and that they humbly submitted themselves to undergo in this world a penalty by which their souls might be saved on the day of the Lord. In place of this, until the same discipline can be restored (which is most to be desired), it has seemed good that at this time the general sentences of the curse of God against impenitent sinners be read before you." What is this other than to wish that the penal works of satisfactions be restored? And it is false that any such custom existed in the primitive Church, unless perhaps you wish to adorn the corrupt Roman Church with that praise. Will not this alone sufficiently indicate that the authors of this book lean towards the present Roman Church?

units.la: Semina etiam idololatriæ libro hoc continentur. Nam 1. Calendarium catalogum habet quorundam virorum & fœminarum, quos speciali ratione ad sanctorum honorem evehit, quid hoc aliud est quam sanctorum Canonizatio, quæ sanctorum invocationi viam sternit? 2. Eodem collimat dedicatio dierum in honorem sanctorum, quæ ab hac ecclesia semper post reformationem judicata fuit Idololatria papistica. 3. Beata virgo Maria vocatur Domina nostra, pag. 14. 4. In oratione consecrationis elementorum S. cœnæ sic habetur. Benedicito & sanctificato verbo tuo & S.Spiritu has tuas creaturas panis & vini, ut sint nobis corpus & sanguis dilecti filii tui: quæ sunt formalia verba Canonis missæ pro transubstantiatione. Dicit quidem Apostolus creaturas Dei sanctificari verbo & precibus, sed an unquam auditum, res spiritualis gratiæ incapaces sanctificari per spiritum. Interim libri hujus architecti satis sensum suum[?] prodiderunt; vid. ut Deus omnipotentia sui spiritus miraculose efficere velit, ut panis ille & vinum mutetur in verum corpus & sanguinem Christi. Nam sanctificatio hæc; quæ verbis illis petitur, est mutatio quædam, eaque vel sacramentalis, vel spiritualis, vel per transubstantiationem: Non est sacramentalis, quia tum non opus esset aliis verbis, quam institutionis Christi: neque spiritualis, nam sic potius cum Anglica liturgia dicendum esset: Sanctificato nos[?] verbo tuo & spiritu, ut participes esse possimus corporis & sanguinis Christi: Restat itaque intelligenda esse de mutatione per transubstantiationem, & in hunc finem mentionem facit liber Corporalis, qua voce notandum est quod non utantur, nisi post consecrationem. 5. In margine ponitur, pag. 208. cum ad verba illa institutionis, panem accepit, presbyter officiaturus devenerit, sumet tu patinam in manus. Et in missali Romano sic habetur. Dum repetit sacerdos, hoc est enim corpus meum, hostiam supra caput elevet, ut ab omnibus conspici & adorari possit. Neque dubitandum quin idem hic sit sensus, praesertim si locus & situs presbyteri & populi attente consideretur, nam presbyter a populo longe remotus ad occidentalem altaris partem facie a populo aversa stat, & populus extra sacrarii cancellos in genua provolvitur: quare necesse est ut patinam & calicem in altum elevet, si a populo conspici velit, alioqui frustra species (uti hic liber loquitur) in manus sumeret. Adde quod ab hoc presbyteri & populi situ sequatur, utrumque facie ad orientem conversa precari. Vah quam subdole subrepat idololatria. 6. Pontificii duplicem habent in missa oblationem, alteram praeparatoriam, panis & vini consecrandi, alteram hostiae post consecrationem: utramque liber hic continet. Prior est in offertorio diserte: secunda in memoriali oblationis post orationem consecrationis; nam praeterquam quod titulus ipse illud clamet, verba etiam memorialis satis demonstrant: & licet mentionem faciat sacrificii laudis seu gratiarum actionis, non tamen per vocem illam intelligi debet spirituale aliquod sacrificium, quod in laude & gratiarum actione consistit, sed corporis Christi sacrificium, sic dictum, quia per illud Deus laudatur, Bellarmino interprete de missa. lib. 2. cap. 21. 7. Licet presbyter ante consecrationem steterit, nunc tamen peracta consecratione genu flectit: & pag. 104. dicit; Comesam esse Christi carnem, & ebibitum sanguinem, ac precatur, ut corpora nostra per ejus corpus mundentur, ac animae in sanguine ejus laventur; phrases admodum crassae sunt hae, cum tam crude sine ulla omnino explicatione aut distinctione a Pontificiis erroribus, proponantur. 8. Episcopus aut presbyter officians jubetur in utraque specie communionem primum recipere priusquam populo tradat, pag. 210. Ubi primum, Papismum redolet vox Species; quasi elementorum materia, panis vid. & vini vere non manerent post consecrationem. 2. Videtur etiam redolere consumptionem sacrificii, in qua formam ejus poni contendit Bellarminus. De missa lib. 1. cap. 27. nam hic peragitur sacrificium & à presbytero consumitur, priusquam admittatur populus. 9. In liturgia baptismi infans baptizatus cruce signatur; nonne hoc est additamentum mere humanum, & ritus symbolicus nullo Christi mandato, institutis ejus superadditus? semen etiam est horrendae idololatriae inter Pontifi-cios, quam ecclesia haec hoc nomine expresse abjuravit. 10. Qui matrimonii vinculo conjunguntur, jubentur pag. 244. genu flectere coram mensa seu altari Dominico; quid, quaeso, hoc aliud est quam quod in solennibus matrimonii jubet Rituale Romanum?
units.tr: Seeds of idolatry are also contained in this book. For (1) the Calendar has a list of certain men and women whom it raises in a special way to the honour of saints. What is this, other than the canonization of saints, which paves the way to the invocation of saints? (2) To the same end is the dedication of days in honour of saints, which this Church has always judged Papist idolatry since the Reformation. (3) The Blessed Virgin Mary is called "Our Lady" (p. 14). (4) In the prayer for the consecration of the elements of the Lord's Supper it is written thus: Bless and sanctify by your word and by your Holy Spirit these your creatures of bread and wine, that they may be to us the body and blood of your dearly beloved Son. These are the formal words of the Canon of the Mass for transubstantiation. The Apostle indeed says that the creatures of God are sanctified by the word and by prayer, but when was it ever heard that things incapable of spiritual grace are sanctified by the Spirit? Meanwhile the architects of this book have sufficiently revealed their meaning, namely that God by the omnipotence of his Spirit is to bring about miraculously that this bread and wine be changed into the true body and blood of Christ. For this sanctification, which is asked for in those words, is a certain change, and it is either sacramental, or spiritual, or by transubstantiation. It is not sacramental, for then there would be no need of other words than the words of Christ's institution. Nor is it spiritual, for then it would have been better to say, with the English liturgy: Sanctify us by your word and Spirit, that we may be able to be partakers of the body and blood of Christ. It remains, therefore, that it must be understood of a change by transubstantiation, and to this end the book makes mention of the Corporal. It should be noted that they do not use this cloth except after the consecration. (5) In the margin it is placed (p. 208) that when the minister, about to officiate, comes to the words of institution, he took bread, he shall take the paten into his hands. And in the Roman missal it is written thus: While the priest repeats, This is my body, he is to raise the host above his head, so that it may be seen and adored by all. Nor is there any doubt that the meaning here is the same, especially if the place and position of the minister and the people are carefully considered. For the minister, standing far removed from the people at the western side of the altar with his face turned away from the people, and the people kneeling outside the chancel of the sacristy, it is necessary that he raise the paten and the chalice on high if he wishes to be seen by the people; otherwise he would take the "species" (as this book speaks) into his hands to no purpose. Add that from this position of the minister and people it follows that both pray with faces turned toward the east. Alas, how craftily idolatry creeps in! (6) The Papists have a twofold offering in the Mass: one preparatory, of the bread and wine to be consecrated, and the other of the host after consecration. This book contains both. The first is expressly in the offertory; the second is in the memorial of the offering after the prayer of consecration. For, besides the fact that the title itself proclaims it, the words of the memorial also show it plainly. And although it makes mention of the sacrifice of praise or thanksgiving, yet by that phrase one must not understand some spiritual sacrifice which consists in praise and thanksgiving, but the sacrifice of the body of Christ, so called because by it God is praised, as Bellarmine interprets it in his work on the Mass, book 2, chapter 21. (7) Although the minister stood before the consecration, now, when the consecration is finished, he kneels; and on p. 104 it says that the flesh of Christ is eaten and his blood drunk, and it prays that our bodies may be cleansed by his body and our souls washed in his blood. These phrases are very crude, since they are put forward so crudely, without any explanation or distinction, from the errors of the Papists. (8) The bishop or the minister officiating is commanded to receive communion in both kinds first, before he delivers it to the people (p. 210). Here the word "Species" at once smells of Popery, as if the matter of the elements, that is, the bread and wine, did not really remain after consecration. (2) It also seems to smell of the consumption of the sacrifice, in which Bellarmine contends that its form consists (On the Mass, book 1, chapter 27), for here the sacrifice is carried out and consumed by the minister before the people are admitted. (9) In the liturgy of baptism the baptized infant is signed with the cross. Is this not a purely human addition, and a symbolic rite added to Christ's institutions without any command from Christ? It is also a seed of horrible idolatry among the Papists, which this Church has expressly abjured by this name. (10) Those who are joined in the bond of marriage are commanded (p. 244) to kneel before the table or the Lord's altar. What, I ask, is this other than what the Roman Ritual commands in the solemnities of marriage?

units.la: Denique liber hic nobis obtrusus in multis Anglica liturgia pejor & corruptior est. Nam. 1. multo plures sancti in Calendario nostro ponuntur, quam in Anglico. 2. Ante communionem liber Anglicus hortatur omnes praesentes ut pauperum memores sint, cujus exhortationis loco, sententias quasdam ex offertorio Romano depromptas recitari jubet noster. 3. Licet quaedam sint in Anglico sententiae, quibus ad eleemosynam excitetur populus, omnes tamen sunt ex novo testamento fere desumptae, & de eleemosyna tantum loquuntur, ita ut nihil periculi sit, ne ad alienam oblationem detorqueantur; noster vero multas profert veteris testamenti sententias, quae tantum intelliguntur de sacrificiis & oblationibus Leviticis. 4. In Anglico jubetur populus precari, ut Deus eleemosynam hanc sui populi sibi acceptam esse velit; & cæt. Noster vero supersuperaddit gratiarum actionem pro iis qui in fide mortui sunt, & cæt. & sic magis accedit ad missam pontificiam, prout supra observatum fuit. 5. In Anglico mensa Dominica in medio navis templi aut sacrarii ponitur, noster vero jubet locari situ altaribus consueto, intra sacrarii cancellos quibus removetur populus, ita ut orientalis ejus pars sacrarii extrema contingat. 6. In Anglicana liturgia post orationem consecrationis elementorum S. cœnæ, jubetur presbyter communicare & populo statim tradere : at in hac nostra, post orationem consecrationis, (longe diversam ab Anglica) secundæ oblationis oratio sequitur, ad ideam Missæ. 7. In Anglica presbyter panem populo tradens jubetur dicere : Accipe & ede in memoriam quod Christus pro te mortuus sit, fide illum edito in corde tuo cum gratiarum actione ; quæ aurea sententia transubstantiationis jugulum secans, hic in nostra prorsus omittitur, quia scil. in Canone missæ non exstat: idem observandum etiam in traditione poculi: Liturgia Anglica habet; Bibe hoc in memoriam sanguinis Christi pro te effusi & gratias agito : Quæ verba in nostra non reperiuntur, quia non in missa Romana. 8. Anglica jubet elementa tradi in manus populi, nostra illud delet, & sic quid vetabit, quin communicantium ori ingerantur? 9. Anglica jubet utrumque elementum in populi manus tradi : nostra vero nihil prorsus loquitur de utriusque elementi traditione, contenta dixisse, populus suo ordine communicet: hoc est, removeri oportet laicos ut vulgus profanum extra sacrarium, ea de causa cancellis septum ; ac quid si innuatur alium esse ordinem populi communicaturi a clericis non solum ratione loci, sed ratione communicationis sub utraque specie, ut Pontificii loquuntur: Non sine causa tale quid propositum fuisse libri nostri architectis suspicamur ; nam diserte hactenus declararunt, fundamentum nullum esse in sacra scriptura quo superstrui possit participatio in coena Domini sub utraque specie: ad traditionem referetur ab Elienfi episcopo Whito, libro nuper impresso, de Sabbato. pag. 97. & expresse Montacutius episcopus, in originum libro pag. 396. Ubi (inquit) jubentur in Scripturis infantes baptizari, aut in coena Domini sub utraque specie communicantes participare? de his possumus profiteri, nihil tale docet scriptura, scriptura haec non praedicat. Nonne merito metuendum nobis est, ne ex consulto utriusque elementi traditionem omiserint, ut immani huic sacrilegio in posteriori libri hujus editione viam parent? 10. In nostra liturgia, reliquiae panis consecrati operiendae sunt Corporali, & mensa Dominica decoro tapete instruenda est: horum vero in Anglica nulla prorsus mentio. Neque vox Corporale, quae lintea quibus elementa teguntur, significat, unquam in ecclesia audita ante natam transubstantiationem. 11. In Anglica liturgia universa fidelis populi eleemosyna pauperum aerario imponi jubetur at in nostra jubetur dividi, cujus altera semissis cedit presbytero. 12. Noster liber mentionem facit, oblationis panis & vini, de qua in Anglico altum silentium. 13. Noster panem azymum rotundum probat, cum Anglicus fermentato & ordinario uti jubet. 14. Anglicus liber jubet reliquias elementorum ad Curati aedes deferri, easque pro ordinario & vulgari pane & vino habet: noster vero vult reliquias illas ut sacras in ipso templo consumi. 15. Quod si elementa consecrata populo communicanti non suffecerint, noster jubet alia de novo consecrari, non ficAnglicus. 16. In prima oratione baptismi haec sententia exstat in libro hoc nobis obtruso, fontem hunc baptismale sanctifica, quae in Ang. deest. 17. Ibidem in margine libri nostri, jubetur aquafontis baptismalis singulis mensibus bis renovari, &c. & tum solenni verborum formula consecrari : utrumque in Anglico deest.
units.tr: Finally, this book, forced upon us, is in many respects worse and more corrupt than the English liturgy. For (1) far more saints are placed in our Calendar than in the English one. (2) Before communion the English book exhorts all those present to remember the poor; in place of this exhortation, our book orders certain sentences taken from the Roman offertory to be recited. (3) Although there are in the English book some sentences by which the people are stirred to almsgiving, they are almost all taken from the New Testament and speak only of almsgiving, so that there is no danger of their being twisted toward another offering. Our book, however, brings forward many sentences of the Old Testament, which are understood only of the sacrifices and offerings of Leviticus. (4) In the English book the people are bidden to pray that God may be pleased to accept this almsgiving of his people; and so on. Our book, however, adds over and above a thanksgiving for those who have died in faith, and so on, and thus comes closer to the Papist Mass, as was noted above. (5) In the English book the Lord's table is placed in the middle of the body of the church or of the sacristy; our book, however, orders it to be placed in the position customary for altars, within the chancel of the sacristy, from which the people are removed, so that its eastern part touches the extreme end of the sacristy. (6) In the English liturgy, after the prayer of consecration of the elements of the Lord's Supper, the minister is bidden to communicate and immediately deliver to the people. But in this book of ours, after the prayer of consecration (very different from the English one), there follows the prayer of the second oblation, in keeping with the idea of the Mass. (7) In the English book, the minister who delivers the bread to the people is bidden to say: Take and eat, in remembrance that Christ died for you, feed on him in your heart by faith with thanksgiving. This golden sentence, which cuts the throat of transubstantiation, is in our book entirely omitted, because, namely, it does not occur in the Canon of the Mass. The same is to be observed in the delivery of the cup. The English liturgy has: Drink this in remembrance of the blood of Christ shed for you, and give thanks. These words are not found in ours, because they are not in the Roman Mass. (8) The English book orders the elements to be delivered into the hands of the people; ours deletes this, and so what will prevent them from being thrust into the mouths of the communicants? (9) The English book orders each element to be delivered into the hands of the people; our book, however, says nothing at all about the delivery of either element, but is content to say that the people communicate in their order. That is to say, the laity must be removed, as the profane crowd, outside the sacristy, and for that reason it is fenced off with chancel rails. And what if it is hinted that there is a different order of the people who are to communicate, distinguished from the clergy not only by place but by the manner of communion under both kinds, as the Papists speak? We suspect that our book's architects had some such thing in mind, and not without cause. For they have hitherto declared plainly that there is no foundation in Holy Scripture on which participation in the Lord's Supper under both kinds may be built. The Bishop of Ely, White, in his recently printed book on the Sabbath, p. 97, refers this to tradition; and Bishop Montagu expressly, in his book Originum, p. 396, says: "Where are infants commanded in the Scriptures to be baptized, or those communicating at the Lord's Supper in both kinds to take part? Concerning these we may declare that Scripture teaches nothing of the kind, Scripture does not preach this." Ought we not rightly to fear that they have deliberately omitted the delivery of each element, so as to prepare the way in a later edition of this book for this monstrous sacrilege? (10) In our liturgy, the remains of the consecrated bread are to be covered with the Corporal, and the Lord's table is to be furnished with a decent cloth; of these things, however, there is no mention at all in the English. Nor does the word Corporale, which signifies the linens with which the elements are covered, appear to have ever been heard in the Church before transubstantiation was born. (11) In the English liturgy the whole alms of the faithful people is commanded to be put into the poor-box; but in ours it is commanded to be divided, one half of which goes to the minister. (12) Our book makes mention of the offering of bread and wine, about which the English is wholly silent. (13) Our book approves round unleavened bread, whereas the English book orders leavened and ordinary bread to be used. (14) The English book orders the remains of the elements to be carried to the curate's house, and holds them as ordinary and common bread and wine; ours, however, wishes those remains, as holy, to be consumed in the church itself. (15) If the consecrated elements do not suffice for the communicating people, our book orders others to be consecrated anew; the English does not. (16) In the first prayer of baptism this sentence stands in this book forced upon us: sanctify this font for baptism, which is lacking in the English. (17) Likewise, in the margin of our book, it is ordered that the water of the baptismal font be renewed twice every month, etc., and then consecrated with a solemn form of words. Both of these are lacking in the English.

units.la: Animadversiones in librum Canonum ab Episcopis obtrusum ecclesiæ Scoticæ.
units.tr: Animadversions on the book of Canons thrust upon the Church of Scotland.

units.la: 1. Liber hic Canonum obtruditur sine ullo ecclesiæ consensu & approbatione in synodo nationali, cum tamen hierarchici ipsi fateantur Canones ecclesiasticos nullibi unquam conditos fuisse quam in synodis ecclesiasticis. D. Lancelotus Andreas Episcopus Wintoniensis, in concione de tubis, edita & revisa ac cum cæteris ejusdem concionibus Regi Serenissimo dedicata per Gulielmum Episcopum Londinensem, nunc Cantuariensem: & ordinaria praxis ecclesiæ Anglicanæ in domo Convocationis, quæ synodi nationalis apud eos vicem supplet, idem docet.
units.tr: 1. This book of Canons is forced upon the Church without any consent or approval from the Church in a national synod, although the hierarchical men themselves confess that ecclesiastical canons were never enacted anywhere except in ecclesiastical synods. Lancelot Andrewes, Bishop of Winchester, in his sermon on the trumpets, published, revised and dedicated to the most serene King with his other sermons by William, Bishop of London, now of Canterbury, and the ordinary practice of the Church of England in the House of Convocation, which among them takes the place of a national synod, teach the same.

units.la: 2. Uno ictu universam ecclesiæ hujus disciplinam, & acta ac decreta octoginta plus minus synodorum nationalium penitus subvertit: ac in ejus locum novam disciplinam substituit, ab episcopis solis, remotis omnibus presbyteris, formatam, qua mera tyrannis Episcoporum Dioecesanorum in omnes ecclesias stabilitur, & quibus conceditur facultas irrefragabilis omnia in ecclesia pro arbitrio circumagendi. Adde quod libro hoc aperte contradictoria contineantur, ac quædam municipalibus regni legibus diserte adversantia, ac errores quosdam graves.
units.tr: 2. At one blow he has utterly overthrown the whole discipline of this Church, and the acts and decrees of some eighty national synods more or less. In its place he has substituted a new discipline, formed by bishops alone with all presbyters removed, by which the sheer tyranny of diocesan bishops is established over all churches, and they are granted the irresistible power to manipulate everything in the Church as they please. Add that this book plainly contains contradictory matter, some things expressly opposed to the civil laws of the kingdom, and certain grave errors.

units.la: Disciplinam receptam & canonibus synodalibus, ac legibus regni sancitam subvertit: 1. Dum interdicit presbyteris, & Laicis ne causas ullas ecclesiasticas tractent; cap. 8. parag. 4. unde sequitur, abrogandas esse sessiones seu consistoria, presbyteria seu classes; neque concedendum esse laicis quibuslibet, licet ecclesiarum senioribus, & ab ecclesiis ad synodos rite ac legitime deputatis, jus suffragii in synodis. 2. Nullam prorsus mentionem facit cujuslibet synodi, præterquam Dioecesanæ,in qua tantum regnabit Episcopus , & pro cujus arbitrio indicenda est : Exercitium etiam spiritualis jurisdictionis in commissarios seu officiales Episcopi, in solidum transfert , quasi vero officiales illi essent à Christo instituti ministri ecclesiastici cap.19. para.1. 3.Interdicit aliis omnibus ecclesiasticorum conventibus pro rebus ecclesiasticis.cap.8.para.2. 3.Semel quidem sed ex obliquo, quasi authoribus incogitantibus excidisset, mentio fit Nationalis synodi;sed altum est silentium , quænam ejus membra sint, unde haud male quis colliget, Episcopis statutum se solos esse legitima synodi illius membra : nam synodus nationalis ecclesias illius nationis repræsentat, & Episcopi se hactenus exornarunt elogio ecclesiæ repræsentativæ. 5. Ordinem Diaconorum prout à Spiritu S. instituitur, & ab hac ecclesia receptus fuit, penitus rejecerunt, & in eorum locum œconomi quidam ab Episcopis eligendi , ( ltirps[?] prorsus novella, Scotis ne vel de nomine cognita) assumuntur.
units.tr: He has subverted the discipline received and sanctioned by synodal canons and the laws of the kingdom: 1. While he forbids presbyters and laymen to deal with any ecclesiastical causes (chap. 8, para. 4), whence it follows that sessions or consistories, presbyteries or classes are to be abolished, and that no laymen whatever, even the elders of the churches and those duly and lawfully deputed by the churches to synods, are to be allowed the right of voting in synods. 2. He makes no mention of any synod except the diocesan one, in which the bishop alone rules and which is to be convened at his discretion. He also transfers the exercise of spiritual jurisdiction wholly to the bishop's commissaries or officials (chap. 19, para. 1), as if those officials were ecclesiastical ministers instituted by Christ. 3. He forbids all other assemblies of churchmen concerning ecclesiastical affairs (chap. 8, para. 2). 3. Once indeed, but obliquely, as if it had slipped from the authors unawares, mention is made of a national synod; but there is a deep silence as to who its members are, whence one may fairly conclude that it is decreed that the bishops alone are the lawful members of that synod. For a national synod represents the churches of that nation, and the bishops have hitherto adorned themselves with the title of a representative church. 5. They have utterly rejected the order of deacons as instituted by the Holy Spirit and received by this Church, and in their place certain stewards, to be chosen by the bishops (a wholly novel breed, not even known to the Scots by name), have been put in.

units.la: Potestatem omnem, imo & tyrannidem Episcopis largitur. Nam. 1. eis solis, aut eorum capellanis attribuitur facultas examinandi promovendos ad S S. ministerii functionem. cap.2.parag.3. 2. Episcopi est literas dimissorias concedere pastoribus. cap. 2. parag.5. 3. Ejus solius est ordinare pastores. cap.2.parag.7.4. potest Episcopus concedere facultatem pastoribus non residendi ad ecclesias suas. cap.3.parag.1. cum tamen residentia sit de jure divino. 5. interdicit pastoribus ne alibi quam in suis ecclesiis concionentur, quæcumque demum extraordinaria occasio sese offerat, aut necessitas urgeat, nisi primum facultatem ab ordinario loci ( sic Episcopum vocant) obtinuerint. cap.2.parag.2. 6.Episcopus potest dispensationes concedere pastoribus, qua liberentur à catechizandis rudibus ecclesiæ suæ. cap.3. pag.6.7. Interdicit pastoribus, ne haereses & errores quoslibet, ab aliis pastoribus publice licet propositos,refutet, nisi facultatem a Dicecesano obtinuerit.cap.3.parag.7.&quid si eosdem errores soveat Episcopus,silendum erit orthodoxis pastoribus, & pereundum populo. 8. Licet statuta civilia, aut ecclesiastica semel sancita sint iniquissima, interdicitur tamen pastoribus,cap.3.parag.8. ne iis contradicat, sed scrupulos suos Episcopo proponat, ejusque determinationi modeste acquiescat. 9. Nulla demigratio conceditur pastoribus de ecclesiis ad ecclesias, cap. 4. parag.4. quæcunque demum utilitas & ædificatio populi urgeat,nisi per episcopum. 10. Potest episcopus facultatem concedere celebrandi matrimonium, licet Bannarum trinundina denunciatio non præcesserit. 11. Episcopi est indicere locum & tempus synodorum. 12. Ejusdem est præceptores scholis,& lectores ecclesiis præficere. 13. Typographis interdicit ne quidlibet imprimant sine faculate visitatorum, hoc est, Episcopi ejusque capellani. cap.12.parag.1. & quid si heterodoxias illi foveant, nonne ad perpetuum silentium orthodoxa scripta damnabuntur? aut saltem exspectandum erit donec fato defunctus Episcopus, orthodoxus in cathedram ejus succedat, quod vix sperandum esse praeteriti temporis experientia demonstrat. 14. Catalogum baptizatorum, matrimonio conjunctorum, praesertim vero demortuorum, a quibus spes lucri Episcopis affulget per approbationem seu confirmationem testamentorum, ad Episcopum quotannis transmittere jubetur presbyter. 15. Episcopi est in suæ Dioecefeos ecclesiis jejunia indicere,cap.14.§.1. Itaut nisi consentiat episcopus nefas fit publicis jejuniis & precibus gravissimamDei iram imminentem deprecari.
units.tr: He grants to bishops all power, indeed tyranny itself. For: 1. The power of examining candidates for the holy ministry is given to bishops alone, or their chaplains (chap. 2, para. 3). 2. It is the bishop's to grant letters dimissory to ministers (chap. 2, para. 5). 3. It is his alone to ordain ministers (chap. 2, para. 7). 4. The bishop may grant ministers permission not to reside at their churches (chap. 3, para. 1), although residence is by divine right. 5. He forbids ministers to preach anywhere other than in their own churches, whatever extraordinary occasion presents itself or necessity presses, unless they first obtain permission from the ordinary of the place (as they call the bishop) (chap. 2, para. 2). 6. The bishop may grant dispensations to ministers, freeing them from catechizing the ignorant of their church (chap. 3, p. 6, 7). 7. He forbids ministers to refute any heresies or errors whatever, even if publicly put forward by other ministers, unless they obtain permission from the diocesan (chap. 3, para. 7). And what if the bishop fosters those same errors? Then orthodox ministers must keep silent and the people must perish. 8. Although civil or ecclesiastical statutes once sanctioned are most unjust, ministers are forbidden to contradict them (chap. 3, para. 8), but must lay their scruples before the bishop and humbly acquiesce in his decision. 9. No transfer of ministers from church to church is permitted (chap. 4, para. 4), however much the advantage and edification of the people may urge it, unless it is done through the bishop. 10. The bishop may grant permission to celebrate a marriage even though the threefold proclamation of banns has not preceded. 11. It is for the bishop to appoint the place and time of synods. 12. It is his to set masters over schools and readers over churches. 13. He forbids printers to print anything without the permission of the visitors, that is, the bishop and his chaplains (chap. 12, para. 1). And what if they foster heterodoxies? Will not orthodox writings be condemned to perpetual silence? Or at least we must wait until the bishop dies and an orthodox man succeeds him in the chair, which the experience of past times shows is scarcely to be hoped for. 14. The minister is ordered to send each year to the bishop a register of the baptized, of those joined in marriage, and especially of the dead, from which the bishops hope for gain through the approval or confirmation of wills. 15. It is for the bishop to appoint fasts in the churches of his diocese (chap. 14, §1), so that unless the bishop consents it is wrong to entreat by public fasts and prayers the most grievous wrath of God hanging over us.

units.la: 16. Episcopi est designare ubi & quomodo ponenda sint templorum pulpita,quæ decora esse oportet. cap. 16. §. 5. hoc est, Episcopo conceditur facultas imperandi lectionemEuangelii de superiori pulpito, quia illud dicunt quidam,aliis omnibus S.script.partibus magis sacrum esse, propter contactum scil. oris Christi: & de inferiori pulpito alias omnes scripturæ partes: & quid si per illam pulpiti decentiam, astringamus ad ligneum pulpitum, propter symbolicam significationem crucis Christi, juxta Amulatrium.lib.3. De divinis officiis.17.Episcopi est providere de bonis omnibus piis usibus dicatis, eique tradentur scripta omnia quæ ad hæc bona pertinent, cap.17. §.5.6.10. & quis pro fide Episcopi spondebit, ac nobis Episcoporum avaritiam expertis persuadebit, à sacrilegio immunes futuros, aut si rei agantur hujus sceleris quomodo convinci poterint, cum facile illis erit scripta illa supprimere ? Itaque ut hic sibi optime cavisse videntur, sic in manifesto crimine deprehensis prospexerunt,nam nullam aliam in sacrilegos pœnam statuunt.cap.17.parag. 1.quam restitutionem.18.Interdicit ne sententia excommunicationis in quemlibet proferatur, nisi chirographo episcopi prius obsignetur,ca.18.parag.3: Aliter certe Christus ecclesiæ suæ consuluit. Matth:18:17. Dic ecclesiæ: Nisi forte Episcopus solus ecclesiâ repræsentet, ut princeps regnum. 19.Interdicitur ne excommunicati satisfaciant ecclesiæ aut absolvantur nisi ex consensu & beneplacito Episcopi; quàm positè,nam ejus est solvere,cujus est ligare. 20.Episcopus potest facultatem concedere conversandi in excommunicatis;cap.18.§.5. An hoc nō est facile concedere dispensandi cum lege Christi? 21.Interdicit ne sententia depositionis contra presbyterum feratur per ullum aliud quam Archiepiscopum aut Episcopos Diœceseos, & sic cautum est profanis & Heterodoxis, modo episcopum benevolum habeant, quem raro adversarium experiantur, si acres ceremoniarum defensores se gesserint, prout ecclesiarum frequentissima gravamina hodie clamant.
units.tr: 16. It is for the bishop to designate where and how the pulpits of the churches are to be placed, which ought to be seemly (chap. 16, §5). That is, the bishop is granted the power of ordering that the Gospel be read from the upper pulpit, because some say it is holier than all other parts of Scripture on account of the contact, namely, of Christ's mouth; and that all other parts of Scripture be read from the lower pulpit. And what if, for the sake of that pulpit decency, we are bound to a wooden pulpit on account of the symbolic signification of Christ's cross, according to Amalarius, book 3, On the Divine Offices? 17. It is for the bishop to provide for all goods dedicated to pious uses, and all writings that pertain to these goods shall be handed over to him (chap. 17, §§5, 6, 10). And who will vouch for the bishop's good faith? Who will persuade us, having experienced the avarice of bishops, that they will be free from sacrilege, or, if they are charged with this crime, how can they be convicted, since it will be easy for them to suppress those writings? So, as they seem to have taken very good care for themselves here, so they have provided for those caught in manifest crime, for they lay down no other penalty for sacrilegious persons (chap. 17, para. 1) than restitution. 18. He forbids that sentence of excommunication be pronounced against anyone unless it has first been sealed by the bishop's hand (chap. 18, para. 3). Otherwise Christ has provided for his Church differently: Matth. 18:17, "Tell it to the Church." Unless perhaps the bishop alone represents the Church, as a prince represents the kingdom. 19. It is forbidden that the excommunicated make satisfaction to the Church or be absolved except by the consent and pleasure of the bishop. How badly this is done, for it belongs to him to loose whose it is to bind. 20. The bishop may grant permission to converse with the excommunicated (chap. 18, §5). Is this not an easy grant of power to dispense with the law of Christ? 21. He forbids that a sentence of deposition be passed against a presbyter by anyone other than the Archbishop or the diocesan bishops; and thus provision is made for the profane and heterodox, provided they have a benevolent bishop, whom they rarely find an adversary, if they have acted as fierce defenders of the ceremonies, as the very frequent grievances of the churches cry out today.

units.la: 22. Episcopi est decernere, quo habitu vestiendi sint Decani, doctores, presbyteri, Diaconi & reliquus clerus: quisnam vero ille futurus sit, haud difficile est divinatu; nam cum urgeant libri hi conformitatem cum ecclesia Anglica, vestitus ille clericorum idem erit cum eo qui in Canone 74. Anglicarum constitutionum imperatur, & si quid ad plenum cum pontificiis syncretissimum in vestitu sacro apud Anglos decerat, nostri episcopi, in melius scilicet indies proficientes, liberaliter addent; & sicuti missam fere totam reposuerunt, vestitum etiam missaticum cur omitterent? nam turpe esset devorato bove in cauda haerere, & camelo absorpto percolare culicem. 23. Denique quasi taederet episcopos, potestatis suae rapidum torrentem intra ullos omnino limites contineri, cap. 19. parag. ultimo: potestatem sibi assumunt pro arbitrio poenas infligendi eorum canonum violatoribus, qui nulla speciali poena sanciuntur: & hunc colophonem superbo huic aedificio superimponunt: ac si quid deest, hoc supplemento coronant: Omnium porro summa est, Episcopos posse judicare omnes, sed a nemine judicari.
units.tr: 22. It is for the bishop to decree in what dress the deans, teachers, presbyters, deacons and the rest of the clergy are to be clothed. Who that will be is not hard to guess: since these books press conformity with the Church of England, that clerical dress will be the same as that commanded in Canon 74 of the English constitutions. And if anything was lacking among the English in the sacred vestments to make them fully syncretistic with the Papists, our bishops, growing better day by day, will liberally add it. Just as they have restored almost the whole Mass, why would they omit the Mass vestments? For it would be shameful, having swallowed the ox, to stick at the tail, and, having gulped down the camel, to strain out a gnat. 23. Finally, as if the bishops were weary of their power's rapid torrent being contained within any limits at all (chap. 19, last para.), they claim for themselves the power of inflicting penalties at will on violators of those canons which are sanctioned by no special penalty. They crown this proud edifice with this finishing touch, and if anything is still lacking they complete it with this supplement: "In sum, bishops can judge all, but be judged by none."

units.la: Tertio. Liber hic contradictoria quaedam continet: Nam summariam excommunicationem, hoc est, quae citationibus non praecedentibus fertur, damnant, cap. 18. parag. 2. cum tamen cap. 8. & 4. qui synodis contradixerint, earumque decretis non acquieverint, qui rubricam, canonem, verba librorum horum, videlicet canonum, liturgiae, ordinationis, homiliarum; (ex quibus solus liber Canonum tum typis commissus prostabat) mutaverint, ipso facto excommunicati declarantur : Dein Residentiam presbyteris injungunt, & tamen cap. 10. Cu-rati inter legitimos ecclesiæ ministros recensentur : quorum nullus alius usus esse potest, quam ut pastoris absentis & non residentis vices suppleant.
units.tr: Third, this book contains some contradictory statements. It condemns summary excommunication, that is, excommunication pronounced without prior citation (chap. 18, para. 2), and yet in chapters 8 and 4 it declares that those who have opposed the synods and not submitted to their decrees, and those who have altered the rubric, canon, or wording of these books (namely the canons, the liturgy, the ordination service, and the homilies, of which only the Book of Canons was then in print), are excommunicated by the very fact. Then it enjoins residence on presbyters, and yet in chapter 10 curates are counted among the lawful ministers of the Church. Yet curates can serve no purpose other than to supply the place of a minister who is absent and does not reside.

units.la: Quarto. Liber hic quædam continet diserte adversantia municipalibus regni legibus. Nam cap. 7. parag. 6. Parti innocenti post legitimum divortium interdicuntur fecundæ nuptiæ vivente adultero. Cum tamen reditus ad nuptias statuto parlamentari sanciatur : Dein cap. 17. parag. 7. Pastores sine liberis morientes astringit, ut magnam bonorum suorum partem, licet à majoribus hæreditario jure transmissa possideat, testamento leget in pios usus, quod multi nihil aliud esse credunt, quam ut in ærarium episcopi conferantur, quippe quod illi soli commissa sit suprema ejusmodi bonorum cura; neque sit qui ad rationes reddendas adigere cum aliquo operæ pretio possit: Sed quicquid sit de administratione: ipsum illud decretum excedit omnem potestatem, quam reges nostri unquam sibi in liberos subditos vendicarunt, & Episcopos constituit Dominos bonorum & fortunarum, quæ alii legitime possident tanquam propria; in quæ nulli alteri jus quodlibet est: ac communi & recepto juris nostri axiomati repugnat, statuentis, ultimam ingenuorum hominum morientium voluntatem esse liberam.
units.tr: Fourth, this book contains some things plainly opposed to the municipal laws of the kingdom. In chapter 7, para. 6, a second marriage is forbidden to the innocent party after a lawful divorce while the adulterer is still alive, although a return to marriage is sanctioned by a parliamentary statute. Then, in chapter 17, para. 7, ministers who die without children are bound to leave by will a large part of their goods, even though they hold them by hereditary right handed down from their ancestors, to pious uses. Many believe this amounts to nothing more than that the goods should be paid into the bishop's treasury, since the supreme oversight of such goods is committed to him alone, and there is no one who could with any profit compel him to render accounts. But whatever may be said of the administration, the decree itself exceeds all the power that our kings have ever claimed over their free subjects. It makes the bishops lords of the goods and fortunes that others lawfully possess as their own, and over which no one else has any right whatsoever. It also contradicts the common and accepted axiom of our law, which holds that the last will of freeborn men who die is free.

units.la: Quinto. Gravissimos aliquot errores continet, inter quos sunt hi. Episcopum posse licentiam concedere conversandi cum excommunicatis; quod adversatur mandato Christi Matth. 18. 17. Sit tibi tanquam Ethnicus & publicanus, & Apostolorum sæpius: 2. Posse licentiam non residendi pastoribus concedere, cum tamen jure divino, si fidi pastores esse velint, residere teneantur. 3. Reditum ad nuptias parti innocenti post legitimum divortium quamdiu adulter maritus vixerit, interdicitur contra Christi expressam mentem. Matth. 5. 32. & 19. 9. quibus locis nuptiae post divortium permittuntur. Nam si maechatur qui novam uxorem ducit, nisi repudiata priore ob adulterium; tum, qui repudiata priore uxore ob adulterium, novam duxerit, non maechatur: nam vis hujus exceptionis, nisi ob adulterium, est, ut contrarium supponat in eo quod excipitur. Uti omnes reformatae ecclesiae differte contra Pontificios tuentur, qui eandem matrimonii indissolubilitatem in synodo Tridentina sessione. 7. cap. 24. decreverunt. 4. Sic loquitur liber cap. 8. parag. 4. quasi ecclesia haec Scotica tam in doctrina quam disciplina nondum reformata esset, judicent vel caeci quam posticam hic sibi aperiant Episcopi, qua impune doctrinam mutare possent; ideoque nullam prorsus mentionem faciunt Confessionis fidei in publicis regni comitiis olim fancitae. 5. Ordinem satis aperte inter sacramenta refert. cap. 2. parag. 7. Nam quae ad integritatem sacramenti, (prout supra definivisse, Catechismum Liturgicum diximus,) requiruntur, hic invenies, nam ritus externus est manuum impositio: Adest etiam internae gratiae promissum, quod per impositionem manuum confertur accipe, inquit Episcopus ordinans, Spiritum S. Et cum Dei gratiam ordinandis precentur, oportet promissum exstare, si preces ex fide esse vellent: Divinam etiam institutionem vendicant, quasi Deus instituisset ut per manus Episcopi gratia illa conferretur. 6. Idem de poenitentia colligere licet, alias, cur ejus partes uti pontificii vocant, Confessionem & Absolutionem sacramentalem vocarent, vocemque hanc majusculis literis depingi curarent. pag. 18. parag. 9? Denique ut fuco speciosiori omnia velarent, Sereniss.[?] Regi nostro adulantur hic Episcopi nostri libri hujus authores. Nam cap. 1. parag. 2. Quamcunque potestatem in rebus ecclesiasticis pii Reges inter Iudaeos unquam obtinuerunt & exercuerunt, eandem simpliciter & sine ulla restrictione Serenissim.[?] Regi & ejus successoribus in hac ecclesia tribuunt: unde sequitur reges nostros Serenissimos authoritatem habere consignandi & scribendi libros Canonicos S. Scripturae, nam nulli ignotum est, Davidem & Salomonem ea munera in ecclesia Iudaica exercuisse, & infallibiles fuisse, eatenus saltem, Spiritus S. amanuenses: & cap. 8. parag. 4. Regem ejusque successores statuunt; supremos Iudices controversiarum omnium ecclesiasticarum tam in doctrina quam disciplina; cum tamen suprema potestas determinandi controversias in qualibet ecclesia sit penes synodum nationalem legitime convocatam & formatam, ut rotunde absque verborum involucris loquuntur Theologi ex magna Britannia à piae memoriae Rege Iacobo ad synodum Dordracenam deputati, sessione. 29. illius synodi, in responsione ad protestationem Remonstrantium.
units.tr: Fifth, it contains several very grave errors, among which are these: (1) that a bishop may grant licence to associate with the excommunicated, which is contrary to Christ's command in Matt. 18. 17, "Let him be to thee as a heathen and a publican", and to the frequent teaching of the Apostles; (2) that licence not to reside may be granted to ministers, although by divine right they are bound to reside if they are to be faithful pastors; (3) that return to marriage is forbidden to the innocent party after a lawful divorce for as long as the adulterous husband lives, contrary to the express mind of Christ in Matt. 5. 32 and 19. 9, where marriage after divorce is permitted. For whoever marries a new wife commits adultery, unless he has put away the former one for adultery; and he who, having put away his wife for adultery, marries again, does not commit adultery. For the force of this exception, unless for adultery, is to imply the contrary of what is excepted. All the reformed churches rightly maintain this against the Papists, who in the Council of Trent, session 7, chapter 24, decreed the same indissolubility of marriage. (4) The book speaks as if this Scottish church, in doctrine as well as discipline, were not yet reformed. Let the blind judge what back door the bishops here open for themselves, by which they could change doctrine with impunity. For this reason they make no mention at all of the Confession of faith once enacted in the public assemblies of the kingdom. (5) It sets out the order quite plainly among the sacraments (chap. 2, para. 7). For what is required for the integrity of a sacrament (as we said above, the Liturgical Catechism defined) you will find here: the external rite is the laying on of hands, and there is also the promise of inward grace, which is conferred through the laying on of hands. "Receive the Holy Spirit," says the ordaining bishop. And since they pray for grace for those being ordained, a promise must exist if the prayers are to be offered in faith. They also claim divine institution, as if God had ordained that this grace should be conferred through the hands of the bishop. (6) The same may be gathered about repentance. Otherwise, why would they call its parts, as the Papists do, Confession and sacramental Absolution, and have these words printed in capitals (p. 18, para. 9?)? Finally, to cover everything with a more specious veneer, the authors of this book flatter our most serene King. In chapter 1, para. 2, they grant to our most serene King and his successors, simply and without any restriction, whatever power pious kings ever held and exercised in ecclesiastical matters among the Jews. From this it follows that our most serene kings have authority to write and set down the canonical books of Holy Scripture, for no one is unaware that David and Solomon exercised those offices in the Jewish church and were infallible, at least insofar as they were amanuenses of the Holy Spirit. And in chapter 8, para. 4, they establish the King and his successors as supreme judges of all ecclesiastical controversies, both in doctrine and discipline. Yet the supreme power of determining controversies in any church rests with a national synod lawfully convened and constituted, as the theologians sent from Great Britain by King James of pious memory to the Synod of Dort plainly say, without verbal wrappings, in session 29 of that synod, in their answer to the Remonstrants' protestation.

units.la: Animadversiones in librum ordinationis Episcoporum, presbyterorum, & Diaconorum.
units.tr: Animadversions on the book of the ordination of bishops, elders, and deacons.

units.la: 1. Liber hic nullo ecclesiarum in synodo consensu praeeunte formatus fuit, neque ulla penitus authoritate ecclesiastica seu civili nititur; licet eo saepius usi fuerint Episcopi: 2. Quod Episcopos tertium ordinem cleri diserte statuat, distinctum à presbyteris. 3. Quod novum ordinem Diaconorum constituat, quibus nulla pauperum cura incumbit, uti prima Diaconorum institutio ab Apostolis Act. 6. jubet, iisque potestatem concedit praedicandi & Baptizandi, 4. Quod promovendos ad ministerium in nova & insolita juramenta adigat, quod est contra expressa regni hujus statuta: neque juramenta ea prius promovendis ostenduntur, quam cum ad momentum ipsum perventum fuerit, quando jurandum illis erit: & sic jurantes non possunt dici jurare in judicio. 5. Quod formam ordinationis pastorum per Episcopum afferat, decreto nationalis synodi niti, quod prorsus falsum est. 6. Quod probationem & examinationem promovendi pastoris ad Episcopum referat, exclusò presbyterio seu classe, ad quam proprie pertinet. 7. Quod episcopus manus subito imponat ordinando; quem sæpenumero prius nunquam conspexit, neque ipsius dona aut vitam cognitam aliter habet, quam ex perfunctoria relatione archidiaconi aut capellani. 8. Quod ordinationis potestatem soli Episcopo attribuat, exclusis omnibus presbyteris, nisi forte admittantur ut testes actionis. 9. Tota forma consecrationis Episcoporum & Archiepiscoporum pontificia est, & ex rituali Romano translata. 10. Episcopos exortem hanc suam potestatem & jurisdictionem à Deo accepisse dicit. Plurima alia addebant alii perpendenda, tam in hoc quam in aliis libris duobus obtrusis, nam quartus ille Homiliarum nondum compositus fuit.
units.tr: 1. This book was drawn up without any prior consent of the churches in a synod, and it rests on no ecclesiastical or civil authority at all, although the bishops have often used it. 2. It states plainly that bishops form a third order of the clergy, distinct from elders. 3. It sets up a new order of deacons, who have no care of the poor, although the first institution of deacons by the Apostles (Acts 6) requires that care, and it grants them the power of preaching and baptizing. 4. It binds those to be advanced to the ministry by new and unusual oaths, which is contrary to the express statutes of this kingdom. Nor are these oaths shown to candidates before the very moment has come when they must swear, and so those who swear cannot be said to swear in judgment. 5. It attributes the form of ordaining ministers by a bishop to a decree of the national synod, which is wholly false. 6. It refers the examination and trial of a candidate for the ministry to the bishop, leaving out the presbytery or classis, to which it properly belongs. 7. It requires the bishop to lay hands suddenly on the one being ordained, whom he has often never seen before, and whose gifts and life he knows only from the perfunctory report of an archdeacon or chaplain. 8. It assigns the power of ordination to the bishop alone, excluding all elders, unless they are perhaps admitted as witnesses of the act. 9. The whole form of consecrating bishops and archbishops is Papist, and it has been carried over from the Roman ritual. 10. It says that bishops have received this power and jurisdiction from God. Others added many more points to be weighed, both in this book and in the two other books thrust upon us, for the fourth of those Homilies was not yet composed.

units.la: Quibus maturo judicio perpensis sic de singulis decretum est unanimi synodalium judicio.
units.tr: When these matters had been weighed with mature judgment, the following decision was made on each point by the unanimous judgment of the members of the synod.

units.la: De libro liturgiæ. Quandoquidem à Pseudoepiscopis formatus & obtrusus sit ecclesiæ, sine ulla ecclesiasticæ authoritatis specie, & præter barbaram phraseologiam, ac insolitam cultus divini formam, mere pontificiam, plurimos pontificiorum errores ab ecclesia Scotica jampridem damnatos, ac semina multiplicis idololatriæ & gravissimarum superstitionum contineat, quæ ex diametro repugnent doctrinæ & disciplinæ, confessionibus fidei, constitutionibus synodalibus; ac statutis parlamentariis, reformatæ religionis professionem sancientibus, ideo liber hic à synodo merito rejicitur ac damnatur, ac severe sub pœna censuræ ecclesiasticæ ejus praxi omnibus hujus ecclesiæ membris interdicitur.
units.tr: Concerning the book of liturgy: since it was formed by pseudo-bishops and thrust upon the Church without any appearance of ecclesiastical authority, and since, apart from its barbarous phraseology and unusual form of divine worship, it is purely Papist, containing many errors of the Papists long since condemned by the Scottish Church, and the seeds of manifold idolatry and very grave superstitions, which are directly opposed to the doctrine and discipline, the confessions of faith, the synodical constitutions, and the parliamentary statutes that establish the profession of the reformed religion, therefore this book is rightly rejected and condemned by the synod, and its use is strictly forbidden to all members of this Church under penalty of ecclesiastical censure.

units.la: De libro Canonum, superaddunt: Destitutum esse ecclesiastica authoritate; Pseudo-episcopos in illo, laudabile ecclesiæ regimen, & disciplinam verbo Dei conformem & ab ipsis reformationis primordiis non fine singulari Dei benedictione hactenus constanter usitatam, uno ictu subruere, ac exoticam disciplinam ejus loco substituere, ac sibi assumpsisse tyrannicam dominationem in cultum Dei, conscientiam, libertatem, & fortunas omnium; ideoque à se rejici, ac damnari.
units.tr: Concerning the book of canons, they add that it is destitute of ecclesiastical authority; that by it the pseudo-bishops at one blow overthrow the praiseworthy government of the Church and a discipline in conformity with the Word of God, which has been constantly observed from the very beginnings of the Reformation, not without a singular blessing of God; that they substitute in its place a foreign discipline; and that they have assumed a tyrannical dominion over the worship of God, over conscience, liberty, and the property of all. Therefore it is rejected and condemned by the synod.

units.la: Librum ordinationis, declarat synodus destitutum esse tam civili, quam ecclesiastica authoritate: ossicia quædam & munera ecclesiastica in ecclesiam, Dei Domum introducere tanquam divina, quæ à Deo tamen nunquam instituta fuerunt, & ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ legibus hic receptis contraria sunt, impedire fidelium & idoneorum pastorum promotionem ad S S. ministerii munus, utpote quod promovendos adigat in juramenta illegitima: ideoque rejici ac damnari declarat.
units.tr: Concerning the book of ordination, the synod declares that it is destitute of both civil and ecclesiastical authority. It introduces into the Church, the House of God, certain offices and ecclesiastical functions as if they were divine, although God never instituted them, and they are contrary to the laws of ecclesiastical discipline received here. It hinders the promotion of faithful and fit ministers to the office of the holy ministry, inasmuch as it binds those to be promoted by illegitimate oaths. Therefore it declares that the book is rejected and condemned.

units.la: Ad examen etiam vocatum fuit Tribunal, vulgo Curia celsæ commissionis; cujus erectione, jurisdictionem omnem ecclesiasticam subverti, & interturbari declarat; ac tribunalia omnia confundi, ac miscere; In ea sententiam non ferri secundum constitutiones Ecclesiasticas (licet supremi fori ecclesiastici speciem mentiatur) nec leges regni municipales: quod legibus regni fundamentalibus repugnat, Iacob. 1. parliam. 3. statut. 48. & Iacob. 4. parliam. 6. stat. 79. quibus expresse cavetur; ne aliis quam regni legibus municipalibus regantur subditi. In ea ecclesiasticis concedi utriusque gladii tam civilis quam ecclesiastici; ac mere Politicis, ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ & clavium potestatem. Tribunal esse extraneum, sine ecclesiæ & ordinum regni consensu erectum, ad tyrannidem episcopalem statuminandam.
units.tr: The Court, commonly called the High Commission, was also brought under examination. The synod declares that by its erection all ecclesiastical jurisdiction has been subverted and thrown into confusion, and that all the courts have been confounded and mixed together. In it sentence is not passed according to the ecclesiastical constitutions (although it pretends to the appearance of the highest ecclesiastical court), nor according to the municipal laws of the kingdom. This is contrary to the fundamental laws of the kingdom (James I, Parliament 3, Statute 48, and James IV, Parliament 6, Statute 79), by which it is expressly provided that subjects shall not be governed by any laws other than the municipal laws of the realm. In it the power of both swords is granted to ecclesiastical men, civil and ecclesiastical alike, and the power of the keys of discipline is handed over to purely political men. The Court is foreign, erected without the consent of the Church and of the estates of the realm, in order to establish episcopal tyranny.

units.la: Sess. 15. Decemb. 7. Die Veneris.
units.tr: Session 15, 7 December, Friday.

units.la: Synodi judicio & censuræ submisit se Episcopus Caledonius per literas, quibus absentiam suam in ætatem ingravescentem rejiciebat, quam tanto & tam difficili itineri jam hyeme suscipiendo imparem omnes noverant.
units.tr: The Bishop of Caithness submitted himself by letter to the judgment and censure of the synod. In it he excused his absence on account of his advancing age, since all knew that he was unequal to so long and so difficult a journey to be undertaken in winter.

units.la: Episcoporum accusatores urgent prosecutionem suæ causæ contra Episcopos.
units.tr: The accusers of the bishops press forward with the prosecution of their cause against the bishops.

units.la: Capita accusationis Episcopo Gallovidiano Thomæ Syncerfio objecta Sess.8. releguntur, eorundemque plena probatio deducitur: qua omnium eorum criminum & pervicaciæ reus esse, ideoque ab ecclesiastica communione excludendus ab omnibus censetur. De modo excommunicationis sententiarum quædam diversitas fuit; aliis summariam urgentibus, aliis vero, admonitiones publicas præmittendas esse statuentibus: Sed cum ostensum fuisset notoriam & flagrantem fuisse hujus pertinaciam, & obstinatam contumaciam contra ecclesiam in synodo hac repræsentatam; cui se præsentem sistere dedignaretur, licet in vicinia hæreret, ac se citatum non ignoraret; omnium fere judiciis summariæ excommunicationis fulmine feriendum esse statutum est.
units.tr: The articles of accusation objected to Thomas Sydserf, Bishop of Galloway, in session 8 are read out again, and their full proof is laid out. He is judged by all to be guilty of all these crimes and of obstinacy, and therefore to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion. There was some difference of opinion about the manner of pronouncing excommunication: some urged a summary sentence, while others held that public admonitions should be sent out first. But since it was shown that his obstinacy and stubborn contumacy against the Church, represented in this synod, was notorious and blazing, and since he disdained to present himself before it, although he was staying nearby and knew he had been summoned, it was resolved, by almost the judgment of all, that he should be struck with the thunderbolt of summary excommunication.

units.la: Examinatur causa Archiepiscopi Andreapolitani, probatur reum esse non solum omnium criminum quæ Episcopis omnibus communia sunt; verum etiam publicæ & ordinariæ profanationis sabbati, immodicæ ad intempestam usque noctem tabernarum frequentationis, atrocium calumniarum & convitiorum in synodos omnes nationales præcedentes, criminis falsi ob interlita & mutata synodi Abredonenfis decreta, facrilegii, fimoniæ, indulgentiæ erga paftores & profeffores heterodoxias (quibus annis præteritis graviter vexata fuit ecclefia) fpargentes; quos licet facile reprimere potuiffet; non coercuit; horumque audaciæ filentio fuo vires addidit; eorumque poenam in fe contraxit, nam poteftas quæ prohibere fcelus poteft & debet, fi fciens patiatur perpetrari, quafi probat debere fieri, ut olim recte Salvianus, Τὸ μὴ κωλύειν[?] τὰς ἁμαρτάνοντας[?] ἴσον τῷ ἁμαρτάνειν[?]. Obtulerunt ipfius accufatores fe liquido demonftraturos eum aliis flagitiis, aut faltem flagranti eorundem fcandalo teneri: Quare confentientibus fuffragiis abdicatur à muneribus & functionibus ecclefiafticis, atque cum præcedentibus flagitiis pervicaciam addidiffet, excommunicandus cenfetur.
units.tr: The case of the Archbishop of St Andrews was examined, and it was proved that he is guilty not only of all the crimes common to all bishops, but also of the public and habitual profanation of the Sabbath, of excessive frequenting of taverns until the unseasonable hour of night, of atrocious calumnies and reproaches against all the earlier national synods, of the crime of forgery through the altering and erasing of the decrees of the Synod of Aberdeen, of sacrilege, of simony, and of showing indulgence to ministers and professors spreading heterodox opinions, by which the Church was grievously troubled in past years. Although he could easily have restrained these men, he did not check them, and by his silence he added strength to their audacity, and so he incurred their punishment himself. For a power that can and ought to prohibit a crime, if it knowingly allows it to be committed, seems to approve that it be done. So Salvian rightly said long ago: To not prevent sinners is the same as sinning [Τὸ μὴ κωλύειν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας ἴσον τῷ ἁμαρτάνειν]. His accusers offered to demonstrate clearly that he is also held by other shameful acts, or at least by the open scandal of the same. Therefore, by the unanimous votes, he is deprived of his ecclesiastical offices and functions, and since he had added obstinacy to his previous shameful acts, he is judged to be excommunicated.

units.la: Eidem poenæ fubjicitur Epifcopus Brechinenfis; quem flagitia plurima omnibus liquido comperta, infamem jampridem reddiderunt;
units.tr: The same penalty is imposed on the Bishop of Brechin, whose many shameful acts, plainly known to all, had long since made him infamous.

units.la: Seffion. 16. Decemb. 8. Die Saturni.
units.tr: Session, 16 December, Saturday 8.

units.la: Comes Vemefius referebat, Archiepifcopum Glafguenfem fecum égiffe, ut apud Synodum in ipfius gratiam intercederet; præfertim cum reftaretur fe contra animi fui fententiam propemodum coactum ab epifcopo Roffenfi & aliis, proteftationi contra Synodum fubfcripfiffe: Quare delegati fuerunt quidam à Synodo qui ferio cum Archiepifcopo agerent, ut, quod familiari fermone protuliffet, fcripto fignaret, ac synodi judicio, à qua æquiffima fperaret, fimpliciter fe fubmitteret: Ac licet fpem aliquam utriufque oftenderet, plus tamen apud inconftantem ipfius animu prævaluit metus, ne amiffione ampliffimorum redituum & penfionis quinq; millium librarŭ fæpius promiffæ, in præfentem paupertatem incideret, quam excommunicationis terror; ad cujus mentionem fefe trepidare, initio præ fe ferebat.
units.tr: The Earl of Wemyss reported that the Archbishop of Glasgow had come with him to intercede on his behalf before the Synod, especially since it was said that he had been forced, almost against his own judgment, by the Bishop of Ross and others to subscribe a protest against the Synod. Therefore certain men were appointed by the Synod to deal earnestly with the Archbishop, so that he would sign in writing what he had said in private conversation and simply submit himself to the judgment of the Synod, from which he hoped for the most just outcome. Although he showed some hope of both, the fear that gripped his inconstant mind prevailed more: that by losing his very ample revenues and the pension of five thousand pounds, often promised, he would fall into present poverty. The terror of excommunication moved him less. At the mention of it, he at first showed himself trembling.

units.la: Dein à fynodo defignati ad verum & genuinum fenfum quorundam articulorum Confeffionis, ex regiftris Synodicis & aliis Ecclefiæ publicis fcriptis eruendum, diligentiæ fuæ rationem prolixiori fcripto exhibent, quod tribus conftabat partibus. Prima, Neceffitatem operis fufcepti demonftrabat. Secunda, farraginem conftitutionum Synodicarum ab anno 1576. ad 1596. quibus rejici videbatur omne genus Epifcopatus, continebat. Tertia vero, refponfiones ad objecta quædam quibus Epifcopatum fulciri quidam putabant: Scripto hoc prælecto & examinato, vifum eft Præfidi Quæftionis hujus de Epifcopatu Determinationem ad fuffragia referre, cujus hic fuit ftatus: An fecundum fidei confeffionem (anno 1580. primitus formatam, & anno 1581. univerfaliter receptam, & 1590. repetitam) jullus alius in hac ecclefia tum approbaretur Epifcopus, quam particularis ecclefiæ feu unius gregis paftor, cui nulla πρωτοδρία, & poteftas in collegas competeret: Et an fecundum genuinum & annis illis publice receptum Confeffionis fenfum; Omne aliud Epifcopatus genus abjuratum fuerit, ideoque nunc etiam removendum: Omnes (uno folum excepto) refpondent; Omnem omnino Epifcopatum qui ab unius gregis paftore differret, fecundum Confeffionis fenfum tum receptum Abjuratum fuiffe, ac nunc eliminandum effe extra ecclefiam: At unus diftinguendum dicebat Epifcopatum; In eum qui tum à quibufdam ufurpatus fuiffet, reluctante ecclefia; cui foli perpetuam fpiritualem præeminentiam & dignitatis primatum in totam Dioecefin, fimul cum potestate ordinationis & jurifdictionis omnimodæ alligare folent Hierarchici: Epifcopatum hunc Ecclefiã condemnaffe, ac in confeffione abjuratum effe; ideoq; de ecclefia penitus removendum, ut errorem Pontificium, S. Scripturæ, & puriori antiquitati inco[?]gnitum : Alium vero esse Episcopatum , quo usi fuerunt pii patres in primitiva ecclesia , quique in officio superintendentium initio reformatæ religionis in Scotia obtinuit, cui, presbyterorum voluntārio consensu , primatus quidam ordinis,isque ἀρχιἐπισκοπῶν[?], concedebatur : Hunc licet non revocandum censeat ;animo tamen suo vix persuasum,ut judicet confessione illa abjuratum esse : Ac facem huic distinctioni prælucere in formalibus verbis Decreti Synodici, anno 1580. Taoduni conditi, & repetiti Glasguæ. 1581. Nam sæpius repetitur Officium Episcopi, prout nunc eo utuntur Episcopi in hoc regno: quod cum sit manifesta determinatio subjecti, videl. Episcopatus, ad illud primum genus Episcoporum, quibus vexabatur tum ecclesia, non poterat extendi ad omnem omnino Episcopatum simpliciter in se consideratum. Quibus adde solum Episcopatum prædictarum synodorum constitutionibus damnari, qui non esset ex Deo, qui in se esset illegitimus, qui efset officium ad quod Episcopi à Deo non vocentur: Atque ab ipsis reformationis primordiis constans fuit ecclesiæ Scoticæ opinio, Officium superintendentium in se non fuisse illegitimum, & qui ad illud munus ab ecclesiis rite vocarentur, à Deo vocatos fuisse, uti in formula ordinationis superintendentium Psalteriis præfixa liquido constat ; Nam quæstio penultima istius formulæ sic se habet ; Agnoscis ne dignitatem hujus officii ad quod Deus te vocavit, requirere vitæ sanctimoniam etiam hostibus Euangelii Conspicuam ? Qua responsione quæstionem propositam non fuisse unam, sed quæ se in plura membra divideret, quam πολυξήτητον[?] vocant, innuere videbatur ; nam aliud est quærere; An tum ullus alius in ecclesia approbaretur Episcopus quam qui esset unius egre-gis pastor ; Aliud vero: An omne aliud omnino Episcopatus genus tum abjuraretur, & in confessione damnetur. Aliud denique an nunc omne illud aliud Episcopatus genus removendum sit: Sed quicquid sit de unius sententia, plurium vicerunt calculi, quæstionique propositæ responderunt affirmative: hisce præsertim fundamentis nixi.
units.tr: Then the men designated by the Synod to draw out the true and genuine sense of certain articles of the Confession from the synodical registers and other public church records presented an account of their diligence in a longer writing, which had three parts. The first demonstrated the necessity of the work undertaken. The second contained a mass of synodical constitutions from 1576 to 1596, by which every kind of episcopacy seemed to be rejected. The third contained replies to certain objections by which some thought episcopacy was supported. When this writing had been read and examined, the Moderator thought fit to put the question of episcopacy to a vote. It was framed thus: whether, according to the Confession of Faith (first drawn up in 1580, universally received in 1581, and repeated in 1590), any bishop in this church was approved other than the pastor of a particular church or single flock, to whom no primacy [πρωτοδρία] and no power over colleagues belonged; and whether, according to the genuine sense of the Confession publicly received in those years, every other kind of episcopacy was renounced and therefore must now also be removed. All of them, with one exception, answered that every episcopacy whatsoever which differed from the pastor of a single flock had been renounced according to the sense of the Confession then received, and must now be eliminated from the church. But one man said episcopacy must be distinguished. There was the kind which some had then usurped against the will of the church, and to which alone the Hierarchists are wont to attach a perpetual spiritual pre-eminence and a primacy of dignity over the whole diocese, together with a power of ordination and jurisdiction in every respect. This episcopacy the Church had condemned and renounced in the Confession, and therefore it must be wholly removed from the church, as a Papist error unknown to Holy Scripture and to purer antiquity. But there was another episcopacy, the one the godly Fathers used in the primitive church, and which held its place at the beginning of the reformed religion in Scotland in the office of superintendent. To this office a certain primacy of order was granted, by the voluntary consent of the presbyters, and that of archbishops [ἀρχιεπισκόπων]. Although he did not think this should be revoked, he was hardly persuaded in his own mind that it had been renounced by that Confession. He said that the formal words of the synodical decree, drawn up at Dundee in 1580 and repeated at Glasgow in 1581, shed light on this distinction. For the phrase "the office of bishop, as bishops in this kingdom now use it" is repeated often. Since this is a clear determination of the subject, namely episcopacy, to that first kind of bishops by whom the church was then troubled, it could not be extended to every episcopacy simply considered in itself. To these points he added that only the episcopacy condemned by the constitutions of the said synods is damned: the kind that is not from God, that is illegitimate in itself, and that is an office to which bishops are not called by God. Moreover, from the very beginnings of the Reformation the opinion of the Scottish church was constant: the office of superintendent was not illegitimate in itself, and those who were duly called to that ministry by the churches were called by God. This is plain from the formula of ordination of superintendents prefixed to the Psalters. For the second-last question of that formula runs: "Do you acknowledge that the dignity of this office, to which God has called you, requires a holiness of life conspicuous even to the enemies of the Gospel?" By this answer it seemed to be hinted that the question proposed was not one question but one that divides itself into several parts, which they call polyzetēton [πολυζήτητον]. For it is one thing to ask whether any other bishop was then approved in the church than one who was the pastor of a single flock; another, whether every other kind of episcopacy was then renounced and condemned in the Confession; and finally, whether all that other kind of episcopacy is now to be removed. But whatever the view of this one man, the votes of the majority prevailed, and they answered the question proposed in the affirmative, relying especially on these grounds.
