units.la: Confessionis hujus optimum interpretem esse librum secundum de politia ecclesiastica, qui post doctissimorum virorum plurimos congressus, & disputationes publicas sæpius in synodis repetitas tandem unanimi omnium consensu comprobatus fuit in Synodo nationali Edenburgena ann. 1578. & publicis synodorum registris insertus, in synodo nationali Glasguensi ann. 1581. mandatumque ut omnes quotquot sint, aut erunt Ecclesiarum pastores eidem libro subscriberent, in synodis Edenburgensis, annor. 1590. & 1591. Atque in hoc libro Hierarchia tota Archiepiscoporum & episcoporum penitus damnatur, & gubernatio ecclesiæ per Sessiones, Presbyteria, Synodos sancitur. 2. Ex registris Nationalium constare dicunt, quod licet aliquandiu titulares illos Episcopos toleraret ecclesia, multorum tandem querelis anno 1575. de licentia & negligentia istorum Episcoporum vexatam ecclesiam, ac compulsam fuisse, altius despicere in ipsum quod tum sibi arripiebant episcopi officium, quos ecclesiæ oneri esse videbant, ac tum decrevisse nomen episcopi proprie competere omnibus pastoribus, quibus unius gregis cura commissa esset, monitosque fuisse titulares Episcopos ut unius gregis curam seriam susciperent; Et qui constitutioni huic non obtemperarent, ac peculiari gregi operam suam non addixissent, censura notatos fuisse Episcopos in synodo anni. 1560. Dein anno 1578. propositæ fuere quæ in titularibus istis Episcopis emendanda censuit Synodus, videl. 1. Quod unius peculiaris gregis curam non suscepissent. 2. Quod jurisdictionem criminalem & 3. Civilem exercuissent. 4. Ac ab ecclesiis non deputati suffragium ferrent in conventu ordinum regni: 5. Bonaque ecclesiastica, pastoribus ecclesiarum, pauperibus ac scholis alendis destinata ad se solos arriperent. 6. Quod fastuosos dignitatum temporalium titulos usurparent, ac se Dominos Lords salutari vellent. 7. Quod principatum in presbyteria. 8. Ac in Sessiones seu consistoria usurparent. Decretumque ut ab hisce corruptionibus sibi caverent, ac sponderent submissuros sese synodi nationalis judicio, si quae alia in Episcopatu emendanda censeret: Posthac cum nullis repagulis eorum licentiam coerceri posse cerneret Ecclesia, in nationali Synodo Taodunensi anni 1580. Sessione 4. radices & fibrae omnes Episcopatus illius penitus evelluntur, corruptionum quarundam ramis antehac excisis, & denuo pullulantibus: Decretum tum plenis omnium suffragiis, Episcoporum officium quo sensu vulgo tum accipiebatur, commentum esse humanum, magno ecclesiae detrimento introductum, nullam habere in scripturis S S. authoritatem, Itaque titulares Episcopi officium hoc statim deponerent, utpote ad quod a Deo vocati non essent: neque functionis ecclesiasticae munia quaelibet attingerent, nisi de novo ad pastoralis officii munus a Synodo Nationali promoverentur: idque sub poena excommunicationis. Ut libellus secundus de disciplina, qua hierarchia confoditur, Regi ac senatui offerretur confirmandus authoritate Senatus regii, donec in conventu ordinum lege sanciretur ad vigorem publicae obsequentiae. Eodemque anno, cum cognitum esset Episcopos Abredonensem & Moravienfem decreto huic Taodunensi sese nondum submisisse, statutum in synodo Edenburgena, ut contra eos & quoslibet jurisdi-
units.tr: The best interpreter of this Confession is the second book on ecclesiastical polity. After very many meetings of the most learned men, and public disputations repeatedly held in the synods, it was at last approved by the unanimous consent of all in the National Synod of Edinburgh in 1578 and inserted in the public synodical registers. In the National Synod of Glasgow in 1581 it was ordered that all who are or will be ministers of the churches should subscribe to this book, and this was repeated in the synods of Edinburgh of 1590 and 1591. In this book the whole hierarchy of archbishops and bishops is utterly condemned, and government of the church through sessions, presbyteries and synods is established. 2. They say the registers of the national synods show that, although the church had for some time tolerated those titular bishops, yet in 1575, after many complaints about the licence and negligence of those bishops, the church, troubled and under pressure, began to look more closely at the very office of bishop which they were then seizing and which they saw to be a burden to the church. It then decreed that the name of bishop properly belonged to all ministers to whom the care of a single flock was committed. The titular bishops were admonished to take up in earnest the care of a single flock, and those who did not obey this constitution and did not devote their labour to a particular flock were marked with censure as bishops in the synod of 1560. Then in 1578 the matters which the Synod judged to need correction in those titular bishops were put forward, namely: (1) that they had not taken up the care of a single flock; (2) that they had exercised criminal jurisdiction, and (3) civil; (4) that, not being appointed by the churches, they gave votes in the convention of the estates of the kingdom; (5) that they seized for themselves alone the ecclesiastical goods destined for the support of the ministers of the churches, the poor and the schools; (6) that they usurped proud titles of temporal dignities and wished to be greeted as Lords; (7) that they claimed a principality in the presbyteries; (8) and usurped it in the sessions or consistories. A decree was made that they should guard themselves against these corruptions, and promise to submit to the judgment of the National Synod if it judged anything else in episcopacy to need emendation. Afterwards, since the Church saw that their licence could not be restrained by any barriers, in the National Synod of Dundee of 1580, session 4, all the roots and fibres of that episcopacy were utterly torn up, the branches of corruption having been cut off before and sprouting again. The decree then passed with the full votes of all: the office of bishop, in the sense then commonly understood, was a human invention, introduced to the great detriment of the church, and had no authority in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore the titular bishops should at once lay down this office, as not being called to it by God, nor should they touch any ecclesiastical functions unless they were newly promoted by the National Synod to the pastoral ministry; and this under penalty of excommunication. The second book on discipline, by which the hierarchy is overthrown, was to be offered to the King and the Privy Council for confirmation by royal authority, until it was sanctioned by law in the convention of the estates for public obedience. In the same year, since it was known that the Bishops of Aberdeen and Moray had not yet submitted to this Dundee decree, it was decided in the Synod of Edinburgh that against them, and against anyone else who usurped that episcopal jurisdiction already condemned, the decree of the Synod of Dundee should simply be enforced.

units.la: ctionem illam Episcopalem jam damnatam usurpantes, Taodunensis synodi decretum simpliciter urgeretur: Quod anno sequenti 1581. in Synodo Glasguensi denuo repetitur, & explicatur: quando etiam Diagramma omnium presbyteriorum seu Classium, simul cum secundo libro politiæ ecclesiasticæ registris synodicis inseruntur, cui immediate nulla interveniente linea subjungitur, ut Confessioni minori, (quæ vulgo Confessio familiæ regiæ vocatur) omnes subscriberent: Ut itaque ex hoc constare dicunt; disciplinam ecclesiæ quam omnium chirographis & juramento obsignari jussit Synodus, fuisse illam quæ libro secundo politiæ continetur, non vero regimen Hierarchicum tum explosum. Ac ne quis in re tam perspicua hæsitet, considerandum quomodo cum iis actum, qui Episcopatum erigere studuerunt; etenim cum anno 1581. spargeretur, Robertum Montgomerium, relicta Sterlinensi ecclesia ambivisse Episcopatum Glasguensem, ac docuisse omnem ecclesiæ disciplinam mutabilem esse, & inter ἀδιαφόρα referendam; gravi censura à Synodo Edenburgena notatus fuit, cumque serio eum admonuisset, ac sub pœnâ excommunicationis eidē interdixisset, ne Episcopatum Glasguensem attingeret; quia ille spreta ecclesiæ authoritate pro Episcopo se gessisset, fretus se aulicorū quorundam gratia ecclesiæ Censuras evasurum: sententia Synodi nationalis Andreapoli 1582. coactæ excommunicandus declaratur, nisi statim pœnitentiam profiteretur: ac Episcopatu relicto, ad suam ecclesiam protinus rediret: quæ licet in se tum recepisset, ad vomitum tamen post rediit; & non obstante intercessione Senatus regii, excommunicatur, Synodusque per deputatos suos regi, regiisque senatoribus necessarii hujus consilii rationes profert: Ac licet densa caligine ecclesiæ facies annis aliquot succesdentidentibus oppressa fuerit, ambitione Adamsoni & Montgomeri, tandem tamen discussis tenebris ad pristinam politiam rediit Ecclesia: ac in synodo nationali anni 1586. unanimi consensu declaratur nomen Episcopi omnibus verbi pastoribus esse commune, ac 1587. denuo Pfeudo-Archiepiscopis Adamfono & Montgomerio litem contestatur ecclefia; quibus omni ecclesiastico munere interdicit, ac in literis ad regem, officium illud Episcoporum, ad quod Robertum Pontanum, vel invitum evehere satagebant aulici, non esse verbo Dei consentaneum, ac frequentibus ecclesiæ decretis jam inde à profligato papifmo damnatum declarat: deputatis ecclefiarum in mandatis datum, ut summa diligentia caverent ne quid sanciretur in comitiis regni, quod disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ, prout ante annum 1584. recepta fuit, præjudicaret. Anno 1590. Decretum, ut pastores omnes & quotquot ad Ecclesiasticum quodvis munus evehendi effent, libro fecundo politiæ subscriberent, præsertim vero capitibus controverfis, illis videl. de rejectione Episcopatus, & approbatione presbyteriorum; quod denuo repetitur in synodo anni 1591. Denique in synodo anni 1592. deputatis synodi mandatum, ut ecclesiarum nomine instarent inductioni & abolitioni statutorum, quibus ecclesiæ disciplina mutata fuit, præsertim vero statuti anni 1584. quo restitutio Episcoporum in comitiis sanciebatur, ac ferio urgerent Confirmationem Disciplinæ in libris politiæ sæpius approbatæ, & ubique receptæ. Quæ omnia à rege & regni ordinibus obtinuerunt; quorum publica authoritate regimen ecclesiæ per conventus Synodorum nationalium, Provincialium, Classicalium, & Sessionum sancitur, ac statuta quælibet præcedentia quæ huic disciplinæ contraria sunt, refiguntur, præsertim vero illud anni 1584. Neque sic contentum fuisse Serenis. Regem, quin ultra procederet, & statutum illud, Θεὸν[?] verè βασιλικὸν[?] ad synodum nationalem quae anno 1595 cogebatur, miserit, quod hodie inter archiva ecclesiae relatum esse cernitur; Ex his, inquiunt, excerptis quivis facile colliget, quae fuerit sententia ecclesiae Scoticae circa Episcopatum.
units.tr: ...jurisdiction, already condemned, and to press simply the decree of the Synod of Dundee against them and against anyone else who usurped that episcopal authority. This was repeated and explained in the following year, 1581, at the Synod of Glasgow. There the diagram of all the presbyteries or classes was entered in the synodal registers together with the second book of the Polity, and immediately beneath it, with no line intervening, was added the signature line, as for the Shorter Confession (commonly called the Confession of the royal household), so that all should subscribe. From this, they say, it is clear that the discipline which the Synod ordered to be confirmed by everyone's signature and oath was the one contained in the second book of the Polity, and not the hierarchical government, which had by then been driven out. Lest anyone hesitate over so plain a matter, consider how those were dealt with who had tried to set up an episcopate. In 1581 it was rumoured that Robert Montgomery, having left the church of Stirling, aspired to the bishopric of Glasgow and taught that all church discipline is changeable and to be counted among the things indifferent [ἀδιαφόρα]. The Synod of Edinburgh censured him severely, and after earnestly admonishing him and forbidding him, under pain of excommunication, to lay hold of the bishopric of Glasgow, he nevertheless, despising the authority of the Church and acting as a bishop, relying on the favour of certain courtiers to escape the Church's censures, was declared by the sentence of the National Synod at St Andrews in 1582 to be excommunicated unless he at once professed repentance and returned forthwith to his own church. Although he accepted this for the time being, he returned to his vomit, and despite the intercession of the royal Senate he was excommunicated. The Synod, through its deputies, set out to the king and the royal senators the reasons for this necessary decision. And although for some years the face of the Church was oppressed by thick darkness through the ambition of Adamson and Montgomery, at length the darkness was dispelled and the Church returned to its former polity. In the National Synod of 1586 it was declared by unanimous consent that the title of bishop is common to all ministers of the Word. In 1587 the Church again brought suit against the pseudo-archbishops Adamson and Montgomery, forbidding them every ecclesiastical office. In letters to the king it declared that the office of bishop, to which the courtiers strove to raise Robert Pont, even against his will, is not consonant with the Word of God, and that it had been condemned from the time of the overthrow of Popery by frequent decrees of the Church. The deputies of the churches were instructed to take the greatest care that nothing be enacted in the assemblies of the realm to prejudice the discipline of the Church as it had been received before the year 1584. In 1590 a decree was passed that all ministers, and all who were to be promoted to any ecclesiastical office, should subscribe the second book of the Polity, especially the controverted chapters, namely those on the rejection of episcopacy and the approval of presbyteries. This was repeated again in the synod of 1591. Finally, in the synod of 1592 the deputies of the synod were ordered to press, in the name of the churches, for the repeal and abolition of the statutes by which the discipline of the Church had been altered, especially the statute of 1584 by which the restoration of bishops was sanctioned in the assemblies, and they were to urge earnestly the confirmation of the discipline often approved in the books of the Polity and received everywhere. All these things were obtained from the king and the estates of the realm, by whose public authority the government of the Church through the assemblies of the National, Provincial, Classical and Session courts is sanctioned, and all earlier statutes contrary to this discipline are annulled, especially that of 1584. Nor was the Most Serene King content with this, but went further, and sent to the National Synod which met in 1595 that statute, a divine and truly royal [θεῖον, βασιλικόν] enactment, which is today seen to be recorded among the archives of the Church. From these extracts, they say, anyone may easily gather what was the opinion of the Scottish Church concerning episcopacy.

units.la: Denique inquiunt; Confessionis hujus verba suo lumine satis perspicua sunt: Detestamur Pontificem Romanum, Antichristum: mundanam ipsius monarchiam, & impiam Hierarchiam: Porro hierarchia haec impia vel, judicio Conciliabuli Tridentini declaratur consistere praecipue ex Episcopis; De Sacramento ordinis. cap. 4. Canon. 6. Idem expresse Bellarminus lib. 7. De clericis. cap. 11. Tres, inquit, sunt Hierarchiae in ecclesia militante, prima pontificum id est, episcoporum, secunda Sacerdotum, tertia, Diaconorum; Atque hi Diaconi licet comparati, ad sacerdotes, sint ministri, ad plebem tamen comparati sunt principes & praesules: Bellarminum vero cum nomino, aut Synodum istam Tridentinam, omnium omnino pontificiorum hanc esse sententiam intelligi volo, nam utcunque in gradibus quibusdam ordinum Hierarchiae Ecclesiasticae diffentiant: omnes tamen conveniunt, Episcopatum ad hierarchiam praecipue referri: Et si Theologis Parisiensibus credendum, pontifex Romanus, Cardinales, Patriarchae, Primates, Archiepiscopi, intra Hierarchiae ambitum censendi non sunt, nisi quatenus sunt Episcopi: In censura propositionum quarundam ex Hibernia delatarum per sacram facultatem Theologiae Parisiensis facta. Quo etiam collimarunt Confessionis hujus authores; nam Hierarchiam, cujus caput est Episcopatus, a Mundana Papae monarchia dilucide distinguentes, innuunt damnari a se hierarchiam papalem, licet absit papalis monarchia: imo omnem illam Episcopatus hierarchiam (licet Papæ tanquam capiti non subordinetur) impiam dicit Confessio, epitheto perpetuo non ἀκεφάλῳ [?] proprietatis non discretionis; pontificisque Romani esse dicitur; licet apud ecclesias quasdam prævaluerit ante plenam & perfectam papatus tyrannidem; etenim corruptiones omnes, quibus doctrina, cultus, aut regimen ecclesiarum vitiata fuerunt, à quo mysterium illud iniquitatis operari cœpit, quæ nunc à Papa retinentur, & pro quibus dimicat, merito ad Papatum referuntur.
units.tr: Finally, they say: the words of this Confession are clear enough in their own light: "We detest the Roman Pontiff as Antichrist, his worldly monarchy, and his impious hierarchy." Moreover, this impious hierarchy is declared, by the judgement of the Council of Trent, to consist chiefly of bishops (On the Sacrament of Order, chapter 4, canon 6). Bellarmine expressly says the same in book 7 of On Clerics, chapter 11: "There are three hierarchies in the militant Church: the first of pontiffs, that is, bishops; the second of priests; the third of deacons." And although these deacons, compared with priests, are ministers, compared with the people they are nonetheless princes and presidents. But when I name Bellarmine, or that Council of Trent, I wish it to be understood that this is the opinion of all Papists without exception; for although they differ in certain grades of the orders of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, yet they all agree that episcopacy is chiefly to be referred to the hierarchy. And if the Parisian theologians are to be believed, the Roman pontiff, cardinals, patriarchs, primates and archbishops are not to be counted within the compass of the hierarchy, except insofar as they are bishops (in the censure of certain propositions brought from Ireland, made by the sacred faculty of theology of Paris). The authors of this Confession aimed at the same thing. For in distinguishing clearly the hierarchy, of which episcopacy is the head, from the worldly monarchy of the Pope, they hint that the papal hierarchy is condemned by them, even though the papal monarchy is not in view. Indeed the Confession calls every hierarchy of episcopacy impious (although it is not subordinate to the Pope as its head), using the perpetual epithet "headless" [ἀκεφάλῳ], a designation of its character, not of its distinction; and it is said to belong to the Roman pontiff, although it prevailed in certain churches before the full and perfect tyranny of the papacy. For all the corruptions by which the doctrine, worship or government of the churches were vitiated, from the time when that mystery of iniquity began to work, which are now retained by the Pope and for which he contends, are rightly referred to the Papacy.

units.la: Fulcris hisce præcipue nitebatur Synodi sententia, uti latius in Canonibus impressis deducuntur: verum antequam ultra progrediar, discutienda sunt ab Episcopis objecta, in libello quem nomine deputati regii tum protruserunt, quo omnibus persuadere satagunt, Episcopatum nec abjuratum fuisse in confessionis prima obsignatione ann. 1580, nec statuto Senatus regii ad 22. Sept. 1638. quo ab omnibus obsignari confessionem hanc denuo imperatur cum clausula illa explicatoria; secundum tenorem ac sensum & publicam professionem, quæ in regno Scotiæ vigebat anno 1580. Prima ratio hæc est. Absit ut cujusvis mentem subeat, Regem aut senatum regium quemlibet velle adigere in juramentum illicitum: Atqui si adegissent in abjurationem Episcopatus, illicitum imperassent, utpote quod Apostolicæ sit institutionis, sanciunturque frequentibus parlamenti legibus, (quæ ad calcem tractatus subjiciuntur) & Canonibus Synodicis. Respondit Synodus: Gratis fine ulla probationis specie asseri Episcopatum Diœcesanum, aut quemlibet primatum perpetuum unius supra reliquos verbi presbyteros, esse Apostolicæ institutionis: Etenim, nihil in sacra scriptura, cui soli fides Christiana firmiter inniti potest, extat, quo probari possit regimen hoc Episcopale ecclesiis traditum; Et quod ad traditiones non scriptas Apostolis affictas attinet, quid ad eos qui reformatis ecclesiis nomina sua dederunt ? Nam præterquam quod patenti hac traditionum non scriptarum porta semel aperta, pontificiis tutum asylum præberetur ; & scripturæ sufficientia in quæstionem vocaretur, quibus quæso argumentis fidem facis hoc tradidisse Apostolos ? Antiquitatem, visibilem perdurationem, perpetuam successionem, unanimem patrum consensum, universæ ecclesiæ præxin, concilliorum authoritatem, uti non repudiant Reformatæ ecclesiæ doctores, ita media esse incerta, fallibilia, invictis argumentis solide demonstrarunt, & in di-gressione de dissimilitudine veterum episcoporum ab hodiernis, vere de episcopatu controversio hæc non posse affirmari, supra ostensum. Sed in materia facti fidem saltem habendam esse probatorum hi-storicorum testimonio: qui omnes seriem episcopo-rum ab apostolis ad sua tempora deducunt: Et cur eadem fides non habetur iisdem historicis fabulosa multa narrantibus, & Apostolis apostolorumque ævo ascribentibus ?v. g. de certamine Petri cum Simone mago, de Monachis, de Petri episcopatu Romano, de Petri adventu Romam, & similibus: Dein quam incerta sunt media illa quibus historici pervenerunt ad cognitionem rerum ab Apostolis aut viris Apostolicis gestarum: audita & fama recepta narrant. An vero famæ credat nisi inconsideratus ? Et Eusebius qui historicorum princeps merito audit, propter rerum antiquarum obscuritatem quæ profundis fere tenebris demersæ jacebant, veniam præfari cogitur in histor. suae proœmio. Nam & primi (inquit) argumentum hoc jam aggressi sumus, ac velut deserta quandam & inusitatam viam ingredi conamur, ubi nusquam nobis nuda eorum hominum vestigia deprehendere licet, qui eandem hanc sint ante nos viam ingressi, nisi exi-guas duntaxat occasiones. Denique attento lectori quam perspectissimum erit, sui sæculi morem præsentem nebulas illis offudisse, & errore eo quasi torrente abreptos, priora sæcula ad præsentis sui pedem metiri solitos fuisse, uniusque exemplum cæteros fere re ἀβασιλευτὸς[?] imitari. Quod de legibus regni parlamentariis & Synodorum Canonibus pro Episcopatu affertur, suo loco respondebitur. Secunda ratio pro Episcopatu hisce continetur. Non potest absolute abjurari illud quod est mutabile, hoc enim esset conscientiis laqueum & miserrimum servitutis jugum imponere. Atqui Episcopatus est mutabilis, nam pertinet ad disciplinam & regimen ecclesiæ, quæ ad ecclesiæ arbitrium mutationi obnoxia esse declarat articulus 20. & 21. majores confessionis fidei ecclesiæ Scotiæ: quare licet largiatur Episcopatum à majoribus anno 1580. abjuratum fuisse quando in disciplinam ecclesiæ jurarunt, unde tum exulabat Episcopatus, id tamen non aliter intelligendum est, quam si ecclesiæ non visum fuerit disciplinam illam mutare, & exemplo illustratur regis coronandi, qui licet juret se populum gubernaturum secundum leges regni, per hoc tamen non stat quin leges illæ mutari possint: Sic abjurarunt majores episcopatum, quamdiu videl: ecclesia judicatura esset eum non sibi fore utilem. Respondit Synodus. Male convenire secundam hanc rationem primæ, & sententiæ Episcoporum in protestatione contra Synodum. Prima ratio dicit Episcopatum esse institutionis Apostolicæ, Episcopi dixerunt esse necessarium, & sibi à Christo commissam esse potestatem in Clerum: Nunc vero dicunt esse mutabilem, & si verbis citatorum articulorum ex confessione præcise adhærere velint, inter ceremonias reponent, ab hominibus excogitatas, quæ pro loco & tempore mutabiles sunt, & mutari debent cum fovendæ superstitioni magis inserviant, quam ecclefiæ ædificandæ: Adversis frontibus hæc prudentioribus concurrere, ac uti. Cadmæa proles mutuo sese perimere videntur. Nam si Episcopatus à Christo institutus, ab Apostolis ecclesiis traditus, & necessarius sit, quomodo referri poterit in censum ceremoniarum ab hominibus pro tempore & loco excogitatarum, & mutabilium? Ad illud vero de mutabilitate disciplinæ & regiminis ecclesiæ, sufe supra responsum à præside synodi, in disputatione contra D. Balcanquellum sessione 7. videl: intelligendum esse articulum de Disciplinæ ac regiminis accidentalibus non essentialibus, de disciplina particulari, non universali; illam enim licet mutabilem statuat Confessio, hanc tamen immobilem declarat, utpote quod tertiam veræ visibilis ecclesiæ notam faciat articul. 19. Confessionis fidei & libro primo de disciplina ab iisdem authoribus formato qui Confessionis authores fuerant, dicitur regimen ecclesiæ per quatuor genera ministrorum, pastores, doctores, presbyteros seu seniores & Diaconos in sacra scriptura traditum esse, ideoque perpetuum ac mutationi non obnoxiū. Nam quod præcipitur (inquit Tertullian.) imperatur quod imperatur necesse est fieri. Ad illud vero Tertulliani ejusdē lib.de veladis virginibus cap. 1. Regula fidei, quæ una omnino est, sola immobilis & irreformabilis, manente, cætera disciplinę & conversationis, admittunt novitatem correctionis, operante scil. & perficiente usque in finem gratia Dei, quem solum locum citat fani Andreæ Archiepiscopus, in refutatione libelli de regimine ecclesiæ Scoticanæ. pag. 37. Responderi potest; Dogma illud Tertulliani prorsus Montanısmum sapere, nam eodem capite ad finem, Montanısmi primarium caput exerte proponit, quuin liberiorem & majorem Dei gratiam somniat subsequentibus sæculis, quam quæ temporibus Apostolorum effusa erat; & comparat ecclesiam Apostolicam arbori germinanti, quæ per adventum paracleti, hoc est, Montani, ad maturitatem perducenda erat. Sed quid pluribus argumentis regiminis ac disciplinæ immutabilitatem astruimus? en Hierarchici regiminis acerrimum propugnatorem Saraviam idem diserte affirmantem contra Bezam.
units.tr: The Synod's judgment rested chiefly on these supports, as is set out more fully in the printed Canons. But before I go further, I must examine the objections the Bishops raised in the little book they then put forward in the name of the royal commissioners. In it they try to persuade everyone that episcopacy was neither renounced in the first subscription of the Confession in the year 1580, nor in the royal Act of the Senate of 22 September 1638, by which all are again commanded to subscribe this Confession, with that explanatory clause: "according to the tenor and sense of the public profession which was in force in the kingdom of Scotland in the year 1580." The first argument is this. Far be it from anyone's mind that the King or any member of the royal Senate should wish to bind anyone to an unlawful oath. But if they had bound men to renounce episcopacy, they would have commanded something unlawful, since it is of apostolic institution, and it is sanctioned by frequent acts of parliament (which are appended at the end of the treatise) and by synodal canons. The Synod replied: it is asserted gratuitously, without any show of proof, that diocesan episcopacy, or any perpetual primacy of one presbyter over the rest, is of apostolic institution. For nothing is found in Holy Scripture, on which alone Christian faith can firmly rest, by which it can be proved that this episcopal government was handed down to the churches. And as for the unwritten traditions supposedly delivered by the Apostles, what has that to do with those who have given their names to the reformed churches? For, besides the fact that once this gate of unwritten traditions was thrown wide open a safe refuge would be offered to the Papists, and the sufficiency of Scripture would be called into question, by what arguments, I ask, will you make it believable that the Apostles handed this down? Antiquity, visible continuance, perpetual succession, the unanimous consent of the Fathers, the practice of the whole Church, and the authority of councils: the teachers of the reformed churches do not reject these, but have solidly demonstrated by unanswerable arguments that these means are uncertain and fallible; and in the digression on the unlikeness of the ancient bishops to the present ones, it was shown above that this controversy cannot truly be about episcopacy. But in a matter of fact, they say, credit must at least be given to the testimony of approved historians, who all trace the succession of bishops from the Apostles down to their own times. Why, then, is the same credit not given to the same historians, who narrate many fabulous things and ascribe them to the Apostles and the age of the Apostles, for example the contest of Peter with Simon Magus, the monks, Peter's episcopate at Rome, Peter's coming to Rome, and similar things? Then, how uncertain are those means by which historians came to know the things done by the Apostles or Apostolic men: they relate things heard and received by report. Would anyone but the thoughtless believe report? And Eusebius, who is rightly called the prince of historians, is obliged to beg pardon in the preface to his history, because of the obscurity of ancient things, which lay sunk in almost deep darkness. For he says: "We are the first to have undertaken this subject, and we attempt to enter, as it were, upon a deserted and unusual road, where nowhere can we find the bare footprints of those men who entered this way before us, except for a few slight hints." Finally, it will be most plainly evident to the attentive reader that the custom of his own age cast those mists over them, and that, carried off by this error as by a torrent, men have been accustomed to measure earlier centuries by the foot of their own present, and that almost all the rest imitate one example in the matter of being without a king [ἀβασιλευτός]. What is alleged for episcopacy from the parliamentary laws of the kingdom and the canons of synods will be answered in its place. The second argument for episcopacy is contained here. That which is mutable cannot be absolutely renounced, for this would lay a snare on consciences and the most wretched yoke of slavery. But episcopacy is mutable, for it pertains to the discipline and government of the Church, which Articles 20 and 21 of the greater Confession of faith of the Church of Scotland declare to be subject to change at the Church's discretion. Hence, even if it is granted that our forefathers renounced episcopacy in 1580, when they swore to the discipline of the Church, from which episcopacy was then excluded, this must nevertheless be understood only to mean that the Church did not then see fit to change that discipline; and the example of a king at his coronation illustrates this: although he swears that he will govern the people according to the laws of the kingdom, this does not prevent those laws from being changed. So our forefathers renounced episcopacy only for as long as the Church judged that it would not be useful to it. The Synod replied: this second argument does ill agree with the first, and with the bishops' statement in their protest against the Synod. The first argument says that episcopacy is of apostolic institution; the bishops said that it is necessary, and that power over the clergy was committed to them by Christ. Now they say it is mutable; and if they wish to cling strictly to the words of the cited articles of the Confession, they will place it among the ceremonies devised by men, which are mutable according to place and time, and ought to be changed since they serve to foster superstition rather than to build up the Church. These positions, so contrary to one another, are being put forward by these men of prudence, and they seem, like the Cadmean brood, to slay one another. For if episcopacy was instituted by Christ, handed down to the churches by the Apostles, and is necessary, how can it be reckoned among the ceremonies devised by men according to time and place, and mutable? As to what concerns the mutability of the discipline and government of the Church, it was answered above by the president of the Synod, in the disputation against Doctor Balcanqual, in the seventh session: the article must be understood of the accidental, not the essential, features of discipline and government, of particular discipline, not universal. For although the Confession declares the former to be mutable, it declares the latter immovable, since it makes it the third mark of the true visible Church (Article 19 of the Confession of faith); and in the first book of discipline, drawn up by the same authors who wrote the Confession, it is said that the government of the Church, as handed down in Holy Scripture, consists of four kinds of ministers: pastors, teachers, elders or seniors, and deacons, and is therefore perpetual and not subject to change. For, as Tertullian says, "what is commanded must necessarily be done." As to that passage of Tertullian in his book On the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 1: "The rule of faith, which alone is entirely one, alone immovable and unalterable, admits novelty of correction in the remaining things of discipline and conduct, the grace of God working and perfecting them even to the end," which the Archbishop of St Andrews alone cites in his refutation of the book on the government of the Scottish Church, p. 37. It can be answered that this dogma of Tertullian savours wholly of Montanism, for in the same chapter, near the end, he openly sets forth the chief point of Montanism, when he dreams of a freer and greater grace of God in later ages than that which was poured out in the times of the Apostles; and he compares the Apostolic Church to a germinating tree, which was to be brought to maturity by the coming of the Paraclete, that is, of Montanus. But why do we assert the immutability of government and discipline with more arguments? Behold the fiercest champion of hierarchical government, Saravia, affirming the same thing expressly against Beza.

units.la: Vt demus, (inquit) quicquid Deus constituit, non ea forte conditione ut perpetuum esset, tamen ea gubernationis ratio, quæ ætate Apostolorum fuit, ea conditione constituta est, ut perpetua esset. Idem alibi. Institutum Apostolorum de regimine ecclesiastico mutari non potest, ut decretum Dei de sacerdotio Aaronico mutari non potuit. Quo etiam telo confoditur ecclesiastico-politicorum dogma, Conformandum videlicet esse regimen ecclesiasticorum politico; quasi alia esset regiminis ecclesiastici ratio instituenda sub Monarchico regimine, quam sub Aristocratico aut Democratico, ac magistratui ecclesiæ administratio ita commissa esset, ut liceat ipsi disciplinam pro arbitratu suo mutare, & quem statui ipsorum præsenti maxime expedire putaverit, obtrudere: Non sic visum Whitakero controvers. 4. quæst. 1. cap. 9. Tot (inquit) possunt esse humanarum πολιτείων [?] formæ, quot ipsi homines voluerint, sed ecclesia regi debet non ut humano ingenio arriserit, sed ut Christo ecclesiæ Domino solique principi placet: quam ergo Christus formam instituit, ea servari atque optima judicari debet, & inepte faciunt qui ex Philosophorum sententiis, aut humano judicio statuunt, quam formam regendæ ecclesiæ Christus præscripserit, qui politias non præscripsit. Et Matthæus Sutclivius de pontifice Roman. lib. 1. cap. 1. dum convellit argumentum illud Bellarmini pro Monarchia ecclesiastica desumptum à Monarchia civili, quasi videlicet una & eadem utriusque esset ratio, sic loquitur: Sicut unus est ecclesiæ summus princeps Iesus Christus, sic una est ecclesiæ vera & essentialis forma: At rerum publicarum ut varij sunt magistratus sic variæ reperiuntur formæ, nam hæc à rege, illa ab optimatibus, alia à potentioribus & locupletioribus de populo regitur: omnesque istæ formæ bonæ sunt. At secus fit in ecclesia: nam & unus est summus ecclesiæ Rex, & una est ecclesiasticæ politiæ ratio, à qua qui discedunt, in labem gubernationis incidunt, & Christi leges transgrediuntur. Deniquè uti doctissimus Feildus de eccl. lib. 5. cap. 45. sub initium arguit contra Papæ potestatem in temporalibus, sic hic. Nemo hominum immutandi rem aliquam, potestatem habet, nisi ille tantummodo cui, gradu eminenti inest, & à quo illa originaliter derivatur. Hæc ille. Atqui regimen ecclesiasticum qua tale, magistratui non inest eminenter, neque ab eo originaliter dependet: nam utrumque regimen à Deo authoritatis suæ originem trahit, & neutrum ab altero in proprii muneris functione dependet, ac distinguuntur ratione formalis objecti, modo agendi, finibus, ita ut fine confusione in unam personam coalescere non possint: unde illud Ambrosii epistol. 33. ad Valentinianum Imperatorem. Noli te gravare imperator, ut putes in ea quæ divina sunt, aliquod imperiale jus habere, politicorum tibi minorum [?] quis commissum [?] est non sacrorum. Ergo regimen ecclesiasticum quod essentiale est, à magistratu immutari non potest: Addo quod essentiale est, nam in politia ecclesiæ externa quatenus spectat adiaphora, magistratui Christiano supremam potestatem cum omnibus reformatis lubenter tribuimus: At vero in rebus necessariis & perpetuis Christum solum ecclesiæ principem agnoscimus. Neque est quod quispiam calumniam collateralitatis hic objiciat, quasi in una republica duas potestates pariter authenticas, hoc est civile, & ecclesiasticum sententiæ hujus fautores ponerent: Nam ut gubernationes vere sint collaterales hæc inprimis necessario requiruntur, quæ hic deprehendi non possunt. 1. Ut eodem eminentiæ gradu utrumque regimen Deo subsit: Politicum vero subordinatur Deo instar Dominatus, ecclesiasticum est tantum famulitium, & simplex ministeriū inferius subjectum : uti loquitur Rollocus Edenburgenæ ecclesiæ pastor & professor ὁμολογείμς[?] in 1. Thessal. 5. 12. 13. 2. ut parem[?] potestatem vice versa in se invicem habeant: ecclesiastica potestas rebus ad politicam potestatem pertinentibus se non immiscet, & si officio suo desit, non potest contra eam, nisi via monitionis procedere, docet solum, suadet, monet, rogat. At potestas politica Christiani magistratus se extendit ad externum ecclesiæ regimen quoad indifferentia & mutabilia, & si deviet potestas ecclesiastica, coactiva vi instruitur. 3. Ut æquali potentia populum sibi concreditum moderentur : potestas ecclesiastica verbo aberrantes oves arcet, & recolligit, persuadendo servit hominibus qui Christo se submiserunt: Politica vero ubi facinorosos legibus subjectos tenuerit, magnam quam obtinet, declarat potestatem, & invitos cogit recedere à perversis suis moribus, cogendo dominatur. Atque hæc ad rationem secundam, qua ostenditur Episcopatum inter mutabilia disciplinæ non fuisse agnitam ab ecclesia Scotica, neque disciplinam omnem mutabilem esse, nec pro arbitrio principis supremi policiti in essentialibus mutari posse, aut ad idæam politici regiminis conformari. Si cui duriora hæc videbuntur, ac calumniis imminutæ majestatis regum arcessat, quasi hujus sententiæ fautores desertis hic reformatis in Iesuitarum castra transfugerent ; (prout non puduit maledicum rabulam inter plaustra illa convitiorum & nequissimarum calumniarum, quibus afflictam ecclesiam Scoticâ frustra onerare satagit, in putido isto famoso libello, quem obstetricantibus furiis non ita pridem extrusit, sub titulo fictitiæ epistolæ con-gratugratuloriæ Lysimachi Nicanoris Iesuitæ ad fœderatos Scotos, quos nebulo mentitur difficiles illas tempestates cum quibus adhuc conflictantur, subiisse, ut excusso legitimi regiminis jugo, cui lubentes parent, Iesuitismum promoverent, quem persecto odio abominantur, ) si, inquam, cuiquam propositum in sententiam hanc debacchari; meminerit in Saraviam, Sutclivium, Feildum, ac Whitakerum, ut alios non nominem, omnem prius iracundiam effundere, qui hanc eandem sententiam jampridem cum laude propugnarunt, in hos quibuscunque velit, convitiis ac contumeliis se exsatiet, & si mortui non possunt, vivi saltem remordebunt, neque patientur orthodoxum dogma impune à scurris traduci.
units.tr: Grant, he says, that whatever God has ordained was not perhaps established on the condition that it should be perpetual; nevertheless, that form of government which existed in the age of the Apostles was established on the condition that it should be perpetual. He says the same elsewhere: The Apostles' institution concerning ecclesiastical government cannot be changed, just as God's decree concerning the Aaronic priesthood could not be changed. This is also the weapon with which the ecclesiastical-political doctrine is pierced, namely that the government of the Church must be conformed to the civil government. As though the rule of ecclesiastical government were one thing under a monarchy and another under an aristocracy or a democracy, and the administration of the Church had been committed to the magistrate in such a way that he may change the discipline as he pleases and impose on the Church whatever he thinks most expedient for his own state at the time. Whitaker did not see it this way, in his Controversies, book 4, question 1, chapter 9: "There may be as many forms of human commonwealths," he says, "as men themselves wish; but the Church must be governed not as human wit pleases, but as pleases Christ, the Lord of the Church and the sole prince. Therefore the form that Christ instituted is what must be kept and judged best. Those who decide from the opinions of philosophers, or from human judgment, which form of governing the Church Christ has prescribed, act foolishly, since Christ did not prescribe the forms of commonwealths." Matthew Sutcliffe too, in his book on the Roman pontiff, book 1, chapter 1, while he overthrows Bellarmine's argument for ecclesiastical monarchy, taken from civil monarchy, as though the reason for each were one and the same, speaks thus: "As Jesus Christ is the one supreme prince of the Church, so there is one true and essential form of the Church. But the forms of commonwealths are various, as the magistracies are various: for one is ruled by a king, another by the nobles, another by the more powerful and wealthy of the people; and all these forms are good. It is otherwise in the Church: for there is both one supreme King of the Church and one rule of ecclesiastical polity, and those who depart from it fall into the ruin of government and transgress Christ's laws." Finally, as the very learned Field argues against the power of the Pope in temporal matters in his book 5 On the Church, chapter 45, near the beginning, so here: "No man has the power to change any thing unless he alone has it, who holds an eminent degree and from whom that power is originally derived." Thus far Field. But ecclesiastical government, as such, does not inhere eminently in the magistrate, nor does it depend originally on him. For each government draws the origin of its authority from God, and neither depends on the other in the discharge of its proper office. They are distinguished by the formal object, the manner of acting and the ends, so that they cannot coalesce into one person without confusion. Hence that saying of Ambrose in Epistle 33 to the Emperor Valentinian: Do not trouble yourself, emperor, to think that you have any imperial right in things divine; the civil things committed to you are the lesser ones, not the sacred. Therefore ecclesiastical government, which is essential, cannot be changed by the magistrate. I add "which is essential," for in the external polity of the Church, so far as it concerns things indifferent, we gladly grant supreme power to the Christian magistrate, together with all the reformed. But in necessary and perpetual matters we acknowledge Christ alone as the prince of the Church. Nor is there reason for anyone to object here the charge of collateral power, as though the supporters of this opinion placed two equally authentic powers in one commonwealth, the civil and the ecclesiastical. For in order that the governments be truly collateral, the following are especially required, and they cannot be found here: (1) that both governments be subject to God at the same degree of eminence. But the civil power is subordinate to God as a lord, while the ecclesiastical is only a service and a simple ministry, lower and subject; as Rollock, minister of the Edinburgh church and professor of divinity, puts it in his commentary on 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13. (2) That they have equal power in turn over one another: ecclesiastical power does not meddle with matters that belong to civil power, and if it fails in its duty, it cannot proceed against it except by way of admonition; it only teaches, persuades, warns and asks. But the civil power of the Christian magistrate extends to the external government of the Church in indifferent and changeable matters, and if the ecclesiastical power goes astray, it is armed with coercive force. (3) That they govern the people entrusted to them with equal power: ecclesiastical power keeps off wandering sheep by the word and gathers them back, serving men who have submitted to Christ by persuading them; but the civil power, when it has held the wicked subject to the laws, displays the great power it possesses, and compels the unwilling to withdraw from their perverse ways, ruling by compulsion. And this is enough for the second reason, by which it is shown that episcopacy was not acknowledged by the Scottish Church as among the changeable matters of discipline, nor is all discipline changeable, nor can it be changed at the will of the supreme civil prince in essentials, or conformed to the idea of civil government. If these harsher points seem hard to anyone, and he summons slanders against the majesty of kings, as though the supporters of this opinion were defecting from the reformed to the camp of the Jesuits, (as the slanderous hack was not ashamed, among those carts of abuse and most wicked calumnies with which he vainly labours to burden the afflicted Scottish Church, in that stinking, infamous little book which he lately thrust out with the furies as midwives, under the title of a fictitious letter of congratulation from the Jesuit Lysimachus Nicanor to the Scottish Covenanters, whom the wretch falsely says have undergone those difficult storms with which they still struggle, so that, having shaken off the yoke of lawful government, which they gladly obey, they might promote Jesuitism, which they utterly abhor): if, I say, anyone is inclined to rage at this opinion, let him remember that before he pours out all his anger on Saravia, Sutcliffe, Field and Whitaker, not to name others, who have long since defended this same opinion with praise, he may glut himself with insults and abuse against them as he wishes; and if the dead cannot answer, the living will at least bite back, and they will not allow the orthodox doctrine to be dragged through the mud by buffoons with impunity.

units.la: Tertia ratio qua probaturEpiscopatum in fœdere & confessione non abjuratũ fuisse, hæc est: Quia ipsi fœderati in disputationibus cum Abredonensibus hoc fassi sunt; & inter alias rationes quibus dissuadebant subscriptionem fœderis à rege imperati, hanc allegabant, quod Regi subscriptione istius fœderis propositum esset Episcopatum tueri. Respond. Licet in disputationibus illis negaverint expresse & specifice abjuratum fuisse Episcopatum in posterior fœderis parte, quæ continet applicationem ad præsentia tempora: Nunquam tamen negarunt virtualiter, eundem abjurari in corpore confessionis ipsius, & specialem quæstionis hujus determinationem ad synodum remiserunt, cujus sententia unanimi declaratur, Hierarchiæ papalis nomine rejici Episcopatum Dioœcesanum hodiernum: Ac licet inter alias recusati fœderis à Rege imperati rationes, hanc allegaverint, regi videlicet propositum fuisse Episcopatum tueri, utpote quod articulum de disciplina restringeret ad eam quæ tum obtinuit, hoc est Episcopatum. Cum tamen senatores regii in statuto explicatorio addidiffent; Se subscribere & imperare aliis subscriptionem hujus fœderis secundum sensum & tenorem majorum fœdus illud primitus obsignantium, Atque jam constat majores Episcopatum tum rejecisse; aperte sequitur, eos qui fœderi & confessioni à Rege imperatæ ex præscripto senatus Regii subscripserunt; episcopatum etiam rejecisse & virtualiter abjurasse.
units.tr: The third reason by which it is to be proved that episcopacy was not abjured in the covenant and the confession is this: the Covenanters themselves admitted this in their disputations with the Aberdonians; and among other reasons by which they dissuaded the subscription of the covenant imposed by the king, they alleged this, that the purpose of subscribing that covenant for the king was to defend episcopacy. Reply: although in those disputations they expressly and specifically denied that episcopacy had been abjured in the latter part of the covenant, which contains the application to present times, they never denied that it was virtually abjured in the body of the confession itself. And they referred the particular determination of this question to a synod, whose judgment was declared unanimously: that the present diocesan episcopacy is rejected under the name of the papal hierarchy. And although, among the other reasons for refusing the covenant imposed by the king, they alleged this, namely that it was proposed to the king to defend episcopacy, since it would restrict the article on discipline to that which then prevailed, that is, episcopacy; yet when the royal senators had added in the explanatory statute: We subscribe, and we command others to subscribe, to this covenant according to the sense and tenor of the elders who first sealed that covenant, and it is now certain that the elders at that time had rejected episcopacy, it plainly follows that those who subscribed the covenant and confession imposed by the king, under the direction of the royal senate, also rejected episcopacy and virtually abjured it.

units.la: Ratio, 4. Qui jurat, tenetur in illum sensum jurare quem scit aut saltem probabiliter credit intendi ab eo qui in sacramentum adigit: Perjuri sunt, (inquit Augustinus) qui servatis verbis exspectationem eorum quibus juratum est deceperunt: Et Cicero. Quod ita juratum est, ut mens deferentis fieri conciperet oportere, id servandum est. Atqui omnibus quam notissimum fuit, Regem in juramentum & subscriptionem fœderis adigentem, intendisse, ut obligatione illius fœderis tueretur Episcopatus in regno & ecclesia Scotica. Itaque quicunque passi sunt se in illud sacramentum adigi, tenentur Episcopatum tueri; tantum abest ut abjuratum esse existiment. Respond. Veram esse majorem de juramentis quæ primum concipiuntur ab eo qui juramentum defert; Aliam tamen longe esse rationem ejus jurisjurandi, quod non primitus concipitur ab eo qui defert; sed a majoribus antea conceptum repeti jubetur idque in majorum sensum, exclusó quolibet alio sensu qui majorum sensum destruat: In quod qui se patiuntur adigi, obligatione juramenti tenentur non tam ad mentem illius qui præsens defert, quam ad mentem eorum qui primitus juramentum illud conceperunt, præsertim si eorundem sensus in ipsa jurisjurandi formula sese perspicue satis prodat. Ad minorem. Quæcunque demum fuerit aut fit fere-
units.tr: Argument 4. One who swears is bound to swear in the sense that he knows, or at least probably believes, is intended by the one who binds him by the oath. "They are perjurers," says Augustine, "who, while keeping the words, deceive the expectation of those to whom they swore." And Cicero: "What has been sworn in such a way that the mind of the one who imposes the oath must be understood, that must be kept." But it was perfectly well known to everyone that the King, in requiring the oath and the subscription to the covenant, intended that by the obligation of that covenant Episcopacy would be protected in the kingdom and the Scottish Church. Therefore whoever has allowed themselves to be bound to that oath are bound to defend Episcopacy, and so far are they from thinking they have abjured it. Reply: the major premise is true of oaths first framed by the one who tenders them. But the case of an oath is quite different when it is not first framed by the one who tenders it, but is ordered to be repeated in the form and sense conceived earlier by the forefathers, with every other sense that would destroy theirs excluded. Those who allow themselves to be bound to such an oath are bound by its obligation not so much to the mind of the one who now tenders it as to the mind of those who first framed it, especially if their sense shows itself clearly enough in the very wording of the oath. As to the minor premise: whatever at last has been or is

units.la: Serenissimi Regis mens de Episcopatu in ecclesiis Anglicanis & Hibernicis, non esse sui muneris inquirere, Optare se iisdem veritatem & pacem: ac ut omnia ibidem ad exemplar in monte ostensum componantur: Subditis hujus regni quam notissimum esse, senatores regios ex quorum praescripto juramentum illud exigitur, clare & perspicue pronuntiasse, Confessioni subscribendum esse secundum sensum majorum qui annis 1580. & 1590. illam primitus obsignarunt, & distertam clausulam expositoriam addidisse, tam in obsignationibus suis, quam in statuto quo aliis omnibus foederis obsignationem imperabant nomine Regio. Qua clausula necessario Episcopatus abjurandus esse intelligitur, utpote, quod sole meridiano illustrius fit, iis qui affectu & praejudiciis abripi se non patiuntur, Episcopatum controversum de ecclesia Scotica prorsus profligatum tum fuisse; neque adhuc legitimae alicujus & liberae Synodi nationalis authoritate revocatum: ac reponendum esse inter corruptelas disciplinae de quibus merito quaesita[?] est ecclesia; Cum vero, mandato renovandi obsignationem antiquae confessionis & foederis, omnium subditorum chirographis & juramento; ex animo instituerit sereniff. Rex, ecclesiae aequissimis & moderatis postulatis satisfacere, removendo corruptiones, quae hactenus irrepserunt, & promovendo puritatem religionis, non doctrinae solum, verum etiam disciplinae, (cui contrarium esse Episcopatum semper judicavit haec ecclesia.) Non dubitandum, quin pro singulari pietate & justitia a Deo majestati ipsius indulta, intellecto vero statu hujus ecclesiae ex vera & perfecta relatione constitutionum Synodicarum, tandem judicaturus sit Episcopatum repugnare confessioni & foederi ex ipsius speciali praescripto obsignatis.
units.tr: the mind of the most serene King concerning Episcopacy in the English and Irish churches is not his business to inquire into. He wishes those churches truth and peace, and that everything there be arranged according to the pattern shown on the mountain. It is well known to the subjects of this kingdom that the royal councillors, by whose direction this oath is required, have clearly and plainly declared that the Confession must be subscribed according to the sense of the forefathers who first ratified it in the years 1580 and 1590, and they added an express explanatory clause, both in their own subscriptions and in the statute by which they required the subscription of all others in the King's name. By that clause it is understood that Episcopacy must necessarily be abjured, since it is clearer than the midday sun that, for those who do not allow themselves to be carried away by feeling and prejudice, the disputed Episcopacy in the Scottish Church was then utterly overthrown, and has not yet been revoked by the authority of any lawful and free national synod. It must be placed among the corruptions of discipline about which the Church has rightly complained. Since the most serene King, by his command to renew the subscription of the old Confession and covenant by the handwriting and oath of all his subjects, has sincerely purposed to satisfy the Church's most just and moderate demands, by removing the corruptions that have crept in until now and by promoting the purity of religion, not only of doctrine but also of discipline (to which this Church has always judged Episcopacy to be contrary), there is no doubt that, by the singular piety and justice granted him by God, once he has a true understanding of the state of this Church from a true and complete account of the synodal constitutions, he will at last judge that Episcopacy is inconsistent with the Confession and covenant sealed under his own special direction.

units.la: Ratio quinta & ultima, quae prioribus firmandis ut plurimum subservit hæc est: Nunquam ostendi poterit quo tempore majores Confessionem illam obsignarunt, abjuratum fuisse ab iis episcopatum: quin contra evidentia exstant indicia quibus stabiliri episcopatum ostenditur, nam sub principio Consessionis hæc habentur verba: Confessionem hanc approbatam esse à plurimis exteris ecclesiis, receptam in ecclesia Scotica, & regis ac trium ordinum regni authoritate sancitam ut Dei æternam veritatem, quæ salutis fundamentum continet: Annon vero Ecclesiastici majores, hoc est, Episcopi, Abbates, Priores, tertium regni membrum faciebant? & cuiquam credibile illos istud sancituros, quod ipsorum ordinem funditus destrueret? Sed largiatur à synodis ecclesiasticis abjuratum tum fuisse episcopatum; statuta tamen parlamentaria adhuc nondum refixa pro Episcopatu faciunt, in quæ Synodi nationales nullam authoritatem arrogabunt nisi in Iesuitarum castra transfugiant: Dein rationibus hisce bene longus Catalogus legum parlamentariarum in gratiam Episcopatus subjicitur. Respon.Ex publicis & authenticis ecclesiarum registris supra perspicue ostensum est, abjuratum fuisse episcopatum, quando à majoribus anno 1580. & 1590. obsignata esset confessio: verbaque quibus canones Synodici episcopatum damnabant, usque adeo evidentia, ut acerrimis hierarchiæ propugnatoribus nullum subterfugium, nullam posticam relictam fuisse pro episcopatu revocando in ecclesiam hanc, apparuerit; neque in hanc rem quidquam expressius à quoliber licet omnes ingenii nervos intenderet, dici potuisse. Ad clausulam illam in ratione contraria allegatam, Confessionem videl. sancitam fuisse authoritate trium ordinum regni; quorum unum Ecclesiasticos fecisse dicitur. Respond. Verba illa intelligenda sunt de majori confessione fidei, & de religionis doctrina, non vero disciplina, nam hæc tandem recepta fuit anno 1580. Atque licet de disciplina intelligeretur, nihil lucri Episcopatui firmando accederet, utpote quod nihil inde elici posset pro Episcopatu ac si tum vigeret, nisi per longissime deductas consequentias; quæ admittendæ non sunt quando dilucide patet consequentias illas seu porismata expressis verbis ab ecclesia damnata fuisse: At cur, inquies, fit mentio trium ordinum regni, nisi admittantur ecclesiastici ? Respond. Verba esse styli[?] curiæ, (ut loquuntur) religiose observata fine ulla mutatione, etiam in iis parlamentis quibus nulli adfuerunt omnino Ecclesiastici, & in quibus à sententiæ dictione penitus exclusi fuere: Quod vero additur destatutis parlamentariis nondum resixis, quæ pro Episcopatu faciunt. Respond. Licet illud concederetur; eorum tamen beneficio destitutum nunc esse Episcopatum, utpote quod unanimi consensu Regis, deputati regii, Senatus, & collectivi corporis regni legibus omnibus renunciatum sit, quæ disciplinæ anno 1580, cum majores confessionem primitus obsignassent, receptæ repugnant; inter quas, si ullæ extent, de episcopatu primas partes facile tenent; quia nempe non solum non convenit cum disciplina quæ tum viguit, verumetiam eandem penitus destruit.
units.tr: The fifth and last argument, which mostly serves to confirm the earlier ones, is this: it can never be shown at what time the forefathers subscribed that Confession, that they had abjured Episcopacy. On the contrary, there are clear indications by which Episcopacy is shown to have been established. For at the beginning of the Confession these words stand: that this Confession has been approved by very many foreign churches, received in the Scottish Church, and sanctioned by the authority of the King and the three estates of the kingdom as the eternal truth of God, which contains the foundation of salvation. But did not the ecclesiastical forefathers, that is, the bishops, abbots and priors, form the third estate of the realm? And who can believe that they would have sanctioned something that would utterly destroy their own order? But grant that Episcopacy was then abjured by the ecclesiastical synods; still the parliamentary statutes, not yet repealed, favour Episcopacy, and national synods will claim no authority to annul them unless they go over to the camp of the Jesuits. Then a long catalogue of parliamentary laws in favour of Episcopacy is added to these arguments. Reply: from the public and authentic registers of the churches it has been clearly shown above that Episcopacy was abjured when the Confession was sealed by the forefathers in 1580 and 1590. The words by which the synodal canons condemned Episcopacy are so plain that the fiercest defenders of the hierarchy have been left no evasion and no back door by which to bring Episcopacy back into this Church; nor could anything more explicit have been said on this matter by anyone, however hard he strained all the sinews of his wit. As to the clause alleged in the opposing argument, namely that the Confession was sanctioned by the authority of the three estates of the kingdom, of which one is said to have been the ecclesiastical: Reply: those words must be understood of the greater Confession of faith and the doctrine of religion, not of discipline, for discipline was only received in 1580. And even if it were understood of discipline, nothing would be gained for confirming Episcopacy, since nothing could be drawn from it for Episcopacy as if it were then in force, except through very remote consequences; and these are not to be admitted when it is evident that those consequences, or corollaries, were expressly condemned by the Church. But, you will ask, why is mention made of the three estates of the kingdom, unless the ecclesiastics are admitted? Reply: these are the words of the court's style, religiously observed without any change, even in those parliaments in which no ecclesiastics were present at all, and in which they were entirely excluded from giving judgment. As to the addition that parliamentary statutes favouring Episcopacy have not yet been repealed: Reply: even if that were conceded, Episcopacy is now without their support, since it has been renounced by the unanimous consent of the King, the royal deputies, the Senate and the collective body of the kingdom, in all the laws which are contrary to the discipline received when the forefathers first sealed the Confession in 1580. Among these laws, if any exist, those concerning Episcopacy easily hold the first place, because they not only do not agree with the discipline then in force, but utterly destroy it.

units.la: Addunt, non recurrendum esse ad statuta parlamentaria ut ostendatur quænam fuerit ecclesiæ sententia de episcopatu, & lubricum esse si non sophisticum arguendi genus, ecclesiæ sententiam affingere ex longe petitis consequentiis, quæ in detorsione sententiolæ ad formam solam usitatæ, fundantur, contra ecclesiæ expressam mentem: ejus genuinam disciplinam ex alveario Canonum Synodicorum, libris politiæ, in hunc solum fere finem consignatis & conscriptis petendam esse; In quibus omnia contra Episcopatum plana & perspicua esse supra fifius oftenfum : At , inquies, quicquid fit de Canonibus ecclefiafticis contra Epifcopatum ; notum tamen eft,in epifcoporum gratiam plurima effe àRege &Ordinibus regni fancita,quibus refigendis nullam authoritatem habet Synodus quælibet ecclefiaftica. Refpond. Quandoquidem poteftas civilis & ecclefiaftica inter fe diftinctæ & feparatæ fint & à fe fubfiftant divifim & fcorfim, neutra ab altera dependens in iis rebus quæ ad utramvis jurifdictionem proprie pertinet, & utraque alteri fubfit in iis rebus quæ ad propriam jurifdictionem alterutrius non pertinent;hoc eft,ratione rerum fpiritualium à Chrifto Ecclefiæ commiffarum ,’ civilis poteftas ecclefiaftica fubeft , ratione vero rerum mundanarum ecclefiaftica poteftas civili fubeft , ita quidem ut ficuti ecclefiafticis non liceat leges civiles fancire aut refigere , neque poffiint regni ordinibus obftare, quin leges de rebus civilibus rogatas aut irritas jubeant , fic nec poffint ordines regni in comitiis leges de rebus quæ ad ecclefiafticam poteftatem proprie pertinēt,originaliter fancire,aut ab ecclefia in re proprie jurifdictionis latas refigere , aut obftare ne à fe latas refigat ecclefia. Etenim licet fynodorum decreta de rebus proprii fori publico civilis poteftatis edicto fanciri poffint , & vero fancita fint , ut fic legis vim habeant , quod veteres κύρωσιν δεσποτικῶν[?] vocarunt , ad vigorem fcil: publicæ obfervantiæ, hoc tamen non impedit, quin ecclefia poffit decretum proprium refcindere,quo refciffo ex confequenti refcindi intelligitur civilis illa fanctio , utpote quod fynodi decreto tanquam fundamento innitatur : Contraria vero affertio eorum,qui tuentur, non poffe ecclefiam femel à fe decreta de rebus proprii fori, & legibus civilibus fancita refcindere, ufque adeo abfurda eft, derogatque prærogativæ & juri Chrifti regio, ejufque facris inftitutis,ac libertati ecclefiæ, cui ut dilectæ sponsæ potestatem illam suam utendam , fruendam , ad verbi sui amussim , in membrorum suorum ædificationem , testamento suo sacro commisit , ejusque potestatis exercitio libero in Synodis ecclesiasticis, denique usque adeo repugnat jurisdictioni ecclesiasticæ, cujus naturam destruit, finem proprium pervertit , ejusque animam quasi vitalem suffocat , ut confidendum sit , paucos eam amplexuros.
units.tr: They add that one must not resort to parliamentary statutes in order to show what the Church's opinion about Episcopacy was, and that it is a slippery, if not sophistical, kind of argument to attribute to the Church an opinion drawn from far-fetched consequences, which rest on twisting a small opinion to the mere form in common use, against the Church's express mind. Its genuine discipline must be sought from the storehouse of the synodal canons and from books of polity, written and composed almost solely for this purpose, in which everything against Episcopacy is plain and clear, as has been shown above. But, you will say, whatever may be the case with the ecclesiastical canons against Episcopacy, it is well known that very many things have been enacted by the King and the estates of the kingdom in favour of bishops, and no ecclesiastical synod has any authority to rescind them. Reply: since civil and ecclesiastical power are distinct and separate, and each subsists on its own and apart, neither depending on the other in those matters that properly belong to its own jurisdiction, and each is subject to the other in matters that do not belong to the other's proper jurisdiction, that is: by reason of spiritual things committed by Christ to the Church, civil power is subject to ecclesiastical power, but by reason of worldly things ecclesiastical power is subject to civil power. Just as ecclesiastics may not enact or rescind civil laws, nor oppose the estates of the kingdom, nor order laws proposed on civil matters to be annulled, so the estates of the kingdom in their assemblies cannot originally enact laws on matters that properly belong to ecclesiastical power, nor rescind what the Church has enacted in a matter of its proper jurisdiction, nor prevent the Church from rescinding what it has itself enacted. For although the decrees of synods about matters of their own forum can be ratified by the public edict of civil power, and indeed have been ratified so as to have the force of law (what the ancients called the ratification of imperial decrees [κύρωσιν δεσποτικῶν], that is, the vigour of public observance), this does not prevent the Church from being able to rescind its own decree. When that decree is rescinded, the civil sanction is understood to be rescinded along with it, since it rests on the synod's decree as its foundation. But the contrary assertion of those who maintain that the Church cannot once rescind decrees it has made about matters of its own forum, decrees sanctioned by civil laws, is so absurd that it derogates from the prerogative and right of Christ the King and from his sacred institutions and the liberty of the Church. To the Church, as his beloved spouse, he committed that power of his, to be used and enjoyed according to the rule of his word, for the building up of his members, by his sacred testament, and for the free exercise of that power in ecclesiastical synods. Finally, it so contradicts ecclesiastical jurisdiction, destroying its nature, perverting its proper end and all but suffocating its vital soul, that one may be confident that few will embrace it.

units.la: Accedamus tandem ad examinationem farraginis legum, quas in comitiis trium ordinum regni sancitas dicunt in gratiam Episcopatus, & quas ad pompam & speciem longo ordine instruunt, ut earum frequentissimo numero, & densa acie eminus terreantur lectores,libellus ille ordinem annorum quibus illæ sanciebantur , sequitur ; qui nobis non est premendus , ne inutili repetitione rerum earundem actum reiterare cogamur. Ego leges illas hoc ordine disponam. Primus continebit eas quibus in reformationis primordiis Episcopatum abolitum non fuisse demonstrare conantur. Secundus , eas quæ confirmationem aut restitutionem privilegiorum politicorum Episcopis sanciunt. Tertius vero, leges illas quibus ecclesiasticam potestatem Episcopis concessam dicunt.
units.tr: Let us at last come to the examination of the heap of laws which they say were enacted by the parliament of the three estates in favour of Episcopacy, and which they set out in a long list for show and display, so that readers may be frightened from a distance by their great number and dense ranks. The pamphlet follows the order of the years in which those laws were enacted, but we need not follow it, lest we be forced to repeat the same matters in useless repetition. I shall arrange those laws in this order. The first group will contain those by which they try to show that Episcopacy was not abolished in the early days of the Reformation. The second group will contain those which confirm or restore political privileges to the Bishops. The third group will contain those laws by which they say ecclesiastical power was granted to the Bishops.

units.la: Primus ordo leges continet , sancitas. in parlament. 1567. stat. 2. quo cavetur ne quis Episcopus aut prælatus quamlibet jurisdictionem exerceat quæ à Romani pontificis authoritate fluat , &stat. 3. Quo rescinduntur statuta omnia præcedentium temporum verbo Dei & confessioni fidei, quam ordines regni tum ratam habuerunt, contraria. Unde colligitur reformatoribus non fuisse tum propositum Episcopatum simpliciter supprimere , sed quatenus solum dependeret à Pontifice Romano ; & stat. 8. quo præscribitur juramentum regi coronando deferendum, se videl. promoturum veram Christianam religionem, & legitimam sacramentorum administrationem, prout illa tunc obtinuerunt; nulla prorsus disciplinae facta mentione, utpote quod Pontificiae ecclesiae disciplina, quae Epi-scopatum fovet, nullam tunc mutationem passa sit, idem etiam innuitur stat.68. parlam.ann.1579.Respond. Notissimum esse Reformatores primos corruptam ecclesiae disciplinam aeque ac doctrinam reformasse; ac Episcopatum rejecisse, non solum quatenus à Pontifice dependet, verum in totum; ac declarasse per nullos alios ecclesiam regendam esse, quam per pastores, doctores, presbyteros seu seniores, & diaconos: ac in singulis hisce ministrorum generibus paritatem agnovisse; Ac licet episcopis quibusdam qui reformationi se adjunxerunt, à regni ordinibus indulti sint reditus, ne jus tamen ecclesiasticum exercerent, severe in Synodis interdixisse ecclesiam; idemque ex verbis primi illius statuti quod citatur, colligitur ordines regni in comitiis sancivisse. Nam cum nulla alia jurisdictione ecclesiastica vestiti essent illi Episcopi, quam quae à Papa flueret; & vero ne eam exercerent interdictum esset, omnem omnino ecclesiasticam jurisdictionem statuto eo ipsis ademptam quis neget? Praesertim cum nulla alia sit Episcoporum jurisdictio quam Pontificia; quod consarcinator hujus libelli non negat, cum asserit, veterem ecclesiae disciplinam hoc est Pontificiam, nullam mutationem passam fuisse, quod licet falsum esse, cuivis reformationis Scoticanae historiam delibanti constet, fatetur tamen author quisquis est, jurisdictionem quam sibi vendicant hodierni Episcopi, eandem esse cum Papalium Episcoporum jurisdictione, ideoq; ad impiam Papae Hierarchiam in foedere majorum abjuratam, referendam esse: quam ex ecclesia Scotica in reformationis primordiis ejectam fuisse, impudens est qui neget ; Etenim mysterium illud papatus primum coepit à corruptione disciplinae , per quam viam sibi stravit ad corruptionem doctrinae ; Quare reformatores Scoti utramque pariter ab Antichristi foribus repurgarunt , & sicuti summam doctrinae in confessione ordinibus regni exhibita, consignarunt, sic fundamenta disciplinae in libro primo de Politia ecclesiae ; simul & semel expresserunt ; neque prius destiterunt quam perfectionem eam Disciplinae tandem promovissent , ac ab omnibus sordibus primaevo suo nitori restituissent.
units.tr: The first group contains laws enacted in the parliament of 1567: act 2, by which it is provided that no Bishop or prelate shall exercise any jurisdiction that flows from the authority of the Roman Pontiff; and act 3, by which all statutes of earlier times that are contrary to the Word of God and to the confession of faith, which the orders of the realm then approved, are rescinded. From this it is inferred that the Reformers did not then intend to suppress Episcopacy altogether, but only insofar as it depended on the Roman Pontiff. Also act 8, by which an oath is prescribed to be taken by the king at his coronation, namely that he will promote the true Christian religion and the lawful administration of the sacraments, as they then stood; with no mention at all of discipline, since the discipline of the Popish Church, which favours Episcopacy, had then suffered no change. The same is implied in act 68 of the parliament of 1579. Reply: it is very well known that the first Reformers reformed the corrupt discipline of the Church just as much as its doctrine; that they rejected Episcopacy, not only insofar as it depended on the Pope, but altogether; and that they declared the Church is to be governed by no others than ministers, teachers, presbyters or elders, and deacons, and that they acknowledged equality among each of these kinds of ministers. And although some bishops who joined the Reformation were granted revenues by the orders of the realm, they were nevertheless strictly forbidden by the Church in the Synods to exercise ecclesiastical right. The same is gathered from the words of that first statute which is cited: the orders of the realm enacted this in parliament. For since those Bishops were clothed with no ecclesiastical jurisdiction other than that which flowed from the Pope, and since it was forbidden for them to exercise even that, who would deny that all ecclesiastical jurisdiction was wholly taken away from them by that statute? Especially since there is no other jurisdiction of Bishops than the Popish one, which the patcher-together of this pamphlet does not deny when he asserts that the ancient discipline of the Church, that is the Popish, suffered no change. Although this is false, as anyone who has tasted the history of the Scottish Reformation knows, the author, whoever he is, nonetheless admits that the jurisdiction which the Bishops of today claim for themselves is the same as the jurisdiction of the Papal bishops, and therefore must be referred to the impious Papal hierarchy, which was renounced in the covenant of our forefathers. That this was cast out of the Scottish Church in the early days of the Reformation, only a shameless man would deny. For that mystery of Popery first began with the corruption of discipline, and by this way it paved its path to the corruption of doctrine. Therefore the Scottish reformers purged both alike from the doorways of Antichrist, and just as they set down the sum of doctrine in the confession presented to the orders of the realm, so they set forth the foundations of discipline in the first book of the Polity of the Church, expressing both at once. Nor did they stop until they had finally advanced that discipline to perfection and restored it to its original brightness, free from all filth.

units.la: Secundus ordo statutorum municipalium quæ pro Episcopatu afferuntur, continet leges quibus status seu ordinis Ecclesiastici privilegia & immunitates sanciuntur. Uti sunt Iacob 6. parl.1. statut.24. & parl.2. stat.35. & parl.11, statut.23. & parliam. 17.statut.231.& parl. anni.1606. stat.2.& parliam. 20.stat.6. Respondit Synodus, Statuta hæc de privilegiis solum politicis & immunitatibus civilibus agere, alia vero de exemptionibus eorum qui titulo Episcoporum & reditibus Abbatiarum ad vitam gauderent. Dein si quæ statuta mentione faciant totius ordinis ecclesiastici, privilegia legibus illis concessa diserte restricta esse iis qui munere & functione ecclesiastica rite fungebantur ; non vero extendi posse ad eos, qui relicta functione ecclesiastica, ad quam nunquam vocati fuerunt ab ecclesiis, inani titulo ac reditibus ecclesiasticorum gaudebant : quo solum nomine Episcopis illis sententiæ dictio in supremis regni Comitiis permissa fuit, quod alibi etiam in quibusdam reformatis provinciis cernitur : Etenim in ditione Ultrajectina Belgii Confœderati, qui titulo & reditibus ecclesiasticorum gaudent, primum provinciæ illius membrum conficiunt, & nomine Ecclesiasticorum veniunt, licet nulla ecclesiastica : funfunctione in ecclesiis gaudeant: Et ut usitatus curiæ stylus conservetur, Præpositorum, Canonicorum & cæt. nomina retinentur, licet politia illa Pontificiorum jamdudum apud eos exoleverit: Sic in regno Scotiæ ordinaria fit mentio Ecclesiasticorum seu Clericorum, ratione videlicet reditum [?] & possessionum, non vero ratione officii alicujus ecclesiastici: Quare statuta illa parliamentaria nihil loquuntur de jurisdictione ecclesiastica titularibus illis Episcopis debita.
