Adde quod in Comitiis regni anno 1597. statuto 231. licet iis qui reditibus Episcopatuum & Abbatiarum gauderent, concessum sit jus suffragii in conventu supremo ordinum, expresse tamen cavetur, ne hoc ordinariæ & sequentibus legibus sanctæ disciplinæ, & jurisdictioni Synodorum, presbyteriorum, ac sessionum detrimento sit; Item ibidem statuitur, ut qui ad titulos illos promoveantur, operam suam particularibus ecclesiis addicant; quod cum infra dignitatem suam putent Episcopi, & deserto verbi ministerio jurisdictionem omnem Ecclesiæ sibi solis arripuerint, iniquum est ut hujus privilegii beneficio fruantur: Ac licet istarum conditionum & reservationum nulla esset expressa facta mentio; ordinaria tamen & recepta consuetudo in Comitiis regni, quæ quicquid sanciunt, salvo jure cujuslibet, sancitum esse declarant; satis ostendit, illorum privilegiorum concessione, non esse ademptum ecclesiæ & sponsæ Christi jus suum: quasi non liceret eos in jus vocare, aut in manifestorum scelerum convictos non animadvertere; præsertim cum privilegium illud suffragii, iis concessum fuisse constet qua essent Ecclesiæ deputati, cui legationis suæ obitæ rationem redderent; à qua exauctorati, jus etiam suffragii in Comitiis regni amitterent:
units.tr: The second group of municipal statutes which are brought forward for Episcopacy contains laws by which the privileges and immunities of the ecclesiastical estate or order are sanctioned. Such are: James 6, parliament 1, act 24; parliament 2, act 35; parliament 11, act 23; parliament 17, act 231; the parliament of 1606, act 2; and parliament 20, act 6. The Synod replied that these statutes deal only with political privileges and civil immunities, and the others with the exemptions of those who enjoyed for life the title of Bishops and the revenues of abbeys. Next, if any statutes make mention of the whole ecclesiastical order, the privileges granted by those laws are expressly restricted to those who rightly discharged the ecclesiastical office and function; they cannot be extended to those who, having left the ecclesiastical function, to which they were never called by the churches, enjoyed an empty title and the revenues of the Church. It was only under this name that the judgment of the highest assemblies of the realm was allowed to those Bishops, as is seen elsewhere also in some reformed provinces. For in the district of Utrecht in the Confederated Netherlands, those who enjoy the title and revenues of the Church form the first member of that province and are called by the name of ecclesiastics, although they have no ecclesiastical function in the churches. And so that the customary style of the court may be preserved, the names of provosts, canons and so forth are retained, although that Popish polity has long since fallen into disuse among them. Likewise in the kingdom of Scotland, mention of ecclesiastics or clerics is made as a matter of course, namely by reason of revenues and possessions, and not by reason of any ecclesiastical office. Therefore those parliamentary statutes say nothing about the ecclesiastical jurisdiction owed to those titular Bishops. Add that in the parliament of the realm in the year 1597, act 231, although the right of voting in the supreme assembly of the orders was granted to those who enjoyed the revenues of bishoprics and abbeys, it is nevertheless expressly provided that this shall not be to the prejudice of the holy discipline ordained by the laws that follow, nor of the jurisdiction of Synods, presbyteries and sessions. Likewise it is laid down in the same place that those who are promoted to those titles shall devote their labour to particular churches. Since the Bishops think this beneath their dignity, and, having deserted the ministry of the Word, have seized for themselves alone all the jurisdiction of the Church, it is unfair that they should enjoy the benefit of this privilege. And although no mention was expressly made of these conditions and reservations, the ordinary and accepted custom of the parliament of the realm, which declares that whatever it enacts is enacted saving the right of every person, sufficiently shows that by the grant of those privileges the right of the Church, the spouse of Christ, was not taken away. It is as if it were not lawful to summon them to judgment, or to take note of them when convicted of manifest crimes; especially since it is established that the privilege of voting was granted to them on the understanding that they were deputed to the Church, to which they should render an account of the discharge of their embassy, and from which, if they were removed from office, they would also lose the right to vote in the parliament of the realm.

units.la: Tertius ordo urget, Episcopis præter privilegia civilia, concessam esse jurisdictionem in pastores, Atque in hunc finem citantur omnia ea statuta quae levissimam mentionem faciunt Episcoporum ; in causis quibuslibet ecclesiasticis ; praesertim in causis quae proprie ecclesiasticae nō sunt, ut sunt matrimoniales: &cæt. Iac. 6. parl. 3. ann. 1572. cap. 46. Archiepifcopis & episcopis conceditur authoritas deponendi à functione ecclesiastica eos qui Confessioni fidei non subscripserint, & Regi juramentum fidelitatis non præstiterint. Et cap. 48. in visitationibus ecclefiarum commodam pastoribus habitationem defignandi. & 54. adigendi parochianos ad templorum fabricam reparandam : & parl. 4. ejusdem Iacobi 6. ann. 1573. cap. admonendi eos qui matrimonii fidem malitiosa desertione violant, & pertinaces admonitionum contemptores per pastorem ecclesiæ excommunicandi. Respondet Synodus: Quæcunque in statutis illis Episcopis deferuntur, expresse etiam delata sunt Superintendentibus, ac Ecclefiarū Commiffariis : quo constare possit Episcopis qua talibus hæc non competere, verum licuisse Ecclesiæ eos qui titulo & reditibus Episcopatuum gaudebant, delegare ad executionem Canonum quorundam ecclefiafticorum ; Dein temporum illorum annales diferte testari dicunt, Ecclesiam ratam non habuisse subdolam & tantum non violentam Episcoporum per Proregem obtrufionem ; Tertio, Posterioribus Comitiorum statutis, quibus regimen ecclesiæ in libro fecundo Politiæ sancitur, omnes illas leges in Episcoporum gratiam conditas, antiquatas fuisse ; Idem etiam responsum refert Synodus ad statuta illa anni 1584: contra quæ Ecclesiarum deputati tum publice protestati sunt, & quæ expressis verbis refiguntur in Comitiis anni 1592. cap. 114. At saltem, inquies, Statuto anni 1584. Episcopi restituuntur ad jus suffragii in Comitiis ; Respondet Synodus ; Non Episcopi solum, verum & omnes majores præláti, inter quos censentur Abbates, Priores, & cæt. ad idem privilegium, statuti illius vigore restituuntur; Neque tamen inde colligi potest; Abbatum, aut Priorum officia ab ecclesiis unquam approbata fuisse: Deinde Episcopis privilegium illud restitutum fuit; non tamen quatenus Ecclesiasticis, sed qua possessores erant Baronarum Episcopatibus Papismi tempore annexarum: Quod vel inde liquido constat, quia qui Episcoporum nomine in Comitiis tum venerunt; sæpius nobiles fuerunt, nulla ecclesiastica functione gaudentes; sic Robertus Comes Marchiæ regis Jacobi avunculus Episcopus Cathanesiæ dicitur: sic alii nobiles Abbatiarum & Prioratuum possessores, ordinario curiæ stilo, abbates vocabantur: Quare cum ratione beneficiorum Episcopis, Abbatibus, & cæt. suffragium in supremo ordinum conventu concessum fit, beneficiis illis coronæ regiæ annexis, (uti cavetur parliam. 11. ann. 1587.cap.29. qua annexatione ordinem Episcoporum indirecte saltem abolitum fuisse constat;) privilegium illud sententiæ dictionis in Comitiis sua sponte corruit, uti in Abbatibus corruisse nullus ignorat: Neque verendum est ne exclusis ecclesiasticis, seu Clero (ut salutari cupiunt Hierarchici) diminutionem integritatis membrorum suorum sentiat Parliamentum: Nam ab ipsis regni primordiis, diu ante incarnatum Christum, tribus membris constitisse regni Scotiæ ordines constat, inter quos nullus fuit ex Clero; & à Rege Donaldo qui regum omnium primus Christianos ritus anno Christi 199 recepit, ad Eugenii usque tempora postrema, Ecclesiæ Scotorum per Monachos, (Culdæos id est Dei cultores vocabant) populi suffragiis electos regebantur, absque Episcopis, quos primum Palladius à Cœlestino Pontifice Romano missus, in Scotia creavit, Eugenio Rege circa annum 450. Itaque toto illo 251. annorum spatio ordinibus regni Scotiæ sua constabat integritas ex tribus membris, videlicet, nobilitate majori, minori, & civitatum legatis; excluso Clero, cui tum religio fuit civilibus negotiis se immiscere: Et qui postea ex Monasteriis electi fuerunt Episcopi, functioni solum ecclesiasticæ; quæ tum nondum quæstuaria erat, sese penitus addixerant, uti referunt annales ad annum Christi 854. Cumque Clerum à pristina sanctimonia & simplicitate degenerasse cerneret Constantinus Rex, luxu corruptum, venationibus, aucupiis, aulicæque pompæ deditum; ad veterem parsimoniam & temperantiam legibus severissime latis reduxit: Tum decretum ut sacris tantum incumberent, prophanis abstinerent: Annotantibus historicis in vita Constantini fecundi ab iisdem proditum, sero admodum Antichristo Romæ in in folium collocato Episcopos ad sæculares dignitates promotos fuisse; etenim licet Gregorius Scotorum rex 73.circa annum Christi 900 leges de libertate ecclesiastica primus fere tulerit; ad tertium ordinum regni membrum non fuisse admissos ecclesiasticos, illarum legum fragmenta, & historiæ testantur; quin contra, immunitas illa ministrorum ecclesiæ,eo fine sanciri dicitur, ut à mundanorum negotiorum molestiis & strepitu exempti,liberiusDeo in vocatione sua servirent: Porro licet posterioribus quibusdam sæculis Episcopis, Abbatibus, Prioribus sententiæ dictio in Comitiis regni ratione ampliffimarum Baroniarum, quas regum improvida prodigalitate possidebant, concessa sit, nunquam tamen dignitatem hanc sibi arrogare ausi fuerant, quasi sibi ut regni membro debitam; nam nobilitatem majorem, minorē seu libere-tenentes, & civitatum legatos, tres regni ordines constituisse negari vix potest: De majori nobilitate & civitatibus, nullus adeo effrons qui in quæstionem vocet: Si quid controversi, illud totum de minori nobilitate, seu libere-tenentibus qui de Domino rege tenent in capite (ut municipalium legum verbis loquar.) Atque Iacobi primi regno, constat jus suffragii iis olim competivisse;parl.7.cap.101.utque decentius omnia in supremo illo conventu peragerentur. Indultum fuisse iisdem ut in singulis provinciis duos delegarent, qui omnes libere-tenentes in istis provinciis repraesentarent; quod repetitur denuo in parlia. 11. sub Iacobo 6.cap.113. anno scil.1587. quo sancitur vocandos esse minores Barones seu Provinciarum deputatos ad parliamentum, literis ex Cancellaria, quo modo alii regni ordines vocari solent; iisque praesentibus eadem cum aliis ordinibus privilegia concedi, ut vid. Articulorum Domini seu Apolecti[?] pari numero ex his eligantur quo ex civitatum legatis eligi solent: Quare licet ex Ecclesiastico ordine nullus interfit Comitiis, tres tamen regni ordines statuto hoc designati, Parliamenti integritatem constituunt, quibus si addas ordinem ecclesiasticum, quartum illud membrum redundabit; Aut si ordinis ecclesiastici praesentia usque adeo necessaria, cur Episcoporum solorum fit mentio? quandoquidem compertum fit, corruptioribus saeculis quibus ecclesiastici ad jus suffragii promovebantur, plures duplo semper interfuisse Abbates & Priores, quam Episcopos: qui omnes simul cum nobilitate majori, cum à regibus Baroniis ditati essent, unum ordinum regni membrum constituebant, sicut hodie in Anglia cernitur.
units.tr: The third order argues that, besides civil privileges, jurisdiction over ministers was granted to the bishops, and to this end they cite every statute that makes even the slightest mention of bishops in any ecclesiastical cause, especially in causes that are not strictly ecclesiastical, such as matrimonial ones, and so on. James VI, Parliament 3, 1572, chapter 46: archbishops and bishops are granted authority to depose from ecclesiastical office those who have not subscribed the Confession of Faith and have not given the King the oath of fidelity. And chapter 48: in visitations of the churches, to assign a suitable dwelling to the ministers. And chapter 54: to compel parishioners to repair the church buildings. And Parliament 4 of the same James VI, 1573, chapter: to admonish those who break the faith of marriage by malicious desertion, and to excommunicate by the minister of the church those who obstinately despise admonition. The Synod replies: whatever is attributed to bishops in those statutes is also expressly attributed to the superintendents and the commissioners of the churches. From this it can be seen that these things do not belong to bishops as such; rather, it was lawful for the Church to delegate to those who enjoyed the title and revenues of the bishoprics the execution of certain ecclesiastical canons. Next, the annals of those times clearly testify that the Church did not ratify the bishops' imposition by the Viceroy, which was crafty and hardly less than violent. Third, by the later statutes of the Assemblies, in which the government of the Church is laid down in the second book of the Polity, all those laws made for the bishops' benefit were abolished. The Synod gives the same answer to the statutes of the year 1584, against which the deputies of the Churches then protested publicly, and which are expressly revoked in the Assemblies of 1592, chapter 114. "But at least," you will say, "by the statute of 1584 the bishops were restored to the right of voting in the Assemblies." The Synod replies: not only bishops but all the greater prelates, among whom are counted abbots, priors and so on, were restored to the same privilege by virtue of that statute. Nor can it be inferred from this that the offices of abbots or priors were ever approved by the churches. Further, that privilege was restored to the bishops, but not in so far as they were ecclesiastics; rather, it was restored in so far as they were the holders of baronies annexed to the bishoprics in the Papist times. This is plain even from the fact that those who came to the Assemblies in the name of the bishops were often laymen, enjoying no ecclesiastical function; thus Robert, Earl of March, uncle of King James, is called Bishop of Caithness; and so other nobles, holders of abbacies and priories, were, in the ordinary style of the court, called abbots. Therefore, since the vote in the supreme assembly of the orders is granted to bishops, abbots and so on by reason of their benefices, and those benefices have been annexed to the Crown (as is provided in Parliament 11, 1587, chapter 29, by which annexation it is certain that the order of bishops was at least indirectly abolished), that privilege of giving judgment in the Assemblies has fallen of its own accord, just as it is well known that it fell for the abbots. Nor need Parliament fear lest, with the ecclesiastics or clergy excluded (as the hierarchs wish, for their own good), it should feel a diminution of the integrity of its members. For from the very beginnings of the kingdom, long before Christ was made flesh, it is certain that the orders of the kingdom of Scotland consisted of three members, among whom there was none from the clergy. And from King Donald, who was the first of all kings to receive the Christian rites, in the year of Christ 199, down to the last times of Eugenius, the churches of the Scots were governed by monks (whom they called Culdees, that is, worshippers of God), chosen by the votes of the people, without bishops, whom Palladius, sent by Pope Celestine of Rome, first created in Scotland in the reign of King Eugenius, about the year 450. Thus throughout that whole span of 251 years the orders of the kingdom of Scotland were made up of three members, namely the greater nobility, the lesser nobility, and the representatives of the towns, the clergy being excluded, since it was then considered a matter of religion for them not to meddle in civil affairs. And those who were afterwards chosen from the monasteries as bishops had wholly devoted themselves to the ecclesiastical function alone, which at that time was not yet a source of profit, as the annals record for the year of Christ 854. And when King Constantine saw that the clergy had degenerated from their former holiness and simplicity, corrupted by luxury and given over to hunting, fowling and courtly pomp, he restored them to their old frugality and temperance by laws enacted most severely. Then he decreed that they should devote themselves only to sacred things and abstain from profane ones. The historians who note this in the life of Constantine the Second record that it was very late, when the Antichrist was set on his throne at Rome, that bishops were promoted to secular dignities. For although King Gregory of the Scots, about the year of Christ 900, was almost the first to enact laws on ecclesiastical liberty (the 73rd), the fragments of those laws and the histories testify that the ecclesiastics were not admitted to the third member of the orders. Indeed, on the contrary, that immunity of the ministers of the Church is said to have been established for this end: that, freed from the troubles and noise of worldly affairs, they might serve God more freely in their calling. Moreover, although in later centuries the giving of judgment in the Assemblies of the kingdom was granted to bishops, abbots and priors by reason of the very large baronies which they held through the improvident prodigality of the kings, they never dared to claim this dignity for themselves as due to them as a member of the kingdom. For it can scarcely be denied that the greater nobility, the lesser nobility or freeholders, and the representatives of the towns constituted the three orders of the kingdom. Concerning the greater nobility and the towns, no one is so brazen as to call it into question. If there is any dispute, it concerns wholly the lesser nobility, or freeholders who hold of the lord King in chief (to use the words of the municipal laws). And in the reign of James I it is established that they had formerly held the right of voting, and, that everything might be done more fittingly in that supreme assembly, it was granted to them that in each province they should appoint two men to represent all the freeholders in those provinces. This was repeated again in Parliament 11, under James VI, chapter 113, in the year 1587, by which it is provided that the lesser barons, or the deputies of the provinces, are to be summoned to Parliament by letters from the Chancery, as the other orders of the kingdom are usually summoned, and that, when they are present, the same privileges as the other orders are to be granted them; as the articles of the Lord, or the Apolectus [?], show, they are to be chosen in the same number from these as are usually chosen from the representatives of the towns. Therefore, although no one from the ecclesiastical order takes part in the Assemblies, nevertheless the three orders designated by this statute constitute the integrity of Parliament; and if you add the ecclesiastical order, there will be a fourth member over and above. Or, if the presence of the ecclesiastical order is so necessary, why is mention made of bishops alone? Since it is well established that in the more corrupt centuries, when ecclesiastics were promoted to the right of voting, there were always twice as many abbots and priors present as bishops; and all of these together with the greater nobility, since they had been enriched with baronies by the kings, constituted one member of the orders of the kingdom, just as is seen today in England.

units.la: Denique à libelli istius authore objicitur: Licet plurimas mutationes passus sit Episcopatus, tandem tamē ann.1606. restitutus fuit Episcopatus & restitutio illa reiterata ac ad majore cautelam confirmata in Comitiis anni 1609. & 1617. Resp.synodus.Ann. 1606. Secularia beneficia illa Episcopatuū concessafuisse quibusdam quos titulo antea rex ornaverat, jurisdictionis autem ecclesiasticæ nulla prorsus mentione facta: sicuti hæc in Comitiis anni 1609. nam expressè dicitur, Episcopos ad temporalem jurisdictionem, & privilegia antecessoribus concessa, quæ à regia majestate fluuisse[?], esse restitutos: quibus clausulis excluditur spiritualis illa jurisdictio quam sibi in Ecclesiâs arrogant Episcopi: tum quia temporalis non est, aut mundana, tum quia à rege fluere non potest, quod non negant Episcopi in protestatione sua contra Synodum; cum se à Christo Episcopos constitutos asserant, nec jurisdictionem suam Synodis, Regi, aut Parliamentis accepta ferant. Quod ad statutum illud anni 1617. quo sancitur, Episcopos per Capitulum eligendos, ac ritibus, ceremoniisque consuetis consecrandos. Respondet Synodus: Leges politicas de rebus ecclesiasticis, cum proprie ratificationes, ut ita loquantur, sint & tantum sanctiones Canonum ecclesiasticorum, ad vigorem publicæ observantiæ, quam sub pœna civili imperant; firmitatem sumunt mutuari à Canonibus, utpote fundamento cui infiltrantur; quibus rescissis, non possunt non esse irritæ leges illæ civiles iis superstructæ. Atque leges & statuta anni 1617. Canonibus Synodi Glasguensis anni 1610. initituntur; quam multis nominibus illegitimam fuisse cum jam demonstratum sit; ex consequentia necessario infertur, leges illas jam non ligare: Præsertim cum nihil unquam decreverit ecclesia de Episcoporum consecratione, aut electione, neque eo usque processerit Pseudo-synodus ista, ut Dioecesanum Episcopatum (qui nunc in quæstione versatur) restitui voluerit, quem ab Ecclesia jampridem damnatum & profligatum sciebat: Sed detur, Synodum illam legitimam fuisse; si ejus beneficio, aut legum municipalium[?] ei superstitiorum frui volunt; cur[?] cautiones à Synodo positas neglexerunt ? in quas etiam jurarunt; ac annuarum Synodorum Nationalium, à quibus se judicari tum sacramentis professi sunt, convocationem impediverunt. Atque hæc præcipua sunt quæ tunc ab Hierarchicis ad Episcopatum fulciendum prolata fuerunt, quibus Episcopalis regiminis in Ecclesia Scotica ab ipsis reformationis exordiis ad præsentia tempora continuationem demonstrare annitebantur; ideoque Episcopatum Dioecesanum immerito damnatum clamabant: quam vere, ex synodi responso facile judicabitur.
units.tr: Finally, the author of this little book objects: although the episcopate suffered many changes, at last, in the year 1606, it was restored; and that restoration was repeated and confirmed, for greater security, in the Assemblies of 1609 and 1617. The Synod replies. In 1606 those secular benefices of the bishoprics were granted to certain men whom the King had previously honoured with the title, but no mention at all was made of ecclesiastical jurisdiction. The same holds for the Assembly of 1609, for it is expressly said that the bishops were restored to temporal jurisdiction and the privileges granted to their predecessors, which are said to have flowed from the royal majesty. By these clauses that spiritual jurisdiction which the bishops arrogate to themselves in the churches is excluded: first, because it is not temporal or worldly; second, because it cannot flow from the king, which the bishops themselves do not deny in their protest against the Synod, since they assert that they were constituted bishops by Christ, and do not hold their jurisdiction from Synods, the King or Parliaments. As for that statute of 1617, by which it is provided that bishops are to be elected by the chapter and consecrated with the customary rites and ceremonies, the Synod replies: political laws concerning ecclesiastical matters are, properly speaking, only ratifications, so to speak, and sanctions of ecclesiastical canons, given civil penalty to enforce public observance; they take their firmness by borrowing from the canons, as from the foundation into which they are inserted. If these are rescinded, those civil laws built upon them cannot but be void. And the laws and statutes of 1617 are founded on the canons of the Synod of Glasgow of 1610, which has already been shown to be illegitimate in many respects. From this it follows necessarily that those laws no longer bind. Especially since the Church has never decreed anything about the consecration or election of bishops, nor has that pseudo-synod gone so far as to want the diocesan episcopate (which is now in question) restored, an episcopate which it knew had long since been condemned and overthrown by the Church. But grant that that Synod was lawful: if they wish to enjoy its benefit, or the advantages of the municipal laws, why have they neglected the safeguards laid down by the Synod, which they also swore to, and hindered the convening of the yearly National Synods, by which they professed with their oaths that they were then to be judged? And these are the chief points which the hierarchs then put forward to support the episcopate, by which they strove to demonstrate that the episcopal government had continued in the Scottish Church from the very beginnings of the Reformation down to the present time; and therefore they cried out that the diocesan episcopate had been condemned undeservedly. How truly this is so will easily be judged from the Synod's reply.

units.la: Sess. 17. Decemb. 10. Die Lunæ.
units.tr: Session 17. December 10. Monday.

units.la: De famosis[?] quinque articulis Perthensibus deliberandum esse proposuit præses, An secundum genuinum Confessionis sensum, qui annis 1580. 1581. & 1590. 1591. obtinuit, quinque isti articuli ex ecclesia removendi essent, vid. 1. Genuflexio in S. Cœna. 2. Quinque dies festi, in memoriam nativitatis, passionis, resurrectionis, ascensionis Christi, ac descensus Spiritus S. in Apostolos instituti. 3. Episcopalis confirmatio. 4. Privata Baptismi. & 5. S. Cœnæ administratio. Antequam ad suffragia deventum esset, prælectum fuit scriptum ex publicis ecclesiæ registris collectum eorum opera, qui ad ea excutienda à Synodo designati fuerunt: Cujus hæc fuit summa:
units.tr: The president proposed that they should deliberate on the five notorious Perth Articles: whether, according to the genuine sense of the Confession that prevailed in the years 1580, 1581, 1590 and 1591, these five articles ought to be removed from the Church. They are: (1) kneeling at the Lord's Supper; (2) the five festival days instituted in memory of the nativity, passion, resurrection and ascension of Christ, and of the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles; (3) episcopal confirmation; (4) private baptism; and (5) the administration of the Lord's Supper in private. Before they came to a vote, a paper was read, drawn up from the public registers of the Church by those whom the Synod had appointed to examine these matters. Its substance was as follows:

units.la: De genuflexione in S. cœna. Sic administranda sunt sacramenta, prout Christus ipse statuit, qui hic solus à nobis imitandus est: (sunt verba formulæ fidei psalteriis præfixa.) Idem repetitur cap. 23. Confessionis Majoris: In liturgia S. cœnæ Psalteriis præfixa; Sessio & distributio per ipsos communicantes conjunguntur ac lib.2. de polit.eccles. gestus hic Sessionis ipsius Christi exemplo, ac huic actioni maxime conformis esse dicitur; ac quæcunque ab hominibus inventa sunt, censentur alterationes institutionis nis Dominicæ, quasi eam imperfectionis arguerent: In Synodo nationali anni 1562. jubentur pastores in administratione S.Cœnæ sequi ritus in Ecclesia Anglicana, Genevensi usitatos, cujus olim pastorem egit D. Knoxius, primarius ecclesiæ Scoticæ reformator; qui Genuflexionem in S. Cœna, aberrationem à simplicitate & puritate sacramenti hujus semper judicavit. In Comitiis regni anno 1567. Sancitur, ut qui nolint participes esse sacramentorum, prout tum in Ecclesia hac reformata administrabantur, ne ecclesiæ hujus membra censeantur; In iisdemque comitiis, juramentum à Rege inaugurando præstandum inter alia continet; Regem procuraturum administrationem sacramentorum legitimam, quæ tum usu recepta fuit. Quod statutum denuo repetitur anno 1581.octobri mense, quo anno brevior hæc fidei confessio (de cujus sensu jam quæritur) obsignata fuit omnium chirographis & juramento solenni: in qua confessione damnantur omnes ritus & ceremoniæ ab hominibus superadditæ legitimæ sacramentorum administrationi; non solum quæ contra, sed quæ præter Dei verbum & reformatæ hujus ecclesiæ doctrinam & disciplinam sunt: Atque Genuflexio in Sacra Cœna Christi exemplo non est conformis, neque ordinariæ praxi hujus ecclesiæ, quo tempore Confessionem illam obsignavit; Sed est ritus ab hominibus præter Dei verbum aut si non contra, introductus tandem anno 1618.
units.tr: On kneeling at the Lord's Supper. The sacraments are to be administered just as Christ himself ordained, who alone is to be imitated by us (these are the words of the formula of faith prefixed to the psalters). The same is repeated in chapter 23 of the Greater Confession, which is prefixed to the Psalters in the liturgy of the Lord's Supper: the sitting and the distribution by the communicants themselves are joined together, and in the second book of the Polity of the Church this posture of sitting is said to be after the example of Christ himself and most in conformity with this action; and whatever has been devised by men is judged to be an alteration of the Lord's institution, as if it indicated imperfection in it. In the national Synod of 1562 it was ordered that the ministers, in administering the Lord's Supper, should follow the rites used in the English Church and at Geneva, whose minister Mr Knox, the chief reformer of the Scottish Church, once was; he always judged kneeling at the Lord's Supper to be a departure from the simplicity and purity of this sacrament. In the parliament of the kingdom in 1567 it was enacted that those who would not take part in the sacraments, as they were then administered in this reformed Church, should not be counted members of this Church. In the same parliament, the oath to be taken by the King at his inauguration contains, among other things, that the King shall procure the lawful administration of the sacraments, which was then received in practice. This statute was repeated again in October 1581, the year in which this shorter confession of faith (whose sense is now under question) was sealed with the signatures and solemn oath of all. In this confession all rites and ceremonies added by men to the lawful administration of the sacraments are condemned, not only those that are contrary to the Word of God and to the doctrine and discipline of this reformed Church, but also those that are beside them. Kneeling at the Lord's Supper does not conform to Christ's example, nor to the ordinary practice of this Church at the time when it sealed that Confession. It is a rite introduced by men, beside the Word of God, or if not against it, and it was finally introduced in 1618.

units.la: De diebus illis festis. Libro primæ disciplinæ, cap.1. Censetur; festa nativitatis, circumcisionis, Epiphaniæ & cæt. Apostolorum, Martyrum & B. Virginis Mariæ penitus abolenda esse, cum eorum observatio nullibi à Deo in scripturis imperetur; rogandos itaque esse magistratus, ut hic obnitentes civili authoritate coerceat: In Synodo nationali Edenburgena anno 1566.Major illa confessio Helvetica in omnibus comprobatur, excepto articulo de diebus festis: Porro cum reformatæ in Helvetia ecclesiæ, licet festa illa celebrent, à superstitione Pontificia sibi caveant; evidenter colligitur, omnem omnimodo dierum illorum observationem rejectam fuisse ab hujus ecclesiæ reformatoribus; quorum vestigia pressêrunt posteri, nam ann. 1575. in Synodo nationali male acceptum fuit, quod Pastores quidam & Lectores in tractu Abredonensi populum convocarent ad conciones & preces publicas diebus illis festivis; ac in mandatis datum à Synodo Nationali anni 1577. Ecclesiarum visitatoribus, ut interdicerent pastoribus administrationem S. Cœnæ temporibus illis festivis; quasi majoris efficaciæ sint sacramenta tum celebrata. Denique constans hæc fuit pastorum omnium sententia; Solum diem Dominicum festivum esse & Deo sacrum. Referebant alii Regem Iacobum in synodoNationali anni 1590. publicè Deo gratias egisse, quod rex esset in ecclesia totius orbis purissima: imo quæ Genevensem ipsam superet, nam (inquit) colunt Genevenses festa Nativitatis & Paschatis, qua autem authoritate id faciant, ipsi viderint.
units.tr: On those festival days. In the first book of discipline, chapter 1, it is judged that the festivals of the Nativity, the Circumcision, the Epiphany, and the rest, and those of the Apostles, the Martyrs and the Blessed Virgin Mary, are to be wholly abolished, since their observance is nowhere commanded by God in Scripture; and therefore the magistrates are to be asked to restrain those who resist this by civil authority. In the national Synod of Edinburgh in 1566 the greater Helvetic Confession was approved in all points, except the article on festival days. Moreover, since the reformed Churches in Helvetia, although they keep those festivals, guard themselves against Papist superstition, it is clearly gathered that the observance of those days in any way whatever was rejected by the reformers of this Church. Their successors followed in their footsteps. For in the national Synod of 1575 it was ill received that certain ministers and readers in the Aberdeen district gathered the people to sermons and public prayers on those festival days. And in 1577 the national Synod gave a mandate to the visitors of the Churches that they should forbid ministers to administer the Lord's Supper at those festal times, as if the sacraments celebrated then were of greater efficacy. Finally, this was the settled opinion of all the ministers: that only the Lord's Day is a festival and sacred to God. Some reported that King James, in the national Synod of 1590, had publicly given thanks to God that the king was in the purest Church in the whole world; indeed, that it surpassed even Geneva itself, for (he said) the Genevans keep the festivals of the Nativity and Easter; but by what authority they do so, they themselves must see.

units.la: De Episcopali Confirmatione. Refertur ad quinque ista Pontificiorum spuria sacramenta, expresse in confessione abjurata: Quia confessione ea damnatur Episcopatus, damnatur etiam Impositio manuum per Episcopos: Neque ulla illius vel levissima mentio fit in Canonibus de Catechizatione juniorum.
units.tr: On episcopal confirmation. This is counted among those five spurious sacraments of the Papists, expressly renounced in the Confession. Because that Confession condemns episcopacy, it also condemns the laying on of hands by bishops. Nor is there any, even the slightest, mention of it in the canons concerning the catechizing of the young.

units.la: De Administratione sacramentorum in privatis locis extra templa publico Dei cultui destinata. In liturgia Psalteriis metricis proposita, expresse dicitur Sacramenta à Deo non esse instituta ut in privatis angulis administrentur, (uti consueverunt magi ac incantatores) verum publice pro populo: Ac 1581. quo anno obsignata fuit haec Confessio, decretum fuit in synodo Nationali, in privatis aedibus Nefas esse Sacramenta administrare; Ac suspensum fuisse postea à functione pastorali pastorem Trajentensem, quod in privatis aedibus infantem baptizasset; hujus culpae publicam poenitentiam professum tantum functioni restituendum decrevit Synodus: Quibus satis compertum est, Ecclesiam Scoticam abominatam fuisse, quaecunque fovérent opinionem heterodoxam de necessitate Baptismi, & S. Cœnæ tanquam viatici.
units.tr: On the administration of the sacraments in private places, outside the churches set apart for public worship of God. In the liturgy, in the metrical psalters, it is expressly said that the sacraments were not instituted by God to be administered in private corners (as magicians and enchanters have been accustomed to do), but publicly, for the people. And in 1581, the year in which this Confession was sealed, it was decreed in the national Synod that it was wrong to administer the sacraments in private houses. The minister of Trajent was afterwards suspended from his pastoral office because he had baptized an infant in a private house; the Synod decreed that he should be restored to his office only after he had professed public repentance for this fault. From these things it is sufficiently clear that the Scottish Church abhorred whatever fostered the heterodox opinion about the necessity of baptism and of the Lord's Supper as viaticum.

units.la: Prælecto hoc scripto, libertas cuilibet concessa fuit arguendi, & de proposito themate libere disputandi; unus solum prodiit, qui quaestus[?] fuit male formatum esse quaestionis statum; Nam quaerere an Articuli hi removendi essent juxta sensum genuinum Confessionis primitus obsignatae juramento solennis, idem esset ac, an quicunque articulos illos in praxin redegerint post nationale illud juramentum perjuri essent? Respondet Praeses. Quaestionem à se propositam nihil tale secum ferre. Ad suffragia cum deventum effet; Omnes (eo solo excepto qui difficultate diffi-cultatē movit de statu quaestionis) respondent, Abjuratos fuisse illos articulos in confessione, & removendos esse: Quare Synodus decrevit ne quis iis posthac uteretur, neque eas defenderet.
units.tr: When this paper had been read, freedom was granted to anyone to argue and to dispute freely on the proposed theme. Only one came forward, who complained that the state of the question had been badly framed. For to ask whether these articles ought to be removed according to the genuine sense of the Confession first sealed by solemn oath would be the same as asking whether all who had put those articles into practice after that national oath were perjured. The president replied that the question he had proposed carried no such implication. When they came to a vote, all (except the one who had raised the difficulty about the state of the question) answered that those articles had been renounced in the Confession and were to be removed. Therefore the Synod decreed that no one should henceforth use them or defend them.

units.la: Remotis corruptelis, consultum esse suggestum fuit novos Canones ordini & disciplinae servientes condere, praesertim cum purioris disciplinae ignari essent complures, ob synodorum quadraginta annis exactis infrequentiam,quando omnia Episcoporum arbitrio circumagerentur. Quare designati sunt quidam à Synodo; qui omnium consilia in hunc finem colligerent, ac in ordinem redacta Synodo proponerent.
units.tr: With the corruptions removed, it was suggested that it was advisable to draw up new canons serving order and discipline, especially since many were ignorant of purer discipline, owing to the infrequency of synods over the forty years that had passed, when everything was managed at the will of the bishops. Therefore certain men were appointed by the Synod, who were to gather the counsels of all to this end, and to bring them into order and propose them to the Synod.

units.la: Posthæc quorundam Episcoporum cáusæ examinantur. Episcopo Edenburgeno objectum, præter illa quæ ipsi cum omnibus Episcopis esset communia, quod libros Canonum & liturgiæ, aliasque novitates non solum exemplo & praxi comprobasset; verum etiam pastoribus severe obtrusisset, quod nullum ad sacri ministerii functionem admitteret, nisi qui prius ordinem Diaconatus suscipiret: quod coram altari genuflecteret, quod rocheto, & aliis istis Missaticorum vestibus in sacris usus esset, quod templa more Romano consecrasset, quod facultatem concesserit celebrandi matrimonia licet trinundina denunciatio non præcessisset; quo quampluribus multum damni cessit: quod ritu Elevationis in S. cœnæ administratione solenniter usus fuisset, quod heterodoxiam in pastoribus quibusdam Edenburgensis, indulgentia sua & conniventia foverit, & quod ipse portentum ubiquitatis in scriptis suis typis commissis defenderit: Ob quæ, cum liquido probata essent; atque protestatione contra Synodum, pervicaciæ crimen addidisset; ab omni ecclesiastica functione deponendum, atque excommunicandum decrevit Synodus.
units.tr: After this the cases of certain bishops were examined. Charged against the bishop of Edinburgh, besides those things which were common to him with all the bishops, was that he had not only approved by example and practice the books of canons and of the liturgy and other novelties, but had also severely imposed upon the ministers that he would admit no one to the function of the sacred ministry unless he first received the order of deacon; that he knelt before the altar; that he used the rochet and other such vestments of the Mass in sacred acts; that he consecrated churches after the Roman manner; that he gave permission to celebrate marriages even when the threefold proclamation had not preceded, from which much harm came to many; that he solemnly used the rite of elevation in administering the Lord's Supper; that by his indulgence and connivance he fostered heterodoxy in certain ministers of Edinburgh; and that in his writings committed to print he defended the monstrous doctrine of ubiquity. Since these charges were clearly proved, and since he had added the crime of obstinacy by a protest against the Synod, the Synod decreed that he should be deposed from all ecclesiastical function and excommunicated.

units.la: Aberdonensi Episcopo objectum præter vulgaria Episcoporum crimina, flagrantis Simoniæ scandalum, quod libros illos Canonum & liturgiæ pastoribus obtrusisset, quod pastores à ministerii functione suspenderit, quia die Dominico jejunium publicum celebrassent; quod in Synodis provincialibus tyrannidem exercuisset, ac in iis Canones de jejuniis condiderit, pastoribus non consultis: quod Capellas superstitiose dedicasset; quod Pontificios, & incestus scandalo flagrantes ab ecclesiasticis censuris, reluctante ecclesia, liberasset: Addebant alii, malitiosæ apostasiæ crimen fœdum; nam licet olim disciplinæ purioris acerrimus esset propugnator, ac præfervido zelo collegis gravis fuisset; postea tamen tempori & scenae serviens, Episcoporum conatibus promovendis sese totum tradiderit: Quare ab omni functione ecclesiastica deponitur ac Excommunicandus decernitur.
units.tr: Charged against the bishop of Aberdeen, besides the common crimes of bishops, was the scandal of flagrant simony; that he had imposed those books of canons and of the liturgy upon the ministers; that he had suspended ministers from the function of the ministry because they had kept a public fast on the Lord's Day; that he had exercised tyranny in the provincial synods, and had drawn up canons on fasts there without consulting the ministers; that he had superstitiously dedicated chapels; and that, against the wishes of the Church, he had freed Papists and persons notorious for incest from ecclesiastical censures. Others added the foul crime of malicious apostasy: for although once he had been a most zealous champion of purer discipline, and had been a severe rebuke to his colleagues with his fervent zeal, afterwards, serving the times and the stage, he gave himself wholly over to promoting the efforts of the bishops. Therefore he is deposed from all ecclesiastical function and decreed to be excommunicated.

units.la: Episcopo Rossensi objectum, praeter ea quae Episcopis omnibus fuere communia quod hisce annis praeteritis liturgiam Anglicanam in ecclesia sua cathedrali praelegerit, coram altari genuflecteret, superstitiosis istis ac sordidis missaticorum vestibus indutus sacra peregisset, pios ac doctos Euangelii ministros deposuisset, surrogatis in eorum locum indoctis ac profanis scortatoribus: quod singulari familiaritate Papistas amplecteretur; quod insignis esset aleator, ac diebus Dominicis, iisque etiam quibus Sacra Domini Coena administrabatur, alearum & chartarum lusu usus fuerit; quod vasallos crudeliter expilasset, multis ad extremam inopiam & miseriam redactis; quod stata jejunia diebus Veneris indixisset; Diem Dominicum ordinarie profanasset, ac deserto verbi ministerio, Politicis negotiis in aula & senatu totum sese mancipasset, quod Pontificiorum errores plurimos eosque crassiores, ac omnes Remonstrantium heterodoxias publice tum per se, tum per asseclas[?] suos defenderit; quod omnium calamitatum, quibus jamdiu praesa[?] fuit tam ecclesia quam regnum, primarius author ac conciliator fuisset; Denique cum criminibus hisce, quae usque adeo aperta fuerunt, ut probatione vix indigerent, extremam pertinaciam, & ecclesiae contemptum probrosa ista protestatione contra Synodum, addidisset, unanimi omnium judicio indignus censetur functione qualibet ecclesiastica, ac pro infami habendus, ac excommunicandus.
units.tr: The Bishop of Ross was charged, besides the faults common to all bishops, with having read the English liturgy in his cathedral church in recent years; with genuflecting before the altar and performing the sacred offices vested in those superstitious and filthy mass vestments; with deposing pious and learned ministers of the gospel and putting in their place ignorant and profane whoremongers; with showing singular familiarity toward the Papists; with being a notorious gambler, and playing games of dice and cards on the Lord's Day, including days on which the Lord's Supper was administered; with cruelly plundering his vassals, reducing many to extreme poverty and misery; with appointing set fasts on Fridays; with habitually profaning the Lord's Day and, neglecting the ministry of the Word, devoting himself entirely to political affairs in the court and the Senate; with publicly defending very many, and very gross, errors of the Papists, and all the heterodoxies of the Remonstrants, both by himself and through his followers; and with being the chief author and promoter of all the calamities by which both the Church and the kingdom have long been afflicted. Finally, to these crimes, which were so open that they hardly needed proof, he added extreme obstinacy and contempt of the Church, by that shameful protest against the Synod. By the unanimous judgment of all he is judged unworthy of any ecclesiastical function, and is to be held infamous and excommunicated.

units.la: Seff. 18. Decemb. 11. Die Martis.
units.tr: Session 18. 11 December, Tuesday.

units.la: Examinatur causa Episcopi Orcadum. Objectum, præter perfidam stipulatarum cautionum violationem, quod illi cum aliis omnibus episcopis commune fuit, quod diem Dominicum publice profanasset; quod ecclesiæ bona in filiorum & generorum gratiam non sine sacrilegio dilapidasset, quod ecclesiasticas censuras non exercuerit in adulteros, ac sortilegos, quod in fabricam Cathedralis templi à pastoribus pecunias extorserit: & cæt. verum cum epistola ad Synodum missa, ejus censuræ sese submissurum, nec unquam novitates ab Episcopis obtrusas sibi placuisse declarasset; ab omni functione ecclesiastica deponitur, ac nisi feriæ pœnitentiæ signa exhibeat, à deputatis synodi excommunicandus declaratur.
units.tr: The case of the Bishop of Orkney was examined. He was charged, besides his treacherous violation of the sworn undertakings, with the faults he shared with all the other bishops: that he publicly profaned the Lord's Day; that he squandered the goods of the Church, not without sacrilege, for the benefit of his sons and sons-in-law; that he did not exercise ecclesiastical censures against adulterers and sorcerers; that he extorted money from the ministers for the building of the cathedral church; and so on. However, since he sent a letter to the Synod declaring that he would submit to its censures, and that he had never approved of the innovations thrust upon the bishops, he is deposed from every ecclesiastical function, and, unless he shows signs of repentance within the set period, he is declared by the Synod's deputies to be excommunicated.

units.la: Moraviensi episcopo præter vulgaria Episcoporum omnium crimina, objicitur, quod ille primus ausus fuerit superpelliceo indutus sacra peragere, in primario Edenburgenæ civitatis templo, anno 1633. professus se in regis gratiam, quem palpabat, viliorem adhuc futurum: Ab omni ecclesiastica functione removetur; nequaquam tamen excommunicandus, nisi Synodi judicio sese submittere renuat:
units.tr: The Bishop of Moray, besides the common crimes of all bishops, was charged with being the first to dare to perform the sacred offices wearing a surplice, in the chief church of the city of Edinburgh, in the year 1633, and with professing that he would become even more worthless for the sake of the king, whom he flattered. He is removed from every ecclesiastical function, but is not to be excommunicated unless he refuses to submit to the judgment of the Synod.

units.la: Glasguensi Archiepiscopo, præter ea quæ ipsi cum collegis essent communia objectum; quod in provinciali synodo pastoribus omnibus fere reclamantibus, decreverit librum Canonum novitatibus refertum, esse recipiendum, quod sub pœna perduellionis pastoribus mandaret, ut librum liturgiæ obtrusum publice legerent, quod à pastoribus pecunias extorserit, quod aliis stipendium non persolvisset, quod officia juridica curiæ commissarionatus (quæ ecclesiastica dicitur) venum expos-uisset; quod vassallos suos avare & crudeliter vexasset, ac ministerii candidatis concionandi facultate interdixisset, nisi primum futiles quasdam juramentorum formulas à se ipso excogitatas, chirographis obsignassent: Quare ab omni functione ecclesiastica deponitur; ac excommunicandus censetur, nisi mature pœnitentiam professus fuerit, ac synodi judicio se submiserit.
units.tr: The Archbishop of Glasgow was charged, besides the faults he shared with his colleagues: that in a provincial synod, when nearly all the ministers objected, he decreed that the book of canons, full of innovations, should be received; that under penalty of treason he commanded the ministers to read publicly the liturgy book thrust upon them; that he extorted money from the ministers; that he did not pay the stipends of others; that he put up for sale the judicial offices of the commissary court, which is called ecclesiastical; that he greedily and cruelly harassed his vassals; and that he forbade ministerial candidates to preach unless they first sealed with their signatures certain trivial formulas of oaths devised by himself. For these reasons he is deposed from every ecclesiastical function, and is judged to be excommunicated unless he promptly professes repentance and submits to the judgment of the Synod.

units.la: Argathelienfi Episcopo crimini datum, præter communia collegarum vitia, quod in illegitima quædam jamenta pastores adegisset, ac librum liturgiæ obtrufiffet; Diem Dominicum profanaffet, atque ut tempori serviret, heterodoxias Arminianorum, quas olim damnabat, publice defendisset; Multorum animos qui hominem antea familiariter noverant, ingens subiit admiratio, quibus artibus factum, ut tam subito mutaretur, nam certissimis indiciis compertum fuit, eorum dogmatum quæ alibi strenue promoventur, nullum ipsi nunc displicere: Sed φιλοπμία δεινὸν κακὸν, vitiorum origo, tinea sanctitatis, excæcatrix cordium; quoisque nulla potuit movere luxuria, nulla subruere avaritia, mentis hæc ærugo Ambitio criminosos facit.
units.tr: The Bishop of Argyll was charged, besides the common vices of his colleagues, with having compelled ministers to take certain illegitimate oaths and with having thrust the liturgy book upon them; with having profaned the Lord's Day; and, to serve the times, with having publicly defended the heterodoxies of the Arminians, which he had once condemned. Many who had formerly known the man intimately were greatly amazed by the means by which he had been so suddenly changed; for it was established by the most certain evidence that he now disliked none of those doctrines which are vigorously promoted elsewhere. But [φιλοπμία δεινὸν κακὸν], "love of power is a dreadful evil," the source of vices, the moth of holiness, the blinder of hearts. What luxury could not move, what avarice could not overthrow, this rust of the mind, ambition, makes criminal.

units.la: Infularum Episcopo nihil objectum præter communia Episcoporum crimina. Censura depositionis in utrumque decernitur:
units.tr: Nothing was charged against the Bishop of the Isles except the crimes common to bishops. Deposition from office is decreed against both of them.

units.la: Episcoporum agmen claudebant censuræ in Paftores quosdam, Episcoporum quorum libidini se mancipaverant, afflectas. Iohannes Matthius gravissima heterodoxias infamia jam pridem celebris, quam ex sinu Sinserfii Gallovidiani & Maxwellii Rollensis episcopi hauserat, tanquam sal infatuatus, ministerii functione deponitur: Probatum, eum publice tutatum fuisse omnes Arminianorum heterodoxias, ac preces pro mortuis, descensum localem animæ Christi ad inferos, damnationem infantum sine baptismo decedentium, baptismi opus operarum; se teneri missam Pontificiam celebrare si ita manmandet rex. Quibus superbum Presbyterii seu Classis despectum superaddidit.
units.tr: Closing the ranks of the bishops were the censures laid upon certain ministers who had given themselves over to the lusts of the bishops. John Mathie, long notorious for the most serious infamy of heterodoxy, which he had drawn in from the bosom of Sinserf, Bishop of Galloway, and Maxwell, Bishop of Ross, like salt that had lost its savour, is deprived of the ministerial function. It was proved that he publicly defended all the heterodoxies of the Arminians, prayers for the dead, the local descent of the soul of Christ into hell, the damnation of infants dying without baptism, and the efficacy of baptism wrought by the act itself; and that he was bound to celebrate Papist mass if the king so commanded. To these he added a proud contempt for the presbytery, or classis.

units.la: Aliorum quorundam pastorum causæ examinatæ, & extrema sententiæ dictio ad Synodi deputatos relata fuit; Verum Thomæ Fosteri Mulrossensis pastoris causa nequaquam silentio involvenda: Classe Mulrossiana accusante probatum fuit, sæpius publice asseruisse, licere opera quaslibet servilia die Dominico peragere; exemploque suo auditoribus suis præivisse; ut messem die illo sacro ex agris in horrea conveherent; Quartum præceptum nullatenus fuisse morale, aliter statuentes, homines ad Iudaismum reducere: quod per templum suum pecora ordinarie deduci juberet; quod demolita mensa lignea celebrationi Dominicæ Cœnæ destinata, & in vilissimos usus conversa, altare cancellis circumclusum erexerit; intra quos ipse stans, populo à sancti hujus sanctorum aditu prohibito, porrigebat sacramentum: Quod dixisset curiosum esse disquirere an Christus ibi præsens esset sacramentaliter, an vero per transubstantiationem & consubstantiationem: Quod profanis contumeliis publicam & ordinariam verbi divini prædicationem lacesseret, eamque nullam publici cultus divini partem necessariam; lectionique liturgiæ obtrusæ postponendam, (quam corruptelis omnibus vacuam, & absolutissimam cultus divini formulam) afferebat. Quod ecclesiarum omnium pastores publice, & Christiani omnes privatim, orationum formulis in libro liturgiæ præscriptis, iisque solis uti debeant: Quod in propriis suis ædibus sæpius baptizasset; Quod Arminianorum & pontificiorum heterodoxias auditoribus suis obtrusisset; Quod convitiorum plaustra in beatos Ecclesiarum reformatores publice & privatim conjecisset, quos plus detrimenti pauculis quibus vixerunt annis, Ecclesiis Christianis intulisse affirmabat, quam PonPontifex Romanus cum factione Papali, decem integris sæculis: Atque hæc sunt tantum specimina, profundæ illius Theologiæ, & insignis pietatis, quam Hierarchici eorumque asseclæ tam plenis buccis crepant; Multorum animos tum subiit recordatio illius quod venerabilis Beza non sine prophetiæ spiritu olim rescripsit Cnoxo, ecclesiæ Scoticæ reformatori, Sicut Episcopi papatum pepererunt, ita oculis pene ipsis jam cernitur Pseudo-Episcopos, Papatus reliquias, Epicureissimum terris invecturos[?]. Cujus certissimi vaticinii eventum parum abfuit quin Ecclesiæ Scoticæ plene expertæ essent, nisi Deus optimus maximus populi sui scelerum oblitus, iram placabilis leniisset, tristitiæque nube repulsa, exerto brachio signum ostendisset liberandi ecclesiam sponsam filii sui ab ejusmodi pestiferis carcinomatibus ejus viscera tamdiu impune exedentibus.
units.tr: The cases of certain other ministers were examined, and the final sentence was referred to the Synod's deputies. But the case of Thomas Foster, minister of Mulross, must not be passed over in silence. The Mulross classis, as accuser, proved that he had often publicly asserted that it is lawful to perform any servile work on the Lord's Day, and by his own example had led his hearers to bring in the harvest from the fields into the barns on that holy day; that the fourth commandment was in no way moral, those who held otherwise leading men back to Judaism; that he ordinarily ordered cattle to be led through his church; that, having demolished the wooden table destined for the celebration of the Lord's Supper and turned to the basest uses, he erected an altar enclosed by rails, within which he himself stood and administered the sacrament, the people being forbidden access to this holy of holies; that he said it was a curious matter to inquire whether Christ is present there sacramentally, or indeed by transubstantiation or consubstantiation; that he assailed the public and regular preaching of the divine Word with profane insults, and declared it to be no necessary part of public worship, and that it ought to be postponed to the reading of the liturgy, which he described as the most perfect form of divine worship, free of all corruptions; that the ministers of all the churches publicly, and all Christians privately, ought to use the prayer forms prescribed in the liturgy book, and those alone; that he often baptized in his own house; that he thrust the heterodoxies of the Arminians and the Papists upon his hearers; and that he publicly and privately heaped carts full of abuse upon the blessed reformers of the Churches, whom he affirmed had done more harm to the Christian Churches in the few years they lived than the Roman Pontiff with the Papal faction had done in ten full centuries. These, then, are only samples of that profound theology and remarkable piety which the hierarchs and their followers boast of with full cheeks. Then many were reminded of what the venerable Beza, not without a spirit of prophecy, once wrote to Knox, the reformer of the Scottish Church: As the bishops gave birth to the papacy, so we now see with our own eyes that pseudo-bishops, remnants of the papacy, will bring the most Epicurean life into the lands. The fulfilment of this most certain prophecy came close to befalling the Scottish Church, fully experienced by it, had not God, the best and greatest, forgotten the sins of his people, and, appeased in his anger, dispelled the cloud of sorrow and, with his arm stretched out, shown the sign of freeing the Church, the bride of his Son, from such pestilential cancers which had so long devoured her vitals with impunity.

units.la: Sess. 19. Decemb. 12. Die Mercurii.
units.tr: Session 19. 12 December, Wednesday.

units.la: Examinantur causæ Episcoporum, Caledonii & Cathanesiæ: præter communia Episcoporum crimina, objectum fuit Simoniæ scandalum utrique. Sed quia Synodi censuræ se submiserant, à functione Episcopali depositi solum sunt: & Caledonio gratia facta est pastoralis functionis in ecclesia Sancti Madoci:
units.tr: The cases of the Bishops of Caithness and of Caledonia were examined. Besides the common crimes of bishops, the scandal of simony was charged against both. But because they had submitted to the censures of the Synod, they were deposed only from the episcopal function; and the favour was granted to the Bishop of Caledonia of retaining the pastoral function in the church of St Madoc.

units.la: Tandem ad examen vocatur Episcopus Dumblanensis:qui non ita pridem in Angliam profugerat: ei objectum, præter communia Episcoporum vitia, quod cum Roffensi episcopo strenuam operam navasset in formandis libris Canonum & liturgiæ; quos severe pastoribus obtrusit, ac toto Episcopatus tempore ita se gesserit, quasi volupe sibi fuisset ecclesiam cum fastu calcasse; quod flagranti ebrietatis, profanationis nominis divini & diei Dominicæ, scandalo teneretur: Quod, cum Professorem egisset S S. Theologiæ in Academia Andreapolitana, solenne illi fuisset pleraque in reformatis ecclesiis recepta dogmata publice privatimque sugillare, & auditoribus suspecta reddere; Pontificiorum & Arminianorum scripta extollere, & discipulis suis imprimis commendare: Quibus sic praeparatis, virus ipsum pleni Arminianismi, & complurium heterodoxiarum Pontificiarum instillabat, unde factum ut multorum auditorum ingenia corruperit, ac pravis opinionibus imbuerit; cujus mali vim omnes regni partes adhuc sentiant: Una voce omnium, ab omni ecclesiastica functione statim deponendus, ac excommunicandus censetur.
units.tr: At last the Bishop of Dunblane, who had not long before fled into England, was called to examination. He was charged, besides the common vices of bishops, with having laboured vigorously with the Bishop of Ross in forming the books of canons and liturgy, which he imposed severely upon the ministers; with having conducted himself throughout his episcopate as if it had been a pleasure to him to trample the Church under pride; with being guilty of a notorious scandal of drunkenness, and of profaning the name of God and the Lord's Day; that, when he was professor of sacred theology in the University of St Andrews, it was his habit to disparage, publicly and privately, most of the doctrines received in the reformed Churches, and to render them suspect to his hearers; to extol the writings of the Papists and Arminians, and especially to commend them to his students. Having thus prepared the way, he instilled the very poison of full Arminianism and of many Papist heterodoxies, whereby he corrupted the minds of many of his hearers and imbued them with pernicious opinions; the force of this evil all parts of the kingdom still feel. By the unanimous voice of all, he is judged to be deposed at once from every ecclesiastical function, and to be excommunicated.

units.la: Decretum fuit Synodi sententiam de Episcopis die sequenti publice pronunciandam esse per Synodi praesidem.
units.tr: It was decreed that the Synod's sentence concerning the bishops was to be publicly pronounced the following day by the president of the Synod.

units.la: Sess. 20. Decemb. 13. Die Iovis.
units.tr: Session 20. 13 December. Thursday.

units.la: Praeses ex Synodi praescripto elegantem & gravem concionem habuit ex Psalmi 110. vers. 1. Dixit Iehova Domino meo, sede ad dexteram meam donec posuero inimicos tuos in scabellum pedum tuorum: Dein sententiam Synodi promulgavit, qua ab omni functione ecclesiastica depositi excommunicabantur. Iohannes Spotswodus Archiepiscopus Andreapolitanus, Patricius Lindesius Archiepiscopus Glasguensis, D. David Lindesius Episcopus Edenburgenus, Thomas Sidserfius Gallovidianus, Iohannes Maxwellus Rossensis, Walterus Whytfoordius Brechinensis, Adamus Bannatinus Abredonensis, Iacobus Wedderburnus Dumblanensis. In alios quatuor sola depositionis ab omni omnino ecclesiastica functione sententia pronunciabatur, vid: in Iohannem Guthereum Moravienfem, Iohannem Gramium Orcadensem, Iacobum Fairlium Argathelienfem seu Lismorensem[?], & Nigellum Cambellum Insularum Episcopos. Praeterea lata est in Episcopos Alexandrü Lindesiü Caledonium,
units.tr: Following the Synod's prescription, the president preached an elegant and weighty sermon on Psalm 110, verse 1: "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool." He then promulgated the Synod's sentence, by which the deposed were excommunicated and removed from every ecclesiastical function. These were John Spottiswood, Archbishop of St Andrews; Patrick Lindsay, Archbishop of Glasgow; Dr David Lindsay, Bishop of Edinburgh; Thomas Sydserf, Bishop of Galloway; John Maxwell, Bishop of Ross; Walter Whitford, Bishop of Brechin; Adam Bannatyne, Bishop of Aberdeen; and James Wedderburn, Bishop of Dunblane. Against four others the sentence pronounced was deposition from every ecclesiastical function, and nothing more: John Guthrie, Bishop of Moray; John Gram, Bishop of Orkney; James Fairlie, Bishop of Argyll or Lismore [?]; and Neil Campbell, Bishop of the Isles. Moreover, a sentence was passed against Alexander Lindsay, Bishop of Caledonia,

units.la: & Ioannem Abrenethium Cathanefium [?] sententia depositionis ab Episcopatu; ita tamen ut legitime vocati ad munus pastorale unius gregis, eam functionem exercendi per synodum iis gratia facta sit: Sententiam synodi in sex primos, decretum est in omnibus totius regni ecclesiis pronunciandam esse ab ecclesiarum pastoribus. Atque hic exitus telae quam tam solerti vafritie tamdiu texebant: Tremendus certe est Dominus in iudiciis suis, dum eorum faciem ignominia opplevit, ac tam subito de culmine mundanae felicitatis praecipitavit, qui mediocri fortuna non contenti, firmam stabilitatem non nisi in extrema tyrannide obtineri posse, futiliter sibi persuaserant: hodie experientia comprobatum illud Psalm.73.
units.tr: and against John Abernethy, Bishop of Caithness [?], a sentence of deposition from the episcopate. Yet this was done in such a way that the Synod granted them leave to exercise the pastoral function of their own flock, since they had been lawfully called to it. It was decreed that the Synod's sentence against the first six was to be pronounced in all the churches of the whole kingdom by the ministers of those churches. And this was the outcome of the web they had woven for so long with such clever cunning. Certainly the Lord is terrible in his judgments: he has covered their faces with shame and so suddenly hurled down from the height of worldly prosperity those who, not content with a moderate fortune, had vainly persuaded themselves that firm stability could be obtained only through extreme tyranny. Today experience has confirmed that saying of Psalm 73:

units.la: Vidi repente quam pede lubrico Starent superbi, quam stabiles parum Opes tenerent, quam fragili loco Fultos ruina praecipiti trahas.
units.tr: I have suddenly seen how on slippery feet the proud stood, how little stable their wealth held, how from a fragile place, by headlong ruin, you drag down those who were propped up.

units.la: Eadem sessione Guilelmus Annahus [?] Airensis ecclesiae pastor multorum criminum arcessitur; malitiosae desertionis ecclesiae suae octo continuis mensibus; quod in Sanctorum honorem festa confecranda asseruisset; quod in synodo Provinciali concione publica librum liturgiae obtrusum summis laudibus prosequutus fuisset, precesque omnes conceptas prout afflaverit spiritus, contumeliis exagitasset, & c cæt. Deponendum à functione pastorali decrevit Synodus: Eademque censura fertur in Thomam Mackenizium; archidiaconum Roffensem, cujus facta est supra mentio, ad Sess. 5. ac in Robertum Hammiltonium, cujus causa sess. 13. examinata fuit.
units.tr: In the same session, William Annand, minister of the church of Ayr, was summoned on many charges: for malicious desertion of his church for eight continuous months; for having maintained that festivals should be kept in honour of the saints; for having praised the printed liturgy book with the highest commendation in a public sermon at the provincial synod; and for having reviled with insults all the prayers he conceived as the spirit moved him, and so on. The Synod decreed that he be deposed from the pastoral function. The same censure was passed against Thomas Mackenzie, archdeacon of Ross, of whom mention was made above, in Session 5, and against Robert Hamilton, whose case was examined in Session 13.

units.la: Sess. 21. Decemb. 14. Die Veneris.
units.tr: Session 21. 14 December. Friday.

units.la: Post examinatas pastorum quorundam presby-terii terii Lanarcensis causas, pastores quidam qui protestationi contra Synodum subscripserant, poenitentiam profitentur; se ignaros ad male sana haec consilia illectos fuisse; quare cum lachrymis Synodum obtestabantur, ut liceret nomina sua expungere, quandoquidem apud se jam decreverint, synodi authoritatem esse legitimam: Horum votis annuit Synodus.
units.tr: After the cases of some ministers of the presbytery of Lanark had been examined, certain ministers who had subscribed the protest against the Synod professed repentance. They said they had been ignorant and had been enticed into these ill-advised counsels. Therefore, with tears, they begged the Synod to allow them to erase their names, since they had now judged within themselves that the authority of the Synod is lawful. The Synod granted their prayers.

units.la: Nobiliss. Victoniæ, seu Wigtomensis Comes, Senator regius, quod antea per Comitem Montis Rosarum synodo Seff. 8. significari curavit, hac sessione, cum Synodo interesset, repetebat; videl. Se quidem Confessioni à Rege imperatae subscripsisse, sed hac expressa conditione, ut secundum mentem majorum primitus sancientium annis 1580.&1590 explicaretur; quare cum necessaria hac opera eruendi genuinum sensum articulorum quorundam controversorum defuncta sit synodus; ejus sententiae libenter se submittere, doctrinamque ac disciplinam, uti à synodo praesenti explicata est, amplecti, summisque votis utriusque authorem Deum obtestari, ne à tam sancto consilio vel tantillum deflectat.
units.tr: The most noble Earl of Wigtown, or Wigtonensis, a royal councillor, who had earlier had the Synod informed of his position through the Earl of Montrose in Session 8, repeated it in this session, being present at the Synod. Namely, he had indeed subscribed the Confession imposed by the King, but on this express condition: that it be explained according to the mind of the fathers who first sanctioned it in the years 1580 and 1590. Therefore, since the Synod had finished this necessary task of bringing out the genuine sense of certain controverted articles, he willingly submitted himself to its judgment, embraced the doctrine and discipline as the present Synod had explained them, and with the most earnest prayers besought God, the author of both, that he would not turn aside even a little from so holy a counsel.

units.la: Alia quaedam minoris momenti negotia de translatione pastorum conclusa fuere; quibus enarrandis, ne taedio sim, lubens supersedeo.
units.tr: Some other matters of lesser importance, concerning the transfer of ministers, were concluded. I gladly pass over these, lest I weary the reader by recounting them.

units.la: Seff. 22. Decemb. 15. Die Saturni.
units.tr: Sessions 22. 15 December. Saturday.

units.la: Quandoquidem Pseudo-episcoporum usurpatione, legitima authoritas conventuum omnium ecclesiasticorum suppressa fuisset, qua ad extremum prope discrimen res ecclesiasticae redactae fuerunt; unanimi omnium sententia conventibus ecclesiasticis, hoc est, Synodis Nationalibus, Provincialibus, Presbyteriis seu Classibus, Sessionibus seu Consistoriis, postliminii jure legitima ea authoritas restituitur, quae in libris politiae ecclesiasticae iisdem competere judicatur : Diagramma presby-teriorum & provincialium synodorum constitutum fuit ; ac quibus statis temporibus synodi Provinciales coirent : Decretum etiam ut viciniores synodi correspondentiam (ut ita loquar) amicam alerent ; mutua delegatione duorum deputatorum.
units.tr: Since, through the usurpation of the pseudo-bishops, the lawful authority of all ecclesiastical assemblies had been suppressed, and ecclesiastical affairs had been brought almost to the brink of ruin, it was agreed unanimously that this lawful authority be restored to the ecclesiastical assemblies, namely the National Synods, Provincial Synods, Presbyteries or Classes, and Sessions or Consistories, by the right of postliminy. This authority is judged in the books of ecclesiastical polity to belong to them. A plan of presbyteries and provincial synods was drawn up, and the times at which the provincial synods were to meet were fixed. It was also decreed that neighbouring synods should maintain a friendly correspondence, so to speak, by the mutual delegation of two deputies each.

units.la: Ut, quæ maturo consilio à synodo hac conclusa fuere, executioni committerentur, ac quædã minoris momenti negotia, quæ in synodo commode satis peragi non potuerunt, felicius, ubi quæstiones ortæ fuerunt, expedirentur ; visum fuit eligere quosdam tum pastores tum seniores, quos Synodi Nationalis authoritate munitos, Synodi Deputatos vocant ; iisque mandatum, ut in provinciis designatis synodi mandata expedirent: Designati etiam qui Academiâ Abredonensem visitarent, ejus ad synodum legato instante, ac querente, tantum non oppressam fuisse miseram illam Academiam usurpatione Episcopi, qui reditus artium liberalium ac scientiarum professoribus destinatos transtulerit in Canonicos, prebendarios, juris Canonici Professores, & id genus damnatas à reformatis ecclesiis functiones.
units.tr: So that what this synod had concluded with mature deliberation might be carried into execution, and so that certain matters of lesser importance, which could not conveniently be finished in the synod, might be dealt with more successfully when questions arose, it was thought fit to choose certain ministers and elders, whom, armed with the authority of the National Synod, they call Deputies of the Synod. They were charged to carry out the synod's mandates in the designated provinces. Men were also appointed to visit the Academy of Aberdeen, at the urging of the synod's envoy, who complained that that wretched Academy had almost been crushed by the usurpation of a bishop, who had transferred the revenues destined for professors of the liberal arts and sciences to canons, prebendaries, professors of canon law, and that kind of office, which the reformed churches condemn.

units.la: Seff. 23. Decemb. 17. Die Lunæ.
units.tr: Session 23. December 17. Monday.

units.la: Decreta ac Canones præcedentium sessionum releguntur, quos concordibus suffragiis denuo ratos habuere quicunque tum aderant : Qui sess. 17. designati fuerant ad colligenda & in ordinem redigenda omnium gravamina vel consilia de novis canonibus ordini & decoro servituris, rationem diligentiæ suæ exhibent,ac significant,pauca fuisse proposita quæ salubri consilio non essent antea constituta, quæ tamen cum temporum iniquitate in desuetudinem abiverint ; consultissimum sibi visum esse eadem renovare ; quæ sententia omnibus probata fuit : Quare antiqui illi Canones ad pristinum vigorem restituti sunt : inter quos hi præcipui sunt :
units.tr: The decrees and canons of the preceding sessions were read out, and all who were then present ratified them again by unanimous vote. Those who had been appointed in session 17 to gather together and arrange in order all the grievances and proposals concerning new canons that would serve order and decorum gave an account of their diligence. They reported that few proposals had been made that had not already been settled by wholesome counsel in the past, but that these had fallen into disuse because of the wickedness of the times. They judged it most advisable to renew them, and this view was approved by all. Accordingly those ancient canons were restored to their former force. Among them the following are the most important:

units.la: De presbyteriis, ut vicinarum ecclesiarum conventus (quem Presbyterium seu Classem vocant) singulis septimanis semel habeatur tam mensibus hiemalibus quam æstivis; ut libri alicujus S. Scripturæ interpretatio publica habeatur, textum alius pastorum exponat, alius vero doctrinas inde eruat, & ad usus applicet; ut recurrente prima uniuscujusque mensis hebdomade, Pastores per vices controversum aliquod doctrinæ caput publice tractent, de quo amice & placide remoto populo inter fratres disputandum fit. De visitatione ecclesiarum: ut singulis annis semel ad minimum ecclesiarum omnium visitatio instituatur; ac tum diligenter inquiratur à visitatoribus, de exercitio cultus divini in familiis privatis; & quæ diligentia adhibeatur in catechizatione juniorum, in ecclesiis præsertim rusticanis. Ut pastores omnes domicilia figant in locis pastorum habitationi destinatis, ut severe non residentia interdicatur omnibus pastoribus. De visitatione Scholarum, Academiarum. De disciplina & moribus pastorum, eorumque prima promotione ad functionem ministerii.
units.tr: Concerning presbyteries: the meeting of neighbouring congregations, which they call the Presbytery or Classis, is to be held once a week, in winter and in summer alike. A public exposition of some book of Holy Scripture is to be given, one minister expounding the text and another drawing out the doctrines from it and applying them to use. In the first week of each month, the ministers in turn are to treat publicly some controverted head of doctrine, and it is to be debated among the brethren in a friendly and calm manner, with the people removed. Concerning the visitation of churches: a visitation of all the churches is to be carried out at least once a year, and the visitors are to inquire diligently into the practice of divine worship in private households, and into the care taken in catechising the young, especially in the country congregations. All ministers are to settle in the houses assigned to ministers' residence, and non-residence is severely forbidden to all ministers. Concerning the visitation of schools and universities. Concerning the discipline and conduct of ministers, and their first promotion to the office of the ministry.

units.la: De frequentiori administratione S. Cœnæ. De modo & viis supprimendi papatus reliquias contra diei Dominicæ profanationem; Et ut cum oppidorum magistratibus serio agatur, ut translatione nundinarum si obtineri possit, aut quovis alio remedio, impediant profanationem diei Dominicæ, quæ celebratione nundinarum diebus Saturni aut Lunæ sæpenumero accidit. Abstinendum esse à societate eorum in quos sententia excommunicationis lata est. Qui confessionem fidei in Synodo explicatam, aut synodum ipsam ejusve decreta petulanter sugillaverit, censuris ecclesiasticis obnoxium futurum. Ne pastores in Consistoriis, suffragii negativi jus sibi arrogent; cum pluralitate suffragiorum æquum fit omnia decerni, quæ ecclesiasticis canonibus non sunt contraria. Ne quis corruptos & fæces Papismi redolentes titulos usurpet, quales sunt: Capituli ejusque electio & consecratio, Abbatum, Priorum, Decanorum, Archidiaconorum, Diaconorum in verbi ministerio laborantium, Cantorum, Subcantorum: & hujus farinæ titulos qui à Pontifice Romano, ejusque jure Canonico dependent. Ne Pastores populo obtrudantur. Ne matrimonia absque trinundina & consueta bannarum (ut vocant) denunciatione celebrentur. Ne funebres conciones habeantur, ac elaborandum esse ne in templis funera sepulturæ tradantur.
