De examine promovendorum ad SS. ministerii functionem, eorumque justa ætate: ne videl. ante ætatis annum 25. promoveantur; nisi Synodo Nationali aut Provinciali compertum fuerit, illustria & singularia dona ætatem superasse: Promovendi exhibeant presbyterio à quo ad ministerii functionem admittendi sunt, testimoniales literas ab Academiis aut Presbyterio in quo vixerunt; quibus cognitum fiet, non solum quomodo se in moribus gesserint, verumetiam an præparatoriis illis privatarum & publicarum concionum exercitiis Presbyterio illi aut Theologiæ Professoribus satisfecerint: Porro hoc ordine examinandi sunt: Primum, specimen peritiæ in publicis concionibus exhibeant; ac exercitium illud classicale pastoribus usitatum peragant: Tum religionis caput controversum à classe designatum Latina oratione tractent, ac thesibus ad disputationem editis defendant: Dein respondeant ad quæstiones de aliis religionis capitibus in controversiam vocatis, de Chronologia Sacræ Scripturæ, de casibus conscientiæ, de sensu locorum S. Scripturæ, de reconciliatione apparentium contradictionum in S. Scriptura, de peritia linguarum Hebraicæ, & Græcæ. Sessione hac designantur visitatores Academiæ Glafguensis; & summa vehementia pastorum quorundam translationes ad frequentiores ecclesias urgentur.
units.tr: Concerning more frequent administration of the Lord's Supper. Concerning the manner and means of suppressing the remnants of popery, and against the profanation of the Lord's Day. The magistrates of the towns are to be dealt with seriously, so that, if it can be obtained, the fairs are transferred, or by some other remedy they prevent the profanation of the Lord's Day, which very often happens when fairs are held on Saturdays or Mondays. One must abstain from fellowship with those against whom the sentence of excommunication has been pronounced. Whoever wantonly reviles the confession of faith set out in the Synod, or the Synod itself or its decrees, shall be liable to ecclesiastical censures. Ministers in consistories are not to claim for themselves a right of negative vote; since it is fitting that everything which is not contrary to the ecclesiastical canons be decided by a majority of votes. No one is to use corrupt titles that smell of the dregs of Popery, such as: chapter and its election and consecration; abbots, priors, deans, archdeacons, deacons labouring in the ministry of the Word, precentors, sub-precentors; and titles of this kind that depend upon the Roman Pontiff and his canon law. Ministers are not to be forced upon the people. Marriages are not to be celebrated without the threefold, or customary, announcement of banns (as they call it). Funeral sermons are not to be held, and care must be taken that in the churches burials are not handed over to the grave. Concerning the examination of those to be promoted to the function of the holy ministry, and their proper age: namely, that they are not to be promoted before the age of twenty-five, unless it has been made known to the National or Provincial Synod that illustrious and singular gifts have outstripped their age. Those to be promoted must present to the presbytery, by which they are to be admitted to the function of the ministry, testimonial letters from the universities or from the presbytery in which they have lived. By these it will be known not only how they have conducted themselves in morals, but also whether they have satisfied that presbytery or the professors of theology in those preparatory exercises of private and public preaching. Moreover, they are to be examined in this order: first, they are to show a sample of their skill in public preaching, and carry through that classical exercise customary for ministers; then they are to treat in Latin speech a controverted head of religion designated by the classis, and defend it by theses published for disputation; after that they are to answer questions on other heads of religion brought into controversy, on the chronology of Holy Scripture, on cases of conscience, on the sense of passages of Holy Scripture, on the reconciliation of apparent contradictions in Holy Scripture, and on skill in the Hebrew and Greek languages. In this session visitors of the University of Glasgow are appointed; and with great vehemence the transfer of certain ministers to more populous churches is urged.

units.la: Seff. 24. Decemb. 18. Die Martis.
units.tr: Session 24. December 18. Tuesday.

units.la: Excommunicandos decrevit Synodus Pastores eos, qui à functione pastorali hujus Synodi sententia depositi, pastoralis tamen muneris functiones obirent, ac contumaces sese contra Synodi authoritatem exhiberent. Alia quædam privata negotia agitata fuere, & discussum gravamen illud: An diebus Dominicis liceret salmonum piscaturam agere? Ex registris profertur Canon Synodi Nationalis ad S. Crucis coenobium anno 1602. quo diebusDominicis omnis omnino piscatura severe interdicitur, cui omnes acquiescendum esse censebant.
units.tr: The Synod decreed that ministers who, having been deposed from the pastoral office by the sentence of this Synod, nevertheless go on performing the functions of the pastoral office, and who show themselves obstinate against the authority of the Synod, are to be excommunicated. Certain other private matters were discussed, and that grievance was examined: whether it was lawful to carry on salmon fishing on the Lord's Days. From the registers was produced a canon of the National Synod held at the abbey of the Holy Cross in the year 1602, by which all fishing on the Lord's Days is severely forbidden, and to which they judged all must submit.

units.la: Seff. 25. Decemb. 19. Die Mercurii.
units.tr: Session 25. December 19. On Wednesday.

units.la: De functionibus civilibus ac authoritate politica eorum ecclesiasticorum qui verbi ministerio defunguntur, actum fuit: An liceret iis ut eirenarchis pro tribunali sedere? an sententiam ferre in parliamentis & senatu regio, in suprema causarum civilium curia, quam Sessionem seu Collegium justitiæ vulgo vocant Scoti, in Camera rationum regia? & similia.
units.tr: The civil functions and political authority of those churchmen who discharge the ministry of the Word were discussed. The questions were whether they might sit on the bench as eirenarchs (justices of the peace), and whether they might pronounce sentence in parliaments and the royal senate, in the supreme court of civil causes that the Scots commonly call the Session or College of Justice, and in the royal Exchequer, and similar matters.

units.la: Hinc inde plurima prolata fuere, verum cum ad suffragia deventum fuisset, omnes unanimi consensu (duobus exceptis) declarant: Quantumvis liceat imo teneantur verbi pastores ex verbo Dei consilia Regi, Ordinum conventui, Senatui regio, aut quibuslibet suggerere de iis negotiis quæ ecclesiam aut conscientiam tangunt; Nullatenus tamen iisdem concedendam esse jurisdictionem & authoritatem civilem, seu ordinariam seu extraordinariam; Cum autem decretum Synodi ad montem Rosarum ann. 1600. objiceretur, quo conclusum fuerat; Licere pastoribus in ordinum conventu sententiam de republica dicere, Responsum fuit, ecclesiam pacis gratia pro tempore coactam fuisse illud permittere; addidisse tamen expressas cautiones quibus tanquam cancellis potestatem illam ferendi suffragium in comitiis coerceret; & has cautiones inferendas fuisse decreto parliamenti, quo sanciendum erat jus suffragii ecclesiae concessum, ut pars illius necessaria; Conditiones autem has foede à Pseudo-episcopis violatas, cum omnes norint, neque ipsi, quantacunque sint impudentia, negent; jure meritoque nunc refigendum esse illud decretum, praesertim cum in Synodo illa multi minis & terroribus, non argumentorum pondere, & rationibus aequa judicii lance pensitatis, sententiam pronunciaverint, alii vero Episcopaturientium obtestationibus decepti quibus nimia credulitate fidem adhibebant, & cautionibus quibus eorum authoritas limitaretur satis cautum esse putantes, nimia simplicitate assenserant, qui alioqui nunquam cessissent, si praevidissent, quae tum sagaciores subodorati fuerunt, & quae hodie omnium oculis cernuntur, vid. Concessione illa suffragii ecclesiasticis in Conventu ordinum, posticam fuisse apertam qua irrepserunt tot malorum iliades quibus ad extremam fere calamitatem redacta est ecclesia.Rationes quibus synodi sententia nitebatur hae praesertim fucrunt. 1. Christum exemplo suo docuisse quid facere debeant Euangelii ministri. Lucae 12.14.Qui haereditatis herciscundae potestatem recusavit ut a munere suo alienam: Quis (inquit) me vobis judicem praefecit? Si Christus Euangelii minister authoritatem hanc civilem exercere noluit, quo modo liceat pastoribus qui pro Christo legatione funguntur, & ecclesiis non suo sed Christi nomine praesunt: Sicut misit me pater ita & ego mitto vos Iohann. 20. 21. Item in adulteram sententiam ferre noluit. Iohann. 8. suumque regnum non fuisse ex hoc mundo saepius testatur. 2. Interdictum fuisse Apostolis dominatum civilem, Matth. 20.25, 26. non solum qui regibus & imperatoribus competit, vid. supremum, verum etiam subalternum, qualem exercent οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν κ) μεγάλοι[?]. Unde illud Bernardi de consideratione ad Eugen. lib. 2. Apostolis interdicitur dominatus: I ergo tu, & tibi usurpare aude aut Dominans Apostolatum, aut Apostolicus dominatum, forma Apostolica haec est, interdicitur dominatio, indicitur ministratio: τὸ κατακυριεύειν[?] κ) τὸ καταξουσιάζειν[?] quo civilis dominatio denotatur, & τὸ δοῦλον κ) ἀλλόγον[?] εἶναι quod Apostolis eorumq; successoribus verbi ministris praecipitur, ita sibi invicem opposita sunt, ut nulla modificatione in uno eodemq; subjecto convenire possint; nam tam personis Apostolorum quam a natura Apostolicae functionis praecepto hoc peremptorio omne Dominium civile removetur: Porro quam ineptum sit illud effugium, quo aciem hujus ancipitis argumenti se hebetasse quidam putant; quasi mysterium aliquod in κατακυριεύειν[?] lateret; doceat locus Lucae, Matthaei citato parallelus: apud quem κυριεύειν[?] leges, Omnem videlicet dominatum in Apostolis damnans; vel cum aliis, Dominatum cum violentia, non injusta per tyrannidem, sed legitima per vim coactivam, quem habet magistratus omnis legitimus in suos subditos, quibus vel invitis dominatur. 3. Non esse eorum qui nomen dederunt sacrae huic militiae vitae hujus negotiis non necessariis implicari, dico non necessariis, quia ad rem familiarem curandam tenentur Pastores nisi infidelibus deteriores esse velint: Itaque non negandum licere pastoribus parare victum propriarum manuum labore, si aliunde non suppetat unde vivant, exemplo Apostoli. 1. Corinth. 4. 12. Quare sicuti legibus politicis cautum est, ne milites alienorum negotiorum procurationem suscipiant, ne a signis suis avocentur. Cod.lib.2. tit.13. sic legibus Apostolicis idem vetatur ecclesiasticis, cœlestis militiæ castra sequentibus. 2.Tim.2. 4. Qui Deo Sacræ hujus militiæ summo imperatori nunquam placebunt, nisi avocamentis sæcularibus non necessariis valedixerint; Præsertim vero cum munus hoc quod obeunt gravius sit quam ut quisquam ei sit par. 2.Cor.2. 16. & labores sustinendi in functione hac continui sint, ac in orbem perpetuo redeuntes; unde in scripturis vocantur vigiles, speculatores, agricolæ, piscatores, pastores, milites, legati, operarii in messem Domini ab ipso emissi, quibus laborandum in verbo & doctrina ἀκαίρως εὐκαίρως[?]; 4. Apostolos ipsos extraordinariis donis instructos agnovisse impares se fuisse mensarum ministrationi, & verbi prædicationi, ideoque Diaconos instituisse, Act. 6.2. erant tamen utraque hæc munia Ecclesiastica; & Gregorius I. citante Gratiano in decreto dist. 89. cap. singula; probat duo ecclesiastica officia uni non esse committenda, à loco Apostoli ad Rom. 12. 6, 7. Sicut, inquit, indecorum est, ut in corpore humano alterum membrum alterius fungatur officio; ita noxium simulque turpissimum, si singula rerum ministeria personis totidem non fuerint distributa: Si duo ecclesiastica officia sunt (ut ita loquar) incompatibilia, multo magis ecclesiasticum & civile: Hujusque sententiæ documenta in veterum scriptis obvia sunt: Canones Apostolorum & spuria ejus generis scripta hic missa facienda essent, nisi specioso antiquitatis titulo ab Hierarchicis æque ac à Pontificiis obtruderentur. In illis tamen mistio hæc civilium cum ecclesiasticis sæpius damnatur. Can. 6. Episcopus vel presbyter sæculares curas non suscipiat, alioqui deponatur, & Can. 81. & 83. Cyprianus lib. 1. epistola. 9. dicit; jampridem in concilio Episcoporum statutum esse, ne quis de clericis & Dei ministris tutorem vel curatorem testamento suo constituat, quando singuli divino sacerdotio honorati non nisi altari & sacrificiis, precibus & orationi vacare debeant; Scriptum enim est: Nemo militans Deo obligat se molestiis sæcularibus: & cæt. Clemens primus (quem Romanum episcopum multi volunt, & ex cujus scriptis hiatum historiæ ecclesiasticæ post Acta Apostolorum supplendum esse dicunt;) in epistola ad Iacobum Domini fratrem quem Episcopum instituit: Neque judicem aut cognitorem sæcularium negotiorum te ordinare vult Christus, ne præfocatus præsentibus hominum curis non possis verbo Dei vacare, & secundum veritatis regulam secernere bonos à malis; Ista namque opera quæ tibi minus congruunt, sibi invicem exhibeant Discentes, hoc est, Laici: Impietatis tibi crimen est neglectis verbi Dei studiis, sollicitudines suscipere sæculares. Synesius Ptolemaidis Episcopus citante Lipsio in politicis dixit; Illicitum esse jungere civilem virtutem cum sacerdotio, nam hoc esset miscere omnino non miscenda, hoc est, sacris civilia confundere. Hilarius Pictavienfis ad Auxentium. Quibusnam suffragiis ad prædicandum Euangelium Apostoli usi sunt ? quibus adjuti potestatibus Christum prædicarunt, gentesque omnes fere ex idolis ad Deum transtulerunt ? Anne aliquam sibi a palatio dignitatem sumpserunt hymnum Deo in carcere inter catenas & post flagella cantantes ? At nunc proh dolor! divinam fidem suffragia terrena commendant, inopsque virtutis suæ Christus arguitur, dum ambitio nomini suo conciliatur. Gregorii Romani sententiam supra produxi, vide, si vis, Gratiani Decreti part. prim. distinct. 88. & 89. Bernardus de consideratione ad Eugenium. Lib. 2. In decretalibus: Clericus qui fecularibus negotiis fe immiscet est Irregularis ; Sed objicies , Augustinum seculi sui ingens lumen, non detrectasse sententiam ferre de causis fecularibus; in Pfalm.118. Concion. 24. Maligni cum suis vitiosis & negotiosis cupiditatibus adjuvandis ut occupemur, & iis nostra tempora impendamus flagitant, & cæt. quibus dicere non audemus. Dic homo quis me constituit judicem inter vos ? Constituit enim talibus causis ecclefiafticos Apostolus cognitores, in foro prohibens jurgare Christianos: Alludit videl. ad locum Apoftoli. 1.Cor.6.4. Et de eo refert Possidonius in ipfius vita cap.19. Quum interpellaretur hoc nomine non solum à Christianis sed & à cujusque sectæ hominibus, secundum Pauli sententiam omnium caufas adeo pie ac diligenter audivisse ut aliquando totum diem huic negotio dederit. Respondeo : Coronam illam testimoniorum ex prima antiquitate productorum Augustini opinioni, quæ ex falsa scripturæ interpretatione fluxit præferendam esse: Etenim Pauli sententia in verbis. 1. Corinth. 6. 4. Perfpicua est, videl. lites inter fratres potius ad ἐξ[?]ἀγῶς in ecclesia, hoc est, contemptibiles qui nullo loco habentur, deferendas esse, quam ut ad forum infidelium disputarent: An contemptibiles illi & viliffimi ex ecclesiasticorum ordine sunt? An vero potius infimi quique laicorum? quod censuit Clemens Romanus in epistola ad Iacobum. Dein obfervantibus jurisconsultis ', licet corruptis ecclesiæ temporibus civiles lites definirent ecclesiastici,(quomodo & quibus artibus eo provecti sint, consule authorem Historiæ Concilii Tridentini. Lib.4.) notandum, primum necessario accedere debuisse consensum utriusque partis litigantis, 2. in civili duntaxat negotio. 3. Sententiam tulisse episcopos more Arbitri, cujus judicio, compromissi vinculo præeunte, sponte se submittebant litigantes: Quid hæc ad ordinariam civilem jurisdictionem? quæ in hoc potissimum consistit, ut vi legum & authoritate magistratus quisque in officio retineatur, etiam invitus.
units.tr: Much was said on both sides, but when the votes were taken, all (with two exceptions) declared with one accord that, although the ministers of the Word may and indeed ought, from the Word of God, to offer counsel to the King, the convention of the Estates, the royal senate, or anyone else concerning those matters which touch the Church or conscience, yet no civil jurisdiction or authority, whether ordinary or extraordinary, is to be granted to them. When the decree of the Synod of Montrose of 1600 was objected, by which it had been concluded that ministers might give their opinion on public affairs in the convention of the Estates, the answer was that the Church had been compelled to permit this for the time being, for the sake of peace; but that express cautions had been added, which, like barriers, restrained that power of casting a vote in the assemblies; and that these cautions had been inserted in the decree of Parliament by which the right of voting granted to the Church was sanctioned, as a necessary part of it. Now these conditions had been shamefully violated by the pseudo-bishops, as everyone knows and as they themselves, however shameless they are, cannot deny. Therefore that decree rightly and justly ought now to be revoked, especially since in that Synod many had pronounced their opinion under threats and terrors, not weighed by the force of arguments and by the balance of fair judgement; others, deceived by the entreaties of those aspiring to bishoprics, to whom they gave credit through excessive gullibility, and thinking that enough caution had been taken by the restrictions by which their authority was limited, had assented through too much simplicity, though they would never otherwise have yielded had they foreseen what the shrewder men then suspected and what is today plain to everyone's eyes. That is, in that concession of a vote to churchmen in the convention of the Estates there was left an open back door, through which crept the whole host of evils by which the Church has been brought almost to utter ruin. The reasons on which the Synod's opinion rested were chiefly these: (1) Christ by his own example taught what the ministers of the Gospel ought to do (Luke 12:14), who refused the power of dividing an inheritance as foreign to his office: "Who (he said) appointed me a judge over you?" If Christ, the minister of the Gospel, was unwilling to exercise this civil authority, how may ministers be permitted it, who discharge an embassy for Christ and preside over churches not in their own name but in Christ's name? "As the Father has sent me, so I send you" (John 20:21). Likewise he was unwilling to pass sentence on the adulteress (John 8), and he often testifies that his kingdom is not of this world. (2) Civil lordship was forbidden to the Apostles (Matt. 20:25–26), not only that which belongs to kings and emperors, the supreme power, but also the subordinate kind, such as "the rulers of the nations" [οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν] and "the great ones" [μεγάλοι] exercise. Hence that saying of Bernard in On Consideration, to Pope Eugenius, book 2: "To the Apostles dominion is forbidden: go then, and dare to usurp for yourself either the apostolate as lordship or lordship as apostolate; the apostolic form is this: lordship is forbidden, ministry is enjoined." The words to lord it over [τὸ κατακυριεύειν] and to exercise authority over [τὸ καταξουσιάζειν], by which civil domination is denoted, and to be a servant [τὸ δοῦλον] and to be a stranger... are set against each other, so that they can in no way be reconciled in one and the same subject. For this peremptory precept removes all civil dominion, both from the persons of the Apostles and from the nature of the apostolic function. Moreover, how absurd is that escape by which some think the force of this two-edged argument has been blunted, as if some mystery lay hidden in to lord it over [κατακυριεύειν]. The passage of Luke parallel to the cited passage of Matthew teaches otherwise, where you will read to rule [κυριεύειν], condemning all lordship in the Apostles; or else, with others, that it means lordship with violence, not unjust by tyranny but legitimate by coercive force, which every lawful magistrate has over his subjects, whom he rules even against their will. (3) It is not for those who have given their names to this sacred warfare to be entangled in the affairs of this life that are not necessary. I say "not necessary", because ministers are bound to look after their household affairs, unless they wish to be worse than unbelievers. Therefore it must not be denied that ministers may get their living by the labour of their own hands, if they have no other means of living, after the example of the Apostle (1 Cor. 4:12). Wherefore, as it is provided by civil laws that soldiers shall not undertake the management of other men's affairs, lest they be drawn away from their standards (Cod. lib. 2, tit. 13), so the apostolic laws forbid the same to churchmen, who follow the camp of the heavenly militia (2 Tim. 2:4). They will never please God, the supreme commander of this ssacred army, unless they have bid farewell to worldly distractions that are not necessary. Especially since the office they discharge is too weighty for anyone to be equal to it (2 Cor. 2:16), and the labours to be borne in this function are continuous and recur in a constant circle. Hence in the Scriptures they are called watchmen, scouts, husbandmen, fishermen, shepherds, soldiers, ambassadors, workers sent out by the Lord himself into his harvest, who must labour in the Word and doctrine in season and out of season [ἀκαίρως εὐκαίρως]. (4) The Apostles themselves, though furnished with extraordinary gifts, acknowledged that they were unequal to the serving of tables and the preaching of the Word, and therefore appointed deacons (Acts 6:2). Yet both these duties were ecclesiastical. Gregory I, quoted by Gratian in the Decretum, dist. 89, chapter Singula, proves from the Apostle's passage in Romans 12:6–7 that two ecclesiastical offices are not to be committed to one man. "As," he says, "it is unseemly that in the human body one member should perform the office of another, so it is harmful and at the same time most shameful if the several ministries of affairs are not distributed among as many persons." If two ecclesiastical offices are (so to speak) incompatible, much more so are the ecclesiastical and the civil. Evidence for this opinion is to be found everywhere in the writings of the ancients. The Canons of the Apostles and the spurious writings of that kind would have to be passed over here, were they not thrust upon us by the hierarchists and the Papists alike under the specious title of antiquity. Yet in these the mixing of civil with ecclesiastical affairs is often condemned. Canon 6: "A bishop or presbyter shall not undertake secular cares; otherwise he shall be deposed." And Canons 81 and 83. Cyprian, book 1, epistle 9, says that it was long ago decreed in a council of bishops that no one should appoint a clergyman or minister of God as guardian or trustee in his will, since those honoured with the divine priesthood ought to be occupied only with the altar and the sacrifices, prayers and devotion: "For it is written: No one who serves God binds himself with secular troubles," etc. Clement the First (whom many hold to have been bishop of Rome, and from whose writings they say the gap in the history of the Church after the Acts of the Apostles is to be filled) says in his epistle to James, the Lord's brother, whom he made bishop: "Christ does not wish you to be appointed a judge or arbiter of secular affairs, lest, choked by the present cares of men, you be unable to devote yourself to the Word of God and to distinguish, according to the rule of truth, the good from the bad. For those works which suit you less let the disciples, that is, the laity, perform for one another. It is a crime of impiety for you, having neglected the study of the Word of God, to take upon yourself secular anxieties." Synesius, bishop of Ptolemais, quoted by Lipsius in his Politics, said: "It is unlawful to join civil virtue with the priesthood, for this would be to mix what must not be mixed, that is, to confound civil with sacred things." Hilary of Poitiers, to Auxentius: "With what votes did the Apostles use to preach the Gospel? By what powers, what aid, did they preach Christ and turn almost all the nations from idols to God? Did they take to themselves any dignity from the palace, singing hymns to God in prison among their chains and after their scourgings? But now, alas! earthly votes commend divine faith, and Christ is accused of lacking his own power, while ambition is reconciled to his name." I have already cited the opinion of Gregory the Roman; see, if you wish, Gratian's Decretum, part 1, distinctions 88 and 89. Bernard, On Consideration, to Eugenius, book 2. In the Decretals: "A clergyman who mixes himself up with secular affairs is irregular." But you will object that Augustine, the great light of his age, did not shrink from passing sentence in secular causes; in Psalm 118, sermon 24: "The malicious urge us to be occupied with the assisting of their wicked and busy lusts, and to devote our time to them," etc., to which we dare not reply: "Say, man, who has appointed me a judge between you?" For the Apostle appointed churchmen as arbiters in such causes, forbidding Christians to go to law in the courts. He alludes, of course, to the passage of 1 Cor. 6:4, and Possidius reports about him in his life, chapter 19, that when he was asked on this matter not only by Christians but also by men of every sect, he heard the causes of all so devoutly and diligently, according to Paul's judgement, that sometimes he gave a whole day to this business. I reply: that crown of testimonies drawn from the earliest antiquity is to be preferred to Augustine's opinion, which flowed from a false interpretation of Scripture. For the meaning of Paul's words in 1 Cor. 6:4 is plain: namely, that disputes between brothers are rather to be referred to the contemptible ones in the Church [ἐξουθενημένους], that is, those who are held of no account, than to be argued before the courts of unbelievers. Are those contemptible and most worthless persons from the order of churchmen? Or rather the lowest of the laity, as Clement of Rome judged in his epistle to James? Then, as the jurists observe, although in the corrupt times of the Church ecclesiastics settled civil disputes (how and by what arts they came to this, consult the author of the History of the Council of Trent, book 4), it must be noted that, first, the consent of both litigating parties had necessarily to be obtained; second, only in a civil matter; third, the bishops gave sentence in the manner of an arbiter, to whose judgement the litigants voluntarily submitted themselves, the bond of a compromise going before. What has this to do with the ordinary civil jurisdiction, which consists chiefly in this: that each person is kept in his duty by the force of the laws and the authority of the magistrate, even against his will?

units.la: Digressionem hanc claudenti occurrit gravissimum celeberrimi Martini Buceri judicium, in libro vere aureo de vi & usu SS. ministerii, nam agens de gravissimis incommodis quibus opprimitur ecclesia, cum Episcopi non abstinent ab omnibus negotiis quæ ipsos in vocatione remorantur, cum non toti vacant iis studiis quibus ad rite obeundum ministerium ecclesiasticum incumbere debent, cum se administrationi Reipublicæ admiscent, sic πολυπραγμοσύνῃ[?] hanc τῶν ἀπολειπομένων[?] per-stringit: Istud (inquit) cum probe nosset Satan, effecit ut Episcopi, Abbates, & præcipui ecclesiarum prælati accerserentur à Regibus & Imperatoribus ad aulam, ad negotia publica & belli & pacis, hinc consequuta hæc sunt mala: Primum neglectus S. ministerii, fermentatio doctrinæ, interitus disciplinæ: Deinde ut prælati satraparum locum tenere cœperunt, eorum etiam luxum & pompam sibi vendicarunt. Ad quam rem cum & opes Satraparum requirebantur, quæ debebant de rebus ecclesiasticis dispensare in fideles ecclesiarum ministros, in scholas, in Christi pauperes, ea omnia per horrendum sacrilegium illis erepta impenderunt in luxum & pompam Satrapalem. Quumque eis ad hunc luxum & pompam Ecclesiæ facultates non essent satis, eblanditi & emendicatique sunt, variisque fraudibus abstulerunt à regibus luculentas ditiones & magna imperia; Quibus deinde accessionibus factis, luxus istorum non fotus tantum & sustentatus fuit, verumetiam in immensum auctus, & cæt. Hæc quidem ille de Clero Pontificio atque Episcopis. Quæ tam vera fuisse in iis qui mundo persuasum volunt se pontifici Romano valedixisse, cæcus est qui non viderit.Fœlix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum. Atque hæc de dignitatibus & functionibus ecclesiasticorum politicis.
units.tr: This digression is closed by the very weighty judgment of the famous Martin Bucer, in his truly golden book on the power and use of the sacred ministry. Speaking of the most serious harms by which the Church is oppressed, when bishops do not refrain from all the business that hinders them in their calling, when they do not devote themselves wholly to those studies which they ought to pursue in order to discharge the ecclesiastical ministry properly, and when they mix themselves into the administration of the commonwealth, he censures this meddling (polypragmosynē) of those who have fallen behind [πολυπραγμοσύνῃ, τῶν ἀπολειπομένων]: "Satan, knowing this well (he says), brought it about that bishops, abbots and the chief prelates of the churches were summoned by kings and emperors to the court, to public business of war and peace. From this these evils followed: first, neglect of the sacred ministry, fermentation of doctrine, and the ruin of discipline. Then the prelates began to hold the place of satraps, and claimed for themselves their luxury and pomp. For this purpose the wealth of the satraps was needed, which ought to have been distributed from ecclesiastical resources to the faithful ministers of the churches, to schools, and to the poor of Christ; all of that, taken away by a dreadful sacrilege, they spent on satrapal luxury and pomp. And since the resources of the Church were not enough for this luxury and pomp, they flattered and begged, and by various frauds they extracted from kings splendid estates and great dominions. Once these accessions had been made, the luxury of these men was not only fostered and sustained but also increased beyond measure," and so on. These things, indeed, he said of the Papist clergy and the bishops. That they were as true in those who want the world persuaded that they have bid farewell to the Roman pontiff, only a blind man would fail to see. Happy is he whom the dangers of others make wary. And so much concerning the political dignities and functions of churchmen.

units.la: Delecti hac sessione legati qui ecclesiarum gravamina & postulata regni ordinibus exhiberent in Comitiis Majo mense celebrandis,quibus in mandatis datum ut sedulo curarent, ne quid damni res ecclesiastica acciperet.
units.tr: In this session there were chosen commissioners who were to present the grievances and demands of the Church to the orders of the realm at the assembly to be held in May, with instructions that they should take careful care that the ecclesiastical cause suffer no harm.

units.la: Sess. 26. Decemb. 20. Die Iovis.
units.tr: Session 26. December 20, Thursday.

units.la: Quia typographorum inaudita & minime serenda licentia plurimum detrimenti annis elapsis passa est ecclesia, ut malo huic obviam iret Synodus, decrevit ne quis tractatus quoslibet de religione, præsertim vero de causis hodie controversis proelo committeret; nisi prius judicio & censura M. Archibaldi Ionstoni, Synodalis scribæ probentur, Atque huic decreto omnes typographi in Scotia obtemperare jubentur sub pœna censuræ ecclesiasticæ.
units.tr: Because the unheard-of and altogether intolerable licence of the printers had in past years done much harm to the Church, the Synod, to meet this evil, decreed that no one should commit to the press any treatise whatever on religion, especially on the causes now in controversy, unless it had first been approved by the judgment and censure of Mr Archibald Johnston, clerk of the Synod. All printers in Scotland are ordered to obey this decree under penalty of ecclesiastical censure.

units.la: Presbyteriis & Synodis provincialibus stricte mandatum, ut quoscunque contra Synodum hanc pervicaces[?], ejusve decretis immorigeros comperient, in jus vocent, ac pro qualitate contumaciæ cum eis agant.
units.tr: The presbyteries and provincial synods are strictly charged that whomever they find to be obstinate against this Synod, or disobedient to its decrees, they are to summon before them and deal with according to the degree of their contumacy.

units.la: Decretum etiam; ut, quicunque in ecclesiis aut scholis hujus regni publicam aliquam professionem sustinentes, confessioni fidei seu fœderi hactenus nondum subscripserunt; eandem nunc chirographis suis ac solenni juramento obsignent: Confessionifque subscribendæ titulo addenda esse sequentia: Quandoquidem in Synodo Nationali Glasguensi habita mense decembri ann. 1638. determinata fit capitum seu articulorum illorum explicatio, qui ad Synodum Nationalem referebantur; ac declaratum sit, quinque articulos Perthenses, regimen ecclesiæ per Episcopos, ejurata fuisse à majoribus confessionem hanc primitus obsignantibus: Nos subscribimus, confessionemque hanc ratam habemus juxta Synodi hujus expressam determinationem.
units.tr: It is also decreed that whoever, holding any public office in the churches or schools of this realm, has not hitherto subscribed the Confession of Faith or the Covenant, shall now seal it with their signatures and a solemn oath. To the title of the Confession to be subscribed the following is to be added: Since in the National Synod held at Glasgow in December 1638 an explanation was settled of those articles of the chapters which were referred to the National Synod, and it was declared that the Five Articles of Perth and government of the Church by bishops were abjured by those elders who first sealed this Confession, we subscribe, and hold this Confession ratified according to the express determination of this Synod.

units.la: Hac sessione;Divina, Ecclesiastica & Civili authoritate licere huic Nationali Ecclesiæ Scoticæ in Synodos Nationales annuas, aut sæpius pro re nata coire, declaratur: Et quandoquidem Deputatus regius nunc absit; cui præsenti, lege municipali competeret loci & temporis subsecuturæ synodi designatio; Synodus ipsa declarat locum Synodi fore Edenburgum, diem autem Mercurii tertiæ septimanæ mensis Iulii ann. 1639. Quod si interim extraordinarii quid occurrat, quod Synodi convocationem ante diem illum postulet, provincia hæc presbyterio Edenburgeno imponitur, ut omnes quorum interest tempestive certiores faciat. Denique si serenissimo Regi visum fuerit ante Iulium mensem Synodum Nationalem indicere, jubet Synodus ut omnes, loco & tempore designatis edicto regio, conveniant.
units.tr: In this session it is declared, by divine, ecclesiastical and civil authority, that it is lawful for this National Church of Scotland to meet in annual National Synods, or more often as occasion requires. And since the king's Commissioner, to whom by municipal law the designation of the place and time of the following synod would belong, is now absent, the Synod itself declares that the place of the Synod shall be Edinburgh, and the day Wednesday of the third week of July in the year 1639. But if meanwhile something extraordinary should arise that calls for the convocation of the Synod before that day, this duty is laid upon the Edinburgh presbytery, that it should inform all whom it concerns in good time. Finally, if it shall please the most serene King to summon the National Synod before the month of July, the Synod orders that all should assemble at the place and time designated by royal edict.

units.la: Supra ad sessionem 16. facta fuit mentio libelli editi authoritate & nomine Deputati regii: quo contendit author persuadere, Episcopatum ejuratum non fuisse annis illis quibus obsignata olim fuit confessio, ideoque per genuinum confes-sionis sensum hodie abjurari non posse, præsertim cum mandato & edicto regio Mensis Septembris hoc primario à Rege intendatur, ut subscriptione fœderis & confessionis, fulciretur Episcopatus: Quare omnibus severe interdicebatur à Marchione Deputato regio, ne confessionem illam obsignent, quolibet sensu qui Episcopatum destruat: Verum huic explicationi firmiter adhæreant : Quod cum synodo innotuisset, quibusdam in mandatis dedit, ut libellum illum serio excuterent, & de omnibus ad Synodum referrent. Atque licet sessione 16. operæ suscepte rationem amplissimam exhibuissent, neque ulli scrupulus hæreret, quin secundum genuinum confessionis sensum annis 1580. 1581. 1590. 1591. publice professum, (quo confessionis hujus obsignatores statuto declaratorio Senatus regii, remittebantur,ut supra sæpius observatum) Episcopatus iste Dicecesanus liquido removendus esset ; hac sessione tamen ad majorem cautelam visum fuit Synodo, declarare Episcopatum illum in Confessione abjuratum esse, ideoque sub poena censuræ ecclesiasticæ vetare, ne quis confessioni à rege imperatæ subscriberet, cum tam insolenti & peregrina glossa, prout ab illustriss. Marchione proponitur,ipsa verba Consessionis evertat, & sic obsignatores juramenti contradictorii labyrintho inextricabili involvat: ac Regem serenissi. humiliter obtestandum esse,ut ecclesiæ hujus ( cui nativitatem utramque debet) in synodo repræsentatæ explicationem confessionis supradictam ratam habere dignetur , quo non solum editurus erit regium & se dignum pietatis ac justitiæ testimonium ; verumetiam arctiori. (si arctius stringi possent) nexu fidelium subditorum animos sibi devinciet.
units.tr: Above, at session 16, mention was made of a little book published with the authority and name of the king's Commissioner, in which the author sought to persuade that episcopacy had not been abjured in those years in which the Confession was once sealed, and therefore could not today be renounced according to the genuine sense of the Confession; especially since the chief purpose of the king's mandate and edict of September was that episcopacy should be supported by the subscription of the Covenant and the Confession. Therefore the Marquis, the king's Commissioner, sternly forbade everyone to sign that Confession in any sense that would destroy episcopacy, and urged them to hold firmly to this explanation. When the Synod learned of this, it gave instructions that the little book be carefully examined and that everything in it be reported to the Synod. And although in session 16 they had given a very ample account of their reasoning, and no doubt remained that according to the genuine sense of the Confession, publicly professed in the years 1580, 1581, 1590 and 1591 (by which statute of the royal Senate the subscribers of this Confession were referred back, as has often been observed above), this diocesan episcopacy ought to be clearly removed, yet in this session the Synod thought it fitting, for greater caution, to declare that episcopacy abjured in the Confession, and therefore, under penalty of ecclesiastical censure, to forbid anyone to subscribe the Confession as imposed by the king, since such an insolent and foreign gloss, as is proposed by the most illustrious Marquis, overturns the very words of the Confession and entangles the signatories in the inextricable labyrinth of a contradictory oath. And the King is to be humbly entreated that he deign to hold ratified the explanation of the aforesaid Confession presented to the Synod by this Church, to which he owes both his natural birth; for by this he will not only give a royal and worthy testimony of piety and justice, but also bind the minds of his faithful subjects to himself with a closer bond, if a closer bond could be drawn.

units.la: Denique quibus sessione præcedenti in mandatis datum fuit, ut epistolæ ad regem perscribendæ formam conciperent,qua gratias agerent ob synodi indictam, & vera relatione omnium quæ conclusa fuerunt,calumniatoribus obviam irent, ( qui omni opera in id intenti erant ut in deterius innocentes synodi actiones traducerent, nam solenne reis judicem calumnjari postquam causa ceciderunt.) Denique qua constitutionum Synodicarum sanctionem obtinerent ; formam epistolæ nunc prælegendam exhibent;quæ cum ab omnibus approbata fuisset,decretū fuit, ut synodi totius nomine, ( quod semper antea fieri consuevit)eidem subscriberent Præses & synodi Scriba ; quæ de verbo fere in verbum translata sic se habet.
units.tr: Finally, those who in the preceding session were instructed to draft the form of a letter to be written to the king, in which they were to give thanks for the summoning of the Synod, and to meet the calumniators with a true account of all that was concluded (for they were intent on every effort to twist the innocent actions of the Synod for the worse; for it is customary for accused men to calumniate the judge once their cause has been lost), and by which they might obtain the sanction of the Synod's constitutions, now present the form of the letter to be read out; which, when it had been approved by all, was decreed to be subscribed, in the name of the whole Synod (as has always been customary before), by the Moderator and the clerk of the Synod. It stands, translated almost word for word, as follows.

units.la: Epistola Synodi ad Regem.
units.tr: The Synod's Letter to the King.

units.la: Serenissime Rex.
units.tr: Most Serene King.

units.la: HUmillimi ac devotissimi Majestatis vestræ subditi, deputati ecclesiarum perantiqui & nativi vestri regni ad Synodum Glasguensem, M. V. speciali indictione coactam: Quum animo volveremus singularem illam fœlicitatem quæ regnis & ecclesiæ pariter accrescit, mutuis religionis ac justitiæ, veritatis ac pacis amplexibus, quando supremæ providentiæ visum fuerit actiones humanas sic procurare, ut regalis ac politica potestas ecclesiasticæ authoritati subsidio sit ; non potuimus nobis temperare, quin gratissimis animis agnosceremus, ore confiteremur, ac in sempiternam M.V. gloriam coram universo orbe testaremur, quantopere totum hoc regnum recreetur ac revirescat suavi sensu pietatis, justitiæ, bonitatis, quæ in M.V. conspicue se se prodiderunt, quando supplicibus nostris literis pro libera & plena Nationali synodo obtinenda tam facilem M.V. se præbuit. Cum vero impræsentiarum nullum verius sinceræ gratitudinis argumentum nobis M. V. devotissimis subditis suppeteret, quam ut regio hoc favore digni incederemus ; sedulo certe in id incubuimus, ac secundum Domini Iesu Christi supremi (quam suo pretioso sanguine redemit) ecclesiæ regis voluntatem, eo omnia nostra studia collimarunt, ut in omnibus nostris actionibus, à prima conventus nostri hora, ea animi moderatione, ordine, ac fidelitate nos gereremus, qua decet subditos tam justi & boni regis, pro cujus incolumitate & fœlici regimine ex animo Deum semper precati fuimus: Neque quidpiam fuit cujus tam anxio renebamur[?] desiderio, quam M.V. præsentia, qua si frui nobis datum fuisset, nihil ambigebamus, quin regia vestra sanctione constitutiones nostras ratas habuisses: animus quippe vere Christianus ac regius, religioni & pietati favens, primo intuitu discernet, ac discernendo rapietur amore singularis pulchritudinis, ac cœlestis ordinis domus Dei, nam utrumque ab uno & eodem spiritu procedit.
units.tr: We, the most humble and most devoted subjects of Your Majesty, the deputies of the very ancient and native churches of your kingdom, gathered at the Synod of Glasgow by your special summons: When we consider that singular happiness which grows equally for kingdoms and for the Church, through the mutual embraces of religion and justice, of truth and peace, when it pleases the supreme providence to so order human affairs that royal and civil power serves as an aid to ecclesiastical authority, we could not restrain ourselves. We acknowledge with the most grateful hearts, we confess with our mouths, and we bear witness before the whole world to the everlasting glory of Your Majesty, how greatly this whole kingdom is refreshed and revived by the sweet sense of piety, justice and goodness, which have plainly shown themselves in Your Majesty, since you showed yourself so easy to persuade in granting our humble petitions for a free and full National Synod. Yet at present we have no truer proof of sincere gratitude available to us, your most devoted subjects, than to walk worthy of this royal favour. Certainly we have applied ourselves diligently to this, and we have directed all our efforts, in accordance with the will of the Lord Jesus Christ, the supreme King of the Church (whom he redeemed with his precious blood), that in all our actions, from the first hour of our meeting, we should conduct ourselves with that moderation of spirit, order and loyalty which befits subjects of so just and good a king, for whose safety and happy reign we have always prayed to God from our hearts. Nor was there anything we longed for so anxiously as Your Majesty's presence; had we been granted the enjoyment of it, we had no doubt that you would have ratified our constitutions with your royal sanction. For a mind that is truly Christian and royal, favouring religion and piety, will at first sight discern, and in discerning will be carried away by love of the singular beauty and heavenly order of the house of God; for both proceed from one and the same Spirit.

units.la: Verum uti gaudium nostrum prope ineffabile fuerat, ac vivida spes, à M. V. clementia tanquam copiosa scaturigine manans, corda nostra repleverat; ita immane quantum animis consternabamur, cum perciperemus non solum ante apertam synodum, quantam operam dedisset M.V. deputatus præliminandæ Synodo in membris suis necessariis, & rebus in ea tractandis, contra expressam M.V. intentionem, qua libera Synodus Nationalis secundum consuetudinem hujus ecclesiæ, & regni statuta indicebatur: verumetiam à primo conventus nostri exordio nihil decerni passus fuit, (quantumlibet necessarium, & ordinarium; quod à nullo in quæstione trahi potuit) sine censura, contradictione aut protestatione; quasi eo solù nomine huc destinatus fuisset ut impedimento non adjumento nobis esset, aut quasi nobis propositum fuisset religioni ac Majestati V. præjudicare, (à quibus quantum abhorreant intimæ nostræ cogitationes, Deus καρδιογνώστης[?] perspectum habet.) Demum post aliquot dies contentionibus hujusmodi transactos, summo nostro cum dolore ac præter omnium spem, ipse de Synodo.discessit[?], nobis etiam severe imperatis ut Synodum statim dimitteremus, ejus generis edicto quod post examen facile probabitur, nulli solido fundamento aut rationi innixum fuisse, quæ supremi conventus Parlamentarii aut M. V. accurati judicii censuram sustinere posset. Cui si obtemperatum à nobis fuisset, cum M. V. speciali mandato in Synodum legitime formatam coivissemus, ecclesia & regnum subito præcipitandum fuisse cernebamus in horrendum confusionum chaos, & miseriarum abyssum, quibus difficulter postea remedium adhiberi potuisset: idque contra M. V. expressam intentionem, prioribus edictis toties declaratam, ac subditorum omnium ordinum spem.
units.tr: But just as our joy was almost beyond words, and a lively hope, flowing from Your Majesty's clemency as from a copious spring, had filled our hearts, so we were dreadfully dismayed when we perceived, not only before the Synod was opened, how much effort the deputy of Your Majesty had expended in arranging, before the Synod, its necessary members and the matters to be treated in it, against Your Majesty's express intention, by which a free National Synod was summoned according to the custom of this Church and the statutes of the kingdom. Indeed, from the very beginning of our meeting he suffered nothing to be decided (however necessary and ordinary it might be, and which no one could draw into question) without censure, contradiction or protest, as if he had been sent here for this purpose alone, to be a hindrance rather than a help to us, or as if it had been our purpose to prejudice religion and Your Majesty's authority (from which our inmost thoughts recoil; God, the heart-knower [καρδιογνώστης], has seen this). At last, after some days spent in such contentions, to our great sorrow and beyond everyone's expectation, he himself departed from the Synod, and we were also severely ordered to dismiss the Synod at once, by an edict of a kind which, on examination, will easily be shown to rest on no solid foundation or reason that could withstand the scrutiny of the supreme Parliament or of Your Majesty's careful judgment. Had we obeyed this, although we had gathered into a Synod lawfully formed by Your Majesty's special mandate, we saw that the Church and the kingdom would be suddenly plunged into a dreadful chaos of confusion and an abyss of miseries, for which a remedy could afterwards hardly be applied. And this would be against Your Majesty's express intention, so often declared in earlier edicts, and against the hope of subjects of every rank.

units.la: Ad has incitas redacti, consultissimum nobis una omnium voce visum fuit, illud potius sequi quod M. V. voluntati nobis per edicta revelatæ magis congrueret; ac quod religioni, M. V. honori, ac regni hujus utilitati conduceret, quam ut morem gereremus mandato Deputati, quod à subitaneo impetu procederet, & omnia in ruinam præsentem traheret. Atque hic tantum abest, ut nobis à luce metuamus ne opera nostra arguantur; quin contra, quo accuratius instituatur examen, quanta animi moderatione usi simus potestate illa à Deo, ejusque in terris supremo deputato M. V. nobis concessa, eo firmius confidimus M. V. actiones ac decreta nostra probatum iri: Præsertim quandoquidem absente M. V. deputato, & nobis vetitis, ne actionem tam piam tam necessariam ulterius promoveremus, diligentiam duplicaverimus, ac intensioribus animis sollicite magis in omnibus, quæ consideratione nostræ objecta fuerunt, incedere nobis propositerimus, ut sine ullius scandalo, tanquam sub Dei ipsius intuitu, ac quasi M. V. oculi nos præsentes spectarent, omnia ageremus secundùm Dei verbum, fidei consessionem, juramentum illud Nationale, ac laudabiles superiorum Synodorum constitutiones: studentes vetera potius decreta, regnante M. V. patre beatæ memoriæ, condita, ac ex publicis ecclesiarum registris singulari Dei providentia luci jam redditis, eruta renovare; quam, vel assensum præbere novationibus absque ordine introductis, avaritia & ambitione eorum, qui in privatos fines authoritate abusi fuerunt; vel novum quemvis ordinem primitus non receptum, cui solenni juramento astricti non fuimus, instituere.
units.tr: Brought to these straits, it seemed to us with one voice most prudent to follow rather what agreed better with Your Majesty's will, as revealed to us by your edicts, and what conduced to religion, to Your Majesty's honour and to the advantage of this kingdom, than to obey a mandate of the deputy, which proceeded from a sudden impulse and would draw everything into present ruin. And here we are so far from fearing the light, lest our works be found wanting, that on the contrary, the more carefully the examination is conducted, the more firmly do we trust that Your Majesty will approve our actions and decrees, with what moderation of spirit we have used that power which God, and Your Majesty, his supreme deputy on earth, has granted us. Especially since, with Your Majesty's deputy absent, and we forbidden to promote this so pious and necessary business any further, we have doubled our diligence and proposed to proceed with more intense minds and greater care in all the matters that were put before our consideration; so that, without scandal to anyone, as under the very eye of God, and as if Your Majesty's eyes were watching us in person, we might do everything according to the Word of God, the confession of faith, that National Covenant, and the praiseworthy constitutions of earlier Synods. We were eager rather to renew older decrees, enacted in the reign of your father of blessed memory, and now, by a singular providence of God, brought to light and drawn out of the public registers of the churches; rather than either to give our assent to innovations introduced without order, through the avarice and ambition of those who abused their authority for private ends, or to set up some new order never received before, to which we were not bound by solemn oath.

units.la: In quibus omnibus tam perspicua lux nobis omnibus affulsit, remotis quibuscunque scrupulis, ut singularis harmonia & unanimitas omnibus admirationi esse posset, atque usque adeo efficacibus argumentis convincebamur, ut aliter decernere non potuissemus, nisi Deo & conscientiæ apertum bellum indixissemus.
units.tr: In all these matters so clear a light has shone upon us all, with every scruple removed, that a singular harmony and unanimity could be a matter of admiration to all; and we were convinced by arguments so compelling that we could not have decided otherwise, unless we had declared open war upon God and our conscience.

units.la: Regius & prudens M. V. animus satis cognitum habet, nihil usitatius esse traductione ac detorsione actionum innocentissimarum & æquissimarum, ac ut male audiant qui optime fecerunt: Balaamo licet Pseudoprophetæ injuria sic impacta, quippe pro eo quod dixerat, Dominus non vult ut vobiscum eam, Moabitarum principes Balaco retulerunt, Balaamum nolle cum iis ire. Sed hoc nobis est solatio, quod veritas temporis sit filia, quodque calumniam celeri cursu veritatem præverteentem, pressis pedibus sequatur tandem veritas, hospitemque se præbeat nobilibus ac regiis animis, in quibus calumniæ diu locus tutus non conceditur: Quare speramus M. V. cum prudenti illo Rege aurium alteram calumniis obseraturam; exemplo prudentissimi Salomonis, qui cum primum specimen exhibiturus esset prudentiæ illius divinæ, utramque partem contendentem sibi sisti jussit, ut utraque pariter audita, ea victrix discederet, cujus æquior esse causa.
units.tr: Your Majesty's royal and prudent mind knows well enough that nothing is more usual than the twisting and distorting of the most innocent and most just actions, so that those who have done best are ill spoken of. Balaam, though a false prophet, was wronged in this way: for, although he had said that the Lord would not let him go with them, the princes of Moab reported to Balak that Balaam was unwilling to go with them. But this is our comfort: that truth is the daughter of time, and that truth will at last follow calumny, which runs swiftly ahead, with unhurried steps, and will show itself a welcome guest to noble and royal minds, in which calumny is not allowed a safe place for long. Therefore we hope that Your Majesty, like that prudent king, will stop the other ear against calumnies, following the example of the most prudent Solomon, who, when he was about to give the first proof of his divine wisdom, ordered both parties contending before him to be brought forward, so that, both being heard alike, the one whose cause was the fairer might depart victorious.

units.la: · Quum à M.V. reconditussimi synodi hujus recefsus prudenti trutina expendentur : habeamur mortalium pessimi, (prout hactenus hostes nostri calumniantur) ac miserrimi; (quod hostium corda vindicta turgentia unice expetunt) habeamur ab omnibus indigni qui vitali aura in hoc M. V. regno fruamur, si causa quam tuemur, & quam huc usque promovimus, alia sit, quam quod nobis cordi sit, ut Deus opt. maxim. qui noster terror & pavor est, rite colatur, & ipsius domus ex ipsius praescripto regatur : nisi in omnibus nostris actionibus post Dei gloriam, M. V. honorem promovere studuerimus: nisi infra reformationis nostrae primitivae limites nos continuerimus, neutiquam perstringendo aliarum reformatarum ecclesiarum constitutiones, quibus veritatem & pacem ex animo optamus, & quarum maturo judicio & Christianae aequitati nostra haec probatum iri speramus : nisi nimia potius censurarum lenitate quam severitate in criminum obnoxios deliquerimus: nisi regimen & disciplina hujus ecclesiae, (omnium chirographis & solenni juramento olim obsignata, ) & nunc unanimi omnium judicio approbata, promovendo Christi regno, obedientiae M. V. a subditis hujus regni debitae, gloriae ac honori coronae vestrae regiae, nostrae paci, ac omnibus hostibus honoris M. V. & nostrae felicitatis terrendis unice serviat. Denique si quid sit a nobis decretum (quantum mens nostra capit, ac humana patitur infirmitas) quod, in trutina rationum a M. V. patre beatae memoriae & nostris majoribus olim feliciter positatum (quas nobis religio fuit violare) expensum mereatur iram & indignationem, qua toties minitamur.
units.tr: When this synod's most secret proceedings are weighed by Your Majesty in a prudent balance, let us be held the worst and most wretched of mortals (as our enemies have hitherto slandered us), which the hearts of enemies, swollen with revenge, alone desire; let us be held by all as unworthy to enjoy the breath of life in this kingdom of Your Majesty, if the cause we defend and have advanced so far is other than what lies close to our hearts: that God, the best and greatest, who is our terror and fear, be duly worshipped, and his house ruled according to his own prescription; unless in all our actions we have sought, after God's glory, to advance the honour of Your Majesty; unless we have kept ourselves within the limits of our first reformation, in no way censuring the constitutions of other reformed churches, which we heartily wish well for truth and peace, and by whose mature judgment and Christian equity we hope this our work will be approved; unless we have dealt with offenders more with excessive gentleness in censures than with severity; unless the government and discipline of this Church (sealed long ago by the signatures of all and by solemn oath, and now approved by the unanimous judgment of all) serve solely to advance the kingdom of Christ, the obedience due from the subjects of this kingdom to Your Majesty, the glory and honour of your royal crown, our peace, and the terror of all enemies of Your Majesty's honour and of our happiness. Finally, if anything has been decided by us (as far as our mind can grasp and human weakness allows) which, when weighed in the balance of reasons by your father of blessed memory and our forefathers, who happily established it (and which we were bound in conscience not to violate), deserves the anger and indignation with which you have so often threatened us.

units.la: Quin contra, cum haec nobis sincero studio proposita fuerint, ut Deo debitus honos, religioni sua puritas, M. V. honor illibatus constaret, ut impietas ac homines ad flagitia prostituti, & tantum non
units.tr: On the contrary, since these matters have been laid before us with sincere zeal, so that the honour due to God, the purity of religion and the unimpaired honour of Your Majesty might stand firm, and so that impiety, and men who have prostituted themselves to crimes and are as good as

units.la: venundati impune non evaderent, ne impunitate alii ad similia perpetranda exstimularentur, ut ecclesia hæc ad pristinam suam & laudabilem politiam reduceretur, sollicite præcaventes ne injuriæ levissima specie quævis alia reformata ecclesia se perstrictam esse merito queri posset: Quare humillimis precibus obsecramus, ac certo sperDamus, omnem hanc tempestatem & sævos turbines mutatum iri in suavem halcyoniam, à radiis pacati vultus M.V. illucescentibus super hoc pervetustum M.V. regnum & populum: Ac decreta hæc in Comitiis ordinum regni, Majo mense anni sequentis, edicto M.V. habendis, sancitum iri: Qua sanctione ea religio nostra firmitate sulfulcietur [?], quæ majori splendore illustre M.V. diadema coruscabit, nosque sub M.V. diuturno & fœlici regimine beatum populum efficiet: Porro ut hisce M.V. coronare velit ille per quem Reges regnant, (cujus præsentiam hactenus experti sumus,) in totius orbis admirationem, hostium M.V. terrorem, piorumque solatium, ardentibus & continuis votis contendemus.
units.tr: sold to them, might not go unpunished, lest impunity encourage others to commit similar offences, and so that this Church might be restored to its former and praiseworthy polity, we take care lest any other reformed church should justly complain that it has been wronged, even in the slightest degree. Therefore we beseech Your Majesty with the humblest prayers and firmly hope that this whole storm and these savage whirlwinds will be turned into a gentle halcyon calm, under the rays of Your Majesty's peaceful countenance shining upon this most ancient kingdom and people of Your Majesty. And we hope that these decrees will be ratified in the assembly of the estates of the kingdom, to be held by Your Majesty's edict in the May of the following year. By this sanction our religion will be supported with firm strength, and it will make the diadem of Your Majesty, already shining with greater splendour, more illustrious, and will make us a blessed people under Your Majesty's long and happy rule. Further, that He by whom kings reign (whose presence we have hitherto experienced) may be pleased to crown these things for Your Majesty, to the wonder of the whole world, the terror of Your Majesty's enemies and the comfort of the godly, we shall strive with burning and unceasing prayers.

units.la: Tandem præses polita & gravi oratione Synodum dimittit, Deo ac regi gratias agendas esse monet, ob singulare hoc synodi liberæ beneficium: Aliis etiam, prout uniuscujusque merita postulabant, idem officium, synodi nomine exhibuit: Ac cum cantu Psalmi 133. quæ fœliciter aperta fuit, fœliciter dissolvitur Synodus, post triginta dierum sessionem; cui intererant cum jure suffragii tam definitivi quam deliberativi, centum quadraginta tres pastores & professores, nonaginta quinque Seniores tam ab urbibus quam à Classibus deputati, inter quos fuere sexdecim ex majori nobilitate, Comites videlicet & Domini Barones; ex minori nobilitate viginti octo, Equites Aurati ut plurimum. Finis.
units.tr: Finally, the moderator, with a polished and weighty speech, dismisses the Synod, and bids them give thanks to God and the king for this singular benefit of a free synod. He also, in the name of the Synod, offered the same duty to others, according to what the merits of each required. Then, with the singing of Psalm 133, the Synod, which had been happily opened, is happily dissolved after thirty days of sessions. Present at it, with both definitive and deliberative vote, were one hundred and forty-three ministers and professors, and ninety-five elders deputed both from the towns and from the classes; among them were sixteen from the higher nobility, namely earls and lords barons, and from the lesser nobility twenty-eight, mostly knights of the golden spur. Finis.

units.la: A Synodo Nationali deputati, provinciam sibi impositam diligenter obeunt; pastores synodi authoritatem pervicaciter rejicientes, aliosque de quibus in meliorem mentem reducendis deploratum effet, & insignibus flagitiis infames loco movent: quorum complures in Angliam profugerant, & hi cum aliis, qui in ruinis patriæ suæ Scotiæ improbas & immodicas suas spes fundabant, quicquid livor aut malitia comminisci poterat, contra Scotos fœderatos impudenter ventilarunt: atque hisce artibus eousque prævaluere, ut non solum plurimis ex plebe, verumetiam magnatibus tandem persuaserint, Scotos quotquot fœderi subscripsissent & Synodum Nationalem ratam habuissent, à regis legitima obedientia defecisse, ac de Anglia invadenda cogitare: Et eousque calumniis hisce fides habita, ut in aula regia, convocato senatu de bello in Scotos rebelles consultatum fuerit; ibi, rege serenissimo non dissimulante quid vellet, & Scotis profugis facilitatem victoriæ futiliter ostentantibus, conclusum fuit, rebellionem hanc Scotorum fœderatorum apertam, armata manu protinus compescendam esse; & bellum terra marique adversus Scotos decernitur: Magni itaque apparatus tam navales quam terrestres in Anglia instrui jubentur; & per emissarios omnia terriculamenta adhibentur quibus à fœdere deficerent Scoti: sublatum fuit commerciorum jus, obsessi omnes viarum ac itinerum aditus, ne ulla rerum Scoticarum certa relatio ad Anglos perveniret: Nobiles Scoti qui aulæ regiæ ministeria obibant, & alii qui aulam sequebantur, in juramentum adiguntur, quo fœderi Nationali & synodo Glasguensi abjurabatur, ac tenebantur omnes suas vires regi subministrare, quandocunque ipsius Majestati visum fuerit eorum opera uti. Adhæc prodeunt regis literæ ad omnes Angliæ provincias 26. Ianuarii datæ, quibus nobilibus Anglis imperabatur,ut Eboraci, (quam ci-vitatem pro exercitus sui diribitorio designaverat Rex) cum suis Regi adessent ad Calend. Aprilis; ut inde ad limites regni Angliæ profecturi objicerent se Scotis Angliam invasuris.
units.tr: Deputies appointed by the National Synod diligently carry out the task laid upon them. They remove from their places those ministers who stubbornly reject the authority of the Synod, and others whom it was despaired of bringing back to a better mind, and who were infamous for notorious crimes. Many of these had fled into England, and these, together with others who were building their wicked and immoderate hopes on the ruin of their country Scotland, shamelessly spread abroad whatever envy or malice could devise against the Scots who had entered the Covenant. By these arts they prevailed so far that they persuaded not only many of the common people but at last even the magnates that the Scots, all who had subscribed the Covenant and had approved the National Synod, had revolted from the lawful obedience of the king, and were planning to invade England. And so much faith was given to these calumnies that in the royal court, with the council summoned, a debate was held about war against the rebel Scots. There, the most serene king not concealing what he wished, and the Scottish exiles vainly displaying the ease of victory, it was concluded that this open rebellion of the Covenanted Scots must be put down at once by armed force, and war by land and sea against the Scots was decreed. Therefore great preparations, both naval and land forces, are ordered to be made ready in England; and through emissaries every kind of threat is employed to turn the Scots from the Covenant. The right of commerce was abolished, all approaches to the roads and highways were blockaded, so that no certain report of Scottish affairs might reach the English. The Scottish nobles who served in the royal court, and others who followed the court, were bound by an oath by which they renounced the National Covenant and the Glasgow Synod, and were held to furnish all their strength to the king whenever His Majesty should see fit to use their service. Besides, letters of the king were issued to all the provinces of England, dated 26 January, by which the English nobles were commanded to be present with their men at York (which city the king had designated as the depot for his army) by the Kalends of April; so that from there they might set out to the borders of the kingdom of England and confront the Scots who were about to invade England.

units.la: In hoc rerum statu publicatum est à Scotis scriptum in Anglorum gratiam, ut ipsos[?] vero controversiæ statu, & serie actionum suarum in[?] serio edocerent, deque communi periculo[illegible, ~1 letter]rique genti à Romanensibus imminente amice [illegible, ~3 letters]monerent, ac omnem malæ suspicionis ansam inter tam vicinas&c unice amicas, ac tot tamque arctis vinculis sibi invicem conjunctas gentes averterent; rumores[?] illos, quod prætextu religionis,regii regiminis jugum excutere, ac Angliam invadere dicerentur, esse meras calumnias,Deumque vindicem in capita sua vovent, si impiis ejusmodi cogitationibus animas suas, regi secundum Deum devotissimas, unquam polluerint: Scriptum porro illud de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: In this state of affairs there was published by the Scots, for the benefit of the English, a writing in which they were to set out sincerely for them the true state of the controversy and the sequence of their actions, and were to warn them in friendly fashion of the common danger threatening both nations from the Romanists; and they were to turn away every occasion of evil suspicion between two such neighbouring and uniquely friendly nations, joined to each other by so many and such close bonds. They declare that those rumours, that under the pretext of religion they were said to be shaking off the yoke of royal government and invading England, are mere calumnies; and they call God to witness against their own heads, if they ever polluted their souls, which are most devoted to the king after God, with such impious designs. The writing itself, translated almost word for word, is as follows.

units.la: Declaratio directa ad omnes sinceros & probos Christia- nos in regno Angliæ degentes, à Nobilibus, Baronibus, civitatibus, ecclesiarum pastoribus,& plebe regni Sco- tiæ, ad vindicandas actiones & intentiones suas ab iniquis hostium calumniis.
units.tr: Declaration addressed directly to all sincere and upright Christians living in the kingdom of England, from the nobles, barons, cities, ministers of the churches, and people of the kingdom of Scotland, to vindicate their actions and intentions from the unjust calumnies of their enemies.

units.la: OPus illud reformationis nunc denuo renovatum, & fœliciter hactenus in hoc regno promotum, ubique obviam habuit, quicquid excogitare potuit emissariorum Romanensium hostium nostrorum astuta malitia: Sed Dominus omnes eorum conatus hactenus frustratus est, ac ab eo infatuata est Ahitophelis prudentia. Nunc vero cum satis videant se non posse aperta vi Hierosolymæ mœnia dejicere, eadem calumniis subvertere moliuntur, freti impio illo axiomate, Calumniare audaciter semper aliquid adhærebit: Ac exemplo Tobiæ, Sanballati, & hujus farinæ similium omni opera readificationi per Ezram & Nehemiam sese opponentium, ac regi suggerentium; Cur civitas hæc rebellis reædificatur ? Eadem premunt vestigia novationum in hac ecclesia authores, qui captata opportunitate (qua nos summo nostro cum dolore destituimur) & freti auxilio & cohortationibus quorundam suæ professionis, male erga religionis nostræ sincéritatem affectorum, regi susurrant, ac in vicina Anglia spargunt salsissimas & impias calumnias (præter illas in edicto 18. Decemb. objectas, quas fuse in protestatione nostra hactenus in publicam lucem evulgata diluimus) majori ne impudentia an malitia haud facile dicas: Religionem videlicet à nobis solum prætendi; propositum tamen nobis esse legitimum authoritatis regiæ jugum penitus excutere, ac vicinam Angliam invadere; ut ejus spoliis ac exuviis ditemur. Atq;licet horum nobis minime conscii simus, ac pro Christiana æquitate confidamus, neminem, cui religionis aut politiæ rationes ullatenus perspectæ sint, calumniis istis, contra integrum regni & ecclesiæ Nationalis corpus confictis, fidem habiturum; cum tamen certiores facti essemus, novationum inter nos authores & reformationis hostes primarios omni conatu adniti, ut sacras Majestatis regiæ aures calumniis hisce inficiant, ac eosdem Anglis persuadeant, cogebamur innocentiam nostram vindicare, ac fidem diluere quam hæ calumniæ apud quemlibet inventuræ essent, tum supplicibus nostris literis exhibitis 31. Ianuarii proxime elapsi, Dominis in sanctiori regis in hoc regno senatu, tum hac nostra præsenti publica declaratione, qua Deum testamur, Religionem unicum esse subjectum, Conscientiam solam motivam, ac Reformationem uni-cum cum esse scopum nostrorum conatuum: quam ut assequeremur, sicuti hactenus nunquam declinavimus ac destitimus ab humillima & legitima via petitionum, quibus serenissimi Regem obsecrati fuimus ut malis nostris ac gravaminibus dignaretur legitimis mediis mederi; sic eadem via adhuc pergimus, ac pro ratione officii nostri denuo rogamus, ut indictione parlamenti ad sanciendam Synodum regia authoritate indictam, coepta nostra felicia coronare velit. Et uti hactenus in supplicibus nostris libellis saepius professi fuimus, ac in solenni nostro foedere cum Deo sacrosancte juravimus, ac publice coram Deo & hominibus, coelo & terra spectantibus in protestationibus nostris declaravimus, nunquam nobis in mentem venisse, submissam & debitam legitimae authoritati regiae obedientiam excutere, sic praesentibus hisce idem repetimus, ac solenniter declaramus, fidelia nostra pectora nunquam hospitium praebuisse cogitationi cuilibet quae clementiss. nostro regi ejusque regimini praejudicio esse posset, cui a Rege regum longaevum & justum super nos regnum precamur: atque eo ad immortalitatem fero demum translato, ut ex ipsius posteris nunquam defuturi sint, qui, quandiu sol ac luna vices suas in mundo obeant, solio huic insideant. Etenim agnoscimus eum esse Dei deputatum regni hujus sceptrum gubernantem, ea continua a tot regibus majoribus suis successione, ut nullus hodie rex sese ejus Majest. hic conferat, neque ulla gens nobis sese aequiparare posset, ratione verae antiquitatis & legitimae successionis unius stemmatis regum apud nos natorum, quam gloriam absit ut foedo quovis & impio contra Dei unctum conatu obliteremus, quin contra serio imprecamur, ut omnes ejus hostes ignominia confundantur, ac ex animis precamur ut felix quaelibet nobis detur occasio, qua cum summo vitae ac fortu-narum narum nostrarum discrimine, fidelitatem, qua in regis personam ac honorem tuendum & promovendum flagramus, testemur. Benignitas & veritas regem semper custodiant.
units.tr: That work of reformation, now renewed again and happily advanced thus far in this kingdom, has met with whatever the crafty malice of our Roman enemies' emissaries could devise. But the Lord has so far frustrated all their attempts, and the counsel of Ahithophel has been turned to foolishness. Now, however, since they see that they cannot pull down the walls of Jerusalem by open force, they strive to overthrow them by calumnies, relying on that impious maxim, Calumniate boldly; something will always stick. Following the example of Tobiah, Sanballat, and others of that stamp, who opposed all rebuilding under Ezra and Nehemiah and suggested to the king, "Why is this rebellious city being rebuilt?", the authors of innovations in this church tread the same path. Seizing the opportunity (which, to our very great sorrow, we lack), and relying on the help and encouragement of some of their own profession who are ill-disposed toward the sincerity of our religion, they whisper to the king and spread in neighbouring England the most bitter and impious calumnies. (Besides those objected in the edict of 18 December, which we have refuted at length in our protestation already published, it is hard to say whether with greater impudence or malice.) Namely, they claim that religion is merely a pretext for us, and that our real purpose is to cast off entirely the yoke of royal authority and invade neighbouring England, so as to be enriched by its spoils. Although we are by no means aware of these things, and trust in Christian fairness that no one whose understanding of religion or politics is at all clear will give credence to these calumnies, fabricated against the whole body of the kingdom and the National Church, nevertheless, since we have been made aware that the chief authors of innovations among us and the primary enemies of reformation strive with every effort to taint the sacred ears of His Royal Majesty with these calumnies and to persuade the English of them, we were compelled to vindicate our innocence and to clear away the stain these calumnies would leave in anyone's mind. We did this both by our supplicatory letters presented on 31 January last to the lords in the more sacred senate of the king in this kingdom, and by this present public declaration, in which we call God to witness that religion is the sole subject, conscience alone the motive, and reformation alone the aim of our endeavours. To attain this, just as we have never departed or withdrawn from the most humble and lawful way of petitions, by which we have repeatedly begged the most serene King to deign to remedy our evils and grievances by lawful means, so we still continue by the same way. According to the duty of our office, we again ask that he be pleased to crown our happy undertakings by calling a parliament to ratify the Synod convened by royal authority. And just as we have often professed in our supplicatory libels, have solemnly sworn in our sacred covenant with God, and have declared publicly in our protestations before God and men, in the sight of heaven and earth, that it never came into our minds to cast off the submissive and due obedience owed to lawful royal authority, so by these present letters we repeat the same and solemnly declare that our faithful hearts have never harboured any thought that could be prejudicial to our most clement king and his government. We pray to the King of kings for a long and just reign over us for him, and that, his throne being carried over into immortality, there may never be lacking from his offspring those who, as long as sun and moon perform their courses in the world, sit upon this throne. For we acknowledge him to be God's deputy, governing the sceptre of this kingdom, by so continuous a succession from so many majestic kings before him, that no king today can compare with His Majesty here, nor could any nation equal us in true antiquity and lawful succession of kings born among us of one line. Far be it from us to blot out this glory by any foul or impious attempt against God's anointed. Rather, we earnestly pray that all his enemies be confounded with shame, and from our hearts we pray that some happy occasion be given us by which we may attest, at the greatest peril of our lives and fortunes, the loyalty which we burn to defend and promote for the king's person and honour. May kindness and truth always preserve the king.

units.la: De Anglia invadenda quod objicitur: Æternum Deum, cui cordium nostrorum intimi recessus explorati sunt, testamur, nunquam nobis in mentem yenisse, ullam gentem damno quolibet afficere, multo minus vicinam Angliam, cum qua in eadem insula, sub eodem rege, remotis omnibus controversiis, & exhibitis tot sinceri amoris indiciis hactenus degimus, ut sperari vix posset, illud unquam eventurum inter gentes sibi invicem olim tam adversas, nunc vero feliciter reconciliatas, ac arctissimis vinculis conjunctas, quibus potius arctius constringendis, quam iniqua hostilitate dissecandis studebimus. Atque licet confidamus, ipsa hujus contra nos calumniæ improbabilitate, apud bonos fidem omnem obstructum iri; ut tamen improbis hisce calumniatoribus os obstruatur, ac pudore, si quis illis reliquus sit, suffundantur, gravamina & metus, conatus & proposita nostra ea libertate & sinceritate breviter delineabimus, qua demonstrari possit quam amice in fratres Anglos feramur, ac vanitas & falsitas calumniæ hujus omnium oculis objiciantur.
