units.tr: As to the charge that England is to be invaded: we call the eternal God, to whom the innermost recesses of our hearts are known, to witness that it never came into our minds to inflict any harm on any nation, much less on neighbouring England. We have lived with England on the same island, under the same king, with all controversies set aside and with so many signs of sincere love shown on both sides, that it could scarcely be hoped this would ever happen between nations once so hostile to each other, now happily reconciled and bound by the closest ties. Those ties we shall rather strive to bind more tightly than to sever by unjust hostility. And although we trust that, by the very improbability of this calumny against us, all belief in it will be shut off among good people, nevertheless, so that the mouths of these wicked calumniators may be stopped, and they may be covered with shame if any shame remains to them, we shall briefly set out our grievances and fears, our endeavours and purposes, with such frankness and sincerity that it may be shown how friendly our feelings are toward our English brethren, and the vanity and falsehood of this calumny be set before everyone's eyes.

units.la: Etenim cum unice dilectis Christianis fratribus vicinæ nobis gentis deflemus, manifestam & palpabilem experientiam periculosarum machinationum, quas moliuntur & promovent Ecclesiastici quidam maximæ authoritatis in Anglia, ut novationes in religione introducant, corruptione doctrinæ, mutatione disciplinæ, & quotidiana alteratione externi & publici cultus divini, publica Arminianismi & quorundam dogmatum papatus defensione, pastorum & Professorum promotione, quibus heterorodoxiæ istæ unice arrident, approbatione & commendatione librorum istis heterodoxiis refertorum; multatione, exilio eorum qui pro munere à Deo imposito hæresibus, disciplinæ, ac cultui Romanensi obviam ire conantur; violatione ac diminutione juris regii; tyrannide in conscientias, bona ac fortunas omnium cujuscunque demum dignitatis subditorum in regno Angliæ: Neque contenti intra proprios limites subsistere authores fuerunt & auxilio, hujus regniPseudo-episcopis ut non solum conformitatem in ceremoniis inter hanc ecclesiam & Anglicanam urgerent, verumetiam cum ipsa ecclesia Romana in articulis papatus substantialibus, uti constat ex libris liturgiæ & Canonum, quos papisticarum superstitionum, doctrinæ, ac tyrannidis cumulum continere deprehensum fuit, quosque confessum fuit, primum formatos, dein interpolatos in Anglia, atque huc demissos ad ipsorum socios Pseudo-Archiepiscopos & Episcopos hujus regni, ut hic impressi, nostris ecclesiis obtruderentur, idque sine ullo ordine aut consensu, ut unica forma divini cultus publici & regiminis ecclesiastici, atque sic per nos facilior via iisdem in Anglia sterneretur: Quod per epistolas egerint cum publicis hujus regni officiariis, nobilibus, ut civitatibus, ut eosdem libros hic promoverent: Quod sereniss. regi persuaserint, ut edicto publico declararet, libros hos, licet pontificia superstitione refertos, ab eâ tamen prorsus immunes esse; quin media esse commodissima ad hujus ecclesiæ ædificationem: Quod regi Authores fuerint, ut severo edicto prohiberet legitimos conventus & humiles supplices libellos subditorum suorum sub pœna rebellionis: &, quia impias has istorum machinationes in lucem apertam protraxerant, ac de iisdem modeste quæsti fuerant, & Nationale majorum cum Deo fœdus renovaverant, quo ad regis legitimam obedientiam sese denuo obligarent; ut Rex Sereniss. fideles hosce suos subditos eo nomine haberet rebelles & perduelles, quibus extremam ruinam interminatus sit: Quod regi persuaserint, ut sub pœna perduellionis interdiceret continuationem liberæ nostræ Nationalis synodi; (regia authoritate indicta, quod post tot supplicationes tandem obtinuimus) utque se verbo regio obstringeret ad eorum tutelam qui contra ecclesiæ legitimam authoritatem pervicaces essent: ut minaretur & se accingeret ad bello invadendum antiquum hoc, fidele, & nativum sibi regnum; ut supplicibus nostris libellis, juramentis solennibus, declarationibus ingenue formatis, dissideret: Quibus factis (quantum penes se fuit) omnem operam impenderunt, ut regis animum à subditis suis, & subditorum studia (si fieri posset) à rege abalienarent. Denique ut malitiæ suæ extremum colophonem imponerent, regi persuaserunt, ut consilium apertorum (ut fertur) papistarum amplecteretur, iisque summam præfecturam exercitus nobis invadendis destinati, traderet. Neque adhuc cessant, discordiarum semina inter utrumque regnum spargere, ut in mutuam cædem nos protrudant; Quod malum avertat Deus, ac speramus istorum malitiam eo usque non posse pertingere, Deo Sereniss. regis & vicinæ gentis oculos aperiente, ut opertam istam vafritiem recludant, qua hoc solum ab iis intenditur, ut duobus regnis in cruentum bellum commissis, reformata religio utrinque facilius deleri, ac Papatus restitui possit; quod haud difficile factu erit, utroque regno belli calamitatibus concusso, & Pontificiis regni vires & præcipua munia militaria obtinentibus (quorum potentia Angliæ antea satis formidabilis erat) & animum nunc sibi sumentibus, haud dubia spe auxilii ab exteris, qui opportunitatem eam lubentes amplectentur.Quæ omnia quamplurimum damnî inferunt honori & potestati regiæ, ipsiusque frequentissimis edictis, in tutelam reformatæ religionis ( cujus assertor est ) publicatis. Iure etiam meritoque querimur, quod sint in regno Angliæ qui magis credant calumniis ad fovendam discordiam, excitandam in nos fratres invasionem hostilem ingeniose excogitatis, quam nostris solennibus protestationibus, libellis supplicibus, declarationibus, & Sacrosancto cum Deo ipso fœderi: Interim, qui in hanc sen-tiam concesserunt, eos, vel falsa relatione rerum nostrarum per adversarios nostros, vel defectu perspicuæ & plenæ relationis fidelium & legitimorum nostrorum, qui Christianos decent, conatuum, eo pertractos esse non dubitamus. Quare summis votis contendimus, ut pro prudentia & Christiana charitate sibi posthac caveant, ne ejusmodi relationibus ad invidiam nobis conflandam confictis temere credant, donec commode de vero rerum nostrarum statu certiores fieri possint. Dolemus insuper cujuslibet animum opinionem hanc subivisse; defensionem, scilicet, episcopatus in Ecclesia Scotica justam posse præbere causam nos hostiliter invadendi, & gentem hanc bello impetendi, ac resuscitandi veterem illam Christiani sanguinis profusionem & infœlices controversias, quæ olim inter utramque gentem exagitatæ fuerunt, nunc vero feliciter permutatæ sunt in suavem animorum conjunctionem: Quandoquidem Episcopatus in hac ecclesia, adversetur primitivæ reformationi, Confessioni fidei, & juramento Nationali, quo regimen illud primitus abjuratum olim fuit; quod in alterius cujuslibet regni aut ecclesiæ damnū cedere nequit, quæ propriis suis statutis & constitutionibus adhærere potest. Verū sicuti in omnibus quæ sub deliberatione cadunt, justitia debet esse causa movens, & utilitas aut honor,fines; sic in negotio hoc momenti maximi ferio hæc perpendenda veniunt, An videl. hostilis hæc regni nostri invasio, quia sacramento Deo omnipotenti præstito de re legitima, adhæremus, & debitam legitimis regni statutis & ecclesiæ decretis obedientiam præstamus; invasoris respectu legitima esse possit & & justa: & an utilitas restituendi inter nos Episcopatum possit præstare tantam Christiani sanguinis profusionem & cruenti belli discrimina, cujus eventus à Domino exercituum dependet. Quin cuivis quam perspectissimum esse poterit, alium longe finem ab adversariis nostris hoc bello intendi, eorumque consilia altius descendere, alioqui certe præsules, si Christianam religionem & patriam sincere & ex animis colerent, facilius ferrent jacturam ambitionis & sæcularis fastus quæ studiose fovent, quam ut subjiciendo faces quibus utrumque arsurum sit regnum, religionem ipsam in manifestum discrimen deducerent.
units.tr: For we grieve, as Christian brethren who love the neighbouring nation dearly, over the plain and tangible experience of the dangerous schemes that certain churchmen of the highest authority in England are contriving and promoting in order to introduce innovations in religion. These include the corruption of doctrine; the alteration of discipline; the daily changing of the external and public worship of God; the public defence of Arminianism and of certain dogmas of Papacy; the promotion of ministers and professors to whom these heterodoxies alone are pleasing; the approval and commendation of books full of these heterodoxies; the fining and exile of those who, by the office laid on them by God, try to oppose heresies, discipline and Roman worship; the violation and diminution of the royal right; and tyranny over the consciences, goods and fortunes of all subjects in the kingdom of England, whatever their rank. Nor have these authors been content to keep within their own bounds. With the help of the pseudo-bishops of this kingdom, they have pressed not only for conformity in ceremonies between this church and the English one, but also with the Roman church itself in the substantial articles of Papacy. This is clear from the books of the liturgy and of the canons, which were found to contain a heap of papal superstitions, doctrine and tyranny. It is admitted that these books were first drawn up and then interpolated in England, and sent hither to their fellows, the pseudo-archbishops and bishops of this kingdom, to be printed here and forced upon our churches. This was done without any order or consent, so that a single form of public worship and of ecclesiastical government might be laid down more easily among us, and by our means a smoother path might be paved for the same things in England. They have worked by letters with the public officers of this kingdom, with the nobles and with the cities, to promote these books here. They persuaded the most serene King to declare by public edict that these books, although stuffed with papal superstition, were nonetheless wholly free from it, and indeed most suitable means for building up this church. They were the authors of the king's forbidding, by a severe edict, lawful assemblies and the humble supplications of his subjects, under penalty of rebellion. And because we had dragged their impious machinations into the open light and had modestly inquired about them, and because the national covenant of our forefathers with God had been renewed, by which we bound ourselves anew to the king's lawful obedience, they made the most serene King count these his faithful subjects, on that account, as rebels and traitors, and threatened them with utter ruin. They persuaded the king, under penalty of treason, to forbid the continuation of our free national synod, which we obtained after so many supplications, though it was called by royal authority. They persuaded him to bind himself by royal word to protect those who were obstinate against the lawful authority of the church; to threaten and prepare to invade by war this ancient, faithful and native kingdom of his; and to reject our supplications, solemn oaths and frankly framed declarations. In all this, as far as lay in them, they spent every effort to estrange the king's mind from his subjects, and the subjects' loyalty from the king, if that could be done. Finally, to crown their malice, they persuaded the king to embrace the counsel of the papists (as it is said, openly so), and to hand over to them the supreme command of the army destined to invade us. Nor do they cease to scatter the seeds of discord between the two kingdoms, to push us into mutual slaughter. May God avert this evil. We hope their malice cannot reach so far, God opening the eyes of the most serene King and of the neighbouring nation, so that they may uncover the hidden craft by which this alone is aimed at: that, with the two kingdoms set against each other in bloody war, the reformed religion may more easily be destroyed on both sides and Papacy restored. This will not be hard to do, with both kingdoms shaken by the calamities of war, and with the papists holding the kingdom's strength and its principal military offices (whose power was already quite formidable in England) and now taking courage, with a confident hope of help from foreigners, who will gladly seize the opportunity. All these things do great harm to the honour and power of the king, and to his very frequent edicts published in defence of the reformed religion, of which he is the champion. We also complain, with justice and reason, that there are in the kingdom of England some who give more credence to calumnies cleverly devised to foment discord and to stir up a hostile invasion of us, their brethren, than to our solemn protestations, supplications, declarations and most sacred covenant with God. Meanwhile, we do not doubt that those who have consented to this opinion have been led to it either by a false account of our affairs given by our adversaries, or by the lack of a clear and full report from our faithful and lawful persons of the endeavours that befit Christians. We therefore earnestly urge that, in prudence and Christian charity, they take care henceforth not to believe rashly such reports, invented to stir up hatred against us, until they can be properly informed of the true state of our affairs. We grieve moreover that anyone's mind has entered upon the opinion that the defence of episcopacy in the Scottish Church could give a just cause to invade us hostilely, to attack this nation with war, and to revive that old shedding of Christian blood and those unhappy controversies which once troubled both peoples, and which have now happily been changed into a sweet union of minds. For episcopacy in this church is opposed to the primitive reformation, to the Confession of faith and to the National Covenant, by which that government was first abjured. Such a thing cannot be harmful to any other kingdom or church, which can keep to its own statutes and constitutions. But just as in all matters that come under deliberation, justice ought to be the moving cause, and utility or honour the aims, so in this matter of the greatest weight these questions must be weighed: whether this hostile invasion of our kingdom can be lawful and just on the part of the invader, because we adhere to what is lawful, sworn to Almighty God, and render due obedience to the lawful statutes of the kingdom and the decrees of the church; and whether the advantage of restoring episcopacy among us can justify so great a shedding of Christian blood and the dangers of cruel war, whose outcome depends on the Lord of hosts. Indeed it will be quite plain to anyone that our adversaries aim at a quite different end by this war, and that their counsels run deeper. Otherwise, certainly, the prelates, if they cherished the Christian religion and their country sincerely and from the heart, would more easily bear the loss of the ambition and worldly pride which they zealously foster, than by setting alight the torches by which both kingdoms would burn, bring religion itself into manifest peril.

units.la: Ne quis vero scrupulus cujuslibet animum suspensum teneat de nostrarum intentionum sinceritate, aut actionum æquitate, aut declarationum & accusationum contra reformationis & pacis nostræ hostes institutarum veritate: Ecce, paratos nos prositemur, ac opportunitatem nobis concedendam obtestamur, iisdem coram toto terrarum orbe asserendis & vindicandis: Etenim nisi nobismet ipsis oculos sponte occlusissemus, ac adversati fuissemus voluntati Dei nobis cognitæ, agnitæ, à nobis obsignatæ, in quam à Rege Serenissimo & majoribus nostris solenni cum Deo fœdere juratum fuit, quæque tot frequentibus regni statutis & ecclesiæ decretis post reformationem sancita fuit; nihil prorsus eorum quæ à nobis facta sunt, ullatenus omittere potuimus: Atque licet regnum hoc & ecclesia, tam libera, antiqua, independentia sint, quam quodlibet ullum aliud. regnum aut ecclesia in toto terrarum orbe, nihilominus ut vicinæ genti scrupuli omnes penitus eximantur, ne conatus & actiones nostras in deteriorem partem interpretetur, & ut demonstretur quam non solum legitima verumetiam simpliciter necessaria fuerint, quæcunque à nobis facta sunt in nupera Nationali Synodo; certo confidimus ordines regni Angliæ (si iisdem in parlamento convocatis actionum nostrarum in hoc negotio progressus & series fideliter, candide, ac plene relata fuerit,) non solum easdem non condemnaturos, verumetiam earundem æquitatem calculo suo approbaturos, ac in nostram gratiam se apud Regem Serenis. interpositurus: Ideoque rogamus, ne quis, cujus animo ingenuus erga Scotiam amor insidet, deteriora interim de nobis suspicetur; qui de actionum & intentionum nostrarum innocentia non dubitamus, quæ hactenus liberæ fuerunt ab omni criminis labe in regem nostrum Serenis. aut vicinam gentem: Et sicuti certiores facti de hisce calumniis contra nos confictis, sacrosancto juramento in frequentissimo conventu nobis invicem declaravimus, ejusmodi fœdis & impiis consiliis locum apud nos nunquam concessum fuisse; ita impense rogamus, ut commoda opportunitas nobis offeratur, qua eandem nostram innocentiam vobis & toti terrarum orbi testatam faciamus.
units.tr: Lest any scruple keep anyone's mind in suspense about the sincerity of our intentions, the fairness of our actions, or the truth of the declarations and accusations made against the enemies of the reformation and of our peace, behold, we profess ourselves ready, and we beg that an opportunity be granted us to assert and vindicate these things before the whole world. For unless we had of our own accord closed our eyes and opposed the will of God, known to us, acknowledged by us and sealed by us, to which the most serene King and our forefathers swore in a solemn covenant with God, and which was sanctioned after the reformation by so many frequent statutes of the kingdom and decrees of the church, we could in no way have omitted anything that we have done. And although this kingdom and church are as free, ancient and independent as any other kingdom or church in the whole world, nevertheless, so that all scruples may be wholly removed from the neighbouring nation, and our endeavours and actions may not be interpreted in a worse sense, and so that it may be shown that whatever was done by us in the recent National Synod was not only lawful but simply necessary, we confidently trust that the estates of the kingdom of England, if the course and sequence of our actions in this business are faithfully, candidly and fully reported to them when they are convened in parliament, will not only not condemn them but will approve their fairness with their votes, and will intercede with the most serene King on our behalf. Therefore we ask that no one whose mind holds a generous love for Scotland should meanwhile suspect worse of us; we who do not doubt the innocence of our actions and intentions, which until now have been free from any stain of crime against our most serene king or the neighbouring nation. And just as, having been informed of these calumnies invented against us, we declared to one another, under a most sacred oath, in a very full assembly, that such foul and impious counsels had never been admitted among us, so we earnestly ask that a convenient opportunity be offered us, by which we may make this our innocence attested to you and to the whole world.

units.la: Quibus votis tam æquis, tam pacificis si damnemur, non erit solum nobis Christianis vestris fratribus ingenti solatio, ac in futurum arctius nos vobis stringet, verumetiam omni dubio procul remoto, æquissimus mundi arbiter beneficii hujus in nos collati fructum uberem rependet, & cui notum quam cito.
units.tr: If they are condemned for these wishes, so just and so peaceful, this will be not only a great consolation to us, your Christian brothers, and will bind us to you more closely in future. Beyond all doubt, the most just Arbiter of the world will also repay abundantly the fruit of this kindness shown to us, and he knows how soon.

units.la: Nobis interim curæ erit omni opportunitate arrepta perspicue demonstrare, quantum ab animis nostris semper hactenus fuerit (& Dei gratia semper futurum sit) ut qualibet hostili actione, vicino regno noceremus, nisi quantum in necessariam nostram defensionem cogemur. Atque licet (quod bonus Deus avertat,) dura necessitas ad illud nos impelleret, illubenter certe in eam opinionem descendemus, ut judicaturi simus tale quid à regni illius corpore procedere, cum quo uti nulla est nobis controversia, sic propositum nobis non est ◆ contentionis[?] funem cum illo ducere, nisi primi ab Anglia invadamur: Quin potius judicabimus turbas hasce primum excogitatas, fotas, ac promotas fuisse ab iis qui neutri alterutrorum regnorum bene volunt, cum quibus solis nobis contendendum erit, quos jure pro meritis accipere possumus; utpote quod ob privatos & turpes suos fines non dubitent utrumque pariter regnum cruenti belli calamitatibus involvere; Atque licet factio domestica ab externis focillata, à quibus nervos suos derivat, nutritur, ac fovetur, nos ad vindictam irritet & solicitet; ejus tamen futilitas & infirmitas ea est, ut, sicuti in flammam nos non concitabit, nisi manifesta hostilitate nos aggrediatur; sic multo minus ad violentiam ullam nos protrudet, qua fraterna duorum horum regnorum concordia interrumpi, aut labe quavis sancta nostra professio aspergi possit: Ita confidimus iniquas communium utrique nostrum adversariorum calumnias, cousque[?] apud charissimos fratres non prævalituras, ut eos in funestam contentionem contra nos deducant, præsertim cum tam amico erga eos animo simus, ut seria sympathia tangamur gravissimorum onerum, & intolerabilium gravaminum, quibus premuntur per tyrannidem Hierarchiæ, & metuendæ istius servitutis, sub cujus jugo gemunt, ad eas incitas redacti impiis ecclesiasticorum consiliis, quæ Romam sapiunt, & pericuipsas tam in negotio religionis quam politiæ innovationes quotidie proferunt.
units.tr: For our part, we will take every opportunity to show plainly how far our hearts have always been (and by the grace of God always will be) from wishing to harm the neighbouring kingdom by any hostile action, except so far as we are forced to it for our necessary defence. Even if (which may good God avert) harsh necessity should drive us to it, we would certainly be unwilling to believe that anything of that kind had come from the body of that kingdom, with which we have no quarrel. Just as we have no quarrel with it, so we do not intend to draw the rope of contention with it, unless England attacks us first. Rather, we will judge that these disturbances were first devised, fostered and promoted by men who wish well to neither kingdom, and with whom alone we must contend, and whom we may rightly regard as deserving of this. For for the sake of their private and base ends they do not hesitate to involve both kingdoms equally in the calamities of a bloody war. And although the domestic faction, encouraged by foreign powers from which it draws its strength, is nourished and cherished, and stirs us and urges us to vengeance, yet its futility and weakness are such that, just as it will not set us aflame unless it attacks us with open hostility, so much less will it drive us to any violence by which the brotherly concord of these two kingdoms could be broken, or our holy profession be tainted with any stain. We trust that the unjust slanders of our common adversaries will not prevail so far with our dearest brothers as to lead them into a deadly contest against us, especially since we are so friendly towards them that we are moved by a sincere sympathy for the most grievous burdens and intolerable oppressions under which they are weighed down by the tyranny of the Hierarchy, and by that dreaded servitude under whose yoke they groan, driven to these straits by the impious counsels of churchmen, which savour of Rome, and which every day bring forth new innovations both in matters of religion and of government.

units.la: Ut ingenuam & apertam hanc intentionum nostrarum declarationem emitteremus, officii nostri ratio nos cogit; ut omnibus saltem probis vicinæ gentis subditis satisfaceremus, uti speramus nihil illis magis in votis esse quam ut confirmentur in bona, quam de nobis conceperunt ac fovent opinione; & ut sic præsumantur[?] contra traductiones & calumnias eorum qui extremam Christi regni ruinam, & ex tota hac insula profligationem sibi proposuerunt. Quam calamitatem Deus avertat, quem ferio[?] precamur, ut pacem & veritatem nobis largiri velit, ultra quæ animorum nostrorum desideria se nunquam extenderunt, quibusque procurandis nullis aliis utemur armis (nisi coacti) quam jejuniis & ad Deum omnipotentem precibus, ac supplicibus obsecrationibus ad Serenis. & Clementissimum nostrum Regem.
units.tr: The duty of our office compels us to make this frank and open declaration of our intentions, so that we may at least satisfy all honest subjects of the neighbouring nation. We hope that nothing is more desired by them than that they may be confirmed in the good opinion they have formed and cherish of us, and so may be protected against the calumnies of those who have proposed to themselves the utter ruin of Christ's kingdom and the overthrow of this whole island. God avert that calamity, whom we earnestly pray to grant us peace and truth, beyond which the desires of our hearts have never extended. To procure these we will use no other weapons (unless compelled) than fasting, prayers to Almighty God, and humble entreaties to our most serene and most gracious King.

units.la: Revisum ex præscripto Nationalis Synodi per me
units.tr: Revised according to the prescription of the National Synod by me

units.la: Mr. A. Ihonstonum[?], Synodi scribam.
units.tr: Mr. A. Johnston, clerk of the Synod.

units.la: Edinburgi 4. Februarij 1639.
units.tr: Edinburgh, 4 February 1639.

units.la: Hoc scriptum avide arreptum à multis in Anglia, sed statim maxima cura suppressum, ne in plures evulgaretur, & contrarium scriptum in Anglia adornatur quod per omnia templa Angliæ, dum ad sacra conveniret populus, è suggestu prælegendum imperatur; aculeatum imprimis, quo fœdus illud Scotorum cum Deo latum, opus diaboli, fœderati Scoti Dei & hominum osores, hypocritæ, seditiosi, rebelles, male sani cerebri, quorum technæ aperte se proderent, qui sibi propositum fuissent Angliam invadere, & læsæ majestatis rei declarantur; ut omnis sexus, omnis ordo hominum in eorum perniciem animaretur, & ad arma, quibus Scoti fœderati obruerentur, prorueret: quod de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: This writing was eagerly seized upon by many in England, but was at once suppressed with the greatest care lest it be spread among more people. Meanwhile a contrary writing was drawn up in England, which was ordered to be read aloud from the pulpit in all the churches of England while the people gathered for worship. It was especially harsh, in that the covenant made by the Scots with God was called the work of the devil, and the covenanting Scots were described as haters of God and men, hypocrites, seditious, rebels, men of unsound mind, whose schemes openly betrayed them, who had proposed to invade England, and who were declared guilty of treason. The purpose was to rouse every sex and every rank of men to their destruction and to drive them to arms by which the covenanting Scots might be overwhelmed. Translated almost word for word, it runs as follows.

units.la: PER REGEM. Edictum & declaratio, qua certiores fiant dilecti nostri subditi in regno nostro Angliæ, de seditiosis actio- nibus quorundam in Scotia, qui falsis religionis prætextibus Regiam nostram authoritatem subvertere co- nantur.
units.tr: BY THE KING. An edict and declaration, by which our beloved subjects in our kingdom of England are informed of the seditious actions of certain men in Scotland, who attempt to overthrow our royal authority under false pretexts of religion.

units.la: QUandoquidem placidis & pacatis mediis diu hactenus omnem operam dedimus, ut tumultus, a quibusdam in nos iniquioribus, excitatos in regno nostro Scotiæ sedaremus; sed frustra.
units.tr: Since we have hitherto taken every pains to quiet, by calm and peaceful means, the tumults stirred up in our kingdom of Scotland by certain men ill-disposed towards us, but in vain.

units.la: Nunc non æquum solum, verumetiam necessarium iudicavimus, subditis nostris in hoc nostro Angliæ regno in genere declarare, quæ fuerit actionum nostrarum veritas; quanta lenitate & clementia erga eos nos gesserimus; & quam maligne & pertinaciter illi sese contra nos gesserint, quemcunque tandem speciosum fucum obducant,quo se ac odiosam suam causam fidelium nostrorum subditorum animis melius insinuare possint.
units.tr: We have now judged it not only fair but necessary to declare to our subjects in this our kingdom of England, in general terms, what the truth of our actions has been, with how much gentleness and clemency we have behaved towards them, and how maliciously and obstinately they have conducted themselves against us, whatever specious colour they may spread over their odious cause, so that they may better insinuate it into the minds of our loyal subjects.

units.la: Tumultus illi & confusiones in Scotia primum excitati fuerunt, & nutriti à seditiosis quibusdam & in perduellionem pronis ingeniis, religionis prætextu, qui à perduellibus solenniter semper ostentatur; nunc tamen manifesto apparet, hominibus istis religionem nō fuisse propositam, (uti præ se falso ferunt & divulgant) sed ut omne Monarchici regiminis genus prorsus excuterent, regiamque nostram Authoritatem, iure hæreditario nobis in eos competentem, contemnerent: Quin ipsorum malignitas eousque processit, ut astute & subdole conati sint corda fidelium nostrorum in hoc regno subditorum inficere, & ad parem rebellionem (si penes eos fuisset) seducere. Nunc licet satis fidamus amori subditorum hujus regni erga nos (cujus perspicua testimonia hactenus exhibuerunt, quando tam paratos & hilares in hac causa nobis se obtulerunt) neq; unquam putemus factiosa & turbulenta ista ingenia scopum suum hic obtentura, nihilominus tamen pernecessarium censemus, iisdem mature significare, quam perduellibus conatibus & conciliis isti ferantur, quæ multifariam se nobis produnt.
units.tr: Those tumults and confusions were first stirred up in Scotland and nourished by certain seditious men, inclined by nature to treason, under the pretext of religion, which rebels always solemnly put forward. Yet it is now plainly evident that these men did not have religion in view (as they falsely pretend and proclaim), but intended to cast off every kind of monarchical government altogether, and to despise our royal authority, which belongs to us over them by hereditary right. Indeed their malice has gone so far that they have craftily and slyly tried to corrupt the hearts of our faithful subjects in this kingdom, and to seduce them into a like rebellion, had it lain in their power. Now, although we trust well enough in the love of the subjects of this kingdom towards us (of which they have given clear proofs hitherto, when they offered themselves so ready and cheerful to us in this matter), and although we never think that these factious and turbulent spirits will attain their aim here, nevertheless we judge it most necessary to make known betimes what rebellious attempts and plots they are pursuing, which show themselves in many ways.

units.la: Uti. 1. Frequentes famosos libellos, calumniis contra regiam nostram authoritatem, & æquas actiones refertos imprimi curarunt, quos in diversis regni hujus partibus sparserunt.
units.tr: For instance: (1) They have caused many infamous libels, full of calumnies against our royal authority and of unjust actions, to be printed, and have scattered them in various parts of this kingdom.

units.la: 2. Literis huc missis quosdam contra nos excitare, & quosdam fœderis sui socios Londinum miserunt, qui in privatis conventiculis, probos nostros subditos ab officio nobis debito seducere conati sunt.
units.tr: (2) By letters sent hither they have tried to stir up some against us, and they have sent some of their covenanting associates to London, who in private conventicles have tried to seduce our good subjects from the duty they owe us.

units.la: 3. Æqua nostra mandata omnia contempserunt, & contra eadem seditiose protestati sunt, quod in regno rite ordinato ferendum non est.
units.tr: (3) They have despised all our just commands and have protested against them seditiously, which is not to be tolerated in a rightly ordered kingdom.

units.la: 4. Fœdus nostrum Authoritate imperatum, eo nomine quod à nobis imperatum esset, rejecerunt, cum tamen nullum fœdus in eo regno unquam fuerit, fit, aut esse, possit legitimum, quod authoritate Regia imperatum non sit, aut saltem assensum ab eadem habeat, v. g. fœdus illud regnante patre nostro, gloriosæ memoriæ, ab eo probatum fuit, & dein permissum ut subditi illud obsignarent; idque Synodo Nationali obsecrante. Repetimus, fœdus nostrum ab iis rejectum fuisse, eo nomine quod à nobis imperaretur, quod vel inde constat, ex harmonia videl. absoluta inter fœdus à nobis imperatum, & illud ab iis obsignatum, quantum ad negotium religionis attinet. Quo istorum fœdere, multis proditorie persuaserunt, ut in societatem fœderis contra nos jurarent : quod fœdus (vel verius conspiratio) cum Deo esse nequit, cum contra nos fit Dei unctum & ipsorum regem, verum fuit & est fœdus cum Deo solum prætensum, ut speciosius perficerent opera diaboli, qualia sunt rebellio & perduellionis crimen.
units.tr: (4) They rejected our covenant, enjoined by royal authority, on the ground that it had been enjoined by us. Yet no covenant in that kingdom has ever been, is, or can be lawful which is not enjoined by royal authority or at least has its assent. For example, that covenant in the reign of our father of glorious memory was approved by him and then permitted to be signed by subjects, at the entreaty of the National Synod. We repeat: they rejected our covenant on the ground that it was imposed by us, which is clear from the complete agreement, so far as religion is concerned, between the covenant enjoined by us and the one they signed. By this covenant of theirs (or rather conspiracy) they treacherously persuaded many to swear to join their fellowship against us. That covenant (or rather conspiracy) cannot be with God, since it is against us, God's anointed and their king. It was and is a covenant only pretended to be with God, so that they might more plausibly carry out the works of the devil, such as rebellion and the crime of treason.

units.la: §. Denique istorum conatus & consilia rebellia ex omni genere hostilis apparatus bellici se produnt; quasi nos ipsis non essemus rex, sed hostis juratus. Et apparatu hoc bellico instructis quid aliud propositum esse potest, quam ut regnum hoc invadant ? nisi nos præmunitos deprehenderint, tam ut eorū armatæ violentiæ resisteremus, quam ut in superbam istorum contumaciam animadverteremus.
units.tr: §. Finally, the rebellious plans and designs of these men reveal themselves through every kind of hostile military preparation, as though we were not their king but their sworn enemy. For men equipped with such a war-machine, what other aim can they have than to invade this kingdom, unless they find us prepared, both to resist their armed violence and to punish their proud obstinacy?

units.la: Nam eorum plurimi & primi, non solum sint ingenio inquieto, sed re familiari disperdita, & unice expetunt, quamlibet occasionem sibi oblatam (præsertim quæ religionis velo tegitur) qua spoliis prædiorum & fortunarum fidelium nobis in regno hoc Angliæ subditorum nostrorum, res suas ad lautiorem statum redigant; quos confidimus sibi & rebus suis melius prospecturos, quam ut eas desperatorum hypocritarum arbitrio permittant, quorum conditio vix deterior reddi potuit, quamque quaerunt nunc meliorem efficere : Iterum quaerimus, quid aliud istis propositum esse potest ? Nam nostris edictis hactenus promulgatis persuasimus, tantum abesse ut de mutanda aut innovanda religione unquam cogitaverimus, ut contra apud nos firmiter statuerimus, eandem, prout legibus regni publicis sancitur, tueri : Et certe licet usque adeo nobis cordi fuerit iisdem hic satisfacere, ut omnibus ipsorum postulatis annueremus, regia tamen nostra clementia nullum aliud effectum apud eos sortita est, quam ut per eam intoleranda eorum superbia aucta sit : Ad omnia nihilominus connivere visum fuit, donec radicem ipsam regii regiminis aperte peterent : Regiam quippe authoritatem nunc sibi assumpserunt, etenim licet in omnibus regnis typographia ad regem pertineat, seditiosi tamen isti ausi fuerunt quicquid ipsis libitum esset, prælo committere nobis etiam vetantibus; & vetare ne imprimeretur quod ipsis displiceret, nobis etiam impressionem imperantibus, nec sine insigni contumelia typographum nostrum dimiserunt. Præterea ausi sunt conventus subditorum nostrorum indicere, exercitus colligere, arces nostras obsidere, subditos nostros censere, non sine minis contra eos qui nobis fideles permanserant. Hisce addemus, quod mandata & authoritatem senatus nostri despectui habeant, & authoritate sua propria senatum erexerint, cui adsunt quidam ex ipsorum primariis specie deputationis à nupera Pseudo-synodo Nationali: Atque sic conveniunt quando & ubi ipsis visum fuerit, agitant & definiunt quæ ipsi volunt, & mandata sua per omnes regni partes emittunt, sine consensu, imo notitia nostra, vel deputati nostri, vel senatus; quod licet directe adversetur plurimis statutis illius regni, nihilominus tamen ausi sunt obtendere violationem legum, quasi vecordis sui furoris causam primariam.
units.tr: For most of them, and the leaders in particular, are not only restless by nature but also ruined in their private fortunes. They desire above all else any opportunity that presents itself, especially one veiled by the cloak of religion, by which they may restore their own affairs to a more comfortable state through the plunder of the estates and fortunes of the faithful subjects we have in this kingdom of England. We trust that our loyal subjects will look after themselves and their property better than to hand them over to the will of desperate hypocrites, whose condition can hardly be made worse, and who now seek to make it better. Again we ask: what else can they intend? For we have persuaded people by our edicts published hitherto that we have never thought of changing or innovating religion. On the contrary, we have firmly resolved to maintain it here as it is sanctioned by the public laws of the realm. And certainly, although we have so much cared to satisfy them on this point that we would have agreed to all their demands, our royal clemency has obtained no other effect with them than that their intolerable arrogance has grown. Nevertheless we thought fit to overlook everything until they openly attacked the very root of royal government. For they have now claimed for themselves royal authority. Although in all kingdoms the printing press belongs to the king, these seditious men have dared to entrust to the press whatever they pleased, even though we forbade it, and to forbid the printing of whatever displeased them, even though we commanded its printing. Nor did they dismiss our printer without signal insult. Moreover, they have dared to summon assemblies of our subjects, to raise armies, to besiege our fortresses, and to tax our subjects, not without threats against those who had remained faithful to us. To these things we add that they hold our mandates and the authority of our council in contempt. By their own authority they have set up a council, to which some of their chief men are attached under the pretext of deputies from the late pseudo-synod of the nation. Thus they meet whenever and wherever it pleases them, debate and decide whatever they wish, and send out their orders through all parts of the kingdom, without the consent, indeed without the knowledge, of ourselves, our deputies, or the council. Although this directly contravenes many statutes of that realm, they have nevertheless dared to allege the violation of the laws as the chief cause of their frenzied rage.

units.la: Hic itaque Deum & orbem universum testamur nos ad arma coactos descendere, non solum ut eos ad saniorem mentem revocemus, & authoritatem nostram regiam in antiquo illo nostro regno restabiliamus,verumetiam ut præsidio & saluti simus huic regno, fidelibus subditis, cum uxoribus, liberis, bonis tam eorundem quam nostrorum, contra istorum rabiem, furorem, ac fœdus. Nobis etiam visum est vobis insuper declarare; sperare nos eorum optimis suo tempore ostensuros, nos fœdus in regno nostro cui assensum non præbemus, nunquam latiuros. Itaque status quæstionis nunc non est; An recipiendus sit liber liturgicus nec ne, neque an continuandum Episcopale regimen, an vero i[?]tud per presbyteros amplectendum; verum, An nos pro rege habeant an secus. Nam licet in quibusdam ab ipsis editis libellis nobis subblandiantur, nosque blanditiis ob suos fines permulcere conentur, praesertim in nupero isto libello Edenburgi impresso Februar. 4. 1639. Quidam tamen ipsorum repudiant tam juramentum fidelitatis quam primatus, ac publice tuentur, non teneri se ut in ea juramenta adigantur; quis vero putabit fideles & devotos nobis subditos esse, qui periculosarum ejusmodi opinionum Authores seu fautores sunt: aut pios & religiosos esse, qui doctrinam eam promovent, quae usque adeo adversatur communi & receptae omnium protestantium Theologorum sententiae de rege & civili magistratu? Atque hoc morbo quamplurimos suorum infecerunt, nam tres Scoti hodie in Wallia in vinculis detinentur, ob rejectionem juramenti fidelitatis & primatus nostri, & allegant se non posse fidem suam illis juramentis obstringere, quia in foedus istorum prius jurarunt. Atque licet hactenus usque adeo clementer & patienter erga eos nos gesserimus, nolumus tamen ut quilibet subditorum nostrorum existimet, nos posse aut velle permittere abrogationem regiminis Episcopalis ex illo nostro regno, tam frequentibus legibus ibidem sancitis, praesertim cum universo Christiano orbi notum sit, regimen illud in se esse maxime Christianum, & paci ac Monarchico regimini imprimis accommodum.
units.tr: Here, therefore, we call God and the whole world to witness that we have taken up arms, not only to call them back to a saner mind and to restore our royal authority in that ancient kingdom of ours, but also to be a protection and safeguard to this kingdom, to our faithful subjects, and to their wives, children, and goods, as well as to ours, against the madness, fury, and covenant of these men. We have also thought fit to declare to you further that we hope to show them, at a suitable time, that we will never permit the covenant in our kingdom, to which we do not give our assent. So the question now is not whether the liturgical book is to be received or not, nor whether episcopal government is to be continued, or rather to be replaced by government by elders. The question is whether they will acknowledge us as king or not. For although in some of the pamphlets they have published they flatter us and try to soothe us with blandishments for their own ends, especially in the recent pamphlet printed at Edinburgh on 4 February 1639, some of them nevertheless reject both the oath of allegiance and the supremacy, and publicly maintain that they are not bound to be bound by those oaths. Yet who will think those men faithful and devoted subjects to us who are authors or supporters of such dangerous opinions? Or who will think those religious and pious who promote a doctrine so opposed to the common and accepted opinion of all Protestant divines concerning the king and the civil magistrate? And they have infected very many of their people with this disease. For three Scots are today held in chains in Wales because they refused the oath of allegiance and our supremacy, and they allege that they cannot bind their faith by those oaths, since they have first sworn to the covenant of those men. And although we have hitherto treated them with such clemency and patience, we do not wish any of our subjects to think that we can or will permit the abolition of episcopal government in that kingdom of ours, government which has been so often sanctioned there by laws, especially since it is well known to the whole Christian world that this government is in itself most Christian and especially suited to peace and to monarchical government.

units.la: Volumus etiam, ut secum perpendant illius regni nostri subditi, quid fiet de tertio membro Parlamenti si aboleatur Episcopatus.
units.tr: We also wish the subjects of that kingdom of ours to consider carefully with themselves what will become of the third estate of Parliament if the episcopate is abolished.

units.la: * Visum insuper est vobis significare, & universo Christiano orbi notum facere, introductione libri liturgici in regno illo, nobis propositum non fuisse religionem seu hic, seu ibi innovare; verum ut esset conformitas in cultu divino publico inter illud regnum & alia nostra duo, licet maligni in deteriorem artem quædam detorserint.
units.tr: * It has further seemed right to us to signify to you, and to make known to the whole Christian world, that in introducing the liturgical book into that kingdom it was not our purpose to innovate in religion either there or here, but to secure uniformity in public divine worship between that kingdom and our two other kingdoms, although the malicious have twisted some things to a worse meaning.

units.la: Certiores vos facimus prodituram statim fusam declarationem quæ singula ab hujus negotii primordiis continebit, ipsorum improbis actionibus testata, ut blandi sed falli ipsorum sermones convincantur & confundantur: Interim quia declaratio ea tam mature componi nequit, necessarium judicavimus, ut præcurreret brevis hæc declaratio, ne fideles nostri subditi hic aut alibi inficiantur falsis,impiis, fucatis, sed admodum seditiosis istorum declarationibus: v. g. in postremo suo libello, (præter plurima falsa, vilia, & assentantia) sunt hæc scandalosa & splendide falsa mendacia: ut cum dicunt, Præfecturam summam exercitus quem nunc contrahimus, commisisse nos professis & apertis papistis, quod non plus nostro honori & nobilibus quibus ista cura demandatur derogat, quam est in se aperte falsum. Rursus dixerunt; Quosdam magnæ authoritatis in Hierarchia Anglicana, persuasisse ut armato exercitu nativum illud nostrum regnum aggrederemur, ac sese cum ipsorum religione intermiscuisse; Cum tamen verissimum sit, eorum nullum quidlibet aggressum fuisse nisi nostro regio mandato: Et de armato exercitu, omnibus nostris senatoribus qui tunc interfuerunt, liquido constat, illorum consilia ad pacem inclinasse, & (quantum penes se fuerat) persuasores fuisse moderationis immeritæ, quam erga tantorum criminum obnoxios hactenus exercuimus.
units.tr: We inform you that a full declaration will shortly be published, setting out each particular from the beginnings of this affair and attested by their wicked actions, so that their smooth but false words may be refuted and confounded. Meanwhile, since that declaration cannot be composed so soon, we have judged it necessary that this brief declaration should go before it, lest our loyal subjects here or elsewhere be infected by their false, impious, and disguised, yet most seditious declarations. For example, in their latest pamphlet (besides very many falsehoods, base things, and flatteries) there are these scandalous and glaringly false lies: that they say we have committed the supreme command of the army we are now raising to professed and open papists, which detracts no more from our honour and from the nobles to whom this charge is entrusted than is plainly false in itself. Again they have said that certain men of great authority in the English hierarchy persuaded us to attack that native kingdom of ours with an armed army, and that they have mixed themselves with their religion. Yet it is most true that none of them undertook anything except by our royal command. And concerning the armed force, it is clear to all our councillors who were then present that their counsels inclined to peace, and that (as far as lay in them) they were advocates of the undeserved moderation which we have hitherto shown towards those guilty of such great crimes.

units.la: Dicunt insuper, se nihil hostile contra Anglian aggressuros, nisi ad necessariam tutelam cogantur: Lubenter hic sciremus. Cujus rei tutelam? An perduellionis, Contra quos? Nonne contra nos verum & le[?]itimum ipsorum regem? Si se contra nos tueri veint, lege illud oportet, non armis, illam nunquam defugiemus, hanc nunquam permittemus. Leges vero nostræ quas præ se ferunt se tanti facere, ab iis quodammodo opprimuntur, & judices nostri ita terrentur, ut vix ac ne vix quidem ausi sint secundum leges sententiam pronunciare.
units.tr: They further say that they will undertake nothing hostile against England unless they are compelled to necessary self-defence. We would gladly know here: defence of what? Against whom? Of treason? Is it not against us, their true and lawful king? If they wish to defend themselves against us, they must do so by law, not by arms; we shall never shun the former, and we shall never permit the latter. But our laws, which they profess to hold in such high esteem, are in some measure oppressed by them, and our judges are so terrified that they have scarcely dared, or hardly even dared, to pronounce sentence according to the laws.

units.la: Hujusce generis seditiosis libellis rogamus ne boni nostri subditi se infici patiantur: utque omnes sciant quam necessario nunc cogamur armis nos instruere; quod nullo alio fine fit, quam ut regno huic nostro securitatem & salutem præstemus, & authoritatem nostram ibi collapsam restituamus, eosque in ordinem cogamus qui obliquis artibus subditos nostros in Scotia seduxerunt, idemque hic moliuntur, nisi ipsorum fraudi mature præveniatur. Nequaquam vero nobis propositum est armata manu urgere innovationem religionis quæ regni illius legibus sancitur, aut ut ejus leges, libertates & privilegia legitima violemus.
units.tr: We ask our good subjects not to allow themselves to be infected by writings of this sort, and so that all may know how necessarily we are now compelled to arm ourselves. This is done for no other end than to secure safety and welfare for this our kingdom, to restore our authority which has fallen there, and to bring to order those who by crooked arts have led our subjects astray in Scotland, and who are attempting the same here unless their deceit is forestalled in good time. Yet it is by no means our purpose to press by armed force an innovation in religion, which is sanctioned by the laws of that kingdom, or to violate its laws, liberties, and lawful privileges.

units.la: Præsentibus ergo hisce volumus & imperamus omnibus hujus regni nostri subditis, ne libellos seditiosos de hisce rebus ex Scotia aut aliunde transmissos recipiant; utpote quorum nullus alius usus esse poterit, quam ut ad parem rebellionem excitentur fideles nostri subditi. Mandamus etiam ut quicunque ejusmodi libellos hactenus receperint, eirenarchæ nostro proximo statim tradant, qui eosdem ad quemlibet nostrorum secretariorum transmittet, sub pœna severissima.
units.tr: Now, by these presents, we will and command all the subjects of this our realm that they receive no seditious pamphlets about these matters, sent from Scotland or from elsewhere, since such pamphlets can have no other use than to stir our loyal subjects to a like rebellion. We also order that whoever has hitherto received any such pamphlets shall at once hand them over to our nearest justice of the peace, who shall forward them to one of our secretaries, under the severest penalty.

units.la: Volumus etiam & jubemus, ut edictum & declaratio hæc nostra prælegatur in singulis per universum hoc regnū templis quando sacra peraguntur, ut infimi etiam & vilissimi perspiciant splendida & improba istorum facinora, actionumque nostrarum æquitatem & clementiam.
units.tr: We will and command also that this our edict and declaration be read aloud in every church throughout this whole kingdom when the sacred services are performed, so that even the lowest and meanest may perceive the shameful and wicked deeds of these men, and the justice and clemency of our actions.

units.la: Datum in Aula nostra. 27.Februar. anno. 14. regni Angliæ, Scotiæ, & Hiberniæ.
units.tr: Given in our Court, 27 February, in the 14th year of the reign of England, Scotland and Ireland.

units.la: Deus custodiat Regem.
units.tr: God save the King.

units.la: Impressum Londini apud Typographum Regium 1638.
units.tr: Printed at London by the King's Printer, 1638.

units.la: Qui annus erat Scotis uti omnibus aliis Christiani orbis incolis. 1639. Sed Angli computum suum annuum inchoant à 25. Martij.
units.tr: This was the year 1639 for the Scots, as for all other inhabitants of the Christian world. But the English begin their civil year on 25 March.

units.la: Classico hoc satis innotuit Scotis quid sibi exspe-ctandum esset, præsertim cum ab iis interceptæ essent tum literæ ad Marchionem Huntilæum, nobilem, clientelæ numerosissimæ, cujus in Borealibus Scotiæ provinciis ultra montem Grampium formidabilis olim consuevit esse potentia; & hisce literis intelligunt fœderati, Huntilæo cum summa authoritate istarum provinciarum præfecturam à rege demandatam fuisse: quam sciebant cupide amplexurum, & nihil reliqui ad summam diligentiam facturum, quo regis desiderio satisfaceret, & familiæ suæ Gordonianæ exsiltimationem augeret: Certis etiam nunciis certiores fiunt fœderati, se in Anglia rebelles declaratos, Berwicum & Carleolum munitas in Anglico limite urbes præsidiario milite impleri, regem sereniss. ingentem exercitum terra marique contra se submittere, Comitem Arundelium huic expeditioni præfectum esse, edicto regio ex singulis Angliæ provinciis justo numero delectos & in armis exercitatos regio vexillo Eboraci adesse, familiam regiam iter Eboracum versus, ad diribitorium designatum, suscipere, regemque ipsum citatis equis subsequuturum, & magnis itineribus Scotiam versus castra promoturum, Marchionem Huntilæum ut septentrionales Scotiæ provincias a reliquis distraheret, paratum habere ex clientibus & aliis quatuor aut quinque millia militum sub signis: Abredonenses, qui ab horum motuum initiis aversi in fœderatos animi aperta signa sæpius prodiderunt, urbem suam maritimam magna festinatione munire, ut regiâ classem amice exciperent, unde auxilia quotidie exspectabat, præmisso hactenus apparatu bellico; Australibus Scotiæ provinciis Marchionem Duglassiæ, Comitem Hethiæ, ac Baronem Parlamentarium Herefium; omnesPontificiæ religionis, cum suis clientelis quæ sane numerosæ sunt, imminere: Proregis Hiberniæ minas, qui præ se ferebat se totum occidentale latus Scotiæ, quod Hiberniam spectat, infestaturum, superaddi. Summa, cum undique metus ab externo hoste tam mari quam terra se ostentaret, nec levis tempestas ab internis hostibus, Pontificiis aulæ adictis, & quotquot in turbidis aquis largam piscaturam sibi promittebant, qui in diversis regni partibus se communiebant oborta est. Accipiunt etiam, hostium consiliis persuasum fuisse Anglis; Scotis in ordinem cogendis, externis copiis vix opus esse, mutuis cædibus semetipsos confecturos; vim tantum in limitibus eminus ostentaret Rex.
units.tr: The Scots had learned well enough from this call what they were to expect, especially since letters addressed to the Marquis of Huntly, a nobleman with a very large following, whose power once used to be formidable in the northern provinces of Scotland beyond the Grampian mountains, had been intercepted. From these letters the Covenanters understood that the command of these provinces, with the highest authority, had been entrusted to Huntly by the king. They knew he would embrace it eagerly and would leave nothing undone with the utmost diligence to satisfy the king's wish and to increase the reputation of his Gordon family. The Covenanters were also more certainly informed, by sure messengers, that they had been declared rebels in England; that Berwick and Carlisle, the fortified towns on the English border, were being filled with garrison soldiers; that the most serene king was sending a huge army by land and sea against them; that the Earl of Arundel had been placed in command of this expedition; that by royal edict a due number of men chosen from each province of England and trained in arms were assembling at York under the royal banner; that the royal household was setting out on the road to York, appointed as the rendezvous; and that the king himself would follow with swift horses and would move his camp towards Scotland by forced marches. Further, that Huntly, in order to cut off the northern provinces of Scotland from the rest, had ready four or five thousand men from his clients and others, under arms. The men of Aberdeen, who from the beginning of these disturbances had turned away from the Covenanters and had often openly shown their hostility to them, were fortifying their seaport in great haste, so as to receive the royal fleet as friends, from which they were daily expecting help, having first prepared their war equipment. In the southern provinces of Scotland, the Marquis of Douglas, the Earl of Hertford and Baron Herries, a member of Parliament, all adherents of the Popish religion, with their clients, who are indeed numerous, were threatening. To this was added the threat of the Lord Deputy of Ireland, who gave out that he would attack the whole western side of Scotland, facing Ireland. In short, while on all sides fear of a foreign enemy showed itself by sea as well as by land, there also arose no slight storm from internal enemies, Papists attached to the court, and all those who hoped for a rich catch in troubled waters, who had fortified themselves in various parts of the kingdom. They also learned that the English had been persuaded by their enemies' counsels that there would be scarcely any need of foreign forces to bring the Scots to order: they would destroy themselves by mutual slaughter, if the king only displayed his power at a distance on the borders.

units.la: Quare fœderatorum primarii Edenburgum convolant ad deliberandum ne quid religio & Respub. detrimenti caperet: Ante omnia statos dies complures per universum regnum publicis precibus ac jejuniis dedicant, ut Rex regum in cujus manu corda regum sunt, Serenis. sui regis animum, inimicorum calumniis à se prope abalienatum, ad mitiora & æquiora consilia flectere dignaretur: à se nihil non sed frustra pertentatum, quo regis immeritam iram deprecarentur; declarationes, Apologias, juramenta sua solennia quibus ab objectis criminibus se vindicabant, rejici querebantur, neque alio adhuc responso dignatum fuisse regem supplices à synodo literas fideliter traditas, quam apparatu hoc bellico: Difficultatibus hisce quibus undique obsepti quamprimum occurrendum esse omnibus persuasum fuit. Ad defensionem itaque sedulo se comparant, cumque plurimum inter arma bonam conscientiam sibi vendicare compertum haberent; nam ut ait ille
units.tr: Therefore the leading men of the Covenant hurried to Edinburgh to consider how religion and the commonwealth might be kept from harm. Above all, they set aside several days throughout the whole kingdom for public prayers and fasts, so that the King of kings, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, might deign to turn the mind of their most serene king, which had been nearly alienated from them by the slanders of their enemies, towards milder and more equitable counsels. They complained that they had tried everything, though in vain, to deprecate the king's undeserved anger; that their declarations, apologies and solemn oaths, by which they vindicated themselves from the crimes laid against them, were rejected; and that the king had not yet deigned to give any other answer to the humble letters faithfully delivered to him by the Assembly than this warlike preparation. All were persuaded that these difficulties, by which they were beset on every side, must be met as soon as possible. They therefore prepared themselves diligently for defence, and since they had found that among arms a good conscience was of the greatest value, for as the poet says:

units.la: Frangit & attollit vires in milite causa,Quæ nisi justa subest, excutit arma pudor.
units.tr: A just cause gives strength and lifts up the soldier's courage; without it, shame strikes the weapons from his hands.

units.la: Scripto demonstrant justitiam & præsentem necefsitatem defensionis contra armatam supremi magistratus vim: Licere videlic. maximæ & incorruptiori nobilitatis parti, cum collectivo regni corpore, religionem legibus publicis sancitam, regni privilegia & libertates armata manu tueri, contra principem qui extra regnum degens, hostium religionis consiliis circumactus, hostili apparatu subditos suos nullius criminis in leges reos aut convictos invadit, idque absque ulla juris divini aut humani violatione.
units.tr: In writing they demonstrated the justice of their cause and the present necessity of defence against the armed force of the supreme magistrate. Namely, that it is lawful for the greatest and most incorruptible part of the nobility, together with the whole body of the kingdom, to defend by armed force the religion established by public laws and the privileges and liberties of the kingdom, against a prince who, living outside the kingdom and swayed by the counsels of the enemies of religion, attacks with hostile preparations his own subjects, who have been neither accused of nor convicted of any crime against the laws; and that this may be done without any violation of divine or human law.

units.la: Scriptū hoc publicis typis & prælo nunquam commissum,oppugnarūtillud multi, sed ex obliquo partes quasdam perstringentes, easque à corpore scripti resecatas, ut facilius de adversario à se convicto triumphos facerent; utramque paginam Iesuitismi criminationibus replebant; contra vero fœderati Scoti immanem inter se & Iesuitas differentiam ostendebant; majorumque suorum ab ipsi regni Scotici primordiis, (quæ in ea tempora conjiciunt Historici quibus Alexander Magnus Babylonem cepit) ac vicinorum omnium regnorum vetera & recentia exempla proferebant, quibus quæstionem hanc extra omnem dubitationis aleam repositam affirmabant; prodiit tunc in lucem libellus quidam in Hibernia impressus, cujus author ut specimen exhi-beret pœnitentiæ quam profitebatur, quod Scotorum fœdus approbasset, ex professo totum illud Scotorum scriptum refutandum in se suscipit, ac ut opimam aliquam conditionem ecclesiasticam adipisceretur, strenue in Scotos fœderatos debacchatur, ut patronis suis munificis placeret, contraria thesi elegans scilicet & politum illud opusculum exornat, videlic. Non licere omnibus omnino subditis licet in unum coëuntibus, armata manu contra regem suum se tueri, licet sursum deorsum omnia tam in religione quam in legibus regni fundamentalibus vertat, omnibus ex regno fugiendum esse aut ferendum; læsæ majestatis reos esse, Iefuitismum reponere merum, qui ullam omnino quibuslibet defensionem armatam relinquat; jus hoc regis secum ferre, cujus absolutam & illimitatam potestatem qui legibus subjiciat, aut juramento, quo reges inaugurati obstringuntur, coërceat, humani & divini juris violatorem esse: Scoti fœderati cum libellum hunc tantas absurditates prima facie præ se ferre conspicerent, ut sperarent desperata ejusmodi dogmata nullos amplexuros, præsertim cum nullis aliis argumentis quam virulentæ linguæ petulantia & impuris verborum bombis instruerentur, indignum judicarunt responso, neque tenebrionum ambitionem, & captandæ gloriolæ immoderatum ardorem subjectis responsionum faculis fovendam esse.
units.tr: This writing was never committed to the public press. Many attacked it, but only obliquely, touching on certain parts and cutting them out of the body of the document, so that they could triumph more easily over an adversary they had supposedly refuted. They filled both pages with accusations of Jesuitism. The Scottish Covenanters, on the other hand, showed the vast difference between themselves and the Jesuits, and set forth the examples, old and recent, of their ancestors from the very beginnings of the Scottish kingdom (which historians, to whom Alexander the Great took Babylon, date to that time), and of all the neighbouring kingdoms, by which they affirmed that this question had been settled beyond every chance of doubt. Then there appeared a certain pamphlet printed in Ireland. Its author, to show a specimen of the repentance he professed for having approved the Scottish Covenant, undertook expressly to refute the whole Scottish document, and, in order to obtain some rich ecclesiastical benefice, he raged vigorously against the Covenanting Scots, so as to please his generous patrons. He adorned his elegant and polished little work with the contrary thesis, namely: that it is not lawful for all subjects, however they may join together, to defend themselves by armed force against their king, even though he overturns everything, in religion as well as in the fundamental laws of the realm; that all must either flee the kingdom or endure; that those who do so are guilty of treason; that this is pure Jesuitism, which leaves no armed defence at all to anyone; that this right belongs to the king, and that whoever subjects his absolute and unlimited power to the laws, or restrains it by the oath with which crowned kings are bound, is a violator of human and divine law. When the Covenanting Scots saw that this pamphlet at first sight presented such absurdities, they hoped that doctrines so desperate would win over no one, especially since it was furnished with no other arguments than the impudence of a venomous tongue and empty bombast of words. They judged it unworthy of a reply, and held that the ambition of little dark-minded men and an immoderate passion for a cheap glory should not be fed by giving them the torches of an answer.

units.la: Ne vero ex improviso opprimerentur provinciæ limitaneæ, legionem peditum conducunt sub ductu fortissimi & solertissimi tribuni Munroi, qui limitibus essent præsidio, priusquam major vis hostium ingrueret; ac in limitaneis istis provinciis locis opportunis dispositi impedirent, ne qua manus domesticorum hostium, qui regiarum essent partium, coiret. Uno etiam condicto die multa regni propugnacula in diversis regni partibus fine cæde & sanguine intercipiunt, Edenburgenam præsertim & Britannodunensem arces regias, in rupibus præcipitibus fitas, quibus aperta vi potiundis si apparatu bellico instructæ fuissent, nulla erat spes, verum necessario apparatu & commeatu tum destitutas facilius fuit in suam potestatem redigere, quas commeatu & omnibus necessariis egregie tunc munivere: Suspectos etiam & dubios fine tumultu exarmant; maritima loca freti Bodotriani ab utroque littore, quæ maritimæ hostilitati maxime obvia fuerunt, subitaria defensione muniunt, Letham præsertim portum Edenburgenum, multis hominum millibus voluntarias operas contribuentium, cum de salute hujus urbis penderet Edenburgum regni metropolis: idque tanta festinatione ut prope die noctuque in opere continuarent.Arcem Dalkethenfem admotis scalis suæ potestatis faciunt, simul cum apparatu bellico qui ibi post Julium mensem anni superioris delituit; Coronam, sceptrum, & ensem regium, regni insignia in conclavi ibidem reposita inveniunt, quæ magna solennitate à primariis nobilibus in arcem Edenburgenam, locum à majoribus destinatum hisce custodiendis, deferunt. Comes Argathelius, ut littora Cantiere & vicinarum provinciarum, ab exscenfionibus ex Hibernia tueretur, & impediret ingentes minas Proregis Hiberniæ, & conatus Comitis Antrum Hiberni ac quorundam insulanorum ex Hebridibus, præsertim Donaldi Gorm cum tribu sua, qui omnes magnifica se præstituros liberaliter promittebant; mille plus minus vassallos & clientes suos in locis opportunis disposuit, & cum aliis quibusdam copiis arcem marchionis Hammultonii in Arania (quæ insula est in æstuario Glottæ Hiberniam spectans, egregiamque ac tutam navibus stationem præbens) illasis custodibus intercepit. Tria millia militum festinato delectu ex Transforthanis provinciis, quibus se adjunxere qui in Angusia & Mernia foederatarum partium erant complures, adversus Huntilæum mittunt, qui tum cum æquali fere suorum numero sub signis prope Abredoniam se continebat, ut foederatos, Forbesios præsertim in illo tractu perpotentes & sibi æmulos, obrueret: Hisce foederatorum copiis præficitur Comes montis Rosarum magnæ spei juvenis, cui in vivido illo juventutis flore non solum non defuit, verumetiam eandem longe superavit: huic comes adfuerat sed fine ulla publica præfectura nobiliss. Alexander Lesslius, Eques Auratus, cui per omnes militiæ gradus illustris virtus & rara fœlicitas ad summam dignitatem & præfecturam militarem in castris SuecoGermanicis viam fecit, ejusque, secundum Deum, providis consiliis hujus expeditionis fœlicitas plurimum debebat.
units.tr: Lest the border provinces be overwhelmed unexpectedly, they hired a legion of infantry under the leadership of the bravest and most skilful tribune Munro, to guard the borders before a greater force of the enemy should rush in; and stationed in these border provinces at suitable places, they were to prevent any band of domestic enemies, who favoured the royal party, from assembling. Also, on one agreed day they seized many of the kingdom's strongholds in various parts of the realm without bloodshed or slaughter, especially the royal castles of Edinburgh and Stirling, which stand on sheer rocks; against these, had they been attacked by open force with a war equipment, there was no hope, but since they were lacking in the necessary equipment and provisions, it was easier to bring them under their own power, and they strongly fortified them then with provisions and everything necessary. They also disarmed, without tumult, those who were suspected or doubtful. They fortified the coastal places of the Firth of Forth on both shores, which were most exposed to hostile attack from the sea, with a hasty defence, and especially the harbour of Leith at Edinburgh, since the safety of Edinburgh, the capital of the kingdom, depended on it; many thousands of men contributed their work voluntarily, and they worked on it nearly day and night, with such haste. They took the castle of Dalkeith by setting up ladders, together with the war equipment that had lain hidden there since July of the previous year. They found the crown, sceptre and sword, the royal insignia, stored in a room there, and with great solemnity the leading nobles carried them to the castle of Edinburgh, the place designated by their ancestors for their safekeeping. The Earl of Argyll, to guard the shores of Kintyre and the neighbouring provinces against landings from Ireland, and to block the great threats of the Lord Deputy of Ireland and the attempts of the Irish Earl of Antrim and of certain islanders from the Hebrides, especially Donald Gorm with his clan, all of whom promised liberally to show magnificent support, placed about a thousand more or less of his vassals and clients at suitable points, and with certain other forces he seized, without any opposition from the guards, the castle of the Marquis of Hamilton in Arran (an island in the estuary of the Clyde, facing Ireland, which offers a splendid and safe anchorage for ships). They sent three thousand soldiers, quickly levied from the Trans-Forth provinces, to whom were joined many from Angus and Mearns who belonged to the Covenanting party, against Huntly, who at that time was keeping himself under arms with nearly an equal number of his men near Aberdeen, in order to overwhelm the Covenanters, especially the Forbes family, who were very powerful in that region and were his rivals. The command of these Covenanting forces was given to the Earl of Montrose, a young man of great promise, who in that vigorous flower of youth lacked nothing and far surpassed his peers. The noble Alexander Leslie, a knight, was present with the earl, but without any public command. His distinguished courage and rare good fortune had opened his way, through every grade of military service, to the highest rank and command in the camps of the Swedes and Germans, and the success of this expedition owed much, under God, to his wise counsels.

units.la: Mandatum fuit ut operam darent ne Huntilæus amplius provincias illas Boreales turbaret, & ut ipsum adorirentur, priusquam cum classe regia vires suas conjungeret, cujus adventum quotidie præstolabatur; ut Abredoniam subitaria defensione à civibus communitam in foederatorum potestatem redigerent, &c æt.[?] Favit Deus incœptis, nam audito copiarum foederatarum, quas Comes montis Rosarum ducebat, adventu, quibus foederati ex adversa Grampii montis parte se conjuncturi erant, dilabitur Huntilæus, nam vel copiis hisce conjunctis se imparem cernebat, quarum conjunctionem impedire non potuit, vel in mandatis fortasse non habebat, ut proelii dubiæ aleæ rem adhuc committeret; & ad munitum castellum Bogium maxima festinatione cum familiaribus & tribus liberis se recepit; Atque cum à selectis quibusdam foederatorum copiis infestatum se cerneret, & castellum ab omnibus ad arcem defendendam necessariis imparatum, ultro se in foederatorum manus tradidit, & non exspectata obsidione pacis conditiones accepit; multi propinquorum & clientium foederi subscribunt; Ipse Marchio Huntilæus cum primogenito, ut obses & pignus solidæ in futurum pacis foret, Edenburgum abductus, atque ibi in firma sed libera custodia fuit: etenim non satis tutum arbitrabantur foederati, nobilem tam potentem, qui iniquioris in se animi indicia complura proderet, liberum dimittere, præsertim cum ipsius proximus natu filius Vicecomes Habonię, magni animi adolescens, accepto paucorum dierum commeatu, & de reditu data fide, non tamen redierit, & prout suspicabantur prudentiores, majorum postea turbarum author & dux fuerit. In regiarum partium fautores inquirunt foederatæ illæ copiæ, iisque apparatum bellicum, quem non ita pridem miserat rex, adimunt. Abredonia etiam ab Huntilæi copiis deserta, sponte se foederatis, quorum copiis imparem se cernebat, submisit, ac (dilapsis primum Episcopo & Theologis, quorum opera vulgo creditum fuit cives à fœdere Scotorum alieniores fuisse redditos, & aliis qui foederatos petulantius lacessiverunt, navibus se in Angliam conferentibus) munitiones suas, quibus frustra antehac se jactabat, adæquavit, civiumque complures fœdus Scotorum chirographis & juramento solenniter obsignarunt.
units.tr: The orders were that they should take care to prevent Huntly from troubling those northern provinces any further, and that they should attack him before he could join his forces with the royal fleet, whose arrival he awaited every day; and that they should bring Aberdeen, which the citizens had fortified with makeshift defences, under the power of the Covenanters, etc. God favoured their undertakings. For when Huntly heard of the coming of the Covenanters' forces, which the Earl of Montrose led, and with which the Covenanters were to join at the far side of the Grampian mountain, he fell back. Either he saw that he was too weak against these combined forces, whose junction he had not been able to prevent, or perhaps he had no orders to risk the outcome of a doubtful battle. He withdrew with his household and three children in great haste to his fortified castle at Bog. There, seeing that he was harassed by select units of the Covenanters, and that the castle was unprepared, lacking everything needed to defend the stronghold, he surrendered himself into the hands of the Covenanters of his own accord. Without waiting for a siege, he accepted the terms of peace. Many of his kinsmen and clients subscribed to the Covenant. Marquis Huntly himself was taken to Edinburgh with his eldest son, to serve as a hostage and pledge of a firm peace in future, and there he was kept under a strict but comfortable confinement. The Covenanters judged it not safe enough to release so powerful a nobleman, who had given many signs of a hostile mind towards them, especially since his next son, Viscount Aboyne, a young man of great spirit, had been granted leave for a few days on promise of returning, but did not return; and, as the wiser men suspected, he later became the author and leader of greater disturbances. Those Covenanting forces then searched out the supporters of the royal party and took from them the military equipment which the king had sent not long before. Aberdeen too, deserted by Huntly's forces, submitted itself of its own accord to the Covenanters, whose forces he saw he could not match. First the bishop and the theologians, by whose efforts it was commonly believed that the citizens had been turned against the Scottish Covenant, and others who had provoked the Covenanters more wantonly, departed by ship for England. Then the citizens levelled the fortifications on which they had vainly prided themselves before, and many of the citizens solemnly sealed the Scottish Covenant with their signatures and an oath.

units.la: Pacatis Borealibus ultra Grampium provinciis, & in Australi, ac Orientali plaga omnibus sic comparatis, ut nullus effet ab hoste intestino metus, arbitrabantur foederati Scoti, satis jam innotuisse Anglis, (quos omni conatu adnitebantur ipsorum adversarii in belli contra Scotos societatem trahere) quam vana & futilia essent illa promissa & relationes de numero & potentia domesticorum hostium in ipsis Scotiæ visceribus latentium; Interim, quia sciebant eosdem suos adversarios, pro ingenio & moribus consuetis, actiones has quam atrocissime infectaturos ; & (quandoquidem commentum illud de summa facilitate conficiendi Scotos, ab ipsis Anglis explosum conspexissent) ad alias artes fe conversuros, ac juraturos, prodere jam fœderatos manifesta rebellionis signa, quâ religionis fucata larva hactenus velarunt, eos prostituere ac tantum non conculcare majestatem regiam, nec intra defensionis limites iis statutum sese continere, notiora esse illa à rege ferenifs.Scotis fœderatis objecta edicto illo Februarii 27. quam quæ negari aut excusatione ulla dilui possent; Scriptum ediderunt fœderati quo ad edictum illud, & singula ejus capita fuse respondent, præcedentium suarum actionum æquitatem demonstrant, ac ab omnibus in edicto objectis vindicant,Defensionem hanc suam armatam licitam docent, & ideoque interceptionem hanc arcium & castellorum legitimam imo necessariam fuisse, cum medium fit ad defensionem simpliciter necessarium. Etenim fi liceat rem alienam, ex qua ingens & certum mihi imminet periculum, citra alienæ culpæ considerationem invadere, & custodire donec fecuritati meæ cautum fit; cur non (inquiebant) liceat collectivo regni corpori contra armatam vim legitime fe tuenti, arces & fortalitia à majoribus suis[?] intra regnum condita, ut effent propugnacula contra externos hostes, intercipere? Cum præfens & ingens ab iis tati regno intentetur periculum: Scriptum vero illud de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic fe habet.
