units.tr: With the provinces beyond the Grampians in the north pacified, and with everything in the south and east so arranged that there was no fear of an enemy within, the Scottish Covenanters judged that the English had now learned well enough how empty and futile were those promises and reports about the number and strength of domestic enemies lying hidden in the very bowels of Scotland, which their adversaries, who strove with all their might to draw the English into a war against the Scots, had put about. Meanwhile, since they knew that these same adversaries, according to their habit and character, would blacken these actions as foully as possible, and since (as the Covenanters had seen that the fiction about the great ease of subduing the Scots had been exploded by the English themselves) those adversaries would turn to other arts and would swear that the Covenanters were now showing manifest signs of rebellion, which hitherto they had concealed behind the painted mask of religion, that they were betraying themselves and all but trampling underfoot the royal majesty, and were not keeping themselves within the limits of defence set for them: the Covenanters, they said, knew well that the charges brought against the Scottish Covenanters by the most serene king in that edict of 27 February could neither be denied nor be refuted by any excuse. The Covenanters therefore published a writing in reply to that edict, answering fully to it and to each of its articles, demonstrating the justice of their earlier actions and vindicating them against all the charges made in the edict. They show that this armed defence of theirs is lawful, and therefore that this seizure of fortresses and castles was lawful, indeed necessary, since it is a means simply necessary for defence. For, they argued, if it is permitted to attack another's property, from which a great and certain danger hangs over me, without considering the fault of the other, and to hold it until my safety is secured, why should it not be permitted to the body politic of the kingdom, which lawfully defends itself against armed force, to seize the citadels and forts built within the kingdom by its ancestors, so that they might be bulwarks against external enemies, since a present and great danger is threatened by them against the whole kingdom? That writing, translated almost word for word, stands thus.

units.la: REMONSTRANTIA
units.tr: Remonstrance

units.la: Nobilium, Baronum, Civium, Pastorum & plebis regni Scotiae, qua se actionesque suas vindicant à criminibus objectis in nupero edicto regio in Anglia promulgato Februar. 27. 1639.
units.tr: The Remonstrance of the nobles, barons, burgesses, ministers and commons of the kingdom of Scotland, in which they vindicate themselves and their actions from the crimes laid against them in the royal edict published in England on 27 February 1639.

units.la: Licet abyssus consiliorum, & secreta viarum quibus omnipotens Deus incedit, nobis impervestigabilia sint, donec ab ipso reclusa divulgentur; quantum tamen concipere possumus de providentiae divinae progressu in praesenti nostro negotio, subit animos Deum ingens aliquod opus in terris meditari: Nam poculum illud irae divinae, reformatis aliis ecclesiis propinatum, nobis nunc offertur: Nihil reliqui ad summam diligentiam à nobis factum est, ut regem nostrum serenissimum qua precibus, qua remonstrantiis, qua humillimis literis supplicibus, de rerum nostrarum vero statu certiorem faceremus, ac immeritam ejus iram deprecaremur: sed frustra fuere omnia; Nam ejus aures praeoccupatas reperimus falsis relationibus Pseudo-episcoporum nostrorum, & aliorum qui in aquis nostris turpidis largam piscaturam sibi promittunt, unde factum ut regis serenissimi ira in dies incalescat, uti nobis devotissimis regi subditis hodie nimis compertum est, qui clemens & benignum responsum ad postremam nostram supplicationem synodi nomine exhibitam anxiis animis exspectabamus; & uti omnibus constare potest ex nupero illo edicto & declaratione in Anglia Februar. 27, in omnibus regni Angliae templis praelegenda.
units.tr: Although the depths of God's counsels and the hidden ways by which almighty God proceeds are unsearchable to us until he himself reveals them, yet as far as we can grasp the course of divine providence in our present affair, it comes to mind that God is planning some great work on earth. For that cup of divine wrath, which has been poured out on the other reformed churches, is now offered to us. We have left nothing undone, with the greatest diligence, to inform our most serene king of the true state of our affairs, both by prayers and by remonstrances and by most humble supplicatory letters, and to beg him to turn away his undeserved anger. But all was in vain. For we found his ears already preoccupied by the false reports of our so-called bishops and of others who hope for a rich catch in our troubled waters. Hence it comes that the anger of our most serene king grows hotter every day, as we, his most devoted subjects, have now learned all too well. We had been waiting with anxious minds for a kind and gracious answer to our last supplication, presented in the name of the Synod. And as can be known to all from that recent edict and declaration, published on 27 February in all the churches of England to be read aloud.

units.la: Hoc tamen nobis superest solatium & certa spes, cui nitimur; Ipsas inferorum portas contra causam hanc quam tuemur non praevalituras, ac testimonio quod exhibebitur regno filii Dei Iesu Christi, de quo tota controversia nunc vertitur, Deo tandem gloriam in altissimis constituram, pacem in terris, & Dei populo benevolentiam. Nobis interim vel quam maxime dolet, ad eas nos incitas redactos esse, ut vel pereundum sit sub intolerabili tot atrocium criminum infamia, aut cogamur edictis, adversariorum nostrorum opera protrusis, & quotidie contra nos promulgatis, contradicere.
units.tr: Yet this consolation and sure hope remains to us, on which we lean: that the gates of hell itself will not prevail against the cause we defend, and that, by the testimony which will be given to the kingdom of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, on whom the whole controversy now turns, God will at last establish glory in the highest, peace on earth, and good will toward his people. Meanwhile it grieves us most deeply that we are driven to such straits that we must either perish under the intolerable infamy of so many atrocious crimes, or be compelled to contradict the edicts, thrust forth by the work of our adversaries and published daily against us.

units.la: Atque licet nupero illo edicto aliorum criminum non arcessamur, quam quæ sincere, plene, & perspicue protestationibus impressis, relationibus, declarationibus, ac responso a nobis dato & exhibito declarationi deputati regii, & Episcoporum protestationi, qua synodi authoritatem subterfugiebant, hactenus diluimus; ne tamen Dei causa, & nostra innocentia dum eam tuemur, nostro silentio præjudicii quid patiatur apud eos qui nobis bene volunt & causæ huic favent, & ut ex abundanti convincantur conscientiæ, si non obstruantur ora ἀντικειμένων[?], non pigebit summa eorum capita repetere, quæ hactenus susè descripta sunt, eademque præsenti instituto accommodare.
units.tr: And although in that recent edict we are charged with no other crimes than those which we have hitherto refuted sincerely, fully and clearly, in our printed protests, reports, declarations, and in the answer we gave and presented to the declaration of the royal deputy, and in the protest of the bishops, by which they sought to escape the authority of the Synod; nevertheless, lest, while we defend the cause of God and our own innocence, anything be harmed by our silence in the judgment of those who wish us well and favour this cause, and so that consciences may be convinced beyond doubt, if the mouths of the opponents [ἀντικειμένων] are not stopped, we will not hesitate to repeat their principal heads, which have been set out at length until now, and to apply them to the present business.

units.la: Titulus edicti præ se fert. 1. Edictum illud regium intendi, Ut per illud certiores fiant subditi Angliæ, quod unice nobis in votis est, & cui obtinendo sedulam hactenus operam navavimus; certa spe freti; eos omnes accepta & perpensa plena & vera rerum nostrarum relatione, actiones nostras judicii sui calculo approbaturos, utpote quod ab amore in Christum, Regem, & patriam (quæ apud nos indivulsim conjunguntur) processerint; quorum zelo usque adeo flagramus, ut ex animis doleamus, & insigni injuria affectos nos putemus, quod amoris & fidelitatis officiis, quibuslibet Christiani orbis subditis inferiores censeamur. Sed quam vera narratio a prælatis nostris, ipsorumque asseclis ac parasitis exspectari nunc possit, (quibus nulla alia spes reliqua est ad priorē fastū redeundi, quam ex nostra ruina) omnes probi in Anglia pro prudētia sua facile judicabūt.
units.tr: The title of the edict declares: 1. That the royal edict is intended "so that by it the subjects of England may be better informed", which is our only wish, and for the obtaining of which we have hitherto laboured with diligence, trusting in the sure hope that all of them, once they have received and weighed a full and true account of our affairs, will approve our actions by the judgment of their own minds, as having proceeded from love of Christ, of the King and of the fatherland, which among us are inseparably joined. We burn so greatly with zeal for these that we grieve from the heart, and we think ourselves gravely wronged that we should be judged inferior, in the duties of love and loyalty, to any subjects of the Christian world. But what a true account may now be expected from our prelates, and from their followers and parasites (who have no other hope of returning to their former pride except from our ruin), all honest men in England will easily judge for themselves with their own prudence.

units.la: 2. Additur in titulo. Seditiosis nostris actionibus speciosò religionis prætextu velatis, in id intentos esse ut jus regium Sereniss. nostri regis subvertamus. Nulla actionum nostrarum tam frequentibus seditionum calumniis impetitur, quam confessionis fidei & fœderis Nationalis necessaria obsignatio, in quo tamen fœdere tantum abest ut regiam authoritatem subvertamus, ut contra Declaremus coram Deo & hominibus, nunquam nobis propositum fuisse quidpiam conari quod cederet in regiæ majestatis & authoritatis diminutionem.
units.tr: 2. It is added in the title: "Our seditious actions, veiled under the specious pretext of religion, are aimed at subverting the royal authority of our most serene king." No action of ours is assailed with such frequent calumnies of sedition as the necessary subscription to the Confession of Faith and to the National Covenant. Yet in that Covenant we are so far from subverting the royal authority that, on the contrary, we declare before God and men that we never purposed to attempt anything which would tend to the diminution of the majesty and authority of the king.

units.la: Ne per somnium quidem animum nostrum unquam subire potuit, recusationem libri liturgici, & episcopatus abdicationem (quæ duo structuram cultus divini & disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ legum authoritate apud nos hic receptæ, subvertunt) à quolibet interpretandam fore tanquam juris regii subversionem. Fundamenta & columnæ veri juris regii, sunt religio & justitia, quæ juramento stabilire conati sumus, neque dubitamus quin si liceat illis cum pace frui, omnibus perspicuum fiet, hæc esse regii solii firmissima columina.
units.tr: Not even in a dream could it ever enter our minds that the refusal of the liturgical book and the abjuration of episcopacy (two things which overthrow the structure of divine worship and of church discipline, established among us here by the authority of law) would be interpreted by anyone as a subversion of royal right. The foundations and pillars of true royal right are religion and justice, which we have sought to establish by oath; nor do we doubt that, if we are permitted to enjoy these in peace, it will become plain to all that these are the firmest pillars of the royal throne.

units.la: Actiones nostræ dicuntur seditio-sæ, perversæ, tumultuosæ; intentiones rebelles: declarationes libelli famosi: protestationes fastiosæ: fœdus nostrum, liga & conspiratio contra Dei unctum, quod pre nobis ferimus esse cum Deo ut honestiori velo[?] perficeremus opera Diaboli, qualia sunt rebellio, seditiones: Præparationes ad innocuam nostri defensionem, hostiles, perinde ac si rex noster esset juratus hostis: actiones nostræ, insolens & audax arrogantia: conatus & consilia nostra hunc scopum habere, ut Angliam invadamus, cujus spoliis[?] res nostras familiares & fortunas disperditas resarciamus: præsens status cerebri intemperies: Nec que ipsi, improbi, ad rebellionem prompti, factiosi & turbones vocāvocamur. Ad quæ respondemus. 1. Dominus forte in nostras grummas[?] oculos conjicere dignabitur, & pro his maledictis bonum rependet. 2.Sam.16.12. Beati critis cum vos convitiis affecerint & persecuti fuerint, ac dixerint quidvis mali adversus vos propter me. Matth. 5. 11.
units.tr: Our actions are called seditious, perverse and tumultuous; our intentions rebellious; our declarations a libel; our protests arrogant; our covenant, league and conspiracy against the Lord's Anointed, which we profess to make with God, so that under a more honourable veil we may carry out the works of the devil, such as rebellion and sedition; our preparations for the harmless defence of ourselves are hostile, as if our king were a sworn enemy; our actions are insolent and bold arrogance; our attempts and plans have the aim of invading England, so that by its spoils we may repair our ruined household goods and fortunes; our present state is a disorder of the brain. And we are called not only these things but also wicked, prompt to rebellion, factious and troublemakers. To these we reply. 1. "Perhaps the Lord will look upon our affliction, and will requite us good for this cursing." 2 Sam. 16.12. "Blessed are ye when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely for my sake." Matth. 5.11.

units.la: 2. Convitia hæc & probra à præsulum nostrorum animis nulla Christiana religione imbutis processerunt, qui undæ maris efferatæ sunt, sua ipsorum despumantes dedecora: atque hisce maledictis testatum faciunt, excommunicationis ecclesiasticæ sententia verè se Satanæ traditos esse, cujus spiritus efficaciter in eis nunc operatur: Omnia hæc ipsorum in nos convitia ne vel unicam voculam à nobis extorquebunt, qua oblique serenissimus noster Rex perstringi possit. Artem istam antiquam edocti sunt, Hierarchiam scil. suam, regis imagini ita caute inserere; ut necesse sit ei qui unam colat, utramq; pariter colere, nullusq; sit qui contra illam hiscere audeat, nisi contemptus in hanc reus audire velit. Verum hæ ipsorum artes nobis sunt quampridem pernotæ; Deusque viam nobis monstravit, qua regi debitum obsequium præstemus, ac rebellionis, seditionis & læsæ majestatis crimina detestemur, Episcopis nullo honore affectis, ac sine perfida abjuratæ ipsorum tyrannidis approbatione. 3. Duo sunt quibus demonstratur præsulibus nostris statutum iras suas in perniciem insignem acuere: alterum est, quod asperrimis verborum contumeliis utantur; hic tamen fine suo frustrantur; nam verba quibus utuntur convitia sunt ex trivio, non propria, magisque student quæcunque ab aliis aut semetipsis excogitari possunt maledicta effundere, quam quidlibet proferre, quod nobis seu causæ nostræ vere officiat: Alterum est, quod Serenissimus regem huic negotio usque adeo implicare satagant, ut cum honore vix liceat illi se extricare;-Et hic etiam spe sua frustratum iri speramus; neque penes eos unquam futurum, ut regem impellant ad illud quod revocari & emendari non poterit.
units.tr: 2. These reproaches and insults have come from the minds of our prelates, who are imbued with no Christian religion, who are like a raging sea, foaming up their own disgraces. By these curses they bear witness that by the sentence of ecclesiastical excommunication they are truly delivered over to Satan, whose spirit now works effectively in them. None of all these insults of theirs against us will extort from us even one little word by which our most serene king could be indirectly assailed. They have been taught that old art: to insert their own hierarchy so cautiously into the image of the king that whoever worships the one must worship the other equally, and there is no one who dares to murmur against it unless he wishes to hear that he is guilty of contempt against it. But these arts of theirs are long since well known to us; and God has shown us the way by which we may render to the king the obedience due to him, and detest the crimes of rebellion, sedition and treason, with the bishops deprived of all honour, and without any approval of their perfidiously abjured tyranny. 3. There are two things by which it is shown that our prelates have resolved to sharpen their wrath to our notable destruction. The first is that they use the harshest verbal insults; yet in this they are frustrated in their aim, for the words they use are the abuse of the street, not their own, and they strive rather to pour out whatever curses can be devised by others or by themselves than to produce anything which truly harms us or our cause. The second is that they labour so hard to entangle the king in this business that he can scarcely extricate himself with honour. And we hope that they will be frustrated in this hope too; nor will it ever be in their power to drive the king to that which cannot be recalled or amended.

units.la: Principes, qui omnibus ex æquo parentes esse debent, sese partem adversam non constituent, hoc enim esset inæquali pondere in alteram cymbæ partem inclinante, cymbam ipsam evertere, neque eos solum qui vehuntur, verum etiam ad clavum sedentem manifesto discrimini exponere; quod desperato prorsus ingenio præsules nostri potius elegerunt, quam ut fera pœnitentia tangerentur, aut ut cum Iona in mare præcipitati soli pereant. Receptus apud eos sermo est, Cum de nobis actum fuerit, quid nobis si mundus incendio pereat?
units.tr: Princes, who ought to be parents equally to all, do not set themselves up as a party against one side. For to lean with unequal weight toward one side of the boat would be to overturn the boat itself, and to expose to manifest danger not only those who are carried in it but also the man sitting at the helm. Our prelates, with a mind utterly desperate, have preferred this to being moved by a deep repentance, or to being hurled into the sea like Jonah and perishing alone. The saying current among them is: "Since it has gone badly for us, what does it matter if the world burns?"

units.la: In ea priori hujus edicti parte quæ narrationem continet; Lætamur, intentiones nostras (Deo soli directe cognitas) per actiones mundo cognitas ab illis examinari: quas spretis eorum calumniis & obloquiis justas esse afferimus: 1.[?] Utpote, quod tam diuturna patientia æquis animis immodicam præsulum arrogantiam passi fuerimus, qui animorum unitatem, synodorum authoritatem, ministerii ordinem, doctrinæ & cultus puritatem, totam denique religionis in hac ecclesia reformationem subverterunt, nullo alio fine quam ut ambitioni & avaritiæ suæ satisfacerent; (quibus tanquam fascinis naturalium[?] hominum animi illaqueantur, quasque sævissimas Harpyas semper experta est religio) ac unitatis fraternæ loco schisma induxerunt, pro ordine ministerii tyrannidem Episcopalem, pro puritate cultus divini, (quam admirandum divinæ erga nos misericordiæ opus, & gentis nostræ veram gloriam merito exosculamur) primum cerebri humani inventa; dein, (cum in plenipotentiam excrevissent per reditus & amplas dignitates, per potestatem in pastores verbi & alios subditos, per sententiæ dictionem in Parlamentis, Senatu regio, Collegio justitiæ, Camera rationum regia, & celsa Commissione) librum Canonum formarunt, quibus regeretur ecclesia, hoc est, liceret ipsis pro arbitrio de religione statuere. Toto tamen hoc tempore nullam aliam experti sunt oppositionem, quam paucorum verbi pastorum zelum, qui spretis fortiter periculis veritati testimonium præbuerunt, quam etiam afflictionibus signarunt; & gemitus ac clamores populi ad Deum, ut tandem aliquando dignaretur eos liberare ab ipsis magis crudelibus pensi exactoribus quam fuere Ægyptiorum [illegible, ~8 letters]. 2. Quod à prima hora qua istis nosmet publice opponere cœpimus, actiones nostræ quietæ, modestæ fuerint, ac pacem spiraverint, idque inde patet: Licet istorum arrogantia usque adeo excreverit, ut sine cognitione nedum consensu ecclesiæ librum liturgiæ formarint, qui in omnibus regni ecclesiis reciperetur tanquam unica divini cultus publici forma, ac obtinuerint severa edicta, quibus pastorum bona publicarentur qui eundem non reciperent; ipsique libro eo usi fuerint publice in cultu divino, neque pastores solum & lectores quosdam submoverint qui librum illum non recipiebant, verumetiam edictum procuraverint, quo sub pœna mortis omnibus interdictum fuit, ne quid contra librum illum & Episcopos quidlibet objicerent. Atque licet modus introducendi librum esset illegitimus, omnibusque notum esset, secum totius cultus divini externi sensibilem mutationem tracturum; Nobiles tamen, Barones, Cives, Pastores, & plebs frequentissimo quidem numero, sed pacate sine ullo tumultu, libellis solum supplicibus senatui regio oblatis rogarunt, ut à maximis hisce gravaminibus liberarentur, opera senatus apud regem serenissimum. 3. Cum supplicationibus hisce ad regem per senatum regium directis aliter non responderetur, quam severissimis edictis, quibus omnes ipsorum actiones, conventus damnarentur; mala, de quibus questi effent, approbarentur; cum ipsorum querimoniæ contra insignia & flagrantia præsulum crimina negligerentur, novisque molestiis succrescentibus premerentur: Illi in malorum horum causas apud fe ferio inquirentes, & unde factum effet ut æquissima sua ad regem postulata rejicerentur, tandem deprehenderunt, à semetipsis & priori sua contra Dei fœdus perfidia profectum fuisse: ideoque unanimi omnium consensu statuerunt renovandum esse Nationale illud fœdus cum folenni jejunio & precibus ad Deum propitiandum, & ut melius ac fœlicius negotia in posterum succederent. Decreverunt etiam renovandum esse postulatum ad Serenifs. Regem, pro Synodo nationali & Parlamento, quæ ordinaria & efficacissima sciebant esse media malis hisce medendis: Neque quidpiam intentatum reliquerunt quo æquis hisce postulatis fatisfieret, aut quod Chriftianos subditos deceret, qui Deum colunt & regem reverentur; suæ[?] etiam ad singula, quæ contra fœdus objici possent, responderunt. 4. Cum multum petita & diu desiderata Synodus tandem concederetur, ac regis speciali mandato coiret, & deputato regio præsente in omnibus suis membris rite constitueretur; interdictum fuit ne ulterius progrederemur, ac severe mandatum fuit, fine ulla à nobis oblata causa, ut Synodum protinus dissolveremus. Hisque angustiis utrinque constricti, hinc quidem præcipitandi regnum & ecclesiam in innumeras confusiones periculo, illinc vero irae regiæ, fi post interdictionem synodum continuaffemus; illud elegimus, quod Christi authoritate muniebatur, & quod nostro judicio regiæ voluntati antea manifestatæ & publico commodo magis conveniret, prout latius hæc deduximus in literis supplicibus à Synodo
units.tr: In the first part of this edict, which contains the narrative, we rejoice that our intentions (known directly to God alone) are being judged by the world through our actions. Despising their calumnies and objections, we declare those actions to be just. 1.[?] For we have borne with calm minds for so long the immoderate arrogance of the bishops, who have overthrown the unity of souls, the authority of synods, the order of the ministry, the purity of doctrine and worship, and finally the whole reformation of religion in this church. They did this for no other end than to satisfy their ambition and greed (by such charms as ensnare the minds of natural men, and by which religion has always been devoured like the most savage Harpies). In place of fraternal unity they have introduced schism; in place of the order of the ministry, episcopal tyranny; in place of the purity of divine worship (which we rightly embrace as a wonderful work of divine mercy towards us and the true glory of our nation), first the inventions of the human brain. Then, when they had grown into full power through revenues and ample dignities, through authority over the ministers of the Word and other subjects, and through the pronouncing of sentences in the Parliaments, the royal Senate, the College of Justice, the royal Exchequer chamber, and the high Commission, they drew up a book of canons by which the church would be governed; that is, by which it would be lawful for them to decree at their own pleasure about religion. Yet throughout all this time they have met with no opposition other than the zeal of a few ministers of the Word, who, bravely disregarding dangers, bore witness to the truth, which they also sealed with afflictions; and with the groans and cries of the people to God, that he would at last deign to free them from exactors more cruel than the taskmasters of the Egyptians [illegible, ~8 letters]. 2. That from the first hour in which we began to oppose them publicly, our actions have been quiet and modest and have breathed peace, and this is plain from the following. Although their arrogance has grown so great that, without knowledge, let alone consent, of the church, they drew up a book of liturgy which was to be received in all the churches of the kingdom as the sole form of public divine worship, and obtained severe edicts by which the goods of ministers who did not receive it were to be confiscated; and although they used that book publicly in divine worship, and not only removed ministers and certain readers who did not receive that book, but also procured an edict by which, on pain of death, it was forbidden to everyone to object anything against that book or the bishops. And although the manner of introducing the book was illegitimate, and it was known to all that it would bring with it a perceptible change in the whole external worship, nevertheless the nobles, barons, citizens, ministers and common people, in a very great number but peacefully and without any tumult, asked only by humble petitions presented to the royal Senate that they be freed from these very great grievances, through the good offices of the Senate with the most serene King. 3. Since no answer was given to these supplications directed to the King through the royal Senate except the most severe edicts, by which all their actions and assemblies were condemned, the evils of which they had complained were approved, their complaints against the notorious and flagrant crimes of the bishops were ignored, and they were oppressed by new troubles piling up, they, examining seriously within themselves the causes of these evils and why their most just requests to the King were rejected, at last discovered that it arose from themselves and from their former faithlessness against the covenant with God. Therefore, by the unanimous consent of all, they resolved that the National Covenant should be renewed, with a solemn fast and prayers to propitiate God, so that affairs might succeed better and more happily in the future. They also decided that the request to the most serene King for a National Synod and Parliament should be renewed, since they knew these to be the ordinary and most effective means of healing these evils. Nor did they leave untried anything by which these just requests might be satisfied, or which befits Christian subjects who worship God and reverence the king; they also answered each thing that could be objected against the covenant. 4. When the National Synod, long sought and long desired, was at last granted and assembled by the king's special command, and was duly constituted in all its members with the royal deputy present, it was forbidden that we proceed any further, and it was sharply ordered, without any cause given by us, that we dissolve the Synod at once. Pressed on both sides by these straits, on the one hand by the danger of hurling the kingdom and the church into innumerable confusions, and on the other by the king's anger if we continued the synod after the prohibition, we chose that course which was supported by the authority of Christ, and which, in our judgement, better agreed with the king's will previously made known and with the public good; as we have explained more fully in the supplicatory letters written by the Synod

units.la: ad Regem fereniff.perscriptis,quarum nullam mentionem facit declaratio hæc regia. Post illa tempora minitamur indies ab Anglia hostili exercitu & invafione, contra quam, prout potuimus, nosmet paramus ac in legitimam & necessariam nostram defenfionem incumbimus, fine ulla cogitatione invadendi aut damno quolibet vicinos afficiendi. Quare post tam obstinatam patientiam & diuturnum silentium, viæ omnes quas adhuc pressimus, quibus gravaminum levamen obtineremus, nullæ aliæ sunt quam humiles ad Deum preces & supplices ad regem libelli, necessariæ protestationes, religiosa fœderis Nationalis cum Deo renovatio, synodi Nationalis authoritate regia indictæ plufquam necessaria continuatio, Innocentiæ nostræ ac æquitatis causæ quam tuemur perspicua declaratio, & præparationes ad necessariàm nostram tutelam contra manifestam vim hostiliter intentatam.
units.tr: to the most serene King, of which letters this royal declaration makes no mention. Since those times we have been threatened daily with a hostile army and invasion from England, against which we prepare ourselves as we can and apply ourselves to our legitimate and necessary defence, without any thought of invading or harming any neighbour. Therefore, after such obstinate patience and long silence, all the ways we have so far pursued to obtain relief from our grievances are none other than humble prayers to God, supplicating petitions to the King, necessary protestations, the religious renewal of the National Covenant with God, the continuation of the National Synod, convened by royal authority, beyond what is strictly necessary, a clear declaration of our innocence and of the cause of justice which we defend, and preparations for our necessary protection against the open force hostilely threatened against us.

units.la: Sed excutiamus quibus argumentis nos læsæ majestatis reos demonstrent nostræ actiones prout in declaratione hac regia proponuntur. Primum, (inquit) est, multitudo infamium libellorum qui calumnis in regiam authoritatem scatent. Si ullus liber qui à nobis prodiit designatus fuisset, specialius hic responderemus; quare in genere audemus afferere, quicquid à nobis prodiit, sicuti per illud nobis propositum fuit conatus nostros a perduellionis macula vindicare, ita nihil continere cur tam gravi censura notaretur, nam tum in materia tum in forma omnia concepta sunt cum singulari erga regem sereniss. reverentia, ejusque actiones in optimam partem ubique interpretantur.
units.tr: But let us examine by what arguments this royal declaration, as it sets out our actions, shows us guilty of treason. First, it says, the multitude of infamous libels which swarm with calumnies against the royal authority. If any book issued by us had been named, we would answer more specifically. So we dare to assert in general that whatever has come from us, since by it we intended to vindicate our endeavours from the stain of treason, contains nothing for which it should be marked with so grave a censure; for both in matter and in form everything has been composed with singular reverence towards the most serene King, and everywhere interprets his actions in the best light.

units.la: Secundo. Literas (dicit declaratio) missas Londinum ad privatos quosdam homines, & missos fuisse nonnullos fœderatos ad privata quædam conventicula Londini, quibus subditi contra regem excitarentur, & ab officio debito deducere ducerentur. Conatum hunc meram rebellionem spirare non negamus, qui apud fideles subditos locum nunquam obtinebit: Atque sicut certi fumus, nullas id genus literas aut nuncios communi fœderatorum nomine unquam missos fuisse, ita vel singularem præsulum vafritiem redolet, illud objicere cujus falsitatem nos demonstrare non possumus; vel insignem eorundem malitiam, illud omnibus imputare, quod privati quidam proprio motu sine nostra notitia forte fecerunt; Neque cuipiam insolens videbitur, si turbulentis hisce temporibus extrudantur libelli in quibus modestiam desideres, si falsa nova discurrent, si prodeant literæ eorum nomina mentientes quibus nunquam visæ fuerunt. An vero tam sedula & curiosa horum inquisitio, ac severa suppressio, an eorundem contemptus aptissimum sit contra ea remedium & antidotum, judicent politici. Notum est aquam obstructam, aggeribus dirutis multifariam prorumpere.
units.tr: Second. Letters (the declaration says) sent to London to certain private men, and some confederates sent to certain private conventicles in London, by which subjects were stirred up against the king and led away from their due duty. We do not deny that this attempt breathes pure rebellion, which will never find a place among faithful subjects. And as we are certain that no letters or messengers of this kind were ever sent in the common name of the confederates, so it either smells of the singular cunning of the bishops to object what we cannot show to be false, or of their notable malice to impute to everyone what certain private persons perhaps did of their own accord and without our knowledge. Nor will it seem strange to anyone that in these turbulent times libels are put out in which you would miss moderation, that false news goes about, and that letters appear bearing names which were never seen by those they name. But whether such diligent and curious inquiry and severe suppression, or contempt of these things, is the most fitting remedy and antidote against them, let the statesmen judge. It is known that water held back by dams bursts out in many directions once the embankments are broken.

units.la: 3. Quod publice æquissima omnia regis mandata contemserimus ac contra ea seditiose protestati fuerimus. Nobis certe maximo semper solatio fuit æquis serenis. regis mandatis humiliter & religiose obsequi: & à nostra sententia quam immane distat ut regis quaelibet mandata despiciamus, aut seditiose contra eadem quantumvis iniqua protestemur: Verum modeste contra ea protestari prout humiles & fideles subditos decet, usitatum semper fuit, legitimum, ordinarium, & aliquando usque adeo necessarium ad jus tuendum, & injustitiam amoliendam, ut omitti nequeat; neque illud unquam justam offensionis & scandali ansam præbere potest.
units.tr: 3. That you publicly scorned all the most just commands of the king and protested against them seditiously. Indeed, for us it has always been the greatest comfort to obey the most serene king's commands humbly and religiously. How far from our opinion it is to despise any command of the king, or to protest seditiously against any command, however unjust! But to protest against such commands modestly, as becomes humble and faithful subjects, has always been usual, lawful and ordinary, and at times so necessary for defending right and removing injustice that it cannot be omitted; nor can it ever give a just cause for offence or scandal.

units.la: Quartum argumentum tria continet quibus sigillatim respondendum. 1. Nullum fœdus inter subditos legitimum esse posse sine mandato supremi magistratus politici. Huic exceptioni abunde à nobis antehac satisfactum est, argumentis ab authoritate divina & humana , eaque tam ecclesiastica quam politica , prolatis ; ab antiqua piorum praxi , à majorum religionem sincere colentium exemplo , à continua & usitata in hac ecclesia subscriptione , & à natura juramenti ipsius & fœderis quod Nationale est ; ita ut non dubitemus , quin omnibus qui in scriptis nostris versati sunt , exceptis præsulibus eorumque fautoribus , satisfactum sit ; qui argutiarum nullum finem aut modum sciunt , & qui subdole adnituntur ad controversiæ hujus initium nos revocare , ut infectum reddant ( si possent ) quod à nobis hactenus factum est. 2. Quod rejecerimus fœdus regia authoritate imperatum , eo nomine quod imperaret rex. Rationes,non quidem rejecti fœderis , sed modestæ retentionis chirographi nostri , cum a rege fœdus illud imperaretur , suse extant in publicis & impressis nostris protestationibus Septembr.22. & Decembr.18. in responsione ad declarationem deputati regii , ac in decretis nuperrimæ Nationalis Synodi , cui proprie competit publica & judiciaria interpretatio Consessionis fidei : Atque cum scriptis illis nominatis perspicue demonstratum sit, Confessionem authoritate regia imperatam , secundum sensum affictum à rege, in negotiis religionis non solum adversari subscriptioni nostræ , mense Februario anni superioris ; verumetiam genuino & vero Confessionis sensui, uti publica ejus professio vigebat anno 1580. Non potuimus confessioni à rege, secundum adulterinum illum sensum imperatæ, subscribere, nisi horrendi perjurii reos nos fecissemus , ac graviorem Dei omnipotentis iram in nostra capita contraxissemus, quam prima illa fuit, & quam fœderis obsignatione amoliri studebamus. 3. Fœdus hoc nostrum esse conspirationem contra regem , quod præ nobis ferimus esse cum Deo, ut opera diaboli perficeremus. Blasphemia hæc est, à qua regem sereniss.& omnes Deum timentes quam longissime abesse nobis persuademus; plurimum etiam fiduciæ nobis sic additur, Dominum in cœlis ratum habuisse Anathema in præsules pronunciatum, atque in convitia & maledicta hæc opportune animadversurum, neque opera hæc ipsorum successura: Quare in Domino Deo nostro nosmet solantes, cui vsum fuit, tot signis & perspicuis argumentis fœdus hoc nostrum ratum habere, non referemus illis maledicta, neque paribus convitiis eos excipiemus, verum dicimus, Domine qui Hierosolymam elegisti increpato eos, & serva regem.
units.tr: The fourth argument contains three points, to which I will reply one by one. 1. No covenant between subjects can be lawful without the command of the supreme civil magistrate. We have already given this objection full satisfaction, with arguments drawn from divine and human authority, both ecclesiastical and civil; from the ancient practice of the godly; from the example of our forefathers who sincerely worshipped God; from the continual and customary subscription in this Church; and from the nature of the oath itself and of the covenant, which is National. We do not doubt, therefore, that everyone who has read our writings has been satisfied, except the bishops and their supporters, who know no end or limit to their quibbling, and who craftily strive to drag us back to the beginning of this controversy, so as to undo (if they could) what we have hitherto done. 2. That we rejected a covenant imposed by royal authority, on the ground that the king imposed it. Our reasons, not for rejecting the covenant but for modestly withholding our own signature when the king required that covenant, are set out in our published and printed protestations of 22 September and 18 December, in our answer to the royal commissioner's declaration, and in the decrees of the recent National Synod, to which the public and judicial interpretation of the Confession of Faith properly belongs. Since it has been clearly shown in those writings that the Confession, imposed by royal authority in the sense devised by the king, conflicts in matters of religion not only with our subscription in February of last year, but also with the genuine and true sense of the Confession, as its public profession stood in 1580, we could not subscribe to the Confession imposed by the king in that spurious sense without making ourselves guilty of a horrible perjury and drawing upon our heads a greater wrath of Almighty God than the first, which we were striving to avert by the signing of the covenant. 3. That our covenant is a conspiracy against the king, which we openly profess to be made with God in order to carry out the works of the devil. This is a blasphemy, from which we are persuaded that the most serene king and all who fear God are far removed. Our confidence is also greatly strengthened by the fact that the Lord in heaven has approved the anathema pronounced against the bishops, and will in due time take notice of these insults and curses, and that their works will not prosper. Therefore, comforting ourselves in the Lord our God, who has shown by so many signs and clear proofs that he approves this our covenant, we will not return their curses, nor answer their insults with like insults; rather we say, The Lord rebuke you, O you who chose Jerusalem, and preserve the king.

units.la: Denique in nostræ rebellionis argumentum afferitur; Hostilis noster apparatus ad Angliam invadendam. Cui diluendo in nupera nostra ad Anglos informatione, quantum viris bonis satisfacere posset, dictum hactenus confidimus, quantumvis posthabitis caritatis regulis, ejusmodi rumoribus temere fidem habuissent; quod nunquam nobis persuadebitur. Absit ut optimæ & legitimæ nostræ actiones, & quibus satisfieri debet illius regni subditis, in tam alienum sensum improbe detorqueantur. Et quamvis præsules paroxismo desperationis correpti (dum cognitum habeant se non posse damna sua resarcire nisi nostra ruina & pernicie) ut desperatos & perditos hypocritas nos traducant; eventus tamen, Dei bona gratia, testabitur, loquutos nos sicut eos decet quibus nomen Dei magnum & tremendum est, cum quo fœdus nostrum renovavimus, & qui suo tempore non impune feret nostram hypocrisin, seu illorum calumnias.
units.tr: Finally, as proof of our rebellion they allege: Our hostile preparation for invading England. In refuting this charge in our recent information to the English, we trust that we have said enough to satisfy good men, however much, having cast aside the rules of charity, they may have rashly given credit to such rumours; this will never be persuaded to us. Far be it from us that our best and lawful actions, which ought to be made clear to the subjects of that kingdom, should be wickedly twisted into so alien a meaning. And although the bishops, seized by a fit of despair (since they know they cannot make good their losses except by our ruin and destruction), label us as desperate and lost hypocrites, the outcome, by God's good grace, will bear witness that we have spoken as becomes those to whom the name of God is great and dreadful, the God with whom we have renewed our covenant, and who in his own time will not let our hypocrisy, or their calumnies, go unpunished.

units.la: Hostes etiam nostri, ut malæ suspicionis semina de nobis licet immeritis jacerent, aperto ore venditarunt; Multos & primarios nostrum, homines esse ingenii turbulenti, & fortunarum decoctarum. Sed hic male sibi consuluerunt & propria vineta cædunts. Suspiciones à prudentioribus nō male comparantur cum vespertilionibus, quod avium genus ad volandum non prodit meridie, sed in diei crepusculo; Etenim omnibus quibus regni hujus status cognitus est, quam perspectissimum est, Universum propemodum regnum huic causæ adhærere; Nobiles, Barones, & cives primarios in singulis ubi degunt locis, ob religionem, prudentiam, potentiam, & opes statui regni hujus conformes, coli; minimos etiam è plebe forte sua, licet tenuiori, contentos esse, modo eadem illis frui liceat cum luce & usura Euangelii. Omnibus etiam pernotiffimum est, Hostes nostros, licet omnes numerentur, nullam notabilem regni partem conficere posse, eorumque primarios (si paucos senatores regios, & qui aulam regiam sequuntur dempseris) esse vel apertos Atheos, aut Papistas, aut æri alieno immersos, quibus aqua & igni jampridem interdictū fit, & quos regia authoritate comprehendere & in arctam custodiam conjicere possint creditores; Atque hi sunt qui vana spe freti prædia nostra & fortunas hactenus inter se partiti sunt, & Anglorum auxiliis eadem se adepturos sibi persuaserunt. Deus interim de cœlo in cordium nostrorum innocentiam prospicere dignatus est, ac pro infinita sua prudentia medium ostendit eandem contra calumnias hafce vindicandi: Nam præter supplicem nostrum libellum senatui regio ob illum finem Ianuarii 13. proxime elapsi oblatum, & nuperam nostram ad Anglos declarationem, Februar. 4. publico senatus regii testimonio innocentia nostra asseritur; Epiftola quædam in Angliam missa à Georgio Sterlino cive Edenburgeno, suasu & consilio Georgii Sterlini commiffionarii seu Officialis Wigtonienfis (quorum uterque proxima affinitate nuperum Pfeudoepiscopum Gallovidianum attingit) ad nos delata fuit, easdem continens calumnias quas nunc prose-runt. runt praesules ; hanc epistolam regio senatui exhibuimus Februar.22. & 28. cum querimonia, supplicatione, obtestatione gravissima divini nominis, conscientiae nostrae testimonio, subscriptione, aut quocunque demum modo foedum istud crimen literis [?]iltis per impudentem calumniam nobis impactum dilui posset: Hinc Domini senatores regii supplicationem illam nostram ad regem transmittendam censuerunt, cum libello supplice à se formato, quo obsecrati fuerunt ne ejusmodi informationibus pateretur se ad duriora consilia flecti, quam quibus hactenus erga antiquum & nativum suum regnum usus esset, & ut pro consueta majestatis suae sollicitudine erga commodum hujus sui regni, medium aliquod despiceret & excogitaret, quo sine armata vi, aut regiae potentiae manifestatione, regni status componi posset, ut fusius in ipsa illa epistola & supplici senatus ad regem libello continetur.
units.tr: Our enemies too, though we deserve no such thing, have openly spread about seeds of ill suspicion concerning us: Many of our leading men are people of turbulent temper and ruined fortunes. But in this they have ill consulted their own interests and cut down their own vineyards. The prudent rightly compare such suspicions to bats, a kind of bird that does not come forth at midday but at the dusk of day. For it is very plain to all who know the state of this kingdom that almost the whole realm adheres to this cause: nobles, barons and the chief burgesses in every place where they live are honoured, on account of their religion, prudence, power and wealth, as conformable to the state of this kingdom; and even the least of the common people, however humble their station, are content, provided they may enjoy the same things along with the light and the fruit of the Gospel. It is also very well known to all that our enemies, however many they are counted, cannot make up any considerable part of the kingdom, and that their leading men (if you leave out the few royal senators and those who follow the royal court) are either open atheists, or Papists, or sunk in debt, men whom fire and water have long since been forbidden, and whom their creditors could seize by royal authority and cast into close custody. These are the men who, relying on a vain hope, have hitherto divided among themselves our estates and fortunes, and have persuaded themselves that they will obtain them by the help of the English. Meanwhile God has deigned to look down from heaven upon the innocence of our hearts, and in his infinite wisdom has shown a means of vindicating it against these calumnies. For, besides our humble petition offered to the royal senate for that purpose on 13 January last, and our recent declaration to the English of 4 February, our innocence has been affirmed by the public testimony of the royal senate. A certain letter sent into England by George Stirling, a citizen of Edinburgh, at the persuasion and advice of George Stirling, commissary or official of Wigtown (both of whom are closely related to the recent pseudo-bishop of Galloway), was brought to us; it contained the same calumnies which the bishops now publish. We presented this letter to the royal senate on 22 and 28 February, with complaint, supplication, most solemn invocation of the divine name, the testimony of our conscience, our signature, or in whatever way this foul crime, fastened on us by shameless calumny, could be cleared up by the letters in question. Hence the lords senators of the king resolved to send our petition to the king, together with a humble petition drawn up by themselves, in which they begged him not to allow himself to be turned by such information towards harsher counsels than those he had hitherto used towards his ancient and native kingdom, and that, according to his customary solicitude for the welfare of his kingdom, he would devise and contrive some means by which the state of the realm might be settled without armed force or any display of royal power, as is set out more fully in that letter itself and in the senate's humble petition to the king.

units.la: Vocamur etiam in crimen usurpatae potestatis regiae. 1. Quia nobis vendicavimus imperium in praela typographorum, & typographo regio primum interdiximus, dein dimisimus. Vetus haec est & rancida Pontificiorum praesulum contra primos ecclesiae hujus reformatores, anno 1559. querela, & salsissime ab ipsorum successoribus contra nos hodie renovata, etenim nec interdiximus typographo regio, nec eum dimisimus, qui pacate Edenburgi adhuc commoratur. Nec decretum nationalis synodi, quod hic perstringi opinamur, quidpiam continet quod merito torqueri posset ad regiae potestatis usurpationem, aut ejusdem in typographorum praela diminutionem: nam synodi decreto interdicitur solum sub poena ecclesiasticae censurae, ne quid imprimatur quod ad Ecclesiam pertinet sine mandato & authoritate ecclesiae: potestas haec ecclesiis ubique competit; & usu recepta est in hac ecclesia non solum sub papa-tu, tu, vetumeriam[?] post reformationem : quod liquido demonstratur compluribus Synodorum decretis contra abusus typographorum, & quibus statuitur quosdam tractatus imprimendos esse, ac designantur quibus provincia examinandi ea quæ typis evulganda essent, committitur. Neque putandum Nationalem ecclesiam authoritate ea non pollere, qua Academiæ omnes nostrates gaudent, quæ libertate hac sine ullo objecto impedimento fruuntur ; Iniquum prorsus judicabunt prudentiores, nationali synodo denegare potestatem typis publicis mandandi decreta & constitutiones suas, cum discipulis Academiarum concessum sit ut theses suas annuatim sine ulla contradictione imprimant : Privatis etiam professoribus nunquam crimini datum, cum tractatus suos emittunt in lucem publicam, quod typographos graviter adjurent (nam amplior illis authoritas non constat) ne alia forma aut characterę imprimant ; Et non licebit ecclesiæ sine regii juris usurpatione, uti authoritate sibi a Deo concredita, in suam pacem & religionis commodum procurandum ?
units.tr: We are also accused of the crime of usurping royal power. 1. Because we claimed authority over the printing presses, and first forbade the royal printer, and then dismissed him. This is an old and stale complaint of the Papist bishops against the first reformers of this Church, dating from 1559, and it has been renewed today against us by their successors, most saltily. For we neither forbade the royal printer nor dismissed him, who still lives peacefully in Edinburgh. Nor does the decree of the National Synod, which we think is here being struck at, contain anything that could rightly be twisted into a usurpation of royal power or a diminution of it over the printing presses: for the decree of the synod only forbids, under penalty of ecclesiastical censure, that anything touching the Church be printed without the command and authority of the Church. This power belongs everywhere to the churches, and it has been received in use in this Church not only under the papacy, but also after the Reformation; this is plainly shown by several decrees of the synods against the abuses of printers, by which it is ordained that certain treatises are to be printed, and by which the task of examining what is to be published in print is committed to designated persons. Nor should it be thought that the National Church lacks that authority which all our universities enjoy, and which they exercise in this freedom without any hindrance. The wiser sort will judge it altogether unfair to deny the National Synod the power to have its decrees and constitutions published in print, when students of the universities are permitted to print their theses every year without any objection. Nor has it ever been charged as a crime against private professors when they send their treatises into the public light that they solemnly charge the printers (for they have no wider authority) not to print them in another form or character. And will it not be permitted to the Church, without usurping royal right, to use the authority committed to her by God for the procuring of her own peace and the advantage of religion?

units.la: 2. Argumentum invasi à nobis juris regii, est, quod Conventus subditorum indicamus, exercitus college-rimus, arces regias obsederimus. Gravibus hisce acculationibus quæ aliquam veri speciem habent, plenè & planè à nobis responsum est in postrema nostra protestatione Decembr. 18. atque ita, sicuti frustra hæc denuo objiciunt præsules, sic non indigent nova & iterata responsione.
units.tr: 2. The charge that we have usurped the royal authority rests on our having called assemblies of the subjects, gathered an army, and besieged the royal castles. We have fully and plainly answered these grave accusations, which have some appearance of truth, in our last protestation of 18 December. So, although the prelates raise them again in vain, they do not need a new and repeated answer.

units.la: In postrema nostra declaratione ad Anglos directa, præterquam quod ingenuitatis & fidelitatis nostræ erga sereniss. regem testimonia distorqueantur in vanam & vilem adulationem, & falsa esse declarentur ; in specie etiam duorum splendidissimorum mendaciorum rei agitur. Primum est, quod exerexercitibus nunc collectis præfici Pontificios, dixerimus: Sic certe nobis relatum fuit, ideoque clausulam hanc addidimus (uti rumoribus ad nos delatum fuit.) Et quid quæso impedit, quo minus exercitus ductores conformes sint primariis authoribus, causæ, & fini operis, quæ omnia Romam & Papismum redolent? Alterum infigne mendacium cujus arcessimur, est: quod dixerimus: Ecclesiasticos quosdam primariæ authoritatis & dignitatis in Anglia authores fuisse regi, ut regnum hoc hostiliter invaderet, noxiæque religionis negotiis importune se immiscuisse.Sed in nos recipimus, nos hoc tum scripto tum testimoniis senatorum regiorum primariæ dignitatis contra quosdam Ecclesiasticos in Anglia probaturos, nominatim contra Cantuariensem ipsum; illique commercium fuisse cum Roma ad formandas hosce libros Canonum & liturgiæ nobis obtrusos, ipsum propria manu mutasse, obliterasse, ac interseruisse complura in iis libris, quæ ad propiorem cum Romana ecclesia conformitatem facerent. Machinatio certe usque adeo periculosa, ut nisi opportune eam frustratus esset Dominus, primum Scotia, dein Anglia, ejus & collegarum qui factionem istam fovent, opera, ad religionem Pontificiam præcipitatæ fuissent. Neque reiterata impressio colloquii cum Iesuita Fischero, famam ejus hic vindicabit.
units.tr: In our last declaration addressed to the English, apart from the fact that the evidence of our sincerity and loyalty towards the most serene king is twisted into empty and base flattery, and our statements are declared false, two most notorious lies are charged against us in particular. The first is that we said that the army now gathered is being placed under Papists. Thus indeed it was reported to us, and so we added the clause (as has been reported to us by rumour). And what, I ask, prevents the army's leaders from being in agreement with the chief authors, the cause and the aim of the work, all of which smell of Rome and Popery? The other notorious lie with which we are charged is this: that we said some ecclesiastics of the highest authority and dignity in England were the instigators of the king to invade this kingdom in a hostile manner, and had meddled unseasonably in the affairs of a harmful religion. But we undertake to prove this, both in writing and by the testimony of royal senators of the highest rank, against certain ecclesiastics in England, namely against the Canterbury man himself. We will show that he had dealings with Rome to shape those books of canons and liturgy forced upon us, and that he himself altered, erased and inserted with his own hand many things in those books which tended to closer conformity with the Roman church. Indeed the scheme was so dangerous that, unless the Lord had opportunely frustrated it, first Scotland and then England would, through the work of him and his colleagues who foster that faction, have been hurled into the Papist religion. Nor will the reprinted account of the conference with the Jesuit Fisher vindicate his reputation here.

units.la: Ideoque omnes in Anglia, quibus religionis veritas, & regis serenis. honor cordi est, & qui libertatis regni amore tenentur, serio obtestamur, ut cum rege serenis. sedulo agant, ac persuadeant Parlamenti in Anglia indictionem, ut mysterium hoc iniquitatis quod hactenus tecte operabantur, tandem retegatur, & in primarios ejus authores inquiratur, ac severe pro meritis animadvertatur; & ut subdola & proditoria hæc astutia, qua utrumque pariter regnum cruento bello immiscere satagunt, (ut videl. utriusque enervatione surgat Roma, & utrinque præficiatur Pontifex Romanus) in apricam tandem lucem proferatur, & opportune frustretur, quo Deo gloria, regi honos, & subditis sua constet securitas ab exteris tyrannis tam in animas quam corpora sæviturus.
units.tr: Therefore we earnestly beseech all in England to whom the truth of religion and the honour of the most serene king are dear, and who are moved by love of the liberty of the kingdom, to work diligently with the most serene king and to persuade him to call a Parliament in England. Then this mystery of iniquity, which until now they have worked in secret, may at last be uncovered, its chief authors sought out and severely punished according to their deserts. And this crafty and treacherous plot, by which they strive to draw both kingdoms alike into bloody war (namely so that Rome may rise from the weakening of both, and the Roman Pontiff be set over both), may at last be brought into the open light and opportunely frustrated. Thus glory may be to God, honour to the king, and security to the subjects against foreign tyrants, who are about to rage against both souls and bodies.

units.la: Præsules, ne quid seu falsi seu veri prætermittant, quo rem suam promoveant, hoc etiam crimen nobis objiciunt: Quod per nos publicarum legum authoritas suffocetur: ita quidem ut non audeant judices sententiam dicere secundum legum præscriptum. Regni hujus primarii judices meminisse possunt, legitimam justitiæ administrationem se nobis denegasse, non quidem proprio motu, & ex animi sui sententia, sed metu ne peccarent in rescripta, ab aula præsulum opera contra nos procurata: Revocandum etiam in memoriam est, quod, cum nuperrime literas, (quæ expediri solent contra eos quibus aqua & igni interdictum est) contra excommunicatos præsules nobis concedi instaremus, juxta expressa statuti parlamentarii verba; quod subditorum minimis conceditur, nobis tamen à Dominis Sessionis concessum non fuerit, qui literis ad serenis. regem perscriptis Martii 2. solam & unicam causam, ob quam legitimum nostrum postulatum non concesserint, fuisse ajebant, regiæ Majestatis beneplacitum, & mandatum; simulque preces addebant, ut regno & ecclesiæ ea pax & tranquillitas restitueretur, qua hactenus erat gavisa: Unde satis constat, non leges solum, verum etiam judices nullo metu aut terrore coactos, sed conscientia officii erga Deum, regem, patriam, causæque nostræ favere.
units.tr: The prelates, so that they may leave nothing untried, whether false or true, to advance their cause, also charge us with this crime: that through us the authority of the public laws is suppressed, so that judges dare not pronounce sentence according to the prescription of the laws. The chief judges of this kingdom can recall that they have denied us the legitimate administration of justice. They did not do so of their own motion or by their own judgment, but from fear of sinning against the rescripts procured against us through the work of the prelates' court. It must also be recalled that when we most recently insisted that letters be granted to us against the excommunicated prelates (letters which are usually issued against those under interdiction of fire and water), according to the express words of the parliamentary statute, which is granted to the least of the subjects, yet they were not granted to us by the Lords of the Session. In their letter written to the most serene king on 2 March, they said that the sole and only reason why they did not grant our lawful request was the pleasure and command of His royal Majesty. At the same time they added prayers that the peace and tranquillity which the kingdom and church had hitherto enjoyed might be restored. Whence it is sufficiently clear that not only the laws but also the judges, coerced by no fear or terror, but by a sense of duty towards God, the king, the country and our cause, favour us.

units.la: Ut superioribus accusationibus probabilitatis quandam speciem superinducant, dicunt, quosdam nostrum utrumque regi præstandum juramentum rejicere, Fidelitatis videl. & Primatus, ac tueri nulla lege nos astrictos ut in [?] illa juramenta adigamur, tres etiam Scotos in Wallia in carcerem conjectos[?] esse, quod juramenta hæc repudiassent. De Scotis in Wallia carceri inclusis nihil respondebimus, quandoquidem tum homines qui sint, tum quæ fuerint ipsorum actiones prorsus ignoremus: Colligimus tamen locis illis Inquisitionem sedulo promoveri. Et ad nos ipsos quod attinet, licet inter se differant juramentum fidelitatis & primatus, neque per conscientiam nobis liceat jurare in verba juramenti primatus prout hodie exponitur & extenditur à supparasitantibus quibusdam præsulibus; quæcunque tamen politico magistratui concedenda esse docent puriores & doctiores reformatæ ecclesiæ Theologi, & quæ verbo Dei regibus debentur, lubentissime ex animis deferimus; nobis quippe non incognitum est, quintum præceptum quo officium subditorum erga reges & magistratus continetur & præscribitur, esse primum secundæ tabulæ mandatum; nostræque fidei confessionem agnoscere Regem nostrum ferenif. esse Dei in terris deputatum, ad quem conservatio & purgatio religionis pertineant.
units.tr: To lend some semblance of probability to their earlier accusations, they say that some of us refuse the oath due to the king on both counts, namely of fidelity and of supremacy, and that we are bound by no law to be compelled to take those oaths; and that three Scots in Wales have been thrown into prison because they rejected these oaths. About the Scots shut up in prison in Wales we will reply nothing, since we are utterly ignorant both of who these men are and of what their actions were. We gather, however, that an inquisition is being diligently promoted in those places. As for ourselves, although the oath of fidelity and the oath of supremacy differ from each other, and it is not lawful for us in conscience to swear to the words of the oath of supremacy as it is today explained and extended by certain obsequious prelates, yet whatever the purer and more learned theologians of the reformed church teach should be granted to the civil magistrate, and whatever is owed to kings by the word of God, we most willingly render from our hearts. For it is not unknown to us that the fifth commandment, by which the duty of subjects towards kings and magistrates is contained and prescribed, is the first commandment of the second table. And in our confession we acknowledge that our most serene king is the deputy of God on earth, to whom the preservation and purification of religion belong.

units.la: Sicuti sinistriorem hanc de nobis opinionem regi persuaserunt hostes nostri, sic declaratione hac satis edocemur quo animo rex ferenif. in ecclesiam & regnum hoc feratur, & quo tandem res hæc eruptura sit, nisi Deus mutatione cordis regii, aut via alia prudentiæ suæ cognita partum hunc abortivum fecerit? aut suffocaverit. Nam 1. pro insanabili superstitione & Vatiniano præsulum in religionem reformatam odio, declaratur: Introductione liturgiæ nunquam propositam fuisse quamlibet religionis mutationem, verum solam cultus divini conformitatem cum aliis duobus regis regnis, licet à malignis quædam sint in iniquiorem sensum detorta. Atque ita liber liturgicus nullam prorsus religionis mutationem secum fert, sed nostro solum interpretamento, obtorto quasi collo, in eum sensum depravatur. Cultus divini conformitas cum aliis regnis urgetur, quasi nos essemus instar tabulae rasae, neque nobis publica legum qua civilium qua ecclesiasticarum authoritate, forma divini cultus constaret; Mera cum aliis regnis conformitas praetenditur, licet frequentissimae liturae & interpolationes liturgiae, in aliis duobus regnis usitatae contrarium testentur; eaeque liturae ac interpolationes praesulum nostrorum ac Cantuariensis ipsius manu propria exaratae sunt: Propter eorum itaque peccata in nos animadvertendum erit, & captata opportunitate innocens scilicet ille liber recipiendus erit.
units.tr: Just as our enemies have persuaded the king of this more unfavourable opinion of us, so this declaration sufficiently teaches us with what mind the most serene king is moved towards the church and this kingdom, and to what end this affair is about to break out, unless God, by a change of the royal heart or by some other way known to His wisdom, makes this abortive birth miscarry or suffocates it. For first, out of an incurable superstition and a Vatinian hatred of the prelates against the reformed religion, it is declared: that by the introduction of the liturgy no change of religion was ever proposed, but only the conformity of divine worship with the king's two other kingdoms, although some things have been twisted by malicious men into a worse sense. And so the liturgical book carries no change of religion whatsoever, but is depraved into that sense solely by our interpretation, as if by a twisted neck. Conformity of divine worship with the other kingdoms is urged, as if we were a blank slate, and as if the form of divine worship did not rest upon the public authority of laws, both civil and ecclesiastical. A bare conformity with other kingdoms is pretended, although the very frequent alterations and interpolations of the liturgy used in the other two kingdoms testify to the contrary; and those alterations and interpolations were written with the own hand of our prelates and of the Canterbury man himself. Therefore on account of their sins we shall have to take vengeance upon them, and when an opportunity is seized, that innocent book shall have to be received.

units.la: 2. Qua sunt ambitione & avaritia praesules, declaratio illa certos nos reddit, Regimen Episcopale retinendum esse prout statutis parlamentariis sancitur; utpote,quod universo orbi notum sit, regimen illud esse in se legitimum, ad pacem politicam procurandam & conservandam convenientissimum, regiminì Monarchico unice consonans, & sine quo tribus parlamenti ordinibus sua integritas non constabit. Licet verum sit, nulla lege parlamentaria, nulla synodi cujusliber decreto officium illud Diœcesani Episcopatus in hoc regno muniri, notumque sit omnibus fere reformatis ecclesiis, esse in se potius Antichristianum, & paci politicae quam maxime adversari, uti & regimini Monarchico; & apud omnes gentes Monarchis fuisse maxime perniciosum: Adde, licet parlamentum fuerit, esse posset, & sua natura sit ex omni sua parte integrum& perfectum, sine membri hujus inutili redundantia; Attamen fovendi sc.sunt[?] necessario Episcopi idq; Iure divino,neq; minori quam antehac fastu,ut regum libidini in cultu Dei inserviant. 3.Declaratur:Nullum fœdus cum rex serenissimus assensum non praebuerit permittendum esse, ac praetendi solum fœderi nostro, quod cum Deo ictum sit, ut honestiori velo tecti opera Diaboli perageremus, qualia sint, perduellionis & rebellionis crimina. Inde est quod sentiant, non posse magis permitti fœdus hoc nostrum quam rebellio & seditio, fœderatisque aut renuntiandum Deo in cujus verba solenniter jurarunt, aut rebellium & perduellium pœnas atroces subeundas esse. 4. Declaratur, Statum quæstionis nunc non esse de libro liturgico, & Episcopatu : Sed an rex sereniss. nobis rex sit, necne ? nobisque statutum esse dicunt, regii regiminis imas radices convellere : imo jus regium nos in regis persona contempsisse, & nobismet ipsis vendicasse objiciunt : Ideoque regem serenis. 5. Cogi jus suum regium armata manu apud nos restabilire, daturumque operam ut maximi nostrum re ipsa experiantur, nunquam se approbaturum tale, quale inter nos sancivimus fœdus. Atque sic omnibus abunde constat, conclusum & promulgatum esse, serenis. regem hostilem exercitum omnibus viribus instructum, qui declaratione hac & id genus mediis in Anglia cogi possit, in nos movere, (nam eo solum nomine declaratio hæc prælegenda est in singulis totius regni templis) nullo alio fine quam ut librum liturgicum & Episcopatum restabiliat, fœdus nostrum cum Deo rescindat, & ut in nos tanquam perduelles & rebelles animadvertat.
units.tr: Second, by their ambition and avarice the prelates make us certain by that declaration: that the episcopal government is to be retained as it is sanctioned by parliamentary statutes; for it is known to the whole world that that government is in itself lawful, most convenient for procuring and preserving political peace, uniquely consonant with monarchical government, and without which the integrity of the three estates of Parliament will not stand. Although it is true that by no parliamentary law, and by no decree of any synod, is that office of diocesan episcopacy fortified in this kingdom; and although it is known to almost all the reformed churches that it is in itself rather antichristian and most hostile to political peace, as also to monarchical government, and among all nations has been most pernicious to monarchs. Add that Parliament, although it may be, and could be, and by its nature is in every part whole and perfect, without the useless redundancy of this member, nevertheless the bishops must necessarily be cherished, and that by divine right, and with no less pride than before, so that they may serve the lust of kings in the worship of God. 3. It is declared: No covenant is to be permitted to which the most serene king has not given assent; and it is only pretended for our covenant, which was struck with God, so that under a more honest veil we might carry out the works of the Devil, which are the crimes of treason and rebellion. Hence they think that this covenant of ours can no more be permitted than rebellion and sedition, and that either the covenant must be renounced, to which God we solemnly swore, or the atrocious penalties of rebels and traitors must be undergone. 4. It is declared that the state of the question is now not about the liturgical book and episcopacy, but whether the most serene king is king to us or not; and they say it has been decided to overthrow the deepest roots of royal government. Indeed they object that we have despised the royal right in the person of the king and claimed it for ourselves; therefore the most serene king 5. is compelled to re-establish his royal right among us by armed hand, and will take care that the greatest of us experience it in fact; he will never approve such a covenant as we have sanctioned among ourselves. And so it is abundantly clear to all that it has been decided and proclaimed that the most serene king will move against us a hostile army, equipped with every resource, which can be assembled in England by this declaration and by such means (for this declaration is to be read out in every church of the whole kingdom for this reason alone). His only purpose is to restore the liturgical book and episcopacy, to rescind our covenant with God, and to punish us as traitors and rebels.

units.la: Quare nostrum nunc est serio perpendere & mature deliberare ac concludere ; An confultum fit, cum peccato & ignominia tot fœdorum & atrocium criminum falso nobis impactorum dedecus intolerabile subire, quorum pessimis etiam temporibus vix arcessebantur Christiani quilibet : Item, recipere librum illum liturgiæ ut unicam divini cultus formulam, quem tamen synodus demonstravit ingentem superstitionis, Idololatriæ, & Antichristianæ tyrannidis cumulum continere : Revocare etiam præsules nostros, ipsorumque regimen maturo consilio abjuratum : Primos illos nostros reformatores, & gloriosum reformationis opus condemnare ; Renunciare fœderi cum Deo inito, totiesque perfidos esse, quoties juramento & chirographo illud obsignavimus: Laborem & operam nostram in tam piam causam tamdiu locatam perdere: Nostrismet manibus patentem portam aperire & exemplo nostro latam viam digito quasi demonstrare, qua papatus & omnes posthac innovationes in religionem nostram irruant: Regi offendiculum ponere in via qua ad cœlum pergitur: Obstaculo esse reginæ ne convertatur: Scandalo esse reformatis omnibus ecclesiis, quæ pro nobis apud Deum seriis precibus hactenus intercesserunt: Obdurare corda, & munire dextras omnium veritatis hostium tam domesticorum quam externorum: Hominibus & Angelis odiosum spectaculum nosmet exhibere: Præteritam servitutem & suspiria ob redemptionem oblivioni tradere: Veritatis, misericordiæ & potentiæ divinæ, toties & tot modis ineffabili nostro solatio hactenus erga nos manifestatæ sensum denegare: Posteros, qui miseriis obvoluti flagitium hoc nostrum sed frustra deflebunt, perdere: Pudorem bonis suffundere: Amicis lachrymas, & hostibus nostris gaudiorum jubilos procurare: Dei in terris progressum interrumpere, & expansum ipsius signum è manibus extorquere: Coronam judici ac regi nostro Christo eripere: Tristari spiritum S. eidemque resistere: Aureum illud candelabrum diripere, ejusque lumen extinguere: Denique omnia illa judicia, quæ in Dei libro exstant in nostra capita contrahere; ita ut omnes gentes dicturæ sint: Quare ita severe agit Dominus cum illa gente, quid sibi vult furor tantæ iræ? Tum respondebitur, quia fœdus Dei dereliquerunt, ideo malis illis merito premuntur; Neque vocula ulla quæ defectionem sapit nobis citius excidet, quin statim inferni horrore corripientur animæ nostræ. Aut contra, nostrum est nunc concludere; An non consultissimum sit potestate à Deo nobis concessa uti ( non ut Angliam invadamus, aut ut Dei populum qui pacem nostram non interturbat, molestia ulla afficiamus ; Anathema quibuscunque ejusmodi arridènt consilia ; aut qui ad ea exequenda operam suam prastabunt, verum ) in nostram solum innocuam tutelam contra vim armatam, & iniquam, à quibus minime debuit, invasionem.
units.tr: It is therefore for us now to weigh this matter seriously, deliberate maturely, and conclude whether it is advisable to bear, with sin and disgrace, the intolerable shame of so many foul and atrocious crimes falsely imputed to us, crimes for which hardly any Christians were charged even in the worst times; likewise, whether to accept that liturgy book as the only form of divine worship, which the synod has shown to contain a huge heap of superstition, idolatry and Antichristian tyranny; to recall our prelates, whose government we abjured after mature counsel; to condemn our first reformers and the glorious work of reformation; to renounce the covenant made with God, and to be faithless as often as we sealed it with oath and signature; to lose the labour and effort we have so long expended on so pious a cause; to open with our own hands a wide gate and, by our example, point out with a finger, as it were, the broad road by which Papacy and all future innovations in our religion may rush in; to place a stumbling block before the king on the way to heaven; to be an obstacle to the queen, lest she be converted; to be a scandal to all the reformed churches, which have hitherto interceded for us with earnest prayers before God; to harden the hearts and strengthen the hands of all enemies of the truth, domestic and foreign alike; to exhibit ourselves as a hateful spectacle to men and angels; to consign our past servitude and our sighs over redemption to oblivion; to deny the sense of truth, mercy and divine power, so often and in so many ways manifested to us for our ineffable comfort; to destroy our posterity, who, wrapped in miseries, will vainly lament this crime of ours; to bring shame upon the good; to cause tears to our friends and shouts of joy to our enemies; to interrupt God's progress on earth and wrench the extended sign from his hands; to snatch the crown from Christ, our judge and king; to grieve the Holy Spirit and resist him; to tear down that golden candlestick and extinguish its light; and finally, to draw upon our own heads all those judgements which stand written in God's book, so that all nations will say: "Why has the Lord dealt so severely with that people? What means the fury of so great a wrath?" And the answer will be given: because they forsook the covenant of God, therefore they are rightly crushed by these evils; and no word savouring of defection will fall quickly from us without our souls being at once seized with the horror of hell. Or, on the contrary, it is for us now to conclude whether it would not be most advisable to use the power granted us by God, not to invade England, nor to inflict any harm upon the people of God who do not disturb our peace (anathema to whoever favours such plans, or lends his effort to carrying them out), but solely for our innocent protection against an armed and unjust invasion, by those from whom it least ought to come.

units.la: Itaque cum in edicto & declaratione regia quaeritur. Quid illud fit ad cujus defensionem nos comparemus? Respondemus ; Religionem, privilegia, vitam denique ipsam ; non vero contumaciam aut rebellionem. Et cum quaeritur, Contra quos haec defendamus? Ne conatus & actiones nostrae, ab iis qui de vero rerum nostrarum statu certiores nondum facti sunt, non recte percipiantur, aut à malignis pervertantur, quasi saniorum Theologorum doctrinae, aut laudabili Christianorum seu veterum seu recentium praxi repugnarent; Antequam ad quaestionem hanc respondeamus, rogamus ut serio & maturo judicio sequentia perpendantur.
units.tr: Therefore, when the edict and royal declaration asks, What is that for whose defence we are arming ourselves? we answer: religion, privileges, and life itself; not, however, contumacy or rebellion. And when it is asked, Against whom are we defending these? we ask that, lest our endeavours and actions be wrongly understood by those who have not yet been informed of the true state of our affairs, or be perverted by malicious men, as if they were contrary to the doctrine of the sounder theologians or to the commendable practice of Christians, both ancient and recent, the following points be weighed with serious and mature judgement before we answer this question.
