units.la: Magnam videlicet differentiam esse inter regem in regno suo commorantem, & facili ab utraque parte contendentium accessu, de vero controversiae statu recte edoctum ; Et regem longe à nobis in altero regno distantem, & aures faciles alteri tantum partium concedentem, à quibus de vero rerum nostrarum statu ei imponitur : Inter regem, quatenus regem, legitimo judicio secundum praescripta legum regni hujus contra rebelles procedentem; & regem, quatenus hominem, de regio solio descendentem (ad cujus pedes ostendi possunt subditorum suorum supplices libelli, quos nullo responso aequo dignatur) & furioso incessu contra devotissimos sibi subditos progredientem: Inter regem à religione prorsus alienum, qui subditis suis religionem profitentibus amplius non astringitur quam sibi beneplacitum fuerit; & nostrum Serenifs.[?] regem communem nobiscum religionem profitentem, patris facto & solenni suo juramento astrictum, ut nos sibi subditos, vitas nostras, religionem, libertates & leges tueretur.
units.tr: There is clearly a great difference between a king dwelling in his own kingdom, with easy access for either side of the disputants, who is rightly informed of the true state of the controversy, and a king far away from us in another kingdom, who lends willing ears to one party only, by whom the true state of our affairs is misrepresented to him. There is a difference between the king as king, proceeding by lawful judgement, according to the prescribed laws of this realm, against rebels, and the king as a man, descending from the royal throne (at whose feet the humble petitions of his subjects may be laid, which he does not deign to answer with any fair reply), advancing with a furious gait against his most devoted subjects. There is a difference between a king wholly alien to religion, who binds his religion-professing subjects no further than pleases him, and our most serene king, who professes the same religion as we do, bound by his father's deed and his solemn oath to protect us as his subjects, our lives, religion, liberties and laws.

units.la: Dein consideranda venit differentia, inter privatos quosdam armatos ad resistendum; & inferiores magistratus, judices, regni senatores, nobiles, primores, quibus nativitatis aut deputationis jure, sententiæ dictio & suffragium in parlamentis competit, Barones, cives spectatos, & totum fere regni corpus (si paucos exceperis eosque vel aulicos, vel publicis muniis regis gratia fungentes, vel papistas, aut ad Papismum inclinantes, eorumque asseclas) in innocuam suam defensionem accinctū: Inter subditos insurgētes aut contumaces contra leges & omnē omnino rationem, ut à jugo obedientiæ magistratui debitæ liberentur; & subditos à debita regi obedientia ne vel minimum deflectentes, sed ei constanter & devote adhærentes, & submissa humilitate obseerantes religionis suæ puritatem & justitiæ administrationem: Inter populum armata manu conantem novationes in religione contra leges introducere; & eum, cui nihil magis in votis est quam ut eadem sanciatur religio, cujus publica professione post reformationis tempora semper gavisi sunt, & in quam non solum olim à rege & subditis juratum est, verumetiam in quam rex speciali mandato senatores adegit, & in quam à senatu regio adacti sunt omnes subditi: Inter populum de ludicris suis inventis & excogitatis à se futilitatibus contendentem; & eum, qui sententiam & praxin de articulis quibusdam controversis ampliandam censuit, donec eos definiret Nationalis Synodus, ( cui soli proprie competit de hujus naturæ rebus sententiam ferre, ) quibus à Synodo legitime definitis constanter adhæret.
units.tr: Next must be considered the difference between certain private persons armed to resist, and the inferior magistrates, judges, senators of the realm, nobles and chief men, to whom, by right of birth or appointment, belongs the pronouncing of sentence and the vote in parliaments, together with the barons, respected citizens, and almost the whole body of the realm (if you except a few, and those either courtiers, or holding public offices by the king's favour, or papists, or those inclined to Popery, and their followers), who have girded themselves for their innocent defence. There is a difference between subjects rising up against the laws and against all reason, so as to be freed from the yoke of obedience owed to the magistrate, and subjects who do not deviate in the least from the obedience due to the king, but adhere to him constantly and devotedly, and with humble submission maintain the purity of their religion and the administration of justice. There is a difference between a people attempting by armed hand to introduce innovations in religion against the laws, and one to whom nothing is more desired than that the same religion be sanctioned, a religion whose public profession they have enjoyed ever since the time of the Reformation, and to which not only the king and subjects once swore, but to which the king also bound the senators by special mandate, and to which the royal senate bound all subjects. There is a difference between a people contending over trifles of their own invention and futilities devised by themselves, and one who judged that opinion and practice on certain controverted articles should be left open until the National Synod, to which alone it properly belongs to pass judgement on matters of this kind, had defined them, and who constantly adheres to them once they have been lawfully defined by the Synod.

units.la: Nunc vero quæstionis statu sic formato, An nobis liceat nosmet defendere? Respondemus licere; idque satis nos docent lex & lumen naturæ, verbum Dei tam in veteri quam novo testamento, fœdus inter Deum & populum initum, finis propter quem magistratus a Deo ordinantur; quod superioribus nostris stationem & ordinem sibi a Deo, cui subordinantur, positum deferentibus, subditis tamen eorum consistendum sit in statione a Deo sibi statuta: Hisce addantur selectissimorum Theologorum, saniorum politicorum ac jurisperitorum, ne iis quidem exceptis qui acerrime contra Monarchomachos pugnant, testimonia; mutuus ille contractus, & pacta conventa inita inter regem coronandum ac populum; statuta parlamenti; & laudabilis majorum nostrorum praxis.
units.tr: Now that the question has been so framed, whether it is lawful for us to defend ourselves, we answer that it is lawful. The law and the light of nature, the word of God in both the Old and the New Testament, the covenant entered between God and the people, and the end for which magistrates are ordained by God, teach us this sufficiently: superiors, who bear the station and order placed on them by God, to whom they are subordinate, must leave their subjects to stand in the station God has appointed for them. To these may be added the testimonies of the most select theologians, of the sounder politicians and jurists, not excepting even those who fight most bitterly against the Monarchomachs; that mutual contract and the agreed pacts entered into between the king to be crowned and the people; the statutes of parliament; and the commendable practice of our forefathers.

units.la: Ad fratres & vicinos in Anglia, quorum aures prælectione edicti hujus in omnibus templis repletæ fuerunt, nostra sese nunc convertit oratio. Pro reverentia & honore quem authoritati utpote Dei instituto, debemus; Pro naturali illo ac devotissimo amore, quo in serenissf. & clementissf. nostrum regem inter nos natum & baptizatum, ferimur; sincere & ex animis gravissime dolemus, quod regium ipsius nomen ab improbis hominibus adeo fœdetur, & sacræ ipsius aures usque adeo præoccupentur, ut tam faciles eas præbeat tot absurdis & fidem omnem excedentibus calumniis contra integram gentem, nativam suam ipsius patriam & regnum; Nimis constat quanta discrimina secum trahant calumniæ præsertim universales, quales hæ sunt, quibus reprimendis summa ope, extremo legum rigore niti deceret: Et pro amore vobis debito, cum quibus pluribus ac firmioribus vinculis in mutuam amicitiam constringimur, quam cum qualibet alia orbis universi gente; ægerrime certe, prout decebat, tulimus, ac ex animis dolemus, vestra templa & aures ejusmodi sermonibus patere, neque facilem credulitatem vestram satis admirabimur, si fidem apud vos invenient: Et quia id genus sermones plantaria ac seminaria seditionum esse possent inter ipsos fratres, qui semel irritati sævius digladiantur, & difficilius conveniunt; Rogamus (si forte apud gentem tam prudentem obsecrationibus opus sit) ne quibuslibet relationibus subito protrudamini ad illud contra nos aggrediendum quod in mutuam utriusque perniciem tendat: aut ut, qualia in hujus generis bellô exspectari poterunt commoda, hoc est, nullius prorsus pretii, aureo hamo piscari velitis; quo facto utramque pariter gentem externorum ludibrio exponeretis, & insulam hanc tam diuturna pace beatam in campum sanguinis mutaretis, hostesque, qui obliquis oculis nostram fœlicitatem intuiti sunt, & nostro exitio quotidie imminent, in prædam promiscue utrosque raperent: Cumque vobis relatum fuerit de nostris ad innocuam tutelam usque adeo necessariis præparationibus ut finé iis nosmet defendere nequeamus, & quibus nihil prorsus damni vobis intenditur aut afferetur, rogamus ut Christiane & prudenter secundum æquitatis regulas Quod tibi fieri non vis id alteri ne feceris, judicare velitis: Et ne rumoribus & relationibus ab adversariis nostris confictis & sparsis subito credatis; præsertim cum authores nequitiæ suæ sibi probe conscii, rumores hos inter solos Anglos spargant, qui eorundem vanitatem & falsitatem nequeunt convincere: & à nostra notitia detineant, ubi lucem & levius examen nequaquam [?]fetre possunt, universa plebe eorundem falsitatem perspectum habente. Atque licet ad nos tandem perveniant, difficulter tamen, neque fine ingenti discrimine nostræ refponfiones & vindicationes ad Anglos perveniunt, prout nunc fese res habent. Denique rogamus ut feriis precibus apud Deum, & supplicationibus apud regem pro nobis intercedere velitis, & fi necesse fit, ut potentiam & vires vestras in nostram tutelam contra mercenarios & impiam Belial progeniem converta-tis. Nonne fratres fumus, eodem sanguine & ofsibus concreti? Nonne sub eodem degimus tecto, uno eodemque navigio ferimur, unius ejufdemque corporis membra fumus? Pii majores vestri religionis reformandæ & stabiliendæ nobis auxilio fuerunt; neque de vobis tam male meriti fumus, aut vos à patriis virtutibus usque adeo degeneraftis, ut metuendum fit ne à vobis nunc deferamur; cum eadem nunc fit causa quæ olim, & mutatis tantum personis casus prope idem, ac incolumitas utrique communis. Serio itaque contendamus pro fide fanctis semel tradita, ut misericordia, pax & amor supra nos multiplicentur.
units.tr: Our speech now turns to our brothers and neighbours in England, whose ears have been filled by the reading of this edict in all their churches. Out of the reverence and honour which we owe to authority as an institution of God, and out of that natural and most devoted love with which we are drawn towards our most serene and most clement king, born and baptized among us, we sincerely and from our hearts grieve most deeply that his royal name is so defiled by wicked men, and his sacred ears so preoccupied that he lends such easy ear to so many absurd calumnies, beyond all belief, against an entire nation, his own native country and kingdom. It is well known what great dangers such calumnies bring with them, especially universal ones such as these, which ought to be repressed with the utmost effort and the strictest rigour of the laws. And out of the love owed to you, with whom we are bound in mutual friendship by more numerous and firmer ties than with any other nation in the whole world, we have taken it very ill, as was fitting, and we grieve from our hearts that your churches and ears lie open to such discourses; nor shall we sufficiently marvel at your easy credulity if they find belief among you. And because such discourses could become seedbeds and nurseries of sedition between the very brothers, who, once provoked, fight more savagely and are reconciled with greater difficulty, we ask (if perhaps a people so prudent needs entreaties) that you not be suddenly driven by any reports into attacking us in a way that tends to the mutual destruction of both. Or that you be willing to fish with a golden hook for such advantages as may be expected from a war of this kind, which are of no value whatsoever; by doing so you would expose both peoples alike to the mockery of foreigners, turn this island, blessed with so long a peace, into a field of blood, and seize both peoples indiscriminately as plunder for enemies who have looked askance at our happiness and who daily threaten our ruin. And since it has been reported to you that our preparations for innocent defence are so necessary that without them we could not defend ourselves, and that they threaten no harm at all to you nor will bring any, we ask that you judge in a Christian and prudent manner, according to the rules of equity: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. And do not believe suddenly the rumours and reports devised and spread by our adversaries, especially since the authors of this wickedness, well aware of their own guilt, spread these rumours among the English alone, who cannot refute their vanity and falsehood, and keep them away from our knowledge, where they could not bear the light or a closer examination, since the whole common people here have a clear view of their falsity. And although our replies and vindications may at last reach you, yet, as things now stand, they reach the English with difficulty and not without great danger. Finally, we ask that you intercede for us with earnest prayers before God and with supplications before the king, and, if need be, turn your power and strength to our protection against mercenaries and the impious brood of Belial. Are we not brothers, knit together of the same blood and bones? Do we not dwell under the same roof, and are we not carried in one and the same ship? Are we not members of one and the same body? Your pious forefathers were our help in reforming and establishing religion; nor have we deserved so ill of you, nor have you so degenerated from your fathers' virtues, that we must fear you will now desert us, since the cause is now the same as it was then, and the situation nearly the same with only the persons changed, and the safety common to both. Let us therefore earnestly contend for the faith once delivered to the saints, so that mercy, peace and love may be multiplied upon us.

units.la: Perpendentibus etiam nobis, quam nuperæ noftræ actiones contra primarios nostros hostes, & præcipua regni fortalitia, ut sunt, arx Edinburgena, & cæt. eorum calumniis pateant, qui omnia nostra præcedentia consilia quantumvis neceffaria in deteriorem partem detorserunt; & quia ab amicis forte nostris hic errari possit, qui longe remoti nequeunt fatis percipere quam mature singula hic gesta sint; necessarium judicavimus, ut illorum ora obstruerentur, & his fatisfieret, omnibus declarare, quo modo ad hæc, in necessariam nostri tutelam, pro præfenti rerum nostrarum statu, adacti fuerimus.
units.tr: Considering also how our recent actions against our chief enemies, and against the principal strongholds of the kingdom such as the castle of Edinburgh, etc., lie open to the slanders of those who have twisted all our earlier counsels, however necessary, to the worst construction; and because our friends, being far away, may perhaps fail to grasp sufficiently how promptly each thing has been done here, we judged it necessary to declare to everyone how we were driven to these measures for our own necessary protection, given the present state of our affairs, so that the mouths of such critics might be stopped and their doubts satisfied.

units.la: Nullis regni hujus subditis ignotum esse potest, quantis minis & quam ingentibus terriculis replete fuerint edicta compluria hic promulgata, uti fuerunt illa Iulii 4. & Decembris 18. Multisque etiam satis innotuerunt literæ ad nobiles & generosos in Anglia à rege missæ, quibus imperabatur ut adesseunt regio vexillo Eboraci ad Aprilis 1. & quæ edicta in Anglia promulgata sunt, tam illud Ianuarii 29. quam hoc quod priora omnia superat, Februar. 27. quibus condemnantur omnes nostræ actiones quantumvis legitimæ, libelli supplices, protestationes, relationes quantumvis veræ & modestæ, quin & intentiones ipsæ, (nobis licet Deum toties & tam solenniter contra astestantibus) ut falsæ, rebelles, proditoriæ, nos vero ut rebelles & perduelles, quibus hostile bellum indicitur. Neque nos fugit, quibus epistolis tepidi nostri amici hic excitati, & aperti hostes animati fuerint, quomodo pecunia & apparatu bellico contra nos instructi fuerint, quæque ad eos transmissa sint mandata, quo modo sese commodissime in nostram perniciem conjunxerint: Quam etiam magnifice ac jactabunde nostratium quidam, tam in aula, quam domi hic apud nos hærentes, qui amorem omnem in patriam suam exuerunt, in se suscepepint, exercitus ingentes tum in Borealibus tum in Australibus regni hujus provinciis sese collecturos, ut nos undique circumcluderent; Scotos nobiles, senatores regni & alios in aula coactos fuisse fœderi regio subscribere cum hac additione; Se repudiare nuperam Synodum Nationalem, nec adhæsuros fœderi & confessioni à nobis subscriptæ, nobisque adversaturos quantum possint, prout mandaturus sit rex; Familiam regiam iter suscepisse Martii 18. regemque ipsum equis citatis subsecuturum Martii 27. ac tertio die Eboracum aut Novum Castrum adventurum, ut in Scotiam cum exercitu moveat: Mandatum nobilibus Scotis, ut cum comitatu peritorum belli ducum domum in Scotiam se conferant, ut amicos & clientes colligant ac sub signis distribuant, sub ductu Marchionis Hammiltonii, qui exteris nostris hostibus in regis comitatu fe adjuncturus fit; Comitem Lind-sejae cum classe 17.regiarum navium instructa tribus militum millibus ad ea hujus regni loca exfcenfionem facturum, quae literae[?] & mandatum resignandum designabunt; fexcentos equites ad limites regni mittendos ut incursionem faciant; domesticos noftros hostes eorundem adventum exspectare, excommunicatos nostros praesules in Angliam profugiffe cum asseclis; Praedia & fortunas Nobilium, Baronum, & opulentiorum Civium designari in spolia & exuvias inter hostes dispartiendas. Quare cum ita fe res habeant, caputque spei quam fovent hostes nostri, situm fit in domesticis nostris divisionibus, in potentia & viribus quorundam pontificiorum & aliorum magnae apud nos dignitatis, ac in locis quibusdam munitis, ad regni tutelam contra externos hostes destinatis, (prout fufius ostendimus in protestatione nostra) praecipue vero in arce Edenburgena, praecipuo societatis[?] nostrae membro, ac conventuum nostrorum loco. Non erat differendum nobis, verum ad has incitas redactis aliquid aggrediedum fuerat in nostram incolumitatem; aut moriendum, aut cogebamur nosmet defendere, aut hostibus nostris, quorum misericordiae crudeles sunt, nofmet submittere; hinc est quod ad illa necessario adacti fuerimus, quae Edinburgi & alibi perfecta esse accepistis.
units.tr: No subject of this kingdom can be unaware how full of threats and how terrifying were the several edicts published here, such as those of July 4 and December 18. Many have also learned well enough of the letters sent by the king to the nobles and gentlemen in England, ordering them to attend at York under the royal standard on April 1; and of the edicts published in England, both that of January 29 and this one of February 27, which surpasses all the earlier ones, by which all our actions, however lawful, our humble petitions, our protestations, and our reports, however true and modest, and indeed even our intentions (although we have so often and so solemnly called God to witness them), are condemned as false, rebellious and treasonous, and we ourselves are declared rebels and traitors against whom war is proclaimed. Nor is it hidden from us by what letters our lukewarm friends here were stirred up and our open enemies encouraged; how they were equipped with money and war matériel against us; what orders were sent to them; and how they joined themselves together most conveniently for our destruction. Nor do we fail to note how magnificently and boastfully certain of our countrymen, who remain at court and at home here among us, having cast off all love for their native land, have undertaken that great armies would be gathered in the northern and southern provinces of this kingdom to surround us on every side. The Scottish nobles, the senators of the kingdom and others compelled at court to subscribe the royal covenant with this addition: that they repudiate the recent National Synod, and will not adhere to the covenant and confession subscribed by us, but will oppose us as far as they can, as the king shall command. The royal family set out on March 18, and the king himself would follow on swift horses on March 27, and would arrive at York or Newcastle on the third day, in order to move into Scotland with an army. The Scottish nobles were ordered to betake themselves home to Scotland with a retinue of experienced war leaders, to gather their friends and clients and distribute them under standards, under the leadership of the Marquis of Hamilton, who would join himself to our foreign enemies in the king's train. The Earl of Lindsay, with a fleet of seventeen royal ships and three thousand soldiers, would make a landing at those places of this kingdom which the letters and the mandate to be handed over will designate. Six hundred horsemen would be sent to the borders of the kingdom to make an incursion, and our domestic enemies await their arrival. Our excommunicated prelates have fled to England with their followers. The estates and fortunes of the nobles, barons and wealthier citizens have been marked out to be divided as spoils and plunder among the enemy. Therefore, since matters stand thus, and since the hope which our enemies cherish rests on our domestic divisions, on the power and strength of certain Papists and others of great standing among us, and on certain fortified places destined for the defence of the kingdom against foreign enemies (as we have shown more fully in our protestation), and above all on the castle of Edinburgh, the chief member of our association and the place of our meetings, it was not to be deferred. Reduced to these straits, we had to undertake something for our safety: either we must die, or we were compelled to defend ourselves, or we must submit to our enemies, whose mercy is cruel. Hence it is that we were necessarily driven to those things which you have heard were carried out at Edinburgh and elsewhere.

units.la: Ubi vero opus hoc Dei cessaturum fit, novit Dominus qui hactenus eo usque nos quasi manuduxit; & sicuti nobis statutum est non ultra procedere quam ubi praesentiam ipsius concomitantem cernimus: mus: ita quicquid nunc à nobis factum est, iure ac legitime factum esse omnium conscientiis demonstrare possumus; Etenim si defensio licita est & necessaria, quomodo potest necessaria media sine quibus defensio peragi nequit esse illicita? & annon licebit ictum tam praevenire quam repellere? Nonne magniloquorum nostrorum hostium exarmatio, & eorundem, qui regem fereniss. ad tam dura contra nos impulerunt, comprehensio tam licita erit, quam ipsa defensio? Et annon praestabit eos sic comprehendere, quam in praelio? Lex tum naturalis tum civilis docet, Quod ad defensionem sufficiat si praecedat offensa vel iustus timor offensae, & quod nec debeat quis exspectare primum ictum: melius enim iura intacta servare, quam post vulneratam causam remedium quaerere. Quando praecedunt signa et actus manifestae offensionis, et quando aliter nosmet tueri non possumus, tum inculpata ac necessaria dicitur tutela, ac in dubio insultatus quicquid facit in incontinenti praesumitur ad sui defensionem facere. Satis est ad defensionem, si quis offensam interminatus fuerit, aut certum periculum & iustus timor ofsensae praecesserit. Rationes omnes à nobis antehac prolatae pro legitima defensione & custodia arcis Edinburgenae, hic nunc valent, & iustam ac legitimam esse demonstrant ejusdem interceptionem. Necessaria haec praeventio, in Gallia, Belgio foederato, Germania, & olim hic apud nos obtinuit, cum ad religionis & libertatis necessariam defensionem in arma protruderentur, quae se deposituros obtulerunt cum primum de securitate cautum sibi foret: Sicut & nos hodie declaramus, Arma nos sumpsisse, non ut quempiam invaderemus, aut ut politicum regimen mutaremus, aut ut cuilibet damnum inferremus, aut in aliena involaremus, verum ut religionem, libertates & vitam nostram tueremur: Atque licet altera manuum exerto in defensionem gladio armetur, altera tamen etiam tunc humillima nostra postulata Regi ferenilf. offeremus; quibus quamprimum satisfactum, nobisque de securitate cautum fuerit, ac quae ad ecclesiae & regni pacem conducunt, stabilita fuerint, de manibus gladios projiciemus, & quantum in nobis est omnia faciemus, quibus perfecta pax procurari possit. Regiis interim legibus obedientiam vovemus, tutelamque personae ac authoritatis regiae; Utque sereniff.nostri regis animum ad haec consilia inclinare velit, antequam malum hoc desperatum & dissidium irreparabile fiat, ex animis Deum optimum maximum serio precamur.
units.tr: But when this work of God will cease, the Lord knows, who has so far led us, as it were, by the hand. Just as it has been settled for us not to proceed further than where we perceive his accompanying presence, so we can demonstrate to the consciences of all that whatever we have now done has been done rightly and lawfully. For if defence is lawful and necessary, how can the necessary means without which defence cannot be carried out be unlawful? And will it not be lawful to forestall a blow as well as to repel it? Will not the disarming of our boastful enemies, and the seizing of those who have driven the most serene king to such harsh measures against us, be as lawful as the defence itself? And will it not be better to seize them in this way than in battle? Natural and civil law teaches: that it suffices for defence if an offence has gone before, or a just fear of offence; and that one ought not to wait for the first blow, for it is better to keep one's rights intact than to seek a remedy after the injury is done. When signs and acts of manifest offence precede, and when we cannot otherwise protect ourselves, then the protection is called blameless and necessary; and in doubt, whatever the one attacked does at once is presumed to be done in his own defence. It is enough for defence if someone has threatened an offence, or if a certain danger and a just fear of offence have gone before. All the reasons we have previously advanced for the lawful defence and guarding of the castle of Edinburgh hold good here, and show that its seizure was just and lawful. This necessary preventive action prevailed in France, in the United Netherlands, in Germany, and once here among us, when men were thrust to arms for the necessary defence of religion and liberty, and offered to lay them down as soon as they were assured of security. Just so we today declare that we have taken up arms not to attack anyone, nor to change the political government, nor to inflict harm on anyone, nor to seize what belongs to others, but to protect our religion, our liberties and our lives. And although one hand is armed with a sword raised in defence, yet with the other we will still present our most humble requests to the most serene King. As soon as these are met and we are assured of security, and whatever conduces to the peace of the Church and the kingdom has been established, we will cast the swords from our hands and do all that is in us to procure perfect peace. Meanwhile we vow obedience to the royal laws, and protection of the person and authority of the king. And before this evil, desperate and irreparable division becomes final, we earnestly pray from our hearts to God, best and greatest, that he may be pleased to incline the mind of our most serene king to these counsels.

units.la: Revisum ex praescripto Nationalis Synodi per me , , Mr.A.Ihonstonum[?],Synodi Scribam.
units.tr: Revised according to the prescript of the National Synod by me, Mr. A. Johnston, Clerk of the Synod.

units.la: Edinburgi 22. Mart. 1639.
units.tr: Edinburgh, 22 March 1639.

units.la: Primo Calendarum Maij conspecta fuit classis Anglica in aestuario Forthae (qui Ptolomeo & antiquis geographis est Bodotria, Lothianam provinciam a Fisa dirimens) in qua erant 28 naves, & praeter classiarios, quinque aut sex mille pedites Angli, cum magno apparatu bellico & ingenti pecuniae summa ad colligendum aere militem, ubi descensum in terram faceret Marchio Hammiltonius, qui huic expeditioni praefuit; hisque copiis colligendis praefuturi fuerant nobiles quidam Scoti, & alii ductores bellici, qui regiarum partium erant, & qui eadem classe vehebantur. Stetit in anchoris classis medio freto, inter Letham & Bruntilandiam; In duabus desertis insulis, Betha & Aemona, (quae à sacello olim S. Columbo sacro & dicato, Insula Sancti Columbi vulgo audit) milites terrestres exponebantur, ut se à nausea & jactatione marina reficerent, & unde alibi sparsus rumor vanus ingentis victoriae de foederatis. Caeterum conspecta hac classe Nobiles quidam, qui libertatis vindicibus antea se non conjunxerant, magno studio & summa alacritate cum suis clientelis accurrunt, & ex utroque freti littore, maritima loca circumjacentia milite replent, ut Anglorum exscensionem prohiberent, aut cum exscendentibus justa acie dimicarent. Prætereunda certe non est illustrissima Heroina Hammiltonia Marchionissa, quæ supra sexum, virilis animi pro tuenda vindicum libertatis & religionis causa, egregia indicia edidit, ac posthabito omni materno affectu in illustrissimum filium Marchionem Hammiltonium, quem tamen unice diligebat, se & sua foederatis laborantibus benigne obtulit. Classis illa regia licet hac & illac discurreret, nunquam tamen ausa est in littus alterum milites exponere, & plus molestiarum discursitationibus quibus Scotos vexabat, attulit, quam terroris aut damni.
units.tr: On the first of May the English fleet was seen in the Firth of Forth (which to Ptolemy and the ancient geographers is the Bodotria, dividing the province of Lothian from Fife), consisting of 28 ships and, besides the sailors, five or six thousand English foot soldiers, with great military equipment and a huge sum of money for raising soldiers. The Marquis of Hamilton, who led this expedition, was to make his landing there, and certain Scottish nobles and other military commanders who were on the royal side, and who were carried in the same fleet, were to be in charge of gathering these forces. The fleet stood at anchor in mid-channel, between Leith and Burntisland. On two deserted islands, Inchkeith and Inchmickery (which, from a chapel once dedicated to St Columba, is commonly called the Isle of St Columba), the land soldiers were put ashore to recover from seasickness and the tossing of the sea; and from there a vain rumour of a great victory over the confederates was spread abroad. Moreover, on seeing this fleet, certain nobles who had not previously joined the defenders of liberty hurried up with great eagerness and the utmost readiness, with their followers, and from both shores of the firth filled the neighbouring coastal places with soldiers, to prevent the English from landing or to fight them in regular battle line as they came ashore. Certainly the most illustrious heroine, the Marchioness of Hamilton, must not be passed over. Beyond her sex, she showed remarkable signs of a manly spirit in defending the cause of the defenders of liberty and religion, and, setting aside all maternal feeling, she kindly offered herself and her possessions to the labouring confederates, and to her most illustrious son the Marquis of Hamilton, whom nevertheless she loved uniquely. That royal fleet, though it ran about here and there, never dared to put soldiers ashore on the other shore, and it caused the Scots more annoyance by its roaming about than terror or damage.

units.la: Literas statim misit Marchio Hammiltonius deputatus regius, ad Edinburgi præfectum, quibus obedientiam regi districte & severe imperat, ut portus aperiret & reliqua omnia mandata statim capesseret, inter quæ præcipuum, ut edictum regium quod antea Eboraci in Anglia 25 Aprilis promulgatum fuit, Edinburgi publicandum curaret, quo venia & gratia offertur omnibus Scotis qui ante elapsum octiduum regi se submitterent, ac ante actorum veniam precarentur, si fœderi & decretis Nationalis Synodi renunciarent, regiæque declarationi denuo renovatæ acquiescerent; secus perduelles & læsæ majestatis rei declarantur, ipsorumque bona fisco addicuntur. Utq; omnes ad eorum ruinam animarentur, non solum promittitur impunitas villicis & vasallis consueta servitia & reditus veteribus dominis denegantibus, & debitoribus fœderatorum debita distrahentibus, verumetiam si regi se adjungerent, profusa spes iisdem ostentatur beneficentiæ regiæ: Sed præstat edictum ipsum inspicere, quo omnes fere Scoti, à rege suo extra Scotiam in Anglia commorante, non citati nec auditi, perduellionis damnantur: Quod de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: The Marquis Hamilton, the king's commissioner, immediately sent a letter to the governor of Edinburgh. In it he strictly and sternly ordered him to obey the king: to open the gates and promptly carry out all the other orders. Chief among these was that he should see to it that the royal proclamation, first published at York in England on 25 April, be made public in Edinburgh. This proclamation offered pardon and favour to all Scots who, within eight days, submitted themselves to the king and asked for forgiveness for their past deeds, provided that they renounced the covenant and the decrees of the National Synod and acquiesced in the king's declaration, now newly renewed. Otherwise they would be declared traitors and guilty of high treason, and their goods would be forfeited to the treasury. To encourage everyone to their own ruin, impunity was promised to bailiffs and vassals who withheld the customary services and rents from their old lords, and to debtors of the covenanters who refused to pay their debts. Moreover, if they joined the king, a generous hope of royal bounty was held out to them. But it is better to look at the proclamation itself, by which almost all the Scots, though neither summoned nor heard, and while their king remained in England outside Scotland, were condemned for treason. It is translated here almost word for word:

units.la: PER REGEM:
units.tr: BY THE KING:

units.la: QUandoquidem benigne & indulgenter omnem hactenus operam dederimus, ut subditos nostros ab aliis in praecipitia & seditionem astute seductos, ad saniorem mentem & legitimam obedientiam nobis praestandam reduceremus, ac authoritatem nostram regiam in eo regno restabiliremus: Sed frustra, nam clementia nostra & erga eos benignitas à multis petulanter admodum excipitur: Atque licet animos ad rebellionem eo usque obfirmaverint[?], ut ausi sint armata manu arces nostras regias, coronam, omnia antiqua regni insignia, apparatum nostrum bellicum, & quicquid ad nos pertinet, intercipere, ac urbes contra nos munire: Nihilominus tamen sincere declaramus ac data fide pollicemur, arma haec quibus nunc instruimur, nunquam vertenda ut nativo nostro huic regno religionis quaelibet mutatio obtrudatur, aut ut ipsius privilegia, leges supprimantur: Etenim animo usque adeo amico in regnum hoc nostrum, ac subditos qui se nobis fideles nunc praestituri sunt, ferimur, (quibus ea amoris nostri & benignitatis indicia promittimus, quae ipsorum merita fuerit fidelitas) ut utriusque curam sedulam habituri simus, cum ad gloriam & splendorem nostrum pertinere judicemus, ut legitimam eorum libertatem & privilegia religiose propugnemus.
units.tr: Since we have hitherto done everything in our power, graciously and indulgently, to bring our subjects back to a saner mind and to the lawful obedience they owe us, having been craftily led astray by others into ruin and sedition, and to re-establish our royal authority in that kingdom: but in vain. For our clemency and kindness towards them are received very wantonly by many. And although they have hardened their minds to rebellion to such a degree that they have dared, with armed hands, to seize our royal castles, the crown, all the ancient insignia of the kingdom, our military stores and whatever else belongs to us, and to fortify towns against us, nevertheless we sincerely declare, and promise on our word, that these arms with which we are now equipped will never be turned so that any change of religion is forced upon this our native kingdom, or so that its privileges and laws are suppressed. For we are so friendly in spirit towards this our kingdom, and towards those subjects who are now about to pledge their loyalty to us (to whom we promise such tokens of our love and kindness as their fidelity deserves), that we consider it both the way to our own glory and splendour, and a matter of our care, to uphold devoutly the lawful liberty and privileges of both.

units.la: Atque in hunc finem praesentibus hisce denuo renovamus priorem nostram fidem datam de tuenda religione & libertatibus; ac subditis nostris quam persuasissimum esse jubemus, nos quæcunque antehac nostris edictis, declarationibus, aut quæ deputatus noster in postrema pseudo-synodo Nationali, nostro nomine in se receperit, candide, ingenue, remota omni fraude, præstituros. Et ut ubique appareat, detestandam seditiosorum istorum malitiâ (qui tumultuum horum primi authores fuerant) nullo solido fundamento innixam fuisse, dum subditos nostros inficerent, ac corrumperent, iisque persuadere adniterentur, propositum nobis fuisse Papismum revocare, eumque nos privatim fovere; licet superfluum sit reiteratis declarationibus testari sincerum nostrum amorem in veram reformatam Protestantium religionem, quam ingenue profitemur: Non incommodum tamen censemus populo significare, Objecta hæc esse splendide falsa, neque alium scopum propositum fuisse excogitatoribus istarum impudentissimarum calumniarum, quam ut fidelium subditorum corda nobis subducerent, ac facilius & securius rebelles & impios suos fines, Monarchici regiminis conculcationem, assequerentur: Et Deum cordium scrutatorem testamur, nos, sicut titulo Defensoris fidei reformatæ utimur, sic eandem sincere & ingenue profiteri, cui, Dei gratia, constanter adhærebimus; neque unquam permissuros, ut quælibet religionis immutatio in regnis nostris subrepat, quin potius eandem, prout Dei verbo & legibus regnorum nostrorum respectivè sancitur, firmiter propugnaturos.
units.tr: And to this end, by these present letters we renew again our former pledge, given to defend the religion and liberties. We order our subjects to be fully persuaded that we will perform, frankly, openly and without any deceit, whatever we have previously promised in our edicts and declarations, or whatever our commissioner has undertaken in our name at the last pseudo-synod, the National one. And so that it may be plain everywhere that the detestable malice of those seditious men (who were the first authors of these tumults) rested on no solid foundation, since they infected and corrupted our subjects and tried to persuade them that it was our purpose to bring back Popery and to favour it in private: although it would be superfluous to testify again and again to our sincere love for the true reformed religion of the Protestants, which we openly profess, we nevertheless think it not inappropriate to inform the people that these charges are shamefully false, and that the inventors of these most impudent calumnies had no other aim than to draw the hearts of our faithful subjects away from us, so that they might more easily and securely achieve their rebellious and impious ends, the overthrow of monarchical government. And we call God, the searcher of hearts, to witness that, just as we use the title Defender of the Reformed Faith, so we sincerely and openly profess that same faith, to which, by the grace of God, we shall constantly adhere; and that we will never permit any change of religion to creep into our kingdoms, but rather will firmly uphold that religion as it is sanctioned by the Word of God and the laws of our kingdoms respectively.

units.la: Et licet prorsus ignoremus, quibus verbis animi nostri sensum in hoc negotio clarius exprimamus; certiores tamen facti sumus, quosdam ad rebellionem pronos, non obstante nostra hac plana & diserta declaratione, summo conatu in id ferri, ut subditis nostris persuadeant, nobis nunquam propositum esse, promissum præstare; Ideo præsentibus
units.tr: And although we are wholly ignorant in what words we might express more clearly the sense of our mind in this matter, nevertheless we have been informed that certain men, prone to rebellion, despite this plain and clear declaration of ours, are striving with the utmost effort to persuade our subjects that it has never been our purpose to keep our promise.

units.la: hisce amplius (fi quid amplius dici possit) omnibus, persuademus; Intentiones omnes nostras esse vere regias, æquas, ac tantum à nobis abesse, ut quorumlibet promiffMorum fidem corrumpesemus, ut contra, eandem sancte & religiose in omnibus liberaturi fimus, eadem, qua religioni ipsi adhæremus, firmitate: Et hisce nobis persuademus abunde fatisfactum iri probis & dilectis nostris subditis, atque illos neglectis seditiosorum susurris, non passuros fe ab obedientiæ nobis debitæ tramite deduci, proditoriis eorum artibus, qui cum ipsi manifestorum flagitiorum teneantur, ingenii fui nervos omnes intendunt, ut sequacium multitudine, perduellionis pœnas effugiant. Sciant tamen pessimam esse ad innocentiam viam, multos seducere, & vel hoc argumento pœnarum severitatem nos infligturos.
units.tr: Therefore by these present letters we persuade all (if anything more can be said) that all our intentions are truly royal and just, and that we are so far from corrupting the faithfulness of any promises whatever that, on the contrary, we shall keep them holily and religiously in every respect, with the same firmness with which we adhere to the religion itself. And we are persuaded that our upright and beloved subjects will be fully satisfied by this, and that, disregarding the whisperings of the seditious, they will not allow themselves to be led off the path of the obedience due to us. Those men, who are themselves bound by manifest crimes, bend every nerve of their wit by their treacherous arts, so that they may escape the penalties of treason through the multitude of their followers. Let them know nevertheless that it is a very bad road to innocence to lead many astray, and that on this very ground we shall inflict the severity of punishments.

units.la: Pernecessarium etiam nobis hic visum est, ut omnibus tam subditis nostris, quam aliis Christiani orbis incolis innotescat, quod, licet ingens fit eorum numerus, quorum actiones in hisce tumultibus rebelles fuerint, ea tamen fit nostra erga eos clementia, ut præteritorum omnium gratiam faciamus, iis qui nunc oblatam amplectentur, modo posthac fe nobis ac æquis nostris mandatis submissuri sint. Atque eo fine, Dei gratia, propositum nobis est, Coronitia regni celebrare, iisdemque interesse, quamprimum pax ea ac tranquillitas regno restituetur, quæ honori nostro conveniat. Quare imperamus ut nobis restituantur palatia, arces, corona regia, ornamenta & insignia nostra regalia, apparatus bellicus, & quicquid denique ad nos antehac pertinebat, & nunc à quolibet subditorum interceptum & detentum est: ut urbium munitiones solo adæquentur; ut prædia, domus, arces, bona fidelibus nobis subditis erepta, dominis suis restituantur; ut omnes ab armis discedant, exercitus dimittant, & pacate singuli ad sua se conferant, ut à conventiculis posthac abstineatur, idque octiduo post decreti huius promulgationem. Quibus bona fide præstitis, & subditis civilem & debitam in omnibus secundum nativi nostri regni leges obedientiam nobis exhibentibus; Tum omnibus & singulis prædictis subditis, liberam & plenam præteritorum omnium gratiam facimus, ac in proximis comitiis ἀμνηστίαν[?] statutum sanciemus. Atque cum, pro innato, regio, tenero in nativum nostrum regnum affectu, visum nobis sit laceri regni illius vulnera tam miti oleo superinfuso obligare, ejusque errores usque adeo leviter corrigere, ut maxime rebelles in misericordiæ nostræ ulnis amplecti non dedignemur; certa spe tenemur, oblatam hanc gratiam omnes submisse, prout debent, amplexuros.
units.tr: It has also seemed most necessary to us here that it be made known both to all our subjects and to the other inhabitants of the Christian world that, although the number of those whose actions in these tumults have been rebellious is great, our clemency towards them is nevertheless such that we grant a pardon for all past offences to those who now embrace the offered favour, provided that henceforth they submit themselves to us and to our just commands. And to this end, by the grace of God, it is our purpose to hold the coronation of the kingdom and to be present at it, as soon as that peace and tranquillity shall be restored to the kingdom which befits our honour. Therefore we command that there be restored to us the palaces, castles, royal crown, our ornaments and royal insignia, the military stores, and in short whatever formerly belonged to us and is now seized and held by any of our subjects; that the fortifications of the towns be levelled with the ground; that the estates, houses, castles and goods taken from our faithful subjects be restored to their lords; that all lay down their arms, disband their armies, and each return peacefully to his own home; and that conventicles be abstained from henceforth, all this within eight days of the publication of this decree. When these things have been faithfully carried out, and our subjects show us civil and due obedience in all things according to the laws of our native kingdom, then to all and each of the aforesaid subjects we grant a free and full pardon for all past offences, and in the next parliament we will enact a statute of oblivion. And since, out of our innate, royal and tender affection for our native kingdom, it has seemed good to us to bind the wounds of that torn kingdom with such gentle oil poured over them, and to correct its errors so lightly that we do not disdain to embrace even the most rebellious in the arms of our mercy, we confidently hope that all will embrace this offered grace humbly, as they ought.

units.la: Quod si quidam usque adeo desperatæ indolis futuri sint, ut nullam medicinam admittant, & posthabita nobis, nativo regi, reverentia, in rebellione cœpta progrediantur, & gratiam hanc oblatam ante octo dies, non amplexi fuerint, (quod nullos ausuros speramus:) Tum eo casu ad violentiorem & acriorem medicinam recurrere, & hanc ipsorum pertinaciam & rebellionem justitiæ gladio propulsare cogemur. Ideoque promulgamus hos omnes posthac apertos rebelles, perduelles, læsæ majestatis reos, omnia ipsorum prædia, agros, fortunas, bona mobilia & immobilia fisco nostro addicta esse, quæ conferemus in bene de nobis merituros, nobiles & alios nobis adhæsuros, & qui æquis nostris mandatis obtemperabunt: Atque in hunc finem, vasallis & villicis rebellium horum interdicimus, ne dominis suis reditus, ac consueta ulla servitia persolvant; sed penes se reservent, alteram semissem pro se, alteram nobis tradituri: villicis horum rebellium, si dominis desertis se nobis ad tuendam nostram authoritatem adjunxerint , pollicemur benefice cum ipsis nos transfacturos de collocatione agrorum& prædiorum per annos plures , remissa etiam triente redituum qui rebellibus Dominis persolvi consueverunt , vasallis rebellium Dominorum idem promittimus,modo defertis Dominis rebellibus , se nobis adjunxerint.Quod si fidelis nobis Dominus permanserit,vasalli vero ac villici rebelles fuerint , & gratiam hanc oblatam intra præfinitum diem nō amplexi fuerint, declaramus , libere licere Domino, rebelles istos ex prædiis extrudere, & quicquid fisco nostro publicatione prædiorum accresceret,illud resignamus,ac libera donatione utendum fruendum concedimus Domino fideli,cui opem nostram impendemus,ut beneficio hoc fruatur.Interdicimus etiam,ne,qui ære ullo alieno rebellium tenetur,illud ejusve quamlibet partem rebellibus persolvant, ac subditis nostris fidelibus persuasum volumus, ex istis pecuniis singulorum in nos merita benefice repensuros.
units.tr: But if some are of so desperate a disposition that they admit no remedy, and, setting aside the reverence owed to us, their native king, go on in the rebellion they have begun, and do not embrace this grace offered them within eight days (which we hope no one will dare to do), then in that case we shall be forced to resort to a more violent and sharper remedy, and to repel their obstinacy and rebellion with the sword of justice. Therefore we proclaim that all those who are henceforth openly rebels, traitors and guilty of high treason, and all their estates, fields, fortunes, movable and immovable goods, are forfeited to our treasury, and these we will bestow on those who deserve well of us, on nobles and others who adhere to us, and who obey our just commands. And to this end we forbid the vassals and bailiffs of these rebels to pay their lords any rents or customary services, but to keep them in their own hands, to hand over one half to us and to keep the other half for themselves. To those bailiffs of these rebels who, having deserted their lords, join us in defending our authority, we promise that we will kindly confirm with them the leasing of fields and estates for several years, and also remit a third of the rents that were customarily paid to the rebel lords. We promise the same to the vassals of rebel lords, provided that they desert their rebel lords and join us. But if a loyal lord has remained faithful to us, while the vassals and bailiffs have been rebels and have not embraced this offered grace within the appointed day, we declare that the lord is free to thrust those rebels out of their estates; and whatever would accrue to our treasury from the confiscation of the estates, we relinquish that to the faithful lord, and grant him free gift and enjoyment of it, and we will lend him our aid so that he may enjoy this benefit. We also forbid anyone who is bound to pay any debt to rebels to pay to the rebels that debt or any part of it; and we wish our faithful subjects to be persuaded that, out of those sums, we will kindly repay the merits of each one towards us.

units.la: Si quod oppidum , urbs, aut civitas gratiam hanc nostram intra præfinitum diem amplexa fuerit, nobisque ad tuendam nostram authoritatem adhaeserit; ejus libertates & privilegia in patrocinium & tutelam nostram recipimus, easque urbes propugnabimus, prout justum regem decet.
units.tr: If any town, city, or borough accepts this our grace within the appointed day and adheres to us in upholding our authority, we take its liberties and privileges under our protection and defence, and we will defend such towns as a just king ought to.

units.la: Denique nobis visum est,& præsentibus hisce declaramus , rebellium proscriptionem, bonorumque omnium quæ ad eos pertinent publicationem , non futuram fraudi & damno probis nostris subditis nobis adhærentibus, & hanc nostram gratiam amplexuris, ac publicationum seu Confiscationum donationes onerandas solutione debitorum, quæ rebelles isti contraxerant, & cet.
units.tr: Finally, it has seemed good to us, and by these presents we declare, that the proscription of the rebels and the forfeiture of all their goods shall not be to the loss or damage of our loyal subjects who adhere to us and accept this our grace. The grants of such forfeitures and confiscations shall be burdened with the payment of the debts which these rebels had incurred, etc.

units.la: Datum & publicatum Eboraci.25.April.1639.
units.tr: Given and published at York, 25 April 1639.

units.la: Præfectus Edinburgenus ad literas Marchionis respondit; Integrum sibi non esse in rebus tanti momenti, meti[?],quæ ad universi regni statum pertinerent quidpiam decernere: Responsum certum exspectandum esse à supremo conventu Ordinum regni seu parlamento, quod indictione regia brevi conventurum fuit.
units.tr: The Provost of Edinburgh replied to the Marquis's letter: that it was not within his power to decide anything on matters of such weight, which concerned the state of the whole kingdom; a definite answer must be awaited from the supreme convention of the Estates of the kingdom, or Parliament, which was to meet shortly by royal summons.

units.la: Qui cum convenissent, Marchioni graviter responderunt, ac rationes enumerarunt complures, propter quas edictum illud evulgari nec debeat nec possit: nisi in leges peccare, regni dedecus propalare, semetipsos perfidos & perjuros, atque omnium atrocissimarum & impudentissimarum calumniarum, quas in se congerunt adversarii, conscios & obnoxios agnoscere vellent. Edictum hoc (dicebant) tam in materia quam forma illegitimum esse; in forma, quod extra regnum conderetur, & ejus promulgatio hic urgeretur, non confulto hujus regni senatu, quod, uti legibus, sic continuæ & receptæ praxi adversatur, prout omnes regni hujus senatores satis norunt: Et ad materiam edicti responderunt: Inauditum esse, ut proceres omnes & universum fere regni corpus hostes publici, perduelles, læsæ majestatis rei declarentur, bona omnia publicentur, sine ullo causæ prævio & legitimo examine in parlamento aut supremo criminalis justitiæ tribunali, quæ tamen fora sola competentia sunt in hujus generis & momenti negotiis. In vilissimum subditorum pœnam hanc atrocem statui non posse, nisi prius citetur, & de reatu ipsius in foro competenti contradictorio plene constiterit: Omnes præcedentes suas actiones edicto hoc declarari rebelles, quas tamen æquas & necessarias demonstraturi essent.
units.tr: When they had assembled, they answered the Marquis sternly and listed many reasons why that edict neither ought nor could be published, unless they were willing to break the laws, disclose the shame of the kingdom, and acknowledge themselves faithless and perjured, and guilty and liable to all the most atrocious and shameless calumnies that their adversaries heap upon them. This edict (they said) was unlawful both in matter and in form: in form, because it was drawn up outside the kingdom and its promulgation was being pressed here without consulting the Senate of this kingdom, which is contrary both to the laws and to the continued and accepted practice, as all the senators of this kingdom know well. And to the matter of the edict they replied: that it was unheard of that all the nobles and almost the whole body of the kingdom should be declared public enemies, traitors, and guilty of treason, and all their goods be confiscated, without any prior cause or lawful examination in Parliament or in the supreme court of criminal justice, which alone are the competent courts in affairs of this kind and weight. Such a cruel penalty could not be imposed on the lowest subjects unless they were first summoned and their guilt fully established in the competent court after a hearing of both sides. All their earlier actions were declared rebellious by this edict, which they would nevertheless show to be just and necessary.

units.la: In regis sereniss.honore impingere hoc edictum; quia illegitimum, cum tamen rex sæpius declaraverit, & vero hoc etiam edicto declaret, sibi statutum leges & regni privilegia tueri. Senatores regios, & collegii justitiæ seu Sessionis edictum hoc illegitimum sæpius pronunciasse.Quare sibi persuasum esse dicebant, regem suum serenissimum et æquissimum ejus authorem non esse, sed subdolis et improbis apertorum ecclesiæ et regni hostium artibus excogitatum esse, ut vincula omnia quibus regnum hoc regi conjungitur, penitus solvant, ac ejus animum a subditis prorsus avertant, et violentis, iniquis, ac extremis hisce contiliis omnia ad extrema præcipitent, unde reditus ullus sperari non possit. Atque licet Regi serenissimo omnem civilem legitimam ac debitam obedientiam lubentissime ac submisse, uti semper, sic nunc deferant, ne huic tamen edicto morem gerant, obstare Nationale illud suum cum Deo fœdus; cujus obliteratio quæritur; et cujus perfidiæ si se reos fecerint, certissimam et horrendam omnipotentis Dei iram in se ac posteros provocabunt. Omnia hactenus à se tentata quibus Regem serenissimum de vero rerum suarum statu certiorem facerent, sed frustra: paratos nihilominus esse omnia adhuc experiri, ac rogare se Illustrissimum Marchionem, ut ejus opera liceret sibi cum Rege ipso coram agere, quem non dubitent tandem probaturum quæcunque à se hactenus facta sint: Neque se faciliorem aut tutiorem ad pacem viam excogitare posse, quam ut serenissimus rex ipse, aut illustrissimus Marchio regis deputatus Parlamento regia indictione nunc convocato adsit; ac tum regi serenissimo et universo terrarum orbi se demonstraturos, in sese recipiunt, Adversarios suos esse regis, regni, ecclesiæ hostes; et vere reos læsæ majestatis divinæ et humanæ: se vero submissos et probos subditos.
units.tr: This edict strikes at the honour of the most serene King, because it is unlawful, although the king has often declared, and indeed declares again in this very edict, that he is bound to uphold the laws and the privileges of the kingdom. The royal senators and the College of Justice, or Court of Session, had often pronounced this edict unlawful. Wherefore, they said, they were persuaded that their most serene and most just king was not its author, but that it had been devised by the crafty and wicked arts of the open enemies of the Church and kingdom, so that all the bonds by which this kingdom is joined to the king might be wholly dissolved, his mind turned entirely away from his subjects, and everything hurled to extremes by these violent, unjust, and extreme counsels, from which no return could be hoped for. And although they render to the most serene King, as always, all civil, lawful, and due obedience, most willingly and humbly, yet they could not comply with this edict, because their national covenant with God stood in the way; its obliteration was being sought, and if they were made guilty of its breach, they would bring upon themselves and their posterity the most certain and dreadful wrath of Almighty God. They had hitherto attempted everything by which they might inform the most serene King of the true state of his affairs, but in vain; nevertheless they were ready to try everything still, and they asked the Most Illustrious Marquis that, through his good offices, they might be allowed to treat with the King himself face to face, whom they did not doubt would at last be persuaded of all that they had hitherto done. Nor could they devise an easier or safer way to peace than that the most serene King himself, or the Most Illustrious Marquis as the king's deputy, should be present at the Parliament now summoned by royal writ; and then they undertook to show to the most serene King and to the whole world that their adversaries were enemies of the king, the kingdom, and the Church, and truly guilty of violating the divine and human majesty, while they themselves were submissive and honest subjects.

units.la: Rex interim Parlamentum differri jubet quo die primum conveniret. Multi qui in Scotos iniquiori animo fuerunt, ubique spargebant, fœderatos et libertatis vindices Rege etiam prohibente parlamentum continuaturos; ut scilicet eorum actiones et causam vulgi odio apud exteros exponerent; qui imprudenter fatis aliorum regnorum utiliffima instituta fui regni legibus aut praxi admetienda judicant. Sed & hanc calumniam dies discussit: ac licet juris regii non esse (dicebant) parlamenta ampliare fine consensu ordinum regni; regiis tamen mandatis fe morem nunc gesturos: Et ne quid detrimeti difficillimis istis temporibus caperet Respub: circumstrepente undique & assultante armorum impetu; classe regiâ littoribus imminente, ac prorege Hiberniæ occidentalibus provinciis; In borealibus vero provinciis Bonæ[?] vicecomite Huntlaei filio tumultus excitante, ægre[?] etiam cum exercitu (fama, ut solet, omnia augente) & frequenti nobilitate Anglica in Scotiam movente: Quia sibi & universo regno pro religione & legibus, aris & focis diminicandum esse prospiciebant, de colligendo justo exercitu deliberarunt. Et ut omnem livoris & odii materiam tollerent, inter tot proceres paris dignitatis & ordinis, communi consensu, & omnium ordinum folenni approbatione & fubfcriptione fupremam in omnes exercitus præfecturam Generali Leslio experto militiæ duci deferunt, quod amplissimum munus ille nulla ambitione aut imperandi cupiditate, sed sola concivium suorum charitate & misericordia suscepit: & cum peregrinis exercitibus fæpius cum laude præfuisset, vitamque suam pro caufa Euangelica in Germania intrepide obtulisset, quod adversorum vulnerum cicatrices clamant; non fatis æquum aut pium judicabat, patriæ suæ & parenti laboranti, officium suum & operam tempore tam difficili obftinatius denegare, præsertim cum de causæ æquitate, & belli defenfivi necessitate abundeilli persuasum effet, ac melior nobilitatis pars reliquique ordines regni suprema omnia promitterent, & vitam ac omnes fortunas suas in hac causa propugnanda sacrosancte devoverent: Debitam illi
units.tr: Meanwhile the King ordered Parliament to be postponed from the day on which it was first to meet. Many who were ill-disposed towards the Scots spread the word everywhere that the covenanters and defenders of liberty would continue the Parliament even though the King forbade it, so that they might expose their actions and cause to the hatred of the common people abroad, people who rashly judge that the most useful institutions of other kingdoms should be measured against the laws or practice of their own kingdom. But the day also dispelled this slander: although (they said) it was not lawful by royal right to extend a Parliament without the consent of the Estates of the kingdom, nevertheless they would now comply with the royal commands. And so that nothing might harm the commonwealth in such most difficult times, with arms clashing on every side and an armed assault threatening; a royal fleet hanging over the shores, the Lord Deputy of Ireland stirring up the western provinces, and in the northern provinces the Viscount of Aboyne, son of Huntly, rousing a disturbance, and an English army also moving into Scotland (rumour, as usual, magnifying everything), and a considerable English nobility on the march; because they foresaw that they must defend themselves and the whole kingdom for religion and laws, altars and hearths, they deliberated on raising a just army. And so that they might remove every matter of envy and hatred, they unanimously, among so many nobles of equal dignity and rank, with the solemn approval and signature of all the Estates, committed the supreme command over all the armies to General Leslie, an experienced soldier. He undertook this most honourable office not from any ambition or lust for command, but from the sole charity and compassion he felt for his fellow citizens; and having often commanded foreign armies with praise, and having boldly offered his life for the Evangelical cause in Germany, as the scars of his enemies' wounds cry out, he judged it neither fair nor pious to deny stubbornly, in such a difficult time, his duty and labour to his fatherland and to a parent in distress, especially since he was thoroughly persuaded of the justice of the cause and of the necessity of a defensive war, and since the better part of the nobility and the other Estates of the kingdom promised all things and solemnly devoted their lives and all their fortunes to defending this cause. Due...

units.la: ut Generalissimo exercituum ductori obedientiam in omnibus iurarunt ordines regni, praeeuntibus proceribus; Ab eo etiam iuramentum ordinum regni nomine exigitur, ut imperium legitime administraret, & se legum praescripto submitteret.
units.tr: The Estates of the kingdom, with the nobles going first, all swore obedience in all things to him as Commander-General of the armies. An oath was also demanded of him in the name of the Estates of the kingdom, that he would administer the command lawfully and submit himself to the prescription of the laws.

units.la: Suscepta praefectura, leges castrenses promulgat, quae typis ubique proflabant, delectum militum ex provinciis vicinioribus imperat, Comitem Argathelium cum suis copiis prope Sterlinum subsistere iussit, ut praesto esset tam Borealibus quam Occidentalibus provinciis, si quid moveret Hibernia. Dumfrisium urbem Scoticam in dimitibus Occidentalibus praesidiario milite instruit, & copiis omnibus in eo tractu praefecit Ionstonum, numerosae familiae principem, & Baronem parlamentarium, cum mandatis ut obviam iret Anglis & Hibernis, qui Carleoli haerentes Scotiae imminebant, & ut Pontificiorum & aliorum ex clientela Maxwellorum conjunctionem prohiberet: Caffilliae & Eglintoniae Comitibus Occidentalium provinciarum praesecturam demandat: Littora aestuarii Forthensis ita instruit ut in terram descendere Hamniltonius Marchio in animum non induxerit; Et cum vicecomes Boinae cum Bamphio ad famam appulsae classis regiae, & properantis terrestri itinere regii exercitus, magnas turbas cierent, & a facinorosissimis latronibus, (qui pacatis etiam temporibus Borealem illam Scotiae plagam latrociniis infestam habuerunt) suppetias lubentes acciperent, ac omnibus foederatis extremam vastitatem interminitarentur, & nonnullos ex Forbesiis & Fraserus (familiarum sunt haec nomina in iis locis admodum potentium, & partium foederatarum) incautos adorti fugassent, lata per eorum agros sufa populatione; Abredoniam haud invitam in suam potestatem & societatem denuo pertraxissent, atque ex clientibus Huntilæi, civibus Abredoniensibus, quibus cum fortuna fidem mutare animus fuerat, ac latronibus, numerum suum ad non contemnendum exercitum auxiliari: Comites Montis Rosarum, (qui primam contra Marchionem Huntilęum[?] expeditionem tam fœliciter perfecerat,) & Marescallum, cum satis magnis copiis ad motus illos sedandos, & tumultuantes in ordinem redigendos mittit: Atque hi adjunctis Comitum Arolii, Fermelodum, Glamesii vasallis selectioribus, & cohorte unica aut altera civium Taodunensium; (qui antehac fidelem & strenuam operam semper exhibuerant) in hostem recta movent, qui statim dilabitur, & ad latebras circumspicere coactus fuit; Abredonia secunda vice à fœderatis intercipitur; castella Nobilium qui regiarum partium in illis locis fuerunt, obsidentur, quibusdam expugnatis: verum cum accepissent classem regiam prope Abredoniam in anchoris stare, & plurimi suorum dilapsi essent, (utpote quod expeditionem putarent prope peractam) veriti ne à reditu in Australes provincias prohiberentur; consultius judicarunt retrocedere; ut copiis auctis & redintegratis turbas istas opportunius prorsus exstinguerent: ita ut expeditione illa secunda hostium suorum furorem magis suppresserint, postea vehementius erupturum, quam oppresserint.
units.tr: Having assumed the command, he promulgated military laws, which were immediately printed and circulated everywhere, and ordered levies of soldiers from the nearer provinces. He directed the Earl of Argyll to remain with his forces near Stirling, so that he would be at hand for the northern as well as the western provinces if Ireland stirred. He garrisoned the Scottish town of Dumfries on the western borders with a garrison soldiery, and set over all the forces in that district Johnstone, prince of a numerous family and a parliamentary baron, with orders to confront the English and Irish who, lodged at Carlisle, threatened Scotland, and to prevent the union of the Papists and others of the Maxwells' following. He entrusted the command of the western provinces to the Earls of Cassillis and Eglinton. He so fortified the shores of the Firth of Forth that the Marquis of Hamilton did not venture to land. And when the Viscount of Aboyne, together with Banff, stirred up great disturbances at the news of the royal fleet's approach and of the royal army hastening by land, and gladly received help from the most wicked brigands (who had kept that northern part of Scotland infested with robberies even in peacetime), and threatened the utmost devastation to all the covenanters, and attacked some of the Forbeses and Frasers, who were powerful in those parts and of the covenanting party, unawares, and put them to flight, the country being ravaged through their fields; they had also drawn Aberdeen, not unwillingly, back into his power and alliance, and had enlisted as auxiliaries, from Huntly's clients, the citizens of Aberdeen, whose loyalty had been changed by fortune, and robbers, a force not to be despised in number: the Earl of Montrose (who had so successfully carried out the first expedition against the Marquis of Huntly) and the Marischal, with fairly large forces, he sent to quell those movements and bring the rioters back to order. These, joined by the choicest vassals of the Earls of Airlie, Fermelodum, and Glamis, and by one or two companies of the citizens of Dundee (who had always shown faithful and vigorous service), moved straight against the enemy, who at once slipped away and was forced to look about for hiding-places. Aberdeen was taken by the covenanters for the second time; the castles of the nobles who were on the royal side in those parts were besieged, some of them being stormed. But when they learned that the royal fleet lay at anchor near Aberdeen, and many of their men had deserted (thinking the expedition almost finished), and fearing that they would be prevented from returning to the southern provinces, they judged it more prudent to fall back, so that, with their forces increased and renewed, they might more conveniently extinguish these disturbances altogether. Thus, by that second expedition, they suppressed the fury of their enemies more than they crushed it, and it would later break out more violently.

units.la: Interea, uti contra armatam vim se pararunt Scoti fœderati, sic nec tum destiterunt, remonstrantiis ac supplicationibus cum rege agere; sed haud facile reperiebantur qui regi sereniss. eas traderent, nam res maximi discriminis tum erat in Scotorum gratiam in aula vel hiscere, & qui à senatu regio in Scotiam eo nomine ad aulam missi fuerant ; aut detinebantur , aut nullo operæ pretio peracto redierunt. Forte advenerat tum in Scotiam Moslejus Anglus, Theologiæ Doctor, ut oculis ipse suis spectaret, an ad eam insaniam proruissent Fœderati libertatis vindices, qua correptos fuisse calumniabantur hostes; & habitu ecclesiastico Anglis consueto vicinas Scotiæ urbes perlustravit : Cumque aliter[?] se omnia habere deprehendisset, utriusque regni miseriam deflevisse fertur ; quod mendacibus paucorum. calumniis utraque sibi invicem tam amica gens in manifestam perniciem protruderetur. Rogat nobiles Scotos, cum quibus olim quædam ei familiaritas fuit, ut libellis supplicibus apud regem adhuc pergerent; eosq; in semet recepit regi se traditurum, ac posthabito omni periculo libere & ingenue eundem de vero rerum & actionum in Scotia statu certiorem facturum, & additurum quæ regi serenissimo leniendo accommoda forent.
units.tr: Meanwhile, just as the confederate Scots prepared themselves against armed force, so at that time they did not cease to deal with the king through remonstrances and supplications. But men could not easily be found who would deliver them to the most serene king, for the matter was then of the greatest danger, so that to open one's mouth at court in the Scots' favour was perilous. Those whom the royal council had sent to the court on that business from Scotland were either detained or returned having accomplished nothing worthwhile. As it happened, John Moseley, an English Doctor of Theology, had then arrived in Scotland, to see with his own eyes whether the defenders of liberty, the Confederates, had run to that madness with which their enemies accused them. Wearing the clerical dress customary among the English, he toured the neighbouring towns of Scotland. When he found everything otherwise than he had been told, he is reported to have lamented the misery of both kingdoms, that two nations so friendly to each other should be thrust into manifest ruin by the lies and calumnies of a few. He asked the Scottish nobles, with whom he had once had some acquaintance, to continue their supplicating petitions to the king. He undertook to present them to the king himself and, disregarding all danger, to inform the king freely and frankly about the true state of affairs and actions in Scotland, and to add whatever would be suitable for soothing the most serene king.

units.la: Literas itaque supplices ad regem illi tradunt, quibus sereniss. regis immeritam iram anxie & sollicite deprecabantur, utpote, cum nullius in regem criminis se sibi conscios esse dicerent; rogant ut æquo judicio liceret sibi experiri contra hostes suos, qui innocentissimas suas actiones detorquentes belli cruenti flammam excitant. In omnibus ex legum civilium & ecclesiasticarum præscripto, obedientiam se nunquam denegaturos, nec adhuc denegasse. Alias etiam literas misere Nobiles Scoti, ad Comitem Effexiæ, Berwici tum præfectum, ut pro sincero in patriam & religionem amore, preces suas apud serenissimum regem interponeret, ne controversiæ hujus definitionem armata violentia aggrederetur. Per eundem Theologum ad Pembrochium & Hollandium Comites Anglos perscribunt in hunc sensum : Quandoquidem quæcunque à se hactenus præstita essent motibus hisce sedandis & flammæ restinguendæ, quam religionis & publicæ utriusque regni pacis hostes excitarunt, non successerint; neque spes ulla reliqua, sit conficiendæ pacis per nobiles Scotos interpretes, quorum opera hactenus frustra usi suissent, recurrere se tandem ad ipsorum Dominationes; quos pio & nobili studio ferri ad continuationem publicæ pacis retulit D. Iohannes Moslejus[?], cujus zelus ad sancti hujus operis promotionem probandus est, licet nulla publica authoritate ad illud procurandum instructus venerit. Præsentibus itaque literis non solum duobus illis nobilibus, verumetiam aliis omnibus regni Angliæ senatoribus religionem reformatam & pacem communem amantibus, quibus hasce literas communicare illis visum fuerit, declarant, nunquam sibi fastidio fuisse Monarchicum regimen, nunquam animos subivisse ut legitimam & debitam sereniss.[?] suo regi denegarent, aut Angliam invaderent. Calumnias has efse ex industria & consulto excogitatas ab improbis suis adversariis, ne justa sua postulata à sereniss. rege obtinerent. Quorum summa est, ut sibi suis legibus vivere, & religionis incorrupta puritate frui liceat. Hæc esse quæ postulent, in quæ juraverint, & quibus obtinendis, fortunas, vitam & quicquid mortalibus carum esse solet, lubentissime devoverint. Neque hæc posse justam ullam causam Nationali controversiæ præbere, quandoquidem tam leges civiles quam decreta ecclesiæ pro nationū varietate varia sint, & sicuti(inquiunt) summo studio adnitimur leges nostras ac institutas religiose tueri, sic iniquum semper judicavimus aliis eo nomine vim quamlibet facere. Generalem illam æquitatis regulam serio meditandam esse, Quod tibi non vis fieri, id alteri ne feceris. Quare rogant ut eorum opera Rex tandem flectatur, neque se æquis subditorum postulatis tam difficilem præbeat, præsertim cum eorum concefsione regis gloria augebitur, controversiis hisce, omnium cum gaudio, finis imponetur, & grata recoletur à posteris eorum memoria, qui ad sanctum hoc opus promovendum operam suam gnaviter impendent.
units.tr: Accordingly they handed him letters of supplication to the king, in which they anxiously and urgently begged the most serene king not to vent undeserved wrath upon them, since they said they were conscious of no crime against the king. They asked that they might be allowed to contest matters by a fair judgment against their enemies, who, twisting their most innocent actions, were kindling the flames of bloody war. They declared that in all things, in accordance with the prescriptions of civil and ecclesiastical laws, they would never refuse obedience, nor had they refused it hitherto. The Scottish nobles also sent other letters to the Earl of Essex, then governor of Berwick, asking him that, out of sincere love for country and religion, he would interpose their prayers with the most serene king, so that the settlement of this controversy would not be attempted by armed violence. Through the same theologian they wrote to the English earls Pembroke and Holland to this effect: since whatever they had hitherto done to calm these disturbances and to quench the flame which the enemies of religion and of public peace in both kingdoms had kindled had not succeeded, and since no hope remained of arranging peace through the Scottish nobles as mediators, whose efforts had hitherto been used in vain, they had at last turned to their lordships. They reported that Dr John Moseley had been moved to this by a pious and noble zeal, and that his zeal for promoting this holy work deserves commendation, although he had come without being instructed by any public authority to bring it about. Therefore by the present letters they declare, not only to those two nobles but also to all the other senators of the kingdom of England who love the reformed religion and common peace, to whom it seems good to communicate these letters, that monarchical government had never been distasteful to them, that they had never entertained the thought of denying their lawful and due obedience to their most serene king, nor of invading England. These calumnies, they say, have been deliberately and craftily devised by their wicked adversaries, so that they might not obtain their just demands from the most serene king. The sum of those demands is that they be allowed to live under their own laws and enjoy the uncorrupted purity of religion. These are the things they demand, the things they have sworn to, and for obtaining which they have most willingly devoted their fortunes, lives, and whatever mortals usually hold dear. Nor can these things give any just cause for a national controversy, since civil laws as well as the decrees of the Church vary according to the diversity of nations; and, as they say, just as they strive with the utmost zeal to uphold their own laws and institutions religiously, so they have always judged it unjust to do violence to others on that account. That general rule of equity is to be seriously pondered: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Therefore they ask that by their efforts the king may at last be moved, and not show himself so hard toward the fair demands of his subjects, especially since by granting them the king's glory will be increased, an end will be put to these controversies to everyone's joy, and the memory of those will be held in grace by posterity who zealously devote their effort to furthering this holy work.

units.la: Cum vero indies augescere rumor, regium exercitum relicto Novo-Castro, Berwicum ad limitem Scotiæ Orientalem contendere, Generalis Leslius versus eundem limitem iter suscepit; ac 21.
