Maij cum parte copiarum Edinburgo egreditur, reliquis subsequi jussis; primum Hadinæ, dein Dumbari considit: ac nunciis in omnes vicinas provincias celeriter missis, ut qui Religionem & Patriam salvam vellent, quam possent celeriter in viam, cum necessario aliquot dierum commeatu se darent: Statim advolant frequentes, instructi commeatu & apparatu bellico supra expectationem, & ad extremam dimicationem pro aris & focis alacres: Quare Dumbato relicto, Dunglassium Angliam versus castra movet, ut regio exercitui qui non procul à limite hærebat, & in quo summa rei versabatur, in ipsis regnorum confiniis occurreret. Ubi cum consedisset, accedit à Comite Hollandiæ, equitatus regii supremo præfecto Caduceator, cum literis ad nobiles Scotos, & aliis ad Comitem Argathelium solum datis, quibus eos seriò invitabat ad civilem obedientiam regi præstandam ex præscripto illius edicti 14. Maij ad Novum-Castrum in Anglia conditi, ubi tunc rex cum exercitu commorabatur: quod simul cum literis detulerat tubicen: Ejus hæc summa fuit. Cum rex ipse venturus esset Berwicum agmine pacato ad sedandas Scotiæ turbas, & ut æquis subditorum postulatis publice in parlamento satisfaceret, & cum maximus rumor in Anglia esset, Scotos hostilem irruptionem in Angliam meditari: ut de bona sua voluntate certiores fierent utriusque regni subditi, se per præsentes literas imperare, ne Scotorum armatæ cohortes intra decem mille passus Berwico appropinquent: si secus fecerint, se exercitus sui præfectis districte mandaturum, ut omnes illos pro rebellibus habeant, & tanquam Angliæ invasores impune perdant.
units.tr: But since the rumour grew daily that the royal army, leaving Newcastle, was making for Berwick, the eastern frontier of Scotland, General Leslie set out towards the same frontier. On 21 May he left Edinburgh with part of the forces, ordering the rest to follow; he first settled at Haddington, then at Dunbar. Having quickly sent messengers to all the neighbouring provinces, bidding those who wished to keep religion and country safe to take to the road as quickly as they could, and to provide themselves with supplies for some days, crowds at once flocked in, equipped with provisions and military gear beyond expectation, and eager for the final struggle for altars and hearths. Therefore, leaving Dunbar, he moved the camp towards England, so as to meet the royal army, which was not far from the border and on which the whole matter turned, on the very borders of the kingdoms. When he had encamped there, a herald came from the Earl of Holland, supreme commander of the royal cavalry, bearing letters to the Scottish nobles, and others addressed to the Earl of Argyll alone. By these he earnestly invited them to render civil obedience to the king according to the prescription of that edict of 14 May issued at Newcastle in England, where the king was then staying with the army. The herald brought this along with the letters. The substance was this: since the king himself was about to come to Berwick with a peaceful force to calm the disturbances of Scotland, and to satisfy publicly in parliament the fair demands of his subjects, and since there was a great rumour in England that the Scots were planning a hostile invasion of England, so that the subjects of both kingdoms might be informed of his good will, he commands by these present letters that the armed cohorts of the Scots not approach within ten thousand paces of Berwick. If they do otherwise, he will strictly order the prefects of his army to hold all of them as rebels and to destroy them with impunity as invaders of England.

units.la: Apud Scotos qui fraudulenter hæc peti putabant, privatim mussitabant: Si huic mandato mos geratur, oportere copias quasdam retrocedere, & hanc retrocessionem hostes pro ingenio & artibus consuetis, interpretaturos esse imbecillitatis & timoris publici confessionem; qua ipsorum audacia ad majora petenda augebitur: velut enim ignis levi aquæ aspersione magis accenditur, ita quicquid initio concesseris, ad ulterius petendum sit gradus, & concessione ea non restingui, sed inflammari hostes dicebant. Verendum etiam ne captata occasione hostes in interiora regni penetrent, urbesque limitaneas præsidiario milite vacuas intercipiant, aut in solo Scotico castra figant, aut cohortes à castris huc & illuc dispersas deleant.
units.tr: Among the Scots, who thought this demand was made with deceit, they murmured privately: if this command were obeyed, it would be necessary to withdraw some forces, and the enemies, according to their wont and tricks, would interpret this retreat as a confession of weakness and public fear; by this their boldness would be increased to seek greater things. For just as fire is kindled more by a light sprinkling of water, so whatever one concedes at the beginning becomes a step toward further demands, and by such a concession the enemies would not be quenched but inflamed, they said. They also feared that, seizing the occasion, the enemies might penetrate into the interior of the kingdom and capture the border towns emptied of garrison soldiers, or pitch camp on Scottish soil, or destroy the cohorts scattered hither and thither from the camps.

units.la: Sed cum res publice ageretur in senatu bellico, statutum fuit regis mandato morem gerere, præsertim, cum superioris edicti asperitas, quo denunciabatur, regem statuisse in Scotos fœderatos animadvertere ut rebelles, læsæ majestatis divinæ & humanæ reos, hic multum leniretur; & mitior aura de longinquo spirare multorum conjectura esset, qua fœdam hanc tempestatem sedatum iri sperabant.
units.tr: But when the matter was discussed in the war council, it was resolved to obey the king's command, especially since the harshness of the earlier edict, by which it had been announced that the king had resolved to punish the Confederate Scots as rebels, guilty of violating divine and human majesty, was here greatly softened. Many conjectured from afar that a milder breeze was blowing, by which they hoped this foul storm would be calmed.

units.la: Itaque ad Hollandiæ comitem literas officii & humanitatis plenas remittunt; paratos se, dicunt, sociorum omnium nomine submissam obedientiam legibus concessam serenis. regi deferre: ac licet nullius sibi sceleris conscii essent, male tamen a regia classe multatos, quæ merces omnes interciperet ac mercimonia tolleret. Quicquid controversi juris inter ipsos & regem esset, non defugere quin ejusdem honorarii arbitri essent nobiles Angli; nec alios pacis interpretes & sequestres quam ipsum Comitem & Nobilissimos suos sodales requirere. In præsentiarum vero experimentum hoc propensæ suæ voluntatis & submissæ erga regem serenissimum observantiæ se daturos, & ex edicti præscripto exercitum intra præscriptos limites retenturos, quanquam merito suspicari possent quo animo hæc sibi imperarentur.
units.tr: Accordingly they sent back to the Earl of Holland letters full of courtesy and humanity. They say they are ready, in the name of all their associates, to offer the most serene king the submissive obedience granted by law; and although they were conscious of no crime, they had nonetheless been unjustly punished by the royal fleet, which intercepted all their goods and cut off their merchandise. Whatever disputed right there was between them and the king, they did not refuse that the English nobles should be arbiters of it in that honourable capacity; and they sought no other peace-makers and mediators than the Earl himself and his most noble companions. For the present, however, they will give this proof of their well-disposed will and submissive respect toward the most serene king, and according to the prescription of the edict they will keep their army within the prescribed limits, although they could reasonably suspect with what intention these things were enjoined upon them.

units.la: Remisso cum hoc responso caduceatore, Iohannem Humium illustrem equitem auratum ad eundem Comitem ablegant, cum mandatis, ut Comitem Hollandiæ & sodales verum controversiæ statum edoceret, videl. An, liceat Scotis suis legibus vivere, et an in negotiis ecclesiasticis, Nationalium Synodorum decretis, in politicis vero supremo ordinum conventui, & parlamenti legibus stare debeant subditi Scotiæ? Horum judiciis se & sua omnia permittere paratos semper fuisse, & fore, ibidemque omnium anteactorum rationem reddituros. Dein ut fidem obligaret quæ à bonis requiri posset, quotquot Scotorum fœdus obsignassent, de minuenda authoritate regia nunquam cogitasse, multo minus de invadenda Anglia, (uti improbe calumniantur adversarii, ut utramque nationem inter se committerent, ac publica ruina & communi incendio privatis suis odiis litarent.) Verum ad justam & necessariam defensionem se armasse ac comparasse, contra injustam & armatam vim, quibuscunque demum, prajudiciis velatam, quam nullo modo subterfugere aut possunt aut debent. Doceret etiam invitos ad arma protrusos esse Scotos, nec se commodiorem viam ad farciendam concordiam & amolienda impendentia mala prospicere, quam si utrinque delecti homines perspectæ fidei & probitatis, quibus cordi esset religio reformata & publica pax, ac regni utriusque salus, in unum coeant, neque dubitandum, quin, Dei gratia, de tota controversia æquissimis conditionibus haud difficulter transfigi possit.
units.tr: Sending the herald back with this answer, they dispatched Sir John Hume, an illustrious knight, to the same Earl, with instructions to inform the Earl of Holland and his companions of the true state of the dispute, namely: whether the Scots may live under their own laws, and whether the subjects of Scotland ought to abide by the decrees of the National Synods in ecclesiastical matters and, in political matters, by the decisions of the supreme convention of the estates and the laws of Parliament. They said they had always been, and would always be, ready to submit themselves and all they had to these men's judgment, and to give an account there of all their past actions. Then, to give a pledge of the kind that good men might require, they said that all who had sealed the Scottish covenant had never thought of diminishing royal authority, much less of invading England, as the adversaries falsely slander them for the purpose of setting the two nations against each other and sacrificing public ruin and a common conflagration to their private hatreds. Rather, they had armed and prepared themselves for a just and necessary defence against an unjust armed force, however veiled under whatever pretexts, which they could in no way avoid or ought to avoid. He should also tell them that the Scots had been driven to arms against their will, and that he saw no more convenient way of restoring concord and averting the threatening evils than for chosen men from each side, of proven good faith and integrity, who held the reformed religion, public peace and the welfare of both kingdoms dear, to meet together. There was no doubt that, by the grace of God, the whole controversy could easily be settled on the most equitable terms.

units.la: Suscepit hoc in se munus Comes, & seriam in illo obeundo operam est pollicitus.
units.tr: The Earl undertook this task and promised to labour earnestly in carrying it out.

units.la: Verum dum hæc ageretur, intervenit occasio quæ nisi successu exspectato destituta fuisset, spem omnem reconciliationis & pacis penitus abrupisset: Deo tamen aliter providente, cui solenne ex tenebris lucem producere, è frustratione illius expeditionis pacificationem cum Anglis maturavit. Etenim in diversa regione, prope Kalsonem, Iedburgum, ab illis locis quibus Generalis Leslius cum primario Scotorum exercitu castra metabatur, dispersa erant quatuor aut quinque millia peditum Scotorum ad commodiorem frumentationem, & ut iis locis præsidio essent in quibus diversabantur: & vero, cum regis superiori edicto, ne infra decem mille passus ad limites regni Angliæ appropinquarent, assensissent Scoti, tum ut sereniss. regi obedientiæ suæ experimentum ostenderent, tum ut testatum facerent paratos se ad omnes concordiæ rationes promovendas, & irritamenta animorum omnia tollerent, quæ facile evitari non potuissent, si in mutuum conspectum venissent duo exercitus; subverebatur tamen Generalis Leslius, ne forte Angli arrepta opportunitate de intercipiendis & delendis dispersis illis cohortibus cogitarent, quod facile illis erat cum equitatu prævalerent, si imparatis supervenissent in regione plana, & in oppidis, ut apud Scotos, ex veteri majorum instituto, vallo, aggeribus, aut fossa non munitis, quare ut huic malo præcaveret, cum nec turmas illas revocare posset, nisi timoris confessionem simul daret, & totam circumjacentem regionem Anglis in prædam exponeret, (quod consultum neutriquam fuisset, cum civilia bella primis momentis maxime constent, & ex primis successibus totius belli spem multi præsagiant) neque ipse castra propius ad limitem promovere posset ob fidem prius interpositam: Quod unum restabat, mandat cohortium istarum præfectis, Comiti Landoniæ, Flaminio, Areskino, Munroo, tribunis militum, ut sine ulla mora omnes in unum convenirent; Kalsonem oppidum in ripa Tuedæ fluminis situm, quantum in se esset, contra subitariam impressionem equitatus regii munirent, ac intensas interim vigilias agerent; nam in vicinia non ultra quatuor mille passus, totus circumjacebat equitatus regius: quod si cum præcipuo exercitus robore, adhibitis majoribus tormentis bellicis, in eos moveret rex, sibimet ipsis tempori consulerent, & per impedita ac equiti impervia loca ad se festinarent. Cæterum sicuti metuebat Leslius, evenit. Nam cum è transfugæ relatione regi innotuisset, unicam tantum Areskini tribuni legionem Kalsoni subsistere, ibique in maxima securitate agere, aliasque cohortes in locis a se invicem longe distantibus dispersas esse, omnes vero facile opprimi posse; negotium datur Comiti Hollandiæ, qui 4. Iunii, assumptis equitum turmis 13. & tribus peditum millibus, ac nonnullis campestribus machinis, rectà Kalsonem iter intendit: Sed commodum superiori nocte Comitis Lothianæ, Flaminii, Munroi copiæ ex Generalis Leslii mandato Kalsonem advenerant, qui nuncio per exploratores accepto de hostili Comitis Hollandiæ contra se adventu, aciem locis opportunis instruunt, & pugnandi copiam faciunt, nullamque Anglis Kalsonem viam patere, nisi per sua viscera, sic ostendunt. Inopinato hoc visu ictus Hollandiæ Comes, primo substitit, dein ordinem & animos-mos mos[?] Scotorum arma expedientium, ex colle edito speculatus, discessum fugæ similem majori quam venisset gradu accelerat; Scoti vero milites gregarii qui ex confuso reditu trepidationem adversi agminis ex propinquo aspiciebant, Anglos hostiliter urgere vehementer cupiebant, & ægre certe à tribunis & præsectis suis contineri in suis stationibus potuerunt, qui cum ad propulsandam non inferendam injuriam arma suos induisse meminissent, extra limites innocuæ tutelæ in hoc primo belli tentamento progrediendum non censuerunt, & confessionem hanc timoris ipsa victoria haud inferiorem judicarunt: præsertim cum ingenue postea agnoverint Angli, penes Scotos fuisse, si hostili in ipsos animo fuissent, indecorum satis reditum efficere potuisse.
units.tr: But while these things were going on, an opportunity arose which, had it not failed to produce the outcome hoped for, would have utterly cut off all hope of reconciliation and peace. God, however, providing otherwise, since it is his custom to bring light out of darkness, used the failure of that expedition to bring about a pacification with the English sooner. For in a different region, near Kelso and Jedburgh, away from the places where General Leslie had pitched camp with the main Scottish army, four or five thousand Scottish foot soldiers had been dispersed, both for more convenient foraging and to garrison the places where they were quartered. The Scots had agreed to the king's recent edict that they not approach within ten thousand paces of the border of England. They did this both to show the most serene king a proof of their obedience and to make clear that they were ready to advance every means of agreement and to remove all causes of irritation, which could easily be avoided if the two armies did not come into sight of each other. Nevertheless, General Leslie feared lest perhaps the English, seizing the opportunity, might plan to intercept and destroy those scattered companies. This would be easy for them, since they excelled in cavalry, if they fell upon them unprepared in open country and in towns not fortified, as the Scots' towns were not, by the ancient custom of their ancestors, with rampart, earthworks or ditch. So, to guard against this danger, since he could not recall those troops without at the same time confessing fear and exposing the whole surrounding region as plunder to the English (which would not have been wise, since civil wars depend most on their first moments, and many foretell the hope of the whole war from the first successes), and since he could not himself move the camp nearer the border because of the faith previously pledged, the only course left was this. He ordered the commanders of those companies, the Earl of Lauderdale, Flemyng, Erskine and Munro, tribunes of the soldiers, to gather together in one place without any delay, and to fortify Kelso, a town on the bank of the river Tweed, as far as in them lay, against a sudden attack by the royal cavalry, and meanwhile to keep close watch. For in the neighbourhood, not more than four thousand paces away, the whole royal cavalry lay around. If the king should move against them with the main strength of the army and heavy siege artillery, they should look to their own safety and hasten to him by difficult routes impassable to cavalry. But, as Leslie feared, it turned out so. For when the king learned from the report of a deserter that only one legion of Erskine's tribunate remained at Kelso, living there in great security, and that the other companies were scattered in places far apart from one another, and that all of them could easily be overwhelmed, the task was given to the Earl of Holland. On 4 June he set out straight for Kelso, taking with him thirteen troops of horse, three thousand foot and some field engines. But the forces of the Earls of Lothian, Flemyng and Munro had arrived at Kelso the previous night by General Leslie's order. Having received word through scouts of the hostile approach of the Earl of Holland against them, they drew up their line in suitable places and offered the chance of fighting, and so showed the English that there was no way into Kelso except through their own bowels. Struck by this unexpected sight, the Earl of Holland first halted. Then, watching the order and spirit of the Scots as they armed themselves from a high hill, he hastened his retreat, which resembled flight, at a greater pace than he had come. The Scottish common soldiers, who saw from close at hand the confused retreat of the opposing column and its panic, were eager to press the English hard, and their tribunes and commanders could scarcely hold them in their posts. Yet, remembering that they had taken up arms to repel injury, not to inflict it, they judged that in this first trial of the war they should not advance beyond the limits of harmless defence. They judged that this victory was no less a confession of fear than the retreat, especially since the English later candidly acknowledged that it had been in the Scots' power, had they intended hostility against them, to make the retreat quite disgraceful.

units.la: Frustrata hac expeditione, non dubium erat Anglos, si qua esset ex tali discessu contracta ignominia, statim reparaturos; rumor etiam fuit eos totis viribus illud moliri; quare postridie illius diei, 5.vid. Iunii Generalis Leslius copias illas Kalsone evocat & ut sibi ad collem Dunsianum medio fere itinere occurrerent, jussit: Etenim cum satis prodidissent Angli expeditione illa in Kalsonem, propositum sibi esse Scotiam invadere, castra propius Angliam promovet Leslius, & ad collem Dunsianum (vulgo Duns Law, Dunsio municipio in Mercia propinquum; quod nativitate Iohannis Scoti Subtilis, & ludibriosa Henrici Percii Northumbriæ Comitis per pastorum crepitacula, fuga anno 1374. insigne est) sex millibus passuum ab Anglia distantem, unde prospectus esset in castra regia, posita ad alteram Tuedę ripam, loco editiori castra metatur. Ad primum Scotorum adventum Anglis prorsus inexspectatum, ad arma clamatum est in castris regiis: Nam licet antea ex profugarum Scotorum relationibus, qui apud eos commeabāt, audivissent Angli, Scotos ex adverso
units.tr: Once this expedition had failed, there was no doubt that the English, if any disgrace had been incurred from such a retreat, would at once try to repair it; there was also a rumour that they were striving for this with all their strength. So on the following day, 5 June, General Leslie summoned those troops from Kelso and ordered them to meet him about halfway, at the hill of Duns Law (commonly so called, near the town of Dunse in Mercia, and famous for the birth of John Duns Scotus and for the ludicrous flight of Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, in 1374, through the rattling of the shepherds' clappers). The English had quite revealed by their expedition against Kelso that they intended to invade Scotland, so Leslie moved his camp nearer to England and pitched it on higher ground at Duns Law, six thousand paces from England, from where there was a view of the royal camp, which was pitched on the other bank of the Tweed. At the first arrival of the Scots, which the English had not at all expected, there was a cry to arms in the royal camp. For although before this, from the reports of fugitive Scots who went to and fro among them, the English had heard that the Scots would not dare to stand opposite

units.la: consistere non ausuros, eorum vires quatuor mille pedites & quadringentos equites non excedere qui ex suis latibulis prodire, aut pugnandi copiam facere nunquam auderent; Nunc tamen cum eosdem tetoria figere in regii exercitus conspectu, & ex ordinatione castrorum fine ullo vallo, ingentis exercitus speciem circumcirca collem dispositi conspicerent, falsos penitus de Scotis sparsos fuisse rumores inter se prudentiores mussitabant: Satis jam constare, Scotos fœderatos nihil hostile in regem aut suam gentem meditari, & si secus molirentur, quid olim obstaret, quominus ante collectum regis exercitum vicinas Angliæ urbes intercepissent, aut Hollandiæ Comitem cum suis non ita pridem in reditu suo male multaffent, aut nunc castra regia in tanta multorum trepidatione adorirentur, præsertim cum commeatuum penuria laborari ibi cœptum fit, & multos morbis castrensibus tentari aut exstingui cognitum esset; contra apud Scotos omnia abundare, vegetum ac validum ipsorum exercitum esse, ita ut ex 24. millibus militum ne unus quidem morbo quovis castrensi affectus fuerit, quod multis forte supra fidem erit, sed pro certissimo deprehensum: Nullum in Scotorum exercitu esse alterius cujuslibet quam purioris reformatæ religionis professorem, & uno excepto Germano tubicine, omnes esse natione Scotos qui pro aris & focis ad extrema pericula subeunda alacres se comparárent. Ita qui non ita pridem Scotorum paucitatem, paupertatem despiciebant, in maximam admirationem conversi fuerunt, unde Scotis tantæ vires, tam constans & innoxia fiducia. Qui in Scotorum exercitu exploratores commeabant, constanter retulere, admirandum ducum & militum animorum conspirationem ad causam hanc promovendam, frequentia privatæ & publicæ pietatis exercitia, ita ut longe abessent quæ alibi in castris grassantur scelera, ebrietas, scortatio, impudici sermones, blasphemiæ, execrationes, rixæ, homicidia: Horas etiam suas distribuisse totum exercitum, in preces, conciones, corporis resectionem, & armorum exercitia.
units.tr: them, that their forces did not exceed four thousand foot and four hundred horse, and that they would never dare come out of their hiding places or offer battle; now, however, when they saw them pitching tents in full view of the royal army, and, from the arrangement of the camp without any rampart, saw the appearance of a huge army spread around the hill, the more prudent men muttered among themselves that the rumours spread about the Scots had been wholly false. It was now sufficiently clear that the confederate Scots planned nothing hostile against the king or his nation. And if they were planning otherwise, what had prevented them from seizing the neighbouring English towns long ago, before the royal army was gathered, or from having severely mauled the Earl of Holland and his men on their return not long before, or from attacking the royal camp now, in such great panic among the many? Especially since the royal camp had begun to suffer a shortage of supplies, and it was known that many were being attacked and carried off by camp diseases. Among the Scots, on the other hand, everything abounded, and their army was vigorous and strong, so that out of 24,000 soldiers not even one had been affected by any camp disease whatever. This will perhaps be beyond belief to many, but it was discovered to be most certain. In the Scottish army there was no one professing any religion other than the purest reformed one, and, with one exception, a German trumpeter, all were Scots by nation, who were prepared eagerly to face the utmost dangers for altars and hearths. Thus those who not long before had despised the Scots' small numbers and poverty were turned to the greatest astonishment, wondering whence the Scots had such strength and such steadfast and harmless confidence. Scouts who went among the Scottish army reported consistently the admirable unanimity of the commanders and soldiers in promoting this cause, and the frequent exercises of private and public piety, so that the crimes which rage elsewhere in camps, drunkenness, whoring, obscene talk, blasphemy, curses, brawls and murders, were far absent. The whole army, they said, had distributed its hours among prayers, sermons, refreshment of the body and exercises of arms.

units.la: Cæterum cum desperatum esse penitus de pace cernerent Scoti,ac non solum se rebelles declaratos, verumetiam omnes occasiones anxie captari & avide arripi quibus funditus obruerentur, suamque innocentiam tam apud exteras & transmarinas gentes, quam apud Anglos vicinos fœde traduci; suggestum fuit a nonnullis, An consultum foret vicinos reges & respublicas de rerum suarum statu certiores facere, ut iis mediatoribus uterentur apud serenifs.suum regem ad controversias hasce pacis potius quam belli consiliis componendas, aut si illud non obtinere possent, innocentiam saltem suam asserent apud exteros quorum aures obrutæ fuerunt falsis & fictis relationibus per quosdam mercenarios venalis ingenii & linguæ. Nobilibus qui in castris fuerunt consilium hoc non usque quaque displicebat: & ante omnes ut cum Galliarum rege agerent, fere persuasum illis erat, propter sacrum illud fœdus per multa sæcula post Caroli Magni Galliarum, & Achaii Scotorum regis tempora fideliter observatum. Literas in eum finem conscribendas decreverunt, quarum hæc capita designabantur: Cum percognitum sit serenissimum Galliarum Regem asylum & refugium esse afflictis Principibus & Rebuspub. ad eum se coactos nunc confugere, ac nobilem D. Colvillum ad eum delegasse, ut vindicet & asserat innocentiam & æquitatem non actionum solum suarum, verumetiam intentionum, quas universo terrarum orbi notissimas esse cuperent: Rogandum esse serenissimum regem ut pro consueta sua justitia & benignitate nobis nunc adesse velit, & ut eidem
units.tr: Meanwhile the Scots, seeing that all hope of peace had utterly failed, and that they had not only been declared rebels but that every opportunity was being anxiously sought and eagerly seized to crush them, and that their innocence was being foully misrepresented both to foreign and overseas nations and to the neighbouring English, were advised by some to inform the neighbouring kings and commonwealths of the state of their affairs. They should use these as mediators with their most serene king, so that the disputes might be settled by counsels of peace rather than by war. Or, if that could not be obtained, they should at least assert their innocence before foreigners whose ears had been stopped with false and fabricated reports by certain mercenaries of venal wit and tongue. The nobles in the camp did not altogether dislike this plan. Above all, they were almost persuaded that they should deal with the king of France, because of that sacred alliance, faithfully observed for many centuries since the times of Charlemagne, king of the French, and Achaius, king of the Scots. They resolved to write letters to that end, the heads of which were drawn up as follows: since it is well known that the most serene king of France is a refuge and asylum for afflicted princes and commonwealths, and since they have now been forced to flee to him, and have sent the noble Colville to him to vindicate and assert the innocence and equity not only of their actions but of their intentions, which they wished to be known to the whole world; the most serene king is to be asked, according to his customary justice and kindness, now to stand by them, and to deign to give credence to Colville in all matters that concern them.

units.la: Colvillo in omnibus quæ ad nos pertinent fidem habere dignetur. Mandata etiam tunc conceperunt Colvillo tradenda, secundum quæ munus hoc imponendum obiret: ex quibus facile intelligitur quid sit illud quod à rege Galliarum postulent, quæ de verbo in verbum translata sic se habent.
units.tr: They then also drew up instructions to be handed to Colville, according to which he should undertake this charge. From these it is easily understood what they asked of the king of France. Translated word for word, they read as follows.

units.la: Mandata seu instructiones tradendæ D. Colvillo.
units.tr: Instructions or directions to be delivered to Lord Colville.

units.la: 1. In memoriam revocabitur perantiquum illud & arctissimum fœdus inter duo regna, Galliæ & Scotiæ, olim sancitum, sæpius renovatum, & religiosé ac inviolate per multas annorum centurias observatum, quo factum est ut alterutra gentium ad incitas redacta, alterius promptum & fidum auxilium semper experta sit, idque successu optimo, quod mutuis nationalibus amicitiæ vicissitudinibus confirmatum esse, utriusque regni annales & publica registra testantur.
units.tr: 1. It shall be recalled that most ancient and very close alliance between the two kingdoms, France and Scotland, once sworn, often renewed, and religiously and inviolably observed through many centuries, by which it came about that whichever nation was reduced to straits always experienced the prompt and faithful aid of the other, and with the best success. The annals and public records of both kingdoms attest that this was confirmed by mutual vicissitudes of national friendship.

units.la: 2. Declarabitur; Intentiones nostras regiminiMonarchico nullatenus adversari, quin contra devotissimos & fidelissimos esse serenif.[?] nostro regi subditos, in ejus personam & authoritatem tuendam, vitam & fortunas lubenter exposituros; Neque in aliud nos ferri quam ut religionem & privilegia ecclesiastica & politica sarta tecta tueamur, prout legibus sancita sunt.
units.tr: 2. It shall be declared that our intentions are in no way opposed to monarchical government. On the contrary, we are most devoted and faithful subjects of our king, and we willingly expose our lives and fortunes in defending his person and authority. Nor are we moved to anything else than to keep our religion and our ecclesiastical and civil privileges safe and intact, as they have been sanctioned by law.

units.la: 3. Declarabitur; Non fidendum esse calumniis ab adversariis nostris contra nos sparsis; quandoquidem splendidissima sint mendacia, eo solum fine improbe excogitata, ut in vicinorum principum, Rerumpubl. ac gentium odia ac immeritam invidiam nos trahant: Cum contra, omnes nostræ cogitationes, verba, actiones legitimæ sint, prout qui præsentes feret, abunde edocebit.
units.tr: 3. It shall be declared that the calumnies spread against us by our adversaries are not to be trusted, since they are most glaring lies, wickedly devised for the sole purpose of drawing us into the hatred and undeserved odium of neighbouring princes, commonwealths and peoples. Whereas all our thoughts, words and actions are lawful, as the bearer who is present will abundantly show.

units.la: 4. Quandoquidem frequentissimis nostris libellis supplicibus apud regem nostrum serenif.[?] nihil profecerimus, Rogandum esse Galliarum regem, ut apud nostrum regem intercedat, quo dimittantur contra nos collecti exercitus, ac nobis liceat religione nostra ac privilegiis frui, pacifice & libere sub serenis. nostri regis legitima authoritate, quantumvis non diffidamus quin Deus nobis adfuturus sit, quandocunque armata manu nosmet tueri cogemur, quam armatam nostri defensionem leges Divinæ, naturæ, & gentium probant.
units.tr: 4. Since by our very frequent humble petitions to our king we have achieved nothing, the French king is to be asked to intercede with our king, so that the armies raised against us may be dismissed, and that we may be permitted to enjoy our religion and privileges peacefully and freely under the lawful authority of our serene king. We do not doubt that God will be with us whenever we are compelled to defend ourselves by force of arms, a defence which the divine, natural and international laws approve.

units.la: Sed conatus hic prorsus evanuit, nunquam transmissæ fuerunt hæ literæ, nunquam D. Colvillo tradita mandata, cum ubique clausi essent portus, & ea præsentis belli moles Scotis ingrueret, cui soli tum vacandum fuerat.
units.tr: But this attempt came to nothing. These letters were never sent, and the instructions were never handed to Colville, since all ports were closed everywhere, and the burden of the present war pressed upon the Scots, to which alone they then had to attend.

units.la: Interim ex multorum ultro citroque commeantium congressibus via ad pacem aperiri cœpit. Nam cum Fermeloduni Comes, ad castra regia excurreret amicis quibusdam salutandis, monetur, desiderari ab Anglis in castris regiis, ut Scoti pacis media proponerent, quibus promovendis operam utilem impenderent: Cumque Scotis illud relatum fuisset, eundem Fermeloduni Comitem cum supplicibus ad regem literis remittunt, quarum summa fuit; Se supplices serenis. regem obsecrare, ut, post alia media frustra tentata, nunc tandem nonnullos Anglos religionis & publicæ pacis studiosos deputare dignetur, qui cum Scotorum deputatis mutuo colloquio de gravaminibus, ac mediis ad pacificationem serio agant, priusquam malum hoc in nervum erumpat; Nunquam sibi propositum fuisse aliud postulare, quam ut liceret suis legibus vivere; daturosque operam ut omnes aperte videant, per se non stetisse quo minus negotium hoc, pacate hactenus conclusum sit. Literas etiam ad Comitem Hollandiæ & senatores regios in Anglia, qui tunc castra sequebantur, dederunt; quibus rogant, ut ad pacem procurandam sese apud regem interponant: Omnia à se ha-ctenus persecta quibus regi serenissimus & Anglis satisfacerent; ac nisi rex negotium pacis delegatis quibusdam mature deputare velit, mala quæ evitari nequeunt, omnem medicam manum superatura esse; quæ sibi imputanda non erunt, quippe, quibus nihil aliud in votis sit, quam ut bona regis cum venia liceat suis legibus vivere, ac religionis puritatem & antiqua regni privilegia sarta tecta tueri; Neque quidlibet antiquius habeant, quam ut regi seren. quam devotissimos subditos, & Anglorum studiosos se ostendant.
units.tr: Meanwhile, through the many meetings of people coming and going on both sides, a way to peace began to open. For when the Earl of Fermeloduni went to the royal camp to greet some friends, he was told that the English in the royal camp wished the Scots to propose means of peace, and that they would give useful help in promoting them. When this had been reported to the Scots, they sent the same Earl of Fermeloduni back to the king with letters of supplication. Their substance was this: they humbly beseech the most serene king that, since other means have been tried in vain, he would now at last deign to appoint some English men zealous for religion and public peace, who might confer seriously with the Scottish deputies about grievances and the means of pacification before this evil breaks out in earnest. They had never intended to ask for anything other than that they might be allowed to live under their own laws, and they would take care that everyone clearly sees that it was not their fault that this business has not yet been peacefully concluded. They also gave letters to the Earl of Holland and to the royal councillors in England who then accompanied the camp, by which they asked them to interpose with the king to procure peace. Everything they had so far done to satisfy the king and the English was complete. Unless the king was willing to appoint certain deputies promptly to the business of peace, the evils that cannot be avoided would overcome every remedy. These evils would not be imputed to them, since they desired nothing else than that, with the king's pardon, they might be allowed to live under their own laws, and to keep the purity of religion and the ancient privileges of the kingdom safe and intact. They held nothing more important than to show themselves most devoted subjects of the king and friends of the English.

units.la: Accepta hac supplicatione serenissimus rex Edmun-dum Vernejum, splendidum Equitem Anglum ad Scotorum castra delegat, qui moneret; regem Scotorum postulatis non prius responsurum, quam edictum illud promulgarent, April. 25. Eboraci conditum, quod hactenus suppressissent Scoti. Respondent à Scotis deputati, rationibus firmis se hactenus ostendisse Illustriss. Marchioni Hamiltonio, quam inconsultum esset edictum illud, tam in materia quam forma illegitimum & prorsus vitiosum, promulgare, vitiorumque objectorum summa capita idemEques in memoriæ suæ subsidium descripsit; ut tamen regi satisfacerent, in privato conclavi coram iis qui omnium nomine responsum expediebant, edictum prælegi jubent, ut ad singulas se-ctiones, ejus vitia (ut ajebant) ostenderent & refutarent. Ad serenissimum regem cum rediisset hic Eques Anglus, tandem nobilium Anglorum serio interventu consentiit rex, ut quos foederati Scoti deputatos nominarent ad regia castra venirent, die Lunæ qui fuit 10 Iunii, quando sex nobiles Angli primariæ dignitatis ipsorum adventum hora octava matutina in tentorio Comitis Arundelii, summi castrorum præfecti exspectarent.
units.tr: On receiving this petition, the most serene king sent Edmund Verney, a distinguished English knight, to the Scottish camp, to warn that the king of Scots would not answer their demands until they published that edict, drawn up at York on 25 April, which the Scots had hitherto suppressed. The Scottish deputies replied that they had already shown the most illustrious Marquis Hamilton, by firm arguments, how unwise it was to publish that edict, which was illegitimate in matter and form and wholly faulty. The knight wrote down the chief heads of the objected faults to aid his memory. Nevertheless, in order to satisfy the king, they asked that in a private room, before those who were preparing the answer on behalf of all, the edict be read aloud, so that they might point out and refute its faults, section by section, as they put it. When this knight had returned to the most serene king, at last, through the earnest intervention of English nobles, the king consented that the Scottish deputies whom the allied Scots named should come to the royal camp on Monday, 10 June, when six English nobles of the highest rank would await their arrival at eight in the morning in the tent of the Earl of Arundel, the chief commander of the camp.

units.la: Quare Scoti statim delegant Comitem Rothusiæ; Laudonium, nobiles supremi ordinis; Gulielmum Duglassium Equitem, Teviotiæ præfectum juridicum; Alexandrum Hendersonum pastorem Edinburgenum, nuperæ synodi Glasguensis Præsidem, & Archibaldum Ionstonum, Advocatum in suprema curia, & synodi nationalis scribam. Quæstio quædam fuit de literis salvi conductus, quia statutis regni Angliæ omnes salvi conductus literæ, læsæ majestatis reis præsertim concessæ, nullius prorsus valoris sunt nisi magno regni sigillo muniantur; & rex sereniss. Scotos fœderatos, rebelles esse sæpius asseruit, iisque facultatem noluit concedere, ut in Angliam adventientes, actionum suarum æquitatem ei demonstrarent: sed deputati Scotorum quicquid sit de literis salvi conductus; unius sereniss. regis fidei confidere satis tutum judicarunt; & ad horam & locum condictum sese contulerunt, ac causam publicam, sereniss. rege præsente, quod unice in votis habebant, luculenter egerunt. Postulata quædam generalia offerunt, vid. 1. Ut rex pro benignitate, clementia, ac justitia sua, vellet nuperam synodum Glasguensem in parlamento ad 23. Iulii indicto, sancire. 2. Ut negotia ecclefiastica synodis, & politica parlamentis secundo aut tertio quoq; anno recurrente habendis definienda permitteret. 3. Ut Classem reuocaret; bona arresto detenta redderet, ac damnum quod interruptione mercaturæ subivissent, rependeret: liberos denique redderet Scotos ab omni metu invasionis seu terra seu mari. 4. Ut excommunicati à Scoticis ecclesiis, & qui privata tantum commoda sectati, calumniis ac falsis relationibus incendium hoc belli excitarunt, in Scotiam remitterentur, sceleribus hisce atrocissimis debitam pœnam subituri. 5. Ut declarationes, edicta ab istis quidem extrusa, sed regis nomine palliata supprimerentur, cum in regis sereniss. regnique sui infamiam tendant.
units.tr: Therefore the Scots at once appointed the Earl of Rothes; Lord Loudoun, nobles of the highest order; Sir William Douglas, judicial sheriff of Teviotdale; Alexander Henderson, minister of Edinburgh and president of the recent Glasgow synod; and Archibald Johnston, advocate in the supreme court and clerk of the national synod. There was a question about letters of safe conduct, because by the statutes of the kingdom of England all letters of safe conduct, especially those granted to persons accused of treason, are of no force at all unless they are secured with the great seal of the realm. The most serene king had often asserted that the Scots were rebels bound by alliance, and he was unwilling to grant them permission to come into England and demonstrate the equity of their actions to him. But the Scottish deputies, whatever the case with the letters of safe conduct, judged it sufficiently safe to trust the word of the most serene king alone. They went to the appointed hour and place, and pleaded their public cause brilliantly, with the most serene king present, which was what they desired above all. They offered certain general demands, namely: (1) that the king, in his kindness, clemency and justice, would ratify the recent Glasgow synod in the parliament summoned for 23 July; (2) that he would permit ecclesiastical matters to be settled by synods, and civil matters by parliaments, to be held every second or third year; (3) that he would recall the fleet, return goods held under arrest, make good the loss suffered through interruption of trade, and finally return the Scots free from all fear of invasion, whether by land or by sea; (4) that those excommunicated by the Scottish churches, and who, pursuing only private advantages, stirred up this fire of war by calumnies and false reports, be sent back to Scotland to undergo the due punishment for these most atrocious crimes; (5) that the declarations and edicts, thrust out by those men but covered with the king's name, be suppressed, since they tend to the infamy of the most serene king and of his kingdom.

units.la: Atque sicut (inquiunt) nobis nunc quam gravissime dolet, seren.nostrum regem contra nos fidelissimos & devotos sibi subditos irritatum fuisse, sic quâ maxīmo posthac nobis erit gaudio, Regi religionis nostræ puritatem & leges tuenti, obedientiam civilem quæ à quibuslibet fidelibus subditis exspectari possit, præstare, imo eam quæ aliis exemplo esse possit. Respondit rex: Quandoquidem subditi sui Scoti nihil aliud sibi in postulatis esse præ se ferant, quam ut libere fruantur religione & libertatibus ex præscripto legum qua civilium qua ecclesiasticarum regni Scotiæ; se exspectare, ut evidenter demonstrent, singula postulatorum capita hujus naturæ esse, ideoque nulla quæ legibus hactenus sancitis non muniuntur, in controversiam vocanda esse.
units.tr: And just as (they say) it grieves us most of all that our most serene King was provoked against us, his most faithful and devoted subjects, so hereafter we will render him, who upholds the purity of our religion and its laws, the civil obedience that may be expected from any faithful subjects, nay, obedience that may serve as an example to others. The King replied: since his Scottish subjects show nothing else in their demands than that they may freely enjoy their religion and liberties according to the prescription of the laws of the kingdom of Scotland, both civil and ecclesiastical, he expects them clearly to demonstrate that each single head of their demands is of this nature, and therefore that nothing which is not secured by laws hitherto enacted is to be called in question.

units.la: Redierunt hac vice ad suos Scotorum deputati laute & magnifice à nobilissimo Arundeliæ Comite semper excepti: ac die Mercurii Iunii 13. ad castra regia cum sociorum responso redeunt: quo superiora postulata legitima demonstrabant. Ac 1. De synodo sancienda postulatum legitimum est, quandoquidem synodus regia authoritate indicta fuisset, ac in omnibus suis membris, secundum receptam ecclesiæ Scoticæ consuetudinem, rite constituta; neque ullum quodvis decretum ab ea conditum fuerit, quod vel expresse vel per consequentiam necessariam & immediatam prius non fuerit decretum in præcedentibus ecclesiarum synodis. Quare cum singula in synodo ordine & legitime processerint, Regis esse, cum utriusque tabulæ custos sit, eandem synodum in parlamento sancire, præsertim cum ecclesia & regnum hoc unum quasi corpus ex iisdem membris conflatum constituant, & sibi invicem ita arctè cohæreant, ut nisi exhortationibus ac censuris urgeant ecclesiastici debitam politico magistratui obedientiam, & nisi magistratus politicus civilem sanctionem ad vigorem publicæ observantiæ, ecclesiasticis constitutionibus superaddat, nulla stabilis & firma pax exspectari possit. Necessarium etiam esse ut die præfinita, regni Comitia celebrentur, cum nullam procrastinationem aut dilationem præsens regni & ecclesiæ status ferre possit. 2. Secundi articuli æquitatem per se patere (dicebant) ut causæ ecclesiasticæ in synodis, civiles in parlamentis definirentur, quia causæ hæ usque adeo diversæ sunt ut nequeant in uno eodemque foro sine extrema confusione definiri. Et ut recurrente biennio aut triennio regni Comitia solenniter & ordinarie habeantur admodum necessarium esse, quandoquidem serenis. regis absentia à regno impediantur subditi, ne gravamina sua regi immediate deferant. Tertium, quartum, & quintum postulatum usque adeo evidentia sunt, ut à nullo in quæstionem vocari possint.
units.tr: The Scottish deputies returned to their people on this occasion, always most lavishly and magnificently entertained by the most noble Earl of Arundel. On Wednesday, 13 June, they came back to the royal camp with the response of their colleagues, which demonstrated that the above demands were lawful. (1) On the ratification of the synod, the demand is lawful, since the synod was convened by royal authority and was duly constituted in all its members according to the received custom of the Scottish Church. No decree was made by it that had not first been decreed, either expressly or by necessary and immediate consequence, in the earlier synods of the churches. Therefore, since everything in the synod proceeded in order and lawfully, it belongs to the King, who is the guardian of both tables, to ratify the same synod in parliament. This is especially so since the Church and the kingdom together form one body, as it were, made up of the same members, and cohere so closely that no stable and firm peace can be expected unless ecclesiastics press the due obedience to the civil magistrate by exhortations and censures, and unless the civil magistrate adds civil sanction to ecclesiastical constitutions to give them the force of public observance. It is also necessary that the assembly of the realm be held on a fixed day, since the present state of the kingdom and Church can bear no procrastination or delay. (2) The fairness of the second article, they said, is evident in itself: ecclesiastical causes should be decided in synods and civil causes in parliaments, since these causes are so different that they cannot be decided in one and the same forum without extreme confusion. And it is very necessary that the assemblies of the realm be held solemnly and regularly, once every two or three years, since the subjects, prevented by the absence of the most serene King from the realm, cannot bring their grievances directly to the King. The third, fourth and fifth demands are so evident that no one can call them into question.

units.la: Hac (ut refertur) vice quæstiones quasdam proposuit rex, ad quas Scotorum deputatos responderere jussit. 1. An regi soli competat synodi Nationalis indictio? 2. An in synodis suffragium negativum regi competat? 3. An liceat synodum continuare rege dissolutionem ejus imperante? Ad quas paratam habuerunt deputati altera vice responsionem, cujus summa hæc fuerat. 1. Quæstionum hujus generis determinationem ad synodum Nationalem proprie pertinere, ita ut si synodo non prius consulta easdem definirent, synodi censuram merito incurrerent. 2. Si ad unam respondeas, ad omnes tres eadem opera respondebitur; nam si regi soli indictio synodi competat, nulla opus erit quæstione de suffragio negativo, aut de dissolutione synodi, dein si regi negativum competat suffragium, inutilis prorsus erit quæstio de indictione & dissolutione, & si regi liceat per se, sua propria authoritate synodum dissolvere, frustra disputabitur de indictione & suffragio negativo. Adse, qua privatos, quod attineret, submisse agnoscere se, licere regi quando & quoties velit, omnis generis synodos tam Nationales quam Provinciales convocare; Agnoscere etiam solennem & publicam indictionem, per modum Compulsionis & editi, ad regem solum proprie pertinere, neque potestatem hanc in pontificem Romanum aut quemlibet externum transferri, nec a subditis sine usurpatione vendicari posse. Interim suos animos subire nunquam posse, dicunt, regis sententiam esse; Nunquam licere ecclesiae convenire, deliberare, & constitutiones proprie ecclesiasticas ad religionis tutelam condere, idque extrema & urgente necessitate, si ecclesiae tum deerit Magistratus; Nam licere rationibus hisce demonstramus; 1. Quia Deus ecclesiae facultatem hanc concessit ut conveniat; Dei filius praesentiam suam ecclesiae convocatae promisit, & ecclesia Christiana Synodis semper usa est ut medio ordinario & necessario ad religionis uniformitatem stabiliendam, haereses exstirpandas, & mala ecclesiam penitus destructura, si Synodis destitueretur. 2. Quia ecclesia Scotica jure hoc divino freta, statas suas Nationales Synodos cum singulari Dei benedictione solenniter celebravit: nam quamdiu Synodorum viguit authoritas, tamdiu sua doctrinae constabat puritas, disciplinae unitas, & ecclesiae pax: eruditio laudem suam & praemia nacta est; impietas & idololatria coercebantur. 3. Quia ecclesia Scotica declaravit licere ecclesiae in synodos convenire, ac locum & tempus celebrandi & habendi definire. 4. Quia idem statuto parlamentario anni 1592. sancitur, quod statutum immutabile esse oportet, prout fundamenta sunt quibus innititur. 5. Quia nullo decreto ecclesiastico, nulla lege municipali ab ipsis reformationis primordiis, ostendi potest, regi per se & absolute licere synodum dissolvere, aut suffragii negativi jus unquam sibi asseruisse: Quin contra diserto & expresso statuto parlamentario declaratur; Ius regium nullo modo præjudicare libertatibus & privilegiis ecclesiæ ministris a Deo concessis, quæ libertates sæpius in parlamentis sanciuntur, præsertim in postremo cui rex serenis. interfuit & præfuit. 6. Quia si hæc tria regibus concederentur, religio tota ecclesiæque jurisdictio penderet absolute ab eorum beneplacito: Cum tamen serenis. rex publico edicto in Anglia declaraverit, jurisdictionem ecclesiasticam in conventibus & synodis ecclesiasticis, non fluere ab authoritate sua regia, non obstante quovis statuto parlamentario in contrarium; verum ab ecclesiasticis ipsis, & ipsorum propria potestate: licere itaque ipsis curias & fora sua propriis suis nominibus indicere, & in iis sententias ferre. Atque hæc summa fuit istius scripti ad regis tria interrogata; sed regi serenis. fortasse huic proposito diutius insistere visum non fuit; Nam responsum a deputatis nunquam requisivit.
units.tr: On this occasion, as is reported, the King put certain questions, to which he ordered the Scottish deputies to reply: (1) Does the power to summon a National Synod belong to the King alone? (2) Does the King have a negative voice in synods? (3) May a synod continue to sit when the King commands its dissolution? To these the deputies had ready on this second occasion a reply, the substance of which was this. (1) The determination of questions of this kind belongs properly to the National Synod, so that if they define such questions without first consulting the synod, they would rightly incur the censure of the synod. (2) If you answer the first, the other three will be answered at the same stroke. For if the power to summon a synod belongs to the King alone, there will be no need for a question about a negative voice or about dissolution. Then, if the King has a negative voice, the question about summoning and dissolving will be wholly pointless; and if the King may by himself, on his own authority, dissolve a synod, it will be vain to dispute about summoning and the negative voice. As for themselves as private persons, they humbly acknowledged that the King may, whenever and as often as he wishes, convene synods of every kind, both National and Provincial. They also acknowledged that the solemn and public summoning, by way of compulsion and edict, belongs properly to the King alone, and that this power is not to be transferred to the Roman pontiff or any foreigner, nor can it be claimed by subjects without usurpation. Meanwhile, they say, it could never enter their minds that it was the King's opinion that it is never lawful for the Church to assemble, to deliberate, and to frame ecclesiastical constitutions for the protection of religion, and that too in extreme and pressing necessity, if the Church then lacks a magistrate. For we demonstrate by these reasons that it is lawful: (1) Because God granted the Church the power to assemble; the Son of God promised his presence to the gathered Church; and the Christian Church has always used synods as the ordinary and necessary means of establishing uniformity of religion, of rooting out heresies, and of preventing evils from utterly destroying the Church, were it deprived of synods. (2) Because the Scottish Church, relying on this divine right, has solemnly held its National Synods with singular blessing from God. For as long as the authority of the synods flourished, so long did the purity of doctrine, the unity of discipline and the peace of the Church endure; learning gained its praise and rewards, and impiety and idolatry were restrained. (3) Because the Scottish Church has declared that it is lawful for the Church to assemble in synods and to fix the place and time of meeting. (4) Because the same is sanctioned by a parliamentary statute of 1592, which ought to be an unchangeable statute, as the foundations on which it rests are unchangeable. (5) Because from the very beginnings of the Reformation no ecclesiastical decree and no municipal law can be shown by which the King may by himself and absolutely dissolve a synod, or ever claimed for himself a right of negative voice. Indeed, the contrary is declared by an express and explicit parliamentary statute: the royal right in no way prejudices the liberties and privileges granted by God to the ministers of the Church, which liberties have been frequently sanctioned in parliaments, especially in the last, at which the most serene King was present and presided. (6) Because if these three things were granted to kings, the whole religion and the jurisdiction of the Church would depend absolutely on their pleasure. Yet the most serene King has declared by public edict in England that ecclesiastical jurisdiction in ecclesiastical conventions and synods does not flow from his royal authority, notwithstanding any parliamentary statute to the contrary, but from the ecclesiastics themselves and their own power; and so it is lawful for them to convene their courts and tribunals under their own names and to pronounce sentences in them. This was the substance of that paper in reply to the King's three questions. But it seemed best to the most serene King perhaps not to dwell longer on this proposal, for he never asked the deputies for an answer.

units.la: Tertia vice ad castra regia revertuntur deputati, quando etiam fuisse de omnibus gravaminibus & quæ hisce motibus causam & occasionem dederunt, agitatum fuit; Serenis. regis ingenuitatem, ac pium candorem omnes deprædicabant, ac prout decuit, dolebant, Optimum Principem contra ingenii sui ad pacem & æquitatem proni impetum, quorundam calumniis & susurris ad extrema & violenta hæc consilia fuisse pertractum: & à nullo dubitatum tum fuit quin pacate omnia componerentur, Nobilibus Anglis stremuam[?] ad id operam navantibus. Sed cum denuo repeterent castra regia ad horam condictam foederatorum deputati, regis animum nonnihil abalienatum deprehendunt, quam inexspectatam mutationem turbulentis quorundam praesulum fortasse Roffensis consiliis imputabant. Quare nullo operae-pretio conventu illo praestito ad Scotorum castra redierunt deputati: Cum vero res ad commune & publicum foederatorum in castris concilium delata fuisset; varii erant animorum motus: Suspicabantur alii, colloquiis hisce nihil aliud quaeri, quam ut bellum protelaretur in adventu majorum copiarum ex Anglia & Hibernia, aut saltem ut commeatus & frumentationis inopia ad retrocessionem cogerentur; adversariorum versutiae veteres & recentes interpretando etiam auctae omnium sermonibus vexabantur. Quare deputatis suis mandarunt libertatis vindices, ut serio negotium urgerent, sibi nulla ratione consultum in dubio haerere, movenda protinus esse castra, & dilatoriis hujus generis tractatibus abruptis, figenda esse intra machinae jactum prope castra regia. Fuerunt qui haec omnia futiliter extulerunt, & forte uti id hominum genus solet, multa nunquam dicta nunquam cogitata de suo addiderunt, ac utrinque hujus farinae homines non deerant. Verum Dei bona gratia regis sereniss. animus prioribus & salubrioribus consiliis adhaesit, ac tandem hoc edicto voluntatem suam declaravit, quod de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: For a third time the deputies returned to the royal camp, and on this occasion all the grievances and whatever had given cause and occasion for these disturbances were discussed. All of them extolled the most serene King's frankness and pious candour, and, as was fitting, lamented that the best of princes, against the natural bent of his disposition towards peace and fairness, had been drawn by the calumnies and whisperings of certain men to these extreme and violent counsels. No one then doubted that everything would be settled peacefully, the English nobles working earnestly to that end. But when the deputies of the Covenanters returned to the royal camp at the appointed hour, they perceived that the King's mind was somewhat estranged, and they attributed this unexpected change perhaps to the turbulent counsels of certain bishops, above all the Bishop of Rochester. Therefore, the deputies returned to the Scottish camp, the conference having achieved nothing worthwhile. When the matter was referred to the common and public council of the Covenanters in the camp, their feelings were varied. Some suspected that these conferences aimed at nothing else than to prolong the war until larger forces arrived from England and Ireland, or at least that the lack of provisions and supplies would force them to retreat. The old and recent stratagems of their adversaries, magnified by everyone's talk and interpretation, troubled them. Therefore the champions of liberty ordered their deputies to press the matter seriously: that they themselves had no reason to hesitate in doubt, that the camps must be moved at once, and that, with negotiations of this dilatory kind broken off, they should be pitched within cannon-shot of the royal camp. There were those who spread all this about with no foundation, and, as that kind of men usually do, added much of their own, things never said and never thought. On both sides there was no lack of men of this stamp. But by the good grace of God, the mind of the most serene King clung to the earlier and more wholesome counsels, and at last he declared his will by this edict, which, translated almost word for word, reads as follows.

units.la: Edictum pacificatorium.
units.tr: The Edict of Pacification.

units.la: Perpensis scriptis & supplicibus libellis nobis exhibitis a subditis nostris in regno Scotiae, quos admisimus ut voluntatis nostrae declarationem in castris nostris exspectarent, iisdemque saepius auditis, in omnibus, quæ in causæ suæ patrocinium proferre potuerunt, quæ senatoribus utriusque regni nostri communicavimus, unanimi & maturo eorundem consilio, visum nobis est plenum & æquum hoc responsum iisdem referre. Quod, licet nolimus ratam habere Pseudo-synodum Glasguensem multis gravibus de causis, quæ tum ante eandem habitam, tum post dimissam acciderunt, quibus ingens præjudicium affertur honori ac securitati veri illius regiminis Monarchici, continua tot majorum serie ad nos devoluti: Nihilominus visum nobis est, præteritis nuperis tumultibus, non solum ratum habere & præstare omne illud, quod nomine nostro concesserit aut promiserit deputatus noster: verum etiam prout postulant submisse subditi nostri, Declarare omnes causas ecclesiasticas definiendas esse synodorum judiciis, & politicas parlamenti & aliorum inferiorum tribunalium: Quæ synodi ecclesiasticæ Nationales, singulis annis semel habebuntur; aut prout ea in re conventum fuerit in proxima synodo. Et ut præsentes hæ animorum alienationes ac motus sedentur, visum nobis est, liberam synodum Nationalem habendam esse Edenburgi 6. Augusti proxime subsecuturi, cui Deo favente, nobis propositum est interesse, & cujus legitimam indictionem senatui nostro imperabimus: ac ibidem parlamentum 20. Augusti mensis habendum esse, ad sancienda Nationalis synodi decreta, & componenda ea omnia quæ ad pacem & commodum antiqui illius nostri regni conducent; Et ad ἀμνηστίας [?] statutum sanciendum.
units.tr: Having carefully weighed the written statements and petitions presented to us by our subjects in the kingdom of Scotland, which we admitted so that they might await the declaration of our will in our camp, and having often heard them, and having shared with the senators of both our kingdoms everything they were able to put forward in defence of their cause, we have, by the unanimous and mature counsel of those same senators, judged it right and fair to give them this reply. Although we are unwilling to ratify the Glasgow Pseudo-synod, for many grave reasons, both those that arose before it was held and those that have arisen since it was dismissed, by which great prejudice is done to the honour and security of that true monarchical government, handed down to us through so long a succession of our forebears, nevertheless we have judged it right, with the recent tumults set aside, not only to ratify and fulfil whatever our deputy has granted or promised in our name, but also, as our subjects humbly ask, to declare that all ecclesiastical causes are to be decided by the judgments of the synods, and civil causes by Parliament and the other lower courts. The national ecclesiastical synods are to be held once a year, or as may be agreed at the next synod. And so that these present alienations of minds and these disturbances may be calmed, we have judged that a free National Synod is to be held at Edinburgh on the sixth of August next, which, God willing, it is our purpose to attend, and whose lawful summons we will order our Council to issue; and there Parliament is to be held on the twentieth of August, to ratify the decrees of the National Synod and to settle all those matters that will conduce to the peace and welfare of that ancient kingdom of ours, and to ratify an act of amnesty [ἀμνηστίας].

units.la: Ad illud vero quo postulatur ut classis nostra à littoribus, & copiæ terrestres à limitibus revocentur, ac ut captivi liberentur, & naves ac bona arresto aut alio quovis modo detenta reddantur, & ut illi denique ab omni invasionis metu liberentur: Nobis clementer & benigne visum est significare ; Quandocunque copias illi suas, conventus ac conventicula dimiserint, nobisque restituerint omnia nostra castella, arces, apparatum bellicum, regalia ornamenta ac insignia ; singulisque aliorum nostrorum fidelium subditorum, libertatem, bona, agros, domus, & quaecunque demum iis erepta sunt post nuperam Pseudo-synodum : Nos tum statim classem ac exercitus omnes revocaturos, naves & bona arresto detenta restituturos: ut appareat propositum nobis non fuisse nativum hoc nostrum regnum hostiliter invadere, aut religionem & leges ejus innovare: sed armis nos instruxisse eo solum nomine ut auctoritatem nostram regiam tueremur ac vindicaremus.
units.tr: As to the demand that our fleet be recalled from the coasts and our land forces from the borders, that the prisoners be released, that ships and goods held under arrest or by any other means be returned, and that our subjects be finally freed from all fear of invasion: it has pleased us to declare graciously and kindly that, as soon as they disband their armies, assemblies and conventicles, and restore to us all our castles, fortresses, military stores, royal ornaments and insignia, and the liberty, goods, lands, houses, and whatever else has been taken from each of our other loyal subjects since the recent Pseudo-synod, we will at once recall the whole fleet and army, and return the ships and goods detained under arrest. This is so that it may be clear that it was never our purpose to invade this native kingdom of ours in hostile fashion, or to alter its religion and laws; rather, we have armed ourselves for the sole purpose of protecting and vindicating our royal authority.

units.la: Atque cum hinc liquido constare possit, nobis uti nunquam antehac, sic neque nunc propositum esse, leges aut religionem mutare, quin contra utrumque illaesum & illibatum defendere ; exspectamus ut fideliter & submisse obedientiam praestent, prout decet probos & fideles subditos, quales se toties professi sunt. Et sicuti nobis persuasum est praesenti hac declaratione satisfactum iri fidelibus & pacis studiosis nostris subditis ; Ita Deum & universum terrarum orbem testamur ; Calamitates quæ necessaria nostra coercitione arrogantiæ eorum qui pertinaciter pervicaces se prodent, evenient, nobis non imputandas esse, sed sibimet ipsis.
units.tr: Since it may therefore be plainly established that our purpose, as never before, so now too, is not to change the laws or the religion, but on the contrary to defend both unharmed and undiminished, we expect them to render obedience faithfully and humbly, as befits upright and loyal subjects, which is what they have so often professed themselves to be. And just as we are persuaded that by this present declaration our loyal subjects who love peace will be satisfied, so we call God and the whole world to witness that the calamities which will come upon those who stubbornly show themselves obstinate, through the necessary restraint of our arrogance, are not to be imputed to us, but to themselves.

units.la: Leges porro & articuli pacificationis in quas conventum fuit in castris regiis, & quas utriusque regni Secretarii postea signarunt, hæ fuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the laws and articles of pacification agreed upon in the royal camp, and afterwards signed by the secretaries of both kingdoms, were these.

units.la: 1. Exercitus Scotorum intra quadraginta & octo horas postquam de promulgatione hujus edicti conventum fuerit, dimittendus est.
units.tr: 1. The Scottish army is to be disbanded within forty-eight hours after agreement has been reached on the publication of this edict.

units.la: 2. Post edicti promulgationem, arces regiæ, castella, omne genus apparatus bellici intercep-ti, inti, insignia coronæ restituenda sunt, quamprimum regi visum fuerit quemlibet deputare cui tradantur.
units.tr: 2. After the publication of the edict, the royal castles, fortresses, all kinds of military equipment seized, and the insignia of the crown are to be restored, as soon as the king has seen fit to appoint someone to whom they may be handed over.

units.la: 3. Hisce restitutis, classis regia primo quoque secundiore vento discedet, quod si ventus secundus non afflaverit, ne mercium subvectio & piscatura impediatur.
units.tr: 3. Once these have been restored, the royal fleet will depart at the first favourable wind; but if a favourable wind does not blow, the carriage of merchandise and fishing are not to be hindered.

units.la: 4. Regi benigne visum est imperare & procurare restitutionem bonorum omnium & navium arresto aut quovis alio modo detentarum ac interceptarum post Calendas Februarias proxime elap-sas.
units.tr: 4. The king has graciously consented to order and to arrange the restitution of all goods and ships held under arrest or seized by any other means, and intercepted since the first of February last past.

units.la: 5. Ne conventus, tractationes, consultationes, aut quaelibet subditorum nostrorum conventicula præter ea quæ legibus approbata sunt, habeantur.
units.tr: 5. No assemblies, negotiations, consultations, or any other conventicles of our subjects are to be held, except those that have been approved by law.

units.la: 6. Desistendum esse à locis muniendis, & munitiones hactenus erectas regis sereniss. arbitrio permittendas esse.
units.tr: 6. Work on fortifying places is to cease, and the fortifications hitherto erected are to be left to the decision of the most serene king.

units.la: 7. Probis nostris subditis restituenda esse prædia, domus, fortunas, & quicquid iis ereptum fuit post diem prædictum.
units.tr: 7. Estates, houses, fortunes, and whatever has been taken from our upright subjects after the aforesaid day, are to be restored to them.

units.la: Quæ cum ad suos retulissent fœderatorum deputati; Convocato frequenti senatu, quæsitum an edicto hoc postulatis suis satisfieret? & cum singula edicti verba & sententias excuterent; ægre tulerunt asperiores illas phrases ubique disper-sas, quibus synodus Glasguensis Pseudo-synodus; priores actiones, tumultus, arrogantiæ, contumaciæ vocabantur: Sed deputatorum, qui pacis interpretes fuerunt, prudentia, difficultates illæ discussæ fuerunt: Nam referebant, omnia hæc sibi perspecta fuisse, ac displicuisse, ideoque serenis. regem obsecratum fuisse, ut phrasium istarum asperitatem leni-ret, ret, & alia quædam difertius exprimeret quibus omnes scrupuli ac suspiciones fidelium subditorum animis eximi possent: Responsum quod à rege obtinuisse se dixerunt, scripto, in conventu illo sociorum commiserunt, ejusque exemplaria nobilibus quibusdam Anglis, quorum nobile & pium in pacis negotio procurando studium se exeruerat, tradituros in se reciperunt, ut si quæ quæstio posthac forte suboriretur ex ambiguitate & generalitate phrasium quarundam in edicto positarum, de ea judicium fieri posset secundum ea quæ in scripto illo continebantur; utpote quod contineret ea quæ privatim transacta fuerunt, ipsis illis Anglis nobilibus præsentibus: Scriptum vero illud sic se habuit.
units.tr: When the deputies of the Covenanters had reported these terms to their own people, the Council was summoned in full, and it was asked whether this edict satisfied their demands. As they went through each word and sentence of the edict, they took it badly that those harsher phrases were scattered everywhere, by which the Glasgow Synod was called a Pseudo-synod, and its earlier proceedings were called tumults, arrogance and obstinacy. But the prudence of the deputies, who were the interpreters of the peace, settled these difficulties. For they reported that they had examined all these things and had found them displeasing, and therefore they had earnestly begged the most serene king to soften the harshness of those phrases, and to express certain other matters more plainly, so that every scruple and suspicion could be removed from the minds of the loyal subjects. The reply which they said they had obtained from the king they committed to writing at that meeting of their associates, and they undertook to hand copies of it to certain noble Englishmen, whose noble and pious zeal in promoting the cause of peace had been shown; so that if any question should later arise from the ambiguity and generality of certain phrases set down in the edict, a judgment could be made about it according to what was contained in that writing, since it contained what had been transacted privately, with those same noble Englishmen present. The writing itself stood as follows.

units.la: 1. Licet præfatio & conclusio edicti regii asperioribus verbis pungeret subditos regni Scotiæ, regem tamen declarasse, nullam se de iis sinistriorem opinionem fovere: rationem habendam esse existimationis suæ apud exteros: frustra de verbis moveri quæstionem cum de re ipsa constiterit; & cum postulata obtinuissent.
units.tr: 1. Although the preface and conclusion of the royal edict pricked the subjects of the kingdom of Scotland with harsher words, the king nevertheless declared that he holds no less favourable opinion of them; that regard must be had for his reputation among foreigners; that it is in vain to raise a question about words when the matter itself has been settled; and that they had obtained what they asked for.

units.la: 2. Licet synodum Glasguensem Pseudo-synodum vocaret, neque ulla ejus decreta approbaret præter illa quibus declaratio sua regia publicis registris inserta esset, apud Scotos tamen se non institurum, ut synodo illi renunciens.
units.tr: 2. Although he calls the Glasgow Synod a Pseudo-synod, and does not approve any of its decrees except those which his royal declaration has been inserted into the public registers, nevertheless among the Scots he will not require them to renounce that synod.

units.la: 3. Ad synodi constitutionem quod attinet, ostensum regi fuisse, nullum pro synodi membro agnosci posse, qui rite delegatus non esset, tres vid. verbi pastores cum unico seniore à singulis presbyteriis seu Classibus, & ab academiis ac civitatibus singulis unus, qui simul cum rege aut regio deputato synodum plenam facerent. Ursisse[?] regem jus suffragii assessoribus suis; & cum in priori hujus edicti forma quædam phrases insertæ suissent quibus mentio fiebat rationum prioribus edictis contra synodum Glasguensem contentarum, quibus seniores à synodo Nationali penitus excluderentur; Postulatum tum à nobis fuit, ut omnes id genus controversiæ, more huic ecclesiæ consueto, ad synodi definitionem remitterentur: Rex vero contra videbatur instare, ut ad se remitterentur; Verum cum significatum fuisset, Adversari ecclesiæ constitutionibus, ut rerum ad se proprie pertinentium alium quemvis judicem agnosceret quam synodum ipsam, cui rex vel per se vel per deputatum interesset & primus sententiam ferret; Tandem conclusum fuisse vocem Liberæ Synodi, in edicto regio, secum ferre ac includere facultatem judicandi de omnibus quæstionibus, quæ circa Synodi constitutionem, membra, aut materiam in ea tractandam moverentur.
units.tr: 3. As to the constitution of the synod, it was shown to the king that no one could be acknowledged as a member of the synod who had not been duly elected: three ministers of the Word, namely, with one elder from each presbytery or classis, and one from each university and each town, who together with the king or his deputy would make a full synod. The king wished to reserve the right of voting to his assessors; and since in the earlier form of this edict certain phrases had been inserted which mentioned the grounds set out in the earlier edicts against the Glasgow Synod, by which elders would be wholly excluded from the National Synod, it was then demanded by us that all controversies of this kind be referred, according to the custom of this Church, to the definition of the synod. The king, on the contrary, seemed to insist that they be referred to himself. But when it had been made clear that it was contrary to the constitutions of the Church for anyone other than the synod itself to judge matters properly belonging to it, in which the king, either in person or through a deputy, would take part and pronounce sentence first, it was at last concluded that the phrase a free synod in the royal edict carries with it and includes the power of judging all questions that may be raised concerning the constitution, membership, or business to be treated in the synod.

units.la: 4. De restitutione arcium regiarum, prout ingenue illud in se receperunt subditi, ita non celarunt quod ad regni incolumitatem pertineret ad parlamentum referendum esse, quando supplicibus literis sereniss. regi postulata sua offerrent: Addiderunt etiam rationem habendam esse sumptuum in arcibus illis muniendis & custodiendis.
units.tr: 4. Concerning the restitution of the royal fortresses, the subjects, while frankly accepting this point, did not conceal that whatever pertained to the safety of the kingdom had to be referred to Parliament when they presented their petitions to the most serene king. They added also that account must be taken of the expenses of fortifying and garrisoning those fortresses.

units.la: 5. In restitutionem bonorum, & aliorum interceptorum, consensum fuit, modo debita nostra in publicum usum contracta ab omnibus pariter dissolverentur, quod aliter fieri non poterit quam speciali regis mandato, aut authoritate parlamentaria. Et cum à nobis objectum fuisset, quædam bona fuisse dispersa & hactenus consumpta; sereniss. regem respondisse, restitutionem intelligendam esse de bonis quæ adhuc supersint.
units.tr: 5. As to the restitution of goods and of other things seized, it was agreed that our debts, contracted for public use, should be discharged equally by all. This could not be done except by a special mandate of the king or by parliamentary authority. When we objected that some goods had been dispersed and hitherto consumed, the most serene king replied that restitution was to be understood of the goods that still remained.

units.la: 6. Quum objiceretur à nobis, præjudicare regem legitimæ constitutioni liberæ synodi, quia in priori hujus edicti forma synodum Glasguensem repudiare se dixisset propter multas rationes, quæ prioribus suis edictis comprehenderentur, inter quas fuerunt illæ contra seniores, eorumque in synodis suffragia: Regem clausulam illam tandem expunxisse.
units.tr: 6.
