When we objected that the king was prejudicing the lawful constitution of a free synod, because in the earlier form of this edict he had said he repudiated the Glasgow synod for many reasons, which were set out in his earlier edicts, among them those against the elders and their votes in synods, the king at last struck out that clause.

units.la: 7. Itidem cum objiceretur à nobis, phrasibus quibusdam in declaratione regia inserta registris synodi Glasguensis, præsupponi Episcopatus continuationem; videl. dum dicitur, initiandos ministerii functione in nullum aliud juramentum adigendos esse quam quod statutis parlamenti continetur, &, Episcopos subjici censuræ nationalis Synodi; cumque illa approbare neutiquam nos posse dixisfemus[?],utpote, quod Episcopatum præsupponerent, Confessioni fidei & constitutionibus ecclesiasticis adversantem: Visum regi fuit utramque illam clausulam delere.
units.tr: 7. Likewise, when we objected that certain phrases inserted in the royal declaration, drawn from the records of the Glasgow synod, presupposed the continuation of episcopacy, namely where it is said that men entering the ministry are to be bound by no other oath than what is contained in the statutes of parliament, and that bishops are subject to the censure of the national synod; and when we said that we could by no means approve those things, since they presupposed episcopacy, which is opposed to the Confession of faith and the ecclesiastical constitutions: it seemed good to the king to delete both those clauses.

units.la: 8. Cum, 15. Iunii, submisse urgeremus, ut tot fidelium subditorum votis rex fereniss. satisfacere dignaretur, declarando se nolle urgere Episcopatum; respondisse regem; In primis nostris postulatis hoc non fuisse comprehensum: Nobis vero instantibus, primis nostris postulatis, quibus synodi Glasguensis sanctionem petebamus, hoc contineri; Regem agnovisse; Ita quidem rem se habere, neque se illud adhuc aperte denegasse, verum de ea re mature deliberaturum intra biduum: Atque cum die illo condicto idem urgeremus, ac dilucide demonstraremus, si vellet Episcopatum in hac ecclesia mordicus retinere, laboraturam ecclesiam schismate, regnum divisionibus & factionibus quibus remedium adhiberi non posset; Contra vero, si regnum & ecclesiam abEpiscopatu liberaret, eam sinceram, promptam, ac submissam obedientiam ab omnibus omnino subditis præstitum iri, qua major à nullis exspectari posset: Respondisse regem serenissi. Non debere nec posse se suffragii sui libertati praejudicare : Indictam esse a se liberam synodum, quae de ecclesiasticis omnibus causis cognosceret, statueret, ac judicaret ; cujus decreta in parlamento sanciturus esset.
units.tr: 8. On 15 June we urged humbly that the most serene king deign to satisfy the wishes of so many faithful subjects by declaring that he did not wish to insist on episcopacy. The king replied that this was not included in our first demands. But when we insisted that our first demands, in which we sought the sanction of the Glasgow synod, did contain this, the king acknowledged that it was so, and that he had not yet openly denied it, but would deliberate on the matter maturely within two days. On that appointed day we pressed the same point and clearly showed that if he wished to retain episcopacy stubbornly in this church, the church would be troubled by schism and the kingdom by divisions and factions for which no remedy could be applied; on the contrary, if he freed the kingdom and the church from episcopacy, sincere, prompt and submissive obedience would be rendered by all subjects without exception, such as no greater obedience could be expected to give. The most serene king replied that he ought not and could not prejudice the freedom of his vote: he had himself summoned a free synod, which would take cognisance of, decide and judge all ecclesiastical causes, and whose decrees he would sanction in Parliament.

units.la: In majorem etiam cautelam foederati frequentissimo omnis generis & ordinis sociorum suorum conventu convocato, ne quis acceptationem hujus edicti regi detorqueret in alienum sensum, quasi synodo Glasguensi renunciarent, aut priores suas actiones ut illegitimas damnarent, scriptum consignarunt, quod de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: For greater caution, the confederates called a very full assembly of their allies of every kind and rank, so that no one might twist the acceptance of this edict by the king into an alien sense, as if they renounced the Glasgow synod or condemned their earlier actions as illegitimate. They signed a document which, translated almost word for word, reads as follows.

units.la: Ne declaratio & edictum regium quo respondetur humilibus nostris postulatis serenissi. nostro regi per deputatos nostros oblatis ; non recte accipiatur a probis, aut ab iniquioribus in alienum sensum detorqueatur, quo serenissi. regis aequitas & clementia supprimantur, aut fideles subditi quidpiam commisse aut nunc admisse videantur, quod solenni cum Deo foederi ac juramento adversetur: Exercitus Generalis, Nobiles, Barones, Cives, Pastores, & cohortium Ductores ante dimissum exercitum convenientes, pernecessarium judicavimus scripto consignare quod a deputatis nostris relatum fuit: videl. regem serenissi. iis significasse; licet non posset ratam habere & agnoscere nuperam synodum Nationalem Glasguensem, unde est quod in edicto illo Pseudo-Synodus vocetur: subditorum tamen acceptationem hujus edicti a se non intelligi, quasi synodo illi abrenunciarent, aut actiones suas praecedentes condemnarent ut tumultuosas, illegitimas, arrogantes, pertinaces. Quare, uti enixe rogamus, ut omnes regis serenissi. fideles subditi, submissis ac gratis animis agnoscant ac confiteantur singularem regis fereniff. gratiam, indicendo liberam synodum Nationalem ad 6. Augufti, & parlamentum ad ejusdem mensis diem vigefimum, ad sanciendum synodi decreta; quod proprium & efficacissimum medium est procurandæ & stabiliendæ pacis ecclesiasticæ & politicæ: Ita etiam iisdem notum facimus, ne acceptatione edicti & articulorum pacificationis annexorum, ullo pacto renuncient aut repudient prædictam synodum, verum sciant fe adhuc teneri ut eidem synodo obtemperent, ac tueantur; Atque ut omnibus detorfionibus obviam eatur; Innotescat & significetur hoc omnibus, ubicunque regium edictum promulgabitur. Etenim sicuti hanc regis nostri esse sententiam fæpius ipse deputatis nostris aperuit, ita nobis abunde persuasum est, sic confultum fore honori regis, acpiorum votis, & beatam hanc pacificationem promotunt[?] iri: Quæ ardentissimis precibus Deo Opt: Maxim: quam commedatiffima facere omnes decet: &ad mentem ferio revocare nuperum & folenne noftrum cum Deo fœdus; ut eo digni incedamus ac inveniamur: Deum etiam obsecrandum esse ut fynodi hujus & parlamenti opera, religio & justitia in hoc regno stabiliantur.
units.tr: Lest the declaration and royal edict in reply to our humble petitions, offered to our most serene king through our deputies, be wrongly taken by the upright or twisted by the less scrupulous into a sense foreign to it, so that the equity and clemency of the most serene king are suppressed, or faithful subjects seem to have committed, or now to admit, anything contrary to their solemn covenant and oath with God: the General Army, Nobles, Barons, Citizens, Ministers and captains of cohorts, meeting before the army was dismissed, judged it most necessary to set down in writing what had been reported by our deputies. Namely, that the most serene king had signified to them that, although he could not ratify and acknowledge the recent National Synod of Glasgow, whence it is that in that edict it is called a pseudo-synod, nevertheless the subjects' acceptance of this edict was not to be understood by him as if they renounced that synod or condemned their previous actions as tumultuous, illegitimate, arrogant and obstinate. Wherefore we earnestly ask that all the most serene king's faithful subjects, with submissive and willing minds, acknowledge and confess the singular grace of the king in calling a free National Synod for 6 August, and a Parliament for the twentieth day of the same month, to sanction the decrees of the synod. This is the proper and most effective means of procuring and establishing ecclesiastical and civil peace. Thus we also make known to the same people that, in accepting the edict and the articles of pacification annexed to it, they must in no way renounce or repudiate the aforesaid synod; rather, let them know that they are still bound to obey and defend that synod. And so that every twisting may be forestalled, let this be known and declared to all, wherever the royal edict is published. For just as our king himself has often revealed to our deputies that this is his opinion, so we are fully persuaded that it will be thus consulted for the honour of the king, will promote the wishes of the godly and this blessed pacification. All ought most earnestly to commend this to God, the Best and Greatest, with prayers, and to call to mind our recent and solemn covenant with God, that we may walk worthily of it and be found so. God is also to be entreated that through the labours of this synod and parliament, religion and justice may be established in this kingdom.

units.la: Tandem edictum seu declaratio hæc regia in Scotorum castris promulgatur 18. Iunii à supremo feciali regio, præfente Comite Mortonio, Vernejo & Boroughbio splendidis Equitibus Anglis à rege ad id deputatis: Cafiliffæ Comes, nomine totius exercitus Scotici ac reliquorum libertatis ecclesiasticæ vindicum, submissas fereniff. regi gratias referebat, quod dignaretur subditis suis fidelibus eatenus gratificari; ac simul addebat, spem omnes certam fovere, Dei bona gratia, fereniff. Regem meliorem opinionem de synodo Nationali Glafguenfi, & subditorum fidelitate, brevi conceptarum[?], quam quæ in declaratione illa expressa effet: Se cum sociis synodo illi adhærere ac fœderi, quæ sine horrendo perjurio abnegare non possent: Et simul feciali obtulit quod in frequentissimo conventu consignatum fuisse statim diximus. Atque cum eadem declaratio regia Edinburgi promulgata fuisset denuo, eandem repetiit D.Lindesius, Baro Parlamentarius.
units.tr: Finally, this royal edict or declaration was published in the Scottish camp on 18 June by the chief royal herald, in the presence of the Earl of Morton, Vernon and Borough, splendid English knights deputed for this purpose by the king. The Earl of Cassillis, in the name of the whole Scottish army and of the other defenders of ecclesiastical liberty, returned submissive thanks to the most serene king that he deigned thus far to favour his faithful subjects; and at the same time he added that everyone cherished the certain hope, by God's good grace, that the most serene king would soon form a better opinion of the national synod of Glasgow and of his subjects' loyalty than that expressed in that declaration. He and his allies adhered to that synod and to the covenant, which they could not renounce without horrible perjury. At the same time he offered to the herald what we said had been signed at the most crowded assembly. And when the same royal declaration was published again at Edinburgh, Lindesey, the Parliamentary Baron, repeated the same.

units.la: Prout conventum fuit, ad dimissionem exercitus se accingunt Scoti: multorum opinio fuit Regem ad eorum castra venturum, sed quibus consiliis non advenerit, varia fuerunt hominum judicia: hoc certum, fœderatis omnibus nihil magis in votis fuisse, quam ut in conspectu serenissi. sui regis atroces illas calumnias spreti regiminis Monarchici, reipsa refutarent, & arma sua, quæ inviti admodum induerant, ut vim armatam contra se arcerent, coram clementissimo suo Rege lubentes deponerent; nunquam assumenda nisi in Regis, Religionis, & patriæ Libertatis nunc denuo pactæ defensionem.
units.tr: As agreed, the Scots prepared to dismiss their army. Many thought the king would come to their camp, but why he did not come, opinions varied. This much is certain: nothing was more in the wishes of the confederates than to refute in fact, in the sight of their most serene king, those atrocious calumnies of a despotic monarchical rule, and gladly to lay down before their most clement king the arms which they had reluctantly taken up to ward off armed force against themselves. These arms were never to be taken up except in the defence of the king, of religion, and of the liberty of the country, now pledged anew.

units.la: Nobiles Angli & cohortium ductores frequentissimi accurrebant; & omnibus, (non sine calumniatorum[?] infamia, & diras in eorum capita execrationes etiam per gregarios Anglos milites) evidenter perspectum fuit, fœderatos Scotos privatis odiis non litasse, neque de præda aut tollendis inimicis cogitasse; aut de augenda re familiari, (nam nulla vox audita fuit in universo tractatu pacificationis, ex qua privatis commodis studuisse fœderatorum capita, vel suspicacissima ingenia colligere potuerant, quod alibi in ejusmodi motibus fieri consuevit:) sed omnia eorum studia de solido religionis statu, pace ac æquitate publica ordinanda fuisse: Qui præsentes aderant, uno ore testabuntur, utramque gentem nunquam amplioribus mutuæ necessitudinis officiis amice se invicem complexam fuisse : quam fœlicem concordiam perennet Dominus.
units.tr: English nobles and captains of cohorts flocked together in great numbers, and it was clearly seen by all (not without infamy for the slanderers, and dire curses against their heads even from the English common soldiers) that the confederate Scots had not sacrificed to private hatreds, nor thought of plunder or of removing enemies, nor of increasing their household wealth. No word was heard throughout the whole treaty of pacification from which the leaders of the confederates, or the most suspicious minds, could gather that they had pursued private advantage, as is usually done in such movements elsewhere. Rather, all their efforts were directed to the solid ordering of the state of religion, public peace and equity. Those who were present will testify with one voice that the two nations never embraced one another more friendly, with greater offices of mutual kindness. May the Lord make that happy concord everlasting.

units.la: Cæterum 20. Junij die condicto Scotorum exercitus dimittitur, & singuli pacatis agminibus ad sua redierunt, læti sine sanguine & cæde tam ingentes motus compositos fuisse, ac Deum laudantes qui belli jacruentum hunc exitum dedisset. Eorum exercitus licet apparatu Equitatus Anglis inferior diceretur, Equorum tamen numero & Equitum fortitudine æquavit: peditatus vero longe superior tam numero quam animis referebatur, utpote qui constaret viginti millibus militum ex flore juventutis vicinarum tantum Angliæ provinciarum, & quotidie advolabant novæ legiones, ita ut dimisso exercitui & domum redeunti sæpius obviam venerint. Omnibus de belli æquitate ac necessitate persuasum fuit, & commeatus abunde suppetebat: Animos etiam addebat, probata ducum rei militaris peritia, & fortitudo ac fœlicitas, quarum frequentia specimina adhuc celebrare poterit Germania, cuius libertati contra superbam & impotentem Austriaco-Hispanicam tyrannidem afferendæ, sub fœliciffimorum Suecorum signis antehac sese devoverant, iisque piis conatibus immorituri suissent, nisi patriæ periclitanti, filiorum suorum auxilia tempore tam necessario advocanti, accurrissent.
units.tr: Meanwhile, on the appointed day, 20 June, the Scottish army was disbanded. The companies went home in peace, glad that such great disturbances had been settled without bloodshed or slaughter, and praising God for giving this bloodless end to the war. Their army was said to be inferior to the English in cavalry equipment, but it matched them in the number of horses and the strength of its horsemen. The infantry, however, was reported to be far superior both in numbers and in spirit, since it consisted of twenty thousand men drawn from the flower of youth in the neighbouring English provinces alone. New companies were flying in every day, so that they often met them on the road as the army was disbanded and returning home. Everyone was persuaded of the justice and necessity of the war, and supplies were plentiful. Their spirits were also raised by the proven military skill of their commanders, and by their courage and good fortune, of which Germany can still show many examples. Germany had earlier vowed itself under the banners of the most fortunate Swedes to win back its liberty from the proud and overbearing Austro-Spanish tyranny, and would have perished in those pious endeavours had its sons not hurried to the aid of their country when it was in danger and called for their help at so necessary a time.

units.la: Dum hæc ad limites & confinia regnorum agerentur, in Borealibus Scotiæ provinciis vice-comes Boinius, adeptus post secundam fugam peritos aliquot belli duces, & apparatum bellicum Berwico cum navibus transmissum, captata Montis Rosarum & Mareschalli absentia, magnas turbas movet, & ducem se factioni exhibet; ad quem convolarunt omnes regiarum partium, ex quibus speciem quandam exercitus confecit, præsertim si numerus & copiarum ductores soli numerarentur : Et horum quidam cum omnem spem suam in celeritate ponerent , magnis itineribus in Auftraliores Merniæ & Angusiæ acTaithiæ provincias contendendum esse suadebant , ut foederatos sub ductu Montis Rosarum & cæt. vel incautos & nihil sinistri metuentes ex improviso opprimerent , aut apparatum saltem bellicum in vicinis oppidis interciperent : Quod factu sibi haud difficile judicabant ; Nisi magno animo prædicti Comites cum suis obviam eis venissent , quorum adventu usque adeo terrebantur Boniæ vice-comes cum suis, ut , mutato priori consilio, ingenti terrore cogerentur ad antiquas latebras confugere , & ut tutius laterent, cum ad Deæ fluminis, ( quod Abredoniam præterlabitur, ) pontem venissent, eundem obstruunt; & dispositis in ripa cohortibus , transitum foederatis prohibere conantur : sed frustra, quippe foederati post paucorum horarum moram , pontem obstructum admotis majoribus machinis intercipiunt , & qui non ita pridem triumphum ante victoriam canebant, ad latebras & tutam fugam,quanta celeritate possent,circumspiciunt , & Abredoniam , foederatorum arbitrio denuo exponunt, qui eam statim interceperunt: Commodum certe Abredonensibus tum fuit , quod celeri nuncio, Montis Rosarum & Marefchalli Comites de icta pace certiores facti sunt , nam alioqui verendum fuisset, ne clementia illa quam, toties experti fuerant , & qua se toties indignos reddiderunt cives quidam Abredonenses ( nam omnibus omnino civibus instabilis hæc mutabilitas imputari non potuit ; quippe quod eorum quidam, licet cum manifesto vitæ & fortunarum periculo, reliquis foederatis serio se olim adjunxerant ; neque fidem datam corruperunt ) in justam iram verteretur, quandoquidem, ne ignem in tecta ipsa conjicerent, difficulter detinebantur milites fœderati; sed ducum authoritate, & pacis certo nuncio asperiora illa consilia & conatus impediebantur. In omnibus illis motibus nihil humani sanguinis effundebatur, præterquam in hoc ad Deæ pontem conflictu, ubi duo fœderati desiderati sunt, sed ex altera parte plus minus quinquaginta, & complures vulneratiinter quos Ionstonus quidam tribunus, vir acris & expediti ingenii.
units.tr: While these events were taking place on the borders and frontiers of the kingdoms, in the northern provinces of Scotland Viscount Aboyne, who after his second flight had gathered some experienced commanders and a store of war supplies brought across from Berwick by ship, took advantage of the absence of Montrose and the Marischal to stir up great disorder and presented himself as leader of the faction. All the men of the royal party flocked to him, and from them he formed something like an army, especially if one counted only the numbers and the commanders of the forces. Some of these men, placing all their hope in speed, urged that they should march with great haste into the more northerly provinces of the Mearns, Angus and Strathtay, and attack the confederates under Montrose and the others, either unprepared and fearing no harm, or at least seize the war supplies in the nearby towns. They judged this not difficult to do. But the earls named above met them in person with their men, and at their coming Aboyne and his followers were so terrified that, changing his earlier plan, he was forced by great fear to retreat to his old hiding places. To hide more safely, they reached the bridge over the River Dee, which flows past Aberdeen, and blocked it. Posting their companies along the bank, they tried to keep the confederates from crossing. But in vain. After a delay of a few hours the confederates brought up heavier siege engines, broke through the obstructed bridge, and those who not long before had been singing of triumph before victory now looked about, as fast as they could, for hiding places and a safe escape. They left Aberdeen again at the discretion of the confederates, who at once took possession of it. It was certainly fortunate for the people of Aberdeen that they were informed by swift messenger of the peace agreed with the Earls of Montrose and the Marischal. Otherwise it would have been feared that some of the citizens of Aberdeen, who had so often experienced that mercy and had so often proved themselves unworthy of it, might have turned the confederates' just anger against them. The confederate soldiers were with difficulty restrained from setting fire to the houses themselves, and only the authority of the commanders and the certain news of peace prevented those harsher plans and attempts. (It cannot be laid to the charge of all the citizens that they were so unstable; for some of them had earlier joined the other confederates in earnest, at manifest risk to their lives and property, and had not broken their pledged faith.) In all these disturbances no human blood was shed, except in this clash at the bridge over the Dee, where two confederates were missed, but on the other side more or less fifty were lost, and many were wounded, among them a certain Johnstone, a tribune, a man of keen and ready wit.

units.la: Motibus sic compositis, ac arcibus regiis cum intercepto apparatu bellico qui adhuc supererat, regi traditis, & Scotorum exercitu dimisso; magnus eos incessit metus, nam cohortes regiæ in limitibus hærebant, & magno præsidiariorum numero instruebantur Berwicum & Carleolum, urbes quidem ditionis Angliæ, sed in ipsis Scotiæ limitibus sitæ; Indictio synodi procrastinabatur; arcis Edinburgenæ custodia perito belli duci committebatur, ac multo commeatu & apparatu muniebatur, Rex etiam serenissim: Berwici adhuc hærebat; & eo evocaverat decem & quatuor primarios confœderatorum, ut cum iis de rebus maximi momenti ageret; ac licet qui in vicinia hærebant, Nobiles fœderati statim advolarent, & sociorum suorum absentiam excusarent, renuisse tamen regem (referebatur) cum illis agere, sed omnium exspectare adventum, ac tum de sua voluntate prolixius omnes simul intellecturos esse: Magnarum suspicionum ansam hæc & plura hujus generis fœderatis præbebant, & gravius aliquid subesse multorum fuit opinio: etenim cum pauciores numero, & minoris dignitatis totum pacificationis negotium antea absolvissent, quorsum jam multo plures evocarentur, præsertim selecta fœderatorum capita? & veteres historias in mentem revocabant; neque novum esse differebant, in minimis fidem præstruere ut postea cum operæ pretiū erit majori cum momento fallas: Atque eo usque prævaluit hic metus, ut duos solummodo ex quatuordecim evocatis selectos Berwicum ad regem remitterent, cum diserta & expressa reliquorum excusatione; quod sereniff. regi ingratum fuisse, multa postea prodiderunt: Duobus tamen illis significavit, sibi tunc integrum non fuisse in Scotiam venire; ut Synodo & parlamento prout apud se constituisset, adesset, alia quædam magni momenti negotia Londini tractanda esse, quæ suam præsentiam requirerent, prout reginæ & senatus sui literis monitus fuit: Deputatum tamen suo nomine qui promissa præstaret, missurum. Alia etiam quædam negotia quæ ad pacem stabiliendam conducere credebantur, pertractata fuere; & Regi tum ostensum, penes fœderatos non esse munitiones Lethæ demoliri, Edinburgenis asserentibus, licere sibi per privilegia sua, Letham'ditionis suæ oppidum, & portum munire: vim etiam & injuriam Comiti Traquario, regni Thesaurario à fæce vulgi aut procacibus mulieribus illatam diligenter excusabant, & per magistratum Edenburgenum non stetisse quominus in reos inquireretur ac levere animadverteretur, quandoquidem Thesaurarius ipse judicaret haud futurum è re sereniff. Regis aut pacis publicæ, si strictius inquisitio instituta fuisset; horum nomine injuriam hanc se levius ferre. Denique nihil intentatum reliquerunt fœderatorum deputati, quo regis sereniffimi animo scrupulos omnes eximerent, ne fœderatos reos aut conscios fuisse aut futuros judicaret cujuslibet facti quo fides Regi data corrumperetur; ipsorumque responsionibus judicatum fuit sereniffimum Regem acquievisse.
units.tr: With the disturbances thus settled, the royal castles were handed over to the king together with the war supplies that still remained, and the Scottish army was disbanded. Yet great fear seized the confederates. For royal cohorts remained on the frontiers, and Berwick and Carlisle, towns indeed under the jurisdiction of England but situated on the very borders of Scotland, were being strongly garrisoned with large numbers of troops. The calling of the synod was delayed. The keeping of Edinburgh Castle was entrusted to an experienced commander and fortified with abundant supplies and equipment. The king himself still remained at Berwick, and had summoned there fourteen of the leading confederates to discuss matters of the greatest importance with them. Although the confederate nobles who were nearby hastened at once to join them and excused the absence of their colleagues, it is reported that the king refused to deal with those present, insisting instead on waiting for all to arrive, when he would make his will known more fully to all together. These and many similar things gave the confederates grounds for great suspicion, and many held the opinion that something more serious lay beneath. For the entire settlement of the pacification had earlier been concluded by fewer men, of lower rank, so why were so many more now summoned, especially the chosen leaders of the confederates? They called to mind older histories and said it was nothing new to lay a foundation of trust in small matters so that later, when it would be worth the effort, one might deceive them in greater ones. This fear prevailed to such an extent that they sent back to the king at Berwick only two of the fourteen summoned, with an explicit and definite excuse for the rest. The most serene king was not pleased with this, as many later reported. Yet he told those two that it was not then in his power to come to Scotland; that other matters of great importance had to be dealt with in London, which required his presence, as he had been warned by letters from the queen and his council. Nevertheless he would send a deputy in his name to carry out the promises. Some other matters thought to be conducive to establishing peace were also discussed, and it was pointed out to the king that the confederates were not to demolish the fortifications of Leith, since the people of Edinburgh asserted that by their privileges they were entitled to fortify Leith, a town and port within their jurisdiction. The confederates also carefully excused the violence and injury done to the Earl of Traquair, the Lord Treasurer, by the dregs of the populace or by insolent women, and claimed that it was not the fault of the magistrates of Edinburgh that the offenders were not searched out and punished severely, since the Treasurer himself judged that a stricter inquiry would be neither in the interest of the most serene king nor of the public peace; on these grounds they bore this injury more lightly. Finally, the deputies of the confederates left nothing untried by which to remove from the most serene king's mind all scruples, so that he might not judge that the confederates had been, or would be, parties or accomplices in any act by which the faith pledged to the king might be broken. And by their answers it was judged that the most serene King had acquiesced.

units.la: Interea indicitur mandato regio ipsis Iulii calendis synodus Nationalis, mandatum Archiepiscopis, Episcopis, ecclesiarum deputatis & aliis quibuscunque jus suffragii in synodo habentibus, ut Edinburgum ad duodecimum Augusti diem in synodum Nationalem coirent, & cæt.Fœderati sæpius instabant, ut nulla in literis indictionis Archiepiscoporum & Episcoporum fieret mentio; utpote, cum nullos tali potestate præditos in ecclesia Scotica agnoscerent; cumque illud obtinere non potuissent contra protestantur, ne silentio suo (ut loquebantur) præsules synodi membra agnoscere viderentur: & sic rei essent violati juramenti detuenda synodo Glasguensi, qua ministrorum verbi imparitas ab ecclesia exulare jubetur, & præsules ipsi variis censuris ecclesiasticis notantur; Atque licet hanc synodum ratam habere noluerit serenis. rex ; tamen (inquiunt) deputatis fœderatorum in castris suis professum fuisse, nolle se cogere aut urgere fœderatos subditos suos synodum illam repudiare, ideoque mandasse ut sententiæ illæ in declaratione sua nupera pacificatoria expungerentur, quæ secum ferrent approbationem Episcopatus aut episcoporum. Quare protestantur & declarant.
units.tr: Meanwhile, by royal command, a National Synod was called for the first day of July, with a mandate to the archbishops, bishops, deputies of the churches and all others who had a right to vote in the synod, that they should assemble at Edinburgh for the National Synod on the twelfth day of August, and so on. The confederates repeatedly urged that no mention of archbishops and bishops be made in the letters of summons, since they did not acknowledge any men endowed with such authority in the Scottish Church. When they could not obtain this, they protested that by their silence (as they put it) the prelates would seem to acknowledge them as members of the synod. Thus they would be guilty of breaking their oath, which bound them to the Glasgow synod, by which the inequality of the ministers of the Word is banished from the Church, and the prelates themselves are branded with various ecclesiastical censures. And although the most serene king was unwilling to ratify that synod, they say that his deputies professed in their camp that he did not wish to compel or press his subjects, the confederates, to repudiate that synod; and therefore he had ordered that the sentences which carried the approval of the episcopacy or the bishops be struck out of his recent pacifying declaration. Wherefore they protest and declare as follows.

units.la: 1. Synodum illam Glasguensem fuisse legitimam, plenam & liberam synodum Nationalem: omnibusque ipsius decretis, præsertim vero quæ contra Episcopatum & Episcopos sunt, obtemperandum esse ab omnibus fœderatis, 2. Fœdus suum cum Deo esse legitimum, cui adhærent. 3. Præsules illos ecclesiasticis censuris merito notatos fuisse, & usurpatione titulorum condemnatorum pervicaciam suam prodere, calumniis improbis serenis. regem contra fideles suos subditos incitasse, & malorum omnium quæ hactenus perpessi essent, incendiarios fuisse; ideoque reversuros, ab omnibus habendos esse, quo loco Christus Ethnicos & publicanos & anathemate notatos haberi jusserit: præsententemque hanc eorum citationem per literas indictionis nihil juris eis in synodo afferre. 4. Quandoquidem regis mandato imperetur collegio justitiae, ut tempore tam importuno judicia exercerent, declarare se, omnes sententias in foro illo serendas hoc tempore nullas esse, cum ex legum praescripto quadraginta dierum citatio praecederet; quod tempus observari nequit: neque subditis causas in hoc foro acturis vacare possit, scripta & causarum documenta quae in locis tutioribus in motuum horum fervore reposuerunt custodienda depromere; cum privatis & domesticis suis negotiis aliquantisper consulere cogantur, quae praeparationibus ad religionem & patriam suam defendendam distenti, mensibus hisce elapsis prorsus neglexerunt.
units.tr: 1. That the Glasgow Synod was a lawful, full and free National Synod, and that all its decrees, especially those against Episcopacy and the bishops, must be obeyed by all the Covenanters. 2. That their Covenant with God is lawful, and that they adhere to it. 3. That those prelates were rightly marked with ecclesiastical censures, and by usurping condemned titles they show their obstinacy; that by wicked calumnies they incited the most serene king against his faithful subjects, and were the firebrands of all the evils suffered until now; and therefore, since they will not repent, they are to be held by all as Christ commanded that heathens and tax-collectors be held, and as those under anathema. And that this present citation of them by letters of summons gives them no right in the Synod. 4. Since the king's command orders the college of justice to exercise judicial functions at so untimely a time, they declare that all sentences to be passed in that court at this time are null, since by the prescription of the laws a forty days' citation must precede them; and this period cannot be observed. Nor can subjects who are to plead causes in that court have leisure to bring out the writings and case documents which, in the heat of these disturbances, they have put away in safer places to be kept; since they are forced to attend for a while to their private and domestic affairs, which, being occupied with preparations to defend their religion and country, they have completely neglected these past months.

units.la: Historica narratio Synodi Nationalis Edin- burgi coactæ.
units.tr: Historical narrative of the National Synod convened at Edinburgh.

units.la: EX praescripto edicti regii Edinburgum convenerunt ecclesiarum deputati ad synodum Nationalem, quae 12. Augusti aperta fuit: Ubi pro recepta consuetudine proximae synodi praeses, ad Deum precibus & oratione ad synodum, sessionem primam auspicatus est: omnesque monuit, ut literas fidei scribae traderent; quo facto sessio illa dimissa fuit.
units.tr: In accordance with the prescription of the royal edict, the deputies of the churches gathered at Edinburgh for the National Synod, which was opened on 12 August. There, according to the custom received from the previous synod, the moderator, with prayers and an address to the synod, began the first session, and he admonished all to hand their letters of faith to the clerk; when this was done, that session was dismissed.

units.la: Sessione secunda, Iohannes Stuartus Traquariae Comes, supremus regni Thesaurarius, Deputatus regius ad synodum, deputationis suae literas praelegendas tradidit, ac synodi registris inferendas: Observatum fuit in literis illis, sereniss. regem hisce formalibus verbis absentiam suam excusasse: Quod gravissimis maximique momenti negotiis reditum in Angliam urgentibus impediretur: Plenam tamen potestatem se concedere praedicto deputato omnia in synodo peragendi: Sicut nos facere potuissemus, si in nostra sacratissima persona adessemus, secundum ecclesiæ consuetudinem, legesque prædicti antiqui nostri regni. Dein quinque pastorum nomina à præside, synodo proposita fuerunt, ex quibus novum præsidem eligeret synodus, plurimorumque suffragiis electus fuit David Dicsonus, pastor magni nominis, qui provinciam capessens, superioris synodi Præsidi Alexandro Henderson publico nomine gratias egit, & oratione ad synodum conversa, scopum quo omnium tunc studia collimare deberent, proponit.
units.tr: In the second session, John Stewart, Earl of Traquair, the chief treasurer of the kingdom and the royal commissioner to the synod, handed over his letters of commission to be read out and entered in the registers of the synod. It was observed in those letters that the most serene king excused his absence with these formal words: because he was hindered by the most grave and weighty matters, which urged his return to England; yet he granted full power to the said commissioner to conduct everything in the synod, as we could have done, had we been present in our most sacred person, according to the custom of the church and the laws of our ancient kingdom. Then the moderator proposed to the synod five names of ministers, from whom the synod was to choose a new moderator, and David Dickson, a minister of great name, was elected by the votes of the greater part. Taking up the office, he thanked Alexander Henderson, the moderator of the previous synod, in the public name, and, turning his address to the synod, he set forth the aim at which all their efforts ought then to be directed.

units.la: Cum prælegerentur delegatorum fiduciariæ li-teræ, rogati sæpius sunt omnes, ut si quid haberent quod objicerent, statim proferrent, alioqui silentium pro approbatione à synodo acceptum iri.; Cumque nullus prodiret qui in specie contrà quemlibet deputatum aut literas fidei quidvis exciperet, Declaratum fuit, synodum completam ac rite formatam esse.
units.tr: When the commissions of the delegates were read out, all were often asked, if they had anything to object, to bring it forward at once, otherwise silence would be taken as approval by the synod. And since no one came forward who raised any specific objection against any deputy or letter of faith, it was declared that the synod was complete and duly constituted.

units.la: Sessione quarta, inter omnia subditorum gravamina quæ hisce motibus occasionem & causam præbuerunt, seu vere seu secus (inquit deputatus regius) quædam sunt quæ rex serenifs.[?] edictis suis hactenus abrogavit; quibus excutiendis frustra nunc insudabitur, duo tantum, suo judicio, restare excutienda: Personalia videl. Episcoporum crimina olim objecta: ac regem velle ut in ea legitime inquireretur: & Episcopatum ipsum: atque hic mature & serio perpendendum omnibus esse, Regem serenifs.[?] cum in ea ecclesia educatus sit in qua approbaretur, solidas rationes exspectare, quid sibi de eo statuendum sit in hac ecclesia: Quare Synodo dandam operam esse, ut regi Serenissimo satisfiat. Ejus orationem excepit præses, & Ecclesiarum gravamina recensuit, quæ videlicet fuerunt.
units.tr: In the fourth session, among all the grievances of the subjects which gave occasion and cause for these disturbances, whether truly or otherwise (said the royal commissioner), there are some which the king has hitherto removed by his edicts; in examining them, labour will now be spent in vain. In his judgement only two remain to be examined: namely, the personal crimes of the bishops once objected, and the king's wish that inquiry be legally made into them; and Episcopacy itself. And here, he said, everyone must weigh the matter early and seriously, since the most serene king, having been brought up in that church in which it was approved, expects solid reasons for what is to be decided about it in this church. Therefore the synod must take care to satisfy the most serene king. The moderator answered his speech and recounted the grievances of the churches, which were these:

units.la: 1. Nationalium synodorum legitime formatarum per annos complures defectus. 2. Approbatio & sanctio synodorum corruptarum, ac non rite formatarum, quales fuerunt, binæ Limnuchenses, Glasguensis, Abredoniana, Andreapolitana, Perthana. 3. Severa obtrusio quinque articulorum Perthensium. 4. Et libri liturgici, ac Canonum, cum curia celsæ commissionis. 5. Violatio fœderis Nationalis cum Deo solenniter sanciti. 6. Episcopatus. 7. Ecclesiasticorum politica munia, ac Episcoporum in synodos & omnes conventus ecclesiasticos tyrannis. Hisce (inquit) mala omnia nostra imputamus; Deumque cordium nostrorum scrutatorem testamur, nobis semper propositum fuisse, regem nostrum sereniss. colere, ejusque mandatis legitimis ex præscripto legum obtemperare, quicquid contra obloquuti sint ac calumnientur adversarii nostri, nam licet reges omnes Christo Dei filio subditos esse agnoscamus, ac quicquid ejus gloriæ ac regno adversetur, eliminandum[?] censeamus; si tam charum nobis esset quam oculus dexter, tam utile ac necessarium quam dextra manus: politicas tamen potestates, utpote à Deo ordinatas, reges & in eminentia constitutos nostro bono, ulla injuria aut contumelia affici nunquam patiemur. Respondit deputatus regius, synodum hanc à rege sereniss. indictam ut mature & in timore domini perpenderent, an hæc omnia ita sese habeant, hoc est, an hæc vera & sola sint ecclesiarum gravamina? Si demonstretur vera & justa esse, ut ex ecclesiis removeantur, sin minus, æquum esse ut adhuc obtineant: verbi gratia (inquit) si Episcopatus sit inter justas & veras causas gravaminum, tum ostendendum erit adversari constitutionibus hujus ecclesiæ: & sic de cæteris. Conditionem hanc Synodi nomine accepit Præses, ac in se recepit, fynodum liquido & ad oculum demonstraturam; ab ipsis reformationis primordiis, ecclesiae Scoticae semper propositum fuisse, Episcopatum profligare, & Apostolico ecclesiae regimini per synodos, & Classes adhaerere: Radices etiam ipsas Episcopatus & omnes ejus fibras foeliciter convulsisse, quae licet saepius postea pullulaverint & succreverint, sup-pressas tamen purioribus temporibus semper fuisse, cum primum capita exererent. Caeterum ut ab intricatis disputationibus abstineretur, monebat deputatus regius consultissimum sibi videri, si ex authenticis synodorum regiistris extracta praelegerentur, quae in hanc rem facerent: Sed quae-stio fuit à quo anno incipiendum esset: aliis instantibus ut ab anno 1560, quando religio reformata publica authoritate sancita fuit; aliis ve-ro urgentibus ut ab anno 1580. quia in con-sessione fidei obsignata illius anni facta est men-tio, initium fieret. Ast tandem visum fuit om-nibus ab anno 1575, Constitutionum synodalium lectionem inchoare: Nam ab illo anno in Synodis Nationalibus frequentissima est Episcoporum mentio, qui tunc temporibus, invitissimis & reluctantibus ecclesiis multa sibi arrogabant, videlicet, titulos dignitatum, civiles functiones, potestatem in pastores, immensos titulos, ac ecclesiastica politicis commiscebant: quæ omnia cum frequentibus synodorum decretis, corruptiones manifestæ regiminis ecclesiastici dicerentur, neque ullis legum repagulis satis coerceri possent, tandem paucorum illorum titularium Episcoporum obstinata pervicacia identidem prorumpente, coactæ fuerunt Synodi Nationales, resecatis antea ramis, radicem ipsam petere, atque anno 1580. declarasse, illicitum esse quicquid ordinarii unius gregis ministri munus excederet : Quare ridiculum esse quod a quibusdam objicitur contra decretum synodi Taodunensis, anno 1580. habitæ, quasi Episcopatum tantum rejiceret ac ex ecclesia Scotica profligaret, quatenus à Pontifice Romano dependeret: Nam si resecentur ea quæ in Episcopatu ante illud synodi decretum damnata fuerunt, quid quæso Episcopo supererit supra ordinarium quemlibet unius gregis pastorem? Addebat alius, non solum profligatum fuisse ex ecclesia Scotica omnem omnino Episcopatum ἐξωχήτως[?] seu singulariter sic dictum, verumetiam exteris Theologis illud quam notissimum fuisse, producta in medium Theodori Bezæ, viri maximi, Epistola ad Iohannem Cnoxum ecclesiæ hujus reformatorem, anno 1571 scriptam. Sed & istud (inquit) mi Cnoxe, te cæterosque fratres meminisse velim, quod jam oculis pene ipsis cernitur, sicut episcopi Papatum pererrerunt, ita Pseudoepiscopos papatus reliquias epicureismum terris invecturos: hanc pestem caveant qui salvam ecclesiam cupiunt; & cum illam in Scotia profligaris, ne quæso illam unquam admittas, &c cæt. Deputatus regius respondebat, sibi minime statutum quidlibet urgere, nisi eo modo qui omnibus probis satisfaceret: sed syrtes & scopulos hic esse à quibus utrinque sollicitè caveretur, eoque nomine venire quæcunque pacem & veritatum impedient: Serenissimum Regem in mandatis sibi dedisse, ut nihil intentatum relinqueret, quo utrumque solide stabiliri posset: Interim synodo providendum, ut regis honorem quam commendatissimum habeat; quod in se recepit præses.
units.tr: 1. The long-standing defects of lawfully constituted National Synods. 2. The approval and sanction of corrupt synods which were not duly constituted, such as the two at Linlithgow, and those at Glasgow, Aberdeen, St Andrews and Perth. 3. The harsh imposition of the Five Articles of Perth. 4. The liturgical books and canons, together with the high commission court. 5. The violation of the National Covenant solemnly sworn with God. 6. Episcopacy. 7. The tyranny of the ecclesiastical bishops over political offices, and over synods and all ecclesiastical assemblies. "For these," he said, "we impute all our evils; and we call God, the searcher of our hearts, to witness that it has always been our purpose to honour our most serene king and to obey his lawful commands according to the prescription of the laws, whatever our adversaries have said against us or falsely charged. For although we acknowledge that all kings are subject to Christ, the Son of God, and we judge that whatever opposes his glory and kingdom ought to be eliminated; yet, if he were as dear to us as our right eye, as useful and necessary as our right hand, we shall never suffer the political powers, as ordained by God, and kings set in eminence, to be wronged or insulted for our good." The royal commissioner replied that this synod, convened by the most serene king, should weigh maturely and in the fear of the Lord whether all these things are so, that is, whether these are the true and only grievances of the churches. If they are shown to be true and just, so that they should be removed from the churches; but if not, it is fair that they should still stand. For example (he said), if Episcopacy is among the just and true causes of grievance, then it must be shown to be contrary to the constitutions of this church; and so with the rest. The moderator accepted this condition in the name of the synod and undertook for it that the synod would demonstrate the matter clearly and openly: that from the very beginnings of the Reformation the Scottish church had always purposed to overthrow Episcopacy and to adhere to the apostolic government of the church by synods and presbyteries; that it had also happily plucked up the very roots of Episcopacy and all its fibres, which, although they often sprouted and grew again afterwards, had nevertheless always been suppressed in purer times as soon as they put forth their heads. Moreover, so that intricate disputes might be avoided, the royal commissioner declared that he thought it most advisable if extracts from the authentic registers of the synods were read out which bore on this matter. But the question arose from which year to begin: some urged from 1560, when the reformed religion was sanctioned by public authority; others more insistently from 1580, because mention was made in the confession of faith signed in that year. At last it seemed best to all to begin the reading of the synodal constitutions from the year 1575. For from that year on, in the National Synods, mention of the bishops is very frequent; for in those times, against the strongest wishes and reluctance of the churches, they claimed many things for themselves, namely titles of dignity, civil functions, power over the ministers, immense titles, and they mixed ecclesiastical matters with political ones. Since all these things, together with frequent decrees of the synods, were called manifest corruptions of church government, and could not be sufficiently restrained by any barriers of law, at last, when the obstinate perversity of a few of those titular bishops kept breaking out again and again, the National Synods were compelled, the branches having first been lopped off, to seek the root itself, and in 1580 to declare unlawful whatever exceeded the office of an ordinary minister of one flock. Hence it is ridiculous that some object against the decree of the synod held at Dundee in 1580, as if it rejected only Episcopacy and cast it out of the Scottish church insofar as it depended on the Roman Pontiff. For if those things that were condemned in Episcopacy before that synodal decree are cut away, what, I ask, will remain for the bishop beyond any ordinary minister of one flock? Another added that not only was every Episcopacy altogether cast out of the Scottish church by excellence, or singularly so called [ἐξοχήν], but also that this was very well known to foreign theologians, the letter of Theodore Beza, that great man, written in 1571 to John Knox, the reformer of this church, being brought forward. "But this also (he said), my Knox, I would have you and the other brethren remember, which is now almost visible to the eyes themselves: just as the bishops have wandered through the papacy, so the pseudo-bishops, the remnants of the papacy, will bring epicureanism into the lands; let those who desire a safe church beware of this plague; and since you have cast it out in Scotland, I beg you never to admit it again, etc." The royal commissioner replied that he had no intention of pressing anything except in a way that would satisfy all honest men; but there are quicksands and rocks here, from which care must be taken on both sides, and for that reason whatever impedes peace and truth must be avoided. The most serene king had commanded him in his instructions to leave nothing untried by which both could be solidly established; meanwhile the synod must provide that the king's honour be held in highest regard; which the moderator undertook.

units.la: Ante sequentem sessionem inter synodi membra absente deputato regio, serio inquisitum fuit qui essent in specie scopuli illi, ac deliberatum quibus mediis ecclesiæ pax stabiliri posset ita ut regi sereniss. satisfieret, & ecclesiæ libertas sarta tecta remaneret.
units.tr: Before the next session, with the royal deputy absent from the members of the synod, they seriously inquired what those rocks in particular were, and deliberated by what means peace could be established in the Church so that the most serene King would be satisfied and the liberty of the Church would remain safe and intact.

units.la: Cumque in synodum convenissent : Deputato regio significavit præses, se omnes in illud intentos fuisse quod tam serio commendasset, neque ullam ad pacem & veritatem convenientiorem viam excogitari à se posse, quam quæ a rege ipso serenissimo demonstrata fuit ; videlicet : Cum nihil fit quod in quæstionem vocari jam possit præter nuperam synodum Glasguensem ; quam quia rex ratam habere noluit, eam nunc non urgere statutum est, ita tamen (inquit) ut nullatenus hoc accipiatur quasi eandem rejiceremus, præsertim cum Rex serenissimus pollicitus sit se illud nolle urgere, quippe, quod ad ejus Synodi authoritatem tuendam quamplurimis arctissimis vinculis subditos constrictos intellexisset : Ab utroque itaque extremo diligenter cavendum esse : Deputatus regius respondit. Fœliciter visas & descriptas esse à quibus metuebat syrtes & scopulos, precatus ut pari fœlicitate præternavigarent, se cursum suum in medio directurum.
units.tr: When they had gathered in the synod, the president told the royal deputy that all of them had been intent on that matter which he had commended so earnestly, and that he could devise no more suitable way to peace and truth than the one the most serene King himself had pointed out, namely: since there is nothing that can now be called into question except the recent Synod of Glasgow, which the King was unwilling to ratify, it has been decided not to press it now. Yet (he said) this must in no way be taken as if we were rejecting it, especially since the most serene King has promised that he will not press it, having learned that many subjects had been bound by the tightest chains in defence of that synod's authority. Thus both extremes must be carefully avoided. The royal deputy replied that he was glad the rocks and shoals he feared had been seen and marked out, and prayed that they would sail past them with equal good fortune, saying that he would steer his own course through the middle.

units.la: Dein synodi scribæ mandatum, ut acta synodalia de Episcopatu fideliter & alta voce prælegeret, aufspicaturus ab anno 1575. Inter legendum autographon sibi tradi sæpius jussit Deputatus regius & oculis ipse suis lustrabat extracta cum originali convenire : Ac scribam pergentem in prælectione Canonum contra Episcopatum, interpellavit ; Quin (inquit) ad alia gravaminum capita transis, nam in hoc abunde mihi satisfactum, habeo hoc pro confesso. Hæc formalia fuerunt ejus verba, quibus innuebat se satis jam conspicere, Episcopatum adversari constitutionibus ecclesiasticis: Interim ut alii omnes perspecta haberent fundamenta, quibus actiones synodi Glasguensis, tam misere traductæ à calumniatoribus, inniterentur, praelectio deducebatur ad synodum Taodunensem, quæ 1580 habebatur.
units.tr: Then the synod's clerk was ordered to read aloud and faithfully the synodal acts concerning episcopacy, beginning from the year 1575. While he read, the royal deputy repeatedly asked that the authentic copy be handed to him, and with his own eyes he checked that the extracts agreed with the original. When the clerk went on reading the canons against episcopacy, he interrupted him: "Why not (he said) move on to the other heads of grievances? For I am fully satisfied on this point, and I take it as conceded." These were his formal words, by which he signified that he now saw plainly enough that episcopacy was contrary to the ecclesiastical constitutions. Meanwhile, so that everyone else might have a clear view of the foundations on which the acts of the Synod of Glasgow rested, so unjustly misrepresented by its slanderers, the reading was carried on to the Synod of Dundee, which was held in 1580.

units.la: Sessionibus subsequentibus prælectæ fuere rationes contra quinque articulos Perthenses, sex Pseudo-synodos, Librum liturgiæ, Canonum, Ordinationis, Celsam Commissionem: quæ cum eadem sint cum illis quæ in synodo Glasguensi propositæ fuerunt, ex illius synodi historia petantur: Et ante dimissam sessionem electi fuerunt ex omni ordine quidam, qui decretum Synodicum de præcedentibus in formam redigerent.
units.tr: In the sessions that followed were read the grounds against the five Perth articles, the six pseudo-synods, the Book of Liturgy, the Canons, the Ordination, and the High Commission. Since these are the same as those that were put forward in the Synod of Glasgow, they may be sought in the history of that synod. And before the session was dismissed, certain men were chosen from every rank to draw up in form the synodal decree on the preceding matters.

units.la: Sessione octava, Literæ ab Episcopo Orcadum ad præsentem synodum missæ prælegebantur: quibus pœnitentiam profitebatur, quod Episcopatus ordinem amplexus fuisset, quem verbo Dei penitus distitutum esse, ac ingentium malorum in multis Christi-ani orbis regnis, præsertim vero in Scotia, primariam fuisse causam confitebatur.
units.tr: In the eighth session, letters sent to the present synod by the Bishop of Orkney were read aloud. In them he professed repentance that he had embraced the episcopal order, which he confessed had been utterly rejected by the Word of God, and that it had been the chief cause of the great evils in many kingdoms of the Christian world, and especially in Scotland.

units.la: Ideoque se abjurasse, ac præsentibus hisce abjurare & rejicere (dicebat) omnem illam Episcopalem potestatem & jurisdictionem; sicuti & ea à majoribus abjurata fuerat anno 1580, quando Nationalis confessio primum obsignata fuit. Pollicebatur itidem, ac per tremendum Dei nomen jurabat, se posthac Episcopali ista potestate directe seu indirecte nunquam usurum, neque illam vel privatis sermonibus asserturum, quin contra nuperæ synodi Glasguensis decreta defensurum ac reformationis opus, quantum penes se foret promoturum. In cujus fidem præsentes literas manu propria obsignavit, testibus quatuor pastoribus, quorum duo cum synodo interessent, genuinum & verum esse auctoris scriptum restati sunt.
units.tr: Therefore, he said, he had renounced it, and by these presents he renounced and rejected all that episcopal power and jurisdiction; just as his predecessors had renounced it in 1580, when the National Confession was first signed. He likewise promised, and swore by the dreadful name of God, that he would never hereafter use that episcopal power, directly or indirectly, nor assert it even in private conversation; rather, he would defend the decrees of the recent Synod of Glasgow and promote the work of reformation as far as lay in him. In witness of this he signed the present letter with his own hand, and four ministers as witnesses, two of whom were attending the synod, declared that the writing was genuine and true, as the author had written it.

units.la: Tum præ-legitur decretum quod à synodi deputatis formatum fuit ac de verbo in verbum sic se habet.
units.tr: Then the decree drawn up by the deputies of the synod was read out, and it runs word for word as follows.

units.la: Quandoquidem sereniss. Rex benigne declaraverit, sibi placere, ut omnes controversiæ de religione & rebus ecclesiasticis per synodos determinentur; ac publico edicto præsentem hanc synodum Nationalem indixerit ad motus præsentes componendos, & perfectam pacem stabiliendam contra divisiones & tumultus ac animorum distractiones, regi non minus ingratis, quam probis subditis graves: Serenissimi Regis deputatus Iohannes Traquariæ comes, sufficientibus literis fiduciariis instructus, præsenti huic synodo, in omnibus suis membris rite formatæ ac constitutæ notum fecit, sincerum serenissimi regis erga reformatam religionem zelum, ac vere regiam sollicitudinē ac paternum amorem erga hanc ecclesiam, cui nativitatem suam & baptismum debet, & insignem animi dolorem ob varias tum in regno tum in ecclesia divisiones, ardentissimum deniq; desiderium omnia nostra vulnera, leni &/paterna quantum fieri poterit manu, perfecte sanandi. Ac licet pro recepta hujus ecclesiæ consuetudine, omnia hæc gravamina in prioribus synodis hactenus ita excusa sint, ut omnibus abunde satisfactum esse possit: Cum tamen illustriss. deputato visum esset, eorundem mentionem denuo facere ac inquirere sedulo in veras omnium quæ perpessi fuimus malorum causas, declaratū eidem fuit per synodum hanc, ex multis has fuisse primarias. Primam, Quod præsules sine ulla authoritate ecclesiastica, huic ecclesiæ obtrusissent Librum liturgicum, qui præter formam mere pontificiam, contineret multiplices ceremonias & errores pontificios, ac femina multiplicis idololatriæ & crafliorum fuperftitionum; fimul cum libro Canonum, nulla etiam authoritate ecclefiaftica munito, quo fubvertitur penitus difciplina hujus ecclefiæ recepta & regimen per fynodos,ac in Episcopos tyrannica poteftas in ecclefiam confertur: Cum Libro ordinationis, fine ulla omnino authoritate feu civili feu ecclefiaftica, quo munia & officia quaedam ecclefiaftica fine ullo verbi Dei fundamento eriguntur in ecclefia; directe adverfantia difciplinæ & decretis hujus ecclefiæ; cum celfa commiffione, quam curiam feu tribunal fine ulla authoritate ecclefiaftica erexerunt, quo jurifdictionem & ordinaria judicia ecclefiaftica fubverterunt, ac mere ecclefiafticis utriufque gladii poteftatem, & mere politicis poteftatem clavium ac cenfuræ ecclefiafticæ commiferunt. Secundam Caufam fuiffe articulos quinq; Perthenfes[?], vid.celebrationem feftorum dierum; genuflexionem in S. Cœna; confirmationem; adminiftrationem facramentorum in locis privatis, qui articuli introducti fuerunt per Pfeudo-Synodum, & adverfantur confeffioni fidei anno 1580. & fæpius poftea obfignatæ, ordini etiam & decretis hujus ecclefiæ. Tertiam caufam fuiffe, Mutationem regiminis ecclefiaftici à synodis ad paucos ecclefiafticos, qui nomine Episcoporum præeminentiam fingularem & poteftatem in fratres fibi arrogarunt, contra prædictam fidei confeffionem, ac ordinem hujus ecclefiæ libris politiæ defcriptum; & conftitutiones ab ipfo reformationis exordio repetitas. Quartam caufam fuiffe, Officia & poteftatem politicam ecclefiafticorum, qua epifcopis conceffum, fuit fententiam ferre in fefsione feu collegio juftitiæ, camera rationum, parlamento; aliis vero eirenarchas agere, quæ non folum adverfantur fpirituali ecclefiafticorum vocationi secundum hujus ecclesiae decreta, verum etiam alio non tendunt, quam ut superbe efferantur supra fratres & collegas, ac ministerium impediant. Quintam vero, quod habitae & sancitae sint Pseudo-Synodi quaedam, videlicet Limnuchensis anno 1606. & ibidem altera 1608. Glasguensis 1610. Abredonensis 1616. Andreapolitana 1617. Perthana 1618. quae illegitimae sunt, quia non solum indictae ac formatae fuerunt contra decreta & ordinem qui in hac ecclesia constanter observatus fuit a reformationis initio, verum etiam novationes contra ordinem & religionem hic sancitam introducunt; omni itaque authoritatis specie destituendae sunt. Sextam causam esse defectus Nationalium & liberarum synodorum, quae legitime formatae ex pastoribus, doctoribus & senioribus annuatim haberentur aut saepius pro re nata, sicuti statuto parlamentario sancitum anno 1592 fuit. Dein synodus universa concordibus omnium suffragiis nullo contradicente aut haesitante declaravit, haec & id genus alia, orta a neglectu & violatione Nationalis foederis hujus ecclesiae & regni cum Deo anno 1580. initi; veras & primarias fuisse omnium nostrorum malorum & distractionum causas. Ideoque decernit secundum constitutiones hujus ecclesiae, & fundamenta respective supra designata, Ut liber liturgicus, Canonum, ordinationis, celsa commissio adhuc rejiciantur; interdicit praxin articulorum Perthensium; statuit ut regimen ecclesiae per episcopos, ac civilia munia & authoritas politica ecclesiasticorum in hac ecclesia illegitima censeantur; ut sex illae synodi posthac nullius prorsus sint authoritatis. Atq; ut religio sarta tecta & incorrupta maneat, ac hujusmodi calamitatibus posthac opportune obviam eatur, decernit, ut synodi Nationales rite formatae, tanquam proprii & competentes rerum omnium ecclesiasticarum judices quotannis posthac semel habeantur, aut sæpius, prout occasio & necessitas postulaverint: ita tamen ut synodorum pro re nata necessitas Regi serenissimo per libellos supplices prius remonstretur: Decernit etiam, ut consistoria (seu seisiones[?], presbyteria (seu Classes) ac Synodi provinciales rite formentur ac celebrentur, secundum ordinem & disciplinam hujus ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Since the most serene King has graciously declared that it pleases him that all controversies concerning religion and ecclesiastical affairs be determined by synods, and by public edict has summoned this present National Synod to settle the present disturbances and to establish a perfect peace against divisions, tumults and the distraction of minds, which are as grievous to the King as they are unwelcome to good subjects; the King's most serene deputy, John, Earl of Traquair, furnished with sufficient letters of trust, made known to this present synod, duly formed and constituted in all its members, the King's sincere zeal for the reformed religion, his truly royal solicitude and paternal love for this Church, to which he owes his birth and baptism, his remarkable grief at the various divisions both in the kingdom and in the Church, and finally his most ardent desire to heal perfectly all our wounds with a gentle and, as far as possible, fatherly hand. And although, according to the accepted custom of this Church, all these grievances have hitherto been so fully dealt with in earlier synods that full satisfaction may be given to everyone, nevertheless, since it seemed good to the most illustrious deputy to mention them again and to inquire carefully into the true causes of all the evils we have suffered, it was declared to him by this synod that the principal causes were these, among many. The first: that the bishops, without any ecclesiastical authority, had imposed on this Church the Liturgical Book, which, apart from a form that is purely Popish, contains manifold ceremonies and Popish errors, and the seeds of manifold idolatry and grosser superstitions; likewise with the Book of Canons, also fortified by no ecclesiastical authority, by which the discipline received in this Church and government by synods are utterly subverted, and tyrannical power over the Church is conferred upon the bishops; with the Book of Ordination, with no authority whatever, civil or ecclesiastical, by which certain ecclesiastical functions and offices are set up in the Church without any foundation in the Word of God, directly opposed to the discipline and decrees of this Church; and with the high commission, which they erected as a court or tribunal without any ecclesiastical authority, by which they subverted the ordinary ecclesiastical jurisdiction and judgments, and committed the power of both swords, purely ecclesiastical, and the power of the keys and of ecclesiastical censure, purely civil. The second cause was the five Perth articles[?], namely the celebration of festival days, kneeling at the Lord's Supper, confirmation, and the administration of the sacraments in private places, which articles were introduced by a pseudo-synod and are opposed to the Confession of Faith of 1580, often signed afterwards, and also to the order and decrees of this Church. The third cause was the change of ecclesiastical government from synods to a few churchmen, who under the name of bishops arrogated to themselves singular pre-eminence and power over their brethren, contrary to the aforesaid Confession of Faith and to the order of this Church described in the books of polity, and to the constitutions repeated from the very beginning of the Reformation. The fourth cause was the offices and civil power of churchmen, granted to the bishops, of giving sentence in the Session or College of Justice, the Exchequer, and Parliament, and for others to act as justices of the peace; which not only conflict with the spiritual calling of churchmen according to the decrees of this Church, but also tend to no other end than that they may be proudly exalted above their brethren and colleagues and hinder the ministry. The fifth, that certain pseudo-synods were held and sanctioned, namely the Synod of Linlithgow in 1606, another there in 1608, Glasgow in 1610, Aberdeen in 1616, St Andrews in 1617, and Perth in 1618, which are illegitimate, because they were not only called and framed contrary to the decrees and order which had been constantly observed in this Church from the beginning of the Reformation, but also introduce innovations contrary to the order and religion sanctioned here; they must therefore be utterly stripped of any semblance of authority. The sixth cause is the failure of national and free synods, which, lawfully formed of ministers, teachers and elders, ought to be held every year, or more often as occasion requires, as was enacted by parliamentary statute in 1592. Then the whole synod, by the unanimous votes of all, without any dissent or hesitation, declared that these and other things of the kind, arising from the neglect and violation of the National Covenant of this Church and kingdom with God, made in 1580, were the true and principal causes of all our evils and divisions. Therefore it decrees, according to the constitutions of this Church and the foundations designated above, that the Liturgical Book, the Canons, the Ordination, and the high commission are to be rejected; it forbids the practice of the Perth articles; it enacts that government of the Church by bishops, and the civil functions and political authority of churchmen in this Church, are to be deemed illegitimate; and that those six synods shall henceforth be of no authority whatever. And so that religion may remain safe, intact and uncorrupted, and that such calamities may be opportunely met in future, it decrees that national synods, duly formed, as the proper and competent judges of all ecclesiastical affairs, shall be held once a year hereafter, or more often as occasion and necessity may require; yet in such a way that the need for a synod as occasion arises shall first be made known to the most serene King by humble petitions. It also decrees that consistories (or sessions[?]), presbyteries (or classes) and provincial synods shall be duly formed and held according to the order and discipline of this Church.

units.la: Antequam decretum hoc in suffragia iret, visum fuit præsidi, veteranos quosdam ex omnibus regni partibus pastores, rogare, an decretum hoc satis placeret? Quod omnes uno ore affirmarunt; ac longius provecti fusius differebant de diverso ecclesiæ Scoticæ statu, quem oculis suis conspexerunt; quanta, fuisset ejus puritas ante astute[?] introductum Episcopatum, quam efficaciter tunc operaretur Spiritus Sanctus per ministerium servorum suorum nullo sæculi typho turgentium, in animis fidelis populi: postea quanta tepiditas omnium invasisset animos, ita ut admirati sæpius sint, Deum de cœlis insigniori aliqua pœna, apostasiam illam non vindicasse: Nunc vero sopitos illos zeli ignes resuscitatos, ac ecclesiam purgatam licet oculis suis aspicerent, vix tamen iis fidere, quippe quod essent veluti qui somniant; Gratias immensas Deo optimo.maximo debere, qui dignatus esset per manum serenissim. regis Caroli, genuinum nitorem castæ suæ sponsæ restituere; & serenam hanc cœli faciem, (nam complures dies elapsos vix confpectus fuerat Sol, cujus coruscantes radii templum in quo convenit synodus tum repleverant) spectatorum oculos non tantum afficere, quantum fœlicis hujus diei memoria piorum animos vero & solido gaudio perfunderet. Singuli sua proferebant, sed omnes læta & fausta serenissim. regi precati sunt.: Tandem præses rogat ut si cujus animo inesset scrupulus, libere eundem nunc proponeret ante colligenda suffragia, & recitata deputatorum nomina: Sed cum nullus prodiret, Deputatus regius primus sententiam rogatus est; qui ursit[?] ut postremi suffragii gratiam synodus illi concedere vellet, quippe quod in mandatis habere se diceret, ut si plurimorum suffragiis hæc proposita gravamina veras ac justas fuisse præcedentium malorum causas concluderetur, & ipse calculum suum adderet, ac ecclesiam ab iis liberaret; licet (inquit) satis hactenus colligere possim ex hilarioribus omnium vultu, ac reverendorum illorum pastorum orationibus, quo tandem res hæc cessura fit. Cum ad suffragia deventum fuisset, singulorumque delegatorum nomina ordine consueto ex Catalogo per scribam recitarentur, Responsum ab omnibus, placet, assentior decreto: Deputatus vero regius in hunc fere modum loquutus est: Sæpius (inquit) venerandæ huic synodo dixi, & nunc repeto, serenissim. regem velle, ac mihi in mandatis dedisse, ut, si Episcopatus synodi hujus judicio declararetur illicitus, ac constitutionibus hujus ecclesiæ adversus, (prout supplicibus vestris libellis sæpius significaltis) synodi judicio consentirem, idque ratum facerem ac sancirem: Quare decretum hoc ex animo probo.
units.tr: Before the decree was put to the vote, the president thought it fitting to ask some veteran ministers from all parts of the kingdom whether the decree pleased them. They all affirmed with one voice that it did. Those who were further advanced spoke at length about the Scottish Church's former condition, which they had seen with their own eyes: how great its purity was before the Episcopacy was craftily introduced, and how effectively the Holy Spirit then worked in the minds of the faithful people through the ministry of his servants, who were puffed up by no worldly pride. Afterwards, they said, such lukewarmness had seized all minds that they often wondered God had not avenged that apostasy from heaven with some more notable punishment. Now, however, although they saw with their own eyes those dormant fires of zeal rekindled and the Church purged, they could hardly trust what they saw, since they were like men dreaming. They said immense thanks were due to God, most good and great, who had deigned, through the hand of the most serene King Charles, to restore the genuine brightness of his chaste spouse. This serene face of heaven (for the sun, whose gleaming rays had filled the church where the synod met, had scarcely been seen for many days) moved the eyes of the onlookers, and the memory of this happy day filled the hearts of the pious with true and solid joy. Each gave his own opinion, but all prayed for the most serene king. At last the president asked that, if anyone had a scruple, he should state it freely before the votes were gathered and the names of the deputies read out. No one came forward, so the royal deputy was asked first for his opinion. He asked the synod to grant him the favour of voting last, since he said he had been instructed that if most votes concluded that the grievances put forward were the true and just causes of the earlier evils, he should add his own vote and so free the Church from them. "Although," he said, "I can already gather enough from the cheerful faces of everyone and from the speeches of those reverend ministers, as to how this matter will end." When it came to the vote, and the clerk read out each delegate's name from the list in the usual order, all answered, "I agree, I assent to the decree." The royal deputy then spoke in roughly this manner: "I have often said to this venerable synod, and now I repeat, that the most serene king wishes, and has instructed me, that if the Episcopacy is declared by this synod's judgment to be unlawful and contrary to the constitutions of this Church (as you have often indicated in your supplicatory petitions), I should consent to the synod's judgment and ratify and confirm it. Therefore I approve this decree from my heart."

units.la: Interim certissime mihi persuadeo, nullum iniquiori animo laturum quod rex noster serenissim. se non tam facilem quam multorum vota poscebant, in hoc negotio exhibuerit, si in memoriam revocaverit ubi & quo modo serenissim.
units.tr: Meanwhile I am quite certain that no one will take it with a worse grace that our most serene king has not shown himself as easy in this business as the wishes of many demanded, if he calls to mind where and how the most serene king was brought up.

units.la: Rex educatus fit: Neque hujus regni solum regem esse, verumetiam aliorum duorum, qui huic rejecta probant: Quare si cujus animum scrupulus aut metus quilibet olim male habuerit , spero nunc exemptum fore : Et vestri mu-neris est qui pastorum officio fungimini, omnem operam dare ut populus serenissim. Regis benignitatem incomparabilem & iustitiam sentiat. Quod voce protuli, scripto sanciam. Regis porro nomine sic subscripsit. 17. Augusti.
units.tr: The king was educated... that he is king not only of this kingdom but also of two others, who approve of what is rejected here. Therefore, if anyone's mind has been troubled by scruple or by some fear, I hope it is now set free. And it is your duty, you who discharge the office of ministers, to take every care that the people feel the incomparable kindness and justice of the most serene king. What I have said by word of mouth, I will confirm in writing. He subscribed in the king's name thus: 17 August.

units.la: Ego Iohannes Comes Traquariae , Deputatus regius ad praesentem hanc Synodum , regis nomine declaro , serenissim. regem pro incomparabili sua benignitate , ut praesentes distractiones componeret , & subditorum votis satisfaceret , decretum hoc approbare , licet contra suadeat regis indoles seu opinio, ac multae aliae graves rationes : Et ego regis serenissim. Deputatus suprascripto decreto assentior , idemque chirographo meo obsigno.
units.tr: I, John, Earl of Traquair, royal deputy to the present synod, declare in the king's name that the most serene king, in his incomparable kindness, in order to settle the present disturbances and satisfy the wishes of his subjects, approves this decree, although the king's disposition or opinion and many other grave reasons speak against it. And I, the most serene king's deputy, assent to the above-written decree and seal it with my own hand.

units.la: Iohannes Comes Traquariae Commissionarius.
units.tr: John, Earl of Traquair, Commissioner.

units.la: Sequenti sessione, quae fuit 19. Augusti, synodo exhibitae fuerunt literae Alexandri Lindesii, quondam Episcopi Caledonii, quibus palinodiam canebat, ac Episcopatui simpliciter renunciabat: quem nullo verbi divini fundamento niti, ac foederi nationali & canonibus ecclesiasticis adversari profitebatur.
units.tr: At the following session, on 19 August, letters from Alexander Lindsay, formerly Bishop of Caledonia, were presented to the synod. In them he recanted and simply renounced the episcopate, which he declared rests on no foundation of the divine word and is contrary to the National Covenant and the ecclesiastical canons.

units.la: A nona ad decimam sextam sessionem agitatae fuerunt privatae quaedam controversiae, & excussa ecclesiarum gravamina; auditi etiam qui sententiis Deputatorum synodi Glasguensis gravatos se affirmarunt, cum quibus varie actum fuit, deputato regio semper praesente.
units.tr: From the ninth to the sixteenth session, certain private disputes were debated and the grievances of the churches were examined. Those who said they were aggrieved by the decisions of the deputies of the Synod of Glasgow were also heard, and various matters were dealt with, the royal deputy being present throughout.

units.la: Sessione decima sexta, propositum fuit synodo, universam ecclesiam Scoticam & complura primaria illius membra, singulari iniuria ac non ferendis contumeliis affici per librum quendam, qui licet regis sereniss. nomine extruderetur, ejus tamen nomen impudenter mentiretur[?], cui titulus, Fusior[?] declaratio; in quo introducit author, regem sereniss. praefe ferret[?] praecedentium actionum seriem deducentem, quasi singulis actionibus interfuissset; calumniis vero, detostionibus, falsitatibus, ita refertum fuisse dicebant, ut nihil supra. Deputatus regius instabat, ut vel huic negotio penitus supersederetur, vel si illud impetrare non posset, ut parce admodum uti probos subditos decet, de eo loquerentur, quod regis titulum prae se ferret. Respondit Comes Rothusius senioris nomine ad synodum deputatus, Regis sereniss. honorem omnibus cordi esse, neque severa censura infamis hujus suppositii libri nullatenus laedi posse, praesertim cum liquido constet, regem ejus authorem non esse, vindicandam itaque esse ecclesiae famam; Neque posse titulum regis, libro praefixum, authorem quisquis sit, a debita censura magis liberare, aut subditorum actiones & querelas justas contra eundem impedire, quam titulus & inscriptio regia a falsario adulterinae monetae impressa, adulteratorem poenis lege sancitis eximere. Addebat alius, a nullo tam graviter laesum esse regem, quam ab illius libri authore, qui regem ea confidenter afferentem introduceret, quorum contraria hisce meis (inquiebat) auribus sereniss. regem affirmantem audivi.
