Cum res ad suffragia relata fuissent, placuit, ut selecti quidam delegarentur, qui librum excuterent, & de omnibus ad synodum referrent: Atque hi postea diligentiae suae rationem publicam dederunt, ac in seriem congesserunt[?] quae animadversione digna judicarunt, quibus praelictis, Praeses quorundam sententias rogabat, quid facti consultissimum esset; Politici quidam ecclesiastica censura non contenti ad asperiores poenas recurrendum suadebant, inter alios Baro de Kircoubrie deputatus senior a Classe ejusdem nominis, dicebat: Dolendum esse, si in viros aliàs bonos, ad aurium usque amputationem & nasi mutilationem, ob libellos quosdam scriptos alicubi se-vere animadvertitur, & si in nebulones sereniss. regis nomen mentiri ausos, libri hujus authores, vel amputatione capitis non animadverteretur: Sed monebat Præses pœnas omnes ejus generis excedere ambitum synodorum Nationalium; Et communibus omnium suffragiis decretum fuit, synodi nomine supplicibus literis regis deputatum compellandum esse, quibus rogabant, ut perpenso specimine crassissimarum absurditatum quibus author libri istius insigni injuria Deum, Regem, Ecclesiam Scoticam, & per ejus latus alias reformatas, ac totum hoc regnum ac primaria ejus membra affecerit; regi omnia repræsentaret, ac Synodi nomine sereniss. regem obsecraret, ut libri revocatione, & publica interdictione notum omnibus faceret, quam sibi displiceret; dein ut authores, ac fautores, saltem qui in hoc regno Scotiæ nati fuerunt, ad hoc regnum amandare vellet, & judicio sese sistere juberet, præsertim vero Gualterum Balcanquellum, decanatu Dunelmensi nuper amplificatum, qui se ejus authorem jactat; ut exemplari pœna deterreantur alii ab improbis omnibus id genus conatibus, quibus seditionem inter regem & subditos ferere satagunt. Supplicem hunc libellum tradit synodus Deputato regio, qui in senatu regio eundem postea præleġit: ac promissum tum fuit eundem regi communicandum fore.
units.tr: At the sixteenth session it was put to the synod that the whole Scottish Church and several of its chief members were being wronged by a singular injury and insults that could not be borne, through a certain book. Although it was published under the king's name, it shamelessly misused his name. It was titled "A Fuller Declaration." In it the author introduces the king as presenting a sequence of earlier proceedings, as though he had been present at each action. The speakers said it was so full of calumnies, slanders and falsehoods that it could be no fuller. The royal deputy urged that either the matter be dropped altogether or, if that could not be obtained, that they speak of it very sparingly, as loyal subjects ought, since the book bore the king's title. Earl Rothes, deputed to the synod in the name of the elder, replied that the king's honour was dear to everyone, and that it could not be harmed by a severe censure of this spurious book, especially since it was clear the king was not its author. The reputation of the Church must therefore be vindicated. A royal title prefixed to the book could no more free its author, whoever he might be, from due censure, or prevent the just actions and complaints of subjects against it, than a royal stamp impressed on counterfeit coin by a forger could exempt the forger from the penalties sanctioned by law. Another added that no one had wounded the king so grievously as the author of that book, who introduced the king confidently asserting things, whereas he (the speaker) had himself heard the king affirm the contrary with his own ears. When the matter was put to the vote, it was agreed that certain selected men should be appointed to examine the book and report everything to the synod. Afterwards these men gave a public account of their diligence and set out in order what they judged worthy of notice. When this had been read, the president asked the opinions of some as to what was most advisable. Certain politicians, not content with ecclesiastical censure, urged recourse to harsher penalties. Among them Baron Kircoubrie, senior deputy from the presbytery of the same name, said it was to be regretted if men otherwise good were severely punished, even to the cutting off of their ears and the mutilation of their noses, for certain libels written somewhere, while the authors of this book, who had dared to lie in the name of the most serene king, were not punished even by the amputation of the head. But the president warned that all penalties of that kind lay beyond the scope of the National Synods. By the common vote of all, it was decided that in the synod's name the deputy should be asked, by a supplicatory letter to the king, to lay everything before the king, having weighed the specimen of crass absurdities by which the author, with notable injury, had offended God, the King, the Scottish Church, and through its side the other reformed churches, and this whole kingdom and its chief members. They asked the king, in the synod's name, to make known to everyone, by recalling the book and publicly prohibiting it, how much he disliked it. They further asked that he would summon the authors and abettors, at least those born in the kingdom of Scotland, back to this kingdom and order them to submit to judgment, especially Walter Balcanquhal, lately enriched with the deanery of Durham, who boasts that he is its author, so that others might be deterred by exemplary punishment from all such wicked attempts, by which they strive to sow sedition between the king and his subjects. The synod handed this supplicatory petition to the royal deputy, who afterwards read it before the royal council. It was promised at that time that it would be communicated to the king.

units.la: Sessione 20. Cum proposuisset præses, Omnium vota eo tendere, ut deputatus regius vellet Confessioni subscribere, ac non solum exemplo suo aliis præire, verum etiam pro authoritate ejusdem ob-signationem imperare; Respondit ille, Scriptum illud cujus obsignationem urgeret synodus duo continere: Confessionem scilic. fidei, de qua (inquit) nulla nunc poterit esse quæstio, quippe quod abunde sibi persuasum esset, tum verba formalia ejusdem, tum explicationem per synodum cui subscripserat 17. Augusti, verum esse: Scrupulum tamen nonnullorum animis hærere de altera scripti parte, mutuo scilic. fœdere, qui suo judicio commoda explicatione facile posset removeri, ita ut regi satisfieret. Præses dicebat, synodum ignorare quid amplius dici posset, quam quod hactenus dictum esset: sed re ad sequentem sessionem dilata, post longam disceptationem, decretum fuit, offerendum esse libellum supplicem senatui regio, quo peteretur ut pro more majorum, senatus fœdus illud sanciret, ejusque obsignationem modo politico omnibus omnino regni subditis imperaret: qui de verbo in verbum translatus sic se habet.
units.tr: At the twentieth session the moderator proposed that the votes of all were tending towards this: that the royal commissioner should be willing to subscribe the Confession, and not only set an example to others but also, by the authority of his office, command its signing. He replied that the document whose signing the synod was urging contained two things. The first was the Confession of faith, about which (he said) there could now be no question, since he was thoroughly persuaded that both its formal words and the explanation by the synod, to which he had subscribed on 17 August, were true. Yet a scruple remained in the minds of some concerning the other part of the document, the mutual covenant, which in his judgment could easily be removed by a sound explanation, so that the king would be satisfied. The moderator said that the synod did not know what more could be said than had been said so far. The matter was deferred to the following session, and after a long debate it was decreed that a supplicatory petition should be offered to the royal Council, asking that, according to the custom of our ancestors, the Council would ratify this covenant and command by civil authority that all the subjects of the kingdom sign it. The petition, translated word for word, reads as follows.

units.la: Nos in synodum hanc Nationalem congregati, submissa & debita animorum gratitudine complures recentes favores à rege serenif.in nos collatos agnoscentes, ac perpendentes, nihil jam reliqui esse, quo regis erga nos benignitas compleri possit, quam ut omnia hujus ecclesiæ & regni membra, una & eadem confessione ac fœdere cum Deo, rege; ac mutuo inter se conjungantur: & in memoriam revocantes primariam remoram & impedimentum tam boni operis, & tot anxiis omnium votis expetiti, fuisse sinistriores relationes Regi serenif. factas de nostris intentionibus, quasi statutum nobis fuisset civilem & debitam supremis potestatibus obedientiâ excutere, ac regis authoritatem & amplitudinem diminuere: Nunc vero cum ex animis anxie deside[?]remus, illud cum aliis omnibus impedimentis removere, quæ obstaculo esse possint tam perfectæ unioni;ac fidelitatem nostram vindicare & asserere: Nostro & reliquorum omnium subditorum quos nunc repræsentamus nomine, Illustriss. deputato regio, ac Dominis honoratissimi secretioris concilii regii, submisse, prout decet, remonstramus, ac coram Deo & universo orbe ingenue declaramus, nunquam nos cogitationem quamlibet in animis nostris fovisse aut fovere, de subducendis nobis ab himili subjectione & obedientia regi ejusque regimini debita; cujus authoritatem à centum & septem regibus, majoribus suis traditam, majorum nostrorum exemplo lubentes agnoscimus: Neque mentem nostram unquam subiisse, ut quidlibet aggrederemur, quod ad diminutionem amplitudinis aut authoritatis regiæ tenderet: quin contra agnoscentes quietem ac felicitatem nostram dependere à salute nostri regis, (tanquam Dei deputati nobis superimpositi ad religionis tuitionem, & justitiæ administrationem) ac amplitudinis & regiæ authoritatis defensione; solenniter juravimus ac juramus, nos non solum in causa religionis, libertatis ac legum hujus regni tuendarum, regi adfuturos, in eumque finem, vitam, fortunas intrepide exposituros; verumetiam in omni causa quæ ad regis serenissimi honorem pertinet, (secundum hujus regni leges & fidelium subditorum officium) cum amicis & clientibus adfuturos, seu armato seu pacato agmine, prout Rex, senatus, aut regis deputatus imperaverit.
units.tr: We, gathered in this National Synod, acknowledging with humble and due gratitude of heart the many recent favours bestowed upon us by the most serene king, and considering that nothing now remains by which the king's kindness towards us can be completed except that all the members of this Church and kingdom be joined together in one and the same confession and covenant with God, the king, and one another; and recalling that the chief hindrance to so good a work, and to what everyone had anxiously desired, was the more sinister reports made to the most serene king about our intentions, as if it had been our purpose to shake off the civil and due obedience owed to the supreme powers and to diminish the king's authority and greatness: now, since we earnestly desire from our hearts to remove that obstacle, along with all other impediments that might stand in the way of so perfect a union, and to vindicate and assert our loyalty, we humbly and as is fitting remonstrate, in the name of ourselves and of all the other subjects whom we now represent, to the Illustrious royal commissioner and to the honourable Lords of the Privy Council. We freely declare before God and the whole world that we have never harboured in our minds, nor do we harbour now, any thought of withdrawing from that subjection and obedience owed to the king and his government, whose authority, handed down to him by one hundred and seven kings, his predecessors, we gladly acknowledge, following the example of our ancestors. Nor has it ever entered our minds to undertake anything that would tend to the diminution of royal greatness or authority. On the contrary, acknowledging that our peace and happiness depend on the safety of our king (as God's deputy set over us for the protection of religion and the administration of justice) and on the defence of his greatness and royal authority, we have solemnly sworn, and do swear, that we will stand by the king not only in defending the cause of religion, liberty and the laws of this kingdom, and will fearlessly expose our lives and fortunes to that end, but also in every cause that pertains to the honour of the most serene king (according to the laws of this kingdom and the duty of faithful subjects). We will stand by him with our friends and clients, whether in armed or peaceful array, as the King, the Council, or the king's commissioner shall command.

units.la: Atque cum nihil nobis antiquius sit, quam ut ab id genus obloquiis innocentiam nostram asseramus; majorum nostrorum exemplo, anno 1589. celsitudinem tuam, regis nostri serenissim. deputatum, & Dominos honoratissimi secretioris regii senatus supplices rogamus, ut edicto senatus confessionem hanc & fœdus, (quibus in tesseram[?] ac pignus fidei erga Deum, & fidelitatis erga Regem hactenus subscripsimus) ab omnibus sereniss. regis hujus regni subditis, cujuscunque demum dignitatis & ordinis fuerint, obsignari imperetis, & cæt.
units.tr: And since nothing is more important to us than to vindicate our innocence against such accusations, we humbly ask your Highness, the deputy of our most serene king, and the honourable Lords of the secret royal Council, following the example of our ancestors in 1589, that by an edict of the Council you command this confession and covenant, to which we have hitherto subscribed as a token and pledge of our faith towards God and our loyalty towards the king, to be signed by all the subjects of this most serene king in this kingdom, of whatever rank or order they may be; et cetera.

units.la: Synodi in hoc libello supplici postulatum concessit senatus, ac registris senatus inseri jussit; quod non solum statuto formato 30. Augusti. demonstravit, verumetiam Deputatus regius sessione synodi penultima publice coram synodo dixit; Libellum illum supplicem senatoribus regiis usque adeo placuisse, ut non potuerint non eidem simpliciter assentiri; Ad se vero quod attinet quatenus deputatum regium, lubenter fœderi subscripturum, sed cum hac addita declaratione.
units.tr: The Council granted the synod's request made in this supplicatory petition and ordered it to be entered in the Council's registers. This it showed not only by its formal statute of 30 August, but the royal commissioner also declared publicly before the synod at its penultimate session that the petition had so pleased the royal Councillors that they could not but simply agree to it. As for himself, as royal commissioner, he would gladly subscribe to the covenant, but with this declaration added.

units.la: Quandoquidem synodus hæc, pro laudata consuetudine antehac observata, deputatum regium, ac Dominos senatores honoratissimos secretioris senatus regii submisse obsecraverit, ut fœderi cum explanatione hujus synodi subscriberetur, ac omnibus hujus regni subditis senatusconsulto idem imperaretur. Atque cum, in supplicatione hac sua ad senatum, clausulam addiderint, qua fœdus hoc declaratur idem esse quoad substantiam cum eo quod a seren. regis Patre beatæ memoriæ annis 1580. 1581. 1590. obsignatum fuit, & sæpius postea renovatum, ut sese ab omni suspicione infidelitatis erga regem, aut diminutionis amplitudinis & authoritatis sereniss. nostri regis vindicarent.
units.tr: Since this synod, according to the praised custom observed before, had humbly besought the royal commissioner and the honourable Lords, the senators of the secret royal Council, that the covenant be subscribed with the explanation of this synod, and that the Council's decree command the same of all the subjects of this kingdom; and since in this supplication to the Council they had added a clause declaring that this covenant is the same in substance as that which was signed in the years 1580, 1581 and 1590 by the most serene king's father, of blessed memory, and often renewed afterwards, so that they might clear themselves of every suspicion of infidelity towards the king, or of diminishing the authority and greatness of our most serene king.

units.la: Quare ego quatenus regius deputatus, quo subditis abunde satisfiat, & plena pax ecclesiæ & regni stabiliatur, approbo & assentior (secundum prædictam meam declarationem decreto synodi subjunctam, quod 17. Augusti conditum fuit) ut ab omnibus hujus regni sub-ditis ditis fœderi subscribatur, in cujus testimonium præsentes has mea manu subscripsi.
units.tr: Therefore I, as royal commissioner, so that the subjects may be fully satisfied and complete peace of Church and kingdom may be established, approve and agree (according to my aforesaid declaration, appended to the synod's decree drawn up on 17 August) that the covenant be subscribed by all the subjects of this kingdom. In witness of this I have subscribed these presents with my own hand.

units.la: Iohannes Comes Traquarius Commissionarius.
units.tr: John Earl of Traquair, Commissioner.

units.la: At quatenus inter alios regni subditos esset, profitebatur se simpliciter cum aliis omnibus ex senatus præscripto sine ulla addita declaratione subscripturum, æquum etiam esse ut omnes subditi idem faciant, quandoquidem rationes quæ regem ad limitatam hanc subscriptionem urgeant, subditorum nullum tangere possint, ne se quidem quatenus Comitem Traquarium eximendum esse: Addebat sibi curæ futurum ut in parlamento præcedentia omnia sancirentur; Quæ vox summo omnium cum gaudio, ac sensu favoris divini & benignitatis regiæ accepta fuit.
units.tr: But inasmuch as he himself was among the other subjects of the kingdom, he declared that he would simply subscribe, like all the others, according to the Council's prescription and without any added declaration. He said it was also fair that all subjects do the same, since the reasons which urge the king to this limited subscription could touch no subject, not even himself, the Earl of Traquair, who ought not to be exempted. He added that it would be his care that all precedence be enacted in parliament. This statement was received with the great joy of all, and with a sense of divine favour and royal kindness.

units.la: Cæterum præses synodum monuit, consultum fore, ut decreto synodico idem sanciretur: quod sic se habuit.
units.tr: Moreover, the moderator advised the synod that it would be advisable to have the same enacted by synodal decree, which ran as follows.

units.la: Synodus exploratum habens singularem fœlicitatem, quæ oritur à plena & perfecta unione regni & ecclesiæ hujus, in unum & idem fœdus cum Deo, rege serenissimo[?] ac mutuum inter se coeuntis; cumque solenni juramento sinceritatem & fidelitatem intentionum nostrarum in universa præcedentium actionum serie declaraverimus, ac supplicibus literis Illustriss. deputatum regium & D. honoratissimi senatus regii obsecrati fuerimus, ut senatusconsulto imperarent omnibus hujus regni subditis obsignationem confessionis fidei & fœderis, cui à nobis antehac subscriptum fuit, ut arrha & pignus esset fidei in Deum, & fidelitatis nostræ erga regem: Atque cum nostris postulatis ab Illustriss. deputato regio, & D. Honoratissimi senatus regii satisfactum sit, omnibusque omnino subditis ejusdem fœderis obsignationem imperaverint authoritate politica, ut uno plenior ac perfectior fit, decreto & constitutione ecclesiastica praedictum foedus in omnibus suis clausulis, & ex omni parte synodus haec probat, ac denuo decernit sub poena ecclesiasticae censurae, ut Academiarum praefecti, professores, scholarum praeceptores, studiosi ad scholasticos gradus promovendi, omnes de papismo aut quovis alio errore suspecti, ac denique omnia & singula huius ecclesiae membra, eidem foederi subscribant, hisce verbis subscriptioni praefixis. (Articulus huius foederis qui in prima subscriptione relatus fuit ad determinationem Nationalis synodi, cum nunc definitus sit, ac quinque articuli Perthenses, regimen ecclesiae per Episcopos, civilia officia & politica ecclesiasticorum potestas, declarata sint in hac ecclesia esse illicita ob rationes decretis ac canonibus Nationalium synodorum comprehensas; Nos subscribimus secundum determinationem praecedentem.) Ac statuit ut foedus cum hac declaratione publicis omnibus huius ecclesiae registris, Nationalibus, provincialibus, & classicalibus, ad perpetuam memoriam inferatur: Submisse etiam rogat Illustriss. deputatum regium, & honoratissimos ac amplissimos regni ordines in parlamento convocatos, ut sua authoritate, eadem sanciant, ac sub poenis civilibus imperent: Quod non dubitamus quin cessurum sit in Dei gloriam, religionis purioris praeservationem, sereniss. regis honorem, ac perfectam regni & ecclesiae pacem.
units.tr: The synod, having ascertained the singular happiness that arises from the full and perfect union of this kingdom and Church, coming together in one and the same covenant with God, the most serene king, and one another; and since we have declared, by solemn oath, the sincerity and fidelity of our intentions throughout the whole course of our previous actions; and since we have been humbly petitioned by letters from the Illustrious royal commissioner and the honourable Lords of the royal Council to command, by decree of the Council, all the subjects of this kingdom to sign the confession of faith and the covenant to which we had previously subscribed, as an earnest and pledge of faith in God and of our loyalty towards the king; and since our requests have been granted by the Illustrious royal commissioner and the honourable Lords of the royal Council, who have commanded all subjects to sign the same covenant by political authority, so that it may become fuller and more perfect as one body: by ecclesiastical decree and constitution, this synod approves the aforesaid covenant in all its clauses and in every respect, and again decrees, under penalty of ecclesiastical censure, that the heads of Universities, professors, schoolmasters, students to be promoted to academic degrees, all those suspected of popery or of any other error, and finally all and each of the members of this Church, subscribe to the same covenant, with these words prefixed to the signature. (The article of this covenant which was related in the first subscription to the determination of the National Synod has now been defined; and the five Articles of Perth, government of the Church by bishops, civil offices, and the political power of churchmen, have been declared unlawful in this Church for the reasons contained in the decrees and canons of the National Synods. We subscribe according to the preceding determination.) It also ordains that the covenant, with this declaration, be entered for perpetual memory in all the public registers of this Church, national, provincial and classical. It further humbly asks the Illustrious royal commissioner and the most honourable and distinguished orders of the kingdom, convened in parliament, that by their authority they ratify the same and command it under civil penalties. We do not doubt that this will tend to the glory of God, the preservation of purer religion, the honour of the most serene king, and the perfect peace of kingdom and Church.

units.la: Proposuit tum Deputatus regius quaestionem, An foederis huius cum praedicta explanatione obsignatio, extra limites regni Scotiae obligaret? Ac negativam speciose astruebat [?], sed cum synodus perspiceret, quo conatus ille tenderet, respondit: Unicuique cum sua conscientia consulendum esse, licet omni metu a censuris ecclesiasticis liber esset. Declarationem tamen ille protulit, qua significabat, prædictorum praxin prohibitam, intelligendam tantum esse intra limites regni; neque obsignatores censuris ullis ecclesiasticis notandos esse, si extra regni limites, hic damnatis uterentur; Ac licet declaratio hæc synodo non arrideret, multorumque judicio putaretur non satis convenire cum iis quæ tam liberaliter promittebat antehac deputatus regius, omnibusque etiam importuna videretur, sub nomine declarationis protestationem reipsa continens; synodi tamen registris ex mandato deputati inseruerunt; sed recitative solum, hoc est, non quasi approbarent, sed quod talia publice protulisset Deputatus.
units.tr: The Royal Commissioner then raised the question whether signing this covenant with the aforesaid explanation bound people outside the limits of the kingdom of Scotland. He argued the negative with some plausibility, but when the synod perceived where this attempt was heading, he replied that each person must consult his own conscience, though he himself was free from any fear of ecclesiastical censures. He nevertheless produced a declaration stating that the practice of the aforesaid things was prohibited only within the limits of the kingdom, and that signatories would not be liable to any ecclesiastical censures if they practised here the things condemned while outside the kingdom's borders. Although this declaration did not please the synod, and many judged that it did not agree well with what the Commissioner had so generously promised before, and it seemed objectionable to everyone, since in effect it contained a protest under the name of a declaration, the synod nevertheless inserted it in its registers by the Commissioner's order. It was entered only as recited, that is, not as if they approved it, but because the Commissioner had publicly put it forward.

units.la: Sessione ultima decretum fuit ut sequens synodus Nationalis, Abredoniæ ad 28. Iulii mensis anni subsequentis 1640.' conveniret, & classi Edenburgenæ commissum fuit, ut interim dispiceret ne quid damni pateretur ecclesia, ac pro ratione gravaminum necessitatem synodi regi sereniss. remonstraret. Statutum tum ut ad regem literæ synodi nomine, perscriberentur, quibus gratiæ agerentur ob beneficia hactenus obtenta, & synodi sanctio per parlamentū postularetur: neq; ullus fuit, cujus animo non fuerit abunde persuasum, omnia hæc in parlamento Deputatum regium rata habituram, quippe quod in articulis pacificationis hoc diserte pactum fuisset, ut quod definiret synodus, illud sanciret parlamentum; ac publice sæpius in synodo deputatus regius in se recepisset publicam synodi sanctionem, cujus omnes actiones suffragio suo comprobassent.
units.tr: At the last session it was decided that the next National Synod should meet at Aberdeen on 28 July of the following year, 1640. The Edinburgh classis was charged with meanwhile taking care that the church suffered no harm, and with informing the most serene king, according to the grievances, of the need for a synod. It was then resolved that letters be written to the king in the name of the synod, giving thanks for the benefits hitherto obtained and requesting that the synod's sanction be ratified by parliament. No one was unconvinced that the Royal Commissioner would make all these things valid in parliament, since it had been expressly agreed in the articles of pacification that parliament would sanction whatever the synod defined; and the Royal Commissioner had often publicly undertaken in the synod to secure the public sanction of the synod, whose acts he had all approved with his vote.

units.la: Peractis omnibus ob quæ convenerat Synodus, luculentam orationem habuit præses, cujus summa capita fuerunt. Dominum mira in oculis suorum operatum esse, ac justitiam & misericordiam suam manifeste nunc exeruisse, Iustitiam. 1. In pastores ecclesiae, in quos Deus merito animadvertit, ob supinam illam rerum divinarum negligentiam. 2. In nobiles & alios regni ordines; qui conniventia sua passi essent, praesules conscendere ad superbam illam dominationem, qua procerum cervicibus arroganter insultarunt, 3. In praesules ipsos, qui statione sua non contenti, Domini non ministri haereditatis Christi haberi se volebant, quorum faciem infamia replevit nunc Dominus. In medio tamen irae memorem fuisse Deum, pro benignitate sua, misericordiarum, idque 1. in nos pastores, quibus oculos opportune aperuit, ne in foveam praecipitaremur, unde vix sperari potuisset exitus: nostrasque animas morti & erroris efficaciae non tradidit.
units.tr: When all the business for which the synod had assembled was finished, the president gave an eloquent speech, whose main heads were these. The Lord has worked wonders in the eyes of his people, and has now clearly displayed his justice and mercy. His justice was shown: (1) against the ministers of the church, on whom God has rightly taken vengeance for their supine neglect of divine things; (2) against the nobles and other orders of the kingdom, who by their connivance allowed the prelates to climb to that proud domination by which they arrogantly trampled on the necks of the great; (3) against the prelates themselves, who, not content with their station, wished to be regarded as lords rather than ministers of Christ's inheritance, and whose faces the Lord has now filled with infamy. Yet in the midst of his anger God remembered mercy, in his kindness, and this toward us ministers: (1) in that he opened our eyes in time, lest we be plunged into the pit from which escape could scarcely have been hoped, and did not hand over our souls to death and the power of error.

units.la: 2. In regem sereniss. quem à fusione innocentis nostri sanguinis retinuit, atque id usque adeo mirifice, ut in nostra defensione humanam potentiam conspici vix voluerit: imo nobis ad incitas saepius redac-tis, & ignaris (inquit) quo nos converteremus, Deus exerto quasi digito exitum semper monstravit, & benigna sua providentia ad nostrum commodum & solatium singula convertit. 3. In Rempub. hanc; à miraculo certe non longe abesse merito dicas, integram gentem praesertim Scoticam, (cujus ingenium apud exteros praefervidum audit) tamdiu commotam & sedibus suis excitam, sine caede & sanguine propemodum sedatam, idque mediis legitimis. Praesules in coelo nidificantes ac se triumphantem ecclesiam venditantes, in contemptum hunc quo hodie merito obruuntur à Deo dejectos, cernere; ac sereniss. Carolum, regem nobis esse, (cui vitam & felicitatem perennet Dominus) licet nulli sint Episcopi, contra ipsorum ἐ[?]ιν ἀ[?]ξην[?] : Nullus Episcopus, nullus Rex.
units.tr: (2) Toward the most serene king, whom he restrained from shedding our innocent blood, and that so wonderfully that he scarcely willed human power to be seen in our defence. Indeed, when we were often driven to straits and did not know (he says) which way to turn, God, as if stretching out a finger, always showed us the way out, and by his kindly providence turned each thing to our advantage and comfort. (3) Toward this commonwealth: one may rightly say it is not far from a miracle that the whole nation, especially the Scots (whose temperament is said to be very fiery among foreigners), so long stirred and roused from their homes, has been calmed almost without slaughter or bloodshed, and by lawful means. We see the prelates, who nested in heaven and boasted of themselves as a triumphant church, cast down by God into this contempt under which they are today rightly overwhelmed. We see Charles, the most serene king (may the Lord grant him life and happiness for ever), as our king, although there are no bishops, contrary to their own maxim: No bishop, no king.

units.la: Dein ad Pastores oratione conversa, serio eos monuit officii fui, ut ita se gererent quasi rationem reddituři Domino de animabus curæ ipsorum creditis, ut depósito typho & fastu sæculari fraterne inter se degerent, obliti præcedentium infœlicium controversiarum, quas æterno silentio sepeliendas dicebat, & quibus soli Satan & Antichristus lucrati fuerunt; Hancque unicam suam gloriam judicarent, multas animas Diaboli laqueis ereptas Christo lucrari: Monebat serio, ut nihil intentatum relinquerent quo populus bonam opinionem de Rege foveret, ac promptam & paratam obedientiam legitimis ejus mandatis præstaret, supra omnia vero, ut ex corde eum diligeret, præsertim cum vix inveniatur princeps iis donis instructus, quæ serenissimi regi concessit Dominus: ita quidem, ut licet abesset dignitas illa regia, qua supra omnes ut Dei in terris deputatus fulget, Chorus tamen ille virtutum vere Heroicarum, in oculis subditorum eum merito amabilem redderet. Abalienationem quandam hactenus fuisse, quæ, cum Dei benignitate mutata sit in suavem reconciliationem, amoris redintegrationem debere secum ferre: præsertim si ipsa abalienatio penitus inspiciatur, satis cuilibet apparitutum[?], per regem solum, secundum Deum ste-tisse, quo minus in majorem flammam incendium illud non proruperit. Nam 1. (inquit) perpendi velim ab omnibus, quænam fuerit serenissimi regis nostri educatio; & an cuipiam mirum videri debeat, si, quibus ab incunabulis prope assuetus fuerit, usque adeo mordicus adhæserit? 2. Regibus necessario utendum esse consiliariis, cum ipsi suis oculis singula conspicere non possint; Ac quorum quaeso[?] consiliariorum opera confidentius uti potuisset Rex noster serenissimus quam eorum qui illi omnia debebant, & ob id solum ad dignitatum fastigia evecti erant, ut salutaribus consiliis ei adessent, ac de subditorum statu vere certiorem facerent? Sed dolendum, quod in Episcopos inciderit, qui gratia qua apud eum pollebant foede abusi sunt; ac sibi tantum prospicientes, & turpibus affectibus abrepti, consiliis suis specie laetis, sed tractatu duris, & eventu, nisi Deus stulta reddidisset, tristioribus, malorum omnium authores fuerunt quae hactenus (inquit) perpessi sumus, & per eos non stetit quominus de nobis conclamatum, & status hic in extremam usque ruinam (quam Deus pro singulari sua providentia tam benigne antevertit) praecipitatus fit. 3. Quantum ex serie tota actionum serenis. regis contra nos colligere possum; videre mihi videor regem hostile quid serio in nos non meditatum fuisse, sed omnia eo spectasse ut probaret quo postulata nostra, ab adversariis nostris misere & foede distorta; revera tenderent, & animorum nostrorum candida & aperta fidelitate penitus perspecta; placabilem se tandem, frendentibus turbidis istis consiliariis, ostendisse, ac halcyoniam hanc, quam diuturnam voveo, concessisse. Sed altius in secreta haec consilia penetrare consultum non judicarem: Regum corda in manu Domini sunt, qui serio precandus est, ut ad ea consilia posthac flectat, quibus glorioso huic operi extrema manus addi possit, & ut regis nostri serenis. folio semper adsit.
units.tr: He then turned his speech to the ministers and seriously admonished them of their duty: they should so conduct themselves as those who must render an account to the Lord for the souls entrusted to their care; laying aside pride and worldly arrogance, they should live together as brothers, forgetting the earlier unhappy controversies, which he said should be buried in eternal silence, and from which only Satan and Antichrist had profited. They should regard this as their sole glory, to win for Christ many souls snatched from the devil's snares. He earnestly urged them to leave nothing untried by which the people might cherish a good opinion of the king and render prompt and ready obedience to his lawful commands; and above all, to love him from the heart, especially since hardly any prince is found endowed with those gifts which the Lord has granted to the most serene king. So, although that royal dignity is absent, which shines above all others as God's deputy on earth, that chorus of truly heroic virtues would nonetheless make him deservedly lovable in the eyes of his subjects. He said that there had hitherto been a certain estrangement, which, now that God's kindness has turned it into a sweet reconciliation, ought to bring with it a renewal of love. Especially if the estrangement itself is examined closely, it is clear enough to anyone that it was through the king alone, under God, that the fire did not break out into a greater blaze. For (he said): (1) I would have everyone consider what the upbringing of our most serene king was, and whether anyone should think it strange if he has clung so stubbornly to what he was almost accustomed to from his cradle. (2) Kings must necessarily use counsellors, since they cannot see every thing with their own eyes. And whose counsel, I ask, could our most serene king have used with more confidence than theirs, who owed him everything and had been raised to the heights of dignity for that very reason alone, so that they might stand by him with wholesome counsel and truly inform him of the condition of his subjects? But it is to be lamented that he fell in with bishops who foully abused the favour they enjoyed with him. Looking only to themselves and carried away by base desires, they gave counsels that were pleasing in appearance but harsh in their handling and, in the outcome, sadder still, unless God had made them foolish. They were the authors of all the evils we have hitherto suffered (he says), and through them it did not stand that we were given up for lost and this state was not hurled into utter ruin, which God by his singular providence so kindly averted. (3) As far as I can gather from the whole series of the most serene king's actions against us, I seem to see that the king never seriously intended anything hostile against us. Rather, all his actions aimed at proving where our demands, wretchedly and foully distorted by our adversaries, truly tended; and, our minds having been thoroughly perceived through our candid and open loyalty, he showed himself at last placable, while those turbulent counsellors gnashed their teeth, and granted this halcyon peace, which I pray may be long-lasting. But I do not judge it wise to penetrate further into these secret counsels. The hearts of kings are in the hand of the Lord, who must earnestly be entreated to turn them henceforth to those counsels by which this glorious work may be brought to completion, and who may always be present at our most serene king's throne.

units.la: Denique quia in synodo mentionem fecerat Deputatus regius eorum nobilium, quorum opera usus fuisset serenis. Rex a motuum horum initiis, ac de eorum studiis candide judicari rogaverat, de iis etiam quaedam loquutus est Praeses, ac in tres Classes distinguebat politicos omnes qui foederi adversati fuerunt, ac praesulibus adhaeserunt, Alii (inquit) erant pontificiis erroribus addicti, qui sub umbra præsulum tuto latere se posse, sibi haud immerito persuaserant: alii vero errore mentis seducti fuerunt, licet papismum aversarentur; & hos commiseratione complectendos sibi videri: Tertius vero ordo eorum, quibus visum fuit politi-cis consiliis incedere, atque hi (inquit) satis ostenderunt, se Regem serenissim. & ecclesiam ac regnum pariter dilexisse, ac semet quasi bipertitos fuisse, nam licet ipsi adessent regi, nobis tamen liberos suos reliquerunt, ut hoc pignore & obside certos nos redderent, pacem sibi ex animo propositam fuisse; hisce, prout decet, prospera omnia vovemus, eorumque actiones candide interpretabimur. Præsertim vero illustrissim. Marchioni Hammiltonio, (quandoquidem studiosissimum pacis fuisse retulisset Deputatus regius) synodi nomine gratias meritas referebat, ac senatoribus regiis, qui Deputato in singulis sessionibus adfuerunt; ac tandem oratione ad illustrissim. Deputatum conversa, licet actionum harum laudem modeste a se amoliretur, ac Echum tantum se agere profiteretur, qui serenissim. regis verba repeteret. Inter alios (inquit) iniquum esset si tua Celsitudo præteriretur, cui plurimum se debere fatetur synodus, quod, antehac in adversam partem proniorem conspexisset, nunc tamen piorum votis & desideriis propemodum satisfecerit: Agnoscenda tibi (inquit) est Dei gratia, qui te ut singulare ac insigne instrumentum elegit perficiendi hujus operis, cui jam nihil deest quam ut sanctione Parlamentaria extremum colophonem addas: Ac animo grato singulares illas ingenii dotes à Deo concessas, in Christi honorem ac ecclesiæ commodum impendas, qui se honorantes honorat, neque ullos se colentes immuneratos unquam dimisit. Post preces ad Deum, & publicum Psalmi vigesimi tertii cantum, Præses benedictionem precatus, synodum dimittit. 30. Augusti mensis. Finis.
units.tr: Finally, since the Royal Commissioner had mentioned in the synod those nobles whose help the most serene king had used, and had asked that their zeal be judged fairly from the beginnings of these disturbances, the president also spoke about them. He divided into three classes all the politicians who opposed the covenant and adhered to the prelates. Some (he said) were addicted to papist errors, and had reasonably persuaded themselves that they could lie safely under the shadow of the prelates. Others were led astray by an error of judgement, although they abhorred popery, and these, he thought, should be embraced with compassion. The third class were those who chose to proceed by political counsels, and these (he said) have sufficiently shown that they loved the most serene king, the church and the kingdom alike, and that they were, as it were, divided in two. For although they stood by the king, they left us their children as free, so that by this pledge and hostage they might assure us that peace was sincerely intended by them. We wish all prosperity to these men, as is fitting, and will interpret their actions candidly. Especially to the most illustrious Marquis of Hamilton (since the Royal Commissioner had reported that he was most zealous for peace), the synod rendered thanks, as was deserved, and likewise to the royal senators who attended the Commissioner at each session. Finally, turning his speech to the most illustrious Commissioner, although he modestly disclaimed praise for these actions, professing that he was merely an echo repeating the words of the most serene king, he said: Among others it would be unfair to pass over your Highness, to whom the synod confesses it owes very much, since it had earlier seen you more inclined to the opposite side, yet now you have nearly satisfied the prayers and desires of the godly. The grace of God must be acknowledged in you, who chose you as a singular and remarkable instrument for completing this work, to which nothing now is lacking except that you add the final seal by parliamentary sanction. And with a grateful mind you should spend those singular gifts of mind granted to you by God for the honour of Christ and the advantage of the church, for he honours those who honour him, and never dismissed unrewarded any who worshipped him. After prayer to God and the public singing of Psalm 23, the president pronounced the blessing and dismissed the synod, 30 August. End.

units.la: Die sequenti post dimissam synodum, regni ordinum conventus, seu parlamentum (prout edicto regio imperatum fuit) cogitur: Alexandro Hendersono luculenta oratione de institutione, fine, utilitate magistratus, actionem auspicante. Dein ad electionem Dominorum ad articulos deventum; (hi vero sunt octo ex singulis ordinibus electi, quibus committi solet præparatio omnium negotiorum quæ ad pleni parlamenti cognitionem deferenda sunt; quæ quia in articulos referunt, Domini articulorum, seu ad articulos videl. formandos, dicti vulgo sunt, & quia ad id munus electi, Apolecti ab historicis vocantur) Deputatus regius in vicinum conclave evocatis supremi ordinis nobilibus secedit, relictis duobus aliis regni ordinibus provinciarum & civitatum deputatis in ordinaria Comitiorum aula, ignaris prorsus quid rerum agendum esset, & ad rei novitatem stupentibus: Qui longioris morae tandem pertæsi, quosdam ablegarunt, qui sciscitarentur, quid sibi vellet illa Nobilium separatio; & cum compertum habuissent, Deputato regio statutum fuisse Apolectos suo & nobilium suffragiis eligere, exclusis provinciarum & civitatum suffragiis; intercedunt, nec satis æquum asserunt, ut Apolecti, qui parlamenti totius nomine publica negotia procurant, ab aliis quam universis regni ordinibus in pleno parlamento eligantur, præsertim cum tota illa, qua vestiuntur authoritas à parlamento dependeat, eamque deputatorum à parlamento nomine exerceant: Ante annum 1617. quando Episcopi electionem hanc sibi primum arripuerunt, in plenis comitiis omnium suffragiis electos semper fuisse; episcopis vero nunc fœliciter ejectis, æquum dicebant fore, ut electio hæc Apolectorum vel ad pristinum suum statum postliminio reduceretur; velfi illud non placeret, à singulis ordinibus fui ordinis deputati eligerentur; cum, quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus approbari debeat: Quod fi insciis ac non confultis & invitis parlamenti ordinibus reliquis, ab uno solum ordine, quisquis is demum fit, eligantur, non posse haberi pro parlamenti deputatis, & eorum acta omnia prorsus fore irrita, cum fiant à non habentibus potestatem.
units.tr: The day after the synod was dismissed, the assembly of the estates of the kingdom, or parliament, was convened as the royal edict had ordered. Alexander Henderson opened the proceedings with an eloquent speech on the institution, purpose and usefulness of the magistracy. Then they came to the election of the Lords of the Articles. These are eight men chosen from each estate, to whom the preparation of all business to be brought before the full parliament is usually committed. They are commonly called the Lords of the Articles because they draw matters up into articles, and historians call them Apolecti because they are the chosen ones. The royal commissioner withdrew into a nearby chamber with the nobles of the highest rank, leaving the other two estates, the deputies of the provinces and burghs, in the ordinary hall of the assembly. Those deputies were quite ignorant of what was to be done and stunned by the novelty of the matter. Growing weary at last of the long delay, they sent some men to ask what that separation of the nobles meant. When they learned that the royal commissioner had decreed that the Apolecti should be chosen by his own votes and those of the nobles, with the votes of the provinces and burghs excluded, they objected. They argued that it was not fair that the Apolecti, who manage public business in the name of the whole parliament, should be chosen by anyone other than all the estates of the kingdom in full parliament. This was especially so because all the authority they hold depends on parliament, and they exercise it in parliament's name as its deputies. Before the year 1617, when the bishops first seized this election for themselves, they said, those chosen had always been elected by the votes of all in full assembly. Now that the bishops had happily been ousted, it would be fair for this election of the Apolecti to be restored to its former state. If that did not please, each estate should choose its own deputies from its own order, since what touches all should be approved by all. But if they were chosen by one estate alone, whichever it might be, without the knowledge, consultation or consent of the other estates of parliament, they could not be regarded as parliament's deputies, and all their acts would be utterly void, since they were done by men without the power to do them.

units.la: Hæc intercessio multis usque adeo æqua visa fuit, ut incorruptior nobilitatis pars in eam sententiam, ut Reipublic. maxime salutarem concesserint; & patri studio urgendum esse omnes statuerint, ut illimitata illa & tantum non absoluta potestas Apolectorum, arctioribus, quam quibus aliquot annis supinâ ordinum regni conniventiâ usi fuerunt, limitibus circumscriberetur: præsertim cum nullo statuto municipali sancitum esset, debere Apolectos esse, aut eorundem potestas ullibi definiretur: Atque cum à parlamento deputati essent, absurdum fore nisi non solum tenerentur eidem rationem reddere omnium quæ ipsis proponentur, verumetiam nisi pro utilitate & necessitate ipsis præscribi posset.
units.tr: This objection seemed so fair to many that the more upright part of the nobility agreed with it as most salutary for the commonwealth. They all resolved to press zealously that the unlimited and almost absolute power of the Apolecti be confined within tighter limits than those under which they had acted for some years through the passive connivance of the estates. This was especially so since no municipal statute had sanctioned that there should be Apolecti at all, or defined their power anywhere. And since they were deputed by parliament, it would be absurd if they were not bound to give parliament an account of everything proposed to them, and if it could not also be prescribed to them what to do for the benefit and need of the occasion.

units.la: De facto quidem à regno Davidis Brucii fuisse quosdam Apolectos, sed in actibus liberis non currere præscriptionem. Addebant civitatum & provinciarum legati, literis ad parlamentum citatoriis, citatos omnes non vocari solum ad sententiam simpliciter ferendam, verumetiam ut singula examinent, ac diligenter discutiant, quod usurpatione Dominorum ad articulos prorsus ademptum est, qui cum omnia definiant, nec solum in articulos discutienda referant, verumetiam statutorum formas inconsultis reliquis parlamenti membris componant, eorumque solum rubricas in pleno parlamento prælegant, quid cæteris quæso relictum est præter simplicem assensum aut dissensum ? Idque sine ulla libertate explicandi & confirmandi sententiam suam, nedum contrariam refutandi. Naturam etiam delegationis suæ, cum personalis sit & inhærens, non ferre ut potestatem sibi à provinciis & civitatibus commissam, in alios præsertim se inconsultis & invitis electos transferant. Quare utilissimum fore regno judicabant, & ad supremi hujus tribunalis splendorem plurimum collaturum; si omnia gravamina in parlamento pleno exhiberentur; & si pro re nata communi omnium authoritate delegarentur; qui eadem excuterent, & singula ad plena comitia referrent, & statutorum formas cum omnibus communicarent, ut sic singuli exacte intelligerent ea de quibus sententia ferenda sit. Sed neutrum à Deputato regio obtineri potuit; interim tamen ne controversiæ hæ de electione & potestate apolectorum, comitiorum progressum in ipso limine impediret, hoc temperamento contenti fuerunt ordines, ut quos deputatus regius cum nobilibus elegisset, iidem etiam ab aliis ordinibus denuo eligerentur, utraque parte in scriptis protestante de salvo suo jure, & quæstio de apolectorum potestate ante dimissa comitia definiretur.
units.tr: It is true that in the reign of David Bruce there were some Apolecti, but prescription does not run against free acts. The envoys of the burghs and provinces added, in the letters summoning parliament, that those summoned were called not merely to pass judgment but also to examine and carefully discuss each matter. This had been entirely taken away by the usurpation of the Lords of the Articles, who settle everything. They do not merely refer matters to be discussed in the articles, but also compose the forms of statutes without consulting the other members of parliament, and read out only their headings in full parliament. What, I ask, is left for the others except simple assent or dissent? And that without any freedom to explain and confirm their own opinion, let alone to refute the contrary one. Moreover, the nature of their delegation, being personal and inherent, does not allow them to transfer the power committed to them by the provinces and burghs to others, especially to men chosen without their consultation and against their will. Therefore they judged it would be most useful to the kingdom, and would greatly add to the splendour of this supreme court, if all grievances were presented in full parliament. If, as occasion required, delegates were appointed by the common authority of all, they would examine these grievances, report each matter to the full assembly, and share the forms of statutes with everyone, so that each might clearly understand the matters on which judgment was to be given. But the royal commissioner could obtain neither. Meanwhile, so that these disputes about the election and power of the Apolecti would not hinder the progress of the assembly at its very threshold, the estates were content with this compromise: those whom the royal commissioner had chosen with the nobles would be chosen again by the other estates, each side protesting in writing for the preservation of its right, and the question of the power of the Apolecti would be settled before the assembly was dismissed.

units.la: Postea actum fuit de constitutione parlamenti præsentis, quomodo pro plenario & omnibus suis membris integro haberi posset, cum deesset tertius ordo, pro clero videlicet episcopi & abbates. Pauci cum Deputato regio dicebant; ideo esse plenarium, quod omnes quorum adesse intererat legitime citati fuissent: alii vero omnes addi volebant, nullum pro clero debere adesse, & ante omnia declarandum esse, Episcopis, Abbatibus, neque ullis ecclesiæ nomine jus suffragii in comitiis esse, cum synodi nuperæ judicio decretum esset, episcopos ex ecclesia ejiciendos esse, qui jure illo suf-fragii se gaudere jactitabant, quod ecclesiæ personam in Comitiis repræsentarent: ac interdictum severe pastoribus, quia eorum functio spiritualis est, & aliis quibuscunque, ne ecclesiæ nomine in Comitiis regni suffragium ferant: quibus decretis cum assensisset Deputatus regius in synodo, rogant ut ante omnia declaretur, præsens hoc parla-mentum omnibus suis legitimis membris ita integrum esse, ut ejus integritas subsequentium sit mensura constans & perpetua: Etenim cum statutis parlamentariis anni 1609. sancitum sit, irrita esse omnia parlamenti statuta nisi consensum habeant trium ordinum regni: & vero clerum ordinem unum fecisse multa sint quæ persuadeant, episcoposque pro Clero sententiam tulisse, cuivis obvium est, primum & ante omnia decernendum esse, Clero nullum jus dicendæ sententiæ nunc esse, & qui contra sentiunt, non videre dicebant, posticam apertam, qua hujus parlamenti statuta à principio irrita fuisse necessario affirmari posset, neque negarunt quin mutatio quædam hæc sit, verum necessaria, originem suam trahens à decreto nuperæ synodi, obsignato à deputato regio, cujus synodi sanctione, cum edicto perpetuo Rex serenissimus pollicitus sit in hisce comitiis, eo præsertim nomine indictis, ejusque edicti beneficium urgeant ecclesiarum à synodo Deputati, absurdum prorsus esse inferebant, nisi ecclesiis quæ regio promisso innituntur flagitantibus satisfiat, ac statuta omnia præcedentium comitiorum de jure suffragii in Comitiis pro Clero penitus refigantur, cum manifesto adversentur nuperæ synodi decretis. Deputatus regius synodi sanctionem aperte non denegabat, sed statuta adversantia ut refigeret, aut ut Clerum à jure suffragii in perpetuum excluderet, nequicquam ei persuaderi potuit, quantam, æquorum postulatorum pertinaci rejectione, conjiciebant complures, fero illum pœnituisse quod in abdicationem episcopatus & subversionem civilis potestatis ecclesiasticorum in synodo tam liberaliter consentiisset: aut novis forte ab aula mandatis instructum fuisse, nam posthac observatum fuit nihil proponi potuisse, quantumvis necessarium & luce sua perspicuum, quin objectis novis difficultatibus aut simpliciter rejiceretur, aut ejus definitio procrastinaretur, donec ab aula rediret tabellarius.
units.tr: Afterwards the matter of the constitution of the present parliament was taken up: how it could be regarded as full and complete in all its members, since the third estate, namely the clergy (bishops and abbots), was missing. A few agreed with the royal commissioner that it was full because all whose presence was required had been lawfully summoned. The others all wanted it added that no one should attend for the clergy. Above all, it must be declared that bishops and abbots, and indeed no one at all, have a right to vote in the assembly in the name of the Church. By the judgment of the recent synod it had been decreed that bishops must be cast out of the Church; they had boasted that they held the right to vote because they represented the person of the Church in the assembly. Ministers were also severely forbidden, because their function is spiritual, and so was anyone else whatever, from giving a vote in the assembly of the kingdom in the name of the Church. When the royal commissioner had assented to these decrees in the synod, they asked that before all else it be declared that the present parliament was so complete in all its lawful members that its completeness should be a constant and perpetual measure for later ones. For since the parliamentary statutes of 1609 sanctioned that all acts of parliament are void unless they have the consent of the three estates of the kingdom, and since there are many indications that the clergy formed a single estate and that the bishops gave a verdict on behalf of the clergy, it is obvious to anyone that it must first and above all be decreed that the clergy now has no right to give a voice. Those who thought otherwise, they said, could not see any open loophole by which the statutes of this parliament could necessarily be affirmed to have been void from the beginning. Nor did they deny that this change was indeed a change, but a necessary one, springing from the decree of the recent synod, which the royal commissioner had sealed. The most serene King had promised, in a perpetual edict sanctioned by that synod, that these assemblies would be held, and the deputies of the churches from the synod press the benefit of that edict. It was therefore utterly absurd, they argued, unless the churches, resting on the royal promise, were satisfied in their demands, and all the statutes of earlier assemblies concerning the clergy's right to vote were wholly annulled, since they manifestly contradict the decrees of the recent synod. The royal commissioner did not openly deny the sanction of the synod, but he could not be persuaded to repeal the contrary statutes or to exclude the clergy from the right to vote for ever. Many conjectured that he regretted, to the great detriment of these just demands which he stubbornly rejected, having so freely consented in the synod to the abdication of episcopacy and the subversion of the civil power of churchmen. Or perhaps he had been furnished with new orders from the court, for afterwards it was observed that nothing could be proposed, however necessary and self-evident, without either being simply rejected by new objections or its settlement being postponed until the courier returned from court.

units.la: Dein summa animorum contentione disputatum fuit de statuto ἀμνηστίας[?] et pacificationis, quo quæcunque post exortos hos motus accidissent, perpetuæ oblivioni traderentur; Deputatus regius: urgebat, ut contenti essent ordines statuto remissionis, quo præteritæ fœderatorum actiones damnabantur ut illegitimæ, severissimas pœnas meritæ, & cæt. quas tamen sereniss. rex pro singulari sua clementia indulgenter remitteret: At ordines regni asserebant, in tractatu pacificationis nuper inito, innocentiam suam fœderatos coram rege vindicasse, qui ideo dignatus esset clausulas quasdam asperiores, quibus in prima edicti pacificatorii formula, innocentia eorum perstringi videretur, expungere: Causam quam tutati fuissent, justam esse, ac in ejusdem prosecutione persuasum sibi esse, quod legum limites non excesserint, & si res denuo postulaverit, (quod avertat dominus) ejusdem causæ defensionem suscepturos, ad quam sacrosancto cum Deo fœdere, cui deputatus regius cum omnibus regni senatoribus subscripsissent, expresse obligati essent: Neque ita male de se meritum esse Christum, ad quem hæc causa proprie pertineret; ut confessione reatus, (cujus licet nondum sibi conscii essent, acceptatio tamen remissionis extorqueret) eum desererent, quem in omnibus difficultatibus præsentem semper experti essent. Quare formulam ἀμνηστίας[?] à se compositam deputato regio offerunt, in qua sereniss.regis æquitatem, bonitatem & clementiam erga regnum Scotiæ, qua tandem permiserit motus hoisce pacificis & legitimis mediis componi, ita deprædicabant, ut suam interim assererent innocentiam, & in alios authores & fautores malorum quibus presi[?] hactenus fuerunt, culpam oblique conjicerent: Sed & hæc formula à deputato regio, non sine verborum asperitate, rejecta fuit.
units.tr: Then, with the greatest contention of spirits, there was debate about the statute of amnesty [ἀμνηστίας] and pacification, by which whatever had happened since these movements arose should be consigned to perpetual oblivion. The royal commissioner urged the estates to be content with a statute of remission, by which the past acts of the covenanters were condemned as illegitimate and deserving the most severe penalties, and so on, which the most serene king, in his singular clemency, would nevertheless indulgently remit. But the estates of the kingdom asserted that in the recently concluded treaty of pacification the covenanters had vindicated their innocence before the king, who had therefore deigned to remove certain harsher clauses by which their innocence seemed to be aspersed in the first formula of the pacifying edict. The cause they had defended was just, and they were persuaded that in pursuing it they had not exceeded the limits of the laws. If the matter should again demand it (which the Lord forbid), they would undertake the defence of the same cause, to which they were expressly bound by the sacrosanct covenant with God, which the royal commissioner had subscribed together with all the senators of the kingdom. Nor had Christ, to whom this cause properly belonged, deserved so ill of them that they should desert him, whom they had always found present in all difficulties, by confessing a guilt which would extort acceptance of a remission, though they were not yet conscious of any. Therefore they offered the royal commissioner a formula of amnesty composed by themselves. In it they so extolled the equity, goodness and clemency of the most serene king towards the kingdom of Scotland, in permitting these movements to be settled by peaceful and lawful means, that meanwhile they asserted their own innocence and obliquely laid the blame on other authors and abettors of the evils by which they had hitherto been oppressed. But this formula too was rejected by the royal commissioner, not without harshness of language.

units.la: Actum postea fuit de salutaribus & efficacibus remediis, contra latrocinia, furta & cædes grassantium latronum in Borealibus montanis prope Grampiū provinciis; De libro illo in Anglia non ita pridem typis publica authoritate excusó, quem gravi censura à synodo notatum supra meminimus; De suffragiis deputatorum à singulis provinciis ad Comitia, an utrique deputatorum (nam duo semper à singulis provinciis delegantur) distinctum & separatum concedendū sit in comitiis suffragium? An non consultum esset sancire, ne majoris nobilitatis honos (cui jus suffragii in comitiis semper adjunctum est) exteris concederetur, nisi annuum censum decem mille marcarum Scoticarum in Scotiæ regno possideant? An senatus regius à parlamento judicari non posset? An consultum esset non concedi remissionem facinorum criminalium, ut furti, cædis, nisi primum parti læsæ satisfiat? De renovatione legum antehac sancitarum; contra protectiones à decoctoribus procuratas cum damno creditorum; De electione eirenarcharum; De mutuo auxilio, hoc est, an æquum non sit ut omnes omnino regni Scotiæ subditi, pro rata bonorum portione censeantur? ad dissolvendos sumptus hisce postremis motibus impensos, præsertim cum causa omnes ex æquo tangeret, conservatio religionis & libertatis subditorum; & omnes regni ordines, paucis quibusdam nobilibus exceptis, jubentes consentirent; De apparatu bellico ab exteris regionibus in Scotiam advecto, an a vectigali liber esse debeat? An, prout legibus olim sancitum est, Prefes collegii justitiae seu sessionis, à collegii illius judicibus eligendus sit? An suffragia nobilium à Comitiis absentium, per procurationes, admittenda & numeranda sint? De abroganda minutiore ista moneta aenea, aut ea saltem ad justum valorem reducenda, & an consultum esset, non mutari valorem monetae nisi ex consensu ordinum regni in Comitiis, prout à majoribus salubri consilio factum fuisse docent comitiorum regiftra publica. An consultum non esset, Ut arces regni munitę, (quales Edinburgena, Britannodunensis, Sterlinensis, cum claves regni sint, in ejusdem tutelam & custodiam contra externum hostem aedificatae,) consensu ordinum regni in Comitiis, traderentur civibus in Scotia natis? neque earum militaris custodia exteris quibuslibet committeretur, ne liberum Scotiae regnum in devictae & subactae provinciae formam redigatur. De mercatura & opificiis promovendis, & de mercimoniorum vectigalibus non augendis, nisi ex consensu ordinum regni. Haec & complura hujus generis quae ad pacem & commodum religionis & regni necessario conferebant, in articulos referri instabant ordines regni per apoelectos, quorum plurima, quae potribus statutis olim sancita non fuere, quum fere semper intercederet deputatus regius & moras necteret, nunc hoc nunc illud objiciens, expressam habebant clausulam referendi eorundem definitionem ad sereniss. regis arbitrium.
units.tr: Afterwards there was discussion of wholesome and effective remedies against the robberies, thefts and murders committed by roaming brigands in the northern mountainous provinces near the Grampians; of that book lately printed in England by public authority, which we mentioned above as having been severely censured by the synod; of the votes of the commissioners sent from each province to the Assembly: whether each of the two commissioners (for two are always chosen from each province) should be granted a distinct and separate vote in the Assembly? Would it not be wise to enact that the honour of the greater nobility (to which the right to vote in the Assembly has always been attached) should not be granted to outsiders unless they possess in the kingdom of Scotland an annual rent of ten thousand Scottish marks? Could the royal senate not be judged by parliament? Would it not be wise not to grant remission of criminal offences, such as theft or murder, unless satisfaction is first made to the injured party? Concerning the renewal of laws enacted before; against protections procured by bankrupts to the loss of creditors; concerning the election of justices of the peace; concerning mutual aid, that is, whether it would not be fair for all subjects of the kingdom of Scotland, without exception, to be assessed in proportion to their goods, to defray the expenses incurred in these recent disturbances, especially since the cause touched everyone equally, namely the preservation of religion and the liberty of the subjects; and all the orders of the kingdom, with a few nobles excepted, were willing to consent. Concerning the war equipment brought into Scotland from foreign lands: should it be free of duty? Whether, as was formerly enacted by law, the President of the College of Justice, or Court of Session, should be chosen by the judges of that college? Whether the votes of nobles absent from the Assembly may be admitted and counted by proxy? Concerning the abolition of this petty copper coinage, or at least its reduction to its just value; and whether it would be wise that the value of the coinage should not be changed except by consent of the orders of the kingdom in the Assembly, as the public registers of the assemblies show was done by our ancestors with sound counsel. Would it not be wise that the fortified strongholds of the kingdom (such as Edinburgh, Dumbarton and Stirling, which are the keys of the kingdom, built for its defence and protection against a foreign enemy) be handed over, by consent of the orders of the kingdom in the Assembly, to citizens born in Scotland? Nor should their military garrison be entrusted to any foreigners whatever, lest the free kingdom of Scotland be reduced to the form of a conquered and subjugated province. Concerning the promotion of trade and manufactures, and that duties on merchandise should not be increased except by consent of the orders of the kingdom. These and many other matters of this kind, which were necessary to the peace and advantage of religion and the kingdom, the orders of the kingdom insisted should be drawn up into articles through the committees chosen for the purpose. Very many of these had not been enacted by former statutes, since the royal commissioner almost always intervened and delayed, now raising this objection and now that; and the articles held an express clause that their final definition be referred to the judgement of the most serene king.

units.la: Cum vero inter deputatum regium & ordines regni nunquam fere conveniret, illo objiciente, ordinum haec postulata regi non innotuisse, eorundemque concessionem mandati sui limites excedere, ac regem prius de singulis monendum esse, neque seren. regi ingratum fore, si procerum quidam omnium nomine ad aulam excurrant, ut coram postulatorum suorum æquitatem demonstrarent, in hunc finem ostensa epistola regia. Ac licet illud novum multis videretur, liberorumque comitiorum libertatem destruere, neque satis conveniret cum promissis regiis, de Deputato cum plena potestate delegando; studio tamen singulari omnia offendicula removendi, & æquitatis suæ conscientiæ confisi, duos nobiles supremi ordinis, Comitem Fermeloduni, & Laudonium ad regem serenissi. mittunt, literas fidei & mandatorum subsignantibus ipsis calend. Novemb. 1639. plurimis omnium nomine: Eo fere spectabant mandata ut articulorum à regni ordinibus postulatorum æquitatem & fundamenta demonstrarent, neque aliud quidpiam quæri, quam sine quo religio & libertas sarta tecta esse nequit: eorumque concessione & sanctione regii juris nihil diminutum iri: (nam audiebant suggestum fuisse ab adversariis, postulata ordinum Scotiæ radicem ipsam regiæ authoritatis petere; quibus concessis umbram tantum regiæ dignitatis regi relictam) in omnibus religiose sibi cavilse ordines ne limites in pacificatione positos transilirent, ac explicite nunc ea solũ petere, quæ in cumulo & implicite tunc concedebantur; ac latebant sub phrasi, concedendi & sanciendi ea quæ ad ecclesiæ & regni commodum & stabilendam pacem conducere judicabit Synodus et parlamentum.
units.tr: But since the royal commissioner and the orders of the kingdom almost never came to agreement, he objecting that these demands had not been made known to the king, that granting them would exceed the limits of their mandate, and that the king must first be informed of each point; and that it would not be unwelcome to the most serene king if some of the nobles went to court in the name of all, to demonstrate before him the fairness of their demands, the royal letter being shown for this purpose. Although this seemed a novelty to many, and a destruction of the liberty of free assemblies, and did not sufficiently accord with the royal promises about appointing a commissioner with full powers, yet, out of singular zeal to remove every obstacle, and trusting in the fairness of their own conscience, the orders sent to the most serene king two nobles of the highest rank, the Earl of Dunfermline and the Earl of Lauderdale, on 1 November 1639, with letters of credence and instructions signed by themselves and by most of the members in the name of all. Their instructions aimed chiefly at showing the fairness and grounds of the articles demanded by the orders of the kingdom, and that nothing else was sought than what religion and liberty cannot be kept safe without; and that by granting and sanctioning these nothing of the royal right would be diminished. (For they had heard it suggested by their adversaries that the demands of the Scottish orders sought the very root of royal authority, and that once these were granted only a shadow of royal dignity would be left to the king.) In everything they had been religiously careful that the orders should not overstep the limits set in the pacification, and that they now sought explicitly only those things which were then conceded in bulk and implicitly; and these lay hidden under the phrase of granting and sanctioning those things which the Synod and Parliament shall judge conducive to the good of the Church and kingdom and to the establishment of peace.

units.la: Verum cum post tam longum & molestum iter nobiles hi à parlamento delegati Londinum pervenissent, ad regem non admissi fuerunt, & imperatum ut confestim inScotiam redirent, hoc prætextu, quod inconsulto deputato regio legationem eam suscipere ausi fuissent, cum tamen omnibus in ore esset, in id maxime delegatos fuisse, ut de Deputato ipso ejusq; in parlamento actionibus quererentur: sagaciores tamen satis videbant alia consilia tum coqui, & Scotorum hostes in aula sedulo in id incumbere, ut modis omnibus Scotorum animi exulcerarentur, ac aliquid committerent, quo bello, quod seminabant, speciem aliquam arriperent: existimantes præfervida gentis illius ingenia tam nobilium internunciorum contemptum æquis animis ferre non posse: verebantur etiam ne consilia quæ meditarentur in aula nondum satis matura per importunos hos internuncios ut speculatores emanarent; quos idcirco procul ablegandos voluerunt. Sed & hæc consilia irrita fuerunt: nam ordinibus regni Scotiæ visum eandem denuo tentare semitam, & cum scirent rem sibi esse non cum extero quovis principe, sed cum rege suo serenissⁱ. injuriam illam non tam internunciis quam sibi illatam dissimulant, ac quendam cum supplicibus ad regem literis denuo mittunt, quibus enixæ & humiliter rogabant ut si regi visum non esset deputato suo imperare comitiorum expeditam conclusionem, saltem rescripto significare dignaretur an vellet aliquot à parlamento deputatos ad se mitti, qui coram plenius edocerent rationes & fundamenta eorum quorum sanctio jam postulatur; atque interim ne hostium suorum, in aliorum miseriis solatium quærentium, contra se obloquiis sideret. Responsum fuit à rege 11. Decemb. & obsignatum à secretario regni Scotiæ in aula commorante Comite Sterlinensi: Se permittere, ut quot vellent ad se delegarent, qui monstraturi essent postulatorum in parlamento rationes et fundamenta.
units.tr: But when these nobles, delegated by parliament, had reached London after so long and troublesome a journey, they were not admitted to the king, and were ordered to return to Scotland at once, on the pretext that they had dared to undertake this embassy without the consent of the royal commissioner; although it was on everyone's lips that they had been sent chiefly to complain about the commissioner himself and his conduct in parliament. The shrewder men, however, saw well enough that other plans were being hatched, and that the enemies of the Scots at court were busily labouring to exasperate the Scots by every means, so that they would commit some act by which the enemies could seize on some appearance of justification for the war they were sowing; reckoning that the hot spirits of that people could not bear the contempt of such noble envoys with calm minds. They also feared that the plans being devised at court, not yet ripe enough, might leak out as spies through these troublesome envoys; and so they wished them sent far away. But these plans also came to nothing, for the orders of the kingdom of Scotland decided to try the same path again. Knowing that the matter was not with some foreign prince but with their own most serene king, they passed over that injury, which was done not so much to the envoys as to themselves, and sent again, with suppliants, a letter to the king, by which they earnestly and humbly asked that if it did not please the king to order his commissioner to bring the sessions to a speedy conclusion, he would at least deign to signify by rescript whether he wished some deputies from parliament to be sent to him, who might more fully explain before him the reasons and grounds of those matters whose sanction is now demanded; and meanwhile that they not be exposed to the mockery of their enemies, who seek comfort in the miseries of others. The king replied on 11 December, and the reply was sealed by the secretary of the kingdom of Scotland, the Earl of Stirling, who was staying at court: that he permitted them to send as many as they wished, who would set out before parliament the reasons and grounds of the demands.

units.la: Quo benigno responso nondum plane conclamatum de fœlici exitu parlamenti sperabant: nisi in sumum protinus abiisset hæc spes.
units.tr: With this kindly reply they did not yet altogether give up hope of a happy outcome to parliament; but this hope soon vanished into smoke.

units.la: Nam 18. Decembris deputatus regius declarat, serenissⁱ. regem sibi imperasse rescripto minori sigillo obsignato, ut comitia hæc statim dissolveret, ac in secundum diem Junii subsequentis anni prorogaret, idque regia tantum authoritate, ad quem solum res hæc pertineret: quandoquidem satis perspectum haberet rex, scopum & intentionem ordinum non esse religionem, sed mutationem & innovationem regiminis politici; Dissolutionem itaque se ordinibus imperare sub poena læsæ majestatis.
units.tr: For on 18 December the royal commissioner declared that the most serene king had ordered him, by a rescript sealed with the lesser seal, to dissolve this assembly at once and to prorogue it to the second day of June of the following year; and that this was by royal authority alone, to which the matter alone pertained, since the king had seen clearly enough that the aim and intention of the orders was not religion but a change and innovation in the political government. He therefore commanded the orders to dissolve, under penalty of treason.

units.la: Ordines vero regni contra declarant; Nunc primum post viginti sæcula in Scotia audiri, ut plenum & in omnibus suis membris legitime constitutum parlamentum, post electionem apolectorum, eorumque quindecim plus minus hebdomadarum continuas sessiones, post formatos & præparatos omnes articulos, sine ordinum regni in comitiis consensu dissolveretur: nullum hujus nunc primum auditæ dissolutionis vestigium vel volam exstare in publicis præcedentium omnium comitiorum registris, ad quæ provocarent: Quicquid à regibus alibi fiat, & sibi vendicent ex plenitudine regii juris, non esse suum disquirere; nec à posse ad esse legitime consequi; quod, ut in divinis ἀλογον est, ita in humanis, imprudentiæ & impotentis judicii proles est, & confusionis mater: fereniff. regem sæpius professum esse, sibi nunquam institutum, subditis suis in regno Scotiæ quidpiam imperare quod legibus regni & majorum praxi conforme non fit: Nullibi vero legem ullam inveniri posse, quæ ab ampliatione & prorogatione comitiorum ordines regni excludat, quin contra perpetuam exstare praxin pro consensu eorundem necessario: ejusdem commatis etiam esse poenam læsæ majestatis pronunciatam, contra universos regni ordines, (penes quos stat potestas definiendi quæ sint læsæ majestatis crimina) ob nullam legum quarumlibet violationem, verum ob id solum quod patriis ab omni ævo receptis institutis adhæreant: Neq; persuaderi sibi posse quin hostium religionis suæ opera prodeat hæc comitiorum prorogatio, qui consilia hæc suggerunt posthabito regis honore, regni commodo & pace, ut cruentum suum scopum quovis modo promoveant: qui si essent quales les haberi se volunt, meminisse possent prorogatione hac corrumpi promissum regium sereniffima majestatis suae manu obsignatum, quo concessum fuit parlamentum ad sancienda synodi decreta, & controversias omnes politicas definiendas: Cumque aliis negotiis advocatus fuisset sereniff. rex, ut sacra sua praesentia synodum & comitia cohonestare non posset;
