(quo uti nihil magis in votis nobis fuerat, ita maximo solatio fuisset) dignatum tamen fuisse verbo suo regio certos nos reddere, se deputatum missurum sufficienter, & plena potestate instructum; qui promissa abunde praestiturus esset: Literas etiam mandati & fidei, quibus Comiti Traquario deputatio illa committebatur, magno sigillo munitas mentionem tantum facere tentionis et observationis parlamenti, fine ulla prorogationis clausula: quibus praevalere nequaquam debent privata quaelibet rescripta minoribus sigillis obsignata. Eum esse praesentem regni statum, qui prorogationis hujus moram ferre non posset, sine manifesto confusionis periculo, cujus non ignari hostes nostri omnia sua studia eo gnaviter collimant, ut discordiarum seminā inter sereniff. regem & nos fideles subditos in utriusque perniciem ferant. Ac licet (inquiunt) recepto majorum more, tum literis indictionis, ac articulis in pacificatione pactis licitum nobis esse declaremus non obstante ampliationis mandato, Comitia continuare; ut tamen maledicis nostris hostibus omnem obloquii ansam praeriperemus, eorumque ora, (quod sperari vix poterit,) obstrueremus, nunc tantum decrevimus regi sereniff. exponere fundamenta & rationem reddere actionum nostrarum in comitiis, ut constet quam nulla nostra culpa factum sit, quod optatum exitum nondum assequuti simus, & quam necesse sit ut posthabita omni mora aliquid tandem operæpretii agatur, quo ecclesia regnum hoc ab extremis miseriis conferventur, quas utriusque & regii simul honoris ac pacis nostræ hostes machinantur: In quem finem selectos ex singulis regni ordinibus delegavimus, cum mandatis ut Edinburgi commorentur, ad accipiendum & referendum quod à rege sereniss. responsum fuerit æquissimis nostris postulatis, utque ea omnia agant quibus regem de æquitate & necessitate nostrorum postulatorum certiorem reddere possint. Quod si obstinata hostium nostrorum malitia eousque prævaleat, ut ipsorum artificiose excogitatis major fides habeatur, quam universæ gentis hujus, in supremis comitiis coactæ, ingenuis & sinceris declarationibus: Deum & homines testamur nobis non imputanda esse, quæ exinde necessario eventura sint mala: nobisque semper licere illud agere quod ecclesiam & regnum ab extrema interminata pernicie vindicare possit. Hæc summa est declarationis prælectæ in magna comitiorum aula, præsentibus omnibus regni ordinibus, & in futuram rei memoriam publicis Comitiorum registris insertæ.
units.tr: The estates of the realm, however, declare the opposite. For the first time in twenty centuries, it is said, a parliament in Scotland, fully and lawfully constituted in all its parts, has been dissolved after the election of its lords of the articles, after some fifteen weeks of continuous sessions, and after all the articles had been drawn up and prepared, without the consent of the estates assembled in parliament. No trace or hint of this dissolution, heard of now for the first time, can be found in the public records of all earlier parliaments, to which they might appeal. Whatever kings may do elsewhere and claim for themselves from the fullness of royal right, it is not for the estates to inquire; but to pass from what is possible to what is lawful does not follow. As that is absurd in divine matters, so in human affairs it is the offspring of imprudence and of an unsound judgement, and the mother of confusion. His most serene majesty the king has often professed that he never intended to command his subjects in the kingdom of Scotland anything that is not in accordance with the laws of the realm and the practice of their ancestors. Nowhere, moreover, can any law be found that excludes the estates of the realm from the prorogation or extension of parliament; on the contrary, there is a constant practice that their consent is necessary. Likewise, the punishment of treason has been pronounced in this very matter against all the estates of the realm (in whose power it lies to define what counts as treason), not for the violation of any law whatever, but solely because they adhere to the institutions of their country, received from all ages. Nor can they be persuaded that this prorogation of parliament does not come about by the work of enemies of their religion, who suggest these measures, setting aside the honour of the king, the good and peace of the kingdom, so that they may advance their bloody purpose by any means. If they were what they wish to be considered, they could remember that the promise of the king, sealed with his most serene majesty's own hand, by which parliament was granted for ratifying the decrees of the synod and for settling all political controversies, is corrupted by this prorogation. And although his most serene majesty the king, being summoned to other business, could not honour the synod and parliament with his sacred presence (which, as nothing was more in our wishes, so it would have been the greatest comfort), he has nevertheless deigned to assure us by his royal word that he would send a sufficient deputy, furnished with full power, who would abundantly perform the promises. Moreover, the letters of commission and trust, by which that deputation was committed to the Earl of Traquair, bearing the great seal, make mention only of the intention and observance of parliament, with no clause of prorogation. Private rescripts sealed with lesser seals ought in no way to prevail over these. The present state of the kingdom is such that it cannot bear the delay of this prorogation without a manifest danger of confusion; our enemies, who are not unaware of this, bend all their efforts vigorously to this end, that they may sow the seeds of discord between his most serene majesty the king and us, his faithful subjects, to the ruin of both. And although (they say) by the received custom of our ancestors, both by the letters of summons and by the articles agreed in the pacification, we may lawfully declare that we may continue the parliament notwithstanding the mandate of prorogation, yet, so that we may take away from our slanderous enemies every occasion for detraction and stop their mouths (which can scarcely be hoped for), we have now resolved only to set out for his most serene majesty the king the foundations and to give an account of our actions in parliament, so that it may be evident how, through no fault of ours, it has come about that we have not yet attained the desired outcome, and how necessary it is that, with all delay set aside, something of worth be at last done, by which the Church and this kingdom may be preserved from the extreme miseries which the enemies of both his royal honour and our peace are plotting. To this end we have chosen delegates from each of the estates of the realm, with instructions to remain at Edinburgh, to receive and report whatever answer shall be given by his most serene majesty the king to our most just requests, and to do all those things by which they may be able to make the king more certain of the equity and necessity of our demands. But if the obstinate malice of our enemies should prevail so far that more credit is given to their artfully devised schemes than to the free and sincere declarations of the whole nation, assembled in the supreme parliament, we call God and men to witness that the evils which will necessarily follow from this are not to be imputed to us, and that it shall always be lawful for us to do that which can deliver the Church and the kingdom from extreme and threatened destruction. This is the sum of the declaration read out in the great hall of parliament, in the presence of all the estates of the realm, and inserted into the public records of parliament for the memory of the matter in future.

units.la: Simul etiam singuli ordines ex instituto supramemorato, suos Deputatos elegerunt: supremus nobilium ordo pro se nominavit, Lothianæ et Dalhufium, Comites; Yesterum, Balmerinonem, Cranstonum, Naperum, Barones parlamentarios: idem etiam à provinciarum & civitatum Deputatis factum.
units.tr: At the same time, each of the estates, according to the custom mentioned above, chose its own deputies. The highest order of the nobles nominated for itself: the Earls of Lothian and Dalhousie; the Lords of Parliament, Yester, Balmerino, Cranstoun and Napier. The same was also done by the deputies of the shires and burghs.

units.la: Ultimo hoc actu dissolutis comitiis, non sine bonorum omnium ingenti mœrore, qui subsequentis anni calamitates prospiciebant, Deputatus regius, confirmatis prius factionis suæ animis, & inita conjuratione cum quibusdam in primariorum procerum fœderatorum, ut ferebatur, perniciem, quæ postea detecta fuit, ad aulam properat, relaturus quam belle personam suam sustinuisset in comitiorum theatro, ejusque rerum Scoticarum relatione fusa, (quam vera & ingenua ea fuerit postea memorabitur) usque adeo incensi fuerunt senatores regni Angliæ, ut universos regni Scotiæ ordines ne auditos quidem statim damnaverint, & ex unius relatione & fœderatorum Scotorum hostis, ut dicebant, dignam judicarent universam gentem, in quam ferro & flamma sæviendum esset: Sed cum deesset pecunia belli nervus, Hierarchicis superioris belli (cujus auctores & suasores erant) impensis exhaustis, indictio parlamenti in Anglia promovetur, summa quidem omnium cum admiratione, quibus cognitum fuerat quam antehac semper factio ista vel ad parlamenti nomen expalleret: idem etiam factum in Hibernia, quo vero successu[?], post memorabitur.
units.tr: When parliament was finally dissolved by this act, not without the great grief of all good men, who foresaw the calamities of the following year, the royal deputy, having first strengthened the spirits of his faction and having entered into a conspiracy with some of the leading nobles who were allied with the Scots (as was reported) for their destruction, which was later discovered, hastened to the court, intending to report how splendidly he had sustained his part in the theatre of parliament. And with his account of Scottish affairs laid out at length (how true and sincere it was will be recorded afterwards), the senators of the kingdom of England were so inflamed that they at once condemned all the estates of the kingdom of Scotland without even hearing them, and, on the strength of one man's report and the word of the Scots' enemies, judged the whole nation worthy, as they said, to be raged against with sword and fire. But since money, the sinew of war, was lacking, and the expenses of the previous war (of which the hierarchs were the authors and advisers) had exhausted the treasury, a summons of parliament was brought forward in England. This was done with the astonishment of all, who had known how this faction had always before turned pale at the very name of parliament. The same was also done in Ireland; with what success, however, will be told later.

units.la: Dum calerent hæc consilia in aula, tandem adveniunt Scotorum internuncii seu legati; Comes Fermelodum & Laudonius, Guilielmus Donglassius, Eques splendidus, & Robertus Barclajus, præfectus Irwinensis vir probæ & spectatæ fidei, cum mandatis tum 1. Novemb. anni 1639, tum novis 20. Ianuar. 1640. à comitiorum deputatis obsignatis: quorum summa fuit. 1. Ne causam hanc agerent coram ullis à rege deputatis, vel ipso senatu Angliæ, quasi judices eos in hac causa agnoscerent, quandoquidem hoc effet violare jus liberi regni Scotiæ, Deo & regi solis subditi: interim tamen non detractarent eosdem aut quovis alios auditores, dum coram rege sereniss. causam dicturi sint, addita semper protestatione de regni Scotiæ & Comitiorum independentia: imo instarent, ut præsente senatu Anglico, sed nullatenus judice, tota hæc causa excutiatur ad removendam pravam illam opinionem, quam regni illius senatores, ex relatione detorta Comitis Traquarii, contra ordines regni conceperunt. 2. Ut scriptis omnia agerent. 3. Ut demonstrarent singula comitiorum postulata, quæ maxime controvertuntur, usque adeo necessaria esse, ut sine eorundem concessione nulla sit religioni aut legibus securitas, & usque adeo æqua, ut legibus municipalibus, majorum continuæ praxi, ac sanæ rationi prorsus consonent, neque regis authoritatem, cui tutandæ (inquiunt) nos & nostra omnia religiose vovimus, ullatenus lædere, quin contra eorundem sanctione dignitatem regiam augeri. 4. Si interrogata ulla ad publicum regni statum spectantia, quorum solutionem adjunctæ mandatis chartæ non exhiberent, propositæ fuerint, ad ea ne respondeant; sed ad deputatos, Edinburgi ex præscripto comitiorum hærentes, transmitterent, eoque quam sæpissime de rerum suarum statu certiores subinde redderent; ac reditum maturarent ante 25. Mensis Martii. 5. Ad faciliorem veritatis manifestationem, instate, ut in apertam lucem proferantur publica comitiorum registra, ad quæ accessus vobis pateat, quæ contra omnem æquitatis speciem nobis hactenus pertinaciter denegata fuerunt. 6. Instate ut, secundum expressum tenorem pacificationis cum rege initæ, liberi parlamenti beneficio promisso fruamur, tam ad synodum sanciendam, quam ad componendas civiles omnes controversias; & ut abruptum sine mora revocetur. 7. Ostendendum, esse contra leges pacis, quod arx Edinburgena muniatur apparatu bellico contra urbem Edinburgum, cui extrema omnia minatur, & triplo majori militum numero instruatur, quam qui defensioni sufficiat: idem etiam de Britannoduno arce, quæ præsidiariis Anglis, contra leges, instruitur. 8. Querendum, quod Scoti in Hibernia, & qui negotiorum conficiendorum gratia in Angliâ excurrunt, in juramenta illicita,& fœdus nostrum, à Deputato regio ejusque senatu approbatum & obsignatum, damnantia adigantur. 9. Denique rogandus est serenifs. rex pro amore & studio in antiquum hoc & nativum sibi regnum, ne iniquis quibuslibet contra nos relationibus, ab apertis hostibus excogitatis & suggestis, credat; nisi prius nostrum contra eas responsum audiverit; quod fieri nequit, nisi dignetur earum copiam nobis facere, & cæt.
units.tr: While these plans were heating up at court, at last the messengers or envoys of the Scots arrived: the Earl of Dunfermline and Lauderdale, William Douglas, a distinguished knight, and Robert Barclay, sheriff of Irvine, a man of proven and tried faith, bearing both the instructions sealed by the parliamentary deputies on 1 November 1639 and newer ones of 20 January 1640. Their substance was as follows: (1) They were not to plead this cause before any deputies appointed by the king, nor before the senate of England itself, as if they acknowledged those men as judges in this matter, since that would be to violate the right of the free kingdom of Scotland, subject only to God and the king. Meanwhile, however, they were not to refuse these or any other hearers, while they were to plead the cause before the most serene king, always adding a protestation of the independence of the kingdom of Scotland and of parliament. Indeed, they were to insist that the whole matter be examined in the presence of the English senate, but in no way as judges, in order to remove the false opinion which the senators of that realm had formed against the estates of the kingdom, from the distorted report of the Earl of Traquair. (2) They were to do everything in writing. (3) They were to demonstrate that each of the demands of parliament that are most disputed is so necessary that without their concession there is no security for religion or for the laws, and so just that it is wholly consonant with the municipal laws, the continuous practice of our ancestors, and sound reason; and that it does not in any way harm the authority of the king, whose defence (they say) we have religiously vowed, together with all that we possess, but that on the contrary royal dignity is increased by their sanction. (4) If any questions concerning the public state of the kingdom were put to them, the solution of which the charters attached to their instructions did not supply, they were not to answer these, but to refer them to the deputies remaining at Edinburgh in accordance with the directive of parliament; and they were to keep these deputies as often as possible informed of the state of their affairs, and to hasten their return before 25 March. (5) For a easier manifestation of the truth, they were to insist that the public records of parliament be brought out into the open light, and that access to them be opened to us; which, against every appearance of equity, have hitherto been stubbornly denied to us. (6) They were to insist that, according to the express terms of the pacification made with the king, we enjoy the promised benefit of a free parliament, both for ratifying the synod and for settling all civil controversies, and that what has been broken off be recalled without delay. (7) It was to be shown that it is contrary to the laws of the peace that the castle of Edinburgh is being fortified with military preparations against the city of Edinburgh, which it threatens with every extremity, and is garrisoned with three times more soldiers than are sufficient for its defence; likewise concerning the castle of Dumbarton, which is furnished with English garrison troops contrary to the laws. (8) It was to be complained of that the Scots in Ireland, and those who go into England on business, are compelled to take illicit oaths condemning our covenant, which was approved and sealed by the royal deputy and his senate. (9) Finally, his most serene majesty the king is to be asked, out of love and zeal for this his ancient and native kingdom, not to believe any unjust reports against us, devised and suggested by open enemies, unless he has first heard our answer to them; which cannot be done unless he deigns to give us copies of them, et cetera.

units.la: Porro cum cognitum satis haberent Scoti machinas omnes admoturos adversarios suos in Anglia, ut regni illius populum universum calumniis & sufsurris contra se commoverent, confultum duxerunt breve quoddam scriptum typis mandare, directum ad probos subditos regni Angliæ, quo calumnias contra se nunc denuo extrulas diluerent, & Anglis ostenderent necessitatem & æquitatem postulatorum in comitiis, atque in eum finem quæ maxime in controversiam vocari ac invidiosissime exagitari apud exteros, legum Scoticarum imperitos acceperant, vindicant. Dein ostendunt in quas angustias regnum Scotiæ hostium artibus redactum sit, & quibus novis injuriis & calamitatibus, etiam post pacem anno superiori initam, contra expressas pacis leges affecti essent regni illius subditi, ita ut, nisi maturo consilio sanguinolentis hostium suorum conatibus obviam eatur, cogendiforent Scoti ad extremam ecclesiæ & regni perniciem vitandam, alia quam quibus hactenus usi essent media & remedia adhibere. Scriptum vero illud, de verbo fere in verbum fideliter translatum, sic se habet.
units.tr: Moreover, since the Scots knew well enough that their adversaries in England would bring every device to bear to stir up the whole population of that kingdom against them with slanders and whispers, they judged it advisable to have printed a short paper addressed to the upright subjects of the kingdom of England, by which they might refute the slanders now again raised against them and show the English the necessity and fairness of their demands in the Parliament. To that end they also vindicate those matters which they had learned were most hotly disputed and most bitterly attacked abroad by those ignorant of Scottish law. Next they show into what straits the kingdom of Scotland has been reduced by the arts of its enemies, and with what new injuries and calamities the subjects of that kingdom have been afflicted, even after the peace concluded last year, contrary to the express laws of the peace; so that, unless their bloody attempts are met with mature counsel, the Scots would be compelled to adopt other measures and remedies than those they have used until now, to avert the extreme ruin of the Church and kingdom. That paper, translated almost word for word and faithfully, reads as follows.

units.la: Informatio directa ab Ordinibus regni Scotiæ ad Anglos. 1640.
units.tr: Information directly issued by the Estates of the kingdom of Scotland to the English. 1640.

units.la: Compositis propemodum qui anno priori regnum hoc afflixerant, tumultibus; ac sedatis tempestatibus quæ utriq; paritur regno ingentia mala minitabantur; pacificatione in castris regiis ad regni limites: Subditi hujus regni ad sua se contulere, non solum certa spe fruendi pace domestica per parlamentum & Synodum, verbo regio pactam, quibus motus omnes, horum defectu hactenus orti, facile componi potuerunt; verumetiam in arctius amicitiæ vinculum cum vicinis Anglis coeundi, quandoquidem calumnias istas atroces nobis impactas tam perspicue diluissemus, non solum actionibus nostris innocentiam spirantibus, verumetiam apertura fontium, unde mala quæ Dei beneficio tum evaseramus, veram suam originem deduxerant. Neque dubitandum, quin fœlices fuissemus, si facta promissis nobis præstitis respondissent, uti nos iisdem ingenue sidebamus.
units.tr: Almost all the tumults that had afflicted this kingdom the previous year were settled, and the storms that threatened the kingdom with great evils had subsided. By the pacification in the royal camp at the borders of the realm, the subjects of this kingdom returned to their own affairs. They did so not only in the firm hope of enjoying domestic peace through the parliament and Synod, which was guaranteed by the royal word, and by which all the disturbances that had arisen hitherto from their failure could easily have been composed. They also hoped to enter into a closer bond of friendship with the neighbouring English. For we had refuted those atrocious calumnies flung at us so clearly, not only by our actions, which breathe innocence, but also by opening the sources from which the evils we had escaped by God's benefit had derived their true origin. And there is no doubt that we would have been happy, if the deeds had matched the promises made to us, as we had sincerely trusted they would.

units.la: Verum adversarii nostri pro constanti sua impietate & malitia tum statim cœperunt, & quotidie pergunt, hostile aliquid secreto contra nos machinari, & sicuti hactenus justam querendi materiam nobis exhibuerunt, procuratione violationis articulorum stipulatorum in pacificatione, & singulari ista dissolutione parlamenti nostri, cujus nullum exemplum ab omni seculo in hoc regno ostendi potest; ita quotidie satagunt, falsa actionum nostrarum relatione, serenissimum nostrum regem contra nos excitare, Anglorumque animos, quorum aures mendacissimis calumniis replent, nobis aversos reddere, quasi legitimæ nostræ actiones seditionem spirarent, ac innocentissimæ nostræ intentiones, ad apertam rebellionem, & profanam civilis obedientiæ conculcationem spectarent :- Quas impudentes & putidas calumnias à se primum excogitatas, in Anglia spargendas ubique curant per emissarios suos, præsertim pontificios, utpote qui ægre ferunt, sincera & legitima hac reformatione se Scotia excludi, metuentes ne eandem brevi fortunam in Anglia etiam experiantur. Atque hic duplici damno contendimus: 1. Quod ipsorum calumniæ contra integrum regni corpus, (licet primitus inventæ ac sparsæ à pauculis profugis, patriæ suæ juratis hostibus; ac corruptis Ecclesiasticis) fidem tamen obtineant apud imperitos sine ullo prævio examine; Contra vero, Declarationibus ordinum hujus regni, actionumque nostrarum vindicationi, nulla habeatur fides, licet sæpius obsecrati simus, ut legitimo judicio liceret nobis contra illos experiri, ipsorumque calumnias refellere, ac nostram innocentiam tueri. 2. Quod libere liceat istis, calumnias habere apud regem & subditos in Anglia spargere, nos vero ab ipsius præsentia, & justa vindicatione penitus excludamur. Nam sicut anno superiori obtinuerunt, ut interdictione tabellariorum & epistolarum, ac severissimis edictis contra informationes ex Scotia missas, omnia media occluderentur, per quæ Angli quovis modo ad veram cognitionem actionum ac intentionum nostrarum devenirent; ita nunc quoque eandem terunt semitam, neque liberum folum epistolarum commeatum interrumpunt, verum etiam effecerunt, ne deputati nostri à conventu regni ordinum delegati, (idque speciali & expresso mandato sereniss. regis per epistolam ad Comitem Traquarium, regis supremum Deputatum seu Commissionarium, missam, & à multis visam) ut regem de statu vero rerum nostrarum certiorem facerent, ad regis præsentiam admitterentur, utque iis statim mandaretur, ut in Scotiam omni mora posthabita redirent; ne, videlicet, eorum opera de vero actionum nostrarum statu certiores fierent Angli: Licentia hac adversariis nostris concessa nobis impune calumniandi, & libertate justa nobis adempta innocentiam nostram vindicandi, facillime putant se posse serenis[?]. regem ac Anglos, qua præjudiciis, qua calumniis in suam sententiam pertrahere, ac tandem renovatis tumultibus utramque gentem sanguinolentis suis consiliis ad arma protrudere; unde duplex sibi cessurum lucrum sperant, prout ex duobus hominum generibus constant. Nam Ecclesiastici, jure meritoque ex hac ecclesia ejecti, cum desperent de reditu ad pristinam conditionem, si legitime ac ordine motus hi in Scotia componantur, omnia hic tumultu & sanguine replere adnituntur; ac per vim, Anglorum opera, restitui: quæ vis aperta utrique pariter regno periculosa erit, ac ingenti damno utrumque regnum afficiet, præsertim si mutuis vulneribus alterutrum concisum, à Pontificiis hostiliter invadatur, qui opportunitatem hanc è manibus elabi non patientur. Alii vero hostium nostrorum sunt politici quidam, animo in patriam suam iniquiore, iique, vel qui tumultibus conditionem suam jam pæne ad extrema redactam, ex aliorum ruinis restaurare se posse putant: vel qui ad insignia publica munia antea provecti; ut judicii aleam effugiant, & pœnas facinoribus suis promeritas, (quas parum abfuit quin subivissent, & optime norunt eas necessario sibi subeundas esse, si rescripto & mandato regio liceret iis diem dicere atque in jus vocare, non ob vetera solum sed & nova male-ficia) summo conatu adlaborant, ut flamma in Republica accensa, ruinam sceleribus suis procuratam evitent, certa spe impune evadendi in mediis bellorum tumultibus. aut vulgata illa ἀφανσία, quæ compositionem magnorum Nationalium tumultuum sequi solet, præteritorum scelerum omnium gratiam obtinendi.
units.tr: But our adversaries, true to their constant impiety and malice, immediately began, and go on daily, to plot something hostile against us in secret. Just as hitherto they have given us a just ground for complaint, by the violation of the articles stipulated in the pacification and by that unparalleled dissolution of our parliament, of which no precedent can be shown in this kingdom from any age, so they daily labour, by a false account of our actions, to stir up our most serene king against us, and to turn the minds of the English, whose ears they fill with the most lying calumnies, away from us. It is as if our lawful actions breathed sedition, and our most innocent intentions aimed at open rebellion and the profane trampling of civil obedience. These impudent and foul calumnies, first devised by themselves, they take care to spread everywhere in England through their emissaries, especially the Papists, who are indignant that Scotland is excluded from this sincere and lawful reformation, and fear lest they themselves soon experience the same fate in England. Here we contend that we suffer a twofold loss: (1) that their calumnies against the whole body of the kingdom (though first invented and spread by a few fugitives, sworn enemies of their country, and corrupt churchmen) nonetheless win credence among the unskilled without any prior examination; whereas, on the contrary, no credence is given to the declarations of the estates of this kingdom or to the vindication of our actions, although we have often entreated that we be allowed to contest those charges by lawful judgment, to refute their calumnies, and to defend our innocence; (2) that they are freely permitted to have their calumnies heard by the king and to spread them among the subjects in England, while we are utterly shut out from his presence and from just vindication. For just as last year they obtained that, by the prohibition of couriers and letters and by the most severe edicts against reports sent from Scotland, all means were closed by which the English might in any way arrive at a true knowledge of our actions and intentions, so now too they tread the same path. They not only interrupt the free passage of letters, but have also brought it about that our deputies, delegated by the convention of the estates of the kingdom (and this by a special and express command of the most serene king, sent by letter to the Earl of Traquair, the king's chief Deputy or Commissioner, and seen by many), who were to be admitted to the king's presence to inform him of the true state of our affairs, were ordered at once, without delay, to return to Scotland. The purpose was, namely, that the English should not be made aware of the true state of our actions through their work. Believing that this licence granted to our adversaries to slander us with impunity, while the just liberty of defending our innocence has been taken from us, will allow them to draw the king and the English very easily into their own opinion, whether by prejudices or by calumnies, and at last, with the tumults renewed, to drive both nations to arms by their bloody counsels, they hope for a double gain, according to the two kinds of men of whom they consist. For the ecclesiastics, rightly and deservedly ejected from this church, despair of a return to their former condition if these disturbances in Scotland are settled lawfully and in good order. They strive to fill everything here with tumult and blood, and to be restored by force with the help of the English. This open force will be dangerous to both kingdoms alike and will inflict great damage on both, especially if, once each has been wounded by the other, they are hostilely invaded by the Papists, who will not allow this opportunity to slip from their hands. The others among our enemies are certain politicians, ill-disposed to their own country, who either think that their position, already reduced almost to extremity by the tumults, can be restored from the ruin of others, or who, having been promoted earlier to public offices, strive with the utmost effort to escape the hazard of judgment and the penalties their crimes have earned. They came close to suffering these penalties, and they know very well that they must necessarily undergo them if it were permitted, by royal rescript and command, to fix a day for them and summon them to law, not only for old misdeeds but also for new ones. They labour so that the flame kindled in the commonwealth may let them escape the ruin procured by their own crimes, in the certain hope of evading punishment with impunity amid the tumults of war, or of obtaining, through that common [ἀφανσία] oblivion which usually follows the settlement of great national tumults, the pardon of all past crimes.

units.la: Interim speramus Anglos non passuros sibi ab impostoribus istis secunda vice illudi: Nobilibus quippe Anglis & aliis qui in captis regiis fuerunt, in memoriam redeat; cum plene & perspicue de nostris actionibus, earumque fundamentis certiores à nobis facti essent, cumque iis abunde cognitum esset nihil aliud à nobis postulatum fuisse, quam ut liceret nobis nostris legibus vivere, ac religionis puritate frui; redeat (inquam) iis in mentem, ingenue se agnovisse falsis informationibus sese deceptos ante hac fuisse, ac supervacaneas tanti temporis & ingentium sumptuum impensas quæstos fuisse; facili ista credulitate sua multorum vitam manifesto periculo objectam fuisse, ac utrumque enervatum regnum ac tantum non destinatum in prædam exteris exercitibus aut classibus, nisi Deus misericordiæ suæ oculos in utramque gentem opportune flectere dignatus fuisset, ac perspiciet ut pacate convenirent ad aperiendam impostorum ejusque authores; & ut Nobiles Angli qui in nostram perniciem destinati fuerant, pro nobis sedulo apud regem intercederent, ut regia authoritate Synodum Nationalem, & parlamentum obtineremus; quibus postulatorum nostrorum summa continebatur, utpote quod per ea, aptissima remedia curandis tam Reipub. quam Ecclesiæ vulneribus, inventum iri sperabamus. In quo conventu hoc nobis præsertim solatio fuit, quod regi pacato agmine discedenti, ac fratribus nostris Anglis, abunde satisfactum fuerit de actionum nostrarum æquitate, & falsitas calumniarum nobis ab hostibus nostris impactarum splendide innotuerit, qui antea impudenter spargereausi fuerunt; Nobis propositam fuisse mutationem tionem regiminis politici, & hostilem in Angliam excursionem & invasionem, qua spoliis ejus ditaremur: quorum utrumque nunquam nobis in mentem venisse,uti antea sæpius declaravimus, sic actionibus nostris tunc testatum fecimus,quanta fidelitate seren. regem,quanto amore Anglos prosequeremur.
units.tr: Meanwhile we hope that the English will not allow themselves to be mocked a second time by these impostors. For may it come back to the minds of the English nobles and others who were in the king's camp: when they had been fully and clearly informed by us about our actions and their foundations, and when it had been thoroughly understood by them that nothing else had been asked of us than that we might be allowed to live under our own laws and enjoy the purity of religion. May it come back to them, I say, that they frankly acknowledged they had been deceived before by false reports, and had incurred fruitless expenses of so much time and such huge sums; that by this readiness to believe, the lives of many had been manifestly exposed to danger, and both kingdoms weakened and almost destined as prey to foreign armies or fleets, unless God had deigned to turn the eyes of his mercy upon both nations at the opportune moment, and to see to it that they should meet in peace to expose the impostors and their authors. And may it come back to them that the English nobles, who had been destined for our ruin, should earnestly intercede for us with the king, so that by royal authority we might obtain a National Synod and a parliament. In these requests the sum of our demands was contained, since we hoped that through them the most fitting remedies would be found for healing the wounds both of the commonwealth and of the Church. In that convention we had this especial consolation: that the king, departing with a peaceful host, and our English brothers, were fully satisfied as to the equity of our actions, and the falsity of the calumnies flung at us by our enemies, who had before shamelessly dared to spread them, became splendidly known. A change of political government, and a hostile incursion and invasion of England by which we might be enriched with its spoils, had been proposed to us. Neither of these had ever come into our minds, as we have often declared before, and as we then made evident by our actions, showing how great a fidelity we owed the most serene king and how great a love we bore the English.

units.la: Quibus consiliis adhærescere nobis adhuc propositum elt,ac ferio & ex animis imprecamur graviffimam omnipotentis Dei iram in eorum capita, qui primi alterutros ut hostes invadent ; idemque devovemus iis qui aliam quamvis regiminis politici formam suam præfentem, desiderent,aut alium Rectorem quam ferenilf.noftrun[?] regem apud nos natum, cui longævum & justum regnum comprecamur:Interim nullus elt qui æquissimum esse non judicabit, fi, hostili invasione seu terra seu mari ad angustias redacti,nobis defendendis,ac vindicandis,sicuti pios Christianos,&patriæ suæ veros cultores deceat,operam dederimus, fi provido ac maturo consilio rationem optimam iniverimus,qua nos regnumq; hoc ab extrema ruina tueamur,ac evitemus confufionesillas quas hostes nostri interminantur sæpius, regem nobis illaturum impediendo publicam justitiæ admi-. niftrationem, differendo mederi præfentibus quibus . premimur gravaminibus molestissimis, ac inter nosmet ipsos divisioném & factiones urgendo. Etenim hostes nostri jactitarunt,fe effecturos, ut Rex maria nostra classe armata occludat, mercaturam omnem maritimam impediat,ut exercitu terrestri agros noftros vel levibus excursionibus depopuletur: quo aut ad iram & vindictam provocemur,& feminaNationalis belli spargãtur,aut continuis motibusexagitati, & re familiari ac fortunis omnibus exhaustis inermes tandè opprimamur.Quod fi obtinuerint,prudentibus rerum æstimatoribus judicandum relinquimus,quid faciendum nobis erit? & annon satius multo fit(licet animo alias prorsus reluctãte)fortiter pugnando angustias & miserũ carceris squalorem effugere, quam ut misere in eo pereas : Atque hic quidem est rerum nostrarum status, quandoquidem plurimi nostratium mercatura familias alant, quibus omnibus inedia pereundum brevi erit, si negotiari ipsis non licet ; & qui mercaturam non tractant, ad illas incitas redigerentur, ut, relictis artibus quibus se suosque alerent; propriis sumptibus armati præsidia agentes, invasionem hostilem exspectarent, & propellerent : aut ut depositis armis, & limitibus præsidio nudatis patriam hostiũ populationibus exponerent. Verum, uti confidimus, Omnes probos & fideles Anglos operam daturos, ne quid hostiliter seu terra seu mari in nos agatur, sic, si ad necessariam nostram defensionem cogamur, non judicaturos, se teneri malis illis vindicandis, quæ hostes nostri in capita sua contrahunt, quin potius se obligari ad eorum improbitatem castigandam, qui summo studio nituntur ut ab iis sejungant nos, in quibus primarium & fidissimum robur situm est, si ab externo hoste invadentur : Neque est quod quivis ægre ferat, quod fidissimum dicamus ; Namuti nos judicamus, nullum vinculum religione arctius stringere, ita etiam qui religioni nostræ adversantur, judicant, & cum axioma illud eos tam arcto vinculo sibi invicem constringat, nonne danda est opera omnibus sinceris Christianis & patriam communem colentibus, qui in hac infula degunt, ut amicitiam mutuam inter nos ac cum reliquis nostræ professionis ecclesiis, sincere colamus ? An non stimulos nobis languentibus adderent fortitudo & fœlix successus gentium non æq; ac nos potentium, ut unitis viribus contra Babylonicam istam meretricem ejusque ,fulcra coiremus ? An non aures tandem aliquando potius aperiendæ sunt questibus regiorum liberorum unicæ sororis sereniff. nostri regis, qui in longe dissitis orbis terrarum partibus,à majorum hæreditate omnes exulantes,nostram opem anxie implorant,quam ut vinculis quibus toties tam arcte constringimur, ruptis, ludos faciamus Pontifici Romano, ac ipsius genuinis liberis, Episcopis, ut mutuis nostris cædibus ipsorum superbiam & tyrannidem tueamur ?
units.tr: We still intend to hold to these counsels, and from our hearts we solemnly pray that the most grievous wrath of Almighty God fall upon the heads of those who first invade one another as enemies. We likewise devote to the same curse those who desire any form of political government other than the present one, or any ruler other than our own most serene king, born among us, whose long and just reign we pray for. Meanwhile there is no one who will not judge it most equitable if, reduced to straits by hostile invasion by land or sea, we have taken pains to defend and vindicate ourselves, as is fitting for pious Christians and true lovers of their country; if we have adopted, with prudent and timely counsel, the best plan by which we may protect ourselves and this kingdom from extreme ruin, and avoid those confusions which our enemies often threaten. These are that the king will bring upon us the hindrance of the public administration of justice, delay in remedying the most troublesome burdens that press upon us, and the fomenting of division and faction among ourselves. For our enemies have boasted that they will bring it about that the king shuts up our seas with an armed fleet, impedes all maritime trade, and with a land army lays waste our fields even by light raids. By this either we are provoked to anger and vengeance, and the seeds of a national war are scattered, or, harassed by continual disturbances and with our household goods and fortunes all exhausted, we are at last oppressed while defenceless. If they succeed, we leave it to prudent judges of affairs to decide what we must do. Is it not much better, though by inclination altogether reluctant, to escape by fighting bravely the straits and the wretched squalor of prison, than to perish miserably in it? And this is indeed the state of our affairs, since most of our merchants support families, all of whom will soon perish from hunger if they are not allowed to trade; and those who do not engage in commerce would be driven to such extremity that, leaving the arts by which they support themselves and theirs, they would stand guard at their own expense, armed, awaiting a hostile invasion and repelling it; or, laying down their arms and leaving the frontiers stripped of defence, they would expose the country to the ravages of enemies. But, as we trust, all honest and faithful English will take care that nothing hostile be done against us either by land or by sea. So, if we are compelled to necessary defence, they will not judge themselves bound to avenge those evils which our enemies bring upon their own heads; rather they will judge themselves obliged to chastise the wickedness of those who strive with the utmost zeal to separate us from them, when in them lies our chief and most trusty strength, should they be attacked by a foreign enemy. Nor should anyone take it amiss that we call it most trusty. For as we judge that no bond binds more tightly than religion, so too do those who oppose our religion judge, and since that axiom binds them so closely to one another, should not all sincere Christians who dwell in this island and cherish the common country take pains to cultivate sincere mutual friendship among us and with the other churches of our profession? Would not the courage and happy success of peoples, not less than ours but mightier, add spurs to us who are languishing, so that with united forces we might gather against that Babylonish harlot and her props? Should not at last the ears rather be opened to the complaints of the royal children of the only sister of our most serene king, who, in the far-distant parts of the world, all exiled from their ancestral inheritance, anxiously implore our aid, than that, with the bonds by which we have so often been tightly constrained broken, we should make a mockery for the Roman Pontiff and his genuine children, the bishops, so that by our mutual slaughter we might protect their pride and tyranny?

units.la: Votorum nostrorum hæc summa est, ut præteriti saltem temporis experientia fratres Anglos edoceat impiam hostium nostrorum perfidiam,neque faciles aures præbendas esse iis crimina contra nos objicientibus.Atque quamvis probabile sit indictionem parlamenti à quibusdam sic accipi, quasi nostro damno intenderetur, (utpote, quia licet parlamentum toties antea summis omnium desideriis expetitum fuisset, semper tamen denegatū fuit,nunc vero illius primum mentio facta sit subito post relationem actionum nostrarum in parlamento nostro, apud senatum regium in Anglia,quæ calumniis tota scatebat, qua relatione author ostendit plus ingenii & acuminis singendo ea quibus gratum se redderet summis quibusdā auditoribus, quam ingenui amoris in patriam suam, eaq; expiaturum se putabat iram in se conceptam,ruinam extremam sibi minitantem,)nunquam tamē metus à parlamento sollicitos nos tenebit;cum perspectū nobis sit summū illud tribunal, pro solita sua prudentia,gravitate,ac æquitate,in justitiæ trutina omnia perpensurū, neq; determinationes & consilia sua fundaturum super falsas criminationes ab apertis nostris hostibus suggestas,nec seimmisturum nostris legibus aut parlamentis : Nam sicuti nosmet nunquam legibus aut parlamentis Anglię permiscuimus, orta inter regem & eos dissensione, (hoc enim esset in alieno choro pedem ponere) ita æquum non est, ut se nostris immiscceant Angli : quandoquidem duo hæc regna sint independentia,nec alterum alteri subalternum, utriusque regimen fit distinctum, neq; alterum alterius exemplo confirmari velit, in rebus etiam necessariis; multo certe iniquius effet, si alterum alteri molestiam facesseret, cum de rebus agitur quibus neutrius juri damnum aliquod intenditur aut afferri potest. Quin contra, prudentiores pronunciabunt, si hic aut ibi illegitimum quodvis perpetretur, curandum esse illud legibus & potestate regni illius cujus jura violantur; neque cum officioChristiani aut politici consistere, mala (si quae sint quantumvis maxima) cruento bello velle curare, quod utriusque regni cives praesentes & posteros maximis calamitatibus involvet, hoc enim esset, remediis, quovis hujus generis morbo deterioribus, mederi velle.
units.tr: This is the sum of our wishes: that the experience of past time at least may teach our English brethren the impious treachery of our enemies, and that they should not lend a ready ear to those who bring charges against us. Although it is probable that some take the summoning of parliament as aimed at our harm (since, although parliament had been sought with the greatest desire of all men many times before and always refused, its mention has now come up suddenly, just after the report of our actions in the parliament of our kingdom before the royal council in England, a report wholly full of slanders, by which its author showed that he was more clever and sharp in inventing things to make himself pleasing to certain highly placed listeners than sincerely loving his country, and thought that he would appease the anger conceived against him, which threatened his utter ruin), nevertheless we shall never be troubled by fear of parliament. For it is clear to us that this supreme tribunal, by its customary prudence, gravity and equity, will weigh all things in the balance of justice, and will not base its decisions and counsels on false accusations suggested by our open enemies, nor will it meddle with our laws or parliaments. For just as we have never mixed ourselves into the laws or parliaments of England, though dissension arose between the king and them (for that would be to set foot in another's dance), so it is not fair that the English should interfere with ours, since these two kingdoms are independent, neither subordinate to the other, each has its own distinct government, and neither wishes to be confirmed by the example of the other, even in necessary matters. It would certainly be far more unjust if one kingdom were to trouble the other in matters in which no harm to the right of either is aimed at or can be done. Rather, wiser men will pronounce that if any illegitimate thing is committed here or there, it must be remedied by the laws and power of that kingdom whose rights are violated; nor is it consistent with the duty of a Christian or a statesman to wish to cure evils, however great they may be, by cruel war, which would plunge the citizens of both kingdoms, present and future, into the greatest calamities. For this would be to wish to heal with remedies that are worse than any disease of this kind.

units.la: Porro animorum abalienatio inter gentes tam arctis vinculis sibi invicem conjunctas a duplici errore oriri poterit; Primus est, si de vicinorum statu certiores se fieri patiantur, per eos a quibus maxime cavendum sit; recenti adhuc experientia comprobatum fuit, quam iniqua & lubrica sit haec via; & in ipsis castris polliciti sunt Angli, se talibus in posterum fidem non habituros, verum ut in hunc errorem falsa relatione unius, (quantacunque demum dignitatis & eminentiae) & pauculorum turbonum, trahantur, abfurdiffimū esset: Intelligimus autem relationem istam quam de nostris actionibus fecit Deputatus regius coram senatoribus regiis in Anglia; cui complures nimia credulitate fidunt: O egregiū, & si quodquod ullum aliud notandum certe vaframentum! Ut negotium scil. hoc nostrum instar pilæ lusoriæ datatim volitet inter manus paucorum astute & improbe colludentium & praevaricantium, aliis hinc remittentibus, aliis vero apud vos excipientibus, parva sua quidem cum jactura; sed insigni utriusq; regni spectantis, & dolo hoc circumventi, dispendio: æquius erit mutuas operas conjungere, ut fraus hæc opportune aperiatur, ne fero tandem utraque gens damnum, in quod turbones isti astuti nos præcipitare satagunt, sentiat, & fortasse frustra resarciat: Neque patiamur, ab istis pauculis improbis præuaricatoribus in belli, quod machinantur, incommoda, nos errore hoc trahi; præsertim cum utriusque regni commodum hic vertatur, seu potius apertum dispendium. Secundus error oritur à legum nostrarum ignorantia; quodque vestro pede nos metiēdos putetis; Etenim accepimus in hoc totos esse nostros hostes, ut vobis persuadeant nos violata civili & temporali obedientia, jus regium invasisse, ac in parlamento statuta quædā proposuisse sancienda, quæ juri regio derogarent, uti sunt statuta, De abrogatione civilis & politicæ potestatis Episcoporum & ecclesiasticorum, ac rescissione legum prius sancitarum, quibus dignitates illæ politicæ concessæ fuerunt. De potestate & personis constituentibus ac ratione eligendi Articulorum Dominos. Contra procurationes absentium a parlamento, (ne vid.licet iis sententiam dicere aut suffragiu per alios quos scripto deputant, ferre.) De pacificatione seu ἀμνηςία. De mutuo auxilio. De moneta ænea. De restituendis presbyteriis seu classibus ad jus ordinationis pastorum. De declaratione ab ordinibus regni facta contra insolitam parlamenti dissolutionem, & hujus generis similia.
units.tr: Furthermore, alienation of minds between nations so closely bound together by ties can arise from a twofold error. The first is if they allow themselves to be informed about their neighbours' condition through those whom they most ought to beware of. Recent experience has proved how unfair and slippery this path is, and the English promised in the camp itself that they would no longer put faith in such men. But it would be most absurd to be drawn into this error by the false report of one man, however great his rank and eminence, and of a few troublemakers. We mean that report which the royal Deputy made about our actions before the royal councillors in England, in which many trust with excessive credulity. O excellent and, if ever there was one, certainly a trick to be noted! Our business is thus tossed about like a ball in play between the hands of a few who collude cunningly and wickedly and betray, some passing it on from here, others receiving it there among you, with little loss to themselves, but with a serious loss, to be expected, to both kingdoms, which is circumvented by this deceit. It will be fairer for us to join our efforts mutually, so that this fraud may be opportunely exposed, lest at last both nations feel the harm into which these cunning troublemakers are striving to plunge us, and perhaps make it good in vain. Nor let us allow ourselves to be drawn into this error, into the disadvantages of the war which they are plotting, by these few wicked betrayers, especially since the advantage of both kingdoms, or rather their manifest loss, is at stake here. The second error arises from ignorance of our laws, and from your supposing that we are to be measured by your foot. For we have learned that all our enemies are busy in this, to persuade you that we, having violated our civil and temporal obedience, have usurped the royal right, and have proposed in parliament certain statutes to be enacted which would derogate from the royal right, such as the statutes: On the abrogation of the civil and political power of bishops and ecclesiastics, and the rescinding of earlier laws by which those political dignities were granted; On the power and persons who constitute, and the manner of choosing, the Lords of the Articles; Against the proxies of those absent from parliament (namely, lest they should give their opinion or cast their vote through others whom they appoint in writing); On pacification or amnesty [ἀμνηστία]. On mutual assistance. On copper coinage. On restoring the presbyteries or classes to the right of ordaining ministers. On the declaration made by the estates of the realm against the unusual dissolution of parliament, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Nobis nunc non est propositum curiosius inquirere, an hæc, ex legum vestrarum præscripto, juri regio derogent: Nobis tamen pernotissimum est ex omnibus regni hujus publicis registris, eorundē cognitionem propriè pertinere ad nostrum parlamentum, ac distinctè demonstrari potest, nos in hisce tractandis aliis fundamentis innixos non fuisse, quam quæ leges nostræ & praxis usitata, nunquam antehac à quolibet in quæstionem vocata, suppeditant; singulisq; demonstrandis jam vacaremus, si certo sciremus de quibus inter vos esset dubitatum: & nisi horum fusa tractatio in majoris molis volumen excresceret; à cujus impressione temporis angustia excludimur.
units.tr: It is not our purpose now to inquire too closely whether these things derogate from the royal right by the prescription of your laws. Yet it is very well known to us, from all the public records of this kingdom, that the knowledge of them belongs properly to our parliament; and it can be clearly shown that in handling these matters we rested on no other foundations than those which our laws and the customary practice, never before called into question by anyone, supply. We would already be turning to demonstrate each point, if we knew for certain which of them were in doubt among you; and were it not that a full treatment of them would grow into a volume of too great a bulk, from whose printing we are shut out by the shortness of time.

units.la: Interim ut constet quantum æquitati causæ nostræ fidamus, ad serenissimum regem deputatos amandavimus, rationibus a lege & continua regni hujus praxi desumptis bene instructos, ut regis animo scrupulos omnes eximant, & respondeant ad omnia & singula, quæ contra nos objici possent: Quos uti nunquam delegassemus, si causæ nostræ justitiæ, & omnium nostrarum actionum æquitati diffisi fuissemus, ita omnes probos enixe rogamus, ut sibi persuadeant, nihil nos aggressos esse, quod non consistat cum fundamentalibus hujus regni legibus, (utcunque ab hostibus calumnias atroces patiamur) quibus religiose observandis, & secundum quas se nos gubernaturum juramento solenni sese obstrinxit rex: Quas confidimus serenissimum regem nunquam violaturum, neque vicinos in quæstionem vocaturos; quibus omnia prospera, & liberum præsertim Parlamentum vovemus, in quo hostium nostrorum, qui calamitatum harum authores unici sunt, subdolæ machinationes in apertam lucem proferantur, ac ostendatur istis suis artibus multa tam in regni quam religionis statu mutare, propositum fuisse; quibus semel cum fautoribus suppressis, ecclesia regnoque à metu novationum quas urgent & promovent liberatis, non dubitandum quin exinde felicitatis plurimum tam regi serenissimo quam utrique regno redundaturum sit. Auferatur improbus coram rege, utique folium ejus justitia stabilietur: Et sicuti parlamenti postulatio est Vox populi, Concessio ejusdem, Vox Regis, sic Deum optimum maximum precamur, ut in conclusione audiatur Vox Dei, qua Christi regnum promoveatur, & Antichristi tyrannis submoveatur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, so that it may be clear how much we trust in the justice of our cause, we have sent deputies to His Most Serene Majesty, well instructed with arguments drawn from the law and the continuous practice of this kingdom, so that they may remove all scruples from the king's mind, and answer every point and each of the things that might be objected against us. We would never have sent them if we distrusted the justice of our cause and the equity of all our actions. So we earnestly ask all honest men to be persuaded that we have undertaken nothing that does not agree with the fundamental laws of this kingdom (however much we suffer atrocious calumnies from our enemies), which the king bound himself by solemn oath to observe religiously, and according to which he would govern us. We trust that His Most Serene Majesty will never violate them, nor call our neighbours into question. To him we vow all prosperity, and above all a free parliament, in which the deceitful machinations of our enemies, who are the sole authors of these calamities, will be brought into the open light, and it will be shown that by these arts they had intended to change many things in the state both of the kingdom and of religion. Once these men and their supporters have been put down, and the Church and kingdom freed from fear of the innovations which they urge and promote, there is no doubt that much happiness will thence flow to His Most Serene Majesty as well as to both kingdoms. Let the wicked be removed from before the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness. And just as the petition of parliament is the voice of the people, and its grant the voice of the king, so we pray to God, best and greatest, that in the end the voice of God may be heard, by which the kingdom of Christ may be advanced and the tyranny of Antichrist removed.

units.la: In certam etiam spem adducimur vicinam gentem hostium nostrorum contra nos susurris & calumniis sibi denuo imponi non passuram; quin potius auxilio nobis futuram, & preces concordes ad regem conjuncturam, ut tandem aliquando liberemur ab innumeris & gravissimis quibus hodie premimur oneribus & gravaminibus, quibus certe sine extrema nostra pernicie diutius ferendis impares sumus, nisi mora omni sublata remedium opportunum sereniss. rex afferat; parliamenti videl. interrupti conclusionem legitimam imperando. Gravaminum autem horum brevem synopsin subjiciemus.
units.tr: We are also brought into a certain hope that our neighbouring nation, our enemies, will not suffer itself to be imposed upon again by whispers and calumnies against us; but rather that it will be of help to us and will join with us in united prayers to the king, so that at last we may be freed from the countless and most grievous burdens and oppressions under which we are pressed today, and which we are certainly unable to bear any longer without our extreme ruin, unless His Serene Majesty, with all delay removed, brings a suitable remedy: namely by commanding the legitimate conclusion of the interrupted parliament. We shall now set out a brief summary of these grievances.

units.la: Etenim cum in articulis pacificationis, mense Iunio in castris regiis inter alia tum obsignata, promissum nobis fuisset, Synodi Nationalis & parlamenti convocatione motus & tumultus omnes compositum iri, omniaque ecclesiastica negotia synodi judicio componenda, & politica authoritate parlamenti ad diem 2o.Aug.indicti, ac synodi decreta parlamentum sanciturum, omnia denique, sine ulla prælimitatione, quæ in pacem & commodum regni hujus conducerent, ad parlamentum remitterentur, idque tabulis signatis : licet omnia in synodo prospere ac legitime procederent.Cum tamen ad parliamentum deventum esset, obstinate remit Deputatus regius se Synodi decreta sanciturum, nisi cum limitationibus, restrictionibus, declarationibus, accepto videl. mandato privato à rege (ut ferebatur) ne Episcoporum abolitioni consentiret : quod adversabatur instructionibus secundum quas, omnes suas actiones in synodo composuerat, priusquam mandatum illud ad manus ejus devenisset. Ut incommodum hoc quovis modo resarciret, nulla habita ratione solennis promissi regii in legibus pacificationis, & sui coram plena synodo sæpius repetiti, Declaratione quandam publicam obtrudere voluit contra decretum Synodi, in quod 17.Augu.ipse cum aliis omnibus ecclesiarum ad synodum deputatis, unanimi suffragio consensit. [Decreto vero illo, secundum Synodicas ecclesiæ hujus constitutiones rejiciebantur libri liturgiæ seu Communium precum, Canonum, ordinationis, nobis obtrusi ; simul cum cels[?] Commissionis foro: Ceremoniæ, seu quinq; articuli Perthenses: Episcopatus: & ecclesiasticorum politicâ munia ac dignitates, in hac ecclesia illicita esse declarantur; Pseudo-Synodi quædam rescindebantur: Synodi nationales rite ac legitimæ constitutæ, quibus proprie verú ecclesiasticarum judicium competit, decernebantur habendæ singulis annis semel ordinarie. Quod si urgente necessitate ob extraordinariam aliquam occasionem sæpius pro re nata convenire oporteat Synodos nationales, licere, modo necessitas ea regi prius remonstretur libello supplici: Sessiones seu consistoria, presbyteria seu Classes, ac Synodos provinciales constituenda esse juxta politiam hujus ecclesiæ declarabantur: Et denique de fœdere nationali.] Qua declaratione admissa synodi sanctio inutilis fuisset, & perspicue præjudicatum fuisset synodi decreto, si aliter sancitum fuisset in parlamento, aliter vero in Synodo. Atque licet astrictus esset Deputatus regius non solum expresse sancire & rata facere synodi decreta, ut vim legis haberent ad vigorem publicæ observantiæ, verum etiam rescindere & refigere quæcunque superiorum temporum statuta seu directe seu indirecte synodi decretis contraria essent, prout semper apud omnes fieri solet, (absurdum quippe esset, ut ea statuta parlamenti, quæ ob id solum condita sunt ut synodi canones sancient, non refigerentur, cum fundamentum cui innituntur, ab ecclesia euersum fuerit, quæ cum ex se non possit civilem sanctionem abolere à parlamento; cum ecclesiæ decreta sancit, necessario refigenda sunt ex consequente, & ex natura rei) Renuerat tamen superiorum temporum statuta, quæ præsentis Synodi decretis contraria essent, abrogare. Renisus est etiam ne ecclesiæ privilegia sua restituerentur. Ordinationis, videlicet, pastorum per presbyteria seu classes, & plantationis quarundam ecclesiarum ab Episcopis vi presbyteriis ereptarum, licet Deputati ecclesiastici obtulissent se statim demonstraturos, jus illud controversum proprie prie ad Ecclesiam pertinere: Denique quicquid ab ecclesiarum deputatis propositum fuit in evidentem ecclesiæ utilitatem,non solum directe rejecit, verumetiam eosdem aspere habuit, sæpius repetendo, pastores tandem futuros pejores Episcopis; & similibus verborum contumeliis: Atque sic spe omni præsentia mala corrigendi excidimus; promissisque manu regia obsignatis prorsus frustramur: Nam quanquam per synodum nationalem, ipso deputato regio assentiente, omnibusque ad synodum deputatis, sine unico contradicente aut hæsitante suffragio, adstipulantibus; Episcopatus ex hac ecclesia submoveatur; retinent tamen Episcopi consuetos titulos & subscriptiones, & pari quo antea dignitatis & honoris gradu coluntur: Iudicet itaque mortalium quilibet, an religioni debita sua securitas præstetur, (quod divisioni & factionibus inter nos procurandis toties frustra objicitur) an non vero potius eadem subvertatur, & spe nostra nos frustremur?
units.tr: For when, in the articles of pacification sealed in the royal camp in June, among other things, it had been promised to us that all the tumults and disturbances arising from the summoning of the National Synod and Parliament would be settled; that all ecclesiastical business would be settled by the judgement of the Synod, and political matters by the authority of Parliament, which was summoned for 2 August, and that Parliament would ratify the decrees of the Synod; and finally that everything which would conduce to the peace and welfare of this kingdom would be referred to Parliament without any prior limitation, and this was sealed in writing. Yet although everything proceeded successfully and lawfully in the Synod, when the matter came to Parliament, the royal commissioner obstinately declared that he would ratify the decrees of the Synod only with limitations, restrictions and declarations, having evidently received a private mandate from the king (as was reported) not to consent to the abolition of the bishops. This conflicted with the instructions under which he had conducted all his actions in the Synod before that mandate reached his hands. To make good this disadvantage in some way, and disregarding altogether the solemn royal promise in the articles of pacification, and the promise he had repeatedly made before the full Synod, he wished to impose a certain public declaration against the decree of the Synod, to which on 17 August he himself, along with all the other deputies of the churches to the Synod, had given unanimous assent. [By that decree, however, according to the synodical constitutions of this church, the liturgy or Book of Common Prayer, the canons and the Book of Ordination, which had been forced upon us, were rejected; together with the Court of High Commission; the ceremonies, or the Five Articles of Perth; episcopacy; and the political offices and dignities of churchmen were declared unlawful in this church; certain pseudo-synods were annulled; national synods, duly and lawfully constituted, to which the true judgement of ecclesiastical matters properly belongs, were ordained to be held ordinarily once a year. And if urgent necessity required that national synods be convened more often on some extraordinary occasion, this was permitted, provided that the necessity was first made known to the king by a humble petition. Sessions or consistories, presbyteries or classes, and provincial synods were declared to be constituted according to the polity of this church; and finally, concerning the National Covenant.] With that declaration admitted, the sanction of the Synod would have been useless, and it would have been plainly prejudged, if one thing were enacted in Parliament and another in the Synod. And although the royal commissioner was bound not only to expressly sanction and ratify the decrees of the Synod so that they would have the force of law and be publicly observed, but also to rescind and repeal whatever statutes of earlier times were directly or indirectly contrary to the decrees of the Synod, as is always the custom with everyone (for it would be absurd that those acts of Parliament which were enacted solely so that they would sanction the canons of the Synod should not be repealed, once the foundation on which they rest has been overthrown by the Church; since, when the Church's decrees are sanctioned by Parliament, those acts must necessarily be repealed as a consequence, and by the nature of the matter), he nevertheless refused to repeal the statutes of earlier times which were contrary to the decrees of the present Synod. He also resisted the restoration of the church's privileges: namely the ordination of ministers by presbyteries or classes, and the planting of certain churches which bishops had by force taken from the presbyteries, although the ecclesiastical commissioners offered to demonstrate at once that this disputed right properly belongs to the Church. Finally, whatever was proposed by the deputies of the churches for the manifest benefit of the Church, he not only directly rejected, but also treated those men harshly, repeatedly saying that ministers would in the end be worse than bishops, and using similar insulting words. And so we have lost all hope of correcting the present evils, and we are utterly disappointed in the promises sealed with the royal hand. For although, through the National Synod, with the royal commissioner himself assenting, and with all the deputies to the Synod supporting it without a single dissenting or hesitating vote, episcopacy was removed from this church, nevertheless the bishops retain their customary titles and signatures, and are honoured with the same degree of dignity and rank as before. Let therefore any man judge whether due security is provided for religion (which is so often and so vainly alleged as a cause of division and faction among us), or whether rather it is being subverted, and we are being cheated of our hope?

units.la: Rebus ad ecclesiam spectantibus sic repudiatis, negotia quædam politica urgebamus (quandoquidem in eum finem coeant parlamenta, ut gravamina corrigant, & leges sanciant, & serenifl.rex indictionis mandato declaraverit se illud convocasse, ut libere sine ulla prælimitatione vacaret determinationi causarum omnium civilium, & procurationi solidæ pacis in regno) præsertim vero illud urgebamus, de Constitutione plenaria membrorum parlamenti & Dominorum pro articulis: ad quæ Episcoporum abdicatione cogebamur. Sed hisce, utcunque summe necessariis, Deputati regii assensum impetrare non potuimus, licet semper obtulerimus, legitimos fuisse nostros hosce conatus, ex ipsis parlamentorum publicis registris demonstrare, quæ cum ex industria nobis subducta fuissent, (& hoc etiam à ratione quam longissime abest, ut non liceat supremo tribunali sua ipsius scripta publica consulere) & nos obtulissemus locum peculiarem designare ubi laterent, Deputatum humiliter ac enixe obsecrantes, ut mandato suo proferri juberet in publicum parlamenti usum, polliciti fine damno eadem nos reposituros;Sed & hoc etiam rejecit, quo satis ostenditur consulto & dedita opera scripta illa nobis tum subducta fuisse. Statutum pacificationis seu legem ἀμνηςίας [?] sancire recusavit: nisi eo tenore formatum amplecteremur, quo ad sempiternam nostram infamiam, foedae rebellionis crimen literis indelebilibus inscriberemus frontibus nostris. Solenne illi fuit, cum argumentis minime dubiis quidpiam urgeremus, reponere, Ast aliter vult rex, et coget vos ad illud, si non pejora, faciendum: argumentum certe periculo plenum, quod in liberis parlamentis audiatur, & quo alii aliquando etiam premi possunt, uti nos hactenus. Cum Deputatus regius objecisset contra ea quae à nobis proposita fuerunt; quod regi vid. antea non innotuissent, nec instructionibus suis comprehensa effent, licet parlamentum nostrum libere possit sententiam pronunciare de omnibus civilibus negotiis ad regni utilitatem pertinentibus, & manifestae servituri subjiceretur regnum hoc, si parlamento magni sigilli obsignatione munito non liceat proponere & determinare de rebus quibuslibet ad se proprie pertinentibus, nisi primum petita venia & rescripto seu mandato ab aula in eum finem misso: Parati tamen fuimus eorundem, contra quae objecisset, relationem in acta differre, seu de quibus dubitatum fuit, regi scrupulum haesisse, donec plene de omnibus ipsius majestatem certiorem fecissemus; dummodo quaedam extra omnem controversiae aleam posita, ac paci stabiliendae multum opportuna, sublata omni procrastinatione concludi pateretur: Et hoc etiam nobis fuit denegatum, & deputati nostri, mandato regio niffi ad aulam, ut regem de statu actionum nostrarum in parlamento, certiorem facerent, ipsiusq; Maj. satisfacerent, statim ab aula dimissi fuerunt sine ulla audientia: ut vobis satis superque notum est. Deputatis etiam expresse imperavit parlamenti continuationem sola regis authoritate, sine consensu ordinum regni (quod legibus & praxi huius regni directe adversatur) atque alias eadem authoritate dissolutionem parlamenti sub poena rebellionis & læsæ maiestatis nobis imperavit, licet excedat ambitum cuiuslibet edicti regii vel minimum subditorum causa non examinata reum declarare rebellionis, multo minus omnes regni ordines, a quibus quæ rebellionis nomine censenda sunt, declarari oportet.
units.tr: With the matters pertaining to the Church thus rejected, we pressed certain political questions (since Parliaments meet for this purpose, to correct grievances and enact laws, and His Most Serene Majesty declared in the writ of summons that he had called it so that it might freely, without any prior limitation, deal with all civil causes and the establishment of solid peace in the kingdom). Above all, however, we pressed the matter of the full constitution of the members of Parliament and the Lords of the Articles, from which we were being forced to remove the bishops. But although these matters were of the utmost necessity, we could not obtain the assent of the royal commissioner, although we always offered to demonstrate from the public registers of Parliament itself that our efforts were lawful. Those registers had been deliberately withheld from us (and it is far from reason that the supreme court should not be allowed to consult its own public records). We offered to name a particular place where they were kept, humbly and earnestly begging the commissioner to order them to be produced by his mandate for the public use of Parliament, promising to return them undamaged; but he rejected this too, which sufficiently shows that those records were withheld from us at that time on purpose and by design. He refused to ratify the Act of Pacification, or the law of amnesty [ἀμνηστίας], unless we accepted it in a form by which we would inscribe the crime of foul rebellion on our foreheads in indelible letters, to our everlasting infamy. It was his habit, whenever we pressed anything with arguments that were by no means doubtful, to reply: But the king wills it otherwise, and will compel you to do it, if not something worse. This is certainly a dangerous argument to hear in free Parliaments, and one by which others too may sometimes be oppressed, as we have hitherto been. When the royal commissioner objected against the things proposed by us, that they were not previously known to the king nor contained in his instructions, although our Parliament may freely pronounce its judgement on all civil matters pertaining to the advantage of the kingdom, and this kingdom would be subjected to manifest servitude if it were not permitted, without first asking pardon and a rescript or mandate sent from the court for that purpose, to propose and determine on any matters properly belonging to itself, which are under the seal of the great seal of Parliament; nevertheless we were ready to defer to the record whatever he had objected against, or, regarding matters about which doubt had been raised, to allow that the king had a scruple until we had fully informed His Majesty of all things; provided only that certain matters placed beyond all dispute, and very useful for establishing peace, were allowed to be concluded without any delay. This too was denied us, and our deputies, having been summoned to court by the royal mandate to inform the king of the state of our proceedings in Parliament and to give His Majesty satisfaction, were at once dismissed from the court without any hearing, as is well and more than sufficiently known to you. He also expressly ordered the deputies to continue Parliament by the king's authority alone, without the consent of the estates of the kingdom (which is directly contrary to the laws and practice of this kingdom), and by the same authority he commanded us to dissolve Parliament under penalty of rebellion and treason against the majesty, although it exceeds the scope of any royal edict to declare a subject guilty of rebellion without examining his cause, much less must all the estates of the kingdom, by whom what is to be counted as rebellion ought to be declared, be so declared.

units.la: Atque quantumvis perspectissimum haberemus licere nobis legitima authoritate in parlamentum semel coeuntibus, non obstante quolibet rescripto in contrarium, parlamenti sessiones continuare[?]? Nihilominus statim morem gessimus, confisi novo hoc ingenui amoris & submissæ fidelitatis exemplo (dum ea tam æquis animis pateremur, ad quæ nulla officii nostri ratio nos cogeret) facilius tandem potituros assensu regio præsentibus nostris æquissimis postulatis, & firmandis in futurum privilegiis, ac satisfacturos Anglis, & re ipsa hostium calumnias diluturos, (qui pro ingenio suo actionem illam nostram in deteriorem partem procul dubio detorsissent.) atque patientiam & animorum nostrorum in omnibus moderationem orbi universo testaturos, licet nulla conditio stipulata nobis sincere præstetur, quod imputamus illis, qui hinc, om-nia in deterius torquentes ad aulam perscribunt, & hostibus nostris qui hæc in aula suadent. Hisce addendum, quod publica justitiæ administratione privemur, quo regnum hoc similitudinem refert navis foeda tempestate jactatæ, & omnibus periculis, sine clavo, velis, puppi, aut funibus expositæ. Quod mutuo subsidio expensarum & sumptuum, quos legitimæ defensionis gratia subivimus, orbemur: hostibus statuentibus nos sic tandem adigendos ad incitas & extremam confusionem. Quod pastores ecclesiis vacuis non præsententur, quo pastorum defectu lupis in prædam exponuntur greges plurimi. Quod postulata nostra, pro restitutione bonorum pauperibus nautis ereptarum, negligantur. Quod senatores & alii publicis regni muniis fungentes, indicta causa & parte non audita, officiis submoveantur, quod non novum solum est, verumetiam legibus regni hujus prorsus adversatur. Quod author fusæ declarationis sive manifesti in jus non vocetur, neque in eum animadvertatur, quod cumulum splendidissimorum mendaciorum & atrocissimarum calumniarum contra nos in librum illum conjecerit, quorum, usque ad 200. numerum, deputati nostri in castris regiis obtulerunt refutationem: Atque licet liber iste mendaciis & calumniis scatens, tum synodi tum parlamenti judicio damnatus sit, ab omni tamen ulteriori censura, & in authores inquisitione abstinuimus, contenti apud serenif. regem hanc nostram querimoniam humiliter deposuisse, quia sub nomine maj. regiæ prodierat: quod tamen ejus verum authorem non magis liberaret ab exemplari pœna, quam regii nominis & insignium impressio falsarios monetæ a severissimis pœnis liberat, neque plus fidei apud quemlibet obtineret, quam adulterata moneta. Quod religiose pacta & conventa omnia præstiterimus, ac omnia restituerimus, præter pauxillum pulveris tormentarii qui consumptus fuerat, & paucas (musketas ut vulgo vocant) de quibus quid factum fit ignoratur; quorum in utriusque pretium non excederet summam quadragentarum librarum, quam obtulimus rationibus nostris deputati, cum nobis satisfactum fuerit de summa nobis debita aut stipulata. Quod nova munimenta erigantur, & magna præsidiariorum militum manus Berwici & Carleoli retineatur, [?]incatur, quo diffidentiæ & suspicionis nota nobis regis serenis. fidelibus subditis immerito inuritur, cum tamen pari diligentia locis aliis, majoris momenti, & hostium externorum incursionibus magis opportunis, non provideatur: Atque ut infamia illa & metu liberaremur, deputati nostri obtulerunt, ordines Scotiæ se obligaturos, quamprimum certiores fierent imminentis cujusliber periculi, sexcentos milites ad urbes eas muniendas statim submissuros ac post duos dies, bis mille, & post sexaut octo dies, 8000, aut 10000. quibus ab omni externo hoste defendi poterunt. Atque cum milites utrinque dimittendos esse articulis in pacificatione stipulatis cautum sit, & nos nostros statim exautoraverimus, ac dimiserimus, satis patet retentione tot militum in locis nobis vicinis, pactorum conventorumque fidem corrumpi. Quod arx Edenburgena ab usu cui destinatur, hoc est, ut urbem tueretur, ac civibus auxilio esset, convertatur in civitatis terrorem, &c. quod in eum finem, (expresse contra conditiones pacificationis, ut videl. omnia in eo statu collocarentur ac retinerentur, in quo ante exortos motus fuerunt,) ita instruatur commeatu & milite; ut sextuplo excedant numerum, qui a rege serenis. & Marchione Hamiltonio arci custodiendæ sufficere tum judicabatur, aut quem comes Traquarius pollicitus erat se submissurum.
units.tr: And although we were fully convinced that we might lawfully, by our own authority, continue the sessions of a parliament once it had met, notwithstanding any rescript to the contrary, we at once complied.
