We trusted that this new example of free love and humble loyalty would make it easier in the end to obtain the king's assent to our most just requests, to secure our privileges for the future, to satisfy the English, and to refute in fact the calumnies of our enemies, who would doubtless have twisted that action of ours for the worse, and to bear witness before the whole world to our patience and moderation of spirit. Yet no stipulated condition has been sincerely honoured towards us. We lay this to the charge of those who, twisting everything for the worse, report it to the court, and of our enemies who advise these things at court. To this must be added that we are deprived of the public administration of justice, so that this kingdom resembles a ship battered by a foul storm and exposed to every danger, without rudder, sails, stern or ropes. We are bereft of mutual help for the expenses and costs which we have incurred for the sake of lawful defence, our enemies deciding that we may in this way at last be driven to utter ruin and extreme confusion. Ministers are not presented to vacant churches, and through this lack of ministers many flocks are exposed as prey to wolves. Our demands for the restitution of the goods taken from poor sailors are neglected. Senators and others who hold public offices in the kingdom are removed from their posts without the case being heard and without the other party being given a hearing, which is not only new but utterly contrary to the laws of this kingdom. The author of the published declaration or manifesto is not summoned to court, nor is any action taken against him, although he has heaped upon that book a pile of most splendid lies and most atrocious calumnies against us. Our deputies offered at the royal camp a refutation of up to two hundred of them. And although that book, full of lies and calumnies, has been condemned by the judgment both of the synod and of parliament, we have nevertheless refrained from any further censure and from inquiry into its authors. We have been content to lay this complaint of ours humbly before the most serene king, since the book had appeared under the name of His Majesty. Yet this does not free its true author from exemplary punishment any more than the stamping of the royal name and emblems frees counterfeiters of coin from the most severe penalties, nor would it win any more credit with anyone than adulterated coin. That we have faithfully kept all the agreements and covenants, and have restored everything, except a little gunpowder which had been used up, and a few muskets (as they are commonly called), about which it is not known what has become of them; the value of both together would not exceed the sum of four hundred pounds, which our deputies have offered to our accounts, once we have been satisfied concerning the sum owed or stipulated to us. That new fortifications are being raised, and a large body of garrison soldiers is kept at Berwick and Carlisle, and [?] this is undeservedly branded upon us, as a mark of distrust and suspicion, on the part of the most serene king's loyal subjects, while no equal care is taken for other places of greater importance and more exposed to incursions by foreign enemies. And so that we might be freed from that disgrace and fear, our deputies offered that the estates of Scotland would bind themselves, as soon as they were informed of any imminent danger, to send at once six hundred soldiers to garrison those cities, then after two days two thousand, and after sixty or eighty days 8,000 or 10,000, by which they could be defended against every foreign enemy. And since it is provided in the articles stipulated in the pacification that soldiers on both sides are to be dismissed, and we have at once discharged and dismissed our own, it is clear enough that by keeping so many soldiers in places near us the faith of the pacts and covenants is being corrupted. That the castle of Edinburgh is being turned from the purpose for which it is destined, namely to guard the city and to be of help to the citizens, into a terror to the city, etc. To that end (expressly contrary to the conditions of the pacification, namely that everything should be placed and kept in the state in which it was before the disturbances broke out), it is so furnished with provisions and soldiers that it exceeds six times the number which was then judged sufficient by the most serene king and the Marquis of Hamilton to guard the castle, or which Earl Traquair had promised to send.

units.la: Imo qui arci jam præest, declaravit 50 aut 60 praefidiarios arci muniendæ sufficere; cum nunc hunc numerum longe superent, quorum quidam exteri sint, (contra disertam legem in parlamentis olim sancitam, quibus cavetur ne exteris quibuslibet arcium custodia committatur:) instructi tormentis ignivomis seu pyrobolaribus & aliis instrumentis bellicis ad urbes perdendas & comburendas idoneis; defendendis vero prorsus inutilibus. Quod solis peregrinis militibus arx Britannodimensis, contra parlamenti statuta, muniatur. Quod in insolita & nova sacramenta adigantur Scoti, qui negotiis suis privatis procurandis in Angliam & Hiberniam excurrunt, in quae nullae aliae exterae nationes adiguntur. Quod dissidiis adhuc ferveat hoc regnum, neque aliquid operaepretii praestetur ad domesticam ejus pacem procurandam. Quod insigni damno & molestiis pauperiores praesertim afficiantur moneta illa aenea, cujus pretium licet senatus edicto diminutum fuisset, sexto tamen post die contrario edicto id rescissum est, quo factum est, ut illubenter ac difficulter monetam illam recipiant cives, quae justum valorem sexies superat: adde quod monetae hujus praetextu, falsarii ab exteris regionibus omnia repleant adulterata moneta, nullius prorsus pretii. Denique, quod nihil intentatum relinquatur, quo divisiones spargantur & succrescant inter nos semina, sed, Deo gratias, nam artes illas infoeliciori quam quo superiori anno, successu promoventur, quando ab hostibus nostris jactitatum fuit, se factionem inter nos insignem excitaturos, quae nos opprimeret, a qua, eventus docuit, non fuisse quod multum metueremus. Neque certe putandum est hostes nostros aliud hisce gravissimis malis, quibus, eorum opera, consulto premimur, sibi proponere, quam ut iis fracti tandem opprimamur. Quare Dei & naturae legibus nobis licet aliquid in nostram salutem suscipere, & innocuam nostram defensionem aggredi, cui coepto benedicat Dominus, quem sero precamur, ut velit tandem excitare serenissimum nostrum regem ad seriam Davidis etiam regis imitationem: ut oculi ipsius attendant ad veraces terrae, ut hos amet, amplectatur, videat libenter, atque his sociis seu ministris seros senectus impleat annos, ut saevi sceleris ministri nunquam illi censeantur inter amicos candidos, ut impios longe, mora nulla, terrae finibus pellat, ac a civitate Iehovae monstra haec flagitiorum rescindat: Deum etiam rogamus, ut spiritu prudentiæ & fortitudinis omnibus probis in Anglia adsit, qui causam nostram posthabito omni discrimine, acturi sunt, ac malum quod imminet impedituri. Amen.
units.tr: Indeed, the man who now commands the castle has declared that fifty or sixty garrison soldiers are enough to guard it; yet now they far exceed this number, some of them being foreigners (contrary to an express law once enacted in parliaments, by which it is provided that the custody of fortresses is not to be entrusted to any foreigners whatever), equipped with fire-throwing and bomb-throwing artillery and other weapons of war suited to destroying and burning cities, but wholly useless for defending them. That Berwick castle is garrisoned by foreign soldiers alone, contrary to the statutes of parliament. That Scots are compelled to take unusual and new oaths when they go to England and Ireland to pursue their private business, which no other foreign nation is forced to take. That this kingdom is still seething with dissensions, and no effort worth the name is made to secure its domestic peace. That the poorer people in particular are heavily damaged and harassed by that copper coinage; although its value had been reduced by an act of the council, six days later a contrary act rescinded this, with the result that the citizens receive that coin unwillingly and with difficulty, although its true value is exceeded six times over. Add to this that under the pretext of this coinage, counterfeiters from foreign regions flood everything with adulterated coin of no value at all. Finally, that nothing is left untried by which divisions may be scattered and the seeds of discord may grow up among us; but, thank God, these arts are being pushed with less success than last year, when our enemies boasted that they would stir up a notable faction among us which would crush us, a faction of which, as events have shown, there was not much to fear. Nor indeed should it be thought that our enemies propose to themselves by these most grievous evils, by which we are deliberately oppressed through their work, anything other than that we should at last be crushed, broken by them. Wherefore by the laws of God and nature we are permitted to undertake something for our own safety and to undertake an innocent defence, to which undertaking may the Lord give his blessing, whom we entreat late, that he may at last be pleased to stir up our most serene king to a serious imitation of King David as well: that his eyes may rest upon the faithful of the land, that he may love them, embrace them and gladly behold them, and that his old age may be filled with years spent with such companions and ministers; that no wicked minister of cruel crime may ever be counted among his sincere friends; that without delay he may drive the impious far off to the ends of the earth, and cut off these monsters of wickedness from the city of Jehovah. We also pray God that the spirit of prudence and fortitude may be with all upright men in England, who are about to take up our cause, setting aside every danger, and to avert the evil that threatens. Amen.

units.la: Scriptum hoc quam benevole a probis acceptum fuit, tam diligenter etiam repræsentata supplicionum[?] acerbitate ab aliis fuit suppressum; qui in id sedulo incumbebant, ne ulla vera rerum Scoticarum relatiq[?] ad Anglos perveniret; & ab impensis belli quod jampridem excitare statuerant, aversos redderet: manu itaque carnificis publice comburenda quæ inveniri potuerunt exemplaria, curarunt, satis acerba in Scotos odia & exulcerati animi indicia exhibentes verum prout nihil aliud ab istis exspectari potuit, ita maximo dolori Scotis fuit, quod vulgo creditum fuisset regii senatus in Anglia decreto id fieri.
units.tr: However kindly this writing was received by upright men, so carefully was it suppressed by others, with the bitterness of the supplications being likewise set forth, who devoted themselves diligently to ensuring that no true account of Scottish affairs reached the English, and so that they would be turned away from the expense of the war which they had long before resolved to stir up. Accordingly they took care that the copies which could be found should be publicly burned by the hangman's hand, thereby displaying quite bitter hatred against the Scots and signs of an embittered spirit. Indeed, as nothing else could be expected from such men, so it was a great grief to the Scots that it was commonly believed this was done by decree of the royal council in England.

units.la: Legati Scotorum cum ad aulam regiam venifsent, 20 Februarii, serenissimo regi se sistunt, ac perorante Laudonio; demonstrant, fidelibus regni Scotiæ subditis ipsa morte acerbius esse, quod nunc denuo post tot illustria fidelitatis suæ in regem exhibita testimonia, eadem in quæstionem vocentur: & innocentissimæ ac æquissimæ ordinum regni in comitiis actiones traducerentur ut illegitimæ, & jus regium diminuentes, idque a comite Traquario; se regis serenissimi permissu nunc delegatos esse, ac ad-esse paratos ad postulatorum æquitatem afferen-dam, & diluendas objectiones & calumnias: Rogant itaque regem serenissimum ut coram ipso, in præsentia senatorum utriusq; regni liceret sibi ordinum innocentiam vindicare: Epistolam a nupera natio-nali synodo regi serenissimo tradunt, in qua postam-pliffimas gratias regi actas, synodicorum decretorum sanctionem postulabant. Responsum fuit a rege, omnia ipsorum postulata tradenda esse in scriptis; seque per comitem Traquarium significaturum quid suæ voluntatis esset. Ominosum fatis videbatur serenissf. regem noluisse altero internuncio aut interprete uti quam Traquario cujus opera ingrata fœderatis & infœlix hactenus fuit; sed difficultates hæ nunc erant negligendæ, & dissimulandæ: & literas supplices quam primum conscribunt, ejusdem fere tenoris cum prima oratione, & rogant etiam, ut relatio illa comitis Traquarii de actionibus parlamenti; iisdem verbis quibus expressa fuit in regio senatu, sibi traderetur, quo commodius ad singula respondere posset, & serenis. regi ac omnibus fascino istius fucatæ orationis seducti s plenius satisfieret; literas has imperante rege obsignant singuli chirographis, rogantes ut idem a Traquario fieret, regium responsum referente.
units.tr: When the Scottish commissioners came to the royal court on 20 February, they presented themselves to the most serene king. With Lauderdale speaking, they showed that it was more bitter to the loyal subjects of the kingdom of Scotland than death itself that, after so many distinguished proofs of their loyalty to the king, the same matters were now being called into question, and that the most innocent and most just actions of the estates in parliament were being represented as illegitimate and as diminishing the royal right. This charge came from Earl Traquair. They said that, with the king's permission, they had now been sent and were ready to set out the justice of their demands and to refute the objections and calumnies. They therefore asked the most serene king that they might be allowed to vindicate the innocence of the estates before him, in the presence of the senators of both kingdoms. They handed the king a letter from the recent national synod, in which, after expressing the warmest thanks to the king, they asked for his sanction of the synod's decrees. The king replied that all their demands should be delivered in writing, and that he would make known through Earl Traquair what his will was. It seemed an ominous sign to many that the most serene king was unwilling to use any other go-between or interpreter than Traquair, whose services had so far been unwelcome and unlucky for the covenanters. But these difficulties were now to be ignored and passed over. They quickly drew up supplicatory letters, of almost the same tenor as their first speech, and also asked that Earl Traquair's report on the acts of parliament be given to them in the same words in which it had been expressed in the royal council, so that they could answer each point more conveniently, and so that the most serene king and everyone else, who had been misled by the charm of that false speech, might be more fully satisfied. At the king's command they sealed these letters individually with their signatures, asking that the same be done by Traquair when he reported the royal reply.

units.la: Significatum fuit legatis regem velle ut die sequenti, qui fuit 3. Martii, coram deputatis ex suo senatu comparerent. verum cum expressis mandatis vetarentur, ne senatum ipsum vel quoslibet deputatos judices admitterent; & compertum etiam haberent, serenissf. regem, cui soli rationem actionum parlamenti reddere possent, ad aulam Hamptonianam eo die profecturum; per Marchionem Hammiltonium regi significant, sibi non integrum esse quempiam in hac causa judicem agnoscere præter solum regem; ideoque enixe se rogare ut rex ipse adesse dignaretur; quod factum fuit. Itaque ad regem præsentibus illis deputatis admissi, primum viva voce, dein scripto declarant, Quanto in honore ordines regni Scotiæ habeant supremam summi magistratus authoritatem, quibusque arctissimis vinculis ad eandem defendendam obligarentur: quam chara ipsis esset religionis suæ puritas & patriæ libertas, quas licet subvertere nonnulli niterentur, quæsita specie promovendi prærogativam regiam, sed revera causam tantum suam agentes; sperare tamen se serenissf. regem pro prudentia sua non permissurum, ut viperae iste [?] & pestes regum & regnorum (prout beatæ memoriæ Rex Iacobus indigitare solebat) umbra authoritatis regiæ abutantur ad impios suos fines consequendos. Quod si peccata (inquiunt) nostra in Deum, gravem hanc pœnam in nos provocaverint (quod absit) cogemur bonæ causæ & Deo constanter niti. Dein priusquam ad specialem causæ vindicationem progrederentur, Rogarunt senatores Anglos præsentes, ut æquis auribus dicenda acciperent, neque protinus damnarent, si quæ fortasse proferantur legibus aut praxi regni Angliæ per omnia non conformia: Nam sui muneris esse, demonstrare actiones comitiorum regni Scotiæ legitimas esse; non ex aliarum nationum institutis, sed ex præscripto domesticarum legum & consuetudinum regni Scotiæ, ex quibus solis earum æquitas aut iniquitas venit nunc dijudicanda: deinde diligenter distinguendum esse inter actiones ordinum regni in comitiis, quibus legum figendarum & refigendarum potestas sine controversia competit: & actiones privatorum civium, qui læsæ majestatis rei futuri sint, si leges latas propria & privata sua authoritate refixerint. Denique si omnibus objectionibus nunc plene non satisfiat; in causa esse adversariorum astutiam, qui licet actiones parlamenti nunc sugillent, summa tamen diligentia laborarūt, ut objectiones omnes & oppositæ difficultates quas nunc ex improviso exprument, ab ordinibus regni supprimerentur; consulto etiam suppressa [?] fuisse publica comitiorum registra, licet ad ea semper appellatum fuisset, uti & adhuc ad eadem constanter appellamus.
units.tr: The legates were told that the king wished them to appear the following day, which was 3 March, before deputies from his council. But since they had express instructions not to admit the council itself or any deputed judges, and since they also knew that the most serene king, to whom alone they could give an account of the acts of parliament, would set out that day for the court at Hampton, they informed the king through the Marquis of Hamilton that it was not right for them to recognise anyone as judge in this cause except the king alone. They therefore earnestly asked that the king himself would deign to be present, and this was done. Accordingly, admitted to the king's presence with those deputies, they declared first by word of mouth and then in writing how highly the estates of the kingdom of Scotland regarded the supreme authority of the highest magistrate, and by what very close bonds they were obliged to defend it; how dear to them was the purity of their religion and the liberty of their country; and that although some men strove to subvert these under the pretext of promoting the royal prerogative, they were in truth pursuing only their own cause. Yet they hoped that the most serene king, in his wisdom, would not permit those vipers and pests of kings and kingdoms (as the late King James of blessed memory used to call them) to abuse the shadow of royal authority to achieve their impious ends. "If our sins against God," they said, "should provoke this heavy punishment upon us (which God forbid), we shall be compelled to rest constantly on the good cause and on God." Then, before proceeding to the particular defence of the cause, they asked the English senators present to hear what was to be said with fair ears, and not to condemn at once if something was perhaps put forward that did not wholly conform to the laws or practice of the kingdom of England. For it was their duty to show that the acts of the Scottish estates were lawful, not by the institutions of other nations, but by the prescription of the domestic laws and customs of the kingdom of Scotland, from which alone their fairness or unfairness was now to be judged. Next, they said, a careful distinction must be made between the acts of the estates of the kingdom in parliament, to which the power of enacting and repealing laws undoubtedly belongs, and the acts of private citizens, who would be guilty of treason if they repealed laws passed by their own private authority. Finally, if all the objections were not now fully answered, the cause lay in the cunning of the adversaries, who, although they now find fault with the acts of parliament, took the greatest pains that all the objections and difficulties which they now bring up unexpectedly should be suppressed by the estates of the kingdom. It was also deliberately suppressed that the public registers of parliament were kept back, although appeal had always been made to them, and still is constantly made to them.

units.la: Post ad specialia postulatorum capita descendunt, inter quæ præcipue illud de exclusione clericorum à comitiis regni, & jure suffragii: nullum inde oriri posse damnum ecclesiæ, cum in synodo, appro-bante deputato regio, unanimi omnium suffragio, renunciatum fit privilegiis omnibus ecclesiæ in hunc finem antehac concessis; ac declaratum pariter fit, jus illud suffragii in comitiis pro clero repugnare ecclesiæ naturæ, quæ spiritualis est, & damnum insigne eidem semper protulisse; ecclesiæ itaque sano judicio volenti se a jure suffragii in comitiis excluđi, nullam hic fieri injuriam: Sic neque regno ulla fiet injuria clericorum seu ecclesiæ exclusione, cum hoc omnium regni subditorum flagrans votum sit, ut synodi decreta, in quæ consentiente deputato regio jurarunt, in comitiis sancirentur. Sed nullum etiam potestati regiæ inde accrescere potest detrimentum; nam cum reges Dei in terris deputati ad tuendam religionem & justitiam, instar stellarum coruscantium sint, quibus a Deo concessus est splendor in orbis commodum, bonorum cordibus hoc infixum semper erit, ut populi sibi subditi commoda pro suis habeant, ac populi salutem supremam legem sibi statuant, uti sereniss. rex sæpius professus est, & ut omnibus idem constaret, monetæ inscribi voluit vere regium illud & aureum lemma, præsum ut prosim. Prærogativa etiam regia legibus regni Scotiæ definitur. Jus illud quod regi, quatenus regi competit in omnium ordinum cujuscunque conditionis & vocationis subditos. Non vere speciale interesse, (ut loquuntur) in unum ordinem magis quam in alium: quæ prærogative[?] regibus competebat, cum nunquam essent in Scotia Episcopi, & non ita pridem jus illud prærogative possedit rex, cum objuratus esset episcopatus. Atque cum nullus alius ordinum regni scopus fit, quam ut religionem & pacem secundum fundamentales regni leges, & articulos pacificationis stabiliant, cumque omnium judicio, parlamentum liberum fit unicum saluberrimum & efficacissimum remedium curandis præteritis & præsentibus malis, resarciendæ concordiæ, ac paci stabiliendæ: rogant enixe omnes subditi, uti serenissi.[?] rex dignaretur imperare progressum & continuationem comitiorum, ut articuli hactenus agitati, diligenter excussi ac formati definiantur: Interim si scrupulus hæreat, paratos nos (inquiunt) profitemur ad eundem eximendum, modo scripto exhibeatur. Multa tum a variis objecta fuerunt, quibus plene responderunt legati, quibus ad hospi-tia reversis responsum affertur, ut post reditum sere-nissi. regis ab aula Hamptoniana mandata sua ostēn-derent.
units.tr: Afterwards they came down to the particular heads of their demands, among which especially that concerning the exclusion of the clergy from the parliament of the kingdom and from the right of voting. No harm to the Church could arise from this, since in the synod, with the royal deputy approving, it was unanimously renounced by all, with a vote of all, that all privileges of the Church formerly granted for this purpose had been surrendered; and it was likewise declared that this right of voting in parliament for the clergy was contrary to the nature of the Church, which is spiritual, and had always brought remarkable harm to it. So the Church, by sound judgement, willing to exclude itself from the right of voting in parliament, suffers no wrong here. Thus the kingdom will also suffer no wrong from the exclusion of the clergy or of the Church, since this is the ardent wish of all the subjects of the kingdom, that the decrees of the synod, which they swore to with the royal deputy's consent, be ratified in parliament. But nor can any loss to the royal power arise from this. For since kings, deputed by God on earth to uphold religion and justice, are like shining stars, to which God has granted splendour for the benefit of the world, it will always be fixed in the hearts of good kings that they should regard the welfare of their subject peoples as their own, and make the safety of the people their supreme law. As the most serene king has often professed, and so that this might be known to all, he wished that truly royal and golden motto, praesum ut prosim, to be inscribed on the coinage. The royal prerogative is also defined by the laws of the kingdom of Scotland: that right which belongs to the king, insofar as he is king, over the subjects of all estates of whatever condition and calling. It is not, as they say, a special interest in one estate more than another. Such a prerogative belonged to kings when there had never been bishops in Scotland, and the king did not long ago hold that prerogative right, since episcopacy had been abjured. And since the sole aim of the estates of the kingdom is to establish religion and peace according to the fundamental laws of the kingdom and the articles of pacification, and since in the judgement of all a free parliament is the one most wholesome and most effective remedy for curing past and present evils, for repairing concord and establishing peace, all the subjects earnestly ask that the most serene king deign to command the continuation and progress of the parliament, so that the articles hitherto debated may be carefully examined, formed and settled. Meanwhile, they declare, if any doubt remains, they are ready to remove it, provided it is set out in writing. Many objections were then raised by various persons, to all of which the legates fully replied. They returned to their lodgings, where it was reported to them that they should show their instructions after the return of the most serene king from the court at Hampton.

units.la: Itaque rege reverso ad palatium Whitehall, a legatis, 9. Martii comparentibus, exhibita fuerant mandata; & objectum fuit, non esse valida & sufficientia, nec subscripta ab iis quorum intererat[?]. Responderunt legati: mandata sua plena esse, secundum tenorem rescripti regii 11. Decemb. 1639. quo permiserat ordinibus, ut quot vellent ad se mitterent, ad demonstrandas postulatorum rationes; & primum subscripta fuisse a compluribus ex singulis regni ordinibus, tam aliorum quam suo nomine, dein obsignata & amplificata, 20. Januarii, anni præsentis, a parlamenti deputatis. Idem denuo agitatum fuit, 12 Martii, legatis de sententia sua nihil remittentibus; cumque quæsitum fuisset, quo jure deputati isti gauderent potestate obsignandi & concipiendi mandata, omnium regni ordinum nomine dimisso nunc parlamento; Responderunt legati, potestatem hanc illis concessam fuisse in plenis comitiis: in cujus subsidium cum scriptum quoddam authenticum citarent; serenissi. rex jussit totum prælegi, quia quædam continere videbatur, quibus dicebat jus suum regium summopere lædi; erat vero scriptum illud Declaratio ordinum regni contra parlamenti prorogationem sola authoritate regia: multâ voce viva hinc & inde in opinionum confirmationem & refutationem proferebantur; & statutum, ut Martii 16. regi demonstrarent rationes & fundamenta quorundam postulatorum, à comite Traquario descriptorum.
units.tr: So when the king had returned to the palace of Whitehall, the instructions were shown by the legates, who appeared on 9 March; and it was objected that they were neither valid nor sufficient, nor signed by those whose concern it was. The legates replied that their instructions were complete, according to the tenor of the royal rescript of 11 December 1639, which had permitted the estates to send as many as they wished to set out the grounds of their demands; and that they had first been signed by many from each of the estates of the kingdom, both in their own names and in the names of others, and afterwards sealed and enlarged on 20 January of this present year by the deputies of parliament. The same matter was debated again on 12 March, the legates not yielding a jot of their view. And when it was asked by what right those deputies had the power to seal and draw up instructions in the name of all the estates of the kingdom, now that parliament had been dismissed, the legates replied that this power had been granted to them in full parliament. In support of this, when they cited a certain authentic document, the most serene king ordered the whole of it to be read aloud, because it seemed to contain certain things by which, he said, his royal right was greatly injured. This document was the Declaration of the estates of the kingdom against the prorogation of parliament by royal authority alone. Much was said aloud on both sides, in confirmation and refutation of opinions. And it was resolved that on 16 March they should show the king the reasons and grounds for certain of the demands, which had been drawn up by Earl Traquair.

units.la: Quibus scripto responderunt fusè, solutis omnibus contrariis objectionibus: De prorogatione parlamenti, per regem solum exclusis regni ordinibus in comitiis, dixerunt, novum prorsus esse, neque ostendi posse ullum Regum in regno Scotiæ fuisse, qui potestatem illam sibi unquam vendicasset, aut exercuisset, quin contra præter antiqua, recentia esse exempla, (& citabatur parlamentum anni 1604, prorogatum à rege cum expresso ordinum consensu) quibus consensus ordinum regni necessario astruitur: Quod si quis objiciat, in prorogatione quorundam comitiorum hanc formulam inveniri, De mandato domini regis; nullam vero fieri ordinum regni mentionem Responderunt deputati: licet statutum aliquod à rege denominationem habeat, ut comitiorum capite, non tamen inde inferri posse, exclusum fuisse ordinum consensum: nam & exstant statuta quædam in quibus ordinum regni solummodo mentio facta sit; puerile esse si quis inferat, regem exclusum fuisse: multa in hanc sententiam nervose pressa[?] fuerunt, quorum summa capita, in ipsa ordinum regni declaratione, expressa sunt, eodem etiam scripto demonstrarunt necessitatem & æquitatem quorundam capitum, quæ à Comite Traquario regis mandato in quæstionem vocata fuerunt, videl. de definienda potestate dominorum ad articulos: de novis vectigalibus non imponendis sine consensu ordinum regni: de constituendo justo & certo valore monetæ: de custodia arcium munitarum: & de explicatione statuti de camera rationum regia. Quod scriptum coram rege præle-ctum. ctum fuit, & ad objectas difficultates viva voce responsum à legatis ; qui tum etiam questi sunt Comitem Traquarium deputatum regium in comitiis renuisse sancire decretum illud nuperæ synodi, de removendo ex ecclesia episcopatu & cæt. 17. Augusti mensis, suo ipsius assensu condito, quod bis obfignafset cum aliis senatoribus simpliciter fine ulla limitatione; rogaruntque ferenifs. regem ut cum benigno responso, redeundi licentiam sibi concedere dignaretur, ac comitiorum interruptorum progressum quamprimum imperare; cum ex longiori mora periculum non leve creari posset.
units.tr: They answered all the contrary objections at length in writing. On the prorogation of parliament by the king alone, with the estates of the realm excluded from the assembly, they said that this was entirely new, and that it could not be shown that any king of Scotland had ever claimed or exercised such a power. On the contrary, there were ancient and recent precedents, and they cited the parliament of 1604, which the king prorogued with the express consent of the estates. This consent of the estates of the realm is, they said, necessarily established by such precedents. If anyone objected that the formula "By command of the lord king" is found in the prorogation of certain assemblies, with no mention of the estates of the realm, the deputies replied that although some statute bears a title from the king, as in the heading of the assemblies, it cannot be inferred from this that the consent of the estates was excluded. For there are also statutes in which only the estates of the realm are mentioned, and it would be childish to infer that the king had been excluded. Many points to this effect were pressed forcefully, and their main heads are set out in the declaration of the estates of the realm itself. In the same paper they demonstrated the necessity and fairness of certain articles which Earl Traquair, by the king's command, had called into question: defining the power of the lords over the articles; not imposing new taxes without the consent of the estates of the realm; fixing a just and certain value for the coinage; the custody of fortified places; and the explanation of the statute concerning the royal exchequer. This paper was read before the king, and the envoys answered the difficulties raised by word of mouth. They also complained that Earl Traquair, the royal commissioner in parliament, had refused to ratify the decree of the recent synod concerning the removal of bishops from the Church, of 17 August, although he had himself agreed to it, having signed it twice with the other senators simply and without any limitation. They begged the most serene king, with a gracious reply, to grant them leave to return home, and to order the interrupted assembly to resume as soon as possible, since a long delay could create serious danger.

units.la: Verum nihil aliud tum responsum fuit, quam comparendum illis esse denuo, ad 23 Martii, ut reliquorum etiam postulatorum rationes ostenderent; Quod præstituta hora, prolixiori scripto præstiterunt: quumque (inquiebant) sinceris & apertis animis pro ratione muneris nobis impositi sinceram explicaverimus intentionem fidelium majestatis tuæ subditorum in æquis & necessariis illis postulatis, quorum sanctionem in comitiis ex pacificationis præscripta flagitent, diesque nostro reditui præfinitus jam fere transierit, rogamus ut redintegratione parlamenti via obstruatur ingentibus ex mora nascituris periculis, nobisque munere nostro perfunctis, bona cum Majeft. tuæ venia liceat ad nostros redire, cum gratiffimo benigni tui responsi nuncio. Respondit rex, fe tempore sibi maxime opportuno rationes ab iis prolatas perpensurum, ac prout rebus suis commodum judicabit, quid suæ voluntatis effet, declaratum: verum nullum ad reditum diem posse adhuc statuere. Neq;postea publice auditi:sed primum retenti, dein tres in custodiam judicum Londinenfium traditi; Laudonius vero turri Londinenfi commissus fuit, & quid regiæ voluntatis effet, ex declaratione regia typis excusa primum innotuit, quaScoti conquisitis undique causis violatæ pacis anno superiori initæ accusantur, postulata ordinum regni læsæ majestatis regiæ damnantur, intentio reducendi rebelles Scotos ad debitam obedientiam per vim armatam declaratur ; Hibernorum alacritas se & sua omnia ad belli hujus profecutionem offerentium in exemplum Anglis proponitur. Sed de his suo loco. Atque hic exitus fuit legationis ex Scoria ad regem, multum certe contra Scotorum spem.
units.tr: Nothing else was answered at that time, except that they were to appear again on 23 March, so that they might also set out the reasons for the remaining demands. At the appointed hour they did so in a longer written paper: "Since," they said, "with sincere and open minds, in keeping with the duty laid upon us, we have explained the sincere intention of your Majesty's loyal subjects regarding those fair and necessary demands, whose sanction they require in parliament under the terms of the pacification, and since the day fixed for our return has almost passed, we beg that the resumption of parliament not be blocked, lest great dangers arise from the delay. And since we have discharged our duty, we ask that, with your Majesty's kind permission, we may be allowed to return to our people with the most welcome news of your gracious answer." The king replied that he would weigh the reasons they had put forward at a time most convenient to himself, and would declare, as he judged fit for his affairs, what his will was; but he could not yet fix any day for their return. Afterwards they were not heard in public. First they were detained, then three of them were handed over into the custody of the judges of London, and Lauderdale was committed to the Tower of London. What the king's will was became known first from a royal declaration printed in type. In it the Scots, having searched out causes everywhere, are accused of violating the peace made the year before; the demands of the estates of the realm are condemned as treason against the royal majesty; and the intention of bringing the rebel Scots back to due obedience by armed force is declared. The eagerness of the Irish, who offered themselves and all they had to the prosecution of this war, is held up to the English as an example. But of these things in their place. Such was the outcome of the embassy from Scotland to the king, certainly far contrary to the hopes of the Scots.

units.la: Dum hæc interim in aula agitarentur, & omnium opinione satis constaret nihil aliud quam bellum contra Scotos parari: ut adhuc magis irritarentur centum præsidiarii Angli cum multo apparatu bellico & commeatu Letham, portum Edinburgenum mittuntur, cum mandato regio ad præfectum urbis, ut in arcem Edinburgenam deduceret, hactenus duplo aut triplo majori militum numero instructam, quam qui ad defensionem sufficeret, Sed cum specimine singularis suæ obedientiæ adversariorum suorum ora occludi posse sperarent Scoti, (quorum corda usque adeo obduruisse contra Regem sereniff.in aula mentiebantur, ut nullis ejus mandatis parere vellent) præsidiarios illos Anglos in arcem admittunt simul cum apparatu bellico & impedimentis, & hoc experimento comprobatum fecerunt, quanta obedientia, etiam supra omne illud quod leges unquam à quopiam exigerent, mandata sui regis quantumvis gravia prosequerentur, suæque saluti præferrent. Sed ne in exemplum postea traheretur, declararunt, directe adversari legibus regni, ut arcium, quæ regni claves sunt, custodia, aliis quam Scotis committeretur ; præsertim vero Edinburgena in qua regni insignia, corona videl. sceptrum, & gladius, simul cum publicis registris custodiuntur. Violationem hanc legum fundamentalium & privilegiorum regni, etiam agnoscente beatæ memoriæ Iacobo 6. in oratione ad parlamentum Angliæ convocatum anno 1607; si non posse licet regem, exterorum præsidia Scotis imponere, qualia Hispanis, Siculis & Neapolitanis, nisi fundamentales regni leges & privilegia violaret, ac liberum & independens regnum in provinciam subastam[?] redigeret.
units.tr: While these matters were being debated at court, and it was generally agreed that nothing else was being prepared but war against the Scots, a hundred English garrison soldiers, with a large military equipment and supplies, were sent to Leith, the port of Edinburgh, to irritate them further. They carried a royal command to the governor of the city to take them into Edinburgh Castle, which until then had been garrisoned by two or three times more soldiers than were enough for its defence. But the Scots hoped that by showing a singular example of their obedience they could silence their adversaries, whose hearts, the lying tales at court said, had become so hardened against the most serene king that they would obey none of his commands. So they admitted those English garrison soldiers into the castle, together with the military equipment and baggage. By this experiment they proved how great their obedience was, beyond anything the laws had ever required of anyone: they followed their king's commands, however burdensome, and preferred them to their own safety. But lest this be drawn into a precedent afterwards, they declared that it was directly contrary to the laws of the realm for the custody of the fortresses, which are the keys of the realm, to be committed to anyone other than Scots, especially at Edinburgh, where the insignia of the realm, namely the crown, sceptre and sword, are kept together with the public records. They also cited the violation of the fundamental laws and privileges of the realm, which King James VI of blessed memory acknowledged in his speech to the parliament of England summoned in 1607. He said that the king may not impose foreign garrisons on the Scots, such as the Spanish, Sicilians and Neapolitans have, unless he violates the fundamental laws and privileges of the realm and reduces a free and independent kingdom to a subjugated province.

units.la: Admirabantur certe complures gentem Scoticam libertatis suæ tenacissimam tam facilem fuisse ad jugum hoc recipiendum, queritabatur etiam vulgus Edinburgenum damna sua futura prospiciens, ab arce omnibus necessariis abunde munita, & bellicis instrumentis ac machinis fundendis granatis, ad urbis conflagrationem instructa: quare cives in tutelam urbis suæ milites conscribunt: ac ut arcis aditum & exitum diligentius observarent, non longe ab exitimo[?] arcis munimento casam[?] militarem exstruunt; cumque arcis præfectus extrema queque indies urbi minitaretur, Deputatorum parlamenti & senatus urbani maturo consilio arctiori obsidione cincta fuit; præsertim cum certissimis nuncis subinde ex Anglia relatum esset, regem ingentes exercitus conscribere, iisdemque summo cum imperio præfecisse Northumbriæ Comitem: & primo vere in Scotiam moturum. Sæviebat interim arcis præfectus, & novo hoc apparatus bellici & præsidiarium supplemento audacior factus, casam[?] illam militarem statim demoliri, urbanos milites ab arcis aditu facessere jubet, quibus mandatis nisi confestim parerent, extremam vastitatem per granatas urbi interminatur: Cumque ad eum à civibus missi essent comes Southefkius cum Ludovico Stuarto Equite, causarum[?] in suprema curia advocato magni nominis, ut eum demulcerent, nihil aliud obtinere potuerunt quam vix horulæ unius moram, intra quam nisi cives mandata capesserent, hostilia omnia experirentur. Quod cum urbis præfecto astantibus civibus relatum esset, ac qui fœderatorum causæ non faverent, vasa colligerent & fugam ex urbe meditarentur; promiscuum vulgus minis istis præfecti arcis summopere irritatum, non solum impedivit superiorum fugam, verumetiam comitem Southeskium cum Ludovico Stuarto & aliis causæ suæ parum æquis comprehendit, & in primariorum civium ædibus custodit, putabat quippe eorum in urbe præsentia & periculo, quum arcis gubernatori grati essent, minarum asperitatem leniendam aut saltem differendam; omnemq; moram in lucro deputabat. Magistratus tamen urbanus simul cum nobilibus fœderatis, qui Edinburgi hærebant, temerarium illud promiscuæ plebis facinus indigne tulerunt, ac satis ostenderunt, se invitis & minime conscis illud commissu; quod nobilis ille senator regius simul cum aliis à plebe retentis, ad regem perscriptis literis testati sunt, ac enixe obsecrati fuerunt, ne vulgi imprudentia magistratui aut nobilibus vitio verteretur, cum per eos steterit, quominus in gravius malum tumultus ille non eruperit. Hæc tamen excusatio surdis[?] auribus in aula excepta fuit; nam inter alia violatæ pacis argumenta, ob quæ extremæ ruinæ devoventur Scoti, & hoc magno verborum apparatu recensetur: etenim vel minutissima avide arripiebant Scotorum hostes, quibus regem sereniss. irritari, & Anglos in eorum perniciem animari posse putabant.
units.tr: Many were indeed amazed that the Scottish nation, most tenacious of its liberty, had been so easily brought to accept this yoke. The common people of Edinburgh also complained, foreseeing their own losses, since the castle was abundantly stocked with everything necessary, and equipped with weapons and engines for hurling grenades, so that the city could be set on fire. Therefore the citizens enlisted soldiers to guard their city, and in order to watch the entrance and exit of the castle more carefully, they built a military hut not far from the outer fortification of the castle. Since the governor of the castle threatened the city with extreme measures daily, the deputies of parliament and the city senate, by mature counsel, had the city surrounded by a closer siege. This was especially so because certain messengers repeatedly reported from England that the king was raising huge armies, had placed the Earl of Northumberland in supreme command of them, and would move into Scotland at the first sign of spring. Meanwhile the governor of the castle raged, and made bolder by this new military equipment and the addition of garrison soldiers, he at once ordered the hut to be pulled down and the citizen soldiers to withdraw from the castle entrance. Unless they obeyed these orders at once, he threatened the city with utter devastation by grenades. When the citizens sent the Earl of Southesk, with Ludovic Stuart, a knight and advocate of great name in the supreme court, to soothe him, they could obtain nothing more than a delay of barely one hour. Within that hour, unless the citizens carried out his orders, he would try every hostile measure. When this was reported to the city governor, while citizens stood by, and those who did not favour the cause of the Covenanters were packing their goods and planning flight from the city, the common crowd was greatly provoked by the governor's threats. They not only prevented the flight of the leading men, but also seized the Earl of Southesk, Ludovic Stuart and others unfavourable to their cause, and kept them under guard in the houses of leading citizens. For the governor thought that their presence and danger in the city, since they were pleasing to him, would soften or at least postpone the harshness of his threats, and he counted all delay as gain. Yet the city magistrates, together with the confederate nobles who stayed in Edinburgh, took this rash deed of the mixed crowd very ill, and made it sufficiently clear that it had been done against their will and without their knowledge. This noble royal senator, together with the others held by the people, testified in letters written to the king, and earnestly begged that the imprudence of the common people not be imputed to the magistrates or nobles, since it was through their efforts that the tumult had not broken out into a graver evil. This excuse, however, fell on deaf ears at court. For among the other proofs of the violated peace, on account of which the Scots are doomed to utter ruin, this too is recounted with a great show of words. The enemies of the Scots eagerly seized even the smallest things, by which they thought the most serene king could be provoked and the English encouraged to their destruction.

units.la: Inter quos Deputatus Hiberniæ palmam aliis præripere sedulo satagebat, & cum provincialibus suis usque adeo prævaluit, ut in parlamento regni illius ingens pecuniæ summa regi in bellum hoc concederetur, ac plurimi omnia sua ad Scotos rebelles in ordinem redigendos offerrent. Lentius tamen res procedebant in Anglia, ubi omnium ordinum complures, anni superioris exemplo satis edocti, quam facile esset Scotos absentes traducere, & convitiorum plaustris apud imperitiores onerare, qui præsentes suam causæque innocentiam & æquitatem luculenter asseruissent: neque ignari fuerunt quorum artibus violenta hæc consilia contra Scotos primum suggesta ac denuo promota essent: necdum exciderant singularia illa fidelitatis documenta à Scotis exhibita, dum arces omnes munitas regi tradidissent, exercitusque dimissent, neque alia postulassent, quam ea sine quibus religio & privilegia sarta tecta esse nequiverant: quare non movendum temere contra vicinos tam arctis vinculis sibi conjunctos putabant, & ad parlamentum a rege sereniss. indictum, & Aprili mense cogendum oculi omnium fuere conversi.
units.tr: Among these, the Deputy of Ireland eagerly strove to snatch the palm from the others, and with his provincials he prevailed so far that a huge sum of money was granted to the king for this war in the parliament of that kingdom, and very many offered all their goods to bring the rebel Scots to order. Matters moved more slowly in England, where many of every rank, sufficiently taught by the example of the previous year how easily the absent Scots could be slandered and loaded with abuse before the ignorant, were wary. They had also clearly asserted their own innocence and the justice of their cause when present. Nor were they unaware by whose arts these violent counsels against the Scots had first been suggested and then pressed again. Nor had those remarkable proofs of loyalty given by the Scots faded from memory: they had handed over all fortified places to the king and disbanded their armies, and asked for nothing except what without which religion and privileges could not be kept safe. Therefore they thought one should not rashly move against neighbours so closely bound to them by strong ties, and the eyes of all turned to the parliament summoned by the most serene king, to be convened in April.

units.la: Quod cum animadverterent Scotorum hostes, ut omnem ad pacem viam penitus obstruerent, regi sereniss. authores fuerunt, ut Scotorum legatos, licet regiis literis, & salvo conductu munitos, in custodiam mandaret; & Laudonium in turri Londinensi arctissime custodiri juberet: prætextus fuit epistola quædam à Scotis fœderatis ad regem Galliæ perscripta; & Laudonii chirographo obsignata: qua qui in Scotos iniquiori animo ferebantur, exquisita verborum pompa colligebant, regique sereniss. persuadebant, Scotos regis sui pertæsos confugere ad Gallum, Regem externum, & pontificiæ religionis, ejusque auxilia militaria in Britanniam advocare: & jam satis detecta esse apertæ rebellionis consilia, quæ religionis velo studiose hactenus obduxissent. Scoti vero contra demonstrabant, nullis fidiculis ex ulla epistolæ ejus literula, etiam prout typis in Anglia excusa fuit, consequentias has colligi posse; etenim, uti in primimo[?] us narratione supra deducitur, cum Scoti, anno 1639, mense Majo, undique certiores fierent, apud omnes exteros causam suam odiosissime traduci, & fastiditi monarchici regiminis accusari; ac verendum esset ne vicini calumniis seducti operam suam contra eos conferrent; visum tunc Scotis fuit, vicinos reges & Respub. certiores facere, quis esset verus controversiæ status, & quam longe abessent ab impietate istâ impudenter iis ascripta; simulque enixè rogare, ut operam suam apud regem serenis. interponerent, qua legitimis & pacificis consiliis, sine Christiani sanguinis effusione, motus exortus componeretur: Ac inter omnes primus occurrebat Galliarum rex, propter antiquissimum illud inter duas gentes fœdus: ad quem literas mittendas judicarunt, mandata etiam conceperunt, secundum quæ literæ illæ essent formandæ, ita ut si quidpiam obscuritatis occurrat in literis, ex adjunctis mandatis interpretandum esset: Nec diffitentur Scoti a quodam perscriptam fuisse epistolam illam tantopere exagitatam: sed ipsius formam sibi non placuisse, ideoque rejectam & repudiatam ab omnibus fuisse, neque in epistolæ formam involutam, signatam, superscriptam, aut datum additum suisse; neque ad eam perfectionem, quamdiu penes Scotos fuit, unquam pervenisse, ut dignam judicaverint quæ mitteretur, licet nunc ἐπιγραφὴ[?], a sycophanta maligno addita sit, & dati absentia in Scotorum præjudicium detorqueatur, quasi post initam superioris anni pacem conscripta fuisset, cum tamen in ipso primorum motuum fervore conscripta sit; & haud satis æquum esse dicunt, ut quæ legibus pacis & ἀμνηστία[?] sepulta essent, nunc in scenam adducantur; & vel inde satis constare prudentioribus factionis studio non occæcatis, quæri ex omnibus angulis renovandi funesti belli occasiones; & veris deficientibus excogitari alias. Duo porro sunt quæ exagitantur in illa epistola: quod superscriptio fit ad Regem; qua superscriptione subditi tantum ad regem suum utuntur: & quod in ipsa epistola mentio facta sit auxilii, quod a rege Gallico petitur. Ad superscriptionem respondent fictam eam esse, & licet (inquiunt) vera esset; quid inde colligi posset? cum titulus sit regibus omnibus communis; si Galli aut Belgæ eo titulo sereniss. Britanniæ regem compellaverint, quam vel pueris ridiculum esset eosdem arcessere fastiditi domestici regiminis: & nunc primum audiri folæcismum aulicum funestis belli calamitatibus expiandum esse: Ad alterum respondent, mentionem quidem factam auxilii a Gallo petiti: sed mandata adjuncta exponere, quod auxilii genus intelligatur, mediationis scil: & intercessionis; & quod si auxilium per pecunias subministratas; an[?] non æque licitum Scotis se defendentibus, a Gallis auxilii illud genus mutuari, quam adversæ factioni ad Scotos immerito oppugnandos ab Hispanis? Deniq; quid si militum subsidia intelligantur, quis nobis (inquiunt) vitio vertet; si undique pressi Dei & hominum auxilia implorēmus[?] in nostram defensionem? Vicini auxilio sic solent esse vicinis, sine ulla juris acquisitione in alios: advocatione Anglorum ut auxilio essent protestantibus Gallis & Belgis, tum patrum tum recenti nostra memoria; & Scotis olim, gentibus illis pressis nunquam (inquiunt) in mentem venerat magistratuum suorum imperium legitimum excutere, & auxiliatoribus colla subdere: Et concedatur tam atrox illud crimen esse, quam calumniantur adversarii, qua juris specie animadverti poterit in Laudonium legatum gentis Scoticæ seu internuncium, regis sereniff. salvo conducto munitum, ob crimen ante susceptam legationem ab eo tum privato extra Angliam in Scotia commissum: cum gentium jure legationis jus sacrum sit, & ut Cicero inquit, divino humanoque vallatum præsidio, cujus tam sanctum & venerabile nomen esse debet, ut inter hostium tela incolume versetur. Porrò licet gentium jure inviolata securitas legatis non esset praestanda, recepta tamen praxis continua inter duo regna Scotiæ & Angliæ, post unionem 1603 factam, suaderet, Laudonum, si quid in Scotiâ criminis commiserit, non puniendum esse eo nomine in Angliâ, verum in Scotiam remittendum, & ab ordinariis judicibus ibi legitime judicandum, &c. Hæc & alia hujus generis complura ad vindicandam suam innocentiam à Scotis relata fuerunt in libellis typis excusis: Inter quos unus est, titulo Remonstrantiæ directæ à conventu Ordinum regni Scotiæ, qui tum frequentes cogebantur, ad parlamentum regni Angliæ apertum 15 April. anni hujus 1640, in quo statum causæ omnium oculis aperte subjiciunt, & motuum horum causam in Cantuariensem Archiepiscopum & Deputatum Hibernia conjiciunt, qui dissensionum authores sunt inter Clementiss:[?] Regem & fideles subditos, ut dignitatem (inquiunt) malè partam, licet cum Regis regnorumque ruinâ, tueantur, &c. De verbo ferè in verbum translatum subjunximus.
units.tr: When the enemies of the Scots noticed this, in order to block every path to peace, they urged the most serene king to commit the Scottish envoys to custody, although they were furnished with royal letters and a safe-conduct, and to order Lauderdale to be kept under the closest guard in the Tower of London. The pretext was a certain letter written by the confederate Scots to the King of France, and sealed with Lauderdale's handwriting. Those who were more hostile to the Scots gathered from it, with an elaborate display of words, and persuaded the most serene king that the Scots, weary of their own king, were fleeing to the French king, a foreign ruler of the Papist religion, and calling his military aid into Britain; and that the plans of open rebellion, which they had hitherto carefully hidden behind the veil of religion, were now sufficiently revealed. The Scots, however, argued to the contrary that no such inferences could be drawn from any single line of that letter, even as it was printed in England. For, as is set out above in the first narrative, when in May 1639 the Scots were informed from every side that their cause was being most odiously represented to all foreigners and that they were accused of despising monarchical government, and when it was to be feared that the neighbours, misled by calumnies, would lend their efforts against them, it then seemed good to the Scots to inform the neighbouring kings and republics what the true state of the dispute was and how far they were from the impiety shamelessly ascribed to them; and at the same time to earnestly ask that they would interpose their good offices with the most serene king, so that the stirred-up movement might be settled by lawful and peaceful counsels, without the shedding of Christian blood. Among all, the first to come to mind was the King of France, on account of the very ancient alliance between the two peoples. To him they judged letters should be sent, and they also drew up instructions according to which those letters were to be framed, so that if any obscurity occurred in the letters, it was to be interpreted from the accompanying instructions. Nor do the Scots deny that a certain person drafted that letter which has been so much harassed, but its form did not please them, and so it was rejected and repudiated by all; it was never put into the form of a letter, sealed, superscribed, or dated, nor did it reach such completion, while it remained in the Scots' hands, that they judged it worthy to be sent. Yet now a superscription [ἐπιγραφή] has been added by a malicious informer, and the absence of a date is twisted to the prejudice of the Scots, as if it had been written after the peace of the previous year had been concluded, whereas it was written in the very heat of the first movements. They say it is not at all fair that things which were buried by the laws of peace and by amnesty [ἀμνηστία] should now be dragged onto the stage; and that from this alone it is sufficiently clear to the more prudent, who are not blinded by factional zeal, that on every side occasions are being sought to renew the deadly war, and when true grounds fail, others are contrived. Moreover, there are two points in that letter that are being harassed: that the superscription is "to the King," a form of address which subjects use only toward their own king; and that the letter mentions the aid sought from the French king. To the superscription they reply that it is fictitious, and even if it were true, what could be inferred from it? Since the title is common to all kings; if the French or the Dutch had addressed the most serene King of Britain by that title, it would be ridiculous even to boys to infer from this that they had summoned the king's domestic government into contempt; and that now for the first time a courtly solecism is heard of that must be expiated by the calamities of deadly war. To the second point they reply that the aid sought from France is indeed mentioned, but that the accompanying instructions explain what kind of aid is meant, namely mediation and intercession; and that if the aid is meant to be supplied by money, is it not equally lawful for the Scots, defending themselves, to borrow that kind of aid from the French, as it was for the opposing faction to borrow aid from the Spaniards to attack the Scots undeservedly? Finally, if military subsidies are meant, they ask, who will find fault with us if, pressed on every side, we implore the aid of God and men for our defence? Neighbours are wont to be such help to neighbours, without any acquisition of right over others. The summoning of the English to be an aid to the Protestant French and Dutch, in our fathers' time and in our own recent memory, is an example of this; and the Scots, they say, though oppressed for a long time, never thought of casting off the lawful authority of their magistrates and submitting their necks to those who came to help them. And even granting that so atrocious a crime exists as our adversaries slander, it could be considered by what legal pretext Lauderdale, envoy or messenger of the Scottish people, protected by the most serene king's safe-conduct, was punished in England for a crime committed in Scotland before he undertook the embassy, when he was then a private person outside England. For by the law of nations the right of an embassy is sacred, and, as Cicero says, it is fortified by divine and human protection, and its name ought to be so holy and venerable that it may dwell unharmed amid the weapons of enemies. Moreover, although by the law of nations inviolable safety is not to be guaranteed to envoys, the continuous practice received between the two kingdoms of Scotland and England since the union made in 1603 would suggest that Lauderdale, if he had committed any crime in Scotland, was not to be punished in England on that account, but sent back to Scotland, and there lawfully judged by the ordinary judges, etc. These and many other arguments of this kind, to vindicate their innocence, were set forth by the Scots in printed pamphlets. Among these is one, entitled Remonstrance, addressed by the convention of the estates of the kingdom of Scotland, which at that time was meeting frequently, to the parliament of the kingdom of England, opened on 15 April of this year 1640, in which they openly set the state of the cause before everyone's eyes, and attribute the cause of these movements to the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Deputy of Ireland, who are the authors of the dissensions between the most merciful king and his faithful subjects, as (they say) they defend a dignity badly acquired, even at the cost of the ruin of the king and the kingdoms, etc. We have appended this translated almost word for word.

units.la: Remonstrantia de postremis motibus, directa à Conventu ordinum regni Scotiæ Aprilis 16. 1640. ad Par- lamentum Angliæ.
units.tr: Remonstrance concerning the recent disturbances, addressed by the Convention of the estates of the kingdom of Scotland, 16 April 1640, to the Parliament of England.

units.la: CUm[?] superiorum temporum historias perscrutamur, ut maxima, quæ Deus in hanc insulam quam colimus, beneficia contulerit, inveniamus; secundum religionem Christianam, omnia alia longè superare duorum regnorum sub uno capite felicissimam unionem, non possumus non agnoscere. Multis quidem artibus conati fuerunt olim reges, ut opus hoc effectum darent: sed frustrà impedient aut prævenient mortales consilium Dei, qui singularem hanc fœlicitatem nobis & patribus nostris reservavit; ut unionis hujus spectatores essemus, quæ nulla promissorum violatione, nullo sanguine inchoaretur; sed ut Dei donum nobis contingeret per ordinariam illam juris januam, regibus cum aliis communem, & ab utraque gente ut utilem, lubenter amplexatam. Quo vero successu inchoata & continuata hactenus sit hæc Vnio, satis testantur pax & rerum omnium ubertas, quibus nos gavisi sumus, dum vicinæ omnes in Europa gentes in campum sanguinis & desolationis commutarentur. Quo etiam animo religionis nostræ hostes fuerint in amicam hanc & pacatam nostram Vnionem, & quam obliquis ac æmulis oculis vicina regna nos aspexerint, satis loquuntur annales. In præsentiarum tamen, cum in memoriam revocamus quæ præterita sunt, & in præsentia mala incumbentia & imminentia oculos conjicimus; Ingenue in nostrum reatum & dedecus agnoscimus; neque Scotiam, neque Angliam in hunc usque diem satis intellexisse, aut, prout decuit usam fuisse singulari hoc beneficio: ita ut existimatio nostra apud exteros augeretur, aut domesticæ securitati melius provideretur, aut ut reformatæ aliæ ecclesiæ præsens illud solatium & auxilium, quod a nobis sub cruce gementesexspectarunt,expertæ fuerint. Quin contrà, licet inviti, facti sumus instar fractæ arundinis, & scopuli ad quem impingerent & naufragium paterentur,quotquot receptum apud nos exspectarunt, quo se à fœda, qua jactabantur, tempestate extricarent: Ad nosmet ipsos vero quod attinet, Altera gens in alteram conversa est in flagellum correctionis & zelotypiæ, a paucis quibusdam improbis dissidia ferentibus, regem à suis subditis, & subditos à suo rege abalienantibus,& fratres in se mutuo concitantibus,ut ipsi interim omnes promiscue perderent.
units.tr: When we search through the histories of earlier times to find the greatest benefits God has bestowed on this island which we inhabit, we cannot but acknowledge that, in terms of the Christian religion, the most happy union of the two kingdoms under one head surpasses all the others by far. Kings indeed in former times tried by many arts to bring this work about, but mortals vainly hindered or anticipated the counsel of God, who reserved this singular happiness for us and our fathers: that we should be witnesses of this union, which was begun without violation of promises and without bloodshed, but came to us as a gift of God through that ordinary gate of law, common to kings and others alike, and gladly embraced by each nation as useful. What success this union has had since its beginning and continuance until now, the peace and abundance of all things which we have enjoyed, while all the neighbouring nations of Europe were turned into a field of blood and desolation, bear sufficient witness. With what mind the enemies of our religion have regarded this friendly and peaceful union of ours, and with how sidelong and envious eyes the neighbouring kingdoms have looked upon us, the annals speak plainly enough. At present, however, when we call to mind what is past and cast our eyes on the evils now bearing down upon us and threatening, we frankly acknowledge our own fault and shame: that neither Scotland nor England until this day has understood this singular benefit, or made use of it as it ought to have been used, so that our reputation abroad might have been increased, or our domestic security better provided for, or the other reformed churches might have experienced that present comfort and help which they, groaning under the cross, expected from us. On the contrary, though unwillingly, we have become like a broken reed and a rock on which all who expected a refuge there from the foul tempest in which they were tossed have struck and suffered shipwreck. As far as we ourselves are concerned, one nation has been turned against the other into a scourge of correction and of jealousy, while a few wicked men bring forth dissensions, estranging the king from his subjects and the subjects from their king, and stirring up brothers against one another, so that meanwhile they all perish together indiscriminately.

units.la: Inter omnes vero authores malorum, sub quibus utrumque regnum jampridem gemuit, & nunc aut nunquam (ut videtur) liberandum est, Nulli sunt qui suo merito primas sibi tam vendicant, quam quidam inter vos, qui se Ecclesiasticos vocant, & deserta propria statione, ignari ac infœlices politici evaserunt; qui ecclesiam ejusque dogmata converterunt subditis in servitutem, sibi in licentiam, regi in iniquam usurpationem seu tyrannidem; à quibus diu antehac nobis merito metuendum fuerat vestro exemplo, & quos, in gravi & solenni remonstrantia, ante annos aliquot regi serenissim.[?] exhibitâ à deputatis ad parlamentum vestrum in inferiori domo, (seu ex plebe) designatos, accepimus, præcipua fuisse instrumenta & objecta vestri metus de mutatione religionis & regiminis politici apud vos: An vero sic cohibiti fuerint, suggesta vestra & libelli ab ista factione posthac editi satis testantur: quinquam pertinaciter impiis suis finibus promovendis adhærent, satis loquuntur eorum contra nos conatus, & horrendæ machinationes; obtrudendo nobis libros liturgiæ & Canonum, qui semina pontificiæ superstitionis & tyrannidis continent, quo perspicue demonstrarunt, quam bene de Romana aula meriti sint, utpote quod quantum in se esset procuraverint, ut ecclesia nostra, quæ longissime à Romana secederet, prima rediret, & exemplo aliis ad redeundum esset. Nec obscurum, quantum adhuc Romanensium & omnium regni utriusque hostium causam promovere possint, si truculento bello religionem & utriusque gentis privilegia exponant, tanquam sacrificium ad præsentem suam rabiem sedandam, qua ob spem elusam feruntur, aut ad consulendum ignominiosæ & meritissimæ suæ ruinæ, à qua sibi metuunt.
units.tr: Among all the authors of evils under which both kingdoms have long groaned, and which must now be freed from, if ever (as it seems), there are none who claim the first place for themselves as justly as certain men among you, who call themselves ecclesiastics, and, having deserted their proper station, have turned out to be ignorant and unhappy politicians. They have turned the church and its doctrines into slavery for subjects, into licence for themselves, and into unjust usurpation or tyranny over the king. We had long before this rightly feared them, by your example; and in a grave and solemn remonstrance presented some years ago to our most serene king by the deputies sent to your Parliament in the lower house (that is, from the commons), we learned that these men were the chief instruments and objects of your fear concerning the change of religion and of the political government among you. Whether you have indeed been restrained in this way, your pronouncements and the pamphlets since published by that faction sufficiently testify. Indeed, they cling stubbornly to advancing their impious ends, as their attempts against us and their horrible machinations speak plainly enough, thrusting upon us the books of the liturgy and the canons, which contain the seeds of papist superstition and tyranny. By this they have clearly shown how well they have deserved of the Roman court, since they have done all in their power that our church, which had seceded farthest from Rome, should return first, and be an example to others for returning. Nor is it obscure how much they can still advance the cause of the Papists and of all enemies of both kingdoms, if they expose religion and the privileges of each nation to savage war, as a sacrifice to calm their present rage, with which they are carried away on account of their frustrated hope, or to provide for their own ignominious and well-deserved ruin, which they fear.

units.la: Posteri certè haud facilè credent, (nam & nos qui vidimus, admiramur) qui factum sit, ut subditi in Scotia (cujus unio cum Anglia cognita est plus conducere ad pacem domesticam, & tuendam exi-stimationem[?] apud exteros, quam ullæ affinitates, fœdera, artes, victoriæ à vestris principibus unquam obtentæ) nativum suum principem inter vos hærentem tamdiu obsecrati sint, ut æquo jure secum ageret (quod subditis suis præstare tenetur) & ut dignaretur æquis auribus accipere justas eorum querelas, contra paucorum tyrannidem, religionis & regni statum cuniculis suffodientium, ac illis permitteret, ut suis legibus viverent; neque unquam tamen æqua hæc postulata obtinere potuerint: Multo minus vel conjecturis unquam colligent posteri, qui factum sit, ut unicus præsul regi serenissimo dissuadere potuerit, quod communibus & flagrantissimis votis ab integra hac gente postulatum fuerit, quoveque sin-gulari merito plus gratiæ & fidei apud regem obti-nuerit, quam subditi omnes hujus gentis tam antiquæ, tam fidelis, quæ decus regium in una linea, & propriam libertatem supra omnia Europæ regna diutissime conservavit ac tutata est.
units.tr: Posterity will certainly find it hard to believe (and we who have seen it are astonished) how it came about that the subjects in Scotland (whose union with England is known to contribute more to domestic peace and to the preservation of their reputation abroad than any marriages, treaties, arts or victories ever obtained by your princes), so long as their native prince remained among you, have begged him so earnestly that he would deal with them on equal terms, as he is bound to do toward his subjects, and that he would deign to hear with fair ears their just complaints against the tyranny of a few men who undermine the state of religion and of the kingdom as with mines, and that he would allow them to live under their own laws; and yet they were never able to obtain these fair demands. Much less will posterity ever be able to conjecture how it came about that a single prelate could persuade our most serene king to refuse what was asked by the common and most ardent prayers of this whole nation, and that by his singular merit he obtained more grace and trust with the king than all the subjects of this people, so ancient, so faithful, which has kept the royal honour in one line and has preserved and defended its own liberty for longest of all the kingdoms of Europe.

units.la: Etenim cum in memoriam revocamus, quantam nobis fortitudinem, & animorum constantiam ab horum motuum initio indulserit Deus, ad religionem & privilegia nostra propugnanda: ne in servitutem tam animæ quam corporis præcipites protrude-deremur, à qua nulla fuisset spes nobis & posteris nostris nosmet extricandi, quæque ob arctam vobiscum eodem sub rege unionem, periculosissimæ fuisset consequentiæ vestris privilegiis, cum tempore & locis suis in controversiam vocarentur: Contra vero, quam violentis & inusitatis mediis usi sint nostri adversarii, ne rerum nostrarum certa cognitio ad Anglos perveniret, & quam iniquis ac falsis calumniis omnes nostræ actiones traducerentur, ut vos ad vindictam istam exercendam irritarent, quæ in capita nostra decreta fuit eorum consiliis, qui regem sereniss. pro arbitrio circumagunt, hancque suam male partam amplitudinem stabilire conantur, oppressione religionis & libertatis fidelium utriusque regni subditorum, Cum haec in memoriam revocamus, non possumus nos continere quin Deum ex animis laudemus, quod nos invicta patientia & constanti hoc animorum proposito hactenus armaverit, ut quantum in nobis esset, Nationalis contra vos controversiae occasionem omnem evitaremus: nam vobis in memoriam recurrat, Rege, licet horum consiliis, cum exercitu contra nostram spem in nos, non ita pridem, movente, neglexisse tamen nos omnia quae incolumitatem nostram egregie promovere potuissent, nec refiliisse a tramite obedientiae; & ne offensionis vel minimam speciem dilectis nostris in Anglia fratribus daremus, patriam nostram ruinae potius objecisse, quam ut vestram periculo cuilibet exponeremus: Imo, cum non absque stupore & horrore accepissemus inusitata neque unquam antehac audita edicta contra universam gentem, quae nunquam rea fuit cujuslibet contumaciae contra regis sui legitima mandata, ea tamen irritatione neglecta, nihil inter nos aliud auditum tum fuit, quam supplices ad Deum preces pro sereniss. nostri regis incolumitate; singulorumque intensissima vota, ut vitam suam exponerent, & sanguinem effunderent ad incrementum honoris & coronae regiae; & qui in illas licet angustias redacti, vix ac ne vix quidem in suam tutelam & salutem se armarent.
units.tr: For when we call to mind how much courage and constancy of spirit God has granted us from the beginning of these disturbances, to defend our religion and privileges, so that we should not be thrust headlong into slavery of soul and body, from which there would have been no hope for us and our posterity of extricating ourselves, and which, because of the close union with you under the same king, would have been of most dangerous consequence for your privileges when they came to be called into question in their own time and places; on the contrary, when we call to mind by what violent and unusual means our adversaries have acted, so that certain knowledge of our affairs should not reach the English, and with what unjust and false calumnies all our actions have been distorted, so as to provoke you to exercise that vengeance which was decreed against our heads by the counsels of those who drive our most serene king at their own will and try to establish their ill-gotten power by the oppression of the religion and liberty of the faithful subjects of both kingdoms, we cannot refrain from praising God from our hearts, who has armed us until now with invincible patience and this constant resolve of spirit, so that, as far as lay in us, we might avoid every occasion of national controversy against you. For let it come back to your memory: though the king, moved not long ago against our hope by their counsels, came against us with an army, we nevertheless neglected all those things which could have greatly promoted our safety, and did not start aside from the path of obedience; and so that we might give not even the slightest appearance of offence to our beloved brothers in England, we chose to expose our own country to ruin rather than to expose yours to danger of any kind. Indeed, when we had heard, not without astonishment and horror, of edicts unusual and never heard of before against the whole nation, which had never been guilty of any contumacy against the lawful commands of its king, yet, having disregarded that provocation, nothing else was then heard among us but suppliant prayers to God for the safety of our most serene king, and the most intense vows of each man that they would expose their lives and shed their blood for the increase of the honour and crown of the king; and those who, though reduced to such straits, scarcely if at all armed themselves for their own protection and safety.

units.la: Difficulter sane persuadebitur exteris; quibus mediis duae gentes sibi invicem tam vicinae, & omnibus amicitiae ac benevolentiae vinculis tam arctis conjunctae, ad eum statum reduci potuerint, in quo non ita pridem fuerunt; & ad eam periculosam ruptionem, quae nostro saeculo haud facile (ut nihil gravius dicatur) coalesceret, præsertim cum nulla probabilis se prodiderit causa, cur in hisce controversiis, quæ vos & vestra privilegia non tangerent, nedum læderent, nobis adversaremini.
units.tr: It will certainly be hard to persuade foreigners by what means two nations so close to each other, and joined by such tight bonds of friendship and goodwill, could have been brought to the state in which they were not long ago, and to that dangerous rupture, which in our age would hardly have come about (to say nothing harsher), especially since no plausible cause has appeared why you should oppose us in these controversies, which did not touch your privileges, let alone harm them.

units.la: Sed Dei opus fuit admirabile in oculis nostris, quod impedimenta ab adversariis nostris in toto hujus negotii progressu objecta, totidem fuerint quasi gradus quibus promoveretur: uti omnes bene norunt, & ingenue agnoscunt, quorum qualicunque opera Deus hic usus est.
units.tr: But it was a wonderful work of God before our eyes that the obstacles thrown in our way by our adversaries throughout the whole progress of this affair became, as it were, just so many steps by which it was advanced. All know this well and freely acknowledge it, whoever they were whose work, however it was done, God used here.
