units.la: Porro ut testaremur tam fidelitatem ac animorum nostrorum sinceritatem, erga famam sereniss. nostri regis, (licet tum armati contra suos subditos,) quam amorem fraternum in nobiles & alios vestræ gentis; (quibus nihil aliud propositum fuisse credimus, quam ut regem comitarentur, licet revera sic satisfacerent ambitioni & crudelissimæ vindictæ miseri Præsulis) Æquissima & humilia nostra postulata regi adhuc obtulimus, prout tam piæ causæ defensores decuit; & in tractatu pacificatorio omnem operam dedimus, ut abunde satisfaceremus omnibus quæ requiri possent à fidelibus subditis, quibus regis nostri honor cordi esset, idque non sine nostro probabili incommodo, (adversariis etiam nostris judicibus) Nam regi sereniss. arces omnes munitas quas voluit, tradidimus, in splendidissimum obedientiæ nostræ testimonium, licet à nobis custodiri potuissent, ut totidem arrhæ quibus certi redderemur præstitum iri articulos concessos, & concludendos in subsequutura synodo & parlamento: quæ tamen arces contra nostram spem conversæ sunt in catenas servitutis & terroris, ne articulis in pacificatione stipulatis frueremur.
units.tr: Furthermore, to testify both our fidelity and the sincerity of our minds towards the good name of our most serene king (although we were then armed against his own subjects), and our brotherly love towards the nobles and others of your nation (whom we believe had no purpose except to accompany the king, although in reality they were gratifying the ambition and the most cruel vengeance of the wretched prelate), we still offered our most just and humble demands to the king, as befitted defenders of so pious a cause. In the pacification treaty we took every pains to satisfy abundantly all that could be required of faithful subjects to whom the king's honour was dear, and we did so not without our own probable inconvenience (even our adversaries being the judges). For we handed over to the most serene king all the fortresses he wished, fortified, as the most splendid testimony of our obedience. We could have kept them, as so many pledges that the agreed articles, to be concluded in the coming synod and parliament, would be carried out. Yet contrary to our hope those fortresses have been turned into chains of slavery and terror, so that we might not enjoy the articles stipulated in the pacification.

units.la: Atque licet promissorum fides corrumpatur, pro singulari tamen & tenero erga serenis. regem assectu, & serio dolore ob dedecus, quod per improba ejusmodi instrumenta rex noster patitur, Ingenue profitemur, nos fraude non fuisse tum circumventos, neque adhuc poenitere quod verbo regio simpliciter confisi fuerimus: Etenim sciebamus nobis tum rem fuisse cum rege nostro, cum quo sicut minime decet subditos de appendicibus contendere, cum de rei summa conventum esset, ita persuasum nobis fuit, (nisi rex tandem sua sponte judicaverit, quantopere seductus fuerit contra nos suos subditos,qui tam egregia exhibuimus testimonia confidentiae nostrae, & juris quod in ipsius gratiam supra alios merito vendicamus,verum perrexerit omnes occasiones nobis laedendis prosequi) persuasum dicimus nobis fuisse, eidem praetextus speciosos & fallaces contra nos nunquam defuturos, cum statuet a pactis & conventis resilire. Decebat etiam damna illa periclitanda esse, ac successum Deo committendum, quibuscunque demum incommodis afficeremur. Etenim nisi verbum regium, quod subditis suis oraculi loco esse debet, & promissorum ac contractuum fides sigillo & subscriptione obsignata (cui in omni societate humana fides superstruitur ac innititur, quaeque apud Ethnicos & Turcas sacra & inviolata manet) regi serenis. tandem persuadeant, ut articulis pacificatoriis promissa reipsa praestet, tum vere judicamus nihil a nobis tunc formari aut peti potuisse, quod nobis nunc conduceret: uti nihil eorum quae pacta fuerunt, conducunt, neque quae a nobis tum concessa, fuerunt, ea animo accipiuntur quo sperabamus; (licet ad ea concedenda nulla alia quaevis ratio nos cogere potuisset, quam ut per eorundem concessionem plene & realiter articuli pacti praestarentur) Quin contra quantum ex praeteritis omnibus colligi poterit, liquido constat, pacem hostibus nostris nunquam propositam fuisse, nec adhuc intendi.
units.tr: And although the faith of promises is corrupted, nevertheless, out of singular and tender affection for the most serene king, and in serious grief at the disgrace which our king suffers through such wicked instruments, we frankly declare that we were not then circumvented by fraud, nor do we now regret that we simply trusted the royal word. For we knew that we then had to do with our king, with whom it is by no means fitting for subjects to contend over details once agreement has been reached on the substance of the matter. So it was persuaded to us (unless the king at last of his own accord judged how greatly he had been led astray against us, his subjects, who have given such splendid proofs of our confidence and of the right which we rightly claim above others to his favour, but has gone on pursuing every occasion of harming us): we say it was persuaded to us that specious and deceptive pretexts against us would never be lacking to him, when he decided to leap back from the pacts and agreements. It was also fitting that those losses be risked and success committed to God, whatever inconveniences might befall us. For unless the royal word, which ought to be an oracle for its subjects, and the faith of promises and contracts sealed with seal and signature (on which all trust in human society is built and rests, and which remains sacred and inviolate even among pagans and Turks) persuade the most serene king at last to actually perform the promises of the pacification articles, then we truly judge that nothing could have been formed or sought by us then which would now benefit us. Just as none of the things agreed benefit us, nor are the things conceded by us then received in the spirit in which we hoped (although no other reason whatever could have compelled us to concede them, than that through their concession the agreed articles might be fully and actually performed). Indeed, on the contrary, as much as can be gathered from all that has gone before, it is clear that peace was never offered to our enemies, nor is it yet intended.

units.la: Nam totum illud pacificationis negotium in stratagema converterunt, quo vafra & astuta sua consilia occultius tegerent, certa spe facilius se impia sua astutia obruituros, quos aperta vi non potuerunt; Ostentantes quidem exercituum dissolutionem, sed replentes interim limites milite praesidiario, ut belli diuturnioris fundamenta ponerent: Et cum arces huius regni munitas a nobis reciperent, ea expressa conditione, ut in eodem statu manerent, quo ante exortos motus fuerunt, statim tamen easdem instruxerunt in nidos violentiae contra primarias regni partes. Evocarunt insuper Berwicum (Angliae oppidum munitum) complures nostrūm eosque ordinis, primi, sub tenui negotiorum quorundam peragendorum praetextu, (cum tamen totum pacificationis negotium a paucis ex illorum evocatorum numero conclusum fuisset) cumque eorum quidam Berwicum advenissent, in caeterorum adventum omnia illa negotia suspensa fuerunt, eosque remiserunt, ut socios tanquam in nassam deducerent. Cumque nec ars illa proficeret, Consultatum fuit inter eos de intercipiendis primariis quibusdam nostris nobilibus; quae occulta & sanguinolenta consilia Deus miraculose postea aperuit, & ad eorum confusionem, qui authores & fautores fuerunt vilissimorum ejusmodi sicariorum, amplius aperiet. Atque, quod artificii sui caput fuerat, & in quo omnem suam spem collocarunt, permiserunt, ut res omnes ecclesiasticas controversas definiret synodus, deputato regio, regis ipsius nomine in omnia decreta consentiente, ac eorundem confirmationem & sanctionem in parlamento proximo subsequuturo, sacrosancte pollicente, qua arte apud se statuerant, alterâ se manu ablaturos quod unâ darent: Etenim species hæc concludendi res ecclesiasticas per synodum, quas tamen in parlamento ratas habere nolunt ad publicæ observantiæ in Repub. vigorem, uti prorsus inefficacem reddit synodi operam, ita prætextum quendam præ se fert, iis consiliis promovendis, ad quæ maxime aspirant, ut videl: sequuntura ruptio & tumultus, ad quem se etiam tunc accingebant, non posset putari futura pro religione, quam in synodo plene compositam fuisse allegabant; sed pro aliis in Repub. quæstionibus: Et judicatum certè fuit satis probabiliter res ecclesiasticas in synodo compositas fuisse, deputato regio assentiente, sed prudentioribus scrupulus statim objectus fuerat de negotii sinceritate, cum per Declarationes & explicationes posticam sibi parare deputatum regium deprehendissent, quibus negare posset quæ antea suo ipsius consensu & suffragio definita fuerant.
units.tr: For they turned that whole business of pacification into a stratagem, by which they might more secretly conceal their crafty and cunning plans, in the sure hope that they would more easily overwhelm by their impious cunning those whom they could not overcome by open force. They showed indeed the dissolution of their armies, but meanwhile filled the borders with garrison soldiers, so that they might lay the foundations of a longer war. And when they received from us the fortresses of this kingdom, on the express condition that they remain in the same state in which they were before the motions arose, they at once fitted those same fortresses out as nests of violence against the chief parts of the kingdom. Moreover, they summoned to Berwick (a fortified town of England) several of our men, and those of the first rank, under the slight pretext of certain business to be transacted, although the whole pacification business had been concluded by a few from the number of those summoned. When some of them had arrived at Berwick, all those affairs were suspended until the others arrived, and then they sent them back so that they might lead their companions as into a trap. When that device did not succeed, they took counsel among themselves about intercepting certain of our chief nobles. God afterwards miraculously revealed these secret and bloody plans, and will reveal them further, to the confusion of those who were the authors and promoters of such vile assassins. And, what was the very head of their artifice and the thing in which they placed all their hope, they allowed the synod to settle all the disputed ecclesiastical matters, with the royal deputy agreeing to all the decrees in the king's own name, and solemnly promising their confirmation and sanction in the next parliament. By the art they had decided upon among themselves, they would take away with one hand what they gave with the other. For this appearance of concluding ecclesiastical matters through the synod, which they are nevertheless unwilling to ratify in parliament so that it might have the force of public observance in the commonwealth, renders the synod's work utterly ineffective. It also bears a certain pretext for promoting those plans to which they especially aspire, namely that a rupture and tumult should follow, for which they were then also preparing themselves. It could not be thought to be for the religion which they alleged had been fully settled in the synod, but for other questions in the commonwealth. And it was certainly judged, quite plausibly, that the ecclesiastical matters had been settled in the synod with the royal deputy assenting. But a scruple was at once raised by the more prudent about the sincerity of the business, since they had perceived that the royal deputy was preparing for himself a back door, through declarations and explanations by which he could deny what had previously been decided with his own consent and vote.

units.la: In hoc rerum statu apertum fuit parlamentum, & continuatum, non tam ut componeret & sanciret res ecclesiasticas, prout promissum fuerat & nos etiam sperabamus, verum ut servitutis exemplum (tam patribus nostris quam nobis inauditum) nobis obtruderet; ac tandem regia authoritate dissolutum & prorogatum fuit sine ordinum regni consensu, quod, cum directe repugnet legi & continuæ praxi hujus regni, legibus pacificationis adversatur.
units.tr: In this state of affairs parliament was opened and continued, not so much to settle and sanction the ecclesiastical matters, as had been promised and as we also hoped, but to impose upon us an example of slavery, unheard of by our fathers as well as by us. At last it was dissolved and prorogued by royal authority without the consent of the orders of the kingdom. Since this directly contradicts the law and continuous practice of this kingdom, it is contrary to the laws of the pacification.

units.la: Atque licet majores nostri in tali rerum statu aliter se gessissent, nos tamen solis precibus & libellis supplicibus cum rege sereniss. egimus; utque constantem & invictam nostram obedientiam regi ostenderemus, Deputatos nostros Londinum ablegavimus, qui tamen rejecti fuerunt, quosque nec videre nec audire dignabatur rex: Nihilominus Iominus ut singulari nostra patientia adversariorum malitiam tandem expugnaremus, deputatos nostros denuo ad aulam delegavimus, æquissimis mandatis instructos, utpote quibus nihil aliud contineretur & peteretur, quam quod antea concessum fuit, & regis sereniss. sigillo & chirographo obsignatum, quodque a tam pio & justo rege rejici non potuit: Etenim summa & subjectum omnium nostrarum supplicationum, protestationum, informationum, declarationum a principio fuit, ut fundamentales regni leges (haactenus violatæ) & religio (aperte haactenus corrupta) in libera synodo nationali & parlamento denuo sancirentur, & in violationis utriusque improbos authores animadverterentur; quæ magis expresse in articulis pacis exprimuntur, quibus cautum fuit, ut res omnes politicæ parlamenti, & Ecclesiasticæ synodi judicio definirentur: porro cum synodus a rege promissa & concessa, controversias omnes ecclesiasticas feliciter composuisset, dignaretur rex sereniss. parlamentum concludere, quo decreta illa ecclesiastica sancirentur, & controversiæ aliæ civiles legitime componerentur, prout diserte pactum fuit in tractatu pacificatorio ad castra regia. Propositiones tamen hæ quantumvis pernecessariæ, a sereniss. & clementissimi regis nostri auribus exclußæ fuerunt, per Archiepiscopum Cantuariensem & Deputatum Hiberniæ, qui (factione papistica circa regem præpotenti valide muniti) omnia negotia tam politica quam ecclesiastica soli expediunt, & ut operæ suæ necessitatem serenis. regi ostendant, prætextu vindicandi honoris regii, justa subditorum privilegia & veram reformatam religionem in omnibus regis regnis opprimunt.
units.tr: Although our forefathers in such a state of affairs had acted otherwise, we nevertheless pleaded with the most serene king by prayers and supplicatory petitions alone. To show our constant and unconquered obedience to the king, we sent our deputies to London, who were nevertheless rejected, and whom the king did not deign to see or hear. Nevertheless, so that by our singular patience we might at last overcome the malice of our adversaries, we again sent our deputies to the court, instructed with most just mandates, since nothing else was contained or sought in them than what had been previously conceded and sealed with the most serene king's seal and signature, and which could not be rejected by so pious and just a king. For the sum and subject of all our supplications, protests, informations and declarations from the beginning was that the fundamental laws of the kingdom (hitherto violated) and the religion (hitherto openly corrupted) should again be sanctioned in a free national synod and parliament, and that the wicked authors of the violation of both should be punished. These things are set out more expressly in the articles of peace, in which it was provided that all the political affairs should be decided by the judgment of parliament, and the ecclesiastical by the synod. Further, since the synod, as promised and conceded by the king, had happily settled all the ecclesiastical controversies, the most serene king deigned to conclude parliament, in which those ecclesiastical decrees would be sanctioned and the other civil controversies lawfully settled, just as it was expressly agreed in the pacification treaty at the royal camp. Yet these proposals, however very necessary, were shut out from the ears of our most serene and most clement king by the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Deputy of Ireland. Strongly fortified by the papist faction, which is very powerful with the king, they alone manage all business, both political and ecclesiastical. And, in order to show the king the necessity of their service, under the pretext of vindicating the king's honour they oppress the just privileges of the subjects and the true reformed religion in all the king's realms.

units.la: In quo impio conatu jure meritoque dicimus ipsos plurimum profecisse, si præsens concessio liberæ synodi & parlamenti (quæ agnita fuerunt in legibus pacis anno superiore ictæ, ut unicum ecclesiæ & Reipub. incommodis aufferendis, & pacem ac utriusque regni incolumitatem procurandi remedium) cum tandem sortiatur successum, quem in Christiana ecclesia olim habuit synodus ista Tridentina, quæ cum ecclesiarum reformationi destinata esset, ambitione tamen & avaritia ecclesiasticorum, & infœlicibus principum tum regnantium suspicionibus, quibus potior fuit propria utilitas quam Christi & ecclesiæ commodum, conversa fuit in primarium & efficax medium, quo papæ & ecclesiasticorum tyrannis stabiliretur.
units.tr: In this impious attempt we rightly and justly say that they have achieved a great deal, if the present grant of a free synod and parliament (which were acknowledged in the laws of the peace struck last year, as the sole remedy for removing the troubles of Church and commonwealth and for securing peace and the safety of both kingdoms) should at last meet with the same success which that synod of Trent once had in the Christian Church. That synod, though it was intended for the reformation of the churches, was turned, through the ambition and greed of churchmen and the unhappy suspicions of the princes then reigning, who preferred their own advantage to the good of Christ and the Church, into the chief and effective means by which the tyranny of the pope and the churchmen was made secure.

units.la: Majori etiam metu nunc tenemur, cum obliquas & sibi invicem oppositas artes intuemur, nam nobis denegatur parlamentum, licet verbo regio promissum sit, idque in utriusque regni salutem; Et vobis conceditur, licet inexspectatum, ob rationes quæ prudentioribus haud facile excident; Et Hiberniæ obtruditur licet non postulatum; prodeunt commissiones quibus nos destruendi potestas conceditur, licet alterius criminis nobis conscii non simus, quam quod constantibus precibus apud regem institerimus, ut parlamentum concluderet, & leges pacis præstaret: parlamentum nostrum, contra leges, & disertos pacificationis articulos, dissolvitur: præsidia militaria nobis obtruduntur, ut cogeremur obedientiam denegare iniquis ejusmodi mandatis, & nostræmet incolumitati consulere; Quæ omnia certo scimus excogitata esse, ut quæstio contra nos quæreretur, & fundamentum falsæ alicujus & longe petitæ ac extortæ contra nos remonstrantiæ: Nunc vero peculiari studio & consilio istorum supra memoratorum, ingens exercitus contra nos paratur, & extrema pernicies ac ruina religioni & patriæ nostræ interminatur.
units.tr: We are held by even greater fear now, when we look upon artful and mutually contradictory dealings. For parliament is denied us, although it was promised by the royal word, and that for the safety of both kingdoms. Yet to you it is granted, though unexpected, for reasons which the more prudent will not easily overlook. And Ireland is forced upon, though it did not ask for it. Commissions go out by which power to destroy us is granted, although we are conscious of no crime other than that we steadily pressed the king by our petitions that parliament be concluded and the laws of peace be secured. Our parliament is dissolved, contrary to law and to the explicit articles of the pacification. Military garrisons are thrust upon us, so that we would be forced to deny obedience to such unjust commands and to look to our own safety. All these things we know for certain were devised so that a charge might be sought against us, and the foundation of some false and far-fetched and extorted remonstrance against us. Now, indeed, by the special zeal and counsel of the men named above, a huge army is being prepared against us, and extreme ruin and destruction are threatened to our religion and our country.

units.la: Quare, ne silentium nostrum, tempore tam necessario, argueret neglectum officii nostri erga Deum & regem, erga incolumitatem & honorem patriæ nostræ, ac communem utriusque regni pacem, quę omnia arubus hisce periculo certissimo exponuntur; Coram Christiano orbe, & dilectis in Anglia fratribus, præsertim vero vobis repræsentativo regni corpori in parlamento fœliciter convocato, ingenue & candide profitemur, Nos non posse aliter judicare, quam quod omnia illa consilia non ita pridem suggesta ab impotentibus quibusdam consiliariis, qui nunc ad clavum sedent, & omnia pro arbitrio circumagunt, non solum proveniant ab iis qui ob fines privatos assumpta specie promovendi juris regii, idem tamen revera debilitant, & regna in confusionum abyssum protrudunt, verumetiam quod consilia illa in Conclavi Romano & in Hispania primitus excogitata fuerint, & transmissa ac commissa subdolis suis inter vos sociis, qui progenies verè viperina semper fuerunt, ac omni opera conati sunt materna viscera fœde dilaniare: quibus solenne est, quamprimum ecclesiam Romanam matrem agnoverint, eique se submiserint, tam cito regem Catholicum patrem agnoscere, propriumque suum regem usurpatorem ac injustum possessorem, si hæreticum æstimaverint. Ita quidem ut nobis abunde persuasum sit; non amplius opus esse invicta classe qualis fuit illa anno 1588, nec proditione sulphurea, aut ulla alia quavis regia classe ab Hispania, (qualis illa fuit quæ anno superiori litoribus vestris imminebat, vobis vel eo nomine magis metuenda, quod tempore tam inexspectato & inopportuno advenerit) quæ infulam hanc obruat; sed satis illis futurum omnem operam impendere, (& quin faciant non dubitamus) ut flamma hæc civilis belli tamdiu fumigans tandem accendatur, utque eandem recte foveant, (quod certissime præstituri sunt) præsertim cum ad manum sint quæcunque fovere, & longissime absint quæ flammæ huic, si semel in incendium erumpat, restinguendæ conducere possent; & quod multo peßimum est, cum satis appareat exstingui non posse sine insigni victoris damno.
units.tr: Wherefore, lest our silence at so necessary a time should appear to show neglect of our duty towards God and the king, towards the safety and honour of our country, and towards the common peace of both kingdoms, all of which are exposed to the most certain danger by these measures, we openly and candidly profess before the Christian world and before our beloved brethren in England, and above all before you, the representative body of the kingdom happily assembled in parliament, that we cannot judge otherwise than this: all those counsels, lately suggested by certain powerless counsellors who now sit at the helm and turn everything at their own pleasure, come not only from men who, under the pretext of promoting the royal right, which in truth they weaken, and for private ends, drive the kingdoms into an abyss of confusion. They also come from the fact that those counsels were first devised in the Roman conclave and in Spain, and were sent over and entrusted to your treacherous associates, who have always been a truly viperous brood and have striven by every means to tear foully the mother's bowels. It is their custom, as soon as they have acknowledged the Church of Rome as mother and submitted to her, to acknowledge the Catholic king as father as quickly as they can, and to count their own king a usurper and unjust possessor if they judge him a heretic. So that we are fully persuaded that there is no longer any need for an invincible fleet such as that of the year 1588, nor for sulphurous treachery, nor for any other royal fleet from Spain (such as the one that threatened your shores last year, the more to be feared by you on that account, that it came at so unexpected and unseasonable a time) to overwhelm this island. Rather, it will be enough for them to take all pains (and we do not doubt that they will do so) that this flame of civil war, long smouldering, may at last be kindled, and that they may rightly nurse it (which they will most certainly do), especially since whatever feeds it is at hand, while whatever could help quench it, should it once break out into a conflagration, is far away. And, what is much worse, it is quite plain that it cannot be put out without a heavy loss even to the victor.

units.la: Præterea licet merito suspicari possemus, convocatione hac vestri parlamenti, quæ eorum consiliis suggesta fuit qui malum hoc civilis discordiæ in clarissima hac insula sine vestro consensu aut consilio excitarunt, intendi, ut oleum potius quam aquam restinguendæ huic flammæ afferatis, & in motuum horum fervore vobis auxiliatoribus utantur ad constantissimorum vestrorum amicorum ruinam procurandam; quos illi interim ut hostes suos ulciscentur. Nihilominus tamen bonis omnibus in celeberrimo vestro coetu non ingratum futurum speramus, quod summo animi gaudio & hilaritate profitemur ac declaremus, vincula amoris & fraternæ charitatis inter nos esse mutua, & sibi invicem in omnibus erga Deum & hominem, principem & populum officiis usque adeo arcte conjuncta, ut communes amicos & inimicos necesse sit habeamus, seu promiscuam utrique salutem contra hostes exteros defendendo, seu alterutrius privilegia contra domesticos subversores tuendo, a quibus maius imminet periculum: nisi ab unica & firma salutis nostræ regula animus nobis fit defcisccre.
units.tr: Moreover, although we might justly suspect that this convocation of your parliament, which was suggested by the counsels of those who stirred up this evil of civil discord in this most famous island without your consent or advice, is intended to bring oil rather than water to quench this flame, and that in the heat of these disturbances they may use you as helpers in bringing about the ruin of your most steadfast friends, whom they meanwhile wish to punish as their enemies, nevertheless we hope that it will not be unwelcome to all good men in your most renowned assembly that we declare and profess with the greatest joy and cheerfulness of mind that the bonds of love and brotherly charity are mutual between us, and so closely joined to one another in all duties towards God and man, prince and people, that we must have common friends and common enemies. This holds whether we defend our common safety against foreign enemies, or guard each other's privileges against domestic subverters, from whom the greater danger threatens; unless our mind should turn away from the one and firm rule of our safety.

units.la: Nam cum ratione situs huius insulæ & unionis sub uno capite, omnes tanquam in una eademque domo simus, qua corruente, in ejusdem ruinis promiscue omnes sepeliemur: omnes tanquam in una eademque navi vehamur, qua naufragium patiente aut ad infames divisionis scopulos impingente, vix enatabimus; Æquis animis feratis, quod tempestate adhuc sæviente de primo hoc salutari signo vobis gratulemur; quod scil. vos navis hujus veros & penitos directores ad clavum adductos conspiciamus. Rogamus insuper pro communi jure quod nobis est in merces pretiosas, pacem videl: libertatem, religionem quæ eadem hac navi vehuntur, ne stationem vestram in fœda hac tempestate deseratis, (licet consultius fuisset ut temporibus pacatioribus conventus ille vester indictus fuisset) vobisque fit solatio quod sereno cælo, quæ sese de longinquo ostentant nubes, supremo nostro Navarcho prænunciaveritis; ac licet à multis non conspecti fuere tum turbines, quibus nunc vexamur, à quam plurimis tamen populo deputatis & aliis omnium ordinum videbantur; Qui nubes illas congregabant, designabantur, & unde venirent; ferventibus etiam & frequentibus precibus apud serenissi. regem tum instabatis, ne suam & regnorum salutem desereret, & cum navigandum esset in periculosissimis & metuendis angustiis, ne navem Reipub. eorum arbitrio exponeret, qui sola ambitione & privato lucro dirigerentur: ac tam regem quam populum ex fida statione & pacis quieto portu in fœdam quæ nunc sævit tempestatem protruserunt, quæ utrisque nobis naufragium minatur, unde illis solis commodi spes affulget. Si in hisce rerum angustiis non licitum sit minimis qui eadem navi vehuntur, admonere imminentis periculi; nos tamen ratione loci nostri, & pro nostro jure in vestram incolumitatem tacere non possumus; & licet primam vigiliam peregerimus, & tempestatis hujus prima & maxima incommoda, vobis interim alta quiete gaudentibus, forti animo pertulerimus, certi tamen sitis, nobis minime statutum vos solos derelinquere cum vices vestras peracturi sitis, ac sortitudinis & prudentiæ vestræ specimen propediem forte daturi; facile quippe ex præcedentibus vobis innotescit, Nullam synodum, nullum parlamentum, nullum fragilem & fallacem articulorum & pacificationis rudentem, quibus spes nostra innitebatur, ullam posse nobis certam salutem promittere, quamdiu communes utrique pariter hostes ad clavum sedent, & omnia proarbitrio apud vos circumagunt.
units.tr: For since, by the situation of this island and its union under one head, we are all as if in one and the same house, which, if it falls, we shall all be buried together in its ruins; we are all carried as if in one and the same ship, which, if it suffers shipwreck or runs upon the infamous rocks of division, we shall scarcely swim out of. Bear with equanimity that, while the storm still rages, we rejoice over this first saving sign, namely that we see you brought to the helm as the true and proper directors of this ship. We further ask, for the common right we have in the precious merchandise, namely peace, liberty and religion, which are carried in this same ship, that you do not desert your post in this foul tempest (although it would have been more advisable that your assembly had been called in more peaceful times). Let it be a comfort to you that the clouds which show themselves from afar in a clear sky you have announced to our supreme Pilot. Although by many the whirlwinds with which we are now troubled were not seen, yet they were plainly visible to very many of the deputies of the people and to others of all orders. Those who gathered those clouds were pointed out, and whence they would come. You also, with fervent and frequent prayers, urged the most serene king then not to desert his own safety and that of his kingdoms, and, since they must sail through most dangerous and fearful straits, not to expose the ship of the commonwealth to the will of those who are guided only by ambition and private gain. They have thrust both king and people out of a faithful station and the quiet harbour of peace into the foul tempest which now rages, a tempest that threatens shipwreck to us both, while for them alone a hope of gain shines forth. If in such straits it is not permitted even to the least of those who sail in the same ship to warn of impending danger, yet we, by reason of our place and for our own right, cannot keep silent for your safety. And although we have kept the first watch and, while you rejoice in deep calm, have borne with brave spirit the first and greatest troubles of this tempest, be assured that we are by no means resolved to leave you alone, since you are about to perform your own turns and perhaps soon give proof of your courage and prudence. For from what has gone before it is easily made known to you that no synod, no parliament, and no fragile and deceptive rudder of articles and pacification, on which our hope rested, can promise us any certain safety, so long as both our common enemies sit at the helm and turn everything at their own pleasure before you.

units.la: Priusquam vero consilium nostrum aperiamus, quæ sint nostro judicio aptissima media malis quibus utrique premimur removendis; Date veniam ut obiter perstringamus primarias, nostrâ opinione, causas, quibus à culmine illo felicitatis, quà olim in Europa fulgebatis, pedetentim dejecti sitis ad miseram hanc & vilem conditionem, cui nunc subjecti estis, & in quam vestro exemplo nos etiam protracti fuimus, ut tristi hac repræsentatione, tanquam in subobscura umbra, coruscans illud diei vestri appropinquantis lumen utrique nostrum solatio esse possit, quod uti ex animis vovent ita certo sperant Charissimi vestri fratres Scoti, propter singularis misericordiæ divinæ sensum erga se qui magis in reatu fuerunt, & animis ante exortos hos motus dejectioribus, quam cujuslibet fere mentem subire poterit. Porro, cum calamitates nostræ antiquæ sint, neque totam hanc insulam tam subito obruere potuerint, Agite, fontem & scaturiginem unde, ac temporis periodum quando primum prodire cœperunt, indagemus.
units.tr: Before we set out our counsel, namely which means we judge most suitable for removing the evils that press on us both, please allow us to touch briefly on what we consider the chief causes by which you, from that height of happiness in which you once shone in Europe, have gradually been cast down into this miserable and base condition you now endure, and into which we too have been dragged by your example. Our hope is that in this sad picture, as in a rather dim shadow, the bright light of your approaching day may be a comfort to us both. Your dearest brothers the Scots vow this from their hearts and firmly hope for it, out of a sense of singular divine mercy towards themselves, who were more guilty and whose spirits were more cast down before these recent movements arose than almost anyone could imagine. Moreover, since our calamities are old and could not have overwhelmed this whole island so suddenly, let us search out their fountain and spring, and the period of time when they first began to emerge.

units.la: Quando ratione unionis duorum regnorum, non effet quod ab exteris metueremus, nostrum erat tum providere, ne à nobismetipsis damni quidpiam pateremur. Astuti insulae hujus hostes cum satis cognitum haberent, arte & occultâ fraude aggrediendum esse, quod aperta vi non auderent, uti sunt hominum quorundam ingeniis, quæ ad temporum conditionem sese ut plurimum accommodant, quo factum est, ut luxuria & longæ pacis quies plus periculi regnis attulerint, quam praecedentiü bellorum angustiæ, nam pedetentim subditis servituti,& regis proprii animi sensum & illimitatæ ac absolutæ potestatis regulas sequi affuefiebant; tum primü perpauci fuerunt, qui ad honorem & gloriam per publicā virtutis viam ascenderent, tum usus salutaris parlamentorum, in quibus regni vestri incolumitas & robur firmum est, suspectus esse coepit; & sic exstinctis illis publicis auribus & oculis tam regis quàm populi, fupremo fcil. & magno illo regni senatu, pedetentim ftrata fuit via ad senatum obscuriorem in Conclavi domeftico convocatum, ubi adulatio, malitia, invidia, & quaecunque mortalium animos in factiones deducere solent, regnabant, cumque omnia à paucis sic instructis circumagerentur, idque fine ulla contradictione,& varii speciosi prætextus obducerentur, quid miramur, fi miseriâ subditi obruantur, & rex hactenus infoelix fuerit? & licet, postquam subobscuri hi senatus obtinuerunt, parlamenta aliquando convenerint, tamen usi sunt, non ut mediis quibus subditorum gravamina tollerentur, sed quibus regum neceffitatibus subveniretur, atque ita morbos regni quos curaffent, auxerunt: Cumque nullus fit malignus humor ufq; adeo pertinax in corpore, qui peritiam veftram superet, fi remediis appositis & probatis vobis visum fuerit uti; laboratum fuit, ut inter vos controverfiæ & lites orirentur de methodo curandi; & cum ad concordiam conspirare vos viderunt, conventus vestri dissolvuntur, & sic fine ullâ remedii spe, languet Refpublica: regum errores ac populi dolores & gravamina pariter crescunt: & singulorum parlamentorum interruptiones ac dissolutiones novi doloris & morbi materiam subditis subministrant; qui vel eo nomine periculosiores & magis fatales sunt, quod istorum abusuum authores vos contemnant (quando non exerceatis eam fortitudinem & constantiam ad tuendam dignitatem & existimationem quam majores vestri vobis tradiderunt, & cujus rationes à vobis exposcent posteri, quippe quibus jure hæreditario competat, neque in ea à vobis lædentur nisi perpetua vestra cum infamia, & insigni ipsorum damno) neque contemnant solum ; verum etiam audeant regiminis vestri olim bene ordinati fundamenta ipsa subvertere, dum apud populum, cujus libertatibus tutandis tamdiu perstitistis, contemptui vos exponere conantur, & odio apud regem, cujus honori & securitati nihil magis consultum esse potest, quam ut nullus tantum apud ipsum prævaleret, quam leges, neque ut ullus ipsi seu loco seu gratiâ proximior sit, quam vos quorum consilia privatis studiis corrumpi non potuerunt. Hi sunt, ( si semel obtinuerint ut publica regni negotia negligentes, de rebus tantum vestris privatis sitis solliciti ) qui regibus instillarunt ac persuaserunt, Omnia privilegia & libertates subditorum esse principum mere gratuita dona, ( neque subditis jure aliquo nativitatis competere , quod in foro contradictorio allegare possent ) continuanda aut mutanda pro eorum arbitrio ; hi sunt qui ut obliquos suos fines promoveant, principes edocuerunt, penes ipsos esse parlamenta inchoare, continuare, dissolvere, & prout sibi utilius aut secus fore judicaturi sunt, eadem sancire, aut rejicere. Atq; sic quantum penes istos fuit, conantur authoritatem & jus regium quod esset instar radii solaris aliis solatium & lucem afferret, mutare in Cometam, hoc est, stupendæ admirationis materiam pro præsenti, & dirum majoris calamitatis subsecuturæ omen.
units.tr: When, by the union of the two kingdoms, there was nothing to fear from abroad, it was our duty then to take care that we suffered no harm from ourselves. The crafty enemies of this island, knowing well enough that what they did not dare to attempt by open force had to be undertaken by art and secret fraud, found the means in the talents of certain men, who for the most part adapt themselves to the condition of the times. The result was that luxury and the quiet of long peace brought more danger to the kingdoms than the hardships of earlier wars. For little by little the subjects grew accustomed to servitude and to following the will of the king and the rules of unlimited and absolute power. Then, first, there were very few who rose to honour and glory by the public path of virtue. Then the salutary use of parliaments, in which the safety and firm strength of your kingdom lies, began to be viewed with suspicion. And so, with those public ears and eyes of king and people extinguished, namely that supreme and great senate of the realm, a way was gradually paved to a more obscure senate, convened in a private chamber, where flattery, malice, envy, and whatever usually draws men's minds into factions held sway. Since everything was directed by a few so instructed, and this without any opposition, and various specious pretexts were drawn over it, why do we wonder that the subjects are overwhelmed with misery and the king has hitherto been unhappy? And although, after these rather obscure senates gained the upper hand, parliaments have sometimes met, they were used not as means by which the grievances of the subjects might be removed, but as means by which the needs of kings might be relieved; and so they increased the diseases of the kingdom which they were meant to cure. And since there is no malignant humour so stubborn in the body that your skill cannot overcome it, if you judged it right to use suitable and tested remedies, effort was made to stir up quarrels and disputes among you over the method of cure. When they saw you agreeing, your assemblies were dissolved, and so, with no hope of remedy, the commonwealth languishes. The errors of kings and the sufferings and grievances of the people grow alike. The interruptions and dissolutions of individual parliaments supply the subjects with fresh matter of pain and disease. These are the more dangerous and deadly for this reason: the authors of these abuses despise you, since you do not exercise that fortitude and constancy in defending the dignity and reputation which your ancestors handed down to you, and for which posterity will call you to account, since by hereditary right it belongs to them, and they will be injured by you only to your everlasting infamy and their own serious loss. Nor do they merely despise you; they even dare to overturn the very foundations of your once well-ordered government, while they try to expose you to contempt before the people, whose liberties you have so long defended, and to hatred before the king, for whose honour and security nothing can be more advantageously secured than that no one should prevail with him more than the laws, and that no one should be nearer to him in place or favour than you, whose counsels private pursuits could not corrupt. These are the men who, if they once succeed in making you careless of public affairs and anxious only about your own private concerns, have instilled into kings and persuaded them that all privileges and liberties of subjects are merely gratuitous gifts of princes (and that subjects have no right by birth which they could plead in an adversarial court), to be continued or changed at the prince's pleasure. These are the men who, to advance their crooked ends, have taught princes that it is for them to begin, continue and dissolve parliaments, and to sanction or reject their enactments as they judge more or less useful to themselves. And so, as far as in them lies, they try to change the authority and royal right, which should be like a ray of the sun bringing comfort and light to others, into a comet: that is, a matter of amazed wonder for the present, and a dire omen of greater calamity to come.

units.la: Equidem regis prærogativa, ( quæ veneratione semper reservata est, & quam temporibus optimis principes prudentissimi tanquam mysterium non recludendum censuerunt ; quam leges ipsi conceffere supra omnes privatos subditos in communem omnium incolumitatem, quæque in alium finem converti non potest quam in populi salutem) tantum detrimenti passa non fuisset, & frequenti ac vulgari de ea tractatione proprium suum splendorem non perdidisset, in manifestum juris subditorum præjudicium, & veri juris regii debilitationem, nisi thema illud in manus quorundam ecclesiasticorum incidisset, qui in ecclesiæ dedecus & Reipublicæ perniciem, omnes homines omnesque leges subjecerunt simpliciter arbitrio principis, quem absolute circumagunt; atque ut ita sub egregia regalis potestatis larva, finem tandem imponant egregio conatui suo de mutatione religionis & regiminis quam jampridem meditati fuerunt & ad quam adhuc anhelant: quo conatu vix poterunt frustrari, cum omnia usque adeo fœlicem successum ipsis promittere videantur.
units.tr: Indeed, the royal prerogative, which has always been kept with reverence, and which the wisest princes in the best times judged should not be unlocked like a mystery, which the laws themselves granted above all private subjects for the common safety of all, and which can be turned to no end other than the welfare of the people, would not have suffered such loss nor lost its proper splendour through frequent and common debate about it, to the manifest prejudice of the subjects' right and the weakening of true royal right. That would not have happened had this theme not fallen into the hands of certain churchmen, who, to the dishonour of the Church and the ruin of the commonwealth, have made all men and all laws subject simply to the will of the prince, whom they drive about at their absolute pleasure. They do this so that, under the splendid mask of royal power, they may at last bring to completion their grand attempt to change religion and government, which they meditated long ago and still pant after. They can hardly fail in this attempt, since everything seems to promise them so happy a success.

units.la: Nam principem optimum contra nativos suos subditos excitarunt, cui persuaserunt, eos illi non esse subditos fideles, quia iis aperte adversantur qui religionem subditorum corruperunt, & regni pacem interturbarunt: necessarium esse ut oblivificatur se esse subditorum nativum principem, quandoquidem ad totius insulæ Monarchiam promotus sit: Controversiamque hanc infœlicem cum subditis continuandam, ut prætextu rebellionis subditorum, opportunius se armis instruat, & unum regnum in alterius perniciem committat; donec utrumque pariter in extremam servitutem redigatur. Quod si hoc non concedatur, Cogitum principem ut peregrinorum auxilia advocet, omnique alia potestate sibi à Deo concessa utatur (hæc certe est egregiorum illorum ecclesiasticorum Theologia) ad stabiliendum illimitatum illud & absolutum regis jus, quod meditantur. Atque ita adjuncto Papistarum auxilio (qui nuper insignem factionem apud vos excreverunt) & aliorum quos fideles & probos subditos vocant, & qui maximum apud vos numerum conficere dicuntur, quorum animos nunquam subit, fe Deo aut hominibus rationem aliquando redditurosinjuriæ cujuslibet qua alios afficiunt, dummodo eâ conditionem suam promovere pofsint, quibus addendi illi qui non renuent vinculis ligari modo aureis, & à fe compositis, ut alios secum in eadem vincula socios habeant, quorum numerus ubique frequens est & potentia non contemnenda: Hisce omnium hominum generibus convenientibus & auxilia sua deferentibus, conatus istos procul dubio perficient. Atque hi sunt qui sese nos nunc perdituros,ac vos in eandem contra nos sententiam pertracturos firmiter sperant.
units.tr: For they have stirred up an excellent prince against his native subjects, persuading him that they are not faithful subjects, because they openly oppose those who have corrupted the religion of the subjects and disturbed the peace of the kingdom. They tell him that he must forget that he is the native prince of his subjects, since he has been raised to the monarchy of the whole island, and that this unhappy quarrel with the subjects must be continued, so that under the pretext of the subjects' rebellion he may arm himself more conveniently, and set one kingdom against the ruin of the other, until both are reduced together to the utmost servitude. But if this is not granted, the prince is to be compelled to summon foreign aid and to use every other power given him by God (this, surely, is the theology of those distinguished churchmen) to establish that unlimited and absolute royal right which they are plotting. And so, with the help of the Papists added, who have recently grown into a notable faction among you, and of others whom they call faithful and upright subjects, and who are said to make up the largest number among you, men whose minds never consider that they will one day give account to God or to men for any injury they inflict on others, provided they can advance their own cause by it; and to these should be added those who will not refuse to be bound with chains, provided they are golden and of their own making, so that they may have others as companions in the same bonds, a class whose numbers are everywhere great and whose power is not to be despised. With all these kinds of men coming together and bringing their support, they will undoubtedly carry through these attempts. And these are the men who firmly hope that they will now ruin us, and will draw you into the same opinion against us.

units.la: Neque ullo alio (ut videtur) fine nunc convocamini: nam post tam frequentes præcedentium Parlamentorum dissolutiones & interruptiones, (quibus factum est ut fidelibus populi fui consiliis & liberis subsidiis rex hactenus carere cogeretur, & subditorum onera & gravamina fine ulla remediorum spe quotidie adaugerentur) nullus est qui non merito admiretur diem illum illuxisse quo Parlamentum conveniret, præsertim vero illi qui actionum præteritarum feriem sedulo contemplati sunt & diligentius obfervarunt quæ nuper facta fuerunt, ut parlamentis non effet opus, ac norunt adauctum numerum & reatum delinquentium, quibus institutum est ut Parlamentis suis honos restitueretur; qua re probabiliter fatis conjicunt, Parlamentum hoc omnium quæ unquam in hac infula fuerunt, aut futurum felicissimum, ejusque pacem & commoda maxime promoturum, aut (quod Deus avertat) hostium nostrorum operâ, fatale futurum instrumentum ad evertendum tum regni statum, tum ecclesiam: dubitationesque nostras in desperationem, nem, & metus in praesentem confusionem conversurum.
units.tr: Nor, as it seems, are you now called together for any other purpose. For after so many frequent dissolutions and interruptions of previous Parliaments, by which the king has been forced to go without the loyal counsel and free aid of his people, and the burdens and grievances of his subjects have daily grown with no hope of remedy, there is no one who would not rightly marvel that the day has dawned on which Parliament should assemble. This is especially so for those who have carefully considered the sequence of past events and observed closely what has lately been done, so that Parliaments were not needed, and who know the growing number and guilt of wrongdoers, for whose sake it was decided that the honour of Parliaments should be restored. For this reason they reasonably conjecture that this Parliament will be either the most fortunate of all that have ever been held in this island, and one that will greatly advance its peace and welfare, or else (which God forbid) through the work of our enemies, a fatal instrument for overthrowing both the state of the kingdom and the Church, turning our doubts into despair and our fears into present confusion.

units.la: Quare probis omnibus, qui religionis sinceram veritatem, regis honorem, utriusque regni incolumitatem tempore tam necessario & difficili ingenue amant, nunc vel maxime incumbit, ut sedulo quâ jejuniis quâ precibus cum Deo agant, ut, sicuti conventus vestri exordium materiam maximi meritus aut spei omnibus subministrat, ita extrema ejusdem conclusio cedat praesenti saeculo in gaudium, & futuro in benedictionem ; Cujus quidem spei multa hactenus indicia se produnt ; Et si spiritus ille prudentiae, fortitudinis & veri zeli, ad religionem, regis regnorumque salutem, in vestris consiliis, uti olim, se exerat, cui cognitum, quid jam paret & meditetur Dominus, quo priorum frustrationum damna vestra resarciat?
units.tr: Therefore it is now above all incumbent on all good men who sincerely love the pure truth of religion, the honour of the king, and the safety of both kingdoms at so necessary and difficult a time, to deal earnestly with God by fasting and by prayers, so that, just as the beginning of your assembly offers to all a matter of great merit and hope, so its final conclusion may turn to joy for the present age and to blessing for the future. Many signs of this hope have shown themselves so far. And if that spirit of prudence, fortitude and true zeal for religion, the king's safety and the kingdoms' welfare should show itself in your counsels, as it did of old, who knows what the Lord is now preparing and planning, so as to make good the losses you have suffered from earlier frustrations?

units.la: In cujus fidem & certam spem eo magis adducimur, quod omnipotenti Dei manu cogantur malorum nostrorum authores & fautores, satis contra animum suum, vestram operam nunc invocare quâ nos opprimant. Nobis etiam certo persuasum est, non defuturum quicquid subdoli & maligni homines seu arte seu ingenio excogitare poterint ut persuadeant, opportunitatem nunc coaptandam esse, & controversias omnes componendas esse, onerum vestrorum levamen quaerendum esse, praesertim cum sine ullis aliis laboribus aut impensis facile obtineri possit, quam ut nostra gravamina duplicentur. Complures etiam speciosi praetextus producentur, quibus iniqua paucorum consilia, & damnosae istae privatorum consequentiae contra publicam regnorum pacem tegi possint. Sed denique certe oportet esse illam nubem praejudiciorum & falsae narrationis rerum nostrarum oculis vestris objicendam, craffissi-[?] mam necesse erit esse istam caliginem, antequam tam prudens, consultum & grave tribunal, ex selectis totius regni ingeniis conflatum, in animum induxerit, consilia illa rata habere, quae religionis & libertatis nostrae ruinam secum trahunt, in quarum ruderibus vestrae tam religioni quam libertati tumulum paratu effodietis, & hoc parlamento efficeretis ne unquam posthac locus aut usus foret alterius.
units.tr: We are the more led into confidence and firm hope of this because the authors and abettors of our evils are compelled, by the hand of almighty God and somewhat against their own will, to invoke your help now to oppress us. We are also certainly persuaded that there will be no lack of whatever crafty and malicious men can devise, by art or by wit, to persuade you that the opportunity must now be seized, that all controversies must be settled, and that relief from your burdens must be sought, especially since it can easily be obtained without any further labours or expense, other than that our grievances be doubled. Many plausible pretexts will also be put forward under which the unjust counsels of a few and these ruinous consequences for private persons may be concealed against the public peace of the kingdoms. But at last that cloud of prejudice and false report about our affairs must surely be set before your eyes; that thick mist must needs be dispelled before so prudent, deliberate and serious a tribunal, formed from the choicest minds of the whole realm, will resolve to hold those counsels valid which drag down the ruin of our religion and liberty, and in whose ruins you would dig a grave for your own liberty as well as your religion, and by this Parliament bring it about that there should never hereafter be place or occasion for another.

units.la: Verum enimvero de vobis ( Honoratissimi & Amplissimi ) meliora speramus, & qualia ad sæ-culi hujus fœlicitatem proprie pertinent, ut videlicet promotione veritatis divinae Deo sit gloria, justitia in impios regi sit honos, regno utrique salus, & ut nostra arctiori unione obruantur qui in nostris discordiis spes suas fundarunt, belloque hoc ad quod vos in fratres vestros excitant, statuunt uti tanquam equo Trojano, quo omnes illae calamitates inveherentur, quae civile bellum in hac insula necessario comitabuntur. Neque dubitamus quin pro vestra singulari prudentia & æquitate (utpote quibus in omnibus deliberationibus nullus alius scopus proponi solet quam regis sereniss. regnorumque salus, quae nullatenus à se invicem divelli possunt) aliter de rerum nostrarum statu judicaturi sitis, quam hactenus judicarunt isti nostri adversarii, qui sicuti malorum nostrorum, & corruptionis, quae tam in ecclesiam quam in politiam irrepebat, authores fuerunt, ita tam vos quam nos plurima ab iis perpessi fuimus, ac jure meritoque queri possumus de incommodo & malignitate remedii ab iis adhibiti magis quam de morbo ipso.
units.tr: Truly, however, we hope better things of you, most honourable and most distinguished sirs, and such things as properly belong to the happiness of this age: namely, that God may have glory through the advancement of divine truth, that the king may have honour through justice against the wicked, that both kingdoms may have safety, and that those who have founded their hopes on our discords may be overwhelmed by our closer union. And as for the war to which they urge you against your brothers, let them regard it as the Trojan horse, by which all those calamities would be carried in which civil war in this island must necessarily be accompanied. Nor do we doubt that, by your singular prudence and equity (since in all your deliberations no other aim is usually proposed than the safety of the most serene king and of the kingdoms, which can in no way be separated from one another), you will judge the state of our affairs otherwise than those our adversaries have judged until now. These men, who were the authors both of our evils and of the corruption which crept into the Church as well as the polity, have inflicted very many injuries on both you and us; and we may justly and rightly complain of the harm and malice of the remedy they applied, more than of the disease itself.

units.la: Impias hasce suas machinationes nudo praetextu zeli & amoris erga regis sereniss. dignitatem frustra tegunt, quandoquidem tendant in manifestam ruinam & perniciem fidelium regis subditorum, quorum opes illi sunt pro thesauro; quorum quies, ejus gloria; quorum corda & amor invicta sunt præsidia, quorum fœlicitas in coronæ prosperitatem cedit; misera contra potestatis istius sunt effecta quæ nihil aliud profert quam regi imbecillitatem, subditis vero calamitatem: neque existimandum, nostro sæculo huic benedictum Dominum, cui superioribus fæculis maledixerit.
units.tr: Those impious machinations of theirs they vainly cover with the bare pretext of zeal and love for the dignity of the most serene king. For they tend to the manifest ruin and destruction of the king's loyal subjects, whose wealth is his treasure, whose quiet is his glory, whose hearts and love are his invincible defences, and whose happiness redounds to the prosperity of the crown. On the contrary, they have made that power wretched, which brings to the king nothing but weakness and to the subjects nothing but calamity. Nor is it to be thought that the Lord who cursed this power in earlier ages blesses it in our own.

units.la: Evolvantur antiquorum sæculorum annales, ac ubique inveniemus, nihil esse quod iram Dei magis contrahat, quam ut Dei cultus & ecclesiæ profanentur; ac in eorum manus incidant qui sefmet mundo vendiderunt, ac politicis principum negotiis manciparunt: ubicunque hoc receptum fuit, certa & evidens demonstratio est mutationis in regimine, ac miseriarum & infamiæ eorum qui potestate illa abutuntur; deprehendetur etiam eorum res in pejora semper ruere.
units.tr: Let the annals of the ancient ages be unrolled, and everywhere we shall find that nothing draws down the wrath of God more than when the worship of God and the Church are profaned and fall into the hands of those who have sold themselves to the world and handed themselves over to the political affairs of princes. Wherever this has been received, there is a certain and evident demonstration of change in government, and of misery and infamy for those who abuse that power; and it will also be found that their affairs always tend to go from bad to worse.

units.la: Neque est quod vobis in memoriam revocemus discordias & atroces controversias optimorum & fortissimorum vestrorum Regum, cum vestris Archiepiscopis in Anglia ipsa, ut in herba supprimerent papatum illum quem sibi inter vos vendicabant, ut videlicet nisi horum arbitrio non liceret regibus ipsis regnare. Qui in præsentia pericula oculos ferio conjiciunt, neque ignorant qui sint, mali quod intenditur, authores, facile perspicient, licet omnibus utriusque regni subditis persuaderi posset, ut onus illud sponte subirémus quod Episcopus Cantuariensis cum factione illi devota nobis imponeret, ac ut agnoscerémus nos teneri obedire omnibus spiritualium illorum patrum mandatis, statim tamen patere, aliquod aliud fundamentum ambitiosæ suæ amplitudinis allegaturos, quam zelum erga regem sereniff. ejusque honorem: Reges etiam posteri experientiā discerent, omnes hosce labores in suam propriam gratiam subiisse, ut tyrannidem suam tam in regem quam subditos firmarent.
units.tr: Nor is there any need to call to your memory the quarrels and fierce controversies between your best and bravest kings and your archbishops in England itself, when those bishops tried to suppress in its infancy that papacy which they claimed for themselves among you, so that, in short, kings could not reign except at their pleasure. Those who look with their eyes on present dangers, and who do not ignore who the authors of the evil intended are, will easily see that, even if all the subjects of both kingdoms could be persuaded to submit willingly to that burden which the Archbishop of Canterbury, with the faction devoted to him, would impose on us, and to acknowledge that we are bound to obey all the mandates of those spiritual fathers, yet they would at once look for some other foundation for their ambitious greatness than zeal for the most serene king and his honour. And kings in later times would learn by experience that all these labours were undertaken for their own private advantage, in order to establish their tyranny over the king as well as over the subjects.

units.la: Etenim non putamus esse quempiam usque adeo ignarum, aut sponte cæcutientem, qui credet, omnem illam rabiem & malitiam qua in Scotorum fœdus feruntur, esse, quia regis potestatem vere diminuit, aut saltem hostibus proponit regis impotentiam; nam fi ita fe res haberet, Pontifex Romanus & Hispaniarum rex multis auri millionibus idem in Anglia & Hibernia redimerent; Non est quod diutius dissimulent; fatis novimus ubi constringantur, Dei quippe manum exertam in nostro fœdere aperte conspiciunt, contra injustam quam exercuerunt tyrannidem, & pompam suam mundanam; ac verentur, ne, ficuti experti sunt fœdus illud esse instar muri ahe-nei, subditis Scotiæ contra malignam suam ra-biem, quando nullam defensionem obtinere potuerunt nec in legibus nec in suo rege (in cujus tamen gratia specialem locum sibi deberi putant) verentur (dicimus) ne ejus exemplo alibi periculum sibi creetur, metuuntque ne simul ac semel infœlicem exitum tandem sortiantur omnes artes quibus religionem reformatam subvertere conantur. Atque hæc unica causa est cur tum fœdus illud tum nos tot atrocibus calumniarum & criminibus arcessant, ut fcil. odium nostri & causæ hujus aliorum animis insculpant, sicut ipsis hactenus impressum est. Nobis tamen abunde persuasum, Amplissimum vestrum tribunal pro. fota sua prudentia, justitia, æquitate nunquam judicaturum, sufficientem esse inter has duas gentes controversiæ causam; quod nos instemus ut nostris legibus vivere, & religionis nostræ exercitio frui nobis liceat, nam fi ob hanc causam quilibet vestræ gentis nos invadet, aut regni vestri vires & potentia in nos vertantur; inique certe non tulisse-tis, neque vos ulla à nobis injuria affectos fuisse judicassetis, si idem nos præstitissemus, quando controversiæ & disputationes de jure & privilegiis subditorum, fuissent inter serenissimum regem & vos in parlamento vestro congregatos: Verum sicut fœlicia omnia vestris parlamentis semper vovimus, ita non judicamus, labores à nobis susceptos & exantlatos ad nostra privilegia defendenda, vobis posse esse gravamina, aut res mali exempli ad vestrum regnum debilitandum; neque vos in nostram perniciem concitare posse.
units.tr: For we do not think there is anyone so ignorant, or so willingly blind, as to believe that all that rage and malice with which they assail the covenant of the Scots is because it has truly diminished the king's power, or at least displays the king's impotence to his enemies. For if that were the case, the Roman Pontiff and the king of Spain would gladly buy the same thing in England and Ireland for many millions of gold. There is no need for them to dissemble any longer; we know well where they are pinched. For they clearly see the hand of God stretched out in our covenant, against the unjust tyranny they have exercised and their worldly pomp; and they fear lest, just as they have found that covenant to be like a brazen wall to the subjects of Scotland against their malignant rage, when they could obtain no defence either in the laws or in their own king (in whose favour they nevertheless think a special place is owed to them), so by its example danger may be created for them elsewhere; and they fear that all the arts by which they strive to overthrow the reformed religion may at length meet an unhappy end at once. This is the sole cause why they assail that covenant and us with so many atrocious calumnies and charges: namely, to engrave hatred of us and of this cause on the minds of others, as it has hitherto been impressed on their own. Yet we are fully persuaded that your most distinguished tribunal, in all its prudence, justice and equity, will never judge that the cause of controversy between these two nations is sufficient, namely that we insist on living under our own laws and enjoying the exercise of our religion. For if on this account any man of your nation should attack us, or the strength and power of your kingdom should be turned against us, you would certainly not have borne it unjustly, nor would you have judged yourselves wronged by us, if we had done the same when disputes and controversies about the right and privileges of subjects had arisen between the most serene king and you, gathered in your Parliament. Indeed, just as we have always wished every happiness for your Parliaments, so we do not judge that the labours we have undertaken and endured to defend our privileges can be grievances to you, or a matter of bad example tending to weaken your kingdom; nor can they stir you up to our destruction.

units.la: Principes malefanis consiliis abrepti facile pro arbitrio bella concitant, sed cum subditorum sanguine controversia definienda sit, necesse esse ut pericula subeuntibus & damna, cognita sit belli causa: & quandoquidem civilia bella & domesticæ discordiæ, ut interni morbi, difficilius curantur externis; omni opera providendum, ne excitentur: Cumque satis ex prædictis constet, primarios turbarum harum authores in id omnem operam posuisse, ut nos inter nos committerent, tanto magis nostri muneris erit nosmet conservare, ita ut illi frustrentur, & apposito & opportuno remedio nostræ & posterorum saluti consulatur.
units.tr: Princes, carried away by wicked counsels, can easily stir up wars at their pleasure. But since the dispute must be settled with the blood of subjects, those who undertake the dangers and losses must first know the cause of the war. Civil wars and domestic discords are, like internal diseases, harder to cure than external ones, so every effort must be made to prevent them from breaking out. Since it is sufficiently clear from what has been said that the chief authors of these troubles have laboured to set us against one another, it will be all the more our duty to preserve ourselves, so that their schemes are defeated and our own safety and that of our posterity is secured by a timely and suitable remedy.

units.la: Aptissimum porro & expeditissimum quod nobis nunc occurrit, remedium est, ut sicut cum de regnorum unione olim ageretur, quæ non successit, utrumque parlamentum conveniebat, & deputatos delegabat qui de ea agerent; (cum expressa clausula reservationis legum & privilegiorum) qui rationem reddituri erant eorum in quibus conveniretur, iis à quibus deputabantur: Ita nunc cum utraque gens in cruentum bellum protrudatur, ad utriusque libertatis eversionem, nihil est quod magis in votis habeamus, quam ut sereniff. rex dignaretur idem aut simile quidpiam decernere, quo libere & fine violentiae metu convenire possint parlamenta quae per deputatos suos locum & tempus definient, ubi diligenti adhibto examine in aequitatem & iniquitatem nostrorum postulatorum plene inquiratur, ne falsis & fictis relationibus diutius premamur; utque liquido constet qualia sint quae petimus, eorumque fraus & hypocrisis (si quae sit) aperiatur, nullum subterfugiemus examen quod cum jure regni hujus liberi & independentis consistat, aut quod vos, in tali casu de controversis vestris legibus & privilegiis, rege apud nos haerente, non recusaretis.
units.tr: The most fitting and speediest remedy that now occurs to us is this: just as when the union of the kingdoms was once under discussion, which did not succeed, both parliaments met and appointed deputies to deal with it, with an express clause reserving the laws and privileges, and these deputies were to give an account of what was discussed to those by whom they were chosen. So now, since both nations are being driven into a bloody war, to the overthrow of the liberty of each, there is nothing we desire more than that his most serene Majesty would deign to decree the same, or something similar, so that the parliaments may meet freely and without fear of violence, at a place and time fixed by their deputies. There, with careful examination, the justice and injustice of our demands may be fully inquired into, so that we are not burdened longer by false and fabricated reports; and so that it may be clearly established what it is that we seek, and their fraud and hypocrisy (if there is any) may be laid bare. We shall shrink from no examination that is consistent with the law of this free and independent kingdom, or that you yourselves would not refuse in such a case, concerning your own laws and privileges, with the King remaining among us.

units.la: Ob quem finem si regis exercitus dimitteretur, neque novi milites interim colligerentur, lubenter nostros exercitus dimittemus, & ab omni apparatu bellico quem in justam & necessariam noftram defensionem comparamus, supersedebimus, quod alia conditione praestare non possumus sine probabili nostra ruina: neque poterit alterutrum parlamentorum commode convenire, si deputati districtum ensem capitibus suis imminere conspexerint. Neque dubitamus quin Parlamento vestro haec arridebunt, ut aequa, imo ut minima quae facile concedi possunt, seque nobis in hac nostra supplici ad regem petitione adjungat ut coram Deo & mundo liberemini, quod armis nos devincere non fitis aggressi, priusquam rationibus conviceritis, omnibusque probis & veris Christianis notum feceritis & aequas ac necessarias belli causas esse.
units.tr: To this end, if the King's army were disbanded, and no new soldiers meanwhile raised, we would gladly disband our armies and lay aside all the warlike preparations which we are making for our just and necessary defence. We cannot grant anything on any other condition without probable ruin to ourselves. Nor can either parliament meet conveniently if its deputies see a drawn sword hanging over their heads. Nor do we doubt that these things will please your Parliament, as fair, nay, as the least things that can easily be granted; and that it will join us in this our humble petition to the King, so that you may be cleared before God and the world, in that you did not attack us with arms before you had convinced us by reason, and so that you may make known to all upright and true Christians that the causes of the war are just and necessary.

units.la: Si hoc nobis non concedatur, (quod metuimus, nam quid aliud exspectandum nobis est quam ut negotii hujus progressus principio respondeat, & sicuti in exterorum gratiam primitus excogitatum fuit, ita continuatum iri? ad insignem utriusque regni enervationem, religionis & civilis libertatis eversionem, si peries hostes nostros fuerit) tum, (ut finis hujus orationis praecedentia omnia breviter comprehendat) fatemur justum esse apud Deum ut cogamur tristes civilis discordiae calamitates praesentire, quia diuturna nostra pace abusi sumus; & ut curationis pericula subeamus, quia tam segni & diuturna conniventia vires addidimus noxio isti humori, qui nunc tam ecclesiae quam regni vitam ipsam tantum non se suffocaturum minatur. Non erit inopportunum antiquam suggerere paræmiam, quae vos summos Reipub. medicos nunc convocatos proprie tangit: Philotimus, Medicus Graecus, cuidam digitum suum curandum petenti, ex cujus vultu, visu, & anhelitu colligebat tabe laborare, sic respondit; Nequaquam te decet (amice) hoc temporis articulo de unguibus tuis tam sollicitum esse. Non ita pridem maxima quaestio inter vos fuerat, An libellus de illo aridorum & liquidorum vectigali, an vero de subditorum in bonis suis proprietate primum excuteretur; mutata sunt jam tempora, aliud est quod hodie in quaestionem trahi debet & excuti, Antequam de rebus quibuslibet sententiam dicatis, aut alios condemnetis, videndum erit an ipsi fitis liberi, & quod jus vobis ad vestra competit: Etenim si religionis nostrae & privilegiorum regni defensio ansam praebere possit controversiae inter duas gentes tam arcte conjunctas, & si sic visum fuerit nobilissimo & amplissimo vestro senatui, Ignoramus prorsus qua ratione vosmet ipsos absolvatis nobis condemnatis; & si olim conventus vestri gloria fuerit subditorum jura tueri, in infamiam vestram redundabit, si subversionem libertatis fratrum vestrorum nunc conemini.
units.tr: If this is not granted to us (which we fear, for what else can we expect than that the progress of this affair will answer its beginning, and, as it was first devised for the benefit of foreigners, so it will be continued to the notable enfeebling of both kingdoms, and the overthrow of religion and civil liberty, if it should fall out according to our enemies' wishes?), then, to sum up briefly all that has gone before, we confess that it is just before God that we should be compelled to foresee the sad calamities of civil discord, because we have abused our long peace; and that we should undergo the dangers of a cure, because by such sluggish and long-continued tolerance we have given strength to that harmful humour, which now threatens almost to suffocate the very life of the Church as well as of the kingdom. It will not be out of place to recall an old proverb, which applies directly to you, now summoned as the chief physicians of the commonwealth. Philotimus, a Greek physician, when a certain man asked him to treat his finger, and from his face, look and breathing gathered that he was suffering from a festering wound, replied thus: "It does not become you, my friend, to be so concerned about your nails at this critical moment." Not long ago the greatest question among you was whether the bill on that tax on dry and liquid goods should be examined first, or the bill on the property rights of subjects in their goods. Times have changed; another matter is now to be brought into question and examined today. Before you pass judgement on any matter whatever, or condemn others, it must be seen whether you yourselves are free, and what right belongs to you. For if the defence of our religion and of the privileges of the kingdom could furnish occasion for dispute between two nations so closely joined, and if it should seem good to your most noble and most ample Senate, we are utterly at a loss to see how you could acquit yourselves while condemning us. And if it was once the glory of your assemblies to protect the rights of subjects, it will redound to your infamy if you now strive for the subversion of the liberty of your brothers.

units.la: Si consilium hoc Scotiam bello aggrediendi, vere dignosceretur suggestum esse ab Hispania aut Roma, non ambigimus, quin vel pro privata vestra utilitate operam diligentem effetis[?] daturi, ut monstrum hoc in ipso foetu opprimeretur, nisi forte quidam vobis persuaserint, medium esse hoc aptissimum ad languorem vestrae Reipub. expellendum, & nobis injuriam inferendo, meliorem posse reddi vestram conditionem. Et licet nobis abunde constet, gravissimis vestris consultationibus fines nobiliores & honestiores semper propositos fuisse, detur tamen hos fines proponi, sed perpendendum an oblata utilitas damnum vestrum praestare possit? Non est quod hoc premamus; exemplum recens vobis ante oculos obversatur, Provinciae omnes & principes Galliae obliquis oculis protestantium conditionem aspiciebant, tribunalium forensium privilegia, & edictorum beneficia quibus fruebantur, singuli alios antevertere conabantur, ut in protestantium ruinam operam suam conferrent, ut gratos se rederent iis quibus istius negotii cura concredita fuit; Quo vero successu, sentiunt ipsi hodie, & quicunque eos intuetur satis videt quam tutelam sibimet ipsis reliquerint contra legiones praesidiarias. Sed haec intelligi nolumus, quasi de vestra prudentia in negotio tanti momenti & quod vos tam proprie tangit, dubitaremus, verum propter adversariorum nostrorum pertinacem malitiam nobis probe cognitam, quae eousque apud serenis. nostrum regem praevaluit, ut oblivi-scatur afflictionis populi sui quamdiu infinitae istorum malitiae cedit, qui nihil non agunt, ut dissecent vinculum illud obedientiae, quo ad legum religiosam obedientiam conscientia ossicii nostri cū nostri erga regem obligamur, quodque firmissimum est amplitudinis regiæ & vnionis regnorum fundamentum, & quod nos coronæ regiæ arctissime constrinxit, contra violentas temporum calamitates tot sæculis elapsis, ac contra adversariorum quorumlibet armatam violentiam: quod quanto nos impensius tueri ac defendere nitimur, tanto illi diligentius dirumpere satagunt, inque illius locum violentiæ catenam substituere.
units.tr: If it were truly established that this plan of attacking Scotland with war had been suggested from Spain or Rome, we do not doubt that you would, if only for your own private advantage, diligently exert yourselves so that this monster might be crushed in the very womb, unless perhaps certain men have persuaded you that this most suitable means of driving out the sickness of your commonwealth exists, and that by doing us injury your own condition can be made better. And although it is abundantly clear to us that in your most serious deliberations the purposes proposed have always been the nobler and more honourable, let us grant that these purposes are put forward; yet it must be weighed whether the advantage offered can outweigh the loss to yourselves. There is no need for us to conceal this. A recent example lies before your eyes: all the provinces and princes of France looked askance at the condition of the Protestants. Each tried to outdo the others in the privileges of the law courts and the benefits of the edicts which they enjoyed, so as to contribute their efforts to the ruin of the Protestants and to make themselves agreeable to those to whom the care of this business had been entrusted. What success they had, they themselves feel today, and anyone who looks at them can see well enough what protection they left for themselves against the garrison legions. But we do not wish these things to be understood as if we doubted your prudence in a matter of such weight, one which touches you so closely. Rather, we speak because of the stubborn malice of our adversaries, which we know well, and which has prevailed so far with our most serene King that he forgets the affliction of his people, so long as he yields to the endless malice of these men, who do everything to sever that bond of obedience by which we are bound to the King, in conscience of our duty, and by the duty of religious obedience to the laws. That bond is the firmest foundation of royal greatness and of the union of the kingdoms, and it has bound us most closely to the royal crown through so many centuries, against the violent calamities of the times and against the armed violence of any adversaries whatever. The more earnestly we strive to protect and defend it, the more diligently they labour to break it, and to put in its place a chain of violence.
