units.la: Rogamus itaque vos (Nobilissimi & DileCtissimi fratres in utraque domo parlamentaria nuuc coacti) ut pro officio & dignitate vestra, à nobismet ipsis accipere velitis vivam & veram gravaminum nostrorum repræsentationem; Atque cum illius catenæ annulus non possit non vos tangere, si nos primos contingat, obtestamur ut sereniss. nostrum regem tempestive divertatis ne in hæc præcipitia amplius proruat, quæ nihil aliud quam nunquam satis deflendam miseriam tam principi quam subditis tandem producent.
units.tr: We therefore beseech you (most noble and most beloved brothers, now gathered in both houses of Parliament) that, in keeping with your office and dignity, you be willing to receive from us ourselves a lively and true representation of our grievances. And since the ring of that chain cannot fail to touch you if it first reaches us, we entreat you to turn our most serene King aside in good time, so that he does not plunge further into these precipices, which can produce nothing but a misery never sufficiently to be lamented, for prince and subjects alike.

units.la: Atque quandoquidem justam metuendi causam habeamus, ne quod sine vestro consensu inchoatum est, sine vestro etiam consilio prosequantur, ad supremi vestri consessus justitiam nostro judicio proprie pertinet, providere, ne qui regi clementissimo authores fuerunt consilii hujus desperati, tam regi quam utrique regno noxii, impune evadant.
units.tr: And since we have just cause to fear that what was begun without your consent may be pursued without your counsel as well, it belongs properly, in our judgement, to the justice of your supreme assembly to take care that those who were the authors of this desperate counsel, harmful both to the King and to each kingdom, do not escape unpunished.

units.la: Præterea nunc accipimus deputatos nostros in custodiis traditos esse, alios scheriforum seu vicecomitum, alios eirenarcharum Londini, multum contra nostram spem; nam si illud vel conjecturis colligere potuissemus, nullum certe delegassemus; neque ullus fuisset qui in deputationem consentiisset: & contra jus gentium; nam duo distincta regna & gentes sumus, illiique delegati fuerunt à parlamento quod rex sereniss. promisit & indixit; regisque speciali mandato muniebantur, ut se illi sisterent, ac postulatorum nostrorum æquitatem ostenderent: Contra tractatus præsentis fundamenta, nam authoritate parlamentaria ex legum præscripto electi fuerunt quidam hic deputati, quos vocant Ane Comitte, idque necessario, ut cum nostris ad regem delegatis correspondentiam alerent, & ab iis regis sereniss. responsa transmissa reciperent; (ita quidem ut satis mirari nequeamus quemlibet esse tam absurdum qui regi suggerere ausit, Parlamento non licere hos deputatos seu Committe constituere, aut adeo impudentem, ut dicat hos regimen civitatis Edenburgenæ arripuisse) diu tamen est ex quo nihil seu verbo seu scripto ab illis nostris ad aulam deputatis acceperimus, & jam fere desperatum est, ne ulterius quidpiam ab ipsis posthac accipiamus; unde factum est ut prorsus ignoremus an in quopiam deficiant ipsorum propositiones, postulatorumque vindiciæ seu rationes, & an à nobis quidpiam supplendum fit quo regi sereniss. amplius satisfiat: Præterea traditio hæc nostrorum deputatorum in custodias, est contra ipsorum meritum: nihil etenim affertur ab iis commissum quod captivitatem istam mereatur: Nam præsens conditio
units.tr: Furthermore, we now learn that our commissioners have been thrown into prison, some into the custody of the sheriffs or viscounts, others into that of the justices of the peace of London. This is very much contrary to our hope. For had we been able to gather even by conjecture that it would happen, we would certainly never have appointed them, and no one would have consented to be appointed. It is also against the law of nations, for we are two distinct kingdoms and peoples, and they were sent by the parliament which the most serene king promised and summoned, and they were furnished with the king's special mandate to appear before him and to set forth the fairness of our demands. It is also against the foundations of the present treaty, for by parliamentary authority and according to the prescription of the laws there were chosen certain men here, whom they call the Ane Comitte, and this was necessary so that they might keep up correspondence with our envoys at the king's court and receive from them the replies sent by his most serene majesty. (We certainly cannot wonder enough that anyone should be so absurd as to dare to tell the king that Parliament may not appoint these commissioners or Committee, or so shameless as to say that they have seized the government of the city of Edinburgh.) Yet it is a long time since we have received anything, either by word or in writing, from those of our commissioners who are at court, and it is now almost despaired of that we shall receive anything further from them hereafter. The result is that we are entirely ignorant whether their proposals, or the defence and reasons of our demands, are deficient in any point, and whether anything must be supplied by us so that greater satisfaction may be given to the most serene king. Moreover, this handing over of our commissioners to prisons is contrary to their merit, for nothing has been alleged that they have committed which would deserve such captivity. For the present condition...

units.la: Comitis de Southefk, & D. Ludovici Steuarti, qui Edenburgi in salvo sunt, huic deputatorum nostrorum captivitati nullum justum fundamentum subminiftrare potest, quippe quod fereniff. regem illi ipsi per literas certiorem fecerint, quo modo innocens illa eorundem detentio subito evenerit, partim fcil. inexspectata imprudentiâ & temeritate gubernatoris arcis Edenburgenæ, minitantis post horum ex urbe difcelfum, fe tormenta arcis bellica contra urbem Edenburgum hostiliter emissurum, feque effecturum ut oppidani audirent insolitum campanarum sonum; (nam hac phrafi visum illi fuit loqui) partim etiam ipsorum præcipitato & celeriori (quam tales decebat) ex urbe discessu, quem aperte meditabantur, ut fe extra civitatis portas ad evitandum commune periculum proriperent: Vulgus interim (non fine suis rationibus) judicabat eorum intra urbem detentionem sibi futuram in tutelam aliqualem, aut gubernatoris furorem saltem procrastinaturam. Verum quam primum à vulgo comprehensi fuerant, à magistratu statim liberabantur, & à nobilibus in civitate tunc præfentibus humaniter accepti sunt, neque ab illa hora ulla vis iis illata fuit; & sponte ut suæ saluti consulerent in civitate remanserunt, ac in publicis compitis, templis, hortis aut ubi volunt, quanta libertate visum est, libere fruuntur. Quam denique ab omni æquitate alienum est, ut peculiaris tumultus paucorum ex unius civitatis vulgo, imputetur deputatis nostris, ab universo parlamenti corpore, totius gentis nomine, delegatis.
units.tr: ...of the Earl of Southesk and Mr Lewis Stewart, who are safe at Edinburgh, can provide no just ground for this captivity of our commissioners, since they themselves have informed the most serene king by letter how that innocent detention of the same men came about suddenly. It arose partly from the unexpected imprudence and rashness of the governor of the Edinburgh castle, who threatened that after these men's departure from the city he would hostilely launch the castle's artillery against the city of Edinburgh, and would make the townsfolk hear an unusual sound of bells (for he thought fit to speak in this figure). It arose partly also from the headlong and quicker departure of these men from the city (which was not becoming for such men), which they openly planned, so that they might hurry beyond the city gates to avoid the common danger. Meanwhile the common people, not without reason, judged that their detention within the city would be a kind of protection for them, or at least would hold back the governor's fury. But as soon as they were seized by the common people, they were at once released by the magistrate, and were received courteously by the nobles then present in the city; from that hour no violence has been done to them, and they remained in the city of their own accord to look to their safety, and they enjoy the freedom they wish in the public streets, churches, gardens, or wherever they please. Lastly, how far is it from all fairness that the private tumult of a few of the common people of one city should be imputed to our commissioners, who were sent by the whole body of Parliament in the name of the whole nation!

units.la: Verum dum hæc scribimus, certiores facti sumus, rem hanc altius difcendere Dom. Lowdonium arcis Londinenfis custodiæ comiffum esse, neque ob levem aliquem prætextum, ut ejus cuftodia aliorum hic comprehensorum saluti consulatur, sed ob suum ipsius gravem reatum: utpote quod deprehensum sit, illum chirographo & subscriptione obsignasse epistolam directam ad regem Gallicum à quibusdam Comitibus & Baronibus parlamentariis Scotiæ, qua ipsius opem implorant. Atq; hoc ab adversariis nostris, qui ruivam nostram antehac conjurarunt, vehementer exaggeratum est, & in montem quasi ingentem amplificatum, qui non solum obruet D. Lowdonium & socios epistolam obsignantes, verumetiam ut omnes nostri amici, & qui æquioribus oculis causam nostram intuebantur, eandem nunc rejiciant, quasi vel hoc unico argumento satis proderemus, nihil minus religione à nobis intendi.
units.tr: But while we are writing these things, we have been informed that this matter is being looked into more deeply: Lord Loudoun has been committed to the custody of the Tower of London, not on any slight pretext, so as to safeguard by his custody the others here seized, but on account of his own grave offence. It has been discovered that he signed, with his hand and seal, a letter addressed to the French king by certain earls and barons of the Scottish parliament, in which they implore his aid. This has been vehemently exaggerated by our adversaries, who had earlier conspired for our ruin, and magnified into a mountain, as it were, so immense that it will not only overwhelm Lord Loudoun and the associates who signed the letter, but will also make all our friends, and those who look upon our cause with fairer eyes, now reject it, as though by this single argument we had sufficiently shown that we pursue nothing less than religion.

units.la: Sed Honoratissimus & Amplissimus Parlamenti confessus, cui cognitæ sunt artes & improba adversariorum nostrorum malitia, cuique innocentia nostra mensibus præteritis penitus incognita esse nequit, pro singulari prudentia & gravitate qua pollet, judicium suum contra nos & integram nostram gentem, propter visam aut auditam ejusmodi epistolam non præcipitabit, priusquam audiamur. Quare ut vobis satisfiat, & nos vindicemur, inviti certe cogimur in memoriam nunc revocare, & oculis subjicere ipsa formalia verba inusitati illius edicti regii, dati Eboraci. 25 Aprilis 1639. perpetuo alias silentio supprimendi; quod edictum absit ut clementissimo & serenissimo nostro regi imputemus, sed infami barbarorum nostrorum hostium crudelitati: Sic autem se habent illius edicti verba.
units.tr: But the most honourable and most distinguished Confession of Parliament, which knows the arts and the wicked malice of our adversaries, and which cannot be wholly ignorant of our innocence in past months, will not, in its singular prudence and gravity, rush to a judgement against us and our whole nation on account of a letter seen or heard of in this way, before we are heard. Therefore, so that you may be satisfied and we may be vindicated, we are, though reluctantly, compelled to recall to memory and set before your eyes the very formal words of that unusual royal edict, given at York on 25 April 1639, which had otherwise been kept in perpetual silence; and far be it from us to impute that edict to our most merciful and most serene king, rather than to the infamous cruelty of our barbarous enemies. The words of that edict run as follows.

units.la: Ad violentiorem & acriorem medicinam recurrere & hanc istorum pervicaciam & rebellionem justitiæ gladio sanare cogimur. Quare eo casu viz.si gratiam hanc oblatam rejecerint, & ante octo dierum tempus præfinitum, civilem & legitimam nobis debitam obedientiam non exhibeant, promulgamus omnes & singulos posthac, apertos rebelles, perduelles ; læsæ majestatis reos, & omnia ipsorum prædia, agros, bona mobilia & immobilia fisco nostro addicta esse, quæ in nobiles, & alios nobis fideles subditos, æquisque nostris mandatis morigeros conferemus. Atque in hunc finem interdicimus vasallis ac villicis horum rebellium, ne dominis suis rebellibus reditus, emolumenta & servitia consueta persolvant, sed mandamus ut penes se omnia reservata detineant, alteram quidem semissem prose[?], nobis vero alteram tradituři; quod si rebellium horum villici, defertis dominis suis, ad tuendam nostram authoritatem se nobis adjunxerint, pollicemur insuper beneficè vos cum ipsis transfacturos, ac prædia in plures annos elocaturos, remissa ad minimum triente redituum qui rebellibus dominis persolvi consueverunt : prout experiemur ipsorum merita & paratam obedientiam. Vasallis etiam rebellium dominorum promittimus, nostras immediatos futuros vasallos, & tricesimam feudi quod nunc solvere tenentur, remissuros, modo nobis adhærent, neque rebellibus suis dominis parerent. Quod si in fidelitate & obedientia nostra permanserint dominis, cujus vasalli & villici perduelles sint, & hanc nostram gratiam rejiciunt, neque nobis aut dominis suis pro nobis militantibus adesse voluerint, Declaramus licere dominis illis, rebelles istos vasallos seu clientes fiduciarios, & villicos ex agris & prædiis extrudere : & quicquid publicatione eorum prædiorum nobis accreverit, illud totum resignarimus, & liberâ donatione utendum fruendum concedimus dominis fidelibus, quibus opem nostram imperdemus ut concesso hoc beneficio fruantur. Interdicimus etiam ne, qui ære alieno rebellium tenentur, illud ejusve quemlibet partem rebellibus creditoribus persolvant, & nostris mandatis obtemperantibus reperiendis non decrimus [?], pro singulorum meritis. & cæt.
units.tr: We are compelled to have recourse to a more violent and sharper remedy, and to cure this obstinacy and rebellion of theirs by the sword of justice. Wherefore, in that case, namely if they reject this offered grace, and do not render the civil and lawful obedience due to us before the eight days' period appointed, we proclaim all and each of them henceforth open rebels, traitors, and guilty of high treason, and all their estates, lands, movable and immovable goods are adjudged to our treasury, which we shall confer upon nobles and other subjects loyal to us and obedient to our commands. And to this end we forbid the vassals and stewards of these rebels to pay their lords, who are rebels, the rents, profits and customary services, but we command them to keep all these reserved in their own hands, delivering one half to [?] and the other half to us; and if the stewards of these rebels, deserting their lords, have joined themselves to us in defending our authority, we further promise to deal kindly with them, and to lease the estates for several years, remitting at least a third of the revenues that were customarily paid to the rebel lords, as we shall judge of their merits and ready obedience. To the vassals of rebel lords also we promise that they shall be our immediate vassals, and that we shall remit the thirtieth part of the fief which they are now bound to pay, provided they adhere to us and do not obey their rebel lords. But if they remain in fidelity and obedience to us, though their lords whose vassals and stewards are traitors reject this our grace, and will not be with us or with their lords who are serving us, we declare that it is lawful for those lords to eject these rebel vassals or fiduciary clients and stewards from the fields and estates; and whatever shall have accrued to us from the confiscation of those estates, we resign and grant wholly to be used and enjoyed as a free gift by the faithful lords, to whom we shall extend our aid so that they may enjoy this benefit granted. We also forbid that those who are bound by debt to rebels should pay that debt, or any part of it, to the rebel creditors; and to those who obey our commands we shall not decree [?], according to the merits of each... etc.

units.la: Licet antehac à nostratibus extra patriam hærentibus sæpius accepissemus, plurimum admirari alios reges, & respub. nihil à nobis fieri quoipsis causæ nostræ æquitas, rerum status, ac præsens conditio innotescere posset, præsertim cum omnium aures obrutæ essent informationibus contra nos: Quia tamen sperabamus frequentibus nostris supplicibus libellis tandem aliquando responsum iri, prorsus abstinuimus. Verum cum insperato illo edicto spes nostra prorsus exstincta esset, sicut domi ad justam & necessariam nostram defensionem nos armavimus, ita deliberabamus non inconsultum futurum si foras causæ nostræ vindicationem & postulata ad regem humillima emitteremus, præsertim vero ad regem Gallicum, quo facto confidimus nihil nobis excidisse quod iram regis nostri in nos merito provocet, aut quod adversetur fidelium subditorum officio: imo ab ulla gente ad tam extremas angustias redacta nihil minus dici potuisse: Consultatio tamen hæc omnis instar imperfecti embrionis fuit, utpote quod ad eam maturitatem nunquam pervenerit, qua ab aliis conspiceretur: Nobis tam severe comminatis, & minarum executione præsente per ingentem exercitum imminente, an æquum est ut nobis tanquam inexpiabile crimen imputetur, ac in nostros deputatos animadverratur, quod scil. ausi fuerimus cogitare de aliis advocandis, utpro nobis intercederent, præsertim cum supplices nostri libelli & humillimæ ac submissæ preces ad regem rejicerentur. O nos terque quaterque miseros! quos flagellari & miseris modis contundi oportet; sed nec resistere, nec queri deceat. Enixe itaque rogamus ut quicunque[?] oculos conjecturi sint in innocentem illam epistolam, eodem etiam intuitu oculos conjiciant in edictum illud tum in Anglia promulgatum, eaque sibi invicem comparet. Monendi insuper sumus, quid tali casu nobis nunc faciendum erit, & cum in nos movent exercitus hostiles, an nobis non liceat Deum & homines in auxilium vocare, ut apud regem nostrum pro nobis intercedant?
units.tr: Although we have often heard from our countrymen living abroad that other kings and commonwealths wonder greatly that nothing has been done by us to make known the fairness of our cause, the state of affairs and our present condition, especially since everyone's ears were deafened by reports against us, we nevertheless hoped that our frequent humble petitions would at last receive an answer, and so we refrained entirely from speaking. But when that unexpected edict destroyed our hope completely, we armed ourselves at home for our just and necessary defence. We then decided it would not be unwise to send abroad a vindication of our cause and our humble demands to the king, especially to the French king. By doing so, we trust that nothing has escaped us that would justly provoke the anger of our king against us, or that is contrary to the duty of loyal subjects. Indeed, no people reduced to such extreme distress could have said less. Yet all this deliberation was like an imperfect embryo, since it never reached the maturity by which it could be seen by others. We have been threatened so severely, and the execution of those threats is imminent through a huge army now present. Is it fair, then, that we should be charged with an inexpiable crime, and our deputies punished, merely because we dared to think of summoning others to intercede on our behalf, especially when our petitions and our humble and submissive prayers were rejected by the king? O us, miserable three and four times over! We must be scourged and battered in wretched ways, yet it is not fitting for us either to resist or to complain. We therefore earnestly ask that whoever casts his eyes on that innocent letter should also cast his eyes on that edict published in England, and compare the two. We must further be told what we are now to do in such a case, and, since hostile armies are moving against us, whether it is not lawful for us to call on God and men for help, so that they may intercede with our king on our behalf.

units.la: Epistola etiam illa scripta fuit ante regis sereniss. in castra adventum, neque illam nobiles nostri ceularunt; verum rem totam nobilibus quibusdam primariæ dignitatis in castris regiis ingenue & candide significarunt, quare si unquam apud se statuissent hostes nostri, ut bona fide pacificationis articuli observarentur, epistola hæc licet missa fuisset, imo quicquid hujus generis excogitari poterit, oblivionis perpetuæ lege sepeliendum esset, neque poterit esse justum cujuslibet actionis contra obsignatores post pacificationem fundamentum, quin contra in improbum sycophantam & nequissimum delatorem, ut turbatæ pacis publicæ reum severe animadvertendum fuisset. Interim ne probo cuilibet scrupulus ullus posthac hæreat, bona fide subjungimus ipsa formalia verba instructionis seu mandatorum tunc obsignatorum quæ adhuc extant, & ad quæ epistola illa se refert, quæque committenda fuerant, designato illius epistolæ latori; sed numquam tradita.
units.tr: That letter was also written before the most serene king came to the camp, and our nobles did not conceal it. Rather, they openly and candidly made the whole matter known to certain nobles of high rank in the royal camp. Therefore, if our enemies had ever resolved to observe the articles of the pacification in good faith, then even though this letter was sent, and indeed whatever of this kind might be devised, it ought to be buried under the law of perpetual oblivion. Nor can there be any just basis for any action against the signatories after the pacification. On the contrary, the disturber of public peace, the shameless informer and most wicked accuser, ought to be severely punished. Meanwhile, so that no scruple may henceforth stick in any honest mind, we add in good faith the very formal words of the instructions or mandates then signed, which still survive, and to which that letter refers. These were to be entrusted to the designated bearer of the letter, but were never handed over.

units.la: Ostendetur vetus & arctissimum illud fœdus inter duo regna Galliæ & Scotiæ, sæpius renovatum & inviolabiliter observatum per complures annorum centurias, quo factum est ut alterutra gentium ad angustias redacta mutuæ amicitiæ officia & parata auxilia opportune experta fit, quod mutuæ nationalium officiorum vicissitudines in annalibus & publicis utriusque regni registris satis testantur.
units.tr: It will be shown that there was an ancient and very close covenant between the two kingdoms of France and Scotland, often renewed and inviolably observed over many centuries of years. As a result, each nation, when reduced to straits, has tested the offices of mutual friendship and ready aid at the right time, as the exchanges of mutual national services in the annals and public records of both kingdoms sufficiently attest.

units.la: Item, Conatus nostros nullatenus unquam adversatos fuisse aut adversari Monarchico regimini: quin contra sereniss. & clementiss. nostro regi fidelissimos nos esse subditos, ad cujus personam, honorem, & authoritatem defendendam, vitam & fortunas nostras lubenter exposituros. Neque humillima nostra postulata alia esse, quam ut nostra religio, & libertates tam ecclesiasticae quam civiles frequentibus legibus regni & ecclesiae sancitae, conserventur. Declarabitur, calumniis ab hostibus nostris in privatos suos fines excogitatis, & contra nos dispersis, fidem nullam adhibendam esse; cum sint splendidissima mendacia, improbe conficta ut nos in immeritum odium trahant apud vicinos reges, regna, & respublicas, Cum tamen ipsa animorum nostrorum consilia, verba, actiones, & conatus legitimi sint, quod peculiari & fusa deductione ostendere poterit qui praesentes has tradet.
units.tr: Likewise, that our endeavours have never in any way been opposed, or are opposed, to monarchical government; on the contrary, we are most loyal subjects of our most serene and most merciful king, for whose person, honour and authority we would gladly expose our lives and fortunes. Nor are our humble demands other than that our religion and our liberties, both ecclesiastical and civil, be preserved, as they have been sanctioned by the frequent laws of the kingdom and the Church. It will be declared that no faith should be placed in the calumnies which our enemies have devised for their own private ends and spread against us. They are most splendid lies, shamelessly fabricated to draw us into undeserved hatred among neighbouring kings, kingdoms and commonwealths. Yet the very counsels, words, actions and endeavours of our minds are lawful. This the person who delivers these presents will be able to show by a particular and full account.

units.la: Atque quandoquidem sereniss. nostrum regem toties frustra obsecrati fuerimus, rogandum[?] esse Galliae regem ut apud sereniss. nostrum regem intercedere dignaretur, in eum finem, ut exercitus quos contra nos colligit, & quos in nos movet, dimittat rex serenissimus & antiquo suo ac nativo suo regno suis legibus vivere, religione ac privilegiis sub authoritate regia pacifice frui permittat: licet confidamus Deum nobis praesenti auxilio affuturum, quandocunque in nostram tutelam nosmet armare cogemur, quam lex Dei, Naturae, Gentium probant.
units.tr: And since we have so often and so vainly entreated our most serene king, we must ask the king of France to deign to intercede with our most serene king, to the end that His Serene Majesty may dismiss the armies which he is raising against us and moving upon us, and may permit us to live under our own laws in our ancient and native kingdom, and to enjoy our religion and privileges peacefully under royal authority. Yet we trust that God will be present to help us, whenever we are forced to arm ourselves for our protection, as the law of God, of nature and of nations approves.

units.la: Adversarii nostri, qui omnes nobis laedendis occasiones & praetextus sollicite quaerunt, & avide arripiunt; satis hic habent quo ingenium suum exerceant, & se solentur. Verum cum prudens ille & magnus vester senatus in animum revocabit, nunquam fuisse missam epistolam illam, neque quidpiam vel ex Galliis vel ex Scotia nostra proferri posset, quo probetur transmissam fuisse: Scriptam insuper fuisse post durum illud edictum, & ante initam pacificationem, ideoque aeternis oblivionis tenebris sepeliendam esse; Munitam & circumscriptam etiam fuisse ejusmodi mandatis seu instructionibus; quas sola carpet malitia; (nullis quippe ab Anglia minis aut speciosis apparatibus bellicis eo unquam deducemur, ut peregrinorum auxilia advocemus, ita ut separari à se invicem possint hæc duo regna) Cum hæc serio perpender prudens vester senatus, certo speramus non observatum iri ullam aliam justam materiam quæ hostibus solatio, & nobis dolori & pudori esse possit, quam quæ in præcedentibus nostris actionibus suppeditetur, & ut diligenter, sine partium studio excutiantur, unice rogamus.
units.tr: Our adversaries, who anxiously seek and eagerly seize every occasion and pretext for injuring us, have here enough to exercise their wit and to console themselves. But when that wise and great senate of yours considers in its mind that this letter was never sent, and that nothing could be produced either from France or from our Scotland to prove that it was sent; that it was written after that harsh edict and before the pacification was entered into, and therefore ought to be buried in the eternal shadows of oblivion; that it was also fenced about and limited by such mandates or instructions, which only malice will carp at (for we shall never be brought, by any threats from England or by any show of military preparations, to the point of calling in foreign aid, so that these two kingdoms could be separated from one another): when the wise senate of yours weighs these things seriously, we certainly hope that no other just cause will be seized upon that could bring comfort to our enemies and grief and shame to us, beyond what is supplied in our previous actions. We earnestly ask only that these be examined diligently and without partisan zeal.

units.la: Nunc vero licet ad innocuam nostram defensionem nos paremus, contra extremam istam adversariorum nostrorum & protervam arrogantiam, quæ indies magis & magis excrescit & exulceratur, ac pro ipsorum arbitrio tandem erumpet, licet in hoc intenti simus ut æquissima nostra postulata toties humiliter oblata tandem obtineamus, nihilominus sola necessitas quæ legem non habet, ultra supplicationum & defensionis terminos nos protrudet. Cumque ad necessitatem illam redigemur, (quod Dominus pro misericordia sua in utrumque regnum avertat) speramus nos factis ipsis hostium calumnias refutaturos, ac re ipsa demonstraturos, nos nostra commoda non quærere: verum omnium in Anglia auxilio quibus sua ipsorum propria & nostra fœlicitas cordi est, regem nostrum serenissimum impensius & majori cum fructu obsecrare, ut tandem se vere edoceri patiatur, ac subjicere tam omnia quæ in controversiam vocantur, quam improbos istos consiliarios (qui fundamenta ipsa ecclesiæ, regni, & dignitatis regiæ concusserunt) judicio & censuræ liberi parlamenti.
units.tr: Now, although we prepare ourselves for our harmless defence against the extreme and insolent arrogance of our adversaries, which grows and festers more and more each day and will at last break out at their pleasure, we are nevertheless intent on obtaining at last our most just demands, which we have so often humbly offered. Still, necessity alone, which has no law, will push us beyond the limits of supplication and defence. And when we are reduced to that necessity (which the Lord in his mercy turn away from both kingdoms), we hope by our very deeds to refute the calumnies of our enemies, and to show in fact that we do not seek our own advantage. But with the help of all in England to whom their own happiness and ours is dear, we will beseech our most serene king more earnestly and with greater effect, that he may at last allow himself to be truly informed, and that all the matters now in dispute, as well as those wicked counsellors who have shaken the very foundations of the Church, the kingdom and the royal dignity, be subjected to the judgement and censure of a free parliament.

units.la: Quo facto certa nobis spes est propagandum iri Christi Domini nostri Evangelium, liberandum ab imminentibus periculis utrumque pariter regnum, regisque nostri clementissimi & serenissimi authoritatem & gloriam supra omnes suos majores auctum iri. Quae sola, sicuti in fines nobis propositum, ita Deum enixe & ingenue eadem omnes rogamus. Amen.
units.tr: When this is done, we have a certain hope that the Gospel of our Lord Christ will be propagated, that both kingdoms alike will be freed from impending dangers, and that the authority and glory of our most merciful and most serene king will be increased above all his predecessors. This alone we all earnestly and sincerely ask of God, as it is the one purpose set before us. Amen.

units.la: Sola gerit Scotus, quibus arma coerceat, arma.
units.tr: The Scot bears only arms, with which to restrain arms.

units.la: SImul etiam prodiit liber alius prolixior, paginas 128 continens, praeter prolixam praefationem ad parlamentum regni Angliae, cui titulus αὐτοκρατεῖς Laudensium: quo author Robertus Baillius Kilwinnini pastor probare nititur, factionem illam, cujus caput est Archiepiscopus Cantuariensis D. Gulielmus Laudus, ream esse aperti Papismi, Arminianismi, & Tyrannidis tam ecclesiasticae quam politicae: cujus breve compendium subjiciam, citatis ipsorum librorum paginis, ex quibus probationes desumptae sunt. Omnes porro illi libri vel habent Cantuariensem ipsum authorem, vel manifestum fautorem, & censura capellani sui approbatorem, quam praestare tenetur; & quam probare, multa sunt quae persuadeant; ut sunt, librorum illorum aperta defensio, auctorum non solum ab omni censura immunitas, verum etiam ad primarias dignitates evectio, scriptorum adversariorum suppressio, & graves poenae in authores qui contra hiscere audent, statutae. Syllogismo unico totum illum tractatum comprehendit author; qui sic se habet: Quicunque subditorum regis, publice promovent aut spargunt dogmata religioni reformatae, legibus regni Angliae fancitae, & legitimae subditorum libertati adversantia, non solum non sunt fovendi, sed in eos severe est animadvertendum: nam introductione novationum seu per armatam violentiam, seu per artes versutas, praesentis reipub. statu pertaesi, omnium turbarum & tumultuum qui novationes illas consequuntur, authores habendi sunt, nam quod est causa causae, est etiam causa causati: & ne quis putet mutationes illas regi fereniff. affcribendas esse: publicis edictis (ut illo de dissolutione Comitiorum Anglicorum anno 1628. & Iunii. 8. 1638. Septemb. 22. & Decemb. 18. ejusdem anni. 1638.) omnibus suis subditis perfuasissimum esse jubet, se nunquam consensurum in quamlibet religionis & receptorum dogmatum mutationem: & re ipsa ostendit, quando Septemb. 22. 1638. imperavit suo nomine renovari & obsignari confessionem ecclesiae Scoticae: qua singula papismi membra abjurantur. Sed Cantuariensis cum sua factione spargunt aperte & promovent dogmata adversantia religioni reformatae prout regni Angliae legibus sancita fuit; atque hujus probationem per tria generalia capita persequitur author: quae sunt Arminianismus, Papismus, & Tyrannis.
units.tr: At the same time another, longer book appeared, of 128 pages, besides a lengthy preface to the Parliament of England. It is titled The Absolute Rulers of the Laudians [αὐτοκρατεῖς]. In it the author, Robert Baillie, minister of Kilwinning, tries to prove that that faction, whose head is the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr William Laud, is guilty of open Popery, Arminianism, and tyranny, both ecclesiastical and political. I shall set out a brief summary of it, with the pages of their own books cited from which the proofs are drawn. Moreover, all those books either have the Canterbury archbishop himself as author, or have him as open supporter and as approver through the censorship of his chaplain, which he is bound to provide. There are many things that persuade one that this is so: the open defence of those books; the authors' complete immunity from any censure; their promotion to the highest dignities; the suppression of the writings of their opponents; and the severe penalties laid down against authors who dare to speak against them. The author sums up his whole treatise in a single syllogism, which runs as follows: Whoever among the king's subjects publicly promotes or spreads doctrines opposed to the reformed religion, to the laws of England as enacted, and to the lawful liberty of the subjects, must not only not be cherished, but must be severely punished. For whoever introduces innovations, whether by armed violence or by crafty arts, and who are weary of the present state of the commonwealth, must be held to be the authors of all the disturbances and tumults that follow such innovations; for what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of the thing caused. And lest anyone think that those changes are to be attributed to the most serene king, he commands by public edicts (such as that of the dissolution of the English Parliament in 1628, and those of 8 June, 22 September, and 18 December 1638) that all his subjects be fully persuaded that he will never consent to any change in religion or in the accepted doctrines. And he shows this in fact when, on 22 September 1638, he ordered in his own name that the Confession of the Scottish Church be renewed and sealed, in which each single element of Popery is abjured. But the Canterbury archbishop with his faction openly spreads and promotes doctrines opposed to the reformed religion as sanctioned by the laws of England. The author pursues the proof of this under three general heads: Arminianism, Popery, and tyranny.

units.la: De Arminianismo quid judicaverit beatae memoriae rex Iacobus 6. in declaratione contra Vorstium aperte testatur: ubi pag. 18. detestandas haereses, mature exstinguendas & ad inferos usque, unde manarunt relegandas esse dicit: Bertiumque afferentem, opinionem de Apostasia sanctorum non differentive à professione ecclesiae Anglicanae, mendacem pag. 15. gnaviter impudentem & ferrei oris. p. 12. vocat: & Arminium pag. 14. Deo inimicum, ejusque discipulos pestes, arrogantes, haereticos, αἱρέσεις, sectarios: quorum heterodoxias qui pacis gratia tolerandas judicarent, à Deo maledictionem, apud ecclesias omnes infamiam, & in repub. perpetuam distractionem procurare. pag. 15. Cujus opinionis ut & regnorum haeredem esse orthodoxum Carolum, contra maledicos susurros edicta recentia satis demonstrant. Arminianismum porro strenue promoveri à Cantuariensi & factione illa, probat, tum indirecte, quia hujus fautores nullo fere alio nomine celebres, neglectis orthodoxis singulari ejus commendatione regi fereniff. obtrufi, ad dignitates ecclesiasticas promoventur. v. g. in Scotia Maxwellus ad epifcopatum Roffenfem, Forbefius ad Edinburgenum, Syd-ferfius ad Brechinenfem, & inde ad Gallovidianum, Wedderburnus ad Dumblanenfem: ut de Anglia & Hibernia in quibus major eft ejus authoritas, taceam: quia in heterodoxias hujus manifefte reos non animadvertit, feverus alias in eos, quos cæremoniis ab hominibus inventis (ut nihil durius dicatur) non fatis æquos judicat, ita ut paftorum verbi ingentia agmina in orbem alio fub fole calentem cum familiis protrudat: quia celebres illas quæftiones de prædeftinatione cum annexis, meras logomachias, & inutilem verborum contentionem de rebus nullius fere momenti habet, in fufiori declarat. pag. 74. Quia fynodum nationalem Glafguenfem inter alia, & ob hoc fugillat, quod aufa fit paftores ob publicam eorum dogmatum defenfionem, & in iifdem pertinaciam deponere. pag. 16. Dein ad directam probationem defcendit, & ordine per univerfos quinque articulos. Primum & fecundum aperte in libro Appello Cæfarem apprtobato cenfura D. Whyti, poftea Elienfis epifcopi, tuetur Montacutius, licet fermento papiftico turgens, fingulari tamen Cantuarienfis commendatione ad Norwicenfem epifcopatum promotus: qui pag. 60. Doctrinam in fynodo Dordracena de prædeftinatione repetitam, defperatam vocat: Idem Montacutius in tertio & quarto. ibid. pag. 89. difertis verbis Arminianis fe jungit: & pag. 95. inter melioris notæ pontificios, & opinionem quam ecclefiæ Anglicanæ affingit de libero arbitrio nullum effe dicit al cujus momenti differentiam. Apoftafiam fanctorum idem Montacutius ex profeffo ibid. tuetur: & Chonæus in collectionibus Theologicis Cantuarienfi dedicatis & fæpius recufis, fidei plerophoriam irridet: pag. 82. & alibi. Sed longa difquisitione hic non eft opus; nam reos habemus confitentes, idque aperte.
units.tr: Concerning Arminianism, the late most blessed King James the Sixth openly bears witness in his declaration against Vorstius, where at page 18 he says that the detestable heresies must be quickly extinguished and banished to the depths from which they sprang; and he calls Bertius, who asserted an opinion on the apostasy of the saints that does not differ from the profession of the English Church, a liar (p. 15), vigorously shameless and of iron face (p. 12). He calls Arminius, at p. 14, an enemy of God, and his disciples pests, arrogant, heretics, heresies [αἱρέσεις], sectaries; and those who judged their heterodoxies to be tolerated for the sake of peace, he says, bring upon themselves God's curse, infamy among all the churches, and perpetual distraction in the commonwealth (p. 15). That the orthodox Charles is heir of the kingdoms in this opinion too, the recent edicts against slanderous whisperers sufficiently demonstrate. That Arminianism is vigorously promoted by the Canterbury archbishop and that faction, he proves both indirectly and directly. Indirectly, because its supporters, who are scarcely famous under any other name, are pushed forward by his singular recommendation to the most serene king, and are promoted to ecclesiastical dignities, while orthodox men are neglected. For example, in Scotland Maxwell to the bishopric of Ross, Forbes to that of Edinburgh, Sydserf to Brechin and thence to Galloway, Wedderburn to Dunblane. I say nothing of England and Ireland, where his authority is greater, since he does not notice those who are manifestly guilty of these heterodoxies, while he is severe toward those whom he judges (to say nothing harsher) insufficiently compliant with ceremonies devised by men, so that he drives great hosts of ministers of the Word into exile in a region that burns under another sun. He declares at greater length that those famous questions on predestination and their attendant matters are mere logomachies and a useless contention of words over things of almost no importance (p. 74). He censures the national Synod of Glasgow among other things, and for this reason, that it dared to depose ministers for publicly defending their doctrines and persisting in them (p. 16). Then he descends to direct proof, and in order through all five articles. Montagu defends the first and second openly in the book I Appeal unto Caesar, approved by the censure of Dr White, later bishop of Ely. Montagu, though swollen with popish leaven, was nevertheless promoted to the bishopric of Norwich by the singular commendation of the Canterbury archbishop. He calls the doctrine of predestination repeated in the Synod of Dort desperate (p. 60). The same Montagu joins himself in express words to the Arminians in the third and fourth articles (ibid., p. 89); and at p. 95 he says that, among the Papists of better repute, and the opinion that the English Church ascribes to free will, there is no difference of any consequence. The same Montagu professedly defends the apostasy of the saints in the same place; and Chonaeus, in the Theological Collections dedicated to the Canterbury archbishop and often reprinted, mocks the full assurance of faith (p. 82 and elsewhere). But there is no need here of a long inquiry, for we have the accused confessing, and that openly.

units.la: Papismum fovere, hæc (inquit) probant, quia omnia factionis hujus consilia tendunt ad henofin[?] inter Papismum & reformatam religionem, sed conditionibus usque adeo iniquis ut reformatis statio sua sit deserenda[?], ac schismatis & errorum venia petenda: aperte quidem postremum hoc nondum audent propalare; ex sequentibus tamen satis patebit & luce meridiana clarius demonstrabitur, hæc à petulanti convitio aut mendaci calumnia (quam nos ipsis inurere, de nobis conqueri possent) quam longissime abesse.
units.tr: That they favour Popery, he says, is proved as follows: all the counsels of this faction tend towards a union between Popery and the reformed religion, but on conditions so unjust that the reformed must abandon their station and beg pardon for schism and errors. Openly, indeed, they do not yet dare to proclaim this last point; yet from what follows it will sufficiently appear, and it will be shown more clearly than the noonday light, that these charges are as far as possible from a bitter insult or a lying calumny, such as they could bring against us, complaining of us.

units.la: Etenim, quia nullam hujus unionis spem concipere potuerunt quamdiu Reformatis persuasum esset, Pontificem Romanum esse Antichristum, ideo omnes ingenii & industriæ nervos intendunt, in id summo studio incumbentes, omnemque lapidem moventes, ut eundem ab hac infamia liberent, prout non ita pridem Shelfoordus peculiari tractatu de Antichristo aggressus est; & inter alia hanc habet sententiam, Papam non magis posse dici Antichristum quam Lutherus aut Calvinus, quos blasphemiæ & hæreseos, os impudens ibidem accusat; argumenta vero reformatorum doctorum, quibus contrarium manifesto demonstrant, & rationes firmissimas, quibus primorum reformatorum facta & scripta à calumniis vindicant, eorumque doctrinam stabiliunt, deliramenta & apocalypticas phrenesis, vocat Montacutius in Appello Cæsar. perstringens proculdubio oblique nervosissima argumenta Iacobi regis, in epistola illa monitoria vere aurea: & ne ullum omnino restaret vestigium Antichristianismi Papæ, Cantuariensis ipse (ut fatetur in oratione habita in Camera Stellata. pag. 32) propria sua manu delevit ex liturgia Anglica, vocem Sectæ Antichristianæ junctam Romanæ : ejusque loco Babylonicæ substituit, ne scil. pontificiis scandalo esset.
units.tr: For since they could conceive no hope of this union as long as the Reformed were persuaded that the Roman Pontiff is Antichrist, therefore they bend every nerve of their wit and industry, applying themselves to this with the greatest zeal and moving every stone, so as to free him from this infamy, just as not long ago Shelford attacked the matter in a special treatise on Antichrist; and among other things he holds this opinion: The Pope cannot be called Antichrist any more than Luther or Calvin, whom in the same place he accuses of blasphemy and heresy with an impudent mouth. But the arguments of the reformed teachers, by which they clearly demonstrate the contrary, and the most solid reasons by which they vindicate the deeds and writings of the first reformers from calumnies and establish their doctrine, Montagu in I Appeal unto Caesar calls ravings and apocalyptic frenzies, undoubtedly glancing obliquely at the most vigorous arguments of King James in that truly golden admonitory epistle. And so that no trace of the Antichristianism of the Pope should remain at all, the Canterbury archbishop himself (as he admits in his speech delivered in the Star Chamber, p. 32) erased with his own hand from the English liturgy the word Antichristian joined to Roman sect, and substituted in its place Babylonian, so that it might not be a scandal to the Papists.

units.la: De Pontifice Romano honorifice loquuntur: & ecclesiam Romanam sedem Petri, cui potentior principatus super omnes tribuendus est, Cantuarien. in relatione colloquii cum Iesuita nuper impressa & aucta. pag. 183. & 154. & 133. Montacutius in antidiatrib. pag. 51. & 116. in hac sede summi pontificatus apicem, & fontem sacerdotii esse. idem ibid. p. 158. à quo nisi successionem suam derivare posset præsens archiepiscopus Cantuariensis, quam misera esset ipsius conditio, inquit Poklingtonus, in altari Christiano. p. 50. & nisi successionem hanc ab ipsa sede Petri aut alterius Apostoli ostendere posset, non audiendus esset. Poklingtonus in libro cui titulus; Dies dominica non est habenda pro sabbato: atque hoc (inquit idem ibid.) est quod inter alia, episcopalis jurisdictioni nosmet submittere facit. Puritanismus est, inquit Montacut. Origin. p. 417. denegare titulum sanctitatis suæ pontifici Romano, etiamsi fuerit prodigium & propudium honestatis, & eundem aut similes titulos reprehendere, est phrenesis hominum solummodo phanaticorum. Pio & prudenti zelo imperatores quidam de equis descendentes venerationem iisdem pontificibus exhibuerunt. Montacutius in antidiat. pag. 40. imo eosdem adorarunt. ibid. pag. 158. ut [illegible, ~9 letters] Christi, ut Dei & hominum [illegible, ~8 letters] singularis illis debetur honor. ibid. pag. 166.
units.tr: They speak honourably of the Roman Pontiff, and the Canterbury archbishop, in his account of a conference with a Jesuit recently printed and enlarged (pp. 183, 154, 133), says that the Roman Church is the seat of Peter, to which a more powerful primacy over all must be ascribed. Montagu, in his Antidiatribe (pp. 51, 116), says that in this seat is the summit of the supreme pontificate and the fountain of priesthood. The same, ibid. p. 158, says that unless the present Archbishop of Canterbury could derive his succession from it, how wretched would be his condition at the Christian altar, says Pocklington (p. 50); and unless he could show this succession from the very seat of Peter or of some other Apostle, he would not be listened to. Pocklington, in the book entitled The Lord's Day is not to be held as the Sabbath, says (in the same place) that this is among other things what makes us submit ourselves to episcopal jurisdiction. To deny the title of holiness to the Roman Pontiff, says Montagu in Origines (p. 417), is Puritanism, even if he be a monster and a disgrace to honesty; and to find fault with that title or similar ones is the frenzy of fanatics only. Some emperors, with pious and prudent zeal, dismounted from their horses and paid reverence to the same pontiffs. Montagu in the Antidiatribe (p. 40) says that they even adored them (ibid., p. 158), as [illegible in scan] of Christ, as of God and men [illegible in scan]; singular honour is owed to them (ibid., p. 166).

units.la: Principatu, dominiis, facultatibus & omni quicquid nomine possessionum Petri venit, fruatur, utatur: modo alienam possessionem non invadat. ibid. pag. 95. Potestatem pontificis, in Galliis & Hispania regibus perutilem esse. Cantuarien. in relat. pag. 202. Si rex Angliæ subditis suis imperaret, ne quid ecclesiastici negotii in regnis suis sine Papæ authoritate decernerent, & ut quicquid sanxit, sanxeritve legis Apostolicæ authoritas, id legis loco sit, tenentur omnes obedire. ibid Montac. pag. 156.
units.tr: Let him enjoy and use the principality, dominions, faculties, and whatever else falls under the name of the possessions of Peter, provided he does not invade another's possession. ibid. p. 95. That the power of the pope is very useful to the kings of France and Spain. Canterbury, in the relation, p. 202. If the king of England commanded his subjects not to decree anything in ecclesiastical business in their kingdoms without the authority of the Pope, and that whatever the authority of the apostolic law has decreed or shall decree should count as law, they are all bound to obey. ibid. Montacute, p. 156.

units.la: De Cardinalatu & Cardinalibus, licet commen-
units.tr: Concerning the Cardinalate and the Cardinals, although

units.la: to patribus ignoto, honorifice sentit Montacut. in appar. pag. 56, & 57. Sibi plaudit, quod Cardinalem Baronium, virum in eminentissima dignitate constitutum, quam non solum eruditione, verumetiam singulari sanctitate & tantum non ascetica, merito quidem sua esset adeptus: nusquam nisi honorificentissime compellarit & Poklingtonus in altar. pag. 34. Baronium summis laudibus effert, ob jejunia, preces, charitatis opera, pietatem exemplarem, qui vanitatem omnem tam in verbis quam factis aspernaretur, episcopum vocat pium, & acriter perstringit adversarium contra sententiam: Itaque Poklingtono idolorum cultus quibus impensè deditus fuit hic cardinalis, nulla est vanitas: & crudeliter sævire in ecclesiam Dei & sponsam Christi, pietatis nomen apud eum meretur, non vero tyrannidis.
units.tr: he speaks honourably of the fathers, a matter unknown to... Montacute, in the appendix, pp. 56 and 57, congratulates himself that he has never addressed Cardinal Baronius, a man placed in the most eminent dignity, who had attained it by merit not only of learning but also of singular holiness and very nearly asceticism, except in the most honourable terms. And Poklington, in the altar, p. 34, extols Baronius with the highest praises for his fasting, prayers, works of charity, and exemplary piety, and says that he spurned all vanity in word and deed. He calls the bishop pious and sharply censures his opponent who held the contrary opinion. So to Poklington, the worship of idols to which this cardinal was excessively devoted is no vanity at all, and to rage cruelly against the Church of God and the spouse of Christ earns with him the name of piety, not of tyranny.

units.la: Quum animo tam amico ferantur in caput, & humeros hujus monstrosi corporis, non dubitandum, quin reliquum corpus honore affecturi sunt: ideoque eandem esse (afferunt) pontificiorum & reformatorum religionem; neque periculo vacare, si quis afferat (uti semper asseruit Anglicanæ ecclesiæ liturgia regnante Iacobo rege) Pontificiam religionem esse rebellionem. Cantuar. in relatione colloquii. pag. 36. & in oratione in Camera Stellata pag. 36. Protestantium ecclesiam non fecisse secessionem ab ecclesia Romana, in qua adhuc sint omnia ad salutem necessaria, & quæ adhuc omnia habeat quæ ad ecclesiæ essentiam necessaria requiruntur. Potterus in vindicatione charitatis ecclesiæ reformatæ. pag. 66. & si qui longius progressi sunt & acrius perstrinxerunt illam ecclesiam; zelotas esse prudentia & charitate destitutos idem. pag. 74. Hinc reformationis opus per Lutherum deplorandum schisma vocat Cantuariens. Controversias in quibus à fe invicem hæ ecclesiæ differunt, tales non esse quæ alterutrius partis salutem impedire possint, cum non sint fundamentales. les. Heilens. in responso contra Burton. pagin. 124. & licet pontificiæ ecclesiæ errores essent fundamentales, cum tamen esset aliarum quas tuetur fundamentalium veritatum efficaciam, ut instar antidoti, admixta errorum venena hebetent. Iosephus Hallus Exonienf. episcopus in veteri religione prope initium, & Butterfeildius in ejus vindiciis. Qui profitentur se Iesum Christum diligere, licet fundamentalibus errent, fratres tamen orthodoxis esse, & salvari posse. Potterus. Vbi supra pag. 109. & ne quis existimaret hæc dici de iis solum qui in ecclesia Romana vixerunt ante reformationem, extendit idem Potterus, ad hodierna tempora, & nunc bene sperandum de omnibus qui simplicitate cordis seducti, Romanam fidem profitentur, in ejusque professione moriuntur, pag. 77: Non sine insigni injuria Pontificios accusari idololatriæ, hæreseos, aut schismatis: Idololatriæ, cum cultum λατρείας creaturis non tribuant. Shelfoordus. pag. 300. Montacut. in apparat. pag. 79. & in Originib. 309. quo factum est, ut Cantuariensis ex liturgia jejunii recepta, expungi curaverit vocem idololatriæ, qua submersi jacuisse dicebantur majores nostri in ecclesia Romana. Dowus in responf. contra Burtonum. pag. 142. hæreseos injuste accusari, cum non peccent in defectu, sed excessu. Potterus. pag. 102. Sic & schismatis, cum per omnia Romanam fidem integerrime profiteantur, Montacut. in appar. 283. à schismate liberos esse & hæresi coram Deo, quia errores, si quos fovent, ipsi non invenerunt, neque primi excogitarunt. Cantuariensis relat. colloq. pag. 316. Schismaticos potius habendos, Scaligerum, Parcum, & alios optimatores, qui contempto spretoque majorum consensu phreneticas suas observationes obtrudunt. Montacut. in appar. pag. 389. Itaque nihil impedire quin in unam coëant ecclesiam papistæ & protestantes, nisi insana intemperies furiosorum quorundam zelotarum obstaret (Iesuitae videlicet & Puritani) qui pharisaica sua instituta in Christianismum revocarunt, quorum utrosque Montacut. in apparat. pag. 245. pietatis vocat carcinomata, Christianismi debonestamenta, pacis & concordiae alastoras & pernicies. Quam miris contra elogiis ornat idem ibid. pag. 45. Cassandrum ipsissimam probitatis & modestiae animam: dolet tam male ab importuno censore Calvino exceptum: Summa, quicunque Samaritanissimum istum fovent, quam cupide eorum scripta complectuntur, & in coelum laudibus efferunt; contra vero quam contemptum loquuntur & contumeliose exagitant exteras reformatas ecclesias, earumque celeberrimos, & de Ecclesia Iesu Christi optimè meritos orthodoxos doctores seu vivos, seu mortuos, eosque praesertim qui elaboratissimis suis scriptis iis larvam detrahere, & ipsorum petulantiam retundere ausi fuerunt, inter quos sunt insignia illa nostri saeculi lumina & ornamenta D. Rivetus & Voetius, quod ille Calvinum a virulentis Lanceloti Andreae morsibus vindicaverit, hic vero Montacutium δυσθεοφορον[?] ad partes modeste vocaverit, nec passus hominem fastu turgidum ecclesias reformatas impune conculcasse: Clariss. Vedelium quam indignis modis tractaverint, referre piget.
units.tr: Since they are carried with such a friendly feeling towards the head and shoulders of this monstrous body, there is no doubt they will also honour the rest of the body. So they assert that "the religion of the Papists and that of the reformed is the same, nor is there any danger if someone should maintain" (as the liturgy of the English Church always maintained under King James) "that the Popish religion is rebellion." Canterbury, in the relation of the conference, p. 36, and in his speech in the Star Chamber, p. 36: "The Protestant Church has not seceded from the Roman Church, in which all things necessary to salvation are still to be found, and which still has all the things required for the essence of a church." Potter, in the Vindication of the Charity of the Reformed Church, p. 66: "And if some have gone further and attacked that church more sharply, they are zealots destitute of prudence and charity," ibid., p. 74. Hence Canterbury calls the work of reformation carried out by Luther "a schism to be deplored." "The controversies in which these churches differ from one another are not such as can hinder the salvation of either party, since they are not fundamental." Heylin, in his answer to Burton, p. 124. And "although the errors of the Roman Church were fundamental, yet, since the other fundamental truths it preserves still retain their efficacy, the poisons of the mixed errors are blunted, like an antidote." Joseph Hall, bishop of Exeter, in the Old Religion, near the beginning, and Butterfield in his Vindications: "Those who profess that they love Jesus Christ, although they err in fundamentals, are nevertheless brothers to the orthodox and can be saved." Potter, ubi supra, p. 109. And lest anyone think this is said only of those who lived in the Roman Church before the Reformation, the same Potter extends it "to present times, and we must now hope well of all who, led astray by simplicity of heart, profess the Roman faith and die in that profession," p. 77. Not without notable injustice are the Papists accused of idolatry, heresy, or schism. Of idolatry, "since they do not give to creatures the worship of latreia." Shelford, p. 300. Montacute, in the appendix, p. 79, and in the Origines, p. 309. Hence it came about that the Archbishop, from the liturgy of the fast which was received, had the word "idolatry" struck out, by which our ancestors were said to have lain sunk in the Roman Church. Dow, in his answer to Burton, p. 142: they are "unjustly accused of heresy, since they sin not by defect but by excess." Potter, p. 102. So also of schism, "since in all respects they most entirely profess the Roman faith," Montacute, in the appendix, p. 283: "they are free before God from schism and heresy, because the errors they cherish, if any, they did not themselves discover nor first devise." Canterbury, relation of the conference, p. 316. Rather, Scaliger, Parkes, and other best men are to be held schismatics, who, despising and scorning the consensus of their elders, thrust forward their frenzied observations. Montacute, in the appendix, p. 389. "Therefore nothing prevents the papists and the protestants from coming together into one church, except the insane intemperance of certain furious zealots (namely the Jesuits and the Puritans), who have recalled their Pharisaic institutions into Christianity," of whom Montacute, in the appendix, p. 245, calls both "cancers of piety, disgraces of Christianity, and poisons and destroyers of peace and concord." With what contrary eulogies the same man, ibid., p. 45, adorns Cassander, "the most genuine soul of probity and modesty"; he grieves that he was so badly received "by the importunate censor Calvin." In sum: whoever cherishes that most Samaritan of men, how eagerly they embrace his writings and raise them to heaven; on the contrary, how contemptuously they speak of and abusively harass the other reformed churches and their most famous orthodox teachers, living or dead, and especially those who have dared with their most elaborate writings to strip off that mask and to blunt their wantonness. Among these are those notable lights and ornaments of our age, D. Rivetus and Voetius: the former because he defended Calvin from the virulent bites of Lancelot Andrewes, the latter because he modestly called Montacute "ill-god-bearing" [δυσθεοφορον] back to his proper place, and did not allow the man, puffed up with arrogance, to trample the reformed churches with impunity. How unworthily they have treated the most distinguished Vedelius, I am sorry to report.

units.la: Et ne quis putet hæc inconsiderantibus excidisse, age (inquit author) exquiratur, quo modo iis arrideant quae in pontificiis, protestantes omnes, maxime qui reformati dicuntur, imprimis exagitant: in quatuor specimen exhibet, videlicet, Idolatria, hæresibus, superstitionibus; & abominando Missae idolo.
units.tr: And lest anyone think that these things slipped out from careless people, come, says the author, let us examine how those things agree with what all Protestants, and especially those who are called reformed, chiefly attack in the Papists. He sets out a sample under four heads: idolatry, heresies, superstitions, and the abominable idol of the Mass.

units.la: Multiplex est Romanæ ecclesiæ idololatria, sed nullibi magis exerte se præbet omnibus conspicuam quam in adoratione altarium, panis sacramentalis seu hostiæ, imaginum, reliquiarum, & sanctorum defunctorum. Altari porro reverentiam exhibendam, docet Cantuarien-sis. in orat. in Camera Stellar. & ex Psalmo profert locum, Venite, adoremus, procumbamus coram Domino & altari ejus. pag. 49. & ne quis dubitaret aliam esse σεβοχύνησιν[?] à Pontificia, in adorationis hujus subsidium allegat Poklingtonus in altar. pag. 160. praxin nobilis. Equitum S. Georgii in ipsis papismi crassissimis tenebris: & additur ratio, ab Heilens. in responsi. contra Burtonum. pag. 30. propter personalem Dei in altari praesentiam, qui ibi tanquam in folio residet, inquit Poklingtonus in altar. pag. 143. Hancque etiam σεβοχύνησιν urgent cum non celebratur S. caena: quotidiana praxis illud testatur.
units.tr: The idolatry of the Roman Church is manifold, but nowhere does it show itself more openly and more conspicuously to all than in the adoration of altars, of the sacramental bread or host, of images, of relics, and of the dead saints. Moreover, Canterbury teaches that reverence is to be shown to the altar, in his speech in the Star Chamber, p. 49, and he quotes the text from the Psalm: "Come, let us worship and fall down before the Lord and his altar." And lest anyone doubt that this adoration is different from the Papist kind, Poklington, in the altar, p. 160, cites in support of this worship the practice of the noble Knights of St George "in the very thickest darkness of Papism." And a reason is added, from Heylin in his answer to Burton, p. 30: "because of God's personal presence at the altar, who there sits as on a throne," says Poklington, in the altar, p. 143. And they urge this worship also when the holy Supper is not being celebrated; daily practice bears witness to this.

units.la: Adorationem elementorum eucharisticorum, non solum in actu communicandi, verumetiam extra eundem urgent; hinc, presbytero vel sacerdoti genuflectendum quater, quum patinam & calicem tollit & deponit, & adorationem hanc ad elementa ipsa dirigi, facile probabitur, nam si adorandum sit altare propter propinquam illam cumChristo communionem, ut differunt, multo magis elementa eucharistica, quia unio hic arctior est, magisque perspicua. Notandum etiam Cantuariensem non tulisse, elementorum illam adorationem vocari Pontificiam: nam cum praesules Scoti cap. 6. Canonum ecclesiasticorum, in exemplari eorundem ad regem misso, adorationem illam vocassent Pontificiam, in exemplari ab aula remisso Cantuariensis manu sua in margine notat, delendam esse vocem Pontificiam.
units.tr: They urge the adoration of the eucharistic elements not only in the act of communicating but also outside it. Hence: "the presbyter or priest must genuflect four times when he lifts and sets down the paten and chalice." And that this adoration is directed at the elements themselves will easily be proved: for if the altar is to be adored on account of its near communion with Christ, as they argue, much more so the eucharistic elements, since the union here is closer and more evident. It should also be noted that the Archbishop did not tolerate that adoration of the elements being called Popish. For when the Scottish prelates, in chapter 6 of the ecclesiastical canons, in a copy of them sent to the king, had called that adoration Popish, the copy sent back from the court bore a note in the Archbishop's own hand in the margin: "the word Popish is to be deleted."

units.la: De imaginibus honorifice loquuntur: earum everfores, Montacut. origin. p. 162. vocat, furiosos iconoclastas, religiosos scil. nebulones: Contumelias illis illatas, in archetypum, id est, Christum & sanctos transfire, & si quis (inquit idem antidiab. p. 28.) sancti alicujus imaginem dedecore afficiat, illum [illegible, ~6 letters] optaverim, & sit[?] fiue temeritatis poenas dare. Nolunt inter iconomachos censeri, & ideo summa cura in templorum cryptis, rariis, parietibus & fenestris, frequentissimas imagines servant, Montacut. antidiat. p. 24. & situ ac squalore rancidas exornavit Couzius prebendarius Dunelmensis: Has externam pulchritudinem ecclesiis afferre, & libros esse Laicorum asserit Montacutius, Antigage, pag. 300. Controversiam inter Pontificios & Protestantes esse σκιομαχίαν[?]. Idem in Antidiatr. pag. 40.
units.tr: They speak of images in honourable terms. Montacutius (Origin. p. 162) calls their destroyers furious iconoclasts, that is, religious scoundrels. He says that the insults offered to images pass over to the archetype, that is, to Christ and the saints. And (the same author, Antidiatr. p. 28) says: "If anyone should dishonour the image of any saint, I would wish that he pay the penalty of his rashness." They do not wish to be counted among the image-breakers, and so with the greatest care they keep very many images in the crypts, corners, walls and windows of churches (Montacutius, Antidiatr. p. 24). Couzius, prebendary of Durham, has decked them out, rancid with dirt and grime. Montacutius asserts that these images bring external beauty to churches and are the books of the laity (Antigage, p. 300). He says the controversy between the Papists and the Protestants is a shadow-fight [σκιομαχία]. The same in Antidiatr. p. 40.

units.la: De reliquis audiatur Montacutius. antidia. p. 17.
units.tr: Let Montacutius be heard on relics (Antidiatr. p. 17).

units.la: Ego certe (inquit) cum Constantino, reliquias illas fasciis involvam, auro includam circumgestandas, admovebo labiis, ac collo suspensas manibus oculisque crebro usurpatas intuebor, vel in apothecas condam & recludam interpretiosissima cimelia censendas. Veneratione relativa exemplo veteris ecclesiæ colendas esse dicit idem. ibid. pag. 16. Neque peregrinationem religiosam ad loca sancta improbandam esse, ibid. pag. 44. item denique omnem de reliquijs inter partes bodie, esse de lana caprina, & asini umbra. idem, in Origin. p. 45.
units.tr: "I, for my part," he says, "with Constantine, will wrap those relics in cloths, enclose them in gold to be carried about, press them to my lips, hang them from my neck, and often use them, gazing at them with my hands and eyes; or I will store them in cabinets and shut them up to be kept as most precious treasures." The same author says that they are to be honoured with relative veneration, following the example of the ancient Church (ibid., p. 16). He says that a religious pilgrimage to holy places is not to be condemned (ibid., p. 44). Finally, he says that all the disputes among the parties today about relics are about goat's wool and the shadow of an ass (Montacutius, Origin. p. 45).

units.la: De sanctorum demortuorum adoratione, docent; Sanctos esse orationis & intercessionis mediatores apud Deum. Montacut. antidiat. pag. 20. ideoque sanctorum festa à se celebrari, ut eorundem intercessionis participes esse possint. Lancelotus Andreas in ftricturis, opere posthumo, cura & censura Cantuariensis excusso. pag. 8. Immerito idololatriae aut superstitionis taxari, si quis oraverit; Sancte angele custos ora pro me. Montacut. De invocat. sanct. pag. 99. Inter omnes vero sanctos demortuos, nullus est quem Pontificii impensius venerentur Beata Virgine Maria. & hujus cultum promovere conatus est Antonius Staffordus, peculiari libello Londini impresso, cui titulus; Fœminei sexus gloria, defenso ab Heilens & Dowo, in scriptis publicis & approbatis. Vbi asserit, immunem fuisse ab omni peccato. pag. 8. reginarum reginam, filiam, matrem, & sponsam Dei. in præfat. illius miraculosam in cœlum assumptionem veritatem esse infallibilem. pagin. 210. quam meritis suis acquisiverat. pag. 21. & 80. Coram ea justorum animas procun.bere. ibid. in panegyrico. ipsi terrena omnia cognita esse ex speculo Trinitatis. ibid. Puritanissimum[?] esse, si quis renuat in ejus honorem salutationem Angelicam repetere. pagin. 220. & nisi boni sumus Mariani, malos esse Christianos. ibid. Pietatem monachorum, monialium, & magnatum ac principum, qui sodalitio Mariæ nomina sua ascribunt, laudandam esse & imitandam. pag.23. Hæc, imo omnia quæ hoc libro continentur, defendunt Heilens in responsione contra Burton. p. 123. & Dowus contra eundem. p. 54. utriusque vero auctoris scripta à Cantuariensi recensita & approbata prostant. Eandem pæne sententiam tenet Montacutius: Aliter in mundum ex utero materno processisse, quam aliæ mulieres. in apparat. p. 301. vixisse mundum[?] ab actuali peccato. ibid. p. 338. Omnium creaturarum esse dominam. p. 321. Majorem mundum Deum potuisse facere, majus etiam cœlum, majorem autem matrem quam est mater Dei, Deum facere non posse. ex Bonaventura citat & probat. p. 302. & recte [?]homam dicere, Beatam virginem ex hoc quod est mater Dei, quandam habere dignitatem infinitam. ibid. Atque hæc de idololatria.
units.tr: On the adoration of the departed saints they teach that the saints are mediators of prayer and intercession before God (Montacutius, Antidiat. p. 20), and therefore that they themselves celebrate the feasts of the saints, so that they may share in their intercession. Lancelotus Andreas, in his Stricturae, a posthumous work edited and censured by the Canterbury (archbishop), p. 8. One is not rightly charged with idolatry or superstition if one prays, "Holy angel, my guardian, pray for me" (Montacutius, De invocat. sanct., p. 99). Among all the departed saints, however, there is none whom the Papists venerate more zealously than the Blessed Virgin Mary. Antonius Stafford has tried to promote her cult in a special little book printed at London, titled The Glory of the Feminine Sex, defended by Heylin and Dow in public and approved writings. There he asserts that she was free from all sin (p. 8), the queen of queens, daughter, mother and bride of God (in the preface); that her miraculous assumption into heaven is an infallible truth (p. 210), which she had earned by her merits (p. 21 and 80); that before her the souls of the just plead (ibid., in the panegyric); that all earthly things are known to her from the mirror of the Trinity (ibid.); that it is most Puritanical if anyone refuses to repeat the Angelic Salutation in her honour (p. 220); and that unless we are good Marians, we are bad Christians (ibid.). The piety of monks, nuns and great men and princes who enrol their names in the fellowship of Mary is to be praised and imitated (p. 23). Heylin, in his answer against Burton (p. 123), and Dow, against the same (p. 54), defend these things, indeed everything contained in this book; and the writings of both authors, reviewed and approved by the Canterbury (archbishop), are in print. Montacutius holds almost the same opinion: that she came into the world from her mother's womb differently from other women (in Apparat., p. 301); that the world lived without actual sin (ibid., p. 338); that she is lady of all creatures (p. 321); and, quoting and approving Bonaventure, that God could make a greater world, and a greater heaven, but could not make a greater mother than the mother of God (p. 302). And he rightly says that the Blessed Virgin, from the fact that she is the mother of God, has a certain infinite dignity (ibid.). And so much for idolatry.

units.la: Proximum est de hæresibus dicendum, quas junctis manibus in Pontificiis acerrime exagitant reformati omnes: has tamen vel extenuant, vel amplectuntur factionis hujus primipili.
units.tr: Next, I must speak of heresies, which all the reformed churches, with joined hands, most bitterly attack among the Papists; yet the leaders of this faction either minimise them or embrace them.

units.la: Nam contra SS. scripturæ perfectionem urgent traditiones dogmaticas, non de ritibus, sed de doctrina ipsa, & harum numero ascribunt baptismum infantium, dei dominicæ sanctificationem; traditionem poculi eucharistici Laicis, orationes in linguis populo cognitis & cæt. Whitus episcopus Elien sis, de sabbatho. p. 97. Montacut. in origin. 396. Ex penu
units.tr: For against the perfection of Holy Scripture they press dogmatic traditions, not concerning rites but concerning doctrine itself. Among these they count the baptism of infants, the sanctification of the Lord's day, the tradition of giving the cup of the Eucharist to the laity, prayers in languages known to the people, and so on (Whitus, bishop of Ely, De sabbatho, p. 97; Montacutius, in Origin., p. 396). From this most abundant storehouse [penus] are drawn all those things which they rigidly insist upon in their visitations,

units.la: hoc locupletissimo deprompta sunt illa omnia quæ in visitationibus rigide urgent, vid. Iurisdictio Episcoporum supra presbyteros, prostratio & genuflexio coram altari, oratio ad orientem, signum crucis in baptismo, formatio crucis in aere, ejusdem super altare positio, & sexcenta alia ejusmodi. Heilens antidot. Lincolniensis p. 87. Samuel Hoardus in concione quam habuit in visitatione metropolitana p. 15. & hisce omnibus auctoritatem scriptæ legis vendicant, Whitus de sabbato. Denique in eo solum scripturæ sensu acquiescendum, qui traditionis & consensus patrum auctoritatem habet: Chounæus in collectionibus Theologicis, Cantuariensi dicatis, neque unquam adhuc improbatis p. 31. Poklington. altar. p. 129. & Cantuariensis ipse in relat. colloq. p. 62. Verbum divinum aliud est scriptum, aliud non scriptum. & ibid. p. 84. Candela scripturæ non est prius lux, quam accensa fuerit per admotionem luminis ecclesiasticæ traditionis, & ibid. p. 114. Lumen scripturæ per se non est clarum satis, nec potest locuples testimonium sibi ipsi perhibere. & pag. 104. Quando patres dicunt se inniti scripturæ, non excludunt traditionem. & ibi quia scriptura est recondita & obscura & potest in diversos sensus trahi, nemo proprriis viribus absq; ecclesia fidat. An hoc non est S. Script. cum pontificiis judicis & norme absolutæ authoritate spoliare, & traditiones ecclesiæ (per quam intelligit pontificiam) non solum æquare, sed & supra scriptum Dei verbū extollere?
units.tr: namely: the jurisdiction of bishops over presbyters; prostration and genuflection before the altar; prayer toward the east; the sign of the cross in baptism; the forming of a cross in the air, and its placing upon the altar; and six hundred other such things (Heylin, Antidotum Lincolniense, p. 87; Samuel Hoard, in the sermon he preached at the metropolitan visitation, p. 15). And for all these they claim the authority of written law (Whitus, De sabbato). Finally, one must rest only in that sense of Scripture which has the authority of tradition and the consent of the Fathers. (Chounaeus, in the Theological Collections dedicated to the Canterbury (archbishop), and never yet disapproved, p. 31; Pocklington, Altar, p. 129; and the Canterbury (archbishop) himself in his Relatio Colloquii, p. 62.) The divine word is one thing written, another unwritten. And ibid., p. 84: The candle of Scripture is not a light until it has been kindled by the approach of the light of ecclesiastical tradition. And ibid., p. 114: The light of Scripture is not clear enough in itself, nor can it bear a sufficient testimony to itself. And p. 104: When the Fathers say that they rest on Scripture, they do not exclude tradition. And there: Because Scripture is hidden and obscure and can be drawn into diverse senses, no one should trust in his own powers apart from the Church. Is this not to strip Holy Scripture of its absolute authority and judge, as the Papists do, and not only to set the traditions of the Church (by which they mean the papal) on a level with it, but even to raise them above the written Word of God?

units.la: De vita monastica docent. Eversionem monasteriorum per Henricum 8. Angliæ regem sacrilegam fuisse θεομαχίαν, facinus flagitiosum. Montacut. in originib. 303. & 384. cum vita hæc originem suam repetat ab Elia, Eliseo, Iohanne Baptista. idem, ibid. 369. & 370. & striæ regulas ab Evangelista Marco. Wats in concione de Apostolica mortificatione, pag. 20. quos si voluntarij cultus aut superstitionis coargueris, eadem opera sanctos instituti illius authores, Eliam, Elisæum, Danielem, Marcum accusabis ejusdem criminis. Kk idem pag. 28. Hodiernos Carthusianos, Franciscanos & caeteram istam monachorum fæcem, pios & bonos ac religiosos esse, etiam ratione ordinis sui. Staffordus in fœminina gloria. p. 236. Virginem Mariam monialem vixisse. idem pag. 22. Processiones discalceatas per urbium compita, monachorum horas canonicas, vigilias, nocturnas ad templa peregrinationes, & similia, nulla ratione reprehendendas esse, dicit Wats, ubi supra.
units.tr: They teach concerning monastic life. The overthrow of the monasteries by Henry VIII, king of England, was a sacrilegious theomachy [θεομαχία], a shameful deed (Montacutius, in Originibus, pp. 303 and 384), although this life traces its origin back to Elijah, Elisha and John the Baptist (the same, ibid., pp. 369 and 370), and its rules to the Evangelist Mark (Wats, in the sermon on apostolic mortification, p. 20). If you accuse them of voluntary worship or superstition, by the same act you will accuse of the same crime the holy founders of that way of life, Elijah, Elisha, Daniel and Mark. The same, p. 28: The present-day Carthusians, Franciscans and that whole dregs of monks are pious, good and religious, even by reason of their order. Stafford, in The Glory of the Feminine Sex, p. 236: The Virgin Mary lived as a nun (the same, p. 22). Barefoot processions through the crossroads of cities, the canonical hours of the monks, night vigils, pilgrimages to churches, and the like, are not to be censured on any ground, says Wats, in the place cited above.

units.la: De limbo patrum, & orationibus pro defunctis, sic Montacutius in apparat. pag. 476. Sanctos ante Christum defunctos cælo non receptos fuisse; sed inferno inclusos unde à Christi descensu ad inferos liberabantur, & in hujus confirmationem locum illum 1. Petr. 3. 19. contra Puritanos adducit, idem in origin.pag. 286. Imo, pium est credere Christum, dum dicitur infernum spoliasse, paganos virtutis commendatione ornatos inde liberasse, ut sint, Socrates, Aristoteles, Hercules, Epaminondas, Plutarchus, & similes, inquit, Maxwallus in demonstratione. pag. 9. Atque licet scriptura mentionem tantum faciat duorum locorum post mortem, neque ullum sit in scriptura indicium alicujus loci tertii, non tamen inde sequi non esse tertium, quia multa sunt quæ non indicantur in scripturis.
