Montacut. in apparat. pag. 135. Oblationes & preces pro demortuis, in pontificiis non solum non damnant, verumetiam authoritatibus patrum confirmant. Lancel. Andreæ strictur. pag. 56. Poklingt. altar. pag. 83. Et omnes veteres liturgias in causæ hujus subsidium advocat Dowus. pag. 56. De sacramentis, in hisce cum Pontificiis consentiunt, quod sacramentorum veteris testamenti vim diminuant, & mera fuisse signa gratiæ. Montacut. in originib. pag. 72. quod cum synodo Tridentina anathema dicant iis, qui dixerint Iohannis baptismum eandem vim habuisse cum baptismo Christi: Quod contraria sententia Calvinii, sit privati hominis παραλήψημα[?]. Idem, ibid. pag. 390. Quod omnes omnino infantes Baptizati in ba-
units.tr: On the limbo of the Fathers and prayers for the dead, Montacutius says thus (Apparat., p. 476): The saints who died before Christ were not received into heaven, but were shut up in hell, from which they were freed at Christ's descent into the underworld; and in confirmation of this he brings forward against the Puritans that passage, 1 Peter 3:19 (the same, Origin., p. 286). Indeed, it is a pious belief that when it is said that Christ despoiled hell, he freed from there pagans adorned with the commendation of virtue, such as Socrates, Aristotle, Hercules, Epaminondas, Plutarch and the like, says Maxwell, in his Demonstration, p. 9. And although Scripture mentions only two places after death, and there is no indication in Scripture of any third place, it does not follow from this that there is no third, because there are many things which are not indicated in the Scriptures (Montacutius, in Apparat., p. 135). The oblations and prayers for the dead, among the Papists, not only do they not condemn, but they even confirm them by the authority of the Fathers (Lancelot Andrewes, Stricturae, p. 56; Pocklington, Altar, p. 83). And he calls on all the ancient liturgies in aid of this cause (Dow, p. 56). Concerning the sacraments, in these matters they agree with the Papists, in that they diminish the force of the sacraments of the Old Testament, and say they were mere signs of grace (Montacutius, in Originibus, p. 72); and that, with the Tridentine Synod, they pronounce an anathema on those who say that the baptism of John had the same power as the baptism of Christ. That the contrary opinion of Calvin is a private man's conceit [παραλήψημα] (the same, ibid., p. 390). That all infants baptised in baptism are truly regenerated, justified, sanctified; and there is no doubt at all of their salvation if they depart from life before committing actual sins (Montacutius, in Appello Caesarem, p. 35).

units.la: [The last line is followed by the catchword "ptismo" at lower right.] ptifmo vere regenerentur, justificentur, sanctificentur; neque ullatenus dubitandum de eorum salute, si ante commissa actualia peccata ex vivis excesserint. Montacut. in Appello Cæsarem. pag. 35. Whitus Eliensis episcop. contra Dialog. pag. 95. Licet idem ante ademptum episcopatum dogma hoc, ut Pontificium rejecerit, in colloquio cum Jesuita Fischero. pag. 176. Quod baptismum simpliciter necessarium ad salutem, non solum ratione præcepti, sed ratione medii, allato in hunc finem loco ex Iohannis Euangelio cap. 3.5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit, & cæt. Contuariens. in relatione Colloquii cum Jesuita. pag. 56. Expositiones vero reformatorum doctorum contrarias, meras esse elusiones excogitatas in contemptum Dei & dispendium animarum, dicit Montacut. in origin. p. 397. Quod ceremoniæ ab hominibus inventæ & baptismo superaddite, (ut vestis alba, oleum, lac, sal, chrisma,) baptismi sint ornamenta, & exercitia, quibus mens externarum rerum sensu & significatione ad divinum cultum, ipsumque Deum attrahitur) retineri debeant; & ubi abrogantur, denuo restituende. Montacut. in antidiatr. p. 15. & 16. Quod tota illa disputatio inter partes de quinque illis (spuriis ut reformati vocant) sacramentis, sit λογομαχία[?]. Andreæ Wintoniens. episcopi strictur. p. 11. Quod Confirmatio per episcopos, plenos & perfectos faciat Christianos. Poklingtonus in Altar. p. 65. Quod nullius momenti sit quæstio de ordinum sacrorum numero, & quod penuria ecclesiarum factum sit, quod in reformatis ecclesiis omnes isti ordines non vigeant. Andreæ strictur. p. 12. Quod jure divino Episcopis, iisque solis, competat pastorum ordinatio, ita ut à nemine non episcopo ordinato & rite consecrato possit adhiberi; & irrita sit omnis ordinatio & missio, quæ à non legitimo & Canonico more non proficiscitur. Quod si à se oriantur aliqui & non missi ingeruant cœlesti huic functioni manus (intelligit hic earum ecclesiarum pastores à quibus Episcopatus exulat) viderint ipsi quid sint responsuri olim summo sacerdoti, cujus partes usurpant, nos nostras, non aliorum tuemur vocationes. Inquit Montacutius, in antidiatr. p. 138. Causas matrimoniales per jus Canonicum pontificiorum dijudicari volunt: cujus juris originem repetunt à primorum paparum decretis; quare ubique urgent Canones Apostolicos, Clementis constitutiones, & similia scripta supposititia, Poklingt. & Heleins de altar. passim. Montacut. ubique: & huic juri Canonico, Basiliensis concilij decreta asscribunt, Ut Staffordus in gloria foeminei sexus. p. 128. Pro festo visitationis Mariae, concilium illud citat: Proh quam verum est illud! Qui modestiae limites semel transilierit, eum gnaviter impudentem esse oportet. De sacramento poenitentiae docent, auricularem illam confessionem plurimas praestare utilitates, ideoque pie frequentandam ab iis qui ad eucharistiam accedunt. Whitus Eliensis episc. in praefatione de sabbato: & dolendum esse quod aboleatur, Sprint. in concione de Confess. p, 18. typis excusa cum approbatione. Neque ulla peccata celanda esse si sacerdotalem absolutionem exspectemus, in qua exercenda sedent sacerdotes ut judices delegati à Deo: Confessionem hanc privatam sacerdoti factam unicum esse medium obtinendi peccatorum remissionem. Idem p. 16. & 19. & 15. diserte & totidem verbis. Praeter privatos confessores, consultum esset ut in singulis ecclesiis revocaretur usus ille publici poenitentiarij (qui olim in usu apud veteres) qui initio quadragesimae in die Cinerum, in reclinatorio residens, omnium confessiones audiret, & singulis, cinere capita primum respersis, poenitentiam in quadragesima praestandam praescriberet; & plenarie satisfacientes exeunte quadragesima ante paschatis festum absolveret, hac (inquit Poklingtonus in altar. pag. 57.) est illa sancta disciplina, quam restitutam cupit liturgia: Atque hac poenitentia vere satisfieri Deo pro peccatis commissionis: ut oratione pro omissionis, inquit Shelfordus, p. 125. & 129. & 129. De extrema unctione nullam fore controversiam cum pontificiis, utantur prout velint, modo ne in censum sacramentorum evangelicorum adscribant: Montacut. in Antigag.p.267.
units.tr: [The last line is followed by the catchword "baptismo" at lower right.] are truly regenerated, justified and sanctified by baptism; and there is no reason at all to doubt their salvation if they die before committing actual sins. Montacut. in Appello Caesarem, p. 35. Whitus, bishop of Ely, against the Dialogue, p. 95. Although before he was deprived of his bishopric he rejected this doctrine as Popish, in a conference with the Jesuit Fisher, p. 176. That baptism is absolutely necessary to salvation, not only by reason of precept but by reason of means, citing to this end the passage from John's Gospel, chapter 3, verse 5: Unless one is born again, etc. Contuariens. in the account of a conference with a Jesuit, p. 56. The contrary expositions of the reformed doctors, he says, are mere evasions devised to the contempt of God and the loss of souls, Montacut. in Origines, p. 397. That the ceremonies devised by men and added to baptism (such as the white robe, oil, milk, salt, chrism) are ornaments and exercises of baptism, by which the mind is drawn through the sense and meaning of external things to divine worship and to God himself; and where they have been abolished they must be restored again. Montacut. in Antidiatribe, pp. 15 and 16. That the whole dispute between the parties over those five so-called spurious sacraments, as the reformed call them, is a verbal quarrel. Andreae, bishop of Winchester, Strictures, p. 11. That Confirmation by bishops makes Christians full and perfect. Poklington in Altar, p. 65. That the question of the number of holy orders is of no importance, and that the lack of churches has caused it that in the reformed churches all these orders do not flourish. Andreae, Strictures, p. 12. That by divine right the ordination of ministers belongs to bishops, and to them alone, so that it may not be employed by anyone who is not a bishop, ordained and duly consecrated; and that every ordination and mission which does not proceed in the legitimate and canonical manner is void. And if some arise of their own accord and, not sent, thrust their hands into this heavenly office (he means here the ministers of those churches from which episcopacy is banished) let them see for themselves what they will answer one day to the high priest whose part they usurp; we defend our own calling, not that of others. Montacutius says so in Antidiatribe, p. 138. They want matrimonial causes to be decided by the Canon Law of the Papists, the origin of which law they trace back to the decrees of the first popes; therefore everywhere they press the Apostolic Canons, the Constitutions of Clement, and similar spurious writings, Poklington and Heylin, in Altar, passim. Montacut., everywhere. And to this canon law they ascribe the decrees of the Council of Basel, as Stafford does in Glory of the Female Sex, p. 128. For the feast of the Visitation of Mary he cites that council. Alas, how true is that! Whoever has once overstepped the limits of modesty must be brazenly shameless. Concerning the sacrament of penance they teach that that auricular confession brings very many advantages, and therefore should be devoutly frequented by those who come to the Eucharist. Whitus, bishop of Ely, in the preface on the Sabbath; and it is to be lamented that it is abolished, Sprint, in a sermon on Confession, p. 18, printed with approval. Nor are any sins to be concealed, if we expect priestly absolution, in the exercise of which priests sit as judges delegated by God; this private confession made to a priest is the only means of obtaining the remission of sins. The same, pp. 16, 19 and 15, expressly and in so many words. Besides private confessors, it would be advisable that in each church that custom of the public penitentiary be revived (which was once in use among the ancients), who at the beginning of Lent, on Ash Wednesday, sitting in a chair, would hear the confessions of all, and sprinkling the heads of each with ashes first, would prescribe penance to be performed in Lent, and at the end of Lent, before Easter, would absolve those who had made full satisfaction; this, says Poklington in Altar, p. 57, is that holy discipline which the liturgy desires to be restored. And by this penance God is truly satisfied for sins of commission, as by prayer for sins of omission, says Shelford, pp. 125, 129 and 129. Concerning extreme unction there will be no controversy with the Papists; let them use it as they wish, provided they do not count it among the evangelical sacraments: Montacut. in Antigag., p. 267.

units.la: De fide, justificatione, legis impletione, & merito, docent. Fidem nudum tantum esse assensum, nullam requirere applicationem, nullam fiduciam personalem; eamque personalem applicationem esse meram præsumptionem, & cerebri non satis sani figmentum. Shelfordus. p. 36. Optimum medium apprehendendi Christum, esse charitatem. Ibidem p 106. Iustificationem quidem ab Apostolo attribui fidei, sed illud intelligendum esse Inchoative tantum. Chounæus in collect. theolog. p. 69. Charitatem esse fidei formam: & per eam primario coram Deo justificari homines, Shelfordus, p. 102. & 106. quod hoc apodictico scilic. syllogismo monstrum illud theologi confirmat, Deus justificat, at Deus est charitas. E. charitas justificat: vah! quanta caligine occæcatos oportuit fuisse eorum oculos; quos non puduit impurum & futilem hunc libellum, in ipsis Academicorum comitiorum solemnitatibus onerare tam splendidis profundæ & raræ eruditionis elogiis; an quos per calumniam solifidianos vocant, tam obesæ naris homines putant isti novatores, ut insulsis ejusmodi nugis scutica aut ferula castigandis; de controversiæ statu se moveri permitterent? Sed me contineo. Docent etiam, justificationem peccatoris coram Deo, nihil aliud esse quam conversionem & sanctificationem per justitiam inhærentem. Idem Shelfordus. p. 107. Montacut. in Antig. p. 142. Legè Dei non solum posse, verumetiam in hac vita facile impleri: Shelfordus. p. 121. Deumque si præstitu[?] impossibilia imperasset, in usum fore & tyrannum. idem p. 136. Whitus de sabbato. p. 157. Extremā blasphemiam esse, si quis dixerit in optimis sanctorum actionibus esse admixtum aliquid peccati. Shelf. p. 147. A quibusdā non solum perfecte in hac vita impleri legem ; verum quosdam supererogare, praestando Consilia illa, (quae vocant) perfectionis, castitatis, paupertatis, & obedientiae: idem p. 184. Bona opera vere & proprie esse meritoria aeternae vitae. idem passim ubi supra. Idque ex condigno. Montacut. Appello Caesar. & in antigag. p. 153. esse veras efficientes causas salutis, uti mala opera sunt damnationis. Chounaeus in collect. Theolog. p. 18. Et quod multo maxime admirandum venit, licet ejusmodi scripta ab orthodoxis pro tribunali exagitata sint, nondum tamen à Cantuariensi obtineri potuit, ut heterodoxias istas sibi displicere significaret, quin contra per hyperas-pitas suos Heilens & Dowum, authores eorumque haec dogmata defendit. Atque haec de erroribus & haeresibus Pontificiis à factione hac resorptis : si cui animus sit eorum scripta legere, primo intuitu perspiciet iisdem argumentis utrosque niti.
units.tr: They teach concerning faith, justification, the fulfilment of the law, and merit. Faith is merely a bare assent, it requires no application, no personal trust; and this personal application is mere presumption, and a figment of a brain not quite sound. Shelford, p. 36. The best means of apprehending Christ is charity. Ibid., p. 106. Justification is indeed attributed by the Apostle to faith, but that must be understood only inchoatively. Chounaeus in Collection of Theology, p. 69. Charity is the form of faith, and through it men are chiefly justified before God, Shelford, pp. 102 and 106. For this monstrous theologian confirms it by this apodictic syllogism: God justifies, but God is charity. Therefore charity justifies. Alas! How blinded must their eyes have been, that were not ashamed to load this unclean and frivolous little book, at the very solemn assemblies of the Academics, with such splendid praises of profound and rare learning! Or do these innovators think that those whom they call solifidians by slander are men of such thick nose that they would permit themselves to be moved from the state of the controversy by such silly trifles, to be chastised with a whip or a rod? But I restrain myself. They also teach that the justification of a sinner before God is nothing other than conversion and sanctification through inherent righteousness. Shelford, p. 107; Montacut. in Antigag., p. 142. That the law of God can not only be fulfilled, but can even easily be fulfilled in this life: Shelford, p. 121. And if God had commanded impossible things, he would be a tyrant and used as one, the same, p. 136. Whitus, on the Sabbath, p. 157. It is the utmost blasphemy if anyone says that some admixture of sin is found in the best actions of the saints. Shelford, p. 147. By some it is taught not only that the law is perfectly fulfilled in this life, but that some men do more than required, performing those so-called counsels of perfection: of chastity, poverty and obedience: the same, p. 184. Good works are truly and properly meritorious of eternal life, the same, passim as above. And this by condign merit, Montacut., Appello Caesarem, and in Antigag., p. 153. They are the true efficient causes of salvation, just as evil works are of damnation, Chounaeus in Collection of Theology, p. 18. And what is to be marvelled at most of all: although such writings have been thoroughly examined by the orthodox before the bar of judgement, it has nevertheless not been possible to obtain from the Archbishop of Canterbury any declaration that he disapproves of these heterodoxies; on the contrary, through his hyperaspistes, Heylin and Dow, the authors, he defends these doctrines. And these things concerning the Popish errors and heresies which this faction has revived. If anyone has the inclination to read their writings, he will perceive at first glance that both rest on the same arguments.

units.la: Sequitur ut, quo animo sint in superstitiones pontificias dicatur : verbo quidem fatentur ecclesiam istam superstitionibus laborare; verum cum in specie ad earum designationem descenditur, aliter rem se habere comperietur : Nam, quid vetabit quominus me signem signo crucis in qualibet corporis parte, quocunque demum tempore ; in omni actione, cum in veteri ecclesia hoc factum fuerit, eodemque ritu sine ullo scandalo & superstitione adhuc uti possumus. inquit Montacut. in appellio Caesar. p. 268. & inter genuinas Apostolicas traditiones recenset Samuel Hoardus, in concion. p. 15. Pontificias superstitiones de reliquiis sanctorum circumgestandis, audivimus supra Montacutio probatas. Modum orandi, eorum (uti canit Mantuanus)
units.tr: It follows that we should say what their attitude is towards the Popish superstitions. In words, indeed, they confess that this church labours under superstitions; but when it comes to specifying them, the matter will be found to be otherwise: For what will prevent me from making the sign of the cross on any part of the body, at whatever time, in every action, since this was done in the ancient church, and by the same rite we can still use it without any scandal or superstition, says Montacut. in Appello Caesarem, p. 268; and Samuel Hoard, in a sermon, p. 15, counts it among the genuine Apostolic traditions. The Popish superstitions about carrying about the relics of saints we heard above, approved by Montacutius. The manner of praying of these people (as Mantuan sings)

units.la: Qui filo infertis numerant sua murmura baccis, seu per globulos, & rosaria, laudat, & sacram arythmeticam vocat Staffordus, in gloria foeminei sexus p. 148. Jejunium quadragesimale usque adeo arridet Montacut. in antidiat. p.9. ut non renuat hæreticus judicari, nisi ab Apostolica authoritate sanctitum fuisse probaverit. Et à divina authoritate descendere dicit Couzenius in devotione. p.221. ut & diei veneris jejunium. idem, ibid. &, si Epiphanio (inquit Guilielmus Wats in concione de Apostolica mortificatione p. 50) credendum, eadem authoritate nititur diei Mercurii jejunium.
units.tr: Those who count their murmured prayers on threads strung with beads, or through globules and rosaries, Staffordus praises and calls sacred arithmetic, in The Glory of the Female Sex p. 148. The Lenten fast so pleases Montacutius in Antidiatribe p. 9, that he does not refuse to be judged a heretic unless he has proved it was sanctioned by Apostolic authority. And Couzenius in Devotion p. 221 says it descends from divine authority, as does the Friday fast. The same, ibid. And if (says Guilielmus Wats in his sermon on Apostolic mortification, p. 50) we are to believe Epiphanius, the Wednesday fast rests on the same authority.

units.la: De locorum sanctitate, profitentur, ante Christianam sepulturam coemiteria necessario consecranda esse ab Episcopis, quomodo vero consecratio ea peragenda fit, ad antiquos canones referunt; & consecrata pollui fecularibus actionibus, aut sepultura hæretici, schismatici, aut excommunicati. Laurentius in concione. p. 9. Iosephus Hallus in concione habita ad consecrationem coemiteri. p. 38. & 40. & exemplo Iudæorum hanc consecrationem obtrudit. ibid. Templa esse peculiaribus ritibus consecranda, & iis consecratis sine periculo adscribi sanctitatem, laudatque illud Bernardi, quis parietes istos sanctos dicere vereatur, quos manus sacratæ pontificum tantis sanctificaverere [?] mysteriis. Tedderus in concione habita coram Episcopo Norwicensi. p. 8. Profanari templa si quis intra eorum parietes caput operiat. Shelfoordus p. 51. altaria speciali ritu consecranda esse, & encaenia celebranda. Poklington. altar. p. 141. Altaria cancellis separanda esse à reliquo templo, inter quos solis sacerdotibus ingredi licet; regibus & imperatoribus aliquando idem concedetur cum creatori dona offerunt. Poklington. Ibid. p. 80. coram altari terse prosternere debere sacerdotes. Laurentius ubi supra. p. 20. Propter arctam illam unionem inter locum illum & humanam Christi naturam. idem p. 12. quæ in altari tanquam in throno resident. Cantuariensis. in oratione habita in Camera Stellata. p.47. Precandum esse facie ad orientem conversa, cum sic tradiderint Apostoli. Heilens antidot. Lincoln. Dum recitatur Decalogus genuflectendum esse; dum symbolum & Euangelium, standum; uti & cum habetur concio apertis capitibus standum esse auditoribus. Shelfoord. p. 20. 22. & ad nomen Iesu genuflectendum, exemplo praesulum licet nulla adhuc lege injungatur. Ibid.Delictum esse contra quintum decalogi praeceptum, si quis festa in honorem B. Virginis Mariae, Angelorum, & sanctorum non religiose observet: Couzenius in devotion: & profanari sacrosancta illa festa operibus: Diem tamen dominicum non profanari aut pollui iisdem operibus si ea magistratus permiserit, cum abstinentia ab operibus saecularibus die dominico nullibi in novo testamento imperetur, & quod non prohibetur ultro permissum est. Whitus Elicnsis episcopus, in libro peculiari quo probat diem Dominicum non habendum esse pro sabbato. p. 217. & ne inficeretur populus judaismo sabbati, imperatum fuit pastoribus omnibus in Anglia ut publice praelegerent scriptum quo omnibus concedebatur licentia ludendi diebus Dominicis post finita sacra, dummodo iis interfuissent, Heilens in Historia sabbatica.
units.tr: Concerning the holiness of places, they profess that cemeteries must necessarily be consecrated by bishops before Christian burial; as to how that consecration is to be performed, they refer to the ancient canons; and consecrated places are polluted by secular actions, or by the burial of a heretic, schismatic or excommunicate person. Laurentius in sermon, p. 9. Joseph Hall in a sermon delivered at the consecration of a cemetery, p. 38 and 40, and by the example of the Jews he forces this consecration upon us, ibid. Temples must be consecrated with particular rites, and once consecrated, holiness may be ascribed to them without danger; and he praises that saying of Bernard: who would dare call those walls holy which the consecrating hands of bishops have sanctified with such mysteries? Tedderus in a sermon delivered before the Bishop of Norwich, p. 8. Temples are profaned if anyone within their walls covers his head. Shelfoord, p. 51. Altars must be consecrated with a special rite, and dedication festivals celebrated. Pocklington, Altar, p. 141. Altars must be separated by rails from the rest of the temple, within which only priests may enter; kings and emperors are sometimes granted the same when they offer gifts to the Creator. Pocklington, ibid., p. 80. Priests ought to prostrate themselves humbly before the altar. Laurentius, above, p. 20. On account of that close union between that place and the human nature of Christ, the same, p. 12, who sit upon the altar as upon a throne. The Canterbury man, in the oration delivered in the Star Chamber, p. 47. One must pray with the face turned toward the east, since the Apostles so taught. Heylin, Antidote, Lincoln. While the Decalogue is being recited one must kneel; while the creed and the Gospel are read, stand; likewise when a sermon is preached, the hearers should stand with their heads uncovered. Shelfoord, p. 20, 22. And at the name of Jesus one must kneel, following the example of prelates, although no law yet enjoins it. Ibid. It is a sin against the fifth commandment if anyone does not religiously observe the feasts in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Angels and the saints; Couzenius in Devotion; and those holy feasts are profaned by works. Yet the Lord's Day is not profaned or polluted by those same works if the magistrate permits them, since abstinence from secular works on the Lord's Day is nowhere commanded in the New Testament, and what is not forbidden is by that very fact permitted. Whitus, bishop of Ely, in a special book in which he proves that the Lord's Day is not to be held as the Sabbath, p. 217. And lest the people be infected with the Jewish Sabbath, it was ordered that all ministers in England publicly read out a written document by which permission was granted to play on the Lord's Days after the sacred services were finished, provided they had attended them. Heylin, in the Sabbath History.

units.la: Restat quartum caput de missa pontificia: Cui ut viam praemuniant, vatiniano [?] odio contra publicas conciones. in ecclesiis reformatis frequentatas feruntur: ut iis extrusis [?] locus fit missae. Itaque docent, minus concionandi publicum paucis tantum quibusdam extraordinariis & eminentibus viris committendum esse, necessarium tantum esse cum reformandi sint errores aut novi canones proponendi: hoc est, in ecclesia constituenda, non constituta: praecipuas partes pastoralis officii esse intelligenter ac distincte legere liturgiam, ejusdemque praelectionem esse efficacem concionem. Shelfoordus. p. 35. 39. 76. & passim ex professo. Non esse publice petendum precibus auxilium spiritus S. ante inchoatam concionem; aut finita concione ejusdem opem ad audita in praxin referenda. Heilens contra Burton. p. 165. Neque consultum esse pastoribus etiam doctissimis, ut privatim etiam in conclavibus, alia precum formula utantur, quam quae in liturgia praescribitur; alias sciant se conatu temerario Dei majestatem contemnere: Couzenius in devotion. praefation. Diebus Dominicis, ad summum semel tantum concionandum esse, pomeridianas superfluas esse. Shelfordus p. 93. Heilens contra Burtonum p. 166. 168. (atque hic non fine singulari seu oscitantia seu impudentia in historia sua sabbatica. parte 2. cap. 6. §. 9. ausus est afferere, Decretum fuisse idem in ecclesiis reformatis belgicis in Synodo Dordrechti convenientibus anno 1574. artic. 46. ex rabula procul dubio Scultingio citans hunc canonem. Publicae vespertinae preces non sunt introducendae, ubi hactenus non sunt, & ubi sunt, tollantur. quasi vero synodus illa loquatur de die Dominico, quod pro confesso sumi vult Heilens, atque inde infert, decreto synodico veritas esse pomeridianas conciones diebus Dominicis, quod certe patribus illis ne per somnium quidem unquam in mentem venerat; Nam revera loquuntur de concionibus quae post meridianis horis haberentur in reliquis septimanae diebus.) Docent etiam, conciones istas publicas magis officere pietati quam prodesse, sanctiusq; victuros homines si essent conciones infrequentiores, cum per eas nascantur schismata, haereses & quicquid vitiorum cernitur in populo. Shelfordus. p. 71. 82. Deus bone quanta verborum amarulentia insectentur hodiernos pastores, qui ex Apostoli praescripto sermonibus ad populum instant tempestive & intempestive, prurigino-sos quidlibet effutientes, qui ecclesiam in tonstrinam vertunt, catulos oblatrantes, clamatores odiosos & molestos, ineptiarum plenos vocat Lancelot. Andreas posthum. oper. p. 32. quia sc. inani verborum tinnitu & saecularis scientiae ostentatio purum Domini verbum corrumpere illis religio est, & luporum adventum ac artes populo sibi commisso demonstrant, veritine torpido silentio pereuntium sanguinis rei essent.
units.tr: There remains the fourth head, concerning the papal mass. To prepare the way for it, out of a Vatinian hatred they are said to attack the public sermons frequented in the reformed churches, so that once these are thrust out, room is made for the mass. They therefore teach that preaching in public should be committed only to a few extraordinary and eminent men, and is necessary only when errors are to be reformed or new canons proposed: that is, when the church is being constituted, not when it is already constituted; that the chief part of the pastoral office is to read the liturgy intelligently and distinctly, and that the reading of it is effective preaching. Shelfoord, p. 35, 39, 76, and passim, expressly. It is not to be publicly sought by prayer the aid of the Holy Spirit before a sermon is begun, nor after it is finished the help to put what was heard into practice. Heylin against Burton, p. 165. Nor is it advisable for ministers, even the most learned, to use, even privately in their studies, any other form of prayer than that prescribed in the liturgy; otherwise they should know that by rash endeavour they despise the majesty of God. Couzenius in Devotion, preface. On the Lord's Days one should preach at most once; afternoon sermons are superfluous. Shelfoord, p. 93. Heylin against Burton, p. 166, 168. (And here, with no small carelessness or impudence, in his Sabbath History, part 2, chap. 6, §9, he has dared to assert that the same was decreed in the Belgic reformed churches meeting in the Synod of Dort in 1574, art. 46, doubtless citing this canon from the scold Scultingius. Public evening prayers are not to be introduced where they have not hitherto been, and where they are, let them be removed. As if that synod spoke of the Lord's Day, which Heylin wishes to be taken for granted, and from this he infers by synodical decree that afternoon sermons on the Lord's Days are lawful. Certainly those fathers never even dreamed of this; for in truth they speak of sermons held in the afternoon hours on the other days of the week.) They also teach: these public sermons do more harm to piety than good, and men would live more holily if sermons were less frequent, since schisms, heresies and whatever vices are seen among the people arise through them. Shelfoord, p. 71, 82. Good God, with what bitterness of words they assail today's ministers, who, following the Apostle's prescription, press the people with the word in season and out of season, calling them babbling, itch-eared fellows who turn the church into a barber's shop, barking puppies, odious and troublesome clamourers, full of trifles, Lancelot Andrewes, posthumous works, p. 32. For these critics it is a matter of religion, since by an empty jingle of words and a display of secular learning they corrupt the pure word of the Lord; and they demonstrate the coming of wolves and their wiles to the people committed to them. Whether they would be guilty of the blood of those who perish through torpid silence is the question.

units.la: Atque sic profligatis concionibus, De Missa docent, satis significanter ipsorum liturgiam ea voce denominari, exemplo veteris. Poklingt. in die Dominico. Et sicuti vocem ipsam non damnant, sic neq; rem voce contentam, modo sano sensu intelligatur. Montacut. antidiatrib. p. 10, hoc est, si sola transubstantiatio a missa removeretur, Poklington. altar. p. 138. Imo nec de voce transubstantiationis certamen moveremus, inquit Montacut. antidiat. p. 10.
units.tr: And so, with sermons demolished, they teach concerning the Mass that their liturgy is quite aptly called by that name, following the example of the ancients. Pocklington, on the Lord's Day. And just as they do not condemn the word itself, so neither do they condemn the thing contained in the word, provided it is understood in a sound sense, Montacutius, Antidiatribe, p. 10. That is to say, if transubstantiation alone were removed from the mass, Pocklington, Altar, p. 138. Indeed we would not even move a dispute over the word transubstantiation, says Montacutius, Antidiatribe, p. 10.

units.la: Vocem cum non aspernentur, videndum an pari affectu in res ipsas ferantur: Atque hic consideretur (inquit author) liturgia Scotis obtrusa, (quem foetum esse Cantuariensem, frequentes per eum liturae, interpunctiones, additiones, quin & quatuordecim literae ipsius ad praesules Scotos, dum libri hujus editionem promoverent, satis licet contra jurantem arguent, & illud Eliae Petlaei praefixum liturgiae Anglicanae a se Graece factae: quo gratulatur Archiepiscopo, Ob restitutam ejus cura liturgiam sive dignitati, ita ut solenni more observetur in omnibus totius insulae regionibus.) Et cum missa componatur; facile apparebit, Omnes Missae pontificiae partes ne una quidem exclusa, contineri in Liturgia hac Scotica vel formaliter vel virtualiter: ejusque parallelum se prodpediem in lucem publicam daturum spondet author. Specimen nunc exhibet in iis missae principalioribus partibus, quas primi reformatores in Anglia ex liturgia Anglica expunxerant, & quas Scotis obtrusos denuo inseruit Cantuariensis: Offertorium videl. Canon,& communio.
units.tr: Since they do not spurn the word, let us see whether they are carried with equal zeal toward the things themselves. Here, says the author, let us consider the liturgy forced upon the Scots. That it is the offspring of the Canterbury man is shown by the frequent erasures, punctuations and additions made through him, and indeed by his fourteen letters to the Scottish prelates while they were promoting the publication of this book, which sufficiently argue against him even under oath; and by the preface prefixed by Elias Petlaeus to the English liturgy, which he made into Greek himself, in which he congratulates the Archbishop on account of its restored liturgy or dignity, so that it is observed with solemn custom in all regions of the whole island. Since the mass is composed of such parts, it will readily appear that all parts of the papal mass, not one even excluded, are contained in this Scottish liturgy, either formally or virtually; and the author promises that he will soon publish its parallel in the light of day. He now offers a specimen in those principal parts of the mass which the first reformers in England had expunged from the English liturgy, and which the Canterbury man, having thrust them upon the Scots, has reinserted: namely the Offertory, the Canon and the Communion.

units.la: Offertorii tum vox, tum res ipsa expresse continetur, eaque saepius repetita, ne lectori incauto & cursim forte legenti excideret, ritum esse Synagogae non negant liturgici pontificii, & huc collimat liturgia Scotica, quae quinque ex veteri testamento locos praefigunt, quorum literalis sensus Judaicam oblationem directe infert: quam usque adeo cupide amplectuntur ut ipsam ejus (ut ita loquar) formalitatem imperent: positio patinae per sacerdotem super altari, repræsentat inquit Durandus in rationali, illud Levitici.14.4. Ponetque manus suas super caput hostiæ & acceptabilis erit: Et ut sciatur præparatoriam hanc oblationem tam esse pro mortuis quam vivis, statim subjungitur mortuorum commemoratio qui in singulis suis ætatibus lumina fuerunt mundi, & ornati singulari gratia ac donis, Couzenius speciatim sanctos quosdam nominat. In devotion. p. 371. Neque hic se continent, verum alios omnes Dei servos addunt, qui quæsum suum in fide perfecerunt, & nunc à laboribus quiescunt: quæ Bellarmino commodissima videtur explicatio eorum qui sunt in purgatorio, pro quibus preces concipere jubet Couzenius Cantuariensis Scholæ egregius discipulus, Devotionis suæ. p. 373. Horum nullum est omnino vestigium in liturgia Anglica.
units.tr: The very word and the thing itself of the Offertory are expressly contained in it, and repeated so often that it should not escape a careless reader who happens to read hastily. The liturgical Papists do not deny that this is a rite of the Synagogue, and the Scottish liturgy aims at the same thing. It prefixes five passages from the Old Testament, whose literal sense directly brings in the Jewish oblation, and they embrace it so eagerly that they even command its very form (so to speak): "The placing of the paten by the priest upon the altar," says Durandus in the Rationale, "represents that passage of Leviticus 14.4: 'And he shall lay his hands upon the head of the victim, and it shall be acceptable.'" And so that it may be known that this preparatory oblation is made for the dead as well as the living, there immediately follows "the commemoration of the dead, who in their several ages were the lights of the world and adorned with singular grace and gifts," and Couzenius names certain saints by name (In Devotion, p. 371). Nor do they stop there, but add "all other servants of God who have finished their course in faith and now rest from their labours." This seems to Bellarmine the most convenient explanation of those who are in purgatory, and for them Couzenius, the outstanding disciple of the Canterbury school, bids us offer prayers (Devotion, p. 373). Of all this there is absolutely no trace in the English liturgy.

units.la: Sequitur Canon missæ, quem non minori odio prosequuntur Protestantes omnes, quam summa reverentia colunt pontificii, fatente Bellarmino. lib.2. de missa cap. 18. Ejus orationes & præfationes pæne omnes sunt in liturgia Scotica: sed supra omnes maxime eminent Orationes consecrationis & oblationis; quas verticem & cor divini sacrificii vocat, Innocentius. lib.4. cap.1. Consecrationis porro nomen quod in Anglica expunctum fuit, (quia sensu pontificio Consecrare est consecratione transubstantiare, inquit Durandus lib.4.) hic in liturgia Scotica inseritur majoribus literis; Oratio consecrationis: Et hæc jubetur recitari à sacerdote ad latus altaris occidentale; facie, à populo qui longe distat, aversa: Et quid differt hoc à secreta murmuratione verborum consecratoriorum inter pontificios? Quare si quis hinc inferet, licere sacerdoti lingua populo incognita sacrum illud peragere, (quandoquidem Deus quem alloquitur omnes linguas æque intelligat, elementa vero ipsa quæ consecrantur nihil intelligant, & populus, in cujus solius gratiam usus linguæ cognitæ urgetur, cancellis ab auditu sacerdotis aversi arceatur, ut audire nequeat) haud facile respondebit factio hæc adversaria, præfertim cum eorum longe doctissimus Whitus Elienfis Episcopus de sabbato. p. 97. neget jure divino peragenda esse sacra lingua populo cognita, & ad ecclesiasticam traditionem referat: longe tamen aliter sentiebat & loquutus fuit, cum ad insulam & mitram nondum promotus fuisset; nam in libro quo doctissimi fratris vindicias contra Jesuitam peregit, cui titulus Orthodoxa fides.cap.2.artic.17. Apostolicum præceptum ex 1.Cor. 14. urget. Sed non tunc aperta fuere factionis hujus mysteria: cui solenne est à se semel posita convellere, & religionem ad ambitionem suam attemperare. In ipsa illa consecratoria oratione ipsa formalia Pontificiorum verba inseruerunt, quibus eorum transubstantiatio innititur, nam Deus rogatur ut velit ita sanctificare oblationes panis & vini, ut fieri nobis possint Christi corpus & sanguis: Consona sunt hæc illis Montacutii in appello Cæsarem.p.289. De modo præsentiæ Christi inanem esse inter pontificios & reformatos litem: concordiam esse facilem, nisi pacis consilia Iesuitæ & Puritani à Diabolo instigati impedirent. & Laurentius, in concion.p.18. Modum præsentiæ non quærendum esse, multo minus determinandum. Antea tamen complura ex Cantuariensi & suis accepimus de corporali præsentia Christi in altari; propter quam altare adorari volunt. Si quis vero elevationem & adorationem elementorum desideret, eam exhibet rubrica marginalis Scoticæ liturgiæ, qua presbyter jubetur tollere in manus patinam & calicem, & an æquum conseri debet, ut sacerdos sacra mysteria in manibus sumat, sine humili reverentia & submissione. Heilens contra Burtonum, p. 137. Post orationem consecrationis immediate subjicitur Oratio oblationis, eo ordine & iis verbis quibus in missali Salisburiensi olim exstabat; & ne quis dubitaret ne cum pontificiis plenum consensum foveret de natura hujus sacrificii, docent, verum, proprium, corporale, visibile hic esse sacrificium, licet incruentum, ob cujus oblationem Apostoli & omnes pastores veri sunt sacerdotes seu sacrifici secundum ordinem Melchisedechi, & mensa eucharistica tam verum & proprium est altare, quam æneum illud Mosis altare fuit. Heylens. antidot. Lincol. p.6. & 17. & Poklintonus ex professo, in altari suo Christiano, authentica Cantuariensis licentia excuso, inter alia quibus ubique turget fermento Papistico cap. 20. sic loquitur. Si nullum habemus Christianum altare, neque etiam ullum habemus Christianum sacrificium; si nullum sacrificium neque etiam ullum habemus Christianum sacerdotem: si nullus est nobis sacerdos, Apage Liturgiam docentem sacerdotem quomodo ad altare assistere debet.
units.tr: Next comes the Canon of the Mass, which all Protestants pursue with no less hatred than the Papists hold it in the highest reverence, as Bellarmine confesses (On the Mass, book 2, ch. 18). Almost all its prayers and prefaces are in the Scottish liturgy, but above all the prayers of consecration and oblation stand out, which Innocent calls the summit and heart of the divine sacrifice (book 4, ch. 1). Moreover, the word "consecration," which was struck out of the English book (because in the papal sense to consecrate means to transubstantiate by consecration, as Durandus says in book 4), is here inserted in the Scottish liturgy in capital letters: "Prayer of consecration." And this is ordered to be recited by the priest at the western side of the altar, with his face turned away from the people, who stand far off. How does this differ from the secret muttering of the consecratory words among the Papists? So if anyone infers from this that it is lawful for the priest to perform that sacred rite in a language the people do not understand (since God, whom he addresses, understands all tongues alike, while the elements which are consecrated understand nothing, and the people, for whose sole benefit the use of a known language is required, are kept from hearing, turned away by the screen so that they cannot hear), this adversarial faction will not readily reply. Especially so, since their by far most learned man, Whitus, Bishop of Ely, in De sabbato (p. 97), "denies that the sacred rites are by divine right to be performed in a language known to the people, and refers it to ecclesiastical tradition." Yet he thought and spoke quite otherwise when he had not yet been promoted to the island and the mitre. For in the book in which he defended his most learned brother against the Jesuit, entitled Orthodox Faith (ch. 2, art. 17), he presses the apostolic precept from 1 Cor. 14. But the mysteries of this faction were not yet open. It is its custom to overturn what it has once laid down, and to adapt religion to its own ambition. In that very consecratory prayer they have inserted the formal words of the Papists on which their transubstantiation rests, for God is asked to will to sanctify the oblations of bread and wine so that they may become for us the body and blood of Christ. Montacute's words in Appeal to Caesar (p. 289) agree with these: "The dispute between Papists and reformed about the manner of Christ's presence is empty; concord would be easy, were it not that the Jesuits and Puritans, instigated by the Devil, hinder the counsels of peace." And Laurentius in his sermon (p. 18): "The manner of the presence is not to be sought, much less determined." Yet before this we had received much from the Canterbury man and his followers about the bodily presence of Christ on the altar, on account of which they wish the altar to be adored. If anyone desires the elevation and adoration of the elements, the marginal rubric of the Scottish liturgy provides it, by which "the presbyter is ordered to take the paten and chalice into his hands." Is it fair that a priest should take the sacred mysteries in his hands without humble reverence and submission? (Heylin against Burton, p. 137.) Immediately after the prayer of consecration there follows the "Prayer of oblation," in the order and words which once stood in the Salisbury missal. And lest anyone should doubt whether they fully agree with the Papists about the nature of this sacrifice, they teach that here is a true, proper, bodily, visible sacrifice, though unbloody, by whose oblation the Apostles and all ministers are true priests, or sacrificers, after the order of Melchizedek; and the eucharistic table is as true and proper an altar as that bronze altar of Moses was (Heylin, Antidote to Lincoln, pp. 6 and 17). And Pocklington, expressly, in his Christian Altar, published under the authentic licence of Canterbury and swelling everywhere with Papistical leaven, speaks thus (ch. 20): "If we have no Christian altar, we also have no Christian sacrifice; if we have no sacrifice, we also have no Christian priest; if we have no priest, away with a Liturgy that teaches a priest how he ought to stand at the altar."

units.la: Tertiam missæ principalem partem facit Communio: cum liber Anglicus opportune adderet sententias quasdam de edendo per fidem, & bibendo in memoriâ, ne corporalem præsentiam conciperent imperitiores ex verbis distributionis, Scotica liturgia sententias hasce delet, quia scil. ejus authoribus propositum fuit ut populus corporalem præsentiam conciperet, & responsione Amen eandem diserte profiteretur. Anglica liturgia jubet tradi elementa in manus communicantium, hoc in Scotica deletur, & ejus loco inseritur, debito ordine communicet populus; quibus verbis complura latent mysteria, nam cum iis innuatur oppositio quædam inter communionem clericorum & laicorum, neque ullibi expressum sit, in quibus differentia ista sita sit, excepto loco in quo actio hæc peragitur; cui dubium quin sic postica aperiatur plurimis Pontificiorum erroribus; quales sunt, ut elementa in os communicantis populi ingerantur; ut altera tantum species laicis tradatur: Nam nullibi mentionem facit liber Scoticus communionis Laicorum sub utraque, quin contra Montacut. in originib. p. 396. aperte profitetur, nihil tale in scripturis inveniri. Ubi (inquit) jubentur infantes in scripturis baptizari, aut in coena Domini sub utraque specie communicantes participare; de his possumus profiteri, Nihil tale docet scriptura, scriptura haec non praedicat: Quid sibi vult nomen illud Corporalis, de linteo quo tegenda sint elementa post consecrationem? nomen illud nunquam ecclesiae innotuit nisi post natam transubstantiationem: Uti & illud, si elementa consecrata non sufficiant communicantibus, presbytero repetenda sunt verba consecrationis super novo pane seu vino. Quid repositoria illa publica? A quorum retentione ecclesiam Anglicanam laudari vult Poklingt. nonne satis docent consultum esse sacramenta reservare? in quem usum viderint ipsi: Andreas Wintoniensis in strictur. Non audet damnare consuetudinem illam reservandi sacramenta, & deferendi ad aegrotos pro viatico.
units.tr: The third principal part of the Mass is the Communion. The English book opportunely adds certain sentences about eating by faith and drinking in memory, lest the more unskilled should conceive a bodily presence from the words of distribution. The Scottish liturgy deletes these sentences, because clearly its authors intended that the people should conceive a bodily presence and openly profess it in the response "Amen." The English liturgy orders the elements to be delivered into the hands of the communicants; this is deleted in the Scottish and in its place is inserted "let the people communicate in due order." Many mysteries lie hidden in these words, for by them a certain distinction between the communion of clergy and laity is hinted at, while it is nowhere expressed in what this difference consists, except in the place where the action is performed. Undoubtedly the back door is thus opened to very many errors of the Papists: such as that the elements are thrust into the mouths of the communicating people, and that only one kind is given to the laity. "For the Scottish book nowhere makes mention of the communion of the laity under both kinds," and on the contrary Montacute openly professes in Origins (p. 396) that nothing of the sort is found in Scripture. "Where," he says, "are infants commanded in Scripture to be baptized, or to partake in the Lord's Supper communicating under both kinds? Concerning these things we can profess: Scripture teaches nothing of the sort; this Scripture does not preach it." What does that word "corporal" mean, in regard to the linen cloth with which the elements are to be covered after consecration? That name never became known to the Church until transubstantiation arose. And likewise, "if the consecrated elements do not suffice for the communicants, the words of consecration are to be repeated by the presbyter over new bread or wine." What of those public repositories, whose retention Pocklington wishes the English Church to be praised for? Do they not sufficiently teach that it is advisable to reserve the sacraments? Let them see to what use. Andrew of Winchester, in his Strictures: "He does not dare to condemn that custom of reserving the sacraments and carrying them to the sick for viaticum."

units.la: Restat jam ut probetur eandem factionem gravissimam tyrannidem promovere tum in ecclesias, tum in subditorum privilegia.
units.tr: It remains now to prove that the same faction promotes a most grievous tyranny, both over the churches and over the privileges of subjects.

units.la: Despoticam authoritatem in ecclesias sibi assumere praeter quotidianam praxin, haec eorum ἀξιώ-ματα[?] demonstrant, Potestatem condendi ecclesiasticas leges solummodo competere Dioecesano episcopo, tam extra Synodum, quam in Synodo, in qua quos ex clero advocare Episcopo visum fuerit, suffragia habent solummodo deliberativa, cum spiritualem jurisdictionem in foro exteriori non solum a regibus, verumetiam a Deo habeant episcopi; quia dicit Apostolus, omnis potestas est a Deo. Samuel Hoardus. conc. p. 8. quam habuit in Metropolitana visitatione.
units.tr: Besides their daily practice, these their axioms show that they assume to themselves a despotic authority over the churches: "The power of making ecclesiastical laws belongs only to the diocesan bishop, both outside the Synod and in the Synod, in which those of the clergy whom it has seemed fit to the bishop to summon have only deliberative votes, since bishops have spiritual jurisdiction in the external forum not only from kings but also from God; because the Apostle says, all power is from God" (Samuel Hoard, Concio, p. 8), which he held in his Metropolitan visitation. [ἀξιώματα]

units.la: Jura omnia quibus reguntur ecclesiae, & quibus reges ipsi, membra & filii ecclesiae permittunt se gubernari, nativam vitalitatem ex præpositis ecclesiæ, hoc est, Episcopis, tanquam ex corde recipiunt, & vivacitatem ex ipsis tanquam ex capitibus derivant. Chounæus in collect. theolog. p. 53. Episcopos solos sine ullo cleri consensu posse abrogare totam ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ formam, licet ea legibus regni municipalibus, ac nationalium Synodorum decretis sancita sit, ac annis 80. frequentata: & ejus loco novam substituere: posse totam externam cultus divini formam unica litura obliterare, & novam à se compositam invitis ecclesiis severe obtrudere: Testatur praxis recens Episcoporum Scoticorum, obtrudentium simul & semel libros Canonum, liturgiæ, ordinationis & homiliarum; non minus monstrosa & barbara Scotis sunt hæc nomina, quam fuerunt ominosa: Ad quod faciendum Cantuariensis consilio & auxilio commoti fuerunt, suisque literis frequentissimis quæ in Scotorum manus devenerunt, ut diligens [?]ἐγχειριώκτης[?] eosdem sollicitavit, ac currentibus calcar addidit: Pari reverentia & cura obsequendum esse mandatis Episcoporum, qua Dei; cum Deo contraria non præceperint. Whitus in examin. dialog. p. 20. ex Bernardo citat & probat; ut & illud ex Eusebio, quicquid in sanctis episcoporum consiliis decernitur, id universum divinæ voluntati debet attribui. Ita quidem, ut si quis ausus fuerit vocare in dubium non solum Canonem, verumetiam rubricam & titulum canonum Episcopalium, excommunicandus sit. Canon. Scotic. p. 8. & ubi nulla pœna quorundam canonum violatoribus designatur, ea ad arbitrium Episcoporum referatur. Ibid. p. 37. quam vero gratiam ab episcopis exspectare possint rei læsæ authoritatis episcopalis, illustria & recentia exempla satis docent; stigmata, perpetuus carcer, aurium amputatio, publica flagellatio, exilium, ingentes multæ pecuniariæ; leves dicunt esse pœnas, respectu earum quas meriti sunt qui audent ministrorum paritatem ex verbo Dei probare, aut, episcopatum juris esse divini, negare: Cum tamen singulari clementia ferantur in Iesuitas, & sacerdotes pontificios: absit. (inquit Cantuariensf. in epistola dedicatoria praefixa relationi colloquii cum Piscatore seu Fishero Jesuita) ut ego unquam author aut suasor effem vel minimae persecutionis contra Iefuitas; aut ut ego ipse eos persequerer: nam quantum memini, neque illum vid.Fisherum,aut illius socios vel verbis acrioribus unquam accepi.
units.tr: All the laws by which the churches are governed, and to which the kings themselves, the members and children of the Church, allow themselves to be governed, receive their native vitality from the prelates of the Church, that is, from the bishops, as from the heart, and derive their life from them as from the heads. Chounus, in Collect. Theolog. p. 53, holds that bishops alone, without any consent of the clergy, can abrogate the whole form of ecclesiastical discipline, even though it has been sanctioned by the municipal laws of the realm and the decrees of national synods and observed for eighty years, and substitute a new one in its place; that they can wipe out the entire external form of divine worship with a single stroke of the pen and severely impose on unwilling churches a new form of their own composing. The recent practice of the Scottish bishops bears witness to this, forcing upon them at one stroke the books of canons, liturgy, ordination and homilies; these names are as monstrous and barbarous to the Scots as they were ominous. For doing this they were moved by the counsel and help of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and by his very frequent letters, which came into Scottish hands; as a diligent agent [ἐγχειριώκτης] he urged them on and added spurs to runners. We must obey the commands of bishops with the same reverence and care as those of God, provided they have not commanded anything contrary to God. Whitus, in Examen Dialog. p. 20, cites and proves this from Bernard, and also that from Eusebius: whatever is decreed in the holy councils of bishops must all be attributed to the divine will. Indeed, so that if anyone dares to call in question not only a canon but even the rubric and title of the Episcopal canons, he is to be excommunicated. Canon. Scotic. p. 8. And where no penalty is assigned to violators of certain canons, it is to be referred to the discretion of the bishops. Ibid. p. 37. What favour those whose episcopal authority has been injured may expect from the bishops, recent and illustrious examples sufficiently teach: branding, perpetual imprisonment, cutting off of ears, public flogging, exile, and huge fines of money. They say these penalties are light compared with those deserved by people who dare to prove from God's Word the parity of ministers, or to deny that episcopacy is of divine right; yet they are inflicted with singular clemency on Jesuits and Popish priests. Far be it (says the Archbishop of Canterbury in the dedicatory epistle prefixed to the account of the conference with the Jesuit Piscator, or Fisher) that I should ever be the author or promoter of even the least persecution against the Jesuits, or that I myself should persecute them; for as far as I remember, I never received from that Fisher, or his companions, even harsher words.

units.la: Potestatem supremi magistratus usque adeo extendunt, ut nullus locus legitimis subditorum privilegiis relictus sit: licet seren.Rex Carolus in oratione sua regia ad parliamentum Angliae ann. 1628. ingenue professus sit, praerogativam regiam in eo sitam esse ut subditorum privilegia tueretur; licet advocatus regius in Anglia non ita pridem nobiles quosdam Anglos in jus vocaverit regis nomine, quod scriptum quoddam ab alio compositum penes se haberent, & divulgassent, quo author scripti regi serenissimo suggerebat, ut omnia ad sui ipsius arbitrium revocaret, subditorum fortunas sine ipsorum consensu arriperet, ac edictis suis sine parlamenti consensu leges figeret & refigeret, Quod scriptum, inquit idem advocatus, si vulgo innotuisset, maximis tumultibus causam praebuisset, ac inevitabile fore damnum tam regi serenissimo quam toti regno excitasset: Licet Bilfonus Wintonienfis episcopus de subjectione. p. 280. fateatur, Licere subditis aliquando sine rebellionis crimine, principibus suis resistere, si imperium & regnum in tyrannidem mutare velint, aut neglectis legibus ex animorum suorum arbitrio agere, his (inquit) & similibus casibus, licet optimates & populus se conjunxerit ad antiqua & recepta privilegia defendenda, nequaquam rebelles censendi sunt. Et ibid. idem, Scotorum, Gallorum, Belgarum protestantium causam contra rebellionis crimen iisdem a Pontificiis objectum fuisse agit, ac diserte asserit, Licere optimatibus & populo tueri antiquam suam & Christianam libertatem, pactam conventam cum principibus, quibus primitus se submiserunt; & confirmatam ac approbatam à subsequentibus regibus; licet serenissimus Rex Carolus, reformatos in Galliis contra illorum regem, & Germanos contra tyrannidem imperatoris juverit, nunquam proculdubio manum periclitantibus tam liberaliter majorum suorum exemplo porrecturus, si putasset nulla ratione licere subditis se tueri contra principes supremos: aut regum potestatem supra omnes leges esse, à quibus non posset limitari. Nihilominus tamen vulgo apud hujus adversæ factionis principes receptum & decantatissimum est, regum potestatem illimitatam esse, nam cum sint Dei Deputati, à quibus quæso limitari possunt? An à legibus? Sed illarum conditores sunt & latores: principes itaque supra leges sunt, & principi lex non est posita, & absolutam habet authoritatem: Heilens in moderato suo responsi.[?] p.28. 32. Abredonenses Theologi in duplic. p. 22. Et non minus læsæ majestatis crimen incurrere qui definiet, quid rex possit aut non possit, quam Atheismi, qui pro & contra disputet quid Deus possit aut non possit. Ait quidam ex factione ista sub larva Lysimachi Nicanoris; p.3. Regum rescripta privata, leges esse. Heilens antidot. Lincol.p.66. Totus liber Iohannis Wemii de primatu regis, tyrannicis hisce paradoxis refertus est; in quo nomine primatus regii omnia tum in repub. tum in ecclesia regibus concedit, Ita ut nullo casu, quicunque demum is sit, subditis liceat principi resistere, adversus quem naturalis juris defensio seu injuriæ depulsio omnibus & singulis ademta est: Quod & Abredonenses Theologi in duplica sua passim effutiunt, & in canones ecclesiasticos in nupera convocatione Anglica, Cantuariensis opera relatum est: & hinc atrocia illa rebellionis, seditionis convitia toties in Scotos jactitata, quia privilegia ecclesiasticis & politicis legibus fancita, à pauculis quibusdam ecclesiasticis iisque exteris & peregrinis, regia gratia abutentibus conculcari, & regnum suum independens & liberum simul cum ecclesia, in provinciæ servilis formam redigi non patiuntur.
units.tr: They extend the power of the supreme magistrate so far that no room is left for the lawful privileges of subjects, although the most serene King Charles, in his royal speech to the Parliament of England in 1628, frankly professed that the royal prerogative consists in this, that it protects the privileges of subjects; and although the King's Advocate in England not long ago summoned certain English nobles to court in the king's name, because they had in their possession and had published a certain writing composed by another, in which the author advised the most serene king to draw everything back to his own judgement, to seize the fortunes of subjects without their consent, and to set and reset laws by his edicts without the consent of Parliament. This writing, said the same Advocate, if it had become known to the public, would have given rise to very great tumults, and would have caused an unavoidable loss both to the most serene king and to the whole realm. Yet Bilson, Bishop of Winchester, in De Subjectione, p. 280, admits that it is sometimes lawful for subjects, without the crime of rebellion, to resist their princes, if they wish to change the empire and kingdom into tyranny, or to act according to the judgement of their own minds with the laws disregarded; in these and similar cases, he says, although the nobles and the people have joined together to defend their ancient and accepted privileges, they are by no means to be judged rebels. And the same author, in the same place, argues the cause of the Scottish, French and Belgian Protestants against the charge of rebellion brought against them by the Papists, and plainly asserts that it is lawful for the nobles and the people to defend their ancient and Christian liberty, agreed upon and covenanted with the princes to whom they first submitted, and confirmed and approved by the kings who followed. Although the most serene King Charles aided the Reformed in France against their king, and the Germans against the tyranny of the emperor, he would undoubtedly never have so generously stretched out a hand to those in danger, following the example of his ancestors, had he thought it in no way lawful for subjects to defend themselves against supreme princes, or that the power of kings is above all laws, by which it cannot be limited. Nevertheless, it is commonly received and very much repeated among the princes of this opposing faction that the power of kings is unlimited; for since they are the deputies of God, by whom, I ask, can they be limited? By the laws? But they are the makers and proposers of those laws. Princes therefore are above the laws, and no law is laid down for a prince, and he has absolute authority. Heylyn, in his Moderate Answer, pp. 28, 32; the Aberdeen Divines in their Duplica, p. 22: And he who defines what the king can or cannot do incurs no less the crime of high treason than the atheist who disputes what God can or cannot do. Someone of that faction, under the mask of Lysimachus Nicanor, says (p. 3): The private rescripts of kings are laws. Heylyn, Antidotum Lincolniense, p. 66. The whole book of John Weemes on the primacy of the king is filled with these tyrannical paradoxes; in it he grants to kings, in both the state and the Church, all the primacy of the royal power, so that in no case, whatever it may be, is it lawful for subjects to resist the prince, from whom the natural right of defence, or the repelling of injury, has been taken from every single one of them. The Aberdeen Divines also babble this throughout their Duplica, and it was reported in the recent English convocation, through the work of the Archbishop of Canterbury, that they were made into canons of the Church. Hence come those atrocious accusations of rebellion and sedition, so often hurled against the Scots, because they will not allow the privileges sanctioned by ecclesiastical and political laws to be trampled by a few churchmen, and those foreign and outsiders, who abuse the royal favour, and because they will not suffer their kingdom, independent and free, together with the Church, to be reduced to the form of a servile province.

units.la: Atque hæc summa est illius libri; an vero nomen titulo contractum author expunxerit, ad lectores partium studio non occæcatos, & librorum paginas ac sectiones intrepide provocat.
units.tr: This is the sum of that book. Whether the author has deleted from the title the name he shortened, he boldly challenges readers who are not blinded by partisanship, and the pages and sections of the books, to judge.

units.la: Quibus vero animis scripta hæc in Anglia à quamplurimis accepta fuerunt, in parlamento Angliæ tum convocato satis constabat. Nam licet ingentia promissa corrigendi omnia gravamina & reformandi omnes abusus ostentarentur, dummodo ordines liberaliter & alacres subsidia pecuniaria contra rebelles Scotos concederent; nihil tamen ab inferiori parlamenti illius domo, hoc est, provinciarum & civitatum deputatis obtineri potuit, itaque semper instabant ut gravamina prius excuterentur; persuasum etiam quamplurimis fuit, nullo exercitu opus esse ad Scotos in ordinem redigendos, ac regiæ obedientiæ subjugandos, cujus legitimum jugum nunquam detrectassent: quibusque nihil aliud propositum esse prospiciebant, quam ut privilegia sua à majoribus transmissa tuerentur; nec paterentur se in vilem servitutem redigi, sub specioso & fallaci fuco moderatæ subjectionis: qualem videl. patitur Hibernia.
units.tr: With what feelings these writings were received in England by very many people was sufficiently clear in the Parliament of England, then summoned. For although vast promises were displayed of correcting all grievances and reforming all abuses, provided the estates would generously and eagerly grant money subsidies against the rebel Scots, nothing could be obtained from the lower house of that Parliament, that is, from the deputies of the counties and cities; they therefore kept insisting that the grievances be examined first. Very many were also persuaded that no army was needed to bring the Scots into line and subdue them to royal obedience, since they had never refused its lawful yoke; and they saw that nothing else was being proposed than that they should protect the privileges handed down by their ancestors, and not suffer themselves to be reduced to vile servitude under the specious and deceptive guise of moderate subjection, such as, namely, Ireland endures.

units.la: Ruptæ à Scotis pacis plurima non sine verborum apparatu indicia proponi videbant, & inter alia referri actiones Scotorum in nupera synodo, à rege indicta, & deputati regii continua præsentia cohonestata, ac ejus consensu rata; quas tamen nunc proditionis nomine venire non sine stupore audiebant: licet synodi sanctionem expresse pollicitus fuisset Sereniff. rex; alia vero vel usque adeo levia, vel dubia, vel aperte contra ipsorum mentem distorta suisse quæ Scotis objecta fuerunt, ut, nisi rex per custodem magni sigilli declarasset sibi quam ingratissimum futurum, si quilibet, quicunque demum is esset, operam suam offerret ad negotium hoc inter se & Scotos componendum, constans prudentiorum opinio fuerit, ordinibus regni Angliæ statutum fuisse, apud regem intercedere pro Scotis, ut positis armis res legitime & ex æquo componi pateretur: præsertim cum armata Scotorum oppressione vincula sibi paratum iri metus multis esset.
units.tr: They saw many signs of the breaking of peace by the Scots being put forward, not without a show of words, and among other things were told of the actions of the Scots in the recent synod convened by the king, and sanctioned by his consent, with the continuous presence of the royal commissioner lending it respectability; yet they heard with astonishment that these were now being called treason. Although the most serene king had expressly promised the sanction of the synod, and the things objected to the Scots were so trivial, or doubtful, or plainly distorted against their meaning, that it was the settled opinion of the more prudent, unless the king had declared through the keeper of the great seal how most unwelcome it would be to him if anyone, whoever he might be, offered his services to settle this matter between himself and the Scots, that it had been resolved by the estates of the realm of England to intercede with the king on behalf of the Scots, so that, with arms laid down, the matter might be settled lawfully and fairly; especially since many feared that chains were being prepared for them by the armed oppression of the Scots.

units.la: Quod cum factioni Scotis adversæ suboluisset, neque ullis rationibus persuaderi potuisse provinciarum & civitatum deputatis, ut subsidia in bellum hoc conferrent; nec immerito metuerent, ne, si parlamento permitteretur altius in gravaminum causas inquirere, incideret in foveam quam Scotis paraverat; regi seren. authorem fuisse omnium calculis referebatur, dimittendi ac dissolvendi parlamenti, maximo bonorum cum mœrore. Clerus interim in domo convocationis sibi sedulo prospiciebat, & (reluctantibus regni comitiis, sine quorum tamen decreto nulla synodus legitima, nulla lex ecclesiastica rata esse solet) nutantem suam authoritatem novis canonibus ac juramentis ambiguis fulcire conabatur, in quæ adigendi essent omnes ecclesiastici. Inter alia papismum damnabant; quid vero eo nomine censendum esset multis dubium fuit; cum nucleum ipsum papismi, non solum in sinu foveri, verumetiam publicis scriptis à primipilis promoveri perspectum esset.
units.tr: When the faction hostile to the Scots learned of this, and the deputies of the provinces and cities could not be persuaded by any argument to contribute subsidies to this war, and when they had good reason to fear that if Parliament were allowed to inquire more deeply into the causes of the grievances, it would fall into the pit the Scots had prepared, it was reported that the most serene king, by the judgment of all, was the author of dismissing and dissolving Parliament, to the great grief of good men. Meanwhile the clergy looked after themselves diligently in the House of Convocation. Although the estates of the realm resisted, and without their decree no synod or ecclesiastical law is usually considered valid, the clergy tried to prop up their wavering authority with new canons and ambiguous oaths, to which all churchmen were to be bound. Among other things they condemned Popery. But what should be counted as Popery under that name was doubtful to many, since the very kernel of Popery was seen to be nurtured not only in their bosom but also openly promoted in public writings by their leading men.

units.la: Scotos vero suspensis animis Comitiorum eventum exspectantes, inexspectata hæc eorundem dissolutio, satis edocuit extrema quæque sibi brevi experienda fore, præsertim cum ubique interciperentur eorum naves, diriperentur bona, inclementius cum miseris nautis captivis ageretur quam cum hostibus, & ut omne penitus maritimum commercium excluderetur, rex navibus aliquot suis majoribus cū aliis Myoparonibus & celocibus fretorum omnes aditus obseruari jam pridem imperasset; certis etiam nunciis compertum fuit in procinctu esse regios exercitus tam terrestres quam maritimos, ingentemque apparatum bellicum & omne genus commeatum Hullam, Novo-castrum, Berwicum, oppida Scotiæ maxime vicina, quotidie, non ex reliqua Anglia solum, verumetiam Flandria & Hollandia ac Dania aduectum fuisse: domi vero extrema quæque experirentur à præsidiariis castelli Edenburgeni, qui in pueros, ac fœminas maxime sæviebant sine ullo humanitatis affectu. Quare & ad suam defensionem se accingunt Scoti, castella & tormentorum suggestus locis opportunis contra arcem Edinburgenam ædificant, nequicquam fremente arcis gubernatore & minitante se universum oppidum incendio consumpturum[?]: Consiliorum vero summam ad tempus comitiorum à rege indictum ad 2. Junij Stylo veteri referunt.
units.tr: The Scots, awaiting the outcome of the Assembly with anxious minds, were taught by this unexpected dissolution that the utmost measures would soon be tried against them. This was especially so because their ships were intercepted everywhere, their goods plundered, and their wretched sailors treated more cruelly as captives than enemies would be. So that all sea trade might be completely shut out, the king had long before ordered that all the approaches to the straits be watched by some of his larger ships, together with other pinnaces and skiffs. Certain reports also showed that royal armies, both land and sea, were ready to march, and that huge stores of arms and every kind of supply were being brought daily to Hull, Newcastle, Berwick, towns very close to Scotland, not only from the rest of England but also from Flanders, Holland and Denmark. At home, meanwhile, they suffered the utmost from the garrison of Edinburgh Castle, which raged especially against boys and women without any feeling of humanity. Therefore the Scots also prepare for their defence, building fortifications and gun platforms in suitable places against Edinburgh Castle, while the governor fumes to no purpose and threatens to burn the whole town[?]. They report the substance of the counsels for the time of the assembly, which the king had summoned for 2 June, Old Style.

units.la: Quando cum conuenissent Edinburgum, propter regis regiique deputati absentiam, D.Burleum Baronem parlamentarium multo civilis prudentiæ usu instructum, præsidè comitiorum per suffragia crearunt, ac sanctis iis quæ ad ordinandam pacem publicam & salutem tam ecclesiæ quam regni necessaria judicarent, ad defensionis contra apertam vim consilia progrediuntur: Generali Leslio in omnes exercitus tam maritimos quam terrestres summum imperium unanimi omnium ordinum suffragio defertur; eorundemque supremum legatum seu vicarium constituunt Aumontium Baronem parlamentarium,virum generis nobilitate, & probata virtute,ac singulari pietate & prudentia jampridem conspicuum,quem sincerus in patriam suam, ac religionem amor ex militia Batavica retraxerat, in qua Scoticæ legionis tribunum summa cum laude annis compluribus egerat. Electi tum fuere duo supremi vigiliatum praefecti, Baillius tribunus, simul cum Munroo; expertae utraque virtutis & plurimorum stipendiorum in castris Sueco-Germanicis: Laudonium extra culpam esse illius criminis, cujus in Anglia arceffitur, statuto peculiari declarant, ac damna ex ipsius infortunio spondent se uxori & liberis praestituros. Legiones statim conscribendas designant, iisdemque alendis pecuniis communibus suffragiis colligendas esse.
units.tr: When they had gathered at Edinburgh, because the king and his deputy were absent, they chose by vote as president of the assembly Baron Burleigh, a parliamentary baron of great practical civil prudence. After they had approved the measures they judged necessary for ordering public peace and the safety of both the Church and the kingdom, they moved on to plans for defence against open force. By the unanimous vote of all estates, the supreme command of all armies, both sea and land, was entrusted to General Leslie. As their supreme legate or vicar they appointed Aumont, a parliamentary baron, a man long distinguished for noble birth, proven virtue, and singular piety and prudence. His sincere love of his country and religion had drawn him back from Dutch military service, in which he had served for several years with great distinction as tribune of the Scottish legion. Then two supreme commanders of the watch were elected, Baillie as tribune together with Munro, both of proven courage and long experience in campaigns in the Swedish and German armies. By a special statute they declared Lauderdale free of that charge for which he is summoned in England, and they pledged to make good to his wife and children the losses arising from his misfortune. They immediately ordered legions to be raised, and decided by common vote that money to support them should be collected.

units.la: Leslius provinciam capessit, &Munroum cum legione sua Abredoniam & ad provincias illas transGrampianas progredi jussit, ut nationes illic seditiosas & latrociniis assuetas in officio contineret, & oram istam ab excursionibus maritimis per classem regiam tueretur, ac interim nobilium adversantium castella munita in suam potestatem redigeret, & pecuniam ad belli sumptus omnibus ex comitiorum praescripto imperatam, invitis & detractantibus extorqueret: & pertinaciter reluctantes comprehenderet atque Edinburgum transmitteret: Quæ usque adeo feliciter praestitit, ut ab istis provinciis nihil adversi metuendum fuerit, & sera poenitentia Abredonenses edocti praeteritam suam contumaciam damnaverint. In Australibus cisForthanis regionibus tres supererant arces regiis praesidiis instructae, quas arctissima obsidione claudi jusserunt. Edinburgę arci praerat Ruvenus; Britannoduno, Henderfonus; & Carleveroco, sito ad orientalem Nithi fluminis ripam Comes ipse Nithiae, Maxwellorum familiae in partibus illis numerosae princeps; & pontificiae religioni addictissimus: Sed & hae arces, licet naturali situ munitissimae, commeatus penuria & extrema fame, post aliquot mensium obsidionem vindicibus libertatis tandem traditae fuerunt. In occidentalibus provinciis Hiberniae oppositis, Argathelium & Eglintonii Comites subsistere jubent, ut adjunctis provincialibus, hominibus strenuissimis, totam illam oram maritimam tuerentur: nam constans rumor fuit diligentia & artibus Deputati Hibernici Scotis infensissimi ingentem exercitum ibi conscriptum & propediem transmittendum in vicinas Scotiae provincias, vel ob id solum ut Scotorum vires distraheret; sed nobilissimorum illorum comitum vigilantia usque adeo provisum fuit provinciarum istarum securitati, ut de suis servandis tantum non desperarent Hiberni, si, ut constanti rumore ferebatur, Argathelius in Hiberniam trajecisset.
units.tr: Leslie took up his province and ordered Munro, with his legion, to proceed to Aberdeen and the provinces beyond the Grampians. There he was to keep the seditious and raid-loving peoples in obedience, to guard that coast against sea raids by the royal fleet, and meanwhile to bring the fortified castles of opposing nobles under his power. He was also to extort the money for the costs of war, as prescribed by the Assembly, from all who were unwilling or objected, and to seize those who stubbornly resisted and send them to Edinburgh. He carried this out so successfully that nothing adverse was to be feared from those provinces, and the people of Aberdeen, taught by late repentance, condemned their earlier obstinacy. In the southern regions on this side of the Forth three castles remained, held by royal garrisons, and they ordered these to be closed in by the tightest siege. Edinburgh Castle was under Ruthven; Dumbarton, Henderson; and Carlaverock, which lies on the eastern bank of the river Nith, was under the Earl of Nithsdale himself, chief of the numerous Maxwell family in those parts and a most devoted adherent of the Popish religion. But these castles, though strongly fortified by their natural position, were at last surrendered to the defenders of liberty after several months of siege, through lack of supplies and extreme hunger. In the western provinces, facing Ireland, the Earls Argyll and Eglinton were ordered to stay in place, so that with the provincial levies, very vigorous men, they might guard the whole coast. For there was a constant rumour that, through the diligence and devices of the Lord Deputy of Ireland, who was most hostile to the Scots, a great army had been raised there and was soon to be sent into the neighbouring provinces of Scotland, if only to divide the strength of the Scots. But the vigilance of those most noble earls so thoroughly provided for the safety of these provinces that the Irish hardly despaired of holding their own, if, as was constantly rumoured, Argyll had crossed over into Ireland.

units.la: Diligenter interim promovetur militum delectus in Cisgrampianis, maxime vero cis Forthanis provinciis: qui tandem 2o:Iulii convenerunt in Marcia, ac prope silvam Chaufleam castrametati sunt, cum omnis generis apparatu bellico, & quadraginta dierum commeatu, uti in comitiis imperatum fuit.
