Ibi re diu multumque deliberata, communibus omnium suffragiis conclusum fuit in Angliam progrediendum esse, non ut vicinos damno ullo afficerent; nam regno Angliae violationem nuperae pacificationis non imputabant; verum ut suae necessariae securitati contra factionem illam sibi adversam mature prospicerent: Æquitatem vero hujus expeditionis scripto typis excuso afferunt, quod de verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: Meanwhile the levying of soldiers was pushed forward vigorously in the provinces on this side of the Grampians, and especially on this side of the Forth. On 2 July they at last assembled in the Merse and encamped near the wood of Chaufleam, with every kind of military equipment and forty days' provisions, as the Assembly had ordered. There, after the matter had been long and thoroughly deliberated, it was concluded by the common vote of all that they must advance into England. This was not to inflict any harm on their neighbours, for they did not charge the kingdom of England with violating the recent pacification. Rather, it was so that they might in good time provide for their necessary security against that faction hostile to them. They set out the justice of this expedition in a printed writing, which, translated almost word for word, reads as follows.

units.la: Æquitas expeditionis Scoticæ in Angliam.
units.tr: The equity of the Scottish expedition into England.

units.la: Uti ab initio magni hujus operis in hodiernum usque diem, nihil temere, sed firmissimis rationum fundamentis ac Deo deducente, hactenus à nobis factum est; ita nunc æquitatis nostrae fiducia confisi, parati sumus ad respondendum cuivis poscenti rationem praesentis hujus expeditionis, quae inter maxime notabiles est admirandi hujus & plane divini operis partes. Quod dum præstamus, omnes rogatos volumus, ut animis supra privata commoda aut incommoda sublatis, absque præjudiciis & partium studio in sequentia diligenter intendant.
units.tr: As we have done from the beginning of this great work up to the present day, nothing has been done by us rashly, but on the firmest foundations of reason and with God leading us; so now, trusting in the justice of our cause, we are ready to give an account of this present expedition to anyone who asks for one. It is among the most remarkable parts of this wondrous and plainly divine work. In doing so, we ask all who read to set aside private advantage or disadvantage, and to attend carefully to what follows, free from prejudice and partisan zeal.

units.la: 1. Sicut omnibus cognitum est, quanta sit extremæ necessitatis vis, & quantum ad actiones etiam dubias justificandas seu afferendas possit; ita negari nequit, quin vel pax nobis nunc fit necessario petenda in Anglia, vel succumbendum sit tribus gravissimis oneribus, quibus ferendis prorsus impares nos profitemur. Nam 1. Alendi nobis erunt exercitus in limitibus & locis aliis manifesto periculo expositis, ad patriæ nostræ defensionem, quam armorum depositione & exercituum dissolutione hostibus invasuris in prædam certissimam exponeremus. 2. Privabimur negotiatione maritima; quo non solum rebus compluribus necessariis regnum hoc destituetur, verumetiam oppida, cives & nautæ, & quicunque mercatura aut piscatura familias alunt periturí[?] sint, nam eorum vitæ institutum defectu mutuorum commerciorum cum aliis gentibus prorsus corruet. 3. Omnes totius regni subditi publica justitiæ administratione carituri sunt; nam quamvis singulari Dei providentia regnum hoc sine ordinaria & consueta justitia administratione publica durantibus hisce motibus hactenus ordinatum & quietum fuerit, idem tamen ordo, eadem quies posthac exspectari non poterit; quin contra metuendum est ne omnia in confusionem ruant. Vel horum unum quanto magis tria hæc conjuncta extremam nobis ruinam minantur, nisi hujus expeditionis remedio uteremur. Neque hæc ex solo probabili metu, verum ex gravi sensu eofundem omnium malorum proserimus: nostro quippe ineffabili damno hactenus experti sumus, quam grave sit exercitus alere, commerciis ac publica justitiæ administratione destitui. Quod si usque adeo nos premant malorum horum initia, quid de eorundem augmento & diuturniori continuatione dicendum erit? Tam miseram vitam omnes sani qualibet morte pejorem judicabunt.
units.tr: 1. As everyone knows, extreme necessity has great force and can justify or vindicate even doubtful actions. So it cannot be denied that either we must now seek peace from England as a matter of necessity, or we must give way under three very grave burdens, which we declare ourselves wholly unable to bear. For, first, armies will have to be maintained on the borders and in other places manifestly exposed to danger, for the defence of our country. By laying down arms and disbanding our forces, we would hand that country over to invading enemies as their certain prey. Second, we will be deprived of maritime trade. This will leave the kingdom without many necessary goods, and the towns, citizens and sailors, and all who support their families by commerce or fishing, will perish, for their way of life will collapse entirely without mutual trade with other nations. Third, all the subjects of the whole kingdom will be deprived of the public administration of justice. Although by a singular providence of God this kingdom has so far been kept in order and at peace during these disturbances without the ordinary and customary public administration of justice, that same order and peace cannot be expected to continue, and on the contrary we must fear that everything will fall into confusion. Even one of these would be grave; how much more do these three together threaten us with utter ruin, unless we apply this expedition as a remedy. Nor do we say this from mere probable fear, but from a keen sense of these same evils. At our unspeakable loss we have already learned how burdensome it is to maintain an army and to be cut off from commerce and from the public administration of justice. But if the beginnings of these evils press us so hard, what must be said of their increase and their longer continuance? All sane people will judge such a miserable life worse than any death.

units.la: 2. Consideretur natura & qualitas hujus expeditionis, quæ cum ad defensionem solummodo tendat, æquior est. In cujus rei argumentum revocetur in memoriam. 1. Non nos, verum sereniss. regem vafris sævissimorum hostium nostrorum consiliis deceptum, hujus anni bellum inchoasse: Nam cum in leges pacis anno superiori conventum fuisset, exercitus etiam dimissi, castella reddita, synodus indicta, habita, ac consensu expresso & præsentia continua Deputati regii conclusa; ejus tamen sanctio in supremo ordinum conventu denegata fuit contra leges pacis. Cum deputatos ad regem misissemus qui rationes & fundamenta actionum nostrarum in comitiis demonstrarent, non admissi fuerunt ne ad regis quidem præsentiam, nedum auditi. Postea cum rex significaret se eos auditurum, bellum tamen contra nos conclusum fuit in sanctiori regis senatu in Anglia; imo priusquam ad aulam venissent nostri deputati; & supremum exercituum contra nos imperium comiti Northumbriæ commissum fuit: Adde quod convocata fuerint comitia in Hibernia & Anglia ut pecuniam in bellum hoc conferrent: Quæ astuta consilia in nostram ruinam destinata sunt, & militares præparationes. Nonne nobis nosmet continentibus plurima illata sunt damna, naves interceptæ, erepta bona? Omnium ordinum & ætatum homines crudeliter interempti à regio præsidio arcis Edinburgenæ: Hæc satis indicant hostes nostros bellū hoc instaurasse, nos vero defensorum partes agere.
units.tr: 2. Let the nature and character of this expedition be considered: since it aims only at defence, it is the more just. To confirm this, let the following be recalled. First, it was not we but our most serene king, deceived by the crafty counsels of our most savage enemies, who began the war of this year. For when terms of peace had been agreed upon last year, the armies were also disbanded, the castles surrendered, and a synod was called and held, and its decisions were concluded with express consent and the continuous presence of the royal commissioner. Yet its sanction was refused in the supreme assembly of the estates, contrary to the terms of peace. When we sent deputies to the king to set out in the assembly the reasons and grounds of our actions, they were not admitted even to the king's presence, let alone heard. Later, when the king declared that he would hear them, war was nevertheless resolved upon in the more secret council of the king in England, indeed before our deputies had come to court; and the supreme command of the armies against us was committed to the Earl of Northumberland. Add that assemblies were summoned in Ireland and in England to contribute money for this war. These cunning counsels and military preparations were aimed at our ruin. Have not very great losses been inflicted on us, who were minding our own affairs: ships seized, goods taken away? Men of every rank and age were cruelly slain by the royal garrison of Edinburgh Castle. These facts sufficiently show that our enemies began this war, and that we are playing the part of defenders.

units.la: 2. Nullius damnum aut injuriam nobis propositam esse; sed pacem tantum & salutem nostram, ideoque nosmet instruxisse necessario commeatu & armis, nō quidem ut pugnemus, aut acie decertemus cum quolibet, nisi ad illud in necessariam nostram defensionem cogamur, prout in declaratione consilii nostri latius exponetur. 3. Consideretur nos retroceßuros & arma lubentissime deposituros, quamprimum æquissimis nostris postulatis satisfiet, hoc est, pacem securam & firmam obtinebimus. Atque vel hac de causa qui se maximos & acres regalistas haberi volunt, tuentur, arma Protestantium in Galliis contra regem seductum factione Guisiana, fuisse legitima, bellumque illud Protestantium fuisse defensivum; quia semper parati fuerunt ad dissolvendum exercitum, quamprimum ipsis cautum fuisset de pace & libertate religionis. Quare cum præsens hæc expeditio sua natura defensiva sit, satis liquet non pugnare cum prioribus nostris protestationibus, relationibus, remonstrantiis, in quibus nulla exstat vocula contra arma defensiva in hac causa, verum contra, firmissimæ ubique ponuntur rationes quæ huic expeditioni favent. Etenim licet prima nostra relatio hoc anno in Angliam missa, arma execretur offensiva & hostilem omnem invasionem, perspicue tamen declarat, quod si terra vel mari invadamur, coactum iri nos illud facere, quod solent qui se in squalidis ergastulis & tetro carcere concludendos animadvertunt, hoc est, armis libertatem nostram afferere; Si privato cuilibet ita undique circumcluso, ut non liceat negotiatione & commerciis se familiamque alere, ac in perpetuo vitæ suæ discrimine versetur, & ignoret qua hora à sævissimis hostibus ad lanienam protrahendus sit; si huic liceat quantis poterit viribus, ædes suas liberas reddere; quanto magis idem licebit universæ genti? Iniquum certe esset, quod in privatis hominibus probatur, in tota gente damnare.
units.tr: 3. That no harm or injury has been proposed to us, but only our peace and safety; and therefore we have equipped ourselves with necessary supplies and arms, not indeed in order to fight, or to contend in battle with anyone, unless we are forced to it for our necessary defence, as will be explained more fully in the declaration of our purpose. Consider also that we will withdraw and lay down our arms most willingly as soon as our most just demands are met, that is, that we obtain a secure and firm peace. And for this very reason, those who wish to be regarded as the greatest and fiercest royalists maintain that the arms of the Protestants in France against the king, misled by the Guisan faction, were lawful, and that that war of the Protestants was defensive, because they were always ready to disband their army as soon as provision had been made for them concerning peace and freedom of religion. Therefore, since this present expedition is by its nature defensive, it is quite clear that it does not conflict with our earlier protestations, reports and remonstrances, in none of which is there a single word against defensive arms in this cause; on the contrary, everywhere the strongest reasons are put forward that favour this expedition. For although our first report, sent to England this year, condemns arms for attack and every hostile invasion, it nevertheless plainly declares that if we are attacked by land or sea, we will be compelled to do what those do who see themselves shut up in squalid dungeons and a foul prison, that is, to assert our liberty by arms. If a private person were so hemmed in on every side that he could not sustain himself and his family by business and commerce, and lived in constant peril of his life, not knowing at what hour he might be dragged by most savage enemies to slaughter, then if he were allowed to set his house free with all the strength he could muster, how much more would the same be allowed to a whole nation? It would certainly be unjust to condemn in a whole people what is approved in private individuals.

units.la: 3. Ad hanc expeditionem invitamur eadem divina providentia & vocatione, qua hactenus directi fuimus in magni hujus negotii legitima profequutione. De ejus utilitate ad Dei gloriam ecclesiae & patriae nostrae pacem, evangelii propagationem promovendam satis nobis constat. Post preces fervidas ad Deum ut cælitus nos dirigere dignaretur, corda nostra eo feruntur. Zelum ac animos ad ejus prosequutionem, vires & opportunitatem ad eam fuscipiendam, instrumenta satis instructa ad executionem, unanimè consensum scrupulis omnibus & dubitationum æstibus remotis, largitus est nobis Dominus: Multa quæ animum nobis addant divina quasi virgula opportune exhibita sunt, inter quæ palmam obtinent actiones nuperi parlamenti Angliæ, cujus postulata & gravamina nostris paria & prorsus consona fuere. Operam omnem sedulo & constanter impendimus per multiplices libellos supplices, relationes ac declarationes veras status nostri, delegationes, & per omnia quæ à quibuslibet exspectari possent, ut ab hac expeditione liberaremur, verù conatu prorsus irrito. A nobis minime præmeditatâ aut desideratam fuisse Deus χαριδοχωσης[?] optime perspectum habet: verum huc protrusi & coacti ab hostibus nostris ut sic scilicet nationalis belli femina spargerent. Sed prout hactenus Dei bonitate & paterna erga nos providentia, omnes eorum subdoli conatus ac consilia in suum ipsorum caput conversa sunt, ac in contrarios quam sibi promiserant eventus; sic expeditione hac nostra in Angliam (ab hostibus nostris summis votis jampridem expetita sibi persuadentibus universam gentem Anglicam in causæ suæ privatæ patrocinium sic statim excitatum iri) spe sua frustrandos hostes usque adeo confidimus, ut utramque gentem arctioribus & firmioribus tam civilis quam Christiani amoris vinculis, quam quibus unquam antehac, uniat. Porro ut divinæ vocationis ad hanc expeditionem invitantis argumenta magis perspicue pateant: observandus est ordo vestigiorum Dei quibus in magno hoc reformationis opere gradiri visum est: Nam incipiens à crassioribus sordibus papismi in libris liturgiæ & canonum, progressus est per omnes defectionis nostræ anfractus, quoad primas & minimas novationes quæ in hanc ecclesiam subrepserant: Neque adhuc cessat, sed ultra progreditur recta ducens ad Episcopatum Dicecesanum Angliæ, fontem videlicet, ipsum & certissimam scaturiginem unde Babylonicæ istæ sordes in nos identidem emanarunt: Deo itaque adhuc progrediente minime nobis consistendum est: Imo speramus Dominum usque adeo feliciter hic progressurum, ut bestiam & falsum prophetam Romam usque protrusurus,si non terrarum orbem iisdem liberaturus sit. Tertia itaque hæc ratio ex duabus prioribus resultat: Etenim si necessaria sit hæc expeditio, & ad defensionem solummodo suscepta, necessario & infallibiliter sequitur nos ad eam à Deo vocari. Nam necessaria nostra defensio non solum legitima est, verumetiam à divina & naturali lege imperatur, & ad eam in fœdere nostro obligamur.
units.tr: 3. We are invited to this expedition by the same divine providence and calling by which we have hitherto been directed in the lawful pursuit of this great undertaking. We know well enough that its usefulness is to promote the glory of God, the peace of the Church and our country, and the spread of the gospel. After fervent prayers to God that he would deign to direct us from heaven, our hearts are inclined to it. The Lord has granted us, with one mind and with all scruples and the heat of doubts removed, the zeal and spirit to pursue it, the strength and opportunity to undertake it, and instruments sufficiently equipped for carrying it out. Many things that give us courage have been opportunely supplied, as if by a divine rod; among them the acts of the recent Parliament of England stand first, whose demands and grievances were the same as ours and entirely in harmony with them. We have diligently and constantly spent every effort on many humble petitions, reports and true declarations of our condition, delegations, and by every means that could be expected from anyone, to be freed from this expedition, but to no effect whatever. That we did not premeditate or desire this, God, the knower of hearts [καρδιογνώστης], sees most clearly; but we were thrust in here and driven by our enemies, so that they might thus scatter the seeds of a national war. But just as, hitherto, by the goodness of God and his fatherly providence towards us, all their sly attempts and counsels have been turned back upon their own heads, and have had outcomes contrary to what they had promised themselves, so we are so confident that by this expedition of ours into England (which our enemies, persuading themselves that the whole English nation would at once be roused to defend their private cause, have long desired with the highest wishes), our enemies will be disappointed in their hope, that we will unite the two nations with bonds of civil and Christian love both closer and firmer than any that have existed before. Further, so that the arguments for this expedition, as an inviting calling of God, may appear more clearly, the order of God's footsteps must be observed, by which it has pleased him to advance in this great work of reformation. For beginning with the grosser filth of papism in the books of liturgy and canons, he has progressed through every turn of our defection, down to the smallest and least innovations that had crept into this Church. Nor does he cease, but goes further, leading straight on to the diocesan episcopacy of England, that is, the very fountain and most certain spring from which those Babylonian filths have repeatedly flowed out upon us. Therefore, while God is still advancing, we must by no means stand still. Indeed we hope the Lord will advance here so happily that he will drive the beast and the false prophet back to Rome, if not free the whole world from them. This third reason therefore follows from the two former. For if this expedition is necessary and undertaken for defence only, it necessarily and infallibly follows that we are called to it by God. For our necessary defence is not only lawful, but is also commanded by divine and natural law, and we are bound to it by our covenant.

units.la: 4. Æquitas hujus expeditionis demonstratur, à consideratione partis adversæ contra quam suscipitur: quæ non est regnum Angliæ, sed factio Cantuariensis, conflata ex pontificiis, atheis, Arminianis, & præ-fulibus, regis nostri serenissimi seductoribus, & utriusque regni hostibus. Hinc est quod nobis persuadeamus, fratres & vicinos Anglos rebus suis usque adeo improvide non consulturos, ut se partem nobis adversam constituant, & tutelam ac patrocinium hostium nostrorum inter se degentium suscipiant, prout olim à Benjamitis factum fuit, dum impium Gibeathitarum facinus contra Israelitas defenderent.
units.tr: 4. The justice of this expedition is shown by considering the party against whom it is undertaken. That party is not the kingdom of England but the Canterbury faction, made up of Papists, atheists, Arminians and prelates, the seducers of our most serene king and the enemies of both kingdoms. So we are persuaded that our brothers and neighbours the English will not be so improvident of their own interests as to set themselves against us and take up the protection and patronage of our enemies living among them, as the Benjamites once did when they defended the impious crime of the Gibeathites against the Israelites.

units.la: Iudic. 20. Deum rogamus ut illis lagiri velit mulieris illius Abelitica prudentiam, quæ Ioabo cum exercitu contra Abelem civitatem movente, consilium suggessit, quo civitatem ac Ioabum à mutua hostilitate detinuit. Ad commeatum vero & apparatum nostri exercitus quod attinet, spondemus eum non alium futurum, quam qui inter amicos fieri consuevit: Æ-quitatis & gratitudinis regula satis iis suggeret, necessaria nobis administranda esse, præsertim vero cum hæc expeditio plurimum iis prodesse possit. Detestari illos novimus duram & morosam Nabalis avaritiam, Davidi cum suis necessarium commeatum denegantis etiam cum convitio & contumelia, licet ergo eum valde bonus fuisset, neque injuria ulla affecisset. 1.Samuel.25. & inhumanitatem Succothano-rum & Penuelitarum detrectantium panes Gideonis exercitui urgenti & persequenti omnium Israelitarum communes hostes. Iudic.8. Agant autem Angli sponte sua, quod humanitatis & æquitatis leges suggerent. Nos interim (ut in declaratione nostra notum fecimus) à nullo commeatum gratis petimus, sed vel præsenti & numerata pecunia, vel certa cautione & sponsione resolvendi interposita. Quod si hoc nobis negabitur, (quod non exspectamus) non minus damnandum foret quam barbara & inhumana crudelitas Edomitarum & Moabitarum obstinate renuentium Israelitis aquam ad bibendum, & transitum per ipsorum ditiones. Numer. 20. quod crimen usque adeo inexpiabile & atrox Deo visum fuit, ut Edomitas ac Moabitas execratus fuerit, ac devoverit, ne decima eorum generatio veniret in congregationem Iehovæ. Deuteron.23.
units.tr: Judg. 20. We pray God to give them the wisdom of that Abelite woman, who, when Joab was moving his army against the city of Abel, suggested a plan by which she held back both the city and Joab from mutual hostility. As for the provisions and equipment of our army, we promise that it will be no different from what is customary among friends. The rule of equity and gratitude will sufficiently suggest to them that what we need must be supplied to us, especially since this expedition can greatly benefit them. We know that they detest the harsh and surly avarice of Nabal, who denied necessary provisions to David and his men, with reproach and insult, although David had been very good to him and had done him no wrong (1 Sam. 25.), and the inhumanity of the men of Succoth and Penuel, who refused bread to Gideon's army, which was pressing and pursuing the common enemies of all Israel (Judg. 8.). Let the English, then, of their own accord do what the laws of humanity and equity suggest. Meanwhile we (as we made known in our declaration) ask for provisions from no one free of charge, but either for present, counted money or with a certain guarantee and pledge of repayment. But if this is denied us (which we do not expect), it would be no less deserving of condemnation than the barbarous and inhuman cruelty of the Edomites and Moabites, who obstinately refused the Israelites water to drink and passage through their lands (Num. 20.). This crime seemed to God so inexpiable and atrocious that he cursed and devoted the Edomites and Moabites, so that their tenth generation should not enter the congregation of Jehovah (Deut. 23.).

units.la: §.[?] Quinta consideratio finem spectat, propter quem expeditio hæc suscepta est. Deum Optimum Maximum cordium scrutatorem religiose sæpius attestati sumus, nobis nunquam propositum fuisse quidlibet contra serenif. nostrum regem aggredi, aut vindictam contra adversarios nostros in Anglia exercere, (quos in amplissimis Angliæ comitiis judicari petimus) aut occupatis Anglorum bonis nosmet locupletare, ullam denique omnino Angliæ injuriam inferre: quin contra operam omnem & facultates nostras in ipsorum Anglorum commodum lubenter profundemus, prout gratitudinis leges postulant, ob auxilia olim nobis præstita in ipsis primæ nostræ reformationis exordiis, quibus à tyrannide factionis Gallico-Guisianæ liberatos nos fuisse grata mente recolimus: firmum manebit hoc æterni in Anglos amoris & pacis vinculum, Conscientia nostra, & Deus conscientiis nostris major nobis testantur, solam nobis propositam esse Dei gloriam, utriusque gentis firmam pacem, & genuinum serenissimi regis nostri honorem; & ut legitime ac ordine in Israelis turbatores animadvertatur, incendiarios istos intelligimus ab inferis excitatos, Corahos, Balaamos, Doegos, Rhabshakeos, Hamanos, Tobiahos, Sanballatos hodiernos; quo peracto nobis abunde satisfiet. Neque militarem hanc expeditionem in Angliam ut medium ad sanctos illos fines obtinendos prius aggressi sumus, quam alia omnia irrita hostium vafritie reddita nobis effent: ita quidem ut hoc ultimum & unicum remedium nobis nunc superfit.
units.tr: §.[?] The fifth consideration concerns the end for which this expedition was undertaken. We have often solemnly called God, the Best and Greatest, the searcher of hearts, to witness that it was never our purpose to attack anything against our most serene king, or to take vengeance on our adversaries in England (whom we ask to be judged in the most ample assembly of England), or to enrich ourselves with the goods of the English, or in short to do England any injury at all. On the contrary, we will gladly spend all our effort and resources for the good of the English themselves, as the laws of gratitude require, on account of the help once given to us at the very beginnings of our first reformation, by which we were freed, as we gratefully recall, from the tyranny of the Franco-Guisan faction. This bond of eternal love and peace toward the English will remain firm. Our conscience, and God, who is greater than our conscience, bear witness to us that the only purpose set before us is the glory of God, the firm peace of both peoples, and the genuine honour of our most serene king; and that the troublers of Israel be punished lawfully and in due order. We understand those incendiaries to have been raised from hell, namely the Korahs, Balaams, Doegs, Rabshakehs, Hamans, Tobiahs and Sanballats of today. When this is done, we shall be fully satisfied. Nor did we undertake this military expedition into England as a means of obtaining those holy ends until all other means had been rendered useless by the enemies' cunning, so that this last and only remedy now remains to us.

units.la: 6. Si Domino visum fuerit expeditioni huic benedicere, & peccata nostra ac Anglorum oppositio non obstent, quam dulces fructus utraque gens simul cum posteris carpet, ac quanto futuri sunt solatio exteris reformatis ecclesiis suaves eventus? Nam reformatio Scotiæ ad primævam suam formam revocabitur, Angliæ vero reformatio, tot piorum precibus frequentissimè expetita, perfectionem suam tandem assequetur; tum in doctrinæ ac cultus, tum in disciplinæ puritate: Pontificii præsules, & membra omnia Antichristianæ istius Hierarchiæ, cum sua idololatria, superstitione, traditionibus ac inventis humanis in exilium sempiternum damnabuntur, neque amplius funesta ista sectarum & separatistarum nomina audientur: Verum unus erit Deus, ejusque nomen ac cultus idem per totam infulam. Sic Deo erit gloria, regi honor, regnis gaudium, posteris solatium, Christianis aliis ecclesiis exemplum quod laudent & imitentur; & obstinatis nostris hostibus confusio. Amen.
units.tr: 6. If it pleases the Lord to bless this expedition, and our sins and the opposition of the English do not stand in the way, how sweet the fruits that both peoples, together with their posterity, will gather! And how welcome will the happy outcome be as a comfort to the other reformed churches abroad! For the reformation of Scotland will be restored to its primitive form, and the reformation of England, so often sought with the prayers of many godly people, will at last reach its perfection, both in the purity of doctrine and worship and in that of discipline. The Papist prelates and all the members of that Antichristian hierarchy, with their idolatry, superstition, traditions and human inventions, will be condemned to everlasting exile, and those baleful names of sects and separatists will no longer be heard. There will be one God, and his name and worship will be the same throughout the whole island. Thus there will be glory to God, honour to the king, joy to the kingdoms, comfort to posterity, an example for the other Christian churches to praise and imitate, and confusion for our obstinate enemies. Amen.

units.la: Aliud etiam scriptum typis excusum in Anglia spargendum curant, quo scopum consiliorum suorum per præsentem hanc[?] expeditionem declarant; & per quos factum fit quod, ad extrema hæc remedia protruderentur. De verbo fere in verbum translatum sic se habet.
units.tr: They also take care to have another writing printed and circulated in England, in which they declare the aim of their plans in this present expedition, and by whose fault it came about that they were driven to these extreme remedies. It is translated here almost word for word.

units.la: Declaratio consilij exercitus Scoticani, ad fratres Anglos.
units.tr: Declaration of the purpose of the Scottish army, to the English brethren.

units.la: Per ordinum regni delegatos, Exercitus Impe- ratorem, Proceres, reliquosque exercitus ductores.
units.tr: By the delegates of the estates of the kingdom, to the commander of the army, the nobles, and the other leaders of the army.

units.la: Moribus ita comparatum est, ut actiones etiam præstantissimas, honestissimo hominum consilio susceptas, præsentissima Dei manu, omnibusque conspicua providentia gubernatas, etsi prudentioribus, pieque sagacibus approbatas, cœcæ tamen hominum maleseriatorum[?] suspiciones in pejorem semper partem rapiant, importunæ cavillantium censuræ viam ubique aut invenientes aut facientes reprehendant, imperitorum denique ociumque amplexorum securitas damnet; præsertim vero pravorum improbitas, quibus nihil unquam placere potest, nequidem quæ Deo maxime placent, & in quibus se omnium conscientiis probare homines studiosissime contendunt, quique inter duas sarcinas procubantes Templum nunquam exædificatum, religionem nunquam instauratam, quam aut consiliis suis in rebus terrenis aucupandis remoram, aut securitati in iisdem possidendis molestiam ullam objectam malunt. Populus Dei ex Ægyptiacæ servitutis ergastulis olim assertus, Ecclesia per sanguinem filii Dei redempta, cultus Christianus per ipsius ministros passim disseminatus, idemque à Romana superstitione vindicatus, immensa illa & stupendaDei opera acerbissimas impiorum odiosissime recalcitrantium calumnias non effugerunt.
units.tr: By the custom of the world it comes about that even the most excellent undertakings, entered upon with the most honourable counsel of men, guided by the very present hand of God and by a providence visible to all, and approved by the wiser and the piously shrewd, are nonetheless seized upon by the blind suspicions of ill-disposed men, always in the worse sense. Importunate fault-finders either find or make an opening everywhere to censure them, and the complacency of the unskilled and of those who love their ease finally condemns them. Above all, the wickedness of the depraved condemns them, for nothing can ever please these people, not even what pleases God most, and in whose consciences men most eagerly strive to prove themselves. They, fighting between two burdens, the Temple never built, religion never restored, prefer to throw some obstacle in the way of their schemes for snatching at earthly gain, or some trouble in the way of their secure possession of such things. The people of God, once rescued from the prison-house of Egyptian slavery, the Church redeemed through the blood of the Son of God, Christian worship spread abroad everywhere through his ministers, and the same worship vindicated from Roman superstition: even those immense and stupendous works of God have not escaped the most bitter calumnies of the impious, who kick back most hatefully.

units.la: Enimvero, sive tam eximii operis, in quo moliendo Deus nostro hactenus ministerio uti dignatus est, conditionem & ingenium spectemus, sive impietatis nusquam nobis hucusque non adversantis pertinaciam recordemur, nisi equi aut muli instar mentis expertes esse volumus, contradictionem peccatorum expectare debemus; ut quicquid infernus parturire, quicquid hominum improbitas ventilare possit, illud omne ad odium nobis & causæ quam propugnamus divinæ, cum apud omnes, tum maximè vicinos fratresque nobis longè charissimos conciliandum, in medium proferatur. Ingressum nostrum in Angliam infamabunt, quasi hostilia omnia meditemur; neque aliud ab initio nostrum fuerit consilium, quam ut obtento Religionis & Libertatis publicæ velo, Anglorum bona ad nosmetipsos locupletandos occupemus. Quanquam qui prudenti moderatoque judicio secum perpenderit, quanto cum obsequio per tot annos ante exortos nuper tumultus publice morigeri vixerimus, quam constanter tot editis libellis assertoriis & declaratoriis hostiliter invadendi consilium à conscientia nostra removerimus, & ex animo nos execrari universo terrarum orbi nuper testatum fecerimus, quam cupide pacem semper petierimus, quam libentibus animis, minimam etiam spem amplexi Religionis & legitimæ libertatis fruendæ, arma sumpta, non iniquissimis conditionibus statim abjecerimus; hæc quisquis æqua statera pensitaverit, longe firmiora consilii nostri argumenta esse deprehendet, quam ut ea omnes omnium malevolorum techinæ & calumniæ mirimum labefactare possint.
units.tr: Indeed, whether we consider the nature and character of so distinguished a work, which God has deigned to bring about through our ministry until now, or whether we recall the obstinacy of impiety, which has never ceased to oppose us until now, we must expect the opposition of sinners, unless we want to be devoid of reason like horses or mules. So whatever hell can bring forth, whatever human wickedness can stir up, all of it is brought forward to make us, and the divine cause we defend, hateful, both to everyone and especially to our neighbouring brethren, who are very dear to us. They will defame our entry into England, as though we were planning every kind of hostility. Our purpose from the beginning, they will say, was nothing other than to seize the goods of the English to enrich ourselves, under the veil of religion and public liberty. Yet whoever weighs these things with a prudent and moderate judgement will consider how obediently we lived, publicly compliant, for so many years before the recent tumults arose; how constantly, through so many published pamphlets asserting and declaring our position, we have kept from our conscience any intention of attacking hostilely, and how we have made it known to the whole world that we from our hearts execrate such a thing; how eagerly we always sought peace; and how, with willing minds, we laid down our arms at once, not on the most unfair terms, when we had taken them up in the slightest hope of enjoying religion and lawful liberty. Whoever weighs these things on an even balance will find our arguments for our purpose far too firm to be greatly weakened by all the cunning and calumnies of all our ill-wishers.

units.la: Neque quæ deinceps intervenere, ab hoc perpetuo proposito nos averterunt: Quinimo nobis animum magis etiam obfirmarunt. Pontificiorum sanè in eo regno, Prælatorumque, & hominum episcopalium, qui ut Ecclesia & Respublica nostra funditus exstirpetur, omni conatu & antehac ambibant,& hodie moliuntur, ea est adversum nos injuriarum atrocitas, ut de iis non aliter nos quam de hostibus, & Dei & nostris sentire merito ipsi expectare debeant: Boni tamen Anglicæ cives, ipsumque adeo regnum universum, cum plurimis antehac benevolentiæ testimoniis nos arctissime sibi devinxere, tum illo inprimis, quo & amplissimam sibi gloriæ apud omnes gentes accessionem peperere, & propiore affectu pietatis sibi conciliatos maximo authoramento tenent obstrictos, cujus beneficii, & ipsi;
units.tr: Nor have the things that have since intervened turned us away from this lasting purpose; rather, they have made our resolve even firmer. Indeed, the Papists in that kingdom, and the prelates and episcopal men, who have always sought, with every effort, and now strive, to root out our Church and commonwealth utterly, have shown such atrocity of injuries against us that they ought rightly to expect us to feel towards them no differently than towards enemies both of God and of ourselves. Yet the good citizens of English birth, and the kingdom as a whole, have bound us most closely to themselves by very many earlier testimonies of goodwill; and above all by that one, by which they have also won for themselves ample increase of glory among all nations, and holding us bound by a closer affection of piety, they keep us obliged by the greatest debt of gratitude, of which benefit they themselves

units.la: Et nati natorum, & qui nascentur ab illis, memoriam usurpabimus, & constanti prædicatione ad omnem æternitatem transmittemus: quod cum Secretioris Concilii Anglicani Senatus falsis relationibus temere credens, vim adversus nos decrevi-set; cum Hiberni in Comitiis & corpora sua & fortunas ad belli in nos subsidium detulissent; cum omnes consiliorum machinæ ad eam causam promovendam admotæ, cum ex authoritate regia publicæ declarationes editæ, cum in hunc ipsum finem Comitia in Anglia indicta essent, cum in omnibus curiis pro concione perduelles nos denunciassent, ea tamen fuerit augusti illius Comitiorum consessus prudentia & gravitas, ea justitia, (cum æterno eorum honore prædicanda) ut nullis minis, nullis terroribus, nullis pollicitationibus, nullius spei delinimentis ad bellum aut pecuniarum subsidium adversus nos decernendum induci potuerint: quin econtra & sermonibus & querimoniis, paria nobiscum gravamina deprecantes, ad nostræ causæ patrocinium accesserint.
units.tr: and the children of their children, and those who will be born of them, we shall keep in memory, and hand down in constant proclamation to all eternity. When the Senate of the English Privy Council, too readily believing false reports, had decreed force against us; when the Irish in their assemblies had offered both their bodies and their fortunes as aid for war against us; when every machine of counsel had been brought to bear to advance that cause; when public declarations had been issued by royal authority; when assemblies had been summoned in England for this very purpose; when in all the courts, from the pulpit, they had proclaimed us traitors: yet such was the prudence and gravity of that august assembly of Parliament (to be proclaimed with their eternal honour), and such its justice, that by no threats, no terrors, no promises, and no enticements of any hope could they be induced to decree war or a grant of money against us. On the contrary, both in speeches and in complaints, pleading grievances equal to our own, they came forward in defence of our cause.

units.la: Hoc recenti beneficio longe amplissimo ita nostros affectus obstrinxerunt, ut quantæcunque vires essent nostræ, cum nobis ad summam ingratitudinem nihil reliquum facere videremur, tum justissimam ab irato Deo vindictam exspectaremus, si gentem publice nobis tam amicam in re minima violemus. Atq; in hac benevolentiæ professione non exiguam gratiæ partem inclytæ civitati Londinensi deferimus, quæ oppugnantibus quantumvis Regis & aulæ corruptoribus in sinu suo degentibus, & seditionis classicum nunquam non incinentibus, constantissimo tamen erga Religionem & communem utriusque regni tranquillitatem studio tot rebus probato eximiæ pietatis gloriam jure promeruerit.
units.tr: By this most ample recent kindness our feelings are so bound that, however great our strength might be, we would seem to leave nothing for ourselves but the highest ingratitude, and we would expect righteous vengeance from an angry God if we should wrong so publicly friendly a nation in a small matter. And in this profession of goodwill we give no small share of thanks to the famous city of London, which, though the corrupters of the King and court who dwell within its walls opposed our cause as much as they could, and never ceased sounding the trumpet of sedition, has nevertheless rightly earned the glory of exceptional piety, proved by so many acts of its most constant zeal for religion and for the common peace of both kingdoms.

units.la: Quod si hæc officii nostri publice testata conscientia bonis Anglię civibus plene non satisfaciat, nos & hic publice universis deferimus, & privatim singulis, quibus postulare visum erit, deferemus augustum sanctissimi jurisjurandi sacramentum, magnum tremendi Iehovæ (quem expeditioni nostræ benedicturum speramus) nomen religiose attestati, nihil hostile nos ausuros, in nullum rapina grassaturos[?], ad prælium nisi coactos non descensuros: quam necessitatem ut à Pontificiorum Prælatorumque factione exspectemus, bonos tamen cives, virofque pios, purioris religionis, honoris regii, publicæque libertatis amantes tale nihil molituros sperare jubet, & charitatis ratio, suspicionem sine conscientia demeriti aversantis, & prudentiæ, communem utriusque regni fortunam, sive prosperam, sive adversam esse demonstrantis.
units.tr: But if this conscience of our duty, publicly attested, does not fully satisfy the good citizens of England, we here publicly offer to all, and will privately offer to each person whom it seems fit to ask, the august sacrament of the most holy oath, religiously attesting the great name of the dreaded Jehovah (whom we hope will bless our expedition): that we shall dare nothing hostile, shall make no plunder against anyone, and shall not go down to battle unless compelled. Though we should expect such a necessity from the faction of Papists and prelates, yet the reasoning of charity, which turns away suspicion where there is no consciousness of wrongdoing, and the reasoning of prudence, which shows that the fortune of both kingdoms is common, whether prosperous or adverse, bids us hope that good citizens and pious men, lovers of purer religion, royal honour and public liberty, will plan nothing of the kind.

units.la: Omnia utriusque regni consilia eo spectant, ut Religionis puritas inviolata conservetur, & legitima libertate cives fruantur: contra hostes publici omnibus & machinis & nervis ad utramque subruendam grassantur; ut religio in superstitionem & atheismum degeneret, & libertatem acerbissima servitute commutare cogamur. Ad hæc perficienda viam invenisse sibi videntur longe certissimam, ut hoc regnum undique mari terraque copiis obsessum teneatur. Commerciis enim exclusos, & fortunis spoliatos, eo inopiæ & miseriæ brevi redactum iri, ut aut conditiones hactenus spretas & repudiatas ultro cum summa turpitudine expetamus, eorumque voluntatem pro lege in Ecclesia juxta & Republica amplectamur; quin & Anglis malis nostris deterrita eandem fortunæ asperitatem subire non renuat, aut certe rerum angustiis coacti in Angliam tumultuarie furibundi perrumpamus. Atque hoc ipsis, ut multo expeditius ad conata patranda compendium ardentius deposci arbitramur. Nec enim dubium est, quin adventum istuc nostrum excipiant clamores, Angarorum tursitationes[?], edictorum per regnum universum promulgationes, ad pium nostrum propositum infamandum (quasi quibus hoc ab initio consilium fuisset) & ad Anglos in nos irritandos, ut cruore semel imbuti religionis suæ radices suis ipsi gladiis succidant, in medio sui Romæ denuo instaurandæ fundamenta suis manibus jaciant, sibique juxta & nobis æternæ servitutis lunam detrahant.
units.tr: All the counsels of both kingdoms aim at this: that the purity of religion be kept inviolate and that the citizens enjoy lawful liberty. The enemies of the public, on the other hand, rage with every device and every nerve to overthrow both. They seem to have found a far surer way of accomplishing these things, namely, that this kingdom be held besieged on every side by sea and land with armed forces. For, shut out from commerce and stripped of their fortunes, the English will soon be reduced to such want and misery that either we ourselves, with the utmost shame, will voluntarily seek out the conditions hitherto scorned and rejected, and embrace their will as law in the Church as well as in the commonwealth; or else the English, deterred by our misfortunes, will not refuse to undergo the same harshness of fortune; or certainly, driven by the straits of our affairs, we will burst into England in a tumultuous and furious rush. And we judge that they very eagerly desire this, as a much quicker shortcut to carrying out their schemes. For there is no doubt that our coming here will be met with outcries, the vexations of forced requisitions, and proclamations of edicts throughout the whole kingdom, intended to defame our pious purpose (as if this had been our design from the beginning) and to stir up the English against us; so that, once steeped in blood, they may cut down the roots of their own religion with their own swords, and with their own hands lay the foundations for restoring Rome anew in the midst of themselves, and pull down for us and for themselves alike the moon of eternal servitude.

units.la: Cæterum in hoc articulo purioris religionis & legitimæ libertatis asserendæ mirando consilio cœlitus oblato, si viri boni Dei timentes, honorisque regii & communis utriusque regni tranquillitatis studiosi divinæ providentiæ auspicia secuti, pro sanctissimæ professionis suæ dignitate se gesserint, etsi hostibus vota hactenus processerint, ut sui operis sunibus nos in Angliam pertraxerint, fieri tamen potest, ut summa consilii frustra fit, faberque (quod ajunt) compedes quos fecerit ipse gerat, & astutia in stultitiam desinat: quod sperare nos jubet suprema illa sapientia & potentia quæ in singulis hujus operis vestigiis callidissima hostium commenta in ipsorum perniciem converterit.
units.tr: Moreover, in this matter of asserting purer religion and lawful liberty, which has been offered from heaven by a marvellous counsel: if good men who fear God, and who are zealous for royal honour and for the common tranquillity of both kingdoms, have followed the auspices of divine providence and conducted themselves in a manner worthy of the dignity of their most holy profession, then although the wishes of our enemies have so far gone forward, so that they might draw us into England with the ropes of their own making, it may nevertheless happen that the sum of their plan comes to nothing, and that (as they say) the smith carries the fetters he has made, and their cunning turns into folly. That supreme wisdom and power bids us hope for this, which in every step of this work has turned the most crafty schemes of the enemy to their own destruction.

units.la: Libellis Assertoriis ac Declaratoriis, & Commentario rerum à nobis post nuperam Pacificationem gestarum, quas hactenus perpessi sumus injurias, quibus hodie premamur angustiis ita patefecimus; ut neminem latere posset, quam necesse sit nobis alia ad incumbentium malorum remedium insistere via, quam Petitionum, Supplicationum, Legationumque semitam, hucusque nobis tritissimam, minore tamen cum fructu, quam qui regni antiquissimi civibus à nativo rege debebatur. Multos prius annos, quam vel libellum supplicem detulimus, non Religionis modo veritatem & virtutem a Prælatis Pontificisque oppugnatam, sed etiam libertatis publicæ privilegia universa violata toleravimus; & Religionis fundamenta tantum non eversa: cujus tamen unius solatio apud Deum nitebamur, & quæ gentem universam gloriosam apud exteras Ecclesias reddebat; quarum Theologis Reformatio nostra summa fuit votorum, quam vel gravissimis rerum terrestrium jacturis redemptam libenter volebant. Mox ubi Canonum & Liturgiæ publicæ libri Ecclesiis invitis obtrusi, crassis Papismi tenebris divini cultus puritatem obnubilare coepissent, & communicata Prœlatorum Pontificiorumque consilia de eodem Papifmo in utraque natione stabiliendo patefacta effent, ad pristinam tolerantiam non alia adjecimus arma, quam effusas ad Deum preces ac lacrymas; & delatos Regi libellos supplices: quibus tamen penitus repudiatis, & libri ac corruptelæ quæ deprecabamur, magnificis elogiis commendabantur, & insolenti fuafione eorum, qui nunc regia moderantur consilia, quique malis artibus acquisitæ potentiæ stabilimentum in Religionis ac libertatis nostræ ruderibus fundare conantur, nobis ultrà supplicare,indicta etiam perduellionis pœna, interdictum. Horum malorum sensu animum vellicante, à demissa supplicandi modestia non recedentes, ad Nationale Juramentum & sanctissimum fœdus cum Deo renovandum nos contulimus, ut Religionem, libertatemque publicam juxta ac Majestatis Regiæ authoritatem fartam tectam conservaremus: quippe conscii fœderis illius violati reatum omnium deinceps malorum fontem & originem nobis fuisse; neque aliter sperandum à Deo prosperum rerum eventum, quam fi ad eum conversi & admissi pœnitentes ad officium intermissum reverteremur. Quum apud Regis nostri Majestatem tantum potuissent improborum consilia, ut adversus nos nec demerentes nec exspectantes cum exercitu armato expeditionem susceperit, nobis facile persuasum est, ut potius quam minima in re ab obedientiæ orbita exerrare, aut Anglis longe charissimis fratribus levissimam of-fenfionis ansam præbere videremur, neglectis rationibus quibus incolumitati & securitati rerum noftrarum consulendum videbatur, collectas copias statim dimiserimus, arces & munitiones quæcunque poscebantur obedientiæ nostræ testes, fine cunctatione dediderimus, eoque obsequii erga Regis nostri Majestatem nos demiserimus, ut quantumvis priore Synodo ex Regis authoritate convocata res Ecclesiasticæ determinatæ fuerant, novæ tamen Synodo, novisque Comitiis quæcunque ad Religionem libertatemque publicam spectarent, dijudicanda permiserimus. Et rebus quidem Ecclesiasticis in legitime constituta Synodo, præsente & assentiente Regiæ Majestatis Legato stabilitis, ac facto ordinum Regni in Comitiis conventu, qui summam operi manum adderet, etsi summo studio caverimus, nequid tractaretur, quod Regiam Majestatem jure irritaret, conventum tamen ordinum, quem per improborum consultorum absentiam tanta cum certitudine promiserat, prava eorundem suasione inducti, contra leges & instituta hujus regni prorogari Rex jussit. Et hoc quoque, ut invictam obediendi voluntatem testatam faceremus, tolerare non abnuimus; missque Londinum Legati, qui postulatorum nostrorum rationem redderent. Hi, delegati licet omnium regni ordinum ab ipsa regia Majestate invitati, ita tamen rejecti fuere, ut neque ipsi in præsentiam admissi, neque petitiones quas à comitiis adferebant auditæ fuerint. Novam postea legationem submisimus cum postulatis nostris, nihil quidem illis complectentibus nisi quæ ad Regni commodum & tranquillitatem facerent, quæque Majestas Regia, etiam adscripta manu, publice concesserat. Et hi quoque sine ullo responso tandem dimissi: Res miranda omnibus aulæ mysteriorum ignaris, nec cogitantibus quanto studio Præsul Cantuariensis, & Regis in Hibernia Legatus, Pontificiorum nimis quam potentis factionis opibus nixi, Regiæ potentiæ promovendæ zelum extincta civium libertate & religionis veritate in omnibus tribus regnis venditare contendant! Horum suasu delegati nostri, dum æquum ad postulata responsum expectatur, in privata hospitia relegati, quartus, vir è primo nobilitatis ordine, arctissima custodia conclusus, exterorum militum præsidia cervicibus nostris imposita, quorum barbara insolentia in mulieres etiam & puerulos cæde debacchatur, naves cum mercibus aut captæ aut demersæ, vectores ad nuditatem spoliati, majore cum feritate à regis nostri subditis cum authoritate sævientibus excipiuntur, quam à Turcis aut infidelibus exspectari posset; magni in nos exercitus conscribuntur cum sævissimis mandatis ad nos debellandos & excidendos, ad religionem, libertatem, leges, fortunas, omnia denique apud nos exstirpanda.
units.tr: By our printed Assertions and Declarations, and by our Commentary on the events carried out since the recent Pacification, we have laid open the wrongs we have suffered until now and the distresses that now press upon us, so clearly that no one could fail to see how necessary it is for us to take another way to remedy the evils at hand, rather than the path of Petitions, Supplications and Embassies. That path has been most worn by us until now, yet with less fruit than was owed to the citizens of this most ancient kingdom by their native king. For many years before we even presented a supplicating petition, we endured not only the attack of the Prelates and the Pope upon the truth and virtue of religion, but also the violation of all the privileges of public liberty, and the foundations of religion were all but overthrown. Yet we relied on God alone for consolation in that matter, and it was this that made the whole nation glorious among foreign Churches, whose theologians regarded our Reformation as the highest of their wishes and were willing to buy it even at the greatest loss of earthly things. Soon after the Canons and the public Liturgy books were forced upon the Churches against their will, and began to obscure the purity of divine worship with the thick darkness of Popery, and the counsels of the Prelates and the Popish men, shared among themselves for establishing the same Popery in both nations, were revealed, we added no other arms to our former patience than prayers and tears poured out to God, and supplicating petitions delivered to the King. Yet these were utterly rejected, and the books and corruptions we were pleading against were commended with magnificent praises. Through the insolent persuasion of those who now govern the royal counsels, and who strive to found the stability of their power, won by evil arts, on the ruins of our religion and liberty, we were even forbidden to supplicate further, and a charge of treason was declared against us. With these evils stinging our minds, yet not departing from the humble modesty of supplication, we betook ourselves to renew the National Covenant and the most sacred covenant with God, so that we might keep religion, public liberty, and the authority of the royal Majesty safe and sound. For we were conscious that the guilt of violating that covenant had been the fount and origin of all the evils that followed, and that no prosperous outcome could be hoped for from God unless we turned to him, repented, and returned to the duty we had abandoned. Since the counsels of the wicked had so much power with the Majesty of our King that he undertook an expedition with an armed army against us, though we neither deserved nor expected it, we were readily persuaded that rather than stray from the path of obedience in the smallest matter, or give our very dear brothers the English the slightest occasion of offence, we should set aside the considerations by which the safety and security of our affairs seemed to call for attention. Accordingly we at once dismissed the troops we had gathered, and without hesitation surrendered the citadels and fortifications, whatever was demanded of us, as witnesses of our obedience. We so humbled ourselves in obsequiousness towards the Majesty of our King that, although matters ecclesiastical had been settled by an earlier Synod convened by royal authority, we nevertheless permitted everything touching religion and public liberty to be judged by a new Synod and new Assemblies. Although the ecclesiastical matters were settled in a lawfully constituted Synod, in the presence and with the assent of the royal Majesty's Legate, and a meeting of the estates of the kingdom was arranged to put the final hand to the work, we took the greatest care that nothing should be treated which might legally anger the royal Majesty. Nevertheless, the King, induced by the perverse persuasion of the same men, ordered the meeting of the estates to be prorogued, against the laws and institutions of this kingdom, though he had promised it with such certainty during the absence of the wicked counsellors. We did not refuse to tolerate this either, in order to show our unconquered willingness to obey, and we sent Legates to London to render an account of our demands. Although these were delegates of all the orders of the kingdom, invited by the royal Majesty himself, they were so rejected that they were neither admitted to his presence nor were the petitions they brought from the Assemblies heard. Afterwards we submitted a new embassy with our demands, containing nothing except what would serve the advantage and tranquillity of the kingdom, and what the royal Majesty had publicly granted, even with his own hand subscribed. These too were at last dismissed without any answer. This is a marvellous thing to all who are ignorant of the mysteries of the court, and who do not consider with what zeal the Archbishop of Canterbury and the King's Legate in Ireland, relying on the resources of the Popish faction, which is far too powerful, strive to pass off their zeal for advancing royal power while extinguishing civil liberty and the truth of religion in all three kingdoms! On their advice our delegates, while a fair answer to our demands was awaited, were relegated to private lodgings, and one of them, a man of the first rank of the nobility, was shut up under the closest custody. Foreign garrisons were imposed upon our necks, and their barbarous insolence rages with slaughter even against women and little children. Ships with their merchandise have been either seized or sunk, and passengers stripped to nakedness, and they are handled with greater savagery by the subjects of our king, raging with authority, than could be expected from Turks or infidels. Great armies are being enrolled against us with the most savage orders to subdue and destroy us, and to root out among us religion, liberty, laws, fortunes, and in a word everything.

units.la: In hoc extremo rerum statu novam delegationem cum petitionibus submittere, sensus communis & experientia prohibet: regiorum consiliorum moderatoribus nihil minus passuris, quam ut civium justissimæ querimoniæ & petitiones supplices æqui quicquam à Rege impetrent: quod prorogatis utriusque regni comitiis luculentissime demonstrarunt: per socordiam ignavos desidere, dum sævissimis hostibus visum fuerit ad lanienam nos protrahere (quod nisi cum Dei causa complicatum esset, minus molestum nobis accideret) non religio modo dissuadet, sed natura insuper, quæ suæ quemque incolumitati studere æterna & inviolabili lege præcipit; At ut minas quotidie acerbissimas feramus, ut diuturno bello crudelissime sævientes hostes quotannis singula carpendo universa tandem labefactare toleremus, (quo artificio ad nos subvertendos aperte grassantur inimici) supra vires nostras esse experimur. Re igitur diu multumque apud nos deliberata,constituimus tandem efficere, ut postulata nostra multoties à multis exagitata, & in Comitiis proximis aliqua ex parte à nobis determinata, regiæ Majestati, orbique universo, ac præsertim Angliæ regno magis innotescant, ut detracta mendaciorum larva, nuda rerum nostrarum veritate detecta, firmiorem ipsi pacem & solidioribus nixam fundamentis, cum religionis & legum nostrarum libertate impetremus. Turbarum architectos eos quidem qui e nobis egressi sunt, remitti volumus, ut ex legibus patriis causa ipsorum cognoscatur, & sententia feratur: At perniciosos consultores Anglos, omnium utriusque regni aerumnarum fontes & capita, ad ejus gentis Comitiorum tribunal remittemus, eorumque supplicium ordinum regni arbitrio permittemus.
units.tr: In this extreme state of affairs, common sense and experience forbid us to send a new delegation with petitions. The managers of the royal councils will allow nothing less than that the most just complaints and supplicating petitions of the citizens should obtain anything fair from the King, as they have most clearly demonstrated in the prorogation of the Assemblies of both kingdoms. To sit idle through sloth while our most savage enemies think fit to drag us to slaughter (which would be less troubling to us were it not bound up with the cause of God) is forbidden not only by religion but also by nature, which by an eternal and inviolable law commands each person to care for his own safety. But we find that we are beyond our strength when it comes to enduring the most bitter threats every day, or tolerating that our enemies, raging most cruelly in a long war, should wear away everything piece by piece, year by year, until at last they overthrow it all (for this is the artifice by which our enemies openly press on to subvert us). Therefore, after a long and careful deliberation among ourselves, we have resolved at last to bring it about that our demands, often vexed by many and in part settled by us in the last Assemblies, may become better known to the royal Majesty, to the whole world, and above all to the kingdom of England. Thus, with the mask of lies removed and the naked truth of our affairs laid bare, we may obtain for ourselves a firmer peace, founded on more solid foundations, together with the liberty of our religion and laws. We wish indeed that the architects of the disturbances, those who have gone out from among us, be sent back, so that their cause may be examined under our national laws and sentence passed. But the pernicious English counsellors, the sources and heads of all the miseries of both kingdoms, we will send back to the tribunal of the Assembly of that nation, and we will leave their punishment to the decision of the orders of the kingdom.

units.la: Quum reformationis hujus progressus ab ultimis usque primordiis, reflexa mentis acie speculamur, & divinæ providentiæ admirando omnia consilio moderantis vestigia observamus, in mediis quantumvis angustiis, paternam Dei erga Ecclesiam patriamque nostram curam & gratiam non possumus non celebrare, & animosioris deinceps ac bonæ spei pleni ejus ductum & auspicia sequi perseverare.
units.tr: When we look back with our mind's eye over the progress of this Reformation from its very first beginnings, and observe the traces of divine providence governing all things with wonderful counsel, we cannot but celebrate the Fatherly care and grace of God towards our Church and our country, even in the midst of however great distress. We must persevere in following his guidance and auspices henceforth with more spirited minds, full of good hope.

units.la: Quum jam immensis opibus, amplissimis honoribus, eminente in omnes omnium conditionum cives, Euangelii ministros juxta & cæteros, potestate, eximia dignitatis Parliamentariæ, Senatoriæ Prætoriæ, Scaccariæ, & in celsa Commissione Delegatoriæ authoritate ad summum dominatus fastigium Prælati ascendissent, & altero pede Ecclesiam, altero Rempublicam complexi, ad intolerandam arrogantiam assurrexissent, in ipso extremitatis articulo (quod Domino tempus opportunum esse solet) opus hoc inchoari cœptum est: initiis quidem tenuibus, & nihil eximium ominantibus: sed majora tamen quotidie, divino consilio, per singula vestigia necessitate quadam ineluctabili premente, pedetentim est progressum.
units.tr: When the Prelates, already possessed of immense resources and most ample honours, eminent over the citizens of every condition, both the ministers of the Gospel and others, with power, with the distinguished authority of Parliament, the Senate, the Courts of Justice, the Exchequer, and the high Commission of delegates, had risen to the highest summit of domination, and having embraced the Church with one foot and the Commonwealth with the other, had risen to intolerable arrogance, this work was begun at the very edge of extremity (which is usually the opportune time for the Lord). It began with slender beginnings, promising nothing remarkable, but by divine counsel it has progressed step by step, and every day with greater things, as an ineluctable necessity pressed upon us.

units.la: Verbis assequi non possumus, qui fuerint animorum motus, quæ lacrymarum profusiones, qui clamores tot millibus hominum ora in hac Ecclesia solverint, ubi amorem & potentiam Dei, quasi ex mortuis exsuscitantis, & post tantum cataclysmum ac vastitatem, ad renovati mundi, in quo Religio cum Justitia vigeret, spem certam excitantis, præsentem sensissent. Sæpenumero in vado hærentibus, nec qua ratione progrediendum esset videntibus, dementium adversariorum timores, furores, & consilia ipsa viam aperuerunt, quasque in exitium nostrum comparaverant machinas, causam ipsi quam defendebant maxime labefactarunt, opusque nobis in manibus promoverunt. Convenimus jam per aliquot annos multa sæpe hominum millia, cum neque interim sanctioris Senatus, neque Iudicum consensus esset, tamen citra motum aut tumultum, pacatiores multo quam temporibus etiam maxime tranquillis apud nos fieri solebat. In nupera Pacificatione ita nos comparavimus, ut arma non inviti abjecerimus, & gravissimo rerum nostrarum damno ad pacatam domi vitam nos contulerimus: cum hostium interim improbitas, maris fervescentis & cœnum perpetuo eructantis instar quiescere non potuerit, sed ad ea nos adegerit, quæ Dei consilio in ipsos decreta esse apparet. Honestæ nobis intentiones ab omni sordido & terreno propósito averse, animi in mediis quamvis periculis propensi, tanti operis administri, non voluntatibus modo sed facultatibus etiam ad impedimenta omnia perrumpenda instructi, pax denique inviolata adversus omnes accusantium petitiones corda nostra firmissime sustentans, persuasionem faciunt certissimam Deo acceptum esse quod faximus, neque esse quod desertionem ab eo vereamur. Non diffitemur posse Deum sceleratorum etiam hominum ministerio uti, quos & facultatibus idoneis instruat, & quibus manu potenti conata provehat. Quod tamen ut nos ad cordium sinceritatem penitius explorandam exstimulare, ita nec fideles Dei servos ex vero ipsius amore gloriam ejus spirantes, semitas ejus calcantes, pacis ipsius solatium, consilii directionem, præsentiæque in negotiis benedictionem sentientes, ulla ex parte absterrere, nec hominibus ad Dei opera vituperanda ansam præbere debet.
units.tr: We cannot put into words the emotions, the floods of tears, or the cries that so many thousands of people in this Church let loose, where they felt the love and power of God present with them, raising the dead as it were, and, after so great a cataclysm and devastation, awakening the sure hope of a renewed world in which religion and justice would flourish. Often when we stuck fast in the shallows and did not see how we ought to proceed, the fears, rages, and schemes of our mad adversaries opened the way for us. The very machines they had prepared for our ruin greatly undermined the cause they were defending and advanced the work that was in our hands. For some years now we have met in large numbers, often many thousands of people, and although there was no agreement of a more holy Senate or of the judges, we met without movement or tumult, far more peacefully than was ever usual among us even in the most tranquil times. In the recent Pacification we conducted ourselves so that we laid down our arms unwillingly and, at the very great loss of our affairs, withdrew to a quiet life at home. Meanwhile the wickedness of our enemies, like a sea that keeps boiling and constantly throwing up mud, could not be still, but drove us to those things which appear to have been decreed by God's counsel against them. Our honest intentions, far removed from every base and earthly purpose, our minds inclined to this work even amid dangers, the ministers of so great a task, equipped with resources as well as wills to break through every obstacle, and finally a peace unbroken against all the petitions of accusers, which firmly sustains our hearts, make us most certainly persuaded that what we have done is acceptable to God, and that there is no reason for us to fear His desertion. We do not deny that God can make use of the service of wicked men too, whom He equips with suitable resources and whose undertakings He advances with a mighty hand. Yet this ought to stir us to search the sincerity of our hearts more deeply, and it ought not, in any way, to frighten the faithful servants of God, who truly love Him, breathe His glory, tread His paths, and feel the solace of His peace, the direction of His counsel, and the blessing of His presence in our affairs. Nor should it give men an occasion to disparage the works of God.

units.la: Atqui isthæc tamen omnia, quantumvis nobis animos addant, & in mediis sæpenumero angustiis hactenus sustentaverint, ingressus tamen in Angliam ut justus nobis videatur efficere non possent, si pacem, quam tanto studio sectamur, aut domi assequi fas esset, aut alibi gentium. Ubiubi terrarum invenire dabitur, eam indagemus necesse est: nec citius ea nobis offeretur, quam depositis armis quantumque à turbulentis consiliis ingenia nobis abhorreant certissimis documentis testati, toti terrarum orbi, præsertim vero Angliæ regno, non aliud nostrum fuisse consilium demonstrabimus; neque aliena occupandi, sed nos & nostra defendendi causa arma à nobis induta. Non eget Necessitas positivarum legum patrocinio. Est hoc omnium cordibus inscriptum, omniumque gentium institutis receptum, Necessitatis supremam esse authoritatem, legem eam esse omnes alias leges transcendentem, nullique legi obnoxiam: cui propterea ferunt, nullam legem esse positam. Imperanti necessitati astipulantur Naturæ gentiumque jura, assurgunt & loco cedunt positivæ hominum leges. Hujus legis vis est nonnunquam in excusando, interdum in elevando posita; interim ut actiones alioqui ambiguas ab injustitiæ macula vindicet. At quæ major esse possit Necessitas, quam ut Religionem quæ anima est; Patriam, quod corpus est; nostram omnium vitam, qui membra sumus; Regis denique, qui caput est, honorem illibatum tueamur? Quæ omnia communi hodie discrimine periclitantur, nec ad ea conservanda aliam sub cœlo rationem ipsi novimus (quod si quis ea sit sapientia, ut aliam agnoscat, ex eo discere flagitamus, & ad eam sequendam promptos & alacres nos spondemus) quam ut in hostes publicos ubiubi demum inveniri possint, animadvertamus; & regni securitatem, unde impetrari possit, deprecemur. Non id agitur, nostrane sorte, quantumvis tenui contenti acquiescamus, an occupatis Anglorum bonis nos locupletemus; dubitare hic impium esset non minus quam absurdum: nec id agitur, nosne & nostra domi tueamur, an in vicinos fratresque nobis charissimos grassemur: Nam de hoc ambigere nec Christianum est, nec rationi consentaneum: Illud demum agitur, num pietas, num prudentia suadeat, intra regni limites nos potius continere, dum nosmetipsos jugulare; sacra, leges, patriamque nostram extirpare hosti visum fuerit; quam excusso torpore securitatem, pacem & libertatem ex Anglia petere: num agendo, vigilandoque incolumitati publicæ consulamus potius quam per socordiam & ignaviam sedentes pereamus: aut ut paucis omnia complectamur, num qui non pauci sumus privati cives,; sed universa regni civitas, tot & tantis criminibus insimulati, quanta vix pessimis etiam seculis hominibus Christianis intentata fuerant, dissimulemus, Liturgiam cum universo Papismi corpore amplectamur, Prælatos cum ejerata ipsorum Hierarchia postliminio recipiamus; sanctissimum & tot sacramentis confirmatum fœdus & jusjurandum abdicemus; laboris omnis & operæ in hac causa positæ fructum amittamus, pristinæ servitutis memoriam abjiciamus, priora studia quantivis etiam nostri asserendi obliviscamur, hostium animis lætitiam suggeramus, violentia dexteras armemus; amicorum cordibus mœrorem, vultibus pudorem, nostro probro suffundamus ; Filii Dei causam quam à nobis susceptam, explicato ipsius vexillo, veritas & potentia ejus ita hactenus tutata sunt, ut plus inde solatii perceperimus, quam omnis pax humana, omnis omnium terrestrium rerum affluentia conciliare possent, cum augusti nominis ipsius dehonestamento, deferamus, eoque poenas omnes hominum omni seculo Apostasiæ irrogatas in capita nostra detrahamus; num complicatis manibus & nostram & posterorum absolutam servitutem animarum pariter corporumque & fortunarum omnium exspectemus; aut ( quod idem est ) ibi pro defensione nostri pugnemus, ubi eam præstari non posse fatis compertum habemus, an Deum vocantem ( quid enim aliud est impositæ neceffitatis vinculum ?) secuti, viamque quam , aliis omnibus occlusis, divina providentia nobis aperuit, ingressi, ad libertatem recuperandam, & incumbentia mala amolienda contendamus.
units.tr: Yet all these things, however much they encourage us and have sustained us so far amid the frequent straits we have been in, could not make our entry into England seem just to us, if the peace which we pursue with such zeal were lawful for us to obtain at home or anywhere else among the nations. Wherever on earth it can be found, we must seek it; and it will not be offered to us sooner than we lay down our arms. By the most certain proofs we have shown how far our minds shrink from turbulent counsels, and we will demonstrate to the whole world, and especially to the kingdom of England, that our purpose has been nothing else: we took up arms not to seize what belongs to others, but to defend ourselves and our own. Necessity does not need the protection of positive laws. This is written in the hearts of all men and received in the institutions of all nations: that the authority of necessity is supreme, that this law surpasses all other laws, and is subject to no law; for this reason, they say, no law has been laid down for it. The laws of nature and of nations support necessity when it commands; positive human laws give way and yield their place. The force of this law lies sometimes in excusing, sometimes in exalting; in any case it clears actions that are otherwise ambiguous of the stain of injustice. But what greater necessity could there be than that we defend the honour of religion, which is the soul; of our country, which is the body; of the life of us all, who are its members; and finally of the king, who is the head, unimpaired? All these things are today endangered by a common peril, and we know no other way under heaven to preserve them (and if anyone has such wisdom that he knows another, we beg him to teach us, and we pledge ourselves ready and eager to follow it) than to turn our attention to the public enemies wherever at last they may be found, and to seek the safety of the kingdom from whatever source it can be obtained. The question is not whether we should be content with our lot, however meagre, or whether we should enrich ourselves with the goods of the English; to doubt this would be impious no less than absurd. Nor is the question whether we should defend ourselves and our own at home, or invade our neighbours and our most dear brothers; for it is neither Christian nor reasonable to be in doubt about this. The real question is whether piety and prudence advise us to keep ourselves within the bounds of our kingdom, while our enemies think it fit to cut our throats and to root out our religion, our laws, and our country; or rather, having shaken off our torpor, to seek security, peace, and liberty from England. Will we better consult the public safety by acting and keeping watch, or perish through sloth and cowardice while sitting still? Or, to embrace everything in few words: shall we, who are not a few private citizens but the whole civil community of the kingdom, accused of so many and such great crimes as were scarcely ever charged against Christian men even in the worst ages, dissemble? Shall we embrace the Liturgy with the whole body of Popery, and receive back the Prelates with their accursed Hierarchy as if by right of return? Shall we renounce the most sacred covenant and oath, confirmed by so many sacraments? Shall we lose the fruit of all the labour and effort put into this cause, cast aside the memory of our former servitude, forget all our earlier endeavours to assert our rights, bring joy to the minds of our enemies, arm violence with our right hands, pour sorrow into the hearts and shame on the faces of our friends, and heap disgrace upon ourselves? Shall we abandon the cause of the Son of God, which we took up, whose banner has been so far defended by His truth and power that we have received from it more comfort than all human peace and all the abundance of earthly things could bring, and in doing so dishonour His august name; and so draw upon our own heads all the penalties of apostasy that men have incurred in every age? Shall we fold our hands and await the absolute servitude of ourselves and our posterity, of souls and bodies and all fortunes alike? Or (which is the same thing) shall we fight there for our own defence where we know well enough that it cannot be secured? Or shall we follow God who calls us (for what else is the bond of necessity laid upon us?), enter the way which divine providence has opened to us when all others were closed, and strive to recover our liberty and to turn away the evils that press upon us?

units.la: Nostri hostes initio , regiæ authoritatis velum ita sibi obtenderunt, quàsi ea, nisi ipsis incolumibus, salva esse non posset, aut quasi eos accusare, Majestatem effet violare : nos econtra demonstravimus,non ita cohærere diadematis regii & Episcopalis mitræ dignitatem , quin hac prostrata , majore illud cum splendore & majestate refulgere possit. Hinc repulsi ad aliud confugiunt latibulum , dum hominibus persuadere conantur , Angliam nos ingredi ad eos quamvis ex ipsis legibus tantorum criminum postulandos , non aliud esse quam regnum in quo ipsi vivunt,hostilibus armis impetere: quasi vero excrescentia tubercula amputare , aut apostemati medicari , effet corpus ipsum perimere. Illi quidem ex cerebri fui figmentis securitatis sibi præsidia fomnient : Nos officii non ita fumus immemores , ut surentium instar , in proximos & primum obvios incursemus. Etsi enim negari non possit, injurias nobis factas (nuperam pacificationem violatam, rebellionis & proditionis infamiam nominibus nostris inuftam, naves cum mercibus interceptas, legatos custodiae inclusos, hostilia ex arcibus nostris ab Anglis praesidiariis perpetrata) si authore regno Angliae patratae fuissent, justas publici inter duas nationes diffidii causas futuras fuisse. Cum tamen regni Anglicani ordines in Comitiorum conventu, subsidium adversus nos decernere negaverint, & paria nostris gravamina sua obnixe deprecati sint (quae tamen Majestas Regia edito libello Declaratorio, extra Comitia curaturum spopondit: quae sane cura privatorum civium gravaminibus satis esse posset; cum publica gravamina publicam omnium ordinum in Comitiis regni curam deposcant: quod ne fieret, conventus ille ordinum prorogatus est, & solutus) neque nos Anglorum nationem illius injustitiae ream postulamus: neque Angli nos incusare debent, quod praepotentem Pontificiorum & Praelatorum factionem tot malis utrique genti gravem oppressum imus. Quicumque Religionem & libertatem publicam asserta volunt, adversus hostem communem operam confiliumque conscisco: qui interim vicinae nationis, qui religionis in ea & legum incolumitatem minore cura quam suam conservare studebunt (quippe conscii communem utrique salutem aut ruinam exspectandam esse) maledictos esse jubemus.
