units.tr: At first our enemies held before themselves the veil of royal authority, as if that authority could not be safe unless they themselves were unharmed, or as if to accuse them would be to violate majesty. We, on the contrary, have shown that the dignity of the royal diadem and of the episcopal mitre are not so bound together that the diadem cannot shine forth with greater splendour and majesty once the mitre has been cast down. Repulsed on this point, they now take refuge in another hiding place, trying to persuade men that our entry into England, even though they are to be called to account for such great crimes by the laws themselves, is nothing other than an attack with hostile arms upon the kingdom in which they live; as if cutting away a growing tumour, or treating an abscess, were to destroy the body itself. Indeed they nourish themselves on the figments of their own brain as protections for their security. We are not so forgetful of our duty that we rush, like madmen, upon our neighbours and the first people we meet. For although it cannot be denied that wrongs have been done to us (the recent Pacification broken, the stain of rebellion and treason branded on our names, ships with their cargoes seized, envoys shut up in custody, and hostile acts committed by English garrison soldiers from our own fortresses), these would have been just grounds for public war between the two nations, had they been carried out at the instigation of the kingdom of England. Yet since the orders of the English kingdom, assembled in Parliament, refused to decree aid against us, and earnestly deprecated grievances like ours (which His Royal Majesty promised by a published Declaratory pamphlet to attend to outside Parliament; a care of private citizens' grievances might indeed have been enough, but public grievances demand the public care of all orders in the Parliament of the kingdom), and since, to prevent this, that assembly of the orders was prorogued and dissolved, we neither accuse the English nation of that injustice, nor should the English blame us for having been oppressed by the overbearing faction of Papists and Prelates, which has burdened both peoples with so many evils. Whoever wishes to assert religion and public liberty, I declare that I join forces and counsel against the common enemy; and those who, meanwhile, will strive less zealously than their own to preserve the neighbouring nation, its religion and the safety of its laws (since they know that a common salvation or ruin awaits both) we command to be accursed.

units.la: Ut ergo Deum Opt. Max. coeli & terrae dominum testem nobis appellamus, ista nec alia nobis esse proposita consilia, ita eodem augustissimo sacramento spondemus, nec vitae, neque labori, neque fortunis, (quae alibi nusquam melius aut honestius insumi possunt) ad ea consequenda parciturosx; ab amicis fratribusque nostris Anglis ligulam (quod ajunt) aut alii caput, nisi justo pretio soluto non exacturos, eorum fines non alio affectu ingressuros quam amicos & fratres, malorum quæ hactenus perpessi sunt, periculorumque quæ ipsis, quæ Religioni, quæ legitimæ libertati apud ipsos impendent, sensu ductos, omnique qua possumus ratione ipsis commodare paratissimos; ab iis etiam exspectantes, ut ex pari sensu angustiarum nostrarum (quas cum ulterius tolerare nequeamus patria egressi ad eos confugimus) justa omnia & honesta consilia nobiscum communicent, per quæ postulata æquissima tandem impetremus: Cumque pecunias & commeatum nostrum absumpserimus, præter ea quæ ad quotidianum exercitus usum necessaria fuerint, eaque bona fide & certa cautione pretii quamprimum fieri potuerit resolvendi interposita, nihil postulaturos: atque ea quidem, ut quibus carere non posse ipsi sciunt, omnes (ita firmiter credimus) religionis & communis duorum regnorum pacis amantes ultro deferent, & quæ sunt providentia, rationem inibunt, qua & nobis necessaria suppetant, & suppeditantibus honesta satisdatione caveri possit. Quibus utrinque observatis, neque fratribus nostris damnum dabitur (quippe queis ad ultimum teruncium satisfiet) neque nobis, qui Deum, cujus causa rerum omnium discrimen adivimus, amplissimum remuneratorem exspectamus. Milites si forte aliqui nonnihil deliquerint, nobis imputatum iri non timemus, qui ne quid tale contingat, omnem dabimus operam, neque paulo majore severitate delicta vindicabimus, quam si adversus cives nostros domi fuissent admissa. Prælatos & Pontificios ejusque factionis populares, quique eorum bona receptaverint, non ita rerum imperitos esse credimus, ut commeatus necessarii copiam nobis facere negaverint; memores quo consilio fortunas omnes & possessiones nostras fisco adjudicatas, sibi tanquam bene meritis civibus concessas regi persuaserint publico edicto promulgare. A Regia Majestate nihil postulabimus, nisi ut purioris religionis & libertatis patriæ securitati ex constitutionibus nuperæ Synodi, & publicorum Comitiorum prospiciatur; quæque alia debet ex lege divina &c. patriis institutis Rex non injustus civibus gravissimorum malorum onere fatiscentibus demissisque precibus opem ejus implorantibus. Moram in Anglia longiorem non trahemus, quam in ejus regni Comitiis justæ nostræ querimoniæ & gravamina cognosci, iis remedium adhiberi, cum malorum nostrorum architectis lege agendum, & in eos animadvertendum satis caveri, Religionisque & libertatis nostræ securitati prospici possit. Quibus patratis sine cunctatione pacato agmine nullique gravi reditum accelerabimus. Atque hujus quidem expeditionis fructum speramus futurum adversus Pontificios Papismi exstirpationem, adversus Præ')atos Ecclesiæ à corruptelis expurgationem, adversus Atheos florentem Euangelii propagationem, denique adversus Proditores & incendiarios, utrique regno societatis & amoris vinculum firmissimum: quæ à Deo consiliorum & honestæ voluntatis nobis conscio, eaque effecta reddere potente demissi precamur: Quod si quid ulterius postuletur, Deus manifestabit; & utrique nationi præibit: cujus præeuntis auspicium sequi, operique Jehovæ collum submittere, quis gravabitur? Finis.
units.tr: Just as we call God Almighty, Lord of heaven and earth, to witness that these and no other purposes have been set before us, so we pledge by the same most solemn sacrament that we will not spare our lives, our labour or our fortunes (which could be spent nowhere else more well or honourably) in pursuing them. We will not demand from our friends and brothers the English so much as a shoelatchet (as they say), or a single head, unless it is paid for in full. We will enter their borders with no other feeling than that of friends and brothers, moved by a sense of the wrongs they have suffered so far and of the dangers now hanging over them, over their religion and over their lawful liberty, and we are most ready to help them by every means we can. We also expect them, from the same sense of our own distress (which we can no longer bear, and which is why we left our country and fled to them), to share with us all just and honourable counsels, by which we may at last obtain our most reasonable demands. Once we have used up our money and our supplies, beyond what the army needs for daily use, we will ask for nothing more, provided that the repayment is made as soon as possible, under a sound bond and a secure guarantee of payment. We firmly believe that all who love religion and the common peace of the two kingdoms will freely offer what they know we cannot do without, and will take care, with foresight, to see that we have what we need, and that those who supply it may be secured by honest surety. If these terms are kept on both sides, our brothers will suffer no loss (since they will be paid to the last penny), and we, who have faced the peril of all things for the sake of God, look for him as our most generous rewarder. If any soldiers should happen to misbehave somewhat, we do not fear that it will be charged to us; we will take every care that nothing of the kind occurs, and we will punish offences with no less severity than if they had been committed against our own citizens at home. We do not think the prelates and Papists, and the followers of that faction, and those who have harboured their goods, are so ignorant of affairs that they will refuse us a supply of necessary provisions, mindful of the plan by which they persuaded the king to publish by public edict that all our fortunes and possessions had been adjudged to the exchequer and granted to themselves as well-deserving citizens. From his Royal Majesty we will ask nothing except that provision be made, in accordance with the constitutions of the late Synod and of the public Parliament, for the safety of a purer religion and of our country's liberty, and for whatever else the divine law and the national institutions require; and that the King, who is not unjust to his subjects, may be moved by humble prayers, since they, sinking under the weight of most grievous evils, implore his help. We will not delay in England longer than is needed for our just complaints and grievances to be heard in the Parliament of that kingdom, for a remedy to be applied to them, for the architects of our evils to be dealt with by law and punished, and for the security of our religion and liberty to be adequately provided for. When these things are done, we will hasten our return without hesitation, in a peaceful column, and injure no one gravely. We hope that the fruit of this expedition will be, against the Papists, the extirpation of Popery; against the prelates, the cleansing of the Church from corruptions; against the atheists, the flourishing spread of the Gospel; and finally, against traitors and incendiaries, a most firm bond of fellowship and love between the two kingdoms. We pray humbly to God, who knows our purposes and our honest will and who is able to make these things effective, that he will show us, if anything further is demanded, and that he will go before both nations. Whose auspices would anyone refuse to follow, or who would refuse to bend his neck to the work of Jehovah? Finis.

units.la: Cum in aula regia certo constitisset Scotis propositum in Angliam progredi, statim dimittitur Classis regia destinata ad maritima Scotiæ loca infestanda, militesque relictis navibus coguntur ad regium exercitum in Eboracensi provincia se conferre, cui summo cum imperio tum præfuit Deputatus Hiberniæ, cujus opera sereniss. regem contra animi sui impetum ad violenta hæc consilia protrusum paucis ignotum fuerat: promulgatur etiam edictum, quo non solum Scoti qui in Angliam cum armato exercitu ingredercntur, verumetiam omnes eorum fautores qui eis pecuniam, apparatum bellicum, commeatum suppeditarent, rebelles & læsæ majestatis rei declarantur, gratia interim iis oblata qui armis depositis domum sese conferrent, ac præterita crimina submisse deprecarentur.
units.tr: When it was firmly settled at court that the Scots intended to advance into England, the royal fleet that had been assigned to harry the maritime places of Scotland was immediately dismissed, and the soldiers, leaving their ships, were ordered to join the royal army in the province of York. This army was commanded in chief by the Deputy of Ireland, through whose efforts the most serene king, who had been driven against the impulse of his own mind to these violent measures, was little known. A proclamation was also issued by which not only the Scots who entered England with an armed force, but also all their supporters who supplied them with money, war matériel or provisions, were declared rebels and guilty of treason; meanwhile, a pardon was offered to those who would lay down their arms, go home, and humbly beg forgiveness for their past offences.

units.la: Verum terriculamentis hisce dimoveri non potuerunt Scoti ab instituto: & exercitu recensito qui 27 aut 28. millibus peditum & quatuor millibus equitum constabat, movere castra Angliam versus præcipite Augusto imperat Leslius, quem patriæ suæ in extremis angustiis laboranti reddidit Dominus: Huic summam belli commisisse Scotos, supra dictum: Totus exercitus ad commodiorem frumentationem in tria agmina divisus: Primum ducebat Aumontius, aliud Baylius tertium ipse Leslius, cum ingenti apparatu bellico & multorum dierum commeatu: Transmittendus erat Tueda fluvius Angliam à Scotia disterminans; & hic honos Comiti montis Rosarum peditum tribuno forte obtigit; qui ex equo descendens, pedes flumen ad ordinarium vadum primus pertransiit, quod ab aliis omnibus peditum ductoribus factitatum, ut gregariis mili-tibus animos adderent, ex æquato scilic. omnium labore & periculo. In hosticum cum castrametarentur, severe omnibus sub pœna capitis interdictum, ne nulla injuria Anglos eorumque villas, agros, bona afficerent: præsidiarii interim Berwicenses huc atilluc discurrebant, ut milites sessos aut palantes ab agminibus interciperent; sed nullo prorsus operæpretio: Nam 28. Augusti, ad condictum locum ericetum videlic. Novocastrense, in sinistra Tinæ fluminis ripa quinque millibus passuum supra Novumcastrum castramentantur. Urbecula ibi sita est quam Neuburnam vocant, ibique recedente æstu marino vadum est satis commodum : Sed dextram ripam ex adverso occupaverant Angli, peditum 5000 & equitum 2500: vallo & aggere subitario muniti: Verum Scotorum tormenta majora usque adeo opportune disposita fuere; ut quem precibus obtinere non potuerint transitum, vi sibi aperuerint: Etenim per fecialem Anglos in adversa ripa enixe rogarunt, ut mature se subducerent, neque amicis transitum præcluderent, nullo hostili animo Angliam ingressis, & qui in hostico pacifice adhuc sese gessissent, sine ullo cujuslibet damno & injuria: Sed fecialem hunc non sine procacibus convitiis facessere confestim jusserunt Angli: Quare arma expediunt Scoti experturi an eorum, qui se manifestos hostes declarassent, dexteræ linguas æquarent: Tormentorum displosionibus usque adeo terrebantur pedites Angli, ut vexilla desererent; eoque metu perculsos cum vidissent Scoti, confertis agminibus transitum meditabantur, & vix Imperatoris imperio contineri potuerunt; Atque hic insidias metuens, paucas Equitum turmas tentare vadum jussit, qui flumine superato in adversa ripa consisterent; & si Angli aggrederentur, regressum simularent: eosque in insidias dispositas allicerent, nam in ripa sinistra fluminis locis opportunis, sed occultis, tormenta bellica disponebantur. Quare cum equitum recedentium simulatam fugam veram putarent Angli equites, effusi sequuntur usque ad fluminis ripam, & in insidias inciderunt, nam tormentorum ictibus frequentissimis ex inopinato ita obruuntur, ut concitatiore cursu retrocesserint, & turmæ illæ Scoticæ quæ fugam antea simularunt, momento obversæ tanto impetu retrocedentes Anglos aggrediuntur, ut in fugam conjecerint, interea universus exercitus Scoticus sine ullo oblato impedimento flumen transmisit, & levioris armaturæ equitibus imperatum ut reliquias exercitus Anglici quæ in vicino colle adhuc hærebant, dissiparent: Ibi acriter aliquandiu pugnatum utrinque; sed Angli tandem cum Scotorum impetum diutius non ferrent, fugam capessivere, nec sine ingenti clade evasissent, nisi sævire in fugientes vetitum fuisset, vel hoc indicio testatum faciebant, nullius Angli sanguinem Scotos sitire. Numerus cæsorum incertus, captivorum tam equitum quam peditum major, inter quos qui ordines ducebant retenti, dimissis gregariis & tenuioribus militibus: Ex Scotis pauci desiderati: ex quibus illustris equitis Comarchæ Largi filius & hæres, qui vexillum regium hostibus eripuit.
units.tr: But the Scots could not be moved from their purpose by these threats. Having reviewed the army, which consisted of twenty-seven or twenty-eight thousand foot and four thousand horse, Leslie, whom the Lord gave to his country when it was labouring in the utmost distress, ordered the camp to move towards England at the beginning of August. The supreme command of the war had been entrusted to him by the Scots, as stated above. The whole army was divided into three columns for more convenient foraging: the first was led by Aumont, another by Baylie, and the third by Leslie himself, with a great train of artillery and provisions for many days. The river Tweed, which separates England from Scotland, had to be crossed, and this honour chanced to fall to the Earl of Montrose, a tribune of foot, who, dismounting, was the first to wade across the river at the usual ford. All the other commanders of the foot had done this, so as to encourage the common soldiers, since the labour and danger were then shared equally by all. When they had pitched camp on hostile soil, it was strictly forbidden to all, on pain of death, to harm the English, their villages, fields or goods in any way. Meanwhile the garrison of Berwick ran hither and thither, to intercept soldiers who had straggled or were wandering away from the columns; but to no effect at all. For on 28 August, they pitched camp at the appointed place, namely the heath of Newcastle, on the left bank of the river Tyne, five thousand paces above Newcastle. There lies a small town there called Newburn, and there, as the sea-tide recedes, the ford is fairly convenient. But the English had occupied the opposite, right bank, with five thousand foot and two thousand five hundred horse, protected by a rampart and a hastily thrown-up earthwork. However, the Scots' heavier artillery was so opportunely placed that they opened by force the passage they could not win by prayers. For first, through a herald, they earnestly asked the English on the opposite bank to withdraw promptly and not to block the way for friends, since they had entered England with no hostile intent, and had so far conducted themselves peacefully on hostile soil, without any harm or injury to anyone. But the English immediately ordered this herald to clear off, not without abusive insults. So the Scots took up arms, to find out whether the right hands of men who had declared themselves open enemies would match their tongues. The English foot were so terrified by the explosions of the artillery that they deserted their standards; and when the Scots saw them struck with such fear, they began to plan a crossing in massed columns, and could scarcely be restrained by the commander's order. Here, fearing an ambush, he ordered a few squadrons of horse to try the ford, so that, having crossed the river, they would take position on the opposite bank; and if the English attacked, they were to feign a retreat and lure them into the ambush that had been laid. For in the left bank of the river, at suitable but hidden places, the artillery had been positioned. Therefore, when the English horse took the feigned flight of the retiring cavalry for a real one, they pursued in disorder right up to the riverbank and fell into the trap. For they were so overwhelmed, by the very frequent blasts of the guns coming unexpectedly, that they fell back at a faster pace; and those Scottish squadrons which had earlier feigned flight, turning about in an instant, attacked the retreating English with such force that they threw them into flight. Meanwhile the whole Scottish army crossed the river without any obstacle being offered, and the light-armed horse were ordered to scatter the remnants of the English army which still held a nearby hill. There was sharp fighting on both sides for some time; but at last the English, unable to withstand the Scots' attack for long, took to flight. They would not have escaped without great slaughter had it not been forbidden to rage against those fleeing, which they showed, by this sign, that the Scots did not thirst for the blood of any Englishman. The number of the slain was uncertain; the captives, both horse and foot, were more numerous. Among them, the officers who led the companies were detained, while the common soldiers and the humbler men were released. Of the Scots, only a few were missed, among them the illustrious knight, the Laird of Largo's son and heir, who snatched the royal standard from the enemy.

units.la: Prælium hoc incidit in 28. diem Augusti.
units.tr: This battle took place on the 28th day of August.

units.la: Victoriam hanc incruentam Scoti adepti, ubi publicas in ipsis castris Deo gratias egissent, in armis insomnem eam noctem sub dio transegerunt; hostium quippe vires magis dissipatas quam fractas noverant: nihilque facilius esse ad victorem exercitum vincendum, quam si post victoriam quam cito fieri possit aggrediaris, quod tum fere soleat esse negligentior, & rerum gestarum prosperitate in nimiam securitatem quæ semper exitialis est, resolutus.
units.tr: Having won this victory without bloodshed, the Scots offered public thanks to God in their own camp, then spent that sleepless night under open sky, under arms. They knew the enemy's forces were scattered rather than broken. They also knew that nothing is easier than defeating a victorious army if you attack it as soon as possible after its victory, since it is then usually more careless and, relaxed by its success, falls into an excessive security, which is always fatal.

units.la: Die sequenti Novum Castrum accedunt Scoti, oppidum hoc tuebantur regii, qui audita suorum clade deserto oppido in interiora Angliæ se receperant, & ad primarium exercitum regium se contulerant, quem ita lente colligebat Hiberniæ deputatus, ut multi judicarent, eum non molestè laturum si Scoti insigni aliqua calamitate copias contra se missas affecissent, & Novo-Castrum interciperent, ratus sic tandem, aliis omnibus consiliis frustra tentatis, universam gentem Anglicam excitatum iri in Scotos, quos ferro & flamma in omnia sævituros judicabat: At Scoti contra, quia pacem quærebant, terrorem solum belli ostentabant, ac sine ulla fere noxa in hostico degebant, victoria modeste & clementer utebantur, captivos humaniter habuerunt: quibus actionibus magnam moderati animi laudem adepti sunt, & ut sibi benevolentiam, ita factioni adversæ odium omnium fere in Anglia conflarunt: Accedebat quod regii milites quacunque transibant, tristia incontinentiæ & rapacitatis vestigia post se reliquerint, agricolas expilarint, ac virginibus stupra intulerint, ut ex literis supplicibus ad regem complurium Angliæ procerum manu obsignatis constat. Itaque Novo-castrenses, qui ante biduum amicas Scotorum literas quibus transitum securum petebant, vel aperire dedignati fuerant, portas suas jam lubentes aperiunt, & exercitui com-meatum suppeditant: prætidiariis bis mille simul cum Imperatore ac proceribus hospitia designant: Ingens hic reperta omnis generis annonæ copia in cellis & penuariis recondita in usum exercitus regii, undique huc non ex Anglia solum, verumetiam ex sinu Baltico advecta: quam ad exercitum suum alendum deprompserunt Scoti: Uti etiam quæ in armamentariis regiis reposita fuerunt arma. Hæc omnia in tabulas referebant; privatis vero civibus nihil damni illatum, nam bona fide ab hospitibus accepta vel præsenti pecunia solvebant, aut syngrapho obsignato de solutione cavebant, licet ab hostibus ut prædones quasi publice permisso latrocinio calumnias atroces passi sunt, quas falsas fuisse dies docuit.
units.tr: On the following day the Scots came to Newcastle. The royalists held this town, but after hearing of their comrades' defeat they had abandoned it, withdrawn into the interior of England and joined the main royal army. The Lord Deputy of Ireland was gathering that army so slowly that many judged he would not be sorry if the Scots had dealt some notable blow to the forces sent against them and had seized Newcastle. He reckoned that, once all other plans had been tried in vain, the whole English nation would be roused against the Scots, whom he believed would rage with fire and sword everywhere. The Scots, however, since they sought peace, displayed only the terror of war, and they lived in the enemy's country with almost no harm done. They used their victory with moderation and mercy, and treated their prisoners humanely. By these actions they won great praise for their restraint, and they gained the goodwill of almost everyone in England while bringing hatred upon the opposing faction. Moreover, the royalist soldiers, wherever they passed, had left behind sad traces of debauchery and plunder: they had stripped the farmers and violated maidens, as is clear from letters of supplication to the king, sealed by the hands of many leading men of England. So the people of Newcastle, who only two days earlier had refused even to open the friendly letters of the Scots in which they asked for safe passage, now gladly opened their gates and supplied the army with provisions. They assigned quarters to two thousand garrison soldiers, together with the commander and the nobles. Here a great abundance of every kind of provision was found, stored in cellars and pantries, brought in not only from England but also from the Baltic. The Scots drew it out to feed their own army, and likewise the weapons stored in the royal arsenals. They recorded all of this in lists. But no harm was done to private citizens: the Scots paid for what they had received in good faith from their hosts, either with ready money or by a sealed bond promising payment. Although they suffered atrocious slanders from their enemies, who claimed they had been let loose as robbers with a sort of public licence, the days have shown those charges to be false.

units.la: Eodem fere tempore Berwicenses prælidiarii putabant sibi rei bene gerendæ occasionem oblatam. Nam ad oppidulum Dunsianum, in Mercia Scotiæ, sibi propinquum audiverant reservari Scotorum commeatum & apparatum bellicum qui ad exercitum transvehendus effet, custodiam militarem admodum infrequentem, & securam esse: Quare re-cta Dunsum tendunt, cum curribus & plaustris ad commeatum illum & apparatum avehendum: rati paucos illos præsidiarios, plus minus centum & sexaginta pedites, non ausuros aleam certaminis experiri contra mille equites & centurias aliquot peditum. Oppidulum itaque magnis animis adoriuntur, sed majoribus repelluntur, & post duarum horarum acre certamen, retrocedunt, ac plaustris militum suorum cadaveribus onustis citatiore quam advenerant cursu Berwicum redeunt: metuebant quippe ne à Scotis in vicinia habitantibus & ad sua defendenda convolantibus Berwico excluderentur, aut ad pugnam in reditu cogerentur. Neque illud frustra, nam Comes Hadinæ orientalis limitis & Marciæ præfectus, intellecto eorum consilio, cum ingenti incolarum omnis ordinis manu Dunsum advolabat: Sed accepto nuncio reditus Berwicum, Dunglassum munitum castrum in littore Forthæ divertit: ubi misere cum compluribus nobilibus periit. Erat in castro illo cella quædam in qua reconditus fuerat pulvis tormentarius, ejusque custodia commissa fuit curæ & fidei Angli cujusdam prædicto Comiti à cubiculis, cujus seu negligentia seu inexpiabili perfidia factum fuit ut incenso pulvere tormentario castrum illud momento subversum fit, & cum castro Comes ipse cum aliis fere octuaginta seu consanguineis, seu familiaribus; inter quos & Anglus iste. Infœlicis hujus calamitatis tristissimus nuncius, præcedentium victoriarum lætitiam minuit.
units.tr: At about the same time the garrison of Berwick thought they had been offered a chance to achieve something. For they had heard that at the little town of Duns, in the Merse of Scotland near them, the Scottish supplies and war matériel were being kept, to be carried across to the army, and that its guard was very thin and considered safe. So they made straight for Duns, with carts and wagons to carry off those supplies and equipment, reckoning that those few garrison men, some hundred and sixty foot, would not dare to try their luck in a fight against a thousand horse and several companies of foot. They attacked the little town with great courage, but were driven back with greater losses, and after a fierce struggle of two hours they withdrew. They returned to Berwick faster than they had come, their wagons loaded with the bodies of their soldiers. They were afraid that the Scots who lived nearby and were flocking to defend their own homes might shut them out of Berwick, or force them to fight on the way back. Nor was this fear groundless, for the Earl of Haddington, governor of the eastern march and of the Merse, learned of their plan and flew to Duns with a great band of inhabitants of every rank. But on receiving word that the enemy had returned to Berwick, he turned aside to Dunglass, a fortified castle on the shore of the Forth. There he perished wretchedly, together with several noblemen. In that castle there was a storeroom in which gunpowder had been kept, and its guard had been entrusted to the care and loyalty of an Englishman, a chamberlain of the aforesaid earl. Whether through his negligence or through an unforgivable treachery, the powder was set alight, and the castle was blown to pieces in an instant. The earl himself perished with the castle, along with almost eighty others, both kinsmen and household servants, among whom was that Englishman. The most grievous news of this unhappy disaster diminished the joy of the earlier victories.

units.la: Sed ad exercitum Scoticum revertamus. Post Novi-castri deditionem, reliquæ vicinæ urbes præsidia Scotica admisere; Dunelmi custodia Comiti Fermelodunt[?] cum valido peditum equitumque praesidio traditur. Portus etiam Novi-Castri qua Tina fluvius se mari Germanico miscet, à Scotis interceptus, & munitus contra subitariam vim: atque hic interceptae naves quaedam onerariae quae annonam regio exercitui advehebant, nautis ignaris subitae mutationis.
units.tr: But let us return to the Scottish army. After the surrender of Newcastle, the other neighbouring towns admitted Scottish garrisons. The custody of Durham was handed over to the Earl of Fermelodunt[?], with a strong force of foot and horse. The port of Newcastle, where the Tyne flows into the German Sea, was also seized by the Scots and fortified against sudden attack. Here some merchant ships were captured, which were bringing provisions to the royal army, their sailors unaware of the sudden change.

units.la: Dein deliberatum suit à Scotis, quid sibi ultra faciendum esset, an protinus Eboracum progrediendum, ubi serenis. rex simul cum exercitu primario haereret, an vero supplicibus literis denuo conveniendus effet, vicit eorum sententia qui supplices literas suadebant; licet non ignari elsent regem publicis edictis omnes nobiles simul cum clientibus evocasse, ac edixisse ut 20. Septemb. ad signa adessent, dimicaturi contra Scotos: Literae porro hae sic se habuerunt.
units.tr: Then the Scots deliberated what further they should do: whether to advance at once to York, where the most serene king was staying with his main army, or to be met again by means of a letter of supplication. The opinion of those who urged the letter prevailed, although they were not unaware that the king had summoned all the nobles together with their retainers by public proclamation, and had ordered them to be present under arms on the 20th of September, ready to fight against the Scots. The letter of supplication was couched as follows.

units.la: Literae supplices Deputatorum à nupero parlamento & aliis serenissimi regis fidelibus subditis.
units.tr: Humble letters from the Deputies of the late parliament and other faithful subjects of the most serene king.

units.la: QUa decet animi submissione repraesentamus; Quod post adversa plurima aequis animis hactenus perpessa, extrema necessitate coacti fuerimus in Angliam venire, ut malis nostris medelam & justa nostra ac humilia postulata ab aequitate Majestatis V. obtineremus; ac prout in tractatu de scopo & intentione hujus expeditionis notum universis fecimus; ita in itinere nostro commeatu nobiscum allato contenti viximus; neque regni hujus publicam pacem turbantes quemlibet serenissimi M. V. subditorum cujuscunque demum ordinis esset damno illo affecimus; & hactenus pacifice & amice nos gessimus donec cogeremur ac sollicitaremur armis submovere violentiam nullo nostro merito contra nos intentatam, qua transitum fluminis Tinae prope Neuburnam nobis prohibere conabantur; Atque hac violentia complures in articulo mortis confessi sunt se peccasse in nos contra suam conscientiam, ac reos semet fecisse sui sanguinis: Ut pari aut majori incommodo obviam eatur, & ut nobis liceat ad sereniss. M. V. sine ulteriori oppositione accedere, quo ab æquitate & bonitate M. V. æquissimis & humillimis nostris postulatis satisfieri possit: Nos humillimi & devotissimi M. V. subditi per supplices literas adhuc instamus, quam semitam a motuum horum initio hactenus constanter trivimus, & a qua nulla irritatio aut provocatio ab hostibus tam M. V. quam nostris, nihil adversi quod perpessi sumus, nihil prosperi quod nobis evenire posset fideles & M. V. devotos animos unquam divertet. Quare humillime obsecramus, ut sereniss. M. V. pro regia sua prudentia tandem velit oculos & animum serio conjicere in gravamina nostra, digneturque damnis & injuriis nostris reparandis providere; ac consilio & consensu ordinum regni Angliæ in Comitiis, firmam & solidam pacem sancire tam terra quam mari: ut sic animo hilari & alacriter M. V. ut nativo nobis regi persolvere possimus legitimam omnem obedientiam quæ a fidelibus subditis exspectari poterit; atque evitentur mala & calamitates utrinque pariter regno nunc imminentes, quorum M. V. proborum subditorum animi meminisse horrent. Rogamus insuper Deum omnipotentem, ut M. V. solium adaugeat, ac in medio nostrum pietatis & justitiæ artibus in æternum stabiliat. M. V. benignum responsum humiliter exspectamus.
units.tr: We present these with the submission that becomes us. After suffering many adverse things hitherto with an even mind, we were forced by extreme necessity to come into England, to obtain a remedy for our evils and our just and humble requests from the equity of Your Majesty. As we made known to all in the treatise on the aim and intention of this expedition, so on our march we have lived content with the provisions brought with us. Nor, disturbing the public peace of this kingdom, have we done harm to any of Your Most Serene Majesty's subjects of whatever rank. Hitherto we have conducted ourselves peaceably and amicably, until we were compelled and urged to remove by arms a violence, undeserved on our part, which was attempted against us to prevent our crossing the river Tyne near Newburn. By this violence many, at the point of death, confessed that they had sinned against us contrary to their conscience, and had made themselves guilty of blood. In order that an equal or greater harm may be averted, and that we may be allowed to approach Your Most Serene Majesty without further opposition, so that our most equitable and most humble requests may be satisfied by the equity and goodness of Your Majesty, we, Your Majesty's most humble and most devoted subjects, still press by this humble letter. We have followed this path constantly from the beginning of these disturbances until now, and no provocation or challenge from enemies, whether of Your Majesty or of ours, no adversity that we have suffered, no prosperity that might befall us, will ever turn our faithful and devoted minds from it. Therefore we humbly beseech that Your Most Serene Majesty, in your royal prudence, may at last be pleased to turn your eyes and mind seriously to our grievances, and deign to provide for the repair of our losses and injuries; and that, by the counsel and consent of the estates of the kingdom of England in Parliament, you would confirm a firm and solid peace both by land and by sea. Thus, with a cheerful and willing spirit, we may be able to render to Your Majesty, as to our native king, all the lawful obedience that can be expected from faithful subjects; and thus the evils and calamities now threatening the kingdom on both sides alike may be avoided, which the minds of Your Majesty's upright subjects shudder to remember. We further pray Almighty God to increase Your Majesty's throne and to establish it forever in the midst of us by the arts of piety and justice. We humbly await a gracious answer from Your Majesty.

units.la: Quibus literis rex per Comitem Lanurci, regni Scotiæ secretarium, Eboraci in aula tum commorantem, Septemb. 5. in hæc verba respondit.
units.tr: To these letters the king, through the Earl of Lanark, secretary of the kingdom of Scotland, then staying at court in York, replied on 5 September in the following words.

units.la: Sereniss. rex vidit & perpendit supplicem hunc libellum & clementer dignatus est responsum hoc per me referre. Usque adeo generalibus terminis conceptum esse, ut donec particularia postulata defignaveritis, directe nequeat respondere; Quare vult ut eadem statim designetis. Paratum hactenus se semper fuisse ad audienda & corrigenda subditorum suorū gravamina. Atq; ut maturo consilio de rebus hisce momenti maximi deliberatio instituatur, jussisse proceres omnes hujus regni sibi adesse Eboraci 24. Septemb. quorum consilio illud postulatis vestris referetis responsum quod maxime futurum sit in regis honorem, & pacem ac salutem regnorum. Interim si pax illud sit quod expetitis, prout prae vobis fertis, rex sereniss. exspectat, & rescripto hoc mandat vobis, ne ulterius cum exercitu procedatis, nam unicum hoc superest ad pacem & concordiam inter duo regna resarciendam, ac infœlices controversias componendas, quod nulli magis in votis est quam seren. [?] & clementissimo nostro regi.
units.tr: His Most Serene Majesty has seen and considered this humble petition, and has graciously deigned to have this answer conveyed through me. The petition is framed in such general terms that it cannot be answered directly until you specify your particular requests; therefore His Majesty wishes you to set them down at once. He has always been ready to hear and correct the grievances of his subjects. And so that deliberation on these matters of the greatest importance may be carried out with mature counsel, he has ordered all the nobles of this kingdom to be present with him at York on 24 September. By their counsel you will receive a reply to your requests, which will be most conducive to the honour of the king and to the peace and welfare of the kingdoms. Meanwhile, if peace is what you seek, as you profess, His Most Serene Majesty expects it, and by this rescript he commands you not to advance further with your army. For this alone remains to restore peace and concord between the two kingdoms and to settle these unhappy controversies, and nothing is more the desire of all than of our most serene and most clement king.

units.la: Accepto hoc responso specialia postulata designarunt, quæ opera Guilielmi Flaminii Victoniensis Comitis filii, ad Lanurci Comitem transmiserunt: quorum summa hæc fuit. 1. Ut nuperi parlamenti statuta rex jubeat promulgari suo nomine, hoc est, ut ea rata habeat & sanciat, quænam vero illa essent ex statutorum exemplari antehac misso satis constare. 2. Ut arx Edenburgensis simul cum aliis omnibus munitis regni arcibus, muniantur & convertantur in tutelam & securitatem regni, cum eo fine primum conditæ sint. 3. Ut Scoti in Anglia & Hibernia liberi pronuncientur ab omni pæna ob fœdus in Scotia obsignatum: neque posthac adigantur in novas jurandi formulas quibus damnetur fœdus Scoticum regia authoritate munitum. Hujus vero articuli ideo mentionem faciebant, quia in Anglia ex incudeCantuarienfi novæ juramentorum formulæ excudebantur, in quæ soli Scoti a publicanis & vectigalium exactoribus, cogebantur sub pæna carceris, cujus diutinū squalorem quidam adhuc experiebantur. Sed in Hibernia novo hoc inquisitionis commento sæviebat contra Scotos omnis sexus & conditionis Hiberniæ prorex, quos in expressam fœderis & confessionis Scoticæ etiam in synodo authoritate regia nuper sancitæ abjurationem conceptis verbis adigebat, licet ipsi compertissimum fuisset eosdem confessionem Scoticam ante annos quadraginta mandato regio obsignasse: renuentes vero in carcerem & vincula abripi jubebat, contra tenorem edicti regii quo renuentium nomina solum notari mandabatur. Unde factum ut complures relictis laribus in Scotiam se proripere cogerentur, non sine notabili coloniarum damno, mulieres vero Scoticæ cum liberis qui nocturna fuga sibi tam commode consulere non poterant, ad judicia protrahebantur, quarum una simul cum infante ab uberibus pendente pro ipso tribunali inter viatorum & lictorum manus expiravit. 4. Ut in belli hujus faces, & incendiarios, sævissimorum horum motuum authores severe ex legum præscripto animadvertatur. 5. Ut naves in Anglia & Hibernia detentæ simul cum bonis interceptis restituantur, ac de damno nautis & mercatoribus illato satisfiat. 6. Ut de injuriis, damnis, sumptibus hoc bello expensis satisfiat. 7. Ut edicta regia contra Scotos promulgata rescindantur & revocentur. Denique, ut, consilio & consensu ordinum regni Angliæ in publicis Comitiis, præsidiarij milites a limitibus removeantur, & quicquid libero commercio moram ullam afferre possit: ac ut communicatis consiliis firmæ & stabili paci ita provideatur; ut sine molestiarum ex anno in annum recurrentium solicitudine, liceat religione & libertatibus a majoribus transmissis frui.
units.tr: On receiving this answer, they drew up specific requests, which they sent through the agency of William Fleming, son of the Earl of Wigtown, to the Earl of Lanark. The substance of them was this. 1. That the king command the statutes of the late parliament to be promulgated in his own name, that is, that he hold them valid and confirm them; what those statutes were, however, is sufficiently clear from the copy of the statutes sent previously. 2. That the castle of Edinburgh, together with all the other fortresses of the kingdom, be fortified and turned to the protection and security of the kingdom, for which purpose they were first built. 3. That the Scots in England and Ireland be declared free from every penalty for the covenant sealed in Scotland, and that they not henceforth be compelled to take new oath-formulas by which the Scottish covenant, fortified by royal authority, is condemned. They mentioned this article because in England, at the anvil of Canterbury, new forms of oaths were being forged, which the Scots alone were compelled by tax-collectors and revenue officers to take under penalty of imprisonment, the long squalor of which some were still undergoing. But in Ireland the Lord Deputy, of every sex and condition, raged against the Scots with this new invention of inquisition, forcing them by express words to abjure the covenant and the Scottish Confession, which had recently been sanctioned by royal authority even in a synod; although he knew full well that these same persons had sealed the Scottish Confession by royal command forty years before. Those who refused he ordered to be dragged off to prison and chains, contrary to the terms of the royal edict, by which only the names of those who refused were to be noted. Hence it came about that many, leaving their homes, were forced to flee to Scotland, not without a notable loss to the colonies; and Scottish women with their children, who could not so conveniently provide for themselves by night flight, were dragged before the courts; one of them, together with an infant hanging at her breast, died before the very tribunal, among the hands of travellers and officers. 4. That the firebrands and incendiaries of this war, the authors of these most savage disturbances, be severely punished according to the prescription of the laws. 5. That ships detained in England and Ireland be restored together with the goods seized, and that satisfaction be made for the loss inflicted on sailors and merchants. 6. That satisfaction be made for the injuries, losses and expenses incurred in this war. 7. That the royal edicts published against the Scots be rescinded and revoked. Finally, that by the counsel and consent of the estates of the kingdom of England in public Parliament, the garrison soldiers be removed from the borders, and whatever may cause any hindrance to free commerce; and that provision be made, with counsels shared, for a firm and stable peace, so that, without anxiety over troubles recurring from year to year, it may be lawful to enjoy the religion and liberties handed down by our ancestors.

units.la: Interea complures Angliæ proceres simul cum Londinensibus supplices literas ad Regem mittunt, quibus miserum regni ad extrema ruentis statum proponunt, qua innovationibus in causa religionis per Episcopos, quæ licet antehac per novatores sedulo promoverentur, nunc tamen severe obtruderentur authoritate Canonum ecclesiasticorum, unde metus esset ne major procella ecclesiam obrueret, papismo praesertim lacertos suos movente, & pontificiis evectis ad militares praefecturas contra expressa legum statuta quibus exarmari jubentur: qua advocatione legionum Hibernicarum, &, ut rumoribus fertur, aliorum etiam exterorum militum in regno: qua monopoliis & exactionibus: qua comitiorum intermissione aut interruptione: Regii etiam aerarii nervos accisos, & periculum sereniss. regi imminens si in expeditione hac contra Scotos progrederetur, libere sed summa verborum cum modestia commemorant. Neque sibi malis hisce gravissimis avertendis praesentius constare remedium, quam ut comitia regni publica quam maturrime indicerentur; ubi in gravaminum horum causas sedulo inquiri & in authores animadverti, ac praesentes hi motus sine caede & sanguine componi possint, ita quidem prout maxime conducet saluti & dignitati regiae, populi solatio, & arctiori utriusque regni unioni contra reformatae religionis hostes.
units.tr: Meanwhile several nobles of England, together with the Londoners, send humble letters to the King, in which they set out the wretched state of the kingdom, which is rushing toward extremity. They freely but with great moderation of language recount the innovations in matters of religion introduced by the bishops, which, although formerly pressed by the innovators with zeal, were now being forcibly thrust upon the people by the authority of the ecclesiastical canons; whence there was fear lest a greater storm overwhelm the Church, especially as the Papists were stirring their strength, and Papists were raised to military commands against the express statutes of the laws by which they are ordered to be disarmed; by the summoning of Irish legions, and, as rumour has it, of other foreign soldiers too, into the kingdom; by monopolies and exactions; by the intermission or interruption of parliaments; by the sinews of the royal treasury being cut; and by the danger hanging over the most serene king if he should proceed with this expedition against the Scots. They add that for averting these most grievous evils no remedy seemed more effective to them than that a public parliament of the kingdom be summoned as soon as possible, where the causes of these grievances might be diligently inquired into and the authors punished, and where the present disturbances might be settled without slaughter and bloodshed, in a manner most conducive to the safety and dignity of the king, the comfort of the people, and a closer union of both kingdoms against the enemies of the reformed religion.

units.la: Literis hisce benigne admodum a sereniss. rege responsum fuit, ac publico edicto solennem omnium Angliae procerum conventum ad 24. Septembris indixit, locumque conventus Eboracum statuit.
units.tr: The most serene king replied to this letter very graciously. By public edict he summoned a solemn assembly of all the nobles of England for 24 September, and he fixed York as the place of the assembly.

units.la: Scoti interim oppida intercepta contra subitariā vim muniebant, & cum metus esset, ne, oblata falsa concordiae specie, Deputatus Hiberniae novis quas ex Hibernia exspectabat auxiliis auctior, captata rei bene gerendae occasione ex improviso eos adoriretur; novum militum delectum praesto esse jubent sub ductu Argathelii comitis, ad quem ex flore nobilitatis maximus concursus undique fiebat. Querebantur tamen complures rerum praeclare agendarum occasiones amitti, lentisque hisce consiliis militum alacritatem obtundi, hostibus a quibus nihil sinceri exspe-ctan[?] standum esset animos addi;itaq;se omnia potius extrema quam moras istas malle, sæpiusque ingeminatum illud Poetæ Semper nocuit differre paratis. Sed vehemens prudentiorum pacis & concordiæ studium, & regii mandati reverentia præfervida militum ingenia sedavit: Ac ad diem præfixum quid a serenifs. rege & proceribus Anglis exspectandum esset inter spem & metum, Deo exitum committentes animis dubiis pendebant.
units.tr: Meanwhile the Scots were fortifying the towns they had seized against a sudden attack. There was fear that the Deputy of Ireland, strengthened by the new auxiliaries he was expecting from Ireland, might offer a false appearance of concord and then, seizing an opportunity to act to advantage, attack them unawares. They ordered a new levy of soldiers to stand ready under the command of the Earl of Argathelius, to whom a very large number of men from the flower of the nobility flocked from every side. Yet many complained that several chances of acting brilliantly were being lost, that the soldiers' eagerness was being blunted by these slow counsels, and that courage was being given to enemies from whom nothing sincere was to be expected. They therefore preferred any extreme course to these delays, and repeated often the saying of the poet: Delay has always harmed those who are ready. But the strong desire of the more prudent for peace and concord, and the reverence for the king's command, calmed the fiery spirits of the soldiers. And so, awaiting the appointed day, they hung in suspense with anxious minds, between hope and fear, committing the outcome to God.

units.la: Proceres Angliæ frequentissimi conveniunt, quibus significatum a rege, se proprio suo motu comitia regni indixisse ad tertium Novembris,de quibusdam tamen jam agendum esse quæ differri non possent: ac primum,perpendendum serio quid respondendū esset rebellium Scotorum postulatis, & quomodo reprimenda ipsorum audacia qui Angliam ipsam explicatis signis invasissent: porro ut omnes statum controversiæ perspicue intelligerent,imperatum a Rege Comiti Traquario Scoto ut totum illud negotium explicaret. Dein,quomodo exercitus,quem sanctioris sui senatus consilio collegisset ad immanem hanc subditorum suorum rebellionem reprimendam,alendus esset, usque dum in comitiis subsidia parlamentaria, ut vocant, concedi possent: atque in hunc finem imperatū Deputato Hiberniæ exercituum supremo præfecto ut belli & exercitus statum explicaret.Hic nobiles quibus concordia & æquitatis studium cordi erat, & cognitæ artes factiosis aulicæ quæ regem contra animi sui impetum ad bellum hoc impulisset, pacifica & moderata consilia suggerebant,neq; Comitis Traquarii sermonibus,Scotorum actiones ad sequiorem sensum detorquentis multum sidebant, Incertus bellorum exitus, exhaustum regis ærarium, Scotorum etiam innocentia per quos non steterat quominus præstarentur in quæ conventum fuerat Berwici, multorum oculis obversabatur. Occurrebat & illud Taciti. Præstat difficilem pugnam evitare, honestis conditionibus hosti concessis: quam se cupiditate vindictæ in incertum Martis eventum conjicere. Dein ex victoria etiamsi certa parum gloriæ, minus lucri comparari posse, cum Scotorum in suis tutandis obstinata pertinacia ab omni ævo satis superque cognita esset. Sed complures maxime movebat manifesta servitutis imago a publicæ salutis hostibus jampridem excogitata, & magis quam boni vellent hactenus promota, velata quidem specie egregia promovendi authoritatem regiam, contra æquissimi regis innatam indolem; sed qua revera nihil aliud peteretur ab ista regum etiam optimorum peste & pernicie, quam ut sibi in præsentia grassandi licentiam, & in futurum securitatem conciliarent: Hisce miseriarum sub quibus utrumque pariter gemit regnum authoribus, nihil magis in votis esse, quam ut utrumque regnum sanguini suo innataret: Eo spectare eorum consilia ut pro inveterata sua malignitate & consuetis artibus, Scotos horrendis calumniis insimulatos omnium odiis objicerent, quia scilicet ausi fuerunt eorum ambitioni remoram & obicem ponere: Quare judicarunt,omnes prius rationes tentandas esse quibus vulnus hoc componi posset, quam ad extremum belli intestini remedium confugiendum esset: mali fontes perscrutandos esse, quando si compertum fuerit Scotis propositum esse regiæ authoritatis jugum petulanter excutere, indignos esse vita qui eam non impenderent ad regis sui authoritatem sartam tectam conservandam. Quod si vero rem aliter se habere constiterit, metuendum esse ne Deum innocentiæ & æquitatis vindicem experiantur, qui belli injusti aut saltem non necessarii authores essent, præsertim cum Scoti profiteantur se paratos esse jure agere: Controversiam itaque hanc legatorum & caduceatorum opera non præliis tractandam esse.
units.tr: The nobles of England assembled in great numbers. The king let them know that he had summoned the parliament of his own accord for 3 November, but that some matters had to be dealt with at once that could not be put off. First, they must seriously consider what answer should be given to the demands of the rebel Scots, and how to check the audacity of those who had invaded England itself with hostile banners. Next, so that everyone might clearly understand the state of the dispute, the king ordered the Scottish Earl Traquarius to explain the whole affair. Then, they must consider how the army, which he had raised on the advice of his more sacred council to put down this monstrous rebellion of his subjects, was to be maintained until the parliamentary subsidies, as they are called, could be granted. To this end the Deputy of Ireland, supreme commander of the armies, was ordered to explain the state of the war and of the army. Here the nobles, to whom concord and the pursuit of fairness were dear, and who understood the arts by which the court faction had driven the king, against the inclination of his own mind, into this war, offered peaceful and moderate counsels. They did not put much trust in the words of Earl Traquarius, who twisted the actions of the Scots to a worse meaning. The uncertain outcome of wars, the king's exhausted treasury, and the innocence of the Scots, who had not failed to perform what had been agreed at Berwick, were before the eyes of many. The saying of Tacitus also came to mind: It is better to avoid a difficult fight by granting the enemy honourable terms than to commit oneself, from the desire for revenge, to the uncertain chance of war. Besides, even a certain victory would bring little glory and less profit, since the obstinate stubbornness of the Scots in defending themselves had been known well enough and more than enough in every age. But many were especially moved by the plain image of slavery, which the enemies of the public welfare had long devised and had promoted more than good men wished. Under the attractive pretext of advancing the royal authority, which is in truth the innate disposition of the most just king, what was really sought by that plague and ruin even of the best kings was the freedom to rage for the present and security for the future. The authors of these miseries, under which both kingdoms alike groan, wished for nothing more than that both kingdoms should swim in their own blood. Their plans aimed at this: that, according to their long-standing malice and customary tricks, they might expose the Scots, charged with dreadful slanders, to the hatred of all, because the Scots had dared to place an obstacle and barrier to their ambition. Therefore they judged that all other means must be tried by which this wound could be healed, before resort was had to the last remedy of civil war. The sources of the evil had to be searched out; for if it were discovered that the Scots intended to throw off the yoke of royal authority wantonly, then those who would not sacrifice their lives to keep their king's authority whole and safe were unworthy of life. But if the matter were found to be otherwise, they feared lest they should experience God as the avenger of innocence and justice, if they were the authors of an unjust war, or at least of an unnecessary one, especially since the Scots declared themselves ready to act by law. This controversy, therefore, was not to be settled by battles, but by the work of envoys and heralds.

units.la: Ast alii, inter quos Deputatus Hiberniæ familiam ducebat, omnes ingenii nervos intendebant, ut præfens hoc negotium vi gereretur, neque socordibus consiliis honorem sereniss. regis à rebellibus fœde concultatum[?], & Anglicæ gentis decus proderent, (honesta quippe hæc nomina occultæ suæ fraudi & ambitioni jampridem assueverunt prætexere) facilitatem etiam victoriæ, suo scilicet ductu, contra inermes pauculos rebelles & inter se discordes jactitabat Hiberniæ deputatus, non sine singulari significatione odii sui in nomen Scoticum, cujus memoriam se aboliturum olim inter suos est minatus; Scotosque vel in cruore suo natitantes ex Anglia compellendos esse. Verum Deo Serenissimi & clementissimi regis ac prudentum procerum corda flectente, pacis consilia ut æquiora & tutiora, vicerunt: ac in hanc sententiam itum est, ut communibus procerum suffragiis decem & sex nobiles pacis studiosi deputarentur qui cum Scotis agerent, & si fieri posset, æquis conditionibus transfigerent: nominati fuerunt octo Comites Bedfordius, Effexius, Hartfordius, Sarisburiensis, Warwicensis, Hollandus, Bristolius, Barcerius. Octo Barones Parlamentarii Whartonius, Pagetus, Kinboltonus, Broukius, Poulettus, Howartus, Savillus, Dunfmorius. Monentur etiam Scoti ut deputatos suo nomine cum plenis mandatis mitterent, quibus literæ salvi conductus in amplissima forma, nulla jam facta rebellium mentione, expedirentur. Atque hi nominarunt Comitem Fermeloduni, Laudonium supremi ordinis, quibus postea additus Rothusius Comes. Patricium Hepburnum, Gulielmum Duglassium, quibus postea additus Gulielmus Dromondus, equestris ordinis; Iohannem Smithum consulem seu, ut vulgo vocant, Balivum Edinburgenum; Alexandrum Wedderburnum: hisque postea additus Hugo Kemedus cives tertii ordinis; & quia controversiæ ecclesiasticæ forte
units.tr: But others, among whom the Deputy of Ireland led the way, strained every nerve to have this affair conducted by force. They would not betray the honour of the most serene king, foully trampled by the rebels, nor the glory of the English nation, by idle counsels. (These honourable names had long been accustomed to cover their hidden deceit and ambition.) The Deputy of Ireland also boasted of the ease of victory, under his own leadership, against a few unarmed rebels who were at odds among themselves. He did not conceal his singular hatred of the Scottish name, and once threatened among his own people that he would wipe out its memory; he said the Scots, even swimming in their own blood, were to be driven out of England. But God, who bends the hearts of the most serene and merciful king and of the wise nobles, carried the day for the counsels of peace as the fairer and safer. It was resolved, by the common votes of the nobles, that sixteen peace-loving nobles should be appointed to deal with the Scots and, if possible, bring the matter to a settlement on fair terms. Eight earls were named: Bedford, Essex, Hertford, Salisbury, Warwick, Holland, Bristol and Berkshire. Eight parliamentary barons: Wharton, Paget, Kimbolton, Brooke, Poulett, Howard, Savile and Dunsmore. The Scots were also advised to send their deputies in their own name with full powers, and letters of safe-conduct were drawn up in the most ample form, with no mention of rebels at all. The Scots named as their deputies the Earl of Fermline, Lauderdale of the highest rank, to whom was later added the Earl of Rothes; Patrick Hepburn and William Douglas, to whom was later added William Drummond, of the knightly order; John Smith, consul or, as the common people call him, bailie of Edinburgh; and Alexander Wedderburn, to whom was later added Hugh Kennedy, a citizen of the third order. And because the ecclesiastical controversies were perhaps to be debated, they ordered Alexander Henderson and Archibald Johnston to attend in the name of the Church, and several others were later added to them.

units.la: te disceptandæ essent, nomine ecclesiæ adesse iusserunt Alexandrum Hendersonum, Archibaldum Ionstonum: quibus postea aliquot additi. Atque hi Ruppone (qui locus conventui destinatus, medio fere inter Eboracum & Novo-Castrum itinere) Kalendis Octobris cum proceribus illis Anglis pacis interpretibus convenere: in quorum comitatu advenerant Traquarius, Mortonius, Lanurci, Comites, simul cum Ludovico Stuarto nobili causarum advocato, hos quatuor natione Scotos conventui interesse voluerat rex: Sed negabant Scoti, cum nulla eorundem in publicis illis fidei literis facta esset mentio, & in mandatis suis haberent ut cum iis solum agerent qui a conventu procerum designati, & literis fiduciariis inserti essent: Comitem etiam Traquarium rejiciebant, ut ineptum & inidoneum pacis interpretem, utpote quem inter belli hujus primos authores censerent.
units.tr: These men met the English nobles, the mediators of peace, at Ripon (the place appointed for the meeting, roughly midway on the road between York and Newcastle) on 1 October. In the company of the English who had come were the Earls Traquair, Morton and Lanark, together with Ludovic Stuart, a noble advocate of causes. The king had wished these four Scots to take part in the meeting. But the Scots refused, since no mention of them had been made in those public letters of safe-conduct, and their instructions were to deal only with those who had been designated by the assembly of the nobles and inserted in the letters of trust. They also rejected Earl Traquair, judging him an unfit and unsuitable mediator of peace, since they considered him among the first authors of this war.

units.la: Cum ad actiones deventum fuisset, placuit scripto & consignatis tabulis summa rerum capita utrinque describi. Pro Anglis ut plurimum perorabat Comes Bristolius, vir subacti ingenii & rarae prudentiæ: pro Scotis Laudonius. Urgent Angli ut legibus pacis anno superiori initæ insisterent Scoti; sed frustra, cum mandata & universus hic tractatus directe referret omnes actiones ad postulata à se transmissa Septemb. 5. ad Comitem Lanurci; quænam vero ea sint vide supra. Verum cum postulata illa varia essent, placuit agi de induciis, quas Scoti ea lege admittebant, modo induciarum tempore stipendia exercitui suo a rege persolverentur, ne dura necessitas famelicos milites ad extrema consilia præcipitaret, quos edicti regii & militaris sacramenti reverentia intra modestiæ & æquitatis limites hactenus continuisset: Atque hic graviter querelis sunt Scoti de calumniis denuo contra se sparsis, & patulis nimium auribus ubi minime decuit acceptis, quasi publica permissa militibus populatione agricolas, & cives Novocastrenses expilarent. Et quod calumniæ indignitatem augebat, sparsæ fuere schedulæ typis excusæ, & approbatæ calculo Wimebankii secretarii regii, hominis factioni Hispanicæ & Pontificiæ penitus mancipati, ut imperitæ plebis animos irarum facibus contra Scotos incenderet. Ad hanc calumniam depellendam rogarunt ut sycophantæ isti procerum judicio se sisterent. Sed nullo ausu tam impudentis calumniæ patrocinium suscipere, statim patuit ex qua mendaciorum officina prodierit, uti & literæ Gubernatoris Berwicensis, quibus a vicinis Mercianis in Scotia tributum sibi pendi jussit etiam calente pacis negotio, severe comminatus se renuentes omnibus belli cladibus eversurum, ac ferro & flamma sæviturum: licet ferociam hanc statim compresserit Munrous, qui pacatis Borealibus in Scotia Provinciis, præsidiariis Berwicensibus usque adeo acriter imminebat, ut quoties egressi essent, trepida fuga toties statim se receperint.
units.tr: When they came to business, it was agreed that the main heads of the matter should be set down in writing and on sealed tablets on both sides. For the English the Earl of Bristol did most of the speaking; he was a man of trained judgement and rare prudence. For the Scots it was Lauderdale. The English urged the Scots to abide by the terms of peace agreed the year before, but in vain, since their instructions and the whole of this negotiation referred all actions directly to the demands they had sent on 5 September to the Earl of Lanark (what those demands were, see above). Since those demands were various, it was agreed to discuss a truce, which the Scots would accept on condition that their army be paid by the king during the period of the truce, so that harsh necessity would not drive the hungry soldiers to desperate measures; hitherto the reverence for the royal proclamation and their military oath had held them within the limits of moderation and fairness. Here the Scots complained bitterly of the slanders spread against them again, which had been received too readily and with open ears where it was least fitting, as if the soldiers, by public permission, were plundering the farmers and the citizens of Newcastle. What added to the disgrace of the slander was that leaflets were printed and approved by the pen of Secretary Windebank, a royal secretary wholly devoted to the Spanish and Papist faction, so that he might inflame the minds of the untrained common people with the torches of anger against the Scots. To refute this slander, the Scots asked that these sycophants be made to appear before the judgement of the nobles. But no one dared to take up the defence of so shameless a slander, and it soon became clear from what workshop of lies it had come. So too did the letter of the Governor of Berwick, in which he ordered the neighbouring Mercians to pay him tribute in Scotland, even while the peace negotiations were heating up, and sternly threatened that he would overthrow with all the disasters of war those who refused, and would rage with sword and fire. Yet Monro quickly checked this fierceness; having pacified the northern provinces of Scotland, he pressed so hard on the Berwick garrisons that, whenever they sallied out, they retreated at once in fearful flight.

units.la: De exercitus Scotici stipendio a rege persolvendo consultatio multum exagitata fuit: & durum ac grave prima specie videbatur proceribus Anglis, regis præsertim exercitu stipendiorum penuria laborante. Quare ad regem referendum judicarunt, apud quem egregiam operam pro Scotis interposuere, gnari eos regii mandati reverentia detentos ne progrederentur & in intima Angliæ penetrarent, quod ipsis haud difficile fuisset in tanta trepidatione regiorum militum, nec incognitum erat quam amicè in hostico se gessissent, contenti pecunia à provincialibus pacta: Cum res hæc in publico procerum conventu agitaretur, egregiam occasionem se denuo nactum fuisse sibi visus est Deputatus Hiberniæ debacchandi contra Scotos, quibus æquiorem futurum spes erat post exoneratam diebus superioribus bilem, nec satiatus eos quibus apertum se hostem jampridem professus fuerat lacerasse, nobilem etiam Anglum pacis studiosum acerbe & salse coram sereniss. rege perstringebat, quia scilicet ausus fuerit profiteri rationes inveniri posse conficiendæ pecuniæ ad Scotici exercitus dissolvenda stipendia, ne remora illâ omnem concordiæ spem præcideret, quam boni omnes non majori studio prosequebantur, quam Deputatus Hiberniæ cum sua factione aversabantur: Serēniss. tamen regi visum bonam pecuniæ summam induciarū tempore Scotis concedere, ac deputatis suis mandare ut finitis ad solidum tractatum præparatoriis absolutam actuum bellicorum cessationem & inducias sancirent, quæ hisce ferme legibus utrinque pactæ fuerant. 1. Ut induciæ essent bimestres usque ad 16. Decembris, & utrinque tam terra quam mari bellicis & hostilibus actibus abstineretur. 2. Ut Scotis bona fide persolverentur in dies singulos induciarū 850 [?] libræ Anglicæ, quam summam præfecti juridici provinciarum Northumbriæ, Cumbriæ, Westmoriæ, & Dunelmi ac Novo-Castri, habito conventu & censu provincialium suorum, conficerent. 3. Quod si mala fide designata hæc summa Scotis penderetur, licitum fore declaratur sine ulla induciarum violatione, prædictarum provinciarum incolas ad præsentem solutionem cogere, & numerandas dilatæ solutionis impensas. 4. Provincias hasce & quicquid fluvium Tefin & Scotiam interjacet rex Scotis ad hybernandum concessit, monitis suis militibus nefrequentiori comitatu transflumen illud vagarentur, & Scotis pariter astrictis ut intra designatos illos limites se continerent, fluvius itaque hic limes fuit utrinque militibus frumentatum prodeuntibus. 5. Ne novæ munitiones, novæ militum conscriptiones utrinque fierent. 6. Privata damna inducias non rumpent modo in reum delatum animadvertatur& damnum illatum resarciatur.
units.tr: The payment of the Scottish army's pay by the king was much debated. At first sight it seemed harsh and burdensome to the English nobles, especially since the king's own army was suffering from a shortage of pay. They therefore resolved to refer the matter to the king, for whom they had earnestly interceded on the Scots' behalf. They knew that the Scots had been held back from advancing and penetrating into the heart of England only by reverence for the royal command, which would not have been difficult for them to do given the great panic among the royal soldiers. Nor was it unknown how friendly they had been in enemy territory, content with the money agreed with the provincials. While this matter was being discussed in a public assembly of the nobles, the Deputy of Ireland thought he had found a fresh opportunity to rage against the Scots, and he hoped they would be more agreeable now that he had unburdened his bile in the preceding days. Not satisfied with having torn to pieces those whom he had long openly declared himself an enemy of, he also sharply and sarcastically attacked, in the presence of the most serene king, a noble Englishman devoted to peace, because he had dared to profess that means could be found of raising money to dissolve the Scottish army's pay, so that this obstacle would not cut off all hope of agreement. All good men pursued that agreement with no less zeal than the Deputy of Ireland and his faction shunned it. The most serene king nevertheless saw fit to grant the Scots a considerable sum of money for the period of the truce, and to instruct his commissioners that, once the preliminaries for a full treaty were completed, they should confirm a complete cessation of hostilities and a truce, which had been agreed on roughly these terms: (1) that the truce should last two months, until 16 December, and that on both sides, by land and by sea, acts of war and hostility should be abstained from; (2) that the Scots should be paid in good faith, each day of the truce, 850 [?] English pounds, a sum which the judicial prefects of the provinces of Northumberland, Cumberland, Westmorland, Durham and Newcastle should fix after holding an assembly and taking a census of their provincials; (3) that if this sum designated for the Scots were paid in bad faith, it is declared lawful, without any violation of the truce, to compel the inhabitants of the said provinces to pay immediately, and the expenses of the delayed payment are to be counted; (4) that the king allowed the Scots to winter in these provinces and in the land lying between the river Tyne and Scotland, and that his soldiers should not roam beyond that river in large numbers, while the Scots were likewise bound to keep within the designated limits; this river therefore became the boundary on both sides for soldiers going out to forage; (5) that no new fortifications and no new levies of soldiers should be made on either side; (6) that private damages should not break the truce, but the offender should be punished and the loss made good.

units.la: 7. Fas esto mercatoribus sine literis salvi conductus in utroque regno mercaturam agere, nefas tamen militibus sine commeatu seu salvo conducto designatos supra limites transgredi. Conditiones hasce & alias aliquot minoris momenti ratas habuit serenissimus rex & consilio procerum Angliæ negotium hoc pacis Londinum transferendum decrevit, (nam ibi publica regni comitia aperiebantur) ubi singula Scotorum postulata ordine excuterentur : eorumque de putatis seu præsentibus, seu aliis quos visum illis esset eligere, literæ salvi conductus in amplissima forma expediuntur. Atque hæc summa præparatorii tractatus.
units.tr: (7) Merchants may trade in either kingdom without letters of safe-conduct, but it is forbidden for soldiers to cross the designated limits without a permit or safe-conduct. The most serene king approved these conditions and some other points of lesser importance, and the council of the English nobles decided that this business of peace should be transferred to London, since the public assemblies of the realm met there, where each of the Scots' demands would be examined in order; and letters of safe-conduct, in the fullest form, were issued for those whom the Scots had chosen, whether present or others whom it seemed good to them to select. And this is the substance of the preparatory negotiation.

units.la: Quid vero in ipso pacis negotio Londini hactenus inter partes peractum & definitum sit, cum omnia adhuc in herba sint, necdum ad perfectam maturitatem adoleverint, imprudentis esset typis committere : Interim satis constat Scotorum omnia & singula postulata 5. Septemb. ad Comitem Lanurci transmissa & octo capitibus comprehensa, usque adeo æqua & moderata visa esse serenissimo regi, cum in ea penitius introspiceret ac excuteret ; uti & proceribus pacis interpretibus, quin Amplissimis comitiorum Anglicorum ordinibus, ut non solum serenissimus rex eadem fere omnia concesserit, verumetiam Comitiorum solenni statuto promissa sint trecenta millia librarum Anglicarum, seu tres milliones florenorum ad dissolvendam partem ingentium istarum impensarum ad quas fratres sui Scoti bello hoc adigebantur; & inter alia crimina objecta Cantuariensi Archiepiscopo & Deputato Hiberniæ, nunc reis ex vinculis ad causam capitis dicendam advocatis, inter postrema non collocetur, quod funesti hujus belli authores fuerint & faces, nihilque intentatum reliquerint quo ad mutuam lanienam protruderent duas gentes mutua societate fœlicissimas. Quæ ut arctius coalescerent, dissidio opus fuisse videtur ut ex belli dispendiis pacis compendia pernoscerent, eamque posthac impensius colerent, perinde ut nusquam lætior dies quam ubi tristes nebulas solis radii dispulere. Qui vero innoxiorum ruinas improba spe præceperant, ac ferro & flamma per summam immanitatem omnia involvere satagebant, semperque obnitebantur ne concordia coalescerent, ecce rebus aliter jam fluentibus, quam amaram rerum vicissitudinem experiuntur! ἐχθρὸν[?] illud ὥμμα[?] vivit & vigilat, justitiæ ille oculus illibatus, hic hic est qui
units.tr: What, however, has so far been transacted and settled between the parties in London concerning the peace itself is not for an unwise person to commit to print, since everything is still in the blade and has not yet grown to full ripeness. Meanwhile it is quite clear that all and each of the Scots' demands, sent on 5 September to the Earl of Lanark and comprised in eight heads, seemed so fair and moderate to the most serene king, when he looked into and examined them more closely, and likewise to the nobles who were the peace commissioners, and indeed to the most distinguished orders of the English parliament, that the most serene king has not only granted almost all of them, but by solemn statute of parliament three hundred thousand English pounds, or three million florins, have been promised towards paying off part of the enormous expenses to which their Scottish brothers were driven by this war. And among the other crimes laid against the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Deputy of Ireland, now summoned as accused from their chains to answer for their lives, it is not the least that they were the authors and firebrands of this deadly war, and left nothing untried to thrust the two nations, most happy in their mutual fellowship, into mutual slaughter. For these to be bound more closely together, it seems there needed to be a quarrel, so that from the costs of war they might learn the advantages of peace and cherish it all the more earnestly hereafter, just as there is never a happier day than when the rays of the sun have dispelled the sad clouds. But those who had seized the ruin of the innocent with wicked hope, and strove to engulf everything in iron and fire with the greatest savagery, and always struggled that the two peoples should not unite in concord: behold, now that affairs are flowing in another direction, they experience a bitter reversal of fortune! That [ἐχθρὸν ὄμμα] hostile eye lives and keeps watch, that unimpaired eye of justice; it is this one here which

units.la: Funesta belli incendia sustulit[?]: Fregit cruentæ spicula lanceæ: Contrivit arcus, & volucres In cinerem minuit quadrigas.
units.tr: It has quenched the deadly fires of war; it has broken the points of the bloody lance; it has crushed the bows, and reduced the swift chariots to ashes.

units.tr: FINIS.
