units.tr: THE SCOTTISH CHURCHES

units.la: Ad Helveticas missa, qua origo & progres-sus motuum breviter ostenditur, usque ad Kalendas Aprilis. 1640.
units.tr: Sent to the Helvetic churches, in which the origin and progress of the disturbances is briefly shown, down to the Kalends of April, 1640.

units.la: Lectori S. P.
units.tr: To the Reader, Greeting

units.la: Quia visum fuit Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi aut asseclis[?], literas suas ad professores & pastores Helveticos, viros pacis & veritatis studiosissimos, in lucem communicatis exemplaribus efferre, quibus motuum horum causas confert in obstinatam Scotorum rebellionem excitatam & sopitam[?] tribunitiis pastorum quorundam concionibus, in quibus potenter operaretur humani generis hostis, & qui totam reformatam ecclesiam pontificis ludibrio exponerent, qui nostris & contentionibus latentur. Non inconsultum judicarunt prudentiores, si audirentur pastores illi causam suam agentes coram iisdem (clarissimis & Reverendis pastoribus, quos selos[?] Zelus domus Dei & pax Sionis ex omnibus reformatis ecclesiis exsuscitavit ut operam suam conferrent ad immane hoc incendium extinguendum. Ac licet bona conscientia facile antistet omnium hostium susurris, & jampridem obsurduissent ad convitia ista ex plaustro jactata, ut accola Nili ad Catadupam, ac opere & facto calumnias illas refutarent, ne tamen famam suam prostituisse viderentur, epistolam hanc conscripsere, ut fratribus suis liquido constaret per quos factum sit quod motus hi primum excitati fuerint, & per quos steterit quominus commode sopirentur. Quare propria vineta[?] cadit Archiepiscopus scandala hinc orta ingeminans, quorum ipsum Authorem esse notius est quam ut a quolibet in dubium trahatur. Contentionibus hisce ludos fieri pontificiis, eosque in suam rem vertere reformatorum discordias nullus negat; sed audi quid olim reposuerit Hierarchicorum ille malleus Parkerus de politia ecclesiastica lib. 1. cap. 34. sectione ultima.
units.tr: Since it seemed good to the Archbishop of Canterbury, or to his followers, to publish in printed copies his letter to the professors and ministers of Helvetia, men most devoted to peace and truth, in which he traces the causes of these troubles to the obstinate rebellion of the Scots, stirred up and then quieted by the seditious sermons of certain ministers, in which the enemy of mankind worked powerfully, and who expose the whole reformed Church to the mockery of the Pope, and who rejoice in our quarrels: the wiser sort judged it not unwise that those ministers be heard, pleading their own cause before the same men (the most distinguished and Reverend ministers whom the zeal for the house of God and the peace of Zion have raised up from all the reformed churches to lend their efforts to quenching this monstrous fire). And although a good conscience easily withstands the whisperings of all enemies, and they had long since grown deaf to those reproaches hurled from the wagon, like the dwellers by the Nile at the Cataract, and would refute those calumnies by their deeds, yet, lest they seem to have prostituted their reputation, they have written this letter, so that it may be clear to their brethren by whom these movements were first stirred up, and by whom it has been prevented from being calmly quieted. Therefore the Archbishop is caught in his own snare, repeating the scandals that arose here, of which he is more notoriously the author than anyone could dispute. That these contentions make sport for the Papists, and turn the discords of the reformed to their own advantage, no one denies; but hear what that hammer of the Hierarchists, Parker, once replied in his book on church polity, book 1, chapter 34, final section. Parker's words, as quoted by the author.

units.la: Quasi vero (inquit) contentione inter castra oborta, lætentur hostes de eorum fortitudine qui in vallo fortiter dimicant, ac non de illis fœderatis potius qui intra vallum delitescentes ipsorum partes promovent? Ii vero in nostris castrisHierarchici sunt, qui & contentionem excitarunt,{*} & pro regimine papistico excitarunt, in qua non leviter gaudent papistæ & lætantur.{*} Hæc ille? quid dicturus si vomicam schola Cantuariensis aperIam hodie cerneret?
units.tr: As if, he says, once contention has arisen between camps, the enemies would rejoice in the courage of those who fight bravely on the rampart, and not rather in those allies who lurk inside the rampart and advance their side? But those are Hierarchicals in our camp who have stirred up the contention, and stirred it up for the papal regime, in which the Papists rejoice and are glad not a little. Thus he. What would he say if he saw today the festering sore opened by the school of Canterbury?

units.la: EPISTOLA AB ECCLESIIS SCOTICIS
units.tr: A Letter from the Scottish Churches

units.la: Ad Helveticas missa, qua origo & progressus motuum breviter ostenditur, usque ad Kalendas Aprilis 1640.
units.tr: Sent to the Helvetic churches, briefly showing the origin and progress of the disturbances, down to the first of April 1640.

units.la: Iteras vestras fratres in Domino plurimum honorandi 10[?] Januar. datas vertente Martio accepimus, cum Apographo Epistolae mense ante Junij[?] exaratae; ex quibus curae esse vobis & cordi Ecclesiae nostrae pacem & salutem percipimus, quod non modo nostrae incolumitatis ergo nos orare hortari pergitis; sed & apud eos qui gratia, & authoritate apud Regem pollent laborem operam & studium ad nos sublevandos interponere non gravamini. Debemus & hoc humanitati vestrae, quod adversariis temere fidem non adhibendam duxeritis, qui nos etiamnum calumniis onerare, & sinistris rumoribus differre satagunt. Quibus arctissimis benevolentiae vinculis nos ita obstrinxistis, ut tanti beneficii memoriam nulla aetas, nulla oblivio delere possit.
units.tr: Brethren most worthy of honour in the Lord, we have received your letter dated the 10th of January, delivered in March, together with a copy of the letter written the month before June. From it we learn that you care for our Church and hold it dear, in peace and in safety. You not only continue to urge us to pray for our safety, but you also do not hesitate to bring your labour, effort and zeal to bear on those who are powerful in favour and influence with the King, so that we may be relieved. We owe this to your kindness as well: you have judged that our adversaries should not be rashly believed, though they still strive to burden us with slanders and to spread sinister rumours. You have bound us to you with the closest ties of goodwill, so that no age and no forgetfulness can wipe out the memory of so great a kindness.

units.la: Quod vero vos angi & cruciari scribitis tristi accepto nuncio, Regem Orthodoxum in subditos orthodoxos, eosque in sui defensionem arma parare; atque idcirco tantorum motuum totiusque controversiae causas edoceri à nobis studiose exoptatis. Quae quia in abdito non sunt reconditae, sed in aperto positae solicita investigatione non egent. Malorum etenim omnium fontes in Regni hujus & Ecclesiae perniciem redundantes ex Episcoporum nostrorum Typho tyrannide & Heterodoxia certo certius promanare cernimus. Non pigebit ergò in vestri gratiam (fratres in Domino plurimum colendi) rem omnem altius repetere, atque à Christianæ fidei initiis in hoc Regno exordium paucis arcessere. Tenete igitur;
units.tr: You write that you are distressed and tormented by the sad news you have received: that a Orthodox King is taking up arms against his Orthodox subjects, and arming them in his own defence. For this reason you earnestly desire to be told by us the causes of these great disturbances and of the whole controversy. These causes are not hidden or concealed, but lie in the open, and they do not need a careful investigation. Indeed, we see with ever greater certainty that the sources of all the evils which have flowed out to the ruin of this kingdom and of the Church come from the tyranny and the heterodoxy of our Typhon, our bishops. Therefore, brethren most worthy of our cultivation in the Lord, we will not hesitate, for your sake, to trace the whole matter from further back, and to draw the beginning in a few words from the first origins of the Christian faith in this kingdom. Hold on, then.

units.la: Depulsis ethnicorum superstitionum tenebris Scotis per Apostolos aut Apostolicos saltem viros saelestem[?] Euangelii lucem assulsisse, & regnante Donaldo anno a salutari partu plus minusve ducentesimo subditos cum Rege, Christo nomen publice dedisse, exinde per totos ducentos annos genti Scoticanæ Episcopi potestatem & nomen non innotuisse, sed Presbyteros Ecclesiæ gubernacula tenuisse. Quo temporis spatio exacto ad annum Christi usque millesimum quatuor titulo tenus Episcopos nullis distinctis limitibus, nullis divisis dioecesibus, non imperio, sed sanctimonia in communi Ecclesiam rexisse tradit Boethius, lib. 10. Historiæ Scotiæ.
units.tr: When the darkness of heathen superstitions had been dispelled, the light of the heavenly Gospel shone upon the Scots through the Apostles, or at least through apostolic men. Under King Donald, about two hundred years after the saving birth, the people together with the King publicly gave their name to Christ. For the following two hundred years, the power and name of a bishop were not known among the Scottish nation, but the elders held the government of the Church. After this period had passed, down to the year of Christ 1000, Boethius (book 10 of his History of Scotland) relates that bishops existed in name only, without any distinct boundaries and without divided dioceses; they ruled the Church in common, not by authority but by holiness.

units.la: Quantum vero à Praesidentia Episcopali abhorruerit nostra Ecclesia testis locuples venerandus Beda lib. 5. Historiæ Ecclesiast. qui in Insula illa in qua sepultus est Columbanus Presbyteri dicto Episcopum esse obedientem refert. Unde tria ista constant. 1. Existimasse majores nostros commodissime sine Episcopis administrari posse Ecclesiam; 2. Censuisse etiam jure divino Episcopum Presbytero non superiorem fuisse. 3. Tantum itidem dioecesium divisionem illis displiciuisse ut dioecesianis Episcopis ad annum Christi millesimum Ecclesia nostra caruerit. Post quæ tempora & tenebrarum carcere vinculis exolutus Satanas Ecclesiam Christi majorem in modum infestare turbare & tantum non pessundare cœpit; perfecitque suis artibus ut perpetuæ errorum nox Ecclesiæ huic incumberet totos quingentos & quod excurrit annos; donec misericordia summa commotus Deus Religionis purioris vindices exitaverit, qui ex Antichristi faucibus Ecclesiam ereptam natalibus suis restituere & Apostolicae simplicitati conformare enixe studentes, Episcopalis ὑπεροχῆς[?] nullam rationem habuerunt, sed eodem esse loco Presbyterum quo Episcopum duxerunt. Politiâ quoque Ecclesiae verbo Dei consentaneam ita descripserunt, ut retinendae puritati, morum & doctrinae, quatuor in ea confessus constituerentur; quorum infimus Parochianus ex unius Ecclesiae pastore cum ejusdem senioribus, cui proximus sed authoritate major ex plurium pastorum in vicinia degentium conventus, quem alii Classem, nos cum veneranda antiquitate Presbyterium indigitamus: subjacet hoc provinciali Synodo atque ea Generali; in quibus ab inferiori ad superiorem datur provocatio. Quam diu stetit integra haec nostra disciplina, nulla emersit cofruptela, quae si non in herba enecata, robur aut maturitatem aliquam non est assecuta. Sed ubi reformatorum antesignani, praecipuè Ioannes Knoxus vir omni laude cumulatissimus & prophetico plane spiritu praeditus, ubi, inquimus, confectis vitae stipendiis ad coelestem Patriam migrasset, Prorcegis auspiciis qui tum rerum potiebatur, atque aulicorum artibus & cupiditate qui suis commodis velificabant, procuratum est ut in Episcopos legerentur qui maxima redituum parte illis cederent, sed factum hoc fuit, reclamante Ecclesia quae Generali Synodo sancivit, ut unus uni tantum Parochiae Episcopus non pluribus praeficeretur; sympresbyteris non se anteferrent; Magnatum titulis abstinerent, nec se seculi negotiis immiscerent, Reditus haberent non ad pompam & luxum, sed ad honestatem tuendam idoneos; verum mox has lineas transilientes, cum neque modum neque modestiam servassent, publicis indictis Comitiis ad jus vocavit Ecclesia, multorum criminum postulatos ad unum omnes damnavit, gradu Episcopali dejecit, gravioribus flagitiis coopertos anathematum [?] vinculis innodavit, Episcopatum denique omnem tollendum decrevit. Eodem quo haec gesta sunt anno videl. 1580 edita est brevis fidei confessio, in qua cum Pontificiae doctrinae corruptelis Antichristiana omnis Hierarchia perpetuum damnata est.
units.tr: How far our Church shrank from episcopal presidency is shown by the weighty witness, the venerable Bede (book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History), who reports that on that island where Columba is buried, a presbyter, called a bishop, was obeyed. From this, three things are established. First, our forefathers judged that the Church could be governed most conveniently without bishops. Second, they also held that by divine right a bishop was not superior to a presbyter. Third, the division of dioceses likewise displeased them so much that our Church was without diocesan bishops until the year of Christ 1000. After these times, Satan, loosed from the prison of darkness and his chains, began to attack, disturb and almost ruin the Church of Christ to a greater degree. By his arts he brought it about that a perpetual night of errors lay over this Church for five hundred and a bit more years. Then at last God, moved by his highest mercy, raised up defenders of the purer religion. Eagerly striving to snatch the Church from the jaws of Antichrist, to restore it to its native state and to conform it to apostolic simplicity, they took no account of episcopal eminence, but judged the presbyter to be in the same place as the bishop. They also described the polity of the Church in agreement with the Word of God, so that four levels of assemblies were set up to keep its purity of morals and doctrine. The lowest is the parish, consisting of the minister of one congregation together with its elders. Next, and superior in authority, is the gathering of the ministers of several neighbouring parishes, which others call a classis, but which we, with the venerable antiquity, call a presbytery. This is subject to the provincial synod, and that to the General Assembly, and from the lower to the higher an appeal is allowed. As long as this our discipline stood intact, no corruption emerged; if any did, it was killed in its infancy and never gained strength or maturity. But when the leaders of the Reformation, above all John Knox, a man crowned with every praise and endowed with a truly prophetic spirit, had completed his life's service and gone to the heavenly fatherland, then, under the auspices of the Regent who was then in charge of affairs, and through the arts and greed of courtiers who were sailing toward their own advantage, it was arranged that bishops should be chosen who would give up to them the greatest part of the revenues. This was done, but the Church protested, and the General Assembly decreed that only one bishop should be set over one parish and not over several; that they should not put themselves above their fellow presbyters; that they should abstain from the titles of nobles and not involve themselves in secular business; and that they should have revenues suited to maintaining honest living, not to display and luxury. But soon, leaping over these lines, and having kept neither measure nor moderation, they were summoned to account by the Church, which called a public assembly. Those accused of many crimes were all condemned together, deprived of episcopal rank, and those guilty of more serious shameful acts were bound with the chains of anathema. Finally, the Church decreed that all episcopacy should be abolished. In the same year in which these things were done, namely 1580, a short confession of faith was published, in which every Antichristian hierarchy was condemned for ever, together with the corruptions of Papist doctrine.

units.la: Ad quam confessionem sartam tectam tuendam quà doctrina qua regiminis forma ante memorata, Rex Serenissimus Iacobus cum augusta familia, & Regni omnes ordines Sanctioris Senatus edicto fidem jurejuando additis chirographis obstrinxerunt. Hinc aurea insecuta sunt tempora in quibus pax & concordia maxima inter fratres vigebat: Orthodoxia florebat, pietas magis & magis invalescebat.
units.tr: To defend this confession, both its doctrine and the form of government mentioned above, the most serene King James, together with his noble family, and all the orders of the kingdom, bound themselves by the edict of the more sacred Senate, adding oaths and signatures. From this there followed golden times, in which the greatest peace and concord flourished among the brethren; orthodoxy prospered, and piety grew stronger and stronger.

units.la: Sed istis Alcyoniis diu frui non tulit Ecclesiam nostram reciprocans adversae fortis æstus. Nam vix emenso integri decennii cursu [?] per clandestinas artes & cuniculos Episcopatus instaurari coeptus est. Ad perjurii autem maculam incrustandam verius quam abstergendam ficus hic est factus; Ut crearentur è pastorum albo non qui Episcopi sed Commissionarii dicerentur, quibus in publicis Regni comitiis sententiae dictio daretur Ecclesiae nomine, ne quid ea detrimenti caperet; Huic cum à sagacioribus restitutum fuisset, ista excogitata est ratio, ut quibus munus hoc mandatum certis finibus & cancellis circumscriberentur, extra quos si pedem efferrent, sibi & officio fraudi futurum. In hos tamen posteaquam Serenissimus Rex Iac. titulos reditus & honores Episcopales contulisset, tum procerum titulis compellari, in foro se jactare, in sanctiori Senatu sedere, exosi vulgo & Ecclesiae formidabiles esse coeperunt: Nec tamen ulla lege vel legis colore dominandi aliquam potestatem in Ecclesiam habere; donec reparatae salutis anno 1610 in Glasguensi conciliabulo conductitiis suffragatoribus divenditis sententiis potestatem ordinandi excommunicandi & praesidendi in Comitiis Ecclesiasticis surripuerunt potius quam acceperunt. Ad hanc [illegible, ~9 letters] ubi per gradus istos ascendissent, ne quid pontificiarum ceremoniarum deesset Pesbyterorum ordinationi Episcopalem consecrationem superadjici voluerunt ƒ[?] quam quia in Ecclesiis nostris consequi non poterant; Londini non sine Patriæ & Ecclesiæ libertatis diminutione ab Episcopo Cantuariensi obtinuerunt. Tum succum sanguinem & calorem pristinæ Ecclesiæ amisimus; hinc omnia in pejus ruere & retro sublapsa referri, adeo ut Antichristiana omnis Hierarchia ante ejerata, bonorum summo cum gemitu & mœrore ab inferis in lucem revocaretur. Non enim vos fugit viri doctissimi & fratres venerandi quatuor istis Ordinationis nempe jurisdictionis, Confirmationis & locorum sanctorum Consecrationis potestate Hierarchiæ illius munia perfici & absolvi. Quæ omnia sacræ paginæ largitioni non humanis institutis accepta ferunt PseudoHierarchiæ istius patroni: quod quam putidum sit commentum refellendi nobis nec locus nec animus. Utut est hæc sibi ut propria vendicarunt Episcopi nostri; quæque sibi vendicarunt licenter ea, aut crudeliter potius in fidos Dei administros exercuerunt; quorum alios exauthorarunt, alios silentio damnarunt, carceri non paucos manciparunt, patrium folum nonnullos vertere compulerunt: quin & eo superbiæ pervenerunt, ut in compitis & plateis magno stipante clientium numero Holosericis amicti se jactarent. Si quæ sacra domi obeunda (quæ perrara) facellanis suis ea demandarunt, jus utriusque gladii sibi arrogarunt, in Sanctioris Consilii Senatu dominabantur, jus in foro dicebant, vectigalibus & fisco Regio præsidebant, Generalis Synodi indictioni, ne male administratæ Ecclesiæ postularentur totos viginti annos intercesserunt: ad Cancellariatus fastigia ubi tandem pervenissent cum ne mutire aut hiscere contra quempiam existimarent, Canonum libellum in lucem ediderunt, quo jus omne Ecclesiæ in se transcripserunt ad suum nutum & renutum omnia geri imperantes, presbyteros [illegible, ~10 letters] esse jusferunt. Præter verbi & sacramentorum administrationem, quæ moralis tantum ut loquuntur in scholis potestas, iis nihil reliqui fecerunt.
units.tr: But our Church, which was being tossed back by the adverse tide, was not allowed to enjoy these halcyon days for long. For scarcely had a full decade run its course when, through secret arts and mines, episcopacy began to be restored. To cover over the stain of perjury, rather than to wipe it away, a fig leaf was devised: men were to be chosen from the roll of ministers who would be called not bishops but commissioners, and who would be given the right to vote in the public assemblies of the kingdom in the name of the Church, so that the Church should suffer no harm. When this had been restored by the more shrewd men, another plan was thought up: they were to be confined within certain fixed limits and boundaries, and if they stepped outside them, it would be to their own and their office's ruin. Yet after the most serene King James had conferred on these men episcopal titles, revenues and honours, they began to be addressed with the titles of nobles, to boast in the marketplace, to sit in the more sacred Senate, and to become hated by the common people and feared by the Church. Still they had no power over the Church under any law or pretext of law to lord it over it; until, in the year of restored salvation 1610, at the Glasgow conventicle, by selling their votes to hired supporters, they seized the power of ordaining, excommunicating and presiding in ecclesiastical assemblies, rather than receiving it. When they had climbed up by these steps, and so that nothing of the Papist ceremonies might be lacking, they wished to add an episcopal consecration to the ordination of presbyters. Since they could not obtain this in our churches, they got it in London from the Archbishop of Canterbury, not without a diminution of the liberty of the country and the Church. From then on we lost the juice, blood and warmth of the former Church. Hence all things began to rush towards worse, and things that had slipped backwards were carried back, so that every Antichristian hierarchy, long since cast out, was called back from the dead into the light, to the great groaning and sorrow of good men. For you, most learned men and venerable brethren, are not unaware that the functions of that hierarchy are completed and carried out by four powers: the power of ordination, of jurisdiction, of confirmation, and of consecrating holy places. The patrons of this false hierarchy ascribe all these to the gift of Holy Scripture, not to human institutions; how putrid a fiction this is, we have neither place nor inclination to refute. However that may be, our bishops claimed these powers for themselves as their own, and what they claimed they exercised without restraint, or rather cruelly, against the faithful servants of God. Some of these they deprived of their office, others they condemned to silence, not a few they handed over to prison, and some they forced to leave their native soil. Indeed they came to such pride that they showed themselves off in the streets and squares, clad in silk, with a great crowd of clients pressing around them. If any sacred duties were to be performed at home (which was very rare), they handed these over to their chaplains, while they claimed for themselves the right of both swords. They ruled in the Senate of the more sacred Council, they pronounced judgement in the courts, they presided over the revenues and the royal treasury, and for twenty years they stood in the way of any summoning of a General Assembly, lest the badly managed Church should call them to account. When at last they had reached the heights of the Chancellorship, and thought that no one would dare to murmur or open their mouth against them, they published a book of canons, by which they transferred every right of the Church into their own hands, ordering that everything should be done at their nod and their refusal, and they decreed that the presbyters should be [...]. Apart from the administration of the Word and the sacraments, which, as they say in the schools, is only a moral power, they left nothing to them.

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus de typho & tyrannide Episcoporum pauca delibavimus; restat Heterodoxia quæ vel hinc constat quod ingrati in gratiam Dei Arminianismum, hoc est, Pelagianismum recoctum ex ambone promulgare & populo ingerere non sunt veriti, manubiisque Dei gratiæ voluntatem humanam exornare non perhorruerunt. De statuis in templis reponendis ambigue pro concione differebant; Pontificem Romanum esse illum Antichristum & purpuratam Meretricem nefas ducebant; Præsentiam Christi in sacra Cæna non objectivam tantum & fide contrectandam, sed subjectivam in terris & loco certo circumscriptam asserebant, & quod horret animus meminisse, Christi justitiæ imputationem in quo salutis cardo vertitur ex eorum numero non postremi pro somnio & figmento habuerunt. Nihil crebrius, nihil frequentius in omni cœtu & congressu quam concordiam inter Orthodoxos & Rom. Ecclesiam iniri facile posse, quod in articulis fidei palmariis & fundamentalibus nullum esset dissidium. Addo quod mensam Domini in aram transformarunt, quam ad Orientem sisti, cancellis circumdari præceperunt; illam flexis genibus, quoties prætereirent, venerabantur, Solis ortum adorabundi spectabant. Liturgiam idolatricis refertam ritibus Ecclesiæ nostræ pro norma cultus divini obtruserunt, quam si amplexa esset, actum de religione actum de cultu Dei fuisset. Tantum enim aberat ut Anglicaà quibus scatet fæcibus repurgarent, ut contaminatiorem multo nobis exhiberent, sanioribus expunctis sequiora inseruerunt[?]; quæque verso stylo D. Bucerus eximiæ pietatis & reconditæ eruditionis Theologus olim delevit, ea reposuerunt; adeo ut nullus sit in farraginea[?] pontificiorum errorum mole cuius in ea fere maturam messem aut fermentem saltem oculatus & judiciosus lector non deprehendet. Hinc novorum motuum & tot malorum origo quæ exterorum aures[?] atque animos implevit. Nam cum Regio diplomate in eas angustias Pastores & populus conjecti essent, ut vel perduellionis crimen subire vel illam liturgiam contra jusjurandum, fidem, Ecclesiæ & Patriæ instituta amplecti cogerentur, effectum est, ut Regni omnes Ordines quorum jamdudum in tolerandis Episcopis patientia obrutuit, hujus liturgiæ experrecti nuncio de profligandis corruptelis & primæva puritate restituenda consilium inierint. Regem itaque Serenissimum complurimis supplicibus libellis & sanctiorem ejus Senatum rogare, orare, hortari non destiterunt, ut afflictæ Ecclesiæ succurrerent, in Episcopos vero tantorum malorum authores serio animadverterent. Dum tardius auxilium parari, supplicibus libellis non responderi, postulata sua nihil pensi haberi cernerent; in se altius descendunt, mentis latebras penitus excutiunt, violati fœderis memoria conscientias pungit, lancinat, perfodit; quare seria pœnitentia ducti fœdus cum fidei confessione renovare statuerunt; quæ Chirographis primo consignarunt, deinde solenni indicto jejunio jurejurando sublatis dexteris multo cum gemitu & lachrymis publice in templis confirmarunt. Dum hæc aguntur missus est à Serenissimo Rege Marchio Hamiltonius ad controversias has cognoscendas, lites componendas & tempestates omnes in tranquillum redigendas: cujus ope & industria hoc confequuti fumus, ut Iis[?] tollendis dissidiis Comitia Ecclesiastica Glasguæ habenda indicerentur. Ad condictum diem & locum conuenerunt frequens Pastorum numerus & Seniores quibus jus ferendi suffragii ab Ecclesiis demandatum. Episcopi citati & adesse jussi superbi renuerunt, Ecclesiam ferre judicem recusarunt. Ventilata itaque eorum causa, quod innumera & ingentia in Ecclesiam mala intulissent, susque deque eam, ejusque judicium habuissent, omnium calculis de Episcopali gradu dejecti fuerunt. Episcopalem etiam Hierarchiam quod ex humano instituto multisque nominibus noxiam & exitialem nostræ Ecclesiæ semper essent experti ex nostris Ecclesiis eliminandam censuerunt. Episcopi ira perciti & efferati ad Regem confugiunt, apud quem partim importunis precibus & clamoribus, partim gratia & potentia Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis (quem conatuum, molitionum & superstitionum omnium Authorem Fautorem & Patronum habent) tantum profecerunt, ut sacrosanctum ejus pectus contra indolis probitatem & innatam clementiā impulerint, ut bellum in nos tanquam perduelles indiceret, imo paludatus ipse in nos ducit, terra marique exercitu cingimur. Cum in procinctu utraque acies staret, & viderent adversarii nec numero nec animis nostros inferiores, conventum est utrinque suffragante Rege, ut Ecclesia ab Ecclesiasticis, Politia suis legibus regeretur, Serenissimus Rex quæ recepit præstare visus est, Ecclesiæ congregandi Synodum potestatem fecit; in qua omnium suffragiis annuente etiam Traquario Comite, qui Regis personam sustinebat, repetita & confirmata est Episcoporum & Episcopalis Hierarchiæ damnatio; Sed salvo aliarum Ecclesiarum judicio. Synodum hanc Parliamentum excepit, in quo ante omnia (quod usu & consuetudine semper obtinuit) postulatur à verbi Dei præconibus, ut canones Ecclesiæ sanciantur & comprimis ille de damnato & conclamato Episcopatu. Ad hoc à Traquario Comite qui Regis nomine Comitiis prærat, cunctanter respondetur, tempus extrahitur, diverticula quæruntur; fallacia tandem hæc reperitur, ut si Episcopis Regii corpus careret, præcipuo membro truncaretur, quare in eorum locum ad absolvendum regni corpus, substituendos censent Abbates, priores & ejus farinæ homines: sed perpaucorum fuit hæc aut pene nullorum sententia, qua quid absurdius dici potest, si antiquitatem consulamus, quam Monachos & mandritas qui in locis subter-raneis aut solitudine latebant in luce multorum, urbium frequentia, publicis congressibus versari.
units.tr: So much, then, on the pride and tyranny of the bishops, which we have touched on briefly. There remains the heterodoxy, which is evident from this alone: these ungrateful men were not ashamed to proclaim from the pulpit Arminianism, that is, Pelagianism reheated, and to force it upon the people. They did not shrink from adorning the human will with the spoils of God's grace. Concerning the placing of statues in churches, they spoke ambiguously in their sermons. To count the Roman Pontiff that Antichrist and the purple harlot they held to be wicked. The presence of Christ in the holy Supper they asserted to be not only objective and to be grasped by faith, but subjective, on earth and circumscribed in a definite place. And, what the mind shudders to recall, the imputation of Christ's righteousness, on which the hinge of salvation turns, they regarded, and not the least of them, as a dream and a fiction. Nothing was said more often or more frequently in every assembly and gathering than that agreement could easily be reached between the Orthodox and the Roman Church, since there was no disagreement on the chief and fundamental articles of faith. I add that they turned the Lord's table into an altar, which they ordered to be set toward the East and surrounded with rails. Whenever they passed it, they venerated it with bended knees, and they gazed in adoration at the rising of the sun. They imposed on our Church, as the norm of divine worship, a liturgy stuffed with idolatrous rites, which, had it been embraced, would have meant the end of religion and the end of the worship of God. So far were they from purging the English liturgy of the dregs with which it teems that they presented us with a much more contaminated one: they struck out the healthier things and inserted worse. What the distinguished Bucer, a theologian of remarkable piety and recondite learning, once removed by changing the wording, they put back. So there is no one in this hodgepodge of the Papists' errors in which an attentive and judicious reader will not detect almost the ripe harvest, or at least the leaven, of them. Hence came the origin of the new disturbances and of so many evils, which filled the ears and minds of foreigners. For when, by royal decree, the ministers and people were driven into such straits that they were forced either to incur the crime of treason or to embrace that liturgy, against their oath, their faith, and the institutions of the Church and country, it came about that all the orders of the kingdom, whose patience in tolerating bishops had long been worn down, were roused by the news of this liturgy and undertook counsel for cutting out the corruptions and restoring primitive purity. Accordingly, they did not cease, by very many supplications, to ask, beseech and exhort the Most Serene King and his more holy Senate to come to the aid of the afflicted Church and to take serious note of the bishops, the authors of such great evils. While help was being prepared too slowly, and no answer was given to their petitions, and they saw their demands disregarded, they descended into themselves more deeply and searched out the hidden corners of the mind. The memory of the broken covenant pricked, tore and pierced their consciences. Wherefore, moved by serious repentance, they resolved to renew the covenant with the confession of faith. They first signed this with their hands, and then, a solemn fast having been proclaimed, they confirmed it publicly in the churches with an oath, hands raised, with much groaning and tears. While these things were being done, the Most Serene King sent the Marquis Hamilton to examine these controversies, settle the disputes and reduce all the storms to calm. Through his help and diligence we have achieved this: that to remove these disagreements a General Assembly of the Church was ordered to be held at Glasgow. On the appointed day and at the place, a large number of ministers and elders gathered, to whom the churches had committed the right of voting. The bishops, summoned and ordered to be present, proudly refused, and refused to acknowledge the Church as judge. Their cause was therefore argued, since they had inflicted countless and huge evils on the Church, and had held it and its judgment in contempt. By the votes of all, they were deposed from the episcopal rank. They also judged that the episcopal hierarchy, being of human institution and, under many names, always proved hurtful and deadly to our Church, should be removed from our churches. The bishops, roused and enraged, fled to the King. With him they prevailed, partly by importunate prayers and clamours, partly by the favour and power of the Archbishop of Canterbury (whom they have as the author, abettor and patron of all these attempts, machinations and superstitions). So far did they prevail that they urged his sacred breast, contrary to the probity of his character and his innate clemency, to declare war on us as rebels. Indeed, he himself leads us in arms, and we are surrounded by an army by land and sea. When both lines stood ready for battle, and the adversaries saw that our men were not inferior to them in numbers or spirit, it was agreed on both sides, with the King's assent, that the Church should be governed by churchmen and the State by its own laws. The Most Serene King seemed to perform what he had undertaken, and he gave the Church power to convene a Synod. In it, with the consent of all, and with Count Traquair also assenting, he who bore the King's person, the condemnation of the bishops and of the episcopal hierarchy was repeated and confirmed, but saving the judgment of the other Churches. This Synod was followed by Parliament. In it, above all (as has always prevailed by use and custom), the heralds of God's Word demanded that the canons of the Church be ratified, and especially that one concerning the condemned and rejected episcopacy. To this, Count Traquair, who presides over the assembly in the King's name, answers hesitantly; time is dragged out and evasions are sought. At last this trick is found: that if the body of the King lacked bishops, it would be cut off from its chief member. Therefore they propose that, to complete the body of the kingdom, abbots, priors and men of that sort be substituted in their place. But this opinion belonged to very few, or to almost none. What could be more absurd, if we consult antiquity, than that monks and hermits, who lay hidden in underground places or in solitude, should be seen in the light of many, in the crowds of cities and in public gatherings?

units.la: Quid à decoro magis alienum quam illos quorum erat non docere sed plangere, in cilicio & cinere sordescere, in suprema Regni Curia murice & bombicina veste splendescere. Sed quia dominante papatu in hoc regno receptum fuit ut abbates & Priores suffragium in his Comitiis ferrent, tolerandum hoc quod nondum exolevit; at novos & inauditos Abbates renunciari, qui Episcoporum vicem supplerent, & numero exæquarent nullo jure nitebatur, eoque spectare videbatur, ut quando recta ad restituendum Episcopatum aditus non pateret, his artibus per posticam intromitteretur. Quamobrem isti de Archimandritis sententiæ jure restitutum fuit à Regni ordinibus. Comitiorum Præses partim metu partim aulica gratia inescatus, Sere-nissimum Regem de eo nec non de Comitiorum ordine suffragatorum numero aliisque subditorum querelis consulendum censuit. Dum rescriptum Principis exspectatur, controversiis omnibus læra catastrophe bonorum votis speratur, præter exspectationem, contra morem majorum, Regis solius auspiciis Regni Comitia dissolvuntur. Magnates reliquique Regni ordines graviter molesteque [?] ferentes vulnera Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ non sanata recrudescere ex primaria nobilitate supplices ad Regem delegarunt, qui omnium nomine (ut par est) omnem illi observantiam & obsequium deferret, sed inanidati [?] sine fructu & effectu in patriam sui reversi. Hanc etsi repulsam tulimus, non cessamus Regi supplicare, viasque omnes quaerere quibus ad ejus benevolentiam aditum aperiamus. Parati [?] itaque pro ejus salute fortunas omnes & vitam profundere, interea certis ad nos perfertur rumoribus Regem exercitum [?] contra nos conscribere, quod non sua sponte sed adversariorum hortatu & impulsu facere persuasissimum habemus. Verum Episcopi nostri aliique Babyloniæ meretricis lenones classicum canere, eadem spirare, Regni & Ecclesiæ eversionem moliri non desinunt; nec harum Tragœdiarum fontes causas alias esse scimus, quam quod nefariis illorum conatibus, typho, tyrannidi, & heterodoxiæ via à nobis præcludatur.
units.tr: What is more foreign to decorum than that those whose task was not to teach but to mourn should grow squalid in sackcloth and ashes, yet shine in the supreme court of the kingdom in purple and silk? But since, under the dominant papacy in this kingdom, it was the custom for abbots and priors to cast votes in these assemblies, this is to be tolerated, as it has not yet fallen into disuse. But the appointing of new and unheard-of abbots, to take the place of the bishops and equal them in number, rested on no right, and seemed to aim at this: that since the direct way to restoring episcopacy was not open, it might be slipped in by the back door through these devices. For this reason, the Estates of the kingdom restored by right the sentence against those Archimandrites. The President of the Assembly, partly through fear and partly enticed by court favour, thought the Most Serene King should be consulted about this, and about the number of voting members of the Assembly, and about the other complaints of the subjects. While the Prince's rescript was awaited, a happy outcome of all controversies was hoped for by good wishes. But, beyond expectation and against the custom of our ancestors, the Assembly of the kingdom was dissolved on the King's sole authority. The nobles and the remaining orders of the kingdom, taking this gravely and with distress, sent as suppliants to the King deputies from the leading nobility, who were to offer him, on behalf of all, due observance and obedience. But they returned home without result or effect. Though we have borne this rebuff, we do not cease to supplicate the King and to seek every way by which we may open access to his goodwill. We are prepared therefore to pour out all our fortunes and our lives for his safety. Meanwhile, certain reports have reached us that the King is levying an army against us, which we are fully persuaded he does not do of his own accord, but at the urging and instigation of our adversaries. But our bishops and others, the pimps of the Babylonian harlot, do not cease to sound the trumpet, to breathe the same spirit, and to plot the overthrow of the kingdom and the Church. Nor do we know any other causes of these tragedies than that by their wicked attempts the way of pride, tyranny and heterodoxy is closed against us.

units.la: Videtis ergo fratres plurimum observandi, quam immerito seditionis & Rebellionis traducamur, quantaque cum injuria nos Pastores, tribunitii Concionatores ab adversariis audiamus; quibus non carceres non cruces, sed mentem meliorem exoptamus. Quid autem in casu inculpatæ tutelæ præstandum quoniam vos viros Doctissimos non latet, insuper habemus scriptis mandare. Vobis autem à quibus solis literas benevolentiæ testes accepimus, gratias quantas quantas possumus agimus, relaturi etiam si facultas dabitur, à vobis autem etiam atque etiam petimus ut innocentiæ nostræ testimonium perhibeatis, causæ patrocinium suscipiatis, ab obtrectatorum calumniis famam vindicetis, & uti nos afflictis Ecclesiis auxilio & adjumento fuimus, benignitatis vicem similiter speramus. Quod superest votis omnibus apud Deum contendit pro nobis nostrarumque Ecclesiarum pace ac salute, quem & nos obnixe oramus, ut Ecclesias vestras æternum incolumes & florentes esse velit, vobisque & vestris laboribus ita propicius sit, ut mortalitatis hoc stadio feliciter in munere decurso, pa[?]nam cœlestem assequamini.
units.tr: You see then, brethren, deserving of the closest attention, how unjustly we are slandered as seditious and rebellious, and with what injury our adversaries hear us, the ministers, called tribunes and sermon-makers of the people; for whom we desire not prisons or crosses, but a better mind. As to what must be done in the case of blameless self-defence, since it is not hidden from you, most learned men, we have decided not to commit it to writing. To you alone, from whom we have received letters as witnesses of goodwill, we give thanks as fully as we can, and we shall repay you, if the opportunity is given. From you, however, we ask again and again that you bear witness to our innocence, take up the defence of our cause, and vindicate our good name from the slanders of our detractors; and just as we gave help and support to the afflicted Churches, we similarly hope for a return of your kindness. For the rest, we pray with all our hearts that God, on behalf of us and of our Churches, may maintain our peace and welfare; and we earnestly pray also that He will keep your Churches safe and flourishing for ever, and be so favourable to you and your labours that, having happily completed your office in the course of this mortal life, you may attain the heavenly reward.

units.la: V.R.W. Addictiss. &c.
units.tr: Your Reverences' most devoted servants, etc.

units.la: CUm typothetæ familiariter satis cognita noit[?] fuerit Authoris manus ; fieri non potuit quin complura subrepserint errata ; nam præter ea quæ in distinctionum notis sunt, occurrent frequentia satis in literis : ita quidem ut sæpius sit numeri singularis pro plurali & vice versa permutatio, quæ humanus Lector condonabit, & facile per se corriget. Ante lectionem vero monendus es ut hæc paucula sic emendes, pag. 193. lin. 6. post ad sess. adde 16. pag. 259. & pag. 197. lin. 2. post ad sess. adde. 16. pag. 241. Et pag. 266. 15. pro quæstus fuit male, legendum, monuit sibi videri non satis commode. & eadem pag. lin. 24. post quæstionis, adde, cujus sententia fuit removendos & abjurandos, licet vix sibi persuaderet antea abjuratos fuisse.
units.tr: Since the typesetter was not sufficiently familiar with the author's handwriting, it could not be helped that several errors crept in. Apart from those in the punctuation marks, there are quite frequent errors in the letters. Thus the singular is often put for the plural and the plural for the singular. The kindly reader will pardon these and easily correct them himself. Before reading, however, you are advised to amend these few as follows. On p. 193, line 6, after "ad sess." add "16." On p. 259, and p. 197, line 2, after "ad sess." add "16." On p. 241, and p. 266, line 15, for "quæstus fuit male" read monuit sibi videri non satis commode. On the same page, line 24, after "quæstionis" add cujus sententia fuit removendos & abjurandos, licet vix sibi persuaderet antea abjuratos fuisse.
